units.la: Atque id egregie cauerunt Romani iam ab ipso Vrbis Natali è Lege Romuli: ex eoque fonte hausit Cicero, cuius verba describemus è Lib. II. de Legibus, vt eadem opera illustremus & interpungamus: Suosque Deos, aut nouos, aut alienigenas coli, confusionem habet religionum & ignotas cærimonias. non à Sacerdotibus, non à patribus acceptos Deos, ita placet coli, sihuic Legi paruerunt ipsi. Editionem Gruteri repræsentauimus.
units.tr: The Romans guarded against this admirably from the very birth of the City, by the law of Romulus. Cicero drew from this source, and we shall set out his words from Book II of the Laws, so that at the same time we may clarify and punctuate them: Suosque Deos, aut novos, aut alienigenas coli, confusionem habet religionum et ignotas caerimonias. Non a Sacerdotibus, non a patribus acceptos Deos, ita placet coli, si huic Legi paruerunt ipsi. We have presented Gruter's edition.

units.la: Addit deinde Tertullianus, quibusdam hebdomadis diebus Romanos ocium & prandium curasse, quibusdam totis ieiunasse, quibusdam ad nonam tantum, quod imitatione Iudaeorum proculdubio vsurpabant. hinc addit Afer nostrer: Quod quidem facitis exorbitantes & ipsi à vestris ad alienas religiones. Nomine alienarum religionum intelligit Iudaicam. Sed verba in mendo cubant, quanquam id non primo venae tactu deprehendas, sed morbi arguunt haec Tertulliani verba ex Apologetici cap. XVI. Æque si diem Solis laetitiae indulgemus, alia longe ratione, quam religione Solis, secundo loco abeis sumus, qui diem Saturni ocio & viElui[?] decernunt; exorbitantes & ipsi à Iudaico more, quem ignorant. Nam optime dixit Tertullianus, Ethnicos exorbitasse à Iudaicis moribus, quos tamen vsurpare videbantur, idque verissimum est; neque enim veri Dei religione ista observabant, sed praua Iudaeos imitandi affectatione, cum tamen mores illorum, eorumque causas ignorarent, quemadmodum Christiani diem Solis laetitiae indulgebant, alia certe longe ratione, quàm religione vlla Solis, atque ita Ethnici exorbitabant à suis moribus, vt & etiam ab alienis, quos tamen admittebant, quia alia religione tacti, quam ii, à quibus acceperant, mores istos vsurpabant. Rescribo igitur: exorbitantes & ipsi à vestris, ab alienis, religione. Exorbitabant enim, vt iam diximus, à suis ritibus ad alienos, Iudaicos nempe, rursumque à Iudaïcis moribus exorbitabant religione, quia Iudæi Saturni diem lætitiæ indulgebant longe alia, quàm Ethnici, religione, quiaisti hæc in honorem Saturni vsurpabant.
units.tr: Tertullian adds that on certain days of the week the Romans kept leisure and dinner, on some they fasted entirely, and on others only until the ninth hour, which they undoubtedly did in imitation of the Jews. Hence our African adds: You who also stray from your own practices into foreign religions do this. By foreign religions he means the Jewish. But the words are corrupt, although you would not detect this at first touch of the pulse; the disease shows itself from Tertullian's own words in Apologeticus chapter 16: Likewise, if we indulge the Sun's day in joy, by a reasoning far different from any religion of the Sun, we are second to those who assign Saturn's day to leisure and ... straying themselves from the Jewish custom, which they do not know. For Tertullian rightly said that the Gentiles strayed from Jewish customs, which they nevertheless seemed to follow, and this is most true. For they did not observe these things from the religion of the true God, but from a perverse eagerness to imitate the Jews, although they did not know those customs or their causes, just as Christians indulged the Sun's day in joy, by a reasoning certainly far different from any religion of the Sun. Thus the Gentiles strayed from their own customs, and also from foreign ones, which they nevertheless admitted, because, moved by a different religion from those from whom they had received those customs, they used them. I therefore rewrite: straying themselves from yours, from foreign ones, by religion. For they strayed, as we have already said, from their own rites to foreign ones, namely Jewish ones; and again they strayed from Jewish customs by religion, because the Jews indulged Saturn's day in joy by a religion quite different from that of the Gentiles, who used these practices in honour of Saturn.

units.la: Post Draconem diu non obtinuit apud Athenienses simplex illa adeoque pauco parabilis Deos frugibus venerandi ratio: nam ante Solonem victimas Diis macta-runt, quantum pretium Legibus æstimauit Solon, vt est apud Plutarchum in Solone: [illegible, ~70 letters] Ita vulgo editur hic locus, sed male, aut ego valde fallor: Quid enim audio? At vero tam paruo non æstimabit; qui animo reputabit, quod paullo post refert ibidem Plutarchus, Atticam [illegible, ~12 letters] Adde quod insecutis temporibus, vt testis est locupletissimus Strattis Comicus dramate, cui titulus est Κινησίας[?], vænibat vt plurimum hordei cophinus drachmis quatuor; A. τὰ δ' ἀλφίτ' ὑμῖν πῶς ἐπώλησιν[?]; B. τετάρων δραχμῶν μάλιστα τὸν κόφινον[?]. A. πάλιν[?];
units.tr: For a long time after Draco, that simple way of honouring the gods with fruits, which costs so little, did not prevail among the Athenians. For before Solon they sacrificed victims to the gods. As to what price Solon set on the laws, it is in Plutarch's Life of Solon: [illegible]. The passage is printed thus in the usual editions, but wrongly, or I am much mistaken. For what do I hear? But surely he would not value it at so small a sum, if he considers what Plutarch reports a little later in the same place, that Attica [illegible]. Add that in the following times, as the most abundant witness Strattis the comic poet testifies in a play titled Kinesias, a basket of barley usually sold for four drachmas: A. [τὰ δ' ἀλφίτ' ὑμῖν πῶς ἐπώλησιν;] "And how did they sell the barley-meal for you?" B. [τετάρων δραχμῶν μάλιστα τὸν κόφινον.] "About four drachmas for the basket." A. [πάλιν;] "Again?"

units.la: Cophinus est choinum siue sextariorum trium: Medimnus vero sextariorum nonaginta sex: Quare si cophinus hordei vænibat quatuor drachmis, Medimnus vænibit drachmis centum viginti octo. Dices ea tempestate longe plura fuisse Athenis capita, quàm fuerunt ætate Solonis, ac proinde pluris quoque væniisse hordeum; itemque maiorem fuisse auri argentique copiam: neque nos id negamus: sed tamen, si cum Strattis suas committebat fabulas, hordei cophinus quatuor drachmis Athenis vænibat, quis tam fungus erit, qui credat Solonis ævo Medimnum vna tantum drachma væniisse? Vænibat medi-mnus hordei drachmis octodecim, vt constat è Demosthene, atque etiam tantidem Solonis ætate, vt è lege, quam, Deo dante, suo loco describemus, liquebit. Certe quod idem Plutarchus ibidem docet ouem vna fuisse æstimatam drachma: [illegible, ~40 letters] facit, vt credam pluribus drachmis hordei Medimnum væniisse: Atque ex his etiam colligo quod hic habetur de vnius æstimatione drachmæ ad ouem esse referendum: nam Demetrius Phalereus auctor est, [illegible, ~25 letters]. Ceterum exciderunt literæ numerales, quibus designabatur numerus drachmarum, quibus hordei Medimnus æstimabatur, easque ita repono: [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: A cophinus is a choinix, or three sextarii; a medimnus, however, is ninety-six sextarii. Therefore, if a cophinus of barley sold for four drachmas, a medimnus will sell for one hundred and twenty-eight drachmas. You will say that at that time there were far more people at Athens than in Solon's age, and therefore barley sold for more, and likewise there was a greater abundance of gold and silver. We do not deny this. But still, if Strattis based his plays on the fact that at Athens a cophinus of barley sold for four drachmas, who will be such a fungus as to believe that in Solon's age a medimnus sold for only one drachma? A medimnus of barley sold for eighteen drachmas, as is clear from Demosthenes, and just as much in Solon's age, as will be clear from the law which, God willing, we shall describe in its place. Certainly what the same Plutarch teaches in that place, that a sheep was valued at one drachma [illegible], makes me believe that a medimnus of barley was sold for more drachmas. And from this too I gather that what is here said about the valuation at one drachma must be referred to the sheep, for Demetrius Phalereus is the authority that [illegible]. Moreover, the numeral letters have dropped out by which the number of drachmas was designated at which the medimnus of barley was valued. I restore them thus: [illegible] [illegible].

units.la: Nemo autem negare potest excidisse è Plutarchi codicibus pretium quo æstimabatur à Solone aut ouis aut medimnus hordei. Atqui non excidit pretium ouis, id enim est drachma, vt Demetrius Phalereus docet: Quare pretium medimni excidisse certum est, reposuimus autem illud, siue drachmarum octodecim numerum, eo quod tantidem vænibat medimnus hordei, & facile fuit omittere hunc numerum litteris scriptum ni'. quia eædem fere cum duabus vltimispræcedentis immediatè dictionis σφαγμὸν. Atque ad hanc frugalitatem exemplo suo Soloni præiuit Epimenides, Athenien-sesque eidem assuefecit. Plutarchus de Epimenide: ἔλεγε δ᾽, καὶ παρὰ Σόλωνι ξενοπάθμως φίλος, πολλὰ συνεπιμεγάσατο, καὶ παρὰ ὡδοποιῶν αὐτοῦ τῆς νομοθεσίας, καὶ γὰρ ὑπὲρ ἔλεξις ἐπίστος τῆς λῃτυρ-γίας[?].
units.tr: No one can deny that the price at which Solon valued either the sheep or the medimnus of barley has dropped out of the copies of Plutarch. But the price of the sheep has not dropped out, for that is drachma, as Demetrius Phalereus teaches. Therefore the price of the medimnus has certainly dropped out. We have restored it, namely the number of eighteen drachmas, because a medimnus of barley sold for exactly that much, and it was easy for this number to be omitted, since it was written in letters that are nearly the same as the last two letters of the immediately preceding word σφαγμὸν. And Epimenides went before Solon in this frugality by his own example, and accustomed the Athenians to it. Plutarch on Epimenides: [ἔλεγε δ᾽, καὶ παρὰ Σόλωνι ξενοπάθμως φίλος, πολλὰ συνεπιμεγάσατο, καὶ παρὰ ὡδοποιῶν αὐτοῦ τῆς νομοθεσίας, καὶ γὰρ ὑπὲρ ἔλεξις ἐπίστος τῆς λῃτυρ-γίας]. The Greek is corrupt here and I can only render the sense: that he was a friend to Solon, contributed much to his legislation, and was himself a model of such frugality in his worship.

units.la: Maius tamen, eodem Solone auctore in sextodecimo Axone eximiarum hostiarum pretium, quanquam & hoc vile nimis, si ad sequentia tempora, quibusistud Solonis institutum proculdubio mutauit, attendas. Plutarchus ibi-dem, ὡς γὰρ ἐν τῷ ἐκκλησιαστικῷ τὴν Ἀξόνων εἰς ζημίας ΤΩΝ ΕΚΚΡΙΤΩΝ ΙΕΡΕΙΩΝ, εἰκὸς μὲν πολλαπλασίας εἴη[?], ἄλλως δὲ καὶ πᾶσες τὰς τῶν ἐπελῆς εἰσιν[?]. Antiquitus autem Deo vnicuique terræ aruipendia dedicabant, vel diuidebant, quorum è locationibus proueniebant impensæ, quæ postea in sacrificiis publice fiebant: non enim κατ᾽ ἰδίαν victimas mactabant, sed μαδομένοι[?]. Isocrates Areopagitico: ἐν δὲ τῆς ἀγωνίας τῆς ἱερᾶς ἀπὸ μισθωμάτων ἔχουσι[?]. Harpo-cration: ἀπὸ μισθωμάτων. Δίδυμος φησιν ὁ Γραμματικὸς, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἐκ τῆς περιφερείας πεποιη-μένα ἐκ τῶν ἀγρῶν[?], πλέοντα τῆς ἀπενέμων, ἐξ ὧν μισθουμένων, αἱ εἰς τὰς θυσίας ἐγένοντο δαπάνας[?]. ἐν γὰρ κατ᾽ ἰδίαν ἔχουσι τὰ ἱερά, ἀλλὰ μισθούμενοι. Atque sumptus hos fa-ciebant maiores, quàm Legibus cautum, prout maiores erant τῶν μισθωμάτων prouentus: itaque Nicomachum Scribam notat Lysias in Oratione, quam aduersus illum scripsit, quòd cùm Leges describeret, maiores in sacra impensas adscripserit, quàm à Solone factum fuerat, cùm ita aliquando fieret, vt expensis illis, quæ ἀπὸ μισθωμάτων proueniebant, in priora, quæ occurrebant sacra, non superesset, vnde sumptus facerent in cetera, quæ superabant, sacra. Atqui necesse semper erat sacra omnia fieri, quæ Legibus imperabantur, τὰ ἐκ τῶν Κυρέων ἱερά, eique rei fuerunt semper satis τὰ μισθώματα. Quod si reliquum erat pecuniæ, poterat impendi in eadem sacra, populo scifcente & distribuente. Lysiæ verba sunt, sed corrupta leuiter: ἑαυτῷ μὲν ζῶ δὲ εἰ μὴ ἐλαῶτας ἐπὶ ἑαυτῷ[?] ὅταν δὲ ἐμὲ φάσκῃ ἀπέξει, λέγοντα ὡς χρὴ ζῆν τὰς ἱερᾶς τὰς ἐκ τῆς Κυρέων καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ πλοῖον, καὶ τὰς συλλεγομένας, ὅπου καὶ τῆς πόλεως καταπεφρ[?]ονήσεις. Ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμεῖς ἐψηφίσασθε. Vox ἐπὶ πλοῖον non est, meo iudicio, huius loci. Rescribo: λέγοντα ὡς χρὴ ζῆν τὰς ἱερᾶς τὰς ἐκ τῆς Κυρέων, καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ πλέων, καὶ τὰς συλλεγομένας. Dicit sacra esse facien-da, quemadmodum Legibus scriptum; atque si plus, quàm rite ex Lege fieret, impendatur, secundum id quod scripto cautum est cum ijs, qui τὰ περιφέρεια aruipendia locarunt: nam si superfit pecunia, & sine damno Reipublicæ fieri possit, iubente populo poterit erogari in sacra, vt lautiora sint, quàm Legibus cauetur: videndum tamen semper est, ne qua sacra, si in præcedentia, plus, quam Legibus imperatur, erogetur, prætermittantur, quo nomine Nicomachum carpit & vexat Lysias: πῶς δὴ αὖ τις ἀπὸ ἐκείνου ἡμῖν εἰ ὅσης ἀξίας, ὥσφ' ὧν μὲν τὰ πάτρια ἐπείτα, ἃ μᾶλλον συμφέρει τῇ πόλει· ἐπὶ δὲ, ἃ ὁ δῆμος ἐψηφίσατο, ἡ δωρεὰ τῶν ἀγρῶν ἐκ τῶν περιφερομένων[?]. οὐ δέ, ὦ Νικόμαχε, ταῦτα ζήτησις ἐποίησας. διαγράφεις πλείω τὰ περιφέρεια, ἀλλὰ τὰ περιφερόμενα ἐκ τῶν ἐπὶ ταῦτα ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ ἐπιτάξας[?]. ἐὰν δὲ τὰς πατρίους θυσίας ἐπαλλαχθῆναι[?]. ἐπὶ δὲ ἐκ τῆς Κυρέων ἐκ τῶν ἀγρῶν ἐκ τῆς ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐπὶ πόλις[?]. ἀλλὰ ὁ ἐστιν εἰ μὴ ἀλλεῖα αὐτὸ ἐξαρτᾶσθαι[?] ταὐτ[?]ῆς, εἰς γὰρ τὰς θυσίας τὰς πατρίους ἀπ᾽ ἐκῃ[?]νοῖ, καὶ τεῖα πάλιν ἑτέρας αὐτ᾽ ἐπὶ πόλει[?].
units.tr: Yet, on the same authority of Solon in the sixteenth axon, the price of choice victims is greater, although this too is far too cheap if you consider later times, when Solon's ordinance was doubtless changed. Plutarch there: [ὡς γὰρ ἐν τῷ ἐκκλησιαστικῷ τὴν Ἀξόνων εἰς ζημίας ΤΩΝ ΕΚΚΡΙΤΩΝ ΙΕΡΕΙΩΝ, εἰκὸς μὲν πολλαπλασίας εἴη, ἄλλως δὲ καὶ πᾶσες τὰς τῶν ἐπελῆς εἰσιν]. Formerly, however, each piece of land was dedicated or divided to God, and from the leases of these came the expenses which were afterwards made publicly in sacrifices. For they did not slaughter victims privately, but [illegible]. Isocrates in the Areopagiticus: [ἐν δὲ τῆς ἀγωνίας τῆς ἱερᾶς ἀπὸ μισθωμάτων ἔχουσι]. Harpocration: from rents. The grammarian Didymus says [Greek], the revenues from the fields, which were assigned to them, from which, when let, the expenses for the sacrifices arose: [ἐν γὰρ κατ᾽ ἰδίαν ἔχουσι τὰ ἱερά, ἀλλὰ μισθούμενοι]. These expenses were made greater than the law prescribed, in proportion as the revenue from the rents was greater. Therefore Lysias, in the speech he wrote against him, censures the scribe Nicomachus, because when he was drawing up the laws he entered larger sacred expenses than Solon had fixed. This sometimes happened, so that from those expenses which came from the rents nothing remained for the earlier sacred rites that fell due, so that the expenses for the other sacrifices that remained could be met. Yet it was always necessary that all the sacrifices the laws commanded be performed, and the rents were always sufficient for this purpose. If money remained, it could be spent on the same sacrifices, by the vote and distribution of the people. Lysias' words are slightly corrupt: [ἑαυτῷ μὲν ζῶ δὲ εἰ μὴ ἐλαῶτας ἐπὶ ἑαυτῷ ὅταν δὲ ἐμὲ φάσκῃ ἀπέξει, λέγοντα ὡς χρὴ ζῆν τὰς ἱερᾶς τὰς ἐκ τῆς Κυρέων καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ πλοῖον, καὶ τὰς συλλεγομένας, ὅπου καὶ τῆς πόλεως καταπεφρονήσεις. Ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμεῖς ἐψηφίσασθε.] The phrase upon the boat does not belong to this place, in my judgment. I restore it: [λέγοντα ὡς χρὴ ζῆν τὰς ἱερᾶς τὰς ἐκ τῆς Κυρέων, καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ πλέων, καὶ τὰς συλλεγομένας]. He says the sacrifices are to be performed as written in the law; and if more is spent than is rightly done under the law, it should be paid according to what was written with those who had leased the revenues. For if money remains and this can be done without loss to the Commonwealth, at the command of the people it may be spent on sacrifices so that they are more lavish than the law provides. Yet one must always take care that no sacrifices are neglected through spending more on the preceding ones than the law commands, and on this account Lysias carps at and harasses Nicomachus: [πῶς δὴ αὖ τις ἀπὸ ἐκείνου ἡμῖν εἰ ὅσης ἀξίας, ὥσφ' ὧν μὲν τὰ πάτρια ἐπείτα, ἃ μᾶλλον συμφέρει τῇ πόλει· ἐπὶ δὲ, ἃ ὁ δῆμος ἐψηφίσατο, ἡ δωρεὰ τῶν ἀγρῶν ἐκ τῶν περιφερομένων]. [οὐ δέ, ὦ Νικόμαχε, ταῦτα ζήτησις ἐποίησας. διαγράφεις πλείω τὰ περιφέρεια, ἀλλὰ τὰ περιφερόμενα ἐκ τῶν ἐπὶ ταῦτα ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ ἐπιτάξας].

units.la: Meminit huius Legis ὁ τοῦ Νεαίρας, εἰ γράφεσθε ὁ λόγος, id est, si titulus auctorem non mentitur, meminit, inquam, Demosthenes his verbis: [illegible, ~60 letters] Quid sint τὰ ἱερὰ τὰ Ἀμφιτρύωνος, optime explicat Hefychius, nempe in quibus sacra fiunt publicis totius ciuitatis impensis, quemadmodum τὰ Ἀμφικτύονα sunt, in quibus sacra fiunt vnius tantum Atheniensis Demi impensis. Hefychii verba sunt: Ἀμφιτρύωνος, ἱερὰ, καὶ Δημοτικά. ( ita e sequentibus supplendum est. ) Ἀμφιτρύωνος, Εἰς ἃ ξυμπαντα διδωσι ἐ πόλις, Δημοτικὰ δὲ, Εἰς ἃ οἱ Δῆμοι. Habuit igitur Atheniensium ciuitas publica sua Templa, in quibus sacra siebant publico totius ciuitatis sumptu ; habuerunt quoque singuli Athenienses Demi, & in sacra illa quisque Demus sua pecuniam conferebant, quemadmodum & Γενέσιαι & Ὀργάδες. Nam diligenter illa sunt distinguenda. Harpocration : Ἀμφιτρύωνος καὶ Δημοτικὰ ἱερὰ, διάφερε ἀλλήλων, καὶ Ὀργάδων, καὶ τὴν Γενεσίαν, ὡς Δείναρχος ἐν ὁλῷ τῷ κα τὰ Ἐπιφάνους. An vero siremplse Lege ius esset peregrinis & seruis Templa hæc Ἀμφιτρύωνος, aut Ὀργάδων, aut Γενέσια adire, quemadmodum licebat illis εἰς τὰ Δημοτικὰ ἐ̓ siam, nobis compertum non est, neque enim hæc Lex de his Templis quicquam præcipit; sed illis eam dicebant Demi ipsi, vel Ορκάδαις[?] vel Γενέθλη[?], de quibus suo loco, Deo dante, dicemus. Addit Legislator licere in Templis his, vt quae asyla sint, supplicibus sedere. Primum apud Athenienses asylum supplicibus collocatum est Templum Misericordiae: nam postquam Hercules, verba sunt Seruii ad VIII. Aeneidos, migrauit è terris, nepotes eius timentes insidias eorum, quos auus adfixerat, Athenis sibi primi asylum, hoc est, Templum Misericordiae, conlocarunt, vnde nullus posset abduci. Meminit Statius Thebaidos Lib. XII. vbi Misericordiae Templum describit:
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this Law in his speech against Neaera, if the title does not lie about the author; he speaks in these words: [illegible] What the sacred rites of Amphitryon are, Hesychius explains excellently: namely those in which the sacred rites are performed at the expense of the whole city, just as the Amphictyonic rites are those performed at the expense of a single Athenian deme. Hesychius' words are: Amphitryonos, hiera, kai Demotika [Ἀμφιτρύωνος, ἱερὰ, καὶ Δημοτικά]; (the following should be supplied from what comes after): Amphitryonos: for which the city gives everything; Demotika: for which the demes [give]. [Εἰς ἃ ξυμπαντα διδωσι ἡ πόλις, Δημοτικὰ δὲ, Εἰς ἃ οἱ Δῆμοι.] Therefore the Athenian state had its own public temples, in which sacred rites were performed at the public expense of the whole city; and the individual Athenian demes also had theirs, and each deme contributed money to those rites, as also at the Genesia and the Orgades. For these must be carefully distinguished. Harpocration: The Amphitryonian and demotic sacred rites differ from each other, and from the Orgades and the Genesia, as Deinarchus says in the whole speech against Epicrates. Whether by the Law itself it was permitted to foreigners and slaves to enter these temples of Amphitryon, or the Orgades, or the Genesia, as it was permitted for them to enter the demotic ones, we have not learned; for this Law does not prescribe anything about these temples. But the demes themselves called them the Orkadai or the Genethlai, about which we shall speak in its place, God willing. The lawgiver adds that in these temples, which are places of asylum, it is permitted to sit as suppliants. The first place of asylum established among the Athenians for suppliants was the Temple of Mercy: for after Hercules, the words of Servius on Aeneid VIII, departed from the earth, his descendants, fearing the plots of those whom their grandfather had struck down, first established for themselves at Athens an asylum, that is, the Temple of Mercy, from which no one could be dragged away. Statius mentions it in Thebaid Book XII, where he describes the Temple of Mercy:

units.la: Urbe fuit media nulli concessa potentum Ara Deum: mitis posuit Clementia sedem, Et miseri fecere sacram. sine supplice nunquam Illa nouo: nullâ damnauit vota repulsâ. Auditi quicumque rogant, noctésque diesque Ire datum, & solus numen placare querelis. Parca superstitio. non thurea flamma, nec altus Accipitur sanguis, lacrymis altaria sudant. Mœstarúmque super libamina serta comarum Pendent, & vestes mutata sorte relictae. Mite nemus circa, cultúque insigne verendo, Vittatae laurus, & supplicis arbor olivae. Nulla autem effigies, nulli concessa metallo Forma Deae, mentes habitare, & pectora gaudet. Semper habet trepidos, semper locus horret egenis Coetibus: ignotae tantum felicibus arae. Fama est defensos acie post busta paterni Numinis, Herculeos sedem fundasse nepotes. Fama minor factis. ipsos, nam credere dignum, Coelicolas, tellus quibus hospita semper Athenae, Ceu leges hominémque nouum, ritúmque sacrorum, Seminaque in vacuas hinc descendentia terras, Sic sacrasse loco commune animantibus aegris Confugium, unde procul starent irasque, minasque, Regnáque, & à iustis Fortuna recederet aris.
units.tr: In the middle of the city was an altar of the gods granted to none of the powerful; gentle Clemency established the seat, and the wretched made it sacred. Never without a suppliant was she new; she condemned no vows with refusal. Whoever asks, to be heard, is given the right to go by night and day, and alone to appease the godhead with complaints. Sparse is the worship: no incense flame, no deep blood is taken; the altars sweat with tears. And garlands of mourners' hair hang upon the offerings, and garments left behind when fortune changed. A gentle grove surrounds it, notable for reverent cultivation: laurels bound with fillets, and the olive tree of suppliants. But there is no image, no form of the goddess allowed in metal; she delights to dwell in minds and hearts. She always holds the trembling; the place always shudders for the needy assemblies; her altars are unknown only to the fortunate. It is said that after the battle, defended by the arms of their father's godhead, the descendants of Hercules founded their seat behind the tombs. The fame is less than the deeds; for it is worthy to believe that the heavenly dwellers, to whom Athens, always hospitable to the earth, as to the laws and the new man and the rite of sacred things, and the seeds descending hence into empty lands, so they consecrated in this place a common refuge for the sick among living creatures, whence wrath and threats and kingdoms should stand far off, and fortune should withdraw from the just altars.

units.la: Vetus Statii Interpres: Hyllus Deianirae & Herculis, & reliqui ex eodem nati, postquam Hercules terris abiit, pulsi ab Eurystheo, Athenas confugerunt, à quibus postquam tam facile auxilium meruerunt, hanc aram Misericordiae consecrasse memorantur. Eratque in foro posita. Pausanias Atticis: Ἀθηναίοις δὲ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ[?] ἔστιν ἐκ ἐς ἀπόρρητα ἐπίσημα[?], καὶ Ἐλέου βωμός. Asyli quoque ius habuerunt Minervae Templum in arce, & Eumenidum ara. Plutarchus Solone: Ὁ δὲ Κυλώνειος ἀγὸς ἦν μὲν ἐκ πολλοῦ διαπεφάνται[?] τὴν πόλιν, ἐξ ἧς τοὺς ἱκετεύοντας τῷ Κύλωνος[?] ἱκετεύοντας τὸν θεὸν Μεγακλῆς ὁ Ἀρχῶν[?] ἐπιστὰς ἐξάγοντας[?] δὲ τὰς ἕδρας κρύψαν[?] ἡλωκώς[?], καὶ τούτῳ ἐξορμίζουσιν[?] ὡς ἐξόρμητοι[?] τοὺς Σεμνὰς θεάς, καὶ ἐλαιώντες[?] αὐτοματώς τῆς ἑορτῆς ῥαχίσεως, ἁρμοστὸς[?] συλλαμβάνων ὁ Μεγακλῆς καὶ οἱ σύνωμόται[?], ὡς ἡ θεὸς ἡ ἱκεσία[?] ἀπολέσαι μὴ[?] καὶ τοὺς λαὸς[?] ἔξω κατηλάσθη[?], οἱ δὲ τῆς βωμοῦ[?] ἀπεσφάγησαν[?]. Hanc candé historiâ narrat Pausanias Achaicis : χρόνῳ δὲ ὕστερον αὖθι οἱ ἐχθροὶ τὰς Ἀθήνας [?], διέφθειρον τῆς Ἀθηναίων ἱκετείας τὴν Κύλωνι ὁμοῦ τῷ ἀκροπόλιν καταλαμφθέντων [?] καὶ αὐτοί τε οἱ ἀποκτείναντες ἐπομ[?]σύσαντες καὶ οἱ ἐκ ἐκείνων συγγενεῖς τῆς θεοῦ [?]. Eumenidum hoc sacellum erat iuxta Areopagum. Pausanias loco laudato : ἅμα δὲ ἡμέρᾳ ἀφιξόμενον ἐπ' αὐτὴν τὴν Ἀθηναίων, καταφυγόντων εἰς τὸν Ἄρειον πάγον, καὶ ὅτι τὴν θεὰν αἱ Σεμναὶ καλούμεναι τοὺς βωμούς, itemque Atticis. Meminit huius Asyli, ut & illius, quod ædes Thesei habuit, Aristophanes Equitibus, cuius verba describimus paullo altius repetita, ut emendemus:
units.tr: The old commentator on Statius: Hyllus, son of Deianira and Hercules, and the others born of the same, after Hercules departed from the earth, were driven out by Eurystheus and fled to Athens; and after they had obtained help there so easily, they are recorded to have consecrated this altar of Mercy. It was placed in the forum. Pausanias in the Attica: For the Athenians in the agora there is [ἐς ἀπόρρητα ἐπίσημα] and an altar of Pity [Ἐλέου βωμός]. The Athenians also had the right of asylum in the temple of Minerva on the citadel, and at the altar of the Eumenides. Plutarch in Solon: The Cylonian pollution had long since defiled the city; Megacles the archon, standing over them, drove out the suppliants of Cylon who had sought refuge at the goddess's altar, and when they had been seized, those who sat at the seats were slain at the altar. Pausanias in the Achaica narrates this same story: later, the enemies destroyed the Athenian suppliants who had been seized together with Cylon near the citadel, and both the killers themselves and their descendants were held accountable to the goddess. This little sanctuary of the Eumenides was near the Areopagus. Pausanias, the passage quoted: at daybreak coming to it, the Athenians having fled to the Areopagus, and because the goddesses called the Semnai the altars; likewise in the Attica. Aristophanes in the Knights mentions this asylum, as well as the one that the temple of Theseus had; we quote his words, taken a little further back, so that we may correct them:

units.la: ἈΠΟΞΗΠΑΙ. οὐ δῆτ' ἐμοῦ γ' ἀρξῇ ποτ'. ἀλλ' ἐάν με χρῇ Ὑπὸ πρηνδὸν [?] Γαπίσι', σὺ [?] καὶ καταγνεφέσομαι. Οὐδὲ Ναυφαίτης γ' ἐς τὴς Νεώσωνος, οὐ δῆτ', ὦ θεοί, Εἴ' ἀρ' ἐκ πεύκης γ' ἐς καχὸ καὶ ξύλων ἐπηρμένου. Εἰσὶ' ἀρέσκει τῶν' Ἀθηναίοισι, καὶ ἡμέραι μοι δοκῶ Εἰς Ὁ Θησεῖον πλεούσας, ἢ 'πὶ τῆ Σεμναῖ θεᾷ.
units.tr: ASPASIA? No, indeed, you will never rule me. But if you need me, I will be laid under the Gapisian ... and I will be covered with a cloud. Nor, by the gods, will I sail to the Nauphaites or to Neosos, no indeed, from the pine-wood and the tree-stump raised up on high. It pleases the Athenians, and it seems good to me that the days ... sail to the Theseion, or sit at the altar of the Holy Goddess. [Ἀποξηπαί. οὐ δῆτ' ἐμοῦ γ' ἀρξῇ ποτ'. ἀλλ' ἐάν με χρῇ ... καὶ καταγνεφέσομαι. Οὐδὲ Ναυφαίτης γ' ἐς τὴς Νεώσωνος, οὐ δῆτ', ὦ θεοί ... ἢ 'πὶ τῆ Σεμναῖ θεᾷ.]

units.la: Cum de se vnatantum hic loquatur triremis, illud plurale πλεούσαις vltimo versu ferri non potest: Adde quod Asylum non erat eorum, qui in Piræo, Eumenidum hoc sacellum, quod plusquam stadiis quadraginta à Piræo distabat. Referibo igitur:
units.tr: Since only the trireme speaks here about itself, the plural "sailing" (πλεούσαις) in the last verse cannot stand. Add that the asylum was not one of those at Piraeus: this was the little shrine of the Eumenides, which was more than forty stadia from Piraeus. I therefore correct the text to read:

units.la: Εἰσὶ' ἀρέσκει τῶν' Ἀθηναίοισι, καὶ ἡμέραι μοι δοκῶ Εἰς Ὁ Θησεῖον πλέουσα, ἵνα ἢ 'πὶ τῆ Σεμναῖ θεᾷ.
units.tr: It pleases the Athenians, and it seems good to me that I sail to the Theseion, to sit at the altar of the Holy Goddess. [Εἰσὶ' ἀρέσκει τῶν' Ἀθηναίοισι, καὶ ἡμέραι μοι δοκῶ Εἰς Ὁ Θησεῖον πλέουσα, ἵνα ἢ 'πὶ τῆ Σεμναῖ θεᾷ.]

units.la: Ego, inquit, si quidem Atheniensibus decretum est navigare εἰς Καρχηδόνα, ad Thesei sacram ædem navigans ibi sedebo supplex, ἵνα ἢ ὅτι τῇ Σεμναῖ θεᾷ, eodem iure quo ea, quæ ad Eumenidum aras sedet. Iam vero non sine causa comparat asyli ius, quod Thesei ædi concessum erat, cum asyli iure, quod habuit Eumenidum sacellum, id autem erat sacrosanctum maxime, itaque esse iusserat oraculo Dodonæus Iupiter. Pausanias Achaicis : Ἀθηναίοις γὰρ ὅτι ἡλικία μάλιστα τῆ Ἀφιδάμπας ἀφίκετο καὶ τῷ ἐν Δωδώνῃ δίχα τὰ ἐπὶ πεδὸ.
units.tr: He says: "If indeed the Athenians have decided to sail to Carthage, I, sailing to the sacred temple of Theseus, will sit there as a suppliant, to be with the Holy Goddess, by the same right by which she sits at the altars of the Eumenides." Now the author compares the right of asylum granted to the temple of Theseus with the right of asylum held by the little shrine of the Eumenides, and that was held to be most sacred; so Jupiter of Dodona had ordered it by oracle. Pausanias in the Achaica: "For the Athenians came at the same time as Aphidamas, and by the oracle at Dodona ..." [Ἀθηναίοις γὰρ ὅτι ἡλικία μάλιστα τῆ Ἀφιδάμπας ἀφίκετο καὶ τῷ ἐν Δωδώνῃ δίχα τὰ ἐπὶ πεδὸ.]

units.la: Φεύξεσθαι δ' Ἄρειον τε πάγον, βωμοῖς τε ξυνᾶδης Εὐμενίδων, ὅτι γὰρ Λακεδαιμόνιοι ἱκετεύσαι Δουεῖ πιεζομένους· τοὺς μὲν σὺ πτῆνε σιδηρῷ, Μηδ' ἱκέτας ἀδικεῖν ἱκέτας δ' ἱερεῖ τε καὶ ἀγνοί.
units.tr: "You will flee to the Areopagus and to the altars of the Eumenides, for the Lacedaemonians came as suppliants, pressed by the Doves: you, winged one, with iron, and do not wrong suppliants; suppliants are holy and sacred." [Φεύξεσθαι δ' Ἄρειον τε πάγον, βωμοῖς τε ξυνᾶδης Εὐμενίδων, ὅτι γὰρ Λακεδαιμόνιοι ἱκετεύσαι Δουεῖ πιεζομένους· τοὺς μὲν σὺ πτῆνε σιδηρῷ, Μηδ' ἱκέτας ἀδικεῖν ἱκέτας δ' ἱερεῖ τε καὶ ἀγνοί.]

units.la: Duo autem fuerunt Athenis Thesei sacella, vnum intra vrbem, alterum extra vrbem. An vtrumque ius asyli habuerit, videndum est. Vrbanum Thesei sacellum erat prope Gymnasium. Pausanias Atticis: πρὸς δὲ τῷ Γυμνασίῳ. Θησεὺς ὅστις ἰερόν. idque media in vrbe, quod docet Plutarchus, vt & ἀσυλίαν habuisse. Κεῖται νῦν ἐν μέσῃ τῇ πόλει, τὸ δὲ νῦν Γυμνάσιον, ἔσι δὲ φύξιον οἰκέταις καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ταπεινοτέροις καὶ ἱκέταις χρείαν. Quæ vero erat extra vrbem Thesei ædicula, non longe à muro longo erat posita: Colligo ex Andocidis Oratione περὶ μυστηρίων. ἀναχαλέσαντες δὲ τοὺς Σπαρτιάτας, ἀφικνοῦντο, Ἀθηναίων τοὺς μὲν οἰκοῦντας ἐναι εἰς τὴν ἀγορὰν, τὰ ὅπλα λαβόντας τοὺς δὲ ἐν μαχρῷ πόλῃ, εἰς τὸ Θησεῖον. Hoc designat Aristophanes versibus, quos hic iterum describemus:
units.tr: There were two shrines of Theseus at Athens, one within the city and the other outside it. It must be considered whether each of them had the right of asylum. The city shrine of Theseus was near the Gymnasium. Pausanias, in the Attica: "Next to the Gymnasium, Theseus' sanctuary ..." And this was in the middle of the city, as Plutarch teaches, who says that it also had asylum: "It now lies in the middle of the city, and the present Gymnasium is a refuge for slaves and for all the lowly and for suppliants in need." [πρὸς δὲ τῷ Γυμνασίῳ. Θησεὺς ὅστις ἰερόν. ... ἱκέταις χρείαν.] But the little shrine of Theseus outside the city was placed not far from the Long Wall. I gather this from Andocides' speech On the Mysteries: "When they summoned the Spartans, they came, some of the Athenians living in the agora taking up arms, and others in the Long Wall, to the Theseion." [ἀναχαλέσαντες δὲ τοὺς Σπαρτιάτας, ... εἰς τὸ Θησεῖον.]

units.la: Εἰ σ' ἀρέσκει τῶν' Ἀθηναίοισι, καὶ ἡμέραι μοι δοκῶ Εἰς Ὁ Θησεῖον πλέουσα, ἵνα ἢ 'πὶ τῆ Σεμναῖ θεᾷ.
units.tr: "If it pleases the Athenians, and it seems good to me that I sail to the Theseion, to sit at the altar of the Holy Goddess." [Εἰ σ' ἀρέσκει τῶν' Ἀθηναίοισι, καὶ ἡμέραι μοι δοκῶ Εἰς Ὁ Θησεῖον πλέουσα, ἵνα ἢ 'πὶ τῆ Σεμναῖ θεᾷ.]

units.la: Quibus è verbis duo colligas, vnum est asylum fuisse, alterum ad mare positum, nempe, si quid iudico, non longe aberat à muro longo, intra μακρὸν τεῖχος sive ὃ Βοφὸν[?], & ὃ Δ[illegible, ~3 letters] μέσον τεῖχος sive ὃ Νόπιον, quod erat medium inter ὃ μακρὸν τεῖχος καὶ ὃ Φαληρικόν. Quod etiam ex Aristophanis versibus confirmatur: nam è Pirææ nauali soluit triremis navigatura in Thraciam, in hac ora habes Phalerum: sed statim ac soluit triremis, ad ipsum μακρὸν τεῖχος confugit in asylum ad Thesei ædem: Erat igitur hoc Thesei sacellum in Piræo ad mare, habebatque ius asyli, quemadmodum & vrbanum Θησεῖον. Quare de vtroque capiendus Diodorus Siculus Lib. IV. οἱ δὲ Αθηναῖοι μεταμεληθέντες τὰ τε ὀστᾶ μετέκομισαν, καὶ πέμψαντες ἐπὶ τὰς Αθήνας ὃ Θησεὺς ἀπὸ τῆς Σκύρου ἀπὸ αὐτοῦ Θησεῖον[?]. Itemque Hesychius his verbis: Θησεῖον, ἡ εἰς Θησέως, ἐφ' ὧν οἱ ἱκέται δεδράσκοντες καταφεύγουσι. Auctor Etymologici: Θησεῖον, τὸ εἰς Θησέα ἐστὶ τὸ Θησεῖ. ἡ ὅσις τῆς οἰκήσεως ἀσυλον ὥσπερ ἐλέγετο δὲ ἱερὰ ἐπὶ ἐν τῷ ἱκέται. ἡ τοῦ Θησέως, ἐφ' οὗ οἱ ἀσεβεῖς τοῦ τῶν καταφεύγουσι. Φιλόχορος δὲ, ἡ μόνον ἱερὰ ἐν εἰς πᾶσιν ἱκέταις ἐπὶ καὶ ἱκετῶν ἔνεκα εἰς ἱκετεύοντες. Scholiastes Comici ad laudata eius verba: εἰς Θησεῖον. ἐπεὶ ἐκ ἱκετῶν καταφυγόντες τῷ οἰκέτῃ ἀσυλίας εἴχον. Ὅτι τῷ Σεμνῷ δῆλον, εἰς ὃ Ἐνυμῶν ἱερὸν, καὶ ἐπὶ ἱερὸν οἰκέτῃ ἐφέρων. Suidas de his Eumenidum & Thesei ædibus sacris. εἰς ἡ ἐν ἱερὰ ἱκέται ἐπὶ καὶ ἡ ἀσυλίας εἶχον. Obseruandum autem est, certis finibus circumscriptam fuisse in his omnibus ædibus sacris asyli sanctitatem. Pollux Lib. I. cap. I. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀσυλὸν τὸ ἕλη, τῶν καὶ χρησφίτοις λέγω, καὶ φύξιμον, καὶ ἱερεῖ ὁ ἱερὸς, ἐφ' ὧν τῆς οἰκήσεως ἀσφαλῶς. Vbi referibo, ἐφ' ὧν τῆς ἱκέτης ἀσφαλῶς non enim soli serui, quanquam & hi frequentissime, sed etiam alij supplices ad templa aræque confugiebant, atque eo tutelæ genere frequenter vtebantur: Quia vero inde neminem licebat vi abripere, vt tamen arcerentur, admouebant ignem, atque ita non ab hominibus, sed à Deo amoueri credebantur. Itaque dicit Hermione apud Euripidem Andromachæ in cognomine fabula sedenti ad Theridis signum:
units.tr: From these words you may gather two things. One is that there was an asylum, and the other is that it was placed by the sea, namely, if I judge rightly, not far from the Long Wall, within the Long Wall, which is called the Bophon, and the Middle Wall, which is called the Nopion, which lay between the Long Wall and the Phalerum. This is also confirmed by the verses of Aristophanes: for when the trireme sets off from the naval station at Piraeus, to sail to Thrace, you have Phalerum on this coast; but as soon as the trireme sets off, it flees for asylum to the Long Wall itself, to the temple of Theseus. This Theseion, therefore, was at Piraeus by the sea, and had the right of asylum, just as the city Theseion did. So Diodorus Siculus, Book IV, must be understood of both: "The Athenians, repenting, carried the bones over and sent them to Athens, Theseus from Scyros ..." Likewise Hesychius, in these words: "Theseion: the (place) of Theseus, where suppliants fleeing take refuge." The author of the Etymologicum: "Theseion: that which belongs to Theseus; a place of dwelling which is an asylum, as was said, and a sacred place for suppliants." The scholiast on the Comic poet, on his words: "to the Theseion: since suppliants who fled there had asylum." Suidas on these sacred buildings of the Eumenides and Theseus: "in which suppliants took refuge and had asylum." It must be noted that in all these sacred buildings the sanctity of the asylum was confined within fixed boundaries. Pollux, Book I, chapter 1: "If also the asylum is a place, and I speak of the things that are granted, and a refuge, and a sacred place, where ..." Here I read "where suppliants are safe"; for not only slaves, although these most often, but also other suppliants fled to temples and altars, and frequently used this kind of protection. And because no one could be dragged out of there by force, yet to keep them away they set fire around, and so they were believed to be removed not by men but by God. Hence Hermione in Euripides' Andromache, in the play of that name, sits beside the statue of Theris:

units.la: πῦρ σὺν τὰς ἐστίσιν.
units.tr: Fire with the hearth-fires.

units.la: Scholia. ἵσως ὧν τῶν εἰς βωμὸν καὶ ἀφ' ἑκάστου πῦρ ἐπὶ τὰ σοφιῶν. Ex eo more Plautus Mostellaria Actu V. Sc. I.
units.tr: Scholia: Perhaps of these, the fire at the altar and from each ... In this custom Plautus, in the Mostellaria, Act V, Scene I:

units.la: Iam iubeboignem & sarmenta, carnifex, circumdari.
units.tr: Now I will order the fire and the faggots, executioner, to be put around.

units.la: Et Rudente Act. III. Sc. IV.
units.tr: And in the Rudens, Act III, Scene IV:

units.la: Ibo hercle aliquo quaeritatum ignem, Ignem magnum hic faciam.
units.tr: I'll go somewhere to look for fire; I'll make a big fire here.

units.la: Sed haec satis: Paene autem adnotasse praeterieram, aliud, praeterquam Thesei fanum, fuisse extra vrbem, Munychiæ, asylum, quò confugiebant qui in Piræo habitabant, item Tricrarchi & nautæ: huc pertinet Demosthenis locus ἐν τῷ ἀξίᾳ ἐφ' αἵς ἐν τῷ ἀσυλῳ ἔχουσι... Vlpianus ad hunc locum; καὶ τῷ ἐφεύγοντι, οἱ πρὸς τῷ πειραιεῖ τῷ ἐπιφανεῖς ἐν τῷ ἀσπίδι ἐν τῷ Μουνιχία ὁ Πειραιεύς. Quæramus vero, quot fuerint Athenis asyla: Atque id commodè vt fiat; videndum est vtrum omnes Deorum aut Heroum aræ, omnia Templa, asyli ius habuerint necne: & quidem habuisse videtur posse colligi, nam passim in Comœdiis palliatis serui tutelæ causa aras occupant: ita apud Plautum Mo-
units.tr: But enough of this. I had almost forgotten to note that, apart from the shrine of Theseus, there was outside the city, at Munychia, another asylum, to which those who lived in Piraeus fled, likewise the trierarchs and sailors. To this pertains the passage of Demosthenes, "in the ... for which they hold in asylum..." Ulpian on this passage: "and to the fleeing man, those at Piraeus, the notables, in the shield, at Munychia, the Piraeus." But let us ask how many asylums there were at Athens. To do this conveniently, it must be considered whether all the altars of the gods or heroes, all temples, had the right of asylum or not. And indeed it seems it may be gathered that they had it, for everywhere in the comedies in cloaks slaves seize altars for protection. So in Plautus' Mostellaria:

units.la: stellaria Act. V. Sce. I. Tranio.
units.tr: Mostellaria, Act V, Scene I. Tranio:

units.la: Ego interim hanc aram occupabo.
units.tr: Meanwhile I will seize this altar.

units.la: Terentius Heautontimorumeno Act. V. Sc. II.
units.tr: Terence, Heautontimorumenos, Act V, Scene II:

units.la: --Nemo accusat, Syre, te, nec tu aram tibi,
units.tr: No one accuses you, Syrus, nor do you prepare an altar for yourself,

units.la: Nec precatorem pararis.
units.tr: nor a suppliant's ... (refuge).

units.la: Undeapud Euripidem Andromache:
units.tr: Hence in Euripides' Andromache:

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Verumtamen certissimum est, non omnes aras, non omnia Templa habuisse ius asyli, nec id probant Euripidis verba, sed id tantum servis, aut aliis supplicibus perfugia fuisse, quia alio confugere non poterant quam ad Templa sive aras, non tamen ad omnes aras, aut omnia Templa: neque enim omnia habebant ius asyli. Comicorum vero exempla non omnibus aris, sed quibusdam, quas designant, ius istud adstruunt: quippe cum in Scena aræ veræ & propriæ fuerint, Bacchi, aut Apollinis, tamen apud Plautum Rudente Palæstra atque Ampelisca ad Veneris aram sedent, &
units.tr: Yet it is most certain that not all altars and not all temples had the right of asylum; Euripides' words do not prove this, but only that there was a refuge for slaves, or other suppliants, because they could not flee elsewhere than to temples or altars, yet not to all altars or all temples: for not all had the right of asylum. The examples of the comic poets support this right not for all altars but for certain ones which they name, since on the stage the altars were real and proper, of Bacchus or Apollo; yet in Plautus' Rudens, Palaestra and Ampelisca sit at the altar of Venus, and

units.la: Hic in fano Veneris signum flentes amplexae tenent.
units.tr: Here at the statue in the temple of Venus they weeping clasp and hold it.

units.la: Et Tranio apud eundem Mostellaria occupando aram designat, ad quam confugit. Quare non fuit asylum in omnibus Templis, verba sunt Servij ad Librum II. Æneid. nisi quibus consecrationis Lege concessum esset. Vnde Legis apud Diodorum Siculum verbis iam ante laudatis, cùm agit de æde, quam Athenienses suo dederunt Theseo, [illegible, ~45 letters] Si omnia Deorum atque Heroum Templa asyli ius habuissent, nihil opus erat addidisse, Athenienses [?]Θησεῖον [?]ποιῆσαι [?]ἄσυλον, cum ius istud asyli habuisset pro omnium Templorum lege: sed non ita est: Solis in Templis asylum fuit, quibus consecrationis Lege concessum fuit. Vnde necessum habuit Diodorus observare Athenienses Templo, quod Theseo consecrarunt, consecrationis Lege asylum concessisse. Quot autem Templa sive sacella fuerint, quibus asylum Lege consecrationis concesserint Athenienses, dicere periculosæ forte plenum opus est aleæ. Audebimus tamen: Quatuor igitur Templorum, quibus asylum concessum fuerit intra vrbem, duorum in Piræeo, mentio occurrit: Eorum, quæ in vrbe, primum est, ara Misericordiæ ad forum: Secundum, Templum Minervæ in arce: Tertium, Eumenidum Sacellum in Areopago: Quartum denique, Thesei fanum prope Gymnasium: Duorum vero quæ extra vrbem vnum est, Thesei fanum in Piræeo ad longum murum: alterum Munychiæ. Plura autem non fuisse facile mihi persuadeo, & vides e sex asylis, quatuor in vrbe fuisse, duo in Piræeo; & id quidem recte atque ordine: Nam Piræus, & adiuncta ei Munychia, (nam hæc sub illo comprehendebatur) tertiam Vrbis partem faciebant, itaque e sex asylis trientem, id est, duo asyla habuit Piræus, reliqui duo trientes, id est, asyla fuerunt intra vrbem: unde emendandi sunt Harpocrationis & Suidæ codices in [?]Ἀγοράνομοι, [?]Ἀγυιαί, [?]Μέζωνες, [?]Σιπφύλακες, ubi hæc proportio non observatur: Sed de his loco commodiore, si Deus dederit, in sequentibus dicemus.
units.tr: And Tranio in the same Mostellaria, by seizing the altar, shows the altar to which he flees. Therefore the asylum was not in all temples; these are the words of Servius on Book II of the Aeneid: unless it had been granted by the law of consecration. Hence, in the law in Diodorus Siculus, quoted above, when he speaks of the temple which the Athenians gave to Theseus, [illegible]. If all temples of gods and heroes had the right of asylum, there was no need to add that the Athenians made the Theseion an asylum, since that right of asylum would have been held by the law of all temples. But it is not so: asylum existed only in those temples to which it had been granted by the law of consecration. Hence Diodorus was bound to note that the Athenians had granted asylum by the law of consecration to the temple they consecrated to Theseus. How many temples or shrines there were to which the Athenians granted asylum by the law of consecration is perhaps a dangerous task, full of risk. Yet I will dare: of temples within the city to which asylum was granted, four are mentioned, and of two at Piraeus: among those in the city, the first is the altar of Mercy in the forum; the second, the temple of Minerva on the citadel; the third, the shrine of the Eumenides on the Areopagus; and fourth, the temple of Theseus near the Gymnasium. Of those outside the city, one is the temple of Theseus at Piraeus by the Long Wall, the other at Munychia. I am easily persuaded that there were no more, and you see that of six asylums, four were in the city and two at Piraeus; and this is indeed correct and in order. For Piraeus, together with Munychia joined to it (for this was included under that name), made up a third part of the city; so of six asylums, a third, that is two asylums, belonged to Piraeus, and the remaining two-thirds, that is, the asylums, were within the city. Hence the manuscripts of Harpocration and Suidas must be emended at [the entries] Agoranomoi, Agyiai, Mezones, Siphylakes, where this proportion is not observed. But of these matters we will speak in a more suitable place in what follows, God willing.

units.la: Asylorum quoque ius apud Romanos obtinuit ab ipso nascentis Vrbis exordio, auctore Romulo, idemque imo longe sanctius confugium præbuerunt Cæsarum statuæ. Meminerunt Iurisconsulti Labeo & Cælius apud Vlpianum Libro I. ad Edictum Ædilium Curulium, cuius verba referuntur Lege XVII. D.de Ædilitio Edicto. Apud Labeonem, & Cælium quæritur; Si quis in alylum confugerit, aut eò se conferat, quò solent venire, qui se venales postulant: an fugitiuus sit? Ego puto, non esse eum fugitiuum, qui id facit, quod publicè facere licere arbitratur. ne eum quidem,qui ad Statuam Cæsaris confugit,fugitiuum arbitror: non enim fugiendi animo hoc facit. Idem puto & in eum, qui in alylum, vel quod aliud confugit, quia non fugiendi animo hoc facit. Interpretantur Clarissimi Viri hæc Legis verba, aut eò se conferat,quò solent venire,qui se venales postulant, de catasta, in qua solebant venire,qui venales producebantur: sed, meo iudicio, in catasta qui veniebant, non seipsos venales postulabant, sed à mangonibus aut dominis producebantur. Aliud igitur intelligendum est;nempe sui se nummis serui emebant,alio emptioni nomen suum accommodante, Lege IV. D.de Manumissionibus: itaque è Lege illa XVII. D. de Ædilitio Edicto, videtur locus fuisse, in quem venire solebant, qui se venales, id est, suis se nummis emi, nomine tantùm emptioni accommodato, postulabant, nam qui suis nummis emebantur, in eam conditionem redigebantur, ut libertatem adipiscerentur. d. Lege IV. D.de Manumissionibus: itaque, si quis suis emptus nummis à Domino, in cuius fidem confugit, non manumittitur; potest queri cum domino suo, quod ab eo non manumittatur, Romæ quidem apud Præfectum Vrbi, in Prouinciis vero apud Præsides, ex sacris constitutionibus Diuorum Fratrum Lege V. D.eod. Lege I.D. de officio Præfecti Vrbi. Huiusmodi igitur seruum, qui hunc in locum se contulit,in quo conueniunt,qui se suis emiummis[?] ab amicis emptioni nomen accommodantibus postulant, fugitiuum non esse pronunciat Vlpianus, nam id facit,quod publicè facere licere arbitratur, ac ne quidem cum ad Statuam Cæsaris confugit, quanquam qui id facit seruus, non jam se suis emere nummis in libertatem quæsiit, sed de domino, cuius imperium refugit,queritur per officium distrahendus: ita enim agebatur cum seruo, qui ad Cæsaris statuam confugerat. Habes apud Vlpianum Lib. VIII. de officio Proconsulis sub titulo, De Dominorum sævitia: cuius verba habentur in Collatione Legum Mosaycarum & Romanarum, itemque Lege II. D.de His,qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt: Si dominus in seruos sæuierit, vel ad impudicitiam turpemque violationem compellat: quæ sint partes Præsidis, ex Rescripto Diui Pij ad Ælium Marcianum Proconsulem Bœticæ manifestabitur, cuius Rescripti verba hæc sunt: Dominorum quidem potestatem in suos seruos illibatam esse oportet, nec cuiquam hominum ius suum detrahi. Sed dominorum interest, ne auxilium contra sæuitiam, vel famem, vel intolerabilem iniuriam denegetur his, qui iuste deprecantur. Ideoque cognosce de querelis eorum,qui ex familia Iulij Sabini ad Statuam confugerunt: & si vel durius habitos, quam æquum est, vel infami iniuria affectos cognoueris: veniri iube ita ut in potestate domini non reuertantur. Idem Rescriptum leges Institutionum in libris tit. eod. sed quædam præmisit à nobis obseruanda. Sed & maior asperitas dominorum eiusdem Principis Constitutione coërcetur: nam Antoninus consultus à quibusdam Præsidibus Prouinciarum de his seruis, qui ad ædem sacram, vel ad statuam Principum confugiunt, præcepit, ut si intolerabilis videatur fœnitia dominorum[?], cogantur seruos suos bonis condicionibus vendere, ut pretium dominis daretur. Addidit hic de suo, quod etiam obseruat maximus vir, addidit, inquam, de suo Iustinianus, ad eandem sacram: nempe Iustiniani aeuo aeque sacrosanctum erat asylum Ecclesiæ, quàm statuæ Principum, imò longè augustius esse voluerunt Imperatores Theodosius atque Valentinianus Augusti his verbis: [illegible, ~150 letters]. Quæ verba immediatè præcedunt Constitutionem, quæ habetur Lege IV. Cod Theod. de his qui ad Ecclesiam confugiunt, & Lege III. Cod. cod. quo titulo asylum tributum est Ecclesiis. Serui autem, qui ad statuas confugerant, audiebat Præfectus Vrbi, Lege I. D. De officio Præfecti Vrbi. Atque hi serui, qui ad statuam confugiebant, dominum infamare censebantur, Lege V. D. de extraordinariis criminibus. Quare venditor si dixerit seruum ad statuam nunquam confugisse, oportet eum id præstare, Lege XIX. D. de Ædilitio Edicto. Cùm enim Leges omnibus hominibus æqualiter securitatem tribuant, merito visum est, in iniuriam potius alterius, quàm sui defensionis gratia, ad statuas vel imagines Principum confugere, nisi si quis ex vinculis vel custodia, detentus à potentioribus, ad huiusmodi præsidium confugerit, Lege XXVIII. D. de pœnis.
units.tr: The right of asylum also held sway among the Romans from the very beginning of the city, under Romulus as its author. The statues of the Caesars offered an even more sacred refuge. The jurists Labeo and Caelius are mentioned by Ulpian in Book 1 on the Edict of the Curule Aediles, whose words are quoted in Law 17, D. de Aedilitio Edicto. Labeo and Caelius ask: If someone takes refuge in an asylum, or betakes himself to where those go who demand to be sold, is he a runaway? I think that he is not a runaway who does what he thinks it lawful to do publicly. Nor do I think a runaway even one who flees to the statue of Caesar, for he does not do this with intent to run away. I think the same of one who flees to an asylum or elsewhere, since he does not do this with intent to run away. The most distinguished men interpret the words of this law, or betakes himself to where those go who demand to be sold, as referring to the auction block (catasta), on which those who were put up for sale were displayed. But in my judgment, those who came to the auction block did not demand to be sold themselves; they were presented by slave-dealers or masters. Something else must therefore be understood: namely, that slaves bought themselves with their own money, another person lending his name to the purchase (Law 4, D. de Manumissionibus). So from that Law 17, D. de Aedilitio Edicto, there seems to have been a place to which those came who demanded to be sold, that is, to be bought with their own money, the purchase being made in name only by lending a name to it. For those who were bought with their own money were brought into that condition so that they might obtain freedom (Law 4, cited, D. de Manumissionibus). Thus, if a slave bought by his master with his own money takes refuge in the protection of the one into whose care he flees, he is not manumitted; he may complain against his master that he is not freed by him, at Rome indeed before the Prefect of the City, and in the provinces before the governors, under the sacred constitutions of the divine brothers (Law 5, D. eod.; Law 1, D. de officio Praefecti Urbi). Ulpian therefore pronounces that a slave of this sort, who has betaken himself to this place where those meet who, through friends lending their names to the purchase, demand to be bought with their own money, is not a runaway, for he does what he thinks it lawful to do publicly. Nor is he one even when he flees to the statue of Caesar. Yet a slave who does this is no longer seeking freedom by buying himself with his own money; he complains of the master whose rule he flees, and asks to be sold by the office. For thus was a slave dealt with who had fled to Caesar's statue. You have this in Ulpian, Book 8, on the office of the Proconsul, under the title On the cruelty of masters. His words are found in the Collatio of Mosaic and Roman Laws, and likewise in Law 2, D. de His qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt: If a master rages against his slaves, or compels them to immorality and shameful violation, what the duties of the governor are will be made clear by the rescript of the divine Pius to Aelius Marcianus, proconsul of Baetica, whose words are these: The power of masters over their slaves ought to remain unimpaired, and no one's right should be taken from him. But it is in the masters' interest that help against cruelty, or hunger, or intolerable injury, not be denied to those who justly appeal. Therefore inquire into the complaints of those from the household of Julius Sabinus who have fled to the statue; and if you find that they have been treated more harshly than is fair, or been subjected to shameful injury, order them to be sold so that they do not return to the power of the master. The same rescript is cited in the Institutes, in the title quoted, but with some additions that we must observe. But the excessive harshness of masters is also restrained by a constitution of the same Prince: for Antoninus, when consulted by certain governors of the provinces about those slaves who flee to a sacred temple or to the statue of the Princes, ordered that if the cruelty of the masters seems intolerable, they be compelled to sell their slaves on good terms, so that a price be given to the masters. Justinian added here, on his own, what the most distinguished man also observes: he added, I say, on his own, to the same sacred [place]. For in Justinian's age the asylum of the Church was just as sacrosanct as the statues of the Princes; indeed the Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian Augusti wished it to be far more august, in these words: …. These words immediately precede the constitution found in Law 4, Cod. Theod., de his qui ad Ecclesiam confugiunt, and in Law 3, Cod. eod., by which the title asylum was granted to churches. But slaves who had fled to statues were heard by the Prefect of the City (Law 1, D. de officio Praefecti Urbi). And those slaves who fled to a statue were considered to defame their master (Law 5, D. de extraordinariis criminibus). Hence, if a seller says that the slave never fled to a statue, he must guarantee it (Law 19, D. de Aedilitio Edicto). For since the laws grant security equally to all men, it has been judged better to flee to statues or images of the Princes in order to injure another rather than for one's own defence, unless someone, held in chains or custody by the more powerful, has fled to such protection (Law 28, D. de poenis).

units.la: Quanquam autem Lege concessum sit peregrinis atque ipsis seruis Atheniensium Templa [illegible, ~12 letters] adire, supplicibusque sedere, tamen non omnibus id concessum est Atheniensibus: nam Lege quibusdam interdicitur omnibus omnino Templis [illegible, ~14 letters], de quibus suo dicemus loco, [illegible, ~8 letters], funitque hi [illegible, ~10 letters], infamia notati. At verò quibusdam vitæ integris & famæ illibatæ Lege interdicebatur aditu sacelli Eumenidum: [illegible, ~24 letters] | Redeuntibus postliminio ab hostibus non licere [illegible, ~26 letters] | sacellum Eumenidum adire.
units.tr: Although by law foreigners and the slaves of the Athenians themselves were permitted to approach the temples and sit as suppliants, not all Athenians were granted this. For by law certain persons were forbidden entry to all temples…, of which we shall speak in its proper place… and these were marked with infamy. But to certain persons whose life was blameless and reputation unstained, the law forbade approach to the shrine of the Eumenides… Those returning by right of postliminium from the enemy were not permitted … to approach the shrine of the Eumenides.

units.la: Legem hanc descripsit Hesychius, sed locus miserè corruptus est, ita editur: [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~70 letters] [illegible, ~65 letters] [illegible, ~55 letters]. Emendabat hunc locum merito suo Clarissimus Meursius: [illegible, ~45 letters]. Nos verò longè aliter emendandum & exponendum hunc locum suspicamur: suspicionem nostram horum rerum studiosos non celabimus. Rescribendum itaque coniicio: [illegible, ~90 letters] [illegible, ~80 letters] [illegible, ~70 letters]. Interpretatur eruditissimus Grammaticus quis sit ὁ Ἀπέφθιμος, nempe is est, cui tanquam mortuo iusta funera facta sunt: Eum reducem per sinum laxae stolae mulier demittebat, tanquam denuo renasci videretur. Quem Atheniensium morem imitati sunt ex parte Romani, vt Illustris Herosad Festum obseruauit. Nam eum, qui postliminio ab hostibus reuertebatur, nolebant Romani limen insistere, quia eo funestari putabant, tam limen vtrumque, & superum & inferum, si a mortuo calcaretur, quam & hominem ipsum: Idcirco tecto perforato in ædes admittebatur, ne ominosum illi esset per ianuam ingredi, per quam tanquam elatuserat. Ij autem, quibus absentibus tanquam mortuis funus factum fuerat, duùm sunt genera: aut enim peregrè erant historiæ vel negotiorum ergo, aut militatum abierant: his domum reducibus Lege non licebat Eumenidum sacellum adire, vt Hesychius hic obseruat.
units.tr: Hesychius also described this law, but the passage is wretchedly corrupted and is printed thus: … The most distinguished Meursius emended this passage with his usual skill: …. We, however, suspect that this passage should be emended and explained quite differently, and we will not hide our suspicion from students of these matters. I conjecture, then, that it should be rewritten thus: … The most learned grammarian explains who the Apephthimos is: namely, he is the one for whom funeral rites were performed as for a dead man. A woman let him back in through the fold of a loose robe, as if he were being born again. The Romans partly imitated this Athenian custom, as the illustrious Heros observed on Festus. For the Romans were unwilling that one who returned from the enemy by postliminium should set foot on the threshold, because they thought that the threshold, both upper and lower, was defiled if trodden by a dead man, just as the man himself would be. Therefore he was admitted to the house through a perforated roof, lest it be ominous for him to enter by the door through which he had been carried out as dead. Those, however, for whom funeral rites had been performed in their absence as if they were dead are of two kinds: either they had been abroad for the sake of study or business, or they had gone off to military service. For these, on returning home, it was not lawful to approach the shrine of the Eumenides, as Hesychius observes here.

units.la: Tem⁄ lorum, quibus concessum fuerat asyli ius, religionem tutati sunt, Lege scripta, qua Supplices sacrosanctos esse sanciebatur.
units.tr: Of the temples to which the right of asylum had been granted, the sanctity was protected by a written law, which decreed that suppliants are inviolable.

units.la: Τοὺς ἱκέτας εἴ] ἀσφαλὲς. Supplices esse sacrosanctos.
units.tr: Suppliants are inviolable. [Τοὺς ἱκέτας ... ἀσφαλὲς]

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Equites his verbis, in Cylonis historia referenda: Τοὺς ἡ ἄλλους φονέας ... ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς βωμοῦ ... (Greek text as printed, partly illegible in scan) ... Sed mendum est in his verbis, ὅτι ἐκ τῶν ἀρχαίων νόμων προσέκοπε, non enim secundum Leges iura asyli temerauerant, imò potius conta Legum sanctiones supplices non habuerant sacrosanctos. Relcribendum itaque putamus apud Interpretem Aristophanis: οἱ καὶ ἐξέβαλον τῆς πόλεως, ὅτι ἐκπὶ ἀρχαίων νόμων προσέκοπε, Τοὺς ἱκέτας φονεύσαντας. Dicit esse sextam Legem inter antiquas, non Solonis illas, sed longè antiquiores: nam hæc asylorum ἀσφάλεια concetta pœnè cum ipsis cultus Deorum primordiis, & Deorum oraculis sancita videtur: ita de asylo concesso Eumenidum ædi sacræ refert Paufanias Achaïcis: Φαίνεται ... Ἀθηναῖοις ... (Greek text as printed, partly illegible in scan) Φεύζετο δ' Ἀρείων τ' πάγον, βωμοῦ τ' Ἰυνάτης Εὐμενίδων, οὔ χρὴ Λακεδαιμονίους ὁ ἱκετεύσαι Δικεῖ πειζούσης· τοὺς μὲν οὖ κτεῖνε σιδήρῳ, Μοῖ' ἱκέτας ἀδικῶν· ἱκέτας δ' ἱερῆ τυχῇ ἀγοῖ.
units.tr: The scholiast on Aristophanes' Knights mentions this law in his account of the story of Cylon: "The others, the murderers … but from the altar …" There is an error in these words, that they offended against the ancient laws. For they had not violated the rights of asylum according to the laws; rather, they had not treated suppliants as inviolable in accordance with the sanctions of the laws. We therefore think the interpreter of Aristophanes should be read thus: "those who also drove them out of the city, because they had offended against the ancient laws by killing suppliants." He says that this is the sixth law among the ancient ones, not those of Solon but much more ancient. For this inviolability of asylums seems to have been granted almost with the very beginnings of the worship of the gods, and sanctioned by the oracles of the gods. Thus Pausanias, in the Achaica, relates concerning the asylum granted to the shrine of the Eumenides: [Φεύζετο δ' Ἀρείων τ' πάγον, βωμοῦ τ' Ἰυνάτης Εὐμενίδων, οὔ χρὴ Λακεδαιμονίους ὁ ἱκετεύσαι Δικεῖ πειζούσης· τοὺς μὲν οὖ κτεῖνε σιδήρῳ, Μοῖ' ἱκέτας ἀδικῶν· ἱκέτας δ' ἱερῆ τυχῇ ἀγοῖ.] (He fled to the hill of Ares and to the altar of the Eumenides, which the Lacedaemonians must not approach, for Justice does not permit it. Whoever harmed a suppliant, one must not strike with iron; but whoever leads a suppliant to a sacred lot…)

units.la: Quænam autem Atheniensium iure sancita fuerit pœna in temeratores huiu
units.tr: What penalty Athenian law fixed for violators of this [law] ...

units.la: Quanquàm ignorare non possimus Festorum celebrationem caussam etiam habuisse, hominum à consuetis laboribus cessationem, tamen vel præcipuam fuisse fatendum est sacrorum curam ad honorem Deorum: Agricolæ prisci, fortes, paruoque beati, Condita post frumenta, leuantes tempore festo Corpora, & ipsum animum spe finis dura ferentem,
units.tr: Although we cannot ignore that the celebration of festivals also had a cause, namely the cessation of men from their customary labours, it must nonetheless be granted that the chief concern was the care of the sacred rites in honour of the gods: Ancient farmers, brave and content with little, when the harvest was stored, relaxed their bodies at the festal time, and their spirit itself, which bore hard labour in hope of its end.

units.la: Cum socijs operum, & pueris, & coniuge fida, Tellurem porco, Siluanum lacte piabant, Floribus & vino Genium, memores brevis aevi.
units.tr: With their fellow workers, their children, and their faithful wives, they propitiated Tellus with a pig and Silvanus with milk, and honoured the Genius with flowers and wine, mindful of the brevity of life.

units.la: Optime Strabo Lib.X. [?]ὁ τῆς πολυρυθμίας [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀπὸ τῆς [?]ἀρχῆς ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ [?], cui praeiuit Aristoteles VIII. Nicomachῶν [?]ἐπὶ τὰς [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐν τοῖς [?]κατὰ τὴν [illegible, ~8 letters] ὡς τὴν [?]χαρὰν συνοικιᾶσθαι, ἡ ἀπόλαυσις [?]μάλιστα γὰρ ἐν τούτοις [?]ἐχρῆσθαι ἐν [?]τοῖς ἡμέραις. Quare inter praecipuas Legislatoris Atheniensium curas, haec fuit, vt diebus Festis Sacra Diis rite fierent, non auocato ad alias curas [?]τὴν ἑορτάζοντων animo, neve cuiquam, qua priuatim, qua publicè, iniuria fieret.
units.tr: Strabo rightly says, in Book X, [illegible] ... which Aristotle went before in Book VIII of the Nicomachean Ethics [illegible] ... that joy is shared, and enjoyment ... for it was in these things especially that they [used] ... on the days. Hence, among the chief concerns of the Athenian lawgiver was this: that on festal days the sacred rites be duly performed for the gods, the minds of those celebrating not being drawn to other cares, and that no wrong be done to anyone, whether privately or publicly.

units.la: [illegible, ~18 letters] μήτε ἰδίᾳ, μήτε κοινῇ μηδὲν ἀλλήλοις ἀδι-κεῖν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ χρόνῳ, μηδὲ χειροτονεῖν [?]ὅ, τι αὐτοῖς μὴ ἐφεστῆκε τῆς ἑορτῆς ἢ.
units.tr: [illegible] neither privately nor publicly to do wrong to one another during this time, nor to vote on anything that does not belong to the festival [μήτε ἰδίᾳ, μήτε κοινῇ μηδὲν ἀλλήλοις ἀδικεῖν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ χρόνῳ, μηδὲ χειροτονεῖν ὅ, τι αὐτοῖς μὴ ἐφεστῆκε τῆς ἑορτῆς ἢ].

units.la: Die populo Atheniensium festo ne cuiquam, sive priuatim, sive publicè iniuria fiat, neve habeatur concio de alijs rebus, quam ijs, quae ad festorum religionem per-tinent.
units.tr: On the festival day of the Athenian people, no one is to be wronged, whether privately or publicly, nor is an assembly to be held about other matters than those that pertain to the religious observance of the festivals.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτους, eaque praecipit diebus festis Deorumque cultui sacratis hoc esse agendum, atque huic uni rei, neque cuiquam alteri, operandum, & animum appellendum. Auocabatur autem animus, vel alterius iniuria prouocatus, vel rogatus & in suffragia missus, concione habita de rebus, quae nihil ad religionem festorum attinerent. Cauet igitur Legislator, ne quis quemquam iniuriosè tractet, aut populo de rebus, quae sacrorum non sint: Poterant quidem Prytaneis ἐπ' ἐγκλήμασι [?]ἐκκλησίας [?]ποιεῖν, poterant quoque Proedri ad populum referre, χρημάτων [?]ζῆν, sed cum hac cautione, ὅ, τι αὐτοῖς ἑορτῆς ἢ, vt est in Lege, μείζονος χρείας [?]Φιλοσόφων alioquin iusticium erat, [?]ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ ἀφειμένοι [?]ποιῶ, vt legitur in veterum Commentariis, ἐπ' οὐδὲν [?]προηγόρευσε τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τῆς βουλῆς. Vnde Demosthenes hac ipsa aduersus Timocratem Oratione: [?]τὰ ἔμπροσθεν Κεφισίων ἐν Ἀθήναις ἀφιέναι τῆς βουλῆς. Et paulò post: ἡ βουλὴς μὲν ἀφιέντων, τῶν ὁ ἄλλων ἐν [?]τῇ ἑορτῇ ἐκκλησιῶν ἀγόντων. Nulla tamen diei festi religione mouebantur, si decernendum aut scitcendum esset de rebus sacris ad religionem pertinen-tibus. Itaque reum peragit Timocratem Demosthenes, quod die festo, ἐν τῇ Κεφισίων ἐκωμῴδησε, non, vt Lege cautum est, ἐπὶ τῆς ἑορτῆς, sed de aerariis. Dixi-mus referri posse ad populum diebus festis de rebus sacris in genere, & quae alicuius festi religionem spectarent, non tantum de rebus, quae ad religionem illius diei festi, quo concio habebatur, pertinerent: id expresse habes apud Demosthenem, nam concionem haberi vult Timocrates die duodecimo mensis Hecatombaeonis, quo celebrabatur τὰ Κρόνια, praetextu Panathenaeo-rum, quasi de rebus illius festi ad populum esset referendum: ἀλλὰ ἐκκλη-σίας, ἐν ᾗ πάντες νόμους ἐπιχειροτονήσατ, ὅπως ἐνδείξητε τῆς Ἐκατομβαιῶνος μένοις, διαδικάζῃ τὸ νόμον εἰσάγειν ἀν' ἡμᾶς τὴν ὑγείαν, ἐπ' ἐκ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἔλεγον. [?]τὰ [?]πιθανολογήσαντος μὲν τὴν ὑμῶν ἐπισκευάζοντας, ἐκ ἀμφισβητήσαν νομοθεσίαν ἀλλ' ὁ ἁ-φίσματος, ὅτι τὴν τῶν Παναθηναίων πεφάσθαι. Habes ibidem ipsum Psephisma.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in his speech against Timocrates, and he prescribes that on festal days, and on days consecrated to the worship of the gods, this alone is to be done and this alone attended to, and the mind directed to nothing else. The mind, however, was diverted either by provocation from another's wrong, or by being asked and sent to the vote, when an assembly had been held on matters that had nothing to do with the religion of the festivals. The lawgiver therefore takes care that no one treat another unjustly, or bring before the people matters that are not sacred. The prytaneis could indeed convene an assembly on accusations, and the presidents could refer matters to the people, but with this caution: that [they should not do so on] whatever pertains to the festival, as is stated in the law, unless of greater need. Otherwise it was unlawful, [illegible], as is read in the ancient commentaries: [the council] proclaimed the assembly for no purpose. Hence Demosthenes, in this same speech against Timocrates: the council dismissed [the assembly] in the earlier days of the Kephisia in Athens. And a little later: the council dismissed [the people], while the others held assemblies during the festival. Yet they were in no way hindered by the religion of the festal day if something had to be decreed or voted on concerning sacred matters pertaining to religion. Therefore Demosthenes indicts Timocrates because on a festal day, in the Kephisia, he [brought forward a matter], not, as the law prescribes, during the festival, but about the treasuries. We have said that on festal days matters of sacred things in general may be referred to the people, and those that concern the religion of some festival, not only those that pertain to the religion of that festal day on which the assembly was held. You have this expressly in Demosthenes, for Timocrates wishes the assembly to be held on the twelfth day of the month Hecatombaeon, on which the Kronia were celebrated, under the pretext of the Panathenaea, as if the business of that festival were to be referred to the people. [The text of the decree follows], by which Demosthenes shows that the assembly was convened for the Panathenaea. You have the decree itself in the same place.

units.la: ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ.
units.tr: DECREE [ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ].

units.la: Ἐπὶ τῆς Παιανιέως, ὅσης ἐνδείξητε τῆς ἀρυτομίας, Τιμοκράτης εἶπεν, ὅπως αὐ[?]τοῖς [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: Under the prytany of Paiania, in so far as you have shown ... Timocrates proposed that ... [illegible].

units.la: Legem, quam dicte lequenti, qui duodecimus erat Hecatombæonis, ... tulit Timocrates, apud Demosthenem in sequentibus habes. Dicitur autem in hac Lege [illegible, ~12 letters], id est, diebus omni Atheniensium populo festis, quia aliæ erant [illegible, ~10 letters] quorundam ex Atheniensibus: nam sua priuataque erant sacra & festa singulis [illegible, ~20 letters], gentibus, familiis: atque soli illi feriabantur, quorum erat sacrum.
units.tr: The law which he proposed on the following day, the twelfth of Hecatombaeon, Timocrates ... you have in what follows in Demosthenes. This law speaks of days festal to the whole Athenian people [illegible], since other days belonged to certain Athenians alone: for each of the clans, gentes and families had their own private sacred rites and festivals, and only those to whom the sacred rite belonged kept the holiday.

units.la: Athenæ, quibus de suo nomen dedit inventrix oleæ Minerua, Deam illam religiosissime, vt par erat, coluerunt, atque inter præcipua festa in eius honorem celebrarunt Panathenæa, de quibus Libro singulari viri præstantissimi: Nemo autem est qui ignoret duplicia fuisse apud Athenienses Panathenæa, Maiora scilicet & Minora: quorum illa quinto quoque anno agitabatur, hæc vero quotannis recurrebant. Sed de tempore disputatur, quo Minora celebrabantur: Nam Viri Clarissimi censent celebrata esse vere: Panathenæis enim aperiri mare, ac navigari iterum coeptum est, quod tamen alij verius adscribunt Dionysiis. XVIII. docens varie accipi præpositionem ἐκ, cum dicitur aliquid ἐκ τῶν [illegible, ~8 letters] ita scribit, ὁ γὰρ ὡς πλεῖ, ἐκ τῆς Πανα-θηναίων ὁ πλεῖ. Incunte vere solita maria aperiri, cum veteribus parum in vsu esset hiberna navigatio, nemo it inficias. Ergo ista Panathenæa, de quibus Aristoteles, vere agitabantur: Maiora autem Panathenæa mense Hecatombæone celebrabantur, id est, per æstatis tempus. Reliqui igitur, vt Minora illa sint Panathenæa, quæ vere agitabantur, & à quibus mare [illegible, ~10 letters] itaque patebat nauibus. units.tr: Athens, to which the inventress of the olive, Minerva, gave its name, worshipped that goddess most devoutly, as was fitting, and among the chief festivals celebrated in her honour were the Panathenaea, about which a distinguished man wrote a separate book. Now, no one is unaware that there were two kinds of Panathenaea among the Athenians, the Greater and the Lesser: the former was held every fifth year, the latter returned every year. But there is dispute about the season when the Lesser were celebrated. Some very distinguished men think they were held in spring, for at the Panathenaea the sea was opened and voyaging began again; others however more truly assign this to the Dionysia. Aristotle, in Book I, chapter XVIII of On the Generation of Animals, teaching that the preposition ἐκ is taken in various senses when one says something ἐκ of something, writes thus: "for he sails as from the Panathenaea" [ὁ γὰρ ὡς πλεῖ, ἐκ τῆς Πανα-θηναίων ὁ πλεῖ]. That at the beginning of spring the seas were customarily opened, when winter navigation was little practised by the ancients, no one denies. Therefore those Panathenaea of which Aristotle speaks were held in spring, while the Greater Panathenaea were celebrated in the month Hecatombaeon, that is, in the summer season. Some therefore suppose that the Lesser Panathenaea, which were held in spring and when the sea was thus open to ships, were those ones. The same most distinguished men add that these Lesser Panathenaea were celebrated the day after the Bendideia, that is, on the twentieth day of the month Thargelion.
