Theophrastus: [illegible, ~30 letters] neque dixit Aristoteles, [illegible, ~22 letters] sed τὸν πλοῦν[?], quod longè aliud est. Trierarchiæ[?] (quod munus fuisse apud Athenienses grauissimum omnes norunt) legitimum tempus annus erat. Strategi autem ad obeundam Trierarchiam vocabant, & centum delectum que habebant: iam vero Strategi magistratum suum adibant Hecatombæone mense, quo novo Trierar-chis triremes instruere imperabant,& iudicia [illegible, ~18 letters] reddebant, ita vt circa vertentem Hecatombæonem triremes è portu soluerent, vnde dixit Aristoteles, [illegible, ~16 letters] Longè autem ante Thar-gelionem (ne Panathenaea dicam) aperiebatur mare, nempe Elaphebolione mense à Dionysiis, vt è Theophrasto diximus, & paria facit cum obseruatione Vegetij Lib. V. cap. IX. Sequitur mensium dierumque tractatus. Neque enim integro anno auis atque acerbitas maris patitur nauigantes, sed quidam menses aptissimi, quidam dubij, reliqui classibus intractabiles sunt lege naturæ. Phaenitæ decursu, id est post ortum Pleiadum à die sexto Kalendarum Iuniarum, vsque ad Arcturi ortum, id est, in diem octauum decimum Kalendarum Octobrium, secura nauigatio creditur, quia assatis[?] ventorum inficio ventorum acerbitas mitigatur: ita post hoc tempus vsque in tertiam Idus Nouembris incerta nauigatio est, & discrimini propior, propterea, quia post Idus Septembris oritur Arcturus vehementissimum sidus. Et octano Kalendas Octobris æquinoctialis euenit acerba tempestas. Circa Nonas verò Octobris Hædi pluuiales, quinto Idus eiusdem Taurus. A Nouembri autem mense crebris tempestatibus nauigia conturbat Vergiliarum hiemalis occasus. Ex die igitur tertio Iduum Nouembris vsque in diem sextum Iduum Martiarum, maria clauduntur: Nam lux minima, noxque prolixa, nubium densitas, aeris obscuritas, ventorum, imbri, vel niuibus geminata sævitia, non solum classes pelago, sed etiam commeantes à terrestri itinere deturbat. Post natalem vero (vt ita dicam) nauigationis, qui solenni certamine, publicoque spectaculo multa-rum gentium celebratur, plurimorum siderum, ipsiusque temporis ratione, vsque in Idus Maias periculosè maria tentantur, non quod negotiatorum cessat industria, sed quia maior adhibenda est cautela, quando exercitus nauigat cum Liburnis, quam cum priuatorum mercium festinat audacia. Mendosum est illud, Phaenitæ decur-su, & MSS. codices habent partim, flagrante decursu, partim pugnitæ[?].
units.tr: The Callipeian and Platonian festivals ... in the commentary on the Republic ... the pretext of the festival for the Athenians. On the day after the Bendidiorum ... the torch race ... The authority of the great man does not stand: ... so that you may receive the words, hence the strongest ... To say it plainly, the opinion of the great man: for the torch race is of Dianae, not of Minervae. Plato's words ... For he does not add anything ... It is certain that in the first words of the Dialogue ... were celebrated in the Piraeus. Add that the rest of the things that follow the procession of the Bendidia, the torch race, and the all-night vigil ... nothing more was left for him to see. ... Plato, if the vigils had been completed ... could not, as if new, Socrates ... were instituted, if, receiving the torch race ..., which is plainly new and unheard of. Both were carried out in the Piraeus. For the house of Polemarchus was in that very place ... the father of Polemarchus, when to his house ... the torch race ... was held in the Ceramicus outside the city, or in ... as the ancients to Aristophanes the teacher ... As for Proclus, whose words he praises ... the Rhodian Panathenaea, but rather was celebrated in honour of Minervae, about which much the great man has written in the books of the Atticarum Lectionum. The Plynteria of Greece are celebrated on the twenty-fifth day of the month Thargelion, as is clear from Plutarch in the Alcibiades. About the Callynteria we have nothing certain to say; yet if conjecture has any place, let that festival be conjectured to fall on the twenty-second day of Thargelion. For on the twentieth day of Thargelion, as Aristotle of Rhodes reports, the Bendidia were celebrated. The day after, discourses on the Republic are held in Plato ... On the following day, which is the twenty-second of Thargelion, a discourse is feigned to be held, which is entitled Timaeus; and that day is sacred to Minerva. The passage of Aristotle the Stagirite seems to be of greater weight for confirming the opinion of the great man, but only seems so, for in truth it proves nothing less than what they maintain. It must not be understood, as they interpret it, as if the seas were then first opened at the Panathenaea; for this is false: the seas were opened in the month Elaphebolion at the Dionysia. Theophrastus ... Aristotle did not say ... but the voyage[?], which is far different. For the Trierarchy (which all know was a most burdensome office among the Athenians) the lawful time was a year. The generals were summoned to undertake the Trierarchy and had a hundred men chosen; now the generals entered upon their magistracy in the month Hekatombaion, when, being new, they ordered the Trierarchs to equip their triremes, and they gave judgments, so that around the turn of Hekatombaion the triremes put out from the harbour; whence Aristotle said ... Far earlier than Thargelion (not to mention the Panathenaea) the sea was opened, namely in the month Elaphebolion at the Dionysia, as we have said from Theophrastus, and this agrees with the observation of Vegetius, Book V, chapter IX: Next follows the treatment of the months and days. For sailors do not suffer the harshness of the sea through the whole year, but some months are very suitable, some doubtful, and the rest are unmanageable for fleets by the law of nature. From the Phaenitae course, that is after the rising of the Pleiades, from the sixth day before the Kalends of June until the rising of Arcturus, that is to the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, safe navigation is believed, because the harshness of the winds is softened by the ... of the winds. Thereafter, from this time until the third day before the Ides of November, navigation is uncertain and closer to danger, because after the Ides of September Arcturus, a most violent star, rises. And on the eighth day before the Kalends of October the equinoctial storm occurs. About the Nones of October the rainy Kids, and on the fifth day before the Ides of the same month Taurus. From the month of November, the wintry setting of the Pleiades disturbs ships with frequent storms. Therefore from the third day before the Ides of November until the sixth day before the Ides of March, the seas are closed. For the least light, the long night, the density of clouds, the darkness of the air, and the savagery of the winds, doubled by rain or snow, drive down not only fleets from the sea but also travellers from the land. After the so-called birthday of navigation, which is celebrated with a solemn contest and public spectacle of many peoples, and by the reckoning of many stars and of the season itself, the seas are attempted dangerously until the Ides of May; not because the diligence of merchants ceases, but because greater caution must be applied when the army sails with the Liburnians than when the haste of private merchandise rushes. That passage, Phaenitae decursu, is faulty, and the manuscripts have it partly as flagrante decursu, partly as pugnitae[?].

units.la: Scholia: τὰ γὰρ Μουνυχιῶνι μιλίῳ [?] οἱ ξένοι [?]. Munychionem vero excipiebat Thargelion. Probat quoque Minora atque Maiora Panathenæa eodem tempore celebrata fuisse, quod in Minoribus eadem agebantur quæ in Maioribus, si excipias peplum, qui inferebatur tantum Maioribus Panathenæis; Sed facile est demonstrare Panathenæa quoque Minora agitata fuisse mense Hecatombæone. Plephisma ab Epicrate scriptum est die vndecimo Hecatombæonis ὅτι τῇ τῷ Παναθηναίων [?]. Habes in ipso Plephismate: ὅτι τῆς Παναδηνίδος [?], ἐπικεχειρηκέναι εἰπεν, ὅπως δὲ τὰ ἱερὰ ξυνταχῆ τῆς [?] [?] ἀδικῆ [?], ἐπεῖ [?] Παναθηναίοις [?], δίκην [?], τοῖς Πρυτάνεσι τῶν Παναθηναΐδος [?] [?] [?] ἔδει. Die sequenti Legem scripsit Timocrates, ob quam dica illi scripta est γραφὴ παρανόμων. Eodem autem anno accusatus est Timocrates, quo Legem scripsit: nam nisi intra vertentem annum, quo Lex scribta erat, accusatio institueretur, in nullam incurrebat pœnam: [illegible, ~30 letters] ἀτιμώσθαι. Atqui ἀτιμώμενος erat Timocrates, vt ex hac oratione constat, itaque Oratio κατὰ Τιμοκράτους inscribitur; Quare intra annum, quo Legem tulit Timocrates, scripta est hæc Oratio κατὰ Τιμοκράτους. Idque accidit Theodemo siue Euthydemo Athenis Archonte. Dionysius Halicarnasseus in Epistola ad Ammæum: ὅτι δὲ Θεοδήμου τῆς μετὰ Διοπίωνος ἀρξάντος, τότε κατὰ Τιμοκράτους λόγον ἐγραφῇ Διοδώρᾳ τῷ κεῖνον ἀφελόμενον τὸν Τιμοκράτην. Vertebat annus quartus Olympiadis sextæ supra centesimam, vt videre est apud Anonymum in Descriptione Olympiadum; ad hunc annum IV. Olympiadis CVI. ΘΕΟΔΗΜΟΣ· οἱ δὲ ΕΥΘΥΔΗΜΟΣ. ὁ κατὰ Τιμοκράτους λόγος Δημοσθένους. Hisita disputatis, certum est Panathenæa, quorum prætextu Legem rogauit Timocrates die duodecimo mensis Hecatombæonis anni quarti Olympiadis centesimæ sextæ, fuisse Panathenæa Minora: nam Maiora tertio quoque anno Olympiadis celebrabantur: Atqui Panathenæa, quorum prætextu Legem rogauit Timocrates, celebrata sunt mense Hecatombæone: Unde necessario sequitur Panathenæa Minora celebrata fuisse mense Hecatombæone, quemadmodum & Maiora, non autem Munychione mense, vt volebant Viri eruditissimi. Atque hoc festo nemini licebat in vestè tincta pompam ludosque spectare:
units.tr: Scholia: "For in the month Munychion the foreigners ..." [Greek]. Thargelion followed Munychion. He also shows that the Lesser and Greater Panathenaea were celebrated at the same time, since the same rites were performed at the Lesser as at the Greater, except the peplos, which was carried only at the Greater Panathenaea. But it is easy to show that the Lesser Panathenaea were also held in the month Hecatombaion. A decree was written by Epicrates on the eleventh day of Hecatombaion, that ... [Greek]. You have in the decree itself: that ... [Greek] ... the Prytanes ... [Greek]. On the following day Timocrates wrote a law, on account of which an indictment for illegal proposals (graphe paranomon) was drawn up against him. Timocrates, however, was accused in the same year in which he wrote the law: for unless the accusation was brought within the year in which the law was written, he incurred no penalty ... [Greek] to be disfranchised. But Timocrates was disfranchised, as is clear from this speech; therefore the speech is entitled Against Timocrates. Hence the speech Against Timocrates was written within the year in which Timocrates proposed the law. This happened at Athens in the archonship of Theodemus, or Euthydemus. Dionysius of Halicarnassus in his letter to Ammaeus: [Greek], that in the archonship of Theodemus, with Diopion, the speech Against Timocrates was then written for Diodorus, who was taking that Timocrates' ... away. The fourth year of the 106th Olympiad was the year; for this year, as is seen in the anonymous Description of the Olympiads, the fourth year of the 106th Olympiad: Theodemus, but others Euthydemus. The speech Against Timocrates is by Demosthenes. These matters having been discussed, it is certain that the Panathenaea, on whose pretext Timocrates proposed the law on the twelfth day of the month Hecatombaion in the fourth year of the 106th Olympiad, were the Lesser Panathenaea: for the Greater were celebrated every fourth year of an Olympiad. But the Panathenaea on whose pretext Timocrates proposed the law were celebrated in the month Hecatombaion. Hence it necessarily follows that the Lesser Panathenaea were celebrated in the month Hecatombaion, as were the Greater, and not in the month Munychion, as learned men maintained. And at this festival no one was permitted to watch the procession and games in a dyed garment:

Hipparchum æmulatus est Aristoteles, vt de eius Peplo mihi nonnulla ὡς ἐν πεπλῷ licear obseruare, atque Homeri studiosus fuit, vt qui maximè; coque factum est, vt Homeri Βοιωτία, vbi Principum Græciæ genus, patriam, classemque recenset, iret illustratum, edito Libro in hanc rem, de quo Eustathius è Porphyrio, neque tantum Heroum genealogias, classem & gesta; sed etiam conscripserat illorum extremi fati genus, supremúmque diem, tumulúmque fecerat, & tumulo superaddiderat carmen; atque ita vniuersæ illi historiæ antiquitati facem præferebat, & Politicum informabat. Descripsisse Aristotelem isto Libro Homericorum Heroum genealogias, itémque classem, testis est Porphyrius apud Eustathium: [illegible, ~50 letters], καὶ νεῶν ἐκ[?] ἀριθμόν. Genealogias cùm dicimus, intellige non tantum Heroum maiores, sed etiam posteros. Auctor Etymologici M. Ἠλις, ἐστὶ δὲ πόλις Πελοποννήσου, ὁ κτίσας δ' αὐτὴν Ἠλεῖος παῖς Ποσειδῶνος καὶ Εὐρυμάλης, Ἠλείου δὲ Ἀλέξις καὶ Ἐπειὸς βασιλεύς· ἀφ' ἧς Ἐπειοὶ Ἠλεῖοι, ὡς φησιν Αἰσχύλος ἐν τῷ Πέπλῳ. Gesta quoque Heroum perscripsisse colligimus è Libri titulo: nam iste Liber ἐκλήθη Πέπλος, & à Peplo, qui Mineruæ Panathenaeis inferebatur, nomen accepit: in illo autem peplo intexebatur Titanomachia, resque à Minerua tum hic cum Ioue patre, cum alibi gestæ: depingebantur quoque quæ strenuè se in bello gessissent, inquit Seruius, qui inde à Comico dicuntur ἄξιοι τῆς Πέπλου. Quare isto Libro Aristoteles vniuersa Heroum gesta in literas retulerat ad supremum vsque diem & exitum, quem etiam recensebat; argumento est, quod omnia illa Epigrammata, quæ de Aristotelis Peplo sunt descripta, carmina sint, quæ tumulis illorum superaddantur: præterea neque illorum, vt qui Dij non sint, nomina aut res gestæ intertexi & legi poterant in hoc Peplo, nisi vitam cum morte commutassent, quemadmodum in Mineruæ Peplo non pingebantur nisi ii, qui in bello fortiter fecerant & occubuerant, si Antigonum & Demetrium excipias, quia Atheniensium scito Dij habiti funt: Superaddidere
units.tr: Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, proposed this law: Lycurgus ... Leocrates ... "wishing that Homer also be recited to you, I approve." [Greek] ... Aelian, Varia Historia, book 8, chapter 2: "Hipparchus, the son of Pisistratus, being ... of Glaucus ..." [Greek] ... Plato in the Hipparchus, concerning Hipparchus: "who indeed displayed many works of wisdom by his hand ..." [Greek] ... Aristotle emulated Hipparchus, so that I may note some things about his Peplos, "as in the peplos" [Greek], and he was as devoted to Homer as anyone; hence it came about that the Boeotia of Homer, where he lists the origin, homeland and fleet of the leaders of Greece, was made famous by a book published on this subject, of which Eustathius speaks, from Porphyry. Aristotle not only wrote the genealogies, fleet and deeds of the heroes, but also recorded the manner of their final fate and last day, and made their tombs, and added a poem to each tomb; and thus he held a torch to all that ancient history and shaped it as a political history. That Aristotle described in that book the genealogies of the Homeric heroes, and likewise the fleet, is attested by Porphyry in Eustathius: [illegible] ... and the number of ships. When we say genealogies, understand not only the ancestors of the heroes but also their descendants. The author of the Etymologicum Magnum, "Elis, is a city of the Peloponnese; its founder was Eleios, son of Poseidon and Eurymale; and Alexis and Epeius were kings of Elis, from whom the Epeians, the Eleans, as Aeschylus says in the Peplos." We gather also from the title of the book that he recorded the deeds of the heroes: for this book was called Peplos, and it took its name from the peplos which was carried to Athena at the Panathenaea. On that peplos was woven the Titanomachy, and the deeds done by Minerva here with her father Jupiter and elsewhere; there were also depicted those who had fought bravely in war, says Servius, who are called by the comic poet "worthy of the peplos." Hence in that book Aristotle had committed to writing all the deeds of the heroes down to their last day and end, which he also listed. The evidence is that all those epigrams which are written about Aristotle's Peplos are poems which are added to their tombs. Moreover, the names and deeds of those men, since they were not gods, could not be woven into or read in this peplos unless they had exchanged life for death, just as in Minerva's peplos only those were depicted who had fought bravely in war and fallen, except Antigonus and Demetrius, because by the Athenians' decree they were regarded as gods. Verum, auctore ipso n quàm Philosophum Aristotelem Stagiritam enim Tzetzis duo elicimus, prius est, eundem Πολιτικά. Atqui certissimum est, nullum aliud Stagiritem Aristotelem: alterum vero est, scri-n, vt Politicum informaret, & Πολιτίας, ma-tius & tutius aggrederetur. Nam pleraque illæ scribebat, erant [?] & coloniæ veterum il-m; intererat autem scire, quæ patria, quæ gens t, quænam illorum gesta & fatum, quod in Pe-ne vniuscuiusque Πολιτίας sacrorum ritus, Le-r, &, si forte, cauffæ illorum ab ipsis Colonia-e institutis patriis repetitæ, aperirentur.
units.tr: Many suspect that the Stagirite was not the author, but in that most carefully made index among the works of Aristotle, John Tzetzes makes Aristotle the author, saying that he was the Philosopher, rather than, I think, the one who wrote on the peploi. And he is perhaps the third whom Diogenes lists, and he commented on the same work. But from Tzetzes' own words we draw two points: first, that the same Aristotle the Stagirite wrote the Politics. Yet it is most certain that no other Aristotle the Stagirite exists; the second is that he wrote, so that he might shape the Politician, and approached the Polities more fully and safely. For those things he wrote were the ... and colonies of the ancients; it was important to know what each one's homeland was, what people, what their deeds and fate were, and in the Polity of each, the rites of the sacred things, the laws, and, if perhaps, their causes were laid open, derived from the ancestral institutions of the colonists themselves.

units.la: emetrius atque Theophrastus apud Harpocra-[?] Ἀγαθοκλέους φησίν. οἱ αἰτὴ σκαφηφόρων [?] εἰς τ' ἀκρόπολιν αἰασθήσονται, ἀχ' ὑμῖν ἔχοντες χάριν ἡ Πολιτείας, ἀλλὰ δ' ἀργυρείων ὅπι γὰρ [?] ἐοικα Φηφόρῳ Αθηναι. Δημήτριος γὰρ ὁ πείτῳ νομοθέτης φησὶν ὅτι ὁ νόμος τοῖς μετοίκοις ἐν ταῖς πομπαῖς, αὐτοῖς μὲν σκιάφας φέρειν· τὰς δ' γυναῖκας αἰσχύνεσθαι ὑφεσία [?], ἐκ σκιάδια. Διδίλεκται τοῖς τούτων ἡ Θεόφραστος ἐν τῷ δικαίῳ τῶν νόμων. Sed corruptus est numerus Libri Theophrastei: Scripserat Theophrastus Legum Libros viginti quatuor, ordine alphabetico, vt narrat Diogenes: Νόμων τῶν στοιχείων καὶ. Iam vero στοιχεῖα siue literae Massignatae sunt Leges illae, quae leguntur περὶ Μετοίκων. Duodecimus igitur Liber siue ὁ Μ erat, reponendúmque est apud Harpocrationem ἐν δωδεκάτῳ τῶν Νόμων. nam Μέτοικοι, de quibus agitur primam literam habent M. Intelligitur autem hic pompa Panathenaica. Hesychius: Σκαφηφόροι, οἱ μέτοικοι οὕτως ἐκαλοῦντο· σκάφας γὰρ ἔφερον ἐν Παναθηναίοις, atque hanc pompam designant Dinarchi verba apud Harpocrationem: οἱ αὐτὶ Σκαφηφόρων ἐφῆβοι εἰς τὴν ἀκρόπολιν αἰασθήσονται. Scripta autem videtur haec Lex τῆς Μετοίκων circa belli Peloponnesiaci tempora, vbi Atheniensis prospero rerum suarum successu corrupti insolescere coeperunt: colligere est ex his Ἀελiani verbis Variae Lib. VI. cap. I. Ἀθηναῖοι δὲ τυχίας λαβόμενοι, τὴν ἡγεμονίαν σωφέρους ἐκ ἐλευθέραν· τὰς γὰρ ὑπὸ τῆς Μετοίκων σκιαδηφόρους ἐν ταῖς πομπαῖς ἐωλίσκεσθαι τὰς ἑαυτῶν χεῖρας, τὰς δὲ γυναῖκας τὰς γυναῖξι, τοὺς δὲ ἀνδρας σκαφηφόρους. In hac Panathenaeorum pompa Ephebos nigram indutos fuisse chlamydem existimat Vir eruditissimus, idque obtinuisse ad Herodem Atticum vsque, qui albas indui iussit. Philostratus Soph. Lib. II. in Herode: μετεχόμενοι δὲ καὶ τὰς Ἀθηναίους ἐφήβους εἰς τὸ νῦν ἅρμα, χλαμύδας ἀμφιέσας λευκὰς, τὰς γὰρ δὴ μεγάλας ἐπιμελεῖσθαι τὰς σχολὰς ἀλλὰ ἐλθὼν, ἢ τὰς πομπὰς ἐπεμπον, πυνθανομένων δημοσία τὴν Ἀθηναίων τὸν κήρυκα τὸν Κοπρέα, ὃν αὐτοὶ ἀπέκτειναν, τοὺς Ἡρακλείδας τῷ βωμῷ ἱκετεύοντα. Ego vero nullus dubito sententiam viri eruditissimi non posse cuiquam probari, qui attenderit ad ea quae iam ante obseruauimus: nam nemini fas erat in veste tincta pompam hanc ludósque Panathenaicos spectare: quanto igitur minus pompam ipsam deducere in veste nigra adeoque funesta: neque est quod quisquam putet Legem hanc ab Herode Attica censeri debere, quasi aut ab ipso Herode lata esset, aut certe ex quo ipse Ephebos iussit albas chlamydes indui: non enim id ita est. Lucianus enim Legis huius meminit tanquam iamdiu ante obseruatae, & scripsit Lucianus meo iudicio hunc Librum, antequam quicquam in Ephebo-rum ornatu innouasset Herodes Atticus. Praeterea, quod caput est, Panathenaeorum dies atra aliqua veste ob memoriam caedis cuiusquam funestatos fuisse, par non est credere: Erant enim laetitiae toti consecrati: neque in hanc anni tempestatem potest cadere caedes Coprei, quem lugebant atrati Ephebi, vt è Philostrato constat, πυνθανομένων δημοσία τὴν Ἀθηναίων τὸν κήρυκα τὸν Κοπρέα, ὃν αὐτοὶ ἀπέκτειναν, τοὺς Ἡρακλείδας τῷ βωμῷ ἱκετεύοντα. Circa Hecatombaeonem mensem mortalitatem exuit Hercules: praecipitata quippe hieme, quare Euenus, vt est apud ingeniosissimum Poëtarum, qui nonnulla in his peccat;
units.tr: Demetrius and Theophrastus, in Harpocration, say: Agathocles says: "Instead of the skaphephoroi, the ephebes will go up to the Acropolis [εἰς τ' ἀκρόπολιν αἰασθήσονται]... you have no thanks... but of the silver-workers... for I seem to resemble a Phegophoros [Φηφόρῳ], O Athenians." For Demetrius, the lawgiver of Phaleron, says that the law for metics in the processions was that the men should carry basins [σκιάφας], and the women should carry parasols [σκιάδια]. Theophrastus discusses these things in the twelfth book of his Laws. But the number of Theophrastus' book has been corrupted. Theophrastus wrote twenty-four books of Laws in alphabetical order, as Diogenes relates [Νόμων τῶν στοιχείων καὶ]. Now those laws which are read concerning metics [περὶ Μετοίκων] are arranged by letters. So the twelfth book, or the letter M, is the right reading, and it should be restored in Harpocration as "in the twelfth book of the Laws," for Μέτοικοι, the subject in question, begins with M. The procession meant here is clearly the Panathenaic procession. Hesychius says: "Skaphephoroi: metics were so called, for they carried basins [σκάφας] at the Panathenaia." This procession is indicated by the words of Dinarchus in Harpocration: "the ephebes, instead of the skaphephoroi, will go up to the Acropolis [οἱ αὐτὶ Σκαφηφόρων ἐφῆβοι εἰς τὴν ἀκρόπολιν αἰασθήσονται]." This law seems to have been written around the time of the Peloponnesian War, when the Athenians, made prosperous by their successes, began to grow corrupt and insolent. This can be gathered from the words of Aelian, Varia Historia, book VI, chapter 1: "The Athenians, seizing upon fortune, did not hold their leadership moderately or freely; for in the processions the metic women were compelled to carry parasols [σκιαδηφόρους], and the men basins [σκαφηφόρους], and their own hands were bound..." In this Panathenaic procession, a very learned man thinks the ephebes wore black cloaks, and that this custom lasted until Herodes Atticus, who ordered them to wear white. Philostratus, in Sophists book II, on Herodes: "And the Athenian ephebes, dressed in white chlamydes, were brought into the present chariot [...]..." I certainly doubt that the learned man's opinion can be approved by anyone who has considered what we observed earlier. For no one was permitted to watch this procession and the Panathenaic games in dyed clothing; how much less to lead the procession itself in black, so funereal a colour. Nor should anyone think that this law should be credited to Herodes Atticus, as if he had proposed it, or at least as if it began when he ordered the ephebes to wear white chlamydes; that is not so. For Lucian mentions this law as one long observed, and in my judgment Lucian wrote this book before Herodes Atticus had changed anything in the ephebes' dress. Moreover, and this is the main point, it is not credible that the days of the Panathenaia were darkened by black dress in memory of some slaughter. They were wholly dedicated to joy. Nor can the killing of Copreus, whom the mourning ephebes lamented, as is clear from Philostratus, fall in this time of year. [Philostratus says:] "When the Athenian herald Copreus was asked publicly, whom they themselves had killed while he was supplicating the Heraclidae at the altar..." [πυνθανομένων δημοσία τὴν Ἀθηναίων τὸν κήρυκα τὸν Κοπρέα, ὃν αὐτοὶ ἀπέκτειναν, τοὺς Ἡρακλείδας τῷ βωμῷ ἱκετεύοντα.] Hercules put off his mortality around the month Hecatombaeon, when winter was over and past. Euenus, in the words of the most ingenious of poets, who errs in some points, says:

units.la: Vberior solito, nimbis hiemalibus auctus, Vorticibusque frequens erat atque imperuius amnis.
units.tr: More abundant than usual, swollen with winter rains, and full of whirlpools, the river was impassable.

units.la: Hiemeigitur praecipitata Thrachinem venit Hercules, ibidémque paululum moratus Omphalæ in seruitutem venditus est, apud quam annum fuit: triennio fuisse scribit Apollodorus his verbis: [illegible, ~40 letters] [?] [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: Therefore, with winter past, Hercules came to Trachis, and having stayed there a little while, was sold into slavery to Omphale, with whom he was for a year. Apollodorus writes that it was three years, in these words: [...]

units.la: Sed tres annos apud Omphalé in seruitute nō fuit: nā impendit Hercules annos octo & menses vnum exsequendis primis decem laboribus ab Eurystheo imperatis. Apollodorus: [illegible, ~35 letters] [?] [illegible, ~20 letters].
units.tr: But he was not in slavery to Omphale for three years, for Hercules spent eight years and one month in carrying out the first ten labours imposed by Eurystheus. Apollodorus: [...]

units.la: Addé hīs [?] triennium, quod, si Apollodori codicibus credimus, exegit apud Omphalem, fiunt annī vndecim & mensis vnus; itaque supererunt vndecim tantum menses reliquis omnibus patrandis, quæ ab Hercule gesta suisse produnter: nam duodecimo tandem anno, ex quo imperata ab Eurystheo obire cœpit, fato functus est: At qui [illegible, ~12 letters] [?] intra tam exiguum temporis spatium, quod ne vnius quidem anni est; tot laboribus fuisse defunctum Herculem, vt mittam nuptias cum Deianira, quæ ad hoc interuallum omnino sunt referenda ex Apollodori sententia: é Deianira autem tres liberos suflulit: Rescribo itaque apud Apollodorum [illegible, ~25 letters] [?], si annum, inquit, ad lanificium siue statmen seruierit: atque huic ministerio deputatus est ab Omphale. Donatus in Eunuchum: Omphale Lydiæ Regina fuit, quæ Herculem sibi seruientem etiam ad lanificium compulit, cum ipsa calathum & colum, allusque femineos, sagittas & clamydem leonisq; tegmine mutasset. Exactum fuisse vnum tantum annum ab Hercule in Omphales seruitio testatur Hyllus apud Sophoclem in Hercule Oetæo:
units.tr: Add to these the three years, which, if we believe the manuscripts of Apollodorus, he spent with Omphale, making eleven years and one month. Thus only eleven months would remain for all the remaining deeds that are reported to have been done by Hercules, for he died in the twelfth year, from when he began to perform the tasks imposed by Eurystheus. But who could believe that Hercules was worn out by so many labours within so short a span of time, less than a single year, not to mention the marriage with Deianira, which must, according to Apollodorus, be placed within this interval, and from Deianira he raised three children? So I reply, following Apollodorus: [...] if he served for a year at wool-working or spinning, and was assigned to this service by Omphale. Donatus on the Eunuchus: Omphale was queen of Lydia, who compelled Hercules, serving her, even to wool-working, while she herself exchanged her distaff and spindle, feminine playthings, for his arrows and cloak, and the lion's skin. Hyllus, in Sophocles' Hercules Oetaeus, bears witness that Hercules served for only one year in the service of Omphale:

units.la: Non enim ipsos duodecim menses, hoc est, neque plures, neque pauciores (id enim significat iltud loquendi genus [illegible, ~10 letters] δυοκαιδεκάμηνον χρόνον.) Trachinæ abfuit, sed paullo plures, scilicet quindecim: itaque referibo:
units.tr: For it was not the twelve months themselves, that is, neither more nor fewer (for that manner of speaking means a period of twelve months), that Hercules was away from Trachis, but somewhat more, namely fifteen. So I shall read:

units.la: Πέντε, δὲ [?] [?] καὶ δυοκαίδεκα μηνῶνἈμμέϊνοσι χρόνον. Fauet hic Trachiniarum Chorus afflictæ Deianiræ, quæ sibi pellicem superinduci ægre ferebat: Quare illud; ἀλλ' ὦ [?]; cum interrogationis nota, interferitur, vt doceat non fuisse tanti illud, cuius causa abfuit Hercules, vt quindecim mensium moram traheret. Quanquam ne hos quidem totos menses abfuit quindecim; nam aduersus Eurytum profecturus Trachinem venit, & Melienses è Trachine secum ad bellum duxit. Apollodorus: ἀφικόμενος δ' εἰς Τραχῖνα, ἐπ' Οἰχαλίας πόλιν, [illegible, ~40 letters]. Eaque de caussa apud Sophoclem Melienses Licham detinent ad Deianiram properantem, vt de suorum, qui ad hoc bellum profecti fuerant, salute certi fiant:
units.tr: Five ... and twelve months ... a time. This Chorus of the Trachiniae favours the afflicted Deianira, who took it badly that a concubine was brought in over her. Hence the words "But, O ..." are inserted with a mark of interrogation, to show that the matter for which Hercules was away was not so great as to delay him for fifteen months. Yet he was not even absent for all these fifteen months, for he came to Trachis on his way to fight against Eurytus, and he led the Melians from Trachis with him to the war. Apollodorus: "But arriving at Trachis, he went to the city of Oechalia ..." [ἀφικόμενος δ' εἰς Τραχῖνα, ἐπ' Οἰχαλίας πόλιν, ...]. For this reason in Sophocles the Melians detain Lichas, who is hurrying to Deianira, so that they may be assured of the safety of their people who had gone out to this war.

units.tr: From these things it is gathered that Hercules was taken up within the month Hecatombaeon. There is also a second argument, and a most weighty one: in the twelfth year, after the completion of the years in which he had been bound to carry out the commands of Eurystheus, he was freed from human affairs, as he had received from the oracle. units.la: Apollodorus: ἡ δὲ Πυθία [illegible, ~60 letters] Quare etiam apud auctorem Herculis Oetei petit Hercules Diis inferri, peractis illis, quæ Eurystheus, imposuerat, certaminibus. Primus Herculis labor fuit in Nemæo leone, qui inter astra à Ioue constitutus est, quod Herculis prima fuerit hæc certatio, & quod inermis cum interfecit; inquit Hyginus Astronomiæ Lib. II. Vbi autem inter astra est constitutus, tunc primum videri siue exoriri cepit. Exoritur autem Leo die tricesimo, quo Sol Cancrum peragrat. Geminus: Καρίνος [?] ὁ ἥλιος [illegible, ~30 letters] Καὶ Λέων [illegible, ~20 letters] quem diem comparat Ill. Scaliger cum septimo Kalendas Augusti. Iam igitur ceperat primus annus ex illis duodecim, quos impendere fatum erat Eurystheii iussis: quare annus duodecimus eodem fere tempore exactus est, ac proinde annus tertiusdecimus, quo ineunte mortalitatem exuit Hercules, cepit circa Hecatombæonem mensem. Hercule cœlis recepto, nihil antiquius habuit Eurystheus, quam Herculis liberos Trachinæ, atque adeo Græciā ipsa pellere, sed ab Atheniensibus recepti illi sunt, & Eurystheus illos sibi dedi postulans pugna commissa in fugam vertitur, ac denique cæditur. Apollodorus: μαστέρα [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~190 letters]
units.tr: Apollodorus: "But the Pythia ..." [The Greek is too corrupt to restore.] Hence also in the author Hercules Oetaeus, Hercules asks that he be taken up to the gods, once the contests imposed by Eurystheus were finished. The first labour of Hercules was the Nemean lion, which Jupiter placed among the stars, because it was the first of Hercules' contests and because he killed it unarmed. So Hyginus says in Book II of the Astronomy: when it was placed among the stars, it first began to be seen or to rise. The Lion rises on the thirtieth day, on which the Sun passes through Cancer. Geminus: "... the sun ... and the Lion ..." [The Greek is too corrupt to restore.] Illustrious Scaliger compares this day with the seventh before the Kalends of August. Now the first year of those twelve, which Fate decreed were to be spent on the commands of Eurystheus, had already begun. Hence the twelfth year was completed at about the same time, and therefore the thirteenth year, at whose beginning Hercules put off mortality, began around the month Hecatombaeon. With Hercules received into heaven, Eurystheus had nothing more at heart than to drive Hercules' children from Trachis, and indeed from Greece itself. But they were received by the Athenians, and when Eurystheus, demanding that they be handed over to him, joined battle, he was put to flight and at last cut down. Apollodorus: "... " [The Greek is too corrupt to restore.] ...

units.la: Quare non potuit Copreus, qui Eurystheo iubente auellere voluit ab aris Heraclidas, circa Hecatombæonem mensem ea de causa occidi: Quare aliud voluit Herodes Atticus, nec quicquam facit eius institutum ad pompam Panathenaicam. Sed Philostrati verba longè aliud sonant: [illegible, ~60 letters] Bene quidem Herodes Atticus Epheborum nigras chlamydes albis mutauit, iure namque cæsus erat Copreus, vt qui âovλίᾳ sacelli Miscricordiæ temerare aggressus fuerit: Ephebi autem hic sunt [illegible, ~30 letters], de quibus, in sequentibus, Deo dante, dicemus: nam illis [illegible, ~20 letters] vt est apud Attemidorum Libro I. cap. LVI & dû in vrbe sunt, excubias agunt populo in concionem coacto, vt hinc patet, easque in transuectionibus suis siue lustrationibus (hæ sunt apud Philostratum [illegible, ~15 letters]) chlamydas induti sunt.
units.tr: Therefore Copreus, who at the command of Eurystheus tried to tear the Heraclidae from the altars, cannot have been killed around the month Hecatombaeon for this reason. Herodes Atticus, however, had another purpose, and his institution does nothing toward the Panathenaic procession. But the words of Philostratus sound quite different: "..." Herodes Atticus rightly changed the black cloaks of the ephebi to white, for Copreus had been justly killed, since he had dared to violate the sanctuary of Mercy. These ephebi are ..., about whom, in what follows, God willing, we shall speak. For as is found in Artemidorus, Book I, chapter LVI, while they are in the city they keep watch when the people are called to assembly, and it is clear from this that in their processions or purifications (these are the terms in Philostratus) they were dressed in cloaks.

units.la: Multa eximia diuinaque videntur Athenæ peperisse, atque in vitam hominum attulisse: tum nihil melius illis mysteriis, quibus ex agresti immanique vita excultiad humanitatem, & mitigati sunt homines, initiaque vt appellantur, ita re vera principia vitæ cognoscuntur, neque solum cum lætitia viuendi rationem tradunt, sed etiam cum spe meliore moriendi: itaque inter maxime veneranda sacra ponit hæc Eleusinia Galenus Libro XVII. de Vsu partium,&c. Dixerat Galenus cognitionem, quæ de Deo habetur ex vsu partium corporis humani eam esse, [illegible, ~40 letters] atque adeo præstantissimam esse [illegible, ~20 letters], vt si qui sacra suscipiant, huic [illegible, ~5 letters] nihil par, ne in ipsis quidem Eleusinis, aut Samothraciis orgiis, reperiant: Erant autem hæc Eleusinia mysteria, alia Minora, alia Maiora, quæ certum est intra eundem annum, & quidem vtraque quotannis, celebrati solita. Atque hæc [?] καθάρσεις fiebat variis modis. Vbi defuncti erant hac Minorum Mysteriorum [?] καθάρσεις, intra eundem annum Mysteriis quoque Maioribus initiabantur, neque quicquam opus erat quinquennium expectare, vt volunt Viri Incomparabiles. Interiecto vero anno post hanc τὴν μεγάλων μυστηρίων [?] μύησιν, sequentibus proxime Maioribus Mysteriis intra sacrorum secretum admittebantur, atque Epoptæ fiebant: nam Maiora Mysteria erant μυστικὰ καὶ ἐποπτικά. Scholia Aristophanis ad Ranas: οἱ δ᾽ [?] μυήσεια [?] μυσταγωγοῦντες, μύσας [?] κηρύττουσιν [?]. οἱ δὲ [?] ἐπόπτας ἐάσαντες [?], ταῦτα αὐτῆς [?] ἐφορῶσι [?] μυ-στήρια καὶ ἐποπτικά. Suidas: οἱ τὰ μυστήρια [?] μυσταγωγοῦντες, λέγοντες ἐν λόγῳ [?] μύσαι, μετ᾽ ἐκείνων δὲ ἐποπτείᾳ καὶ ἐφορᾷ. Harpocration: οἱ μυηθέντες ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ μυήσει, ἐποπτεύειν λέγονται. Plutarchus in Demetrio: τότε δὲ οὖν εἰσαζόμενοι εἰς τὰ Ἀθῆναι, ἔγραψεν ὅτι βούλεται [?] μυσταγωγῶν [?] μυητῶν, καὶ τὴν τελετὴν ἀπαθῆ [?] τῆς μικρᾶς ἄχρι τῆς ἐποπτικῆς μυήσεως [?]. τῶν δὲ ἡ ἡμέρα [?] ἐφ᾽ ὧν, ἀλλὰ τὰ μικρὰ τῆς Ἀνθεστηριῶνος ἐπελθῶν, τὰ δὲ μεγάλα τῆς Βοηδρομιῶνος · ἐπώσθησαν δὲ Μουνιχίων ἀπὸ τῶν μεγάλων ἑαυτὸν ἀμαλλίποντες.
units.tr: Athens seems to have produced many excellent and divine things and brought them into human life. Among these, nothing is better than those mysteries by which men, drawn from a rough and savage life to civility, were softened. These initiations, as they are called, truly reveal the first principles of life; they teach not only how to live with joy, but also how to die with better hope. Therefore Galen, in Book XVII of On the Use of the Parts, etc., places these Eleusinian rites among the most venerable sacred things. [The corrupt text is too damaged to restore.] No one can doubt that these words are corrupt, and they are corrected in various ways, which I judge no more faithful to Galen's mind. We think it should be emended ... Galen had said that the knowledge of God obtained from the use of the parts of the human body is ..., and therefore most excellent ..., so that if anyone undertakes the sacred rites, they will find nothing comparable to this, not even in the Eleusinian or Samothracian mysteries. Now these Eleusinian mysteries were of two kinds, the Lesser and the Greater, and it is certain that both were celebrated every year, within the same year. The old scholiasts on Aristophanes say: the Lesser were celebrated in the month Anthesterion, the Greater in Boedromion. Plutarch in Demetrius: ... The Lesser Mysteries were used as a purification before admission to the Greater. The scholiast on the comic poet: "... as purifications ... of the Greater." Now these purifications were carried out in various ways. Once those who had gone through the purifications of the Lesser Mysteries were finished, within the same year they were also initiated into the Greater Mysteries, and there was no need to wait five years, as those incomparable men maintain. But when a year had intervened after this initiation into the greater mysteries, at the next Greater Mysteries they were admitted into the secret rites and became epoptae; for the Greater Mysteries were mystical and epoptic. The scholia on Aristophanes' Frogs: "But those who lead the initiations, having let the epoptae ... proclaim the mysteries ... and they oversee these mysteries, both mystical and epoptic." Suidas: "those who lead the mysteries, saying that they are initiated by word, and with them there is epoptia and oversight." Harpocration: "Those initiated at Eleusis in the second initiation are said to be epoptae." Plutarch in Demetrius: "Then, being admitted into Athens, he wrote that he wished to lead the initiated, and the rite, unhindered, from the lesser to the epoptic initiation ..." [The corrupt Greek is not fully restored.] ... they were moved to ... Munychion, having taken away ... from the greater ...

units.la: Eximius est hic locus, è quo non tantum constat annum fuisse à Maiorum Mysteriorum acceptione interpositum ad eorundem τὰ ἐποπτικά, sed etiam, quod caput est, non fuisse interiectum quinquennij interuallum inter Minorum Mysteriorum acceptionem & Maiorum: nam Maiorum τὰ μυστικά codem anno tradebantur, quo Minora Mysteria accipiebantur: neque id culpat Plutarchus in Demetrio, sed hoc tantum, quòd cum Minora Mysteria nonnisi Anthesterione mense celebrentur, in gratiam Demetrij, qui Munychione mense venerat Athenas, Munychion factus sit Anthesterion; rursus vt eodem tempore suscipere posset Maiorum Mysteriorum, quæ Boëdromione mense agitabantur, τὰ μυστικά, Munychion de Anthesterione Boëdromion factus sit: nulla hic culpa, quod is, qui Minoribus Mysteriis initiatus fuerat Anthesterione mense, intra eundem annum vertentem Boedromione mense acceperit τὰ μυστικὰ Maiorum, id enim pro more fieri solebat: nota tamen non vacat, quod de Munychione Anthesterionem, ac rursum de Anthesterione Boedromionem fecerint, sed longè istud gravissimum, quod eodem Boedromione Maiorum Mysteriorum τὰ μυστικά, καὶ τὰ ἐποπτικὰ tradiderint, quum nonnisi interiecto anno acceptione τὴν μυστικὴν Maiorum Mysteriorum fieri soleret. Quare id exprobrat Philippides Comicus Stratocli, qui in hanc rem decretum scripserat, illiusque faciendi Athenienfibus auctor fuerat,
units.tr: This is a striking passage. From it it is clear not only that a year lay between the admission to the Greater Mysteries and their epoptic rites, but also, what is the main point, that there was no five-year interval between admission to the Lesser Mysteries and admission to the Greater. For the mystical rites of the Greater Mysteries were handed on in the same year in which the Lesser Mysteries were received. Plutarch does not blame this in Demetrius, but only this: since the Lesser Mysteries were celebrated only in the month Anthesterion, to please Demetrius, who had come to Athens in the month Munychion, Munychion was made into Anthesterion; and again, so that he could receive the mystical rites of the Greater Mysteries, which were celebrated in the month Boedromion, at the same time, Anthesterion was made into Boedromion. There is no fault here in that one who had been initiated into the Lesser Mysteries in Anthesterion received the mystical rites of the Greater in Boedromion within the same turning year, for this was customarily done. Yet it is not unworthy of note that they made Munychion into Anthesterion and again Anthesterion into Boedromion; but much more serious is that in the same Boedromion they handed over the mystical rites and the epoptic rites of the Greater Mysteries, whereas they were accustomed to do this only after a year had intervened. Therefore the comic poet Philippides reproaches Stratocles for this, who had written the decree on this matter and had been the author of this measure for the Athenians.

units.la: Ὁ τὸν ἑαυτὸν σὺν τὸ εἰς μίαν ἔτα.
units.tr: He who [himself] together with the ... into one year. [Ὁ τὸν ἑαυτὸν σὺν τὸ εἰς μίαν ἔτα.]

units.la: Sed adscribenda sunt Plutarchi verba, emendatione enim illis opus est: Ἀλλὰ Σπερπλέους γράμμα εἶπόντος, Ἀντιγενιῶνα τὸν Μουνυχίωνα ἐπιφαίνουσιν καὶ λείπειν καὶ νομίζειν, ἐτέλεσεν Δημητρίῳ τὰ μικρὰ ἀγερ-ρ. καὶ μὴ ταῦτα πάλιν ἐκ Ἀνθεστηριῶνος ὁ Μουνυχίων ἡμέρας Βοηδρομιῶν, ἐδίξατο τὴν λοιπὴν τελετὴν, ἅμα καὶ τὴν ἐποπτείαν τὰ Δημητρίου μεγαπαλέσθαι. Sed quid hoc est: ἐτέλεσεν Δημητρίῳ τὰ μικρὰ ἀγερ-ῶν; neque hic audiendus est Incomparabilis Casaubonus: multo minus eruditissimus Meursius, qui μικρὰ ἀγυρμῶν refert: Est autem ἀγυρμὸς primus Maiorum Mysteriorum dies, quare Minoribus non debet imputati. Rescribimus : ἐπίλογω Δημητρίας τὰ μεγάλα Ἀγγεῖα. Minora enim Mysteria Agræ siue Agris percipiebantur. Superest expendendus Tertulliani locus, quem in sententiæ suæ patrocinium aduocant viri magni. Verba eius sunt è Libro I. aduersus Valentinianos primore. Nam & illa Eleusina, hæresis & ipsa Atticæ superstitionis, quod tacent, pudor est. Idcirco aditum prius cruciant, diutius initiant, quàm consignant, quum Epoptas ante quinquennium instituunt, vt opinionem suspendio cognitionis ædificent: atque ita tantam maiestatem exhibere videantur, quantam præstruxerunt cupiditatem. Sequitur iam silentij officium, attente custoditur, quod tarde inuenitur. Ceterum tota in adytis diminitas, tot suspiria Epoptarum, totum signaculum linguæ, simulacrum membri virilis revelatur. Distincte Tertullianus his verbis totam Mysteriorum Atticorum scenam atque apparatū describit & explicat, [?]. Singula eius verba videamus & excutiamus: Idcirco & aditu prius cruciant: ita enim legimus cum viris summis. Aditum appellat [?] μικρὰ μυστήρια, quibus præpurgabātur & præparabantur mentes ad Maiorum acceptionem: Cruciare autem dixit, quia hæc [?] fieri solebat cum incantationibus, salibus, lauro, hordeo, mari, transitione per ignem, [?], [?], [?]. Quæ sequuntur Maiora spectat Mysteria, & ita legenda nobis videntur: Diutius initiant, quàm consignant, quum Epoptas ante [?] instituunt, vt opinionem suspendio cognitionis ædificent, atque ita tantam maiestatem exhibere videantur, quantam præstruxerunt cupiditatem: [?] Maiorum Mysteriorum nominat Tertullian[?] initiationem: Diuturnius autem esse tempus [?] ad [?], quàm fuerit [?] ad [?] Maiorum Mysteriorum acceptionem, indicat Tertullianus, adita prius cruciant, diutius initiant, quod omnino verum est. Nam intra eundem annum acceptis Minoribus Mysteriis Anthesterione mense, septimo post mese, nempe Boedromione, tradebantur [?] Maiorum Mysteriorum. Post accepta vero hæc Maiorum Mysteriorum [?], interponebatur annus, quo elapso [?] eorundem Maiorum Mysteriorū [?], mense Boedromione, tradebantur. Addit Tertullianus, quum consignant, quum Epoptas ante [?] instituunt. Vocat consignationem [?] noras, & symbola, quæ rogati sacrorum in acceptionibus respondebant. Eorum meminit Clemens Alexandrinus Protreptico: [?], [?]. Arnobius Lib. V. Eleusinorum vestrorum notas & origines produnt urbes, & antiquarum elogia literarum: Ipsa denique symbola, quæ rogati sacrorum in acceptionibus respondetis. Ieiunaui, atque ebibi cyceonem, ex cista sumsi, & in calathum misi. accepi rursùs, & in cistulam transtuli. Atque ex his patet, quare apud Tertullianū rescripserimus, quum Epoptas ante [?] instituunt. Hoc enim erat vnū de symbolis, quæ futuri Epoptæ [?], respondebant [?] eorundem. Ebibi cyceonem: [?]. Quum autem imperiti librarij nō intelligerent vocem Tertullianeam [?], mutarunt, facili lapsu, fecerūt-que, quinquennium. Symbola autem hæc esse Maiorum Mysteriorum, probat quod Clemens & Arnobius scribant esse Ἐλευσινίων μυστηρίων. ergo Maiorum, Minora [?] Ἀγγεῖα ἐπόπτικά. De Maioribus his Libanius Declamatione XIX, [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~70 letters] [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~50 letters]
units.tr: But the words of Plutarch must be quoted, for they need correction. "But when Sperplus wrote a letter saying that they show Antigenes [Ἀντιγενιῶνα] the Munychion both leaving and observing [λείπειν καὶ νομίζειν], he performed for Demetrius the small ... [ἐτέλεσεν Δημητρίῳ τὰ μικρὰ ἀγερ-ρ.]; and again after these things the Munychion, on the day of the Boedromia, from the Anthesterion, received the remaining rite, and at the same time the observation of the Demetrian rites [ἅμα καὶ τὴν ἐποπτείαν τὰ Δημητρίου μεγαπαλέσθαι]." But what is this, "he performed for Demetrius the small ... [ἐτέλεσεν Δημητρίῳ τὰ μικρὰ ἀγερ-ῶν]"? Here we should not follow the incomparable Casaubon, much less the most learned Meursius, who reads "small agyrmoi" [μικρὰ ἀγυρμῶν]. Now the agyrmos is the first day of the Greater Mysteries, so it should not be imputed to the Lesser. We rewrite it: "for the Demetrian Greater Vessels" [ἐπίλογω Δημητρίας τὰ μεγάλα Ἀγγεῖα]. For the Lesser Mysteries were celebrated at Agrae or Agrai. There remains the passage of Tertullian to be weighed, which great men summon in defence of their opinion. Its words are from the first book Against the Valentinians: "For that Eleusinian rite, too, a heresy of Attic superstition itself, what they keep silent about is shameful. Therefore they torment the candidate at the entrance first and initiate him for longer than they seal him, since they install the epoptae five years earlier, so that they may build up expectation by the delay of knowledge; and thus they seem to display as great a majesty as they have prepared desire. Then comes the duty of silence, carefully guarded, which is slowly discovered. Moreover, the whole inner sanctuary is in darkness, so many sighs of the epoptae, the whole seal of the tongue, the image of the male member is revealed." Tertullian here describes and explains distinctly the whole scene and apparatus of the Attic Mysteries. Let us look at and examine each word. "Idcirco et aditu prius cruciant": for so we read it with the greatest scholars. He calls the aditus [?] the Lesser Mysteries, by which minds were purged and prepared beforehand for the reception of the Greater. He says "torment" because this was done with incantations, salt, laurel, barley, sea water, passage through fire [?]. What follows concerns the Greater Mysteries, and so we think it should be read: "they initiate for longer than they seal, since they install the epoptae before [?], so that they may build up expectation by the delay of knowledge, and thus seem to display as great a majesty as they have prepared desire": [?] Tertullian names the initiation of the Greater Mysteries [?]; and that the time [?] was longer for [?] than it was for [?] the reception of the Greater Mysteries, Tertullian indicates in the words "they torment at the entrance first, they initiate for longer," which is wholly true. For within the same year, after receiving the Lesser Mysteries in the month of Anthesterion, the Greater Mysteries [?] were handed over in the seventh month after, namely Boedromion. After these Greater Mysteries [?] had been received, a year intervened, and when that had elapsed [?] of the same Greater Mysteries [?] were handed over in the month of Boedromion. Tertullian adds, "when they seal, since they install the epoptae before [?]." He calls the sealing [?] tokens and symbols, which those asked about the rites answered at the receptions. Clement of Alexandria mentions these in the Protrepticus: [?], [?]. Arnobius, Book V: "Your Eleusinian tokens and origins are revealed by cities and by the praises of ancient letters; finally, the symbols themselves, which you answer when asked about the rites at the receptions: I fasted, and drank the kykeon, I took from the chest and put into the basket; I took again and transferred into the small chest." From these things it is clear why we have rewritten, in Tertullian, "since they install the epoptae before [?]." For this was one of the symbols, which the future epoptae [?] answered [?] of the same. "I drank the kykeon": [?]. But since the unlearned copyists did not understand the Tertullianic word [?], they changed it through an easy slip, and made it "quinquennium" (five years). That these symbols belong to the Greater Mysteries is proved by the fact that Clement and Arnobius write that they are of the Eleusinian mysteries, therefore of the Greater; the Lesser [?] are the epoptic vessels. About these Greater Mysteries Libanius, in Declamation XIX, [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~70 letters] [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~50 letters]

units.la: Posteriora illa sana non sunt: ἰδία πάλιν, ὅ, σὺ π[?]ὸ [illegible, ~20 letters]. Quid enim praecipit [illegible, ~12 letters] cum sequatur, [illegible, ~15 letters]. Rescribo, [illegible, ~10 letters] nominatim ἰδία, [illegible, ~8 letters] singulos compellari dicit, [illegible, ~10 letters] exempli gratia, Δημοσθένης Δημοσθένους, nam ita compellare solebant, ὁ Demosthenes Demosthenis fili. Sed ad Tertulliani verba redeamus, qui nihil hac in parte de silentio: neque enim erant [illegible, ~12 letters], vt constat è Libanio, sed tantum de morae caussa, dicit enim annum interpositum fuisse inter [illegible, ~10 letters] Mysteriis, [illegible, ~10 letters], vt opinionem maiestatis his Mysteriis conciliaret suspendio cognitionis, & cupiditatem differendo atque procrastinando praestruerent. Postrema horum Mysteriorum scena [?]ἐποπτεία restat, quae his verbis explicatur: Sequitur iam silentij officium, attente custoditur, quod tarde inueniter. Ceterum tota in adytis diuinitas, tot suspiria Epoptarum, totum signaculum linguae, simulacrum membri virilis reuelatur. Quibus verbis significat, grande illud arcanum, quod in adytis seruabatur, quodque tantopere sibi Epoptis reuelari exoptabant, & precibus multisque suspiriis contendebant Mystae, neque prodere licebat, simulacrum membri virilis fuisse. Non solebant autem olim eos, qui ciues Athenienses non essent, his initiare Mysteriis:
units.tr: Those last words are not sound: [...] For what does [...] command, since it follows [...]? I propose to read [...] by name, "[...] is addressed individually," for example, Demosthenes son of Demosthenes, for they used to address (people) thus: "O Demosthenes, son of Demosthenes." But let us return to Tertullian's words, who in this part says nothing about silence; for these were not [...], as is clear from Libanius, but he speaks only of the cause of the delay. For he says that a year was placed between [...] the Mysteries, [...], so that they might win for these Mysteries the sense of majesty through the postponement of knowledge, and through deferring and procrastinating they might prepare desire. The last scene of these Mysteries remains, the epopteia, which is explained in these words: Then comes the duty of silence, carefully kept, which is slowly discovered. Otherwise the whole divinity is shown in the sanctuaries, so many sighs of the Epoptae, the whole seal of the tongue, the image of the male member is revealed. By these words he indicates that the great secret which was kept in the sanctuaries, which the Epoptae longed to have revealed to them so eagerly, and for which the initiates strove with prayers and many sighs, and which it was not allowed to betray, was an image of the male member. But in earlier times they did not customarily initiate into these Mysteries those who were not Athenian citizens:

units.la: Μυσίνα ξένον μύειν, Peregrinum Mysterijs ne initiato.
units.tr: Do not initiate a foreigner into the Mysteries. [μυσίνα ξένον μύειν]

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Plutum: [illegible, ~12 letters] Ἀλκιβιάδης, μυσίνα ξένον μύειν. Apollodorus Lib.II.agens de Hercule: [illegible, ~12 letters]. Optime autem dixit ἐπὶ, non enim aetate sua id obseruabant: sed primitus nemo initiabatur, qui ciuis Atheniensis non esset: quare Hercules, itemque Castor & Pollux in ciuitatem adsciti sunt adoptati, hi quidem ab Aphidno, ille vero à Pylio. Plutarchus in Thefeo: [illegible, ~20 letters] Castor & Pollux, [illegible, ~25 letters] Hercules [illegible, ~10 letters], atq; ciues Δημοτικοὶ Eleusiniis Mysteriis initiati sunt: estque ex his emaculandus Apollodori codex loco laudato: [illegible, ~30 letters], Ευμολπος, [illegible, ~10 letters] Ελλοῦσα, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Ἐπεὶ δὲ Ἄμπος Πυλίῳ πᾶς ἀφιέμενος ἐμυεῖτο. Thespius Herculis coxeus is non est, qui à Pylio adoptatus est, itaque reponendum est: Ἴσ μὲν Πυλίῳ πᾶς ἀφιέμενος ἐμυεῖτο. Legitimus factus adoptione Pylij filius, ac proinde ciuis Atheniensis, initiatus est. Postea omnibus Graecis id concessum est, vt his Mysteriis possent initiari. Herodotus Lib. VIII. [illegible, ~30 letters] Μηδείας [illegible, ~10 letters] Κόρῃ, [illegible, ~15 letters] ἄλλων Ἑλλήνων, μυείσθαι. Neque tantū Graeci initiati sunt, sed quaecumque etiam aliae gentes. Cicero de Nat.Deorum Lib.I. Omitto Eleusinam sanctam illam, & angustam,
units.tr: The scholiast on Aristophanes' Plutus mentions this law: [...] Alcibiades, do not initiate a foreigner [μυσίνα ξένον μύειν]. Apollodorus, Book II, speaking of Hercules: [...]. He said "at that time" (ἐπί) very rightly, for they did not observe this in their own age; but originally no one was initiated who was not an Athenian citizen. Therefore Hercules, and likewise Castor and Pollux, were received and adopted into the state: the one indeed by Aphidnus, the other by Pylius. Plutarch in Theseus: [...] Castor and Pollux, [...] Hercules [...], and the demotic citizens were initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries; and the text of Apollodorus at the place cited must be emended from this: [...] Eumolpus [...] Hellousa [...]. "Since Pylius adopted everyone who came, he was initiated." Thespius is not the Hercules who was adopted by Pylius; therefore it must be restored: "Since Pylius adopted everyone who came, he was initiated." Having been legitimately made a son by adoption of Pylius, and therefore an Athenian citizen, he was initiated. Afterwards this was granted to all the Greeks, that they might be initiated into these Mysteries. Herodotus, Book VIII: [...] Medea [...] the maiden, [...] of the other Greeks, to be initiated. Not only Greeks were initiated, but any other nations whatever. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, Book I: I pass over that holy and narrow Eleusis,

units.la: Vbi initiantur gentes orarum vltimae.
units.tr: where the peoples of the furthest shores are initiated.

units.la: Cùm hac tamen, puto, cautione, si Graecè scirent: colligo ex his Libanij verbis iam ante laudatis, Declamatione XIX. [illegible, ~20 letters] Ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ Ἀπάτης [illegible, ~10 letters] Ἑλλήνων, μυείσθαι. Neque tantū Graeci initiati sunt, sed quaecumque etiam aliae gentes. Submouebantur tamen voce praeconis omnes barbari, & exesse iubebantur, quemadmodum & homicidae, aliique impij, & scelerati. Isocrates Panegyrico de Medis & Persis agens: [illegible, ~45 letters] Lucianus in Demonacte: [illegible, ~60 letters] Theon in Progymnas-matis: [illegible, ~50 letters] homicidam, [illegible, ~20 letters].
units.tr: Yet with this caution, I think, if they knew Greek; I gather it from these words of Libanius already cited, Declamation XIX: [...] To the [...] of the Greeks, to be initiated. Not only Greeks were initiated, but any other nations whatever. Yet all barbarians were removed by the herald's voice, and ordered to depart, just as murderers and other impious and wicked persons were. Isocrates, speaking in the Panegyricus about the Medes and Persians: [...] Lucian in Demonax: [...] Theon in the Progymnasmata: [...] a murderer [...].

units.la: Diximus in superioribus Mysteria Cereris in initiorum sacra nullo magis quam silentio, solennia fuisse, itaque neque dicere, neque audire licebat, cum parem noxam contraherent aures, & linguae, temerariae curiositatis. Quare si quis arcanae Mysteria Cereris sacra vulgasset, Lege morti addicebatur: Τὸν ἐξειπόντα τὰ Μυστήρια πεθήναι[?] Qui Mysteria vulgarit, capite luat.
units.tr: We have said above that in the Mysteries of Ceres the rites of the initiations were solemnly kept by silence more than by anything else; so it was permitted neither to speak nor to hear, since the ears and tongue would contract an equal guilt of rash curiosity. Therefore if anyone had divulged the secret Mysteries of the rites of Ceres, he was given over to death by law: "The one who reveals the Mysteries shall be put to death." [Τὸν ἐξειπόντα τὰ Μυστήρια θανατοῦσθαι] Whoever has divulged the Mysteries shall pay with his head.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Sopater in Diuisione Quaestionis, nosque ex eo descripsimus, [illegible, ~30 letters], aliunde namque nobis constat capitale fuisse Athenis vulgare haec initia: Ea quippe de causa proscriptus fuit ab Athenien-sibus Diagoras Melius, ac propositum talentum vnum eiusqui Diagoram interfecisset, duo, qui viuum adduxisset. Interpres Comici ad Aues, & ex eo Suidas: [illegible, ~70 letters]
units.tr: Sopater mentions this law in his Division of the Question, and we have copied it from him. [illegible] For it is otherwise established that at Athens it was a capital offence to divulge these rites. For this reason Diagoras of Melos was outlawed by the Athenians, and a talent was offered for whoever killed Diagoras, and two talents for whoever brought him in alive. The commentator on Aristophanes' Birds says this, and Suidas after him: [illegible]

units.la: Etiam Æschylus in vitae discrimen venit, cum in Tragoediis nonnulla, quaeque initia spectabant, euulgasse credderetur. Clemens Alexandrinus Stromat. II. [illegible, ~50 letters] Eustrathius in cap.I. Libri III. Ethicor. Nicomach. [illegible, ~120 letters] Pollux Lib. VIII. c.XII. [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: Aeschylus too came into danger of his life, since he was thought to have divulged some things in his tragedies that concerned the rites. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II: [illegible]. Eustathius on chapter 1 of Book III of the Nicomachean Ethics: [illegible]. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter XII: [illegible]

units.la: Haec tamen Mysteria vocat Ἀναχαλυπτήρια[?], Synesius in Calvitiei encomio: nam vbi nonnulla de frugibus obseruauit, addit, [illegible, ~40 letters]. Putat Cl Meursius Synesium ludentem, quae Mysteria alij, Anakalyptheia dixisse, in quibus nempe Cereris acta reuelarentur. Nuperus Synesii Interpres causam appellationis hanc esse exististimat, quod in Cereris prodeuntis, atq; è gluma & inuolucris explicitae, ac retectae, honore celebrarentur: Nam postea caluorum capita effluentibus pilis [illegible, ~25 letters], ait, ob idq; eorum Anakalyptheia celebrata. Ad hoc pertinere videntur Ouidiani illis versus X. Metam. Festa piae Cereris celebrabant orgia matres, illa, quibus nivea velatae corpora veste, Primitias frugum dant spicea ferta suarum.
units.tr: Yet Synesius, in his Praise of Baldness, calls these Mysteries the Anakalypteria [?]. After noting some things about the crops, he adds [illegible]. Meursius thinks that Synesius, playing, called Anakalyptheia what others called Mysteries, in which the acts of Ceres were unveiled. The recent interpreter of Synesius thinks the name arose because they were celebrated with honour when the grain of Ceres came forth, uncovered and laid bare from husk and wrapping. For afterwards, when the hair of bald heads flows out [illegible], he says, and for this reason their Anakalyptheia was celebrated. To this seem to belong those verses of Ovid in Metamorphoses X: The mothers celebrated the sacred rites of pious Ceres, those who were covered in snow-white garments, and they gave the first-fruits of their crops in garlands of ears.

units.la: Ego vero existimo locum leuiter esse corruptum, maximo tamen cum sententiae damno; emendamus: ὅτι τοῖς Ἐλευσ[?]ινίοις ἀγὰ τὰ Δήμητρος, ἅμα καλύπτειν [?] ῥοιαί, nam in hac Eleusina pompa cistis condebantur mala Punica: Clemens Protreptico: εἶτα δὲ [?] καὶ αἱ χίτες αἱ μυστικαί; οὐχὶ δὲ ῥοιαί, &c. cuius rei causam hanc accipe ab Ouidio Metamorph. Libro V.
units.tr: I, however, think the passage has been slightly corrupted, though with great damage to the sense. Let us emend it: that at the Eleusinian rites of Demeter pomegranates were carried together with the sacred vessels [?], for in this Eleusinian procession pomegranates were stored in baskets. Clement in the Protrepticus: "then also the mystic tunics; not pomegranates," etc. Take the reason for this from Ovid, Metamorphoses Book V.

units.la: —sed tanta cupido Si tibi dissidij est, repetere Proserpina caelum, Lege tamen certa, si nullos contigit illic Ore cibos: nam sic Parcarum foedere cautum est. Dixerat: at Cereri certum est educere natam. Non ita fata sinunt: quoniam ieiunia virgo Soluerat, & cultis dum simplex errat in hortis, Puniceam curua decerpserat arbore pomum: Sumptaque pallenti septem de cortice grana Presserat ore suo.
units.tr: "But if you are so eager to have a quarrel, Proserpina, to return to heaven, yet on this condition, that you have touched no food there; for it is so provided by the covenant of the Fates." She had spoken; but it was resolved to lead the daughter back to Ceres. The Fates did not allow it, since the maiden had broken her fast, and while she wandered simply in the cultivated gardens, she had plucked a pomegranate from the curved tree, and taken seven seeds from its pale rind and pressed them with her mouth.

units.la: Initiati vestem, qua tunc essent amicti, usu iam detritam Cereri & Proserpinae consecrabant ex hac Lege.
units.tr: Initiates consecrated to Ceres and Proserpina the garment they were then wearing, already worn out with use, in accordance with this law.

units.la: Ἐν οἷς ὡς ἱματίοις μυηθῆναι, εἰς τὴν [?] Initiati, qua tunc essent amicti veste, Deabus consecranto. ἀναθέναι [?] Κόρην [?]
units.tr: [Greek fragment, garbled in the source; sense:] Those who are initiated should dedicate to the goddesses the garment in which they were clothed at that time. [ἐν οἷς ὡς ἱματίοις μυηθῆναι, εἰς τὴν ... Κόρην]

units.la: Hanc Legem descripsit è Melanthio Græcus Aristophanis Interpres ad hæc Pluti verba, quæ eo alluduntur:
units.tr: A Greek writer took this law from Melanthius and set it down in his commentary on Aristophanes, at these words of the Plutus to which the passage alludes:

units.la: Καρ. Τὸ τελεσθὲν δ᾽ ἐὰ διώσαι πρὸς τὴν ἡλίκην [?], Ὁ φέρει μὴ σοὶ δ᾽ παιδάρια τοῦτ᾽ [?], φράσον [?], Δικ. Καὶ τὸν διαθῆσαι ἔρχεσαι πρὸς τὸν [?]. Καρ. Μὴ τῶν ἰμανιῶν [?] ἐὰ αὐτὰ τὰ μεγάλα [?]; Δικ. Οὐκ. Ἀλλ᾽ ἐκεῖ ἐπὶ τελετῶν [?].
units.tr: [Greek dialogue of Carion and Dikaiopolis, badly corrupted in the source. Sense:] Carion: "...the one who has been initiated, you should not send your child..." Dikaiopolis: "...and do you come to..." Carion: "Do not the great ... ?" Dikaiopolis: "No, but there, at the rites..."

units.la: Παίζει τὰ [?] τὸν Ἐλευσίνιοι νέμων. ἔτος γὰρ ὧ; ἀ εἰς τῆς ἱματίοις μυηθῆν, εἰς Θεοῦ [?] νος ἀναθέναι τῶν, ὥσπερ Δήλιοι καὶ Μελάνθιος ἐν πα[?] ἐκεῖ μυστηρίων. πάντεινὸν δὲ τῆς ῥαίας ἐλάσεως καὶ τὰς τολμᾶς τῆς μύσεως ἐν ἂς τῆσι μυηθέντας. Sed fallitur Interpres cum consecrari dicit Deo alicui, nam Cereris Proserpinaeque tantum meminit Melanthius, à quo accepit Scholiastes Comici: Nonnulli illas ad infantum sibi fascias reseruabant. Scholia ibidem: ἔνιοι δὲ τὰ τοιαῦτα τολλὰς εἰς τέχνων αὐτ[?]ργανα Φυλάττοιτο. Non autem eas initiati, nisi longo iam usu tritas & laceras deponebant. Scholia ibidem: ὁ δὲ μυήσας ὁ ἱμάτιον, ὁ ἐφο-ρεῖ ἐν τῇ μυήσει, σὺν ποτὲ ἀπέδυεν, μέχρις δὲ τελέως ἀφανιοῦ ἀφρύνει. At vero paulò ante idem Scholiastes videtur indicare vesteshuiusmodi, quae dedicarentur ab initiatis, aut etiam forte ab aliis, fuisse non tantum à fullone candentes, sed etiam nouas: ἀκάπλων εἰς τὰ ἱμάλια τῶν φοινῶν, ὁ[?] ρυ-[?] ἔστιν. ἔνιοι δὲ τὰ τοιαῦτα τολλὰς εἰς τέχνων αὐτ[?]ργανα Φυλάττοιτο. καθαρεῖ δὲ πᾶν ἀπαρχῆσι χὴ νέα. Sed misere corruptus est hic locus, nam hic latet mos antiquus, quem nos docet Hesychius: Καταχύσας, καταχύσας, sed legendum est καταχύσας· οἱ δὲ ἀναθέντες ἱμάτια καταχύζον αὐτά, ἵνα μὴ ἀρθῶν [?] ἀρθῶν [?]. Quando vestes consecrabant, eas prius quam suspenderent, lacerabant & scindebant, ne quis posset in vsum suum conuertere: hoc ipsum docebat Scholiastes his verbis, quæ ita emendo, καταρρύοι δ' ἐπὶ ταραχθῆσαι [?] καὶ νέα. etiamsi nouæ essent vestes, nihilo tamen minus eas lacerabant.
units.tr: The commentator plays on the Eleusinians' custom: for it was a year when, having been initiated in garments, they dedicated them to the god, as the Delians and Melanthius, in his work on the mysteries, [say]. The rites of the ... and the bold acts of the initiation in which they were initiated. But the Interpreter is mistaken when he says they are consecrated to some god, for Melanthius mentions only Ceres and Proserpina, from whom the scholiast on the comic poet took it. Some kept those cloths for their children's swaddling bands. Scholion on the same passage: some of them kept such garments, once dedicated, as ... for the sons. But they did not deposit them except when they were already long worn out and torn. The scholiast on the same passage: the one who initiated him ... the garment he wore in the initiation, once taken off, was ... until it had completely vanished. But a little earlier the same scholiast seems to indicate that garments of this kind, which were dedicated by initiates, or perhaps by others, were not only brightened by the fuller, but were also new: [Greek]. But this passage is wretchedly corrupted, for here lies an ancient custom, which Hesychius teaches: "Katachysas, katachysas," but it must be read as "katachysas"; those who dedicate garments pour them over... When they consecrated garments, they tore and cut them before hanging them up, so that no one could turn them to their own use. The scholiast himself teaches this in the following words, which I emend thus: [Greek]. Even if the garments were new, they nevertheless tore them.

units.la: Quum autem Cereri Eleusiniæ atque Proserpinæ initiarentur æque pauperes atque diuites, viri fœmineque, ne quod inter fœminas discrimen haberetur, hac consultum est Lege,
units.tr: Since both the poor and the rich, men and women alike, were initiated into the Eleusinian Ceres and Proserpina, this law was made so that no distinction should be drawn between women:

units.la: Ἐπὶ ζεύγεις μὴ ἀπιέναι γυναῖκα Ἐλευσινάδε, εἰ δέ τις φωραθείη, ἀπολύειν δραχμὰς ἑξακισχιλίας. [?]
units.tr: [Greek:] "A woman shall not go to Eleusis on a chariot drawn by a yoke; if anyone is caught, she shall pay six thousand drachmas."

units.la: Femina bigis ad sacra Eleusinia ne vehitor: si qua secus faxit, multa drachmarum sex mille irrogator.
units.tr: A woman shall not be carried to the Eleusinian rites in a two-horse carriage; if any woman does otherwise, let a fine of six thousand drachmas be imposed.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Plutarchus in Lycurgo Rhetore, ubi recenset Leges ab eo latas suis Atheniensibus, in eamque Legem prima feminarum commisit ipsius uxor Lycurgi: εἰσαγωγὰς δὲ νόμων, Ἐπὶ ζεύγεις μὴ ἀπιέναι γυναῖκα Ἐλευσινάδε, ὅπως μὴ ἐκφέρωνται [?] τοῦ τῆς πλουσίων· εἰ δέ τις φωραθείη, ἀπολύειν δραχμὰς ἑξακισχιλίας. τῆς δὲ γυναικὸς αὐτοῦ μὴ πειθομένης, τῆς συνοφαντῶν φωραθομένην [?] ἀλλὰ ἐδωκε. Refert quoque Ælianus Variæ Libro XIII. cap. XXIV. vbi tamen male ψήφισμα dixit, quæ reuera Lex erat; Olim currû vehebantur feminæ Eleusinem. Aristophanes Pluto:
units.tr: Plutarch mentions this law in his Life of the orator Lycurgus, where he lists the laws proposed by him for his Athenians. Among them: "A law that a woman shall not go to Eleusis on a yoked carriage, so that they should not be carried out of the ..., and if anyone is caught, a fine of six thousand drachmas. When his own wife did not obey, she was caught ..." Aelian also reports it in Varia Historia Book XIII, chapter XXIV, where he wrongly calls it a decree (psephisma), though it was really a law: "Formerly women were carried to Eleusis in carriages." Aristophanes, in Plutus: "For the great Mysteries, a woman who is carried in a cart, lest she should ..., let us ... for the whole day."

units.la: Μυστηίοις ὃ ἴσις μεγάλοις ὀργυμάλιου / Ἐπὶ τῆς ἀμάξης, ὅτι καταφεύγει μή ἔας, / Ἐντυπῶμεν ἀλ' τῶν ὅλων ἡμέραν.
units.tr: [Greek verses of Aristophanes, quoted above in Latin rendering.] Their sense: the Athenian women went to the great Eleusinian rites riding in a cart.

units.la: Scholia: αἱ τῶν Ἀθηναίων γυναῖκες ἐπὶ ἀμάξαν ὀχούμεναι εἰς τὰ μεγάλα Ἐλευσίνια ἀπήεσαν. Demosthenes quoque in Midianæ Midiæ luxum notat, non quod uxorem suam Eleusinem deduceret bigis, id enim solenne erat, sed insolens illud fuit, quod bigis albis Sicyoniis deduceret: καὶ εἰς μυστήρια τῶν γυναῖκα ἀγέ, κἂν ἀῆρ ὅτι που βάλλεται, ὅτι τῆς Λύκου ζεύγεις τῆς ἐκ Σικυῶνος. Quibus è verbis colligere licet, nondum hanc à Lycurgo latam fuisse Legem, qua fanciebatur, ne qua femina bigis Eleusinem veheretur, Midianam autem scripsit Demosthenes Callimacho Athenis Prætore. Dionysius Halicarnasseus Epistola ad Ammæum: ςὴ Καλλίμαχον γενέσθαι τὴν Ἀρχοντα καὶ ὁ ςὴ Μειδίας λόγος, ὃν συνεπάξατο μὴ τῶν χθονίων [?] κατηγορήσθη. Fuit autem Callimachus Archon anno quarto Olympiadis centesimæ septimæ. Quare post annum quartum Olympiadis centesimæ septimæ lata est hæc Lex à Lycurgo, viro & generis nobilitate & actibus illustri, qui malis terrori, bonis præsidio fuit: itaque urbis custodia, & malefi corum hominum coercitio illi commissa est. Plutarchus in eius vita: ἔφη δὲ καὶ τῆς ἀγρᾶς τῶν Φυλακῶν, καὶ τῆς κακούργων τὴν σύλληψιν, οἷς ὀξύηγεῖτο ἀπολύσεως. Atque hinc cognomen inuenit: nam Ibis cognominatus est. Plutarchus: ἐπικαλεῖτο δὲ ὁ Λυκοῦργος, Ἴβις Λυκούργῳ, Ξενοφάνη ἐκπεπρίεις [?]. Sed misere corrupta sunt Plutarchi verba, exciditque cognomen Lycurgi, quia ab eo incipit versus, quem ita restitues: ἐπικαλεῖτο δὲ ὁ Λυκοῦργος Ἴβις.
units.tr: The scholia say that the women of Athens went to the great Eleusinian rites riding on a wagon. Demosthenes also censures the extravagance of Midias, not because he took his wife to Eleusis in a two-horse carriage, for that was customary, but because it was unusual that he did so with white horses from Sicyon: [Greek]. From these words it may be gathered that this law, which ordained that no woman should be carried to Eleusis in a two-horse carriage, had not yet been proposed by Lycurgus, and that Demosthenes wrote the speech Against Midias when Callimachus was praetor at Athens. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in his letter to Ammaeus: "Callimachus became archon, and the speech of Midias, which he [Demosthenes] composed ... was brought against him." Callimachus was archon in the fourth year of the 107th Olympiad. Therefore this law was proposed by Lycurgus after the fourth year of the 107th Olympiad, a man both illustrious in family and in his deeds, who was a terror to the wicked and a protection to the good; so the guarding of the city and the restraint of evildoers were entrusted to him. Plutarch, in his Life: "He is said to have been in charge of the guard and the arrest of the criminals, on whom he was severe, and so he had no release." And from this he gained a nickname, for he was called Ibis. Plutarch: "Lycurgus was called Ibis, ..." But Plutarch's words are wretchedly corrupted, and the nickname of Lycurgus has dropped out, because the verse begins with it, which you will restore thus: "Lycurgus was called Ibis."

units.la: Ἴβις Λυκοῦργος ξένῳ, Φασὶ νυκτερίς.
units.tr: Lycurgus the Ibis, to the stranger; they call him the bat. [Ἴβις Λυκοῦργος ξένῳ, Φασὶ νυκτερίς]

units.la: Inuocant Ægyptij Ibes suas contra serpentum aduentum, inquit Plinius Libro X. cap. XXVIII. Erat igitur Lycurgus peregrinis & inquilinis, tanquam Ibis Ægyptiis aduersus serpentium aduentum: quod vel Xenocratis, quem tutatus est, exemplum comprobat: at vero nocturnis grassatoribus, qui caedes patrant, est tanquam vespertilio, fruftra enim noctem suis obtendunt caedibus, oculos Lycurgi namque effugere possunt. Elegans & venustum proculdubio de Lycurgo dicterium, & quod illum maximè commendet: nam & peregrinos tutatur, & homicidas mediis in tenebris latentes in solem profert, vt merităs dent poenas.
units.tr: The Egyptians invoke their ibises against the coming of serpents, says Pliny in Book X, chapter XXVIII. So Lycurgus was to foreigners and resident aliens what the ibis is to the Egyptians against the approach of serpents. The example of Xenocrates, whom he defended, confirms this. But to nocturnal robbers who commit murders he is like a bat, for they vainly cover the night with their slaughters, since they cannot escape the eyes of Lycurgus. This is surely an elegant and charming saying about Lycurgus, and one that greatly commends him: he protects foreigners, and he brings murderers who lie hidden in the midst of darkness out into the sun, so that they may pay the penalty they deserve.

units.la: Tam religiosè autem hi Mysteriorum dies obseruabantur, vt ne libellum quidem supplicem per eos offerre Lege liceret.
units.tr: These days of the Mysteries were observed so strictly that, by law, it was not even permitted to offer a suppliant petition on them.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Andocides ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν Μυστηρίων, cuius inimici dicebant capital esse ei qui aduersus hanc Legem commisisset: Κατηγόρουν δὲ μὴ καὶ περὶ τῆς ἱκετηρίας, ὡς καλ[?]εῖλων ἐγὼ ἐν τοῖς Ἐλευσινίων νόμοις δὲ τῶν πάτερος, ὡς αἱ ἐν ἱκετηρίαν μυστηρίοις, [illegible, ~6 letters]. Rursum: πάλιν ὁ Κοδρίας [?] ἔλεγε, ὅτι εἰη νόμος πάτερος, εἰ ἡς ἱκετηρίας [?] ἐν τοῖς Ἐλευσινίοις, ἀχρίτον [?]. Sed id negat Andocides, scribitque ibidem multam tantum mille drachmarum illi irrogari: ἐπιτιμᾷ δὲ νόμων πάτερων λέγεις. ἡ δὲ ζημία, παρ' ἡ ἔσηκας, χιλίας δραχμάς κελεύει ὀφείλειν, ἐαὶ ἡς ἱκετη-ρίας ἦ ἐν τοῖς Ἐλευσινίοις.
units.tr: Andocides mentions this law in his speech On the Mysteries [ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν Μυστηρίων], whose enemies said that it was a capital offence for anyone who transgressed against this law. [Κατηγόρουν δὲ μὴ καὶ περὶ τῆς ἱκετηρίας, ὡς καλ[?]εῖλων ἐγὼ ἐν τοῖς Ἐλευσινίων νόμοις δὲ τῶν πάτερος, ὡς αἱ ἐν ἱκετηρίαν μυστηρίοις] His accusers also charged him concerning the suppliant petition, that I had (?) under the laws of the Eleusinian mysteries, and of the fathers, that the suppliant petition in the mysteries... Again: [πάλιν ὁ Κοδρίας [?] ἔλεγε, ὅτι εἰη νόμος πάτερος, εἰ ἡς ἱκετηρίας [?] ἐν τοῖς Ἐλευσινίοις, ἀχρίτον [?]] Again, Codrias (?) said that there was a law of the fathers, that if the suppliant petition... in the Eleusinia... unjudged. But Andocides denies this, and he writes in the same place that only a fine of a thousand drachmas was imposed on him. [ἐπιτιμᾷ δὲ νόμων πάτερων λέγεις. ἡ δὲ ζημία, παρ' ἡ ἔσηκας, χιλίας δραχμάς κελεύει ὀφείλειν, ἐαὶ ἡς ἱκετη-ρίας ἦ ἐν τοῖς Ἐλευσινίοις.] The penalty, he says, orders a thousand drachmas to be owed, if the suppliant petition were in the Eleusinia.

units.la: Neque item his Mysteriorum diebus Lege licebat cuiquam manum injicere.
units.tr: Nor, likewise, on these days of the Mysteries was it lawful by law for anyone to lay hands on another.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Μειδίου: ἐγὼ τὸν μὲν εἶπον, ἵνα ἀφέστης τῆς πόλεως ἀγορᾶς μισθῶν κατα[?]ώσεως, ἐπὶ τὰ μυστήρια ἀδικεῖ, Εὐαίνδρῳ κατηγορήσαντος ὁ δῆμος, τῆς Θεαπίας, [illegible, ~8 letters], ἀποφυγῆς καὶ τῆς Μενίππου. Vlpianus: ἱ[?]ως τῷ ἐορτῇ ἀσέβημα καὶ ἀσφάλειαν ἡγησάμενος, ἐπιλαμβάνει ὀφείλων. Praecipuis quoque festis Christianorum hanc haberi voluerunt reverentiam Imperatores Christiani. Imperatores Valentinianus Theodosius & Arcadius: In quindecim autem Paschalibus diebus compulsio annonariae functionis, & omnium publicorum & privatorum debitorum differatur exactio. Dat. II. Id. Aug. Romae Timasio & Promoto Coss. Lege VII.C.de Ferijs. Constantinus Magnus die Dominico itemque Veneris omnes caussas & lites reliquaque negotia quiescere iussit Lege, quam laudat Sozomenus Hist. Eccl. Lib.I.cap.VIII. τῷ ἡ Κυριακῷ καλουμένῳ ἡμέραν τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἐφ' ἑαυτῶν ἐδόμασιν, Ἑλλῆνες ἡ ἡλίου ἀπαθείας, καὶ ἡ τῶν ἐδόμης σωματείας δικαστῶν καὶ τῶν ἄλλων πραγμάτων σχολῇ ἀγὼν πάντας, καὶ ὁ θάνατος καὶ λιτῆς ὁ ἡμέρα ἀγαπῶν. Eiusque Legis nonnulla leguntur Lege I.C. Theod. cod. in haec verba: Imp.Constantinus Aug. Helpidio. Sicut indignissimum videbatur, diem Solis venerationis suae celebrem altercantibus iurgijs & noxiis partium contentionibus occupari: ita gratum ac iocundum est, eo die quae sunt maxime votiva compleri. Atque ideo emancipandi & manumittendi die festo cuncti licentiam habeant, & super his rebus actu non prohibeantur. PP. V. Non. Iunij. Caralis Crispo II. & Constantino II. Coff. Habes etiam Leonis & Anthemij Constitutionem Leg. X. C. cod. Impp. Leo & Anthemius AA. Armafio Praef. Praet.
