Long before those things happened, he says that he neither fined anyone nor seized any pledge, plainly when he was choosing the chorus which was to dance at the Thargelijs; the best interpreter himself says in these words: [illegible]. So it was not while the festival of the Thargeliorum was being celebrated, and therefore he did not attend to this law. Add that he does not deny in these words, if I take them rightly, that he could have fined or seized a pledge, but from the fact that he did not do so he proves [illegible]. Finally, even if all those things had happened during the Thargelijs, he could not have turned his mind to this law, since it had not yet been written; Antiphon had already died long before it was passed. This is enough on these matters, but since so convenient an opportunity presents itself, I cannot pass over certain points in the same speech of Antiphon without emending and illustrating them. So in what follows, in the person of the choregus, Antiphon teaches when it was written before the king, who took office the following year, and says: [illegible]. But this does not agree well with these figures, since in what follows he shows that he was one of the Council of Five Hundred, whose tribe had only two days left to finish its prytany. His tribe had drawn the first prytany when his name was laid before the king: [illegible]. Now the prytany was a period of thirty-five days. Harpocration: [illegible]. So the name of our choregus was laid before the king [illegible] on the thirty-fourth day of the prytany, which was the fifth of Metagitnion; for Hecatombaeon is hollow. Thus it was neither on the twentieth of Metagitnion that he was denounced, nor had the king been in office fifty days since he entered it. I therefore read: [Greek: Ἀλλὰ πρῶτον τῆς Ἰούνου τῆς μιᾶς ἢ εἰ κ' ἔσται, ἡμέρας]. He says that five days of the month Metagitnion had passed, if indeed they have. Very good, as is shown by the reckoning. Twenty-nine days must be counted for Hecatombaeon; add five days of Metagitnion, making thirty-four, and on the thirty-fourth day of the prytany he was denounced before the king; so barely the fifth day had come. From these things it also follows that in what follows we must read: [Greek: ὥστε αἱ συμπάσαι ἡμέραι ἡμέραι ἕξ ἡμέρα ὠφέλιμοι εἴκοσι ὀκτὼ, πλέον ἢ πεντεκαίδεκα τοῦ ἑκάστου τῆς Βασιλέως]. It is an easy slip in numerals, so that the letter nu is written as the numeral thirty.

units.la: Peradtis Liberalium ludis concio cogebatur ad Bacchi aedem, referebaturque de Praetoris circa hoc festum cura, iniuriisque festi tempore factis, de quibus inter partes non erat tranfactum: Legis haec sunt verba:
units.tr: When the Liberalia games were over, an assembly was convened at the temple of Bacchus, and there was a report on the praetor's care regarding this festival, and on the wrongs done during the festival time, about which there had been no settlement between the parties. The words of the law are these:

units.la: ΤΟΥΣ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΣ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΝ ΕΝ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΟΥ ΤΗι ΤΣΤΕΡΑΙΑι ΕΝ ΠΑΝ-ΔΙΟΙΣ, ΕΝ ΔΕ ΤΑΥΤΗΙ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΙΖΕΙΝ ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΙΕΡΩΝ, ΕΠΕΙΤΑ ΤΑΣ ΠΡΟΒΟΛΑΣ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΤΩΣΑΝ ΤΑΣ ΓΕ-ΓΕΝΗΜΕΝΑΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΤΗΣ ΠΟΜΠΗΣ, Η ΤΩΝ ΑΓΩΝΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΔΙΟΝΥ-ΣΙΟΙΣ, ΟΣΑΙ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΚΤΕΤΙΣΜΕΝΑΙ ΩΣΙΝ.
units.tr: [Greek: ΤΟΥΣ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΣ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΝ ΕΝ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΟΥ ΤΗι ΤΣΤΕΡΑΙΑι ΕΝ ΠΑΝΔΙΟΙΣ, ΕΝ ΔΕ ΤΑΥΤΗΙ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΙΖΕΙΝ ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΙΕΡΩΝ, ΕΠΕΙΤΑ ΤΑΣ ΠΡΟΒΟΛΑΣ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΤΩΣΑΝ ΤΑΣ ΓΕΓΕΝΗΜΕΝΑΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΤΗΣ ΠΟΜΠΗΣ, Η ΤΩΝ ΑΓΩΝΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΙΟΙΣ, ΟΣΑΙ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΚΤΕΤΙΣΜΕΝΑΙ ΩΣΙΝ.] The Prytaneis shall hold an assembly in the shrine of Dionysus on the day after the Pandia; at this assembly they shall first deal with sacred matters, then hand over the proposals concerning the procession or the contests at the Dionysia, and whatever wrongs have not been settled.

units.la: Prytaneis concionem in Bacchi cogunto, Pandys, postridie Dionysiorum, & de sacris primum referunto, probole deinde dantor, de iniuriis illatis pompae vel Ludorum Dionysiacorum causa, de quibus transfactum non fuerit.
units.tr: The Prytaneis shall convene the assembly in the shrine of Bacchus on the day after the Pandia, and shall first report on sacred matters; then proposals shall be put forward concerning wrongs done on account of the procession or the Dionysiac games, which have not been settled.

units.la: Refert hanc Legem Demosthenes in Midiana, è cuius verbis constat in Legę legendum esse, ΜΕΤΑ ΠΑΝΔΙΑ, non autem ΕΝ ΠΑΝΔΙΟΙΣ, nam ita habet Demosthenes in sequentibus: ὁ μὲν νόμος ἔστ' ἔστι, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, καὶ τὰς ἑορτὰς ... ἐν αἷς παρασκευάζεσθαι γίγνονται, λέγων, ἀσπὶς ἡνιοχοῦντες, ποιεῖν τῶν Συκιώνιος ... ἐν Διονύσου μὴ τὰ Γαμηλίων. Erant autem Pandia, Iouis, siue potius Lunae festa post Liberalia agitatum, vt docent Vlpianus, Harpocration, alij. Postridie igitur Pandiorum cogebatur concio in Theatro ad Bacchi fanum. Vlpianus: ἐν Διονύσου μὲν τὰ παῖ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀκρόπολις ... Ad populum referebatur, an Archon, ὃς ἀρχηγὸς τὰ Διονύσια, religiosè curasset ea omnia, quae festi erant, atq; ea administraret. Demosthenes: ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ... Vlpianus: ἐξαιτίζεται ὁ Ἀρχων ... Paulò post: καὶ Γεωρίων ... Rursum: ἰδίᾳ ... His peradtis referebant quoque de iis, qui diebus festis illis sibi non temperauerant ab inferendis iniuriis, quod vocat. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. VI. ... Demosthenes: ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ... Ἀρχων ... Vlpianus: ἐξαιτίζεται ὁ Ἀρχων ...
units.tr: Demosthenes quotes this law in the Midiana, and from his words it is clear that in the law we must read [Greek: ΜΕΤΑ ΠΑΝΔΙΑ], not [Greek: ΕΝ ΠΑΝΔΙΟΙΣ], for Demosthenes says the following: [Greek: ὁ μὲν νόμος ἔστ' ἔστι, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, καὶ τὰς ἑορτὰς ... ἐν αἷς παρασκευάζεσθαι γίγνονται, λέγων, ἀσπὶς ἡνιοχοῦντες, ποιεῖν τῶν Συκιώνιος ... ἐν Διονύσου μὴ τὰ Γαμηλίων]. The Pandia were a festival of Jupiter, or rather of the Moon, celebrated after the Liberalia, as Ulpian, Harpocration and others teach. So the assembly was convened on the day after the Pandia, in the theatre at the shrine of Bacchus. Ulpian: [Greek: ἐν Διονύσου μὲν τὰ παῖ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀκρόπολις ...]. It was referred to the people whether the archon, who was the leader of the Dionysia, had carefully attended to all that belonged to the festival and was administering it. Demosthenes: [Greek: ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ...]. Ulpian: [Greek: ἐξαιτίζεται ὁ Ἀρχων ...]. Shortly after: [Greek: καὶ Γεωρίων ...]. Again: [Greek: ἰδίᾳ ...]. When these things were done, they also reported on those who had not restrained themselves during those festival days from inflicting wrongs, as it is called. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter VI. ... Demosthenes: [Greek: ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ...] [Greek: Ἀρχων ...]. Ulpian: [Greek: ἐξαιτίζεται ὁ Ἀρχων ...].

units.la: Non licebat festis Liberalium diebus cuiquam manum iniicere, vt hac Lege cautum est.
units.tr: It was not lawful on the festival days of the Liberalia to lay hands on anyone, as this law provides.

units.la: Μηδεὶς τοῖς Διονυσίοις ἐπιχειρείτω. Nemini diebus Liberalium festis manum iniicito.
units.tr: Let no one make an attack during the Dionysia [Μηδεὶς τοῖς Διονυσίοις ἐπιχειρείτω]. Let no one lay hands on anyone on the festival days of the Liberalia.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ Μ... doceatque scriptam esse post Legem sirempsem de Mysteriis: [illegible, ~40 letters: Greek, opening words of a Greek quotation]. Vlpianus: [illegible, ~30 letters: Greek]
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in his speech (the passage is illegible in the scan), and he shows that it was enacted after the law of Sirempses concerning the Mysteries: [illegible Greek quotation]. Ulpian: [illegible Greek quotation].

units.la: Atheniensibus eximie cultus est Apollo, eique passim tota urbe ædes sacræ constitutæ,& festa in eius honorem instituta: sed Deliorum maxime toto tempore sacris operata Urbs noluit,quenquam capitis damnatum, dum Delum eunt redeuntque Theori, pœnas [?]lare:
units.tr: The Athenians paid especial honour to Apollo, and shrines were set up for him throughout the whole city, with festivals instituted in his honour. But the city, during the whole time when the Theori were engaged in the sacred rites of Delos, would not allow anyone condemned to death to be put to punishment while they were going to Delos and returning.

units.la: [illegible, ~45 letters: Greek, Δημοσία ... ] | Deliorum festos dies,dum Delum itur,re-ditur,damnatorum supplicijs ne funestato.
units.tr: [illegible Greek quotation, beginning Δημοσία ...] Let the festival days of Delos not be defiled by the punishment of the condemned, while the journey to Delos and back is being made.

units.la: Meminerunt huius Legis Xenophon ac Plato, qui obseruant Socratem triginta dies in carcere & in expectatione mortis exegisse post damnationem, quia Delia festa interuenerunt. Verba Xenophontis sunt [illegible, ~60 letters: Greek]. Lib.IV. [illegible, ~50 letters: Greek]. Plato Phaedone: [illegible, ~120 letters: Greek].
units.tr: Xenophon and Plato also mention this law. They observe that Socrates, after his condemnation, spent thirty days in prison and awaiting death, because the Delia festival fell in that time. The words of Xenophon are [illegible Greek quotation], in Book IV [illegible Greek quotation]. Plato, in the Phaedo: [illegible Greek quotation].

units.la: Quod hic obseruant Atheniensis, ne funestent damnatorum pœnis Deliorum dies festos atque lætos, honōri[?] Apollinis id datũ, quem non tantum Græci,sed etiam ultimarum terrarum homines in Græcia coluerunt,primitiasque obtulerunt, quod vel Abaridis testatur historia, & Tyriorum exemplum probat apud Euripidem Phœnissis,cuius versus è persona Chori merentur hic expendi, multum enim conferent ad præferendã lucem iis quæ de Tyriorum coloniis in Africa vicinisque Insulis dicuntur: [illegible, ~25 letters: Greek] (ἀχροδίνια Λεξία Φοινίσσας ἀπὸ κάσσω, Φοίβα δούλα μηδ[?]ε[?]ς, ἵ[?] ... [illegible, ~20 letters: Greek] Γαριασοῦ κατασιδοῦ[?]ν) Ἰόνιοι ... [illegible, ~15 letters: Greek] ἀλσὰς πλεύσασα, ἀξιρρύτων γὰρ ἀχαρίστων πεδίων Σικελίας, Ζεφύρου πνοαῖς ἱππεύσομαι ἐν θεσμῷ κόμισον χεράδμα.
units.tr: The Athenians observed this so that the festal and joyful days of Delos should not be defiled by the punishment of the condemned. This was granted in honour of Apollo, whom not only the Greeks but also the peoples of the farthest lands worshipped in Greece, and to whom they offered first-fruits. The history of Abaris bears witness to this, and the example of the Tyrians in Euripides' Phoenissae proves it. The verses of that play, spoken by the Chorus, deserve to be weighed here, for they will contribute much to shedding light on what is said of the Tyrian colonies in Africa and the neighbouring islands: [illegible Greek] (the first-fruits ... Phoenician women, sent from afar ... Phoebus' slaves ... Ionian ... sailed through the salt sea, for across the fertile plains of Sicily, with the breezes of Zephyrus, I shall ride in the course, bringing an offering.)

units.la: Male ista veteres Græci Magistri interpretantur de Tyro; quasi Tyrus ab Agenoris nepotibus vi fuerit capta, & delecta puellarum, quæ in seruitutem redactæ fuerant, manus Apollini Delphico consecrata: sed Tyrus semper fuit in potestate Regum Phœniciæ totius tractus Metropolis : Adde quod huic sententiæ plane aduersantur verba Chori, Phœnissas Tyro, si Dis.placet, Bœotiam petentes Siciliam præteruehi, vt vt istud itineris tempestatibus tri-buas: nam Tyro Bœotiam nauigantes, nunquam in Siciliam aget tempestas Zephyro flante: Zephyrus autem flabat, vt testatur Chorus, isque non adeo validus, vt tempestatem excitaret, si Euripidi credimus,
units.tr: The ancient Greek teachers wrongly interpret these verses as referring to Tyre, as if Tyre had been taken by force by the descendants of Agenor, and the chosen maidens, reduced to slavery, had been consecrated to the Delphic Apollo. But Tyre was always under the power of the kings of Phoenicia, the metropolis of the whole region. Add that the words of the Chorus plainly contradict this view: the Phoenician women, travelling to Boeotia, if it please the gods, sail past Sicily. Attribute this to the storms of the journey, if you like; but ships sailing from Tyre to Boeotia would never be driven to Sicily when Zephyrus is blowing. Zephyrus, however, was blowing, as the Chorus testifies, and it was not so strong as to raise a storm, if we believe Euripides.

units.la: Non est tempestas, sed potius prosper ventus atque secundus. Quare aliud investigandum est. Diuersè refertur tempus conditæ Carthaginis propter diuersos conditores: Phœnicum primi, qui in illo Africæ tractu sedes suas posuerunt, ij sunt, qui Cananitide pulsi sunt à Iosua, vt à Procopio Vandalicor. Lib. II. refertur, & nos alibi diximus. Neque tantum Africani insederunt, sed etiam progressu temporis, negotiandi caussa, Insulas, quæ interiacent inter Africam & Siciliam, adeoque etiam nonnullam Siciliæ partem, vt scribit Thucydides Lib. VI. inter ceteras Insulas recenset Diodorus Siculus Lib. V. Melitam itemque Gaulum: itaque Anna Carthagine pulsa ad Melites insulæ Regè hospitio confisa vetusto se recipit apud Ouidium Lib. III. Fastorum. Insecutis deinde temporibus etiam alij coloni à Tyriis eodem deducti sunt, quâ sæpissime autem Carthaginem: nam & ante captum Ilium, & post eiusdem excidium, Carthaginem conditam à Tyriis fuisse produnt veteres memoriæ: Est igitur apud Euripidem, [illegible, ~12 letters] nomine, intelligenda non Tyrus, sed aliquâ illarum Insularum, quæ inter Africam & Siciliam sitæ sunt: [illegible, ~10 letters] autè dicitur, non quod sit in Phœnicia, sed quia Phœnicibus habitabatur coloni, quemadmodum apud Latinum Poëtam Carthaginis arces Tyriæ dicuntur, atque ipsa Carthago Tyria vrbs, quia scilicet Tyrij tenuere Coloni. Melitam igitur aut Gaulum designat Poëta, in quas colonias deduxerant Phœnices [illegible, ~14 letters] vt loquuntur Thucydides & Diodorus, etiam longè ante Troiana tempora. Sed videntur boni isti coloni Tyrios, quorum erant [illegible, ~10 letters] suis noluisse consistere littoribus, & portubus prohibuisse; itaque Tyrij classe instructa illos adorti expugnarunt, primitiasque prædæ Apollini Delphico consecrarunt:
units.tr: It was not a storm, but rather a favourable and fair wind. Therefore something else must be sought. The time of the founding of Carthage is reported differently because of the different founders. The first Phoenicians who settled in that part of Africa were those who were driven out of Canaan by Joshua, as is reported by Procopius, Vandalic. Wars Book II, and as we have said elsewhere. Nor did only Africans settle there; but also, as time went on, for the sake of trade, they occupied the islands lying between Africa and Sicily, and indeed some part of Sicily, as Thucydides writes in Book VI. Diodorus Siculus in Book V counts among the other islands Melita and Gaulus. Thus Anna, driven out of Carthage, trusted in the hospitality of the ancient king of the island of Melita and took refuge there, as Ovid tells in Book III of the Fasti. In later times other colonists were also led there from Tyre, and most often to Carthage; for ancient records report that Carthage was founded by the Tyrians both before the capture of Troy and after its destruction. Therefore in Euripides the name [illegible] must be understood not as Tyre but as one of those islands which lie between Africa and Sicily. [Illegible word] is said not because it lies in Phoenicia but because it was inhabited by Phoenician colonists, just as in the Latin poet the citadels of Carthage are called "Tyrian," and Carthage itself "the Tyrian city," because, of course, "Tyrians held its colonists." So the poet means Melita or Gaulus, into which the Phoenicians had led colonies [illegible], as Thucydides and Diodorus say, even long before the Trojan times. But these good colonists seem to have refused to let the Tyrians, to whom they belonged [illegible], settle on their shores, and to have barred them from their harbours. So the Tyrians, with a fleet equipped, attacked them, took them by storm, and consecrated the first-fruits of the spoil to the Delphic Apollo.

[illegible, ~5 letters] autem apud Euripidem significat vendo. Tempus conuenit, quo refert Appianus Phœnices in Africam, adde vicinas Insulas, nouos deduxisse colonos, cum priores illi scilicet deseciuissent: [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters]. Bellum autem istud Thebanū prius est Ilij excidio annis quinquaginta. Quare vnius anni prochronismus est apud Eusebium, cuius hæc est nota ad numerum IↄCCLXXXIIII. Septem, qui aduersus Thebas pugnauerunt: οἱ ἑπτὰ ἐπὶ Θήβας [?]. Numero enim DCCLXXXV. allignandum est hoc bellū. Quod vero diximus intelligi Insulam, si forte Meliten, quae inter Africam & Siciliam interiacet, facile probare est ex itinere: Siciliam quippe praeteruehuntur, nō tempestate acti, sed secundo vento, quem Zephyrum esse dicit Euripides, impellente:
units.tr: [Largely illegible passage.] ... The word used by Euripides means "selling." The time agrees with the period in which Appian reports that the Phoenicians led new colonists into Africa and the neighbouring islands, once their earlier colonists had of course revolted. But that Theban war is fifty years earlier than the fall of Troy. So there is a one-year anachronism in Eusebius, whose note at the number 1284 reads: "Seven who fought against Thebes" [οἱ ἑπτὰ ἐπὶ Θήβας]. For this war should be assigned to the number 1285. But that we said the island should be understood as perhaps Melita, which lies between Africa and Sicily, is easy to prove from the route: they sailed past Sicily, not driven by a storm but by a favourable wind, which Euripides says was Zephyrus.

units.la: Soluisse igitur ex Insula constat, è qua in Boeotiam nauigantes necesse fuerit Siciliam praeteruehi, Zephyrumque nauigantibus fuisse ventum secundū: Ergo ex Insula aliqua soluerunt, quae erat in mari Africo inter Africam & Siciliam sita, è qua in Boeotiam nauigantes Siciliam necesse erat praeteruehi, vētusque secundus est Zephyrus. Quare suspicio nostra est Phoeniciam hac Insulam fuisse Meliten, è qua soluerunt. Sed in Atticam reuertamur: Honori Apollinis id datum esse diximus, ne Deliorum dies vltimo damnatorum suppliciō polluerentur: nam non omnibus diebus festis id obseruatū: nam quando Phocion veneno sublatus est ex plebiscito dies erat festus. Plutarch. Phocion: ὣ δ᾽ ἡμέρα μὲν ὡς Μουνυχιῶνος ἑκάτη [?] ἐπὶ ἡμέρα ἀπὸ [?] ἐκ τῆς πόλεως [?], μετὰ δ᾽ ἐκ τοῦ ἡμέρα [?] ἐκ τῶν ὡς ἐκ [?]. Neque certē poenis conuenit cum diei festi ac laeti religione: itaque Romani hac in parte religiosores exemplo edocti: nam anno, quo Coriolanus in exilium pulsus est, Ludi Magni Romae hac de causa instaurati sunt. Mane ferunt quidam paterfamiliae nondū commissō spectaculo sub furca cæsum medio egerat Circo. capti inde Ludi, velut ea res nihil ad religionem pertinuisset, haud ita multo post, T. Latinio de plebe homini somnium fuit. Visus Iupiter dicere, sibi Ludis praesulatorem displicuisse, nisi magnifice instaurarentur hi Ludi, periculum Vrbi fore. iret, ea Consulibus nunciaret: vt est apud Liuium Lib. II.Itaque diebus feriatis, nedum festiv, dabatur vocatio ab omnibus forensibus negotiis. Diuus Traianus, inquit Vlpianus Lib. VII. de Officio Proconsulis: Minucio Natali rescripsit, ferias à forensibus tantum negotiis dare vocationem: eo autem, quae ad disciplinam militarem pertinent, etiam feriatis diebus peragenda: inter quae custodiarum quoque cognitionem esse. Lege IX. D. de Feriis. Sed non possum ire in sententiam viri longe praestantissimi, qui custodiarum interpretatur eorum, qui in custodia & carcere sunt, vt & latronum Lib. X. C. eod. Nam siue illi sint milites, qui sub custodia vel in carcere sint, siue quicumque alij, non poterat quaestio eorum haberi, ex hoc quidem Diui Traiani Rescripto, cū feriae ab omnibus forensibus negotiis dent vacationem, cognitio autem eorū, qui sub custodia vel in carcere sunt, nō poterit non censeri in negotiis forensibus; sola illa excipiuntur, quae ad disciplinam militarem pertinent, disciplinae autem militaris erat haec custodiarum cognitio. Igitur custodiae hic sunt, cum excubiae, cum vigiliae: quas interdum circumire Tribunum vel eum qui exercitui praeest, disciplinæ esse militaris docet Macer Leg. XII. D. de Re militari. Quemadmodum autem anxie seruatæ sunt hæ stationes custodiarum; ita etiam accurate de illis quæstio habita, si deruissent, itaque feriatis diebus earum quæstionem haberi rescripto hoc cauit Diuus Traianus, nam istud omissum nocuisset. Quanquam postea Honorius & Theodosius Imperatores in Constitutione ad Anthemium Præfectum Prætorio quæstionem haberi de latronibus, etiam per tormenta, præceperunt, nullo, ne sanctissimo quidem, die festo excepto. Prouinciarum Præsides moneantur, vt in quæstionibus latronum, & maxime Isaurorum, nullum quadragesimæ tempus, nec venerabilem Paschæ diem exsistiment excipiendum: ne differatur sceleratorum proditio consiliorum, quæ per latronum tormenta quærenda est: cum facillime & in hoc summi numinis spectetur venia, per quod multorum salus & incolumitas procuratur. Dat. V. Kal. Mart. Basso & Philippo Conss. Leg. X. C. de Ferijs. Descripta est hæc Lex è Codice Theodosiano, estque vltima tituli de Quæstionibus. Sed data legitur Constantinopoli V. Kal. May, Basso & Philippo Coss. Atqui vel subscriptio hæc, vel Constitutionis inscriptio est corrupta: vt & Legis IV. Cod. Theod. de Equorum conlatione, quæ scripta dicitur ab Honorio & Theodosio AA. ad Herculium Præfectum Prætorio Illyrici, Dat. III. Id. April. Consp. Bass. & Philippo Coss.
units.tr: It is therefore established that they set sail from an island, from which, to sail to Boeotia, they had necessarily to pass Sicily, and that the wind for those sailing was a favourable Zephyrus. So they set out from some island lying in the African sea between Africa and Sicily, from which those sailing to Boeotia had to pass Sicily, and the wind was a favourable Zephyrus. Hence our suspicion is that this island in Phoenicia was Melita, from which they set sail. But let us return to Attica. We have said that this honour was given to Apollo, so that the days of Delos should not be polluted by the final punishment of the condemned. For this was not observed on all festival days: when Phocion was put to death by poison, by a decree of the people, the day was a festival. [Plutarch, Phocion: Greek quotation, garbled.] Nor do punishments certainly agree with the religious observance of a festive and joyful day. So the Romans, taught by this example, were more scrupulous in this matter: in the year when Coriolanus was driven into exile, the Great Games were restored at Rome for this reason. Some say a householder, early in the morning, before the spectacle had begun, had a man beaten under the yoke in the middle of the Circus. Thereupon the Games were halted, as if the matter had had nothing to do with religion; but not long afterwards a dream came to Titus Latinius, a man of the plebs. He seemed to see Jupiter saying that the leader of the Games had displeased him, and that unless these Games were restored magnificently, there would be danger to the City. He was to go and tell the consuls this; as is found in Livy, Book II. Therefore on holidays, let alone festival days, a summons was not given in any public business. "The Divine Trajan," says Ulpian in Book VII of On the Duty of the Proconsul, "in a rescript to Minucius Natalis, wrote that holidays give exemption only from public legal business, but that matters which pertain to military discipline must be transacted even on holidays; and among these is the hearing of guards." See law IX, D. de Feriis. But I cannot agree with the view of a very distinguished man, who interprets "guards" as those who are in custody and in prison, as also in the law of brigands, Book X, C. of the same title. For whether they are soldiers held under guard or in prison, or anyone else, their case could not be heard on the basis of this rescript of the Divine Trajan, since holidays give exemption from all public business, while the hearing of those held under guard or in prison cannot but be counted as public business. Only those matters are excepted which pertain to military discipline; and the hearing of guards was a matter of military discipline. Therefore "guards" here means sentries and watches, which, as Macer shows in Law XII, D. de Re militari, a tribune or the commander of the army may sometimes go round to inspect, as a matter of military discipline. Just as these guard-posts were kept with anxious care, so too inquiry was made into them with equal precision, if they had been neglected; and so the Divine Trajan provided by this rescript that such inquiries be held on holidays, for that omission would have done harm. Yet afterwards the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in a constitution addressed to Anthemius the Praetorian Prefect, ordered that inquiries into brigands be held, even under torture, with no exception even for the most sacred festival day: "Let the governors of the provinces be advised that in the inquiries into brigands, and especially the Isaurians, they should not regard any season of Lent, nor the venerable day of Easter, as to be excluded; lest the betrayal of the criminals' plans, which is to be sought through the torture of brigands, be delayed; since pardon is most easily obtained from the supreme Divinity in this too, through which the safety and well-being of many is secured. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Bassus and Philip." Law X, C. de Feriis. This law was copied from the Theodosian Code, and is the last of the title On Inquiries. But it is read as given at Constantinople on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Bassus and Philip. Yet either this subscription or the inscription of the constitution is corrupt, as also in Law IV of the Theodosian Code, On the Collection of Horses, which is said to have been written by Honorius and Theodosius Augusti to Herculius, Praetorian Prefect of Illyricum, "Given on the third day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Bassus and Philip."

units.la: Nam Arcadius mortuus est Kalendis Maij huius anni, vt auctor est Socrates Historia VI. Καταλιπὼν δ' ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἀρκάδιος τὸν μὲν Θεοδόσιον ἐκπεπτωκότα τυχόντα, ἐπελθὼν δὲ εἰς Ἰσαυρίαν Βάσσου καὶ Φιλίππου, τῇ αὐτῇ τῆς Μαΐου μηνὸς, τῷ δὲ ἐν τῷ 'Ολυμπιάδος ἐν τῷ 'Ἰωάννου ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ ἔδομ' ἐν Ὀλυμπιά- δος. Quanquam etiam Theophanes confert, & recte meo quidem animo, in diem vndecimum Kalendas Septembris huius anni. Nec dissentit admodum Socrates, vt prima fronte videri posset: nam his quæ iam descripsimus ista subijcit: [?]συμβασιλέως δὲ τῷ πατρὶ Θεοδοσίῳ, ἐπὶ δικαιοσύνῃ. μὴ ὃ τῷ τελευτῶντι τῆς πατρίδος, ἐπὶ δικαιοσύνῃ [?]. Sed postrema ista, αὐτάρ ἡ βίβλος χρόνον ἐπὶ ἐξ, μηνὶ ἐξ, corrupta sunt indubie: nam Liber hic complectitur res gestas ab obitu Theodosij ad mortem Arcadij: primaque hæc sunt capitis primi verba: τῆς δὲ βασιλείας Θεοδοσίου πελευτήσαντος, ἐν Ἰσαυρίᾳ Ολυμπιάδος καὶ Πεδίνου τῆς ἐκκλησίας τῆς Ἰανουαρίου μηνός, &c. Quare referendum est extremo hoc Libro: αὐτάρ ἡ βίβλος χρόνον ἐπὶ πεντεκαιδέκα, μηνὶ ἐξ. Quod vero hic additur de sex mensibus supra annos tredecim, indicat conferendam esse mortem Arcadij in diem vndecimum Kalendas Septembris: nam à die decimoseptimo Ianuarii, quo Theodosius obiit, ad vicesimum secundum Augusti, qui de natali est Arcadii, septem sunt menses, & qui excurrunt dies: itaque reponendum est μηνὶ ἑπτά, nam facile mutarunt hic literæ numerales ς'. ἡ ζ'. Quare etiam Arcadio adscribit Socrates annos quatuordecim post excessum Theodosii, quia supra annos tredecim mensibus septem, diebus quinque imperauerat. Sed his vi letur obstare, quod intra annum secundum Olympiadis ducentesimæ nonagesimæ septimæ fato functum esse Arcadium tradat Socrates: τῷ δ' ὧν ἐν τῷ ἐπὶ ἐνδ... Ολυμπιάδος. Ego vero nullus dubito annos Olympicos Socrati cepisse à Septembri, siue autumno. Nam Valentis cædem confert in annum vertentem quartum Olympiadis ducentesimae octagesimae nonae, diemque nonum Augusti. Verba eius sunt Lib. IV. extremo. [illegible, ~60 letters] Annus hic quartus Olympiadis est affectus: eodemque anno Iuliano à diebus autumnalibus coepit annus primus Olympiadis ducentesimae nonagesimae, alioqui Kalendis Maii anni Christi Dionysiani quadringentesimi octaui, Basso & Philippo Coss. non verteret annus secundus Olympiadis ducentesimae nonagesimae septimae. Dicendum igitur est, his disputatis, in inscriptione harum Legum reponendum esse Arcadij nomen, quod exciderat.
units.tr: For Arcadius died on the Kalends of May of this year, as Socrates reports in Book VI of his History: "The emperor Arcadius left behind Theodosius, who had been exiled and happened to be ... and went into Isauria, in the consulship of Bassus and Philip, in the month of May [Καταλιπὼν δ' ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἀρκάδιος τὸν μὲν Θεοδόσιον ἐκπεπτωκότα τυχόντα, ἐπελθὼν δὲ εἰς Ἰσαυρίαν Βάσσου καὶ Φιλίππου, τῇ αὐτῇ τῆς Μαΐου μηνὸς]." Yet Theophanes also places it, and in my view rightly, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September of this year. Nor does Socrates really disagree with him, although it might seem so at first sight. For after the passages just quoted he adds: "[...] as co-emperor with his father Theodosius, [...] for justice's sake [...]." But the final words, "[...] but the book covers a period of six years, μηνὶ ἑπτά [six months, ...]", are undoubtedly corrupt. For this Book embraces the events from the death of Theodosius to the death of Arcadius, and the first words of the first chapter are these: "After the death of Theodosius, in the second year of the Olympiad and in the month of January [...]." Therefore the passage at the end of this Book should be read as "a period of fifteen years, six months." As for what is added here about six months beyond thirteen years, it shows that the death of Arcadius must be placed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September. For from the seventeenth day of January, when Theodosius died, to the twenty-second of August, the anniversary of Arcadius's birth, there are seven months and some days over. So μηνὶ ἑπτά [seven months] should be restored, since the numeral letters ς' and ζ' were easily confused here. This is also why Socrates assigns Arcadius fourteen years after the departure of Theodosius, since he had ruled for thirteen years, seven months and five days. But this seems to be contradicted by Socrates' statement that Arcadius died within the second year of the two hundred and ninety-seventh Olympiad: "[...] in the year of the Olympiad [...]." I, however, have no doubt that Socrates began his Olympic years from September, or autumn. For he places the murder of Valens in the fourth year of the two hundred and eighty-ninth Olympiad, on the ninth day of August. His words are at the end of Book IV: "[illegible in the scan]." This fourth year of the Olympiad had ended, and in the same year, by the Julian reckoning, the first year of the two hundred and ninetieth Olympiad began from the autumnal days. Otherwise, if the Kalends of May of the year of Christ 408 in the consulship of Bassus and Philip did not fall in the second year of the two hundred and ninety-seventh Olympiad, it would not be so. It must therefore be concluded, after this discussion, that the name of Arcadius, which had dropped out, should be restored in the inscription of these Laws.

units.la: Mense Posideone celebrabatur quoque Cereri atque Baccho festum, cui Aloa nomen fecerunt: coque die Lege non licebat victimam mactare.
units.tr: In the month of Posideon there was also a festival celebrated for Ceres and Bacchus, which they called Aloa, and on that day it was not lawful by law to slaughter a victim.

units.la: Ἀλοῖς ἱερὰ μὴ θύειν. Alois victimam ne mactato.
units.tr: On the Aloa, do not sacrifice victims [Ἀλοῖς ἱερὰ μὴ θύειν]. Do not slaughter a victim at the Aloa.

units.la: Non semel instituta fuisse atque instaurata Olympica ludicra in veterum Commentariis legimus, sed ij, quorum potior ratio habenda videtur, sunt Pelops, Hercules, atque Iphitus; Ac quidem quod ad Pelopem attinet, Olympicum agonem ab eo institutum fuisse numero Eusebiano septingentesimo primo, id est, anno Periodi Iulianae termillesimo[?] tercentesimo nonagesimo octauo, Cyclo Solis decimo, facile nobis probat Ill. Scaliger auctoritate codicis Eusebiani V. A. Pauli Petauij Senatoris Parisiensis, nec negant alij, vt qui sciant in duplici membranaceo codice Eusebiani Chronici sane vetustissimo ista legi ad numerum Eusebianum IOCCI[?]. Pelops Peloponnesijs regnauit, Olympijs quoque praefuit. Eo anno Nouilunium commissum fuit die nono Iulij (nam Graeci dies numerant ab Occaso Sole) ac proinde Plenilunium fuit die vicesimo tertio. units.tr: We read in the older commentaries that the Olympic games were not instituted only once, but were established and restored several times. Those to whom the stronger claim seems to belong are Pelops, Hercules and Iphitus. As for Pelops, that he founded the Olympic contest in the Eusebian number 701, that is, in the year 3998 of the Julian Period, in the tenth Cycle of the Sun, is easily shown by the authority of the great Scaliger, and by the codex of Eusebius which belonged to A. Paulus Petavius, a Senator of Paris. Others too do not deny it, since they know that in a two-column parchment codex of Eusebius's Chronicle, certainly very ancient, these words are read against the Eusebian number: "Pelops reigned over the Peloponnesians and also presided over the Olympic games." In that year the new moon fell on the ninth day of July (for the Greeks reckon days from sunset), and so the full moon fell on the twenty-third day. [Here follows a table of the years of the Period, days, hours, new moons and full moons, in July, which is too corrupt in the scan to be reliably reproduced.]

units.la: Quod vero hinc concludendum putat maximus Heros Olympicum Nouilunium nunquam promotum fuisse citra nonum Iulij diem, cum pridie statutum esset solstitium, nobis non probat, tum quod aetate Pelopis solstitium nondum committebatur die octauo Iulij, sed id obseruatum est aetate Iphiti, qui Olympia instaurauit, cum etiam quia primo Elidensium mensi, vt & Atheniensium Hecatombæoni adscribuntur [illegible, ~6 letters], & certe primum Nouilunium Iphiti Olympicum historicum, quod in anno Periodi Iulianæ termillesimum nongentesimum tricesimum octauum cadit, commissum est ipso solstitij die, vt infra, Deo dante, sumus[?] dicturi, hoc est, die octauo Iulij. Sed de ludicro Olympico ab Hercule instaurato maior oritur difficultas: nam Scaliger [illegible, ~5 letters] ad numerum Eusebianum octingentesimum quintumdecimum adscribit, id est, ad annum Periodi Iulianæ termillesimum quingentesimum duodecimum: cui nullus codex adstipulatur. Nu-perus scriptor conijcit in annum Periodi Iulianæ termillesimum quadringentesimum nonagesimum sextum. Ego vero ibo potius in sententiam eorum, qui adsignant anno Periodi Iulianæ termillesimo quingentesimo septimo, siue numero Eusebiano octingentesimo decimo, vt habet editio Pontacii ad hunc numerum IↃCCCCX[?]. Hercules agonem Olympicum constituit: à quo vsque ad primam Olympiadem supputantur anni quadringenti triginta. Eo anno Nouilunium Olympicum commissum est quarto Iulij die: Plenilunium vero die de-cimonono ineunte, vt Græci suos numerant dies. IVL. | DIES. HOR. I II | NOVILVNIVM. DIES HOR. units.tr: As for what the greatest hero concludes from this, that the Olympic new moon was never moved later than the ninth day of July, since the solstice had been fixed for the day before, this does not convince me. Partly because in the age of Pelops the solstice was not yet set on the eighth day of July, but this was observed in the age of Iphitus, who restored the Olympic games; and partly because the first Olympic new moon, which is historically recorded and falls in the year 1938 of the Julian Period, was held on the very day of the solstice, as I shall show below, God willing, namely on the eighth day of July. But a greater difficulty arises concerning the Olympic games restored by Hercules. For Scaliger assigns them to the Eusebian number 815, that is, to the year 1512 of the Julian Period, and no codex supports him. A recent writer conjectures the year 1496 of the Julian Period. I, however, prefer to follow those who assign it to the year 1507 of the Julian Period, or the Eusebian number 810, as the edition of Pontacus has it at this number. "Hercules established the Olympic contest, from which to the first Olympiad four hundred and thirty years are counted." In that year the Olympic new moon was held on the fourth day of July, and the full moon on the nineteenth day, beginning as the Greeks count their days. [Here follows a further table of days and hours for July, also too corrupt to reproduce reliably.]

units.la: Quod huic anno Olympicum agonem ab Hercule instauratum adscribamus, facit non tantum Eusebius, sed etiam Seneca Agamemnone, & isà[?] quo accepit. Nam eo, quo occisus est Agamemnon, anno fingitur Strophius Pyladis pater coronam ex Olympico agone reportasse, paucisante quam Agamemnonem reducem salutatum veniret diebus:
units.tr: That we assign the Olympic contest restored by Hercules to this year is supported not only by Eusebius, but also by Seneca in his Agamemnon, and by the year in which he received it. For in the year in which Agamemnon was killed, Strophius, the father of Pylades, is imagined to have brought back a crown from the Olympic contest, a few days before Agamemnon returned home and was greeted:

units.la: Phocide relicta Strophius, Elea inclytus Palma reuertor. causa ueniendi fuit, Gratari amico, cuius impulsum manu Cecidit decenni Marte concussum Ilium.
units.tr: Strophius, having left Phocis, returns renowned with the Elean palm. The reason for my coming was to visit my friend Gratarus, by whose hand Ilium fell, shaken by a ten-year war.

units.la: & paullo post:
units.tr: And a little later:

units.la: Cape hoc decorum ludicri certaminis Infigne frontis. læua victricem tenens Frondem, virenti protegat ramo caput. Et ista, donum palma Pisæi Iouis, Velamen eadem præstet atque omen tibi.
units.tr: Take this, the becoming badge of the contest's glory, holding the victor's wreath in your left hand; let the green branch shield your head. And may this palm, the gift of Pisaean Jove, grant you the same covering and the same omen.

units.la: Agamemnon autem occisus est eodem anno Iuliano, quo captum est Ilium, è Senecæ quidem sententia: nempe anno Periodi Iulianæ termillesimo quin-gentesimo tricesimo primo: nam decem tantum annos abfuit, vndecimo ineunte domum rediit, ita Clytemnestra ad Eurybatem·
units.tr: Agamemnon was killed in the same Julian year in which Ilium was taken, according to Seneca's view, namely in the year 1531 of the Julian Period. For he was absent only ten years, and returned home at the beginning of the eleventh. So Clytemnestra says to Eurybates:

units.la: Felix ad aures nuncius venit meas, Vbinam petitus per decem coniux mihi Annos moratur? pelagus an terras premit?
units.tr: Happy news came to my ears: where is my husband, sought for ten years, delayed? Does the sea or the land hold him?

units.la: Adde quod narrat Eurybates Græcos statim atque prœda diuisa est, naues conscendisse in patriam reuersuros, sed fœda tempestate coorta, huc illuc classis acta dispersaque est, Agamemnone cum sociis ad Caphareum Eubœæ pœne in scopulos impacto & allisô[?], unde tandem in patriam appulit:
units.tr: Add that Eurybates relates how the Greeks, as soon as the booty was divided, boarded their ships to return to their homeland. But a foul storm arose, and the fleet was driven hither and thither and scattered, so that Agamemnon with his companions was almost dashed against the rocks at Caphareus in Euboea, and from there at last he made it home.

units.la: Vt Pergamum Dorica cecidit face, Diuisa præda est, maria properantes petunt. * * * * Omnisque nimium longa properanti mora est. * * * *
units.tr: As Pergamum fell to the Dorian torch, the spoils were divided, and they hastened to the seas. * * * * And every delay seems too long to one who is hurrying. * * * *

units.la: Iam littus omne tegitur, & campi latent, Et dubia parent montis Idæi iuga. Et iam, quod unum pernicax acies videt, Iliacus atra fumus apparet nota. Iam lassa Titan colla releuabat iugo, In astra iam lux prona, iam præceps dies, Exigua nubes sordido crescens globo, Nitidum cadentis inquinat Phœbi iubar. Suspecta varius occidens fecit freta. Nox prima cælum sparserat stellis, iacent Deserta vento vela, tum murmur graue Maiora minitans collibus summis cadit, Tractúque longo littus ac petræ gemunt. Agitata ventis unda venturis tumet. Cum Luna subito conditur, stellæ latent, In astra pontus tollitur, cælum perit. * * * * * * * *
units.tr: Now every shore is covered, and the plains are hidden, and the ridges of Mount Ida prepare their uncertain shapes. And now the swift eye of the army sees the smoke of Troy appear as a black mark. Now Titan, weary, was lifting his neck from the yoke; now the light sinks toward the stars, now the day is rushing headlong. A small cloud, growing into a dirty ball, stains the bright beam of the setting Phoebus. The changeable west made the seas suspicious. The first night had strewn the sky with stars; the sails hang idle in the wind. Then a deep murmur falls on the highest hills, threatening greater things, and the shore and the rocks groan with a long drag. The water, stirred by winds that are coming, swells. Suddenly the moon is hidden, the stars are gone, the sea is lifted to the stars, and the sky perishes. * * * * * * * *

units.la: Nos alia maior naufragos pestis vocat. Est humilis unda, scrupeis mendax vadis, Vbi saxa rapidis clausa vorticibus tegit Fallax Caphareus. * * *
units.tr: Another, greater plague calls us, shipwrecked. There is a low wave, deceptive over rocky shallows, where the treacherous Caphareus hides rocks shut in by swift whirlpools. * * *

units.la: Hanc arcem occupat Palamedis ille genitor, & clarum manu Lumen nefanda vertice è summo efferens, In saxa ducit perfida classem face. * * *
units.tr: That height is seized by the father of Palamedes, and, holding a bright light in his unspeakable hand at the top, he leads the fleet, treacherously, onto the rocks with his torch. * * *

units.la: Iam timent terram rates, Voluuntque maria, cedit in luctum furor. Postquam litatum est, Phœbus in lucem redit, Et damna noctis tristis ostendit dies.
units.tr: Now the ships fear the land, and the seas roll; their rage gives way to mourning. After the sacrifice was made, Phoebus returned to the light, and the sad day shows the losses of the night.

units.la: Anid[?] factum sit commode, & ex vero, non disputo, quanquam longe prudentius Seneca, quam Æschylus, qui eodem die euersum Ilium, & reducem Agamemnonem præstat: nam quo facem die vidisse accensam refert speculator ad Clytæmnestram:
units.tr: Whether it happened conveniently and truly, I do not dispute, although Seneca is far more prudent than Aeschylus, who has Troy overthrown and Agamemnon returned on the same day. For the watchman reports seeing the torch lit on the day he sends word to Clytemnestra:

units.la: Καὶ νῦν φυλάσσω λαμπάδος ὁ σύμβολον, Αὐχῶ[?] πυρὸς, φέρουσά σε ἐξίας[?] φάτιν, Ἀλώσιμόν τε βάξιν.
units.tr: And now I keep watch, the sign of the lamp, the fire's signal, bringing word of the capture and the news that the city has fallen. [Καὶ νῦν φυλάσσω λαμπάδος ὁ σύμβολον, Αὐχῶ πυρὸς, φέρουσά σε ἐξίας φάτιν, Ἀλώσιμόν τε βάξιν.]

units.la: Ὦ χαῖρε λαμπτὴρ νυκτὸς, ἡμέρησιον Φάος πεφαύσκων, καὶ χορῶν καταστάσιν Πολλῶν ἐν Ἄργει, τῆσδε συμφορᾶς χάριν. Ἰού, ἰού. Ἀγαμέμνονος γυναικὶ σημαίνων τορῶς, Εὐνῆς ἐπυπτιλάσσειν[?] ὡς Ἄρης, δόμοις Ὀλολυγμὸν δ' ἀφημῶσῶτα[?] τῇδε λαμπάδι Ἐπορθάξειν, εἴωσ' Ἰλίου πόλις Ἑάλωκεν, ὡς ὁ φρυκτὸς ἀγγέλων ἕρπει.
units.tr: O hail, lamp of the night, showing a daylight-like brightness, and the setting up of many dances in Argos in honour of this event. Iou, iou! Clearly signalling to Agamemnon's wife that, like Ares, she should kindle the bed, and that the house should send up a shout of joy at this torch, since the city of Ilium has been taken, as the beacon's messenger runs. [Ὦ χαῖρε λαμπτὴρ νυκτὸς, ἡμέρησιον Φάος πεφαύσκων, καὶ χορῶν καταστάσιν Πολλῶν ἐν Ἄργει, τῆσδε συμφορᾶς χάριν. Ἰού, ἰού. Ἀγαμέμνονος γυναικὶ σημαίνων τορῶς, Εὐνῆς ἐπυπτιλάσσειν ὡς Ἄρης, δόμοις Ὀλολυγμὸν δ' ἀφημῶσῶτα τῇδε λαμπάδι Ἐπορθάξειν, εἴωσ' Ἰλίου πόλις Ἑάλωκεν, ὡς ὁ φρυκτὸς ἀγγέλων ἕρπει.]

units.la: Auctor Argumenti: Ἀγαμέμνων εἰς Ἴλιον ἀπιὼν τῇ Κλυταιμνήστρα, εἴπερ ἡσὶ δὲ Ἴλιον, ὑπατέχετο[?] τῆς αὐτῆς ἡμέρας σημαίνειν λαμπάδι πυρσοῦ. ὅθεν σκηπὸν[?] ἐκάθιον ὅτι μὲν Κλυταιμνήστρα, ἵνα τηρῇ τὸν πυρσὸν. καὶ ὁ μὲν ἰδὼν ἀπῆλλαγεν. Eodem, in-quam, die redit Agamemnon, ipso decimo à profectione anno finiente, vt in his Talthybii habes.
units.tr: The author of the argument: Agamemnon, going off to Ilium, told Clytemnestra that if Ilium was taken on that same day she should signal with a torch; hence the scholiast notes that Clytemnestra was to keep watch on the beacon, and that when he saw it he departed. On the same day, I say, Agamemnon returns, the tenth year from his departure ending, as you have in the words of Talthybius. [Ἰὼ πανηγύρων οὐδὰς Ἀργείας ξένος. Δεκάτῳ σε φέλγὴ πρὸς δ' ἀφικόμην ἔτος.]

units.la: Ἰὼ πανηγύρων οὐδὰς Ἀργείας ξένος. Δεκάτῳ σε φέλγὴ πρὸς δ' ἀφικόμην ἔτος[?]
units.tr: See above: the Greek verse, "Io, threshold of Argive festivals, stranger..., in the tenth year I arrived."

units.la: Quo nomine veterum meruit censuram. Scholia: τινὲς μεμφονται τῷ ποιητῇ, ὅτι ἀυδήμεροι[?] ποιεῖ τοὺς Ἕλληνας ἠκούσας. Sed longe pudentius, vt diximus, Seneca, qui pòene vnius mensis interuallum facit à capto Ilio ad reditum Agamemnonis in patriam, itque in eorum sententiam, qui apud Clementem Alexandrinum Florido I. Ilium volunt esse captum τῇ εἰδὴ φθίνοντος Σκιροφορεῶνος, vltimo Lunæ quadrante:
units.tr: For this reason he earned the censure of the ancients. The scholia: some blame the poet, because he makes the Greeks return on the same day. But, as we said, Seneca is far more prudent, who places an interval of nearly one month between the capture of Ilium and Agamemnon's return to his homeland, and agrees with those who, in Clement of Alexandria, Florido I, hold that Ilium was taken on the ... of the last quarter of the moon. [Νὺξ μὲν εἶτω μεσάτα, λαμπτὴρ δ' ἐπίπλεε σελήνας.]

units.la: Νὺξ μὲν εἶτω μεσάτα, λαμπτὴρ δ' ἐπίπλεε σελήνας.
units.tr: Night stood in the middle, and the lamp of the moon was full.

units.la: In eorum sententiam, inquam, iuit Seneca. Troia soluunt Graeci Luna septima, circiter: nam nocte prima Luna lucebat, quando coorta est maris tempestas,
units.tr: I say Seneca went along with their opinion. The Greeks destroyed Troy about the seventh day of the moon, for on the first night the moon was shining when the storm at sea arose.

units.la: Cum Luna subito conditur, stellæ latent.
units.tr: When suddenly the moon is hidden, the stars are gone.

units.la: Intra tempus quod est à quintadecima Luna (nam in Ludis Olympicis τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τῆς σελήνης ἢ ἡ κείσας.) ad vicesimam secundam redit Agamemnon, Strophius venit ad eum salutandum post reportatam ex agone Olympico victoriam. Cum igitur anno Periodi Iulianæ MMMDXXXI. statim à capto Ilio domum redierit Agamemnon, & Strophius Olympia vicerit, vt auctor est Seneca, omnino sequitur Olympia ab Hercule instaurata fuisse anno eiusdem Periodi Iulianæ MMMDVII. à diebus æstiuis, à quibus septima sunt, si Olympia fingas iam tum quinto quoque anno ineunte celebrata fuisse, vt facit Seneca, ea quæ anno Periodi Iulianæ MMMDXXXI. agitata sunt, qui Olympiadum contextus texi non poterit, si vel anno Periodi Iulianæ MMMDXII. cum Ill. viro, vel anno eiusdem Periodi MMMCCCXCVI. cum nupero scriptore, agonem hunc Olympicum ab Hercule constitutum fuisse dixerimus. Olympias vero, quam primam memorant Graeci, ab Iphito celebrata est numero Eusebiano MCCXLI. siue anno Periodi Iulianæ termillesimo nongentesimo tricesimo octauo: Quanquam non intelligitur prima tempore, sed dignitate. Eusebius Chronic. Lib.1. in Græcis Scaligeri: [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~55 letters] [illegible, ~50 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~50 letters] Prima igitur reuera non fuit, quia viginti septem, si Aristodemo & Polybio fides, aut tredecim, si Callimachum sequimur auctorem, Olympiades ante hanc, quam Coroebus vicit stadio, celebratæ fuerant: atque huic Aristodemi & Polybij calculo accedere videtur Eusebianus: hæc enim Olympias, quæ dicitur prima, erat-que vicesima octaua, confertur ab Eusebio in numerum MCCXXXII. de quo detractis viginti septem Olympiadibus, aut, quod idem, annis centum octo, relinquetur numerus Eusebij CIOCXXXIII. in quo Lycurgus cum Iphito primam Olympiadem instituerit. Sane hoc numero CIOCXXXIII. notatum est, Lycurgus insignis habebatur. Annus autem hic erat Periodi Iulianæ termillesimus octingentesimus tricesimus, Nouilunium commissum est die, vt Græci numerant ab occaso Sole, tertio Iulij: Plenilunium die decimo septimo. ANNI. PER. IVL. DIES. HOR. I I | NOVILVNIVM. | PLENILVNIVM. DIES.HOR. I. II. DIES. HOR. I. II. 3830. 3801. | 2. 17. 55. 23. | 30. 11. 44. 3. | 45. 7. 6. 5. 29. | 21. 1. 8. 7. | 27. 14. 39. 10. | 27. 14. 39. 10. Iulius. | 3. 19. 35. 40. | 2. 22. 4. 53. | 17. 16. 26. 55. 27. 14. 39. 10.
units.tr: Within the period from the fifteenth day of the moon (for at the Olympic Games the assembly of the moon is the ... ) to the twenty-second, Agamemnon returns; Strophius came to greet him after bringing back victory from the Olympic contest. Since therefore in the year 3831 of the Julian Period, immediately after the capture of Ilium Agamemnon returned home, and Strophius won at Olympia, as Seneca reports, it follows that the Olympic games, restored by Hercules, were held in the year 3807 of the same Julian Period, counting from the summer days, from which the seventh days are reckoned, if you imagine that the Olympics were already celebrated every fifth year from the beginning, as Seneca does. Those events which took place in the year 3831 of the Julian Period cannot be fitted into the sequence of Olympiads, if we say that this Olympic contest was established by Hercules either in the year 3812 of the Julian Period, with the most distinguished man, or in the year 3396 of the same Period, with the recent writer. But the first Olympiad, which the Greeks mention, was celebrated by Iphitus in the Eusebian number 1241, that is, in the year 3938 of the Julian Period. Although it is not understood to be first in time, but in dignity. Eusebius, Chronicle, Book 1, in Scaliger's Greek text: [illegible passage]. It was therefore not truly the first, because twenty-seven Olympiads, if we trust Aristodemus and Polybius, or thirteen, if we follow Callimachus, had been celebrated before this one, which Coroebus won in the stadion. And Eusebius seems to agree with this calculation of Aristodemus and Polybius: for this Olympiad, which is called the first, was the twenty-eighth, and Eusebius reckons it as the number 1232. If twenty-seven Olympiads are subtracted from this, or, what amounts to the same, one hundred and eight years, there remains Eusebius' number 1133, in which Lycurgus, together with Iphitus, established the first Olympiad. Indeed this number 1133 has been marked: "Lycurgus was held in high esteem." This year was the year 3830 of the Julian Period; the new moon fell, as the Greeks count from sunset, on the third of July, the full moon on the seventeenth day. [Table of years, Julian Period days, hours, new moon and full moon dates, garbled in the scan.]

units.la: Vicesima octaua Olympias, quæ dignitate prima est, atque titulus temporis historici Græcorum, celebrata est, vt iam diximus, anno Periodi Iulianæ termillesimo nongentesimo tricesimo octauo: Nouilunium incidit in diem octauum Iulij, paullo ante occasum Solem: Plenilunium commissum est die vicesimo tertio Iulij. ANNI. PER.IVL. DIES.HOR. I. II. NOVILVNIVM. PLENILVNIVM. 3938. 3901. | 27. 22. 22. 43. | 60. 1. 28. 7. | 74. 19. 50. 8. 37. | 19. 11. 26. 37. | 51. 6. 25. 0. | 51. 6. 25. 0. Iulius. | 3. 19. 35. 40. | 8. 19. 3. 7. | 23. 13. 25. 8. 51. 6. 25. 0.
units.tr: The twenty-eighth Olympiad, which is first in dignity and the title of the Greek historical chronology, was celebrated, as we have already said, in the year 3938 of the Julian Period. The new moon fell on the eighth of July, a little before sunset; the full moon fell on the twenty-third of July. [Table of years, days, hours, new moon and full moon, garbled in the scan.]

units.la: Nouilunium commissum fuisse diximus die octauo Iulij, nam vertebat adhuc dies Iulij octauus, etiam apud Græcos, qui suos numerant dies ab occaso Sole: quinque enim ante mediam noctem horis Sol nondum erat occasus. Quæ autem à nobis de hac Olympiade, vt & altera, quæ instaurata est anno Periodi Iulianæ, vt diximus, cIↄcIↄcIↄCCCXXX. auctorem & fundum habent Africanum, cuius ista leguntur apud Eusebium loco laudato in Græcis Scaligeri.
units.tr: We said the new moon fell on the eighth of July, for it was still the eighth day of July even among the Greeks, who count their days from sunset; for five hours before midnight the sun had not yet set. The things we have said about this Olympiad, and about the other, which was restored in the year of the Julian Period, as we said, 1 1 1 330 [garbled], have as their author and foundation Africanus, whose words are read in Eusebius, in the place cited, in Scaliger's Greek text: [ΑΦΡΙΚΑΝΟΥ].

units.la: ΑΦΡΙΚΑΝΟΥ.
units.tr: Of Africanus.

units.la: Οὐκ ἄμεσυον δ' αὐ εἴη τὸ τῷ πρὸ Αἰγυπτίοις [?] Ολυμπιά[?]δων ἐνοίδῳ τινὰ ἄλλῳ τῆς [?]ς Ἀθηναίοις ἔστιν ὁ ἀρχὴ δηλοῦσαι τοῖς ἀγροοῖς. [?] γὰρ σελήνη πρὸ Αἰγυπτίοις ἀπὸ ἐσὶν ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... Ολυμπίαν σκάλυσις. αὕτη γὰρ ἀπὸ καρκίνου τῆς ἰδίου οἴκου, ἢ ἀπὸ λέοντος περιέρχομένη τὰ ιϛ'. καταπλάσσει ζωὴ ἐν νυχθημέρῳ κθ'. ᾧ λεπτοῖς λγ'. γ'. τῷ δὲ ἐνεωτῷ ὅλῳ δωδεκάτῳ [?] ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ... ιγ'. ἀ ἀ λόγος ... [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: It would not be out of place here to explain for the Egyptians the Olympiads... for the Athenians the beginning... For the moon, among the Egyptians... [illegible]... Olympic... This moon, moving round from the sign of Cancer, its own house, or from Leo, completes its circuit in 16... Life in a day and night... 29... 33... 12... 13... [remainder illegible]

units.la: Atque in his quaedam sunt, cum bono Deo, à nobis diligenter animaduertenda. Primum est, existimasse Africanum praecise ἀποκατάστασιν fieri Solis & Lunae intra Octaeteridem, & utriusque sideris rationes paria facere, interkalatis tribus mensibus tricenarijs in Octaeteride Lunari, cuius sunt nonaginta nouem syzygiae, vt optime obseruat Africanus, apud quem potior fuit ratio Octaeteridis, quam Enneadecaeteridis, vt & apud ceteros Christianos, qui ante Anatolium ex Octaeteride Paschalem festiuitatem inuestigarunt. Alterum est, Africanum existimasse cardines committi in illis signorum partibus, quibus adscribit Eudoxus. Iam vero adnotat Geminus brumam committi ex Eudoxi sententia in quarta Capricorni parte: τὴν δὲ αἰγόκερων ὁ ἥλιος ἀφαπο[?]ρεῖται ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κθ'. ὁ δὲ τῇ ἀ'. ΕΥδόξῳ ἔσπα[?] χεμεινῶν. æquinoctium vero vernum in sexta Arietis parte: τὴν ἡ χειμῶν ἀφαπορεῖται ὁ ἥλιος ἐν ἡμέρᾳ λα'. ὁ ἡ τῇ ς'. ΕΥδόξῳ ἰσημερία. Vnde coniecturam facere licet solstitium quoque commissum fuisse in sexta Cancri parte ex Eudoxi, quem sequitur Africanus, mente. Tertium est, eundem Africanum solstitium constituisse eodem mensis Iuliani die, quo commissum fuisse Iphiti aetate persuasum erat prioribus, nempe die octauo Iulij, quanquam veteres illi huic octauo Iulij diei adscripserint, quia cardines committi putabant in octauis signorum partibus, contra quam Africanus Eudoxum secutus sentiebat. His ita positis, facile est nosse, quare dixerit Africanus apud Eusebium: αὐτὴ γὰρ ἀπὸ καρκίνου τῆς ἰδίου οἴκου, ἢ ἀπὸ λέοντος περιερχομένη τὰ ιβ'. καταπλάσσει ζωΐα, &c. Dicit Lunam, cuius Nouilunium obseruatum fuit, vbi instaurata est Olympias ab Iphito, cepisse peragrare Zodiacum à primo Cancri gradu, vel ab ipso solstitio, quod omnino verum est: nam, vt ὕστερον πρότερον de posteriori prius dicamus, primae illius, quae est titulus temporis historici apud Graecos, Olympiadis Nouilunium Olympicum commissum est octauo Iulij die vertente apud Graecos, id est, ipso solstitij die: Ergo vere dixit Africanus Lunam περιελληλυθέναι ἀπὸ καρκίνου. Rursum quia centum & octo ante annis celebratum fuisse agonem Olympicum ab Iphito & Lycurgo traditum est, & Nouilunium illud Olympicum incidit in diem, qui tertius Iulij dicendus est Graecis, nam iam iniuerat, optime adnotauit Africanus Lunam περιελληλυθέναι ἀπὸ καρκίνου. Etenim, si octauo Iulij die committitur solstitium, idemque committitur in sexta Cancri parte, vt cum Eudoxo fiscebat Africanus, sequitur necessario primam Cancri partem adscribendam esse diei tertio Iulij: Atque ex his duo elicimus corollaria, quorum prius est solstitium è veterum sententia adsignandum esse diei octauo Iulij: alterum colligitur è doctrina Octaeteridis, nempe remotissimum Nouilunium Olympicum incidisse in diem Iulij octauum.
units.tr: And among these points there are some which, God willing, we must note carefully. First, Africanus thought that the restoration [ἀποκατάστασιν] of the Sun and Moon took place exactly within an octaeteris, and that the two luminaries' cycles came out equal, with three thirty-day months intercalated in the lunar octaeteris, which has ninety-nine syzygies, as Africanus rightly observes. He preferred the octaeteris to the enneadecaeteris, as did the other Christians who, before Anatolius, worked out the date of Easter from the octaeteris. Second, Africanus thought the cardinal points fell in those parts of the signs to which Eudoxus assigns them. Geminus indeed notes that, according to Eudoxus' opinion, the winter solstice falls in the fourth part of Capricorn: "The sun leaves Capricorn on the 29th day, and on the [?] day of ... of Eudoxus the winter..."; and the spring equinox in the sixth part of Aries: "The sun leaves winter on the 31st day, and on the [?] day ... of Eudoxus the equinox." From this one may conjecture that the solstice too was assigned to the sixth part of Cancer, according to the view of Eudoxus, whom Africanus follows. Third, Africanus placed the solstice on the same day of the Julian month on which the earlier writers were persuaded it fell in the time of Iphitus, namely the eighth of July. Yet those older writers assigned it to the eighth of July because they thought the cardinal points fell in the eighth parts of the signs, whereas Africanus, following Eudoxus, held otherwise. With these points settled, it is easy to see why Africanus said in Eusebius: "For this moon, moving round from the sign of Cancer, its own house, or from Leo, completes its circuit in 12..., and life..." etc. He says that the moon, whose new moon was observed when the Olympiad was re-established by Iphitus, began to traverse the zodiac from the first degree of Cancer, or from the solstice itself, which is entirely true. For, to speak of the later event before the earlier, the new moon of the first Olympiad, which is the mark of historical time among the Greeks, fell on the eighth of July as the Greeks reckoned it, that is, on the very day of the solstice. So Africanus was right to say that the moon "had come round from Cancer." Again, since it is recorded that the Olympic games were celebrated a hundred and eight years earlier by Iphitus and Lycurgus, and that Olympic new moon fell on the day which the Greeks call the third of July, for it had already begun, Africanus rightly noted that the moon "had come round from Cancer." For if the solstice falls on the eighth of July, and is also placed in the sixth part of Cancer, as Africanus with Eudoxus held, it necessarily follows that the first part of Cancer must be assigned to the third of July. From this we draw two corollaries: first, that the solstice, according to the opinion of the ancients, is to be fixed on the eighth of July; second, from the doctrine of the octaeteris, that the most remote Olympic new moon fell on the eighth of July.

units.la: Celebratissima autem fuit haec Olympica Panegyris, ad quam ficebat concursus omnium Graeci nominis populorum, & Barbarorum quoque: itaque qui ex illo agone victoriam reportabant, etiam & nomen sibi conciliabant magnum, nec sibi tantum, sed & patriae, quae in partem victoriae praeconio veniebat. Plato Apologia Socratis: [illegible, ~40 letters] [?] [illegible, ~60 letters] Vnde Pindarus Pythionicarum Ode I.
units.tr: This Olympic festival was most famous, and to it flocked crowds of all the peoples bearing the Greek name, and of barbarians too. Those who won victory in that contest gained great renown for themselves, and not for themselves alone but also for their homeland, which shared in the glory of the victory by the proclamation. Plato, Apology of Socrates: [illegible]. Hence Pindar, Pythian Ode I:

units.la: —Τοῦ μὲν ἐπωνυμίαν [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: "Of him the name..." [illegible]

units.la: Κλεινὸς οἰκιστὴρ ἐκ̈ύδαμε πόλιν[?] Γείτονα. Πυθιάδος[?] δ' ἐν δρόμῳ χαρύξ[?] [illegible, ~20 letters] Ἱερωνος [?] [illegible, ~10 letters] ἀρμάτων[?]
units.tr: "Glorious founder of the neighbouring city... in the race of the Pythian... of Hieron... of the chariots..." [remainder illegible]

units.la: Habes quoque apud Heliodorum, alios, quos non exscribo, nam occuparunt iampridem Amplissimi eruditissimique viri. Cum igitur vrbes è victoriis ciuium suorum Olympionicarum honorem consequerentur, Athenienses ne ingrati viderentur, Olympionicis honorem habuerunt vel magno suae Reipublicae dispendio & sumptu, quem coercendum censuit Solon. Dio-genes in eius Vita. ἀθλητὰς δὲ καὶ ἀσκυμάζους, πολυδάπανους, ὧ νικῆσαντες ἐπίζημιοι, καὶ φαινοῦσι τῆς πατρίδος μᾶλλον, ἢ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν λέγοντες τε [?] τὸν Εὐριπίδην,
units.tr: You have this also in Heliodorus, and in others, which I do not copy out, since distinguished and very learned men have long since dealt with them. So when cities gained honour from the victories of their citizens who were Olympic victors, the Athenians, lest they seem ungrateful, paid honour to the Olympic victors even at great cost and expense to their state, which Solon judged must be restrained. Diogenes, in his Life of Solon: "Athletes and those who train, costly people, who, when they win, are a burden, and who appear more to their homeland than to ..." And Euripides says: "Walls ... not leaving behind, they depart..."

units.la: Τείχονες οὐ λείποντες οἴχονται κέχηκας.
units.tr: "Walls, not leaving behind, they depart..." [remainder illegible]

units.la: Ὅταν σοιῶνδὲ ὁ Σόλων, μετεῖως αὐτοῖς ἀπέδεξατο, scripta haec Lege: Τῷ Ὀλύμπια νικήσαντι δραχμὰς πεντακοσίας δίδοσθαι. Olympionicis quingentae de publico drachmae dantur.
units.tr: When Solon ... received them, he set down these writings in the law: "To the Olympic victor let five hundred drachmas be given." Five hundred drachmas are given from the public treasury to Olympic victors.

units.la: Legem hanc habes apud Plutarchum in Solone: τῷ δ' Ἰσθμια νικήσαντι δραχμὰς ἑκατὸν δίδοσθαι. τῷ δ' Ὀλύμπια, πεντακοσίας. Diogenes loco laudato: σιωϊσχλε δὲ καὶ τὰς ἡμας τῶν ἀθλητῶν, Ὀλυμπιονίκῃ μὲν τάξας πεντακοσίας δραχμάς. Verum haec Solonis Lex diu non obtinuit: nam non longe post Olympionicae publice sunt excepti in Prytaneio. Callisthenes apud Plutarchum in Aristide de Polycrita Lysimachi filia: ἡ ζωὴ σιτήσιν ἰσως ἡ τῆς Ὀλυμπιονίκης ὁ δῆμος ἐψηφίσατο. Antiphanes Poëta Comicus:
units.tr: You have this law in Plutarch's Solon: "To the Isthmian victor let one hundred drachmas be given; to the Olympic victor, five hundred." Diogenes, in the passage cited: "He also set the honoraria of the athletes, appointing five hundred drachmas for the Olympic victor..." But this law of Solon did not hold for long, for not long afterwards Olympic victors were received at public expense in the Prytaneum. Callisthenes, in Plutarch's Aristides, on Polycrita, daughter of Lysimachus: "The people voted her food, perhaps, as the Olympic victress." The comic poet Antiphanes:

units.la: Γέρα γὰρ αὐτοῖς ταῦτα τῆς τ' Ολύμπια Νικῶσι δίδοται, ζῳσότητος ἕνεκα, Σίτησις, οὐ γὰρ μὴ πέντε συμβολαί. Γρυτμφα ταῦτα πόρῳ παρεσκευάσθαι[?].
units.tr: "For these are the prizes given to Olympic victors upon winning: maintenance for their life at public expense, for they would not have five ... contributions. These things were prepared ..." [remainder unclear]

units.la: Duos vltimos versus ita interpungo, & rescribo:
units.tr: I punctuate the last two verses thus, and rewrite them:

units.la: Οὐ γὰρ μὴ πέντε συμβολαί. [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: "For they would not have five contributions..." [remainder illegible]

units.la: Itaque vt ad epulum admitterentur, symbola fidem faciebant, & niceteria de collo gestabant. Iuuenalis:
units.tr: Thus, to be admitted to the feast, their tokens (symbola) gave proof, and they wore niceteria round their necks. Juvenal:

units.la: Rusticus ille tuus sumit trechedipna, Quirine,Et ceromatico fert niceteria collo.
units.tr: "That rustic of yours, Quirinus, takes his trechedipna, and wears the niceteria on his oiled neck."

units.la: Atque istæ σπυρίδες [?] an quotidianæ fuerint dubitari potest, fuisse tamen facile mihi persuadeo, inductus auctoritate Æliani περὶ ζῴων ἰδιότητος, Lib. VI. cap. XLIX. in historia muli illius veteli, qui iuniores & robustiores ad vecturam comitabatur, atque adeo qua poterat cohortabatur, cum ædem Minervæ Athenienses conderent: ὁ δῆμος τῶν μαθητῶν ζῴων, τοῦ χώρου [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters].
units.tr: Whether those [?] were daily there is room for doubt; yet I am easily persuaded that they were, moved by the authority of Aelian, On the Peculiar Nature of Animals, Book VI, chapter 49, in the story of that old mule which accompanied the younger and stronger ones to the carting, and encouraged them as far as it could, when the Athenians were building the temple of Minerva: "the people of the learned animals, of the place ..." [remainder illegible]

units.la: Non solis autem Olympionicis, verum etiam Isthmionicis Solonis Lege datum honorarium è fisco: Τῷ Ἰσθμίᾳ νικήσαντι δραχμὰς ἑκατὸν δι-δόναι.
units.tr: Not only Olympic victors, but also Isthmian victors, received an honorarium from the treasury by Solon's law: "To the Isthmian victor let one hundred drachmas be given" [Τῷ Ἰσθμίᾳ νικήσαντι δραχμὰς ἑκατὸν διδόναι].

units.la: Laudat hanc Legem Plutarchus in Solone: τὸ δὲ Ἰσθμίᾳ νικήσαντι, δραχμὰς ἑκατὸν διδόναι. Diogenes loco laudato: [illegible, ~30 letters] Ολυμπιονίκῃ μὲν ἕξεις πεντακοσίας δραχμάς· Ἰσθμιονίκῃ δὲ ἑκατὸν, καὶ αἰδλο-γον [?] τὴν ἄλλων. Vnde disces etiam aliis Hieronicis ceterorum certaminum, Pythiorum puta & Nemeorum constituta esse à Solone honoraria; sed quátailla [?] fuerint non referunt, satis quippe illis fuit, meo iudicio, nos docere quantum fuerit honorarium Olympionicarum, qui omnium maximo in pretio ac fama, quantum etiam fuerit Isthmionicarum, qui infra dignitatem Pythionicarum, & Nemeonicarum: itaque maximi atque infimi pretij honorarium in literas retulerunt, quod horum scriptorum instituto satis erat.
units.tr: Plutarch in Solon praises this law: "But to the Isthmian victor, let one hundred drachmas be given." Diogenes, in the passage cited: "... to the Olympic victor you shall give five hundred drachmas; to the Isthmian victor one hundred, and to the others..." From this you will learn that honoraria were also fixed by Solon for the victors of the other contests, the Pythian and Nemean games. But what amounts they were they do not record; it was enough, in my judgement, for these writers to teach us how great the honorarium of the Olympic victors was, who held the highest value and fame of all, and how great that of the Isthmian victors was, who stood below the dignity of the Pythian and Nemean victors. So they recorded the honoraria of the highest and lowest value, which was sufficient for the purpose of these writers.

units.la: Habuerunt quoque honorem Hieronicis Imperatores Romani Augusti vestigia legentes, præmiaque siue opsonia pro Ifelasticis certaminibus constituerunt, eaque de re extant Plinij & Traiani amœbæa Epistolæ in hæc verba:
units.tr: The Roman emperors also honoured the victors of the sacred games, following the footsteps of Augustus, and established prizes or allowances for the Isolympic contests; and concerning this matter there survive the exchanged letters of Pliny and Trajan, in these words:

units.la: C. PLINIVS TRAIANO IMP. S.
units.tr: C. Pliny to the Emperor Trajan, greetings.

units.la: Athleta, Domine, ea quæ pro Ifelasticis certaminibus constituisti, deberi sibi putant statim ex eo die quo sunt coronati. Nihil enim referre, quando sint patriam inuecti, sed quando certamine vicerint, ex quo inuehi possint. Ego contra Scribo Ifelasticorum nomine. Itaque eorum vehementer addubitem an sit potius id tempus quo εἰσάγεσθαι intuendum, &c.
units.tr: Lord, the athletes think that what you have decreed for the Iselastic contests is owed to them from the very day on which they were crowned. For it makes no difference when they were brought home to their country, but when they won in the contest, from which they can be brought home. I, on the contrary, write on behalf of the Iselastics. And so I am very doubtful whether it is rather the time of being led in [εἰσάγεσθαι] that should be considered, etc.

units.la: TRAIANVS PLINIO S.
units.tr: Trajan to Pliny, greetings.

units.la: Ifelasticum tunc primum mihi videtur incipere deberi, quum quis in ciuitatem suam ipse εἰσάγεσθαι, &c. Plinij verba describimus, vt emendemus: Rescribo: Ego cum transcribo, Iselasticorum, nomine itaque eorum vehementer addubitem, an sit potius id tempus, quo [illegible, ~12 letters] intuendum. Nempe cum libellum ab Iselasticis sibi oblatum Imperatori mittendum transcriberet Plinius, ipso eorum nomine monitus facile vidit Iselasticos dictos fuisse, non ex eo tempore, quo sunt coronati, sed ex quo patriam inuecti sunt, [illegible, ~10 letters]. Atque haec praemia Hieronicarum abiis capi poterant, qui pecuniam Hieronicis crediderant, auctore Papiniano Libro X. Responsorum: Commodis praemiorum, quae propter coronas sacras praestantur, condemnato placuit interdici, & eam pecuniam iure pignoris in causam iudicati capi. Lege XL. De re iudicata: quanquam non poterat, qui nondum e sacro certamine coronam reportauerat, pignori obligare praemia, quae sibi pensitanda sperabat. Pro coronis: Imp. Alexander A. Septimio. Spem eorum praemiorum, quae pro coronis athletis pensitanda sunt, priuata pactione pignorari minime admittendum est: & ideo nec si generale pactum de omnibus bonis pignori obligandis interuenerit, tenet. PP. Kal. Maij, Maximo II. & Paterno Conss. Lege V.C. Quae res pignori obligari possunt. Quinetiam qui tribus coronis erant coronati, ciuilium munerum vacatio illis tribuebatur. Impp. Diocletianus & Maxim. Augusti & Caes Hermeti. Athletis ita demum, si per omnem aetatem certasse, coronis quoque non minus tribus certaminis sacri, (in quibus vel semel Romae, seu antiquae Graeciae) merito coronati, non aemulis corruptis ac redemptis probentur, ciuilium munerum tribui solet vacatio. Lege vnica C. de Athletis. Excusantur quoque a tutelis, vt docet Modestinus Libro II. Excusationum, ex Vlpiano Lib. singulari de officio Praetoris tutelaris: Athletae habent a tutela excusationem, sed qui sacris certaminibus coronati sunt. Lege V I. §. XIII. D. de Excusationibus. Neque vlla notantur infamia. Vlpianus Libro VI. ad Edictum, cuius verba hic repraesentabimus, vt mendum tollamus. Athletas autem Sabinus, & Cassius responderunt omnino artem ludicram non facere: virtutis enim gratia hoc facere, & generaliter ita omnes opinantur, & utile videtur, vt neque Thymelici, neque excusti, neque agitatores, nec qui aquam equis sparsunt, ceteraque eorum ministeria, qui certaminibus sacris deseruiunt, ignominiosi habeantur. Lege IV. De his, qui notantur infamia. Non potest hic ferri [illegible, ~2 letters] Thymelici, neque ita legerunt Graeci, qui vertunt in Basilicis Libro XXI. Titulo II. cap. II. [illegible, ~70 letters, Greek] [illegible, ~60 letters, Greek] [illegible, ~80 letters, Greek] Non ignoro praestantissimum Iureconsultorum longe aliter interpretari in Notis ad Legem III. C. de Spectaculis: Scenici, inquit, a Graecis appellantur Thymelici, veluti mimi, histriones, ludiones. Hos constat esse famosos, & tribu moueri. Specialiter Thymelici dicuntur cantores, qui modos faciebant & saltationes. Hi non sunt famosi, & hos videntur intellexisse Graeci l. IV. D. de his qui not. inf. quam praeceptoris quondam sui sententiam Amplissimus, &, quod pluris facimus, eruditissimus Faber in Agonistico amplectitur: sed vix est, vt credam Thymelicos cosensu hic vsurpari, cum nusquam alibi id significet: sed semper de scanicis dicatur, qui infames sunt. Putem igitur corruptam esse hanc vocem, eique corrumpendæ compendiosam scribendi rationem fuisse. Scriptum igitur olim apud Vlpianum, vt neque ΘΟΔ μύκοι[?], siue thymelici, id est, illi qui τὴν Γυμνικὴν νόμων τῶν αὐλητικῶν ἀδεῖα[?], de quibus Pollux Libro IV, cap. X. τὴν δὲ πυθικὴν νόμου τῆς αὐλητικοῦ, μάχη πέντε, πύξ[?], καλλιχόρου[?], ἰαμβικὸν, ἀσυδῖον[?], καλλιχόρβιος[?]. Ἀλλ' ὅμως ἡ Ἀπόλλωνος μάχης πρὸς τὸν δράκοντα[?]. καὶ ὁ μὲν τῇ πύξι[?], ἀλλ' ἕκαστος[?] τὸν τόπον, εἰ ἄξιος ἐστὶ τὸ ἀγῶνος[?]. ὁ δὲ τῆς καλλιαυλ[?] ἀγῶνος, ἀλλὰ ἐκλείπει τὸν δράκοντα. καὶ δὲ τῆς ἰαμβικῆς, μάχη[?] ἐμάσσειλησθη ἡ ὁ ἰαμβικὸν, καὶ τὰ Γαλατικὰ χρήματα[?] καὶ τὸν ἱδρυσμὸν, ὡς τὰ δράκοντος, ὁ τὰ πλῆξιδὴ συμφορᾶς ἕως ἰδίως[?]. ὁ ἡ ἀσυδῖον δηλοῖ τῶν νίκης τῶν Θεοῦ. ὁ ἡ τὴν καλλιχόρβιον, ὁ ἡς τὰ ὑπὸ-λέκα χοράν[?]. Neque hinc abeunt Græci, si leuiter vnicam vocem emendes, præterquam quod Olympiis attribuunt quæ sunt Pythiorum: καὶ τῶν λεγόντων ὁ ὀλυμπίοις τῶν ἀγῶνα, quæ ad pugnam scilicet Apollinis cum Pythone spectant.
units.tr: It seems to me that the Iselastic reward first begins to be owed when someone is led into his own city [εἰσάγεσθαι], etc. We set out Pliny's words so that we may emend them. I reply: "I, when I transcribe, [write] Iselastics; therefore I am very doubtful whether it is rather the time at which [illegible] should be considered." Clearly, when Pliny was copying out a petition that the Iselastics had handed him to send to the Emperor, he was warned by their very name and easily saw that they were called Iselastics not from the time they were crowned, but from when they were brought home to their country, [illegible]. These rewards of the victors could be seized from those who had lent money to the victors, on the authority of Papinian, Book X of the Responsa: "It has been decided that the condemned man be forbidden the rewards paid on account of sacred crowns, and that this money be seized by right of pledge in the cause of the judgment debtor." Law 40, On Res Judicata: although one who had not yet returned from the sacred contest with a crown could not pledge as security the rewards which he hoped would be paid to him. On crowns: the Emperor Alexander Augustus to Septimius: "The hope of those rewards which are to be paid to athletes for their crowns may by no means be pledged by private agreement; and therefore, even if a general agreement to pledge all goods has intervened, it does not hold. Given on the first day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Maximus (for the second time) and Paternus." Law 5, C., Which Things May Be Pledged. Indeed, those who had been crowned with three crowns were also granted exemption from civic duties. The Emperors Diocletian and Maximian Augusti and the Caesar Hermes: "Athletes are, in the end, usually granted exemption from civic duties only if they have competed throughout their whole lives and have been rightly crowned with no fewer than three crowns of sacred contests (either once at Rome, or in ancient Greece), and have not been approved through corrupted or bought rivals." Single law, C., On Athletes. They are also excused from guardianships, as Modestinus teaches in Book II of the Excusations, drawing on Ulpian's single book On the Duty of the Praetor concerning Guardianships: "Athletes have excuse from guardianship, but only those who have been crowned in sacred contests." Law 6, §13, D., On Excusations. Nor are they marked with any infamy. Ulpian, Book VI on the Edict, whose words I shall set out here so as to remove the error: "Sabinus and Cassius, however, have answered that athletes do not practise a theatrical art at all: for they do this for the sake of virtue, and generally all think so, and it seems useful that neither the Thymelici, nor the trainers, nor the charioteers, nor those who sprinkle water on the horses, nor their other attendants, who serve sacred contests, be considered infamous." Law 4, On Those Who Are Marked with Infamy. Here [illegible] "Thymelici" cannot be accepted, and the Greeks who translate in the Basilica, Book XXI, Title II, chapter II, did not read it so. [illegible Greek]. I am aware that the most distinguished jurist interprets this quite differently, in his notes on Law 3, C., On Spectacles: "Scenici," he says, "are called Thymelici by the Greeks, as mimes, actors and buffoons. It is established that these are infamous and are removed from their tribe. Thymelici are specifically called singers who composed melodies and dances. These are not infamous, and the Greeks seem to have meant these in Law 4, D., On Those Who Are Marked with Infamy." Yet the most distinguished, and, what is worth more to us, the most learned Faber in his Agonisticon embraces the opinion of his former teacher. But I can hardly believe that "Thymelici" is used here in this sense, since it never means that elsewhere, but is always said of stage performers, who are infamous. I think, therefore, that this word has been corrupted, and that a shorthand way of writing it made the corruption easy. So it was once written in Ulpian, that neither [illegible] nor Thymelici, that is, those who [illegible] the Gymnic nomes of the flute-players, of whom Pollux speaks in Book IV, chapter X: the Pythian nome of the flute, the battle, the Pythian, the Cyclic ... the iambic, the [illegible]... Nor do the Greeks depart from this if you lightly emend the single word, except that they assign to the Olympic games what belongs to the Pythian; and [they speak] of the Olympic contest, which of course concerns Apollo's battle with the Python.

units.la: Atque hæc erant satis, adeoque plura quàm instituti nostri ratio exigit: non possumus tamen nonnulla prætermittere, quæ Pythia, Nemeaque spectant: cum enim nobis non constet pro certo, quot drachmas de filco voluerit dari Solon Pythionicis aut Nemeonicu[?], saltem inuestigabimus tempus, quo hæc ludicra peragebantur. Ac quidem quod ad Pythia attinet, longè fallitur meo iudicio Vir Illustris, qui celebrata scribit anno tertio Olympiadis vertente: quanquam enim auctorem laudet Eusebium, qui ad annum tertium Olympiadis XLVIII. notat prima Pythia celebrata fuisse, tamen potior apud me est auctoritas Thucydidis, è quo discimus Pythia celebrata fuisse secundo quoque anno vertente Olympiadis: Nam ineunte anno nono belli Peloponnesiaci annuæ inducíæ inter Athenienses & Lacedæmonios pactæ sunt. Thucydides Libro IV. καὶ τῆς χρόνως διελύθησαν, ὀγδόῳ ἔτος ἐπὶ ἀλλὰ τὰ πολέμῳ. Λακεδαιμόνιοι δὲ καὶ Ἀθηναῖοι, ἅμα δὲ τῆς Ὑπὸ-γυμνασίου Ἱερῷ[?], ὅτι ἐκεχείρηται ἐπὶ πρῶτον ἐπαίνω.
