Cepitque hic annus inducíarum à quartodecimo mensis Elaphebolionis die: habes in pfephismate Athenienfium ibidem: καὶ ἀμολόγησαν εἰς τὰ δίκην τῶν ἐκεχείρια[?] ἐπαύτῳ[?]. ἀρχὴ δὲ τῶν ὅλων τῶν ἡμέρων, πεμπάδα ὅτι δίκα τῆς Ἐλαφηβολιῶνος μηνός[?]. Annus erat primus vertens Olympiadis octagesimæ nonæ, Ilarcho Athenis Prætore: Inciditque hic dies quartusdecimus, siue potius tertiusdecimus Elaphebolionis in diem septimum Aprilis, vt alibi diximus. Quare annus induciarum finiebatur die quartodecimo Elaphebolionis, vertente anno secundo eiusdem Olympiadis octagesimæ nonæ, Amynia Archonte: Atqui durarunt induciæ ad Pythia vsque: Thucydides primis Libri V. verbis: τῆς δὲ Ὑπογυμνασίου ἡμέρας, ἀφ᾽ οὗ ἐκεχείρησαν ἀπέλαυον μάχῃ Πυθίων. Quare Pythia celebrata sunt secundo quoque anno Olympiadis vertente, circa medium Elaphebolionem mensem. Atque id optime etiam obseruauit nuperus scriptor: sed pessime tempus confert peractorum Nemeorum in annum primum Olympiadis: non ignorum Liuium laudare in hanc rem, qui Libro XXVII. Nemea, inquit, celebrata narrat eo anno, quo T. Quinctius Crispinus & M. Marcellus Coss. fuerunt: qui est Vrbis DXLVI. quo Olympiadis CXLIII. cæpit annus primus: Sed de Leuij loco agemus postea.
units.tr: These things are enough, and indeed more than the plan of our work requires. Nevertheless I cannot pass over some points concerning the Pythian and Nemean games. For since it is not certain to us how many drachmas Solon wished to be given from the treasury to the Pythian and Nemean victors, at least we shall investigate the time at which these games were celebrated. As for the Pythian games, that distinguished man, in my judgment, is far wrong who writes that they were celebrated in the third year of the Olympiad, the year turning. For although he cites Eusebius, who notes that the first Pythian games were celebrated in the third year of the forty-eighth Olympiad, yet the authority of Thucydides is weightier with me, from whom we learn that the Pythian games were celebrated in every second year of the Olympiad, the year turning. For at the beginning of the ninth year of the Peloponnesian War, annual truces were agreed between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians. Thucydides, Book IV: "And the truce ended in the eighth year of the war." The Lacedaemonians and the Athenians, at the same time, on the sacred Olympic festival... [illegible]. That year of truce began on the fourteenth day of the month Elaphebolion; you have this in the decree of the Athenians there as well: "And they agreed for a year of truce, from the fourteenth day of the month Elaphebolion." It was the first year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad, with Ilarchus as Praetor at Athens, and this fourteenth, or rather thirteenth, day of Elaphebolion falls on the seventh day of April, as I have said elsewhere. Therefore the year of truce ended on the fourteenth day of Elaphebolion, in the second year of the same eighty-ninth Olympiad, the year turning, with Amynias as Archon. But the truce lasted until the Pythian games; Thucydides in the first words of Book V: "On the day of the sacred festival of the Olympic games, from which they had abstained..." Therefore the Pythian games were celebrated in every second year of the Olympiad, the year turning, about the middle of the month Elaphebolion. The recent writer also observed this rightly, but he very badly assigns the time of the Nemean games to the first year of the Olympiad. I am not unaware that Livy is cited for this matter, who in Book XXVII says: "The Nemean games were celebrated in the year in which T. Quinctius Crispinus and M. Marcellus were consuls," which is the year 546 from the founding of the City, in which the first year of the 143rd Olympiad began. But we shall deal with the passage of Livy later.

units.la: Diodorus Siculus Libro XIX. ad annum secundum Olympiadis centesimæ sextædecimæ, Praxibulo Archonte, Nemea à Cassandro celebrata fuisse referт: Scio quid respondeat nuperus scriptor, Diodori Chronologiam tardidare peccare, itaque Nemea in annum primum esse conijcienda. Sed huic effugio non est locus: Nam si quis penitus attendat ad Liuij historiam, facile videbit Nemea celebrata fuisse anno quarto vertente Olympiadis: itaque mire hic res turbat Liuius. Atqui si anno quarto Olympiadis celebrabatur Nemea, ergo secundo quoque non primo: nam tertio quoque anno instaurabatur hic agon. Scholia Pindari ad Nemeonicas: [illegible, ~70 letters] Panemus hic, ut puto, Corinthiorum est, qui Hecatombæoni respondet, non autem Macedonum: nam tempus non conuenit. Nemea namque, ante Pythia celebrabatur, (quod fieri non posset, si Panemo Macedonum celebrarentur,) idque eodem anno: qua de re eximius est Aristotelis locus Libro V. Metaphysf. cap. XI. ubi [illegible, ~25 letters] docet. [illegible, ~90 letters] Quod enim eodem anno ludicra hæc duo celebrarentur, coniungit Philosophus: Pythia autem secundo quoque anno vertente Olympiadi instaurabantur: ergo etiá & Nemea. Unde etiam colliges Librum hunc ab Aristotele scriptum fuisse incunte anno secundo Olympiadis, idque, ut puto, si audiamus Scriptorem Noctium Atticarum de editis in vulgus ab Aristotele Libris [illegible, ~12 letters] Olympiadis centesimæ undecimæ.
units.tr: Diodorus Siculus, in Book XIX, reports that under the Archon Praxibulus, in the second year of the 116th Olympiad, the Nemean games were celebrated by Cassander. I know what the recent writer will reply: that Diodorus's chronology is slow and in error, and so the Nemean games should be placed in the first year. But this escape has no place. For if anyone attends carefully to Livy's history, he will easily see that the Nemean games were celebrated in the fourth year of the Olympiad, the year turning; and so Livy troubles this matter strangely. But if the Nemean games were celebrated in the fourth year of the Olympiad, then they were held in every second year, not the first; for this contest was renewed every third year. Scholia of Pindar on the Nemean Odes: [illegible]. Panemus here, I think, belongs to the Corinthians, and corresponds to Hecatombaeon, not to the Macedonians; for the time does not agree. For the Nemean games were celebrated before the Pythian, which could not have happened if they were celebrated by the Macedonians in the month Panemus, and in the same year. On this point there is a notable passage of Aristotle, Book V of the Metaphysics, chapter XI, where [illegible] he teaches [illegible]. For the Philosopher joins these two festivals, saying that they were celebrated in the same year; but the Pythian games were renewed in every second year of the Olympiad, the year turning; therefore the Nemean games too. From this you may also infer that this book was written by Aristotle at the beginning of the second year of the Olympiad, and that, as I think, if we follow the writer of the Attic Nights concerning the books published by Aristotle [illegible], in the 111th Olympiad.

units.la: Inter præcipua dierum festorum oblectamenta numerandæ veniunt commissiones Tragœdiarum, quibus tum delectare, cum prodesse volebat Poëtæ, qui illas docebant, [illegible, ~25 letters] ut loquitur Aristoteles in Libello de Poetica. Itaque plerique eorum, qui in scenam inducuntur à Tragicis, boni sunt, longeque adeo meliores quam nunc sunt, si viris summis, quibusipsam pœne dixerim vitam, lucem certe debet aureolus hic Aristotelis libellus, assensum præbeamus. Sed non possumus in illorum ire sententiam: nam qui in Tragœdus inducuntur, non sunt adeo probi, ut meliores, quam qui nunc sunt, dici possint, quia si in aduersam fortunam mutetur eorum felicitas, id nec terrorem incutit, nec miserationem mouet, sed scelestum est: Improbus vero neque cum infelix est affectum mouet, & felicitas commiserationem excludit, horrorem auté multo magis: neque enim improbum miseratur quisquam, quia dignum existimat, nec terrorem excitat eius calamitas: nam nemo sibi euenturum idem putat, quippe optime sentit quisque de probitate sua. Sed inducuntur, qui nec virtute admodum excellant, nec vitiis turpentur, quique inter probü atque improbum sint constituti, id est, qui cum imprudentes peccent, boni viri nomen non tuentur, neque merentur, quia illius officiü sunt transgressi, neque contrà improbi, quia inconsulto peccant. Præterea similes iis qui nunc sunt repræsentat Tragœdia, neque enim alioqui terror excitaretur, nam terror est [illegible, ~14 letters]. Verû, inquies, scripsit Aristoteles cap. II. eos, qui repræsentantur esse aut probos, aut improbos, itaque exprimi vel meliores quam nunc sunt, vel deteriores, vel similes: [illegible, ~25 letters] χί[illegible, ~40 letters] & paulò post: [illegible, ~45 letters] Comœdia deteriores, Tragœdia meliores quâ nunc sit imitari conantur. Sed videndum est iam, quomodo ipse se interpretetur Aristoteles, scribatq; Tragœdiam imitari meliores. Plutarchus de Menandri agens gnomis, [illegible, ~25 letters] inquit, [illegible, ~20 letters]. De Tragœdia verò speciatim scribens Aristoteles docet bonos pictores esse imitandos, qui cùm vultus alicuius exprimant, & similē quidem, pulchriorem tamen pingunt. Poëtas quoque ad hoc exemplū debere, cū iracundos exempli gratia inducūt, æquitatis potius, quā alperitatis habere rationem, atque ita meliores quam fuerunt exhibere: [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: Among the chief pleasures of the festival days must be counted the performances of tragedies, by which the poets who staged them wished both to delight and to benefit [...] as Aristotle says in his little book on Poetics. Therefore most of the characters brought onto the stage by the tragic poets are good, and far better than people now are, if we give our assent to those great men to whom this little golden book of Aristotle owes its very life, I might almost say, and certainly its light. But we cannot go along with their opinion. For those who are introduced as tragic heroes are not so upright that they can be called better than the men of today. If their good fortune were turned to adversity, this would neither strike terror nor arouse pity, but would be wicked. A wicked man, however, does not stir emotion when he is unfortunate, and prosperity excludes pity, and horror much more so. For no one pities a wicked man, since he thinks him deserving, and his calamity does not stir fear, for no one thinks the same will happen to himself, since each person judges his own uprightness very favourably. Rather, the characters introduced are those who are not outstanding in virtue, nor stained by vices, and who are placed between the upright and the wicked: that is, those who, sinning through ignorance, do not keep the name of good men and do not deserve it, because they have transgressed the duty of their office, yet are not wicked either, because they sin without deliberate intent. Besides, tragedy presents men similar to those who now exist, for otherwise terror would not be aroused [...]. But, you will say, Aristotle wrote in chapter 2 that those who are represented are either good or wicked, and so they are portrayed either better than they now are, or worse, or similar [...] and a little later: [...] comedy tries to imitate men worse, tragedy better than they now are. But we must now see how Aristotle himself explains himself, and writes that tragedy imitates better men. Plutarch, speaking of the sentiments of Menander, [...] says [...]. Aristotle, writing specifically about tragedy, teaches that good painters are to be imitated, who, when they portray someone's face, paint it similar indeed, yet more beautiful. Poets too, on this model, when they introduce angry men, for example, ought to have regard for fairness rather than harshness, and thus present them better than they were [...].

units.la: Quare cum dixit Aristoteles Tragœdiam imitari meliores, voluit significare meliores eos esse, qui exhibentur, quam olim fuerant, ita tamen ut semper vitæ suæ institutū morefq; referant, & vultum exprimant similem. Quare ita legendū est verbis laudatis: [illegible, ~30 letters] id est, debet meliores exprimere, quatenus in nostra positu est potestate, aut improbiores: nempe penes Poëtam non est, ut alios mores affingat, & plane dissimile. Meliores igitur inducet Poeta, quatenus illi per imitationis leges licebit, quā reuera fuerunt, id est, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Inducet quoq; Comœdia deteriores, id est, magis ridiculos quam fuerat: Non enim improbi dicuntur [illegible, ~25 letters]. Quod verò ad posteriora Aristotelis verba attinet, ita lego, [illegible, ~40 letters] Comœdia, inquit, deteriores, Tragœdia verò meliores, nunc quidem, imitari conatur. Quod certe verum est. Nā Tragœdiæ initia non solum humilia, sed etiā cum lasciuia & petulantia Satyrica coniuncta fuerunt: testis est locupletissimus Aristoteles ipse, ubi agit de Tragœdia: [illegible, ~50 letters] Sero, inquit, ad maiestatis suæ splendorem peruenit Tragœdia, sed prius habebat multa [illegible, ~30 letters] quæ [illegible, ~20 letters] imitatur. Ergo olim Tragœdia, nō minus quā Comœdia deteriores imitabatur: Et certè olim etiā scribebdis Tragœdiis adhuc ita sunt Tetrametra, quia tota illa Poësis erat Satyrica: [illegible, ~45 letters] Nūc verò, id est, ex quo splendorem suū est cōlecuta, meliores inducit Tragœdia, deterioribus ad Comicos & Satyricos Poëtas amādatis: Itaq; plerique, qui in Tragœdiis inducūtur, boni sunt, ac proinde bene morati, at si quādo improbos cōdignis exhibēt moribus & sententiis, pœnas quoq; extremo dramate dantes reprælentantur. Quare cum hi versus, inquit Seneca Epistola CXV
units.tr: Therefore, when Aristotle said that tragedy imitates better men, he meant that those who are presented are better than they once were, yet in such a way that they always preserve the pattern and character of their life and portray a similar face. Hence the words cited must be read thus: [...] that is, the poet must portray them better, so far as it lies in our power, or worse. Certainly it is not for the poet to invent other manners, entirely unlike. The poet will therefore introduce better men, so far as the laws of imitation allow, than they really were, that is, [...]. Comedy too will introduce worse men, that is, more ridiculous than they were, for they are not called wicked [...]. As for the latter words of Aristotle, I read them thus: [...] comedy, he says, worse, but tragedy better, now indeed, tries to imitate. This is certainly true. For the beginnings of tragedy were not only humble, but were also joined with the wantonness and boldness of satyr-play. Aristotle himself is a most abundant witness to this, where he treats of tragedy: [...] Tragedy, he says, came late to the splendour of its dignity, but earlier it had many [...] which [...] imitates. Therefore tragedy once imitated worse men no less than comedy did. And indeed, even when tragedies were written, they were still in trimeters, because that whole poetry was satyric. [...] But now, that is, since it has gathered its splendour, tragedy introduces better men, having handed over the worse ones to comic and satyric poets. Thus most of those who are introduced in tragedies are good, and therefore of sound character; but if at any time they present wicked men with characters and sentiments befitting them, they are also shown paying their penalty at the end of the drama. Wherefore, when these verses, says Seneca in Epistle 115,

units.la: Pecunia ingens generis humani bonum, Cui non voluptas matris, aut blandæ prolis, Par esse prolis, non sacer meritis parens. Tam dulce si quid Veneris in vultu micat, Merito illa amores cœlitum atque hominum movet.
units.tr: Money, the great good of the human race, to which neither the pleasure of a mother, nor a sweet offspring, is equal, nor a parent holy in merit. If anything of Venus's charm gleams in the face, rightly does it stir the loves of gods and men.

units.la: in Tragœdia Euripidis pronunciati essent, totus populus ad excipiendum & ad clamorem & carmen consurrexit uno impetu: donec Euripides ipse in medium prosiluit, petens, ut expectarent, viderentque quem admirator asperi exitum facerent. Dabatur[?] in illa fabula poenas Bellerophontes, quas in sua quisque dat. Nam hic Bellerophontes animo ferox & elatus, ob prosperos successus, magna opum vim, & regnū, impie in Deos debacchatur, quo refero illa quæ leguntur ex hoc dramate apud Iustinum Martyrem περὶ μοναρχίας [?] & opes commendat, huc spectat hoc fragmentum, quod vertit Seneca. Sunt enim illius, qui aduersus Venerem alioquin invictus, cedit & frangitur animo ob opes. Quare desinat mirari Cl. Lipsius, quid huic cum auro. Opibus enim elatus in cœlum affectat viam. Sed Iupiter ira commotus cum Pegaso ita subuolantem excutit & deturbat, unde crus sibi fregit, regnoque excidit: Vide Aristophanem Ranis, & eius Scholiastem: itemque Eustathium ad Iliad. Z. Atqui hæc est huius dramatis [illegible, ~8 letters]. Atqui ex his habebat unusquisque unde exemplum sumeret sibi, meliorque fieret, maxime cuiusta viris contingant principibus, hi enim in Tragœdiis inducūtur: Unde, cum in Athenienses sæuirent Triginta Tyranni, & viros civitatis primores sint de medio sublatum, Antisthenem docet Socrates non esse causam, cur tenuis conditionis homo viris principibus invideat, si attendamus quales exitus faciant apud Tragicas Atrei, Thyestę, Agamemnones, & Ægysthi: at Tragicorum nullus in scena matari fecit de plebe homine: Hoc nobis repræsentauerat Ælianus Variæ Lib. II. c. XI. sed olim, nā hodie ita editur: [Greek, illegible, ~12 letters] Referibo [Greek, illegible, ~8 letters]. Nā Tragœdia imitatur [Greek, illegible, ~4 letters], non autem [Greek, illegible, ~4 letters], non tantum eo sensu, quo iam diximus, sed etiā ea significatione, qua [Greek, illegible, ~3 letters] omne, id est, quod [Greek, illegible, ~4 letters] splendidum & regale est [Greek, illegible, ~3 letters] vero est vulgus, & exponūt apud Homerū Interpretes [Greek, illegible, ~4 letters]. Incōpositus autē fuit olim Tragicorū Chorus præ personarū multitudine, e quibus constituebatur. Quinquaginta fuisse testantur veteres: sed coractior factus est, & quindecim tantū personarum ex hac Lege: Τὸν Τραγικὸν Χορὸν σώων [?] | Tragicorum Chorus e quindecim personis constituitur.
units.tr: When these lines were delivered in Euripides' tragedy, the whole people rose up together in one rush to applaud and to sing along, until Euripides himself leapt into the middle and asked them to wait and see what harsh end the admirer would meet. In that play Bellerophon pays the penalty, which each man pays in his own way. For here Bellerophon, proud and haughty because of his prosperous successes, with a great mass of wealth and a kingdom, rages impiously against the gods. To this belong the words read from this drama in Justin Martyr's On Monarchy, which commend wealth, and to this points the fragment that Seneca translated. For these are the words of one who, otherwise invincible against Venus, yields and is broken in spirit on account of riches. Therefore let the illustrious Lipsius cease to wonder what this has to do with gold. For, puffed up by his wealth, he aspires to heaven. But Jupiter, stirred to anger, shakes him off and hurls him down as he flies up thus on Pegasus, so that he breaks his leg and falls from his kingdom. See Aristophanes' Frogs and its scholiast, and likewise Eustathius on Iliad Z. Yet this is the [illegible] of this drama. Yet from these, each man had something from which to take an example for himself and become better, especially since these things befall men of the first rank, for such men are brought onto the stage in tragedies. Hence, when the Thirty Tyrants raged against the Athenians and the leading men of the state were removed, Socrates taught Antisthenes that there was no reason for a man of humble condition to envy princely men, if we consider what ends the Atreidae, Thyestes, Agamemnon and Aegisthus meet in the tragedies. Yet none of the tragic poets made a man of the common people die on stage. Aelianus, Varia, Lib. II. c. XI., has reported this, but the text is now printed differently from the old reading, and I restore it. For tragedy imitates the noble, not the base, not only in the sense we have already mentioned, but also in that meaning by which the noble is everything splendid and regal, whereas the common people are the opposite; and the interpreters of Homer explain it so. The chorus of the tragedians was formerly unfixed in number because of the multitude of characters from which it was made up. The ancients testify that there were fifty; but it was made more restrained, and by this law the tragic chorus is constituted of fifteen persons.

units.la: Lex ista lata est occasione Eumenidū fabulæ, quam docuit Aeschylus Pollux Lib. IV. c. XV. [Greek, illegible, ~20 letters] Commode igitur intelligendus Aristoteles, qui Aeschylū huius instituti auctorem laudat Lib. de Poetica cap. IV. [Greek, illegible, ~10 letters]. Imo potius causam dedit ferendæ huius Legis Aeschylus, non ipse tulit, nisi forte dicam ipsum etiā Aeschylū suo prætiuisse exemplo, qui in sua Agamemnone e quindecim tantū personis Chorū constituit, qui numerus Lege ista fit postea constitutus. Referunt Scholia Aristophanis ad Equites: [Greek, illegible, ~6 letters] Τραγικὸς Χορὸς εἰκὼν ὡς Αἰσχύλος Ἀγαμέμνων. Neq; idem tamen numerus vsurpatus postea ab eodem Aeschylo in constituendo Choro: Nam cum Eumenidas docuit Aeschylus, Furias in scenam tanto numero, erat enim Chorus constitutus e quinquaginta personis, adeo horribili ornatu induxit, ut populum vniuersum terror inuaderet, pueri e pauore exanimarentur, grauidæ mulieres abortum facerent; habes in laudatis Pollucis verbis, & testatur Auctor vitæ Aeschyli: [Greek, illegible, ~30 letters]. Agamemnonem autem in scenam produxit Aeschylus ante Eumenidas, quanquam eodem anno, nam utraque fabula erat in Tetralogia, quæ Oresteia dicebatur. Docent veteres Didascaliæ in Agamemnonis Argumento, ut mittam ea, quæ ex illis referuntur ab Aristophanis Interprete ad Ranas: ἐλλάξῃ ὃ ἁρμόττει ἐπί Ἀργότης Φιλοκλέους, Ὀλυμπιάδι εἰκάζῃ ὀγδόῃ, ἐπὶ δεκάτῳ, ἐπὶ Αἰσχύλος Ἀγαμέμνων, Χοηφόροις, Εὐμενίσι, Πρωτεῖ, Σατυρικῷ, ἐργαστῆ ξενοκλῆς Ἀφιδνάι. Annus erat secundus Olympiadis, non XXVIII. sed octuagesimae, Philocle Athenis Praetore, cum commissa est ab Æschylo Oresteia Tetralogia, itaq; referendum est, Ὀλυμπιάδι ὀγδόῃ. Unde colligimus novam istam Legem, qua personarum, e quibus Chorus constituebatur, numerus contractior factus est, & sancitum, ne plures essent quindecim, latam fuisse anno sequenti. Chorus autem hic Tragicus personarum quindecim in quinque iuga distribuebatur, tres scilicet personae in singula iuga; aut in tres ordines, quorum unicuique quinque adscribebantur personae: Atque ubi in scenam prodibat Chorus, tres nonnunquam ex illo prodibant, aliquando quinque, est & ubi una tantum persona. Pollux loco laudato: μίρη δὲ χορεῖ, τρίχες, ζυγὸς. καὶ τεταγμένοι μὲν χορεῖ, ζυγὰ πίντε ἐκ τεσσάρων, καὶ τρίχει τρεῖς ἐκ πέντε πεντηκοντάκις ὅ ὑπὸ ὁ χορὸς. καὶ τρεῖς τρεῖς μὲν εἰσέσθω, εἰ δὲ ζυγὰ γίγνοιτο ἡ πάσῃ δὸς. εἰ δὲ τρεῖς τρίχες, αὐ πίντε εἰσέσθω. ἐὰν ἐπὶ δὲ καὶ καὶ ἑνὶ ἐπιούσῃ τῷ πάσῃ. Ex his illustranda atque emendanda sunt Ciceronis verba in Epistola ad Trebatium, quae est VI. Libri VII. Hoc tibi tam ignoscemus nos amici, quam ignouerunt Medea, quae Corinthum arcem altam habebant, matronae opulentae, optimates: quibus illa manibus gypsatissimis persuasit, ne sibi vitio illae verterent, quod abesset a patria: Nam multi iustam rem bene gessere, & publicam, patria procul. Multi, qui domi aetatem agerent, propterea sunt improbati. Quid hic est, manibus gypsatissimis? Notavit vir doctus ad editionem principem talem glossam: id est, fugitivus, improbissimus. Gypsati enim de catasta venalicij. Talis & Medea fugitiva erat patris & patriae proditrix. Sed quid illa de cretatis sive gypsatis in catasta venalicij, ad Medeam? Numquid illa inter venalicios? Non certe unquam. Inter feminas Tragicas optimates censebantur anus illae, quas πολιὰς κατακόμους nominant Graeci, quibus cani erant crines, & totae nitebant candebantque, unde etiam olim [?] nomen invenerunt. Pollux Lib.IV.cap.XIX. τὰ ὃ ἡ γυναικὶ ... πολιὰ κατακόμως, γεραιὰ ἐλαφρῶς, &c. ἰ μὲν πολιὰ κατακόμως, ἔχη ταῖς ἄλλαις τῷ τε ηλικίᾳ καὶ τῷ ἀξιώσει, λευκόκομος, μετὰ τ' ὄρκον, ὑπωχρὸς. πάλαι δὲ ... χρώμως ἐκαλεῖτο. Hinc illustrandus & emaculandus M.Tullius. Chorus in hac Tragoedia est mulierum Corinthiarum, id est, matronarum opulentarum, optimatum, ut loquitur Cicero; quare plerasque fuerunt inter illas πολιαὶ κατακόμαι, certe eae quas compellat Medea, & quae tunc in scenam prodierant: Videntur autem καὶ ζυγὸν prodiisse, ac proinde tres tantum, idque scripserat Cicero, sed numerales notae loco fuerunt corrumpendo: Olim ita scriptum; quibus illa iii anibus gypsatissimis: quod cum sequentes librarij non intelligerent, pessimo exemplo e numerali nota III id est, tribus, literam m fecerunt, quod erat in procliui. Quare autem hę tres anus dicatur gypsatissima, facile est demonstrare e laudatis Pollucis verbis: nam hae anus non tantum erant canis capillis λευκόκομοι, sed etiam [?], & totę cădebăr. Quod vero attinet ad verba Medeae, desupta sunt e dramate, quod Euripidis nomen praefert, nec male reddita sunt a Latino Poeta, aut praeter Graeci mentem. Quanquam enim prima fronte videatur Medea hoc tantum dicere, se ex aedibus prodiisse, attamen, si quis attedat,
units.tr: This law was passed on the occasion of the Eumenides, the play Aeschylus produced (Pollux, Book IV, ch. XV) [Greek, illegible]. Aristotle, who praises Aeschylus as the author of this practice in the Poetics, ch. IV [Greek, illegible], is therefore rightly understood here. Indeed, Aeschylus gave the occasion for enacting this law rather than enacting it himself, unless perhaps one should say that Aeschylus himself set the precedent by his own example, since in his Agamemnon he made the chorus fifteen persons only, a number later fixed by this law. The scholia of Aristophanes on the Knights report: [Greek, illegible] "The tragic chorus is fifteen persons, as in Aeschylus' Agamemnon." The same number was not, however, used by Aeschylus himself later in constituting a chorus. For when he produced the Eumenides, he brought the Furies onto the stage in a number of fifty, for the chorus then consisted of fifty persons, and he dressed them in such a horrifying costume that terror seized the whole people, boys were frightened to death, and pregnant women miscarried. You have this in the words of Pollux cited above, and the author of the life of Aeschylus bears witness to it: [Greek, illegible]. Aeschylus produced the Agamemnon before the Eumenides, though in the same year, for both plays belonged to the tetralogy called the Oresteia. The ancient Didascaliae teach this in the argument to the Agamemnon, to say nothing of what is reported from them by the interpreter of Aristophanes on the Frogs: [Greek, illegible: "...in the archonship of Philocles, in the eighty-first(?) Olympiad, in the tenth(?) year, when Aeschylus' Agamemnon, Choephori, Eumenides, Proteus, satyr play, and Xenocles' Aphidnae were produced."] The year was the second of the Olympiad, not the twenty-eighth but the eightieth, when Philocles was archon at Athens and Aeschylus' Oresteia tetralogy was staged; so it must be read as "the eightieth Olympiad." From this we gather that this new law, by which the number of persons constituting the chorus was reduced, and by which it was enacted that there should be no more than fifteen, was passed in the following year. This tragic chorus of fifteen persons was divided into five groups, namely three persons to each group, or into three ranks, each of which was assigned five persons. When the chorus came on stage, sometimes three came forward from it, sometimes five, and sometimes only one person. Pollux, in the passage cited: [Greek, garbled: "The chorus is divided into 'files' and 'yokes'; the yokes are arranged five by four, and the files three by five...; if the yokes are three, let them come in threes, and if five, let five come in; if one file, one."] From these words the words of Cicero in his letter to Trebatius, Book VII, letter VI, must be explained and corrected: "You will forgive me, as friends forgive, just as the matrons and wealthy nobles of Corinth forgave Medea, who held the lofty citadel of Corinth, when with her most plastered hands she persuaded them not to blame her for being away from her country. For many have carried on just and public affairs far from their country, and many who lived at home have been condemned for that very reason." What are "manibus gypsatissimis"? A learned man, in his note on the first edition, offered this gloss: that is, "fugitive, most wicked." For the plastered ones were from the slave-auction block. And Medea was such a fugitive, a betrayer of her father and her country. But what has the chalked or plastered ones on the slave-block to do with Medea? Surely she was not among the slaves for sale? Certainly never. Among the tragic women, those old women were counted as nobles whom the Greeks call polias katakomous, whose hair was white and who shone and glistened all over, whence they also at one time found the name [illegible]. Pollux, Book IV, ch. XIX: [Greek, "...grey-haired, with white hair arranged, old and lightly ... [illegible]..."] Thus Marcus Tullius is to be illustrated and emended by this. The chorus in this tragedy is of Corinthian women, that is, wealthy matrons and nobles, as Cicero calls them; so most of them were polias katakomai, certainly those whom Medea addresses and who had then come on stage. They seem to have come out as a yoke or a file, and so only three; and Cicero had written this, but numeral signs were corrupted in place of words. Originally it was written: "quibus illa iii anibus gypsatissimis" ("with three most plastered old women"). When the later copyists did not understand this, through a very bad error they turned the numeral sign III, that is tribus ("three"), into the letter m, which was an easy slip. Why these three old women are called most plastered is easy to show from the words of Pollux cited above: for these old women were not only white-haired [Greek], but also [illegible], and shone all over. As for Medea's words, they are taken from the drama which bears Euripides' name, and they are not badly rendered by the Latin poet nor contrary to the sense of the Greek. For although at first sight Medea seems to say only that she has come out of the house, yet if anyone attends to what follows, [illegible] he will see that Medea is also at pains that they should not hold it against her that she was away from her country. But the passage must be read and punctuated thus:

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] sequentia, videbit & id satagere Medeam, ne sibi vitio verterent, quod abesset à patria. Sed locus ita est legendus, atque interpungendus:
units.tr: [illegible] the following words, he will see that Medea is also at pains that they should not hold it against her that she was away from her country. But the passage must be read and punctuated thus:

units.la: Κοειλίας γυναῖκες, ἐξῆλθον δῆμον· Μὴ μοι ἃ μέμνησαι· οἷα γὰρ πολλοὶ βροτῶν Σεμνοὺς γελῶσας τοὺς μὲν ὀμμάτων ἄπο. Τοῖς δ' ἐν ξυγγείοις οἶσι, ἀφ' ἡσύχου ποδὸς Δυσκλέας ἐκ πόδων τε καὶ ῥᾳθυμίας.[?]
units.tr: Women of Corinth, I have come out of the house; do not blame me. For, as I see, many mortals have been reputed respectable, some because of their eyes' lack of exposure, others who, in their private lives, have lived quietly and without ambition, have been thought ill of through their idleness. [Greek: "Κοειλίας γυναῖκες, ἐξῆλθον δῆμον· Μὴ μοι ἃ μέμνησαι· οἷα γὰρ πολλοὶ βροτῶν Σεμνοὺς γελῶσας τοὺς μὲν ὀμμάτων ἄπο. Τοῖς δ' ἐν ξυγγείοις οἶσι, ἀφ' ἡσύχου ποδὸς Δυσκλέας ἐκ πόδων τε καὶ ῥᾳθυμίας."]

units.la: Honorem haberi voluit Lycurgus Rhetor Poetis Tragicis, Æschylo, Sophocli, & Euripidi hac Lege lata:
units.tr: Lycurgus the orator wished honour to be paid to the tragic poets Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, by a law which he passed:

units.la: Τὰς Τραγῳδίας τῶν ποιητῶν, Αἰσχύλου, Σοφο- κλέους, Εὐριπίδου, † Γραμματεία τῆς πόλεως [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀναγινώσκειν, ὡς ὑποχρινομένοις οὐκ ἐξ- εναι αὐτὰς ὑποχρίνεσθαι.[?]
units.tr: [Greek: "Τὰς Τραγῳδίας τῶν ποιητῶν, Αἰσχύλου, Σοφοκλέους, Εὐριπίδου, Γραμματεία τῆς πόλεως [illegible] ἀναγινώσκειν, ὡς ὑποκρινομένοις οὐκ ἐξεῖναι αὐτὰς ὑποκρίνεσθαι."] The tragedies of the poets Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides are to be read aloud by the city's clerk, since it is not permitted for actors to perform them.

units.la: Æschyli, Sophoclis, & Euripidis Tragedias Vrbis Scriba publice prae- legio: Histriones eas ne agunto.
units.tr: Let the city's clerk publicly read the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides: let actors not perform them.

units.la: Statuas his Poetis statui iussit Lycurgus, eorumque Tragœdias publice asseruari, & Lege cauit ne quis eas histrio doceret, sed vt publice ab Vrbis Scriba recitarentur. Plutarchus in Lycurgi vita: εἰσώθει δὲ καὶ τὸ νόμων, ὡς χαλκᾶς εἰκόνας ἀναστῆναι τῶν ποιητῶν, Αἰσχύλου, Σοφοκλέους, Εὐριπίδου, καὶ ἃς τραγῳδίας αὐτῶν ἐν κοινῷ γραμματείῳ φυλάττειν, καὶ τὴν γραμματεία τῆς πόλεως ἀναγινώσκειν. ὡς ὑποχρινομένοις οὐκ ἐξεῖναι γὰρ αὐτὰς ὑποχρίνεσθαι. Statuarum quae his tribus Poetis in Theatro positae sunt, meminit Paulanias in Atticis: εἰσὶ δὲ Ἀθηναίοις εἰκόνες ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ καὶ Τραγῳδίας καὶ Κωμῳδίας ποιητῶν. Τραγῳδίας δὲ χαίτην τῶν φανερὰ Εὐριπίδης καὶ Σοφοκλῆς. πρὸς γὰρ εἰκόνα τῆ Αἰσχύλου, πολλῷ πύργῳ τῆς πλάτης δοκεῖ ποιητὴν, καὶ τῆς γραφῆς, ἐν ὅ ἔργον ἐχ ὃ ἐν Μαρα̃θῶν. Existimat Vir Cl. excidisse nomen Æschyli, esseque reponendum: Τραγῳδίας δὲ χαίτην τῶν φανερὰ Αἰσχύλες, Εὐριπίδης, ἡ Σοφοκλῆς. Sed nihil esse addendum arguunt sequentia, quia satis indicat statuam ibidem positam Æschylo, cum suum de ea iudicium exponat. Neque item mutilum esse Harpocrationem putem in his: Φιλῖνος δὲ ἐν τῇ πόλει Σοφοκλέους καὶ Εὐριπίδου εἰκόνας, (ita optime restituit Vir Amplissimus & eruditissimus Maussacus noster) πρὸς Εὐβούλου λέγων. Cl. Meursius reponit, ἐν τῇ πόλει Αἰσχύλου, καὶ Σοφοκλέους, καὶ Εὐριπίδου εἰκόνας. Quia, inquit, Lycurgus legem tulit, vt Æschylo, Sophocli, & Euripidi æneæ statuæ ponerentur. Ego verò nullus dubito hanc rationem non adeo firmam esse, vt ei sit standum.
units.tr: Lycurgus ordered statues to be erected to these poets, and ordered their tragedies to be preserved publicly, and by law he provided that no actor should stage them, but that they should be recited publicly by the city's clerk. Plutarch in the Life of Lycurgus: [Greek: "He also proposed a decree that bronze statues of the poets Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides be erected, and that their tragedies be kept in the public archive, and that the city's clerk read them aloud, since actors were not permitted to perform them."] Pausanias in the Attica mentions the statues of these three poets set up in the theatre: [Greek: "The Athenians have images in the agora of the tragic and comic poets. Of the tragic poets, the best known are Euripides and Sophocles; for the statue of Aeschylus, it seems to me, is ..."] The learned man thinks the name of Aeschylus has dropped out and must be restored: "Of the tragic poets the best known are Aeschylus, Euripides or Sophocles." But the following words show that nothing needs to be added, since the passage already sufficiently indicates that a statue was set up there for Aeschylus, when he expresses his own judgement about it. Nor do I think Harpocration is defective in this: [Greek: "Philinus, in his work on the city, [mentions] the statues of Sophocles and Euripides" (so the most distinguished and learned Maussac, our friend, restored it), speaking against Eubulus.] The learned Meursius proposes [Greek: "the statues of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides in the city."] Because, he says, Lycurgus passed a law that bronze statues should be set up to Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides. But I have no doubt that this argument is not so firm that it must be accepted.

units.la: Quamuis enim Æschylo, non minus, quàm Sophocli & Euripidi, statua posita sit, auctore Lycurgo, quod vetat dicere neminem fuisse, qui huic Lycurgi siue Legi siue psephismati de ponenda Æschylo statua, aduersaretur, fuisse, quibus non placeret poni Sophocli atque Euripidi? In his fuit, meo iudicio, Philinus Rhetor, qui aduersus partem hanc Legis Lycurgi orationem habuit, inscriptam itaque πρὸς Σοφοκλέους καὶ Εὐριπίδου εἰκόνας. Nam quod ad Æschylum spectat, fuit suis Atheniensibus magno in pretio.Narrat Auctor Vitae eius Athenienses psephismate pretium posuisse arti illorum, qui Aeschyli fabulas docerent: Ἀθηναῖοι δὲ τοῦτον ἡγάπησαν Αἰσχύλον ὡς ἀφίεσθαι μὴ ἐκ ἠνάγκασαν αὐτὸ, τ' βυκλώσθων ἀδιδάσκει τὰ Αἰσχύλου, χρυσοῦ ἀμυνσαιδῆ. Huc facit Comicus Acharnensibus:
units.tr: For although a statue was set up to Aeschylus, no less than to Sophocles and Euripides, on the proposal of Lycurgus, must we not say that there were people who opposed the Lycurgan law, or the decree about setting up a statue of Aeschylus, and who did not want statues set up to Sophocles and Euripides? Among them was, in my judgment, the rhetorician Philinus, who delivered a speech against this part of Lycurgus' law, and it is therefore titled Against the statues of Sophocles and Euripides (πρὸς Σοφοκλέους καὶ Εὐριπίδου εἰκόνας). As for Aeschylus, he was held in great esteem by his own Athenians. The biographer of Aeschylus reports that the Athenians, by decree, fixed a reward for those who performed Aeschylus' plays: "The Athenians so loved Aeschylus that they did not allow his plays to be performed, but to be ... with gold for the one who performed them."

units.la: Οπε δὲ χαλκὸν πρὸς ἀδοχὴν τὸν Αἰσχύλον, Ο δ' αἰεὶ πιπη, εἴπαι' ὦ Θεόγνι τὸν ἔχεῖν.[?]
units.tr: Aristophanes in the Acharnians is relevant here: "When the bronze coin was [given] for the reception of Aeschylus, and the other one always falls, say, O Theognis, to hold it."

units.la: Ad quæ notant veteres Magistri: τιμῆς δὲ μεγίστης ἔτυχε παρὰ Ἀθηναίοις ὁ Αἰσχύλος. ἢ μόνου αὐτῶν τὰ δράματα ψηφίσματι κοινῷ ἢ μὴ ζῆν ἔτι διδάσκειν. Verum hoc quidem est, id primum datum fuisse uni Æschylo Athenien-sium plebiscito; postea Lycurgi Lege Æschyli, Sophoclis, Euripidisque Tragœdiæ histrionibus datæ non sunt agendæ, sed recitandæ ab Urbis Scriba. Sed quia hic sumus, illustranda sunt nonnulla quæ Sophoclis ætatem, numerumque dramatum eius spectant. Natum cum referunt anno secundo Olympiadis septuagesimæ primæ, Philippo Athenis Prætore. Anonymus in eius Vita: [?] Φασὶν ἐξεδημεῖν [?] Ὀλυμπιάδι, ἐπὶ δὲ Ἀρχίου Ἀθήνησι Φιλίππου. Habes quoque apud Anonymum in Descriptione Olympiadum ad hunc annum II. Olympiadis LXXI. Σοφοκλῆς ὁ τραγῳδοποιὸς ἐγεννήθη. Paria facit Diodorus Siculus Lib. XIII. nam denatum scribit anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimæ tertiæ, Callia Archonte, annos natum nonaginta: [?] τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον ἐπλεύτησε Σοφοκλῆς Σοφίλου, ποιητὴς τραγῳδιῶν, ἐτῶν βιώσας ἐννενήκοντα. Quare anno secundo Olympiadis septuagesimæ primæ, ab eo enim ad annum tertium Olympiadis nonagesimæ tertiæ, utrôque termino inclusô, interuallum est annorum nonaginta, adscribendus est Natalis Sophoclis è Diodori Siculi sententia. Alij tamen natum volebant anno tertio Olympiadis septuagesimæ tertiæ. Anonymus in Descriptione Olympiadum ad hunc annum, Σοφοκλῆς ἐγεννήθη κατὰ ὥρας. Suidas annum non adnotat, sed tamen in Olympiadem septuagesimam tertiam eius natalem conijcit. Σοφοκλῆς Σοφίλου, Κολωνῆθεν, Ἀθηναῖος, τραγικὸς, πρῶτος τῷ ογ'. Ὀλυμπιάδι. Quod ad mortem eius attinet, conferunt in annum tertium Olympiadis nonagesimæ tertiæ, Callia Athenis Prætore. Anonymus ad hunc annum in Descriptione Olympiadum. Σοφοκλῆς ἐν Εὐριπίδης οἱ τραγῳδοποιοὶ ἐπλεύτησαν. Idem habet Diodorus Siculus ad hunc annum Lib. XIII. ὡς δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον ἐπλεύτησε Σοφοκλῆς Σοφίλου, ποιητὴς τραγῳδιῶν, ἐτῶν βιώσας ἐννενήκοντα, ἰσχὺς δ' ἔχων ἀκμὴν [?]. Ἀπολλόδωρος δὲ, τῷ χρονικῷ συντάξει τραγῳδιῶν, φησὶ, ἐν τῶν Εὐριπίδου καὶ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐπιαυτὸν ἐπλεύτησε. Hunc quoque annum indicat Anonymus in Sophoclis Vita. Huicque anno adscribendam esse Sophoclis mortem unicè probat coætuus Poëta Aristophanes, qui Ranas, quo dramate testatur iam tum cum ista scriberet in viuis esse desisse Sophoclem, docuit hoc anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimæ tertiæ, Callia Athenis Prætore, post Antigenem, Lenæis Liberalibus. Eo dramate primore ista leguntur de Sophoclis obitu, quæ non sunt omittenda, ut à nobis illustrentur obiter atque emendentur. Δι. Τοιοῦτοί [?] με δαρδαλῶσι πόθος Εὐριπίδου, καὶ ζῶντα τῆς πτηνικοῦς. Κουδὲν γέ με δὴ πίστιν αἰδέσεσθαι, ὅμ' ἡ ἐπὶ Ἐλθὼν ἐπ' ἐκ ἐφόρου. ῥ. πόπερ, εἰς ἅδου κάτω; Δι. Καὶ γὰρ ἀμ' ἐγὼ. εἴ τί γ' ἔστιν ἐπὶ κατωτέρω. ῥ. Τί βούλόμενος; Δι. ἀξιῶ ποιητὴν δυσχερῆ, Οἱ μὲν γὰρ οὐκ ἔτ' εἰσὶν, οἱ δ' ὄντες κακοί. ῥ. Τί δ' οὐχ Ἰοφῶν ζῇ; Δι. τῶν γὰρ τι ἐ μόνοι Ἐτ' ἔτι λοιπὸς ἀγαθὸν εἰ καὶ τὴν τέχνην [?]
units.tr: The old scholiasts note on this: "Aeschylus enjoyed the highest honour among the Athenians; alone of them his plays were, by a common decree, to be performed even after his death." This is true, that this was first granted to Aeschylus alone by an Athenian plebiscite; later, by the law of Lycurgus, the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides were not to be acted by the players but recited by the city clerk. But since we are here, some points must be illustrated which concern the age of Sophocles and the number of his plays. They report his birth in the second year of the seventy-first Olympiad, when Philip was archon at Athens. The anonymous writer on his life says: "They say he was born in the Olympiad..., and in the archonship of Archias at Athens, Philip." You also have in the anonymous Description of the Olympiads, for this year, the second of the seventy-first Olympiad: "Sophocles the tragic poet was born." Diodorus Siculus agrees in Book XIII, for he writes that he died in the third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, in the archonship of Callias, at the age of ninety: "At the same time died Sophocles, son of Sophilus, the writer of tragedies, having lived ninety years." Therefore, since from the second year of the seventy-first Olympiad to the third year of the ninety-third, both ends included, is an interval of ninety years, the birth of Sophocles must be assigned to that year according to the opinion of Diodorus. Others, however, wanted him born in the third year of the seventy-third Olympiad. The anonymous Description of the Olympiads, for this year, says: "Sophocles was born in the hours (?)." Suidas does not note the year, but nonetheless conjectures his birth to be in the seventy-third Olympiad: "Sophocles, son of Sophilus, of Colonus, an Athenian, tragic poet, first in the ninetieth(?) Olympiad." As for his death, they agree on the third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, with Callias as the Athenian archon. The anonymous writer, for this year, in the Description of the Olympiads: "Sophocles and Euripides, the tragic poets, died." Diodorus Siculus has the same for this year in Book XIII: "At the same time died Sophocles, son of Sophilus, the writer of tragedies, having lived ninety years, still strong in his prime." Apollodorus, in his chronological work on tragedies, says that Euripides also died in that same year. The anonymous writer on the life of Sophocles also indicates this year. And that Sophocles' death must be assigned to this very year is proved beyond doubt by the contemporary poet Aristophanes, who in the Frogs*, a play in which he testifies that Sophocles had already ceased to live when he wrote it, produced it in the third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, with Callias as Athenian archon, after Antigenes, at the Lenaea of Dionysus. In this play, early on, there are words about the death of Sophocles which should not be omitted, so that they may be illustrated and corrected by us along the way. Dionysus: "Such longing for Euripides grips me, and [for him] while alive ..." Heracles: "Not that I would ever have respect for ... but for Euripides? ..." Dionysus: "I think a difficult poet..., for the ones who are no more, and the ones who are alive are bad." Heracles: "Why, is Iophon not alive?" Dionysus: "Of them alone, the only one left is good, if at least ... the art."

units.la: Οὐ γὰρ σαφῶς εἶδ', οὐδ' αὐτὸ τοῦθ' ὅπως ἔχει. Εἶτ' ἤχ' Σοφοκλέα [?] ὅτι Εὐριπίδου Μέλλῃς ἀλαζονεῖν, εἴπερ ἐχθρὸν δεῖ σ' ἀχθῆν; Οὐ, πρὶν γ' ἂν δὴ Ἰοφῶντ' ἀπολέσῃ αὐτὸν μόνον, Ἀνδ' Σοφοκλέος, ὅ, τί ποιῇ χαΐδονίσῳ. Κάλλως. ὁ μὲν γ' Εὐριπίδης πάνυ σοφὸς ὤν, Καὶ ξυναπολοῦσαί [?] δ' ἐπιχάρτως μοι. Ὁ δ' εὔχιλος μὲν οὐδ' ἀδήλως, εὔχολος δ' ἐκ [?].
units.tr: "For I did not clearly see, nor how that very thing stands." Then: "Are you going to boast about Sophocles, since Euripides ... if you must be hated? No, before he destroys Iophon alone, the son of Sophocles, what he does, I will tease with ... The one, Euripides, being very wise, and ... with pleasure for me. And the other, not without a clear ... good-tempered, but ..."

units.la: Horum versuum tertiusdecimus cum sequenti, vt quidem eduntur & interpunguntur, tenebris sunt offusi, sed facile est ex historia illustrare & emendare. Lego:
units.tr: Of these verses, the thirteenth together with the following, as they are printed and punctuated, are shrouded in darkness, but it is easy to illustrate and emend them from history. I read:

units.la: Οὐ, πρὶν γ' ἂν δὴ Ἰοφῶντ' ἀπολέσῃ αὐτὸν μόνον,
units.tr: "No, before he destroys Iophon alone [Iophon/ Iophontem] [Οὐ, πρὶν γ' ἂν δὴ Ἰοφῶντ' ἀπολέσῃ αὐτὸν μόνον,]"

units.la: Ἀ νδ' Σοφοκλέος, ὅ, τί ποιῇ, χαΐδονίσω.
units.tr: "the son of Sophocles, what he does, I will tease [Ἀνδ' Σοφοκλέος, ὅ, τί ποιῇ, χαΐδονίσω.]"

units.la: Oblique carpit Comicus Iophontem cum patre Sophocle: nam accusaverat patrem Iophon quasi desipientem apud iudices, vt à re familiari remouerent cum, sibique potestatem darent in eo, eiusque bonis; habes apud Ciceronem Lib. de Senectute. Scholiastem Comici ad hæc verba, itemque Anonymum in Sophoclis Vita. Suspicio autem erat Iophontem patris fabulas tanquam à se compositas in scenam producere. Ἰοφῶν ὣ ὡς Σοφοκλέους ἐκ Νικοφάνης ἐς δόκησιν προῆγεν, ὅτι τοῖς τῶ πατρὸς ἐχρῆτο ποιήμασιν ὡς οἰκείοις. Atque ex his quæsitus est Comico πατρικός. Caussam enim reddit Bacchus, quare ex inferis non educat Sophoclem, nam prius, inquit, Iophon mihi solus esset conueniendus, & explorandum, ἀ νδ' quid annueret: neque enim Sophocles ipse quicquam sine filii auctoritate, qui in eo tanquam desipiente ciusque bonis potestatem habebat, poterat polliceri, Σοφοκλέους ὅ, τί ποιῇ. Videtur prima fronte idem dicere, quid de Sophocle faceret, sed tamen alludit ad id quod Iophonti diximus obijci, nempe paterna dramata pro suis edere, quid faciat eorum, quæ sunt Sophoclis. Atque hinc factum puto partim, vt nonnulla quæ Sophoclis non sunt, Sophocli adscribantur dramata, de quorum numero paucis est iam disputandum. Primam suarum fabularum docuit Sophocles anno tertio Olympiadis septuagesimæ septimæ, Demotione Archonte, vt alibi diximus, & tunc primum Tetralogiam edidit, vt & alij Tragici, quo labore perterritus, ceteris insequentibus annis nonnisi vnum drama quorannis in scenam produxit: itaque Antigone quam commisit anno tertio Olympiadis octogesimæ quartæ, Diphilo Athenis Prætore, λέλεκτη δράμα τετραλογίαν [?], inquit Aristophanes Grammaticus, ordine est tricesimum secundum eorum dramatum quæ edidit Sophocles. Philoctetes eiusdem productus in scenam est anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimæ secundæ, Glaucippo Archonte. Anonymus in Argumento Philoctetæ: ἐδιδάχθη ὅτι Γλαυκίππου ἄρχοντος, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς. Postremum drama edidit paullo ante supremum suum diem: nam cum in commissione illius victor renunciatus esset, prægaudio animam efflavit. Anonymus in eius Vita: οἱ ὅ, ὅτι μὴ τὸ τῶ δράματος αἰσχύνειν, ὅτε νικῶν συκοφάντη, χαρᾷ νικηθεὶς ἐξέλιπε. Diodorus Siculus loco laudato. Φασὶ δὲ τὸν ἀνδρα τῶν τὸ ἐχάτου πεποιῆσθαι εἰσαγωγὴν ἢ νικήσαντα, χαρᾷ ἀπεπνίγη, ὅ ἐν πλέον τῆς αὐτοῦ ἀνεψύχησεν. Dramata eius recenset Suidas centum viginti tria, quanquam alij longe plura referant: ἐδίδαξε ὁ δράματα ρκγ. ὡς δέ τινες, ἢ πολλῷ πλείω. Anonymus in eius Vita numerat ex Aristophanis Grammatici sententia centum triginta: ἐγκαλεῖ ὁ, ὡς φησιν Ἀ[?]ριστοφάνης, δράματα ἑκατὸν τεσσαράκοντα. Sed numerum hunc corruptum esse suspicor, neque plura recensuisse, quam numeret Suidas, sed cum literis numeralibus scriptum esset, δράματα ρκγ. procliui lapsu mutauit in ρχλ. unde factum ἑκατοντατεσσαράκοντα. Verum tot fabulas non docuit Sophocles, si quidem singulis annis, si primum, quo docere coepit, excipias, vnum tantum drama commisit, quod, teste Suida, omnino verum est, & ex Antigones editione probatur. Quare cum anno tertio Olympiadis septuagesimae septimae Dionysiis docere coeperit, & anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimae tertiae fato sit functus, dicendum est docuisse tantum sexaginta sex dramata. Videbitur tamen nonnemini, plura, etiam e nostro calculo, adtribuenda esse dramata Sophocli, nempe sexaginta octo. Sed nos putamus produxisse tantum in scenam sexaginta sex: nam certe anno quarto Olympiadis octogesimae quartae, quo Strategus fuit, & praefuit bello Anaensi, non potuit rei musicae vacare, cum res Atheniensium bello tueretur, ita vt etiam, neque anno sequenti, qui primus est Olympiadis octogesimae quintae, potuerit drama in scenam producere; solenne enim illi fuit, vt mox dicemus, dramata sua edere quotannis Panathenaeis. Non igitur tot dramata edidit Sophocles, quot recensent Suidas & Anonymus in eius Vita: sed adscribunt illi fabulas minoris Sophoclis, qui eius fuit filius, siue, vt alij volunt, ex Aristone filio nepos, adscribunt, inquam, maiori Sophocli: Nam maior Sophocles dramata docuit sexaginta sex, vt iam diximus: minor vero produxit in scenam quadraginta: non desunt tamen qui minoris Sophoclis fabulas numerent quinquaginta & vnam, eltque hic numerus rescribendus. Suidas ; Σοφοκλῆς Αἰσχύλου, ἰωνὸς δὲ τῆς [?]ἀρχαιοτέρου Σοφοκλέους τῆς πρεσβυτέρου, Ἀθηναῖος, Τραγικὸς. ἐδίδαξε δὲ δράματα μ. οἱ δὲ φασιν ια. Rescribo: οἱ δὲ φασιν ια. Fiunt igitur in vniuersum vtriusque Sophoclis fabulae numero centum & sex. Adde septemdecim illas, quas spurias esse pronunciat Aristophanes Grammaticus, fiunt centum viginti tres. Anonymus in Sophoclis Vita è nostra emendatione. ἐγκαλεῖ ὁ, ὡς φησιν Ἀ[?]ριστοφάνης, δράματα ρκγ. Τοῦτον δὲ νοῦν[?] ἀκριβῶς. Quem fabularum numerum centum viginti trium habet Suidas, qui addit multo plures etiam a nonnullis numerari, ὡς δέ τινες πολλῷ πλείω. Nempe minori Sophocli adscribebant, non quadraginta tantum, sed quinquaginta & vnam: Ex illis vero, quas Iophon docuit, multas Sophocli patris esse volebant, atque ex his non tantum ille spuriarum septemdecim fabularum, quas obelo suo notauit & transfixit Aristophanes Grammaticus, numerus, sed etiam longe plurium conflabatur: nam Iophon docuit dramata quinquaginta, e quibus multa Sophoclis patris fuerunt. Suidas: Ἰοφῶν Ἀθηναῖος Τραγικὸς υἱὸς Σοφοκλέους τῆς πρεσβυτέρου γένος ἀπὸ Νικοστράτης. δράματα ὁ Ἰοφῶν ἐδίδαξε γ. ὧν ἐστιν Ἀχιλλεύς, Τήλεφος, Ἀκταίων, Ἰλίου πόρθησις, Δεξάμενος, Βάκχαι, Πενθεύς. καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ τῆς πατρὸς Σοφοκλέους. Diximus Sophoclem, vbi singulis annis vnum tantum drama in scenam produxit, ea docuisse Panathenaeis, quod maxime illustratur ex iis, quae de morte eius referunt Ister & Neanthes apud Anonymum in Sophoclis Vita: Τελευτῆσαι δὲ αὐτὸν Ἰσχυς καὶ Νεάνθης φασί τὸν τ' ἐξ τῶν. Κ[?]ηιππ[?]ίδης ἐν τ[?]ῳ ε[?]ὶ τὰ[?] πέμψαι ἀπὸ ἐρχ[?]ας ἐξ Ὀπωῶν ἥκοντα [?]ἀ[?]ὸ Ἰεὶ Χ[?]ὰ πέμψ[?]αι αὐτῷ γαῦλῶ · τὸν δ' Σοφοκλέα λεξοῖτα καὶ βαλδύιτα ρ[?]ά ἐπὶ ὀμφαχίζοντ[?] εἰς ὃ σῶμα, ὑπὸ τὸ ἀ[?]ῆν [?]ήρως ἀπο[?]ιῶνα τελευτῆσαι. Corruptus est hic locus; nam, ut editur, mortuus est Choum festo, sive Liberalibus Anthesteriis, atque tunc nullae sunt uvae, nisi passae forte, non autem acerbae. Callippides autem Sophocli attulerat uvas nondum plane maturas, sed pubescentes, & adhuc acerbas. Quare Sophocles obiit paullo ante vindemiam, uvis pubescentibus. Adde quod periit Sophocles, Callia Archonte, anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimae tertiae, antequam Ranas doceret Aristophanes. Ranas autem edidit Comicus hoc ipso anno Lenaeis Liberalibus: ergo non abiit in communem locum Choum festo, quod sequebatur Lenaea Liberalia. Sed rescribendum est, ὁ δ' ἐν τοῖς χοαῖς, id est, inter ipsas mensas secundas, cum libaretur. Anno hoc tertio Olympiadis nonagesimae tertiae, Callia Archonte, cum celebrarentur maiora Panathenaea mense Hecatombaeone, postremum hoc suum drama commisit Sophocles, victorque renunciatus est, ea de causa correptum gaudio expirasse volunt nonnulli, sed Ister atque Neanthes paullo aliter referunt: scilicet victor Sophocles convivio, ut moris erat, excepit amicos, cum autem appositae essent mensae secundae, commodum Callippides uvas dono misit Sophocli, quarum acinis adhuc acerbis suffocatus est. Optime tempus convenit. Erat annus quintus Octaeteridis Harpalcae, cuius Gamelion cepit decimo octavo Kalendas Ianuarias anno secundo Olympiadis nonagesimae tertiae, Hecatombaeon vero cepit quarto Eidus Iulias, ineunte anno tertio eiusdem Olympiadis nonagesimae tertiae. Circa medium Hecatombaeonem celebrata sunt Panathenaea, id est, extremo fere mense Iulio. Quod si iam tum vsurpabatur Enneadecaeteris Metonica, erat annus illius octauus, cuius Hecatombaeon coepit quarto Kalendas Iulij: ergo Panathenaea peracta sunt circa medium mensem Iulium: paullo post celebratum est a Sophocle convivium, quo ex dono Callippidis appositae sunt uvae, quas nil mirum per anni tempestatem fuisse adhuc acerbiusculas. Postea fabulae Aeschyli, permittente populo, correctae a posterioribus Poetis in scenam productae sunt. Quintilianus Lib. X. Sed rudis in plerisque & incompositus Aeschylus, propter quod correctas eius fabulas in certamen deferre posterioribus Poetis Athenienses permisere: suntque eo modo multi coronati.
units.tr: The comic poet mocks Iophon obliquely, together with his father Sophocles. Iophon had accused his father before the judges as a man out of his mind, so that they would remove him from the management of his property and give Iophon power over him and his goods. You have this in Cicero, On Old Age. See the scholiast on the comic poet at these words, and likewise the anonymous writer in the Life of Sophocles. There was, however, a suspicion that Iophon was staging his father's plays as if they were his own. The Greek scholiast says that Iophon used his father's poems as his own [Ἰοφῶν ... ὡς οἰκείοις], and from this the comic poet's allusion to the father is drawn [πατρικός]. For Bacchus gives the reason why he does not bring Sophocles back from the dead: first, he says, he must meet Iophon alone and find out what he will agree to, "what Sophocles is doing" [Σοφοκλέους ὅ, τί ποιῇ], since Sophocles himself could promise nothing without the consent of his son, who had power over him as a man out of his mind and over his goods. At first sight the line seems to mean only what Sophocles is doing, but it alludes to what we said Iophon was charged with, namely producing his father's dramas as his own, and so asks what he is doing with the works that belong to Sophocles. I think this is partly why some plays that are not Sophocles' are ascribed to him, and I must now discuss their number briefly. Sophocles first produced his plays in the third year of the seventy-seventh Olympiad, in the archonship of Demotion, as we said elsewhere, and then for the first time he put on a tetralogy, as the other tragic poets did. Frightened by this labour, in the following years he produced only one drama each year. Thus the Antigone, which he staged in the third year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad, when Diphilus was praetor at Athens, is, according to the grammarian Aristophanes, the thirty-second in order of the dramas Sophocles produced. His Philoctetes was staged in the third year of the ninety-second Olympiad, in the archonship of Glaucippus. The anonymous writer on the argument of the Philoctetes says it was produced under Glaucippus, the archon. He produced his last drama shortly before his final day, for when he was declared victor in the contest he died of excessive joy. The anonymous writer in his Life says: "Some say that he died from joy when he was declared victor, because the play was not disgraceful" [ἐξέλιπε]. Diodorus Siculus, in the passage cited, says: "They say that the man, having brought out his last play, died of joy on winning, and breathed out his soul in that moment." His dramas, Suidas lists as one hundred and twenty-three, though others report far more: "He produced 123 dramas, though some say many more" [ἐδίδαξε δράματα ρκγ. ὡς δέ τινες, ἢ πολλῷ πλείω]. The anonymous writer in his Life, following the opinion of the grammarian Aristophanes, counts one hundred and forty: "he is charged with one hundred and forty dramas, as Aristophanes says" [ἐγκαλεῖ ... δράματα ἑκατὸν τεσσαράκοντα]. I suspect, however, that this number is corrupt, and that it does not list more than Suidas does, but that when the numerals were written as letters, δράματα ρκγ, it was easily altered to ρχλ, whence came "one hundred and forty." Yet Sophocles did not produce so many plays, since, if you except the first year in which he began to produce, he put on only one drama each year, as Suidas also attests, and as the edition of the Antigone confirms. So, since he began to produce at the Dionysia in the third year of the seventy-seventh Olympiad and died in the third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, we must say that he produced only sixty-six dramas. Some will think that more should be assigned to Sophocles even on our reckoning, namely sixty-eight. But I think he brought only sixty-six on the stage. In the fourth year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad, when he was general and commanded in the war against Samos, he could not have been free for the art of music, since he was defending the affairs of the Athenians in war. Nor could he have produced a drama in the following year, which is the first of the eighty-fifth Olympiad, since, as we shall say shortly, it was his custom to produce his dramas every year at the Panathenaea. Therefore Sophocles did not produce as many dramas as Suidas and the anonymous writer in his Life list. Rather, they ascribe to him the plays of the younger Sophocles, who was his son, or, as others want, his grandson through Ariston his son. I say they ascribe them to the elder Sophocles. For the elder Sophocles produced sixty-six dramas, as we have said. The younger produced forty, but there are those who count fifty-one of the younger Sophocles' plays, and this number must be restored. Suidas: "Sophocles, son of Aeschylus, of the elder Sophocles' lineage, an Athenian, tragic poet. He produced forty dramas; others say eleven." I restore: "others say eleven." So altogether the plays of both Sophocles come to one hundred and six. Add the seventeen that the grammarian Aristophanes declares spurious, and you get one hundred and twenty-three. The anonymous writer in the Life of Sophocles, corrected by my emendation, says: "he is charged with one hundred and twenty-three dramas, as Aristophanes says" [ἐγκαλεῖ ... δράματα ρκγ]. This is the number of one hundred and twenty-three plays that Suidas has, and he adds that some count far more: "as some say, much more" [ὡς δέ τινες πολλῷ πλείω]. Indeed, they ascribed to the younger Sophocles not forty only but fifty-one. From the plays Iophon produced, many were claimed to be the elder Sophocles'. From these came not only the number of the seventeen spurious plays, which the grammarian Aristophanes marked with his obelus and pierced, but also a far greater number. For Iophon produced fifty dramas, many of which were his father Sophocles'. Suidas: "Iophon, Athenian tragic poet, son of the elder Sophocles, his mother being Nicostrate. Iophon produced three dramas. Among them are Achilles, Telephus, Actaeon, The Sack of Troy, Dexamenus, The Bacchae, Pentheus, and some others of his father Sophocles." I said that Sophocles, when he produced only one drama a year, staged those plays at the Panathenaea. This is best illustrated by what Ister and Neanthes report about his death, in the Anonymous writer's Life of Sophocles: "Ister and Neanthes say that he died in this way..." The text here is corrupt. As it reads, he died at the Choes festival, or the Liberal Anthesteria, and at that time there are no grapes, unless perhaps dried ones, not unripe ones. But Callippides had brought Sophocles grapes that were not yet fully ripe, but still growing and sour. So Sophocles died shortly before the vintage, when the grapes were only swelling. Add that Sophocles died in the archonship of Callias, in the third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, before Aristophanes produced the Frogs. The comic poet produced the Frogs in the same year at the Lenaea, the Liberal festival. So he did not die at the general Choes, which was followed by the Lenaean Liberalia. But the reading must be restored as: "while he was at the Choes" [ὁ δ' ἐν τοῖς χοαῖς], that is, during the second course itself, while libations were being poured. In this third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, in the archonship of Callias, when the Greater Panathenaea were celebrated in the month Hecatombaeon, Sophocles put on his last drama and was declared victor. For this reason some say he died overcome with joy, but Ister and Neanthes report it rather differently: namely, that the victorious Sophocles entertained his friends at a banquet, as was customary, and when the second course had been served, Callippides happened to send Sophocles grapes as a gift, and he choked on their still-sour berries. The time fits perfectly. It was the fifth year of the Octaeteris of Harpalcus, whose Gamelion began on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January in the second year of the ninety-third Olympiad, while Hecatombaeon began on the fourth day before the Ides of July, at the start of the third year of the same ninety-third Olympiad. The Panathenaea were celebrated around the middle of Hecatombaeon, that is, at about the end of July. If the Metonic Enneadecaeteris was already in use, it was its eighth year, whose Hecatombaeon began on the fourth day before the Kalends of July. So the Panathenaea were finished around the middle of July, and shortly afterwards Sophocles gave the banquet at which the grapes sent by Callippides were served, which is no wonder, since in that season of the year they were still rather sour. Afterwards the plays of Aeschylus, with the people's permission, were revised by later poets and staged. Quintilian, Book X: "But Aeschylus was rough and unpolished in most respects, for which reason the Athenians allowed later poets to bring his revised plays to competition, and in this way many were crowned."

units.la: Institutum primum fuit anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimae tertiae, Archonte Athenis Callia, qui in Praetura excepit Antigonem, ut Anthesteria Dionysia celebrarentur agone Comicorum. Scribit Aristoteles apud Graecum Aristophanis Interpretem ad haec Comici verba Ranis: Σὺ γὰρ καταχέαι[?] ὁμῶ[?] ὅπ[?]ι ᾄσ[?]ει Κα[?]τ' ἀ[?]ππελεῖα, τὸν δὲ[?] Τὸν σαμδαλίσκην καὶ ὃ ῥάκος.
units.tr: This was first instituted in the third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, when Callias was archon at Athens. He succeeded Antigones in the praetorship, so that the Anthesteria and the Dionysia might be celebrated with a contest of comic poets. Aristotle, in the Greek commentary of Aristophanes' interpreter on these words of the comic poet in the Frogs, writes: "For you will pour... [Σὺ γὰρ καταχέαι ὁμῶ ὅπ ᾄσει Κατ' ἀππελεῖα, τὸν δὲ Τὸν σαμδαλίσκην καὶ ὃ ῥάκος]."

units.la: Εοικε ὁ Ἀρεμφάνης ὅτι ἦδν λιτὰς ἐχρήσατο πρὸς πεπτὰς. ὅτι χωὶ τῆς Καλλίου τοῦ πότου φησὶν Ἀειστὰλης, ὅτι σιώδυο ἐδέξε χορηγῶν τε Διονύσια τῆς Τραγῳδῆς καὶ Κωμῳδῆς. ὥστε τῷ τις καὶ ἀπέξ[?]ε τὸν Λεωϊκὸν συσολὴ χορηγῶ. δ' οὐ πολλοὶ ὑπερ ἀπέσας τὰς χορηγίας ἀπειλὴ Κωπαί. Hic ὁ σιῶδυο referendum esse ad Dionysia non autem ad Choragos qui sumptus facerent, dubium esse non potest: nam si duo, non autem unus tantum, sumptus fecissent, nullus poterat esse metus fore; ut progressu temporis non ita splendide Lenaici Comicorum Ludi celebrarentur; imo contra spes fuisset fore splendidiores, cum duo essent collaturi in sumptus, quos antea unus tantum faciebat. Quod igitur metuebant, ne progressu temporis Lenaici Ludi aeque atque antea splendidi forent, hinc fiebat: quod Dionysia Anthesteria, quae antea non celebrabantur editione Comoediarum, essent in posterum celebranda: unde oportebat colligere, cum hi sumptus de nouo essent accessuri, illos iri minutum, qui fiebant in celebrandis Lenaicis ludis, nam non tanta habebatur ratio Lenaicorum, quam Dionysiorum Διονυσίων ἐν ἄστει[?], aut Panathenaicorum, quibus intererant tota Graecia populi. De Dionysiis autem Anthesteriis hic agi, vel hinc liquet, quod diu ante & post Calliam Praetorem, ut constat ex historia Attica, Διονύσοις τῆς κατ' ἄστυ[?], καὶ τῆς κατ' ἀγροῖς[?], sive Lenaeis, exhibitae sint populo Comoediae: At vero tunc primum Callia post Antigenem Archontem Anthesteriis Liberalibus. Sed paullo post mutauit hic mos, neque amplius datae sunt Comoediae Anthesterijs Liberalibus, cum progressu temporis fieret, ut pauci docerent, Cinesia ea de re populum rogante. Aristoteles verbis laudatis, quae ita emendabis: ἀπ' οὗ (χρόνου) πολλοὶ ὑστέρων[?], καὶ τὰ [?] τῆς χορηγίας [?] Κινησίας[?]. Cinesias hic Aristophanis erat aequalis, cuius passim meminit. Sustulit autem quae addita de nouo, nempe editionem Comoediarum Liberalibus Anthesterijs: atque hinc intelligi debet idem Scholiastes ad hanc ipsam fabulam: ὁ Κινησίας [?] τὴν Κωμικὴν, ὡς εἶτα ἀχρήστως[?]. Tandem obsoletum hunc morem Lycurgus Rhetor renouauit, Legemque hanc tulit.
units.tr: Aristophanes seems to have used the word "lit" for "bold" [Εοικε ὁ Ἀρεμφάνης ὅτι ἦδν λιτὰς ἐχρήσατο πρὸς πεπτὰς]. Aristotle says that in the time of Callias the drinker, two were admitted as choregoi of the tragic and comic Dionysia [ὅτι σιώδυο ἐδέξε χορηγῶν τε Διονύσια τῆς Τραγῳδῆς καὶ Κωμῳδῆς], so that someone could be appointed to bear the expense of the Lenaean festival, though few ... [ἀπέξε τὸν Λεωϊκὸν συσολὴ χορηγῶ]. There can be no doubt that this "two" refers to the Dionysia, not to the Choragoi who bore the expense. For if two, and not just one, had borne the expense, there could have been no fear; the fear was that, as time went on, the Lenaicis... that is, the comic games at the Lenaea would not be celebrated as splendidly as before; on the contrary, it would have been hoped they would be more splendid, since two would now contribute to the expense that one alone had previously borne. So what they feared was that, as time went on, the Lenaea would not be as splendid as before. This came about because the Anthesteria, at which comedies had not previously been performed, were now to be celebrated with them. From this it had to be inferred that, since these new expenses were to be added, those for the Lenaea would be reduced, for the Lenaea did not receive as much regard as the Dionysia in the city, or the Panathenaea, which drew the people of all Greece. That the Dionysia of the Anthesteria is meant here is clear from this: long before and after the praetor Callias, as is established from Attic history, comedies were presented to the people at the Dionysia of the city and of the countryside, that is, at the Lenaea. But only then, under Callias, after Antigenes the archon, were comedies first given at the Anthesteria as Liberalia. But soon this custom changed, and comedies were no longer given at the Liberal Anthesteria, as time went on, when few taught, at the request of the people concerning this matter, Cinesias. Aristotle's words quoted above should be emended thus: "from which time many later..., and the expense of the choregia... Cinesias." Cinesias here was a contemporary of Aristophanes, and is often mentioned. He removed what had been newly added, namely the presentation of comedies at the Liberal Anthesteria; and hence the same scholiast on this very play should be understood: "Cinesias [removed] comedy, as then useless." Finally, the Rhetor Lycurgus restored this neglected custom and proposed this law.

units.la: Τὸν [?] τῆς Κωμῳδῶν ἀγῶνα τῆς Χύτρεως [?] ἐπιπλὴν ἐφαμίλλον[?] ὡς τῷ ϑεάτρῳ[?], καὶ τὸν νικήσαντα εἰς ἄστυ [?] καλλιστεύσθαι[?].
units.tr: The contest of comic poets at the Chytri was to be contested in the theatre with rivalry, and the winner was to be honoured in the city [Τὸν τῆς Κωμῳδῶν ἀγῶνα τῆς Χύτρεως ἐπιπλὴν ἐφαμίλλον ὡς τῷ ϑεάτρῳ, καὶ τὸν νικήσαντα εἰς ἄστυ καλλιστεύσθαι].

units.la: Comoedi Anthesterijs fabulas docento atque committunto in Theatro. Victo-rem ciuitate donato.
units.tr: Comic poets are to produce and stage their plays in the Theatre at the Anthesteria. The victor is to be rewarded with citizenship.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Plutarchus in Lycurgi Vita: εἰσῄνεγκε δὲ ἡ τοὺς νόμους, τὸν [?] Κωμῳδῶν ἀγῶνα τῆς Χύτρεως ὑπὸ πολλῶν ἐφαμίλλον ἐν τῷ ϑεάτρῳ, καὶ τὸν νικήσαντα εἰς ἄστυ καλλιστεύσθαι, [?] ἀλλ' ἀλλαχοῦ [?] παιδαγωγῶν[?] [?]. Confunduntur hic, ut & apud alios Scriptores saepius, Chytri cum Liberalibus Anthesterijs, quia Anthesteria die tantum uno Chytros praecedebant: die enim duodecimo Anthesterionis Anthesteria celebrabantur. (hytri vero die tertiodecimo: praeterea Chytri erant Bacchi festum, ut ipse prodit Bacchus apud Aristophanem Ranis:
units.tr: Plutarch mentions this law in the Life of Lycurgus: "He also introduced the law that the contest of comic poets at the Chytri, contested by many in the theatre, and the winner be honoured in the city, but elsewhere..." Here, as often in other writers, the Chytri and the Liberal Anthesterijs are confused, because the Anthesteria came only one day before the Chytri: the Anthesteria were celebrated on the twelfth day of Anthesterion, while the Chytri fell on the thirteenth. Moreover the Chytri were a festival of Bacchus, as Bacchus himself declares in Aristophanes' Frogs:

units.la: Ἡνίχ' ἱερὸν Χύτροι[?] / Χωρὶς κατ' ἐμὲν πίνωσι λαλεῖν ὄχλος[?].
units.tr: When the sacred Chytroi [Ἡνίχ' ἱερὸν Χύτροι] ... drink apart from me, the crowd chatters [Χωρὶς κατ' ἐμὲν πίνωσι λαλεῖν ὄχλος].

units.la: Scholia: Χύτροι[?], ἑορτὴ περὶ Ἀθηναίοις γινομένη τῷ Διονύσῳ[?].
units.tr: Scholia: Chytroi [Χύτροι], a festival celebrated among the Athenians in honour of Dionysus.

units.la: Nullus autem histrio poterat in scenam prodire minor annorum triginta ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Under this law, no actor could come onto the stage who was under thirty years of age:

units.la: Μὴ εἰσιέναι τὴν εἰς [?] τῆς ἑορτῆς, μήτε παιδάριον [?] ἔτι γεγονότα[?].
units.tr: [Μὴ εἰσιέναι τὴν εἰς τῆς ἑορτῆς, μήτε παιδάριον ἔτι γεγονότα]: not to enter ... of the festival, nor one still a boy.

units.la: Histrio fabulam ne agito annorum tri-ginta minor.
units.tr: An actor is not to perform a play if he is under thirty years old.

units.la: Referendam esse hanc Legem ad Histriones omnino constat ex Graeco Aristophanis Interprete, qui obseruat nonnullos existimasse annum quadragesimum, non autem tricesimum, Lege hac fuisse definitum. Aristophanis verba sunt in eximia illa Nubium Parecbasi:
units.tr: That this law applies to actors in general is clear from the Greek interpreter of Aristophanes, who observes that some thought the law had fixed the fortieth year, not the thirtieth. The words of Aristophanes are in that famous parabasis of the Clouds:

units.la: Κἀγὼ πρῶτος γὰρ ἔτ' ὢν, κοὐκ ἐξὸν πω μοι πεκτεῖν[?].
units.tr: "And I was first, for I was still young, and it was not yet permitted for me to..." [Κἀγὼ πρῶτος γὰρ ἔτ' ὢν, κοὐκ ἐξὸν πω μοι πεκτεῖν].

units.la: Scholia: ἔπω ἐπέτρεπον ἐμφωτῇ[?] ὁ λέγει δημοσίᾳ[?], ἀλλ' ὁ νέον τῆς ἡλικίας[?]· ἢ γὰρ [illegible, ~6 letters] ἑαυτῷ κεχρὴ[?] τὰ δράματα ὁ ποιητὴς ἀλλαβούμενος[?]. ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν Ἱππέων ἡρξα-[?] τα εἰσένεγ[?]. νόμος δὲ ὧ, μὴ εἰσελθεῖν τινα εἰπεῖν, μήπω πεπεσχημένον[?] τὴν γεγονότα[?], ὡς δή τινες τεῖχοντα[?].
units.tr: Scholia: "It was not yet permitted to speak publicly to one who was of a young age; for the poet had ... his plays. From the Knights onward ... there was a law that no one might come forward to speak before having reached the age [...], as some said."

units.la: Longe autem dispar Romanorum iudicium ab illo Atheniensium hac in parte: nam Athenis histriones omni nota erant vacui, itaque etiam Poetae ipsi ciues Attici in scenam prodibant, quod de Sophocle, Aristophane, aliis, observatum est veteribus. Romae contra histriones notabantur infamia: unde Laberij querela, quem asperae libertatis Equitem Romanum Caesar invitavit quingentis millibus, ut prodiret in scenam, & ipse Mimos ageret, quos scriptitabat:
units.tr: The Roman judgement in this respect was very different from that of the Athenians. At Athens actors were free of every stigma, so that even the poets themselves, Attic citizens, came onto the stage; this was observed of Sophocles, Aristophanes and others by the ancients. At Rome, by contrast, actors were marked with infamy. Hence the complaint of Laberius, a Roman knight of harsh freedom, whom Caesar invited with five hundred thousand to come onto the stage and act the mimes he himself wrote:

units.la: Ergo bis tricenis annis actis sine nota Eques Romanus Lare egressus meo Domum revertar Mimus, nimirum hoc die Vno plus vixi mihi quam viuendum fuit.
units.tr: Therefore, having spent thirty-odd years without disgrace, a Roman knight, I have left my home and shall return a mime. Surely on this day I have lived one day more than I should have lived.

units.la: Scilicet: Ait Praetor: qui in scenam prodierit, infamis est. Scena est, ut Labeo definit, quae ludorum faciendorum causa, quolibet loco, ubi quis consistit, moveaturque spectaculum sui praebiturus, posita sit in publico, privatorc, vel in vico: quo tamen loco passim homines spectaculi causa admittantur: eos enim, qui quaestus causa in certamina descendunt, & omnes propter praemium in scenam prodeuntes, & famosos esse, Pegasus & Nerua filius responderunt. Lib. II. §. vlt. D. De his, qui notantur infamia. Unde factum est, ut Scenici spectaculorum debeantur obsequiis; eaque Scenicis nati non possint detrectare, sed vel inuiti ad ea praestanda adigantur. Primus, quod sciam, Valentinianus Princeps optimus, anno Christi Dionysiano tercentesimo septuagesimo primo, constituit, liceret Scenicos in extremo vitae periculo constitutos baptizare, & si forte euasissent, noluit ad scenam reuocari: ne autem fraus aliqua fieret, inspicere iussit iudices, aut Vrbium Curatores, an vitae periculum adiissent Scenici: non enim volebat eos baptizari nisi salute conclamata, ne consideratio sacratissimae religionis & Christianae Legis reuerentia scenae emanciparet. Leg. I. Cod. Theod. de Scenicis. Anno Christi Dionysiano tercentesimo octogesimo lata est haec Lex, quae legitur Leg. IV. Cod. Theod. cod. Imppp. Gratianus, Valentinianus, & Theodosius AAA. ad Paulinum P.V. Mulieres, quae ex viliori sorte progenitae spectaculorum debentur obsequiis, si scenica officia declinarint, iudicris ministeriis deputentur, quas necdum tamen consideratio sacratissimae religionis & Christianae Legis reuerentia suae fidei mancipauit. Eas enim quas melior viuendi vsus vinculo naturalis conditionis euoluit, retrahi vetamus. Dat. VIII. Kalend. Maij, Med. Gratiano V. & Theodosio II. AA. Coss. Quid appellent Imperatores, iudicris ministeriis deputari, paullo post videbimus. Haec Lex mulieres spectat, quae cum Scenicis essent progenitae, debebantur, natalium iure, spectaculorum obsequiis: illae vero ea detrectabant, & declinabant: iuberit itaque Imperatores eas in pulpitum retrahi, iudicrisque deputari ministeriis, nisi, antequam possent scenae inseruire, Christo dixissent sacramento. Vnde colligas licitum fuisse tunc Scenicis progenitas, antequam possent scenica præstare officia, sacro tingere lauacro, cum nondum tamen Scenicos & Scenicas liceret baptizare, nisi in extremo vitæ periculo constitutos. Postea de Scenicis ipsis scenæ obsequiis, quæ debebant, præstantibus ab iisdem Imperatoribus scripta Lex est, quæ VIII. legitur Cod. Theod. eod. anno Christi Dionysiano tercentesimo octogesimo primo. Imppp. Gratianus, Valentinianus, & Theodosius AAA. ad Valerianum P.V. Scena mulier, si vacationem religionis nomine postularit, obtentu quidem petitionis veniæ non deest, verum si post turpibus voluptatu complexibus, & religionem, quam expetierit, prodidisse, & gerere, quod officio desierat, animo tamen scenica detegetur, detracta in pulpitum, sine spe absolutionis ullius, ibi cousque permaneat, donec anus ridicula senectute deformis. Nec tunc quidem absolutione potiatur, cum aliud quam casta esse non possit. Dat. VIII. Id. Maij, Aquila, Syagrio & Eucherio Coss.
units.tr: That is: The Praetor says: whoever has come onto the stage is infamous. A stage is, as Labeo defines it, a place set up for the purpose of holding games, in any spot where someone stands and moves to present a spectacle, whether in public, private, or in a street; though people are commonly admitted to such places to watch. For those who go down into contests for gain, and all who come onto the stage for a prize, are infamous, as Pegasus and Nerva the son replied. Book II, last section, Digest, On those who are marked with infamy. Hence it came about that stage people were bound to the service of spectacles, and those born to the stage could not refuse these duties but were compelled to perform them even against their will. The first, as far as I know, was the excellent Emperor Valentinian, in the year of Christ 371, who decreed that stage people in mortal danger might be baptized, and if by chance they recovered, he would not have them recalled to the stage. To prevent any fraud, he ordered judges or the curators of cities to examine whether the stage people had truly come into mortal danger; for he did not want them baptized unless their recovery had been proclaimed, lest reverence for the most sacred religion and the Christian law be surrendered to the stage. Law I, Theodosian Code, On Stage People. In the year of Christ 380 this law was issued, which is read as Law IV of the Theodosian Code: the Emperors Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius Augusti to Paulinus, Praetorian Prefect. Women born of a lower class, who are bound to the service of spectacles by birth, if they evade stage duties, are to be assigned to judicial service; yet the regard for the most sacred religion and the reverence for Christian law has not yet entrusted them to its faith. For we forbid that those whom a better manner of living has drawn out from the bond of natural condition be dragged back. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Gratian for the fifth time and Theodosius for the second. What the Emperors call being assigned to judicial service we shall see a little later. This law concerns women who, having been born of stage people, were bound by birth right to serve spectacles, but who refused and evaded these duties. The Emperors therefore order them to be dragged back onto the stage and assigned to judicial service, unless, before they could serve the stage, they had taken the Christian oath. From this you may gather that it was then lawful for women born of stage people, before they could perform stage duties, to be washed in the sacred bath, though men and women of the stage could be baptized only if they were in mortal danger. Later, a law was written by the same Emperors concerning the stage people themselves performing the stage services they owed; it is read as Law VIII of the Theodosian Code, in the same year of Christ 381: the Emperors Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius Augusti to Valerianus, Praetorian Prefect.
