"If a stage woman asks for exemption on the ground of religion, she is not lacking a pretext for her petition; but if afterwards, having given herself to shameful pleasures, she has betrayed the religion she had sought, and does what she had given up, and is detected in her heart as still on the stage, let her be dragged back onto the stage, without hope of any absolution, and let her remain there until she is an old woman, ridiculous and deformed by age." Nor is she to obtain absolution even then, since she cannot be anything but unchaste. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Aquila and Syagrius and Eucherius.

units.la: Hac Lege constituitur, ut si qua mulier Scenica, quæ velit in Ecclesiam Christi admitti, & baptismate tingi, postulet eo nomine vacationem officiorum scenicorum, impetret; poena tamen sancitur aduersus eam, quæ cum vacationem scenicorum officiorum impetrauerit, sui copiam fecerit: poena ea est, quam iidem appellant Imperatores Lege proxime ante hanc descripta, meo quidem iudicio, ludicris ministeriis deputari. Sed quænam sint hæc ludicra ministeria inuestigandum est ex hac Lege: Detracta in pulpitum, inquiunt, ibi cousque permaneat, donec anus ridicula senectute deformis. Inter Comicas personas erant anus, quæ ridicula repræsentabantur: habes apud Pollucem titulo Lib. IV. cap. XIX. [?] τὰς δὲ γυναῖκας γραῦς ... [?] ... ἡ λυγίνη, γραῦς παιγνία, γραῦς δὲ οἰκουρὸν, ἡ οἰκιακὴ, ἡ ὀξύ· ὃ μὲν λυγισμὸν, ἐπὶ πυρὶ ... [illegible, ~6 letters] ... πυπ- ... ἐν ... ἐπὶ ... τὴν ... ἐν ... αὐτῆ, ... [?] ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ... ἡ δὲ οἰκουρὸς γραῦς δὲ, ... [illegible, ~10 letters] ... ἐν ἑκάτερα τῇ ... ἐν τῇ ... δύο ἐν γυμνῷ. Scenæ igitur mulieres, quæ officiorum scenicorum vocationem impetrauerant religionis obtentu, si quæstum corpore fecissent, in scenam reuocabantur, ut scenica præstarent ministeria; verum ministeria nonnisi ludicra, pœnæ ergo, illis deputabantur, id est, non repræsentabant nisi γραΐδας, quæ ridicula erant, ut γραΐδες λυχνία ἡ οἰκουρες. Volebant igitur Imperatores, ut ad officia scenæ reuocarentur, illisque ministeria ludicra deputarentur, id est, ut cogerentur ridiculas anus repræsentare, donec ipsæ reuera senectute fierent deformes, nec tunc tamen absolverentur, quanquam non possent non pudice, quod æni reliquum superrerat, agere propter senectutem & deformitatem: Putamus igitur in Lege unicam vocem transponendam esse hoc modo. Detracta in pulpitum sine spe absolutionis ullius, ibi cousque permaneat anus ridicula, donec senectute deformis. Inter histriones tamen infames non censebantur, qui agebant Atellanas, de quibus, seruque Exodys pauca dicemus: Exodio Atellanarum in fabularum fine non dicebantur, siue potius iactabantur, & plane erant alia & diuersa ab Atellanis, quibus conserta erant, fabulis Exodia: id liquet manifesto è Liuij verbis Lib. VII. Postquam lege hac fabularum abrisu ac soluto ioco res anucabatur, & paullatim ludus, in artem verterat, iuuentus histrionibus fabellarum actu relicto, ipsa inter se more antiquo ridicula intexta uersibus iactitare cepit, quæ inde Exodia postea appellata, conferta que fabellis potissimum Atellanis sunt. Ex his duo illa elicimus, quorum prius est, Exodia ista non fuisse de argumento fabularum, sed iis tantum inserta, alterum est, non iactitata fuisse in fine fabularum, sed sparsim conserta suisse fabulis. Objicies Scholiastem Juvenalis docere Exodiarios intrasse in fine ludorum. Verum id quidem est, illud dici à Scholiaste, sed nimirum ille confundit Atellanas fabulas cum Exodiis, quae illis erant conserta. Atellanae enim fabulae docebantur in fine ludorum, ut postea dicemus. Opponi quoque potest ratio nominis: Exodium namque exitum significat, & in ludis scenicis μῖμος ἢ Ἐξόδιον appellatur, ὁ ἐξιόντες ἦδον? Sed Exodia Atellanarum alia ratione dicebantur, ut constat è Livio, verbis laudatis: ex quo enim risus atque solutus iocus à re fabularum avocatus est, Exodia, quae risus & soluti ille iocus ridiculaque sunt, exinde dici ceperunt, quasi dicas, quae ἐξοδικὰς, id est, obiter & praeter argumentum fabulae iactitata sunt: neque enim de argumento Atellanarum fabularum erant Exodia; verum illis inserebantur. Significat hîc igitur Exodium ὁ ὁδὸς πρέψιν?, quod non est de fabulae argumento, sed illi inseritur: Constat è Livij verbis Exodia esse iocularia & ridicula versibus intexta, quae iuventus inter se more antiquo iactitabant; ac primum quidem, ut paullo ante docet Livius, inconditis inter se iocularia fundentes versibus cepere. Postea non sicut ante Fescennuno versu similem incompositum temere ac rudem alternis iaciebant, sed impletas modis satyras descripto iam ad tibicinem cantu, motúque congruenti peragebant. Demum ubi Livius post aliquot annos à Satyris ausus est primus argumento fabulam serere, atque ita fabularum res à risu & soluto ioco avocata est, & ludus in artem vertit, iuventus histrionibus fabularum actu relicto, ipsa inter se more antiquo ridicula versibus intexta iactitare cepit, quae exinde Exodia postea appellata sunt, confertaq; fabulis potissimum Atellanis. Vera haec sunt & τὰ ἀρχαῖα? Exodiorum principia, itemque verum Exodiorum argumentum, iocularia nempe & ridicula versibus intexta, sed antiqua simplicitate, quam designat Donatus his verbis. Atellanae salibus & iocis compositae, quae in se non habent nisi vetustam eleganiam. Hinc dicebantur ἐξοδιασταί? Glossae. Atellani, καλωνικοί?, ἀσχαλολάχαι?, βιολάπτοι? Quod autem βιολάπται appellantur, non inde est, quod in Exodijs sententias βιωφελὴς ad vitam viles iacerent, sed quia repraesentabant & ludebant τὰ ἡθοῖα & opprobria φωλάπτων (è quibus certe non negamus posse comparari πολλά, ut loquitur Epicharmus, πολλὰ ζωὰ? ἐγένετο?. Nam
units.tr: By this law it is laid down that if any actress (scenica) who wishes to be admitted into the Church of Christ and baptized asks for exemption from theatrical duties on that ground and obtains it, a penalty is nonetheless imposed on her if, once exempted, she makes herself available again. The penalty is the one that the same emperors, in my opinion, call in the law described just before this one assignment to ludicrous ministries. But what these ludicra ministeria are must be investigated from this law: "Dragged onto the stage, they say, let her remain there so long as the ridiculous old woman, deformed by age." Among the comic characters there were old women who were represented as ridiculous. You have this in Pollux, book IV, chapter XIX: "the old women ... the lamp-woman, the old woman playthings, the old woman who keeps the house, the domestic one, the sharp one ... [the Greek is partly illegible in the scan]... the old woman who keeps the house ... both ... naked." So the actresses who had obtained exemption from stage duties on grounds of religion, if they had made a living by their bodies, were recalled to the stage to perform theatrical services; but the ministries assigned to them as punishment were only ludicra, that is, they were to represent nothing but old women (γραΐδας), who were ridiculous, such as "old women lamp-sellers or housekeepers" [γραΐδες λυχνία ἡ οἰκουρες]. The emperors therefore wanted them to be recalled to the stage services and assigned to ludicrous ministries, that is, to be compelled to represent ridiculous old women until they themselves really became deformed by age; and even then they would not be released, although because of their age and deformity they could no longer perform in a chaste manner what remained of their lives. I think, then, that in the law a single word must be transposed in this way: "Dragged onto the stage without any hope of release, let the ridiculous old woman remain there until she is deformed by age." Yet the actors of the Atellan farces were not counted among the infamous performers. Of these, and of the Exodia, I shall say a few things. The Exodia of the Atellan farces were recited, or rather thrown out, at the end of the plays, and they were plainly different from the Atellan farces into which they were inserted. This is clear from the words of Livy, book VII: "After this law had ended the ridiculing and loosened jesting of the plays, and the spectacle had gradually turned into an art, the young men, leaving the actors to perform the plays, began to throw out among themselves, in the old manner, ridiculous things woven into verses; these were afterwards called Exodia, and were inserted chiefly into Atellan farces." From these words we draw two conclusions: first, that these Exodia were not about the subject of the plays but were inserted into them; second, that they were not thrown out at the end of the plays but were scattered through them. You may object that the scholiast on Juvenal teaches that the Exodiarii came on at the end of the games. That is indeed what the scholiast says, but he evidently confuses the Atellan farces with the Exodia that were inserted into them. For the Atellan farces were performed at the end of the games, as I shall say later. The meaning of the name may also be raised as an objection, since Exodium means an exit, and in the scenic games it is called a mimus or Exodium, from those who went out singing (ὁ ἐξιόντες ἦδον). But the Exodia of the Atellan farces were called so for another reason, as is clear from Livy's words quoted above: since, from the time when laughter and loosened jesting were drawn away from the subject of the plays, the Exodia, which were of laughter and loose jesting and ridiculous things, began to be so called, as if you were to say, they were things thrown out (ἐξοδικὰς), that is, incidentally and beside the plot of the play; for the Exodia were not about the subject of the Atellan farces but were inserted into them. So Exodium here means something that is not part of the plot of the play but is added to it. It is clear from Livy's words that the Exodia were jocular and ridiculous things woven into verses, which the young men threw out among themselves in the old manner. At first, as Livy shows a little earlier, they began by throwing out jocular things in unpolished verses. Afterwards, not like the earlier Fescennine verse, a crude and random exchange of unarranged lines, they performed satires filled with measures, sung to the flute with matching movement. Finally, when Livy, some years after the Satires, first ventured to weave a plot into the play, and the subject of the plays was thus drawn away from laughter and loose jesting and the spectacle turned into an art, the young men, leaving the actors to perform the plays, began to throw out among themselves, in the old manner, ridiculous things woven into verses, which were afterwards called Exodia, and were inserted chiefly into Atellan farces. These things are true, and they are the early beginnings (τὰ ἀρχαῖα) of the Exodia, and their true content was jocular and ridiculous things woven into verses, but in the ancient simplicity that Donatus describes in these words: "The Atellan farces were composed of wit and jokes, and contain nothing but an ancient elegance." Hence they were called ἐξοδιασταί, according to the glosses. Atellani, καλωνικοί, ἀσχαλολάχαι, βιολάπτοι. That they are called βιολάπται is not because in the Exodia they threw out sayings useful for life, but because they represented and mocked the morals and disgraces of φωλάπτων, from which, certainly, we do not deny that many things can be gathered, as Epicharmus says, "many living things came into being" [πολλὰ ζωὰ ἐγένετο]. For

units.la: teneros animos aliena opprobria saepe Exterrent vitiis.)
units.tr: "Other people's disgraces often frighten tender minds away from vices."

units.la: Id liquet maxime ex eo quod eadem fuerant olim Exodia cum Satyra, ut auctor est T. Livius, at certe Satyra tangit & carpit hominum, etiá singulorum ὀνομαστί? opprobria & ἡθοῖα. Quod factitatum in Exodijs fuisse nullus dubito, & en tibi exemplu apud Suet. in Tiberio de obscoenitate oris hirsuto atq; olido illi seni exprobrata. Unde nata in Atellanico Exodio proximis ludis assensu maximo exceptâ, percrebuit: Hircum vetulum capris naturam ligurire. En tibi aliud apud Juvenal. Sat. IV.
units.tr: This is shown most clearly by the fact that the Exodia were formerly the same as satire, as T. Livy testifies; and satire certainly touches on and criticizes the disgraces and morals of men, even of individuals named by name (ὀνομαστί). I have no doubt that this was often done in the Exodia, and here is an example from Suetonius in Tiberius, where an old man with a hairy and foul mouth was reproached for the obscenity of his mouth: "Hence arose, in an Atellan Exodium at the next games, which was received with the greatest applause, the saying spread: 'the old goat licks the nature of the she-goats.'" Here is another from Juvenal, Satire IV:

units.la: Urbicis Exodio risum movet Atellanae, Gestibus Autonoës.
units.tr: "With the Exodium of the Atellan farce he moves the city to laughter, with the gestures of Autonoë."

units.la: Quae verba ita interpretor, Mimum movisse spectatoribus risum, cum in alicuius Atellanae fabulae Exodio ad manum saltaret nescio cuius Autonoës opprobria & ridicula quædam. Sed iam quoque dicenda, vt doceamus quinam illi sint qui Exodia fabulis intertexta, & sparsim conserta fuisse è Li[?] tyricò dramati respondet Atellana fabula. Dior[?] cies est, fabularum Latinarum, quæ à ciuitate Oscorum Atellanæ dictæ sunt, argumentis dictisque iocularibus [?] cis. & paulò post: Latina Atellana à Græca Satyrica Satyrorum personæ inducuntur, aut si quæ sunt ridicula Burrhi. (ita alibi emendauimus) In Atellanæ Oscæ tantum argumento inter se conueniunt Satyrica lanaque, Latinorum fabulæ, sed etiam quod cum dramatis subijciebantur. Diomedes de Satyricis bula, in quaitem Tragici Poetæ non Reges aut Heroas dendi causa iocandique, vt simul [spectator inter res T quoque locis & lusibus delectaretur, vt & Horatius se Carmine qui Tragico vilem certauit ob hircum Mox etiam agrestes Satyros nudauit, & aspe Incolumi grauitate iocum tentauit, eo quod Illecebris erat & grata nouitate morandus Spectator.
units.tr: I interpret these words as meaning that the mime moved the spectators to laughter when, in the Exodium of some Atellan farce, he danced on the stage, mocking, with the gestures of a certain Autonoë, certain disgraces and ridiculous things. But now I must also say what I shall say next, to show who those are who were interwoven with the farces and scattered through them. The Atellan farce corresponds to the lyric drama. ... It is a difference of the Latin farces, which were called Atellan from the town of the Osci, in their plots and jocular sayings ... and a little later: The Latin Atellan [farce] differs from the Greek satiric drama, in which Satyrs are introduced, or in which there are ridiculous ... (as I have emended elsewhere). The Atellan farces of the Oscans agree with the satiric plays only in subject, but also in that they were added to the drama. Diomedes, on satiric plays, [says] that tragic poets did not [use] kings or heroes for the sake of jesting, so that the spectator might be delighted at the same time by places and playful things, as Horace also [says]: "... who contended with a goat for a worthless prize in tragic song; soon he also stripped the rustic Satyrs, and attempted jesting with undiminished dignity, because the spectator must be detained by allurements and by pleasing novelty."

units.la: Idemque videtur non obscurè Horatius significa præcipiens, his vtitur verbis, Ne quicumque Deus, quicumque adhibebitur Regali conspectus in auro nuper & ostro, Migret in obscœnas humili sermone tabernas,
units.tr: Horace also seems to signify this not obscurely when he advises, using these words: "Let no god, or any hero shown in royal splendour of gold and purple, migrate into obscene taverns with humble speech,"

units.la: Atellanas fabulas, quæ Exodijs erant confertæ & rum dramatum commissiones, datàs fuisse pro verba: Exodiarius apud veteres in fine ludorum intraba[t] quid lacrymarum atque tristitiæ coegisset ex Tragicis a[ctoribus] deterget[?]. Illas autem Atellanas fabulas, & iis sparsim olim Romana iuuentus. Liuius loco laudato addit genus ludorum (fabularum Atellanarum) ab Oscis ac ab histrionibus pollui passa est. Postea tamen illas fab[ulas] earum Exodia iactitarunt. Sed & hi histriones, qui ceteros ludiones honestissimi, & cum cæteri, qui caussa in scenam prodirent, infamia notarentur: vt est D. De bis, qui notantur infamia, neque pro ciuibus actores omni nota vacui erat. Liuius: Eo instituto nec tribus moueantur, & stipendia tanquam experties aMaximus Libro II. cap I. Atellani autem ab Oscis a tionis Italica seueritate temperatum, ideoque vacuum uetur, neque à militaribus stipendijs repelluntur. Quinan & quo nomine designati videamus. Putamus itaq iuuenes appellantur, & quorum ludos meminerun de his Calliftratus Libro VI. de Cognitionibus e de Atellanis fabulis pauca ia iactarent, quæ Atellanis uio diximus. Græcorum Sancdes Libro III Tertia spe- n Atella, in qua primum cepe, similes Satyricus fabulis Græ- a differt, quod in Satyrica fere le similes Satyris, Autolycus, persona, ut Maccus. Neque dramata Græcorum Atel- hæ tum illa editis Tragicis Satyrica est apud Græcos fased Satyros induxerunt, lu- ragicas feriasque Satyrorum ntis his versibus, m,
units.tr: The Atellan farces, which were joined to the Exodia (the afterpieces) of the dramas, were called by that name. Among the ancients, the Exodiarius came on at the end of the games to wipe away the tears and sadness that the tragic actors had caused. Those Atellan farces, and the Roman youth who once performed them here and there, are mentioned in Livy at the passage cited, where he adds that the kind of games (the Atellan farces) was defiled by the Oscans and by actors. Afterwards, however, they used to introduce those farces as their Exodia. But these actors, who were the most respectable of the other stage-players and who came on the stage for money, were marked with infamy, as Digest 3.2 says concerning those who are marked with infamy. Actors were not free of every mark of disgrace in the eyes of citizens. Livy says: by this arrangement neither were the tribes moved, nor were they excluded from military pay as though they were disqualified. Maximus, Book 2, chapter 1. The Atellani, however, from the Oscans, were tempered by the Italian severity of the regime, and so they were left free of the infamy, and are not repelled from military pay. By what name are they designated? We think, therefore, that they are called iuvenes, and Callistratus, Book 6 of On Cognitions, mentions their games. Concerning these, we have said a little already in our discussion of the Atellanae. Sandes, in Book 3 of the Greeks, mentions the third kind of play, Atella, in which the actors first appeared with masks, similar to the satyr plays. It differs from the satyr play in that in the satyr play the actors are mostly similar to satyrs; Autolycus, in the character of Maccus, and the Greek dramas of this kind are not Atellan. Thus, when the tragedies were produced, the Greeks had satyric plays, but they introduced satyrs, playing the tragic and festive Satyr scenes, as in these verses,

units.la: [?]are, cum de Satyricis salibus
units.tr: ...are, when concerning satyric jests

units.la: [?]eros,
units.tr: ...eros,

units.la: intertextæ, post Tragico- bant Scholiastæ Iuuenalis i, quod ridiculus foret: ut quic- ffectibus huius spectaculi risus im-conserta Exodia tenuit iis quæ descripsimus. Quod ceptum tenuis iuuentus: nec ulas egerunt histriones, & i Atellanæ docebant, inter artis ludicræ, pronunciandiue in Edicto Prætoris Lege I. s habe rentur, Atellanarum nianct, ut actores Atellanarū rtis ludicræ faciant. Valerius iccis junt quod genus delecta- ota est: nam neque trium mo- n autem histriones isti sint, que histriones illos esse, qui t veteres Inscriptiones: & apud Iurisconsultos Lege
units.tr: interwoven, after the tragedies, as the scholiasts of Juvenal say, because it would be ridiculous; by the effects of this spectacle laughter... The Exodia, joined to the tragedies, were held by the young men of humble station, and they performed the Atellan farces, which the actors taught among the arts of the stage and of delivery, as in the praetor's Edict, Digest 1.? Valerius says what kind of selected ... for neither were the tribes moved... Whether these actors are the ones called iuvenes, and whether they were those actors whom the old inscriptions name; and among the jurists, in Digest 3.? [text corrupt].

units.la: XXVIII. §. III. D. De Tœnis. Solent quidam, qui vulgo se iuuenes appellant, in quibusdam ciuitatibus turbulentissimis sc acclamationibus popularium accommodare. Omnino enim hos iuuenes ad ludos histrioniamque pertinere, cuincunt sequentia paulò post verba: nam spectaculis eis interdicitur, si turbas in Theatro fecerint. Sed frustra sunt Viri eruditissimi, qui iuuenes istos ad Neronis institutum referunt, qui delectos Equites, quos iuuenes Augustanos appellari voluit, vt constat è comparatis Suetonij Nerone, & Tacitj Annalium Libro XIV. locis, habuit, qui plausus ederent: nam iuuenes illi, de quibus Callistratus, si quid peccarent fecissent, quo in poenam incurrerent, fustibus caesi dimittuntur, inquit Iurisconsultus. At vero haec poena hominum tenuiorum erat, vt constat è verbis Callistrati hac ipsa Lege §. II. Non omnes fustibus caedi solent, sed hi dumtaxat, qui liberi sunt, & quidem tenuiores homines. Non ergo poena erat Equitum, ac proinde iuuenes illi non sunt Equitesilli Augustani iuuenes dicti, de quibus Tacitus & Suetonius. Cum autem constet iuuenes hos histriones fuisse, & rursum histriones omnes, praeter Atellanarum actores, insamia notatos, & tribu motos fuisse: iuuenes vero illos inter liberos homines & famae integros, sed tenuiores censitos fuisse (quod liquet ex eo quod caesi fustibus dimittantur.) inde quoque constabit, meo quidem iudicio, histriones istos, qui iuuenes dicuntur, Atellanarum actores fuisse, vt qui essent omni nota vacui. Ita autem appellatos fuisse exiltimo, vt vel saltem nomine referrent eos, qui primi Atellanarum, quibus conserta erant Exodia, ludos tenuerant, iuuentutem nempe Romanam. Callistrati autem verba de iuuenibus, ad scenicos tantum ludos referimus. Nemo autem ignorat, histriones inuicem de victoria certasse, quae victoria, non virtute semper, sed etiam fauore parabatur, & affectu in hunc vel illum histrionem, aut Poetam, qui fabulam docebat, aut Choragum, qui sumptum faciebat, itaque fautores delegabant, qui in subselliis & cuneis Theatri sedentes applaudebant huic vel illi histrioni, & extorquebant plausum spectatorum, quos Popularium nomine intelligit Callistratus, vt & Vlpianus Lege I. §. XII. D. de officio Praefecti Vrbi. Quies quoque Popularium, & disciplina spectaculorum ad Praefecti Vrbi curam pertinere videtur. Appellant Populares, quia in popularibus, vt Suetonius in Domitiano loquitur, sedebant. Plausus autem iste comites saepe habebat rixasatque verbera[?]. Quare prouidendum erat, ne quis histrioni in scena agenti operam suam nauaret in edendo plausu, eliciendoque illo Popularium, i. spectatorum clamore. At, vt liquet Callistrato, iuuenes id praestabant histrionibus, & Theatrum suo plausu commouebant, vt spectatores suum darent ei histrioni, cui iuuenes applaudebant, & factum vellent. Quia autem iuuenes non agebant Atellanas, nisi in fine ludorum, poterant illi inter spectatores sedere, vt essent signiferi motuum & clamorum Theatralium, in gratiam illius histrionis, aut Poetae, cui studebant, & post cuius commissam fabulam ij Atellanam edebant.
units.tr: Digest 28.3 concerning Taenia: Certain men who commonly call themselves young men, in some very turbulent cities, accommodate themselves to the shouts of the people. For it is clear that these young men belonged to the games and the stage, as the words that follow a little later show: for they are forbidden the spectacles if they cause disturbances in the theatre. But those very learned men are wrong who refer these young men to the institution of Nero, who wanted chosen knights, whom he called Augustan youths, to make applause, as is clear from comparing the passages of Suetonius' Nero and Tacitus' Annals Book 14. For those young men of whom Callistratus speaks, if they committed any fault by which they incurred punishment, are dismissed after being beaten with rods, says the jurist. But this punishment belonged to men of humble rank, as is clear from the words of Callistratus in this same law, §2: Not all are usually beaten with rods, but only those who are free, and indeed men of humbler rank. So this was not the punishment of knights, and therefore those Augustan youths of whom Tacitus and Suetonius speak were not knights. Since it is established that these young men were actors, and conversely that all actors, except the actors of the Atellan farces, were stigmatised with infamy and removed from their tribe, while those young men were counted among free men of unimpaired reputation, but of humbler rank (as is clear from the fact that they are dismissed after being beaten with rods), it will also follow from this, in my judgement, that these actors who are called young men were actors of the Atellan farces, being free of every mark. I think they were so named so that they might at least by name refer to those who first held the Atellan games, to which the Exodia were joined, namely the Roman youth. We refer Callistratus' words about the young men only to the stage games. No one is unaware that the actors competed with one another for victory, which was won not always by skill but also by favour and partiality toward this or that actor, or the poet who taught the play, or the choragus who paid the expense. Thus they chose supporters who, sitting on the benches and seats of the theatre, applauded this or that actor and drew applause from the spectators, whom Callistratus calls by the name Populares, as does Ulpian in Digest 1.12, concerning the office of the Prefect of the City: The quiet of the Populares and the discipline of the spectacles seem to belong to the care of the Prefect of the City. They are called Populares because, as Suetonius says of Domitian, they sat in the popular seats. That applause often brought quarrels and blows. Therefore care had to be taken that no one lend his efforts to an actor performing on the stage by raising applause and drawing out that shout of the Populares, that is, of the spectators. But, as is clear from Callistratus, the young men provided this service to the actors, and moved the theatre by their applause, so that the spectators would give their support to the actor whom the young men applauded, and wish it done. And since the young men did not perform the Atellan farces except at the end of the games, they could sit among the spectators, to be standard-bearers of the theatrical movements and shouts, in favour of that actor or poet whom they supported, after whose play they performed the Atellan.

units.la: Quam licenter Comici apud Athenienses, quo iure quave iniuria, bonos malos carperent & vexarent, notum est omnibus vel ex vnius pagellae Aristophanis lectione, neque Magistratus ipsi, qui Reipublicae praerant, ab illorum censura erant immunes, quod cum graue atque iniquum videretur, vt par erat, Lege cautum ne id posterum auderent Comici:
units.tr: How freely the comic poets among the Athenians attacked and harassed good and bad men, by what right or wrong, is known to all, even from reading a single page of Aristophanes. Nor were the magistrates themselves, who presided over the commonwealth, immune from their censure. Since this seemed grievous and unjust, as it indeed was, a law was made to ensure that the comic poets should not dare this in future:

units.la: Τὸν Ἀρχίλοχον μὴ φανερῶς κωμῳδεῖν.
units.tr: Not to mock Archilochus openly. [Τὸν Ἀρχίλοχον μὴ φανερῶς κωμῳδεῖν.]

units.la: Legitur hæc Lex apud Græcum Aristophanis Interpretem ad Nubes: Τῆς Ἀθηναίοις ὁ νόμος, φανερῶς ἐκώλυε τὸν Ἀρχίλοχον κωμῳδεῖν[?]. Qui enim Magi-stratum carpebat, toti vrbi conuicium faciebat, quod cum fecisset dramate, cui titulus est Babylonij Aristophanes, dicam ei scripsit Cleon. Interpres Comici ad Acharnenses: Βαβυλωνίοις δράματα πολλοῖς χαχῶς εἶπεν[?]. ἐκωμῴδησε γὰρ τὰς τε πληρωτὰς καὶ χρήστας ἀρχάς[?], καὶ Κλέωνα, παρόντων τῶν ξένων. καὶ ἀλλ' ἐς τοῦτο ὀργιζεῖς ὁ Κλέων, ἐγράψατο αὐτὸν ἀδικίας εἰς τοὺς πολίτας, ὡς εἰς ὕβριν τῇ δήμου ζώπα ποιητὴν[?]. Quare damnati serio sunt, qui iocose scripserant. Hinc intelligenda Apollonij verba, quæ leguntur in Scholiis Comici ad Ranas: Ἀπολλώνιος δὲ οὐ χαχῶς ὑπονοεῖσθαί φησί, ὁ κωμῳδεῖσθαί ἵνα[?]. Καλλίας δ' ὁ Ἱππονίκου ἐν Μελίτῃ φησί[?]. Callia autem Præture Ranas docuit Aristophanes, vnde dixit tantum,
units.tr: This law is read in the Greek commentator on Aristophanes' Clouds: The law of the Athenians openly forbade mocking Archilochus. [Τῆς Ἀθηναίοις ὁ νόμος, φανερῶς ἐκώλυε τὸν Ἀρχίλοχον κωμῳδεῖν.] For he who carped at a magistrate insulted the whole city. When Aristophanes had done this in the play entitled The Babylonians, Cleon indicted him. The commentator on the Acharnians says: He spoke ill of many in the Babylonians dramas; he ridiculed the paid officials and the officials who received payment [Βαβυλωνίοις δράματα πολλοῖς χαχῶς εἶπεν], and Cleon, with foreigners present [ἐκωμῴδησε γὰρ τὰς τε πληρωτὰς καὶ χρήστας ἀρχάς, καὶ Κλέωνα, παρόντων τῶν ξένων]. And since Cleon was angered at this, he indicted him for injustice against the citizens, as an outrage against the people's poet. [καὶ ἀλλ' ἐς τοῦτο ὀργιζεῖς ὁ Κλέων, ἐγράψατο αὐτὸν ἀδικίας εἰς τοὺς πολίτας, ὡς εἰς ὕβριν τῇ δήμου ζώπα ποιητὴν.] Hence those who had written jokingly were condemned in earnest. From this must be understood the words of Apollonius, read in the scholia on Aristophanes' Frogs: Apollonius says, not badly, that he is insinuated to be mocked [Ἀπολλώνιος δὲ οὐ χαχῶς ὑπονοεῖσθαί φησί, ὁ κωμῳδεῖσθαί ἵνα]. Callias, son of Hipponicus, in the Melite, says [Καλλίας δ' ὁ Ἱππονίκου ἐν Μελίτῃ φησί]. For in the archonship of Callias, Aristophanes produced the Frogs, whence he said only:

units.la: Μὰ Δί', ἀλλ' ἀληθῶς οὐκ Μελίτης μαστίας.
units.tr: No, by Zeus, but truly not of Melite's whips. [Μὰ Δί', ἀλλ' ἀληθῶς οὐκ Μελίτης μαστίας.]

units.la: Neque Calliam Archontem notauit ἐξ ὁμολογίας. Quando autem lata fuerit hæc Lex, inquiramus. Babylonios docuit Aristophanes, vt alibi probauimus, anno secundo Olympiadis octagesimæ octauæ, Prætore Athenis Euclide; eo dramate ἐκωμῴδησε τὰς τε πληρωτὰς καὶ χρήστας ἀρχάς, καὶ Κλέωνα, παρόντων τῶν ξένων. Quo nomine dicam illi scripsit, ea autem erat ἀδικίας εἰς τοὺς πολίτας. nempe nondum Lex ista erat scripta, & Cleonis si forte, de causa, anno ab hinc tertio lata est: nam anno quarto Olympiadis octagesimæ octauæ, Stratocle Archonte, Lenæis docuit Equites Aristophanes, quo inuehitur in Strategum Cleonem. Ergo anno primo Olympiadis octagesimæ nonæ lata est: nam certè obtinebat Lex hæc anno secundo Olympiadis octagesimæ nonæ, Aminia Archonte, quando docuit τὰς διδασκαλίας Νεφέλας, e quibus ista leguntur, quæ indicant iam tum hanc Legem latam fuisse.
units.tr: Nor did he mark Callias the archon by name, by agreement. Let us inquire when this law was passed. Aristophanes produced the Babylonians, as we have proved elsewhere, in the second year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad, when Euclides was praetor at Athens. In that drama he ridiculed the paid officials and the officials who received payment, and Cleon, with foreigners present [ἐκωμῴδησε τὰς τε πληρωτὰς καὶ χρήστας ἀρχάς, καὶ Κλέωνα, παρόντων τῶν ξένων]. For this he indicted him; the charge was injustice against the citizens [ἀδικίας εἰς τοὺς πολίτας]. Thus that law was not yet written, and it was passed perhaps on Cleon's account three years later. For in the fourth year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad, when Stratocles was archon, Aristophanes produced the Knights at the Lenaea, in which he attacks the general Cleon. Therefore the law was passed in the first year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad. For it certainly was in force in the second year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad, under the archon Aminias, when he produced the Clouds, from which these lines are read, which show that this law had already been passed by then.

units.la: Τρεῖς μὲν διδάσκουσι, καὶ ἔχρην Ἀμινίᾳ[?].
units.tr: Three poets produce plays, and it ought to have been in the archonship of Aminias [?].

units.la: Scholia : ποτὲ γὰρ ἦρχεν Ἀμινίας Ἰσογράπου υἱὸς[?], ἐπὶ πρὸ Ἀθηναίοις ὁ νόμος, φανερῶς ἐκώλυε τὸν Ἀρχίλοχον κωμῳδεῖν. Ἀμινίαν ὁ αὐτὸν εἶπεν, αὐτὴ τῆς Ἀμινίας[?].
units.tr: Scholia: For once Aminias, son of Isographus, was archon, when the law, publicly and in the open, forbade Archilochus to write comedy. Aminias said that he himself ... of Aminias [garbled in the source].

units.la: Cum antiquæ Comœdiæ libertas in vitium excidisset, & vim dignam Lege regi, Olympiade octagesima quinta, Prætore Athenis Myrichida; Ἀφίσμα τῆς μὴ κωμῳδεῖν ἐγράφη[?]. Quod tamen antiquatum est, cum Euthymenes Athenis Archon esset, anno quarto eiusdem Olympiadis octagesimæ quintæ. Anonymus in Descriptione Olympiadum ad hunc annum; ὁ ἀφίσμα τῆς μὴ κωμῳδεῖν ἐγράφεν ὅτι Μυεχίδου ἐλυθη[?]. Idem testantur Comici Scholia ad Acharnenses: sed locus male affectus est, nos medebimur: ἐπὶ Εὐξυμένους Ἀρχόντος καπελύθη ὁ ἀφίσμα τῆς μὴ κωμῳδεῖν ἐγράφεν ὅτι Μορυχίδου (scribe Μυεχίδου,) καὶ ἰσχυρῶς ἐκφύσιον τε τὸν ἑαυτῶν καὶ δύο τοὺς ἐξῆς, Ἐπιγίνου, (lego Γλαυκίδου. nam Diodoro Siculo & Anonymo in Descriptione Olympiadum, hic est Archon anni secundi Olympiadis octagesimæ quintæ, à quo ἀρχὴ τῆς Κοσυτικοῦ πολέμου,) τα καὶ Θεοδώρου, ἀλλ' ὡς ἐπ' Εὐθυμένους κατλύσῃ[?]. Posta omnino vetitum est cuiquam conuicium facere.
units.tr: When the freedom of Old Comedy had degenerated into abuse and needed to be checked by a law suited to it, in the eighty-fifth Olympiad, with Myrichides as prætor at Athens, a decree was drawn up forbidding comedy [Ἀφίσμα τῆς μὴ κωμῳδεῖν ἐγράφη]. This decree, however, was abolished when Euthymenes was archon at Athens, in the fourth year of the same eighty-fifth Olympiad. The anonymous author of the Description of the Olympiads says at this year that the decree forbidding comedy was written [ὁ ἀφίσμα τῆς μὴ κωμῳδεῖν ἐγράφεν ὅτι Μυεχίδου ἐλυθη]. The comic scholia on the Acharnians attest the same, but the passage is corrupt and I shall emend it: in the archonship of Euxymenes the decree forbidding comedy, written when Myrichides [read Myechides] was ..., was abolished [ἐπὶ Εὐξυμένους Ἀρχόντος καπελύθη ὁ ἀφίσμα τῆς μὴ κωμῳδεῖν ἐγράφεν ὅτι Μορυχίδου (scribe Μυεχίδου,) καὶ ἰσχυρῶς ἐκφύσιον τε τὸν ἑαυτῶν καὶ δύο τοὺς ἐξῆς, Ἐπιγίνου, (lego Γλαυκίδου ...) τα καὶ Θεοδώρου, ἀλλ' ὡς ἐπ' Εὐθυμένους κατλύσῃ]. In short, it was altogether forbidden for anyone to make a public insult.

units.la: Μὴ κωμῳδεῖν ἐξ ὀνόματος[?]. Nemini in Comœdia nominatim facito.
units.tr: Not to mock by name: let no one be named in comedy.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis, sed non solus, Hermogenes. Ὁ δὲ νόμος ἐκώλυσεν[?]. Horatius Epistola ad Augustum:
units.tr: Hermogenes also mentions this law, though not alone. "But the law forbade ..." [Ὁ δὲ νόμος ἐκώλυσεν]. Horace, in his Epistle to Augustus:

units.la: Fescennina per hunc inuenta licentia mor Versibus alternis opprobria rustica fudit, Libertasque recurrentes accepta per anno Lusit amabiliter: donec iam saeuus aperta In rabiem verti coepit iocus, & per honest Ire domos impune minax. doluere cruento Dente lacessiti, fuit intactis quoque cura Conditione super communi. quinetiam Le Poenaque lata, malo qua nollet carmine q Describi.
units.tr: Fescennine licence, invented through this law, poured out rustic insults in alternating verses, and, received with a freedom that returned year by year, it played amiably; until at last the savage jest, turning into open madness, began to go about threateningly through respectable homes with impunity. Those bitten by its bloody teeth grieved, and even those left untouched were concerned about the common condition. Moreover a law was passed and a penalty, so that no one would want to be described in a malicious song.

units.la: Idem ad Pisones:
units.tr: Horace again, in the Art of Poetry:

units.la: Successit vetus his Comœdia non sine multa Laude; sed in vitium libertas excidit, & Chor Dignam Lege regi. Lex est accepta, Chor Turpiter obticuit, sublato iure nocendi.
units.tr: Old Comedy succeeded these, not without much praise; but its freedom degenerated into abuse, and the Chorus deserved to be restrained by law. The law was accepted, and the Chorus shamefully fell silent, its right to harm taken away.

units.la: Donatus: Vetus Comœdia ἐπωνύμως[?] dicta est, quia vera narrationis, & denominatio omnium, de quibus per priscos Poetas, non, ut nunc, penitus ficta argumenta, iam cum eorum saepe, qui gesserant, nomine decantabantur; centius stylo, & passim laedere ex libidine coepissent, prorum carmen infame proponerer, Lege lata silucre[?]. Chus Poeta Aristophanis aequalis. Comici Ἰφίσματα[?], imo potius Legem, πιτοποιεῖσθαι[?] μὴ ἐν τῇ Olympiadem: tra nonagesimam septimam Olympiadem: nonagesimam septimam Cocalum & Æoloficon; nes. Plutus enim postrema est fabularum, qua to Olympiadis nonagesimæ septimæ, Antipater[?] rentur Cocalus & Æoloficon, ut est in argumento[?]. Inquiunt veteres Magistri, Ἰφίσματος[?] ἐν τῇ ... Præterea ipse Πλάτων[?] δὲ πέμπεις[?] (etsi etiam ...) οὐδὲν tantum est, ἐπωπεῖζε[?] ... propter hanc Legem, χορὸν[?] ... Chorum n... bebat ὁ Πλάτων[?], ut neque Cocalus & ... que Nova Comœdia omnis: nam
units.tr: Donatus: Old Comedy was so called from the name of the place [ἐπωνύμως], because it took its plots not, as now, from wholly fictional material, but from true narrative and the naming of all the people about whom the early poets sang, often with their names attached to those who had acted. When they began to hurt people freely and openly out of wantonness, a law was passed to silence their infamous song. Chus was a poet contemporary with Aristophanes. The comic decrees [Ἰφίσματα], or rather the law, were made ... in the ninety-seventh Olympiad. For Plutus is the last of the plays ... in the ninety-seventh Olympiad, Cocalus and Aeolosicon ... as is said in the argument. The ancient teachers say ... Besides, Plato himself ... on account of this law, the chorus ... Plato ... so that neither Cocalus nor Aeolosicon [...], nor all New Comedy: for [garbled in the source].

units.la: Lex est accepta, Chorusq; Turpiter obticuit, sublato iure nocendi.
units.tr: The law was accepted, and the Chorus shamefully fell silent, its right to harm taken away.

units.la: Quia hæ præcipue erant Chori, λιδωρῶν[?], τοὺς ... ἐκ ἀνὴρ δημοσίᾳ μάστιγι τῇ κωμῳδίᾳ καλίζειν[?]. Qu mœdia expresso nomine connicium gencs ἐάσεων. ἀνομαςὶ κωμῳ[?] Augustum: rem s m as x , uenquam ta uim usque a inest in ea velut historica fides us libere describebatur. Etenim [?]menta, sed res gestæ à ciuibus pa-bantur. Sed cum Poetæ abuti li-lures bonos, ne quisquam in alte-Legem hanc tulit Antima-terpres: ἐδίδαξε δὲ ὁ Ἀντίμαχος ἐξῆς κωμῳδῶν ἐξ ὀνομάτων. Idque in-Nam post Olympiadem no-na fabulas scripsit Aristopha-is ipse docuit, acta anno quar-tro Archonte, antequam edc-mento Pluti: atqui ἔγραψε Κό-ωμον, ὥστε μὴ ὀνομάσῃ κωμῳδὸν prior, cuius hic [illegible, ~6 letters] ἀλφ-on habet, (quem tamen ha-Æolosicon Aristophanis, neue κακῶς [illegible, ~5 letters] ἀξάβαλλειν, uare intra nonagesimam seputam primam Olympiadem videtur scripta hæc lex ante editionem [?]τὰ ἐδ[?] πέγου Γλαύκου. Ante nonagesimam septimam Olympiadem lata non est, quia τὰς Ἐκκλησιαζούσας drama, quod Chorum habet, καὶ [illegible, ~6 letters] docuit anno quarto Olympiadis nonagesimæ sextæ, Archonte Demostrato μετ᾽ Εὐβουλίδου. Ergo non ante, neque post Olympiadem nonagesimam septimam, sed intra ipsam rogata & lata est hæc Lex. Cui qui impunè fraudem facere volebant, nomina omittebant, personas seruabant, id est, laruas, quibus singuli, quos traducebant, exprimebantur, quod [illegible, ~8 letters] dicebant: non nominabantur enim ca ratione, sed repræsentabantur tantum; unde lites sæpe atque controuersiæ. Hermogenes loco laudato: [?]αὐτοπροσώπως εἰσάγων τὰς τὰς κωμῳδουμένους, [?]ἀπαγαγὼν τοῦ ἰδίου, ὡς ὀνομάζει κωμῳδῶν. Quanquam etiam, dum licebat ὀνομαστὶ κωμῳδεῖν, licebat quoque αὐτοπροσώπως, atque id ita fiebat. Habes in Excerptis Platonij: [?]ὁ γὰρ τὰ παρὰ τὰ κωμῳδία εἶναι ζῶν τὰ προσωπεῖα τοῖς κωμῳδουμένοις, ἵνα πρὸς τὴν [?]ἀπαγωγὴν εἰπεῖν ὁ κωμῳδούμενος οὐκ ἔστι ἀμφισβητοῦς τῆς ἀνδρὸς καλλιφῶνος. Hucpertinet quod in Aristophanis Vita legitur, habeturque partim in Equitum Argumento: καὶ χρ[?]ε[?]ας τῷ Κλέωνος, πρὸς Ἱππίας, ὁ ὁ[?]τις διελέγχῳ αὐτὸν τοῖς κλοπαῖς, καὶ ὁ τυρᾶν[?]ικὸν, γρᾶτος ὁ[?] τὴν σκευωρίαν [?]ἐλμισθὸς ὁ προσώπων αὐτὸν ὀνομαστὶ, διὰ τὸ φόβου ἀπὸ δὲ τυρᾶν, μηδὲ τὴν ἐπιχειρεῖσθαι ἕνας ἐλμιῶντες, δὲ ἑαυτῷ Ἀσκηφάνης, ἐπιχειρῆσαι αὐτὸν ὁ προσώπων μιλήτῳ χεῖσις. καὶ αὐτὰς αὐτὸ γεγονὼς ζημίας πέντε παρέσχεν ἃ [?]ἐπὶ τὸν Ἱππέων καὶ πελληκίου. Itaque cum Lege sublata est libertas [?]ὀνόματος, κωμῳδεῖν, sublata quoque & hæc est, τὸ αὐτοπροσώπως. Quare neque in Media neque in Noua Comœdia vsurpatum est αὐτοπροσώπως κωμῳδεῖν. Platonius ibidem: ὁ δὲ τὴν μέσην καὶ νέαν κωμῳδίαν, διὰ τὰς τὸ προσωπεῖα πρὸς ὁ ἡγεμόνων ἐδημιούργησεν, διδοῦσης τοῖς Μακεδόνας, καὶ τοῖς ἐπὶ τῶν φίλου ἐξ ἐκείνων φίλους, ἵνα δὲ μὴ ἐκ τῆς τινὸς ἄνεμος ὁμοιότητος προσώπου συμπιέζειν Μακεδόνων Ἀρχέλαον, καὶ ἔξω ὁ ποιητής ἐκ τοῦ αἰσχροῦ? καὶ κωμῳδεῖν, δίκας ἐχρῶντο.
units.tr: Because these were chiefly the choruses, ... [garbled in the source] ... to be whipped publicly by comedy. Comedy, naming names, cast insults ... Augustus ... There is in it, as it were, a historical truth, and things done by citizens were freely described. But since the poets began to abuse this freedom, to harm good men, a law was passed so that no one would be attacked in ... The translator Antimachus [garbled]: Antimachus taught that comedy should not be made from names. Aristophanes wrote plays after the ninety-first Olympiad; he himself produced [them], acted in the fourth year of Archon Demostratus, before the Plutus, and wrote the Cocalus ... Before the ninety-seventh Olympiad the law was not passed, because the Ecclesiazusae, which has a chorus, was produced in the fourth year of the ninety-sixth Olympiad, under Archon Demostratus with Euboulides. So neither before nor after the ninety-seventh Olympiad, but within it, was this law proposed and passed. Those who wanted to commit slander with impunity omitted names but kept the characters, that is, the masks, by which each person they were portraying was displayed; this they called [garbled]. For they were not named in this way but only represented; whence often lawsuits and disputes. Hermogenes, in the passage quoted: bringing in the persons who were mocked in their own persons ... as he names the comedian. Although, while it was permitted to mock by name, it was also permitted to do so in person, and this was done. You have it in the Excerpts of Plato: for the actor in comedy wore masks for the persons mocked, so that the one mocked could say that it was not ... the man of ... For the Life of Aristophanes says this, and it is partly in the Argument of the Knights: Cleon ... was berated by Hippias, who refuted him with thefts ... he was forced to bring him onto the stage by name, through fear ... and when he did so, he received a fine of five talents, as in the Knights and the Peace. Therefore, when the freedom to mock by name was removed by the law, the freedom to do so in person was removed too. Hence neither in Middle nor in New Comedy was it used to mock in person. Platonius in the same place: the middle and new comedy, because of the masks, ... Macedonians ... so that no one should be defamed by resemblance of face, as with Archelaus of Macedon; and the poet, as a result of the ... they went to trial.

units.la: Vetustissima Atheniensium Lege Musica distributa erat in species suas, quas non licebat temere confundere; qui secus fecisset, in illum à peritis artis ad hanc rem constitutis, indicio peracto, animaduertebatur.
units.tr: In the most ancient law of the Athenians, music was divided into its kinds, which it was not lawful to confuse rashly; whoever did otherwise was punished, once the matter had been reported, by experts in the art appointed for this purpose.

units.la: Τῶν μουσικῶν καὶ εἰδῶν ἑαυτῆς ἀφορίζεσθαι, καὶ οὐκ ἐξεῖναι ἄλλο εἰς ἄλλο μεταβάλλειν, ῥήσεις εἴδους.
units.tr: Of musical kinds, they are separated from one another, and it is not allowed to change one into another [Τῶν μουσικῶν ... εἴδους], the rules of the kind.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Plato Libro III. de Legibus: οὐκ ἴσως, ὦ φίλοι, ἀλλὰ τὴν παλαιὰν νόμων ὁ δῆμος ἦν κύριος, ἀλλὰ ἕτερον ἐκεῖνο ἐκ ἀκούουσιν ἰδίᾳ λέγειν τοῖς νόμοις. ΜΕΓ. ποίοις δὲ λέγεις; ΑΘΗΝ. Τῆς ἀεὶ τῆς Μουσικῆς ἐξ ἀρχῆς διελθεῖν τὸν τῆς ἐλευθερίου λόγον ἐπίδοσιν ἕκαστον. δηλονότι γάρ τότε, ὡς τῶν ἡ Μουσικὴ καὶ εἰδή τι ἑαυτῆς ἄλλα καὶ φθόγγοι, καὶ ἃ ἐν ᾧ εἴδος ᾠδῆς; ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ ἁπλῶς Θεσσαλὸς ὄνομα δὲ Ὕμνοι ἐπενάλαιτο. καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ὁ εὐαλὸν ἐπὶ ὠδῆς ἐπεισιν εἴδος. Ὀρφεύς δὲ τις ἐκ αὐτῶν μαλίστα ἐκάλεσε καὶ Παιῶνες, ἐπεισι καὶ ἀλλο, Διονύσου Τέλεσις, ἐκ δὲ ᾠδεμάσος λεγομένος, νόμοις τε αὐτὸ τῆς ἰῶνα ἐκάλεσι, ἐξ ἀλλὸ ὡς πινα ἑτέρως. ἐπὶ λέγειν δὲ κιθαρῳδικοὶ. Τούτων δὲ ἔχῃ συντεταγμένον, καὶ ἀμφὶ τῶν ἁρμονιῶν, ἐξ ἐξ ἕκαστῳ ἂν ὁ ἀμφὶ ὁ ἀμφὶ λόγοις εἴδος. ὁ δὲ κῶς τούτων γιγνὼ τε καὶ ἅμα γιγνόντα δικαιοῦ.
units.tr: Plato mentions this law in Book III of the Laws: "Not, my friends, but the people was master of the ancient laws, unless ... they hear the laws spoken in private." MEG. "Which laws do you mean?" ATH. "Those of music, which from the beginning went through each development of the free word ... for clearly then music and its kinds were ... tunes and ... and the form of song. But the Thessalian name of hymns was added ... and this is the form of song. Orpheus ... Paeans ... Dionysian ... and nomes ... the citharodic ... These are arranged in order, and concerning the modes ... for each ... the kind of words. Whoever ... becoming and at the same time ... is right."

units.tr: Of the tragic poets there were ten judges, also sworn, chosen by lot from among the Athenians, one from each tribe, as is clear from Plutarch's account in the Life of Cimon. Aristotle mentions these judges in Book III of the Rhetoric, saying that Euripides, once publicly accused, appealed to the judges of the theatre. Before them, if anything seemed to have been said dishonourably, impiously, or improperly, the case was argued and the speaker fined. [Greek, illegible]

units.tr: Plutarch described this law in the Life of Lycurgus: Spectators sitting in the theatre are to keep quiet and not brawl. Those who act otherwise are to be removed by the attendants on the archon's order, and if they do not obey, they are to be fined.
