units.tr: These games of the trainers of birds were held in Scyros; for that they were held in Chaeroneia is attested beyond any exception by Aeschines, in the passage cited. But the lame man was in Scyros: in Scyros..., say the ancient masters.

units.la: Pugna autem & commissio gallorum fiebat in pegmate quadrangulari. Auctor Etymologici é Rhetorico Lexico: Ἡ τηλία, πῆγμα τετράγωνον, ἐφ᾽ οὗ ἀλεκτρυόνες συμβάλλοντα, & in laudatis Æschinis verbis: ... [?]. Victorem autem gallum victus sequebatur. Hinc Aristophanes Auibus Ἡ. ὅρις ἔχαιρε ... Θ. πάππος ... [?] ἀλεκτρυόνος;
units.tr: The fight and the pairing of the cocks took place on a square platform. The author of the Etymologicum, from the Rhetorical Lexicon: The telia, a square platform on which cocks fight; and in the words of Aeschines cited: [illegible]. The defeated cock used to follow the victor. Hence Aristophanes in the Birds: [illegible].

units.la: Græcus Interpres: Φειδικὸν τῶν ... [?] [?]. Hinc quoque Theocriti iftain Diofcuris. π. ἡ ... αἴθαλον ... [?] α. σὺς ... [?] π. ὁρίστων Φοινικολόφων ... [?]
units.tr: The Greek interpreter: [illegible]. Hence also the idyll of Theocritus on the Dioscuri: [illegible].

units.la: Tempus, quo lata est hæc Lex, docet Ælianus, ᾧ ... τῷ Περσῶν ἥκει, & cauffam præbuit gallorum pugnæ, quæ Athenienfibus oblata eft, cum duce Themistocle arma inferrent Barbaris: fuit quippe illis exemplo & incitamento ad fortitudinem, quodimitari quoque potterøs voluerunt, vt fortiter agerent, fortiter paterentur. Ælianus: πῶν δὲ τῶν ἀρχαίων ἔλαβεν ὁ νόμος ὠδὲ, ἐρῶ[?]. ὅτε Θεμιστοκλῆς ἐπὶ τοὺς βαρβάρους ἐξῆλθε τῆς πολιτικῆς διοικήσεως[?], ἀλεκτηνόνας ἐπάσατο μαχιμοῦς[?]. Οὐδὲ λόγως αὐτοῖς εἶδεν, ἐπίσης δὲ τῶν γραφῶν[?]. Ὃ τοῖ-νυν ἡμῖν ὁμοίως ἡμῶν[?], ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τοῦ ἀγῶνος ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων, ἐβούλετο Διαφυλάττειν[?] ἐς τὰ ὅμοια ἔργα ἐκοιμήσαν[?]. atque in hunc finem laudat & probat Solon apud Lucianum loco laudato: Ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ τὸν ἡλιον. Ἐπιδύεται γὰρ τὴς ἡμέρας τῆς ψυχῆς ὁρμὴ ἐς ὃ κινδυνώδεις, ὡς μὴ ἀμελῶς ἐχει καὶ ἀπολυμῶσι[?] Φαίνοιντο τὴν ἀλεκτηνόνων, μηδὲ παρα-παρρησιάζειν τὸ πεῖσμα[?], ἢ καμῶς[?], ἢ τὰ ἄλλου δυσχέρειας.
units.tr: Aelian shows the time when this law was passed, when the Persians came, and it gave the occasion for the cock fight, which was offered to the Athenians when they took up arms against the barbarians under the leader Themistocles. It was for them an example and incitement to courage, which they also wished to imitate, so that they might act bravely and endure bravely. Aelian: [Greek, largely illegible: of the ancients the law took its origin... when Themistocles went out against the barbarians...cocks...to preserve these things for the same works]. And to this end Solon, in Lucian, in the passage cited, praises and approves: "But not even the sun...for the impulse of the soul...so that they are not careless, and are not...the cocks, nor [illegible]."

units.la: Romanis in usu quoque fuisse hoc delectationis genus, si non publice, priuatim saltem, constat ex his Plutarchi in Antonio: πολλάκις δὲ συμβαινόντων ἀλεκτηνόνας, πολλάκις ὁ μαχίμους ὀρτυγας, ἐπιχων οἱ Καίσαρος.
units.tr: That the Romans too had this kind of entertainment in use, if not publicly then at least privately, is clear from this passage of Plutarch's Life of Antony: "Often they staged a cockfight, often a fight between quail, in the presence of Caesar's men" [πολλάκις δὲ συμβαινόντων ἀλεκτηνόνας, πολλάκις ὁ μαχίμους ὀρτυγας, ἐπιχων οἱ Καίσαρος].

units.la: Singulæ mensium Kalendæ sacratissimæ erant, quod testatur Plutarchus Lib. de vitando ære alieno: ἐπὶ δὲ αἰσχυνῆ τῶν Καλανδῶν, καὶ τῆς νουμηνίας, ἐς ἱεροπαρτίαν ἡμέρας οὐδὲν, ἀποφύδα ποιοῦνται δύναμιν[?], ἡ ζῆλον. Neque tamen inter festa censebatur. Suidas: ἔξω γὰρ ἐορτὴν ἡμέραι ἐνίας νομίζοντο Αθηναῖοι, ὅτι, Νουμηνία, ἡ ἑβδόμη, Ἀπόλλωνος. Quanquam non tam Apollini sacra erat, quam omnibus Diis. Scholiastes Homeri ad Odyss. Υ. ἐπὶ δὲ πᾶσιν ἑορτὴ τῶν Νεομηνίας πάντων τῶν θεῶν νομίζοντο εἶ[?]. Τοιαύτη γὰρ οἱ πεσόντες τῆς θεὸς δύνασθαι, ἀλλ᾽ ὃ πεσόντων αὐτῷ εἶ[?] τὰ μῆνος. Plutarchus in Quæst. Rom. Ἐλληνες ἐν τῇ Νουμηνία τοὺς θεοὺς σεβόμενοι, τὸν δ᾽ ὕστερον Ἡρωα, ἢ Δαίμονα ἀποδιδόασι. Eo die sacra Diis ex hac Lege faciebant: Τὰς Νουμηνίας θύειν. Mensium Kalendis sacra faciito.
units.tr: Each month's Kalends was held sacred, as Plutarch attests in his book on avoiding debt: "On the Kalends and the New Moon they make no day of business, but they hold it as a day of rest and of honour to the gods" [ἐπὶ δὲ αἰσχυνῆ τῶν Καλανδῶν, καὶ τῆς νουμηνίας, ἐς ἱεροπαρτίαν ἡμέρας οὐδὲν, ἀποφύδα ποιοῦνται δύναμιν[?], ἡ ζῆλον]. Yet it was not counted among the festivals. Suidas: "The Athenians considered certain days outside the festival days, namely the New Moon, the seventh day, and that of Apollo." Although it was not so much sacred to Apollo as to all the gods. The scholiast on Homer, Odyssey 1 (Υ): "A festival of the New Moon was held for all the gods" [ἐπὶ δὲ πᾶσιν ἑορτὴ τῶν Νεομηνίας πάντων τῶν θεῶν νομίζοντο]. Plutarch in the Roman Questions: "The Greeks worship the gods on the New Moon, but the next day they assign to a hero or a demon" [Ἐλληνες ἐν τῇ Νουμηνία τοὺς θεοὺς σεβόμενοι, τὸν δ᾽ ὕστερον Ἡρωα, ἢ Δαίμονα ἀποδιδόασι]. On that day they offered sacrifices to the gods under this law: "On the New Moons to sacrifice" [Τὰς Νουμηνίας θύειν]. The law reads: "On the Kalends of the months let sacrifice be made."

units.la: Legitur hæc Lex apud Libanium Declamat. VIII. quæ Athenis fingitur habita, ut ex toto illius contextu liquet: τῆς Νουμηνίας νόμῳ μὲν πόλεως ἐξιόντων. In arcem tunc ascendebant, & vota faciebant, ut Urbi publice, & sibi priuatim, fausta omnia evenirent. Demosthenes orat. in Aristogitonem I. τῶν ἐκ τῆς νουμηνίας εἰς τὴν ἀκρόπολιν ἀναβαίνοντας, ταχέως τὴν πόλιν διδόναι, καὶ ἕκαστος ἑαυτῷ τοῖς θεοῖς ἀξίως. Atque hæc Sacra Επιμηνία dicebantur. Harpo-cration: Επιμηνία, ἢ ἐπὶ τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον μηνὸς θυσίαι, ἢ τὰ ὑπὲρ ὅλου μηνὸς ἀπαξ ποτὲ γινόμενα θύματα. Eratque tunc Agon. Theophrastus in Charact. Eth. cap. Περὶ ἀγοραίας. εἰ σημεῖον ὁ ἀγὼν Νουμηνίας ἀγῆ. Præbebaturque Pauonum spectaculum, atque id circa Antiphontis ætatem institutum. Antiphon ὁ πᾶ ἐπὶ Σαῶν, ἀλλὰ τὰς μὲν Νουμηνίας ὁ βουλεύομος εἰσιν, τὰς ἄλλας ἡμέρας εἰ ἐς ἐλπίδι βουλόμενος ἡδονῇ, οὐκ ἔστιν ὃς τις ἐτύγχαν, καὶ τῶν τε οὐκ ἐχρῆν τὸ ἀγῶνα ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ πλέον ἡ τεταχότα δεῖν. Huc possunt referri Dicæopolis verba apud Comicum Acharnensibus.
units.tr: This law is read in Libanius, Declamation 8, which is set, as the whole context makes plain, at Athens: "On the New Moon, by the law of the city, the people went out..." [τῆς Νουμηνίας νόμῳ μὲν πόλεως ἐξιόντων]. They then went up to the citadel and made vows, that all things might turn out well for the city publicly and for each man privately. Demosthenes, Against Aristogiton I: "Those who went up to the Acropolis on the New Moon quickly give the city, and each gives himself worthily to the gods" [τῶν ἐκ τῆς νουμηνίας εἰς τὴν ἀκρόπολιν ἀναβαίνοντας, ταχέως τὴν πόλιν διδόναι, καὶ ἕκαστος ἑαυτῷ τοῖς θεοῖς ἀξίως]. These sacrifices were called Epimenia [Επιμηνία]. Harpocration: "Epimenia are either the sacrifices made for each month, or the offerings made once in the course of a whole month" [Επιμηνία, ἢ ἐπὶ τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον μηνὸς θυσίαι, ἢ τὰ ὑπὲρ ὅλου μηνὸς ἀπαξ ποτὲ γινόμενα θύματα]. There was then also a contest. Theophrastus, in the Characters, chapter "On the Man Fond of the Market": "if the contest of the New Moon is a sign" [εἰ σημεῖον ὁ ἀγὼν Νουμηνίας ἀγῆ]. A spectacle of peacocks was also provided, and this was instituted around the time of Antiphon's life. Antiphon, "who was in the Saeoi," says: "but on the New Moons the councillors are there, while on the other days one who wishes, hoping for pleasure, cannot be there, and the contest is not to be held in the way it has been ordered, but more than was ordered." These words of Dicaeopolis in the comedian's Acharnians may be referred here.

units.la: xn. Οἱ παρὰ Βασιλέως πρέσβεις.
units.tr: The ambassadors from the King.

units.la: δι. Ποίου Βασιλέως; ἀξιοῦμαι ἐγὼ πρέσβεσι,
units.tr: Dicaeopolis: From what king? Do I think myself worthy of ambassadors?

units.la: Καὶ τῆς Ταῦσι, πῶς τ᾽ ἀλαζονικῶς.
units.tr: And of the peacocks [Taws], how boastfully!

units.la: Non negarim alludere Comicum his verbis ad ornatum Perfarum: sed facile mihi persuadeo Dicæopolim ruris plenum & inficetiarum eadem notasse spectaculum illud Pauonum, quod non ita pridem institutum erat, & singulis Neomeniis præbebatur: nam dicuntur ista Neomeniæ Metagitnionis. Haberi quippe fingitur χώρια ἐκκλησία audiendis Legatis.
units.tr: I would not deny that the comic poet, with these words, alludes to the finery of the Persians; but I am easily persuaded that Dicaeopolis, full of the country and rustic in his wit, was also pointing at that spectacle of peacocks, which had not long been instituted and was provided at each New Moon; for these New Moons are said to be those of Metageitnion. Of course the scene is imagined as an assembly held apart to hear the ambassadors.

units.la: Οἱ παρὰ Βασιλέως πρέσβεις. Erat hæc concio [illegible, ~10 letters] [?] ἀρχείας, cogebaturque [illegible, ~6 letters], vt infra, Deo dante, suo loco dicemus, τῆς ἀφυπνίας.
units.tr: The ambassadors from the King. This was an assembly [illegible, ~10 letters] of the magistracy, and it was compelled [illegible, ~6 letters], as we shall say in its proper place below, God willing, concerning the awakening [τῆς ἀφυπνίας].

units.la: DE SACRORVM MINISTRIS.
units.tr: ON THE MINISTERS OF THE SACRED RITES.

units.la: TITVLVS SECVNDVS.
units.tr: TITLE TWO.

units.la: Vanquam inter Magistratus, cosque præcipuos, censeretur apud Athenienses is, cui nomen fecerent REGI, tamen vna è multis illi fuit sacrorum cura, quod testantur varia illa Legis, quæ de eo scripta est, Kapita. Eorum vnum illud est:
units.tr: Although the one called king at Athens was counted among the magistrates, and among the chief of them, he had many duties, and one of them was the care of sacred matters. Several chapters of the law written about him attest this. One of them reads:

units.la: ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΟΝΤΑ ΤΩΝΤΕ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΚΑΘΙ-ΣΤΩΝΤΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΔΗΜΩΝ ΑΙΡΩΝΤΑΙ, ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΓΕ-ΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ. ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΚΟΛΙΑΣ ΕΚΛΕΓΕΙΝ ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΜΕ-ΡΟΥΣ ΤΟΥ ΕΑΥΤΩΝ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΝ ΕΚΤΕΑ ΚΡΙΘΩΝ ΔΑΙΝΥΣΘΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΟΝΤΑΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΥΣ ΕΝ ΤΩ ΙΕΡΩ· ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΠΑ-ΤΡΙΑ. ΤΟΝ ΔΕ ΕΚΤΕΑ ΠΑΡΕΧΕΙΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΑΡΧΕΙΑ ΤΩ ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΕΚΛΟΓΗΣ ΤΩΝ ΚΡΙΘΩΝ.
units.tr: "The king shall see to it, along with the archons, that the parasites are installed as the written laws direct, and that they are chosen from the demes. The parasites are to be chosen from the Boukolia, each of them from his own tribe, and the one who is chosen shall be examined in the sanctuary, according to ancestral custom, to see that he is an Athenian. The one who is chosen shall supply to the public granaries for Apollo the Acharnian parasites, selected from the lot of the judges." [ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΟΝΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΤΕ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΚΑΘΙΣΤΩΝΤΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΔΗΜΩΝ ΑΙΡΩΝΤΑΙ, ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ. ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΚΟΛΙΑΣ ΕΚΛΕΓΕΙΝ ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΜΕΡΟΥΣ ΤΟΥ ΕΑΥΤΩΝ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΝ ΕΚΤΕΑ ΚΡΙΘΩΝ ΔΑΙΝΥΣΘΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΟΝΤΑΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΥΣ ΕΝ ΤΩ ΙΕΡΩ· ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ. ΤΟΝ ΔΕ ΕΚΤΕΑ ΠΑΡΕΧΕΙΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΑΡΧΕΙΑ ΤΩ ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΕΚΛΟΓΗΣ ΤΩΝ ΚΡΙΘΩΝ.]

units.la: Descripsit hanc Legem Athenaeus Lib. VI. docetque Kaput esse Legis de Rege latæ. [?] ὡς ἐν τῷ τῶν Βασιλέως νόμων γεγραμμένων ζητ[?]. ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΝ, &c. Sed prima verba male, meo iudicio, interpretatur Vir doctus, cum vertit: Hoc Regi curæ sit, vt Magistratus creentur. Nam, vt mittam Regem non præfuisse creationi [illegible, ~6 letters] Ἀρχόντων, qui Nouem illi ceterorum omnium principes erant, vnusque de illis Rex ipse, tota hac Lege de sacris agitur, præcipuumque munus Regis erat, τὰ περὶ τὰς πατρίας θυσίας [?]. Addit Pollux: [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐπιτιμίας, ἱεροσύνης, ἀμφισβητήσεως, [illegible, ~8 letters] τῆς ἡμέ-ρας, ἢ τοῖς ἱερεῦσι τῶν αὐτῶν δικαίως. Sed mendosa sunt ista: ἡ τῆς ἡμέρας, ἢ τοῖς ἱε-ρεῦσι. Nam non omnibus ἡμέραις Rex ius dicebat: itaque emendo, vna litera expuncta: τῆς ἡμέρας [?] ἱερεῦσι τῶν αὐτῶν δικαίως, & gentibus siue familiis; sed sacris, omnibus iis dicit: Gentes & familiæ hieraticæ erant Athenis, quibus sacrorum quorundam cura erat de mandata, & è quibus Sacerdotes capiebantur: vbi igitur inter gentiles fiebat controuersia ἱεροσύνης, Rex illis iudicium reddebat: Sed ista obiter: Legis nostræ verba expendamus. Cauet Legislator hoc Kapite, vt Rex videat, ne Parasiti aduersus Leges scriptas constituantur, atque è singulis eligantur populis: Nempe, vt puto, nam de hac re nihil certi pronunciare possumus, singuli populi suos è suis popularibus Parasitos eligebant, atque praeficiebant. Parasiti apud Athenienses ij sunt, quos Romani Vires epulones in suis titulis dixerunt: Nam ὁ τῆς Παρασίτου ὄνομα, inquit Athenaeus Lib. VI. [illegible, ~12 letters]. Crates Lib. II. de Attica Dialecto ita munus illorum describit: ὁ Παρασίτος πᾶν ἐκ ἀλλοτρίων [illegible, ~20 letters]. Pollux Lib. VI. cap. VII. [illegible, ~30 letters] Παρασίτος. [illegible, ~25 letters]. Hesychius: Παρασιτεῖν ἐπὶ τὸν τῆς ἱερᾶς σίτου ἐκλέγειν ἀφορισμένου. Sed quis est hic σῖτος; Dicemusne illud esse frumentum sive hordeum, quod è Rhatio defecabatur campo? Id ut credamus facit Pausanias Atticis, cuius haec sunt verba: Ὅτι πλὴν δὲ Ῥαρίου ἀπαρχὰς ἀπαρχῶν λέγοιτο, ἡ ἔχεται τὴν ἀλλοῖα καρπός, ἡ ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν ἐλαῖς ἐξ αὐτῆς χάρισμα σπ᾽ εἰ, ἡ πυρῶν τῶν ἱερῶν αὐτοῦ πάντα τὰ ἐς ἱερὰ ἐκ ἀλλαχοῦ. [illegible, ~10 letters]. [?]
units.tr: Athenaeus, in Book VI, has copied out this law and states that it is a chapter of the law concerning the king. But I think a learned man has interpreted the first words badly when he renders them: "Let the king take care that magistrates are appointed." For, to say nothing of the fact that the king did not preside over the appointment of the archons, who were the nine chiefs of all the others, and of whom the king himself was one, the whole of this law deals with sacred matters, and the king's chief duty was the care of the ancestral sacrifices. Pollux adds that the king had charge of penalties, priesthoods, and disputes [concerning] the day, or [concerning] the priests of the same. But these words are corrupt: "the day, or the priests." For the king did not judge on every day, so, by emending and removing one letter, we get "of the day," and "for the priests of the same by right," and "for the gentes or families." The king judged all those [disputes] concerning sacred rites. The gentes and hieratic families existed at Athens, and to them was entrusted the care of certain sacred rites, and from them the priests were taken. So when a dispute about priesthood arose among the members of the gentes, the king gave judgment to them. But this is a digression. Let us weigh the words of our law. The lawgiver takes care in this chapter that the king see to it that the parasites are not appointed against the written laws, and that they are chosen from the individual peoples. Namely, as I suppose (for we can say nothing certain about this matter), each people chose and set over itself parasites from among its own fellow citizens. Among the Athenians, the parasites are those whom the Romans called what they call viri epulones in their inscriptions. For, as Athenaeus says in Book VI, the name of parasite [...]. Crates, in Book II of his work on the Attic dialect, describes their office thus: the parasite [...] everything from others [...]. Pollux, Book VI, chapter VII, [...] parasite [...]. Hesychius: "to be a parasite is to choose from the sacred grain set aside." But what is this grain? Shall we say it is the wheat or barley that was harvested from the Rharian plain? Pausanias in his Attica leads us to think so, and his words are these: [...] Besides the Rharian field, the first-fruits of the first-fruits were said to be [...] and the sacred grain was all brought to the sanctuaries from elsewhere. [...]

units.la: An vero illud est, quod nauce batur in illis teni aruipendiis, quae unicuique Deo dedicabant, vel diuidebant, è quorum locationibus proueniebant impensae, quae postea in sacrificiis publice fiebant. Grammatici è Didymo. Δίδυμος φησιν ὁ Γραμματικός, αὐτὴ τὸ ἐκ τῆς τεμένους ἀρχῆς, ἐκ ἐπὶ ἱερᾶς ἐκλέγειν τὴν λοιπὴν τῆς ἀφορμῆς; ἐκ ὧν αὐτοῖς οὐκ ἐδίδοντο, ὧν ἐκ τῆς ἱερᾶς ἐκλέγειν, ἔτι τὸ σάκκος ἀπορρίψαντες ἐξ ἐπὶ ἔχουσι ἱερὰ ἐκ ἀλλαχοῦ. Atque ex his aruipendiis eius Dei, cui erant dedicata, vel diuita, Parasiti ἐξέλεγον τὸν ἱερὸν σῖτον. Est quoque ὁ ἱερὸς σῖτος frumentum sive hordeum, quod a priuatis, pro suo modulo, religionis ergo, dabatur Templis, atque conferebatur. Huc facit locus è Lib. XVIII. Digestorum Scaevola, qui legitur D. de Annuis legatis Lib. XX. §. 1. Attia fidei commissum his verbis reliquit: Quisquis mihi heres erit, fidei eius commitio, uti det ex reditu cenaculi mei & horrei, post obitum, Sacerdoti, & Hierophylaco, & Libertis, qui in illo Templo erunt, denaria decem die nundinarum, quas ibi posui. Exstitiho [?] Libertos vocati, quos veteres dixere Tarasitos. Cum enim parasitari insecutis postea temporibus in vitium excidisset, nec esset ingenui hominis, sed vilis potius, & libertino patre nati, quos Parasitos in veterum monumentis & scriptis nominatos repererat Scaevola, Libertos vocauit.
units.tr: Or is it rather what was being taken in those allotted revenues which they dedicated or assigned to each god, from whose leases the expenses were derived that were afterwards spent on public sacrifices? Didymus the grammarian says: [...] from the beginning of the sacred precinct, [...] they were not given to them, but from which they chose the sacred [grain], and having thrown off their sacks they then held sacred [grain] from elsewhere. And from these revenues of that god to whom they were dedicated or assigned, the parasites chose the sacred grain. The sacred grain is also wheat or barley which was given to the temples by private persons, each according to his means, for the sake of religion, and was brought together. A passage in Book XVIII of the Digest of Scaevola is relevant here; it is read in D. De annuis legatis, Book XX, §1. Attia left a trust in these words: "Whoever shall be my heir, I entrust to his good faith that from the income of my dining room and granary he give, after death, to the priest, and to the hierophylax, and to the libertos who will be in that temple, ten denarii on each market day, which I have set aside there." Here the libertos are those whom the ancients called parasitos. For when parasitari had in later times fallen into disrepute, and it was not the mark of a free man but rather of a base one, and of a man born of a freedman father, Scaevola, who had found the parasitos named in the monuments and writings of the ancients, called them libertos.

units.la: Sequitur in Lege: ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΚΟΛΙΑΣ ΕΚΛΕΓΕΙΝ, &c. Incomparabilis Casaubonus suspicabatur βουκολίαν hic dici vel iugerum, vel alium agri modum, ex quo fas fuit cuique Parasito hordei hecteum exigere: Sed suspicabatur tantum: Nos plane contra sentimus. Neque enim iubetur Parasiti ἐκλέγειν ἐκ τῆς βουκολίας, exigere ex agri modo, qui βουκολία dicatur, hordei hecteum: sed potius Parasitos praecipitur, ut singuli seponant hordei hecteum ἐκ τῆς μέσης τῆς ἱερᾶς σίτου, cuius [?] τῶν ἐκλέγειν ἀφορισθῆναι ἔτι. Quod bona fide praestandum esse à Parasitis cauet Legislator verbis istum, quae Virum Incomparabilem habuerunt exercitum: Ea ita sunt legenda: ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΒΟΥΚΟΛΙΑΣ ΕΚΛΕΙΝ, &c. Seponant, inquit, Parasiti hecteum hordei ἐντὸς βουκολίας, bona fide, siue dolo malo, aut fraude: βουκολία hic idem significat quod ἀπάτη, atque βουκολέω, ἀπατάω, decipio, fallo, interpretatur Hesychius. Hic, puto, Legislator est: sed iudicent eruditi. Hordei hecteum, quem seponere hac Lege iubebantur Parasiti, Apollini reponebant in apothecis Parasiti, qui ex Acharnensium populo fuerant electi: ΤΟΝ ΔΕ ΕΚΤΕΛΕΙ ΠΑΡΕΧΤΙΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΑΡΧΕΙΑ ΤΩΙ ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΕΚΛΟΓΗΣ ΤΩΝ ΚΡΙΘΩΝ. Atque hi Acharnensium Parasiti sacra Apollini faciebant, ut constat ex altero huius Legis Kapite in haec verba: ΘΥΕΙΝ ΤΩΙ ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ Parasiti Acharnensium sacra Apollini faciunto.
units.tr: The law continues: "and the parasites are to be chosen from the Boukolia," and so on. The incomparable Casaubon suspected that Boukolia here means either a iugerum or some other measure of land, from which each parasite was allowed to exact a hecteus of barley. But that was only a suspicion, and we take the opposite view. For the parasites are not ordered to choose from the Boukolia, that is, to exact a hecteus of barley from a measure of land called Boukolia. Rather, the parasites are instructed that each one is to set aside a hecteus of barley from the sacred grain in the middle [...], of which the choosing is to be set apart. The lawgiver takes care that the parasites perform this in good faith, in words which that incomparable man has rendered as follows, and which should be read thus: "and the parasites are to choose within the Boukolia," and so on. Let them set aside, he says, a hecteus of barley within the Boukolia, in good faith, or with evil intent, or by fraud. Here Boukolia means the same as deceit, and Hesychius explains boukoleō as apatāō, to deceive or cheat. This, I think, is the lawgiver's meaning, but let the learned judge. The hecteus of barley which the parasites were ordered by this law to set aside was deposited for Apollo in the storehouses by the parasites who had been chosen from the people of Acharnae: "and the parasites shall supply to the public granaries for Apollo the Acharnian parasites, selected from the lot of the judges." And these Acharnian parasites performed sacrifices to Apollo, as is clear from the other chapter of this law, in these words: "The Acharnian parasites shall sacrifice to Apollo." [...] Parasites of the Acharnians shall sacrifice to Apollo.

units.la: Vnum esse ex huius Legis Kapitibus ex Athenaeo constat, qui laudato Lib. VI. καὶ τοῖς τὸ Βασιλέως ... [?] Θύειν τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι τῆς Ἀχαρνικῆς Παρασίτης. Habuerunt singuli suos Parasitos Dij: Hic habes Apollinis Parasitos, & infe-quentibus Herculi quoque fuisse dicemus: Eligebantur autem è populis qui-que suis, ut iam diximus: Quare hic dicuntur ΟΙ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙ-ΤΟΙ nempe ex Acharnensibus capti. Unde intelligenda & emendanda sunt quae verbis praecedentibus apud Athenaeum è Themistone, quamquam is non laudetur, referuntur: ... [?] Παρασίτους ... ἄρχοντες ... Παλλήνης ... Ἀνοχαρίου ... Ἀναγυρασίους ... Πιτθεύς ... Χαρίνος Δημοχάρους, Γαργήττιος. Optime Vt magnus ebleruat, nullam senofle Athenis sacram tribum, quomodo interpretatus est Dalecampius: itaque ipse putat relinquendum esse vacuum spacium, ad capiendum tribus nomen, quod deest: fenibas, ἡγεμόνες, vel ἱερᾶς. Tali Tribu rem diuinam faciente, Lycofrato Archonte: Gargettio. (referibit enim ΟΥΙ Λυκοφράτου Γαργηττίου.) Vel Phyle est nomen proprium Sacerdotis, id est, Phyle Sacerdote: Erant enim sacra, quibus Sacerdos femina praerat. Gargettius & Pitthaeus ex consuetudine Attica [?] indicant. Agitur hic de donariis, quae visebantur in Atticae populo Pallene, à Parasitis consecrata. Quorundam haec erat inscriptio. ΑΡΧΟΝΤΕΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΙ ΑΝΕΘΕΣΑΝ ΟΙ ΕΠΙ ΠΥΘΟΔΩΡΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΘΕΝΤΕΣ ΧΡΥΣΩ. ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΙ. Alia praeterea recentebat donaria Themistone, ex eoque Athenaeus, inter cetera, puto, phialam sacram, cui sua erat inscripta epigraphe: itaque re-scribo: ΤΩΙ Φιάλης ἱερᾶς, supple ἀνέθηκε ... τῷ. Phialae autem sacra inscriptum erat: ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΙ, ΕΠΙ ΛΥΚΟΣΤΡΑΤΟΥ, ΓΑΡΓΗΤΤΙΟΙ ΠΕΡΙΚΛΗΣ ΠΕΡΙΚΛΕΙΤΟΥ ΠΙΤΘΕΥΣ, ΧΑΡΙΝΟΣ ΔΗΜΟΧΑΡΟΥΣ ΓΑΡΓΗΤΤΙΟΙ. Parasiti, Lycofrato Archonte, Gargettiorum, Pericles Periclis Pitheus, F. Pitthaeus, Charinus Democharis F. Gargettij. ΠΙΤΘΕΥΣ Pitthaeus hic, meo iudicio, non est appellatio ... sed viri nomen: Neque enim verisimile est, idem donarium appensum fuisse à duobus Parasitis, qui non tantum eiusdem non ... sed ne tribus quidem. Atqui Parasiti eligebantur è singulis populis, nec confundebantur inter se. Omnes igitur isti erant Gargettij: neque rescribendum est, ut volunt praestantissimi viri ΕΠΙ ΛΥΚΟΣΤΡΑΤΟΥ ΓΑΡΓΗΤΤΙΟΥ. Non enim apponi solet Archontis nomini, cuius δῆμος ille sit popularis. Sed ad Acharnenses nostros redeamus, quos huius Legis Kaputiubet ΘΥΕΙΝ ΤΩΙ ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΙ Apollo hic cognominabatur ΑΓΥΙΕΥΣ. nam hunc colebant Acharnenses. Paufanias Atticis: ἐν ... Ἀχαρνικὰ δῆμος. οἱ ... Ἀπόλλωνα πυθοῦ ... ἀγυιεύς.
units.tr: It is clear from Athenaeus that this is one of the chapters of this law, for he quotes Book VI, where [...] the king [...] to sacrifice to Apollo, the parasite of the Acharnians. Each god had his own parasites. Here you have the parasites of Apollo, and below we shall say that Heracles too had them. They were chosen from their own peoples, as we have already said. Hence they are here called "the parasites of the Acharnians," that is, taken from the Acharnians. From this, the words that Athenaeus quotes from Themistocles earlier should be understood and emended, though he himself is not cited for this: [...] parasites [...] archons [...] Pallene [...] Anocharius [...] Anagyrasians [...] Pitthaeus [...] Charinus son of Demochares, of Gargettus. Vincent Maggi, a great scholar, rightly observed that there was no sacred tribe at Athens, as Dalechamps translated it. So he thinks a blank space should be left for the name of a tribe, which is missing; [perhaps supply] phylē [the tribe], hēgemones [the leaders], or hieras [sacred]. [It reads] "the tribe performing the sacrifice, under the archon Lycophratus, of Gargettus." (For it refers to the phrase "of Lycophratus of Gargettus.") Or Phyle is the proper name of a priestess, that is, "Phyle, priestess," for there were sacred rites presided over by a woman priest. According to Attic custom, Gargettius and Pitthaeus indicate [the demes]. The passage here concerns the votive offerings in the Attic deme of Pallene, which were dedicated by the parasites. The inscription of one of them read: "The archons and parasites dedicated [this], those under Pythodorus the archon, having been crowned with gold, [...] crown." Themistocles mentions other votive offerings, and from him Athenaeus records, among other things, I think, a sacred phiale with its own inscription; so I rewrite it: [the dedication] of the sacred phiale, [supply] "dedicated" [...] to. The inscription on the sacred phiale read: "Parasites, under Lycostratus, Gargettians: Pericles son of Pericleitus, of Pitthaeus; Charinus son of Demochares, Gargettian." Parasites, under Lycostratus; Gargettians; Pericles son of Pericles, Pitthaeus; Charinus son of Demochares, Gargettian. In my judgment, "Pitthaeus" here is not an appellation [of a deme], but the name of a man. For it is not likely that the same votive offering was hung up by two parasites who did not belong to the same deme, nor even to the same tribe. And yet the parasites were chosen from individual peoples, and were not mixed up with one another. All of them, then, were Gargettians, and it need not be rewritten, as certain very distinguished men would have it, as "under Lycostratus, of Gargettus." For the name of the archon is not usually followed by the name of the deme to which he belongs. But let us return to our Acharnians, whom this chapter of the law orders to sacrifice to Apollo. Apollo was here surnamed Agyieus, for the Acharnians worshipped him. Pausanias, in his Attica: [...] the deme of the Acharnians [...] Apollo [...] Agyieus.

units.la: Sequitur ex eadem Lege aliud Caput, quod ita habet: ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΑ ΤΩΝ ΑΕΙ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΟΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ, ΟΥΣ ΑΝ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΔΗΜΩΝ ΠΡΟΑΙΡΩΝ- ΤΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΓΕΡΟΝΤΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑΣ ΤΑΣ ΠΡΩΤΟ- ΓΟΝΕΙΣ.
units.tr: There follows from the same Law another chapter, which reads thus: "Let the king take care of the one who always holds the kingship, and of the parasites whom they choose from the demes, and of the old men, and of the women who hold the first place" [ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΑ ΤΩΝ ΑΕΙ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΟΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΥΣ, ΟΥΣ ΑΝ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΔΗΜΩΝ ΠΡΟΑΙΡΩΝΤΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΓΕΡΟΝΤΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑΣ ΤΑΣ ΠΡΩΤΟΓΟΝΕΙΣ].

units.la: Describit Athenaeus Lib. VI. ex Themistone in Paraphrasi ΤΩΝ ΘΕΣΜΩΝ ἐν Παναθηναίοις, ΓΙΝΕΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΑ, &c cetera, quae iam descripsimus. Caput de Legis Regiae attestatione Pollucis constat, vbi quid sit [?] interpretatur Lib. III. cap. III. [illegible, ~12 letters]. Sed inquiramus, de quibus hic agatur Sacris, quorum cura non tantum Regi, sed etiam Paraficis, Senibus, & feminis demandata est. Regis curae videntur fuisse communia Panathenaea: nam, vt est apud Pollucem Lib. VIII. cap. VIII. [illegible, ~10 letters]. Panathenaea autem erant in hoc censu. Panathenaeis praeterea Senes forma eximii eligebantur. Habes apud Xenophontem in Symposio: & ex eo Iuncus Libro de Senectute: cuius verba suo loco reddemus: atque hic [illegible, ~8 letters] inquit Iuncus. Hos Senes puto designari hac Lege ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΓΕΡΟΝΤΑΣ. Quemadmodum & cum dixit, ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑΣ ΤΑΣ ΠΡΩΤΟΓΟΝΕΙΣ. intelligi puto anus illas, quae, quemadmodum Senes, in Panathenaeorum pompa oleae ramum gestabant: de quibus Dicaearchus in Panathenaico. Scholiastes Comici ad Vespas: [illegible, ~30 letters]. Atque de his tantum est.
units.tr: Athenaeus in Book VI, from Themistones's paraphrase of the laws at the Panathenaea, describes the words "let the king take charge," etc., and the rest, which we have already set out. The chapter on the king's duties is attested by Pollux, where he explains what it is in Book III, chapter III [illegible]. But let us inquire which sacred rites are here meant, whose care was entrusted not only to the king, but also to the parasites, old men, and women. The king's care seems to have concerned the common Panathenaea: for, as Pollux says in Book VIII, chapter VIII [illegible], the Panathenaea were in this category. Moreover, old men of outstanding appearance were chosen for the Panathenaea. You have this in Xenophon's Symposium, and from it Juncus in his book on old age, whose words we shall render in their place; and here [illegible] says Juncus. I think these old men are meant by this Law, "and the old men." Likewise when it says, "and the foremost women," I think those old women are meant who, like the old men, carried olive branches in the procession of the Panathenaea; Dicaearchus speaks of them in his Panathenaicus. The scholiast on the comic poet's Wasps [illegible]. And so much for these.

units.la: Inter has Leges locum dedimus huic pfephifmati, quod vim Legis habuif- se nulli dubitamus.
units.tr: We have placed among these Laws this decree, which we do not doubt had the force of law.

units.la: ΤΑ ΔΕ ΕΠΙΜΗΝΙΑ ΘΥΕΤΩ Ο ΙΕ- ΡΕΥΣ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΩΝ· ΟΙ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΙ ΕΝΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΘΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΠΑΙ- ΔΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ. ΟΣ Δ' ΑΝ ΜΗ ΘΕΛΗ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΕΥΕΙΝ, ΕΙΣΑΙ ΕΓΩ [?] ΚΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΔΙΚΑ- ΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ.
units.tr: "The parasite shall sacrifice with the priest; the parasites shall be one of those from the bastards and the children of these, according to their country. Whoever does not wish to be a parasite, let him be brought also concerning these before the court" [ΤΑ ΔΕ ΕΠΙΜΗΝΙΑ ΘΥΕΤΩ Ο ΙΕΡΕΥΣ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΩΝ· ΟΙ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΙ ΕΝΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΘΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ. ΟΣ Δ' ΑΝ ΜΗ ΘΕΛΗ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΕΥΕΙΝ, ΕΙΣΑΓΕΤΩ ΚΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ].

units.la: Meminit e Polemone Athenaeus Lib. VI. [illegible, ~40 letters]. ΤΑ ΔΕ ΕΠΙΜΗ- ΝΙΑ ΘΥΕΤΩ Ο ΙΕΡΕΥΣ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΩΝ· & quæ sequuntur iam à nobis descripta. Huc spectant Diodori Sinopensis, versus, è dramate, cuius titulus [?] τοὺς Ἡρακλέους παῖδας [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: Athenaeus mentions this, quoting Polemon, Book VI [illegible]. "The priest shall sacrifice the monthly rites with the parasites," and what follows, which we have already set out. To this relate the verses of Diodorus of Sinope, from a drama whose title is [?] "The Children of Heracles" [illegible lines].

units.la: Diodori mentem allecutus non videtur Casaubonus [illegible, ~12 letters], cuius hæc est animaduersio. Quod ait Poëta de Parasitorum origine, sententiam continet hanc: Olim publice Athenis alebantur in singulis pagis, in honorem Herculis: postea Magistratus, vt hoc sumptu liberarent Rempub. diuites elegerunt, quibus alendos Parasitos tradierent: [illegible, ~12 letters], de Magistratu intelligendum, vtique si legas [illegible, ~12 letters] sin scribas, [?] paululum diuersa sententia expones: ipsi diuites horrabantur sese ad exhibendos Parasitos. Hactenus Vir magnus, qui nescio vnde acceperit sententiam, quam Poëta attingit, non certe, aut ego valde fallor, è verbis ipsius: Hoc enim ex illis colligas, è singulis Atticæ pagis duodecim captos fuisse Herculi Parasitos, non è plebe vulgi, sed apprime nobiles, quibus & res esset, & fama, de his intelligendum esse nostrum pluralem [?]. Nam quia de Parasitis Herculis agebatur, propositum erat in Herculis fano, quod erat ἐν Κυνοσάργει Atticæ populo, duodecim eligebantur è singulis populis, quot scilicet erant anni menses, qui singulis mensium Kalendis facta Herculi faciebant. habes in Plebiscitmate ΤΑ ΔΕ ΕΡΙΜΙΝΙΑ ΟΥΕΤΩ Ο ΙΕΡΕΥΣ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΩΝ. Quod sequitur apud Diodorum: [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] (ita legendum) [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: Casaubon does not seem to have grasped Diodorus's meaning [illegible], and his remark is this. What the poet says about the origin of the parasites contains this sense: Formerly the parasites were maintained at public expense at Athens in the individual districts, in honour of Hercules; later the magistrates, in order to free the commonwealth from this expense, chose the wealthy and handed over to them the parasites to be maintained [illegible], which must be understood of the magistrate, especially if you read [illegible]; but if you write [?], you will explain it in a slightly different sense: the wealthy themselves vied with one another to provide the parasites. So far that great man; I do not know whence he took the view that the poet touches on, but certainly, unless I am much mistaken, not from the poet's own words. For from them you may infer that twelve parasites were taken for Hercules from the individual districts of Attica, not from the common crowd, but men of the highest rank, who had both wealth and reputation; and our plural must be understood of these. For since the discussion concerned the parasites of Hercules, it was the rule that in the temple of Hercules, which was at Cynosarges in the people of Attica, twelve were chosen from the individual districts, namely as many as there were months in the year, who made the offerings to Hercules on the first day of each month. You have in the decree: "The priest shall sacrifice the monthly rites with the parasites." What follows in Diodorus [illegible lines] (so it should be read) [illegible lines].

units.la: Dicitur, vt probet quomodo [illegible, ~12 letters]. Nam, cum olim Parasiti essent tantum Deorum, Herculis puta, facti quoque sunt hominum potentiorum, qui Herculem imitari voluerunt; & Parasitos ipsi habere, non illos quidem [illegible, ~8 letters], sed qui adulandi artem haberent penitus cognitam. Hic est sensus verborum Diodori, quem paucis indicasse non erit praeter rem, quæ de agimus Parasitorum Herculis meminit Chidemus [?] in A-[?], his verbis [illegible, ~20 letters] Σπονδῶν τῷ Ἡρακλῆ[?] Sed agit Psephisma, puto, de Parasitis Herculis, qui ἐκ τῆς Δήμου Κυνοσάργες[?]. Itaque Nothorum meminit, qui Cynosargis censebantur: Κυνοσάργης, τόπος ὧν ἐν Ἀθήναις, ἐν ᾧ καὶ οἱ νόθοι ἐγγενόμενοι ἐκείνοντο[?], ἐπὶ τῆς δὲ τῆς ὅπως γίγνεται[?] ὡς, itemque exercebantur, quia etiam Hercules inter Deos Nothus censebatur. Plutarchus in Themistocle: καὶ τῶν Νόθων εἰς ὃ Κυνοσάργης σωτηρίων[?]. τὴν δ' ἐπὶ ἕξω πυλῶν γυμνάσιον Ἡρακλέους, ἐπὶ κάκιππος[?] εἰς ἡ ψηφίω[?] ἐκ ὑπὸ ἰοῖς, ἀλλ' ἐνείχετο νέα, ἀλλ' ἐπ' ἡ μητέρα ἱστορία ἐπὶ ὁδῷ. Herculani huius Templi, quod erat Cynosargis, Parasiti iubentur hac Lege unum è Nothis aut Nothorum liberis in suum ordinem cooptare: ΟΙ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΙ ΕΝΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΘΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ. plena non est haec oratio, & deest aliquid: sed tamen facile sensus hic, quem diximus, elicitur. ΟΣ Δ' ΑΝ ΜΗ ΘΕΛΗ, ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΕΙΝ ΕΙΣΑΓΕΤΩ ΚΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ. Si quis nollet cooptari & ὃ ἀποδιδράσκειν defugeret, nomen illius apud Magistratum deferebatur, & in iudicium vocabatur. Quod autem de Nothorum cooptatione in hac Lege habes, non aduersatur Legi ab Euclide latae, quae de Nothis est: μηδὲ Νόθων, μηδὲ νόθῃ ἀπογραφέντι εἴη, μηδ' ἱερεῖ, μηδ' οἰκίων ἀπ' Εὐχρείδου Ἀρχοντος. Lex enim haec Nothos arcet ab omnibus sacris, sed gentilitiis tantum.
units.tr: It is said, to prove how [illegible]. For since at first the parasites were only those of the gods, of Hercules that is, they also became those of more powerful men, who wished to imitate Hercules, and to have parasites of their own, not indeed [illegible], but men who had a thoroughly learned art of flattery. This is the sense of Diodorus's words, which it will not be beside the point to indicate briefly; Chidemus [?] in his [?] mentions the parasites of Hercules in these words [illegible]. But the decree, I think, deals with the parasites of Hercules, who were from the deme of Cynosarges. Hence it mentions the nothoi, who were registered at Cynosarges: Cynosarges is a place at Athens, in which also the bastards who were born there were trained, and as they were exercised there, because Hercules too was counted among the gods as a bastard. Plutarch in Themistocles: "and of the bastards, that is, of the Cynosarges [ones], ... the gymnasium of Heracles outside the gates, ... to which the mother ... on the road." Of this temple of Hercules, which was at Cynosarges, the parasites are ordered by this Law to co-opt one of the nothoi or of the children of the nothoi into their order: "the parasites shall be one of those from the bastards and the children of these, according to their country." The sentence is not complete, and something is missing; yet the sense we have stated is easily drawn out. "Whoever does not wish to be a parasite, let him be brought also concerning these before the court." If anyone was unwilling to be co-opted and tried to escape, his name was reported to the magistrate and he was summoned to court. What you have in this Law about the co-optation of nothoi does not conflict with the law proposed by Euclides, which concerns the nothoi: "Let no bastard, nor the son of a bastard, be enrolled, nor be a priest, nor hold any office, under the archon Euclides." For this Law excludes the nothoi from all sacred rites, but only from the gentile ones.

units.la: Praecedenti Titulo demonstrauimus Apollinem summo in honore fuisse apud Athenienses, & Θεωρούς in insulam Delum missos fuisse Athenis, in his erant duo è Cerycum Mysticorum gente, qui annum in Delio Templo Apollini Parasitabantur, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: In the preceding title we have shown that Apollo was held in the highest honour among the Athenians, and that the sacred envoys were sent from Athens to the island of Delos; among these were two from the family of the Cerycae of the Mysteries, who for a year served as parasites in the Delian temple of Apollo, by this Law:

units.la: ΚΑΙ ΤΩ ΚΗΡΥΚΕ ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΓΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΚΗΡΥΚΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΜΥΣΤΗΡΙΩΤΙΔΟΣ, ΤΟΥΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΕΙΝ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΔΗΛΙΩι ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΝ.
units.tr: "And to the herald from the family of the heralds of the Mysteries, these shall serve as parasites in the Delian temple each for a year" [ΚΑΙ ΤΩ ΚΗΡΥΚΕ ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΓΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΚΗΡΥΚΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΜΥΣΤΗΡΙΩΤΙΔΟΣ, ΤΟΥΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΕΙΝ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΔΗΛΙΩι ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΝ].

units.la: Duo Ceryces funto è gente Cerycum Mysticorum : ĭdémque annum in Delio Templo Parasiti funto.
units.tr: Let two Ceryces be from the family of the Cerycae of the Mysteries, and let them be parasites in the Delian temple for the same year.

units.la: Huius Legis meminit Athenaeus Lib. VI. ἐν δὲ τοῖς Κύρβεσι τοῖς περὶ τὴν Δηλιάδων, οὕτως γέγραπται. ΚΑΙ ΤΩ ΚΗΡΥΚΕ, &c. e quibus vides Legem hanc esse de Theoris, qui in insulam Delum mittebantur; nam scripta est περὶ τὴν Δηλιάδων. Sunt enim, vt e Grammaticis constat, Δηλιασταί, οἱ εἰς Δῆλον ἐξελαύνοντες Θεωρούς. Optime animaduertit Vir Incomparabilis, inter antiquissimas gentes populi Athenienfium fuisse gentem Κηρύκων, qui non erant caduceatores, neque praecones, sed sacrorum Ministri: Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. Κῆρυξ, ὁ μὲν τῆς τῶν Μυστικῶν, ἀπὸ Κήρυκος τῆς Ἑρμοῦ, ἡ Παλλάδος τῆς Κέκροπος. ὁ δὲ περὶ τὰς ἀγῶνας, οἱ δὲ περὶ τὰς πομπάς, ἐκ τῆς Ἐλευσίνιων ἡμέρας, οἱ δ', κατ' ἀρχὰν τὰ ὠνια προκηρύττοντες. Verba haec Pollucis indicant, quare in Lege scriptum sit ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΓΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΚΗΡΥΚΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΜΥΣΤΗΡΙΩΤΙΔΟΣ, ne quis putet esse è gente Eunonidarum: itaque perinde est ac si scriptum fuisset: ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΓΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΚΗΡΥΚΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΜΥΣΤΙΚΩΝ. ne quis exiftimet cum summo viro, gentem hanc in plures familias fuisse distinctam, quarum etiam diuisae fuerunt functiones, quod nullo auctore probatur. Verum ex hac gente erat vnus è quatuor illis Ἐπιμελητὴς τῆς Μυστηίων. Erat quoque ἱεροκῆρυξ. Eusebius Præparat. Euangel. Lib. III. ἐν ᾗ τῆς κατ' Ἐλευσῖνα Μυστηρίοις ὁ μὲν Ἱε[?]ροφάντης, εἰς εἰκόνα τῆς δημιουργοῦ ἀνοκλάζε[?]ται. Δαδοῦχος, εἰς τὸν Ἡλίου· ὁ δὲ μὲν [?] βωμῷ, εἰς τὸν σελήνης· ὁ δὲ Ἱεροκήρυξ, Ἑρμῆς.
units.tr: Athenaeus, Book VI, mentions this Law: "in the Cyrbes concerning the Delian women, it is written thus: 'And to the herald,' etc." From which you see that this Law concerns the Theori, who were sent to the island of Delos; for it is written concerning the Delian women. For there are, as is established from the grammarians, Deliastae, those who sent the Theori out to Delos. The Incomparable man rightly observed that among the most ancient peoples of the Athenians there was the family of the Cerykes, who were not heralds with staffs, nor criers, but ministers of sacred rites: Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: "The herald, one of the Mysteries, from Keryx son of Hermes, and of Pallas, from Cecrops; another for the games, others for the processions, from the day of Eleusinian..., others who at first proclaimed the sales." These words of Pollux indicate why it is written in the Law "from the family of the heralds of the Mysteries," lest anyone think it is from the family of the Eunonidae; so it is just as if it had been written: "from the family of the heralds of the Mysteries." Lest anyone should think, with that great man, that this family was divided into several households, whose functions were also divided, which is proved by no authority. But from this family was one of those four Epimeletai of the Mysteries. He was also the sacred herald. Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book III: in the Mysteries at Eleusis, the hierophant is dedicated to the image of the Creator, the torch-bearer to the Sun, the one at the altar to the Moon, and the sacred herald to Hermes.

units.la: Extat Legis fragmentum apud Athenæum Lib. VI. quod huc reiecimus, quia de Parasitis est, in hæc verba:
units.tr: There is a fragment of the law preserved in Athenaeus, Book VI. I have put it here, although it concerns the Parasites, and it reads as follows:

units.la: TOIN ΔΕ BOOIN TOIN HΓEMONOIN TOIN EΞAIPOYMENOIN, TO MEN TPITON MEPOΣ EIΣ TON AΓΩNA, TA ΔE ΔYO MEPH, TO MEN ETEPON TΩ/ IEPEI, TO ΔE, TOIΣ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΙΣ.
units.tr: Of the oxen that the leaders take out, one third goes to the contest, and of the other two parts one goes to the priest and the other to the Parasites, let them yield [ΤΩΝ ΒΟΩΝ ΤΩΝ ἡγεμόνων ΤΩΝ ἐξαιρουμένων, ΤΟ ΜΕΝ ΤΡΙΤΟΝ ΜΕΡΟΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ἈΓΩΝΑ, ΤΑ ΔΕ ΔΥΟ ΜΕΡΗ, ΤΟ ΜΕΝ ἙΤΕΡΟΝ ΤΩ ἹΕΡΕΙ, ΤΟ ΔΕ, ΤΟΙΣ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΟΙΣ].

units.la: Duorum boum præcidaneorum eximiorum tertia pars in certamen: reliquarum duarum vna Sacerdoti: altera Parasitis, cedanto.
units.tr: A third part of the choice oxen, the first-fruit oxen, goes to the contest; of the remaining two parts, one goes to the priest and the other to the Parasites, let them yield.

units.la: Lex hæc erat inscripta columnæ in Anacæo siue Dioscurorum Templo: Athenæus Lib. VI. ἀλλὰ μὴν, ἐπεὶ γὰρ τῶν Παρασίτων ὁ λόγος, καὶ τῷ Ἀναξίῳ ἐπί τινος φήσας γεγράφθαι [?].
units.tr: This law was inscribed on a column in the Anaceum, or temple of the Dioscuri. Athenaeus, Book VI: "But indeed, since the discussion concerns the Parasites, and he said that Anaxios had been written in a certain place [ἀλλὰ μὴν, ἐπεὶ γὰρ τῶν Παρασίτων ὁ λόγος, καὶ τῷ Ἀναξίῳ ἐπί τινος φήσας γεγράφθαι]..." and the rest, as above: "Of the oxen, etc."

units.la: TOIN ΔE BOOIN. &c. Huius ædis mentio apud Harpocrationem his verbis: Ἀναξίου, ὃ ἀάκτρεγον. Δημοσθένης ἐν τῇ κατὰ Στεφάνου, ἱερὸν τῶν Διοσκούρων. Locus quem indicauit Harpocration, hic est è priore in Stephanum Oratione: πονηρὸς, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, πονηρὸς ἐστιν ἐκ τῆς ἀναξίου καὶ ἀδίκως. σημεῖον δὲ εἰ γὰρ ὁ ὧν δίκαιος, πέμπε αὐτῷ, τὰ τῆς δεκαπάτου δημοκρατίας. νῦν δὲ Ἔστουτον χρημάτων ὁ πλήθος κύριος καταφυγὴ, ὥστε Ἔστουτον λαβεῖν ἀπ' αὐτῶν χαλεπὸς ὅσα νῦν κίκτησθαι, οὐχ ὀφείλει Ἔστω, ἀλλὰ παντὸς ἔχειν ἡγεῖσθαι. Locus hic etiam olim legebatur, ἐν τῷ ἀναξίου, vt constat è glossa, quæ in editione Parisiensi è Suida adscribitur: ἀάκτιον διομωτήριον, εἰς ὃ καταπίπτει τῶν πονηρῶν δούλους, & ad hanc διπλογραφίαν spectant verba Etymologici M. ἀάκτιον ἡ διομωτήριον. ἀξιοῦσι δὲ τινες ἀάκτιον γράφεσθαι· ὅπερ ἔστι ὁ Διοσκούρων. Ἀναξας γὰρ εἰ Διόσκουροι. Sed legi non potest ἐν τῷ ἀναξίου eo sensu, quo interpretantur, ἐν τῷ διομωτηρίου, nam Apollodorus obiicit Phormioni vitam anteactam, non quam egerat in ergastulo, sed vbi à Pasione Apollodori patre artem collybisticam edoctus est, quod in præcedentibus dixit: ἐπὶ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ὁ ἡμέτερος τραπεζίτης ὢν ἐκτήσατο αὐτὸν, ἡ γράμματα ἐπαίδευσε, καὶ τὴν τέχνην ἐδίδαξε, ἡ χρημάτων ἐποίησε κύκλον. Nostræ assertionis fundus est ipse Apollodorus, qui vbi Phormionem dixit esse πονηρὸν αὐτὸν ἐκ τῆς ἀναξίου, ἐ ἄδικον, addit immediate: σημεῖον δὲ, εἰ γὰρ δίκαιος ὢν, πέμπε αὐτῷ, τὰ τῆς δεκαπάτου δημοκρατίας. Neque item audiendus est eruditissimus Volfius, qui legit quidem ἐν τῷ Ἀναξίου, sed vertit, ædem Castoris & Pollucis, siue Dioscurorum, ad quam seruos olim væniisse tradit, sed sine auctore & teste: adde quod, vt iam diximus, non obijcitur Phormioni quid egerit antequam à Pasione emeretur, sed quid fecerit, cum Pasioni seruitutem seruiret, & rebus admoueretur illius. Quare etiam existimo nullomodo hanc vocem esse exponendam de æde Dioscurorum, nisi quis dixerit mensam Pasionis argentariam fuisse ad Dioscurorum ædem, id est, Castoris & Pollucis, quæ ad forum erat, vt ex Pausania Atticis constat: quanquam & hoc loquendi genus, si quidem de re ipsa liqueret, nobis non posset probari, vt plane insolens. Dicam igitur, quod conijcio, iudicium esto penes eruditos. Quare Dioscuri dicti sint Ἀναξῆς, variæ adferuntur causæ è variis huius vocis originationibus, quas videre est apud Plutarchum & alios: earum vna hæc est, quam non prætermisit in Theseo[?] Plutarchus: Ἐτὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες, ἀφ᾽ τῶν ἀρχόντων ὑπὸ φάσιν Ἀναξὼς ὀνομάζεσθαι, ὃ γὰρ αὐτὸς τὰς Ἀθηναίους αἰτίας ὀνομάζειν, καὶ αἰτιᾶσθαι ὃ αἰτιᾷ. Ex hac voce αἰτίας, siue potius αἰάχας, quod ostendit deductum hinc Αἰάχων nomen, putem deducendum nomen Αἰάχειος, non tamen eodem significatu, quo vbi fit à nomine Αἴαχες, sed idem significabit, quod superius siue prius, ita vt idem fit ἐν τῷ ἀἰαχείῳ, hoc in loco apud Demosthenem, quod ἀὶ ὤν: & certè redundat hic ὁ ἀὶ ὤν, estque glossema sequentis loquendi modi, quod è margine in contextum irrepsit: itaque locus sic est legendus: [illegible, ~40 letters]. Sed de hoc loco satis est: ad Legem reuertamur, in qua ista TOIN ΔE BOOIN TOIN HΓEMONOIN, interpretati fumus de bobus praecidaneis, quanquam forte intelliguntur armentorum duces. Age vero quia iam conijcere coepimus, inuestigemus & hic coniecturis ad quod sacrum Legis huius fragmentum spectet: quae in eo leguntur ista: TO MEN TPITON MEPOΣ EIΣ TON AΓΩNA, faciunt vt referam ad Panathenaicum sacrum: nam ad haec Sacra omnes Atticae vrbes, siue quae coloniae Athenarum essent, bouem immolandum mittere tenebantur: vnde viscceratio atque epulum populo: inde Aristophanes Nubibus:
units.tr: The mention of this temple in Harpocration is in these words: "Anaxiou, which is 'aaktregon.' Demosthenes in the speech against Stephanus: the temple of the Dioscuri" [Ἀναξίου, ὃ ἀάκτρεγον. Δημοσθένης ἐν τῇ κατὰ Στεφάνου, ἱερὸν τῶν Διοσκούρων]. The passage that Harpocration indicated is from the earlier speech against Stephanus: "Wicked, men of Athens, is he, wicked by reason of his unworthiness and injustice. The proof: if he were just, he would send to him the goods of the ten-tribe democracy. But now the mob is master of his money, so that it is hard for Stephanus to take from them whatever he now possesses; he ought not to have it, but to regard it as belonging to everyone" [πονηρὸς, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, πονηρὸς ἐστιν ἐκ τῆς ἀναξίου καὶ ἀδίκως. σημεῖον δὲ εἰ γὰρ ὁ ὧν δίκαιος, πέμπε αὐτῷ, τὰ τῆς δεκαπάτου δημοκρατίας. νῦν δὲ Ἔστουτον χρημάτων ὁ πλήθος κύριος καταφυγὴ...]. This passage was also once read "en tō Anaxiou", as is clear from a gloss that in the Paris edition is added from Suidas: "aaktion, a place of oath-taking, where the slaves of the wicked fall", and to this double reading the words of the Etymologicum Magnum refer: "aaktion or dioskourion. Some think it should be written aaktion, which is the Dioscurion, for Anaxas is Dioskouroi." But it cannot be read "en tō Anaxiou" in the sense in which they interpret it, "en tō dioskouriou", for Apollodorus charges Phormio with his former life, not with what he did in the workhouse, but where he was taught the collybistic art by Pasion, Apollodorus' father, as he said earlier: "For when our father, being a banker, acquired him, taught him letters and taught him the craft, and made money from it." The foundation of our assertion is Apollodorus himself, who, having called Phormio wicked by reason of his unworthiness and not just, adds immediately: "The proof: if he were just, he would send to him the goods of the ten-tribe democracy." Nor is the very learned Wolf to be heeded, who indeed reads "en tō Anaxiou" but translates it as the temple of Castor and Pollux, or the Dioscuri, to which, he says, slaves once came, but without any author or witness. Add that, as we have already said, Phormio is not charged with what he did before he was bought by Pasion, but with what he did while he served Pasion as a slave and was employed in his affairs. Therefore I also think this word must in no way be explained of the temple of the Dioscuri, unless someone should say that Pasion's banking table was at the temple of the Dioscuri, that is, of Castor and Pollux, which stood in the forum, as is clear from Pausanias for the Athenians; yet even this way of speaking, if the fact itself were certain, could not be proved to us, as it is quite unusual. I will therefore state what I conjecture, and let judgment rest with the learned. Why the Dioscuri were called Anaxes: various causes are brought forward from various derivations of this word, which may be seen in Plutarch and others. One of these, which Plutarch did not omit in his Theseus, is this: "Moreover, those who say that they were named Anaxos from the rulers under whose authority..." and the rest of the Greek, which turns on the verbs "to accuse" [αἰτίας, αἰτιᾶσθαι]. From this word aitias, or rather aiakhas, which shows that the name Aiakhōn is derived from it, I think the name Aiakheios should be derived, not with the same meaning as where it is derived from the name Aiakes, but it will signify the same as "above" or "before," so that the same thing is "en tō aiakheiō" here in Demosthenes, which means "ai ōn." Certainly this "ai ōn" is superfluous here, and is a gloss on the following expression, which crept from the margin into the text; so the passage must be read thus: [illegible, about forty letters]. But enough about this passage. Let us return to the law, in which the words "of the oxen, the leaders" we have interpreted as the first-fruit oxen, though perhaps they are understood as the leaders of the herds. Come now, since we have begun to conjecture, let us also here investigate by conjecture to what sacred rite this fragment of the law refers. The words read in it, "the third part for the contest," lead me to refer it to the Panathenaic festival. For to these sacrifices all the cities of Attica, or those that were colonies of Athens, were bound to send an ox for sacrifice, whence came the distribution of meat and a feast for the people. Hence Aristophanes in the Clouds:

units.la: Ἥδη ζωμοῦ Παναθηναίοις ἐμπλησθείς, εἶτ᾽ ἐπαφής Τὴν γαστέρα.
units.tr: "Already, having filled myself with broth at the Panathenaea, then I touch my belly" [ἤδη ζωμοῦ Παναθηναίοις ἐμπλησθείς, εἶτ' ἐπαφῆς τὴν γαστέρα].

units.la: Scholia: [illegible, ~230 letters]. Pars aliqua quoque cedebat Ludorum victoribus, vt ex hac Lege constat, qui sodalibus epulum praebebant: de Phoco Phocionis filio Athenaeus Libro IV. [illegible, ~60 letters]. de Autolyco idem Libro V. [illegible, ~70 letters]. Sed maxime nostram coniecturam confirmat, quod Lex ista inscripta sit columnae in Dioscurorum aede: nam id factu propter Pyrrhichistas, qui Panathenaeis dabantur. Lysias, [illegible, ~60 letters], Scholiastes Comici ad Nubes: [illegible, ~70 letters]. Hos autem modulos Minerua Dioscuris tibia accinuit. Scholiastes Pindari Pythionic. Ode II. [illegible, ~50 letters]. Aristides Orat. in Mineruam: [illegible, ~30 letters] Minerua [illegible, ~12 letters].
units.tr: Scholia: [illegible, about two hundred and thirty letters]. Some part also went to the victors in the games, as this law shows, who provided a feast for their companions. Concerning Phocus, son of Phocion, Athenaeus, Book IV: [illegible, about sixty letters]. Concerning Autolycus, the same author, Book V: [illegible, about seventy letters]. But what most confirms our conjecture is that this law was inscribed on a column in the temple of the Dioscuri, for that was done because of the Pyrrhichists, who were given at the Panathenaea. Lysias, [illegible, about sixty letters], the scholiast of the comic poet on the Clouds: [illegible, about seventy letters]. Minerva played these measures on the pipe for the Dioscuri. The scholiast of Pindar, Pythian Ode II: [illegible, about fifty letters]. Aristides, in his oration to Minerva: [illegible, about thirty letters]. Minerva [illegible, about twelve letters].

units.la: Parasiti suas habebant apothecas, sua Parasitia, ad quorum, vt & Templi & aedis sacra, sarta tecta tantum argenti dandum erat, quanto faciundū opus locauerant illi Sacerdotes, quibus ea cura erat mandata, qua de re Legem habes in hæc verba:
units.tr: The Parasites had their own storehouses and their own Parasitium. For the upkeep of these, as well as of the temple and the sacred house, the roof and fabric, they were to give as much silver as the priests who had been entrusted with this care contracted for the work to cost. On this matter you have a law in these words:

units.la: ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΕΥΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΝΕΩ ΤΟΥ ΑΡΧΕΙΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΙΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΟΙΚΙΑΣ ΤΗΣ ΙΕΡΑΣ ΔΙΔΟΝΑΙ ΤΟ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΝ, ΟΠΟΣΟΥ ΑΝ ΟΙ ΤΩΝ
units.tr: For the repair of the temple's new storehouse and of the Parasitium, and of the sacred house, let him give silver, as much as the priests who undertake the repair are to pay [ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΕΥΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΝΕΩ ΤΟΥ ΑΡΧΕΙΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΣΙΤΙΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΟΙΚΙΑΣ ΤΗΣ ΙΕΡΑΣ ΔΙΔΟΝΑΙ ΤΟ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΝ, ΟΠΟΣΟΥ ΑΝ ΟΙ ΤΩΝ ΙΕΡΕΩΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΕΥΑΣΤΑΙ ΜΙΣΘΩΣΩΣΙΝ].

units.la: Ad sarta tecta Templi, apo-thecæ, Parasitij, & aedis sacrę, tantum argenti dator, quanto faciendum opus locaΙΕΡΕΩΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΕΥΑΣΤΑΙ ΜΙΣΘΩΣΩ-ΣΙΝ.
units.tr: For the sarta tecta of the temple, the storehouses, the Parasitium and the sacred house, let him give as much silver as the priests who undertake the repair contract for the work to cost [ΙΕΡΕΩΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΕΥΑΣΤΑΙ ΜΙΣΘΩΣΩΣΙΝ].

units.la: Kaput istud est Legis Regiæ, quod legitur apud Athenæum Libro IV. ἐπὶ δὲ καὶ ἀρχῶν ὧν αὐτῆς Παρασίτης ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ νόμῳ Regis παιδὶ γιγαμπλαν, ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΕΥΗΝ, &c. Meminit Pollux Libro VI.cap.VII. καὶ ἀρχῶν Ἀθηναῖοι Γαρασίτιον καλούμενον, ὡς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τῆς Βασιλέως ἐστὶν εἴρειν. Verba Legis, quæ habes apud Athenæum, ita legisse videtur Pollux: ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΕΥΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΝΕΩ ΤΟΥ ΑΡΧΕΙΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΓΑΡΑΣΙΤΙΟΥ, quod etiam Incomparabilis Casaubonus animaduertere occupauit.
units.tr: This is the head of the Royal Law, which is read in Athenaeus, Book IV: "Moreover, of the offices of the Parasite, in the same law concerning the king's child..., FOR THE REPAIR..." Pollux mentions it in Book VI, chapter VII: "And the Athenians have an office called Garasitium, as can be found in the law of the king." The words of the law which you have in Athenaeus Pollux appears to have read thus: "FOR THE REPAIR OF THE NEW STOREHOUSE OF THE GARASITIUM," which the incomparable Casaubon also took care to notice.

units.la: Vetus est in senes dicterium, qui munia vitæ obire nequeunt, ΘΑΛΛΗΦΟΡΟΙ, vt est apud Aristophanem Vespis:
units.tr: There is an old saying about the elderly who cannot perform the duties of life: they are called THALLOPHOROI, as in Aristophanes' Wasps:

units.la: ἐκεῖ πρεσβυτὴν ὄχλος[?]ξενισμὸς εἰς ὁδὸν ἀκμῆ[?].σκωπτόμενοι γὰρ ἂν εἰ[?]ζῶντι ὁδοῖς ἀπάσης[?]Θεσμοφόρῳ καλούμενα[?].
units.tr: "There the old man... a crowd... hospitality... on the road... mocked... for if one were living... Thesmophoros called..." [ἐκεῖ πρεσβυτὴν ὄχλος... ξενισμὸς εἰς ὁδὸν... σκωπτόμενοι γὰρ... Θεσμοφόρῳ καλούμενα]. [Passage much corrupted.]

units.la: Quanquam in hanc rem non legebantur, nisi forma florenti ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Although they were not read for this purpose, except as to the flourishing form in this law:

units.la: Θαλλοφόρεις τῇ Ἀθηνᾷ τὰς καλὰς γεγρ-[?]ᾶς ἐκλέγεσθαι.
units.tr: "Thallophoroi for Athena: the beautiful [women?] are to be chosen" [Θαλλοφόρεις τῇ Ἀθηνᾷ τὰς καλὰς γεγραμμένας ἐκλέγεσθαι].

units.la: Senes Minervæ oleæ ramum Panathenais gestantes, forma florenti eliguntor[?].
units.tr: Old men bearing olive boughs for Minerva at the Panathenaea are chosen for the flourishing beauty of their form.

units.la: Legem hanc habes apud Xenophontem in Sympofio: ἀλλ' οὐδὲ μάνθανεν τῆ ἀπιμαστὸν ὃ κάλλος, ὡς ἔχω παρεχόμεν. ἐπὶ ὥσπερ πολύς γὰρ γίγνεσθαι καλὸς, οὕτως καὶ μειράκιον, ἐ αὐτὴρ, ἡ πρεσβύτης. τεκμήριον δὲ, Θεμοφόρους δὲ τῇ Ἀθηνᾷ ὡς καλὰς γεγρᾶς ἐκλέγοντας, ἐ Xenophonte accepit Iuncus Libro de Senectute: Ἀλλὰ δὲ ἐ ὃ ἀνορεπὶς ἀπηλλάχθη... senibus, ὡς ἡ ἐς ἀγέ[?]κ, καὶ που ἐ Ἱπ[?]ξις ὀφθαλμῶν, οἷα δὲ ἐ ἀπλάνῃ[?]. μάλιστα δ' ἐ ... Ἀθηνᾷ, ὡς φησὶ Ξενοφῶν ὁ Φιλόσοφος, Θεμοφόρους.
units.tr: You have this law in Xenophon's Symposium: "But neither did he learn... as I offer beauty... for just as a man becomes beautiful, so also a youth, and a woman, and an old woman. The proof: the Thesmophoroi for Athena are chosen as beautiful old women [ἀλλ' οὐδὲ μάνθανεν... Θεμοφόρους δὲ τῇ Ἀθηνᾷ ὡς καλὰς γεγρᾶς ἐκλέγοντας]." Junius took it from Xenophon in his book On Old Age: "But ... old age ... is released from..., as the sight of the eyes..., but [illegible] ... Athena, as the philosopher Xenophon says, Thesmophoroi."

units.la: Rex uxorem ciuem atque uirginem ducere tenebatur, ne quid secus fieret in sacris: eaque de re Lex hæc scripta:
units.tr: The king was bound to marry a wife who was a citizen and a virgin, so that nothing would go wrong in the sacred rites; and on this matter this law was written:

units.la: Τῶν γυναικα τῆς Βασιλέως ἀγῶν εἰ, καὶ μὴ ἐπιμιγνυμένων ἑτέρῳ αἰδρὶ, ἀλλὰ παρ-θένον γαμεῖν.
units.tr: "The king's wife shall be an Athenian, and shall not have intercourse with another man, but shall marry a virgin." [Τῶν γυναικα τῆς Βασιλέως ἀγῶν εἰ, καὶ μὴ ἐπιμιγνυμένων ἑτέρῳ αἰδρὶ, ἀλλὰ παρ-θένον γαμεῖν.]

units.la: Laudat hanc Legem Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Νεαίρας, ἐ quo discès eam columnæ lapideæ iuxta aram Bacchi ἐν Λίμναις fuisse inscriptam: Ἐάν δὲ Θνητὸς σεισμῷ κ' αὐτοῦ, ἐ δημοκρατίαν ἐποίησε, καὶ ἡ πόλις πολυαρχέρπος ἐγένετο, τὸν μὲν Βασιλέα ἀνεῖδεν ἦν ὁ δῆμος ἡρεῖτο ἐκ προσκρίτων κατ' ἀσφαλείαν χειροτονῶν. τῶ γυναῖκα αὐτῷ νόμον ἔσται ἀσφαλεῖ[?], καὶ μὴ ἐπιμιγνυμένῳ ἑτέρῳ αἰδρὶ, ἀλλὰ παρθένον γαμεῖν, ἵνα χρὴ τὰ πάντεια ξύνεξαι τὰ ἀρρητα ἱερὰ ... τῆς πόλεως, καὶ τὰ νομιζόμενα γίγνηται τῆς θεοῖς ὕσιώσεων, καὶ μηδὲν καταλύσῃ, μηδὲ χαριστομένῳ. καὶ τῶν τὸν ἱερῶν χρᾶ[?]ντας ἐς τὴν λίθῳ ἔχοντ' ἐν τοῦ ἱερᾶ τῆς Διονύσου ἀγὸ τὸν βωμὸν ἐν Λίμναις. Tenebatur quisquis Rex erat, si maritus fieret intra τῆς ἀρχῆς annum, vxorem ducere ciuem, quod illi cum ceteris omnibus Athenien-sibus commune erat, & praeterea virginem illibatam, aut si iam maritus esset, in ἀγα-χρίοις videbatur, an ciuem & virginem in vxorem duxisset.
units.tr: Demosthenes praises this law in his speech against Neaera, from which you may learn that the law was inscribed on a stone column beside the altar of Bacchus in the Marshes (Limnae). "If the people, after overthrowing the ... , established a democracy and the city became ruled by many magistrates, they should appoint a king, whom the people chose from among those selected, electing him by vote for security. His wife shall be ... and he shall not have intercourse with another man, but shall marry a virgin, so that he may perform for the city all the secret rites ... and the customary sacrifices to the gods, and omit nothing, nor ..." and "those who perform the sacred rites shall ... at the altar of Dionysus in the Marshes." Whoever was king was bound, if he became married within the year of his office, to take a wife who was a citizen, which was common to him with all the other Athenians, and besides a virgin undefiled; or, if he was already married, he was examined at his scrutiny to see whether he had taken a citizen virgin as his wife. [Demosthenes' Greek is quoted above in the original.]

units.la: Tantam patriorum rationem institutorum in faciendis sacris habendi voluerunt Athenienses, vt Lege iubeantur Sacerdotes quisque singillatim suae rationes ἱερωσυνης reddere.
units.tr: The Athenians wished the ancestral practice of their institutions in conducting sacred rites to be kept so strictly that by law each priest was ordered to render an individual account of his priesthood [ἱερωσυνης].

units.la: Τοὺς ἱερεῖς καὶ τὰς ἱερείας ... ἰδία, ἀλλὰ ἐν κοινῇ τὰ ἱερά.
units.tr: "The priests and priestesses ... not privately, but the sacred rites in common." [Τοὺς ἱερεῖς καὶ τὰς ἱερείας ... ἰδία, ἀλλὰ ἐν κοινῇ τὰ ἱερά.]

units.la: Sacerdotes priuatim singuli, totaque gentes & familiae, Sacerdotij suae rationes reddunto.
units.tr: Priests shall each render an account of their priesthood privately, and whole peoples and families likewise.

units.la: Nemo erat, qui exciperetur, ne ij quidem, qui titulo tenus sacrorum curae praeficiebantur, aut pro vrbe vota tantum concipiebant & preces apud Deos. Aeschines id docet ex hac Lege ὁ τῶν κ... ἱερεῖς καὶ τὰς ἱερείας ... ἐὰν ... ὁ νόμος ...
units.tr: No one was exempt, not even those who were set over the care of sacred things in name only, or who merely uttered vows and prayers to the gods on behalf of the city. Aeschines shows this from this law: "The priests and priestesses of ... if ... the law ..." [ὁ τῶν κ... ἱερεῖς καὶ τὰς ἱερείας ... ἐὰν ... ὁ νόμος ...]

units.la: Cum Deos nonnisi caste adiri à quouis fas sit, eorum Ministros castos quoque esse iebere quis sanus negabit? ne quis tamen sibi non dictum putaret, Legeid cautum est.
units.tr: Since it is lawful for anyone to approach the gods only in purity, who of sound mind would deny that their ministers too should be pure? Yet lest anyone think this was not said to him, the law has provided for it.

units.la: Μηδεὶ ἱεροσυνῶν ... ὅστις ... ἁγνὸς ... ἐστι?
units.tr: "Let no one of the priesthoods ... who ... is pure?" [Μηδεὶ ἱεροσυνῶν ... ὅστις ... ἁγνὸς ... ἐστι?]

units.la: Legem laudat Aeschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμάρχου, ἣ (ὡς ἔοικεν) ἡ αὐτὴ ... ἱερωσύνην ... ἡ σῶμα. Praeteredintegros esse corporis oportuit nulloque membro captos: nam ἐν τῇ ... ἐπιμελείᾳ Sacerdotum, id exquirebatur. Auctor Etymologi: ἀφέλης, ἐ ἱερὸς ὁ σῶμα ἢ ἀλοκληρος ... ἀπὸ τῶν ... Ἀλκιβιάδης? ... Vnde praeterea discimus Sacerdotes, siue puro, sorte legerentur, siue crearentur, ἐπιμελητὴν, quem admodum Magistratus.
units.tr: Aeschines quotes the law in his speech against Timarchus, which (as it seems) is the same ... priesthood ... body. It was necessary that priests be whole in body and not disabled in any limb; for this was examined in the scrutiny of priests. The author of the Etymologicum: "... sacred ... whole in body ..., from ..." [ἀφέλης, ἐ ἱερὸς ὁ σῶμα ἢ ἀλοκληρος ... ἀπὸ τῶν ... Ἀλκιβιάδης?] From this we also learn that priests, whether they were chosen by lot or appointed, were subjected to scrutiny by the overseer [ἐπιμελητὴν], just as magistrates were.

units.la: Habes apud Stephanum in Athos fragmentum quod sacra huius populi spectat.
units.tr: In Stephanus, under the word Athos, you have a fragment that concerns the sacred rites of this people.

units.la: ΕΙΡΕΙΔΗ ΑΓΝΟΥΝΤΙ ΘΥΣΙΑ ΕΣΤΙ ΤΩ ΛΕΩ
units.tr: Since a sacrifice made for the people by one who is not pure is ... [ΕΙΡΕΙΔΗ ΑΓΝΟΥΝΤΙ ΘΥΣΙΑ ΕΣΤΙ ΤΩ ΛΕΩ]

units.la: Stephani verba sunt; & ea ... ἐν τῷ πόλει Ἀθηνῶν, ἐν τῇ Ἀξίῳ. ΕΙΡΕΙΔΗ ΑΓΝΟΥΝΤΙ ΘΥΣΙΑ ΕΣΤΙ ΤΩ ΛΕΩ.
units.tr: These are the words of Stephanus, and they ... in the city of Athens, in Axius. Since a sacrifice made for the people by one who is not pure is ... [ΕΙΡΕΙΔΗ ΑΓΝΟΥΝΤΙ ΘΥΣΙΑ ΕΣΤΙ ΤΩ ΛΕΩ.]

units.la: PTIME[?] Papinianus libro I. Definitionum scripsit: Legem esse commune praeceptum, virorum prudentium consultum, delictorum, quae sponte vel ignorantia contrahuntur, coercitionem communem Reipublicae sponsionem. Nam et Demosthenes Orator Orat adueri[?]. [illegible, ~40 letters]. [illegible, ~30 letters] Ἀπὸ [?]
units.tr: Papinian, in the first book of his Definitions, wrote: A law is a common precept, the counsel of prudent men, a common restraint of crimes committed either willingly or through ignorance, a common pledge of the commonwealth. For Demosthenes the orator also [illegible]. [illegible]. [illegible] [Ἀπὸ] [?]
