units.la: Sed ex Philosopho[?], verba sunt Marciani libro I. Institutionum, summa. [illegible, ~25 letters] sapiente Chrysippus sic incipit libro[?] [illegible, ~50 letters]
units.tr: But from the Philosopher [?] are the words of Marcian in the first book of the Institutes: summa. [illegible] the wise man Chrysippus begins thus in the book [illegible].

units.la: Nominauit Marcianus Chrysippum, philosophum sapientiae, quod interpretatur in linguam Stoicam lectio, quam Stoicam sapientiam[?] philosophorum est praecipia; alii legunt summus. Ego putem aduersum esse, summe, quod scribi per e diphthongum non est solitum[?]; Philosophi, inquit summa Stoica sapientiae Chrysippi, dicuntur ista in laudem ipsius Chrysippi, qui Philosophus sit summe, et ea ratione Stoicae sapientiam sapere patuit[?] priorem Stoicorum, ut est apud Ciceronem, de eo re ille olim dictum apud Diogenem Laertium:
units.tr: Marcian named Chrysippus the philosopher of wisdom, which in the Stoic tongue is rendered as a reading, which the Stoic wisdom of the philosophers prescribes; others read summus. I think it is wrong to read summe, since it is not customary to write it with the diphthong e. "The Stoic summa of the wisdom of Chrysippus," he says, "are called philosophers' precepts in praise of Chrysippus himself, who is a philosopher summe, and by that reasoning the Stoic wisdom was seen to be wise," as in Cicero, concerning which that earlier man of the Stoics once said, as is reported by Diogenes Laertius:

units.la: [illegible, ~45 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Sed Chrysippum mittamus, ut de Legibus agamus, quae ita scripta non sunt, ut omnes casus, qui quandoque inciderint, comprehendantur. Lege XII. T. De Legibus. Sed iura constituuntur, ut dixit Theophrastus in his, quae [illegible, ~10 letters] accidunt, non quae [illegible, ~10 letters], et ut ait Theophylactus, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Itaque in ferendis Legibus admodum cauti fuerunt Athenienses, quod ex hac illarum [illegible, ~12 letters] liquido constabit.
units.tr: But let us set Chrysippus aside and turn to the laws, which have not been written in such a way as to cover every case that may at some time arise. Law XII, Tables, On Laws. But laws are established, as Theophrastus said in these matters, that happen, not those that [illegible], and as Theophylactus says [illegible]. Therefore the Athenians were very cautious in enacting laws, as will be clear from this [illegible] of those laws.

units.la: ΕΠΙΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΙΑ ΝΟΜΩΝ.
units.tr: EPICHEIROTONIA OF THE LAWS. [ΕΠΙΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΙΑ ΝΟΜΩΝ.]

units.la: ΕΠΙ ΔΕ ΤΗΣ ΠΡΩΤΗΣ ΠΡΥΤΑ-ΝΕΙΑΣ ΤΗΙ ΕΝΔΕΚΑΤΗΙ, ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ, ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΕΥΞΗΤΑΙ Ο ΚΗΡΥΞ ΕΠΙΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΙΑΝ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ, ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΒΟΥΛΕΥΤΙΚΩΝ · ΔΕΥΤΕΡΟΝ ΔΕ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΚΟΙΝΩΝ, ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΚΕΙΝΤΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΥΣΙΝ ΕΙΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΑΛΛΩΝ ΑΡΧΩΝ. Η Δ' ΕΠΙΧΕΙΡΟΤΟ-ΝΙΑ ΕΣΤΩ Η ΠΡΟΤΕΡΑ ΟΤΩΙ ΔΟΚΟΥΣΙΝ ΑΡΧΕΙΝ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΙ ΟΙ ΒΟΥΛΕΥΤΙΚΟΙ, Η Δ' ΥΣΤΕΡΑ ΟΤΩΙ ΜΗ ΔΟΚΟΥΣΙΝ ΕΙΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΚΟΙΝΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ. ΤΗΝ Δ' ΕΠΙΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΙΑΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΥΣ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΩΝ ΑΠΟΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΗΘΩΣΙ, ΤΟΥΣ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΑΣ ΕΦ' ΩΝ ΑΝ Η ΕΠΙΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΙΑ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΑΠΟΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΗΘΕΝΤΩΝ ΤΗΝ ΤΕΛΕΥΤΑΙΑΝ ΤΩΝ ΤΡΙΩΝ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΩΝ. ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΡΟΕΔΡΟΥΣ ΟΙ ΑΝ ΤΥΧΩ-ΣΙ ΠΡΟΕΔΡΕΥΟΝΤΕΣ ΕΝ ΤΑΥΤΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΙ, ΧΡΗΜΑΤΙΣΕΙΝ ΕΠΑΝΑΓΚΕΣ ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΩΝ, ΚΑΘ' Ο ΤΙ ΚΑΘΕΔΟΥΝΤΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΥ ΟΡΟΘΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ ΕΣΤΑΙ. ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΟΜΩΜΟΚΟΤΩΝ ΤΟΝ ΗΛΙΑΣΤΙΚΟΝ ΟΡΚΟΝ. ΕΑΝ Δ' ΟΙ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΣ ΜΗ ΠΟΙΩΣΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ ΤΗΝ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΝ Ή ΟΙ ΠΡΟΕΔΡΟΙ ΜΗ ΧΡΗ-ΜΑΤΙΣΩΣΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΙΝ ΤΩΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΩΝ ΕΚΑ-ΣΤΟΝ ΧΙΛΙΑΣ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ΙΕΡΑΣ ΤΗΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙ. ΤΩΝ ΔΕ ΠΡΟΕΔΡΩΝ ΕΚΑΣ-ΤΟΣ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΤΩ ΤΕΤΤΑΡΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΔΡΑ-ΧΜΑΣ ΙΕΡΑΣ ΤΗΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΕΝΔΕΙ-ΞΙΣ ΑΥΤΩΝ ΕΣΤΩ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣ-ΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ, ΚΑΘΑΠΕΡ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΡΧΗΙ vota voce præconis peracta, Leges ordine recensentur, primum eæ quæ sunt de Senatu: deinde de Republica: tum de Nouembris; demum de reliquis Magistratibus. Primũque sciscitor, an satis sit Legũ de Senatu: deinde, an non sit satis: atque ita deinceps de Legibus, quæ Rempublicam spectant. Concio habetor secundum Leges, quæ obtinet, ad recensendas Leges. Si quæ autem Leges, quæ obtinent, improbentur, Prytaneis, qui huic Legum recensioni præsunt, vltimam trium concionum habento de improbatis Legibus. Proëdri, quibus concioni huic præesse sortito contigerit, omnino referunto, post relationem primam, quæ est de rebus sacris, de Nomothetis, de quibus scilicet Legibus sententiam sint laturi, & unâ de stipis illis supperet. Nomothetæ autem de iis sunto, qui Heliasticum iusiurandū iurarunt. Si vero Prytaneis concionem non habeant, aut Proëdri non referant, secundum has Leges, Prytanum quisque mille drachmis Minervæ sacris, Proëdrorum vero singuli quadraginta drachmis, Minervæ item sacris, multantor. Eorum nomina apud Thesmothetas deferuntor, quemadmodum eorum, quia ærarij cum sint, tamen ΟΦΕΙΛΩΝ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩι. ΟΙ ΔΕ ΘΕΣ-ΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΝΔΕΙΧΘΕΝΤΑΣ ΕΙ-ΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΔΕΣΜΩΤΗΡΙΟΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ, Η ΜΗ ΑΝΙΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΑΡΕΙΟΝ ΠΑΓΟΝ ΩΣ ΚΑΤΑΛΥΟΝ-ΤΕΣ ΤΗΝ ΕΠΑΝΟΡΘΩΣΙΝ ΤΩΝ ΝΟ-ΜΩΝ. ΠΡΟ ΔΕ ΤΗΣ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΣ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΝΟΜΟΘΕ-ΤΕΙΝ ΕΚΤΙΘΕΤΩ ΠΡΟΣΘΕΝ ΤΩΝ ΕΠΩ-ΝΥΜΩΝ ΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΟΥΣ ΑΝ ΤΙΘΗι, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟ ΠΛΗ-ΘΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΕΚΤΕΘΕΝΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΨΗΦΙΣΗΤΑΙ Ο ΔΗΜΟΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΧΡΟΝΟΥ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ. Ο ΔΕ ΤΙΘΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΚΑΙΝΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΑΝΑ-ΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΕΙΣ ΛΕΥΚΩΜΑ ΕΚΤΙΘΕΤΩ ΠΡΟΣΤΕΝ ΤΩΝ ΕΠΩΝΥΜΩΝ ΟΣΗΜΕ-ΡΑΙ, ΕΩΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ, ΑΙ-ΡΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΣΥΝΑΠΟΛΟ-ΓΗΣΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΔΗΜΩΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΟΙ ΑΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΘΕ-ΤΑΙΣ ΛΥΩΝΤΑΙ ΠΕΝΤΕ ΑΝΔΡΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΑΠΑΝΤΩΝ ΤΗι ΕΝΔΕΚΑ-ΤΗι ΤΟΥ ΕΚΑΤΟΜΒΑΙΩΝΟΣ ΜΗΝΟΣ.
units.tr: In the first prytany, on the eleventh day, in the assembly, when the herald has proclaimed the epicheirotonia of the laws: first concerning the laws of the Council, second concerning the common laws, then those concerning the nine archons, and then those concerning the other magistrates. The epicheirotonia is to be held, or before that, whether the laws which seem to govern the Council are to be held. The epicheirotonia of the laws is to be carried out according to the laws that are written. If some of the written laws are rejected, the prytaneis under whose presidency the epicheirotonia takes place are to bring the rejected laws before the last of the three assemblies. The proedri who happen to preside over this assembly must necessarily put to a vote first, after the sacred matters, concerning the nomothetai, about whom they are to sit, and also concerning the silver, to be placed before the nomothetai. The nomothetai are to be drawn from those who have sworn the Heliastic oath. If the prytaneis do not hold the assembly according to what is written, or the proedri do not put it to a vote according to what is written, each of the prytaneis is to be fined a thousand drachmas sacred to Athena, and each of the proedri forty drachmas, likewise sacred to Athena. Their names are to be laid before the thesmothetai, as is done for those who are debtors to the public treasury. The thesmothetai are to bring those who have been named into the bond-court according to the law, or, if they do not appear, into the Areopagus, so that the amendment of the laws may be completed. Before the assembly, any Athenian who wishes to propose a law is to set forth in writing, in addition to the names of the Eponymoi, the laws which he proposes, so that the people may vote on the time to be prescribed for the nomothetai, according to the number of laws proposed. Whoever proposes a new law is to register it on a white board and set it out daily at the statues of the Eponymoi until the assembly is held. The man who has proposed the new law, when it has been written up on the white board, is to set it forth before the Eponymoi for as many days as it takes until the assembly is held. Five men are chosen from the whole Athenian people, on the eleventh day of Hecatombaion, to be advocates of the laws which are to be repealed by the nomothetai.

units.la: Magistratum gerunt. Si vero Thesmothetae delatos in iudicium non rapiant, ex hac Lege, in Senatu Areopagitico ne cooptantor, ut qui Legum emendationem perverterint. Ante concionem quisquis Atheniensium Legem ferre voluerit, proponat scriptas ad Eponymorum statuas Leges, quas rogaturus est, ut pro numero propositarum Legum, populus decernat de tempore, quod No-mothetis erit praescribendum. Qui vero novâ Legem fert, in album describito, & proponito quotidie ad Eponymorum statuas, donec concio habeatur. Eliguntur autem ex universo Atheniensium populo, die Hecatombaeonis undecimo, viri quinque, qui patroni futuri sint Legum, quae à Nomothetis abrogandae erunt.
units.tr: They hold office. But if the thesmothetai do not bring the accused before the court, then by this law they shall not be co-opted into the Areopagite Council, since they have perverted the amendment of the laws. Before the assembly, whoever among the Athenians wishes to propose a law shall set out in writing the laws which he intends to propose, at the statues of the Eponymoi, so that the people may decree, according to the number of the laws set out, the time to be prescribed for the nomothetai. The one who proposes a new law shall register it on a white board and set it out daily at the statues of the Eponymoi until the assembly is held. Five men are to be chosen from all the Athenians on the eleventh day of Hecatombaion, to be advocates of the laws which are to be repealed by the nomothetai.

units.la: Hæc Legis verba referuntur à Demosthene in Timocratea. Dicitque istam in ferendis Legibus Legem esse observandam: ut Quotannis primo primæ Prytanciæ conventu, qui incidit in diem mensis Hecatombæonis undecimum, ut optime adnotat Ulpianus ad hunc locum: ἡ [?] τῆς [?] πρυτανείας ἐκ-κλησία [?] ἐγίνετο τῇ ἐνδεκάτῃ τῆς ἐκατομβαιῶνος μηνός, ferantur Leges, primum περὶ τῆς Βουλευτικῆς, de Senatu Quingentorum. Ulpianus περὶ τῆς Βουλευτικῆς· περὶ τῆς βουλῆς τῶν Πεντακοσίων. Deinde de ipsa Republica, περὶ τῆς κοινῆς, hoc est, περὶ τῶν δημοσίων πραγμάτων. Postremo περὶ τῶν πολιτευομένων, de Magistratibus. Idque hoc fiebat ordine. Primum cogebatur populus, an satis esset Legum περὶ τῆς βουλευτικῆς, necne, atque an ea placerent: postea περὶ τῆς κοινῆς. demum περὶ τῶν πολιτευομένων, idque eodem ordine. Quod si Legum satis non esset, novæ ferebantur, si quæ jam ante latæ erant, non placerent, improbarenturque, has antiquabat veteres & abrogabant, novasque in veterum locum ἀντικατέστησαν [?] atque sufficiebant. Eligebantur autem decem numero, è singulis Tribubus unus, qui Leges scriberent, & Scriba qui in Senatu, proque concione recitaret: non enim videtur quibusvis promiscue permissum Legem rogare. Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Vespas: εἴρηται δὲ ἑκάστῃ φυλῇ ἕνα Θεσμοθέτην καὶ Γραμματέα εἰς ὃ τις ῥήματα [?]. Huc facit Psephisma scriptum post exactos Athenis Triginta Tyrannos, quod hic inter Leges legi mercetur, quippe cum Legis vim obtineat.
units.tr: These words of the law are cited by Demosthenes in the Timocratea, and he says that this law is to be observed in enacting laws: that each year, at the first assembly of the first prytany, which falls on the eleventh day of the month Hecatombaion, as Ulpian rightly notes on this passage, [ἡ τῆς πρυτανείας ἐκκλησία ἐγίνετο τῇ ἐνδεκάτῃ τῆς ἑκατομβαιῶνος μηνός], the laws are to be brought forward, first concerning the Council [περὶ τῆς βουλευτικῆς], that is, concerning the Council of Five Hundred. Ulpian: [περὶ τῆς βουλευτικῆς· περὶ τῆς βουλῆς τῶν πεντακοσίων]. Then concerning the commonwealth itself [περὶ τῆς κοινῆς], that is, [περὶ τῶν δημοσίων πραγμάτων]. Finally, concerning the magistrates [περὶ τῶν πολιτευομένων]. And this was done in this order. First the people were asked whether there were enough laws concerning the Council [περὶ τῆς βουλευτικῆς] or not, and whether these pleased them; afterwards concerning the common matters, and last concerning the magistrates, in the same order. But if there were not enough laws, new ones were brought forward; if any laws already passed did not please and were rejected, they abolished and repealed the old ones and set new ones in their place [ἀντικατέστησαν] and substituted them. Ten men were chosen, one from each tribe, to write the laws, and a clerk who would read them in the Senate and before the assembly; for it seems that it was not permitted to propose a law to just anyone. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Wasps: [εἴρηται δὲ ἑκάστῃ φυλῇ ἕνα θεσμοθέτην καὶ γραμματέα εἰς ὃ τις ῥήματα]. To this relates the decree written after the Thirty Tyrants were expelled from Athens, which he deserves to have read here among the laws, since it has the force of law.

units.la: ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ.
units.tr: The Decree [ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ]

units.la: ΕΔΟΞΕ ΤΩι ΛΗΜΩι. ΤΙΣΑΜΕΝΟΣ ΕΙΠΕ. ΠΟΛΙΤΕΥΕΣΘΑΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΥΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ, ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΧΡΗ-ΣΘΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΣΟΛΩΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΕΤΡΟΙΣ ΚΑΙ ΣΤΑΘΜΟΙΣ, ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΔΡΑΚΟΝΤΟΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΙΣ, ΟΙΣ-ΠΕΡ ΕΧΡΩΜΕΘΑ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΠΡΟΣΘΕΝ ΧΡΟΝΩι ΟΠΟΣΩΝ Δ' ΑΝ ΠΡΟΣΔΕΟΙ ΟΙΔΕ ΗΡΗΜΕΝΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΥΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΑΝΑΓΡΑΦΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΣΑΝΙΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΕΚΤΙΘΕΝΤΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΠΩΝΥΜΟΥΣ ΣΚΟΠΕΙΝ ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι ΚΑΙ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΝΤΩΝ ΤΑΙΣ ΑΡΧΑΙΣ ΕΝ ΤΩΙΔΕ ΤΩι ΜΗΝΙ, ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟ-ΜΟΥΣ ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΑΤΩ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΩΝ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ, ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΟΙ ΠΕΝ-ΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ, ΟΥΣ ΟΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ ΕΙΛΟΝ-ΤΟ, ΕΠΕΙΔΗ ΟΜΩΜΟΚΑΣΙΝ. ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΙΔΙΩΤΗι ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι, ΕΙΣΙΟΝΤΙ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΒΟΥΛΗΝ ΒΟΥ-ΛΕΥΕΙΝ Ο,ΤΙ ΑΝ ΑΓΑΘΩΝ ΕΧΗι ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ. ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΕΘΩ-ΣΙΝ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΙ, ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΩ Η ΒΟΥ-ΛΗ Η ΕΞ ΑΡΕΙΟΥ ΠΑΓΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΝΟ-ΜΩΝ, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΑΙ ΑΡΧΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΚΕΙ-ΜΕΝΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΩΝΤΑΙ. ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΟΥΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΑΝΑΓΡΑΦΕΙΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΤΟΙΧΟΝ, ΙΝΑ ΠΕΡ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΑΝΕΓΡΑΦΗΣΑΝ ΣΚΟ-ΠΕΙΝ ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι.
units.tr: It seemed good to the People. Tisamenus proposed and said: "The Athenians shall govern the commonwealth according to their ancestral customs. They shall use the laws of Solon, and the measures and weights, and also the ordinances of Draco, which we too have used in former times. If any laws are needed, the Nomothetae chosen from the Senate shall write them on a tablet and set them up before the statues of the Eponymous heroes, so that anyone who wishes may read them. In this same month they shall hand them over to the magistrates. The laws handed over shall first be scrutinised by the Senate and by the Nomothetae whom the People chose, and they shall approve them under oath. Before the Senate, any private citizen who wishes may enter and give whatever good advice he has about the laws. Once the laws have been enacted, the Council of the Areopagus shall ensure that the magistrates use the enacted laws. Enacted laws shall be written on the wall where the earlier ones were written, so that anyone who wishes may read them." [ΕΔΟΞΕ ΤΩι ΛΗΜΩι. ΤΙΣΑΜΕΝΟΣ ΕΙΠΕ. ΠΟΛΙΤΕΥΕΣΘΑΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΥΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ, ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΣΟΛΩΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΕΤΡΟΙΣ ΚΑΙ ΣΤΑΘΜΟΙΣ, ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΔΡΑΚΟΝΤΟΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΙΣ, ΟΙΣΠΕΡ ΕΧΡΩΜΕΘΑ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΠΡΟΣΘΕΝ ΧΡΟΝΩι. ΟΠΟΣΩΝ Δ' ΑΝ ΠΡΟΣΔΕΟΙ ΟΙΔΕ ΗΡΗΜΕΝΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΥΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΑΝΑΓΡΑΦΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΣΑΝΙΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΕΚΤΙΘΕΝΤΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΠΩΝΥΜΟΥΣ ΣΚΟΠΕΙΝ ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι. ΚΑΙ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΝΤΩΝ ΤΑΙΣ ΑΡΧΑΙΣ ΕΝ ΤΩΙΔΕ ΤΩι ΜΗΝΙ, ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΑΤΩ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΩΝ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ, ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ, ΟΥΣ ΟΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ ΕΙΛΟΝΤΟ, ΕΠΕΙΔΗ ΟΜΩΜΟΚΑΣΙΝ. ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΙΔΙΩΤΗι ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι, ΕΙΣΙΟΝΤΙ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΒΟΥΛΗΝ ΒΟΥΛΕΥΕΙΝ Ο,ΤΙ ΑΝ ΑΓΑΘΩΝ ΕΧΗι ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ. ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΕΘΩΣΙΝ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΙ, ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΩ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ Η ΕΞ ΑΡΕΙΟΥ ΠΑΓΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΑΙ ΑΡΧΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΩΝΤΑΙ. ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΟΥΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΑΝΑΓΡΑΦΕΙΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΤΟΙΧΟΝ, ΙΝΑ ΠΕΡ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΑΝΕΓΡΑΦΗΣΑΝ ΣΚΟΠΕΙΝ ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι.]

units.la: Populus sciuit. Tisamenus scripsit. Athenienses Rem-publicam secundum patria instituta gerunto. Legibus autem Solonis, & mensuris, & ponderibus utuntor, ut & Draconis sanctionibus, quibus etiam olim usi sumus. Si quibus vero opus fuerit Legibus eas electi a Senatu Nomothetae in tabella describunto, & ad Eponymorum statuas proponunto, ut a quouis legi possint: eodem-que hoc mense Magistratibus in manus danto: datas prius Senatus Quingentorū, & Nomothetae, quos populares elegerint, iurati approbanto. Cuius priusquam Senatum adire liceto, & quod sibi bonum videbitur de illis Legibus consulere. Vbi latae erunt Leges, Senatus Areopagiticus prouideto, ut Magistratus latis Legibus utantur. Latae Leges in pariete describuntor, ubi prius sunt descriptae, ut a quouis legi possint.
units.tr: The People resolved. Tisamenus proposed. The Athenians shall conduct the commonwealth according to the institutions of their fathers. They shall use the laws of Solon, and the measures and weights, as also the enactments of Draco, which we too have used in former times. If any laws are needed, the Nomothetae chosen by the Senate shall write them in a tablet and set them up before the statues of the Eponymi, so that anyone may read them. In this same month they shall hand them over to the magistrates. The laws handed over shall first be approved by the Senate of Five Hundred and by the Nomothetae whom the people have chosen, under oath. Before the Senate, any private citizen who wishes shall be permitted to enter and to advise whatever seems good to him about those laws. When the laws have been enacted, the Areopagite Senate shall see to it that the magistrates use the enacted laws. The enacted laws shall be written on the wall where they were previously written, so that anyone may read them.

units.la: Descripsit hoc Plephisma Andocides [illegible, ~12 letters] quod paulò post asserram[?] in libertatem a Thrasybulo Athenarum urbem scriptum est, ut ex Andocide constat: [illegible, ~70 letters] Varij autem & diuersi hoc Plephisma nominatur Nomothetae. Priores illi sunt, qui Thesmothetae Graeco Interpreti Aristophanis dicuntur, & a Senatu Quingentorum e singulis Tribubus singuli eligebantur, ad nouas, si quidem illis esset opus, scribendas Leges: Posteriores, qui dicuntur Nomo-
units.tr: Andocides copied out this decree [illegible, about 12 letters], which was written shortly after the city of Athens was freed by Thrasybulus, as is clear from Andocides: [illegible, about 70 letters]. The decree is called by various and different names: Nomothetae. The earlier ones are those who are called Thesmothetae by the Greek interpreter of Aristophanes, and one of each tribe was chosen by the Senate of Five Hundred to write new laws, if indeed there was need of them. The later ones, who are called Nomo-

units.la: [The Greek fragments within the commentary paragraph are illegible on this scan and are given as spans.] thetæ illi sunt, qui iurati Leges à prioribus illis scriptas & publicè propositas debebant δια[?]ζειν [?] ψήφῳ χωρεῖν suo calculo, vel ἐπιχειροτονεῖν [?] ἐπιδοκιμάζειν. Sed vbi de his agitur, transposita sunt Psephismatis verba, quæ ita repono:
units.tr: [The Greek fragments within the commentary paragraph are illegible on this scan and are given as spans.] thetae, are those who, sworn in, were to approve by their vote, or to ratify by their show of hands, the laws written by those earlier men and published publicly. But where these matters are discussed, the words of the decree have been transposed, which I restore thus:

units.la: ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΔΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΑΤΩ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ Ἡ ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ, ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΟΥΣ ΟΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ ΕΙΛΟΝΤΟ. Nam, ut paulò post, Deo dante, dicemus, non quingenti, sed unus & mille Nomothetæ eligebantur. Sed redeamus ad [illegible, ~12 letters], ut illam, eademque opera hoc Psephisma illustremus. Nomothetæ igitur illi decem, qui novam ferre Legem volebant, in senatu causam dicebant, deque ea primum disceptabant apud τὴς Πεντακοσίας, ut illam iis approbarent. Habes in Psephismate: ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΑΤΩ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ Ἡ ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ. Unde etiam scripsit Pollux: [illegible, ~10 letters] Βουλή. Demosthenes in Timocratea: [illegible, ~30 letters] Τιμοκράτης, εἰδὼς [?] ὅτι ὁ [?] ἐν τῇ βουλῇ [?] δῆμος, ἔφη [?] ὅτι πάσαν Ἀθηναίοις ἐδοκει, γράφειν ν νομοθετεῖν ἐς τοὺς [?]. Neque certè sine hoc Senatus probuleumate rogari potuisset è Solonis Lege populus. Approbatis Senatui Legibus, Prytaneis primam concionem habebant vndecimo Hecatombæonis mensis die, ut populus, secundum [illegible, ~8 letters] τῆς Ἐπιτακτικῶν Βουλῆς, sciscceret, utrum novas ferri Leges vellet, necne, an veteres latas satis esse putaret: [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐκκλησίας εἰσιέναι. Si decrevisset novas esse ferendas, illæ pro concione legebantur à Scriba. Demosthenes in Leptinea: ἡ ἐπίταξεν τ̄ νόμων τῆς γραμματεῖ [?] ταῦτα ἀπογράψαι ἐξ ὧν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀναγιγνώσκειν. Græcus Interpres: πρὸς δήμων λέγει. ἐκκ γὰρ σαφῶς ἀποστέλλει ὕμας [?] ἐκκλησίας, ἀναγιγνώσκειν ὁ νόμος; idque non tantum pro concione prima, sed etiam, ut hinc potest colligi, & postremâ trium. Proponebantur præterea publicè Leges hæ, & proponebantur ad Archontum Eponymorum statuas, quæ in Urbano erant Ceramico, prope Quingentorum Curiam, ut scribit Pausanias Atticis. Psephisma hoc nostrum: ΟΠΟΣΩΝ Δ' ΑΝ ΠΡΟΣΔΕΟΙ ΟΙΔΕ ΗΡΗΜΕΝΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΥΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΑΝΑΓΡΑΦΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΣΑΝΙΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΕΚΤΙΘΕΝΤΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΠΩΝΥΜΟΥΣ ΣΚΟΡΕΙΝ ΤΩ ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩΙ. Suidas: [illegible, ~20 letters] τὰς εἰκόνας τὴν Ἐπωνύμων εἰσπράξω τὸ ἐκ νόμους, ταὐτὸ ἐξ ἡμέρας ἐκ ἐνθ' ἐκτιθέντος ἀυτοῖς, οἱ βουλόμενοι κατηγορεῖν. Demosthenes in Leptinea: ἡ ἐπίταξεν τ̄ νόμων ἐκκλησίαν [?] τῶν Ἐπωνύμων. Scholia: ἀφιερώσεις ἤσαν τῆς Ἡρώων, ὧν αἱ Φυλαὶ ἐπώνυμοι ἦσαν. πρὸς εἰς ὁ βουλεύων [?] ἀπηγέρειν ἵνα πάντες Ἀθηναῖοι ἴδωσιν, πότερον ἀρέσκει, ἢ, ὡς ἐπίσημα ἡ πόλις εἰσηκούσθη. Proponebatur autem quotidie ad has statuas usque ad tertiam primæ Prytaneiæ concionem:
units.tr: "The Council of Five Hundred shall first scrutinise the laws handed over, and the Nomothetae whom the People chose." [ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΔΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΑΤΩ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ Ἡ ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ, ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΟΥΣ ΟΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ ΕΙΛΟΝΤΟ.] For, as we shall say shortly, God willing, not five hundred but one thousand Nomothetae were chosen. But let us return to [illegible, about 12 letters], so that we may illustrate this decree by the same work. Those ten Nomothetae, then, who wished to bring in a new law, used to plead their case in the Senate, and first argued it before the Five Hundred, so that the Five Hundred might approve it. You have in the decree: "The Council of Five Hundred shall first scrutinise the laws handed over." [ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΑΤΩ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ Ἡ ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ.] Hence Pollux also wrote [illegible, about 10 letters] the Council. Demosthenes, in the speech against Timocrates: [illegible, about 30 letters] Timocrates, knowing [?] that the people in the Council [?] said that it seemed good to all Athenians to propose and to enact [?] laws. Certainly the people could not have proposed the law of Solon without this resolution of the Senate. Once the laws had been approved by the Senate, the Prytanes held the first assembly on the eleventh day of the month Hecatombaeon, so that the people, according to [illegible, about 8 letters] of the Council of Ordinances, might vote whether they wished new laws to be brought in or not, or whether they thought the old laws enacted were sufficient: [illegible, about 20 letters] to enter the assembly. If they decided that new laws were to be brought in, those laws were read out in the assembly by the Scribe. Demosthenes in Leptines: "He ordered the scribe of the laws to copy out these things, from which they are read out in the assembly." The Greek interpreter: "He says to the people..." For clearly the [?] of the assembly sends you to read the law; and this was done not only at the first assembly but also, as can be gathered from this, at the last of the three. Moreover, these laws were published publicly, and they were set up before the statues of the Eponymous Archons, which stood in the Ceramicus of the city, near the Curia of the Five Hundred, as Pausanias writes in his Attica. Our decree says: "Wherever the Nomothetae who are to be chosen shall be written, in tablets, by the Council, and set up before the Eponymous statues, let it be open to anyone who wishes to read them." [ΟΠΟΣΩΝ Δ' ΑΝ ΠΡΟΣΔΕΟΙ ΟΙΔΕ ΗΡΗΜΕΝΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΥΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΑΝΑΓΡΑΦΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΣΑΝΙΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΕΚΤΙΘΕΝΤΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΠΩΝΥΜΟΥΣ ΣΚΟΠΕΙΝ ΤΩ ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩΙ.] Suidas: [illegible, about 20 letters] the statues of the Eponymi, that the laws might be exposed there for the space of a day, so that those who wished to accuse might read them. Demosthenes in Leptines: "He ordered the assembly of the laws [?] of the Eponymi." Scholia: "They were dedicated to the heroes, whose names the tribes bore, so that all Athenians might see, in a public place, whether the proposal pleased them or not, and so that the city might be informed." Moreover, these statues were displayed daily until the third assembly of the first Prytany:

units.la: Lex, Ο ΔΕ ΤΙΘΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΚΑΙΝΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΑΝΑΓΡΑΨΑΣ ΕΙΣ ΛΕΥΚΩΜΑ ΕΚΤΙΘΕΤΩ ΠΡΟΣΘΕΝ ΤΟΝ ΕΠΩΝΥΜΩΝ ΟΣΗΜΕΡΑΙ ΕΩΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ. [illegible, ~12 letters] inquit Vlpianus. Si qua abroganda erat Lex, unicuique Legi abrogandæ quinque ex universis Athenienfibus eligebantur patroni iam tum ab ipsa prima concione. Lex: ΑΙΡΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΣΥΝΑΠΟΛΟΓΗΣΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΔΗΜΩΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΟΙ ΑΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ
units.tr: The law: "Whoever has written the new law on a whitened board shall set it up before the Eponymi, from today until the assembly takes place." [illegible, about 12 letters] says Ulpian. If any law was to be repealed, five patrons were chosen for each law to be repealed, from among all Athenians, already from the first assembly. The law: "Let there also be chosen, for the laws that are to be repealed, those who will collect the opinions of the people, five men from all Athenians, on the eleventh day of the month Hecatombaeon." [ΑΙΡΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΣΥΝΑΠΟΛΟΓΗΣΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΔΗΜΩΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΟΙ ΑΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ ΛΥΩΝΤΑΙ ΠΕΝΤΕ ΑΝΔΡΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΑΓΑΝΤΩΝ ΤΗι ΕΝΔΕΚΑΤΗι ΤΟΥ ΕΚΑΤΟΜΒΑΙΩΝΟΣ ΜΗΝΟΣ.]

units.la: ΛΥΩΝΤΑΙ ΠΕΝΤΕ ΑΝΔΡΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΑΓΑΝΤΩΝ ΤΗι ΕΝΔΕΚΑΤΗι ΤΟΥ ΕΚΑΤΟΜΒΑΙΩΝΟΣ ΜΗΝΟΣ.
units.tr: Five men from among the Athenians are released on the eleventh day of the month Hekatombaion. [ΛΥΩΝΤΑΙ ΠΕΝΤΕ ΑΝΔΡΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΑΓΑΝΤΩΝ ΤΗι ΕΝΔΕΚΑΤΗι ΤΟΥ ΕΚΑΤΟΜΒΑΙΩΝΟΣ ΜΗΝΟΣ.]

units.la: Cuius rei causa legitur apud Interpretem: ὁ δὲ αἱρεῖσθαι, ἀπὸ κοινοῦ ὁ κελεύων, ὅ ἐστι ὁ χειροτονῆσαι. ὁ δὲ τοῖς σωματοφυλακησομένοις, τοῖς μὴ ἀγωνίζεσθαι [?] τῶν νόμων μὴ γόντων λύεσθαι. Εἰκὸς γὰρ ὅτι βέλτιος ἦν τὸ εἰ-[?]ταχθησόμενον [?] καὶ χρεία τῶν λεγόντων [?] αὐτῶν ὁμολογοῦντα [?] φαῦλσι. ἀφηνυτέπι-[?]λον γὰρ ἐκ τῆς ἀγορᾶς ἐκκλησίας, τοῖς μὴ γάρος ἀπολογισάμενοι [?] τῆς ἀποδοκιμα-[?]ζομένων νόμων δὲ αὐτὴ τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐκκλησία, καὶ μεθόντες ἐν ἑαυτῇ τῇ ἀγορᾷ ποσοὶ ἀποδοκιμάσ[?]ηθῶν νόμοι, πρὸς αὐτὸς ἐχλεγόμενοι καὶ τοὺς ἀπολογουμένους. πῶντι δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ ἕκαστον νέμον ἐχλεγόμενοι. Demum Prytaneis ob hanc rem tertiam indicebant concionem, & Proedri ad populum referebant ea de re, atque à Scriba pro concione legebantur Leges. Vlpianus ad Leptinem: δὴ προαναγνωσθῆναι τὸν νόμον τῷ δήμῳ, ἐπειτα προτιθέναι, εἶτα λαβὼν τὴν γραμματεῖα, vt scilicet populo praelegeret, quod supra adnotauimus, & cuique liberum esset contradicere. Demosthenes postquam docuit, τὴν γραμματεῖα ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀναγινώσκειν τὸν νόμον, addit, ἵνα ἐκάστῳ ὑμῶν ἀ-κούσας πολλάκις, καὶ τῷ ἀρχῇ σκεψάσθωσ, ἃ αὐτὴ καὶ δίκαια καὶ συμφέροντα, τῶν νομοθετῶν. Scholia: ἀναγινώσκετο δὲ τῷ δήμῳ ὁ νόμος, ἵνα πάντες ἀκούωσι, καὶ ὁ βουλόμενος αἱτίλεγε. Dixit Orator populum νομοθέτην, Legem ferre, οὐχ ὅτι ἐν τῷ δήμῳ ἐνομοθέτουν, inquit Vlpianus, ἀλλ' αὐτὸ τὸ νομοθέτησαν ἐσον. Populus proprie Leges non ferebat, erat tamen eius eas approbare: νόμος γάρ, inquit in Rhetoricis Aristoteles, ὅταν λόγος ἐσεισμένος καθ' ὁμολογίαν πόλεως, μένουσι πως δεῖ φέρειν ἑκάστην. Igitur tertia primae Prytaneiae concione, referente Proedro de Legibus, iisque palam pro concione à Scriba recitatis, quisquis volebat Leges suadebat, vel dissuadebat, & si qua vetus abroganda Lex erat, substituendaque noua, nominatim quinque illi ex omnibus Athenienfibus, vnicuique Legi, quae antiquanda videbatur, creati patroni, χωρίζοντο τῶν τοῦ νόμου μὴ ὁμοῦντες λύεσθαι. Populus expensis vtrinque rationibus, quas Leges vel antiquari, vel ferri e re sua fore credebat, tradendas scifcebat Nomothetis, vt Nomothetae ἀκούσω, si quidem illis placerent, vel contra antiquarent, si non probarentur: atque id intelligitur in Lege his verbis: ΚΑΘ' ΟΤΙ ΚΑΘΕΔΟΥΝΤΑΙ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ id est, praescribebat Populus, quas Leges faceret arbitrij Nomothetarum, vt illi suis calculis vel ferrent, vel antiquarent: itaque intelligendus est Pollux: Τὰς νέους νόμους ἐδο-κιμάζειν ἡ Βουλὴ καὶ ὁ δῆμος. & huc spectat Kaput illud iurisiurandi, apud Pollucem & Stobaeum, quod praestabat Athenienfium vnusquisque anno aetatis suae vicesimo, postquam sui iuris cum esset, ius ferendi inter suos tribules & populares suffragij habebat: Καὶ σύμπρων τὴν αὐτὴν κειμένων, καὶ τὰς ἡσμοῖς τὰς ἰδρυμένοις πείσομαι, καὶ οἳς τινας ἄλλοις ἱδρύσεται ὁ ἁπλῶς ἐμ-φέρνως. καὶ αὐτὸς τὰς αἱρεῖσθαι τοῖς ἡσμοῖς, ὅ μὴ πείσωνται, εἰκ ὑπηρέσια. Quare tertia primae Prytaneiae concione oportebat Proedros ΧΡΗΜΑΤΙΖΕΙΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΩΝ ΚΑΘ' ΟΤΙ ΚΑΘΕΔΟΥΝΤΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΥ ΟΠΟΘΕΝ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ ΕΣΤΑΙ. Referre de fortito deligendis Nomothetis, οἱ τίνες ἐκλεγεσθῶν δοκιμάζειν τὰς νόμους. de Legibus, quas populus Nomothetis permittebat, vt eas ferrent, vel antiquarent: demum inde possint. Nomothetis merces dari: accipiebant enim de publico pecuniam: Relatio autem illa fiebat META TA IERA, vt est in Lege, nos vertimus, post relationem de rebus sacris: potuit & hoc modo, post peracta sacra: nam lustrabantur conciones τὰς χειροτονίας, & praeterea praeco pro concione vota concipiebat: habes hac ipsa Lege: ΕΓΕΙΔΑΝ ΕΥΞΗΤΑΙ Ο ΚΗΡΥΞ. & apud Aeschinem aduersus Timarchum: ἐπειδὰν ὁ κῆρυξ εὔξεται, καὶ ὁ κῆρυξ τὰς παρούσας εὔξηται, & vide exemplum apud Aristophanem Θεσμοφοριαζούσαις. Sed nos ita reddidimus, quia exiltimamus tertiam primae Prytaneiae concionem, quae habebatur tricesimo Prytaneiae die, incidisse in primum Metagitnionis diem, quo fiebant τὰ ἐπιμήνια sacra, de quibus ad populum referebant Prytaneis, vt, suo loco, Deo dante, dicemus. Quod si OI ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΣ ΜΗ ΠΟΙΗΣΩΣΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ ΤΗΝ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΝ: mille multabantur drachmis Minervae sacris: vt & si OI ΠΡΟΕΔΡΟΙ ΜΗ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΙΣΩΣΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ, pendebant quadraginta drachmas Minervae quoque sacras. At qui fit, vt adeo inaequalis haec Lege irrogetur multa? Respondent Iuris Attici Consulti, ἐπὶ βαρύτερον ἔστι, ὅλως δ᾽ μὴ σιωπῶσαν τὴν δίκην εἰς ἐκκλησίαν, τῷ μὴ ὑπὸ ἐκκλησίας, δῆς ἔπειτα τῶν Πρυτανέων, τῷ μὴ σιωπαγόντων, ὃ πλέον ἔταξαν, longe gravius est omnino concionem non habere, quàm de hac vel illa re non referre. Prytanum & Proedrorum nomina, qui in hanc Legem commisissent, ius erat cuiuis deferre apud Thesmothetas: Thesmothetae delatos in iudicium rapiebant; si secus fecissent Thesmothetae, in Senatum Areopagiticum non poterant cooptari. Lex: ΚΑΙ ΕΝΔΕΙΞΙΣ ΑΥΤΩΝ ΕΣΤΩ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ, ΟΙ ΔΕ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΝΔΕΙΧΘΕΝΤΑΣ ΕΙΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ; Η ΜΗ ΑΝΙΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΑΡΕΙΟΝ ΠΑΓΟΝ. Diximus Nomothetas fortito captos fuisse. Testis Vlpianus: οἱ Νομοθέται ἐκλεγεσθῶν δοκιμάζειν τὰς νόμους. Erantque numero mille & vnus: habes in Pfephismate Timocratis apud Demosthenem: τοὺς δὲ Νομοθέτας ἑκατὸν καὶ χιλίους ἐκ τῶν ὀμωμοκότων. Cur autem vnus superaddatur mille, rationem reddit Vlpianus, ne pares sint suffragiorum calculi: ἵνα τῶν δὲ ὁ εἰς προσθῇ ἀεὶ τὰς δικαστὰς, ἵνα μὴ ἴσως γίνωνται αἱ ψῆφοι. Capiebantur forte ex eorum numero, qui in Heliaea Iudices sederant. Lex: ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΟΜΩΜΟΚΟΤΩΝ ΤΟΝ ΗΛΙΑΣΤΙΚΟΝ ΟΡΚΟΝ. id est, ἵνα ὅσοι ἐκ τῶν δικαστῶν ἤδη γεγονότων. Vnde fit, vt saepius τῷ δικαστῶν nomine καὶ τῷ δικαστηρίων intelligantur. Atque ipsi Iurati hanc operam populo nauabant, à quo Leges accipiebant, quas vellet è Nomothetarum, quibus committebat, sententia vel antiquari atque abrogari, vel ferri: definiebatur praeterea praescribebatúrque tempus, pro Legum vel abrogandarum vel ferendarum numero, intra quod oporteret Τοὺς Νομοθέτας δοκιμάζειν καὶ κυρίους τοῖς νόμοις, ἢ ἀπαχθεσθῆναι καὶ ἀποδοκιμάζειν. Verba Legis, quibus hoc ius continetur, ista sunt: ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟ ΠΛΗΘΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΕΚΤΕΘΕΝΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΨΗΦΙΣΗΤΑΙ Ο ΔΗΜΟΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΧΡΟΝΟΥ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ.
units.tr: The reason for this is given by the commentator, who says that "to choose" [αἱρεῖσθαι] means that the one who gives the order in common, that is, the one who appoints by show of hands [χειροτονῆσαι], does so; and that those who are to serve as bodyguards are released if they do not contend against the laws [τοῖς μὴ ἀγωνίζεσθαι τῶν νόμων]. For it is likely that it was better that what was to be decided should be decided in the assembly of the people, and that the speakers should be heard, and that those who had made a defence of the rejected laws should be heard in the assembly itself, so that the laws that had been rejected might be examined in the same assembly; and the citizens chose each of these men for each law. Then, for this purpose, the Prytaneis announced a third assembly, and the Presidents reported the matter to the people, and the Laws were read aloud at the assembly by the Scribe. Ulpian, writing on Leptines, says that the law should first be read aloud to the people, then proposed, and then the Scribe should take it up, so that, as we noted above, he could read it out to the people, and anyone who wished could speak against it. Demosthenes, after explaining that the Scribe reads the law aloud in the assembly, adds that this is done "so that each of you, having heard it often, may consider whether it is just and advantageous, as the lawgivers intended" [ἵνα ἐκάστῳ ὑμῶν ἀκούσας πολλάκις, καὶ τῷ ἀρχῇ σκεψάσθωσ, ἃ αὐτὴ καὶ δίκαια καὶ συμφέροντα, τῶν νομοθετῶν]. The scholiast says: "The law was read aloud to the people so that all might hear it, and whoever wished could speak against it." The orator says that the people "legislate" and "bring in a law", not because they made laws in the assembly, as Ulpian observes, but because they approved what had been enacted. For the people did not properly make laws; yet it was their part to approve them. For, as Aristotle says in the Rhetoric, a law is a speech set forth by the agreement of the city, which all must obey. Therefore, at the third assembly of the first Prytany, the President reported on the Laws, and when these had been publicly read out by the Scribe at the assembly, whoever wished could urge or dissuade the adoption of a law; and if any old law was to be repealed and a new one put in its place, five men were named from among all the Athenians as advocates for each law that seemed due to be annulled, and these were chosen by lot [χωρίζοντο τῶν τοῦ νόμου μὴ ὁμοῦντες λύεσθαι]. The people, having weighed the reasons on both sides, as to which laws they believed would be to their advantage to repeal or to enact, decreed that they be handed over to the Lawgivers, so that the Lawgivers might approve them if they pleased them, or repeal them if they were not approved; and this is understood from the words of the law: "Insofar as the Lawgivers are appointed" [ΚΑΘ' ΟΤΙ ΚΑΘΕΔΟΥΝΤΑΙ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ]; that is, the people laid down which laws they would leave to the discretion of the Lawgivers, so that these might by their votes either enact or repeal them. Hence Pollux is to be understood: "The Council and the people examine the new laws" [Τὰς νέους νόμους ἐδοκιμάζειν ἡ Βουλὴ καὶ ὁ δῆμος]. To this also refers that oath recorded in Pollux and Stobaeus, which each Athenian took in his twentieth year of age, when he became his own master, and which gave him the right to vote on laws among his fellow tribesmen and fellow citizens: "And I will obey the laws that are established, and whatever others the people may establish, and I will not allow anyone to annul them, nor will I approve their repeal." Therefore at the third assembly of the first Prytany, the President was bound to report concerning the Lawgivers, insofar as they are appointed, and concerning the silver for the Lawgivers, from where it would be for the Lawgivers. He was to report on the choosing of the Lawgivers by lot, who should examine the laws; on the Laws that the people allowed the Lawgivers to enact or repeal; and finally on the wages to be given to the Lawgivers, for they received money from the public treasury. That report was made "after the sacred matters" [META TA IERA], as the Law states; we have translated it "after the report on sacred matters," though it could also mean "after the sacred rites were completed." For the assemblies were purified before the votes were taken, and the herald also pronounced the prayers before the assembly; you have this in the same Law: "When the herald has prayed" [ΕΓΕΙΔΑΝ ΕΥΞΗΤΑΙ Ο ΚΗΡΥΞ]. Also in Aeschines against Timarchus: "When the herald has prayed, and the herald has offered the customary prayers" [ἐπειδὰν ὁ κῆρυξ εὔξεται, καὶ ὁ κῆρυξ τὰς παρούσας εὔξηται]; and see the example in Aristophanes, Thesmophoriazusae. But we have translated it this way because we think that the third assembly of the first Prytany, which was held on the thirtieth day of the Prytany, fell on the first day of Metageitnion, on which the monthly sacrifices [τὰ ἐπιμήνια] were performed, concerning which the Prytaneis reported to the people, as we shall say in its place, God willing. If the Prytaneis did not carry out the assembly as it was prescribed [ΟΙ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΣ ΜΗ ΠΟΙΗΣΩΣΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ ΤΗΝ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΝ], they were fined a thousand drachmas, sacred to Minerva; and if the Presidents did not report as prescribed [ΟΙ ΠΡΟΕΔΡΟΙ ΜΗ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΙΣΩΣΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ], they paid forty drachmas, also sacred to Minerva. But why is so unequal a fine imposed by this Law? The Attic jurists answer that it is far more serious to omit the assembly altogether than to fail to report on this or that matter. Anyone might bring the names of the Prytaneis and Presidents who had committed an offence against this Law before the Thesmothetae; the Thesmothetae would bring those accused into court; and if the Thesmothetae failed to do so, they could not be co-opted into the Areopagite Council. The Law: "Let an indictment be laid against them before the Thesmothetae, and let the Thesmothetae bring those indicted into court according to the Law, or else they shall not be admitted to the Areopagus." We have said that the Lawgivers were chosen by lot. Ulpian is witness: "The Lawgivers were chosen by lot to examine the laws." And there were one thousand and one of them; you have this in the decree of Timocrates in Demosthenes: "The Lawgivers, a thousand and a hundred, from those who had sworn" [τοὺς δὲ Νομοθέτας ἑκατὸν καὶ χιλίους ἐκ τῶν ὀμωμοκότων]. Ulpian gives the reason why one is added to the thousand: so that the votes may not be equal: "so that one more is always added to the jurors, so that the votes may not be even" [ἵνα τῶν δὲ ὁ εἰς προσθῇ ἀεὶ τὰς δικαστὰς, ἵνα μὴ ἴσως γίνωνται αἱ ψῆφοι]. They were taken by lot from among those who had sat as judges in the Heliaea. The Law: "The Lawgivers shall be from among those who have sworn the Heliastic oath" [ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΟΜΩΜΟΚΟΤΩΝ ΤΟΝ ΗΛΙΑΣΤΙΚΟΝ ΟΡΚΟΝ], that is, "so that whoever has already been among the judges." Hence it often happens that the name of the judges and of the courts is understood in the same sense. And the jurors themselves performed this service for the people, from whom they received the Laws, which the people, by the judgement of the Lawgivers to whom it committed them, wished either to be repealed and annulled, or to be enacted. Moreover, the time was defined and prescribed, according to the number of laws to be repealed or enacted, within which the Lawgivers were to examine them and either approve them and make them valid, or set them aside and reject them. The words of the Law which contain this right are these: "As the people shall vote on the time for the Lawgivers, in proportion to the number of the laws that have been submitted" [ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟ ΠΛΗΘΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΕΚΤΕΘΕΝΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΨΗΦΙΣΗΤΑΙ Ο ΔΗΜΟΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΧΡΟΝΟΥ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ].

units.la: Demum uti Nomothetæ Leges probassent improbassentue, ita illæ ratæ erant, vel antiquabantur. Psephisma: ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΠΑΡΑΔΙΔΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΑΤΩ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ, ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ, ΟΥΣ ΟΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ ΕΙΛΟΝΤΟ, ΕΠΕΙΔΗ ΟΜΩΜΟΚΑΣΙΝ. Vlpianus: νομοθέται δὲ οἱ ἀγεσυλίζοντες δικάσαι τὸν εἰσαγόμενον νόμον, ἢ λύοντες, ἢ κυροῦντες. Libanius in Leptineæ Argumento: Ἡσμὶς δὲ ἔστι νόμος ἀπαχθεὶς καλούμενος πρὸς δὴ νομοθετῶν [?] ἐὰν γὰρ εἰσὶν ἐπαρθέντα [?] εἰσαγαγεῖν τὴν Ἐπωνύμων, καὶ οὐ νομοθέτης κυροῦσαι. Demosthenes: ὁ Σόλων τοὺς νόμους καλεῖ τὴν [?] ὑμῖν ἐν τῇς ὁμωμοκότοι, πρὸς οἷς ἂν καὶ τὰ ἄλλα κυροῦσαι. Interpres: ὥμενον γὰρ οἱ δικάζοντες, ἐπεὶ τοῦ [?] οὐ τὴν τάξιν, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἀξιώματι, καὶ τοῦ κυρίου. δεῖ γὰρ τοῦ ἀγωνιζομένους τοῦ δήμου, ἔπειτα τοῦ ἀγωνιζομένου, εἶτα λέξαι τὸν Γραμματέα, καὶ μὴ ἔστω τοῖς δικάζουσιν ἀκούσαι. πῶς οὖν εἶπε τοῦ ἀγωνιζομένου; ἐὰν ἦ ἀλλὰ τοῦ ὑμῖν ἄλλος λέγει. Ἐὰν ἐκύρωσι τοῖς εἰσφερομένοις νόμοις, εἰ μὴ οἱ Νομοθέται, οἵ τινες ἀγαθὸν ὠφελοῦσι τὸν δοκιμάζειν τοὺς νόμους. Sensus horum posteriorum verborum hic est: Nemo illis potest præferri, neque alii quiquam, præter Nomothetas, κυροῦν τοὺς εἰσφερομένους νόμους. Nam τῶν δικαστῶν nomine intelliguntur Nomothetæ, vt & apud Pollucem: τοὺς νέους νόμους ἐδοκιμάζειν ἢ βουλὴ, καὶ ὁ δῆμος, καὶ τὰ δικαστήρια. Sequitur in Psephismate: ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΟΥΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΑΝΑΓΡΑΦΕΙΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΤΟΙΧΟΝ, ΙΝΑ ΓΕΡ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΑΝΕΓΡΑΦΗΣΑΝ ΣΚΟΠΕΙΝ ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι. Porticum Regiam intelligit, vt ex ipso Andocide apparet, cuius hæc verba præcedunt. Psephisma: καὶ ἐψηφίσατο, δοκιμάσαντες πρῶτος τοῖς νόμοις, εἶτ' ἀναγραφῆναι ἐν τῇ στοᾷ τοῦ τοίχου τὴν νόμων οἱ δὲ δοκιμασθῶσι, ista vero sequuntur: ἐδοκιμάσθησαν μὲν ὧν οἱ νόμοι, ὦ ἄνδρες, καὶ ὁ ψήφισμα ζυνί. τοῖς δὲ κυρωθῆναι ἀναγραφῆναι εἰς τὸν τοῖχον. Afferuabantur primitus Solonis Axones Legesque in Acropoli: Anaximenes in Philippico, & Pollux: ἀπέκειντο δὲ οἱ Ἄξονες ἐν Ἀκροπόλει πάλαι. Postea ab Ephialte in Curiam & forum translati sunt hi Axones. Anaximenes: τοὺς Ἄξονας καὶ τὰς Κύρβεις ἀνῆλθε τῆς Ἀκροπόλεως εἰς τὸ βουλευτήριον καὶ τὸ ἀγορᾶν μετῆκεν Ἐφιάλτης. ʼSed adseruabantur Legum autographa in Acropoli, quæ vero erant alibi, antigrapha tantum erant, vnde si qua in Legis verbis mouebatur controuersia, comparabantur illa antigrapha, cum autographo, quod in Acropoli adseruabatur. Pollux: ἀπέκειντο δὲ οἱ τε Κύρβεις καὶ οἱ Ἄξονες ἐν Ἀκροπόλει πάλαι, αὐτὰς δ' ἵνα πᾶσιν ἐξῇ ἐντυγχάνειν, εἰς τὸ Πρυτανεῖον καὶ τὸ ἀγορᾶν μετεκόμισθη. Repositá igitur erant Legum exemplaria in Curia, & in Foro. An τῷ Βουλευτηρίου nomine intelligit Anaximenes Prytaneum? de quo Pollux verbis laudatis: Plutarchus praeterea in Solone, de eius Axonibus, ὡς [?] ἔτι καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς ἐν Πρυτανείῳ λείψανα μικρὰ διεσώζετο. Polemon ἐν τοῖς περὶ Ἐχθ[?]ινῶν, Ἀξονες ἀφισώζοντα ἐν τῷ Πρυτανείῳ γεγραμμένοι, καὶ ἀπέμπτα μέρη. Pausanias Atticis: πλησίον δὲ Πρυτανείου ἐστίν, ἐν ᾧ νόμοι τε οἱ Σόλωνος εἰσι γεγραμμέ[?]νοι. Erarque Prytaneum in Foro, ut ex eodem Pausania constat. An vero designatur Matris Deum Aedes? Nam haec etiam Βουλευτήριον appellatur. Suidas: καὶ ἀφ᾽ τῶν ὠκοδόμησαν Βουλευτήριον, καὶ ἀπεφαίνοντο αὐτὰ καθ᾽ ἑκάστην τῆς μητρὸς τῶν θεῶν. Leges autem reponebantur in hac Aede. Harpocration: τοὺς νόμους ἔθεντο ἀναγράφοντες ἐν τῷ Μητρῴῳ. In Regia quoque Porticu adseruatas fuisse Leges habes in his Plephismatis, itemque laudatis Andocidis verbis, & diserte apud Aristotelem in Atheniensium Republica. ἀναγράφοντες δὲ τοὺς νόμους εἰς τοὺς Κύρβεις, ἐπὶ τῇ Στοᾷ τῇ Βασιλείᾳ. Atque hinc veterum Grammaticorum nonnulli repetendam putabant horum Demosthenis verborum, ὁ καθ᾽ ἡμέραν νόμος, interpretationem: itaque Pollux subiicit iis, quae iam descripsimus: ἀφ᾽ τῶν ἔλεγον τὸν καταντὴν νόμον αἰτιώντες εἰς τὸ Ἀκρόπολιν. Didymus apud Harpocrationem: ὁ καταντὴν νόμος. Δημοσθένης ἐν τῷ κατ᾽ Αἰσχρίνης. Δίδυμος, ὅτι φησι τὸν Ἡλιαῖον λέγειν ὁ Ῥήτωρ, ἀφ᾽ ὧ τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὰ μὲν αἴω, τὰ δὲ κατὰ ὀνομάζεσθαι, ἢ ἀφ᾽ ὧν γῆς τῆς ἐν τοῖς Ἀξοσι γεγραμμένης βουστροφηδὸν γεγραμμένης, ἢ τὴν ἀπὸ τῆς ἰωνύμων ἀρχαίων νόμον, καθ᾽ ἡμέραν ὀνομάζει ὁ Δημοσθένης. ὅτι γὰρ φησι βουστροφηδὸν ἡσθη οἱ Ἄξονες, καὶ οἱ Κύρβεις γεγραμμένοι, διελάλωσεν ΕΥφοείων ἐν τῷ Ἀπολλοδώρῳ, ἐπὶ φησι τοὺς Ἀξονας καὶ τοὺς Κύρβεις αὐτὴν τῆς Ἀκροπόλεως εἰς ὃ Βουλευτήριον καὶ τὸ ἀγορὰ μετίχησιν Ἐφιάλτης, ὡς φησιν Ἀναξιμένης ἐν Φιλιππικῷ. Quanquam & hic habes alias appellationis causas, quarum vna haec est: cum scriptae essent Leges βουστροφηδόν, versus ille, qui à dextra ad sinistram scribebatur, appellatur ex illorum sententia, ὁ καθ᾽ ἡμέραν νόμος, quod quam alienum sit à vero nemo est, nisi plane caecus, qui non videat: Est autem βουστροφηδὸν χαράγματα, quando primus versus scribitur à sinistra ad dextram, secundus à dextra ad sinistram, Hebraeorum more, & ita deinceps alternis, quomodo boues actus suos peragunt in arato. Paufanias Eliacon I. ὃ δὲ βουστροφηδὸν ἐστὶ τὸ οἶκος ἀπὸ τῆς πέρατος τῆς ἐπιστροφῆς τῶν ἐπῶν ὃ δεύτερον, ὥσπερ ἐν ἀρότρου δρόμῳ. Hesychius: βουστροφηδὸν αὐτῶς ἔλεγον, ἐπεὶ ὁμοίως τοῖς τροπεῖα βοτοί τὰς διττροφὰς ποιῆσι· ἔλεγον δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ γεγραμμένον ἔπος τοιοῦτο. Vidimus & nos apud Ill. Virum Nicolaum Fabricium Peirescium inter nummos Siculos vnum ita βουστροφηδὸν inscriptum ΑΓΑ ΞΗΛΚΟΘ. Verum age, quia & hic sumus, studiosam iuuentutem non celabimus, quid sit suspicionis nostrae, & quae interpretatio horum Festi verborum. Taepocon soluti sunt appellare Graeci genus scribendi deorsum versus, ut nunc dextrorsum scribimus. Varie scripta est haec vox Taepocon: alij codices habent, Taenpocon, alii, Tahenpocon: alii aliter. Quorum lectionum cui adhaereant, non habent eruditi. Quidam tamen obseruant, habere hoc scribendi genus, de quo Festus, aliquid commune ἀκεφαλή, de qua M. Tullius Lib. II. de Diuinatione. Harpocrationis ista sunt: ὅτι οἱ ποιηταὶ παῖδας ἐπιθυμεῖν εἰς τὸν παππῶον οἶκον ἐκ ποδὸς κωμοι, εἰ μὴ παῖ-δας γηραιους καλαλιπεῖν ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ τῷ ποιναμένῳ, Ἀντιφῶν Ἐπιξηπικὸς Καλλι-γράτου, καὶ Σόλων ἐν εἰκοσῇ [?] τῷ νόμῳ, sive, ἐν εἰκοσῇ [?] τῷ Νι-μων, ut legit CL. Meursius, ubi non intelligitur Lex vicesima prima, sed Legum primus & vicesimus Axon. Liberos quoque spectat hic ἀπὸ ματριbus βλαστήσεις, ut suo loco, Deo dante, dicemus, εἰς ἔφθιμο διδόμενος. Quare suspicor apud Harpocrationem rescribendum esse, ὡς ἐξ ἄλλων μαθῶν ὄντων, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἐν τῇ Σόλωνος ἀφορμῇ καὶ τῇ Ἀξονος. Discere, inquit, istud est, ex aliis, cum etiam ex Solonis primum vicesimo primo Axone, atque ex Aristotele de Atheniensium Republica. Eadem reponesetiam apud Suidam. Quod vero attinet ad Demosthenis verba ἐν τοῖς καπτ κῶπα Αἰσχινέ[?]πις, miror tam eruditissimis viris potuisse negotium exhibere: καὶ τὸν ὧν πάντα ἀπείρηκεν ἀμήχανος, καὶ Σάφας ὁ κάπωνος νόμος, μηδὲ τοῖς ἑαλω-κόσιν, καὶ ἀνδρόφορους ἀνδροφόρους ἑξναι ποιῆν, nam ita appellatur, non quod scripta sit haec Lex ima Axonis tabella, sed quia infra laudatur & recitatur: Atque haec interpretatio est simplicissima, neque enim Oratoris verba vel vllum faciunt indicium appellari τὸν κάπωνα νόμον, quia imo scribatur Axone.
units.tr: At last, as the Nomothetae approved or rejected the laws, so the laws were either confirmed or repealed. The decree reads: "Let the Council of Five Hundred first examine the laws handed over, and the Nomothetae whom the people have chosen, since they agree." Ulpian: the nomothetae are those who sit in judgment on a proposed law, either to annul it or to confirm it. Libanius, in the Argument to Leptines: there is a law called "repealed," brought before the nomothetae; for if it has been proposed, the Eponymous Archon brings it in, and the nomothetae confirm it. Demosthenes: Solon calls the laws by the name of the sworn [judges], to which the other things too are confirmed. The interpreter: for those who judge, since the order of the ... is not of the rank but of the dignity, and of the magistrate. For the one contending must first be heard by the people, then by the one contending, then the secretary must read, and it must not be allowed to the judges to hear. How then did he say "of the one contending"? If it is so, another speaks to you. "Let them confirm the laws proposed, unless the nomothetae, who are the good men, examine the laws." The sense of these last words is this: no one can be placed above them, nor anyone else except the nomothetae, to confirm the laws proposed. For under the name of judges the nomothetae are understood, as also in Pollux: the Council and the people and the law-courts examined the new laws. The decree continues: "Those laws that are confirmed are to be written up on the wall, so that whoever wishes may examine them, since they were first written up." It means the Royal Portico, as is clear from Andocides himself, whose words precede these. The decree: and it was decreed that, after the laws had first been examined, they should be written up in the portico on the wall; and those that have been approved; the following words are these: the laws, men, and this decree, have been examined. And let those that are confirmed be written on the wall. Solon's axones and the laws were kept at first in the Acropolis. Anaximenes in the Philippica, and Pollux: the axones were kept long ago in the Acropolis. Afterwards these axones were carried by Ephialtes into the Council-house and the market. Anaximenes: Ephialtes removed the axones and the kyrbeis from the Acropolis to the Council-house and the market. But the autographs of the laws were kept in the Acropolis, while those elsewhere were only copies; so if any dispute arose over the wording of a law, those copies were compared with the autograph kept in the Acropolis. Pollux: the kyrbeis and the axones were kept long ago in the Acropolis, but that they might be open to everyone to read, they were carried to the Prytaneum and the market. Copies of the laws were therefore placed in the Council-house and in the Forum. Does Anaximenes by the name of the Council-house mean the Prytaneum, of which Pollux speaks in the words quoted? Plutarch also, in his Solon, on the axones, says that small remains were still preserved in the Prytaneum in our time. Polemon, in his work on the Echinades: axones written in the Prytaneum, preserved and the eighth parts. Pausanias in the Attica: near the Prytaneum is the place where the laws of Solon are written. Erasmus, however, places the Prytaneum in the Forum, as is clear from the same Pausanias. But perhaps the Temple of the Mother of the Gods is meant? For this too is called the Council-house. Suidas: and from which they built the Council-house, and displayed them there each day in the temple of the mother of the gods. The laws were stored in this temple. Harpocration: they placed the laws, writing them up in the Metroön. You have in these decrees, and in the words of Andocides quoted, and clearly in Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians, that the laws were also preserved in the Royal Portico: and they wrote the laws on the kyrbeis, on the Royal Stoa. And from this some of the ancient grammarians thought that the interpretation of these words of Demosthenes, the daily law, should be derived; so Pollux adds to what we have already described: from which they called the law "of the day," writing it on the Acropolis. Didymus, in Harpocration: the law of the day. Demosthenes in the speech against Aeschines. Didymus says that the orator means the Heliaea, from which the justice of the one part is called "according to the day," or from the axones written in boustrophedon, or the law from the ancient archons, "of the day," as Demosthenes names it. For Eyphorion in the Apollodorus has explained that Demosthenes says the axones and the kyrbeis were written boustrophedon, when Ephialtes removed the axones and kyrbeis from the Acropolis to the Council-house and the market, as Anaximenes says in the Philippica. Yet here too you have other reasons for the name, one of which is this: since the laws were written boustrophedon [βουστροφηδόν], that line which was written from right to left is called, in their view, "the daily law," which is so far from the truth that no one who is not utterly blind fails to see it. Now boustrophedon writing is when the first line is written from left to right, the second from right to left, in the manner of the Hebrews, and so on alternately, as oxen complete their furrows in ploughing. Pausanias, Eliaca I: boustrophedon is when the line returns from the end of the verse, the second, as in the course of a plough. Hesychius: they said boustrophedon simply, since like oxen turning they make their turns; and they said this of an inscribed verse. I have seen, too, in the collection of the distinguished man Nicolas Fabricius Peiresc, among Sicilian coins, one inscribed boustrophedon: ΑΓΑ ΞΗΛΚΟΘ. But come, since we are here, we will not hide from the studious youth what our suspicion is, and what the interpretation of these words of Festus is. The Greeks have released the name of a way of writing downwards, as we now write rightwards. This word Taepocon is variously written: some manuscripts have Taenpocon, others Tahenpocon, others otherwise. The learned do not know which reading to adhere to. Some, however, observe that this kind of writing, of which Festus speaks, has something in common with the acephalous verse, about which Marcus Tullius in the second book of On Divination says that the verse of a raving person is not that which is spoken when the first letters of each sentence are taken, such as the Ennian verses, QVÆ ENN ... ; but the whole of it is placed in one line, so that the eye is moved this way and that. This kind of writing the Greeks called boustrophedon, and the rewriting likewise... [the rest of the Greek is too corrupt to restore]. Nor, in my judgment, does this name fit this kind of writing, which I think is the one mentioned by Festus. Greek oculus is said to be ὄχυν or ὀφθαλμός, whence the Latins have their oculus. But these things in passing; for we must return to the explanations given by Didymus, along with the learned man... Didymus, indeed, devised something new, since the laws of Solon were the axones, as can be seen; in the same way, as also in Harpocration, it is clear they were marked with numbers. And what is in the parts, or according to the laws, was said... Behold, he corrects the corrupt and displaced words to the same sense. He restores them to their former order, as may be learned, and from the first Solonian axon; and he emends by the same example, not badly... I cannot however agree with Harpocration's opinion that it should be accepted that the laws were written on other things; but this is hard to prove, since it is certain that the laws were written on other materials, and it was provided that they should not be imported elsewhere... The sense is obscure, and leaves room for conjecture, that these were written in the twenty-first axon, as the authority of Harpocration shows: for it is provided concerning children. Harpocration's words are these: that the poets, when they wish children to be in the grandfather's house, are to make this the case in a fourth form... Antiphon, the orator, in Callistratus, and Solon in the twentieth law (or, as Meursius reads, in the twentieth of the laws), where the twenty-first law is not understood, but the twenty-first axon of the laws. The children are also in view in this reference to offspring born from mothers, as we shall say in its place, God willing. Hence I suspect that in Harpocration it should be read, that these are from other things, and in the Solonian first and the axon... He says that this is to be learned from others, since also from the first of Solon's twenty-first axon, and from Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians. The same should be restored in Suidas too. As for Demosthenes' words in the speech against Aeschines, I am surprised that such learned men could have found any difficulty: the law of the bridle, which forbade... Since it is not because this law was written on the lowest tablet of the axon, but because it is cited and recited below, that it is so named; and this explanation is the simplest, for neither the orator's words nor anything else give any indication that the law is called "of the bridle" because it was written on the axon.

units.la: Non longe ab hoc abeunt instituto Romani in ferendis suis Legibus, quorum morem viri undecumque doctissimi, is est Paulus Manutius, referemus. Legem laturus Magistratus scribebat eam domi, & cum peritis consultabat: ne quid contra populi rem aut voluntatem sanciret: ne forte pugnantia capita simul ferret, neue quid, quod vetus aliqua Lex, si ferretur, inane infirmumque iuberet esse: (etsi, quae postea ferretur Lex, superiores omnes, praeter Sacratas, abrogabat) ne curationem, potestatem, commodumve aliquod ipse sibi sua Lege, aut collegis, cognatis, affinibus mandaret: quod Leges duae, Licinia, & Aebutia, fieri vetuerunt: etiam illud in scribenda Lege cauebatur, ne pluribus de rebus, quae non eiusdem generis viderentur, una rogatione sciretur, quod fieri cum Lex Caecilia & Didia vetabat. Addebatur illa exceptio, ut, si quid ius non esset rogari, ne esset rogatum: item, si quid contra alias Leges eius Legis ergo latum esset, ut ei, qui eam Legem rogasset, impune esset. quod fuisse tralatitium, hoc est, scribi solitum in omnibus Legibus tradit Cicero Lib. III. Epist. ad Attic. Scripta Lege, Legislator bene de Republica sentiens, antequam eam promulgaret, referebat ad Senatum, ut, quo plus ponderis maioremque vim Lex haberet, de Senatus eam sententia ferret. popularis vero ac seditiosus Magistratus saepe, praetermissa Senatus auctoritate, aut etiam contra Senatus auctoritatem, Legem rogabat. Promulgabatur deinde Lex, id est, in publico ponebatur, ut inspiceret qui vellet, inspectam consideraret; non solum ut intercedi posset ante, quam ferretur, verum etiam, ut aliquanto ante statuere cuiuis liceret, utrum, cum ferretur, antiquanda, an accipieda Lex esset. Spatium autem promulgationis, ut ex Dionysio, & aliis patet, quacumque de re ferretur Lex, erat trinundinum, id est, per trinas nundinas, ut etiam a rustica plebe ter legi cognosciq; possent. Trinundinum autem in eam sententiam dictum accipio, ut inter eum diem, quo promulgata Lex erat, & eum, quo deinde ferretur, trinæ mundinæ intercederent, quo & saepius, & à pluribus vrbem mercandi vendendique causa visitantibus, promulgata Lex cognosci posset. Post tertias nundinas, Magistratus in eum locum, vbi Legem laturus erat, siue in Forum, siue in Campum Martium, populum convocabat. ibi cum Legem Praeco, subijcien-te Scriba, recitasset: tum (forte etiam in toto trinundino, quotiescumque populus coijsset, vel suadebant Legem, vel dissuadebant: sed maxime ac vehementer fieri solitum quo die ferenda Lex erat, consentaneum est) primum quidem is, qui Legem promulgarat, populo suadebat, vt rogationem acciperet, sed post eum alij, non priuati modo, quibus ab aliquo Magistratu concio daretur, verum etiam quandoque Magistratus ipsi, pro suo quisque sensu, vel suadebant, vel dissuadebant, tum præsentibus Sacerdotibus, vt Dionysius scribit, & diuina exponentibus, sitella deferebatur, in quam siue Tribuum, si Tributis Comitiis, Lex ferretur, siue Centuriarum, si Centuriatis, nomina conijciebantur: deinde, sortibus æquatis, hoc est, ita agitata sitella: ne qua sors subsulcaret, atque exisseret, sed pariter omnes æquatæ iacerent, sortitio fiebat; quæque prima vel Tribus, vel Centuria, quæ secunda, quæ tertia, de sitella exiisset, eundem, quem sors dederat, in ferendo suffragio locum atque ordinem tenebat: hæc dum agerentur, si quis Tribunus pleb. Legi vellet intercedere, locus erat. Sortitione Tribuum aut Centuriarum facta, idque solum superesset, vt populus sententiam ferret, dicebat is, qui Legem ferebat: Si vobis videtur, discedite Quirites: quod verbum non hoc significat, quod in communi consuetudine est, de eo loco, vbi Lex fertur, sed in suam quisque Tribum discedat, in qua est suffragium laturus. populus enim confusus, vt semper alias, ita & in concione. Cum suffragia lata essent, etiam priuati homines, qui de Lege laborabant, ne quid fallaciæ committeretur, ipsi aut tabellas dinumerabant, aut dinumerantibus aliis præerant: idque dirimere proprio vocabulo dicebatur. Cistis autem suffragiorum custodiendis certi homines in Comitiis præerant, qui Nongenti sunt appellati. Suffragiis in vtramque sententiam dinumeratis, & diribitis, numeróque eorum punctis notato, eius Tribus aut Centuriæ voluntas cognoscebatur, eaque à præcone renunciabatur, & eadem in reliquis Tribubus aut Centuriis ratione seruata, ex maiore Tribuum Centuriarúmve numero vel antiquabatur, vel sciscebatur Lex: scita atque accepta, omnium ciuium iureiurando confirmabatur, post iusiurandum in æs incidebatur. Vbi vero vnius imperio Respublica Romana paruit, plane istud mutauit; nam quod Principi placuit, Legis habet vigorem, vtpote cum Lege Regia; quæ de imperio eius lata est, populus ei & in eum omne suum imperium & potestatem conferat. Quodcumque igitur Imperator per epistolam & subscriptionem statuit, vel cognoscens decreuit, vel de plano interlocutus est, vel edicto præcepit, Legem esse constat. Leg. I. D. de Constitutionibus Principum. In promulganda tamen Lege laudatissimi Principes Theodosius & Valentinianus hanc voluerunt obseruari formam, quæ præscribitur Leg. VIII. Cod. de Legibus & Constitutionibus Principum.
units.tr: Not far from this practice were the Romans in enacting their laws. Paulus Manutius, the most learned man of any nation, has described their custom, and I shall set it out. A magistrate about to propose a law would write it at home and consult with experts, so that he would not enact anything contrary to the interest or will of the people, and so that he would not carry clauses that clashed with one another, or anything that an older law, if it were passed, would declare void and ineffective. (Though any law passed later abrogated all earlier laws except the Sacred Laws.) He was also not to assign to himself, by his own law, any office, power or advantage, or to his colleagues, kinsmen or relatives. The two laws, the Licinian and the Aebutian, forbade this. It was also guarded against in drafting a law that several matters of different kinds should not be brought under one proposal; the Caecilian and Didian law forbade this. The following exception was added: if it was not lawful to propose something, it was not to be proposed; likewise, if anything was carried in virtue of this law against other laws, the proposer of that law was to be unpunished. Cicero, in Book III of the Letters to Atticus, reports that this was a customary formula, that is, that it was usually written into all laws. A legislator who had the good of the Republic at heart, before he published the law, referred it to the Senate, so that the law might carry more weight and greater force because it was passed on the Senate's opinion. A popular and seditious magistrate, however, often proposed a law while passing over the authority of the Senate, or even against it. The law was then published, that is, placed in public so that whoever wished might inspect it and, having inspected it, consider it. This allowed anyone, some time before the vote, to decide whether the law should be opposed or accepted when it came to be voted on, and not only to intervene before it was brought forward. The period of publication, as Dionysius and others make clear, whatever the subject of the law, was the trinundinum, that is, three market-days, so that even the country plebs could read and learn it three times. I take the word trinundinum to mean that three market-days intervened between the day on which the law was published and the day on which it was afterwards brought forward, so that the published law could be learned more often and by more people who came to the city for buying and selling. After the third market-day, the magistrate summoned the people to the place where he was to propose the law, whether the Forum or the Campus Martius. There the herald read out the law, the clerk prompting him, and then (perhaps also throughout the whole trinundinum, whenever the people assembled, men spoke for or against the law, but it is reasonable to suppose that this was done most vigorously on the day when the law was to be carried) first the man who had published the law urged the people to accept the proposal. After him others spoke, not only private citizens to whom a magistrate had granted a hearing before the assembly, but sometimes the magistrates themselves, each according to his own judgment, urged acceptance or opposition. Then, as Dionysius writes, with the priests present and expounding the divine auspices, a ballot box was brought in, into which the names were thrown, either of the tribes if the law was being passed in the Tribal Assembly, or of the centuries if in the Centuriate Assembly. Then by lot, the box being shaken so that no lot could be pushed up and come out first, but all were thrown in equally, the drawing was made. The tribe or century whose lot came out first, and likewise second, third and so on, kept the place and order in casting its vote that the lot had given it. While this was going on, any tribune of the plebs who wished to oppose the law had the right to do so. When the drawing of tribes or centuries was complete and nothing remained but for the people to give their verdict, the man proposing the law said: Si vobis videtur, discedite Quirites ("If it seems good to you, depart, Quirites"). This phrase does not mean, as it does in ordinary usage, that they should leave the place where the law is being proposed, but that each should go off to his own tribe in which he was to cast his vote, for the people, as always elsewhere, were in confusion even in an assembly. When the votes had been cast, even private citizens who had an interest in the law, to guard against any trickery, either counted the tablets themselves or stood over others who did the counting; this was called dirimere in a special term. Certain men presided over the assembly to guard the ballot boxes of the votes; they were called the Nongenti. When the votes for each side had been counted and sorted, and their number marked with dots, the will of that tribe or century was known, and it was announced by the herald. The same procedure being followed in the remaining tribes or centuries, the law was then either repealed or passed, according to the greater number of tribes or centuries. Once passed and accepted, it was confirmed by the oath of all the citizens, and after the oath it was engraved on bronze. But when the Roman Republic came to obey the rule of one man, this was entirely changed; for what has pleased the Prince has the force of law, inasmuch as by the Royal Law, which was passed concerning his authority, the people have conferred on him all their authority and power. Therefore whatever the Emperor has decided by letter and subscription, or has determined on examination, or has given judgment on in an informal hearing, or has ordered by edict, is plainly law. Digest, Law 1, on the Constitutions of the Emperors. In promulgating a law, however, the most praiseworthy Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian wished this form to be observed, which is prescribed in Law 8 of the Code, on Laws and Constitutions of the Emperors.

units.la: Impp. Theodosius & Valentinianus AA. ad Senatum.
units.tr: The Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian Augustus to the Senate.

units.la: Humanum esse probamus. si quid de cetero in publica priuatáque causa, emerserit necessarium, quod formam generalem, & antiquis Legibus non insertam expofcat, id ab omnibus antea tam proceribus noftri palatij, quam gloriofiffimo coetu veftro, Patres Conscripti, tractari, & fi vniuerfis tam iudicibus, quàm nobis placuerit, tunc legatur[?] dictari. & fic ea denuo collectis omnibus recenseri: & cùm omnes consenserint, tunc demum in sacro noftri numinis consistorio recitari: vt vniuerforum consensus noftrae serenitatis auctoritate firmetur. Scitote igitur, Patres Conscripti, non aliter in posterum Legem noftra clementia promulgandam, nisi suprădicta forma fuerit obseruata. Bene enim cognoscimus, quod cum vestro consilio fuerit ordinatum, id ad beatitudinem noftri imperij, & ad noftram gloriam redundare. Dat. XVI. Kal. Nouemb. Ætio III. & Symmacho Conss.
units.tr: We hold it to be fitting that, if anything in future arises in public or private affairs that is necessary and calls for a general form not contained in the ancient laws, it shall first be discussed by all: by the nobles of our palace and by your most glorious assembly, Conscript Fathers. If it pleases all the judges as well as ourselves, it shall then be read out and dictated, and then, once everything has been gathered together again, it shall be recited in the sacred consistory of our majesty, so that the consent of all may be confirmed by the authority of our serenity. Know therefore, Conscript Fathers, that our clemency will not in future promulgate a law except with the aforesaid form observed. For we well know that what has been ordained by your counsel redounds to the felicity of our empire and to our glory. Given on the 16th day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Aëtius III and Symmachus.

units.la: Periculosæ plenum opus erat aleæ Athenis Legem rogare, nam si ea damnosa iudicaretur, qui rogabat multabatur, itaque Lege licebat dicam ei scribere, qui Legem rogabat, quod damnosam ferret:
units.tr: At Athens it was a dangerous game to propose a law, for if it was judged harmful, the proposer was fined. Therefore, by a law, anyone could write an indictment against the man who proposed a law, on the ground that he had proposed a harmful one.

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΜΗ ΕΠΙΤΗΔΕΙΟΝ ΘΗ ΝΟΜΟΝ, ΤΑΣ ΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΚΑΤ' ΑΥΤΟΥ.
units.tr: If anyone proposes a law that is not expedient, the indictments shall lie against him [ἐὰν τις μὴ ἐπιτήδειον θῇ νόμον, τὰς γραφὰς εἶναι κατ' αὐτοῦ].

units.la: Meminit huius Legis alia apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτους[?] Lex, quam in sequentibus, si Deus dederit, describemus. Cùm autem accusabatur aliquis, quod Legem rogaret vel damnosam, vel alteri Legi aduersariam, non scisce-batur Lex, priusquam iudices sententiam tulissent, vtrum παρανόμος vel ἀσεβὴς εἴη[?] esset, necne. Pollux: Παρανομία δ' ἐστίν, ὅταν τις ἢ ψήφισμα, ἢ νόμον γράφῃ, ὡς ἀνεπιτήδειον. τοῦτο γὰρ Παρανομισθῆναι λέγεται. ἡ γὰρ ὡς μὴ τῷ Παρανομίσθαι ὁ γραφεὶς, πρὶν κριθῆναι, κύριος[?]. Acculari autem debebat ante exactum à Lege lata annum, alioqui non multabatur: nam elapso quidem anno accusari poterant qui Leges scripserant, sed erant ex hac Lege indemnes:
units.tr: Another passage of this law is mentioned by Demosthenes in the speech against Timocrates; we shall describe that law in what follows, God willing. When anyone was accused of proposing a law that was harmful or contrary to another law, the law was not sanctioned until the judges had given sentence on whether it was contrary to law (paranomos) or impious. Pollux: "Paranomia occurs when someone writes a decree or a law as unsuitable; for this is called being made paranomos…" Indeed the accusation had to be brought before a year had passed since the law was proposed; otherwise the accused was not fined. For once the year had elapsed, those who had written the laws could indeed be accused, but by this law they were safe from liability:

units.la: Τὸν γράφοντα νόμον μὴ ἐπ' αὐτὸν μὴ εἰ[?] ἐαυτοῦ ἀδικίου ἡμφελεία[?]· ὅμως δὲ ἐξεῖναι ποιή-σαι τὰς κατηγορίας.
units.tr: The one who proposes a law shall not be liable to indictment on his own account, unless…; nevertheless it is permitted to bring the accusations [τὸν γράφοντα νόμον μὴ ἐπ' αὐτὸν … ὅμως δὲ ἐξεῖναι ποιήσασθαι τὰς κατηγορίας].

units.la: Legitur hæc Lex in Leptinea Argumento: τὰ νόμων οὖν οὕτως ἔχοντες, ἐγράψατο μὲν παρὰ τὸν Βάθιππος Λεπτίνην, ὃς ἀπέφηνε περὶ εἰσελθὼν τῷ γραφῷ. καὶ διεσείσθη χρόνος, καὶ χρόνῳ Λεπτίνης ἀδίκους[?]. νόμως γὰρ ὧν, τὸν γράφοντα νόμον, ἡ ψήφισμα, μὴ ἐπ' αὐτὸν μὴ εἰ[?] ἐαυτοῦ ἀδίκου[?]. ὅμως δ' ἢ καὶ οὕτω τὴν νόμον ἐξὼ ποιῆσαι τὰς κατηγο-ρίας, καὶ οἱ γράφοντες ἐξω κινδυνῶν ὦσι. Itaque Demosthenis Oratio inscribitur κατὰ Λεπτίνου, non κατὰ Λεπτίνου, ἐπειδὴ ἀπελθόντος τῆς χρόνου, ἐν ᾧ ἀνδρὶ ἐμφανής καὶ ἡμφελεία, & in ea non addit, ἀ δὲ παράγγων τὸν ἀποδεδαίνοντα, ἃ δ' ὃ μὴ ὑπεύθυνοί[?] τῇ κατηγορίᾳ. male hic editur, τῇ κατηγορίᾳ. Nam etiam anno elapso è Lege licebat ποιῆσαι τὰς κατηγορίας. Relcribendum igitur est, τῇ ὑμφελείᾳ, aut quid simile: tunc quippe ἐξω κινδυνῶν ἦσαν. Nomen illius, qui accusabatur, quod Legem ferret siue rogaret παρανόμων, ἢ ἀνεπιτήδειον, deferebatur, meo iudicio apud Themosthetas: nam οἱ Θεσμοθέται τῶν νόμων τὸν ἐπιμελητὴν εἶχον. Præterea si Prytaneis, aut Proedri, qui, cùm Leges essent ferendæ, concionem non habuerant, aut ad populum de iis non retulerant τῷ τὰ γεγραμμένα, prout Legibus erat cautum, deferebantur apud Thesmothetas, dubitandum non est nomina eorum apud Thesmothetas delata fuisse, qui Leges non ferebant ξ̄ τὰ γεγραμμένα[?], prout Legibus cauetur. Sed quid dubitamus? Thesmothetae iis, qui huius criminis accusabantur, iudices dabant. Pollux: Θεσμοθέται εἰσάγειν τὰς τῶν παρανόμων γραφὰς[?], καὶ εἰ ὡς μὴ ἐπιτίμιον νόμον γράψαι[?]. Vlpianus in Leptineam: τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας τοὺς εἰσάγοντας τὰς γραφὰς[?] ὁ παρανόμων[?] ὅτι τῶν τῶν παρανόμων γραφῶ εἰσὶν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον[?]. Quanquam non omnes τῶν παρανόμων dicae apud Thesmothetas scribebantur. Exemplo sit dica Cresiphonti ab Æschine scripta: ὅτι Χαιρώνδου Ἀρχῆς, Ἐλαφοβολιάδος ἐκτὴ ἱσταμένου[?], Αἰχίνης Αξιμάπου Καθαρίδης ἀπέλυσε τὰς τὴν Ἀρχὴν παρανόμων γραφῶ τῷ Κτησιφῶντι τὸ Λεωδίνους Ἀναφλυστὸν[?]· ὅτι ἔγραψε παρανόμων ψηφίσματα. Nempe pro ratione παρανόμων, & Legis in quam commiserant, deferebantur modo ad Archontem, modò ad Thesmothetas; etiam ad reliquos τῶν εἰσὶ Ἀρχόντων. Iudicii huius totum ordinem moremque paucis, sed significantissimis expressit verbis Æschines ἐν τῷ ξ̄ Κτησιφῶντος· ἐὰν μὲν ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... καὶ τῆς δημοκρατίας. Ὃ δὲ δεύτερον ὕδωρ, τῷ τῶν γραφῶν φθείρει, καὶ τῶς εἰς αὖ ὃ παράγραμμα λέγειν. & tunc suffragia ferebant iudices, an violatae essent Leges: ἐπειδὴ δὲ τῇ αὐτῇ ψήφῳ μὴ λυθῇ ὁ παρανόμων, ἐὰν ὁ τεῖνον ὕδωρ ἐγχέῃ τῇ ὑμνῳ, καὶ τῷ μεγίστῃ τῆς ὀργῆς τῆς ὑμετέρας. Si accusatus violatarum Legum à iudicibus damnabatur, postea à missis iterum in suffragia multabatur. Quod si multatus non esset soluendo, notabatur infamia, & prohibebatur concionem habere. Plutarchus in Demosthene: Δημάδης ὁ, μηδὲν μέγας ὢν ὤφελε γενέσθαι ἐπὶ τὰς καταδίκης ἐκ-πῆσαι τῆς πόλεως δωκάμωσ[?], (ἠλώκει γὰρ ἐπὶ γραφὰς παρανόμων,) καὶ γεγονὼς ἄλμος ἀξέιρχετο τὸ λέγειν. Imo etiam ex Antiphane Comico constat, non tantum ære luisse, aut infamia, si non esset soluendo: sed omnino infamia notatum fuisse, & concione prohibitum, qui ter fuerat iudicio damnatus παρανόμων. Antiphanis verba sunt Sappho:
units.tr: This law is read in the Leptines argument: "Since matters stood thus, Bathippus indicted Leptines, who had proposed a law contrary to the laws; time was allowed to pass, and in time Leptines…; for according to the law, the one who writes a law or decree shall not be liable to indictment on his own account. Nevertheless, even so, it is permitted to bring the accusations, and those who write are not in danger." Hence the speech of Demosthenes is entitled "Against Leptines", not "Against Leptines" in the sense of…; and in it he adds that the one who proposes the law is not liable to the accusation. The text is wrongly printed here as "to the accusation." For even after the year had elapsed, it was permitted under the law to bring the accusations. It must therefore be read as "to the advantage" or something similar, for then they were out of danger. The name of the man who was accused, because he proposed or moved a law that was paranomos or unsuitable, was lodged, in my judgment, before the Thesmothetae, for the Thesmothetae had charge of the lawgivers' supervision. Moreover, if the Prytaneis or Proedri, who when laws were to be proposed had not held an assembly or reported on them to the people, were denounced before the Thesmothetae, there is no doubt that the names of those who did not bring the laws forward as the laws prescribe were lodged before the Thesmothetae. But why do we hesitate? The Thesmothetae gave judges to those accused of this crime. Pollux: "The Thesmothetae bring in the indictments for paranomia, and if one has proposed an unsuitable law…" Vlpian on Leptines: "the Thesmothetae who bring in the indictments of paranomia…, for the indictments of paranomia are before that court." Yet not all actions for paranomia were written before the Thesmothetae. An example is the action brought by Aeschines against Ctesiphon: "in the archonship of Chaeron, in the month of Elaphebolion, Aeschines, son of Atrometus, of the deme Cathari, brought the indictment for paranomia against Ctesiphon of Leontini of the deme Anaphlystus, because he proposed unlawful decrees." Thus, according to the nature of the paranomia and of the law which had been violated, the case was lodged sometimes before the Archon, sometimes before the Thesmothetae, and sometimes before the other archons. Aeschines, in the speech against Ctesiphon, briefly but very clearly set out the whole order and custom of this trial: if… and of democracy. Then, if it is found that the laws were violated, the judges cast their votes on whether the laws had been violated; and if the accused is convicted, the second vote is taken by the same judges on the penalty.

units.la: πῶς γὰρ ἡμοῖν' αὖ, ὦ πάππ[?]. . .
units.tr: For how, O father… [πῶς γὰρ ἡμοῖν' αὖ, ὦ πάππ…].

units.la: ῥῆταρ ἀφωνῆς, ὦ μὴ ἀλλῷ τεῖς παρανόμων.
units.tr: a speechless orator, you who are not of the paranomoi [ῥῆταρ ἀφωνῆς, ὦ μὴ ἀλλῷ τεῖς παρανόμων].

units.la: Si vero accusator, qui Legi interdicebat, causa caderet, multabatur mille drachmis. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτης ἡμεῖ ἀνὴρ ἐν χιλίας ὑπὸ ἡμῶν ἔλαβ' ὁ κίνδυνος[?]. Ad quem locum Vlpianus: φησὶ γὰρ ὅτι ἐὰν πίπτῃ, ὡς συνοφαντῆς πρὸς ἔγχωρ τὰς χιλίας.
units.tr: If, however, the accuser who opposed the law lost his case, he was fined a thousand drachmas. Demosthenes in the speech against Timocrates: "if he falls, the danger for the man is a thousand drachmas from us." On this passage Vlpian says: "for he says that if he fails, as a sycophant, he pays the thousand to the state."

units.la: Omnino autem non licebat Legem alteri, quae obtinebat; contrariam rogare, si quis enim rogasset, dica ei scribebatur. Quare Lex, quae obtinebat, abroganda erat, in eiusque locum altera roganda, quae si damnosa esset, periculum creabatur ei, qui illam ferebat: dica enim scripta, in ius rapiebatur: qua de re Lex ista regitur apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτης, αἰσχύνθη δὲ μοι λαβὼν τοῦτον ἄνθρωπον... [illegible, ~12 letters] ... νόμων, ὡς ἀναγνώσθη εἰσφέρειν, ἐὰν δὲ τῆς εἰσφορᾶς, γραφέσθαι τελευτᾷ. Νόμος: ΤΩΝ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΩΝ Legum nullam antiquare liΜΗ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΛΥΣΑΙ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ, ΕΑΝ cet, nisi apud Nomothetas: ΜΗ ΕΝ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ ΤΟΤΕ Δ' apud illos cuius AtheniensΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΛΥΕΙΝ ΕΤΕΡΟΝ ΤΙ ΤΙΘΕΝΤΙ ΑΝΘ' ΟΤΟΥ ΑΝ ΛΥΗι, ΔΙΑΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΙΑΝ ΔΕ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΡΟΕΔΡΟΥΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ, ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΥ, ΕΙ ΔΟΚΕΙ ΕΠΙΤΗΔΕΙΟΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, Η ΟΥ. ΕΠΕΙΤΑ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΤΙΘΕΜΕΝΟΥ. ΟΠΟΤΕΡΟΝ Δ' ΑΝ ΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΗΣΩΣΙΝ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΕΝΑΝΤΙΟΝ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΙΘΕΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΩΝ ΜΗΔΕΝΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΛΥΣΑΣ ΤΙΝΑ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΩΝ, ΕΤΕΡΟΝ ΑΝΤΙΤΙΘΗι ΜΗ ΕΠΙΤΗΔΕΙΟΝ ΤΩι ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΔΗΜΩι, Η ΕΝΑΝΤΙΟΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΔΗΜΩι sium cui libuerit, antiquare liceto, si modo alteram Legem rogarit, vicem illius, quam esse censet antiquandam. Proedri autem, quid de his Legibus fieri velint iubeant, in suffragia mittunto: & primum quidem de Lege, quae iam obtinet, an utilis[?] videatur Athieniensium populo, necne: deinde de Lege, quae rogatur.
