Quarum autem alteram iam sciuerint Nomothetæ, ea rata esto.
units.tr: In general, however, it was not permitted to propose a law contrary to one that was in force; for if anyone proposed one, an indictment was written against him. Therefore the law in force had to be repealed, and another proposed in its place; if that proposed law was harmful, danger was created for the one who proposed it, for an indictment was brought and he was dragged into court. Concerning this matter the law is given in Demosthenes' speech against Timocrates: "…and if anyone, having taken this man… of the laws, when it is read out, is to be brought forward, and if he has brought it forward, let him be indicted…" The law: "Of the laws now in force, let none be repealed, unless the Nomothetae have so decided; and when they have been repealed, the one who wishes of the Athenian people may repeal another law, if he proposes another law in place of the one he thinks should be repealed. The Proedri shall, concerning these laws, put to the vote what the people wish to be done: first concerning the law now in force, whether it seems expedient to the Athenian people or not; then concerning the law proposed. Whichever of the two the Nomothetae decide is to be valid. Let no one propose a law contrary to the laws now in force. If anyone repeals any of the laws now in force and proposes another that the Athenian people does not consider expedient, or contrary to the laws of the Athenians, let the indictments lie against him according to the law that is in force." Hence the Latin may be rendered: "…let anyone who wishes repeal, provided he proposes another law in place of the one he judges should be repealed."

units.la: Legem vero contrariam alicui Legum, quae iam obtinent, rogare ne liceto. Si quis vero Legem iam latam antiquans, al- ΤΩΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΩΝ, ΤΩι ΤΑΣ ΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΚΑΤ' ΑΥΤΟΥ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ, ΟΣ ΚΕΙΤΑΙ· ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΜΗ ΕΠΙΤΗΔΕΙΟΝ ΘΗι ΝΟΜΟΝ. teram eius[?] vicem rogarit, quae utilis non sit Atheniensium populo, aut contraria sit alicui earum, quae iam obtinent, ei dicam scribito, secundum Legem, quae lata est aduersus eum qui damnosam Legem rogauerit.
units.tr: Moreover, it shall not be permitted to propose a law contrary to any of the laws now in force. If anyone, while abrogating a law already passed, proposes in its place another that is not useful to the Athenian people, or that is contrary to any of those laws now in force, he shall be prosecuted by a written charge in accordance with the law passed against the one who proposes a harmful law. [The Greek inscription, in substance: concerning the laws now in force, the indictment against him shall be made according to the law now in force; if anyone proposes a law that is not expedient...]

units.la: Cautur igitur hac Lege, quae Solonem habet auctorem, ne quis Legem rogat ceteris Legibus, quae obtinent, contrariam, aut Legem ne abroget, altera lata damnosa: qui secus faxit, ei dica scribatur: Eius alibi meminit Demosthenes, nempe in Leptinea: καὶ ταῦτα ἐπίεγυ κελεύοντος λέγειν[?], ἢ κατ' αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐνοχὴν εἰς τὴν γραφὴν[?], ἐὰν εἰσάγῃ ἢ τις παρέγειν κελεύῃ νόμος. Vlpianus ad eandem: εἶπα αἰαγινώσκει ἐπὶ ἐπέγειν νόμων τὸν κελεύοντα ταὐθὶ[?] ἐπὶ γραφὴν τὸν αὐτὸν εἰσφέρειν τῆς ὑπαρχούσης νόμως[?]. Legis huius haec ratio apud Demosthenem adfertur, ut rebus de singulis Leges sint singulae, neque viri rerum imperiti duarum obtentu Legum contrariarum ab Oratoribus decipiantur. ὁ Σόλων τοὺς νόμους κελῶς κελεύει λέγειν, λέγοντας τὰς ἐπιστείας[?]· ἵν' εἰς ἢ κατὰ τὴν ἑκάστου νόμος[?], καὶ μὴ τοὺς ἰδιώτας αὐτὸ τῶν ... ἀπορίας εἰδότων τοὺς νόμους ἔλαττον ἔχειν[?]· ἀλλὰ πάντων ἢ ταῦτ' ἀναγνῶναι[?], ἐ μαθητ ἁπλᾶ τῇ γραφῇ τὴν δίκην. Praecipit igitur haec Lex primum abrogare Legem, sive contraria ea sit, sive non, deinde alteram in eius locum rogare: αἱρεῖν ... τὸν ... νόμον[?], ἵνα μὴ ἀλλήλοις ἐναντίοι νόμοι διέξωσιν[?]. Lex : Τ ΩΝ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΩΝ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΛΥΣΑΙ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΝ ΝΟΜΟΘΕΤΑΙΣ, ΤΟΤΕ Δ' ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΩι Τ ΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΛΥΕΙΝ ΕΤΕΡΟΝ ΤΙΘΕΝΤΙ, (ita rescribendum est, supple autem NOMON( ΑΝΘ' ΟΤΟΥ ΑΝ ΛΥΗι. Idem Demosthenes in [Leptinea: ὁ παλαιὸς νόμος αὕτω κελεύει νομοθετεῖν. γεγράφθαι μὲν, ἂν τις πιὰ τῶν ὑπ[?]ἐόντων νόμων μὴ κελᾶς ἐχὴν ἡγήσασθαι. Πεισθφέρειν δὲ αὐτὸν ἄλλων, οὐ αὖ ξῆν λύων ἐκξ-[?]ον. Vlpianus ad hanc Orationem: ὁ Σόλων [?]ἐσόπαξε τὸν λύοντα τινα τῶν νομέων [?]νόμων ὠδέναι ἐπεγείρειν ὅπου μὲν ὧν κυρίως, αἰτιασφέρειν δὲ ὅπου δὲ οὐ, λύειν μόνον. Quorum verborum hic est sensus: Legum earum, quae scitae sunt à Nomothetis, abroganda si qua est, is qui abrogationem eius suader, alteram Legem in abrogatae locum rogare debet: quod si Lex nondum scita est à Nomothetis, nihil opus est alteram rogare in eius locum. Prius vero non licebat nouam ferre Legem, quam antiqua fuerit abrogata. Vlpianus ad eandem: ἐπεγειν καλώντος νόμου, μὴ ἐσόπεγειν τιθέναι νόμον, πρὶν τὸν εἰσφέρειν λύειν. Abrogata veteri noua, etiamsi forte nollet, qui tulerat. Demosthenes in Leptinea: ἐν δὲ ὅτι μὲν τῇ ὑματέρᾳ ὑφῳ ἔστιν τὸ νόμον λυθέντος τὸν πεισανεδέσθαι κύριον εἴη, Ἀφας δ' ἀλαῖος κελεύει νόμος. Vlpianus: πάντως γὰρ λυθέντος, ὁ εἰσφερόμενος ἐλθὼν χώριος.
units.tr: This law, which has Solon as its author, therefore provides that no one may propose a law contrary to the other laws in force, or propose to repeal a law without at the same time proposing another in its place; whoever acts otherwise shall be prosecuted by a written charge. Demosthenes mentions this law elsewhere, namely in the Leptinea: "and this is the case when he orders that a law be proposed, or lays himself open to a charge on this very ground, if anyone introduces or proposes a law" [καὶ ταῦτα ἐπίεγυ κελεύοντος λέγειν, ἢ κατ' αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐνοχὴν εἰς τὴν γραφὴν, ἐὰν εἰσάγῃ ἢ τις παρέγειν κελεύῃ νόμος]. Ulpian, on the same speech: "the law requires that he who proposes a law be subject to a charge if he brings forward a law against an existing law" [εἶπα αἰαγινώσκει ἐπὶ ἐπέγειν νόμων τὸν κελεύοντα ταὐθὶ ἐπὶ γραφὴν τὸν αὐτὸν εἰσφέρειν τῆς ὑπαρχούσης νόμως]. The reason for this law, as Demosthenes gives it, is that each matter should have its own law, so that unskilled men are not deceived by the Orators through the support of two contrary laws. Solon ordered that laws be proposed in such a way that each law concerns one matter [ὁ Σόλων τοὺς νόμους κελῶς κελεύει λέγειν, λέγοντας τὰς ἐπιστείας]; and that private citizens, who do not know the difficulties of the laws, should not be at a disadvantage, but that all should read these laws and the charge be simply written. This law therefore prescribes that a law be repealed first, whether or not it is contrary to another, and only then that another be proposed in its place [αἱρεῖν τὸν νόμον], so that contrary laws do not stand side by side. The law reads: "Of the laws now in force, let no one be permitted to repeal any, unless the Nomothetae have ... but then it shall be permitted to the one who wishes, of the Athenians, to repeal one, proposing another in its place" (the text is to be read thus, and the words "from which law" supplied). Demosthenes, in the same Leptinea: "The ancient law orders that laws be enacted thus: it is written that if anyone thinks any of the existing laws should not be in force..." Ulpian on this speech: "Solon forbade one who repeals any of the laws to propose a law, unless he proposes one in its place; where it is proposed that a law be repealed, he must also propose another, but where it is not, he may only repeal." The sense of these words is this: if any of the laws enacted by the Nomothetae is to be repealed, the one urging its repeal must propose another law in its place; but if the law has not yet been enacted by the Nomothetae, there is no need to propose another in its place. Moreover, it was not permitted to bring in a new law before the old one had been repealed. Ulpian on the same: "when a law is proposed, one may not propose a law before repealing the one he brings in" [ἐπεγειν καλώντος νόμου, μὴ ἐσόπεγειν τιθέναι νόμον, πρὶν τὸν εἰσφέρειν λύειν]. The old law being repealed, the new one was enacted even if he who had proposed it were unwilling. Demosthenes in the Leptinea: "in the Athenian democracy, once the law is repealed, the one who proposed the replacement shall be its master" [ἐν δὲ ὅτι μὲν τῇ ὑματέρᾳ ὑφῳ ἔστιν τὸ νόμον λυθέντος τὸν πεισανεδέσθαι κύριον εἴη]. Ulpian: "for once the law is repealed, the one who has proposed it is the one who is entitled" [πάντως γὰρ λυθέντος, ὁ εἰσφερόμενος ἐλθὼν χώριος].

units.la: Quinetiam si quis, vt veterem Legem abrogaret, se nouam simularet laturum, neque ferret, multabatur, ex hac Lege, . .
units.tr: Moreover, if anyone, in order to repeal an old law, pretended that he would propose a new one, and then did not propose it, he was fined under this law.

units.la: [?]Τὸν λέγοντα τινα νόμον, καὶ μὴ ἀντισφέ-ρειν, καλάζεσθαι.
units.tr: [Whoever proposes some law and does not bring it forward for a vote shall be punished.]

units.la: Qui Legem promulgat, nec rogat, in eum animadvertitor.
units.tr: Whoever promulgates a law but does not propose it shall be punished.

units.la: Legitur ista Lex apud Vlpianum loco proxime laudato: ὁ δὲ Φησὶ, καὶ μὴ θέλωμεν, οὐ δυνησόμεθα. Εἰσπλέοι γὰρ ἴδια ἀφὰ τῆς Γραμματικῆς. ἀλλὰ ἔτι νόμως ἑῷ, τλέγοντα τινα νόμον, καὶ μὴ ἀντισφέρειν, καλάζεσθαι.
units.tr: This law is read in Ulpian in the passage quoted just above: "He says, even if we are unwilling, we shall not be able to. For it is a special rule of the grammar..." But the law is still in force: whoever proposes a law and does not bring it forward shall be punished.

units.la: Quanquam autem ista obseruarentur, fieri tamen non poterat, quin obreperent Leges aliæ aliis contrariæ, aut quæ ratæ non erant inter ratas, aut de vna re plures: cui malo vt subueniret Legislator, Legem hanc tu-lit:
units.tr: Although these provisions were observed, it could still not be prevented that laws contrary to one another should creep in, or laws not ratified among those ratified, or several laws on one and the same matter. To remedy this evil the lawgiver brought in this law:

units.la: Τοὺς Νομοθέτας καὶ ἕκαστον ἐναυτὸν ὁρῶν ὃ τὰ δημόσια τῶν νόμους, ἀκριβῶς ἐξεπισκέψασθαι καὶ σκεψαμένους, εἴ τις ἀπαγ-γεγραμμένος νόμος ἕτερος νόμῳ, ἐὰν ἀκύ-ρως ὃ τοῖς χωρίοις. Ἐὰν εἴπου εἰσὶ νόμοι πλείους ἑνὸς ἀναγεγραμμένοι ἐκάστης τῆς ἐξέσεως. καὶ ἢν ἢ ἰσοτὸν δείξωσιν, ἀναγεγράφως ὃ ὀρισμοῖς ἐκλθέναι τῶν Ἐπωνύμων. Πρυτάνεις συγκαλεῖν ἐκκλησίαν, ὑπαγε-ὑμοῖς Νομοθέτας. τὸν δὲ Ἐπιστάτην τῶν Πρόεδρων ἀξέλαγκετος ἀποδεῖναι τὰ ψήφισμα, καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἀιρεῖν τῶν νόμων, τοὺς δὲ καταλείπειν.
units.tr: "The Nomothetae and each of the Thesmothetae, seeing the public laws, shall examine them carefully, and having examined them, if any written law is contrary to another law, or is invalid among the laws... If there are several laws written on each single matter, and they show them to be equal, they shall write them up on the statues of the Eponymous archons. The Prytaneis shall convene an assembly and bring in the Nomothetae. The Epistates of the Proedri shall put the decree to the vote, and the people shall choose some of the laws to abolish and leave others." [Greek text as printed.]

units.la: Thesmothetæ quotannis in publico tabulario conuenientes in Leges inquirunto, & cum cura vidento, vtrum Lex vlla alteri contraria obtineat, aut quæ rata non sit: aut plures sint scriptæ vna eademque de re: Quod si quam huiusmodi deprehenderint, describant in tabella ad Eponymorum statuas proponunto. Prytaneis concionem habento, & Nomothetas designanto. Proedrorum Epistates populum in suffragia mittito de Legibus, quæ vel abrogandæ, vel ratæ habenda sint.
units.tr: The Thesmothetae, meeting each year in the public archive, shall inquire into the laws and with care see whether any law is in force that is contrary to another, or that has not been ratified, or whether several have been written on one and the same matter. If they find any such, they shall copy it on a tablet and set it up by the statues of the Eponymous archons. The Prytaneis shall hold an assembly and designate the Nomothetae. The Epistates of the Proedri shall put to the vote of the people the laws that are to be repealed or to be held as ratified.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Æschines ὁ τῶν ἐξ Κτησιφῶντος. εἰ γὰρ τῶτι ἐστὶν ἀλη-θὴς, καὶ ἐκαστον ἑαυτὸν ἐἶς τὸν πολίτην, ἀλλ' ἀκούεις νόμως ὃ τοῖς χωρίοις ἀναγεγραμμένας ἐφεῖναι, καὶ ἡνὲ μιᾶς κωπελαῖνοι ἐπανεσείονται ἀλλὰ, ἡ ἐλ ἑαυτῶν εἰπεῖ τῆς ἐτ' ἐτὴ τῷ πολίτη, εἰ ἢ ἑαυτὸν ἐκπαν παν πεισθη, οἱ νόμοι ποιεῖν τὸ μὴ ποιῆς ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔχει ταῦτα οὔτως· μὴ ὑμῖς ποτ' εἰς τοσαύτην ἀπαξίαν τῶν νόμων κεφαλ-ῆται, οὔτε ἡμελαγ' ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων τῶν Νομοθετῶν τὰ τῷ δημοκρατίαν καταστάσεω, ἀλλὰ ἀλφρόνων ἐξ ἐπαγγελ-οῖς Θεσμοθέτας καὶ ἐκαστον ἐναυτὸν ἀρθρωῶ ἐν τὰ δημοσίᾳ τοὺς νόμους, &c. Lex hæc præcipit, vt quotannis Thesmothetæ in Leges inquirant, emendationis illarum ergo: τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας καὶ ἐκάστων εἰσαγωγὰς [?] τὸν δῆμον ἐν τῷ δημοσίῳ τοὺς νόμους, ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάσαι [?]. Harpocration : ὅτι δὲ τοὺς νόμους ὅτι Thesmothetae, διὰ ταῦτα καὶ ἕκαστον ἐκρινεν, εἴρηκε Ἀριστίης τὸ ἐν τῷ Κτησιφῶντος, καὶ Θεόφραστος ἐν πείτῳ Νόμων. Sed corruptus est numerus Libri Theophrastei. Scripserat enim Theophrastus Libros νόμων, καὶ ψηφισμάτων, καὶ. Quare tertius non erat Liber, in quo agebatur de hac Legum emendatione, quae ad Thesmothetas, aut Nomothetas spectabat: putem igitur de his actum fuisse a Theophrasto Libro tertiodecimo, quia Leges hae maximè ad Nomothetas referuntur, itaque coniectae sunt in Librum cui numerus erat litera N. sed facilis lapsus fuit literae ν in literam γ. Conueniebant ἐν τῷ δημοσίῳ. Eruditissimus Vvolsius vertit publice : Ego existimo intelligi publicum tabularium, τὸν οἶκον ἐν ᾧ οἱ δημόσιοι χρῆται ἔκειντο, ut loquitur Vlpianus ad haec Demosthenis verba in ea oratione, quae est τῷ ψηφῖσαι, ὅτι καὶ γεγράμματ' ἔχων ἐν τῷ δημοσίῳ κείμενα. In illa autem domo conueniebant Thesmothetae correcturi Leges: nam ibi publice asseruabantur: ut viderent ne qua Lex alteri contraria Legi extaret, ne qua irrita inter ratas, neve plures de vna & eadem re. Quod si quas huiusmodi deprehendissent, descriptas in tabella proponebant publice ad Archontum Eponymorum statuas: Prytaneis vero concionem habebant, ut Nomothetas designarent: τοὺς δὲ Πρυτάνεις ἐκκλησίαν ποιεῖν, ὑπάρχειν [?] Νομοθέτας. Proedrorum autem Epistates populum in suffragia mittebat, ut sciscerent, quae Leges abrogandae forent, quae ratae habendae: τὸν δὲ Ἐπιστάτην τὴν Γερουσίαν ἀναγράφεσθαι ἐν τῷ δήμῳ, καὶ τοὺς μὲν αἱρεῖσθαι τὴν νόμων, τοὺς δὲ καταλείπειν. Scilicet, quemadmodum antea in pari argumento diximus, populus sciscebat quas Leges vellet è Nomothetarum, quibus tamen rem omnem integram committebat, sententia vel antiquari, vel ratas haberi. Hoc enim erat horum Nomothetarum munus. Pollux: νομοθέται δ' ἦσαν χίλιοι, οἳς ἐξὸν λέσσαι παλαιῶν νόμων, ἀλλ' οὐ ξένας νέον· τοὺς δὲ νέους ἐδικίμαζεν ἡ βουλὴ, καὶ ὁ δῆμος, καὶ τὰ δικαστήρια. Itaque Æschines in sequentibus latis indicat penes hos Nomothetas ius fuisse antiquandi veteres Leges alteris, quas ratas esse volebant, contrarias : καὶ ἥσαν δύο χίλιοι νόμοι περὶ τὴν χειρογράφων, ἐξ αἰτίας (οἶμαι) τὴν μὲν Θεσμοθετῶν ἀξιωθέντων, τὴν δὲ Γραμμάτων ἀποδιδόντων τοῖς Νομοθέταις, αὐτοῦ αὐ ὁ ἐτέρος τὴν νόμων. Sed erant nehi Nomothetae alij ab iis, qui Legum ferendarum causla fuerant eiudicum numero forte capti? Distinctum certè erat eorum munus, vt iam diximus, & plane diuersum. Nam hi abrogabant τοὺς χιλίους καὶ χιλίους παλαιοὺς νόμους ἀλλήλοις ἑαυτοῖς, ἵ' ἀκούσῃ ἐν κυκλίοις, ἵ' πλείας ἐνὸς τοῦ ἐκάστης ἀρξέως. Illi vero, ἐκληρώσαντο δικιμάζειν καὶ χωρὶς τοὺς νόμους. etsi idem esset numerus, nempe mille & vnus, quanquam Pollux vnum illum supra mille non recenseat: Νομοθέται δ' ἦσαν χίλιοι, οἳς ἐξὸν λέσσαι νόμων παλαιῶν, ἀλλ' οὐ ξένας νέον. De vtrisque Vlpianus ad III. Olynthiacam : Νομοθέτης ἐλέγετο παρ' Ἀθηναίοις, καὶ ὁ νόμον χειρὸν ἐσφέρων, καὶ πάλιν ὁ χρίνων τοῖς νόμοις, μὴ πῶς ἑαυτοὶ ἕνες ἀλλήλοις ἐλαβον ὄντες. τοῦτο δὲ ὅ ἔργον ἐν τῷ Θεσμοθετῶν. Quod dicit Vlpianus, χρίνειν τοὺς νόμους, μὴ πῶς ἑαυτοὶ ἀλλήλοις ἐλαβον ὄντες, fuisse Thesmothetis cum Nomothetis commune, verum est, imo Thesmothetæ huic rei caput & auctores præcipui erant, vt qui tenerentur τῶν ἐκα-σαν ἐκιωτῶν ἀχριβῶς ἐξεπέζειν, εἰ τῆς ἀμαρτήματι νόμος ἐτῆρε νόμῳ. [?] Præterea Nomothetæ οἱ λύοντες παλαιὸν νόμον diuerso, meo quidem iudicio, eligebantur tempore, atque alio ab eo, quo Nomothetæ, οἱ νόμοι γραφόντες [?] forte capiebantur: Nam hi stata temperdie, hoc est, tertia primæ Prytaneias concione, siue die primo Metagitnionis, fortito capiebantur: Illi verò incerto neque definito tempore, postquam scilicet Thesmothetæ deprehendissent τὸ παρὰ νόμους ἐξω τῆς παρ' ἡμῶν νόμους [?] ... τῆς παραγγελίας. Quas Leges intra tam paucos Magistratus sui dies obseruasse non poterant, vt qui etiam alia, quæ agerent, haberent. Quanquam etiam fieri poterat, neque id quicquam, puto, vetabat, vt iidem, qui iam ante, [illegible, ~12 letters] affecto illo tempore, intra quod oportebat illos [illegible, ~20 letters], etiam abrogationi παλαιῶν νόμων ἀλλήλοις ἐπαγγελίαν præficerentur.
units.tr: Aeschines, in his speech against Ctesiphon, mentions this law: "For if this is true, and each of you examines the public laws, as the law written on the pillars requires, and if the laws are to be repealed or ratified by one assembly, but ... [Greek]... the laws will do what you do not do..." He goes on: "Let us never come to such contempt for the laws, nor let us put in charge of the democracy those who have been neglected, but let the Thesmothetae and each of you examine the public laws..." This law prescribes that each year the Thesmothetae inquire into the laws for the sake of their correction, and that the people, through the assembly, carefully examine the public laws [τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας καὶ ἐκάστων εἰσαγωγὰς τὸν δῆμον ἐν τῷ δημοσίῳ τοὺς νόμους, ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάσαι]. Harpocration: "that the Thesmothetae examined the laws each year, Aristides in his speech against Ctesiphon has said, and Theophrastus in his book on Laws." But the number of the Theophrastean book is corrupt. For Theophrastus wrote books on laws and decrees and... Hence the third book cannot have been the one in which this revision of the laws, which concerned the Thesmothetae or Nomothetae, was treated; I therefore suppose that Theophrastus dealt with these matters in the thirteenth book, since these laws refer chiefly to the Nomothetae, and so they have been assigned to the book whose number was the letter N; an easy slip from the letter ν to γ. "They met in the public" [ἐν τῷ δημοσίῳ]. The most learned Wolfius translates "publicly", but I think "the public archive" is meant, the house in which the public documents were kept, as Ulpian says in commenting on these words of Demosthenes in the speech which is entitled "On the Crown", that they also have documents placed in the public archive. In that house the Thesmothetae used to meet to correct the laws, for there they were kept publicly, so that they could see that no law stood contrary to another law, that no invalid law stood among the ratified ones, and that there were not several on one and the same matter. If they found any of this kind, they had them copied on a tablet and publicly set up by the statues of the Eponymous archons. The Prytaneis held an assembly so that they might designate the Nomothetae [τοὺς δὲ Πρυτάνεις ἐκκλησίαν ποιεῖν, ὑπάρχειν Νομοθέτας]. The Epistates of the Proedri sent the people to the vote, so that they might decide which laws were to be repealed and which held as ratified [τὸν δὲ Ἐπιστάτην τὴν Γερουσίαν ἀναγράφεσθαι ἐν τῷ δήμῳ, καὶ τοὺς μὲν αἱρεῖσθαι τὴν νόμων, τοὺς δὲ καταλείπειν]. Clearly, as we said earlier on a similar matter, the people voted on which laws they wished from the Nomothetae, yet they committed the whole matter, undivided, to them to decide whether to repeal or to ratify. For this was the office of these Nomothetae. Pollux: "There were a thousand Nomothetae, who were permitted to repeal old laws, but not to propose new ones; the Council, the people and the law courts examined the new ones." Accordingly Aeschines, in the subsequent speech, indicates that the power of repealing old laws contrary to others that they wished to be ratified lay with these Nomothetae: "and there were two thousand laws concerning the written ... from the cause (I think) that the Thesmothetae were asked, and the others gave the writings to the Nomothetae, and the other [examined] the laws." But were these Nomothetae different from those who were chosen by lot from the number of judges for the purpose of proposing laws? Their office was certainly distinct, as we have said, and quite different. For these repealed the thousand old laws in turn, so that they might be heard in the circle, if more than one on each matter... But the others were chosen by lot to examine the laws separately. Although the number was the same, namely one thousand and one, though Pollux does not count that one above the thousand: "There were a thousand Nomothetae, who were permitted to repeal old laws but not to propose new ones." Of both kinds Ulpian, on the Third Olynthiac: "among the Athenians a Nomothetes was called both one who brought in a new law, and again one who judges the laws, so that they should not be contrary to one another." That the judging of laws, so that they should not be contrary to one another, was common to the Thesmothetae and the Nomothetae, as Ulpian says, is true; indeed the Thesmothetae were the chief authors and leaders of this business, since they were bound to examine carefully the laws, whether any law stood against a law [εἰ τῆς ἀμαρτήματι νόμος ἐτῆρε νόμῳ]. Moreover, the Nomothetae who repealed an old law were, in my judgement, chosen at a different time from that at which the Nomothetae who proposed laws were drawn by lot: for these were drawn on a fixed day, that is, the third day of the first Prytaneia assembly, or the first day of Metageitnion; but the others were chosen at an uncertain and undefined time, after the Thesmothetae had detected what was contrary to the laws... of the proclamation. The Thesmothetae, having so many other matters to attend to, could not have observed these laws within their short term of office. Although it could also have happened, and I think nothing forbade it, that the same men who had already before... were placed in charge of the repeal of old laws in turn, at that time, within which it was necessary for them...

units.la: Optimè obseruatum est Vlpiano Iurisconsulto Libro III. ad Sabinum, iura non in singulas personas, sed generaliter constituit. Lege VIII. D. de Legibus: Ἐστὶς γὰρ νόμος ἐφ' ἑκάς, ἀλλὰ κρίνος · itaque hac de re Solonis Lege cautum,
units.tr: Ulpian the jurist rightly observed, in Book 3 on Sabinus, that laws are laid down not for individual persons but in general terms. In Digest 1.3.8, De legibus, he says: "For law is not for each one, but common" [Ἐστὶς γὰρ νόμος ἐφ' ἑκάς, ἀλλὰ κρίνος]. Accordingly, Solon's law provides on this matter:

units.la: ΜΗΔΕ ΕΠ' ΑΝΔΡΙ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΘΕΙΝΑΙ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΠΙ ΠΑΣΙΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΙΣ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΞΑΚΙΣΧΙΛΙΟΙΣ ΔΟΞΗ ΚΡΥΒΔΗΝ ΤΗΦΙ-ΖΟΜΕΝΟΙΣ.
units.tr: "Let no law be passed against an individual unless it is the same for all Athenians, unless it be approved by six thousand voting in secret." [ΜΗΔΕ ΕΠ' ΑΝΔΡΙ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΘΕΙΝΑΙ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΠΙ ΠΑΣΙΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΙΣ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΞΑΚΙΣΧΙΛΙΟΙΣ ΔΟΞΗ ΚΡΥΒΔΗΝ ΤΗΦΙΖΟΜΕΝΟΙΣ.]

units.la: Legem hanc descripsimus ex Andocide ἐκ τοῦ λόγου [?] Meminit quoque Demosthenes ἐκ τοῦ ἐχ' Ἀεσχεσίνου. λέγει δὲ τὴν ἐφεξῆς NOMOΣ, μηδὲ νόμον ἐπ' ἀμφοτέρα ἐξέναι ἢ ἐπιτ[?], ἐαν μὴ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐφ' ἅπασιν Αθηναίοις. Sed Orator δουλεύειν τῇ Ἀσσυρίᾳ [?] vltimum prætermisit membrum, ἐαν μὴ ἐξακισχιλίοις ἐδ̣ξη χρύβδηλων ἐπιζημιώσει, quod etiam misere corruptum est apud eundem in Timocratea: λέγε ἐπεσον νόμον. NOMOΣ, μηδὲ νόμον ἐξέναι ἐαν ἀλλά Ἀθηναίοις, ἐαν μὴ ἐ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσιν Αθηναίοις, ἀφ' ἑπισθ̣ὸν ἐξακισχιλίων, οἷς ἂν δῶξη, χρύβδηλων ἐπιζημιώσει, ὅτι ἐὰν νόμον, ἀλλ' ἐπ' τὸν αὐτὸν ἐξέναι ἐξ' τὴν πολιτείαν πᾶντων, καὶ ἀλλ' ἐν' ἀκ' ἐκ δήμους μάντες ἐπὶ αἰῶνι καὶ ἐλλ' ἐπ' ἐκ ἐξ' πολλὰ μὴ ἐπὶ σύνδ' ἐ[?]. Sed proculdubio rescribendum est, ἐαν μὴ ἐφιπιτέων [?] Meminit rursum in eadem huius Legis: ἐὰν ἀλλὰ ἐξ' ἡ ἐπιδογί ἀρχὴν [?] Item in II. ἐξ' Ἐπιφανὴ [?] ἁμαρτίαν ὁ ἐπὶ ἐδ[?] νόμος, μηδὲ νόμον ἐαν' αὐτὸν ἐξέναι ἢ ἐαν μὴ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐφ' ἅπασιν Αθηναίοις. Solonis hanc esse Legem tellatur Æneas Gazæusin Theophrasto: ὁ ἀλλ' τὸν Σόλωνος ὅτι ἐὰν νόμον ἐαν' ἀμέρη ἀδίκεια, ἀλλ' ἐ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐπ' ἅπασι κ... ἐ Priuilegia tamen irrogabantur, si id scisceret populus, vnde in Lege hac habes. EAN MH EΞAKIΣXIΛΙΟΙΣ ΔΟΞΗ ΚΡΥΒΔΗΝ ΤΗΦΙΖΟΜΕΝΟΙΣ. Nisi id videatur sex mille ciuibus suffragia clam ferentibus: isque numerus omnino exigebatur, vnde Demosthenes, μὴ ἐλαττον ἐξακισχιλίων, ὡς ἂν δοξῇ κρύβδην ψηφιζομένοις. Quod vt commodè intelligatur, sciendum est Atheniensium ciuium fuisse viginti millia. Hesychius: ἀνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι δημόσιοι ὁμόφωνες. Demosthenes Oratione contra Aristogitonem: σχεδὸν γὰρ, εἰσὶν ὁμοῦ δημόσιοι πλὴν Ἀθηναῖοι. Ipsque numerusiam ab ipso Cecrope, vt auctor est Philochorus apud Græcum Pindari Interpretem ad Olympion. Od. IX. Φιλόχορος φησὶ Κέκροπα βυλόμενον τὴν τῶν Ἀθηναίων δύναμιν καὶ ὁ πλῆθος ὑπογράψαι, κελεῦσαι αὐτοῖς λίθους ἰσοφεῖν, καὶ βοῆλ[?] εἰς ὃ μέσον. ἐξ ἂν ὑπογραφὰς, δημοσίους αὐτοῖς ὧν[?]. Idemque numerus Olympiadis centesimæ decimæ anno primo, cum Demetrius Phalereus Reipubl. præesset. Anonymus in Descriptione Olympiadum ad hunc annum. Ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἀθηναίων ἡγεμόνος τοῦ Δημητρίου τῆς Φαληρέως, ἀριθμὸν Ἀθηναίων μὲν δημόσιοι, εἰκοσὶ ὃ μυριάδες παραχοήσαι. Ctesicles Libro Chronicorum III. apud Athenæum Libro VI. mille his addit: Κτησικλῆς δὲ ἐν τετάρτῃ Χρονικῶν, τὴν δὲ ἐκ πάσης φησὶν Ολυμπιάδι Ἀθηναῖοι ἐξεπεμψαν ἡμέδαν τοῦ Δημητρίου τῆς Φαληρέως τῶν καταλιπόντων τὸ Ἀθηναῖον. καὶ διρισθέντων Ἀθηναῖοι μὲν δημοσίους εἰς χιλίους, μυρίους ὃ μυριάδας παραχοήσαι. In ferendis autem suffragiis maior pars obtinebat: itaque necesse erat Athenis, vt plures decem millia, siquidem duas in partes tantum scinderetur populus, in eandem irent sententiam: At verò Solon vult, vbi de irrogando priuilegio agitur, vt in his eiusdem sententiæ, qui plures sunt decem mille, sint sex mille minimum, qui suffragium clam ferant, ne quis gratiæ locus sit: nam ἡ[?] χάρις τοῖς ὀν ἐχρῆζετο ἀδηλος γεγονότα. ἡ γὰρ ψῆφος ἀφανὴς φέρεται, vt est apud Æschinem ὡς τῷ Κτησιφῶντι.
units.tr: I have taken this law from Andocides, in his speech [ἐκ τοῦ λόγου]. Demosthenes also mentions it, in his speech against Aeschines, where he quotes the following clause: "Nor shall any law be passed against an individual, unless it is the same for all Athenians." The orator, however, omitted the last clause, "unless it be approved by six thousand voting in secret, with a penalty of ...", which is also badly corrupted in the same orator's speech against Timocrates, where it reads: "Read the law: Nor shall any law be passed against an individual unless it is the same for all Athenians, unless six thousand, whatever they decide, vote in secret..." It is clear that the reading must be emended; and in another passage of the same law he speaks of ... In Book II of the same work, the law reads: nor any law against an individual, unless it is the same for all Athenians. Aeneas of Gaza, in his work on Theophrastus, says that this is the law of Solon: that if any injustice is done to an individual, the law must not be passed against him unless it applies to all. Privileges, however, were still imposed if the people approved, and so this law reads: "Unless it seem good to six thousand voting in secret." Demosthenes has the phrase not fewer than six thousand, as it seems good to those voting in secret. To understand this properly, one must know that the citizens of Athens numbered twenty thousand. Hesychius: men of Athens, the public, of one voice. Demosthenes, in his speech against Aristogiton: for almost all are together the public, except the Athenians. This very number is traced to Cecrops himself, as Philochorus reports, cited by the Greek interpreter of Pindar on Olympian Ode 9: Philochorus says that Cecrops, wishing to set out the power of the Athenians and the people, ordered them to cast stones into a vessel in the middle... The same number is given for the first year of the 110th Olympiad, when Demetrius of Phalerum presided over the state. The anonymous author of the Description of the Olympiads, on this year: Under the leadership of Demetrius of Phalerum, the Athenian public numbered twenty myriads. Ctesicles, in Book III of his Chronicles, cited by Athenaeus in Book VI, adds a thousand: Ctesicles, in the fourth book of his Chronicles, says that in every Olympiad the Athenians sent out... In counting votes, the greater part prevailed; so at Athens, if the people were divided into only two parts, it was necessary that more than ten thousand should go into the same opinion. But Solon wills that, when the granting of a privilege is under discussion, among those of the same opinion who are more than ten thousand there must be at least six thousand who vote in secret, so that there be no room for favour: for the favour toward the man it concerns has become unknown; for the vote is cast invisibly, as is said in Aeschines against Ctesiphon.

units.la: A Solone acceperunt Decemviri, quorum hæc est e XII. Tabulis Lex: PRIVILEGIA NE IRROGANTO. Cui Legi addi non vult maximus Iureconsultorum, NISI MAGNO COMITIATV. docetque optime, meo iudicio priuilegia quæ vocant XII. Tabulæ, de vna tantum persona concipi in omnia tempora: nam alioqui in præsens tempus de singulis ferri Leges possunt, inquit Quintilianus Declamat. CLIV. vt de Menandro Lege V.D. de Captiuis. de Holtilio Mancino Lege vlt. D. de Legationibus. At verò is, qui Legis XII. Tabularum collectam & interpretamentum edidit, putat Priuilegia ea esse inlicita quæ inrogantur, non quæ rogantur: Nam Xviri voluere pro singulis hominibus & priuis rogari licere, in siue contra non licere. Quæ distinctio, si quid iudico, non est huius loci: Romani enim hi Solones cum ab Atheniensi acceperint, PRIVILEGIA NON IRROGARI, eo non dixerunt sensu, quo interpretatur nuperus ille editor. Scripserat enim Solon: MHΑΕ ΑΝΔΡΙ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΘΕΙΝΑΙ, quod non tantum significat, Legem in priuum aliquem rogare non licere, sed etiam non licere de singulis Legem ferre priuam. Atque id expresserunt in XII. Tabulis Xviri hac Lege: PRIVILEGIA NE IRROGANTO. Cui, contra quâ putat vir sumus, addi puto, NISI MAGNO COMITIATV, idq; respödet his Solonis verbis: EAN MH ΕΞΑΚΙΣΧΙΛΙΟΙΣ ΔΟΞΗ ΚΡΥΒΔΗΝ ΨΗΦΙΖΟΜΕΝΟΙΣ. quibus cauet, qua ratione possint priuilegia inrogari, nempe COMITIATV MAGNO, apud Romanos ex interpretatione Xvirorum. Neque hinc abit M. Tullius extremo Libro III. de Legibus, cuius verba describemus, vt commodè interpretemur, interpungamus, & emendemus. Tum Leges praeclarissimae de XII. Tabulis tralata duae: quarum altera priuilegia tollit: altera de capite ciuis rogari, nisi maximo Comitiatu, vetat. nondum initiis seditiosis Trib. pleb. Negotialis quidem admirandum tantum maiores in posterum prouidisse: in priuatos homines Leges ferri noluerunt: id est enim priuilegium: quo quid est iniustius? cum Legis haec vis sit, scitum est iussum in omnes? ferri de singulis? nisi Comitys Centuriatis noluerunt. descriptus enim populus censu, ordinibus, aetatibus, plus adhibet ad suffragium consilij, quàm fuse in Tribus conuocatus. Quo verius in nostra causa vir magni ingenij, summaque prudentia, L. Cotta, dicebat, nihil omnino actum esse de nobis: praeter enim quam quod Comitia illa essent armis gesta seruilibus, praeterea neque Tributa capitis Comitia, rata esse possent, neque vlla priuilegij: quocirca nihil nobis opus esse Lege, de quibus nihil omnino actum effet Legibus. Repraesentauimus hic editionem V. Cl. Gruteri: e cuius Notis variantes lectiones huius loci, & Virorum magnorum conatus in eo emendando, disces. Nos ita rescribendum suspicamur. Tum Leges praeclarissimae de XII. Tabulis tralata duae: quarum altera priuilegia tollit: altera de capite ciuis rogari, nisi maximo Comitiatu, vetat. nondum initiis seditiosis Trib. pleb. negat, aliis: siquidem admirandum tantum maiores in posterum prouidisse: in priuatos homines Leges ferri noluerunt: id est enim priuilegium: quo quid est iniustius? cum Legis haec vis sit, scitum est, iussum in omnes? ferri de singulis? nisi Centuriatis Comitiis noluerunt. descriptus enim populus censu, ordinibus, aetatibus, plus adhibet ad suffragium consilij, quam fuse in Tribus conuocatus. Quo verius in nostra causa vir magni ingenij, summaque prudentia, L. Cotta, dicebat, nihil omnino actum esse de nobis. praeter enim quam quod Comitia illa essent armis gesta seruilibus, praeterea neque Tributa capitis Comitia, rata esse possent, neque vlla: priuilegii quocirca nihil nobis opus esse Lege, de quibus nihil omnino actum effet Legibus. Ista Ciceronis verba, nondum initiis seditiosis Trib. pleb. negat, aliis, dicuntur propter P. Clodiu, qui certè nondum inierat Tribunatum plebis: illud verò, ferri de singulis? referendum est ad id quod praecedit, quo quid est iniustius? eìque priuilegium, quod Legi opponitur, cum Lex sit scitum siue iussum in omnes: Verba vero ista optime, si quid iudico, interpunximus: praeterea neque Tributa capitis Comitia, rata esse possent, neque vlla: Priuilegii quocirca nihil nobis opus esse Legi, &c.
units.tr: The Decemvirs took this from Solon, and this is the law of the Twelve Tables: "Let no privileges be imposed." To this law the greatest of the jurists does not wish unless by a great assembly to be added, and he teaches very well, in my judgment, that the so-called privileges of the Twelve Tables are framed for one person and for all time; for otherwise laws may be passed about individuals for the present time, as Quintilian says in Declamation 154, as in the law of Menander, D. 5, On Captives, and the law of Holtilius Mancinus, last D., On Embassies. But he who published a collection and commentary on the Laws of the Twelve Tables thinks that those privileges are forbidden which are imposed, not those which are requested; for the Decemvirs wished that it be lawful to request laws for individual men and private persons, and not lawful either in or against them. This distinction, if I judge rightly, does not belong to this place: for when these Roman Solons received from the Athenians that privileges are not to be imposed, they did not mean it in the sense that the recent editor interprets. For Solon had written: "Nor shall any law be passed against an individual", which means not only that it is not lawful to request a private law against someone, but also that it is not lawful to enact a private law about individuals. And this the Decemvirs expressed in the Twelve Tables by this law: "Let no privileges be imposed." To this, against what that man thinks, I think should be added: "Unless by a great assembly", and this answers to Solon's words: "unless it seem good to six thousand voting in secret." By these words he provides in what way privileges may be imposed, namely by a great assembly, among the Romans according to the interpretation of the Decemvirs. Nor does Marcus Tullius depart from this at the end of Book III of On the Laws, whose words we shall set out, punctuate and emend, so that they may be properly interpreted. Then the two most excellent laws taken from the Twelve Tables: one of which abolishes privileges; the other forbids that a citizen be brought to trial for his life, except by the greatest assembly. Not yet, by seditious beginnings, does the tribune of the plebs deny others: since indeed the ancestors only provided for the future to be admirable: they did not wish laws to be passed against private men: for this is a privilege: what is more unjust than this? since the force of a law is that a decree is an order upon all: to be passed about individuals? Unless they did not wish it by the Centuriate Assemblies. For the people, enrolled by census, orders, and ages, gives more weight to the counsel of the vote than when called together by tribes without distinction. In our cause, Lucius Cotta, a man of great talent and supreme prudence, said more truly that nothing at all had been done about us: for apart from the fact that those assemblies were carried out with servile arms, moreover neither the Tribal assembly nor the assembly concerning a man's life could be valid, nor any privilege; therefore we had no need of a law about those people about whom nothing at all had been done by law. Here I have presented the edition of the most learned Gruter: from his notes you will learn the variant readings of this passage and the efforts of great men in emending it. We suspect that it should be rewritten thus. Then the two most excellent laws taken from the Twelve Tables: one of which abolishes privileges; the other forbids that a citizen be brought to trial for his life, except by the greatest assembly. Not yet, by seditious beginnings, does the tribune of the plebs deny, to others: since indeed the ancestors only provided for the future to be admirable: they did not wish laws to be passed against private men: for this is a privilege: what is more unjust than this? since the force of a law is that a decree, an order, is upon all: to be passed about individuals? Unless they did not wish it by the Centuriate Assemblies. For the people, enrolled by census, orders, and ages, gives more weight to the counsel of the vote than when called together by tribes without distinction. In our cause, Lucius Cotta, a man of great talent and supreme prudence, said more truly that nothing at all had been done about us. For apart from the fact that those assemblies were carried out with servile arms, moreover neither the Tribal assembly nor the assembly concerning a man's life could be valid, nor any privilege; therefore we had no need of a law about those people about whom nothing at all had been done by law. These words of Cicero, "Not yet, by seditious beginnings, does the tribune of the plebs deny others," are said with reference to P. Clodius, who certainly had not yet entered the tribunate of the plebs. But "to be passed about individuals?" must be referred to what precedes: "What is more unjust than this?" and so the privilege, which is opposed to law, since a law is a decree or order upon all. These words, if I judge rightly, we have punctuated best: moreover neither the Tribal assembly nor the assembly concerning a man's life could be valid, nor any privilege. Therefore we had no need of a law, etc.

units.la: Nam quando Cicero in exilium pulsus est à P. Clodio, factum, id est, nō irrogato priuilegio, sed Lege rogata, quam P. Clodius tulit, verba sunt Velleii Paterculi, vt qui ciuem Romanum indemnatum interemissent, ei aqua & igni interdiceretur. Cuius verbis etsi non nominabatur Cicero, tamen solus petebatur. Qua ex Lege Tributis Comitiis de capite Ciceronis rogauit P. Clodius, atqui Tributa illa Comitia neque rata esse poterant, atque adeo neque vlla, cum Tributis Comitiis non liceat de capite ciuis Romani rogare. Atque hic obiter castigabimus ἀντεξετάσωμεν[?] illius, de quo modo locuti sumus, Editoris collectae Legis XII. Tabularum & cum interpretamento: nam miserè confundit Ephesiorum Legem, secundum quam multandus erat Heraclitus, cum Lege, qua lata, quia in eam incurrerat, pulsus est in exilium Hermodorus Heracliti familiaris: atque ea lex, qua Heraclitus petebatur, posterior est ea Lege, quia in exilium miserunt Hermodorum Ephesii: Legem in se πλεονέκτης[?] scriptam expressit Heraclitus ipse sua Epistola ad Hermodorum: [illegible, ~150 letters]
units.tr: For when Cicero was driven into exile by P. Clodius, this was done not by an imposed privilege but by a law proposed, which P. Clodius carried. These are the words of Velleius Paterculus: that whoever had put a Roman citizen to death without trial should be interdicted from water and fire. Although Cicero was not named in these words, he was the only one targeted. By this law P. Clodius proposed, in the Tribal Assemblies, a measure concerning Cicero's life. Yet those Tribal Assemblies could not validly enact it, nor indeed any law, since the Tribal Assemblies may not legislate concerning the life of a Roman citizen. Here in passing we shall take issue with that editor of the collected Law of the Twelve Tables, with commentary, whom we mentioned just now. He badly confuses the law of the Ephesians, under which Heraclitus was to be punished, with the law under which Hermodorus, a friend of Heraclitus, was proposed and driven into exile because he had fallen under it. The law by which Heraclitus was targeted is later than that law, since the Ephesians sent Hermodorus into exile. Heraclitus himself set out in his letter to Hermodorus the law written against himself.

units.la: Ex his verbis licet colligere hanc Legem, [illegible, ~40 letters] quia in exilium pulsus est Hermodorus: itaque Hermodorum iam Epheso exulantem certiorem facit, quid aduersum se molirentur boni illi Ephesii, nempe, inquit, ἔτι ἄδικα [?], adhuc iniusta statuunt, prius scilicet in Hermodorum lata Lege, cuius meminit apud Strabonem Libro XIV. Heraclitus: [illegible, ~120 letters] Diogenes Laertius in Heraclito: [illegible, ~110 letters] Latinè expressit Cicero Tusculanarum Quaestionum Libro V. Est apud Heraclitum physicum de principe Ephesiorum Hermodoro, universos ait Ephesios esse morte multandos, quod, cum civitate expellerent Hermodorum, ita locuti sunt, Nemo de nobis unus excellat: sin quis extiterit, alio in loco, & apud alios sit. Atque utraque haec Lex oblique, καὶ ἐχηματισμένως lata est.
units.tr: From these words one may gather this law, because Hermodorus was driven into exile. So Heraclitus informs Hermodorus, already exiled from Ephesus, what those good Ephesians were plotting against him: "still," he says, "they decree unjust things" [ἔτι ἄδικα], namely, before the law was passed against Hermodorus, which Heraclitus mentions in Strabo, Book XIV. Diogenes Laertius, in his life of Heraclitus, [...] Cicero expressed it in Latin in the Tusculan Disputations, Book V: There is in the natural philosopher Heraclitus, concerning Hermodorus, the leading man of the Ephesians, a saying that all the Ephesians are to be put to death, because when they expelled Hermodorus from the city they said: Let no one among us be outstanding; but if anyone should arise, let him be elsewhere and among others. Both these laws were passed obliquely and in a disguised form.

units.la: Constat mortalium antiquissimos, literas cum nescirent, Leges, quas in tabulis non habebant descriptas, cantasse, ne obliviscerentur, quod etiam sua aetate apud Agathyrsos moribus obseruatum fuisse testis est Aristoteles Problematum Tmemate XIX. Problemate XXVIII. [illegible, ~60 letters] Verum ubi in tabulas relatae sunt Leges, Magistratui concessum non fuit ius dicere secundum Leges non scriptas: ΑΓΡΑΦΟΙ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΩΙ ΤΑΣ Magistratus iudicia ne reddunto ΑΡΧΑΣ ΜΗ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ, ΜΗ- secundum Leges non scriptas, ne vulΔΕ ΓΕΡΙ ΕΝΟΣ. la quidem de re.
units.tr: It is agreed that the most ancient mortals, since they did not know letters, sang their laws, which were not written down in tablets, so that they would not forget them. That this custom was still observed in Aristotle's own day among the Agathyrsi is attested by Aristotle, Problems, Section XIX, Problem XXVIII. [...] But once the laws were transferred to tablets, the magistrate was no longer permitted to give judgment according to unwritten laws. Magistrates shall not render judgments [ΑΓΡΑΦΟΙ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΩΙ ΤΑΣ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΜΗ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ, ΜΗΔΕ ΓΕΡΙ ΕΝΟΣ] according to unwritten laws, not even in any matter whatever.

units.la: Habes hanc Legem apud Andocidem ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν μυστηρίων. [illegible, ~70 letters] ΑΓΡΑΦΩΙ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΩΙ ΤΑΣ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΜΗ ΧΡΗΣΤΑΙ ΜΗΔΕ ΓΕΡΙ ΕΝΟΣ. iterumque laudat paulò post: Habuerunt tamen Graeci Leges suas non scriptas: unde Ulpianus Libro I. Institutionum: Hoc igitur ius nostram constat aut ex scripto, aut sine scripto: ut apud Graecos, τὸ νόμων οἱ μὲν ἐγγεγραμμένοι, οἱ δὲ ἄγραφοι. Lege VI. D. de iustitia[?] & iure. Quare Aristoteles Libro III. Eth.
units.tr: You have this law in Andocides, in his speech On the Mysteries: [...] "Magistrates shall not use unwritten laws, not even in any matter" [ΑΓΡΑΦΩΙ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΩΙ ΤΑΣ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΜΗ ΧΡΗΣΤΑΙ ΜΗΔΕ ΓΕΡΙ ΕΝΟΣ]. He cites it again a little later. Yet the Greeks did have their unwritten laws. Hence Ulpian, Institutes, Book I: "This law of ours consists either of written or of unwritten law, as among the Greeks: some laws are written, others unwritten" [τὸ νόμων οἱ μὲν ἐγγεγραμμένοι, οἱ δὲ ἄγραφοι]. Law 6, D. de iustitia et iure. Wherefore Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book III,

units.la: Nicomach. meminit [?] τὰ νόμων τῶν κ[?] τὰ γράμματα, καὶ τῶν κ[?] τὰ ἐν [?]. Adeoque multæ sunt Leges [?] τὰ ἐν [?], etiam in tabulas relatæ, quæ vix est vt intelligan-turei, cui [?] sunt ignotæ: qua de re eximius est Aristotelis locus Lib. II. Metaphys. vt vulgo quidem eduntur hi Libri, cap. III. cum adscribemus, vt eadem emendemus, & illustremus. [illegible, ~20 letters] [Greek, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters]. Quod de Legibus interpretantur, in quibus fabulosa multa & puerilia sint, optime explodit Vir Iummus, qui ideo de Nomis exponit, & vertit: Qualis sit consuetudinis vis, etiam ipsi Nomi demonstrant, in quibus fabulosa & puerilia, eo quod eis assueti sumus, plus valent, quam vera eorum cognitio. Ego vero facile mihi persuadeo locum de Legibus esse intelligendum, sed ita emendatum [Greek, ~25 letters] id est. Quanta sit consuetudinis vis, ipsæ Leges demonstrant veteres: fabulosa enim puerilíaque, e quibus ortum habuit consuetudo, ad cognitionem eorum, quæ Legibus cauentur, plus conferunt, quàm Leges ipsæ, quibus causam dedit hæc consuetudo. Hic est sensus, meo iudicio, loci intricatissimi: vel forte retinendum est, [Greek, ~6 letters]: vertendúmque hoc modo: fabulosa enim & puerilia plus conferunt per consuetudinem ad cognitionem eorum, quæ Legibus cauentur, quam Leges ipsæ, quibus causam dedit hæc consuetudo. Quam multæ autem Leges scriptæ sint, quarum causa consuetudo, consuetudo autem originem ducat è fabulosis & puerilibus narrationibus, [Greek, ~5 letters] τυφλῶν. Quoquo autem modo, & qua de causa, scriptæ sint Leges, dummodo ratæ atque scriptæ sint [Greek, ~4 letters] τὰ γράμματα, earum vsus atque auctoritas in Iure dicundo fuit: cum omnem consuetudini siue [Greek, ~4 letters] abroget hæc Athenien-sium Lex: nam Magistratus Iudicia reddere vel de re vlla minima non poterant secundum Legem non scriptam. Qua in re diuersi abeunt, boni Quirites ab Athenien-sibus: Inueterata namque consuetudo pro Lege non immerito custoditur, inquit Iulianus Lib. XCIV. Digestorum: & hoc est Ius, quod dicitur moribus constitutum. Nam cum ipsæ Leges nulla alia ex causa nos teneant, quam quod Iudicio populi receptæ sunt: merito & ea, quæ sine vllo scripto populus probauit, tenebunt omnes: nam quid interest, suffragio populus voluntatem suam declaret, an rebus ipsis & factis? Leg. XXXII. D. de Legibus. atque ex eo, quod scriptum non sit Iusistud moribus constitutum, Paulus, Lib. VII. ad Sabinum, auctoritatem illius probat: Imo magnæ auctoritatis, verba sunt Pauli, hoc Ius habetur: quod in tantum probatum est, vt non fuerit necesse scripto id comprehendere: Leg. XXXVI. D. eod. Obseruabatur igitur, vimque Legis obtinebat diuturna consuetudo, non tamen in his causis, quæ ex scripto descendebant, vt docet Vlpianus Lib. I. de officio Proconsulis. Eius verba hæc sunt. Diuturna consuetudo pro iure & Lege in his, quæ non ex scripto descendunt, obseruari solet: Leg. XXXIII. D. eod.
units.tr: mentions [...] the laws [...] the writings, and [...] Many laws, even those transferred into tablets, are hardly intelligible to those to whom they are unknown. On this matter there is an outstanding passage in Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book II, chapter III, which I shall cite so that we may correct and illustrate the same text as it is commonly printed. [...] As for those who interpret it of laws, in which there are many fabulous and childish things, the excellent man who on that account explains and translates it of customs, Nomi, has rightly exploded it: What great force custom has, the very customs themselves demonstrate, in which fabulous and childish things carry more weight, because we are accustomed to them, than their true knowledge. I, however, am easily persuaded that the passage must be understood of laws, but emended thus: How great is the force of custom, the ancient laws themselves demonstrate; for fabulous and childish stories, from which custom arose, contribute more to the knowledge of what is laid down in the laws than the laws themselves, to which this custom gave cause. This, in my judgement, is the sense of this most intricate passage; or perhaps [...] must be retained, and rendered in this way: For fabulous and childish stories contribute more, through custom, to the knowledge of what is laid down in the laws, than the laws themselves, to which this custom gave cause. How many written laws there are whose cause is custom, and custom in turn derives its origin from fabulous and childish narratives [...] of the blind. However, in whatever manner, and for whatever reason, the laws were written, provided they were ratified and written down, their use and authority in judging was established; for this Athenian law abrogates all custom or [...]: for magistrates could not render judgment on any matter, however minor, according to an unwritten law. In this respect our good Quirites differ from the Athenians. For long-established custom is not unjustly maintained in place of law, says Julian, Digest, Book XCIV: and this is the law which is said to be established by custom. For since the laws themselves bind us for no other reason than that they have been received by the judgement of the people, rightly will all men also be bound by those things which the people has approved without any writing. For what difference does it make whether the people declares its will by vote or by the things themselves and deeds? Law 32, D. de Legibus. And from the fact that this law, established by custom, is not written, Paul, Book VII on Sabinus, proves its authority: Indeed this law is held in great authority, are Paul's words, because it has been approved to such an extent that it was not necessary to comprise it in writing: Law 36, D. eod. Therefore the long-standing custom was observed and held the force of law, but not in those cases which descended from written law, as Ulpian teaches in Book I, de officio Proconsulis. His words are these: Long-standing custom is wont to be observed as law and right in those matters which do not descend from writing: Law 33, D. eod.

units.la: Cum igitur secundum Leges scriptas tantum Iudicia Athenis redderentur, capitalis erat commentitiam Legem apud Iudices laudasse:
units.tr: Since, therefore, judgments at Athens were rendered only according to written laws, it was a capital offence to cite a fabricated law before the judges.

units.la: [Greek, ~12 letters]. Ei, qui in Iudicio commentitiam Legem laudarit, capitalis esto.
units.tr: [...] If anyone cites a fabricated law in a trial, let him be liable to capital punishment.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes [Greek, ~8 letters] τῶν Αἰσχίνης [?]. Καὶ [?] [Greek, ~6 letters] [illegible, ~12 letters] Nam hac ratione Iudicibus, qui secundum Leges se ius dicturos iureiurando affirmaverant, imponeba-tur.
units.tr: Demosthenes cites this law [...] against Aeschines. In this way, judges who had sworn that they would give judgment according to the laws were bound.

units.la: Scitum est Atheniensium factum post exactos Triginta Tyrannos, cum enim metuerent ne, si propter ea quae praecesserant, iudicia redderentur secundum Leges, turbas darent qui in ius vocarentur, hanc Legem tulerunt:
units.tr: This is an Athenian enactment made after the expulsion of the Thirty Tyrants. For since they feared that, if judgments were rendered according to the laws, because of what had gone before, there would be disturbances among those summoned to court, they passed this law:

units.la: ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΗ-ΣΘΑΙ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡ-ΧΟΝΤΟΣ.
units.tr: AND THE LAWS ARE TO BE USED FROM THE ARCHONSHIP OF EUCLIDES [ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ.]

units.la: Quae legitur apud Andocidem [illegible, ~10 letters] μυστηρίων, è quo discés & tempus & causam latae huius Legis. Tempus ubi descripsit, nempe post exactos Athenis Triginta Tyrannos, addit: [illegible, ~120 letters]
units.tr: This is what is read in Andocides [illegible] of the Mysteries, from which you will learn both the time and the reason for passing this law. Where he describes the time, namely after the expulsion of the Thirty Tyrants at Athens, he adds: [illegible]

units.la: NOMOΣ.
units.tr: LAW [NOMOΣ.]

units.la: ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ. & paullo post: [illegible, ~90 letters]. Legum igitur sua auctoritas fuit à Praetura Euclidis. Praetor fuit hic Euclides paullo post exactos Triginta Tyrannos. Ulpianus ad Timocrateam. ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΗΣ ἄρχων ἐγένετο [?] Ἀθηναῖος μετ᾽ ὀλίγον χρόνον τῆς Τεϊάκοντα. At in Fastis Atticis, & apud Diodorum Siculum Lib. XIV. Euclidis Praetura coniicitur in annum secundum Olympiadis nonagesimae quartae, potientibus adhuc rerum Triginta Tyrannis: Nam anno primo Olympiadis nonagesimae quartae οἱ Τεϊάκοντα Τυράννοι Ἀθήναι κατέσχηκαν. Affecto anno quarto eiusdem Olympiadis nonagesimae quartae, ἐπ᾽ ἄρχοντος Ἐξαιρέτου, sive Ἐπαινέτου, τὴν Τεϊάκοντα Τυραννικαλυθέντων, οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι τὴν πάτριον πολιτείαν ἀνεκομίσαντο, ἡ τῆς ἰδίας νομίμοις ἐπολιτεύοντο, sive, ut est apud Diodorum, οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι τὴν πατρίδα ἀνεκομίσαντο, ἡ τῆς ἰδίας νόμοις ἐπολιτεύοντο. Sed Praetoris nomen corruptum est tum Fastis Atticis, cum apud Diodorum: Itaque si Eusebium audimus, Euclidis Praetura coniicienda erit in annum secundum Olympiadis nonagesimae quintae.
units.tr: "And the laws are to be used from the archonship of Euclides" [ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ.] And a little later: [illegible]. The authority of the laws therefore dates from the magistracy of Euclides. This Euclides was archon a little after the expulsion of the Thirty Tyrants. Ulpian, on the Timocratea: "Euclides became archon of the Athenians a short time after the Thirty" [ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΗΣ ἄρχων ἐγένετο [?] Ἀθηναῖος μετ᾽ ὀλίγον χρόνον τῆς Τεϊάκοντα.] But in the Attic Fasti, and in Diodorus Siculus, book 14, Euclides' archonship is placed in the second year of the ninety-fourth Olympiad, while the Thirty still held power. For in the first year of the ninety-fourth Olympiad the Thirty Tyrants seized Athens. In the fourth year of the same Olympiad, under the archon Exaretos or Epainetos, when the Thirty Tyrants had been abolished, the Athenians recovered their ancestral constitution and lived under their own laws [ἡ τῆς ἰδίας νομίμοις ἐπολιτεύοντο]; or, as it is in Diodorus, the Athenians recovered their fatherland and lived under their own laws. But the name of the archon is corrupted, both in the Attic Fasti and in Diodorus. So if we follow Eusebius, Euclides' archonship must be placed in the second year of the ninety-fifth Olympiad.

units.la: Anno enim primo huius Olympiadis nonagesimae quintae dicuntur Tyranni Athenis oppressi. Anno vero sequenti, qui secundus erat huius Olympiadis nonagesimae quintae, Athenienses viginti quatuor literis uti ceperunt, quum ante sedecim tantum literas haberent. Atqui id contigit Archonte Euclide. Suidas & Apostolius: [illegible, ~40 letters] Ἀρχῖνος Ἀθηναίου, ὅτι Ἀρχῖνος ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ. Quare Euclides Archon fuerit anno secundo Olympiadis nonagesimae quintae. Sed tamen idem Eusebius in Graecis Scaligeri in annum quartum Olympiadis nonagesimae quartae confert ista de usu. viginti quatuor literarum apud Athenienses: οἱ δὲ Ἀθωνὰς Τυρσηνοὶ κ[?] ἐαν, Ἀθηναῖοι ἤρξαντο φοινικοῖς καὶ [?] Optime quidem anno quarto Olympiadis nonagesimae quartae adscribit vindicatam Athenien-sium libertatem à servitute Triginta Tyrannorum, sed non bene eidem anno adtribuit vsum literarum Ionicarum ab Athenien-sibus acceptum; longe melius certe Latina B. Hieronymi editio conijcit in annum secundum Olympiadis nonagesimae quintae: nam certum est, accepisse has viginti quatuor literas Athenienses, Praetore Euclide. Euclides autem Praetor fuit anno vt plurimum interiecto post exactos Triginta Tyrannos; Ἀρχὴν ἐλάβετο μετ' ὀλίγον χρόνον τὴν Τριάκοντα[?]. Sed de his satis. Lex autem haec non statim ac Triginta Tyranni exacti sunt, scripta est, sed Euclide Archonte, quod ipsa testatur: ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ. & certe necessum fuit aliquod intercedere tempus, intra quod dicae scriptae, turbarum & rerum nouarum metu, huic scribendae Legi causam dederunt.
units.tr: For in the first year of this ninety-fifth Olympiad the tyrants are said to have been overthrown at Athens. In the following year, the second of this ninety-fifth Olympiad, the Athenians began to use twenty-four letters, when before they had only sixteen. And this happened under the archon Euclides. Suidas and Apostolius [illegible] Archinos of Athens, because Archinos [was the archon] of Euclides. Hence Euclides must have been archon in the second year of the ninety-fifth Olympiad. Yet the same Eusebius, in the Greek text of Scaliger, assigns this account of the use of twenty-four letters among the Athenians to the fourth year of the ninety-fourth Olympiad: the Tyrsenoi ... the Athenians began with Phoenician ... Eusebius rightly assigns to the fourth year of the ninety-fourth Olympiad the liberation of the Athenians from the slavery of the Thirty Tyrants, but he does not correctly assign to the same year the adoption of the Ionic letters by the Athenians. The Latin edition of St Jerome certainly conjectures much better, placing it in the second year of the ninety-fifth Olympiad. For it is certain that the Athenians received these twenty-four letters while Euclides was praetor. Euclides was praetor usually in the year after the expulsion of the Thirty Tyrants: he assumed office a short time after the Thirty [Ἀρχὴν ἐλάβετο μετ' ὀλίγον χρόνον τὴν Τριάκοντα[?]]. But enough of this. This law, however, was not written as soon as the Thirty Tyrants were expelled, but under the archon Euclides, as the law itself testifies: "And the laws are to be used from the archonship of Euclides" [ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ.]. Certainly some interval of time must have intervened, during which the decrees were written, and the fear of disorders and of revolutionary change gave occasion for writing this law.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem Athenienses Legibus suis suam voluerunt esse auctoritatem ab anno, quo Euclides Praetor fuit, ita etiam hanc earundem Legum, illarum quae Euclide Archonte, latae sunt, atque in posterum ferentur, auctoritatem aeternam esse voluerunt hac Lege, cuius auctor Diocles:
units.tr: Just as the Athenians wished their laws to have authority from the year in which Euclides was praetor, so too they wished the lasting authority of those same laws, both those passed under Euclides as archon and those to be passed in future, to be established by this law, whose author was Diocles:

units.la: ΔΙΟΚΛΗΣ ΕΙΠΕ, ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΡΟ ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΤΕΘΕΝΤΑΣ ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑ, ΚΑΙ ΟΣΟΙ ΕΦ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΕΤΕΘΗΣΑΝ ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣΙΝ ΑΝΑΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΟΙ, ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΜΕΤ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΗΝ ΤΕΘΕΝΤΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟ ΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΤΙΘΕΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ, ΗΣ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΣ ΕΤΕΘΗ ΠΛΗΝ ΕΙ ΤΩ ΠΡΟΣΓΕΓΡΑΠΤΑΙ ΧΡΟΝΟΣ, ΟΝΤΙΝΑ ΔΕΙ ΑΡΧΕΙΝ, ΕΠΙΓΡΑΨΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΥΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΑ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΗΜΕΡΩΝ· ΤΟ ΔΕ ΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΟΣ ΑΝ ΤΥΓΧΑΝΗ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΩΝ ΠΡΟΣΓΡΑΦΕΤΩ ΓΡΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΗΣ ΕΤΕΘΗ.
units.tr: DIOKLES SAID: The laws laid down before Euclides under the democracy, and all those laid down under Euclides and now inscribed, shall be valid; but those laid down after Euclides and setting the time from which each one is to begin, shall be valid from the day on which each was laid down, unless a time is added at which it is to begin to operate. And the secretary of the Council shall add to the existing laws, within thirty days, [an inscription]. Thereafter whoever is secretary shall at once add that the law is valid from the day on which it was laid down. [ΔΙΟΚΛΗΣ ΕΙΠΕ, ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΡΟ ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΤΕΘΕΝΤΑΣ ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑ, ΚΑΙ ΟΣΟΙ ΕΦ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΕΤΕΘΗΣΑΝ ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣΙΝ ΑΝΑΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΟΙ, ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΜΕΤ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΗΝ ΤΕΘΕΝΤΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟ ΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΤΙΘΕΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ, ΗΣ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΣ ΕΤΕΘΗ ΠΛΗΝ ΕΙ ΤΩ ΠΡΟΣΓΕΓΡΑΠΤΑΙ ΧΡΟΝΟΣ, ΟΝΤΙΝΑ ΔΕΙ ΑΡΧΕΙΝ, ΕΠΙΓΡΑΨΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΥΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΑ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΗΜΕΡΩΝ· ΤΟ ΔΕ ΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΟΣ ΑΝ ΤΥΓΧΑΝΗ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΩΝ ΠΡΟΣΓΡΑΦΕΤΩ ΓΡΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΗΣ ΕΤΕΘΗ.]

units.la: Dixit Diocles. Leges ante Euclidem libera Republica, eodémque Euclide Archonte, latæ, ac in tabulas relatæ, ratæ sunto. Quæ vero post Euclidis Præturam scriptæ sunt, & in posterum ferentur, ratæ sunto ab ea die, qua vnaquaeque earum lata est, praeter quam si cui adscriptum est tempus, à quo debet incipere. Iis vero, quae iam obtinent, Scriba Senatus intra triginta dies inscribito. In posterum quicumque Scriba erit, adscribito statim, Legem ratam esse ab ea die, qua lata est.
units.tr: Diocles said: Laws laid down before Euclides, while the republic was free, and laws passed under Euclides as archon and entered on the tablets, shall be valid. But laws written after Euclides' praetorship and to be brought forward in future shall be valid from the day on which each was passed, unless a time is specified from which it ought to begin. As for those laws which already hold force, the secretary of the Senate shall inscribe them within thirty days. In future, whoever is secretary shall at once add that the law is valid from the day on which it was passed.

units.la: Refert hanc Legem Demosthenes in Timocratea, agens de Legum auctoritate. Solon apud Plutarchum suas Leges ratas esse iusserat in annos centum: ἐχω τὰς νόμους πᾶσιν εἰς ἐκάστην [?] Sed Diocles hac Lege, Legum omnium, quae ante Euclidis Praeturam libera Republica, & post Euclidem Praetorem latae sunt, & in tabulas siue columnas relatae, aeternam sanxit esse auctoritatem, verum cum distinctione: Nam quibusdam Legibus adscribebatur: Hæc Lex rata esto tum demum, cum hunc Praetorem alius exceperit. Demosthenes ibid. πολλοῖς τὴν νόμων ἀναγραφὴν [?], τὸν δὲ νόμον [?] ἀπὸ τῆς μιᾶς τῶν νῦν Ἀρχόντα[?]. Has itaque Leges vult esse ratas, non ab eo die, quo latæ sunt, sed ab eo tempore, quod præscripsit Legislator; Etenim oportet τὸν γεγραμμένον χρόνον κύριον εἶναι[?]. Ceteras vero omnes, quibus à Legislatore tempus non est præscriptum, eas, inquam, omnes vult ratas esse ab eo, quo latæ sunt, dic: πλὴν ἡμέραν, ἀφ' ἧς ἂν τὸ ψήφισμα κύριον εἶναι[?]. Unde habes in Lege non semel: ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ, ΗΣ ΕΤΕΘΗ. Itaque Senatu Scribæ hac Lege præcipitur, ut unicuique Legi adscribat deinceps ratam eam esse à die quo lata est: ΤΟ ΔΕ ΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΟΣ ΑΝΤΥΓΧΑΝΗ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΩΝ ΠΡΟΣΓΡΑΦΕΤΩ ΠΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΗΣ ΕΤΕΘΗ. Sed quid intelligit hac voce ΕΤΕΘΗ; An id vult, quando οἱ νομοθέται ἐδοκίμασαν ἢ ἐκύρωσαν; Vix puto; Sed potius quando is qui Legem fert, eam rogat apud Quingentorum Senatum. Id ut suspicer, facit descripta Lex cum hac adnotatione temporis apud Andocidem ὅτι πᾶς ἀεὶ τὴν μυστηρίων[?]. Καὶ ἀπαγωγὴ τὸν νόμον τὸν ἐκ τῆς γῆς[?].
units.tr: Demosthenes quotes this law in the Timocratea, when he treats of the authority of the laws. Solon, according to Plutarch, had ordered that his laws should be valid for a hundred years [ἐχω τὰς νόμους πᾶσιν εἰς ἐκάστην [?]]. But Diocles, by this law, established the lasting authority of all laws which were passed while the republic was free before the praetorship of Euclides, and those passed after Euclides' praetorship and entered on the tablets or columns; yet with a distinction. For to some laws this was added: this law shall be valid only when another praetor has succeeded this one. Demosthenes, in the same place: [many ... the inscription of the laws ...] [τὸν δὲ νόμον [?]] from the one of the present archons [?]. He therefore wishes these laws to be valid not from the day on which they were passed, but from the time which the lawgiver prescribed; for [the time written down ought to be authoritative] [τὸν γεγραμμένον χρόνον κύριον εἶναι [?]]. As for all the others, for which no time was prescribed by the lawgiver, he wishes them all, I say, to be valid from the day on which they were passed, [except the day from which the decree shall be valid] [πλὴν ἡμέραν, ἀφ' ἧς ἂν τὸ ψήφισμα κύριον εἶναι [?]]. Hence you have in the law, more than once: THE LAW SHALL BE VALID FROM THE DAY ON WHICH IT WAS PASSED [ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ, ΗΣ ΕΤΕΘΗ]. So by this law the secretary of the Senate is commanded to add to each law, from now on, that it is valid from the day on which it was passed: [ΤΟ ΔΕ ΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΟΣ ΑΝΤΥΓΧΑΝΗ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΩΝ ΠΡΟΣΓΡΑΦΕΤΩ ΠΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΗΣ ΕΤΕΘΗ.] But what does he mean by the word ΕΤΕΘΗ? Does he mean when the lawgivers approved or ratified it? I scarcely think so; rather, when the man who proposes the law puts it to the Council of Five Hundred. To suspect this, the law as written down with this note of time in Andocides makes it plain: [...] and the law taken from the land [?].

units.la: ΝΟΜΟΣ ΕΔΟΞΕ ΤΗι ΒΟΥΛΗι, ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΕΠΙΤΑΝΕΥΕ ΚΑΕΟΓΕΝΗΣ, ΕΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΕ ΒΟΗΘΟΣ ΕΠΕΣΤΑΤΕΙ ΤΑΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΦΑΝΤΟΣ ΣΥΝΕΓΡΑΨΕΝ, ΑΡΧΕΙ ΧΡΟΝΟΣ ΤΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΟΣ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ ΛΑΧΟΤΕΣ ΤΩι ΚΥΑΜΩι, ΟΤΕ ΚΑΕΟΓΕΝΗΣ ΠΡΩΤΟΣ ΕΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΕΝ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΝ, &c. Verba ista: ΑΡΧΕΙ ΧΡΟΝΟΣ ΤΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΟΣ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ ΛΑΧΟΤΕΣ ΤΩι ΚΥΑΜΩι, ΟΤΕ ΚΑΕΟΓΕΝΗΣ ΠΡΩΤΟΣ ΕΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΕΝ. non sunt de Lege, sed ex hac Dioclis Lege addita sunt ad denotandum tempus, ex quo rata esse cepit, postquam eam Nomothetæ ἐκύρωσαν. Tempus autem adnotatur, adscripto nomine Scribæ Senatus, & quando primum ceperit eo munere fungi: nempe scripta est, quando primum Cleogenes Senatui ἐγραμμάτευεν. eo enim die rogaverat suam Legem Demophantus apud Quingentorum Senatum: postea Lege approbata Senatu, è Senatusconsulto rogatus est populus: unde in Lege scribitur: ΕΔΟΞΕ ΤΗι ΒΟΥΛΗι ΚΑΙ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι. Approbata Lex populi suffragiis tradita est Nomothetis, eorum quoque calculis confirmanda: atque Nomothetæ iubebant τὸν νόμον κύριον εἶναι. Sed tempus, à quo incipiebat ὁ νόμος κύριος εἶναι, repetebatur ab illo die, quo primum Lex scripta atque rogata est apud Quingentorum Senatum. Habes igitur hic illustre exemplum huius observationis, sed ita rescribendum. ΑΡΧΕΙ ΧΡΟΝΟΣ ΤΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥ ΝΟΜΟΥ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ ΛΑΧΟΤΕΣ ΤΩι ΚΥΑΜΩι, ΟΤΕ ΚΑΕΟΓΕΝΗΣ ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΕΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΕΝ. Scilicet ἡ Βουλή, οἱ Πεντακόσιοι, λαχόντες τῷ κυάμῳ, ἐδοκίμασαν, atque hinc repetendum est tempus, quo ὁ νόμος ἐπεδόθη, ac proinde ex quo cepit κύριος εἶναι. Si quæ vero iam latæ sunt Leges, & in tabulas relatæ, quibus adscriptum non sit dies, quo ἐπεδόθη, cautetur hac Lege, ut Scriba Senatus intra dies triginta adscribat: ΕΠΙΓΡΑΦΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΙΣ ΜΕΝ ΝΥΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΑ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ.
units.tr: THE LAW WAS RESOLVED BY THE COUNCIL AND THE PEOPLE: IF ANYONE PROPOSES ... CLEOGENES ... HELPER ... SECRETARY ... THE TIME BEGINS FROM THIS DECREE, THE COUNCIL OF FIVE HUNDRED, HAVING DRAWN LOTS BY BEAN, WHEN CLEOGENES FIRST SERVED AS SECRETARY, IF ANYONE CHANGES THE DEMOCRACY, etc. [ΝΟΜΟΣ ΕΔΟΞΕ ΤΗι ΒΟΥΛΗι, ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΕΠΙΤΑΝΕΥΕ ΚΑΕΟΓΕΝΗΣ, ΕΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΕ ΒΟΗΘΟΣ ΕΠΕΣΤΑΤΕΙ ΤΑΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΦΑΝΤΟΣ ΣΥΝΕΓΡΑΨΕΝ, ΑΡΧΕΙ ΧΡΟΝΟΣ ΤΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΟΣ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ ΛΑΧΟΤΕΣ ΤΩι ΚΥΑΜΩι, ΟΤΕ ΚΑΕΟΓΕΝΗΣ ΠΡΩΤΟΣ ΕΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΥΕΝ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΝ, &c.] The words: "The time begins from this decree: the Council of Five Hundred, having drawn lots by bean, when Cleogenes first served as secretary", are not part of the law, but were added from this law of Diocles to mark the time from which it began to be valid, after the lawgivers had ratified it [ἐκύρωσαν]. The time is noted by adding the name of the secretary of the Senate, and the date when he first began to hold that office: namely, it was written down when Cleogenes first served as secretary to the Senate [ἐγραμμάτευεν]. For on that day Demophantus had proposed his law before the Council of Five Hundred; afterwards, once the law was approved by the Senate, the people were asked to vote on a decree of the Senate. Hence the law reads: "It seemed good to the Council and to the People." The law approved by the votes of the people was handed to the lawgivers, to be confirmed also by their ballots; and the lawgivers ordered that the law be valid [τὸν νόμον κύριον εἶναι]. But the time from which the law began to be valid was reckoned from the day on which the law was first written and proposed before the Council of Five Hundred. You have here, therefore, a clear example of this observation, but it must be read thus: "The time begins from this law: the Council of Five Hundred, having drawn lots by bean, when Cleogenes first served as secretary." That is, the Council, the Five Hundred, having drawn lots by bean, approved it [ἐδοκίμασαν], and from this the time must be counted when the law was submitted [ἐπεδόθη], and so from when it began to be valid [κύριος εἶναι]. But if any laws already passed and entered on the tablets lack the day on which they were submitted [ἐπεδόθη], it is provided by this law that the secretary of the Senate shall add it within thirty days: [ΕΠΙΓΡΑΦΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΙΣ ΜΕΝ ΝΥΝ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΑ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ] thirty days.

units.la: ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΗΜΕΡΩΝ. Quod facile fuit ex actis publicis τὰ γράμματα, quae publice ἐν δημοσίῳ asseruabantur. Scripta autem videtur haec Lex, anno, si forte, altero, post Euclidis Praeturam: nam annum hic habes, qui illum excepit, quo Euclides Archon fuit, ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΜΕΤ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΗΝ ΤΕΘΕΝΤΑΣ. Sequentem vero annum, qui tunc primum ceperat, designat his verbis, quae sunt de praesenti: ΚΑΙ ΤΟ ΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΤΙΘΕΜΕΝΟΥΣ. Dixit autem Diocles de Legibus, quae ante Euclidis Praeturam latae sunt: ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΡΟ ΕΥΚΛΕΙ-ΔΟΥ ΤΕΘΕΝΤΑΣ ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΙ. Nam si non addita esset haec exceptio, ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΙ, non potuissent non censeri ἄκυροι. Namque ita vulgo, quae ante Euclidis Praeturam fuisse dicebantur, audiebant: Αἰσχίνης ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμάρχου· ἢ ἔστω τοῦτα ἄκυρα, ὥσπερ τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν Τριάκοντα, ἢ τὰ πρὸ Εὐκλείδου, ἢ εἴ τις ἄλλη πώποτε τοιαύτη ψήφισμα ἐγένετο [?].
units.tr: Thirty days [ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΗΜΕΡΩΝ]. This could easily be learned from the public records, the documents [τὰ γράμματα] that were kept in public [ἐν δημοσίῳ]. This law, if I am not mistaken, seems to have been written a year, or perhaps two, after the Praetorship of Euclides. For you have the year that followed the archonship of Euclides, when the text says "those who were installed after Euclides" [ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΜΕΤ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΗΝ ΤΕΘΕΝΤΑΣ]. He indicates the year that had just begun at that time with the words in the present tense: "and placing the rest in future" [ΚΑΙ ΤΟ ΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΤΙΘΕΜΕΝΟΥΣ]. Diocles, however, spoke of the laws that were enacted before the Praetorship of Euclides: "the laws enacted before Euclides in a democracy" [ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΡΟ ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΤΕΘΕΝΤΑΣ ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΙ]. For if this exception, "in a democracy" [ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΙ], had not been added, they could not have failed to be judged void [ἄκυροι]. For this is how people commonly understood those things said to have been before the Praetorship of Euclides. Aeschines, in his speech against Timarchus: "Let these be void, like those under the Thirty, or those before Euclides, or whatever other such decree was ever made" [ἢ ἔστω ταῦτα ἄκυρα, ὥσπερ τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν Τριάκοντα, ἢ τὰ πρὸ Εὐκλείδου, ἢ εἴ τις ἄλλη πώποτε τοιαύτη ψήφισμα ἐγένετο].

units.la: DE SENATVSCONSVLTIS ET PLEBISCITIS TITVLVS SECVNDVS.
units.tr: ON SENATUS-CONSULTS AND PLEBISCITES, TITLE TWO.

units.la: Vanquam magna esset, vt par erat, Senatus Quingentorum auctoritas, non tamen ius, quod esset perpetuum, faciebat: sed in vertentem tantum annum, ex hac Lege.
units.tr: Although the authority of the Senate of Five Hundred was great, as it rightly was, it did not make a law that was permanent. Its decrees held force only for the coming year, under this law.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes: ἐν τῷ κατ' Αἰσχίνην· εἶπεν αὐτὸν χαλεπὸν ἐρῆν τὸν λόγον, ὡς στρέφει τοῦτο ζητήσει ἐξαπατᾶν ἡμᾶς, ὡς ἄκυρόν ἐστι τὸ ψήφισμα. προβούλευμα γάρ ἐστιν ὁ νόμος ἡ ἐπίταξις κελεύει τὰ τῆς Βουλῆς εἰς ψηφίσματα. Senatus Quingentorum consulta erant, vel προβούλευμα, vt hic loquitur Demosthenes, quae ad populum deferebantur, & in concione populi promulgabantur, vt Plebiscito confirmarentur. Alia erant Psephismata & Senatusconsulta, ad quae confirmanda non mittebatur in suffragia populus, sed sine illius auctoritate fiebant à Senatu Quingentorum: atque haec Senatusconsulta rata erant, iusque faciebant in vnum tantum annum, quamdiu scilicet ille Quingentorum Senatus, qui illa decreuerat, Reipublicae praeesset. Vlpianus adhunc locum: ὁ νόμος ἡ ἐπίταξις κελεύει τὰ τῆς Βουλῆς εἰς ψηφίσματα. ἐχέον δὲ ὅτι τὰ προβουλεύματα καὶ κυρωθέντα ὑπὸ τῆς Βουλῆς ψηφισμῶν, τὰ μὲν ἄχρι αὐτῆς ἴσατο τῆς Βουλῆς. τὰ δὲ, εἰς τὸν δῆμον ἐπέμπετο, ὅσα μὲν οὖν ἴσα τῆς Βουλῆς ψηφίσματα ἦν, τῶν ... [?] & paullo post: ἀλλ' ἃ μὲν ἡ βουλὴ ἰσχύει χωρεῖ τῷ δήμῳ εως ἂν χρὴ, ἐπικέκριται, ἡ ὧν ὅπως ἐπίταξις. τὰ δὲ ... τοῦ δήμου γιγνόμενα, ἡ πλείονα ἐ-μένε χρόνον. ἐπειδὴ τὰ προβουλεύματα τῆς βουλῆς οὐκ εἰσῆγετο εἰς τὸν δῆμον, ἀλλ' ὡ κύκλα ἡ χωρὶς τῇ δήμῳ· ὡ δὲ ἐπίπτειν, αὐτῇ τῇ ἐπ' οἰκιῶν[?]. Atque ex his, puto, lucem accipiet Athenæus, qui Lib. XIII. quærit, quomodo Athenis tibicina Nemea dicta sit à Nemea ludis, cùm cautum esset Psephismate, ne qua infamis mulier Πανηγύρεως alicuius nomen acciperet: ἡ Νεμεάδος τῆς αὐληπείδος Υαξί[?]δης μνημονεύει ἐν τῷ χ[?] Παξηχῆς[?], καὶ ἡς ἄξιον ἰσμαύδ[?]ν, πῶς καὶ ἐκέδει Ἀθηναῖοι ὅτω πος ἐπαγγελλομένων τῶν τῆρ[?] πανηγύρεως ἐπάξ[?] ὀνόματι χ[?]λ[?]. κεκώλυται γὰρ τὰ τοιαῦτα ὀνόματα, ὃ μόνον τῆς ἐπαιρὸ[?]νσίας, ἀλλὰ ἢ τῆς ἄλλας δούλης, ὡς φησι Πολέμων ἐν τῇ περὶ Ἀκροπόλεως. Locum hunc expressit, quamquam imperitè, Harpocration his verbis: Νεμέας αὐληπείδος μνημονεύει Υαξίδης ἐν τῷ χ[?] Παξηχῆς, εἰ γήποις. ὁ δὲ Πολέμων ἐν τῇ περὶ Ἀκροπόλεως, ψηφίσματα, ψήφισμα, καθ' ὃ ἀπίρηπο Ἀθηναίων ὄνομα πεντεπεῖδος πίαδαγ δούλη, ἢ ἀπελευθέρα, ἢ πόρνη, ἢ αὐληπείδ. ἄξιον δὲ ἐπιρρῆσαι, πῶς ὅτως ὠνομάζετο αἱ αὐληπείδες. Lex hæc non fuit, sed Psephisma, quo cavebatur, ne qua serua, sive liberta, aut meretrix, aut tibicina, id est, uno ut absoluam verbo, infamis femina Panegyreos alicuius illustris nomen acciperet, ut optimè nominauit Harpocration: atqui Psephismata sive Senatusconsulta, quæ in concione populi non promulgabantur, cuiusmodi fuit Psephisma illud, καθ' ὃ ἀπίρηπο Ἀθηναίων ὄνομα πεντεπεῖδος πίαδαγ δούλη, ἢ ἀπελευθέρα, ἢ πόρνη, ἢ αὐληπείδ, ius non faciebant nisi in eum tantum, quo facta erant, annum. Quare nil mirum si Pythionicæ, si Isthmiæ, & si quæ sunt huiusmodi bonæ merces, ista fuerint impositæ nomina, post hoc Psephisma, quod ἐπ' ἔτος, & unius tantum anni erat: Nam Aphroditis solebant noua meretricibus tunc primum quæstum corpore facientibus nomina imponere, ut testis est Plautus Pœuulo.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in the speech against Aeschines: "He said it was hard to speak the argument, since he twists this to deceive us, that the decree is invalid. For the law, the ordinance, commands that the business of the Council be turned into decrees" [ἐν τῷ κατ' Αἰσχίνην· εἶπεν αὐτὸν χαλεπὸν ἐρῆν τὸν λόγον, ὡς στρέφει τοῦτο ζητήσει ἐξαπατᾶν ἡμᾶς, ὡς ἄκυρόν ἐστι τὸ ψήφισμα. προβούλευμα γάρ ἐστιν· ὁ νόμος ἡ ἐπίταξις κελεύει τὰ τῆς Βουλῆς εἰς ψηφίσματα]. The Senate of Five Hundred's decrees were either a preliminary resolution (προβούλευμα), as Demosthenes here calls it, which were brought before the people and proclaimed at an assembly of the people, so that they might be confirmed by plebiscite. Others were psephisms and senatus-consults, which were not sent to the people for a vote to be confirmed, but were made by the Senate of Five Hundred on its own authority. These senatus-consults were valid and had the force of law only for one year, that is, for as long as that Senate of Five Hundred which had decreed them governed the commonwealth. Ulpian, on this passage: "The law, the ordinance, commands that the business of the Council be turned into decrees." And it should be noted that the preliminary resolutions, when confirmed by a decree of the Council, remained in force up to the Council itself; but those which were sent to the people, as many as were decrees of the Council... [the text here is corrupt]. And a little later: "But those things which the Council holds in force pass to the people until..., or they are ordered...; and those of the people which were made... remained for a longer time. Since the preliminary resolutions of the Council were not brought before the people, but were...". From these things, I think, Athenaeus will receive light, who in Book XIII asks how in Athens a flute-girl was called "Nemea" from the Nemean games, when a psephism had provided that no infamous woman should take the name of any panegyris: "Hermippus mentions a flute-girl Nemea in the ... of Paxechus, and it is worth asking how the Athenians..., when the festival was proclaimed, took the name..." For such names were forbidden, not only of the free, but also of the other slaves, as Polemon says in his work on the Acropolis. Harpocration expressed this passage, though without skill, in these words: "Hyxides mentions a flute-girl Nemea in the ... of Paxechus, if I am not mistaken. But Polemon, in his work on the Acropolis, [cites] a decree by which it was forbidden for any Athenian to give a slave, or freedwoman, or harlot, or flute-girl the name of..." It is worth asking how the flute-girls were named in this way. This was not a law but a psephism, by which it was provided that no slave, whether servant or freedwoman, or harlot, or flute-girl, that is, to say it in one word, no infamous woman, should take the name of any famous panegyris, as Harpocration rightly named it. Yet psephisms or senatus-consults which were not proclaimed at an assembly of the people, of which kind was that psephism by which it was forbidden for any Athenian to give a name... to a slave, freedwoman, harlot, or flute-girl, had force of law only for that one year in which they were made. Hence it is no wonder if such fine names as Pythionike, Isthmia, and others of that kind were imposed after this psephism, which was for one year only. For they used to give new names to harlots who were then for the first time making gain with their bodies, as Plautus attests in the Pseudolus:

units.la: Aphrodisia, hodie Veneris est festus dies. Tua pietas nobis plane auxilio fuit, Cum huc aduenisti hodie in ipso tempore. Namque hodie earum mutarentur nomina, Facerentque indignum genere quæstum corpore.
units.tr: "Aphrodisia! Today is the feast day of Venus. Your piety has been truly a help to us, since you came here today at just the right time. For today their names were to be changed, and they were to make an unworthy trade with their bodies."

units.la: Sed dubium mouet Athenæus de Nemea, quæ, ut mea fert opinio, hoc nomen accepit, quando istud Psephisma auctoritatem habebat suam, id est, intra annum, quo factum est: itaque excidisse vocem πότε, facile mihi persuadeo, reponendam inter hæc verba: κεκώλυται γὰρ πότε τὰ τοιαῦτα πίαδαγ ὀνόματα[?].
units.tr: But Athenaeus raises a doubt about "Nemea," which, in my opinion, received this name when that psephism had its authority, that is, within the year in which it was made.
