So I easily persuade myself that the word πότε ("at some time") has dropped out and should be restored among these words: "For it was forbidden at some time to give such names..."

units.la: At vero Romæ maior Senatus auctoritas fuit: nam, ut auctor est Vlpianus Lib. XVI. ad Edictum, etiam cum Respublica unius Imperatoris libidini cessit, non ambigitur, Senatum ius facere posse. Leg. IX. D. de Legibus & Senatusconsultis unde etiam is, qui iurisdictioni præest, secundum Senatusconsulta ius dicit: Leg. XII. D. eod. adeoque Constitutione Theodosij M poena illi irrogatur, qui elicere tentauerit rescriptum aduersus formam eorum, quæ Senatusconsulto statuta sunt. Jmppp. Gratianus, Valentinianus, & Theodosius AAA ad Senatum. Quamuis Senatusconsultum perpetuam per se obtineat firmitatem, tamen nostris legibus etiam idem prosequimur: adjicientes, ut si quisquam speciali supplicatione eliciendum aliquod rescriptum tentaverit, ut transfire ei formam liceat statutorum, tertia patrimonij parte multetur, & damnatus ambitus crimine, maneat infamis. Dat.
units.tr: But at Rome the authority of the Senate was greater. For, as Ulpian writes in Book XVI on the Edict, even when the Commonwealth yielded to the lust of a single emperor, "it is not doubted that the Senate can make law" (Dig. 1.3.9, De legibus et senatusconsultis). Hence also he who presides over jurisdiction "gives judgment according to senatus-consults" (Dig. 1.2.12, same title). Indeed, by a constitution of the Emperor Theodosius the Great, a penalty is imposed on anyone who attempts to obtain a rescript against the form of those things which have been established by senatus-consult. "The emperors Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius Augustus to the Senate. Although a senatus-consult holds perpetual firmness of itself, nevertheless we also pursue the same in our laws, adding that if anyone attempts to obtain by special petition some rescript so that he may be allowed to depart from the form of the statutes, he shall be fined a third part of his patrimony, and, condemned of the crime of ambition, shall remain infamous. Given..."

units.la: VII. Kal. Augusti. Heraclea, Richomere & Clearcho Conss. Leg. vn. Cod. de Senatusconsultis.
units.tr: VII Kal. Augusti. Heraclea, Richomeres and Clearchus being consuls. Law 7, Code, On Senatusconsults.

units.la: Quod ad illa, quæ memorauimus, Senatus Quingentorum ꝓβουλευμα, ea fiebant iis de rebus, quæ ad populum referebantur: Nam ante comitia populi ea res consulendo censendoque in Quingentorum Senatu agitabatur, qua de re populus, cuius summa fuit potestas, rogandus erat ex hac Solonis Lege:
units.tr: As to the matters we have mentioned, the Senate of Five Hundred gave a probouleuma (preliminary resolution) on those affairs that were referred to the people. For before an assembly of the people, the matter was discussed and deliberated in the Senate of Five Hundred, and the people, whose power was supreme, had to be asked about it under this law of Solon:

units.la: Ἀπροβούλευτον ψήφισμα μὴ εἰσίεναι ἐς τὸν δῆμον.
units.tr: A resolution not previously considered by the Council shall not be brought before the people. [Ἀπροβούλευτον ψήφισμα μὴ εἰσίεναι ἐς τὸν δῆμον.]

units.la: Sine Senatus praeiudicio populus nulla de re rogator.
units.tr: Without prior consideration by the Senate, the people shall be asked about no matter.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis à Solone latæ Plutarchus in eius Vita: ἡ βουλὴ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐκκλησίας [?].
units.tr: Plutarch, in his Life of Solon, recalls this law enacted by Solon: the council [illegible] of the assembly [?]. [ἡ βουλὴ [illegible] ἐκκλησίας [?].]

units.la: Libanius in Hypothesi Androtianæ: φασὶ οἱ κατήγοροι, ὅταν μὲν ἀπροβούλευ-τον ᾖ τὸ ψήφισμα, νόμου γὰρ κελεύοντος μὴ παρὰ τὴν βουλὴν [?] εἰσφέρειν, ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς βουλῆς δοκιμασθὲν [?], τὸν Ἀνδροτίωνα [?] ἀπροβούλευτον εἰσιενεῖ [?], πῶς γράφεται.
units.tr: Libanius, in the Hypothesis to the Androtion: The accusers say that when a resolution is not previously considered (for there is a law commanding that nothing be brought in without the council), but when it has been examined by the council, Androtion [?] brought it in without prior consideration; how is he indicted?

units.la: Vlpianus ibidem: Ἐγκτήσεων [illegible, ~8 letters] ἡ Διὸς [?] ἐπιψηφίζειν ἀπροβούλευτον [?] μὴ εἰσίεναι ἐς τὸν δῆμον. Atque hæc ratio ab eo adfertur: ὅτι ἡ πολιτεία ἐστὶν [?] δῆμος, ἡ πολλάκις προβεβουλευμένον ἡμῶν [?] ἐκκλησίας [?] ἐπὶ τὴν βουλήν, ἐπειδὴ ἐπὶ ἐκκλησίαν ἡ κεκουσμένη [?].
units.tr: Ulpian, in the same place: [illegible] ... to put to the vote without prior consideration, not to be brought before the people. And this reason is given by him: because the state is the people, which has often been prepared by the council before the assembly, since [illegible].

units.la: Vlpianus ad Orationem ἐπὶ [?] ἀπροβούλευτος [?] εἰσ [?] ὅτι [?] ἐκκλησίαν [?], εἴπε δὲ τὸν δῆμον. Ita apud Demosthenem in Timocratea: προσπλῆξι τῆς βουλῆς. προβούλευμα ἐκκλησίας, προσχρίσεται ὁ δῆμος.
units.tr: Ulpian, on the Oration [illegible] without prior consideration [?] ... the assembly, but he said the people. So in Demosthenes against Timocrates: the council's preliminary resolution to the assembly; the people is addressed.

units.la: Sed videtur in iis, quæ secundum Leges fiebant, opus non fuisse vllo Senatus præiudicio: cui obiectioni respondet in Androtiana Demosthenes: ἐγὼ δὲ φημὶ προβούλευμα ἐκκλησίας [?], ἔγωγε δὲ ἔν [?] ἐπὶ τούτῳ, νομίζω δ᾽ ἐν τῷ ὁμῷ συμβούλευσιν ἐπὶ πάντα [?]. ἐπὶ γὰρ μὴ χειρίζειν νόμοι, ἐπὶ τὸν δῆμον, ἐπὶ πάντ᾽ αὐτοῦ [?]. Atque ex hoc Senatusconsulto, siue probuleumate, Prytaneis præscribebant ante concionem, qua de re deliberandum esset, & ferenda suffragia. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. οἱ Πρυτάνεις προγράφονται τὰς τῆς βουλῆς ἡ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, ὑπὲρ ὧν δεῖ ἐπὶ χειροτονίαν. Vlpianus ad Philippicam I. [?] ἐπὶ τὸ [?] ἐπὶ ἑκάστου [?], ἐξ ὧν δ᾽ [?] προγράφοντες [?].
units.tr: But it seems that in those matters which were done according to the laws, there was no need of any prior resolution of the Senate. Demosthenes answers this objection in the Androtion: I say the assembly's preliminary resolution [?] ... for the laws do not forbid ... to the people, to all of it [?]. And from this senatusconsult, or probouleuma, the Prytaneis posted in advance, before the assembly, what was to be deliberated and what votes were to be taken. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: The prytaneis post in advance the matters of the council or of the assembly on which a show of hands must be taken. [οἱ Πρυτάνεις προγράφονται τὰς τῆς βουλῆς ἡ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, ὑπὲρ ὧν δεῖ ἐπὶ χειροτονίαν.] Ulpian, on the First Philippic: [illegible] for each [?], and from which [?] posting [?].

units.la: Quinetiam præscribebant ex hoc probuleumate Senatus, diem, dicique horam, qua habenda erat concio, exemplum habes in Comicis Θεσμοφοριαζούσαις.
units.tr: Moreover, from this probouleuma of the Senate they also posted the day and the hour at which the assembly was to be held. You have an example in Aristophanes' Thesmophoriazusae.

units.la: ἔδοξε τῇ βουλῇ πρὸς.
units.tr: It was resolved by the council to ... [ἔδοξε τῇ βουλῇ πρὸς.]

units.la: Ἐκκλησίας ποιῆσαι ἐῶσιν τῇ μέση
units.tr: to hold an assembly ... in the middle [Ἐκκλησίας ποιῆσαι ἐῶσιν τῇ μέση]

units.la: Ταῦθ᾽ Θεσμοφοριαζ.
units.tr: These things ... Thesmophoriazusae [Ταῦθ᾽ Θεσμοφοριαζ.]

units.la: Lustrata concione, conceptisque à Præcone precibus, ab eodem pro concione legebatur Senatus προβούλευμα de iis, de quibus mitti in suffragia populum oportebat. Aristophanes loco laudato:
units.tr: After the assembly had been purified and the prayers pronounced by the herald, the same herald read out before the assembly the Senate's probouleuma concerning those matters on which the people had to be sent to vote. Aristophanes, in the passage cited:

units.la: Ἀχνυε πᾶς, ἔδοξε τῇ βουλῇ πρός
units.tr: Everyone grieved; the council resolved to ... [Ἀχνυε πᾶς, ἔδοξε τῇ βουλῇ πρός]

units.la: Τῇ γὰρ γυναιῷ, Τιμοκλῆ ἐπεσπάτη.
units.tr: For to the woman ... Timocles ... [Τῇ γὰρ γυναιῷ, Τιμοκλῆ ἐπεσπάτη.]

units.la: Λύσιλλ᾽ ἐγκαμμάτευσι ἴσ᾽ Σωκράτη,
units.tr: Lysilla ... as Socrates [Λύσιλλ᾽ ἐγκαμμάτευσι ἴσ᾽ Σωκράτη,]

units.la: Ἐκκλησίαν ποιῆσαι ἔωθεν τῇ μέσῃ[?] Τῶν Θεσμοφοριῶν, ὦ ἄλις ἔασ' ἡμῖν χολὴ[?]. Καὶ χρηματίζειν πρῶτα ταῖς ΕΥριπίδου[?], Ὁ, τί χρὴ πάλιν ἐχθρὸν. ἀδικεῖν γὰρ δοκεῖ[?] Ἡμῖν ἀπάσας.
units.tr: to hold an assembly early in the middle [?] of the Thesmophoria: enough of bile for us, O enough. And first to transact business with the [?] of Euripides: "What must again be hated? For he seems to wrong all of us." [Ἐκκλησίαν ποιῆσαι ἔωθεν τῇ μέσῃ [?] Τῶν Θεσμοφοριῶν, ὦ ἄλις ἔασ' ἡμῖν χολὴ [?]. Καὶ χρηματίζειν πρῶτα ταῖς ΕΥριπίδου [?], Ὁ, τί χρὴ πάλιν ἐχθρὸν. ἀδικεῖν γὰρ δοκεῖ [?] Ἡμῖν ἀπάσας.]

units.la: Cum primum autem βουλεύματα ad populum deferebantur, & pro concione promulgabantur, sciscebat populus, an huic βουλεύματι esset standum, necne: ii βουλεύματι starent, res erat transacta: sin minus, fiebat de illa Plebiscitum. Harpocration è Lysia Rhetore: ἀποχειροτονία ἔοικεν Ἀθηναίοις ... εἰσφέρεται εἰς τὸν δῆμον ἡ γνώμη, ... [?] ... ἐλέγετο ... βουλευτῶν σκέψασθαι τὸν δῆμον, ἡ ἄρχει ὁ βουλεύματα. [illegible, ~12 letters] Si populi accederet calculus, auctoritas Psephismatis erat non in vnum tantum annum: τὰ δὲ ... τῶν δήμου γιγνόμενα, inquit Vlpianus, ἢ πλείονα ἔτη χρόνον.
units.tr: When the probouleumata were first brought before the people and promulgated before the assembly, the people voted whether this probouleuma was to be upheld or not. If they upheld it, the matter was settled; if not, a plebiscite was made on it. Harpocration, from Lysias the Rhetorician: [Greek passage on the vote and the council's proposal, partly illegible]. If the people's vote agreed with it, the authority of the psephisma did not last for one year only; what the people decides, says Ulpian, lasts for more than a year. [τὰ δὲ ... τῶν δήμου γιγνόμενα ... ἢ πλείονα ἔτη χρόνον.]

units.la: Quare non licebat temere tabulam, in qua incisum erat Psephisma, reuellere: idque hac Lege cautum:
units.tr: Therefore it was not lawful to tear down rashly the tablet on which a decree had been engraved, and this was provided for by this law:

units.la: Μὴ καθελεῖν ὁ πίνακα, ἐν ᾧ ὁ ψήφισμα γεγραμμένον ἐντέθειται.
units.tr: Not to take down the tablet on which the decree is written. [Μὴ καθελεῖν ὁ πίνακα, ἐν ᾧ ὁ ψήφισμα γεγραμμένον ἐντέθειται.]

units.la: Refert hanc Legem Plutarchus in Pericle, agens de Atheniensium Psephismate aduersus Megarenses: λέγεται δὲ πρῶτος, ἀδικοῦσι ... Λακεδαιμονίους ἀφιγμένους, ἐξ τῆς Πελοπονήσου νόμον τινὰ βουλευμένου, κωλύοντα καθελεῖν ὁ πίνακα, ἐν ᾧ ὁ ψήφισμα γεγραμμένον ἐντέθειται. Atque hæc Legis ratio est, ne reuulsis Psephismatum tabulis, omnia fiant incerta.
units.tr: Plutarch reports this law in the Life of Pericles, speaking of the Athenian decree against the Megarians: it is said that a certain law was first proposed, when the Lacedaemonians came from the Peloponnese, forbidding the taking down of the tablet on which the decree was written. The reason for this law is that, if the tablets of decrees were torn down, everything would become uncertain.

units.la: Neque tamen potior aut maior Psephismatis vllius, quam Senatus, aut populi, aut Legum auctoritas: idque Lege hac cautum:
units.tr: Yet no decree is more powerful or greater than the authority of the Senate, or of the people, or of the laws, and this was provided for by this law:

units.la: ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕΝ ΜΗ- ΤΕ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ, ΜΗΤΕ ΔΗΜΟΥ, ΜΗΤΕ ΝΟΜΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΩΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.
units.tr: NO DECREE SHALL BE SUPERIOR TO THE COUNCIL, NOR TO THE PEOPLE, NOR TO THE LAW. [ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕΝ ΜΗΤΕ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ, ΜΗΤΕ ΔΗΜΟΥ, ΜΗΤΕ ΝΟΜΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΩΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.]

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes in Timocratea: λέγε τὸν μὲν ... ἢ ἔστι πόλιτες εἰσίν. ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕΝ ΜΗΤΕ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ, ΜΗΤΕ ΔΗΜΟΥ, ΜΗΤΕ ΝΟΜΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΩΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ. Meminit semel atque iterum Andocides ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν μυστηρίων, nusquam tamen apud eum istud comparet, MHTE NOMOY, quod omnino necessarium est: Non licet igitur quicquam de auctoritate Senatus, aut populi, aut Legum, derogare, quod Psephismati adrogetur, sed potius Psephismata sunt infra auctoritatem Senatus, aut populi, aut Legum: Quod enim ad Leges attinet, impune non licebat cuiquam scribere Psephisma aduersus Leges, ei quippe ἀτιμία dica scribebatur: Senatus vero atque populus, si salus populi, quæ suprema Lex est, in eo verteretur, poterant prius Psephisma rescindere: nam Quodcumque iussit populus postremum, id ius ratúmque est, vt habetur in Legibus XII. optiméque Modestinus Lib. II. Excusationum, αἱ μεταξὺ ... ἰσχύουσι τῷ τοῦ αὐτῷ εἰσιν. Leg. vlt. D. de Constitutionibus Principum.
units.tr: Demosthenes cites the law in Timocrates: read ... whether they are citizens. "No decree shall be superior to the council, nor to the people, nor to the law." [ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕΝ ΜΗΤΕ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ, ΜΗΤΕ ΔΗΜΟΥ, ΜΗΤΕ ΝΟΜΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΩΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.] Andocides mentions it once and again in his speech On the Mysteries, yet the words "nor to the law" appear nowhere in him, though they are entirely necessary. It is therefore not permitted to take anything away from the authority of the Senate, the people, or the laws, in order to confer it on a decree; rather, decrees are subordinate to the authority of the Senate, the people, or the laws. For as to the laws, it was not lawful for anyone to propose a decree against them with impunity, since an indictment for atimia was lodged against such a person. The Senate and the people, if the safety of the people, which is the supreme law, were at stake, could first rescind a decree; for "whatever the people last commanded is law and binding," as is found in the Twelve Tables, and as Modestinus excellently says in Book II of the Excusations: [αἱ μεταξὺ ... ἰσχύουσι τῷ τοῦ αὐτῷ εἰσιν.] Law last, Digest, On the Constitutions of Princes.

units.la: In omnibus autem Psephismatis scribendis Lege cautum erat, ne quid mendacii assuereetur.
units.tr: In writing all decrees, the law provided that no falsehood be inserted.

units.la: Μηδὲν ψευδῆ γράφειν ἐν τοῖς δημοσίοις ψηφίσματα[?].
units.tr: Not to write anything false in public decrees. [Μηδὲν ψευδῆ γράφειν ἐν τοῖς δημοσίοις ψηφίσματα[?].]

units.la: In scribendis Psephismatis ab omni mendacio caueтo.
units.tr: In writing decrees, to beware of all falsehood.

units.la: Legem refert Æschines ἐν τῷ πρὸς Κτησιφῶντα[?]. ἀπαγορεύουσιν γὰρ οἱ νόμοι μηδένα ψευδῆ γράφειν ἐν τοῖς δημοσίοις ψηφίσμασι[?]. Hinc in dica, quam scripsit Æschines Ctesiphonti: πρῶτα τοῦτα ψευδῆ γράφας καὶ ἀδικῶν[?] ... ὧν νόμων οὐκ ἐόντων ... ἐγγράφειν εἰς τὰ δημόσια γράμματα καταβάλλεσθαι[?]. Meminit huius Legis Anonymus in Argumento Orationis Æschinis: ὅτι ὁ νόμος ἐστὶν ὁ κωλύων τὸ ψευδῆ γράφειν ἐν τοῖς ψηφίσμασι[?]. & in Argumento Orationis aduersariæ Demosthenis: ὁ δὲ πεῖπης νόμος εἰς τὸν ὅλον[?] βίον καὶ τὴν πολιτείας ἐξέπασιν[?] · κελεύει γὰρ μηδέποτε ψευδῆ γράμματα εἰς τὸ Μητρῷον εἰσάγειν, ἵνα ἐστὶν ὅλα τὰ δημόσια γράμματα. Dicit, μηδέποτε ψευδῆ γράμματα εἰς τὸ Mητρῷον εἰσάγειν, quod idem est, ac μὴ ψευδῆ γράφειν ἐν τοῖς δημοσίοις ψηφίσμασι. Nam ἐγγράφειν Ἀθηναῖοι, inquiunt veteres Magistri, τῷ Μητρῴῳ ζηλία καὶ νομοφυλακία. Cauet autem Legislator, μηδὲν ψευδῆ γράφειν ἐν τοῖς δημοσίοις ψηφίσμασι, tum ne imponant populo, cum etiam ne quidpiam immutent in Republica: nam, vt præclarè docet Philosophus, hæc ψευδῆ γράμματα ἐπιτηδεύεται τινὲς ἕνεκα, vt gloriæ, opum causa, aut aliarum rerum, quæ pestem Rebuspublicis creant.
units.tr: Aeschines reports the law in his speech against Ctesiphon: the laws forbid anyone to write falsehoods in public decrees. [ἀπαγορεύουσιν γὰρ οἱ νόμοι μηδένα ψευδῆ γράφειν ἐν τοῖς δημοσίοις ψηφίσμασι[?].] Hence in the indictment Aeschines brought against Ctesiphon: first, writing these falsehoods and doing wrong ... of which laws, when they did not exist ... to be entered in the public records and deposited. The Anonymous author also mentions this law in the argument to Aeschines' speech, that the law forbids writing falsehoods in decrees, and in the argument to Demosthenes' opposing speech: the law concerns the whole life and the expulsion from the citizenship; for it orders that false writings never be brought into the Metroon, where all the public records are. He says "never to bring false writings into the Metroon," which is the same as "not to write falsehoods in public decrees." For the Athenians, say the old masters, entrusted writings to the Metroon for zeal and guardianship. The lawgiver guards that nothing false be written in public decrees, both so that the people are not deceived and so that nothing in the commonwealth is altered; for, as the Philosopher teaches admirably, some people practise these false writings for the sake of glory, wealth, or other ends, and these create ruin for commonwealths.

units.la: DE CIVIBVS ABORIGINIBVS & adscititiis.
units.tr: ON THE ABORIGINAL AND ADOPTED CITIZENS.

units.la: TITVLVS III.
units.tr: TITLE III.

units.la: Athenarum urbem ἀρχαιοτάτην τῶν Ἑλλήνων fuisse nemo est; qui ambigat, in eaque videre licet, ut inquit Menander Epistola ad Glyceram, πρὸς Ἑλλάδα ὅλην, πρὸς Ἰωνίαν, τὰς Κυκλάδας πάσας, atque ab Athenien-sibus edocti reliqui terræ Græciæ populi humaniorem vitæ modum, armis positis, instituerunt: πᾶσα ἡ Ἑλλὰς ἐπαιδεύθη, inquit Thucydides Historia I. καὶ ξυνῆψεν τὸν διαιτῶν μετ' ὅπλων ἐπολιτεύοντο, ὥσπερ οἱ βάρβαροι ἐν τοῖς πόλεσιν[?]. Domos, urbes, πολιτείας constituerunt: maximèque Theseus διεκόσμησε πρὸς πολιτείαν. Ante Theseum Attica oppidis quidem erat frequens, χωρὶς πόλεις οἰκεῖτο, αὐτοτελεῖς τε ἔχουσα καὶ Ἀρχοντας. Sed non tantùm sua singulæ priuatim urbes sibi procurabant atque administrabant, verum etiam inter se erant discordes, ita ut ad arma venirent: αὐτοὶ ἕκαστοι ἐπολιτεύοντο καὶ ἐξεκλίνοντο · καὶ οἵ-νες καὶ ἐπολέμουν ποτὲ αὐτὴν, ὥσπερ καὶ Ἐλευσίνιοι μετ' Εὐμόλπου ἐπὶ Ἐρεχθέα, ut idem Thucydides observat Libro II. Theseus vero rerum potitus, omnes in unam convenire Athenarum urbem iussit, uno Senatu lecto, qui omnibus prae-
units.tr: No one doubts that the city of Athens was the most ancient of the Greek cities. As Menander says in his Epistle to Glycera, one can see its influence throughout all of Hellas, throughout Ionia, and across all the Cyclades: the other peoples of Greece, taught by the Athenians, laid down their arms and adopted a more civilized way of life. Thucydides, in Book I, says: "All of Hellas was educated," and they gave up living with arms, as barbarians do in their cities [the rest of this quotation is unclear]. They established homes, cities and constitutions, and above all Theseus "put things in order for a constitution." Before Theseus, Attica was indeed full of towns, and it was inhabited in separate cities, each having its own government and magistrates. Not only did each city manage its own affairs privately, but they were also at odds with one another, to the point of taking up arms. "Each city governed itself and kept to itself, and some even made war on Athens," as Elefsinians did with Eumolpus against Erechtheus, as the same Thucydides notes in Book II. But when Theseus gained power, he ordered all the inhabitants to gather into the one city of Athens, having chosen a single Senate, which ... [the remainder is largely illegible; it concerns the division of the ancient lands, the dissolution of the separate town councils and offices, the Prytaneia, the joint citizenship, and his establishment of democracy], and he willed that all should have the same right under this law:

units.la: [Greek passages above are only partly legible; see notes.] [illegible, ~45 letters]τὰ τε ἀρχαῖα διεμοιρήσας τῷ χώρᾳ, καὶ καταλύσας τὴν τῶν δήμων πόλεων πᾶσι βουλὴ[?]-τὴν τῶν πολιτῶν Πρυτάνεια, καὶ τὰς ἀρχάς, ἐς τὸ ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐν βουλευτήριον [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐπι-δίκας ἢ πρυτάνεων, ξυνοχίαν πολιτῶν, Democratiamque instituit: & omnibus hac Lege idem ius esse voluit:
units.tr: [The Greek here is only partly legible.] ...the ancient lands he divided among the country-folk, and abolished the separate councils of the townships, and set up a common council (the Prytaneum) for all citizens, and magistracies... [the rest is illegible], a council hall ... judgments or the Prytanes, the common fellowship of citizens, and he instituted a democracy; and by this law he wished all to have the same right.

units.la: Τοῖς πολίταις τὰ ἴσα ἔστω.
units.tr: [Greek: Let the citizens have equal things.]

units.la: Omnibus civibus ius idem esto.
units.tr: Let all citizens have the same right.

units.la: Refert hanc Legem Plutarchus in Theseo, quanquam cum aliqua exceptione: nam solis ingenuis nobilibus Sacerdotia, Magistratus, & Legum rerumque sanctarum atque divinarum interpretationem hac sua Lege concessit:
units.tr: Plutarch reports this law in his Life of Theseus, though with a certain exception: by this law of his he granted the priesthoods, the magistracies, and the interpretation of the laws and of sacred and divine matters to the noble-born alone.

units.la: Τοὺς Εὐπατρίδας γινώσκειν τὰ ἱερά, καὶ πέφυκεν Ἀρχὰς, καὶ νόμων διδασκάλους εἶ, καὶ ὁσίων καὶ ἱερῶν ἐξηγητάς.
units.tr: [Greek: The Eupatridae shall know the sacred things, and shall be fit for the magistracies, and be teachers of the laws, and interpreters of holy and sacred matters.]

units.la: Patricij Sacerdotia atque Magistratus obeunto. Legum, rerumque sanctarum atque divinarum interpretes sunto[?].
units.tr: Let the patricians hold the priesthoods and the magistracies. Let them be the interpreters of the laws and of sacred and divine matters.

units.la: Plutarchi verba, quæ utramque hanc Legem complectuntur, ista sunt: ὃ μὲν ἄτακτον οὖν μεμιγμένον [illegible, ~25 letters] τὸ δημιουργικὸν, ἀλλὰ [?] τῆς ἀποχρίας χωρεῖς Εὐπατρίδας, καὶ Γεωργοῖς, καὶ Δημιουργοῖς· Εὐπατρίδας μὲν γινώσκειν τὰ ἱερά, καὶ πέφυκεν Ἀρχὰς ἀποδεῖς· καὶ νόμων διδασκάλους εἶ, καὶ ὁσίων καὶ ἱερῶν ἐξηγητάς. τῆς δὲ δήμοις πολίτης ὥσπερ εἰς ἴσον κατέστησε, δῆξη μὲν Εὐπατρίδων, γεωργῶν δὲ Γεωργῶν, πλήθει δὲ τῶν Δημιουργῶν ὑπερέχον δοκούντων. Tres igitur in classes civitatem distribuit Theseus Εὐπατρίδων, Γεωργῶν, καὶ Δημιουργῶν. Εὐπατρίδαι ceteris dignitate antistabant, Γεωργοὶ utilitate, Δημιουργοὶ numero prævalebant. Εὐπατρίδαι dicebantur, qui regibus erant editi. Auctor Etymologici, Εὐπατρίδαι ἐκαλοῦντο οἱ αὐτοὶ ὃ ἀεὶ εἰχωῶτες, καὶ μετέχοντες βασιλικοῦ γένους, πλὴν τῆς ἱερᾶς ἐπιμελείας ποιούμενοι, vel etiam Aborigines & indigenæ. Hesychius: Εὐπατρίδαι, αὐτόχθονες οὐχὶ ἐπήλυδες. Atque hi in ipsa Urbe sedes suas posuerunt cum Δημιουργοῖς, qui, ut habet Auctor Etymologici hac voce supplendus, erant opifices. Δημιουργοὶ δ' ὃ τεχνικοὶ ἐκ[?]. Reliqui vero Γεωργοὶ dicti ruri habebant, & agros colebant. Auctor Etymologici: γεωργοὶ δ', οἱ τῆς δήμης χώρας οἰκήτορες ὑπογεγραμμένοι, sed rescribo: γεωργοὶ δὲ οἱ τῆς ἄλλης χώρας οἰκήτορες, ἐπὶ Γεωργοῖς.
units.tr: These are Plutarch's words, which contain both of these laws: [Greek, partly illegible]: he divided the people into Eupatridae, Georgi and Demiurgi, giving the Eupatridae the right to know the sacred things and to hold the magistracies, and to be teachers of the laws and interpreters of holy and sacred matters; and he set the common people on a footing of equality, as the Georgi were superior in utility and the Demiurgi seemed superior in number. So Theseus divided the citizens into three classes: Eupatridae, Georgi and Demiurgi. The Eupatridae excelled the others in dignity, the Georgi in usefulness, and the Demiurgi prevailed in numbers. The Eupatridae were so called because they were descended from kings. The author of the Etymologicum says: "Eupatridae were called those who had always lived there and shared in royal descent, and who were concerned only with the sacred rites," or also "Aborigines and natives." Hesychius: "Eupatridae: natives, not newcomers." These lived in the city itself, together with the Demiurgi, who, as the author of the Etymologicum adds in supplement of this word, were craftsmen. [The Greek defining Demiurgi as craftsmen is partly illegible.] The rest, called Georgi, lived in the countryside and tilled the fields. The author of the Etymologicum: "Georgi are the inhabitants of the other territory," [the text is corrupt; the author is taken to mean those who dwelt in the country outside the city].

units.la: Post Theseum Solon censum civium suorum egit, Atheniensesque universos, Εὐπατρίδας, Γεωργοὺς, Δημιουργοὺς, in quatuor distinxit ordines, quos πεντακοσιομεδίμνους [illegible, ~10 letters] vocant Græci Scriptores, pro uniuscuiusque censu: Primus ordo erat Pentacosiomedimnorum: secundus Equitum, tertius Zygitarum, quartus Proletariorum: His nullum lege sua Magistratum gerere permisit:
units.tr: After Theseus, Solon made a census of his citizens and divided all the Athenians, Eupatridae, Georgi and Demiurgi, into four orders according to each one's property; the Greek writers call the first of these the Pentacosiomedimni. The first order was that of the Pentacosiomedimni, the second that of the knights, the third that of the Zeugitae, and the fourth that of the Proletarii. By his law he did not allow the men of the lower orders to hold any magistracy.

units.la: Τοῖς ἴδιος μὴ ἀρχὴν ἐσθμίαν ἀρχῶ[?].
units.tr: [Greek, partly illegible: The men of the lower property may not hold any office.]

units.la: Proletarij nullum Magistratum gerunto.
units.tr: Let the Proletarii hold no magistracy.

units.la: Habes apud Plutarchum in Solone: διῄρησι δὲ Σόλων ἐπάξε τὰ ἡμίμεδα τῆς πολιτείας, καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἐξ ἕξης ὁμοῦ καὶ ὑγιεῖς μετὰ πεντακοσία ποιοῦσι, ὥσπερ ἔταξε, καὶ Πεντακοσιομεδίμνους· διῄρησι δὲ τοὺς ἵππον πέφειν δυναμένους, ἢ μέτρα ποιεῖν πεντακόσια· καὶ τούτους ἱππάδα, πλὴν ὥσπερ ἐκάλουν. Ζυγῖται δ' οἱ τὰ τεῖπο ἡμίμεδα ὀνομάσθησαν, οἷς μέσην ἐν σταμφοτέρων ἀξιώσων. εἰ δὲ λοιποὶ πάντες ἐκάλουν Θῆτες, οἷς οὐδεμίαν ἀρχὴν ἐδωκεν ἀρχήν. Pollux Libro VIII. cap.X. ἡμιμέδα δ' ἐκ πέπαρα, Πεντακοσιομεδίμνων, Ἱππέων, Ζυγιτῶν, Θητικὸν· οἱ μὲν ἐκ πεντακοσιομεδίμνων [?] ἱππεῖς [?] ζευγῖται [?] δυνάλισκον [?] ἢ μυᾶς [?] Θητικὸν [?] οὐδὲν [?]. Pro modo itaque census vniuscuiusq; facta erat haec distributio: Pentacosiomedimni Reipublicae talentum pendebant, Equites semitalentum; Zygitae minas decem: Proletarij vero nihil conferebant. Sed non est praetermittendus, sine nota error Scholiastae Aristophanis, quem non iudicarunt viri praestantissimi, cum caeteia illius errata castigarent: ἱππεῖς δὲ αὐτῶν ὠνόμαζον [?], ἀλλ' ὁ δωδεκάδραχμος [?] εἶπε [?] αὐτῶν ἐκ [?] ἵππων, ἕκαστος αὐτῶν τρέφειν. ποσὸν δὲ ὁ μὲν ποιητὴς χ. τὸν ἀριθμόν. οὔτε δὲ μὴ ζῶντα τῆς πόλεως πληθωρίσεως, ἐλλοῦντο ἀξιώσει ποιεῖς τὰς χιλίας. Quod ad hunc Equitum numerum attinet, confundit viros Equestris census cum Equitibus, qui lecti ad bellum: Hi quippe qui militarent tot erant, primum sexcenti, deinde mille, demum mille ducenti: At non plures fuisse Equestris census, & ordinis in tantum ciuium numero, vix mihi persuadeo. Inter hos autem Equestris census vere Equites, qui habebant equum publicum, id est, quibus nullo bello data e publico pecunia ad alendum equum. Vlpianus: καὶ γὰρ καὶ οἱ ἐκ τῆς μισθῶν ἱππεῖς [?] ἐλάμβανον δὲ ἐξ Εἰρωνὴν ὑπὸ τῆς τρέφειν εἰς ἵππους. Poterant autem, pro census modulo, ex vno in alium ailegi ordinem, cuius rei illustre legitur exemplum apud Pollucem Libro VIII. cap. X. de Anthemione Diphili Filio, qui in Equitum ordinem ex illo Proletariorum adlectus est: Ἀνθεμίων δὲ ὁ Διφίλου κωμῳδοποιὸς [?] δὲ ὑπογράμματος, ἐπὶ τὸ τῶν Θητικῶν τέλεις εἰς τὴν ἱππάδα μετέστη, καὶ εἰκὼν ἔστιν ἐν Ἀκροπόλει, ἵππους αἰδοῖ πρέσχηκώς, καὶ ὁ ὑπογεγραμμένος [?]. Διφίλου Ἀνθεμίων τὸν δ' ἵππον ἔκτισε [?] εἰς ἀθήναι, Θητικοῦ ἀντὶ τέλεις Ἱππάδ' ἐμείλαλλον [?].
units.tr: In Plutarch's Life of Solon you have: Solon divided the citizens by property into four classes, and those who had five hundred measures of produce, dry and liquid, he placed in the first class, as he had ordained, and called them Pentacosiomedimni; those who could keep a horse, or who had three hundred measures, he placed among the knights, and called them so; the Zeugitae were those who had two hundred measures and were thought fit for a middle rank; and the rest were called Thetes, to whom he gave no share in the magistracies, only the right to attend the assembly and to sit in judgment. [Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 10, on the same classes: the Pentacosiomedimni, the Knights, the Zeugitae and the Thetic class (the text here is partly illegible).] So, according to the amount of each man's property, this division was made: the Pentacosiomedimni paid a talent to the Republic, the Knights half a talent, the Zeugitae ten minae, and the Proletarii nothing at all. But the error of the scholiast on Aristophanes must not pass without remark, which those most distinguished men did not notice when they corrected his other mistakes: [the Greek is largely illegible; the scholiast is taken to have wrongly identified the knights with the cavalry, and to have confused the equestrian property class with the knights who were enrolled for war]. Indeed, those enrolled for war were of such number that they were at first six hundred, then a thousand, and finally twelve hundred; but I can hardly believe there were so many citizens of the equestrian property class and order in addition. Among these, however, were the true Equites, who had a public horse, that is, those to whom public money was given in war for feeding a horse. Ulpian: [Greek, partly illegible; the Equites received money from the public treasury for feeding horses]. They could, according to the measure of their property, be moved from one order into another, and a famous example of this is found in Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 10, concerning Anthemion, son of Diphilus, who was transferred from the class of the Proletarii into the order of the Knights: [Greek, partly illegible: Anthemion, the son of Diphilus the comic poet, moved from the rank of the Thetes into the equestrian class, and there is a statue of him on the Acropolis, a horse having been granted to him by reason of his merit; and he was enrolled among the Knights in place of the Thetes.]

units.la: Proletarios autem è Solonis Lege nullum gessisse Magistratum, constat è laudatis Plutarchi & Pollucis verbis, quod idem testatum reliquit Aristoteles in Athenienfium Republica: Θῆτες δὲ ὁ ἀπαλλαγμένος μετέχειν ἀρχῆς, ὡς καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης διηλθε ἐν Ἀθηναίων Πολιτείᾳ. Neque tamen Proletarios omnium omnino partium Reipublicae expertes esse voluit Solon, nam & cum ceteris in concione sua illos ferre suffragia voluit, atque inter iudices adlegi.
units.tr: That the Proletarii were barred from every magistracy by Solon's law is clear from the words of Plutarch and Pollux already quoted, and Aristotle also left the same testimony in his Constitution of the Athenians: the Thetes were excluded from sharing in office, as Aristotle also explained in the Athenian Constitution. Yet Solon did not wish the Proletarii to be wholly excluded from every part of the Republic, for he also wished them to cast their votes with the others in his assembly, and to be enrolled among the judges.

units.la: Τοὺς Θήτας ἐκκλησιάζειν, καὶ δικάζειν. Proletarij in concione suffragia sua ferunto, & inter iudices legantor.
units.tr: [Greek: The Thetes shall attend the assembly and sit in judgment.] The Proletarii shall cast their votes in the assembly, and be chosen as judges.

units.la: Habes apud Plutarchum loco laudato: οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ πάντες ἐκκλησιῶν Θῆτες, οἷς ἀπονέμειν ἀρχὴν ἔδωκεν ἀρχήν, ἀλλὰ ὁ σωεκκλησιάζειν καὶ δικάζειν, μόνον μετέχειν τῆς πολιτείας. ut haberent unde viverent: nam οἱ Δικασταὶ ἐλάμβανον μισθόν. Quanquam autem primo hoc videretur leue, maximae tamen fuit auctoritatis, quippe penes illos omnium fere rerum fuit arbitrium: siue quia à Magistratibus ad iudices dabatur prouocatio. Plutarchus ibidem: τὰ γὰρ πλεῖστα τῆς ἀξιοφορᾶς εἰσπράττειν εἰς τοὺς δικαστάς. καὶ γὰρ ὅσα ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐτάξε χρίνειν. ἡμίας καὶ σὺ ἐκείνων εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον ἐφιστὰς ἔδωκε τῆς βουλομένοις, siue quia summum ius penes concionem populi fuit: & certè nisi has saltem partes Reipublicæ attigissent, vix ac ne vix quidem inter ciues fuissent censendi: nam, vt est apud Aristotelem Politic. Libro III. πολίτης ἁπλῶς ὁρᾶσθαι τὴν ἄλλων ἐείζεται μᾶλλον, ἢ τὰς μετοχὰς χρίσεως καὶ ἀρχῆς.
units.tr: You have it in Plutarch, in the passage cited: all the rest, the Thetes, to whom he gave no office, but only the right to attend the assembly and to sit in judgment, and so share in the Republic, that they might have a means of living, for the judges received pay. Though at first this may seem a slight privilege, it was of the greatest authority, since almost all matters were decided by them, either because appeals were made from the magistrates to the judges, as Plutarch says in the same place: for most of the business of the state was transacted by the judges, and whatever he had ordained the magistrates should decide, he also gave to these men, to whom the people had granted the right of judging; or because the highest right lay with the assembly of the people. And certainly, unless they had taken at least these parts in the Republic, they could hardly, if at all, have been counted as citizens: for, as Aristotle says in Politics Book III, a citizen is defined rather by his share in judgment and office than by anything else.

units.la: Post Solonis autem tempora mutauit ius istud, nam cum difficillimis temporibus bello aduersus Persas plebs Atheniensis egregiam nauasset afferendæ libertati operam, elata tam prosperis successibus, ab ipsisque animum ducens, instigantibus præterea seditiosis Demagogis & Oratoribus, iuit suo Psephismate, quod vim Legis obtinuit, sublatum discrimen, quod erat inter Proletarios, ceterosque Atheniensis ciues, & nullo discrimine omnes ad Magistratus capessendos admissi sunt; innuit Aristoteles Politic. Libro II. extremo: καὶ πᾶσιν δὲ τὰν ἔπειτα ἐκάστοις τὸν Δημαγωγῶν ἀσεινάζει, αὔξων εἰς τὸ νῦν δημοκρατίαν. Φαίνεται δὲ οὐ χρὴ τὸ Σόλωνος ἡγεῖσθαι τὸ πρῶτος, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἀπὸ συμπτώματος. τῆς ναυαρχίας γὰρ εἰς τῆς Μιλτιάδης ὁ δῆμος αἰτίας ἡγεμόνας, ἐφεγμένης, καὶ Δημαγωγῆς ἐλαβε Φαύλοις αἰτιοπολιτευομένων τὴν ὑπόθεσιν. Psephisma istud est:
units.tr: After Solon's time this law was changed. When the Athenian commons, in very difficult times, had rendered distinguished service in the war against the Persians to secure freedom, they grew proud of their successes and, encouraged by seditious demagogues and orators, passed a decree (psephisma) which had the force of law. It removed the distinction between the Proletarians and the other Athenian citizens, and all without exception were admitted to hold magistracies. Aristotle hints at this in the last part of Politics Book II: "and afterwards, for each of the demagogues, he [Solon's constitution] increased democracy to its present form. It appears that this was not the work of Solon at first, but rather arose by chance: when Miltiades and others had been condemned for treason, and the people took the cause of the demagogues..." The decree reads as follows:

units.la: Κοινῷ τῇ πολιτείας, καὶ τὰς Ἀρχὰς ἐξ Ἀθηναίων πάντων αἱρεῖσθαι.
units.tr: Let the constitution be common, and let the magistracies be chosen from all the Athenians. [Κοινῷ τῇ πολιτείας, καὶ τὰς Ἀρχὰς ἐξ Ἀθηναίων πάντων αἱρεῖσθαι.]

units.la: Ad Rempublicam quinis ciuis accedito, Magistratusque nullo discrimine ex omnibus Athenienfibus eliguntor.
units.tr: Let a citizen be admitted to the commonwealth at the fifth level, and magistrates shall be chosen from all Athenians without distinction.

units.la: Scripsit hoc Psephisma vir cordatissimus Aristides ἐκὼν ἀέκοντι δὲ ἡμῶν, vbi domum redierunt Athenienses è bello aduersus Persas. Plutarchus in Aristide: ἐπὶ δὲ ἀμφοτέρων χρὴ εἰς τὸ ἄγειν τὰς Ἀθηναίους ὁ Αεισίδης ξυνεπαίνων ἐὰν ἐκ πόλεως βαλεῖν τὴν δημοκρατίαν, ἅμα μὲν ἀξίων ἡγεμόνων ἐξ αὐτοῦ πρὸς ἡδονὴν ἐπιμελείας τὸν δῆμον, ἅμα δὲ οὐκ ἐν ῥᾳδίῳ, ἰσχύοντα τῆς ἐπιλοπής, καὶ μέγα Φειδιῶντα τῆς νίκης, ἐκβιαζώμενος, γράφει ψήφισμα, Κοινῷ τῇ πολιτείας, καὶ τὰς Ἀρχὰς ἐξ Ἀθηναίων πάντων αἱρεῖσθαι. Quanquam autem plebi ius fuerit quemuis Magistratum capessere, tanta tamen fuit illius modestia, vt optimatibus volens cesserit vltro, nec Magistratus illos gerat, penes quos rei summa est publicæ. Xenophon de Republica Atheniensium: ὅπως δὲ ταῦτα οὔτως ἔχῃ, δεῖ δίκαιον εἶ παῦσι τὴν ἀρχῶν μετεῖναι, εἰ τι πᾶς κλήρῳ καὶ ἐκ τῆς χειροτονίας. καὶ λέγειν ἐξεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ τὴν πολιτείαν. ἐπειπὲ ὅπως σωτηρίαν φέρειν τὴν ἀρχῶν, γενέσθαι οὖσαν, καὶ μὴ γένεσθαι, ἐν κινδύνῳ τοῦ δήμου ἀπόλυ, τούτων μὲν τὴν ἀρχῶν ἐπιλογὴν ὁ δῆμος μετεῖναι, οὗτε τῆς γραμματικῆς κληρῳ εἰσιέναι σοφίαν χρῆσθαι μετεῖναι, ὅτε τὴν ἰσοπρόχλην. (γιγνώσκει γὰρ ὁ δῆμος ὅτι πλείω ὠφελεῖσθαι ἐκ τοῦ μὴ αὐτὸς ἀρχὴν ταύτας ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐὰν ταῖς δυναστωτάτοις ἀρχὴν) ὁπόσον οἱ εἰσὶ ἀρ-χαὶ μεταφορᾶς ἕνεκα καὶ ὠφελείας εἰς τὸν εἶναι, ταύτας ζητεῖ ὁ δῆμος ἀρ-χεῖ.
units.tr: The decree was written by the most judicious man Aristides, when the Athenians returned home from the war against the Persians. Plutarch, in the Life of Aristides, says: "Aristides, seeing that the Athenians were in two minds, wanted on the one hand to remove democracy from the city, but on the other hand to win the people's goodwill by giving them a share in the government; and since this was not easy, given the people's strength and their sense of the greatness of their victory, he forced the issue and wrote a decree: 'Let the constitution be common, and let the magistracies be chosen from all Athenians.'" Although the commons had the right to take up any magistracy, their modesty was so great that they willingly yielded to the aristocrats and did not hold those offices in which the supreme power of the state lay. Xenophon, in his Constitution of the Athenians, says: "For this to be so, it is right that the people should have a share in the magistracies, to be chosen by lot and by election; and that anyone who wishes may speak on the constitution. For those magistracies which bring safety to the city, if they do not exist, put the people in danger, the people do not take part in choosing them, neither by lot nor by election; for the people know that they gain more by not holding these offices themselves but by leaving them to the more powerful. Magistracies that exist for show and for the people's profit, these the people seek to hold for themselves." [Greek as printed in the source]

units.la: Constabat autem Athenienfis populus in hos ordines distributus, vel ex iis qui aborigines, & indigenæ erant, πολίται φύσει, vel ex aduenis, qui ciuitatis iure donabantur, δημοπόπται, ξένοι μὲν ὄντες τῇ φύσει, τοῦ δὲ τῆς δήμου, τοῦτο, χρὴ ὃ ψήφισμα δήμου πολλῷ γεγυμνασμένοι. de quibus Thesei, Solonis, aliorum Legibus cautum est.
units.tr: The Athenian people were divided into these orders: either those who were natives and autochthonous, citizens by nature (πολίται φύσει), or those who were newcomers and were granted the right of citizenship (δημοπόπται), who were foreigners by birth but were made members of the people by decree of the people, after long training. Laws of Theseus, Solon and others dealt with both groups.

units.la: Ac Thesei quidem ita Lex est,
units.tr: And the law of Theseus is indeed as follows:

units.la: Γᾶν [?] τὰ ἴσα ἔσῃ[?]. Omnes pari iure sunto.
units.tr: All shall have equal rights. [ἴσα ἔστω] Let all be under the same law.

units.la: Sua hac Lege Theseus quosvis aduenas pari cum ciuibus indigenis, si paucissima illa excipias, de quibus iam diximus in praecedentibus, proposito iure Athenas inuitauit, vnde vsurpata praeconij formula, de qua Plutarchus in Theseo: ἐπὶ δὲ μᾶλλον αὐξῆσαι τὴν πόλιν βουλόμενος, ἐκάλει πάντας ἐπὶ τῆς ἴσης [?], καὶ ὅ, ὅδ᾿ ἴτε πάντες λεὼ [?], κήρυγμα Θησέως φασὶ, πανδημίαν [?] ἵνα κλη[?]-σάντες[?].
units.tr: By this law Theseus invited to Athens all newcomers on the same footing as the native citizens, apart from the very few exceptions I have already mentioned. This is why the proclamation formula, which Plutarch mentions in the Life of Theseus, was used: "Wishing to make the city greater still, he called all to an equal share, and proclaimed 'Come hither, all you people'; this, they say, was the proclamation of Theseus, the summons of the whole people..." [Greek as printed in the source]

units.la: Solon vero quendam habuit delectum, neque indiscriminatim quibusvis aduenis ciuitatis ius dedit ἐπὶ τῆς ἴσης, sed iis tantum, qui vel patria in perpetuum exacti sunt exilium, vel Athenas πρόσοικοι commigrarunt artis exercendæ causa:
units.tr: Solon, however, made a selection and did not give the right of citizenship indiscriminately to every newcomer on equal terms; he gave it only to those who had been driven into perpetual exile from their own country, or who had come to Athens with their households to practise a trade.

units.la: Μὴ ξυνεῖναι πολίτας, πλὴν τὰς φύσεως ἀέ[?]-Φυγίας τῆς ἐαυτῶν, ἢ πρὸ ἐσχάτου Ἀθηναῖς μετα-[?]χειρίζουσι ἐπὶ τέχνῃ. Ii soli, qui perpetuum in exilium patria pulsi sunt, aut tota cum familia Athenas commigrarunt artis exercendæ causa, iure ciuitatis donantur.
units.tr: "Let no one share in citizenship except those who have been exiled from their native land for good, or who have come to Athens with their whole household to practise a trade." [Greek as printed in the source] Only those who have been driven from their country into perpetual exile, or who have migrated to Athens with their whole family to practise a craft, are granted the right of citizenship.

units.la: Refert hanc Solonis Legem Plutarchus in eius vita, simulque caufas aperit, quare hanc Legem scripserit, nempe melius animatos fore putauit, si vel propria voluntate impulsi, vel necessitate coacti eo commigrassent. Plutarchi verba sunt: προέχει δ᾿ ἀπελάν καὶ ὁ τῶν Δημοποιητῶν νόμος, ὅπ ἡ ἀπόλιτος[?] ... ὡς ἀπελαύνειν τὰς ἄλλης[?], ὡς ἀπελαύνειν Σύνεις Ἀθηναῖος ἐπὶ βεβαίᾳ τῆς μετέξεως τῆς πολιτείας· καὶ ἅμα πάντες νομιζόμενοι, τοῖς μὲν ἀπολελυμένοις τῷ ἐαυτῶν ἀφὸ τοῦ ἀνάγκῃ· τοῖς δ᾿ ἀπολειπομένοις ἀφὸ τοῦ χωρίου.
units.tr: Plutarch reports this law of Solon in his life and at the same time explains why Solon enacted it: he thought that men would be better disposed if they had come there either by their own choice or driven by necessity. Plutarch's words are: "The law of the Demopoietae (the law on those who make citizens) also stands out, which, ... to drive out ... so that many Athenians should be expelled for the sake of the stability of citizenship; and all were thought to be exiles, the former by their own necessity, the latter by the place of their birth." [Greek as printed in the source]

units.la: Clisthenes vero, qui Pififtratidas Athenis exegit, quibusvis peregrinis aut seruis inquilinis ius ciuitatis concessit : habes apud Aristotelem Polit. Libro III. ἀλλ᾿ ἴσως ἐκεῖνο μᾶλλον ἐχρῆν ὑπάρχειν, ὅσοι μετέχειν, μεταβολῆς γιγνομένης πολιτείας· οἷς Ἀθηναῖοι ἐποίησαν Κλεισθένης μὴ τῶν Τυραννῶν ἐκβολαί. πολλοί, ἂν δ᾿ ἐφυλέττουσι ξένοις καὶ δούλοις μετέχοντες. Optime autem obseruat Aristoteles seruos illos, qui iuris ciuitatis confecuti sunt, fuisse μετοίκους. Nam ne promiscuè omnibus seruis id concederetur, Lege postea cautum, qua vernis denegatum est in ciues posse cooptari:
units.tr: Cleisthenes, who drove the Pisistratidae out of Athens, granted the right of citizenship to all kinds of foreigners and resident slaves. You have this in Aristotle, Politics Book III: "But perhaps it was more fitting that those should share in citizenship who, when the constitution changed, ... the Athenians, after the expulsion of the tyrants, admitted many foreigners and slaves to citizenship." [Greek as printed in the source] Aristotle rightly observes that those slaves who obtained the right of citizenship were metics. For lest this be granted indiscriminately to all slaves, a law was later made forbidding home-born slaves to be enrolled as citizens:

units.la: Τὸν φύσει δοῦλον, ἡμῶν μὴ μετέχειν τῆς πολιτείας. Vernis ius ciuitatis ne danto.
units.tr: A slave by nature shall not share in the citizenship. [Τὸν φύσει δοῦλον, ἡμῶν μὴ μετέχειν τῆς πολιτείας.] Let home-born slaves not be given the right of citizenship.

units.la: Laudat hanc Legem Dio Chrysostomus Oratione XV. οὐκ εἶδε τὸν Ἀθηναῖον, ἔφη, νόμων, ἀλλὰ πολλοῖς δὲ καὶ δήλοις οὖν τὸν φύσει δοῦλον ἡμῶν, οὐκ ἐᾶ μετέχειν τῆς πολιτείας. Negat licere eos, qui serui natura geniti sint, ius ciuitatis Athenienfis adipisci. Seruos natura genitos eosdem non intelligit Legislator cum Aristotele Polit. Lib. I. Philosopho enim οἱ φύσει δοῦλοι ii sunt, qui minus rationis sunt participes, facultate quippe siue naturali potentia & actu definiuntur, vtilitatis atque conseruationis causa, ad parendum sollertioribus: sed ii qui seruis sunt geniti, siue vernæ, intelliguntur: Tres enim sunt modi seruos comparádi, vt docet eadem Orat. Dio: οἱ μὲν γὰρ, ἄλλως λαμβάνονται ἢ γενόμενοι τινὲς, ἢ κλη-ρονομήσαντες, ἢ ἁρπάσαντες, οἷς οἰκονομίας καλῶς. τείης δὲ κτήσεως ἔσπος, ὅταν σὲ πολέμῳ λαβὼν αἰχμάλωτον, [?] καὶ λιποστάμενος [?] τὴν ἔσπον ἔχῃ καταδουλωσάμενος. Lege itaque soli illi Serui οἰκογενεῖς, non alij, ciues fieri vetantur, id est, vernæ, siue seruis geniti in seruitutem, quos Solon in suis Legibus οἰκέας nominabat, vt restis est Ammonius de Differentiis vocum: οἰκότεις μὲν γὰρ, ὁ δὲ τῇ οἰκίᾳ ἀλλαχοῦ ἀφιέμενος, ὃν ἡμεῖς ἀρεπᾶν καλοῦμεν. οἰκέτης δέ, ὁ δοῦλος ὁ ὠνητός. τοῦτο δὲ Σόλων ἐν τοῖς Ἀξοσιν οἰκεῖς κεκλημένους ὁ οἰκότεις.
units.tr: Dio Chrysostom praises this law in his fifteenth oration: "He [Solon] did not see the Athenian law," he says, "but he said that a slave by nature shall not share in the citizenship." [Greek as printed in the source] It denies that those who are slaves by nature may acquire the right of Athenian citizenship. The lawgiver does not understand "slaves by nature" as Aristotle does in Politics Book I. For the Philosopher defines "natural slaves" as those who have less share in reason, being defined by their natural faculty or power in act, for the sake of usefulness and preservation, to serve the more skilful. Rather, the term is understood to mean those born of slaves, or home-born slaves. For there are three ways of acquiring slaves, as the same Dio teaches in his oration: "For some are obtained otherwise than by being born, or by inheritance, or by seizure, which are proper ways of household management; and one way of acquiring is when, having taken someone captive in war, one holds him as a slave." [Greek as printed in the source] Therefore the law forbids only those slaves born in the household to become citizens, not others; that is, home-born slaves, or those born of slaves into servitude, whom Solon in his laws called oikeis, as Ammonius says in his On the Differences of Words: "The oiketes is one who has been released from the household elsewhere, whom we call a freedman; the oiketes is a slave bought for money. Solon in his Axones called the oikeis those called oiketai." [Greek as printed in the source]

units.la: Oportebat autem aduenas, cùm primùm Athenas venissent, aut certè intra breue tempus, ambire à populo ius ciuitatis: idque hac erat cautum lege:
units.tr: Strangers, when they first came to Athens, or at least within a short time, ought to petition the people for the right of citizenship, and this was provided for by the following law:

units.la: Τοὺς ἐξ ἀλλοδαπῆς Ἀθήνησι κατοικεῖν ἐθέλοντας, εἰς πολίτας οὐ χρόνου ὀλίγου ἀφαιρεῖσθαι ἐξελεγχθέντας.
units.tr: Those from abroad who wish to live at Athens are to be admitted as citizens within a short time, if they have been found to qualify. [Τοὺς ἐξ ἀλλοδαπῆς Ἀθήνησι κατοικεῖν ἐθέλοντας, εἰς πολίτας οὐ χρόνου ὀλίγου ἀφαιρεῖσθαι ἐξελεγχθέντας.]

units.la: Aduenae, qui Athenas habitandi ergo commigrarunt, intra breue tempus, in ciues cooptantor.
units.tr: Strangers who have come to Athens to settle there are to be enrolled as citizens within a short time.

units.la: Legem hanc refert Aristophanis Græcus Interpres ad hos Comici versus Ranis:
units.tr: The Greek interpreter of Aristophanes cites this law on the following comic verses from the Frogs:

units.la: βάλεσθε δὴ πῶς κοινῇ σκώψωμεν Ἀρχέδημον; ὃς ἑσθίει ὧν οὐκ ἔφυσε Φέρεσπερ.
units.tr: "Come, let us all together mock Archedemus, who eats what he did not produce, like Hesperus." [Greek as printed in the source]

units.la: Scholiastæ verba sunt: ὁ δὲ Ἀρχέδημος ὡς ξένος πρὸς αὐτὸ καμωδεῖται, ἡμᾶς γὰρ ὧν τοῖς ἀλλοδαποῖς Ἀθήνησι κατοικεῖν ἐθέλοντας, εἰς πολίτας οὐ χρόνου ὀλίγου ἀφαιρεῖσθαι ἐξελεγχθέντας. ὅταν Ἀρχέδημος οὐκ ἐποίησε. διὸ οὖν εἶπεν, ὅτι οὐκ ἐπολι-τογραφήθη, ὥσπερ τοῖς πολίταις ὡσαύτως συγγενεῖς ἦσαν, οὐκ ἔφυσεν εἶπεν· λέγεται οὖν ὅλως χρονίσας δὲ τῆς Ἀθήνας, οὐκ ἰδιωτὴν ἀπαγραφῶν εἰς τοὺς πολίτας. Comici mentem non vidit Interpres, cum hæc intelligantur de relatione Archidemi in tribules, bene sit tamen illius Manibus, qui non est passus nos hanc Legem ignorare. Atque hoc institutum mihi videtur præposter o, quod pace sapientissimi Legislatoris dictum velim, iudicio: Nam, vt diuinitus monet Philosophus Politic. Libro V. cap. III. σταυρωνικὸν δὲ μὴ ὁμόφυλον, ἐὰν εἰ συμπολίτευσιν, neque ciuitas fit ἐν τῇ τυραννίδι πλήθους, neque ἐν τῷ τυραννίδι χρόνῳ. Hinc Sybaritarum, Thuriorum, aliorum, quos enumerare longum esset, clades. Sed Atheniensium Lex ista diu non obtinuit, vt constat è Thucydidis Scholiaste ad hæc verba è Libro I. καὶ πολῖται γεγονότας ἀφ' ὧν ἔδωκαν ἀπὸ παλαιοῦ, ] οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι δ' παλαιοὶ ἀφ' ὧν μετεδίδοσαν πολιτείας · ὕστερον δ' οὐκ ἐπί.
units.tr: The words of the scholiast are: "Archedemus is mocked as a foreigner, for the law says that those foreigners who wish to live at Athens shall, if convicted, be deprived of citizenship after a short time. Since Archedemus did not do so, the comic poet says that he was not enrolled as a citizen, just as he was not born of citizens; he has therefore stayed in Athens a long time without being entered on the citizen rolls as a private person." The interpreter has not grasped the poet's meaning, since these words are understood of Archedemus' enrolment in the tribes; yet he deserves thanks for making us aware of this law. This institution seems to me ill-advised, though I say this with respect for the wisest of lawgivers, for, as the Philosopher divinely warns in Politics Book V, chapter 3: a state is not made up of people not of one kin, if they share citizenship, nor does it exist in a long time of tyranny. Hence the ruin of the Sybarites, the Thurians and others, which would take too long to list. But this Athenian law did not hold good for long, as is clear from the scholiast on Thucydides on these words from Book I: "and having become citizens from those to whom they had long given the right..." The Athenians of old, from whom they used to grant citizenship, later did not.

units.la: Infecutis postea temporibus Leges sunt, ne ciuitate Atheniensi donarentur, nisi διεργεσιῶντες τῷ πόλιν,
units.tr: In later times laws were passed that no one should be made an Athenian citizen unless (the Greek fragment is unclear: διεργεσιῶντες τῷ πόλιν).

units.la: Μὴ ἐξεῖναι ποιήσασθαι Ἀθηναῖον, οὐ ἀν μὴ δὴ αἰσθαγαθίας εἰς τὸ δῆμον τῆς Ἀθηναίων, ἄξιον ἢ ἡλικίας πολιτείας, ἐπὶ ἐπιδοῦ πειθῆ ὁ δῆμος, καὶ δῶ τῷ δωρεᾷ, μὴ χωρίαν ἡλικίας τῷ ποίησιν, ἐὰν μὴ τῇ ψήφῳ εἰς τὸ ἐπὶ τῷ σὺν ἐκκλησίαν ἐξαιρεῖ Ἀθηναῖοι ψηφίσασθαι χρύσεον ψηφιζόμενοι.
units.tr: "It shall not be permitted to make a man an Athenian citizen unless he has been granted a benefit to the Athenian people, worthy of citizenship, by a decree of the people, and unless the vote has been taken in the assembly by the Athenians, six thousand having voted, and in a secret ballot" [Μὴ ἐξεῖναι ποιήσασθαι Ἀθηναῖον, οὐ ἀν μὴ δὴ αἰσθαγαθίας εἰς τὸ δῆμον τῆς Ἀθηναίων, ἄξιον ἢ ἡλικίας πολιτείας, ἐπὶ ἐπιδοῦ πειθῆ ὁ δῆμος, καὶ δῶ τῷ δωρεᾷ, μὴ χωρίαν ἡλικίας τῷ ποίησιν, ἐὰν μὴ τῇ ψήφῳ εἰς τὸ ἐπὶ τῷ σὺν ἐκκλησίαν ἐξαιρεῖ Ἀθηναῖοι ψηφίσασθαι χρύσεον ψηφιζόμενοι] (the Greek as printed is corrupt).

units.la: Atheniensium ciuitate nemo nisi de ea bene meritus donator. Donum populi ratum non esto, nisi sequenti concione plus quam sex mille Athenienses latis clanculum suffragijs id sciuerint.
units.tr: No one shall be made a citizen of Athens except one who has deserved well of it. A gift of the people shall not stand unless, at the next assembly, more than six thousand Athenians have secretly confirmed it by their votes.

units.la: Τοὺς δὲ Πρυτάνεις πὰς κλίσεως, καὶ τὸ [?] ἀφεῖναι ἀπὸ [?] τῶν ξένων, ὁ [?] ἐκ [?] [?], ὅτις ἂν ὁ δῆμος [?] τῶν [?] [?] [?] [?] ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας [?] [?] [?] ἕνα [?] ἀπὸ [?] [?] [?] [?] καὶ ἐκ τούτων ἐξιέναι, καὶ ὅσοι ἐκ γυναικὸς αὐτῶν ἐγένοντο [?] τὴν νόμον.
units.tr: "The prytanes shall ... of the strangers, ... whoever the people ... in the assembly ... and from these shall go out, and as many as were born of their wives ... the law." [Τοὺς δὲ Πρυτάνεις πὰς κλίσεως, καὶ τὸ [?] ἀφεῖναι ἀπὸ [?] τῶν ξένων, ὁ [?] ἐκ [?] [?], ὅτις ἂν ὁ δῆμος [?] τῶν [?] [?] [?] [?] ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας [?] [?] [?] ἕνα [?] ἀπὸ [?] [?] [?] [?] καὶ ἐκ τούτων ἐξιέναι, καὶ ὅσοι ἐκ γυναικὸς αὐτῶν ἐγένοντο [?] τὴν νόμον.] (the text is too damaged to recover fully).

units.la: Prytaneis cados destituunto, & accedenti populo calculos danto, antequam peregrini, de quibus agitur, ad populum accedant, & clypeos offerant. Adscitiij autem isti ciues ne Nouemviratum soruntur, aut Sacerdotium Vllum. Id tamen ius esto eius liberis, matre ciue, & secundum Leges desponsata, natis.
units.tr: The prytanes shall set out the urns, and give pebbles to the people as they approach, before the foreigners in question come forward to the people and offer their shields. These adopted citizens, however, shall not be eligible for the board of Nine, nor for any priesthood. This right, nevertheless, shall belong to their children, if born of a citizen mother and lawfully betrothed.

units.la: Descripsit istam Legem Demosthenes, aut quisquis ille est, qui scripsit Orationem [illegible, ~12 letters] Νεαίρας, & explicat satis suse: [illegible, ~20 letters] A Ϲ [illegible, ~10 letters], μὴ [illegible, ~12 letters], ἐκ [illegible, ~8 letters] A Ϲ [illegible, ~10 letters]. Dicitur ὁ νόμος κείμενος τοῦ δήμου, quia ciuitas nisi plebiscito non poterat dari, idque benemeritis de ea: vnde de Pasione dicitur hac Oratione primore: [illegible, ~24 letters] A Ϲ [illegible, ~6 letters] Παϲίων, καὶ ἐκγόνοις [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐκ [illegible, ~8 letters] πόλιν. Iraque δημοπέπλης à iuris Attici Consultis dicitur πολίτης [illegible, ~8 letters] ψηφισμάτων τῆς δήμου. Sequitur in Lege , siquidem persuasum fuerit populo Atheniensi aliquem ciuitate donare, ratam non esse eam nisi [illegible, ~6 letters], nisi sequenti concione Atheniensium plus quam sex millia clam suffragia tu-lerint.sua: ἐπὶ ἐπιψηφίσῃ [illegible, ~10 letters] δὲ τῶν δήμου, [illegible, ~14 letters] τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν, [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐπὶ [illegible, ~8 letters], ἐὰν μὴ τὸ ψῆφος ἐκ τῶν ἐπὶ [illegible, ~8 letters] ἐκκλησίας ἐπιψηφίσαι, ἀπὸ ὑπὸ [illegible, ~10 letters]. Praescribit deinde Legislator modum suffragia clam ferendi: ἐὰν δὲ Πρυτάνεις κελεύσει ἀπὸ ταῖς ξένοις ὁ νόμος, [illegible, ~12 letters] τῶν ψῆφον ἀθέναι προσοίσουσι τῶν δήμου, ὅπως τοῖς ξένοις ἐξιέναι, καὶ τὰ χέρρα ἀπιέναι. In horum verborum expositione multum æstuat Harpocration: [illegible, ~30 letters]. Sed quid mirum, si missus sit in suffragia populus, ὅπως ἀπαμεῖδωσι τὰ ἀσφέρεματα; An non id semper fiebat? Nonne septum cancellis forum, dum suffragia populus ferebat? dum in concione populus? Vnde in Legibus mentio toties septi, in quo conuenerat populus, loci, quo quendam [illegible, ~10 letters] accedere nefas erat, [illegible, ~12 letters]. Verum de his gratiam facimus Grammatico, aliud enim agit. Videntur illi, qui ciuium numero adscribebantur, clypeos dedisse populo. Demosthenes [illegible, ~20 letters] ὁ ἐμὸς ὑμῖν πατρὸς χιλίας ἔδωκεν ἀσπίδας. Nam hos mille clypeos, quos dedit Pafio ciuis factus, opponit impensis ceteris, quas idem Pafio in Rempublicam Atheniensium contulit: ita tamen χιλίας ἀσπίδας, mille clypeos dedit, vt quod mille dederit, Pafionis liberalitati, quod clypeos, Legis necessitati sic imputandum: & certè quemadmodum ὁ τὴν ἀσπίδα ἀπολωλυῖα? erat e Lege ignominiosus, ἄτιμος, id est, non poterat πολιτεύεσθαι, neque ἐκκλησιάζειν, ita contrà adscititius ciuis, Δημοσθένης Αθηναῖος, qui poterat ἐκκλησιάζειν καὶ πολιτεύεσθαι, docebat clypeos dare, vt vel hinc offenderet, se posse ὡς τῆς πόλεως τὰ ὅπλα ληψόμενος καὶ ἐπαμύνειν, καὶ συμβουλεύειν. Ex his pendet Legis interpretatio, cuius sensus est. Debent Prytanes mittere populum in suffragia, antequam hospites, οὐχ ἕνας μὴ ἐκ πόλεως ποιήσασθαι, in concionem veniant, & offerant τὰ ὅπλα, id est, τὰς ἀσπίδας, clypeos, (quos oportebat τὸν Δημοσθένην dare,) quibus sibi populum demereantur, atque concilient: itaque sequitur apud Demosthenem: ἵνα κύκλος ὢν εὐνοίας ἐκείνος, σκοπῶν παρὰ ἑαυτὸν, ὥστε ἵνα μὴ ἐκ πολίτου ποιήσας, εἰ ἄξιος ὅτι τῆς δωρεᾶς ὁ μόνον λαμβάνεσθαι. Vox autem ὅπλα clypeos, eosque Persicos, significat, teste ipso Harpocratione: Ne mireris autem hanc vocem à Legislatore vsurpatam fuisse. Lata enim Lex haec est (quae nihil quicquam ad Solonis illam τὴν Δημοσθένους, quam in superioribus descripsimus,) post fusum Mardonium & victos Persas ad Plataeas, vt constat è sequenti Demosthenis narratione. Hac igitur Lege cauetur, μὴ ἐξεῖναι ποιήσασθαι Αθηναῖον, ὃς ἂν μὴ δι' ἀπόδοσιν εἰς τὸν δῆμον τῶν Αθηναίων, ἀξιον ἢ ἡμέας πολίτῃ. Nullo autem potiori argumento suam ἀποδοχὴν εἰς τὸν δῆμον τῶν Αθηναίων, quam ἀποδιδόντες τὰ ὅπλα, id est, offerentes Athenien-si populo clypeos Persicos, quasi illos Persis infensissimis Athenien-sium hostibus eripuissent. Addit denique Demosthenes: ἐὰν καὶ ὁ δῆμος ποιήσῃ ὁ Αθηναίων πολίτας, ὁ νόμος ἀπαγορεύει, μὴ ἐξεῖναι αὐτοῖς τὴν εἰσέα Αρχόντων ἡμέσθαι, μηδὲ ἱερωσύνης μεταδιδόναι, ἐὰν μὴ ἐκ γυναικὸς ἀσπίς καὶ ἐμψυχῆς τῷ νόμῳ. Adscriptitij ciues participes erant non minus, quàm indigenae Athenienses, ἱερῶν καὶ ὁσίων, sed cum exceptione, nam quod ad ἔτα siue Rempublicam spectat, non poterant sortiri Nouemviratum, quod ad ἱερέα non poterant capi Sacerdotes. Quae exceptio legitur etiam in Pshephismate de adscribendis in ciues Plataensibus, viris adeo bene de Atheniensibus Republica meritis, vt nec ipsis quidem Atheniensibus charitate in patriam essent inferiores. Psephismate extat apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ κατὰ Νεαίρας, quod integrum meretur hic legi
units.tr: Demosthenes, or whoever it was that wrote the speech Against Neaera, set down this law and explains it fairly fully: [illegible]. The law is said to be laid down by the people, because citizenship could not be given except by a decree of the people, and that only to those who had deserved well of the state. Hence of Pasion it is said in the first part of that speech: [illegible] Πασίων, and to his descendants [illegible] the city. Therefore a citizen created by a people's decree is called by the jurists of Attic law δημοποίητος, by a decree of the people. The law goes on: if it has been resolved by the Athenian people to give anyone citizenship, the grant shall not be valid unless, at the next assembly of the Athenians, more than six thousand have cast secret votes. [Greek fragments illegible.] The lawgiver then prescribes the manner of casting secret votes: if the prytanes order it, the officials of the people shall bring the urns for the voters, so that the strangers may go out and the baskets be removed. Harpocration frets much over the explanation of these words. But what wonder if the people were sent to the vote, so that they might remove the shields? Did this not always happen? Was not the forum enclosed with barriers while the people voted? while the people were in assembly? Hence in the laws there is so frequent mention of the enclosure in which the people gathered, and of a place which it was forbidden for anyone to approach. But we grant these matters to the grammarian, for he is off on another track. Those who were enrolled among the citizens seem to have given shields to the people. Demosthenes [illegible] says: "My father gave you a thousand shields." For he sets these thousand shields, which Pasion gave when he became a citizen, against the other expenses which the same Pasion contributed to the Athenian commonwealth. Yet he gave a thousand shields in such a way that what he gave as a thousand shields is to be credited to Pasion's generosity, and the shields to the necessity of the law. Certainly, just as one who had lost his shield was by the law disgraced (ἄτιμος), that is, could not take part in public life or in the assembly, so, on the contrary, an adopted citizen, Demosthenes, an Athenian, who could attend the assembly and take part in public life, showed by giving shields that he could, as one about to take up the city's arms, defend it and advise it. From this depends the interpretation of the law, whose sense is this: the prytanes must send the people to the vote before the foreigners come into the assembly, so that they may not make anyone a citizen who is not worthy, and so that they may present their arms, that is, their shields, which Demosthenes ought to give, by which they may win over and conciliate the people. Accordingly Demosthenes goes on: [Greek fragment]. The word ὅπλα (arms) means shields, and Persian ones at that, as Harpocration himself attests. Do not wonder that this word was used by the lawgiver. This law was passed (having nothing whatever to do with that law of Solon's of Demosthenes which we described above) after the defeat of Mardonius and the Persians at Plataea, as is clear from the following narrative of Demosthenes. By this law, therefore, it is provided that it shall not be permitted to make an Athenian of anyone who has not given himself over to the Athenian people as worthy to be our citizen. No stronger proof of his devotion to the Athenian people can be given than by giving up his arms, that is, offering to the Athenian people Persian shields, as though he had snatched them from the Persians, the most hostile enemies of the Athenians. Finally, Demosthenes adds: "If the people has made any of the Athenian citizens, the law forbids them to enter the office of the archons or to share in the priesthoods, unless they are of a family with a Persian shield, and in accordance with the law." The adopted citizens shared no less than the native Athenians in sacred and holy things, but with an exception: for as regards the state or public office they could not be chosen to the board of Nine, and as regards the priesthoods they could not be appointed priests. This exception is also read in the decree concerning the enrolment of the Plataeans as citizens, men so well deserving of the Athenian commonwealth that they were not at all inferior to the Athenians themselves in love for their country. The decree is found in Demosthenes, in the speech Against Neaera, and it deserves to be read here in full.

units.la: ΙΠΠΟΚΡΑΤΗΣ ΕΙΠΕ, ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΥΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΔΕ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΕΝΤΙΜΟΥΣ, ΚΑΤΑΠΕΡ ΟΙ ΑΛΛΟΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΙ, ΚΑΙ ΜΕΤΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΙΣ ΩΝΠΕΡ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΙΣ ΜΕΤΕΣΤΙ ΓΑΝΤΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΙΕΡΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΟΣΙΩΝ, ΠΑΛΙΝ ΕΙ ΤΙΣ ΙΕΡΩΣΥΝΗ Η ΤΕΛΕΤΗ ΕΣΤΙΝ ΕΚ ΓΕΝΟΥΣ, ΜΗΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ, ΤΟΙΣ Δ' ΕΚ ΤΟΥΤΩ, ΝΚΑΤΑΝΕΙΜΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΑΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΔΗΜΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΦΥΛΑΣ ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΔΕ ΝΕΜΗΘΩΣΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΕΤΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩ· ΜΗΔΕΝΙ ΓΙΓΝΕΣΘΑΙ ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΩΝ Μ Η ΕΥΡΟΜΕΝΟΥ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΩΝ. Mendose hic legitur: ΠΑΛΙΝ ΕΙ ΤΙΣ ΙΕΡΩΣΥΝΗ Η ΤΕΛΕΤΗ ΕΣΤΙΝ ΕΚ ΓΕΝΟΥΣ. Nam frustra excipitur ἱερωσύνη [?] πάλιν [?] ἐκ γένους, nam nec indigenae quidè ciues AtheniensES poterant capi Sacerdotes, vbi Sacerdotium erat alicuius gentis aut familiae proprium, nisi de ea gente aut familia essent: Praeterea Demosthenes in sequentibus satisclare explicat, omnia Sacerdotia excipi non illa tantum, quae <bl>ἐν δήμοις</bl> erant. ἐπειτα καὶ τὸν νόμον διωρίσατο ἐν τῷ ψηφίσματι πρὸς αὐτοὺς δήμους [?], ἵνα τε τῆς πόλεως ᾗ τὴν ἀρχὴν [illegible, ~12 letters] Ἀρχόντων λαχεῖν, μηδὲ ἱεροποιῶν μυστηρίας [?], τοῖς δὲ ἐκ Τύτων [?], αἱ ἐξ ἀσπὶς γενα[?]χὰς καὶ ἐπιστῆς τῷ τῶν νόμων. Quare rescribendum puto in Plephismate. ΓΑΗΝ ΕΙ ΤΙΣ ΙΕΡΩΣΥΝΗ Η ΤΕΛΕΤΗ ΕΣΤΙΝ ΕΥΓΕΝΩΝ ΜΗΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ. hoc sensu: Plataeensium nulli in ciuem Atheniensem cooptato liceat vlla obire Sacerdotia, neque vel nobilium vlli Nouem viratum sortiri: Erant enim ciuitatis principes, qui, vt plurimum, Nouemviratum sortiebantur. Adscriptitij hi ciues in tribus, populosque referebantur: vnde habes in hoc Plephismate: ΚΑΤΑΝΕΙΜΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΑΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΔΗΜΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΦΥΛΑΣ. atque hinc explicandus titulus Orationis Lysianae, ΚΑΤΑ ΠΑΓΚΛΕΩΝΟΣ . ΟΤΙ ΟΥΚ ΗΝ ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΥΣ, quod à nobis factum est in nostris MISCELLANEIS. Hinc quoque factum est, vt Pasio <bl>δημοποίητος</bl> ACHARNENSIS dicatur, quia relatus est in hunc populum. Relatos quoque fuisse in varios illos ordines Pentacosiome-dimnorum, Equitum, & Zygitarum, pro censu sui quemque modulo, nullus dubito.
units.tr: "Hippocrates proposed: the Plataeans shall from this day be Athenians, honoured as the other Athenians are, and shall share with them in all the gifts and sacred and holy things which the Athenians share; but if a priesthood or rite is by descent from a family, they shall not hold it, nor any of the nine archons; and the Plataeans shall be enrolled in the demes and tribes; and if they are later wronged, no Athenian shall be allowed to be a Plataean unless he is found by the Plataean people." [ΙΠΠΟΚΡΑΤΗΣ ΕΙΠΕ, ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΥΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΔΕ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΕΝΤΙΜΟΥΣ, ΚΑΤΑΠΕΡ ΟΙ ΑΛΛΟΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΙ, ΚΑΙ ΜΕΤΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΙΣ ΩΝΠΕΡ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΙΣ ΜΕΤΕΣΤΙ ΓΑΝΤΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΙΕΡΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΟΣΙΩΝ, ΠΑΛΙΝ ΕΙ ΤΙΣ ΙΕΡΩΣΥΝΗ Η ΤΕΛΕΤΗ ΕΣΤΙΝ ΕΚ ΓΕΝΟΥΣ, ΜΗΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ, ΤΟΙΣ Δ' ΕΚ ΤΟΥΤΩ, ΝΚΑΤΑΝΕΙΜΑΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΑΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΔΗΜΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΦΥΛΑΣ ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΔΕ ΝΕΜΗΘΩΣΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΕΤΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩ· ΜΗΔΕΝΙ ΓΙΓΝΕΣΘΑΙ ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΩΝ Μ Η ΕΥΡΟΜΕΝΟΥ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΠΛΑΤΑΙΕΩΝ.] The text is badly corrupted here: the passage reads "if a priesthood or rite is by descent from a family", which must be corrected to read "if a priesthood or rite is by descent from a family" as the sense requires; the Greek is printed as found.

units.la: Quanquam autem iteratis suffragiis populi ciuitatis ius fuisset datum, nondum tamen per Leges ita ratum erat hoc donum, vt eo iure non possent iudicum sententia excidere οἱ δημοποίητοι [?]. Nam licebat Lege Atheniensium cuiuis in ius vocare adscitiium ciuem, deque iure ciuitatis illi concesso apud iudices disceptare, vt quod praeter Leges esset datum.
units.tr: Although the citizenship had been granted by repeated votes of the people, the gift was not yet so firmly secured by law that, on the strength of that right, the sentence of the judges could not cast out the newly enfranchised (οἱ δημοποίητοι). For Athenian law allowed anyone to summon an adopted citizen to court and to dispute before the judges about the citizenship granted to him, on the ground that it had been given contrary to the laws.

units.la: Ἐξεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ Ἀθηναίων Παρανό-μων γράφειν τῇ δημοποιήτου γραφῇ, ὡς οὐκ ἀξιός ἐστι τῆς δωρεᾶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἀλλ᾽ τοὺς νόμους Ἀθηναῖος γίγνοιτο [?]. Atheniensium cuiuis ius esto adscitiium ciuem in ius vocare, & accusare, quod praeter meritum Legesque ius ciuitatis consecutus sit.
units.tr: "It is permitted to anyone of the Athenians who wishes to bring an indictment for illegality against the newly enfranchised, on the ground that he is not worthy of the gift but became an Athenian contrary to the laws" [Ἐξεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ Ἀθηναίων Παρανόμων γράφειν τῇ δημοποιήτου γραφῇ, ὡς οὐκ ἀξιός ἐστι τῆς δωρεᾶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἀλλ᾽ τοὺς νόμους Ἀθηναῖος γίγνοιτο]. In Latin terms: let it be lawful for any Athenian to summon an adopted citizen to court and accuse him, on the ground that he has obtained the right of citizenship beyond his deserts and contrary to the laws.

units.la: Refert hac Legem loco iam ante laudato Demosthenes Oratione aduersus Neaeram, & obseruat saepe fuisse factum, vt qui plebiscito ciuitate donati fuerant, Iudicum calculis atque sententia hoc exciderint iure: <bl>ἐπειτα μὴ τῶν Παρανόμων γραφὴν ὁ νόμος ἐποίησε κατ᾽ αὐτὸν (δημοποιήτου) τῆς βουλομένῳ Ἀθηναίων, ᾧ ἔστιν</bl> <bl>εἰσελθόντας εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον ἐξελέγξαι, ὡς οὐκ ἀξιός ἐστι τῆς δωρεᾶς, ἀλλὰ ταῖς τοὺς νόμους Ἀθηναῖος γίγνοιτο</bl> [?]. Cuius rei exempla ibidem leguntur.
units.tr: Demosthenes reports this law in the speech against Neaera already cited, and observes that it often happened that those who had been granted citizenship by plebiscite lost that right through the votes and sentence of the judges. The law provided that the indictment for illegality against the newly enfranchised was open to any Athenian who wished, who, entering the court, could prove that he was not worthy of the gift but had become an Athenian contrary to the laws [ἐπειτα μὴ τῶν Παρανόμων γραφὴν ὁ νόμος ἐποίησε κατ᾽ αὐτὸν (δημοποιήτου) τῆς βουλομένῳ Ἀθηναίων, ᾧ ἔστιν εἰσελθόντας εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον ἐξελέγξαι, ὡς οὐκ ἀξιός ἐστι τῆς δωρεᾶς, ἀλλὰ ταῖς τοὺς νόμους Ἀθηναῖος γίγνοιτο]. Examples of this are read in the same place.

units.la: Ne quis vero, qui Atheniensis non esset, in ciuitatem falso adscriptus obreperet, diligentissime cauebant, lata in hunc finem hac <bl>Διαψηφίσεως</bl> [?] Lege.
units.tr: Lest anyone who was not an Athenian should slip into the citizen body by false enrolment, they took the greatest care, and to this end they passed the law concerning the scrutiny (diapsephesis).

units.la: Γενέσθαι ζήτησιν πάντων τῶν ἐγγεγραμμένων τοῖς ληξιαρχικοῖς γραμματεῖοις, εἴτε γνήσιοι πολῖταί εἰσιν, εἴτε μή· τοὺς δὲ μὴ γεγονότας ἐξ ἀστοῦ καὶ ἐξ ἀστῆς, ἐξαλείφεσθαι [?]. Quaestio de omnibus in ciuium albo inscriptis habetur, vtrum vere ciues sint, necne. Qui vtroque parente ciue nati non erunt, ex albo expunguntor.
units.tr: Let there be an inquiry into all who are enrolled in the registers of the ληξιαρχικὰ γραμματεῖα [lexiarchika grammateia], whether they are genuine citizens or not; those who were not born of a citizen father and a citizen mother are to be struck off [?]. An inquiry is held into everyone entered on the citizen roll, whether they really are citizens. Those not born of two citizen parents are expunged from the roll.

units.la: ἀποψηφίζεσθαι δὲ αὐτὸ πάντων τοὺς δημότας, καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἀποψηφισθέντας καὶ ἐμμένειν τὴν ψῆφον τῆς δημοτῶν, ὀξαλαλίσθαι, καὶ τοὺς μετοίκους· τοὺς δὲ βουλομένους ἐφέσιν εἰς δικαστὰς ἀδοῦναι, καὶ μὴ ἀλῶσι, καὶ τὸ τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, πωλεῖσθαι. ἐὰν δὲ ἀποφύγωσι, εἰς πολίτας. [?]
units.tr: The demesmen themselves are to vote on all of them. Those who are rejected, and whose rejection the demesmen's vote confirms, are struck off, and likewise the metics. Those who wish may appeal to the jurors, and if they are not convicted, the court sells them. If they are acquitted, they become citizens. [ἀποψηφίζεσθαι δὲ αὐτὸ πάντων τοὺς δημότας, καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἀποψηφισθέντας καὶ ἐμμένειν τὴν ψῆφον τῆς δημοτῶν, ὀξαλαλίσθαι, καὶ τοὺς μετοίκους· τοὺς δὲ βουλομένους ἐφέσιν εἰς δικαστὰς ἀδοῦναι, καὶ μὴ ἀλῶσι, καὶ τὸ τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, πωλεῖσθαι. ἐὰν δὲ ἀποφύγωσι, εἰς πολίτας.]

units.la: Populares de suis popularibus iudicium ferunto. A popularibus damnati peregrinitatis, neque ad iudices prouocantes, expunguntor, & in censum inquilinorum referuntur. Prouocatio ad popularibus ad iudices datur. Damnati ad iudicibus venduntur. Si secundum illos iudices pronuntiarint, cines censen-tur.
units.tr: Let the demesmen pass judgment on their own fellow demesmen. Those condemned by the demesmen as not really citizens, and who do not appeal to the judges, are expunged and entered among the resident aliens. An appeal from the demesmen to the judges is allowed. Those condemned are sold by the judges. If the judges pronounce in their favour, they are counted as citizens.

units.la: Habes hanc Legem in Hypothesi Orationis Demosthenicæ πρὸς ΕΥΒουλίδην Εφέσιος. γράφεται νόμος περὶ Ἀθηναίοις, ἀρισταν ζήτησιν, & cætera, quæ iam hic habes. Fiebat hæc Διαψήφισις à Popularibus. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. VI. διαψήφισις δὲ ὧν, ὅ τοὺς δημότας τῶν ψῆφον ... [?] ... δικαιωμάτων ἐκβλη-χῶν. Harpocration: Διαψήφισις ἰδίως λέγεται ὅτι τὴν ὡς τὰς δήμους ἐξεπίσων, ἐὰν γίνονται ἐκ ἐκείνου τὴν δημοτελομένων, εἰ τις ἐστι πολίτης καὶ δημότης ἐστιν, ἢ ἀποψηφισθέντα, ξένος ὤν. Vlpianus ad Orationem Demosthenis de Corona: γινομένων δὲ τῶν κεκλημένων Διαψηφίσεων, ὅ ὅστιν ἐξεπάσιον ὁ τῆς δήμου, ὡς ἴσος, εἰ ἀρα φύσει Ἀθηναῖος οὐκ ὢν ἀνέγραφεν ἑαυτὸν, ἐκ ἀπουδῆς ζωῆν, εἰς τοὺς ἀσφῶς. Si peregrinitatis convinceretur, ex albo popularium expungebatur, atque inter inquilinos referebatur: Si ad iudices provocasset, conuictus vendebatur. Suidas: εἴ τις ξένος ἐδόξεν εἶναι ἡ πολίτης, τοῦτον ὁ τῆς Διαψηφίσεως τὴν δήμων ἀποψηφίζοντι οἱ δημόται, καὶ ἐλέγετο ἀποψηφισμένος. εἶτα εἰσῆγετο εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον, καὶ ἐκείνετο ξενίας, ἡ εἰ μὴ ἐάλω, ὑποστρέφακετο ὡς ξένος, εἰ δὲ ἐκφέρει, αἰσλαμβάνετο εἰς τὴν πολιτείαν. Auctor Etymologici: ἐγήμεσε ὁ Ἀθηναῖον ὅτι τὴν ὁ ὁ ἐν τοῖς δήμοις ἀποψηφισθέντων, ἐφάσαν γὰρ αὐτῆς ἐξῶ αὐτῆς εἰς δικαστήριον καὶ τῆς πολιτείας, ἡ εἰ μὴ ἐάλωσαν ἐπωλοῦντο ὡς ξένοι· εἰ δὲ μὴ ἐπεμίσαν εἰς τοὺς ἐξ ὧν ἀξιώσωσιν δήμοις. Iudices autem dabant Thesmothetæ iis, qui à Popularibus prouocauerant. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. VIII. εἰσῆγεσιν ὁ οἱ Θεσμοθέται καὶ τοῖς ἀποψηφισμένοις. Quomodo autem fieret ἀποψηφισις, ostenditur à Demosthene Orat. πρὸς ΕΥΒουλίδην Εφέσιος. Demarchus, penes quem erat ὁ Ληξιαρχικὸν γραμματεῖον, populares suos conuocabat, vnusquisque è Lexiarchico citabatur, si à popularium suorum aliquo peregrinitatis postularetur, testibus, καὶ ὡς γραμματείῳ, (οἱ γὰρ ἀξιωνύμωμι inquiunt veteres ad Aristophanem Magistri, ὡς ξένοι, ὀφείλειν τοὺς ἰδίους πάντας ἐπιδεικνύειν ἐκ τε φρατρίας αὐτῶν ὄντας,) & id genus aliis, (adscititii ciues & eorum posteri præterea è Psephismatibus, quæ publicè adseruabantur.) genus suum, ciuitatisque ius probabat: Ceteri populares iurati ante occasum Solem, quæ suprema erat tempestas, calculum ferebant: ΕΥΒουλίδης ὁ κύριος ὢν τῷ τι ὅρκου, καὶ τὴν γραμματεῖον, ὀξ ὧν ἐσεκάλε τοὺς δημότας, ὅτι ἐπ' αὐτοὺς ἐλεγόντων οἱ δημόται· καὶ τὴν μὲν δημοτῶν οἱ ὁμόσφυτες, ἐχθρῶνῶς ἐπιδῆς ἡ εἰσδημαίνοντος ἠρξάμην· δὲ τῷ Διαψηφίσεως, δίλης ὀφίας, ὥστε οὔ τι ἐδῷ τὸν ἐδαφυλοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὸ ... ἐκκλήτουσσιν τὸ ἴνομα σκαλή, ὅ σκῆπος ἦδη εἶ, ὁ ἠ τὸ ἐξήκοσον. ἡ ἐκλῆθη ὕστερος ἀπόντων τὴν ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ καλοῦντο. ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐκλῄθη ὁ ἡμὸν ὄνομα, ἀδακρύωσα ἐστί, ἐξῆκνοφήμει κατ' ἐμοῦ ἐζὼ· μάρτυρα μὲν ὧν κατηγόρησεν οὐδέν ἐπαγόρευσεν, οὔτε δημότῃ, ὑπὸ τὴν ἄλλων πολιτῶν. Προσεκαλέσατο δὲ τοῖς δημόταις ἀποψηφίσασθαι, ἀξιοῦντος δὲ μου εἰς τὴν ὑπερμίαν ἀπαλαλέσθαι, ἀρά τε τὴν ὥραν, ἡ ὃ μηδέν μου [illegible, ~60 letters] ἀποψηφισμὸς [illegible, ~220 letters] Suidas: οἱ πολῖται συνιάσιν ἑκάστοι [illegible, ~250 letters] ἀποψηφισμός.
units.tr: You have this law in the Hypothesis of Demosthenes' speech against Euboulides of Ephesus: "a law is enacted concerning the Athenians, that there shall be the strictest inquiry," and so on, as you have it there. This scrutiny (diapsephesis) was carried out by the demesmen. Pollux, book 8, chapter 6: the scrutiny is of those whom the demesmen vote upon... Harpocration: "diapsephesis" is used in a particular sense, namely the examination of those who were enrolled in the demes, whether anyone is a citizen and a demesman, or, if he was voted out, is a foreigner. Ulpian, on Demosthenes' speech On the Crown: when the scrutinies were held, which were the examinations of the demesmen, whether anyone who was not by birth an Athenian had enrolled himself... Anyone convicted of being a foreigner was struck from the roll of the demesmen and listed among the resident aliens; if he appealed to the judges and was convicted, he was sold. Suidas: if anyone seemed to be a foreigner or not a citizen, the demesmen voted him out of the deme in the scrutiny, and he was said to be voted out. Then he was brought into court, and he was prosecuted for alienage; if he was not convicted, he was returned to his status as a foreigner, but if he was convicted, he was enrolled in the citizenship. The author of the Etymologicum: the Athenians... for those voted out in the demes were brought before the court and lost their citizenship; if they were not acquitted they were sold as foreigners, but if they were not condemned they were restored to the demes. The Thesmothetae gave the judges to those who had appealed from the demesmen. Pollux, book 8, chapter 8: the Thesmothetae brought the judges to those who had been voted out. How the apopsephisis was carried out is shown by Demosthenes in his speech against Euboulides of Ephesus. The demarch, in whose keeping was the lexiarchic register, summoned his demesmen; each one was called from the lexiarchic register, and if anyone was accused by one of his demesmen of being a foreigner, he proved his descent and citizenship by witnesses and by the register (for the ancient scholiasts on Aristophanes say that those who were challenged as aliens had to show all their people from their own phratry...), and by other such means (adopted citizens and their descendants also proved it from the decrees, which were publicly preserved). The other demesmen, sworn before sunset, which was the final time limit, cast their ballots. Euboulides, who was in charge of the register, read out the names of the demesmen... Further passages from Demosthenes' speech follow, in which the speaker complains that he was called by the demesmen to be voted out, that he brought no witness, and that the accuser's charge was unfounded. Suidas: the citizens gather each in their own... apopsephismos. The rest is too damaged to be read.

units.la: Vtebantur etiam fabis calculorum vicem. Hesychius: [illegible, ~40 letters] ἀποψηφίσεται κυάμοις ἐχρῶντο. albaque fabula signum erant victoriae: οἱ λευκοὶ κύαμοι, inquit in Timocrateam Vlpianus, [?] σὺν ζωῇ, siue foliis. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. V. Φύλλοις δ' ἐψηφίζοντο οἱ ἐν δήμοις δικάζοντες, οἷς ἐπήρξαφον, εἰ τῆς ὡς πρότερον ἐργαστῆς ἐκείνου. In singulos autem ferebantur sententiae, etiam nullo accusante, nullo teste. Æschines aduersus Timarchum. [illegible, ~70 letters] ἀποψήφιστος δὲ τῆς δήμου, ἐ ἑκάστου ἠμῶν ψῆφον δέδωκε τῷ σώματος, ὃς τῆς Ἀθηναῖος ὄντως ἔστι, ἡ ὃς ἀπ' μὴ, ἡ ἐγὼ, ἐπιδεῖ πρὸς τὸ δικαστήριον, ἐ ἀκροάσαιμεν τῶν ἀγωνιζομένων, ὁρᾷ ὅτι ἀεὶ ὁ αὐτὸ ἰσχὺς πρὸς ὑμῖν. ἐπιδεῖ δὲ εἶπη ὁ κατήγορος, ἄνδρες δικασταί, Τούτου κατεψηφίσατο οἱ δημόται, ὁμῶς ἔμπης ὁποῖον δὲ δεῖπνον, ὅτε κατηγορήσατε, ὅτε κατεμαρτυρήσατε, ἀλλ' αὐτοὶ σιωπῶντες δίκας, εἶμαι, ἵνα ὑμεῖς, ὡς ὑ μὲν τὸ κενωμένον τῆς πόλεως. ἴσως γὰρ, εἶμαι, δοκεῖ παρεσκευάσθαι ὑμῖν λόγων σοῦ μαρτυρίας ὅσα τῆς Γραφῆς εἰσὶν ἀσπὶς. Institura primum est haec ἀποψήφισις Archia Athenis Praetore, vt ex Androtione & Philochoro docet Harpocratio. [illegible, ~50 letters] ἀποψηφισμῶν, ὡς γινώσκειν ὅτι Ἀρχίου Ἀρχοντος, Ἀνδροτίων ἐν τῇ Ἀτθίδι, ἡ Φιλόχορος ἐν ἕκτῳ τῆς Ἀτθίδος. Praetura autem Archiae incidit in annum secundum Olympiadis nonagesimae, vt constat e Diodoro Siculo & Anonymo in Descriptione Olympiadum, qui ad hunc annum ista adscribit: αἱ ἀποψηφίσεις, ἵνα αἱ τῶν ἐν δήμοις ἐξεταστῆς εἰσηγήσαντο.
units.tr: They also used beans in place of counters. Hesychius: they used beans in voting... and white beans were the sign of victory: "the white beans," says Ulpian in his commentary on Timocrates, or leaves. Pollux, book 8, chapter 5: those who judged in the demes voted with leaves, as in the earlier fashion. Individual verdicts were given even when no one accused and no one testified. Aeschines against Timarchus: "...being voted out of the deme, each of us gave his vote, a man who is truly an Athenian or not, ...; when the accuser said, 'Men judges, the demesmen have condemned this man,' yet none of you accused or testified, but they themselves kept silent..." For this reason it is thought that they had prepared for you a speech of testimony as a shield.
