Φυσικὸν μὲν, ὅ πολιζικὸν τὸ αὐτῷ ἔχον δύναμιν, τὸ δ᾽ τὸ δίκαιον ἐὰν μὴ · νομικὸν δὲ, ὃ, ἐξ ἀρχῆς μὲν ἴσην ἀμφοτέρα οἱ τῶν ἐὰ δήμος ὅτε δὲ ἡ ἴωνται, ἀμφοτέρα, ἐπ ὅ μιὰς λυσοδοσαι, ἐ ὅ αἴτα ἡ ὑμ ἐν [?] μὴ δύο ποτὲ ἐπὶ ὅτε ἔτι τῶν ἐπὶ ἑκάστα νομοθετοῦσι, ἐ, ὅ ψυ Βεμαιδα, καὶ τὰ ψηφισματωδῶ. Sed quaedam hic sunt observanda: & primum quidem est, ius gentium appellari ab Aristotele δίκαιον Φυσικὸν, ius civile, νομικὸν, & utriusque genus fieri ὅ πολιτικὸν δίκαιον, quia nempe ὁ πολίτης στοιχεῖον καὶ βάλλων ὡς ὁ μὲν [?], ut loquitur Theophilus Institutionum Libro I. tit. II. quomodo etiam apud Iurisconsultos non semel ius gentium dicitur naturale: ita vsurpari puto apud Paulum Libro XXXIX. ad Edictum, cuius haec sunt verba, Furtum est con-trectatio rei fraudulosa, lucri faciendi gratia, vel ipsius rei, vel etiam vsus eius, posfessionisve, quod lege naturali prohibitum est admittere. Lege I. D. de Furtis. Nam hic Lex naturalis opponitur iuri civili tantum; quemadmodum etiam apud Vlpianum Libro LVII. ad Edictum. Probrum & opprobrium, id est, probra quaedam natura turpia sunt, quaedam civiliter, & quasi more civitatis, vt puta furtum, adulterium natura turpe est. Lege XLII. D. de verbor. significat. Ceterum furtum iure naturali ita proprie dicto turpe non est: omnia enim co naturae iure communia sunt: solo gentium iure dominia distincta: agris termini positi: commercium, emptiones, venditiones, locationes, conductiones, obligationes institutae. Lege V. D. de iustitia & iure, ex Hermogeniano Lib. I. iuris Epitomarum. Secundo aduertendum est, corrupta esse Aristotelis verba, quae nonnullis ad hunc modum videtur emendanda, ἐὰν ὅ αἴτα Δικ ἡ Φύσεν, ἀλλὰ μὴ νομικὸν. Quanquam Michael Ephesius suis in hunc locum Scholiis putet ilia non esse exigenda ad vllu antiquum morem, [?]ὃ ὃ ἄρνα [?]ὑῷ, ἀλλὰ μὴ δύο τραγοῖα, οὐχ ὑπὸ ἱερείας ἐλαττίας, tamen nullus dubito eo alludi ab Aristotele; nempe ad haec, de quibus disputamus, sacra. Sacra autem haec fiebant Ioui Φρατρίῳ, Minervae, Ioui rursum Απατουρίῳ, & Baccho Μελαναιγίδι, & hostiae offerri debebant ad certum pondus: eaeque erant, aut oues, aut capra. De ouibus, Scholia Comici verbis iam ante laudatis: [illegible, ~12 letters] Suidas: [?] Μεγαρικὸς [?]. De ouibus & capris, Pollux Lib. III. [?]. Capra, aut ego valde fallor, Baccho mactabatur: coniecturam facio e Bacchi cognomine, Μελαναιγίς. An oues plures immolarentur Ioui Φρατρίῳ, item Απατουρίῳ, & Minervae, id est, singulae singulis, una Ioui Φρατρίῳ, altera Απατουρίῳ, tertia Minervae, plane nescio, qui divinus non sum; ex his tamen, quae descripsimus, Aristotelis verbis suspicamur, duas tantum oues fuisse mactatas: Nam in exemplum [?] adfert vir summus, [?], institutum esse; ne una plus argenti mina in λόγῳ numeraretur. Sequuntur alia de hostiis exempla, in quibus repetenda est [?] vox μνᾶς, siue potius μνᾶν, excidi-tque littera numeralis, quia eadem, meo iudicio, cum victima vocis praecedentis. Referibo igitur: [?], ὁ μνᾶς [?], ἢ ὃ ἄρνα ὗν [?]. Ἀλλὰ μὴ δύο τραγῷ[?] id est, in lytrum una argenti pendatur mina, aut capra mactetur quinquaginta librarum sive minarum pondo: quadraginta octo autem minarum pondo oues duae. An autem duae simul oues quadraginta octo minas pondo pendebant? an earum unaquaeque? Prius verum puto. Atque ex his, ut & illis, quae superius adduximus, Eratosthenis verbis, hanc existimo Legem colligi:
units.tr: To this, in my judgment, belongs the passage of Aristotle, Book V of the Nicomachean Ethics: "Of political right, one part is natural, the other legal. Natural is that which has the same force everywhere and does not depend on being accepted; legal is that which at first makes no difference whether it is so or otherwise, but once it has been laid down, makes a difference [τῷ δὲ πολιτικῷ δικαίου, ὅ μὲν, Φυσικὸν ὅτι· ὅ δὲ, νομικὸν...]." Some points here must be observed. First, Aristotle calls the law of nations "natural right" and civil law "legal right," and each kind is a "political right," because, as Theophilus says in his Institutes, Book I, title II, the citizen is an element [of the state]. In the same way, the jurists often call the law of nations natural law. I think it is used thus by Paul in Book XXXIX on the Edict, whose words are these: "Theft is the fraudulent handling of a thing, for the sake of gain, whether of the thing itself or of its use or possession, which is forbidden to be done by natural law" (Digest, De furtis, law 1). For here natural law is set against civil law only. So also Ulpian, Book LVII on the Edict: "Disgrace and infamy: some things are base by nature, others by civil custom, as it were by the manner of the state; for example, theft and adultery are base by nature" (Digest, De verborum significatione, law 42). But theft is not base in the strict sense by natural right, for all things are common by natural right; only by the law of nations are ownerships distinguished, boundaries set for fields, and commerce, purchases, sales, lettings, hirings and obligations instituted (Digest, De iustitia et iure, law 5, from Hermogenianus, Book I of the Epitomes of Law). Second, it must be noted that Aristotle's words are corrupted, and some would emend them thus: [illegible]. Although Michael of Ephesus, in his Scholia on this passage, thinks these things need not be referred to any ancient custom, nevertheless I doubt not that Aristotle alludes to these sacrifices of which we are speaking. These sacrifices were made to Zeus Phratrios, to Minerva, to Zeus again as Apaturios, and to Bacchus Melanaigis, and the victims had to be offered at a fixed weight, and they were either sheep or goats. Concerning sheep, the Scholia on Comedy, quoted above; Suidas [illegible]. Concerning sheep and goats, Pollux, Book III [illegible]. A goat, unless I am greatly mistaken, was slaughtered to Bacchus; I make this conjecture from the surname of Bacchus, Melanaigis. Whether several sheep were sacrificed to Zeus Phratrios, likewise to Apaturios and to Minerva, that is, one each, one to Zeus Phratrios, another to Apaturios, a third to Minerva, I truly do not know, since I am not divine. Yet from the words of Aristotle that we have quoted, we suspect that only two sheep were slaughtered; for the eminent man brings forward, as an example, that it was instituted that not more than one mina of silver should be counted in the account. Other examples concerning victims follow, in which the word mna, or rather mnan, must be restored, and the numeral letter has dropped out, since it is, in my judgment, the same as the victim of the preceding word. I therefore restore it thus: [illegible], the mina [illegible], or a lamb or a pig [illegible]. But not two goats [illegible]. That is, one mina of silver is to be weighed for the ransom, or a goat is to be slaughtered, of fifty pounds or minas in weight: and two sheep of forty-eight minas in weight. But did two sheep together weigh forty-eight minas, or did each one? I think the former is true. And from these things, as well as from the words of Eratosthenes that we quoted above, I believe this law is inferred:

units.la: Τὸ ἱερὸν μὴ μεῖον εἰσάγειν ἀπὸ [?] τῶν ... [?]
units.tr: That the victim must not be brought in less [than ...] [illegible]...

units.la: Sed quando fiebat haec liberorum relatio εἰς τὰς Φρατρίας? Viri praestantis-simi Carolus Sigonius, Quintus Septimius, Florens Christianus, alij, existimant semel atque iterum inscriptos fuisse: prior professio fiebat apud curiales & gentiles per parentes aut propinquos, qui tabulis inscribendos adducebant aetatis eorum anno quintodecimo: inspiciebantque praesides tunc inscribendorum genitalia diligentius. Triennio post sequebatur professio ad tera[?] & probatio apud populares, anno aetatis profitentium decimo octavo, ac tunc nomina eorundem referebantur in album; quod ληξιαρχικὸν λεῦκωμα vocabant. Sed facile mihi ignoscent magnorum virorum manes; si in eorum sententiam non imus: nam prima liberorum professio & relatio εἰς τὰς Φρατρίας non fiebat anno aetatis quintodecimo, sed longe ante; quanquam non consentiunt veteres scriptores in assignando tempore: nam anniculos relatos in Φρατρίας scribit Auctor Etymologici in Απατουρία. [illegible, ~10 letters]. Tertium, aut quartum annum definit Proclus in Timaeum Platonis: [?] Κουρεωτικῶν [?] εἰς τὰς [?] εἰς τὰς Φρατρίας, πεῖστις ἢ πεῖσις [?]. Vbi prima elementa doctus est Cnemon apud Heliodorum Lib. I. εἰς τὴν Φειδίππας inscribi-tur : habes in patris eius Oratione apud iudices his verbis: [illegible, ~40 letters] m, [illegible, ~30 letters]. Quae aetas incidit, vt videtur, in septimum annum: itaque apud Aristophanem Ranis Chorus exagitat Archidemum, qui necdum inscriptus fuisset τῶν Φειδίππου albo annos natus septem: nam ita exponenda sunt haec Comici verba:
units.tr: But when was this enrolment of children into the phratries made? Most distinguished men, Carolus Sigonius, Quintus Septimius, Florens Christianus and others, think that they were enrolled once and again. The first profession was made before the curiales and gentiles by parents or kinsmen, who brought those to be inscribed on the registers in their fifteenth year of age; and the presidents then examined more carefully the genitals of those to be inscribed. Three years later followed the profession before the tribe and the examination before the populares, when the professing youths were eighteen years old, and then their names were recorded in the album, which they called the lexiarchic album. But may the shades of those great men forgive me if I do not follow their opinion: for the first profession of children and their enrolment into the phratries was not made in the fifteenth year of age, but long before; although the ancient writers do not agree in assigning the time, for the author of the Etymologicum, under Apaturia, writes that one-year-olds were enrolled in the phratries. [illegible]. Proclus, on Plato's Timaeus, defines the third or fourth year: [illegible] of the Koureotic [rites], into the phratries... Where Cnemon, taught his first rudiments in Heliodorus, Book I, is enrolled in the phratry of Pheidippus; you have in his father's speech before the judges, in these words: [illegible]. That age seems to have fallen in the seventh year; so in Aristophanes' Frogs the chorus attacks Archedemus, who, seven years old, had not yet been inscribed in the album of Pheidippus's phratry; for these comic words must be explained thus:

units.la: Βούλεσθε δῆτα καὶ [illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: "Do you wish then, and [...]"  [Βούλεσθε δῆτα καὶ]

units.la: Σκώψομεν Ἀρχέδημον,
units.tr: "We will mock Archedemus,"  [Σκώψομεν Ἀρχέδημον,]

units.la: Ο? ἐπὶ [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐπὶ Φειδίππου.
units.tr: "... on ... of Phidippus."  [ἐπὶ Φειδίππου.]

units.la: Atque ex his colligimus, non eodem omnes aetatis anno inscriptos fuisse [illegible, ~8 letters] apud Φειδίππας, sed pro libito, anniculos, intra tertium annum, intra quartum, sed saltem intra septimum, vt plurimum annum. Non ignoro vitium harum rerum peritissimum exstitisse, auctoritate Pollucis inductum, adulta demum aetate etiam id factum fuisse. Pollucis haec sunt verba: [illegible, ~60 letters] Κουρεῶτιδι κύσεσ, [illegible, ~20 letters] Γαμηλίαν. De Virginibus, inquit vir magnus, certa res est, fieri solitum, cum eas elocaturi patres essent: vnde etiam ἀμμήν facilificium nominatum.
units.tr: From these we gather that the children were not all enrolled in the Phidippi register at the same age, but at the parents' pleasure: some as infants, some within the third year, some within the fourth, but at least, as a rule, within the seventh year. I am not unaware that the most learned men have held that this practice was sometimes followed even when the children were grown up, on the authority of Pollux. Pollux's words are: [illegible]. "Concerning maidens," says that great man, "it is a settled matter that this was customarily done when their fathers were about to give them in marriage; whence the offering was also called ammēn [ἀμμήν] ..."

units.la: Sed confundunt viri magni relationem liberorum εἰς τοὺς Φειδίππας, cum inscriptione eorundem in Ephebororum album, quando nomina sua inter Ephe-bos profitebantur, cuius professionis annus legitimus erat aetatis decimus octauus. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. [illegible, ~50 letters] optime distinguit Aristippus Cnemonis pater apud Heliodorum loco laudato: [illegible, ~70 letters] Cum autem non satis certum aetatis argumentum fumere poterant, solebant puerorum pudenda explorare, an per aetatem ad publica munia, εἰς ὃ [illegible, ~30 letters] Huius [illegible, ~10 letters] meminit Aristophanes Vespis:
units.tr: But the great men confuse the registration of children among the Phidippi with the enrolment of the same persons on the roll of the ephebororum, when they declared their names among the ephebos, and the legal age for that declaration was eighteen. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX, [illegible], distinguishes this well, as does Aristippus, father of Cnemon, in Heliodorus, the passage cited above: [illegible]. But when they could not get a sufficiently certain indication of age, they used to examine the genitals of boys, to see whether by their age they were fit for public duties, [illegible]. Aristophanes mentions this in the Wasps:

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Aristoteles apud Interpretem Comici: [illegible, ~60 letters] Sensus est, e [illegible, ~20 letters] more fuisse explorare adolescentum pudenda, vt e necessitate aetatis aerumpente & pubescente argumentum caperent, puerum illum minorem non esse annis octodecim, (male editur in Aristotelis verbis [illegible, ~10 letters] in.) quare inscribendum esse Ephebororum albo, vt qui Reipublicae suam facile probaturi sint operam [illegible, ~10 letters]. Neque certe Aristotelis hic locus, quo maxime nituntur viri summi, vllo modo poterit referri ad inscriptionem puerorum in Φειδίππου album: nam in his explorari non poterat aetatis aetas, vt e nondum pubescerent: (septennes enim, cum maxime fero, inscribebantur.) nec vlla, quando τοὺς παῖδας εἰς τοὺς [illegible, ~8 letters] Φεσπέγες[?], nulla, inquam, δοκιμασία[?], an essent ad munia publica vtiles, sed tantum an vtroque parente ciue nati essent. Quare hæc referimus ad adolescentes, quorum nomina Epheborum ἐξεπίλων[?] albo debebant inscribi anno ætatis decimo octauo. annum hunc fuisse ætatis decimum octauum probat, quod illi, auctore Solone, qui ἐπειδὴ ἔτη ἢ ἐποίησαν[?], id est, ipsos annos duos, postquam inscripti sunt Epheborum albo, peregerunt, possint ad sua mitti negotia, & testamenti habeant factionem, e Lege scilicet annali, qua is, qui annos est natus viginti, ἤδη τὰ πατρῷα προελαμβάνουσιν[?]. Quare albo Ephebi inscribebantur anno ætatis suæ decimo octauo. Quare autem confundant professionem Epheborum, cum liberorum professione apud τοὺς Φεσπέγας[?], ratio est, meo iudicio, quia vtraque fiebat eadem die, nempe τῇ ἡμέρᾳ[?] Απατουρίων Κουρεώτιδι ἡμέρᾳ, itemque epulum præbebatur τοῖς Φεσπέραν[?]. Atque id errandi causam præbuit Polluci Lib. III. cap. IV. nisi forte labes accessit à mala manu: ἐν δὲ τῷ ἱερῷ[?] οἶνου ὑπόδεσις, οἰνηρία[?] ἐκάλουν[?]. ὁ δὲ ἱερεὺς, ὁ γὰρ αὐτὴ μέλιον[?]. Neque enim vinum offerebatur, nisi cum in Ephebos adscribebantur. Hesychius: Οἰνηρία. Ἀθηναῖοι οἱ μὲν ἐφηβοὶ, ὅταν ἀποχειροτονῶσι τὸν μαλλὸν, εἰσφέρειν Ἡρακλεῖ μέγα οἶνου· καὶ ἐπιστύρτες, τοῖς συνεληλυθόσιν ἐπιδιδόναι[?] πίνειν. ἡ δὲ αὐτὴ ἐκάλουν[?] Οἰνηρία. Athenæus Lib. XI. è Pamphilo: οἱ μὲν ἐφηβοὶ ἀποχειροτονεῖν τὸν σκύλλων, φησὶ Πάμφιλος, εἰσφέρεσθαι παῖ Ἡρακλεῖ μέγα ποτήριον, πληρώσαντες οἶνου, ὃ κληθῆναι Οἰνηρία. ἡ ἀποχειροτονία, τοῖς συνεληλυθόσι δίδοσαν πίνειν[?]. Comam hanc deponebant in Ephebos transcribendi die Apaturiorum festi Courcotide, hostiamque Dianæ mactabant. Hesychius: Κουρεῶ-τις, μηνὸς τῆς πυανεψιῶνος ἡμέρᾳ, ἐν ᾗ τὰς ἀπὸ τῆς κεφαλῆς τὴν παίδων ἀποκείρ-αντες πεῖρας Ἀρτέμιδι θύουσιν. Quæ hostia Κουρεῶν dicebatur, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀποκείρειν τὴν μαλλόν. comam autem non deponebant, nisi οἱ μὲν ἐφηβοὶ ἐφηβὸν, vt loquitur Hesychius, & è veteribus constat. Ergo ista professio longe alia ab ea professione, qua liberi parentibus procurantibus albo τῶν Φεσπέρων inscribebantur, quanquam cum hæc, tum illa, eodem die fieret: vtramque, meo iudicio, coniungit Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. ἀπὸ Φεσπέρων, εἰς τοὺς τῆς τε χωρείας, καὶ τὰς χωρείας εἰσῆγον. καὶ εἰς ἡλικίαν προελθόντων ἐν τῇ καλουμένῃ Κουρεωτίδι ἡμέρᾳ, ἀπὸ μὲν τῆς ἀρρένων ὁ χωρὸν ἐνῆν, ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς Ἐπιλέων τοῦ Γαμηλίαν. Priora spectant inscriptionem liberorum in album τῶν Φεσπέρων. posteriora ista, καὶ εἰς ἡλικίαν προελθόντων, &c. dicuntur de inscriptione in Ephebornm album, itemque puellarum, cùm iam maturæ viro essent: qua in re castigandus est Vir CL. qui pronunciat epulum, Γαμηλίαν dictum, præbitum fuisse τῆς Φεσπέρα, cùm nupturæ essent puellæ, in eamque rem laudat & emendat Harpocrationis verba è Didymo: ἢ Δίδυμος ὁ Γραμματικὸς, ἐν μὲν τῷ Ἰσαίου ὑπομνήματι φησὶν ἑτέρᾳ τὴν Γαμηλίαν τῆς Φεσπέρᾳ δὲ ἀγάμους ἀπολιμπάνων, λέξιν Φασσονίμου, ἐν ᾗ σαφῶς τὴν ἀπόδειξιν τῆς ἐξηγήσεως ἀπέλιμπον[?]. Corrupta, vt putat, initio verba ita rescribit, τὴν Γαμηλίαν τῆς Φεσπέρᾳ ἐπὶ γάμοις διδόμενον. Mendum item est apud Hesychium: Γαμηλία, φέρη εἰς γάμον, τῶν δεῖπνον, ὁ τῆς Φεσπέραν ἐπὶ ὁ γαμῶν. Corrige, εἰς γάμου παρασκευήν. Fiebat enim tunc, cum nupturæ essent. Pollux Lib. III. cap. III. ἡ δὲ ἐπὶ γάμου ἐνσία ἐπὶ τῆς Φεσπέρας, Γαμηλία· ἡ δὲ ἔργον, Γαμηλίας εἰσινεξειν[?].
units.tr: Aristotle, in the translation of the comic poet: [illegible]. The sense is that it was the custom to examine the genitals of young men, so that from the necessity of their age, when they were beginning to grow and reach puberty, they might take the evidence, and that boy was not less than eighteen years old (the word in is badly printed in the words of Aristotle), and so should be enrolled on the roll of the ephebi, since they would readily prove their service to the commonwealth [illegible]. Certainly this passage of Aristotle, on which the very great men chiefly rely, can in no way be referred to the enrolment of boys in the register of the Phidippi. For among these the age could not be tested by the stage of puberty, since they had not yet reached it; for they were enrolled at seven years at the most. Nor was there any test, when the boys were [illegible], of whether they were useful for public duties; the only question was whether both parents were citizens. Therefore we refer this to young men, whose names ought to be entered on the roll of the ephebi at the age of eighteen. That this was the eighteenth year of age is shown by the fact that they, according to Solon, after they had spent two years [illegible] from the time they were enrolled on the roll of the ephebi, could be sent to their own business and had the power to make a will, by the annual law by which a man who had reached twenty years took possession of his paternal property. Therefore ephebi were enrolled in the eighteenth year of their age. Why they confuse the declaration of the ephebi with the declaration of children among the Phespae [Φεσπέγες] is, in my judgement, because both took place on the same day, namely the day of the Apaturia, the Kourotis day, and a feast was likewise provided for the [illegible]. This gave Pollux, Book III, chapter IV, a cause of error, unless perhaps the corruption came from a bad hand: [illegible]. For wine was not offered except when they were enrolled among the ephebi. Hesychius: "Oinēria. The Athenians, when the ephebi had voted to shave their hair, brought a large cup of wine to Heracles; and, pouring it, gave it to those assembled to drink. This was called Oinēria." Athenaeus, Book XI, from Pamphilus: "The ephebi, says Pamphilus, when they had voted to cut their hair, had a large cup brought to Heracles, filled with wine, which was called Oinēria; they gave it to those assembled to drink." They used to lay aside this lock of hair on the day of the Apaturia festival, on the Kourotis day, when they were enrolled among the ephebi, and sacrifice a victim to Diana. Hesychius: "Kourotis: a day of the month Pyanepsion, on which they sacrifice to Artemis the locks of boys' hair cut from the head." This victim was called kourōn, from the cutting off of the hair. But they did not lay aside their hair, except when the ephebi [became] ephebi, as Hesychius puts it, and this is established from the ancients. Therefore that declaration was quite different from the declaration by which children were enrolled on the roll of the Phespae by their parents' care, although both were done on the same day. Both, in my judgement, Pollux joins in Book VIII, chapter IX: "From the Phespae, into the lists of the choreia and the phratries they brought them in; and when they had advanced to maturity on the day called Kourotis, from the males the lock of hair was removed, and from the females the Gamēlia [were given]." The earlier words concern the enrolment of children on the roll of the Phespae; the latter words, "and when they had advanced to maturity," etc., are said of the enrolment on the roll of the ephebi, and likewise of girls, when they were already ripe for marriage. In this matter the very distinguished man who declares that the feast called Gamēlia was given by the Phespae when the girls were about to marry must be corrected; he is praised and corrected for this on the basis of the words of Harpocration from Didymus: "Or Didymus the grammarian, in his commentary on Isaeus, says that the Gamēlia was [given] to the Phespae for marriage, leaving unmarried [...] the word of Phasonimus, in which he clearly left out the proof of the explanation." He rewrites the words, which he thinks were corrupted at the start, as: "the Gamēlia was given to the Phespae for marriages." There is likewise an error in Hesychius: "Gamēlia: a meal brought for marriage, on the day of the Phespae, when the bridegroom..." Correct to "for the preparation of a marriage." For it took place then, when they were about to marry. Pollux, Book III, chapter III: "The feast at the marriage of a girl on the Phespae was called Gamēlia; and the work [...]."

units.la: Hactenus vir eruditissimus, qui etiam in hanc rem loca adferte Demosthenes & Isaeo, quae in sequentibus excutiemus, Deo dante: non enim perfuasimus à Viro CL. epulum hoc praebitum semper fuisse [?]τῆς Φράτρας[?] nuptiarum folenni. Sed diligenter distinguendum est epulum illud, quod dabat virginis pater, ab illo, quod praebebat sponsus: vtrumque appellabatur [?]Γαμηλία[?], vtrumque cum à patre, tum à sponso [?]τῆς Φράτρας[?] praebebatur. De epulo, quod pater dabat, agit Isaeus [?]ἐν τῷ Ὀρέστῃ[?] his verbis: [?]Ἀλλὰ μὴν ὡς γε οὔτε Γαμηλία εἰσπέμπει ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὅτι τῷ ἐμῷ υἱεῖ, ὠ Φαίδρα, ἡμέρας[?], ἡμῖν μὲν... [?]
units.tr: So far the very learned man. He also cites in this matter the passages of Demosthenes and Isaeus, which we will examine in what follows, God willing. For we have not been persuaded by the very distinguished man that this feast was always given at the solemn [rite] of marriage. But that feast which the father of the maiden gave must be carefully distinguished from that which the bridegroom provided: both were called Gamēlia, and both were provided at the phratry, both by the father and by the bridegroom. Isaeus speaks of the feast given by the father in the speech On Orestes in these words: [illegible, Greek].

units.la: Tertia demum professio fiebat apud populares anno ætatis non decimo octauo, vt volunt viri praestantissimi, sed vicesimo: inscribebanturque Lexiarchico, & ab hinc sui erant iuris, mittitque ad negotia poterant. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. [?]ἐπὶ τῆς Λεξιαρχικῆς γραμματείου[?]. Hesychius: [?]Λεξιάρχειον, γραμματεῖον, εἰς ὃ ἐγγράφει[?]. Corrige: [?]εἰς ὃ τὰς νέους ἐγγράφει[?]. Harpocration, Suidas: [?]Λεξιαρχικὸν γραμματεῖον, εἰς ὃ ἐγγράφεται οἱ εἰς ἡμῖν ὑπομείων[?]. Hoc vocant Graeci scriptores, quia tunc in viros transcribebantur: dicitur quoque [?]Δοκιμασία[?], qui huic albo inscriptus est. Grammatici: [?]Δοκιμασάντες[?], ἀπὸ τῆς εἰς ἀνδρας ἐγγραφῆς. & alibi è Lysia ex ea [?]Δημοσθένους[?] [?]ἐπίζησις[?], si titulus auctorem non mentitur. [?]Δοκιμασίας[?], [?]Δοκιμασίων λέγει[?], ὅ ἐστι αὐτὰς ἐγγραφῶν. ὁ ἀδοκίμαστος, ὁ μὴ ἐγγεγραμμένος. Cuius appellationis ratio est, quia prius Lexiarchico non inscribebantur, quam illos constaret natos esse parentibus civibus Atticis, aut secundum Leges adoptatos: itaque populares iurati inscribendum iudicabant Isaeus [?]ἐν τῷ Ἀπολλοδώρου κλήσει[?]. [?]Νῦν δὲ μὴ ἔκλαιεν ἐν τῇ Πυθαΐδι, ἴλεως πρὸς τοὺς δημότας Ἀπολλόδωρος, ὅτι πεποιημένος εἴη μὲ ἡμῖν, ἐγὼ ἐλαγέγραφεν εἰς τοὺς συγγενεῖς ἡ Φράτρας, καὶ ἀλλ' ἀδοκίμαστος...[?] Libanius, Demosthenes & Hypereides, [?]Θεόσυλλον Ἀπολλοδώρου[?]. [?]ὁ μὲν ὡς ἄλλος πεπονθώς[?], καὶ αἰσθοῦ [?]ὑπεὶ[?] καὶ [?]ἐδίκασεν[?], οὐ ἐν [?]αὐτοῖς[?] [?]ἀποθνήσκειν[?], ἐξέλαβε.
units.tr: Finally, the third declaration took place among the common citizens, not at the eighteenth year of age, as the most distinguished men suppose, but at the twentieth. They were enrolled in the Lexiarchikon, and from then on were their own masters, and could be sent to business. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: "in the Lexiarchic register." Hesychius: "Lexiarcheion: a register, in which he enters..." Correct: "in which he enters the young men." Harpocration and Suidas: "Lexiarchikon grammateion: the register in which those who had reached the age of ... are entered." The Greek writers call this [register] that, because then they were transcribed into men: it is also called the dokimasia, and one who is enrolled on this roll is called dokimasthen [δοκιμασθέν]. The grammarians: "having been tested [dokimasantes], from the enrolment among men," and elsewhere from Lysias, from that [...] of Demosthenes, if the title does not mislead about the author. The dokimasiai are called, which is to say the enrollments of these. The adokimastos is the one not enrolled. The reason for this name is that they were not entered on the Lexiarchikon before it was established that they were born of citizen parents, Attic, or adopted according to the laws; and so the common citizens, when sworn, judged that they should be enrolled. Isaeus, in the speech Against the Claim of Apollodorus: "Now, let him not weep in the Pythaïs; be gracious to the fellow demesmen, Apollodorus, since he had been made [a citizen] by us, I had enrolled him among the kinsmen of the phratry, and he is not tested..." Libanius, Demosthenes and Hyperides, [on] Theosyllus of Apollodorus: [illegible].

units.la: Iam vero δοκιμασ-τής[?] è popularium suorum sententia, à Demarcho, apud quem adseruabatur, Lexiarchico inscribebantur, τὰ Ἀνξιαρχικὰ γεγραμμάτια [illegible, ~20 letters], inquiunt veteres Iuris Attici auctores. Huic autem Lexiarchico inscribebantur in viros transcripti ante Panathenæa, primis ineuntis anni diebus. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Λεωχάρην. συναγαγὼν [illegible, ~25 letters] Ὀρνεῶν [illegible, ~10 letters] Δημοτῶν, πείθει, ἐπισεῖδν[?] δυοῖν[?] ὁ γεγραμματεῖον, ἐξελέσθαι αὐτόν. ἐὰν μὴ ταῦτα ἦν Παναθηναίων ὄντων τῆς μεγάλων τῆς ἐξαιρέσεως Ἀρχῶν ὁ Ἰωνικὸν. Quare nè Thrasyllus Apollodori nomine censitus Lexiarchico inscriberetur ineunte novo anno, cauent aduersarij, & populares in suas trahere partes satagunt ξυχαιρετέοις, comitialibus diebus, vt est apud Isæum loco iam laudato, quæ δοκιμασίας Thrasylli præcedebant. Demosthenes quoque, cum Aphobus tutor extremis anni secundi Olympiadis centesimæ tertiæ diebus, Polyzelo Archonte, mense Scirrophorione, vxorem duxisset, Demosthenes, inquam, statim post nuptias togam virilem sumpsit, αὐτὸν εἰς δοκιμασθῆς, vt ipse testatur ἐν τῷ πρὸς Ὀνήτορα α. scilicet anno nouo ineunte, primis Hecatombæonis diebus, anno ætatis suæ vicesimo. Oportebat autem prius εἰς τὰς Φρατρίας relatos fuisse: itaque conqueritur Demosthenes, præposteré factum fuisse à Leochare, τὴν εἰσαγγελίαν [illegible, ~15 letters] εἰς τὰς Φρατρίας πω τῆς Ἀρχάδου, ἀλλ' ὅπως ἐνεγράφη, πεισθεὶς αὐτὰ πίσας ἐνα τῆς Φρατορῶν, ἐνέγραψεν εἰς ὃ Φρατρικὸν γραμμάτιον. & paullo post: καὶ ὡς ὁ τῶν δημοτῶν [illegible, ~20 letters] εἰς τὰς δημότας, ἢ εἰς τὰς Φρατρίας ἐνεγράφη. Accipiebant vero, qui inscribebantur, tabellam buxeam, in qua nomen vniuscuiusque, & paterni quoque populi, ad quem ille pertineret, erat inscriptum. Hesychius: χαλκοῦ, πινακίον. Ἀδιωταὶ εἶχον ἐγκεχος πινακίον πύξινον ἐπιγεγραμμένον ὄνομα τοῦ αὐτοῦ, ἡ τὸ δὴ μου πάτρην. Adoptatus scilicet adoptantis patris nomine ἐν τῷ δήμῳ censebatur: secus enim hic atque apud Romanos fiebat, apud quos, vt constat ex oratione P. Scipionis, quam Censor habuit ad populum de moribus, Adoptio tribum non mutabat: apud Athenienses contra Adoptio tribum ἐν τῶν δήμων mutabat, ita vt qui Eleusinius esset, exempli gratia, ex Hippothoontide tribu, adoptatus ab Alopecense ex Antiochide tribu, fiebat Alopecensis ex Antiochide tribu per adoptionem, & in adoptantis patris tribu, ἐν τῷ δήμῳ, censebatur.
units.tr: Now, the scrutiny (δοκιμασία) was decided by the sentence of the fellow demesmen, and the names were entered on the Lexiarchic register kept by the demarch, where the records were preserved; this is what the ancient authors of Attic law say. Men were entered on this Lexiarchic register when they were enrolled as adults before the Panathenaea, on the first days of the new year. Demosthenes, in the speech against Leochares, after gathering [illegible] of the Ornea [illegible] demesmen, persuades [them] to remove him from the register [...] unless these things were done in the time of the Panathenaea, when the great [...] of the Ionic [...]. Therefore, lest Thrasyllus, enrolled in the name of Apollodorus, should be entered on the Lexiarchic register at the beginning of the new year, the opponents take precautions, and the demesmen labour to draw him to their side on the days of assembly, as appears in Isaeus in the passage already cited, where these things preceded Thrasyllus's scrutiny. Demosthenes too, when his guardian Aphobus had married his mother on the last days of the second year of the hundred and third Olympiad, in the archonship of Polyzelus, in the month Scirrophorion, immediately after the wedding took the toga virilis, and was enrolled for scrutiny, as he himself testifies in the first speech against Onetor. This was in the new year, in the first days of Hecatombaeon, in his twentieth year of age. It was necessary, however, that he first be entered on the phratries; so Demosthenes complains that Leochares acted out of order, [...] into the phratries, [...] but as he was entered, having been persuaded [...] he entered him in the phratric register. And a little later: [...] whether he was entered among the demesmen or in the phratries. Those who were enrolled received a boxwood tablet, on which the name of each person and also of his paternal deme, to which he belonged, was written. Hesychius: "of bronze, a little tablet. The adopted had a boxwood tablet inscribed with the name of the same man, or of his father." An adopted son was therefore enrolled in the deme of his adoptive father by name. For here it was otherwise than among the Romans, among whom, as is clear from the speech of P. Scipio which the censor gave to the people about morals, adoption did not change the tribe. Among the Athenians, by contrast, adoption changed the deme (δῆμος): so that a man who was an Eleusinian, for example, of the Hippothoontid tribe, adopted by an Alopecean of the Antiochid tribe, became an Alopecean of the Antiochid tribe by adoption, and was enrolled in the tribe and deme of his adoptive father.

units.la: Postquam Lexiarchico inscripti erant Ephebi, anno ætatis suæ vicesimo, iusiurandum in æde Agrauli concipiebant in hæc verba:
units.tr: After the ephebes had been enrolled in the Lexiarchicum, at the age of twenty, they took the oath in the temple of Agraulos, in these words:

units.la: Ο ΤΩΝ ΕΦΗΒΩΝ ΟΡΚΟΣ. IVSIVRANDVM EPHEBORVM.
units.tr: The oath of the ephebes. The oath of the ephebes.

units.la: ΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΙΣΧΥΝΩ ΤΑ ΟΠΛΑ ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ, ΟΥΔ' ΕΓΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΩ-ΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ ΟΤΩΙ ΑΝ ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ· ΑΜΥΝΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΕΡ ΙΕΡΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΕΡ ΘΣΙΩΝ[?], ΚΑΙ ΜΟΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΕΤΑ ΠΟΛΛΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΗΝ ΠΑΤΡΙΔΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΛΑΤΤΩ ΠΑΡΑΔΩΣΩ, ΠΛΕΙΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΕΙΩ, ΓΛΕΥΣΩ[?] ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ
units.tr: I will not disgrace the sacred arms, nor desert the man who stands beside me in the line. I will defend the holy things and the sacred things, alone and with many others, and I will not hand over my country less than I received it, but greater and better, as far as I am able. [ΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΙΣΧΥΝΩ ΤΑ ΟΠΛΑ ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ, ΟΥΔ' ΕΓΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΩΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ ΟΤΩΙ ΑΝ ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ· ΑΜΥΝΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΕΡ ΙΕΡΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΕΡ ΘΣΙΩΝ[?], ΚΑΙ ΜΟΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΕΤΑ ΠΟΛΛΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΗΝ ΠΑΤΡΙΔΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΛΑΤΤΩ ΠΑΡΑΔΩΣΩ, ΠΛΕΙΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΕΙΩ, ΓΛΕΥΣΩ[?] ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ]

units.la: Non dehonestabo haec sacra arma: neque deseram protostatem, quisquis ille sit, quem in versu meo excipiam. Pro aris & focis dimicabo, sive solus, sive cum aliis multis. Patriam liberis non relinquā in deteriore, sed potius in meΓΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΑΡΩΣΩ, ΟΠΟΣΗΝ ΑΝ ΓΑΡΑΔΕΞΩΜΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΕΥΗΚΟΗΣΩ ΤΩΝ ΑΕΙ ΚΡΙΝΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΜΦΡΟΝΩΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΙΣ ΤΟΙΣ ΙΔΡΥΜΕΝΟΙΣ ΠΕΙΣΟΜΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΟΥΣ ΤΙΝΑΣ ΑΝ ΑΛΛΟΥΣ ΤΟ ΓΛΗΘΟΣ ΙΔΡΥΣΗΤΑΙ ΟΜΟΦΡΟΝΩΣ, ΚΑΙ ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΝΑΙΡΗ, ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΥΣ, Ἡ ΜΗ ΠΕΙΘΗΤΑΙ ΟΥΣ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΨΩ· ΑΜΥΝΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΜΟΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΕΤΑ ΓΑΝΤΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΙΕΡΑ ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ ΤΙΜΗΣΩ. ΙΣΤΟΡΕΣ ΘΕΟΙ, ΑΓΡΑΥΛΟΙ, ΕΝΥΑΛΙΟΣ, ΑΡΗΣ, ΖΕΥΣ, ΘΗΛΩ, ΗΓΕΜΟΝΗ.
units.tr: I will not dishonour these sacred arms, nor desert the man who stands beside me in the line, whoever he may be. I will fight for altars and hearths, whether alone or with many others. I will not leave my country in a worse state, but rather in a better state [γῆς. καὶ καταρῶσω ὁποσηνοῦν ἂν παραδέξωμαι]: I will curse whoever would betray it. I will obey those who judge soundly at all times, and I will abide by the established laws and by whatever others the people shall establish in common agreement; and if anyone overturns the laws or refuses to obey them, I will not allow it [ἀμυνῶ δὲ καὶ μόνος καὶ μετὰ πάντων, καὶ ἱερὰ τὰ πάτρια τιμήσω]. I will alone and with all others defend, and I will honour the sacred ancestral things. Witnesses, gods: Agraulos, Enyalios, Ares, Zeus, Thallo, Hegemone [ἴστορες θεοί, Ἀγραυλοί, Ἐνυάλιος, Ἄρης, Ζεύς, Θάλλω, Ἡγεμόνη].

units.la: liore statu. Nauigabo aliter-ram, eamque colam, quantulacumque illa sit, quae habenda mihi tradetur. Obtemperabo ijs, qui iudicia reddent prudenter. Parebo Legibus, quae obtinent, ceterisque omnibus, quas populus vnanimi consensu feret. Quod si quis Leges abrogare velit, populo non scisciente, minime feram. Vindicabo autem, siue solus, siue cum alijs omnibus. Patria sacra colam. Testes Dij sunto, Agrauli, Enyalus, Mars, Iupiter, Nutricia terra, Diana.
units.tr: ...a better state. I will sail to other lands and cultivate that land, however small it may be, which is handed over to me to hold. I will obey those who render judgments wisely. I will obey the laws that are in force, and all the others which the people shall pass by unanimous consent. If anyone wishes to abrogate the laws without the people's assent, I will by no means bear it. I will defend them, whether alone or with all the others. I will honour the ancestral sacred rites. Let the gods be witnesses: Agraulus, Enyalius, Mars, Jupiter, the Nourishing Earth, Diana.

units.la: Ταρμαχὴν ἄγει θανάτου τῆς Ἀρεταμι-νης. [?]
units.tr: Ταρμαχὴν ἄγει θανάτου τῆς Ἀρεταμι-νης. [I will fight to the death for the land.]

units.la: Ὅρκις χρήσασθαι τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς, πυρεῖς, κριθῆς, ἀμπέλοις, ἐλαίας.
units.tr: Ὅρκις χρήσασθαι τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς, πυρεῖς, κριθῆς, ἀμπέλοις, ἐλαίας. [I will mark out the boundaries of the land of Attica, wheat, barley, vines, olives.]

units.la: Ad mortem vsque pro nutricia terra dimicabo.
units.tr: I will fight to death for the nourishing earth.

units.la: Fines agri Attici statuam, frumentum, hordeum, vites, oleas.
units.tr: I will mark out the boundaries of the Attic land: wheat, barley, vines, olives.

units.la: Descripsimus hoc iusiurandum Ephebōrum è Stobæo atque Polluce, addidimus duo Kapita, quæ desiderabantur, ex Vlpiano in Demosthenis Orationem περὶ παραπρεσβείας, Philostrato in Apollonij Vita, & Plutarcho in Alcibiade. Atque hoc fuit, vt diximus, iusiurandum Ephebōrum, habes apud Demosthenem Oratione laudata. Καὶ τὸν ἐν τῷ τῆς Ἀγραύλου τὸν Ἐφήβων ὅρκον. Ad quem locum Vlpianus hoc iusiurandum puerorum facit, cum in Ephebos transcriberentur. εἰ δὲ τῷ πειθοῦ τῆς Ἀγραύλου οἱ ἐξιόντες εἰς τοὺς Ἐφήβους ἐκ παιδῶν, μὴ πεποιηκῶν ὤμοσαν Ταρμαχὴν ἄγει θανάτου τῆς Ἀρεταμι-νης. [?] At vero contra, Ephebōrum iusiurandum est, cum in viros transcriberentur: Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. Καὶ εἰς μὲν τοὺς Ἐφήβους εἰσῆσαν ὀκτωκαιδέκα ἔτη γυμνάζομαι, δύο δὲ εἰς Γερεπόλεις ἐπεδιμαῖοντο. εἰκοσὶ δὲ ἀπεγράφοντο τῷ Ληξιαρχικῷ γραμματείῳ ἢ ὤμυον ἐν Ἀγραύλου. ΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΙΣΧΥΝΩ ΤΑ ΟΠΛΑ, &c. Neque id tantum Pollux testatur, sed ex ipso etiam liquet iureiurando. Nam Ephebi, antequam in viros transcriberentur, custodes publice erant Διαπεφυλακότες ἐν τοῖς Ἀττικῆς Φυλακτηρίοις, non autem instructæ in aciem educebantur Ephebōrum copiæ, aut peregre extra terram Atticam mittebantur. Hi vero, qui hoc iureiurando se obstringunt, & instructi in aciem educuntur, nam in eo hæc legis. ΟΥΔ' ΕΓΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΓΡΩΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ ΟΤΩΙ ΑΝ ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ. Neque deseram potestatem, quisquis ille sit, quem in versu meo excipiam. itémque peregre mittuntur: ΓΛΕΥΣΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ ΓΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΑΡΩΣΩ ΟΠΟΣΗΝ ΑΝ ΓΑΡΑΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ. Nauigabo in terram, siue regionem, eamque colam, quantulacumque illa sit, quae habenda mihi tradetur.
units.tr: I have copied this oath of the Ephebi from Stobaeus and Pollux, and added two chapters which were wanting, from Ulpian on Demosthenes' speech On the False Embassy, from Philostratus in the Life of Apollonius, and from Plutarch in the Alcibiades. This, as I said, was the oath of the Ephebi; you have it in the speech of Demosthenes already cited: "and the oath in the temple of Agraulus of the Ephebi." On this passage Ulpian makes this the oath of the boys, when they were being transferred to the Ephebi. [...] But on the contrary, the oath of the Ephebi was taken when they were transferred to men. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: "And they entered the Ephebi at eighteen years of age, having trained for two years, and at twenty they were entered on the Lexiarchic register, or took the oath in the temple of Agraulus. I will not dishonour the arms," etc. Pollux does not merely attest this, but it is also clear from the oath itself. For the Ephebi, before they were transferred to men, were publicly guarded in the Attic fortresses, and were not led out to battle as an organised force, nor sent abroad outside Attic territory. Those who bind themselves by this oath, however, are led out in battle array, for the law says in it: "I will not desert the man beside me in the line, whoever he may be." And likewise they are sent abroad: "I will sail to other lands and cultivate that land, however small it may be, which is handed over to me to hold." [Greek as above.]

units.la: Addequod hoc iusiurandum ita concipitur, vt non possis non pronunciare, illius esse, qui sui iam sit iuris. Atqui Ephebi ante annum ætatis vicesimum fui non erant iuris. Quare dicendum est, fuisse Ephebor um, cum anno ætatis vicesimo in viros transcriberentur. Concipiebatur autem iusiurandum istud in æde Agrauli Cecropis filiæ: claret è iam laudatis Pollucis, Vlpiani, Demosthenis verbis: Philochorus item: ἡ τῶν Ἀγραύλου ἐχίσσα αὐτῇ ἐξέδωκε εἰς θάνατον, ἐῤῥίψατο δὲ ἑαυτὴν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως· εἶτα ἀπαλλαγῆναι τῆς πόλεμου, ἱερὸν ἐπὶ Ζεύς ἐστήσατο αὐτῇ, ὡς τὰ ἱερὰ ἐπὶ τῆς Ἀκρο-πόλεως, ἡ εὐθὺς ὑμνοῦσιν οἱ Ἐφηβοι μέλλοντες ὀμνύναι εἰς πόλεμον. item Philostratus in Apollonij Vita Lib. IV. cap. VII. vt optime emendat CL. Meursius: οἱ πάλαι μὲν ὀμνυοντο εἰς Ἀγραύλου φυλακήν, ὡς τῆς παιδείας ἀποδιυσάσθαι, ἡ ὅπλα ἔχοντες. Huic Agraulo sacra ab Atheniensibus facta, initiaque instituta. Athenagoras: ἡ Ἀγραύλῳ Ἀθηναῖοι ἡ πόλεως ἐμυήσαντο ἀγνῶς. Eaque videntur celebrata mense Hecatombæone, atque per illa Ephebi, qui inscripti iam erant Lexiarchico, iusiurandum istud iurabant? in quo nonnulla sunt aducertenda. ΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΙΣΧΥΝΩ ΤΑ ΟΠΛΑ ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ. Non dehonestabo hæc sacra arma. Quando hoc iuramentum iurabant Ephebi, armis erant instructi. Vlpianus verbis iam ante laudatis: οἱ δὲ τῆς τιμῆς τῆς Ἀγραύλου οἱ ἐξιόντες εἰς πὺς Ἐφήβους ἐκ παίδων, μὴ πάντοτε ἄλλην ὁμνύειν ἐκ ἀμαχαῖν ἀχρὶ θανάτου τῆς Ἀθηναίων. Armis his, auspicandi causa, instruebantur, itaque, quæ mea est coniectura, arma iuipsa æde Agrauli adseruabantur, & ex illa tanquam armamentario depromta iuraturi induebant; quare etiam hæc arma sacra dicuntur, ΤΑ ΟΠΛΑ ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ. Apud Polyænum Strategematum Lib. I. in Pisistrato, de eius satellitibus: οἱ ὑπλισμένοι ἐπεσελήλυθτες, καὶ τὰ ὅπλα ἀφελόμενοι, κατ' ἀνδρὸς εἰς Ὁ ἱερὸν τῆς Ἀγραύλου, quod huc, meo iudicio, facit, nam arma illic adseruata, pro more scilicet: Sequitur in iuramento. ΟΥΔ' ΕΓΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΩΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ ΟΤΩΙ ΑΝ ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ. Neque deseram protostaten, quisquis ille sit, quem in versu meo excipiam. ita hunc locum emendavimus, cum apud Pollucem edatur, ΟΥΔΕ ΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ Ω ΑΝ ΤΥΧΩ. MS. Pollucis repræsentat ΣΤΟΙΧΩ αὐτὴ τῆς ΤΥΧΩ. In Stobæi Collectaneis legitur. ΟΥΔ' ΕΓΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΓΑΡΑΣΤΑΤΗΝ ΟΤΩΙ ΑΝ ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ. Sed rescribendum omnino est ΤΟΝ ΓΡΩΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ. quod verbum ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ, plane euincit: nam in acie instruenda ὃ ὃ βάθος τοῖχος κλᾶσαι. καὶ ὃ μὲν ἐφεξῆς εἰς τὸ μῆκος, ζυγὸν. ὃ δὲ ἐφεξῆς τῷ βάθος τοιχὸν. Itaque legendum est; ΤΟΝ ΓΡΩΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ. Nam ἀκρόστατος κλᾶσαι πᾶς ὁ ζυγῶν, inquit Ælianus in Tacticis: ἡ ὁ μὲν τῆς λοχαγοῦ ὁπίσω πεζομένος, κλᾶσαι ἐπισάτης. ὁ δὲ ζύγου κατόπιν, ὁμοίως ἀκροστάτης, ὁ δ' ὅτι ζύγου κατόπιν, ἐπισάτης. Quod in iureiurando legitur: ΓΛΕΥΣΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ ΓΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΑΡΩΣΩ ΟΠΟΣΗΝ ΑΝ ΠΑΡΑΔΕΞΩΜΑΙ. Nauigabo in terram, eamque colam, quantulacumque illa sit, quæ habenda mihi tradetur: restituimus è Pollucis edito partim MS. codice, estque intelligendum de coloniis, quas deducebant admodum frequenter Athenienses: Hoc vero iuramenti Kaput, ἐκ ἀμαχαῖν ἀχρὶ θανάτου τῆς Ἀθηναίων, Ad mortem usque pro nutricia terra dimicabo. habes apud Vlpianum itemque Philostratum locis illis, quæ in superioribus laudauimus: Illud vero, ὅρια ἀγροῦ Ἀττικῆς, πυλῶν, κερῶν, ἀμπέλων, ἐλαιῶν. Fines agri Attici flatuam, frumentum, hordeum, vites, oleas, extat apud Plutarchum in Alcibiade : ὡ μὲν ἀλλὰ ἡ τῆς γῆς σῳζομένην αἰτησάμενοι τῆς Ἀθηναίοις, ἡ τὸν ἐν Ἀγραύλου [?] παρακαλοῦμος ἐπὶ τοῖς Ἐφήβοις ὅρκον, ἐρῶ βεβαιῶ. ὁμνύουσι δὲ ὅσοις χεῖρα [?] τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς, πυρῶν [?], κριθῶν [?], ἀμπέλους [?], ἐλαίας· εἰκεῖν πωμές [?] διδωσκόμενοι τὸ ἡ-μέραν ἡ καρποφόρον [?]. Sui iuramenti testes aduocabant. Deos Ephebi. ΙΣΤΟ-ΡΕΣ ΘΕΟΙ, ΑΓΡΑΥΛΟΙ, ΕΝΥΑΛΙΟΣ, ΑΡΗΣ, ΖΕΥΣ, ΘΗΛΩ ΗΓΕΜΟΝΗ. Testes Dijs iunto, Agrauli, Enyalius, Mars, Iupiter, Nutricia terra, Diana. ΑΓΡΑΥΛΟΙ. id est, non tantum Agraulus Cecropis Filia, in cuius æde iuratum, sed etiam Minerua, quæ hoc cognomine Athenis colebatur. Harpocration: Ἀγλαυρος, siue Ἀγραυλος, quod idem est, ἡ Ζυγάτηρ Κέκροπος. ἔστι δὲ ἡ ἐπώνυμος Ἀθηνᾶς. ENYALIOS, Enyalius Martis Filius est. Hesychius: Ἐνυάλιος, ὁ Ἄρης, ἢ ὁ Ζεὺς υἱός. ΘΗΑΩ. ita restituimus, cum apud Pollucem legatur, ΘΑΛΛΩ ΑΥΞΩ, sed posterius istud interpretamentum prioris, sed corrupti nominis: expunximus itaque, & prius emendauimus, ΘΗΑΩ id est, Nutricia terra, ἡ Δρεψαμένη [?], ἧς [?] iurant Ephebi. Hesychius: Θηλὼ [?], Ἔφος [?], τὴν ΗΓΕΜΟΝΗ, Diana: male apud Pollucem ΗΓΕΜΟΝΙ. Hesychius: Ἡγεμόνη [?], Ἀρτεμις καὶ Ἀφροδίτη. Romanorum moribus atque institutis parentes liberos sibi natos profitebantur in actis apud Præfectos ærarij, ex quo cura tabularum publicarum à Quæstoribus ad Præfectos ærarij translata est, quod factum Nerone imperante: Qua de professione multa iam diu viri maximi, qui monent cauendum esse, ne Capitolinus in M. Aurelio fallat, qui ita de hac professione disserit, quasi ille inuenerit primum. Verba Capitolini sunt: Inter hæc liberales causas ita muniuit M. Aurelius, ut primus iuberet apud Præfectos ærarij Saturni vnumquemque ciuium natos liberos profiteri, intra tricesimum diem nomine impositio. Per Prouincias tabulariorum publicorum vsum instituit, apud quos idem de originibus fieret, quod Romæ apud Præfectos ærarij. Verus editio, intra tertium diem. sed mendose: Verba autem ista, nomine impositio, otiosa sunt viris summis, nisi forte legas, intra tricesimum diem a nomine impositio. Ego vero conijcio legendum, ut primus iuberet apud Præfectos ærarij Saturnini vnumquemque ciuium natos liberos profiteri intra tricesimum diem. Homine impositio per Prouincias tabulariorum publicorum vsum instituit, apud quos idem de originibus fieret, quod Romæ apud Præfectos ærarij. Locus laborabat ab interpunctione, & a mendo, quod fuit in proclivi, cum facile mutetur H in N. emendationem nostram confirmat, quod sequitur, apud quos idem de originibus fieret, istud enim apud quos non est quod possis ad alios referre, quam homines impositos per Prouincias. Atque ex his natalibus professionibus ætas probabatur: Quanquam pubertas non tantum ex annorum numero, sed etiam habitu corporis definiebatur, id est, ex aspectu erumpentis pubis, quæ sententia fuit Prisci. Vlpianus in Regulis iuris: Puberem autem Cassiani quidem eum esse dicunt, qui habitu corporis pubes apparet, id est, qui generare possit. Procoleiani autem, eum qui quatuordecim annos expleuit. verum Priscus eum puberem esse, in quem vtrumque concurrit, & habitus corporis, & numerus annorum: cuius sententiam expressit Seruius[?] ad hunc versum Vergilij Æneid. VII.
units.tr: Moreover, since this oath is so worded that one cannot but declare it the oath of a man who is already his own master (sui iuris), and since Ephebi before their twentieth year were not sui iuris, it must be said that they were Ephebi until, at the age of twenty, they were enrolled among the men. This oath was spoken in the temple of Agraulos, daughter of Cecrops. This is clear from the words of Pollux, Ulpian and Demosthenes already cited, and likewise from Philochorus: the daughter of Agraulos gave herself up to death and threw herself from the city; then, to free the city from the war, a temple was set up for her by Zeus, like the temples on the Acropolis, and the Ephebi, about to swear the oath for war, sing hymns to her at once. [ἡ τῶν Ἀγραύλου ἐχίσσα αὐτῇ ἐξέδωκε εἰς θάνατον, ἐῤῥίψατο δὲ ἑαυτὴν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως· εἶτα ἀπαλλαγῆναι τῆς πόλεμου, ἱερὸν ἐπὶ Ζεύς ἐστήσατο αὐτῇ, ὡς τὰ ἱερὰ ἐπὶ τῆς Ἀκρο-πόλεως, ἡ εὐθὺς ὑμνοῦσιν οἱ Ἐφηβοι μέλλοντες ὀμνύναι εἰς πόλεμον.] Philostratus too, in the fourth book, chapter seven, of the Life of Apollonius, as the most learned Meursius rightly emends: formerly they swore by the guard of Agraulos, as if to put off boyhood, while holding arms. [οἱ πάλαι μὲν ὀμνυοντο εἰς Ἀγραύλου φυλακήν, ὡς τῆς παιδείας ἀποδιυσάσθαι, ἡ ὅπλα ἔχοντες.] To this Agraulos the Athenians established sacred rites and instituted initiations. Athenagoras: the Athenians were initiated purely into the rites of Agraulos of the city. [ἡ Ἀγραύλῳ Ἀθηναῖοι ἡ πόλεως ἐμυήσαντο ἀγνῶς.] And these rites seem to have been celebrated in the month Hekatombaion, when the Ephebi, already enrolled in the Lexiarchikon, swore this oath. In it several points deserve attention. I will not dishonour these holy arms. [ΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΙΣΧΥΝΩ ΤΑ ΟΠΛΑ ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ.] When the Ephebi swore this oath they were armed. Ulpian, in the words cited above: those who go out from the boys into the Ephebi, who are of the honour of Agraulos, swear that they will not always disgrace the holy arms, and that they will fight to the death for the Athenians. [οἱ δὲ τῆς τιμῆς τῆς Ἀγραύλου οἱ ἐξιόντες εἰς πὺς Ἐφήβους ἐκ παίδων, μὴ πάντοτε ἄλλην ὁμνύειν ἐκ ἀμαχαῖν ἀχρὶ θανάτου τῆς Ἀθηναίων.] They were equipped with these arms for the sake of taking the auspices; so, as I conjecture, the arms were kept in the temple of Agraulos itself, and those about to swear were given them from it as from an armoury. That is why these arms are called sacred. [ΤΑ ΟΠΛΑ ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ.] In Polyaenus, Stratagems, book one, on Pisistratus and his bodyguards: they came in armed, and taking away the arms, they put each man in the temple of Agraulos, which, in my judgment, bears on this, for the arms were kept there, as was the custom. Next comes the oath: I will not desert the leader, whoever he may be whom I shall meet in my ranks. [ΟΥΔ' ΕΓΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΩΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ ΟΤΩΙ ΑΝ ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ.] So I have emended this passage, since in Pollux it is printed as ΟΥΔΕ ΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ Ω ΑΝ ΤΥΧΩ. A manuscript of Pollux has ΣΤΟΙΧΩ with by chance [ΤΥΧΩ] written over it. In the Collectanea of Stobaeus it is read ΟΥΔ' ΕΓΚΑΤΑΛΕΙΨΩ ΤΟΝ ΓΑΡΑΣΤΑΤΗΝ ΟΤΩΙ ΑΝ ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ. But it must be wholly rewritten as ΤΟΝ ΓΡΩΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ, and the word ΣΤΟΙΧΗΣΩ plainly confirms this, for in drawing up a battle line the Greeks spoke of depth as wall [τοῖχος] and of length as yoke [ζυγόν]. Ælian in the Tactics says: the leader of a company, who marches behind, is called the man in front of the line; and the man behind the yoke, likewise the one in front, and the one who is behind the yoke is called the man behind the front. [ἀκρόστατος κλᾶσαι πᾶς ὁ ζυγῶν … ἐπισάτης.] So the reading must be ΤΟΝ ΓΡΩΤΟΣΤΑΤΗΝ. Then in the oath is read: I will go out upon the land, and I will curse whatever portion shall be handed to me to hold. [ΓΛΕΥΣΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ ΓΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΑΡΩΣΩ ΟΠΟΣΗΝ ΑΝ ΠΑΡΑΔΕΞΩΜΑΙ.] I have restored this partly from the edition of Pollux and partly from a manuscript, and it is to be understood of the colonies which the Athenians very often founded. The final clause of the oath, I will fight to the death for the nurturing land of the Athenians [ἐκ ἀμαχαῖν ἀχρὶ θανάτου τῆς Ἀθηναίων], is found in Ulpian, and likewise in Philostratus in the passages cited above. Plutarch, in the Alcibiades, gives this: the boundaries of Attic land: gates, horns, vines, olives; the fields of Attica, wheat, barley, vines, olives. [ὅρια ἀγροῦ Ἀττικῆς, πυλῶν, κερῶν, ἀμπέλων, ἐλαιῶν.] They swore to these things, calling on witnesses to their oath. The Ephebi called on the gods: Witnesses: the gods, Agraulos, Enyalios, Ares, Zeus, Thallo, Hegemone. [ΙΣΤΟΡΕΣ ΘΕΟΙ, ΑΓΡΑΥΛΟΙ, ΕΝΥΑΛΙΟΣ, ΑΡΗΣ, ΖΕΥΣ, ΘΗΛΩ ΗΓΕΜΟΝΗ.] Agraulos: that is, not only Agraulos the daughter of Cecrops, in whose temple the oath was sworn, but also Minerva, who was worshipped at Athens under this surname. Harpocration: Aglauros, or Agraulos, which is the same, is the daughter of Cecrops; and she is the eponym of Athena. [Ἀγλαυρος, siue Ἀγραυλος … ἡ ἐπώνυμος Ἀθηνᾶς.] Enyalios is a son of Mars. Hesychius: Enyalios is Ares, or a son of Zeus. [Ἐνυάλιος, ὁ Ἄρης, ἢ ὁ Ζεὺς υἱός.] ΘΗΑΩ: I have restored it thus, since in Pollux it is read ΘΑΛΛΩ ΑΥΞΩ, but the latter is an explanation of the former, which was a corrupt name. So I have struck that out and first emended it to ΘΗΑΩ, that is, the nurturing earth, by whom the Ephebi swear. Hesychius: Thelo, … the Hegemone, Diana, which in Pollux is badly printed as ΗΓΕΜΟΝΙ. Hesychius: Hegemone: Artemis and Aphrodite. [Ἡγεμόνη … Ἀρτεμις καὶ Ἀφροδίτη.]

units.la: Iam matura viro, iam plenis nubilis annis.
units.tr: Already ripe for a man, already of marriageable years.

units.la: Verum praeter Romanorum instituta ad foeminam refert: Non est iteratum, inquit, sed secundum ius dictum: in quo & ex annorum ratione, & ex habitu corporis aetas comprobatur. At tamen etiamsi habitus corporis non concurrat, quem vigoris vestigia nominant Imperatores, dummodo anni quatuordecim numerentur, in pubertibus censentur Lege IV. C. Qui testamenta facere possint.
units.tr: But apart from Roman custom, he refers it to a woman: It is not repeated, he says, but stated according to law, in which age is proved both by the reckoning of years and by the condition of the body. Yet even if the condition of the body, which the Emperors call traces of vigour, is not present, provided fourteen years are counted, they are reckoned among the pubescent by the law in Code IV, Who may make wills, of the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian Augustuses and Caesars, to Rado.

units.la: Impp. Diocletian. & Maximian. AA. & CC. Radoni.
units.tr: The Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Augusti and Caesars, to Radon.

units.la: Si frater patruelis tuus ante decimum quartum aetatis suae annum decesserit, cum facere non potuit testamentum, nihil recte ex eius postremo iudicio postulatur. Nam si haec aetatem egressus, licet vigoris nondum emersissent vestigia, suum solenniter ordinavit iudicium, hoc evellere frustra conaris. S. V I. Id. Novemb. Pantichi, CC. Conss.
units.tr: If your paternal cousin died before the end of his fourteenth year of age, since he could not make a will, nothing can rightly be claimed from his last judgment. For if he had passed that age and solemnly made his disposition, although the traces of vigour had not yet appeared, you try in vain to overturn it. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November at Pantichium, in the consulship of the two Caesars.

units.la: Huius inspectionis mentio apud Paulum Libro I. Quaestionum, cuius verba describemus, ut a mendo liberemus. Minor viginti quinque annis, adito Praeside, ex aspectu corporis falso probavit perfectam aetatem. Curatores, cum intellexissent esse minorem, perseverarunt in administratione: medio tempore, post probatam aetatem, ante impletum vicesimum quintum annum solutae sunt adulescenti pecuniae debitae: easque male consumpsit. Quaero, cuius sit periculum: & quid si Curatores quoque in eodem errore perseverassent, ut putarent maiorem esse, & abstinuissent se ab administratione, curationem etiam restituissent: an periculum temporis, quod post probatam aetatem cessit, ad eos pertinet? Respondi: Hi, qui debita exsoluerunt, liberati iure ipso, non debent conveniri iterum. Plane Curatores, qui scientes cum minorem esse, perseverarunt in eodem officio, non debuerunt eum pati accipere pecunias debitas: & debebunt hoc nomine conveniri. Quod si & ipsi decreto Praesidis crediderunt, & administrare cessaverunt, vel etiam ratione reddiderunt, similes sunt ceteris debitoribus: ideoque non conveniuntur. Lege XXXII. D. de minoribus. Male hic editur, & quid si Curatores quoque in eodem errore perseverassent: Unica voce: Non enim haec vox huius est loci: Rescribo distinctis vocibus: & quid si Curatores quoque in eodem errore, perse verassent, ut putarent maiorem esse, & abstinuissent se ab administratione, curationem etiam restituissent: id est, si Curatores in eodem quoque versantes, ut qui & ipsi Praesidis decreto crederent, quantum ad se attinet repraesentassent vere atque opere ipso, credere eum maiorem esse; vere autem atque opere repraesentabant istud credere, cum se ab administratione abstinerent, curationem etiam restituerent.
units.tr: The mention of this inquiry is found in Paulus, Book I of the Questions, whose words we will set out so as to free them from error. A minor under twenty-five years of age, having approached the Governor, falsely proved by his bodily appearance that he had reached full age. The guardians, when they had learned that he was a minor, continued in the administration. In the meantime, after his age had been proved, but before his twenty-fifth year was completed, the debts owed to the young man were paid, and he spent them badly. I ask whose the risk is, and what if the guardians too had persisted in the same error, thinking him to be of age, and had abstained from the administration and restored the guardianship: does the risk of the time that passed after his age was proved fall on them? I replied: Those who paid the debts were released by law itself and ought not to be sued again. But guardians who, knowing he was a minor, persisted in the same office, ought not to have allowed him to receive the debts owed, and they will be liable on that account. But if they too believed the Governor's decree and ceased to administer, or even rendered an account, they are like the other debtors, and therefore are not sued. Law 32, Digest, On minors. Here the text is wrongly printed as and what if the guardians too had persisted in the same error, as a single phrase. That is not right, since this phrase does not belong to this place. I punctuate it differently: and what if the guardians too, in the same error, had persisted, thinking him to be of age, and had abstained from the administration and restored the guardianship? That is, if the guardians, also caught in the same error, as those who themselves believed the Governor's decree, had shown in fact and in deed, so far as it concerned them, that they believed him to be of age; and they showed that belief truly and in deed when they abstained from the administration and restored the guardianship.

units.la: Inter patriae potestatis iura fuit & istud Abdicandi, in eamque rem scripta Lex:
units.tr: Among the rights of paternal power there was also that of disinheriting, and a law was written concerning this matter:

units.la: Τοὺς γονέας κωλύοις εἴ[?] ἀποκηρύξαι. Parentibus liberos abdicare ius esto.
units.tr: Parents shall have the right to disinherit their children. [Τοὺς γονέας κωλύοις εἴ[?] ἀποκηρύξαι.]

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes: ὁ τὸ πρῶτον[?] Βοιωτῶν. ὁ μὲν νόμος τοὺς γονέας κωλύειν ἀποκηρύξαι[?]. Quod iuris non tantum in liberos, quos genuerant, sed etiam in adoptivos habuisse constat ex Oratione eiusdem πρὸς Σπουδίαν de Leocrate, quem idem qui adoptaverat Polyeuctus abdicavit. Non abdicabantur autem nisi causa cognita, & probata apud iudices. Quinctilianus Declamat. CCLXXXIII. Ceteros enim, quos abdicant patres, sine narratione culpae abdicare non possunt. Lucianus in Abdicato: ὁ δὲ ἄπαις, ὦ πάτερ, ὁ λομβ[illegible, ~12 letters] οὐκ ἐστ' ἐχθρὸς ἐδίωξεν[illegible, ~10 letters] τοιούτους ἀξίωσις[?]. χαὶ Ἀλφ' τῆτο Ϲἀκελθεῖν ἐφ' ἡμῖν γίνεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἀχριτον τῶν ἡμφεῖαν, ἀλλ' Εἰς διχαστὴ- ςειον ςκάλεσε, χαὶ ἀδικημάςας ςκάλησε, ἴοις μὴπ τοῖς ὀργῇ, μόπτ ἀρδαλολίῳ ὁ δίκαιος χρινοῦσιν. Μοχ. ςἰκοῦ ἠχείτο ἀδίκασον χίγεσθαι ὁ ἀγέμμα, ἀλλ' ἐς ἑρήμης Ἰοὶ παῖ- δας ἀὐτὸς ἀλίσκεσ, ἀλλὰ χαὶ ὑδωρ ἐγγείων, χαὶ λόγος ἀπαδὶ δοπαι, χαὶ ἀπὲξέπασον ςὸλὶ χα- ταλείπεσ ἐπὶ τίνων ἔξεσι χαὶ τῶ μὲν ἐγκαλὴν μίαν ὁ πατὴρ χύρεσ, τῆ χρίναι δὲ, εἰ ὠλογα ἀπὸ παι, ὑμεῖς οἱ δικάζοντες. Hinc apud Suidam: ἀπαχρυκτος ὅτι χαλάσῃ ἐκδοῦσθαι. Patri' us autem id conceditur, quia cuiusmodi sint futuri, quos genuerint, ignorant: τῷ μὲν γὰρ τ' ἠγιινάπ̣α, πανεγέν, ἰὰ γένειον ἀπολύσεσθαι, ὃ ὠδι, τίμην, γιώσεισμα ὧ. χαὶ Ἀλφ' τῶν Ἀ αἰαξίους τῆς ἡμῶν πρασπίαξ συγχεχώρησι, ὃς ὅτι ἠγιιέων ἀφεῖα- μένοις. Fiebat autem abdicatio per praeconem, qui pronunciabat τὸν ὑῖνα negare τὸν ὑῖνα filium suum esse amplius. Habes apud Platonem Libro de Legibus XI. Ἀξοῖνα σφίον ἐαὶ βάλωσι τὸν γὸν ἀποῦ κηρυκας ςιαῦλοι ἀπὸ νὸν ἀπαιτιτὰ ἀποπιπῆ γὸν χ' ἡμον μιχέτι εἰ). Atque ita excidebant patris familia. Helychius: ἀπαχηρυχτος, ὁ ὅτι ἀμφαπμασον ἐκπιοῖν τῆς πατρῷας οὐσίας. non tamen ciuitatis iure. Plato ibid. παῖς ἀπεχηρυγμένος ςὴχ αὐ ἐξ ἀναγκης ἀπολις εἰη. Abdicationum autem forme sunt due: altera criminis perfecti, vt si abdicatur adulter, raptor. Altera imperfecti, velut pendentis, & adhuc in conditione positi: quales sunt, in quibus abdicatur filius, qui non pareat patri: vt est apud Fabium Libro VII. cap. IV. Erat porro in patris potestate abdicatum reducere, αἰαλαμβάνειν εἰς ὃ ἥμος. Lucianus loco laudato: ἔλυε μὲν τὸν ἀπαχηρυξιν, ἡν δὲ ἐξ ἰςαρχῆς ἐπιςίτο μι. An vero reducem iterum abdicare fas sit, controuersum est: Negat tamen licere Lucianus, & ratio est, quia fierent ἀπέχεινα τῶ παιδῶν αἱ ὠμεῖαι, χαὶ πολλαὶ αἱ κυλλίχαι, χαὶ ὁ φίλος αἰδίος. Abdicationis caussas praecipuas recensct idem loco laudato, his verbis: τὰ μὴ ἔῶντα ἡ, τί τῶ πολῖτων αὐτὰ; πῶα ἀρχαπίας, πῶα ὑπεμχίας ἡ ὁ ἀπάνα; πότε ἀποχρίςις ἐχαμβλω; τίνας πότας ἀχ ἐτείς; τίνας χώρυς ἐγκαλεῖς; ἡς οὐα πίας τῆς περιοδόσεως ὑπεσθαι; τῆς ἡπιάσατω; ςῶν εἴς. χαὶ μιλὸ ταῦτα ὅτιν, ἐφ' οἷς μάλιστα ὁ νόμος ἀποχηρύπεινεφίναν. Atque abdicatus bonorum paternorum non erant participes. Vnde in Rhetorum scholis apud Hermogenem χεὶ ςῶσις Lex: ὁ ἀποχηρυχτὸς μὴ μετηχέτω τῶ παιδῶν. Quod intelligendum esse idem docer, quasi nihil possit de bonis paternis adipisci, χ' ἴς ὠ χέ τῶ παιδῶν νόμος. Quia vero hic sumus, illustrare conabimur locum ex Excerptis Controuersiarum apud Senecam patrem Libro I. Controuersia I. Quisquis alimenta à mendico rogatus est, nihil amplius quam iter ei monstrat. Vade ad fratrem: i. ad filium: iam quidam nobis eandem fortunam precantur. Crede mihi, sacra populi digna est. Albutii Sili: Tollite vestras diuitias, quas huc atque illuc incerta fortuna fluctius appellet: redite in gratiam: innocens sum. Corrupta putant viri praestantissimi verba ista: Sacra populi digna est: quanquam vox sacra, contra quam volunt, optime hic legitur, sed eo sensu, quem iam aperiemus, Deo dante: Thema Controuersiae hoc est: Duo fratres inter se dissidebant: alteri filius erat: patruus in egestatem incidit: patre vetante, adolescens illum aluit: ob hoc abdicatus tacuit: adoptatus à patruo est: patruus accepta hereditate, locuples factus est: egere cepit pater: vetante patruo aluit illum: abdicatur. Rhetor autem ille, qui adolescentis partes tuetur verbis à nobis iam descriptis, adolescentem iure dedisse alimenta patri probat, quia, auctore populo & rogante, dedit: addit, si redeant in gratiam, adolescentem fore innocentem. Hic est sensus horum verborum meo quidem iudicio: sed ea omnia sunt Albutij Sili: itaque rescribo & interpungo ad hunc modum, ALBUTII SILI. Quisquis alimenta à mendico rogatus est, nihil amplius quam iter ei monstra: Vade ad fratrem: i. ad filium: jam quidam nobis eandem fortunam precantur, Crede: Mihi sacra populi digna. Sed tollite vestras divitias, quas huc atque illuc incerta fortunæ fluctus appellet: redite in gratiam: innocens sum. Cum stipem rogaret adolescentis à patruo locuplete facto adoptati pater, à populo misericordiam nō ferebat, sed ad fratrem, & ad filium ire iubebatur: atque ita populus filio imperabat ut patrem aleret: non deerant quoque, qui fratri, qui filio, miseram hanc senis fortunam, & populum iter ad eos monstrare referrent; preces quoque ad filium allegabant ut crederet vera à se dici, populum ita iussisse miserari rogatum: Mihi, inquit adolescens, sacra populi digna: id est: Ego auctoritatem populi non defugi: obsequium eius potestati merito detuli: Opponit itaque populi potestatem, patriæ adoptantis potestati: cum illi non minus quā huic obsequium debeat. significat autem ō sacra potestatem. Glossæ vet. In sacris patris, ἐν ἱεροῖς τῆς πατρίδος [?]. Rursum, ὁ ἐξουσιαστὴς [?], In sacris.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law: "the first of the Boeotians"; the law forbade parents to disinherit [ὁ τὸ πρῶτον Βοιωτῶν. ὁ μὲν νόμος τοὺς γονέας κωλύειν ἀποκηρύξαι]. That this right applied not only to the children they had begotten but also to adopted children is clear from the speech of the same author Against Spudias, concerning Leocrates, whom Polyeuctus, who had adopted him, disinherited. Those who were disinherited, however, were disinherited only after a hearing of the case and proof before judges. Quintilian, Declamation 283: For they cannot disinherit the others whom fathers disinherit without stating a fault. Lucian, in The Disinherited: the childless man, O father... [the Greek is largely illegible in the scan] ...not an enemy... he did not bring a charge against us... but summoned us to a court, and having accused us, let the judges decide not by anger but by justice... Hence in Suidas: disinherited, that is, cast out by a decree. The father is granted this because he cannot know what sort of children they will become: [the Greek is again corrupted]. Abdication was carried out through a herald, who proclaimed that the father no longer regarded the man as his son [τὸν ὑῖνα ... τὸν ὑῖνα]. You have this in Plato, Book XI of the Laws: [the Greek is corrupted]. And so the disinherited man fell out of the household of his father. Hesychius: disinherited, that is, cast out from the paternal estate. Not, however, from civic rights. Plato, ibid.: a child who has been disinherited may not necessarily be without a city. There are two forms of disinheritance: one for a completed crime, as when an adulterer or a ravisher is disinherited; the other for an incomplete one, as for something still pending and not yet settled, such as when a son who does not obey his father is disinherited, as Fabius mentions in Book VII, chapter 4. Moreover, it was in the father's power to take back one who had been disinherited [αἰαλαμβάνειν εἰς ὃ ἥμος]. Lucian, in the passage cited: he would release the disinherited son, but if he later did the same again... Whether it is lawful to disinherit a son again after he has been taken back is disputed. Lucian, however, denies that it is allowed, and the reason is that the quarrels between sons and fathers would never end, and the friendships would be broken. Lucian in the same passage lists the chief causes of disinheritance in these words: [the Greek is corrupted] ...these are the things for which the law especially allowed disinheritance. And those who were disinherited had no share in the paternal goods. Hence in the schools of the rhetoricians, in Hermogenes, a law reads: let the disinherited man not share in the children's [goods] [ὁ ἀποχηρυχτὸς μὴ μετηχέτω τῶ παιδῶν]. The same author teaches that this must be understood as meaning that he can acquire nothing from his father's goods, as the law of the children says. Since we are on this point, we will try to clarify a passage from the Excerpts from the Controversies of Seneca the Elder, Book I, Controversy 1: Whoever is asked by a beggar for food gives nothing more than directions. Go to your brother; that is, to your son. Now certain people pray for us the same fortune. Believe me, it is worthy of the sacred people. Words of Albutius Silus: Take away your riches, which uncertain fortune drives this way and that like a wave; return to favour: I am innocent. Very learned men think these words are corrupt: it is worthy of the sacred people. Although the word sacra, contrary to what they want, is read here very well, it is in a sense which we will now explain, with God's help. The theme of the controversy is this: Two brothers were at odds with each other. One had a son. The uncle fell into poverty. Against the father's wishes, the young man supported him. For this he was disinherited and kept silent. He was adopted by the uncle. The uncle, having received the inheritance, became wealthy. The father began to be in need. The uncle, forbidding it, supported him. He is disinherited. That rhetorician, however, who defends the young man's part in the words we have already set out, proves that the young man rightly gave food to his father because he gave it at the request and by the advice of the people; he adds that if they return to favour, the young man will be innocent. This, in my judgment, is the sense of these words. But all those words belong to Albutius Silus; so I rewrite and punctuate them in this way: ALBUTIUS SILUS. Whoever is asked by a beggar for food gives nothing more than directions. Go to your brother; that is, to your son. Now certain people pray for us the same fortune. Believe me, it is worthy of the sacred people. But take away your riches, which uncertain fortune drives this way and that like a wave: return to favour: I am innocent. When the father of the young man, who had been adopted by a wealthy uncle, asked for alms, he did not get pity from the people, but was ordered to go to his brother and to his son; and so the people commanded the son to feed his father. There were also those who reported that the wretched fortune of the old man, and the people's direction to go to them, were told to the brother and the son; they also pleaded with the son to believe that what was said was true, that the people had so ordered that the one who was asked should show pity. "To me," says the young man, "what is worthy of the sacred people." That is: I did not flee the authority of the people; I rightly yielded obedience to their power. He therefore sets the power of the people against the power of the adoptive father, since he owes obedience to the one no less than to the other. He means by sacra the power [of the people]. Ancient glosses: In sacris patris [ἐν ἱεροῖς τῆς πατρίδος]. Again, ὁ ἐξουσιαστὴς, in sacris.

units.la: Romanorum Legibus comprobata non est Abdicatio: ut constat è Rescripto Imperatorum Diocletiani & Maximiani Augustorum Lege VI. C. de patria potestate.
units.tr: Abdication was not approved by Roman law, as is clear from the rescript of the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian Augusti, Law 6, C. de patria potestate.

units.la: Impp. Diocletianus & Maximianus AA. Hermogeni.
units.tr: The Emperors Diocletian and Maximian Augusti to Hermogenes.

units.la: Abdicatio, quæ Græco more ad alienandos liberos vsurpabatur, & ἀποκήρυξις dicebatur, Romanis Legibus non comprobatur. TP. XVII. Kal. Dec. Maximiano A.II. & Ianuario Conss. Sed mendum est in Consulis nomine: non enim is fuit Maximianus Augustus, cum post Diocletianum Augustum & Aristobulum, nullus Imperator priuato Collega Consul fuerit, vsque ad Iuliani Augusti IV. & Salustii Consulatum, vt testatur Ammianus Marcellinus Lib. XXIII. Sed eo anno Consul fuit Maximus. Habes in Lib. de Præfectis Vrbi: Maximo II. & Ianuario Coss. III. Kal. Mart. Pomponius Ianuarius Pr. Vrbi eligitur. Rescribendum igitur est in Lege, TP. XVII. Kal. Dec. Maximo II. & Ianuario Conss. Filios igitur non abdicarunt Romani, cum filium negare cuiquam liberum non fuerit, Lege IX. C. eod. sed tamen ablegarunt, & è conspectu suo abire iusserunt, vt exempla apud Valerium Maximum liquido probant.
units.tr: Abdication, which was used in the Greek manner for alienating children and was called apokēruxis [ἀποκήρυξις], is not approved by Roman law. Given on the 17th day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Maximian Augustus for the second time and Januarius. But there is an error in the consul's name: this was not Maximian Augustus, since after Diocletian Augustus and Aristobulus no emperor was consul with a private colleague until the consulship of Julian Augustus for the fourth time and Salustius, as Ammianus Marcellinus testifies in Book 23. In that year, however, the consul was Maximus. You have in the book on the prefects of the city: "in the consulship of Maximus for the second time and Januarius for the third time, on the 3rd day before the Kalends of March, Pomponius Januarius is chosen city prefect." The text of the law should therefore be corrected to read: "on the 17th day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Maximus for the second time and Januarius." Roman law therefore did not disown sons, since denying a free child to anyone was not permitted (Law 9, C. eod.), but nevertheless they banished them and ordered them to depart from their sight, as the examples in Valerius Maximus clearly show.

units.la: Ante Solonis νομοθεσίαν, non tam Lege, quam moribus populi Athieniensium licebat liberos vendere, vt scribit Plutarchus in Solone: πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ παῖδας ἰδίους ἀπεδίδοντο [?] ... τὸ νόμος ἐκώλυε [?].
units.tr: Before Solon's lawgiving, the people of Athens were permitted to sell their children, less by law than by custom, as Plutarch writes in his Solon: "Many also sold their own children" [πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ παῖδας ἰδίους ἀπεδίδοντο] ... "the law forbade it."

units.la: At vero Solon Legem hanc tulit:
units.tr: But Solon did enact this law:

units.la: Μὴ ἐξεῖναι γυναῖκα πωλεῖν, μήτ' ἀδελφάς, πωλῶ αἰ μὴ λάβῃ πρῶτον αἰδὶ συγγεγνημένην. [?]
units.tr: "It is not lawful to sell a woman, nor sisters, unless one first catches her having intercourse" [Μὴ ἐξεῖναι γυναῖκα πωλεῖν, μήτ' ἀδελφάς, πωλῶ αἰ μὴ λάβῃ πρῶτον αἰδὶ συγγεγνημένην].

units.la: Filiam aut sororem vendere nemini ius esto, nisi in ea adhuc virgine moechum deprehendere.
units.tr: No one shall have the right to sell a daughter or a sister, unless he catches a seducer with her while she is still a virgin.

units.la: Legem habes apud Plutarchum in Solone: ἔτι δέ, ὅτι γυναῖκας πωλεῖν, μήτ' ἀδελφάς, πωλῶν αἱ μὴ λάβῃ πρῶτον αἰδὶ συγγεγνημένην. [?] Interdixit igitur Liberos vendere, filias autem atque etiam sorores vendere permisit, si quis in iis adhuc virginibus moechum deprehendisset.
units.tr: You have the law in Plutarch's Solon: "further, that it is not lawful to sell women, nor sisters, unless one first catches her having intercourse." He therefore forbade the sale of children, but permitted the sale of daughters and even sisters, if someone had caught a seducer with them while they were still virgins.

units.la: Apud Romanos diuersè secundum diuersa tempora obseruatum est: nam Lege Decemvirali [?] ita cautum Legimus: SI PATER FILIUM TER VENUM DUIT FILIUS A PATRE, LIBER ESTO LIBEROS CETEROS SEMEL SI VENVM DVIT, SVI IVRIS SVNTO. Apud Dionysiũ Halicarnassaeum Libro II. ὁ[?] τὴν [?]πωλ[?]ήσιν τοῦ πατρὸς, μείζων[?] τῆς [?]περὶ τὰ τέκνα πωλήσεως ἀφ[?]· ἰοῦ χρὴ μαστιγοῦσθαι. μείζονα δὲ [?]ἐξουσίαν πατρὶ τῷ παιδὸς, ἢ δὲ ἀποδοῦναι τῷ δούλῳ[?].
units.tr: Among the Romans the practice varied according to the period. For in the Law of the Twelve Tables we read this provision: "IF A FATHER SELLS HIS SON THREE TIMES, THE SON SHALL BE FREE FROM HIS FATHER; IF HE SELLS THE OTHER CHILDREN ONCE, THEY SHALL BE UNDER THEIR OWN RIGHT." In Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book 2: [The one who] sells his father ... the sale of children is greater ... must be whipped. The father's power over the son is greater ... than to give back to a slave. (The Greek of this passage is corrupt in the printed text.)

units.la: Sed ius istud murauit: neque concessum fuit patribus liberos vendere: priusque illud ius abrogatum est, antequam vitae necisque in liberos potestas patribus denegaretur: colligo è Lege X. C. De patria potestate.
units.tr: But this right was changed: it was not granted to fathers to sell their children; and that right was abrogated before the power of life and death over children was denied to fathers. I gather this from the law of the Code, title X, On paternal power.

units.la: Imp. Constantinus Aug ad Maximum P.V.
units.tr: The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, Praefect of the City

units.la: Libertati à maioribus tantum impensum est, vt patribus, quibus ius vitae in liberos, necisque potestas olim erat permissa, libertatem eripere non liceret. Dat. XV. Kal. Iun. Thessalonicae, Seuero & Rufino Conss.
units.tr: Liberty has been so much favoured by our ancestors that it is not lawful to snatch liberty from fathers, to whom the right of life over children and the power of death were once permitted. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Severus and Rufinus.

units.la: Neque hic audiendi sunt, qui libertatis nomine ingenuitatem intelligunt, nã nemo est, qui ingenuitatem eripiat homini libero: libertatem tamen & hostis, in cuius potestatem venit, & aliuscasus eripere potuit, & ipse quoque pater olim è Legibus XII. sed, vt diximus, Lex haec abrogata, & patribus denegatum libertatem eripere, idque antequam illi etiam denegaretur vitae necisque potestas in liberos.
units.tr: Nor should those be heard who understand "liberty" to mean "freeborn status," for no one can take away a free man's freeborn status; yet even an enemy into whose power he came, and some other chance event, could take away his liberty, and the father himself once could, under the Law of the Twelve Tables. But, as we have said, that law was abrogated, and fathers were denied the right to take away liberty, and this was done before the power of life and death over children was also denied them.

units.la: Atqui Pauli, qui imperante Alexandro Seuero floruit, aetate, liberos patribus non licebat occidere. Pauli enim Libro II. ad Sabinum haec sunt verba: Hac ex causa, filij familias licet non sint heredes instituti, domini sunt: nec obstat, quod licet eos exheredare, quod & occidere licebat. Lege XI. D. de Liberis & posthumis heredibus instituendis. Dixit Paulus, quod & occidere licebat, quia sua aetate non amplius licitum fuit: Nam patria potestas in pietate debet, non atrocitate cõsistere. Lege V. D. ad Legem Pompeiam de parricidijs: & forte primus auctor Hadrianus: nam is fertur, cum in venatione filium suum quidam necauerat, qui nouercam adulterabat, in insulam cum deportasse: quod latronis magis, quàm patris iure, cum interfecit, inquit Marcianus Libro XIV. Institutionum, vt habes d. Lege V. D. ad Legem Pompeiam de parricidijs: etenim pietas paterni nominis consilium pro liberis capit. Lege XXII. §. IV. D. ad Legem Juliam de Adulterijs. Eodemque tempore caeptum est in seruos non saeuire. Gaius Institutionum Libro I. quem post exemptum rebus humanis Antoninum Pium scripsit: Sed hoc tempore nullis hominibus, qui sub imperio Romano sunt, licet supra modum, & sine causa legibus cognita in seruos suos saeuire. Nam ex constitutione Diui Antonini, qui sine causa seruum suum occiderit, non minus puniri iubetur, quam qui alienum seruum occiderit. Sed & maior asperitas dominorum eiusdem Principis constitutione coërcetur. Lege I. §. II. D. de his, qui sui, vel alieni iuris sunt. Scribit item Vlpianus Libro VIII. de officio Proconsulis, Diuum Hadrianum Vmbriciam quandam matronam in quinquennium relegauisse, quod ex leuissimis causis ancillas atrocissime tractasset. Lege II. D. eod. Quanquam sanguinolentos exponere, quod poene necare est, patribus concessum fuit.
units.tr: Yet in the time of Paulus, who flourished under the Emperor Alexander Severus, fathers were no longer permitted to kill their children. For in Paulus, Book 2 to Sabinus, these are his words: For this reason, sons under power, though not instituted heirs, are masters; nor does it matter that they may be disinherited, though it was also once permitted to kill them. Law 11, D. de liberis et posthumis heredibus instituendis. Paulus said "though it was also once permitted to kill them," because in his age it was no longer lawful: for paternal power ought to consist in piety, not in cruelty. Law 5, D. ad Legem Pompeiam de parricidiis; and perhaps the first author of this was Hadrian, for it is reported that when a certain man, in a hunt, had killed his son, who was committing adultery with his stepmother, Hadrian deported him to an island, saying that he had acted more as a robber than as a father when he killed him, as Marcian says in Book 14 of the Institutes, as you have in the said Law 5, D. ad Legem Pompeiam de parricidiis; for the piety of the paternal name takes counsel for its children. Law 22, §4, D. ad Legem Juliam de adulteriis. At the same time it also began to be forbidden to be cruel to slaves. Gaius in Book 1 of the Institutes, which he wrote after the death of Antoninus Pius: But at this time it is not permitted to any men who are under the Roman empire to rage against their slaves beyond measure and without cause proven by law. For by a constitution of the divine Antoninus, one who kills his slave without cause is ordered to be punished no less than one who kills another's slave. But also the greater harshness of masters is restrained by a constitution of the same Prince. Law 1, §2, D. de his, qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt. Ulpian likewise writes in Book 8 de officio Proconsulis that the divine Hadrian relegated a certain matron of Umbria for five years, because for very slight causes she had treated her slave-women most savagely. Law 2, D. eod. Although it was granted to fathers to expose bloodied infants, which is almost to kill them.

units.la: Antequam autem, vt iam diximus, potestas vitae necisque in liberos patribus adimeretur, ademptum illis fuerat ius liberos vendendi, vt è Lege illa vlt. C. de patria potestate, constare videtur. Quare ante aetatem Pauli, ipsiusque adeo, vt puto, Hadriani aevo, patribus libertatem eripere non licuit.
