Quanquam aliquid paulò post hac in re immutatum est: nam Pauli temporibus, si cogeret egestas, adeo vt ipse pater non posset alendis liberis sufficere, vendere eos illi licebat. Paulus Libro V. Sententiarum Tit.I.§.I. Qui contemplatione extremæ necessitatis, aut alimentorum gratia, filios suos vendiderint, statui ingenuitatis eorum non præiudicant. Homo enim liber nullo pretio æstimatur. Idem nec pignori ab his, aut fiduciæ dari possunt. Ex quo facto sciens creditor deportatur. Opera tamen eorum locari possunt. Neque tamen id etiam postea concessum est: sed omnino omnino liberorum venditione patribus interdictum est: ut constat è Diocletiani Constitutione Lege I. C. de patribus, qui filios suos distraxerunt.
units.tr: But before, as we have already said, the power of life and death over children was taken from fathers, the right to sell children had been taken from them, as seems clear from that last Law, C. de patria potestate. Therefore, before the age of Paulus, and indeed, I think, in the age of Hadrian, it was not lawful for fathers to take away liberty. Yet something was changed in this matter a little later: in the times of Paulus, if want compelled, so that the father himself could not suffice to feed his children, it was lawful for him to sell them. Paulus, Book 5 of the Sentences, Title 1, §1: Those who, in view of extreme necessity or for the sake of food, have sold their sons do not prejudice their children's status of free birth. For a free man is valued at no price. Nor can the same children be given in pledge or in fiduciary trust by them. If a creditor knowingly does this, he is deported. Yet their labour may be let out. But this was not later permitted either; rather, the sale of children was absolutely forbidden to fathers altogether, as is clear from the Constitution of Diocletian, Law 1, C. de patribus, qui filios suos distraxerunt.

units.la: Impp, Diocletianus & Maximianus Augusti Papiniano.
units.tr: The Emperors Diocletian and Maximian Augusti to Papinian.

units.la: Liberos à parentibus neque venditionis, neque donationis titulo, neque pignoris iure, aut aliquo quolibet modo, nec sub prætextu ignorantiæ accipientis in alium transferri posse, manifestissimi iuris est.
units.tr: It is most manifest law that children may not be transferred from their parents to another, by title of sale, of gift, or by right of pledge, or in any other way, nor under the pretext of ignorance on the part of the recipient.

units.la: Cùm tamen obtineri non posset, ut patres egestate laborantes ab oppignoratione, si non venditione liberorum, abstinerent: utraque hac patribus interdixit Constantinus Magnus Lege II. Cod. Theod. de alimentis, quæ inopes parentes de publico petere debent.
units.tr: Since, however, it could not be obtained that fathers suffering from want should abstain from pledging their children, if not from selling them, Constantine the Great forbade both of these to fathers, in Law 2, Cod. Theod. de alimentis, quae inopes parentes de publico petere debent.

units.la: Imp. Constantinus Augustus Menandro.
units.tr: The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Menander.

units.la: Provinciales egestate victus atque alimoniæ inopia laborantes, liberos suos vendere vel obpignorare cognouimus. Quisquis igitur huiusmodi reperietur, qui nulla rei familiaris substantia fultus est, quique liberos suos ægre ac difficile sustentet: per fiscum nostrum antequam fiat calamitati obnoxius, adiuetur[?]: ita ut Proconsules, Præsidesque & Rationales per universam Africam habeant potestatem, & vniuersis quos aduerterint, in egestate miserabili constitutos, stipem[?] necessariam largiantur: atque ex horreis substantiam protinus tribuant competentem. abhorret enim nostris moribus, ut quenquam fame confici, vel ad indignum facinus prorumpere concedamus. Dat. prid. Non. Iul. Romæ, Probiano & Iuliano Coss. Anni sequentis, id est, Christianæ æræ tercentesimi vicesimi tertij, Constitutio eiusdem Constantini, qua nullo modo eripi posse libertatem testatur[?] de Lege X.C. de patria potestate.
units.tr: We have learned that provincials, suffering from want of food and lack of sustenance, sell or pledge their children. Whoever, therefore, is found to be of this kind, who is supported by no substance of family property, and who can scarcely and with difficulty sustain his children: let him be helped by our treasury before he is exposed to calamity; so that the proconsuls, governors and fiscal officers throughout all Africa have the power to give necessary alms to all whom they find placed in miserable want, and immediately to grant from the granaries a suitable provision. For it is contrary to our morals that we should allow anyone to be worn down by hunger or driven to an unworthy crime. Given on the day before the Nones of July at Rome, in the consulship of Probianus and Julianus. Of the following year, that is, of the Christian era 323, there is a constitution of the same Constantine, which testifies that liberty can in no way be taken away, from Law 10, C. de patria potestate.

units.la: Imp. Constantinus Augustus ad Maximum T.V.
units.tr: The Emperor Constantine Augustus to Maximus, his Vicar.

units.la: Libertati à maioribus tantum impensum est, ut patribus, quibus ius vitæ in liberos, necisque potestas olim erat permissa, libertatem eripere non liceret. Dat. XV. Kal. Iun. Thessalonicæ, Seuero & Rufino Coss.
units.tr: So much was granted to liberty by our ancestors that it was not lawful to take freedom away from fathers, to whom the right of life and death over their children once was permitted. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Severus and Rufinus.

units.la: Non potuit tamen extorquere Constantinus à populo, quin patres in egestate destituti liberos suos venderent victus causa, quantùuis ipse ne id fieret, Legibus cauisset: itaque sanguinolentos & adhuc à matre rubentes liberos patribus vendere victus causa permisit Lege II.C. de patribus, qui filios suos distraxerunt.
units.tr: Yet Constantine could not prevent the people from wringing out of him that fathers, reduced to destitution, sold their children for the sake of sustenance, although he himself had provided by law that this should not happen. Accordingly he permitted fathers to sell their children for sustenance even when they were still bloody and red from the mother's womb: Law 2, C., "On fathers who sold their sons."

units.la: Imp. Constantinus Augustus Prouincialibus salutem.
units.tr: The Emperor Constantine Augustus to the provincials, greetings.

units.la: Si quis propter nimiam paupertatem egestatemque victus causa filium filiamve, sanguinolentos[?] nolentos vendiderit, venditione in hoc tantummodo casu valente, emptor obtinendi eius seruitij habeat facultatem. liceat autem ipsi qui vendidit, vel alienatus est, aut cuilibet alij ad ingenuitatem eum proprium repetere: modo si aut precium afferat, quod potest valere, aut mancipium pro eiusmodi præstet.
units.tr: If anyone, on account of extreme poverty and need, sells a son or daughter for the sake of sustenance, whether the child is newly born or unwilling, the sale being valid in this case alone, the buyer shall have the right to keep that service. But it shall be lawful for the seller, or for the one to whom the child was transferred, or for anyone else, to reclaim the child for freedom, provided that they either offer a price that can be accepted, or hand over a slave in exchange.

units.la: Atque hæc Constantini Constitutio obtinuit, quod ad liberorum venditionem victus causa attinet, Theodosii Magni temporibus, non autè quod spectat pretium offerendum, vt venditus ingenuitati pristinæ reformetur. Legem habes Cod. Theod. cod.
units.tr: This constitution of Constantine held, as far as the sale of children for sustenance is concerned, in the times of Theodosius the Great; but not as regards the price to be offered so that the one sold may be restored to his former freeborn status. You have the law in the Theodosian Code, same title.

units.la: Inter præcipuas Solonis curas fuit liberorum educatio atque institutio, de qua hæc eius Lex habetur:
units.tr: Among the chief concerns of Solon was the upbringing and education of children, concerning which this law of his is recorded:

units.la: Τοὺς παῖδας διδάσκειν [?] γράμ-μαῖα, καὶ τοὺς μὲν [?] ἐπι-τὰ περὶ τὰ γεωργίας, καὶ τὰς ἐμπορίας, καὶ τὸ τέχνῳ. τοὺς δὲ βίον ἔχοντας κεκτημένους περὶ τι μουσικὴν, καὶ ἱππικὴν, καὶ τὰ γυμνάσια, καὶ τὰ χωρηγίσια, καὶ τὸ φιλοσοφίαν διδάσκειν.
units.tr: Τοὺς παῖδας διδάσκειν γράμματα, καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἐπὶ τὰ περὶ τὰ γεωργίας, καὶ τὰς ἐμπορίας, καὶ τὸ τέχνῳ. τοὺς δὲ βίον ἔχοντας κεκτημένους περὶ τι μουσικὴν, καὶ ἱππικὴν, καὶ τὰ γυμνάσια, καὶ τὰ χωρηγίσια, καὶ τὸ φιλοσοφίαν διδάσκειν. [Translation: the law directs that children be taught letters; that those of modest means be trained for farming, trade and a craft; and that those possessing an independent livelihood be taught music, horsemanship, gymnastics, hunting and philosophy.]

units.la: Pueri natare & literas primum docentor. Tenuiores deinde rure opus facere, aut peregre ad mercatum ire, aut artem exercere: Honestiores vero in Musicis, in re equestri, in Gymnicis, ad venandum, in Philosophia, instituuntor.
units.tr: Boys are first taught to swim and to read and write. Then those of humbler means are made to work on the land, or sent abroad to market, or trained in a craft; but those of higher rank are instructed in music, in horsemanship, in gymnastics, in hunting, and in philosophy.

units.la: Primum igitur natare & literas docebantur, vnde natum Prouerbium, de quo Diogenianus; μήτε νῆϊ, μήτε γράμματα, ὅτι τὴν ἁμαξῶν. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἐκπαιδεύεν ἐν τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις ἐμάθησαν. Suidas, & Vaticana Proverbiorum Appendix: τοῦ Ἀθηναίοις δ' ὑπὸ πᾶσιν κολυμβᾶν καὶ γράμματα ἐδιδάσκοντο. Anonymus ad Aphthonium cur id docerentur, aperit, nempe vt possent Leges nosse, & Reipublicæ operam, quam debent, præstare in bellis nauali-bus: οἱ γὰρ Ἀ-θηναῖοι ὁ παλαιὸν τοὺς ἑαυτῶν παῖδας γράμματα καὶ μουσικὴν ἐκπαίδευον. ὅ μὲν ἀλλ' τοὺς νόμους· ὃ δὲ δὴ [?] ναυμαχίας. Seneca Controuersia XXVII. ex emendatione Viri Cl. Schotti: Scribam hoc te facturum, & matri tuae quarenti de tua desidia dixeram, ἀξιῶσαν τὴν κολυμβᾶν, δώσειν ὃ γράμματα. Vbi proue-ctiores facti fuerant, pro facultatum modulo in ceteris institue-bantur. Nam tenuiores fortunæ homines liberos suos ruri opus facere docebant, vt est in palliata Menandri apud Terentium fabula Adelphis, aut artificium discebant, vt è sequenti Lege constabit; aut peregre ad mercatum ablegabantur, vt habes in Comœdiis: Honestiores vero instituebantur in musicis, in gymnicis, in re equestri, ad venandum, in Philosophia. Isocratis Orat. Areopagitica de Solone & Clisthene Atheniensibus Legumlatoribus: ἀπέφηνε μὲν οὖν ἐφεῖτιζον τὴν πολιτὴν, μάλιστα δὲ τὴν νεωτέρων. ὡς ὃ παῖς τὸν ἀνδρα ἡμῶν εἶναι, ὅτως ἐκ ἐχέσθαι παιδεύειν [?] Ἀ-παιδείας. Τοὺς μὲν γὰρ ὑποδιέστερον παιδαγωγοὺς ἐπὶ τὰ γεωργίας καὶ τὰς ἐμπορίας ἑτέρου· εἰδότες, τοὺς μὲν ἐμπορίας, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχίας γιγνομένας· τοὺς δ' ἀκαυρχίας ἀπὸ τῆς ἀπειρίας. Τοὺς δὲ βίον ἔχοντας κεκτημένους, περὶ τὸ ἱππικὸν, καὶ τὰ γυμνάσια, καὶ τὰ χωρηγίσια, καὶ τὸ φιλοσοφίαν, ὡἀγκαῖόν Ἀ-παιδεύειν. De his honestiorum iuuenum studiis Terentianus Simo in Andria:
units.tr: First, then, they were taught to swim and to read and write, whence the proverb arose, which Diogenianus records: "Neither swimming nor letters," since these things were learned by the Athenians in their boyhood. Suidas and the Vatican Appendix to the Proverbs: "The Athenians were taught to swim and to read and write" [τοῦ Ἀθηναίοις δ' ὑπὸ πᾶσιν κολυμβᾶν καὶ γράμματα ἐδιδάσκοντο]. The anonymous commentator on Aphthonius explains why they were taught this, namely that they might know the laws and render the service they owe the commonwealth in naval wars: "for the Athenians of old educated their own children in letters and music; the former so that they might know the laws, the latter for sea battles" [οἱ γὰρ Ἀθηναῖοι ὁ παλαιὸν τοὺς ἑαυτῶν παῖδας γράμματα καὶ μουσικὴν ἐκπαίδευον. ὅ μὲν ἀλλ' τοὺς νόμους· ὃ δὲ δὴ ναυμαχίας]. Seneca, Controversy 27, in the emendation of the learned Schott: "I shall do this, that I shall teach you to swim and give you letters," [ἀξιῶσαν τὴν κολυμβᾶν, δώσειν ὃ γράμματα] as I had said to your mother when she asked about your idleness. Once they had grown older, they were trained in other things according to the measure of their means. For men of humble fortune taught their sons to work the land, as in Menander's palliata fable, the Adelphi, as shown by Terence; or they taught them a trade, as the following law will make clear; or they were sent abroad to market, as you find in the comedies. But those of higher rank were trained in music, in gymnastics, in horsemanship, in hunting, and in philosophy. Isocrates, in his Areopagiticus, on the Athenian lawgivers Solon and Clisthenes: he made clear that they cared for the citizens, and especially for the young, so that the child would become a man among us, and so that they would not be without education. For they assigned the lesser teachers to farming and trade, knowing that the one came from ... (the scan here is corrupt), and the other from inexperience; while those who possessed an independent livelihood they had taught horsemanship, gymnastics, hunting and philosophy, as is fitting. On these studies of the more honourable youths, Terence's Simo, in the Andria:

units.la: Quod plerique omnes faciunt adolescentuli,
units.tr: As most young men do,

units.la: Vt animum ad aliquod studium adiungant, aut equos
units.tr: that they might apply their minds to some pursuit, or keep

units.la: Alere, aut canes ad venandum, aut ad Philosophos:
units.tr: horses, or hounds for hunting, or follow the philosophers:

units.la: Horum ille nihil egregie præter cetera
units.tr: of these he pursued none outstandingly above the rest,

units.la: Studebat: & tamen omnia hæc mediocriter.
units.tr: yet he pursued all of them moderately.

units.la: Rursum idem Eunucho:
units.tr: Again, the same author in the Eunuch:

units.la: Fac periculum in literis,
units.tr: Try him in letters,

units.la: Fac in palæstra, in musicis: quæ liberum
units.tr: try him in the wrestling-school and in music, which it is fitting

units.la: Scire æquum est adolescentem, sollertem dabo.
units.tr: a free young man should know; I shall give you a clever one.

units.la: Quanta pietate colendi sint parentes secundum Deum sanxit suis Legibus Solon, poena irrogata si quis secus fecisset: haec enim eius Lex est:
units.tr: How devoutly parents are to be honoured, after God, Solon sanctioned in his laws, with a penalty imposed on anyone who acted otherwise. For this is his law:

units.la: Ὁ τοὺς γονέας τύπτων, ἐὰν μὴ τρέφῃ, ἐὰν μὴ παρέχῃ οἴκησιν, καὶ τὰ ἐπιτήδεια, ἄτιμος ἔστω. | Si quis parentes pulsauerit, aut non aluerit, aut tectum ad habitandum ceteraque necessaria non praebuerit, ignominiosus esto.
units.tr: Ὁ τοὺς γονέας τύπτων, ἐὰν μὴ τρέφῃ, ἐὰν μὴ παρέχῃ οἴκησιν, καὶ τὰ ἐπιτήδεια, ἄτιμος ἔστω. | If anyone strikes his parents, or does not feed them, or does not provide them with a dwelling and other necessities, let him be disgraced. [Translation: whoever strikes his parents, or does not feed them, or does not provide them with lodging and the necessities, let him be dishonoured.]

units.tr: The Attic jurists call this law, concerning the ill-treatment of parents, [text illegible in scan], not only by nature but also by adoption, which Lysias mentions [text illegible in scan] [text illegible in scan].

units.la: Sed morte non luebat, qui in hanc Legem incurrerat, verùm ignominia notabatur: neque capite luisse dixit Lysias, mortem tamen commeritum fuisse Agoratum pronunciat, quia non tantùm in hanc malae parentum tractationis Legem commiserat, sed etiam aliorum reus erat criminum. Ignominiosus igitur erat, qui hanc Legem temerarat. Aeschynes [illegible, ~30 letters] Τιμάρχου. δίκημα (Φησί) Ῥητῶρ. [illegible, ~60 letters] Itaque expressis verbis habes apud Diogenem Laertium in Solone: [illegible, ~40 letters] Quae sit haec capitis minutio, ostendit comparatio Legum ἀπραπίας, & malae parentum tractationis, quas coniungit Demosthenes [illegible, ~30 letters] nempe [illegible, ~20 letters]. Nam cos [illegible, ~70 letters] inquit Vlpianus ad Demosthenem. Certe, ne quid de pulsatis parentibus dicam, iniquissimum est patrem egere, cum filius sit in facultatibus. Lege V.§.XIII.D. de agnoscendis & alendis liberis vel parentibus. Meminit huius Kapitis Legis Demosthenes [illegible, ~50 letters] ludens suo more dixit Aristophanes Auibus.
units.tr: But one who had transgressed this law did not pay with his life; he was marked with disgrace instead. Lysias did not say that he paid with his head, yet he declares that Agoratus had deserved death, because he was not only guilty under this law on the ill-treatment of parents but was also a defendant on other charges. So he who had violated this law was liable to disgrace. Aeschines [text illegible in scan] of Timarchus. The orator says this was a wrong (crime). [text illegible in scan]. Thus you have it in plain words in Diogenes Laertius, in his Solon: [text illegible in scan]. What this loss of civil standing is, the comparison shows between the laws on apraxia and on ill-treatment of parents, which Demosthenes joins [text illegible in scan], namely [text illegible in scan]. For ... as Ulpian says in his commentary on Demosthenes. Certainly, to say nothing of parents who have been struck, it is most unjust for a father to be in want while the son has means. Law 5, §13, D., "On acknowledging and supporting children or parents." Demosthenes mentions this chapter of the law [text illegible in scan], and Aristophanes in the Birds made a playful reference to it in his usual way.

units.tr: Παῖδας ποιῶν [?] τοῖς παλαιοῖς τὴν πέφυκε [?], Δεῖ [?] τοὺς νεωτέρους τὸν πατέρα πάλιν τιμᾶν [?]. [Translation: "Having made children for the old, as nature has ordained, the younger must in turn honour the father."]

units.la: Meminit Legis Isaeus ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς Κίρωνος κλήρου. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς κακώσεως νόμου δηλοῦσιν [?] εἶναι. Εἰ γὰρ ἔζη μὲν ὁ πάππος, σὺ δὲ τῷ πατρὶ ἐπιτιμῶν [?], οὐκ ἂν δύνασθαι [?] κακώσεως, ἀλλ' ἡμεῖς κελεύει γὰρ πεφυκέναι τοὺς γονέας γονῆς σὺ εἶπη μήτηρ καὶ πατήρ, πάππους καὶ τήθη καὶ τούτων μήτηρ καὶ πατήρ, ἐαὶ ἐπὶ ζῶσιν. ἐκεῖνοι γὰρ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἡλίκων εἰσὶ, ἐ[?] τὰ ἐκείνων ἀπολιπόντες [?]. Δὸς ἀπὸ ἀνάγκη πέφυκε αὐτοὺς ὄστι, καὶ μηδὲν καταλίπωσι. Quare vere Plato Libro de Legibus IV. νομίζειν δὲ, ἃ κ[?] πολλὰ [?] τῶν ἡμετέρων, ἴσως ὁ πρέσχον αὐτὰ ἐκ ἐαυτῶν ἐπὶ ὑπηρεσίαν ἐκείνοις χρῆ δύναμιν πᾶσαν. & Theophrastus apud Stobaeum: γονεῖς γονέων ἐποιεῖν χάριν. ὁ γὰρ μὲν Τεύκρος, ἀλλὰ τὴν τῆς φύσεως, ἡ τῆς πόλεως νόμων ὀλίγον ἀμφότερα τοῖς τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἔργοις ἀπεκλείσθαι ἀπ' Harpocration: Κακώσεως, δίκης ὄνομά ἐστι, χρῆ τὴν παίδων τῶν γονέων. Apud Praetorem, qui signabat Fastos, scribebatur haec dica. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. IX. δίκη δὲ τοῖς Ἀρχῶν [?] κακώσεως. Scribebat autem dicam, qui vellet: ἐξὸν καὶ πάντα τῷ βουλομένῳ γράφεσθαι κακώσεως γονέων, ut ex Hyperide ἐν τῷ ὑπὲρ τῆς Πυρρίνου κλήρου, & Lysia περὶ Φιλωνίδου βιαίων, εἰ γονέως, docet Harpocration. Qui autem hanc dicam iudicarint, pro certo compertum dicere non habeo: Mihi quidem videntur, quemadmodum illam τῆς εὐφημίας, quam scribebant liberi parentibus, ita quoque τῆς κακώσεως γονέων iudicasse οἱ Φεάτορες. Additur quoque ab Harpocratione: ὧν δὲ καὶ αὐτὸ ὕδατος. Quae verba Amplissimus Mauffacus noster fidem secutus codicis MS. cum in aliis editionibus deessent, tanquam legitima reposuit: nempe haec lis malae parentum tractationis ad clepsydram, siue μεμψιμοιρίας ἡμέρας non agebatur, ut verba haec sonant: Sed nullus dubito inemendata esse: Nam ad clepsydram agebantur causae, quae magni esse censebantur momenti. Harpocration: Ἀφημελτηρικῶν ἡμέρας, μέχρι τὸ ὕδατος ἐστί, περὶ μεμψιμοιρίας ἡμέρας Ἀφίστημα ῥέον· ἐμετρεῖτο δὲ τοῦ Ποσειδῶνι μίλιν· περὶ δὲ τῶν πηλίζοιντο οἱ μέγιστοι καὶ ἀεὶ τὴν μεγίστων ἀγῶνες· διὰ νέμεται δὲ εἰς πεῖα μέρη ὃ ὕδωρ, ὃ μὲν τοῦ διακονοῦ· ὃ δὲ τοῦ φόρου· ὃ τέλος τῆς δικαιώσεως. Atqui hic ἀγὼν malae parentum tractionis erat περὶ τὴν μεγίστων. nam conuictus malae tractationis, infamia notabatur, quae maxima erat capitis minutio, καὶ μηδεὶς μετεῖχε τὴν κοινωνίαν, ut scribit Ulpianus. Quare dubium esse non potest, quin ad clepsydam, καὶ περὶ Ἀφημελτηρικῶν ἡμέραν, ageretur ἡ τῆς κακώσεως τῶν γονέων δίκη. quomodo etiam apud iudices probabantur abdicationis causae, & περὶ ὕδωρ disceptabatur. Lucianus Abdicato. ὡς ἐκ ἡμῖν ἀδίκασεν γὰρ ἐεσθαι ὃ ταχεῖμα, ὅτι ὃ ἐρίμης ἐκ παῖδας δὲ ὑμῖν ἀλίσκεται, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὕδωρ ἐγχέον, καὶ λόγῳ ἀποδοῦναι, καὶ ἀνεξέταστον ἐδει καταλείπειν. Sed latet in mendo & mensurae, qua aquam dimetiebantur, modus numerusque: Coniicio igitur ita olim ab Harpocratione scriptum fuisse: ὧν ἢ καὶ αὖ ἐκ κ. ὕδατος, id est, ὧν ἢ αὖ πίντε κοτυλῶν ὕδατος. Quinetiam erat quinque cotylarum aquae.
units.tr: Isaeus mentions the law in his speech on the estate of Kiron. But they also show, in the speech on the law of ill-treatment, that: "for if the grandfather were living, and you were reproaching your father, you could not be charged with ill-treatment; for the law commands that parents be honoured by their offspring, mother and father, grandparents and great-grandparents, while they are alive; for those are the rulers of the younger, and they must not leave their own... they are bound by necessity to be honoured, and leave nothing behind." Hence Plato rightly says in Book IV of the Laws: "one must think that ... our ancestors, perhaps... to them one should render every service" [νομίζειν δὲ ...]; and Theophrastus, quoted by Stobaeus: "parents should be honoured for the sake of their parents" [γονεῖς γονέων ἐποιεῖν χάριν]. Harpocration: "Kakōsis is the name of a legal action, for ill-treatment of parents by children." Before the Praetor, who signed the Fasti, this indictment was written. Pollux, Book VIII, ch. 9: "the action of the magistrates for ill-treatment." Anyone who wished could bring the indictment, since it was permitted for anyone who wished to bring a charge of ill-treatment of parents, as Harpocration teaches from Hyperides, in his speech on the estate of Pyrrhinus, and from Lysias, On Philonides, concerning violence against parents. I have no certain knowledge of which magistrates judged this indictment. It seems to me that, as they judged the indictment for slander which children brought against parents, so too the Thesmothetae judged the charge of ill-treatment of parents. Harpocration adds: "of which also [there is a measure] of water." Since these words were missing in the other editions, our most distinguished Mauffac, following a manuscript, restored them as genuine: namely, that this suit for ill-treatment of parents was not brought at the water-clock, or on the day of complaint (μεμψιμοιρία), as these words would sound. But I have no doubt they are corrupt: for causes were pleaded at the water-clock that were considered of great importance. Harpocration: "The day of Aphēmeltērikē extends as far as the water, a flowing stream on the complaint day; it was measured out for Poseidon with a mile; and the greatest were contested about the greatest matters; and the water was distributed into parts, one for the servant, one for the..., and the end of the trial." But this contest over ill-treatment of parents concerned the greatest matters: for a convicted person of ill-treatment was marked with infamy, which was the greatest loss of civil standing, and he was shut out from common fellowship, as Ulpian writes. Hence there can be no doubt that the action for the ill-treatment of parents was pleaded at the water-clock, on the day of Aphēmeltērikē, just as causes of disinheritance were approved before the judges and contested by water. Lucian, in Disinheritance: "for it was not lawful for us to be tried without the water-clock being poured, since he is not caught in the act by the children, but also he must pour the water and give an account of his speech, and not leave it unexamined." But the measure by which the water was measured out, its quantity and number, lies hidden in a corruption. I conjecture, therefore, that Harpocration originally wrote thus: "of which also [there is a measure] of water," that is, "of which also [there is] five cotylae of water." Indeed there was a measure of five cotylae of water.

units.la: Nempe unicuique litigantium dabatur mensura quinque cotylarum aquae, ad quam mensuram causam orabat suam. Neque enim in omnibus causis totidem eaedemque mensurae aquae dabantur. Ita apud Demosthenem ἐν τῇ πρὸς Μακάρτατον, cum de Hagniae haereditate disceptaretur: ἢ ὅπως ἢ ἤλθ' ὁ Ἀρχὼν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον, ἐὰν ἐπὶ ἀγωνίζεσθαι· τὰ τ' ἄλλα ὡ αὐτοῖς ἀ-πωτα [?] πρεσκ[?]ἀσμένα εἰς τὸν ἀγῶνα, καὶ ὃ ὕδωρ, πρὸς ὃ εἰδὲ ἀγωνίζεσθαι, πέτρα-πλέποτ[?] ἡμῖν ἔλεσθαι[?], ἐξαιλαξις γὰρ ἰῶ; ὦ ἀνδρες δικασταί, περὶ ἀξιοῦ[?], ἀμφορία, ἐκ[?] ἐξέαν ἐξέαι περὶ ἀμφισβητουμένων, καὶ τῆς Χοᾶς περὶ ὑστέρου λόγου. Quae postrema verba obseruanda sunt, vnice enim faciunt, meo quidem iudicio, ad praefe-rendam facem tenebricosissimis Harpocrationis verbis: [?]σκεωλίον δὲ περὶ Ἰσαίου ἐν τῷ κατ' Ἐλπαρχόν δὲ Δημοφαίους, πῶς. Suidas habet ἐς, μεμνησμένης τῆς ἡ-μέρας, ὅτι μὲν φασι, Suidas φησι, χωρὶς ὕδατος γίνεσθαι τὰς ἀγῶνας, ὅτι δὲ πρὸς ὕδωρ. Nam quod scribit Isaeus fieri, vt aliquando μεμνησμένης τῆς ἡμέρας causae ad clepsydram perorentur, aliquando sine clepsydra, id ita intelligendum est: In grauioribus & maioris momenti causis erat πρὸς πέρας λόγος, erat etiam πρὸς λόγος, vt è laudatis Demosthenis verbis manifesto constat: τοῦ πρὸς πέρας λόγῳ nullum dubium est, quin causae agerentur πρὸς ὕδωρ. At vero etiamsi aliquando, vt habes apud Demosthenem, τοῦ ὑπὲρ λόγῳ daretur clepsydra, tamen, vt ex Isaei loco ab Harpocratione laudato conijcio, etiam sine aqua causae perorabantur.
units.tr: Each litigant was evidently given a measure of five cotylae of water, and he pleaded his case within that measure. Nor were the same amounts of water allotted in every case. So in Demosthenes, in the speech against Macartatus, when the inheritance of Hagnias was in dispute, the speaker says: "...and the water by which we were to plead..., for the case is of the greatest weight, O judges, concerning the disputed matters, and about the later speech." These last words must be noted, for in my judgment they chiefly serve to clarify the very obscure words of Harpocration: "...but about Isaeus in the speech against Elpharchus..., as Suidas says, the cases were heard without water, but ... by water." What Isaeus writes, that sometimes causes were pleaded by the clepsydra with the day recalled, and sometimes without the clepsydra, should be understood thus. In the more serious and weightier cases there was a pros peras logos and also a pros logos, as is clear from the passage of Demosthenes quoted above. Concerning the pros peras logos there is no doubt that the cases were pleaded pros hydor, that is, by water. But even if sometimes, as you find in Demosthenes, a clepsydra was allowed for a hyper logos, nevertheless, as I conjecture from the passage of Isaeus cited by Harpocration, cases were also pleaded without water.

units.la: Apud Romanos Legibus quidem cogebantur liberi parentes alere, sed id tantum, nulla poena ei irrogata, qui secus fecisset. Imp. Antoninus Pius Augustus, Basso. Parentum necessitatibus liberos succurrere iustum est. Leg. I. C. de alendis liberis & parentibus. Neque tantum ad exhibendos parentes cogebantur, sed etiam auum, proauumque, & ceteros per virumque sexum contingentes. Leg. V. §. II. D. eod. quinetiam à milite quoque filio, qui in facultatibus sit, exhibendos parentes esse, pietatis exigimat ratio. Leg. cad. §. XV. D. eod. Si filius igitur parentes non exhiberet, adibantur competentes iudices, qui alere iubebant: Sed qui competentes sint isti iudices, quaerit Vir CL. & forte, inquit, Consules sunt: vt inscriptio huius Legis quintae D. de alendis liberis & parentibus, innuit, descripta quippe est è Libro secundo Vlpiani de officio Consuli. Eo quoque potest rescripti Lex secunda C. eod. Diui Fratres & AA. Celeri. Competens iudex à filio te ali iubebit, si in ea facultate est, vt tibi alimenta praestare possit. Dat. Id. Aprl. ipsis & Conss. Quasi enim ad ipsos Consules, tanquam competentes iudices, eodem, quo ad (elerem, exemplo rescripserint Diui Fratres, additur, ipsis & Conss. Nisi quis exstimet esse notationem temporis, quo datum est hoc Rescriptum à Diuis Fratribus, nempe ipsis Consulibus, anno, quo primum imperare ceperunt, itaque rescribendum esset, ipsis etiam Conss. At tamen cum cogito Antoninum Pium obiisse hoc ipso anno, Nonis Martiis, atque animo reputo Marci Aurelij in consecrando patre Antonino, in designando Lucio Vero fratre imperij participe, in ordinanda Republica, impensas curas, vix mihi persuadeo intra tam breue tempus, (vnius enim mensis & aliquot dierum interuallum est) fieri potuisse, vt vacarent priuatorum negotiis. Sed haec arbitraria sunt. An vero semper Consules aditi sint in hoc negotio si quaeras, mihi non videtur: nam famulos ingo seruuli soluere reliquum solum illis factum est, vt constat è Leg. vnica D. de officio Consulis. & e formula Consulatus apud Cassiodorum. Inter patronos & libertos, si de illis alendis agebatur, solebat cognoscere Praefectus Vrbi: Habes apud Vlpianum Lib. singulari de officio Praefecti Vrbi: Sed & patronos egentes de suis libertis quaerentes audiet: maximè si ægros se esse dicant, desiderentque à libertis exhiberi. Leg. I. §. II. D. de officio Præfecti Vrbi. An idem obseruatum inter parentes & liberos, nescio. Atque ex his patet Legem illam, quæ sæpius apud Senecam patrem occurrit, Liberi parentes alant, aut vinciantur, non esse desumptam ē iure Athenien-sium, siue Romanorum: sunt in illis è Syria petitæ, exempli gratia hæc legitur apud eundem Senecam. Cum filio tricenario pater patrimonium diuidat: ex hac Lege ista habentur apud Lucam Euangelij cap. XV. ἀνθρωπός τις εἶχε δύο υἱοί. καὶ εἶπεν ὁ νεώτερος αὐτῶν τῷ πατρί, πάτερ, δός μοι τὸ ἐπιβάλλον μέρος τῆς οὐσίας. ὁ δὲ διεῖλεν αὐτοῖς τὸν βίον. Sed de his nos plura, si Deus dederit, ad ipsos Rhetores Græcos & Latinos.
units.tr: Among the Romans, by the laws, children were indeed compelled to support their parents, but only that, and no penalty was imposed on one who acted otherwise. The Emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus, to Bassus: It is just that children should come to the aid of their parents' needs. Code, law 1, On the feeding of children and parents. Nor were they compelled only to provide for their parents, but also for grandfather, great-grandfather, and the others related through either sex. Digest, law 5, §2, same title. Moreover, that even a son who is serving as a soldier, if he has means, must support his parents, the reason of duty requires. Digest, same law, §15, same title. If a son therefore did not support his parents, the competent judges were approached, who ordered him to provide maintenance. But who these competent judges were, a certain most distinguished man asks, and perhaps, he says, they are the consuls, as the inscription of this fifth law of the Digest, On the feeding of children and parents, suggests, since it was indeed taken from the second book of Ulpian On the Duty of the Consul. From this a second law of the Code under the same title may also be taken, a rescript: The divine brothers and the Augusti to Celer: a competent judge will order you to be supported by your son, if he has the means to be able to provide maintenance for you. Given on the Ides of April, to them and the consuls. For as if the divine brothers had given this rescript in the same manner to the consuls themselves as competent judges, the words to them and the consuls are added. Unless someone thinks that this is a notation of the time when the rescript was given by the divine brothers, namely to the consuls themselves in the year in which they first began to rule, and so it would have had to be written to them also, the consuls. But when I consider that Antoninus Pius died in this very year, on the Nones of March, and reflect on Marcus Aurelius's anxious cares in consecrating his father Antoninus, in designating his brother Lucius Verus as partner in the empire, and in ordering the commonwealth, I can hardly persuade myself that within so short a time (for the interval is one month and some days) they could have been free of private business. But these are conjectures. Whether the consuls were always approached in this matter, if you ask, does not seem so to me; for the only thing left to them was to release the slaves and servants, as is clear from the single law of the Digest On the Office of the Consul, and from the formula of the consulate in Cassiodorus. Between patrons and freedmen, if the question was about supporting them, the Prefect of the City used to hear the case. You have in Ulpian, in his single book On the Office of the Prefect of the City: But he will also hear patrons who are needy and who ask about their freedmen, especially if they say they are sick and desire to be supported by their freedmen. Digest, law 1, §2, On the Office of the Prefect of the City. Whether the same was observed between parents and children, I do not know. And from these things it is clear that that law which often occurs in Seneca the Elder, Let children support their parents, or be put in chains, was not taken from the law of the Athenians or of the Romans. It derives from Syria; for example, this is read in the same Seneca: When a father divides his patrimony with a son of thirty. From this law such things are found in Luke, chapter 15 of the Gospel: A certain man had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falls to me. And he divided unto them his living. But concerning these matters we shall say more, God willing, in dealing with the Greek and Latin rhetoricians themselves.

units.la: Liberi, qui parentes suos non exhibuerant, infamia notati, arcebantur concione, Templorum publicorum ingressu, & omni coronarum in publicis festiuitatibus vsu: ὁ νόμος ἐξω τῆς ἀξιώσεως τῆς ἀρχῆς ἀξιῶσαι, ἡ ὁσα... ἐπὶ τὰς χοινὰς φιλοσοφείας, οὐδ' εἰσιέναι εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν τὸ δημόσιον. Si his non abstinerent, hac cum illis agebatur Lege
units.tr: Children who had not supported their parents, marked with infamy, were excluded from the assembly, from entering public temples, and from the use of crowns at public festivals. The law says that such a person is not to be admitted to the office... to public sacrifices, nor to enter the public temple. [ὁ νόμος ἐξω τῆς ἀξιώσεως τῆς ἀρχῆς ἀξιῶσαι, ἡ ὁσα... ἐπὶ τὰς χοινὰς φιλοσοφείας, οὐδ' εἰσιέναι εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν τὸ δημόσιον.] If they did not abstain from these things, proceedings were brought against them under this law:

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΑΡΑΧΘΗ ΤΩΝ ΓΟΝΕΩΝ ΚΑΚΩΣΕΩΣ ΗΛΩΚΩΣ ΕΙΣΙΩΝ ΟΠΗ, ΜΗ ΧΡΗ, ΔΗΣΑΝΤΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΟΙ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ, ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΑΙΑΝ, ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΕΙΤΩ ΔΕ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΛΛΩ, ΤΙΜΑΤΩ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ Ο ΤΙ ΧΡΗ ΠΑΘΕΙΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ Η ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΥ ΤΙΜΗΘΗ, ΔΕΔΕΣΤΩ ΤΕΩΣ, ΕΩΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΤΙΣΗ.
units.tr: "If anyone is convicted of ill-treating his parents, and is found entering where he is not permitted, the Eleven shall bind him and lead him to the Heliaea, and whoever wishes to may accuse him. If he is convicted, the court shall fix his penalty or fine. If he is condemned to pay a sum of silver, he shall remain in bonds until he pays it." [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΑΡΑΧΘΗ ΤΩΝ ΓΟΝΕΩΝ ΚΑΚΩΣΕΩΣ ΗΛΩΚΩΣ ΕΙΣΙΩΝ ΟΠΗ, ΜΗ ΧΡΗ, ΔΗΣΑΝΤΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΟΙ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ, ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΑΙΑΝ, ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΕΙΤΩ ΔΕ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΛΛΩ, ΤΙΜΑΤΩ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ Ο ΤΙ ΧΡΗ ΠΑΘΕΙΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ Η ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΥ ΤΙΜΗΘΗ, ΔΕΔΕΣΤΩ ΤΕΩΣ, ΕΩΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΤΙΣΗ.]

units.la: Si quis damnatus malæ parentum tractationis, ea deprehendatur ingredi loca, quibus arceantur, Vndecimuri capitales cum vinciunto, & in iudicium apud Heliæam rapiunto: quicumque voluerit, cui licet, accusato. Heliæa ei conuictlo pœnam vel multam irrogato. Si multa irrogata fuerit, quousque eam soluerit, in vinculis esto.
units.tr: If anyone condemned for ill-treating his parents is found entering the places from which such people are excluded, the Eleven shall bind him and bring him to judgment before the Heliaea; whoever wishes, and is permitted, shall accuse him. The Heliaea, upon conviction, shall impose a penalty or a fine. If a fine is imposed, he shall remain in chains until he has paid it.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτους, docetque à Solone latam fuisse: ταῦτα γὰρ ὑπάρχουσας ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ ... κατα-λύ[?]. λέγοντων γὰρ τὸν νόμων, οὐς ἔθηκε Σόλων, ὅτι ὁμοίως ὧν τούτῳ νομοθέτης, ἐπὶ τῆς ἀλλης τῆς κακώσεως τῶν γονέων, εἰς τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐμβάλλειν. Addit deinde verba ipsa Legis, quæ describimus.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in the speech against Timocrates, and teaches that it was proposed by Solon. For the laws which Solon established are said to have ... Then he adds the very words of the law, which we have described.

units.la: Non tulit autem Solon hanc de exhibendis parentibus Legem indefinite, sed aliquot adiecit exceptiones: Quarum vna hæc est:
units.tr: Solon, however, did not enact this law on supporting parents without qualification, but added several exceptions. One of them is this:

units.la: Τῷ πέφθι τὸν πατέρα μὴ διδαξάμενον τέχνην ἐπιψαλιες μὴ ἐ[?].
units.tr: "A son whose father has not taught him a craft is not to be compelled to support him." [Τῷ πέφθι τὸν πατέρα μὴ διδαξάμενον τέχνην ἐπιψαλιες μὴ ἐ[?].]

units.la: Filius, quem pater artem non docuerit, ad eum exhibendum ne cogitor.
units.tr: A son whom his father has not taught a craft is not to be compelled to support him.

units.la: Plutarchus in Solone hanc eius Legem refert: ὁ νόμων ἔγραψεν, ὡς πέφθι τὸν πατέρα μὴ διδαξάμενον τέχνην ἐπιψαλιες μὴ ἐ[?]. Legis ferendæ ratio fuit, τὸ πλῆθος τῆς χώρας ἀρκεῖ ἡ φαῦλα. Quare neque quenquam nisi ἐπὶ τῆν ἀ-thenas volebat commigrare, neque impunitam fiuit lentitudinem. Meminit Legis Galenus in Protrepti-co. ἐπαινεῖ δὲ αὐτὸν τῷ Ἀθηναίῳ νομοθέτῃ, ὡς τὸν μὴ διδάξαντα τέχνην, ἐκώλυε τοὺς τῆς παιδὸς πέφθαι, τέχνης ἀπάσης κατ' ἐκεῖνον μάλιστα τὴν χρείαν ἀσχολιμένης.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his Life of Solon, reports this law of his: "...the law which he wrote, that a son is not compelled to support his father if the father has not taught him a craft..." The reason for enacting the law was that the number of the citizens was large and the idle were many; so he did not want anyone to migrate to Athens without a trade, nor did he allow idleness to go unpunished. Galen also mentions the law in his Protrepticus: he praises the Athenian lawgiver for forbidding that a son be compelled to support a father who had not taught him a craft, since among them, above all, every craft was of use. [ἐπαινεῖ δὲ αὐτὸν τῷ Ἀθηναίῳ νομοθέτῃ, ὡς τὸν μὴ διδάξαντα τέχνην, ἐκώλυε τοὺς τῆς παιδὸς πέφθαι, τέχνης ἀπάσης κατ' ἐκεῖνον μάλιστα τὴν χρείαν ἀσχολιμένης.]

units.la: Fuit & altera exceptio hanc in Legem relata,
units.tr: There was also another exception, related in this law:

units.la: Μηδὲ τοὺς ἐκ ἐπίκληρος ὑφορμένους ἐπιψαλιες
units.tr: "Nor are those born of an heiress to be compelled to support..." [Μηδὲ τοὺς ἐκ ἐπίκληρος ὑφορμένους ἐπιψαλιες]

units.la: Nothi patres alere ne cogunter.
units.tr: Fathers of illegitimate children are not to be compelled to support them.

units.la: ἐὰν τῶν πατέρων πέφθι.
units.tr: "If … of the fathers …"

units.la: Descripserat hanc Solonis Legem ex eius Axonibus Heraclides Ponticus, ab eoque mutuatus est, & transcripsit Plutarchus in Solone: [illegible, ~30 letters] , ως Ἡρακλείδης ἱστόρηκεν ὁ Ποντικός. Qui enim è meretrice liberos tollit, illis ὄνομα [illegible, ~8 letters], neque vnquam in animo habuit ὁ ἐν γάμῳ καλὸν, non enim ἐπ᾽ ἀρότῳ παίδων, sed ἡδονῆς ἕνεκα cum illa consuevèrat mulierè. An vero matres alere cogantur liberi quanuis non ex legitimis nuptiis suscepti, si quis quaerat, è Graecorum iure negabit Rhetor apud Synesium Epistola III. posse cogi ad exhibendam matrem, qui non est è legitimis nuptiis susceptus: ὁ υἱὸς ὁ ῥήτωρ, ἀφοσιοῦται φησι τῆς αἰτίας τὸ νόμου μητέρα τρέφειν ἐπαναγκ. [illegible, ~45 letters]. Fuit & tertia exceptio, de qua, suo loco, dicemus.
units.tr: Heraclides of Pontus copied this law of Solon from his axones, and Plutarch borrowed it and transcribed it in his Solon: … as Heraclides of Pontus has recorded. For whoever has children by a prostitute gives them … of the father, and he never had in mind the fair name of lawful marriage. He did not have children for the sake of ploughing (the field) but for pleasure, since he lived with that woman. If anyone asks whether mothers are compelled to support children not born of lawful marriage, the rhetor in Synesius, Letter III, will deny, by the law of the Greeks, that a son who was not born of lawful marriage can be forced to support his mother. The rhetor says the son is freed from the disgrace of the law that obliges him to feed his mother: "Away with such a law! For he who was born of a prostitute cannot shake off the mother, while the rest of the obligation belongs to the parents…". Since both are owed by those who have been born, the duty passes from the fathers to the mothers … There was also a third exception, which we will discuss in its place.

units.la: Apud Romanos autem iure ciuili mater cogitur, vt loquitur Vlpianus Lib. II. de officio Consulis, praesertim vulgo quaesitos liberos alere, nec non ipsi eam. Leg. V. §. IV. D. de agnoscendis & alendis liberis & parentibus.
units.tr: Among the Romans, under civil law, the mother is compelled, as Ulpian says in Book II, On the Duty of the Consul: "especially to support children born out of wedlock, and likewise the father himself to do so." Law V, §4, D., On Acknowledging and Supporting Children and Parents.

units.la: Ea praeterea reuerentia atque pietate in parentes liberos esse voluit Atheniensium Legislator, vt si quis patrem defunctum criminaretur, eaque de re cum filio siue haerede ageret, filius pro patre iusiurandum daret, Lex haec est:
units.tr: The Athenian lawgiver also wished children to have such reverence and piety toward their parents that, if anyone accused a dead father and brought a suit concerning it against the son or heir, the son should swear an oath on his father's behalf. The law reads:

units.la: [illegible, ~60 letters] | Filius pro patre iusiurandum dato, si quis mortuum criminatus [?] cum haerede agat.
units.tr: "The son shall swear an oath on behalf of his father, if anyone brings an action against the heir after accusing the dead man."

units.la: Laudat hanc Legem Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Καλλίππον. ὅτι δὲ ἐγὼ ὑμῖν τῆς παῖδος ἠδύνασθε αὐτὸ πίστιν δοῦναι, ὥσπερ ὁ νόμος κελεύει, ἐὰν τις πεισθεὶ ὑπακαλῶν δικαζέσθαι τοῦ κληρονόμου.
units.tr: Demosthenes praises this law in his speech against Callippus: "that I was able to give you an oath concerning the child, as the law commands, if anyone, having been persuaded, brings a suit against the heir."

units.la: Solon praeuerat Triptolemus, cuius Lex fuit,
units.tr: Triptolemus came before Solon, and his law was:

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] | Honoranto parentes. [?]
units.tr: "Honour your parents."

units.la: Legem hanc in templo Eleusiniae Cereris residere scripsit Xenocrates Philosophus, vt auctor est Hermippus apud Porphyrium [illegible, ~50 letters], ἐν τῷ Ἀθηναίων νομοθετῶν Τειπτόλεμον παλαιότατον πρῶτον ἀπολιφάμου, καὶ ἐν Ἐρμιππος ἐν δευτέρῳ ὅπου τῶν νομοθετῶν χρόφει ἔφη δ᾽ ἀσφαλῆ [illegible, ~40 letters]. B. Hieronymus Libro aduersus Iouinianum II. Xenocrates Philosophus de Triptolemi Legibus apud Atheniensis tria tantum praecepta in Templo Eleusinae residere scribit: Honorandos parentes: Venerandos Deos: Carnibus non vescendum.
units.tr: The philosopher Xenocrates wrote that this law was inscribed in the temple of Eleusinian Ceres. Hermippus, as cited by Porphyry, reports this, and in the Athenian lawgivers … the most ancient Triptolemus … and Hermippus in his second book, where he writes on the lawgivers … Jerome, Book II Against Jovinian: "The philosopher Xenocrates writes that only three precepts of the laws of Triptolemus were inscribed among the Athenians in the temple of Eleusinian Ceres: honour parents; venerate the gods; abstain from eating flesh."

units.la: Quare etiam Legibus Atheniensium ingrati actio dabatur aduersus liberos, qui parentes suos non honorassent:
units.tr: For this reason, under the laws of the Athenians, an action for ingratitude was also granted against children who had not honoured their parents.

units.la: [illegible, ~55 letters] | Si quis parentes non honorarit, dicat il-li scribitor; neque Magistratum gerito.
units.tr: "If anyone has not honoured his parents, let the clerk tell him … and let him not hold office."

units.la: Ex hac Lege, qui inter Magistratus, Nouem uiros puto, allecti erant, Magistratuum albo expungebantur, si, quando in illorum vitam morésque inquirebatur ἐπὶ τὰς δοκιμασίας, in hanc Legem incurrisse arguerentur. Xenophon ἀπομνημονεύματ Lib. II. Οἶδα οὖν ὅτι ἐν ἡ πόλις ἄλλης μὲν ἀρχείας στέ[illegible, ~25 letters]. audiet: maxime si aegros se esse dicant, desiderentque à libertis exhiberi. Leg. I. §. II. D. de officio Praefecti Vrbi. An idem obseruatum inter parentes & liberos, nescio. Atque ex his patet Legem illam, quae saepius apud Senecam patrem occurrit, Liberi parentes alant, aut vinciantur, non esse defunctam è iure Atheniensium, siue Romanorum: sunt in illis è Syria petitae, exempli gratia haec legitur apud eundem Senecam. Cum filio tricenario pater patrimonium diuidat: ex hac Lege ista habentur apud Lucam Euangelij cap. XV. ἀὐδεπὸς τις εἶχε δύο υἱοὶ. ἡ εἶπεν ὁ νεώτερος αὐτῶν τῷ πατρὶ, πάτερ, δός μοι τὸ ἐπιβάλλον μέρος τῆς οὐσίας. ὁ δὲ διεῖλεν αὐτοῖς τὸν βίον. Sed de his nos plura, si Deus dederit, ad ipsos Rhetores Graecos & Latinos.
units.tr: By this law, those who had been chosen among the magistrates (I think nine men) were struck from the list of magistrates if, when their life and conduct were examined at the scrutiny, they were proved to have violated it. Xenophon, Memorabilia, Book II: "I know that in this city … will hear, especially if they say they are sick and ask to be supported by freedmen" (Law I, §2, D., On the Duty of the Prefect of the City). I do not know whether the same was observed between parents and children. From this it is clear that the law which often appears in Seneca the Elder, "Let children feed their parents, or be bound in chains," has not fallen out of use under Athenian or Roman law. Those (laws) are taken from Syria. For example, the following is read in the same Seneca: "With his thirty-year-old son the father divides the patrimony." From this law those things are found in Luke ch. 15: "A certain man had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me. And he divided unto them his living." But we shall say more about these matters, God willing, when we come to the Greek and Latin rhetors themselves.

units.la: Liberi, qui parentes suos non exhibuerant, infamia notati, arcebantur concione, Templorum publicorum ingressu, & omni coronarum in publicis festiuitatibus usu: ὁ νόμος ἐξῶ τὴν ἀπερρίψεως τῆς ἀγρέσεως ξείρχει, ἡ ὅτι ἐὰν φασοδῶσι εἰ τὰς χοινὰς φιλοφορίας, ὅτι εἰσένειν εἰς τὰ ἱερὰ τὰ δημοτικά. Si his non abstinerent, hac cum illis agebatur Lege
units.tr: Children who had not supported their parents, marked with infamy, were excluded from the assembly, from entering public temples, and from wearing crowns at public festivals. The law says: "…if they should come to the common gatherings or enter the public temples." If they did not abstain from these, proceedings were brought against them under this law:

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΑΓΑΧΘΗ, ΤΩΝ ΓΟΝΕΩΝ ΚΑΚΩΣΕΩΣ ΗΛΩΚΩΣ ΕΙΣΙΩΝ ΟΠΗ, ΜΗ ΧΡΗ, ΔΗΣΑΝΤΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΟΙ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ, ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΑΙΑΝ, ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΕΙΤΩ ΔΕ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΛΛΩΙ, ΤΙΜΑΤΩ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ Ο ΤΙ ΧΡΗ ΠΑΘΕΙΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ Η ΑΡΟΤΙΣΑΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΥ ΤΙΜΗΘΗ, ΔΕΔΕΣΤΩ ΤΕΩΣ, ΕΩΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΤΙΣΗ.
units.tr: "If anyone is found mistreating his parents, and is caught entering the places from which he is barred, let the Eleven arrest him and bring him to the Heliaea for trial. Whoever wishes, and is permitted, may bring the accusation. If he is convicted, the Heliaea shall impose a penalty or a fine on him. If he is fined, he shall be held in custody until he pays it." [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΑΓΑΧΘΗ … ΕΩΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΤΙΣΗ]

units.la: Si quis damnatus male parentum tractationis, ea deprehendatur ingredi loca, quibus arcentur, Vndecimuiri capitales cum vinciunto, & in iudicium apud Heliaeam rapiunto: quicumque voluerit, cui licet, accusato. Heliaea ei conuicto poenam vel multam irrogato. Si multa irrogata fuerit, quousque eam soluerit, in vinculis esto.
units.tr: "If a condemned man is found to have mistreated his parents and is caught entering the places from which he is barred, let the Eleven in charge of capital cases bind him and drag him to trial before the Heliaea. Whoever wishes, and is permitted, may bring the accusation. Let the Heliaea impose on him, if convicted, a penalty or a fine. If a fine is imposed, he shall remain in chains until he pays it."

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτους, docetque à Solone latam fuisse: ... καταλύει. λέγοντων δὲ τὴν νόμων, οὐ ἔθηκε Σόλων, ὅτι ὁμοίως ὧν τούτω νομοθέτης, ἐαὶ τῆς ἀλύσεως τῆς κακώσεως τὴν γονέων, εἰς τὴν ἀγρὸν ἐμβάλλη, φιλιάζει. Addit deinde verba ipsa Legis, quae descripsimus.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in his speech against Timocrates, and he teaches that it was proposed by Solon: "…dissolves. And when the law which Solon established is read, which says that a lawgiver, if one bound in chains for mistreating his parents enters the forum, is liable…" He then adds the very words of the law that we have set out.

units.la: Non tulit autem Solon hanc de exhibendis parentibus Legem indefinite, sed aliquot adiecit exceptiones: Quarum vna haec est:
units.tr: But Solon did not enact this law about supporting parents without limit; he added several exceptions. One of them is this:

units.la: Υιὸν πεῖσθαι τὸν πατέρα μὴ διδαξάμενον τέχνην ἐπιθυμεῖν μὴ εἶ. Filius, quem pater artem non docuerit, adeum exhibendum ne cogitor.
units.tr: "A son whom his father has not taught a craft shall not be compelled to support him." [Υιὸν … μὴ ἐπιθυμεῖν]

units.la: Plutarchus in Solone hanc eius Legem refert: ἡ νόμου ἔγραψεν, ὡς πεῖσθαι τὸν πατέρα μὴ διδαξάμενον τέχνην ἐπιθυμεῖν μὴ εἶ. Legis ferendae ratio fuit, τὰ πλῆσα τῆς χώρας ἀλμυρὰ ἡ φαῦλα εἶ. Quare neque quenquam nisi εἰς τὴν πόλιν Athenas volebat commigrare, neque impunitam fuit lentitudinem. Meminit Legis Galenus in Protreptico. ἐπαγγελία δ᾽ αὖ τῆς ἡ τὸν Ἀθηναῖον νομοθέτην, ὡς τὸν μὴ διδάξαντα τέχνην, ἐκώλυε παῖς τὸ παιδὸς πεῖσθαι, τέχνης ἀπάσης κατ᾽ ἐκ-εῖνον μάλιστα τὸν χρείαν ἀσχολιάν.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his Solon, reports this law of his: "He wrote the law that a son is not to be compelled to support a father who has not taught him a trade." The reason for the law was that the land of Attica was poor and barren. For this reason he did not want anyone to migrate except to the city of Athens, and idleness was not left unpunished. Galen mentions the law in his Protrepticus: the Athenian lawgiver, when he forbade a son to be compelled to support a father who had not taught him a craft, made the son especially free from all the cares of a craft.

units.la: Fuit & altera exceptio hanc in Legem relata,
units.tr: There was also a second exception, related in this law:

units.la: Μηδὲ τῆς ἐξ ἐπαρχής ἡμιωθέντος ἐπιθυμεῖν, Nothi patres alere ne cogunter. εἰ, ὃς παῖδας πέφυκεν.
units.tr: Nor to desire what was half of the share from the estate [Μηδὲ τῆς ἐξ ἐπαρχής ἡμιωθέντος ἐπιθυμεῖν]; the fathers of bastards are not to be compelled to support them, if he has begotten children [εἰ, ὃς παῖδας πέφυκεν].

units.la: Descripserat hanc Solonis Legem ex eius Axonibus Heraclides Ponticus, ab eoque mutuatus est, & transcripsit Plutarchus in Solone: <bl>[illegible, ~40 letters]</bl> ὡς Ἡρακλείδης ἱστόρηκεν ὁ Ποντικός. Qui enim è meretrice liberos tollit, illis <bl>[illegible, ~12 letters]</bl> πατρὸς, neque vnquam in animo habuit <bl>[illegible, ~10 letters]</bl> non enim ἐπὶ <bl>[illegible, ~8 letters]</bl> παίδων, sed ἡδονῆς ἕνεκα cum illa consueverat muliere. An vero matres alere cogantur liberi quanuis non ex legitimis nuptiis suscepti, si quis quaerat, è Graecorum iure negabit Rhetor apud Synesium Epistola III. posse cogi ad exhibendam matrem, qui non est è legitimis nuptiis susceptus: ὁ υἱὸς ὁ πάτωρ, ἀφεδαὶ φησι τῆς αἰσχύνης τὸ νόμου μητέρα τρέφειν ἐπαίρειν. ἄπαγε τὸ νόμου, τῆς γὰρ ἡ-πτω γεγονότι, ἀποσείσασθαι μὴ ἡ μήτηρ, ὁ δὲ λοιπὸς τῇ γονέων, ἀμφισβητήσεως. ὅ-σον οὖν ἀμφοτέρους ἐχέδα τῆς δὲ γεγονότων ὀφείλεται, τὸ πρῶ ἡκειν εἰς ἀπατόρων εἰς τὰς μητέρας. Fuit & tertia exceptio, de qua, suo loco, dicemus.
units.tr: Heraclides of Pontus copied this law of Solon from his axones, and Plutarch borrowed it and transcribed it in his Solon: … as Heraclides of Pontus has recorded. For whoever has children by a prostitute gives them … of the father, and he never had in mind the fair name of lawful marriage; for he did not have children for the sake of ploughing (the field) but for pleasure, since he lived with that woman. Whether mothers are compelled to support children not born of lawful marriage, if anyone asks, the rhetor in Synesius, Letter III, denies by Greek law that a son not born of lawful marriage can be forced to support his mother: the son, the rhetor says, is freed from the disgrace of a law that obliges him to feed his mother. Away with such a law! For one born of a prostitute cannot shake off his mother, while the rest of the obligation belongs to the parents… Since both are owed by those who have been born, the duty passes from the fathers to the mothers… There was also a third exception, which we will discuss in its place.

units.la: Apud Romanos autem iure ciuili mater cogitur, vt loquitur Vlpianus Lib. II. de officio Consulis, praefertim vulgo quaesitos liberos alere, nec non ipsi eam. Leg. V. §. IV. D. de agnoscendis & alendis liberis & parentibus.
units.tr: Among the Romans, by civil law, the mother is compelled, as Ulpian says in book 2 of his work on the office of the consul, especially to support children born out of wedlock, and indeed to support them herself. Law 5, §4, D. de agnoscendis et alendis liberis et parentibus.

units.la: Ea praeterea reuerentia atque pietate in parentes liberos esse voluit Atheniensium Legislator, vt si quis patrem defunctum criminaretur, eaque de re cum filio siue haerede ageret, filius pro patre iusiurandum daret, Lex haec est:
units.tr: The Athenian lawgiver also wished children to show such reverence and piety toward their parents that, if anyone brought a charge against a dead father and sued the son or heir over it, the son should swear an oath on his father's behalf. The law reads:

units.la: Υἱὸς γὰρ τῆς παιδὸς τὸν υἱὸν πίστιν δοῦναι, εἰ τις τεθνεῶτι ὑπολαλῶν δικάζηται τὰ κληρονόμω.
units.tr: "The son shall give the oath on behalf of the father, if anyone, slandering the dead man, brings a suit against the heir." [Υἱὸν ὑπὲρ πατρὸς πίστιν δοῦναι, εἰ τις τεθνεῶτι ὑπολαλῶν δικάζηται τῷ κληρονόμῳ]

units.la: Filius pro patre iusiurandum dato, si quis mortuum criminatus cum haere-de agat.
units.tr: Let the son swear for the father, if anyone, accusing the dead man, brings a suit against the heir.

units.la: Laudat hanc Legem Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Καλλίππων. ὅτι δὲ ἐγὼ ὑπὲρ τῆς πόλεως ἡδέλησε αὐτοῖς πίστιν δοῦναι, ὥσπερ ὁ νόμος κελεύει, εἰ τις τεθνεῶτι ὑπικαλῶν δικάζηται τὰ κληρονόμω.
units.tr: Demosthenes praises this law in his speech against Callippus: "that I wished to give them an oath on behalf of the city, as the law commands, if anyone, calling the dead man to account, brings a suit against the heir." [ὅτι δὲ ἐγὼ ὑπὲρ τῆς πόλεως ἠθέλησα αὐτοῖς πίστιν δοῦναι, ὥσπερ ὁ νόμος κελεύει, εἰ τις τεθνεῶτι ὑπολαλῶν δικάζηται τῷ κληρονόμῳ]

units.la: Solonis praeiuerat Triptolemus, cuius Lex fuit,
units.tr: Before Solon there was Triptolemus, whose law was:

units.la: Τοὺς γονεῖς τιμᾶν.
units.tr: "To honour parents." [Τοὺς γονεῖς τιμᾶν]

units.la: Honoranto parentes.
units.tr: Let them honour their parents.

units.la: Legem Iani in templo Eleusiniae Cereris residere scripsit Xenocrates Philosophus, vt auctor est Hermippus apud Porphyrium ὡς ἐν τῷ πόλει ἐνδεικτηρίου, ἐν τῷ πόλει Ἀθηναίων νομοθέτην Τριπτόλεμον παλαιοτάτον ὀφειλόμενον, ὡς δὲ Ἑρμίππου ἐν δευτέρῳ ὡς ἐν νομοθετῶν γράφει τῶν, φασὶ δὲ ἡ Τριπτόλεμον Ἀθηναίων νομοθέτην, καὶ τῶν νόμων εἶναι πρὸς ἐπὶ Ξενοκράτης ὁ Φιλόσοφος λέγει ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι, τοὺς γονεῖς τιμᾶν, ἴσως καρπῶν ἀχαλὰν, ζᾶα μὴ σιτεῖσθαι. B. Hieronymus Libro aduersus Iouinianum II. Xenocrates Philosophus de Triptolemi Legibus apud Atheniensis tria tantum praecepta in Templo Eleusinae residere scribit: Honorandos parentes: Venerandos Deos: Carnibus non vescendum.
units.tr: The philosopher Xenocrates wrote that the law of Triptolemus was inscribed in the temple of Eleusinian Ceres among the Athenians, as Hermippus reports in Porphyry; Triptolemus was the most ancient lawgiver of the Athenians, and Xenocrates says that three precepts of his laws were inscribed at Eleusis: to honour parents, to worship the gods, and to abstain from eating flesh. Jerome, in book 2 against Jovinian: The philosopher Xenocrates writes that only three precepts of the laws of Triptolemus were inscribed among the Athenians in the temple at Eleusis: honour your parents; venerate the gods; do not eat flesh. [Ξενοκράτης ὁ φιλόσοφος ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι τοὺς γονεῖς τιμᾶν, θεοὺς σέβειν, ἐμψύχων ἀπέχεσθαι]

units.la: Quare etiam Legibus Atheniensium ingrati actio dabatur aduersus liberos, qui parentes suos non honorasset: Εἀν τις γονέας μὴ θεραπεύῃ, τοῦτο δίκλιν τῷ ὑπηρέτῃ, ἢ εἴς ἐὰν ἀρχὴν τῆς.
units.tr: Hence, under the laws of the Athenians, an action for ingratitude was granted against children who had not honoured their parents: "If anyone does not serve his parents, let an action be brought against him before the magistrate, and let him hold no office." [Ἐάν τις γονέας μὴ θεραπεύῃ, τούτῳ δίκη ἔστω...]

units.la: Si quis parentes non honorarit, dica illi scribitor; neque Magistratum gerito.
units.tr: If anyone has not honoured his parents, let an indictment be written against him; and let him not hold office.

units.la: Ex hac Lege, qui inter Magistratus, Nouemuiros puto, allecti erant, Magistratuum albo expungebantur, si, quando in illorum vitam morésque inquirebatur ἐπὶ τῆς δοκιμασίας, in hanc Legem incurrisse arguerentur. Xenophon <bl>[illegible, ~8 letters]</bl> Lib. II. <bl>[illegible, ~30 letters]</bl>
units.tr: By this law, those who had been enrolled among the magistrates, I think the nine archons, were struck off the list of magistrates if, when their life and conduct were examined at the scrutiny (ἐπὶ τῆς δοκιμασίας), they were shown to have violated this law. Xenophon [illegible, ~8 letters] book 2 [illegible, ~30 letters]

units.tr: [Illegible annotation under the text; only fragments can be read with any confidence: a Greek note concerning a "dica" written before the archon, as in the other case, of which law, in my judgement, this is the head.]

units.la: Hactenus actum est de potestate patria in liberos, sequitur vt quid iuris potestatisque fuerit liberis in parentes dicamus. Qua de re Lex hæc legitur:
units.tr: So far we have spoken of paternal power over children. It follows that we should say what right and power children had over parents. A law on this matter is read:

units.la: [?]Χιῶ τὸν πατέρα ἐάν νέων, ἢ γήρως δεσ[?]πότας [?] ἐξέστω ἢ ἐμπλήσας [?] ἐξέστω δὲ ἐλόντα τὸν πατέρα ἐξ[?]ειν τοῦ δῆσαι.
units.tr: [Partly illegible Greek law:] Let the son be allowed to seize his father, if he is out of his mind through youth or old age, and having seized him, to lead him away to be bound.

units.la: Filio ius esto patri tanquam desipienti ob morbum vel senectutem dicam scribere: desipere conuicium in vinculis habeto.
units.tr: The son shall have the right over his father, as over one who is out of his mind through sickness or old age, to bring an indictment; let "being out of one's mind" count as an insult, to be punished with chains.

units.la: Huius meminit Aristophanes Nubibus:
units.tr: Aristophanes mentions this law in the Clouds:

units.la: [?]Οἴ μοι, τί δράσω, σαφέστερον τῆς παιδείας;
units.tr: "Alas, what shall I do? More plainly than my schooling?" [Οἴμοι, τί δράσω; σαφέστερον τῆς παιδείας;]

units.la: [?]Πόσην ἐν ἐλαύνοις αὐτὸν εἰσαγαγὼν ἔλω;
units.tr: "How much of a [...] shall I lead him in and seize him?" [Πόσην ἐλαύνων αὐτὸν εἰσαγαγὼν ἕλω;]

units.la: Xenophon [?]ἀπομνημονεύματα Lib. I. Φάσκων δὲ χρῆναι νόμον ἐξεῖναι ἐλόντα τὸν πατέρα δῆσαι. Hinc Plato Lib. XI. de Legibus, ὡς τ' αὐ σοφίᾳ πατέρες [?]νέων ἢ γήρως δεσπότας ἀρχῶς, ἐξεῖναι δ' ἐλόντα γράφεσθαι. Conuictus autem pater, à re familiari remouebatur, potestate data liberis in eius bonis. Cicero Lib. de Senectute. Sophocles ad summam senectutem Tragoedias fecit: quod propter studium cum rem familiarem negligere videretur, à filijs in iudicium vocatus est, vt quemadmodum nostro more, Male rem gerentibus patribus bonis interdici solet: sic illum, quasi desipientem, à re familiari remouerent iudices. Tum senex dicitur eam fabulam, quam in manibus habebat, & proxime scripserat, O Edipum Coloneum recitasse iudicibus, quaesisseque, num illud carmen desipientis videretur. Quo recitato, sententijs iudicum est liberatus. Iudicabant ei Φρένηρες, colligere est è Græco Comici Interprete ad Ranas. [?]εἰσήγαγε δὲ ποτὲ Σοφοκλῆς ἐν δράματι τὸν Ἰοφῶντα αὐτοῦ φρενοῦντα, ἢ πρὸς τὰς Φρένηρες ἐπικαλοῦντα τοῦ πατρὸς, ὡς ἐπὶ γήρως ἀφαφεῖ[?]τῶ, εἰ ἢ τοῦ Ἰοφῶντος ἐπιπίμισθεν. Σάτυρες ἢ φησὶν αὐτὸν εἰπεῖν. εἰ μὲν εἰμί Σοφοκλῆς ἢ ἀφαφεῖ, εἰ ἢ ἀφαφεῖ, Σοφοκλῆς σὺ εἰμί. ἢ πῶς Οἰδίποδα ἀφαγαλ[?]ναι. Eadem habet Auctor Anonymus Vitæ Sophoclis.
units.tr: Xenophon in the Memorabilia, book 1, says that the law allows a son to seize his father and bind him. Hence Plato, in book 11 of the Laws, says that fathers who are out of their minds through youth or old age are to be ruled, and it is permitted, having seized them, to bring an indictment. A father who was convicted was removed from management of his family property, and the children were given power over his goods. Cicero, in the book On Old Age: Sophocles wrote tragedies into extreme old age; because of his devotion to this, he seemed to neglect his household property, and he was summoned to court by his sons, so that, as with us, when fathers squander their goods they are usually forbidden to manage them, so the judges would remove him from his property as if he were out of his mind. Then the old man is said to have recited to the judges the play he had in hand and had recently written, the Oedipus at Colonus, and asked whether that poem seemed to be the work of a madman. When it had been read, he was acquitted by the votes of the judges. They called him "Phrenes" (sound of mind); this can be gathered from the Greek scholiast on Aristophanes' Frogs. [εἰσήγαγε δέ ποτε Σοφοκλῆς ἐν δράματι τὸν Ἰοφῶντα αὐτοῦ φρενοῦντα ... Σάτυρες ἤ φησιν αὐτὸν εἰπεῖν· εἰ μὲν εἰμὶ Σοφοκλῆς, οὐ φρενῶ· εἰ δὲ φρενῶ, Σοφοκλῆς οὐκ εἰμί] The same is given by the anonymous author of the Life of Sophocles.

units.la: DE INQVILINIS.
units.tr: ON INQUILINES.

units.la: TITVLVS QVINTVS
units.tr: TITLE FIVE

units.la: E[?]verunt præter ciues Athenis Μέτοικοι, quorum inter se non idem ius, neque par conditio: Præter ciues diximus, quia πολίτης negat esse summus vir Aristoteles Politic. Libro III. Ait enim tantum [?]κοινωνὸς τῆς οἰκήσεως, vt & serui, neque [?]εἶναι facere τὰ πολιτικά. Non poterant autem recipi nisi è Senatus Areopagitici sententia, vt potest colligi è Sophoclis OEdipo [?]ἐπὶ Κολωνῷ.
units.tr: There were, besides the citizens of Athens, the Metoikoi (resident aliens), who did not all share the same rights or the same condition. I said "besides the citizens" because Aristotle, in Politics Book III, denies that they are citizens [πολίτης]. He says they are only co-residents [κοινωνὸς τῆς οἰκήσεως], like slaves, and so cannot perform civic functions. They could not be admitted except by decree of the Areopagite Council, as can be gathered from Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus.

units.la: Τοιοῦτον αὐτοῖς Ἄρεος ἐξ οὐλου πάγου [?] Ἐγὼ ξυνῳδὸς ξύνοιον ἀνθ', ὡς Σεμ [?] ἐξ Τοιοῖς δ' ἀλλήλαις τῇ οἰκουμένῃ καὶ ἡν πόλει [?].
units.tr: Such a council for them, from the Areopagus of the whole hill... [the Greek verses are too corrupt in the scan to restore with certainty; the sense is that the Areopagite council, and not the people at large, decided on their admission, and that they were settled among the citizens by that council's judgment].

units.la: Atque haec forte ratio est, quia Solon, ut refert Plutarchus, τῷ ἐξ Ἀρείου πάγου βουλὴν ἔπαξεν ἐπίσκοπον, ὅπως ἕκαστος ἐχ' τὸ ἐπιτήδευμα, καὶ τοὺς ὄρχους καλά-ζων. Itaque videbat quoque hic Areopagiticus Senatus, ne quis Athenas commigraret renuere, nisi ἔπι πέξει, aut rei alterius utilis ergo. Inscribebantúrque eorum nomina γεγραμμένα. Aristophanis Scholiastes ad Aves. τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν ξένων γεγραφένα εἰς τοὺς πίνακας. Horum Metoicon alij eodem cum civibus utebantur iure, qui ἰσοτελεῖς dicebantur: Nam μετοίκιον non pendebant, ut docuerant Isaeus ἐν τῷ κατ' Ἐλπιφέρων καὶ Δημοφάνη, & Lysias; aut quisquis alius auctor est Orationis πρὸς Σώφρονα ὑπὲρ ἕως. πολλάκις ἀμὴ τῆς ἀξιώσεως ... Φάνεσθαι τὴν Μετοίκων, καθ' ὦ ἐ τὴ ... μετοίκιον ἀφεῖναι αὐτοῖς ἐτίμησεν. Praeterea ἐν τῷ ἄλλων, ὧν ἐπεχείρησαν οἱ Μέτοικοι, ἀφεσιν εἶχον οἱ ἰσοτελεῖς, ut narrat Theophrastus ἐν ἐπιδείξει τῆς νόμων. ita hodie editur apud Harpocrationem, quasi Liber XI. laudetur, qui revera IX. est. Erroris haec causa est. Scripserat Theophrastus Legum Libros XXIV. ordine Alphabetico, apud Diogenem Laertium, νόμων ξ' στοιχεῖον καὶ στοιχεῖα ί. adsignatae Leges illae sunt, quae leguntur περὶ τῆς ἰσοπολιτῶν. Itaque cum legeret imperitus librarius ἐν ί τῶν νόμων, putavit numerum esse Libri X. non Librum, qui inscriberetur ξ' στοιχεῖον ί. Haec prima malilabes: hinc scripsit ἐν δεκάτῳ νόμων. Hunc errorem alter excepit: geminata quippe est à librario syllaba, & scriptum ἐν ἐνδεκάτῳ τῶν νόμων. Sed nos veram lectionem ἐν ί à corrupte a vindicavimus & asseruimus: Nam ἰσοπολίτης primam literam habent ί. Ἀεratio tamen οἱ ἰσοπολίτης aliquid pendebant. ὁ ἰσοπολίτης, ὠσχυμένος ὅ τέλος ἐδίδου. Idem videlicet cum civibus Hesychius: ἰσοπολίτης, Μετοίκοι ἴσα τῆς ἀσφαλείας τὰν διδόντες. Neque hoc ius cuiquam concessum, nisi plebiscito. Suidas: ἰσοπολίτης. οἱ ἀπὸ τῶν μετοίκων καὶ τινα ἡμῖν ἀπὸ τῆς δήμου ἡμωλήψεως, καὶ ψήφισμα μεταλαμβάνοντες εἰς ὅ τῶν δημοποιητῶν ἐχωρεῖν, ἰσοπολίτης ὠνομάζοντο. ἐγίνετο δὲ τοῦτο τῆς μετοικῆς ἐκ τῆς πόλεως, ὅτε ἐδέχοιντο δὲ πέμπτη χειροῦν ... νόμων. Quod dicit Grammaticus, ἰσοπολίτης μεταξὺ εἰς ὅ τῶν δημοποιητῶν διαχέειν, non vsquequaque verum est; Nam οἱ δημοποιηταὶ praeterea ad Rempublicam gerendam accedebant. Pollux Lib. III. cap. V. ἐνοὶ δὲ τῆς Μετοίκων ἰσοπολίτης εἰσὶν, οἷς αἱ τῶν ἐν ψηφισμάτοις χειροτονίαι εἰ ἡ δημοποίητοι, ὅποτε ἐν δόγματος καινοῦ πολιτείας τύχοιεν.
units.tr: This is perhaps the reason why Solon, as Plutarch reports, set up the council from the Areopagus as overseer, so that each man would follow his own trade [ἐπιτήδευμα] and be punished for idleness. So this Areopagite Council also saw to it that no one who wished to settle at Athens should be refused, unless for some skill or other useful reason. Their names were entered in writing [γεγραμμένα]. The Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds: "the names of the foreigners written on the tablets" [τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν ξένων γεγραμμένα εἰς τοὺς πίνακας]. Some of these Metoikoi enjoyed the same rights as the citizens and were called "equal in taxes" [ἰσοτελεῖς], for they did not pay the metoikion, as Isaeus in his speech against Euphiletus and Demophanes taught, and Lysias too, or whichever other author wrote the speech against Sophron. ... [the rest of this passage is too garbled to restore]. Moreover, the equal-tax men [ἰσοτελεῖς] were exempt from the levies that the Metoikoi undertook, as Theophrastus relates in his work on laws. This is printed today in Harpocration as if from Book XI, though it is really Book IX; the error arose thus. Theophrastus wrote twenty-four books of Laws, arranged alphabetically, as Diogenes Laertius reports [νόμων ξ' στοιχεῖον καὶ στοιχεῖα ί]. The laws in question, those read "on the equal-citizens" [περὶ τῆς ἰσοπολιτῶν], are assigned to that letter. So when an ignorant copyist read "in book ί of the laws," he took the number to be Book X, not Book IX, which was headed with the letter ξ and the letter ί. This was the first small slip; from it he wrote "in the tenth of the laws" [ἐν δεκάτῳ νόμων]. A second error followed: the copyist doubled a syllable and wrote "in the eleventh of the laws" [ἐν ἐνδεκάτῳ τῶν νόμων]. But I have restored and vindicated the true reading ἐν ί against this corruption, since the word ἰσοπολίτης begins with the letter ί. Nevertheless the equal-citizens [οἱ ἰσοπολῖται] did pay something; the ἰσοπολίτης paid a fixed tax. Hesychius likewise says of the equal-citizens: the Metoikoi who gave an equal payment for their protection [ἰσοπολίτης, Μετοίκοι ἴσα τῆς ἀσφαλείας τὰ διδόντες]. Nor was this right granted to anyone except by a plebiscite. Suidas: the equal-citizens [ἰσοπολίτης] were those from among the Metoikoi who, by a vote of the people, were admitted to the rights of the demes and who received a decree allowing them to enter the demes; they were called equal-citizens. This happened to those who had lived in the city, when they were received by the citizens... [the rest is corrupt]. What the grammarian says, that the equal-citizens were admitted among the demesmen, is not entirely true, for the demesmen also came forward to manage the commonwealth. Pollux, Book III, chapter 5: some of the Metoikoi are equal-citizens, to whom the election of the magistrates by vote is open, whenever they obtain the rights of citizenship by a new decree.

units.la: Alij vero τῶν Μετοίκων quotannis pendebant duodecim drachmas, quod μετοίκιον dicebatur. Nicephorus ad haec Synesij verba de Insomniis. ὅτι ἰσοπολίτης, ὁ ὠνὴς ὁ μετοίκιον. ἔγω ὠ ταῖς Ἀθηναίοις λαμβάνει καὶ ἕκαστον ἐτῆς δραχμὰς ιβ'. ἐν τῇ ἐξώσῃ ἐρχομένων εἰς Ἀθήνας ξένων κατοικίας ἐνεκα, τὴν τοῦτο ὀνομάζοντες μετοίκιον. Harpocration: Μέτοικός μὲν ἐστι, ὁ ἐξ ἑτέρας πόλεως μετοικῶν ἐγ ἑτέρα, καὶ μὴ πρὸς ἐλαχίστην ὡς ξένος ἐπιδημῶν, ἀλλὰ τὴν οἰκίαν αὐτοῦ ἀνακτασπαρῆμένος, ἐτίδοντο ὁ ἕκαστον ἐκ δραχμὴν δώδεκα, ὅθ' ὠνόμασεν μετοίκιον, ὡς δηλοῖ ΕΥ̓ξουλος ἐν Πλάτωνι. Pollux Lib. III. cap. IV. Μέτοικος ὁ ὃ μετοίκιον σιωπᾷ ... ὁ ἡ ὠ συνοικοῦσα τῷ δημοσίῳ δραχμῇ, ἡ τῷ Γραμματεῖ, περιάδολον. Hesychius: Μέτοικοι, οἱ συνοικοῦντες ξένοι ἐν τῇ πόλει, ἐ τελοῦντες ἀντὶ δώδεκα τῶν σύνευξ εἰς ὅ δημόσιον, & paullo ante μετοίκιον, πρὸς ἕτερα ἐκάλλο, ὁ ἐπήξεν δραχμὰς δώδεκα. (ita legendum, non δίκα.) τῆς δὲ πλοίης [illegible, ~12 letters]. Sed de hoc triobolo, quod superaddunt Pollux & Hesychius, dicemus infra, Deo dante, suo loco. Isæus Oratione κατ' Ἐλπαγόρου ἐν Δημοφαίους viros drachmas duodecim, feminas sex tantum pependisse ait: atque pendente matre, μετοίκιον non pendebat filius: & contra pendente filio, non pendebat mater. Harpocration ex Isæo: Ἰσαῖος δ' ἐν τῷ κατ' Ἐλπαγόρου ἐν Δημοφαίους [?] δραχμὰς ἐτέλει μετοίκιον, ἡ δὲ γυνὴ ἐξ, ἡ ὅτι τὴς ὁμοῦ πλουσίως, ἡ μήτηρ οὐκ ἐπέλει· μὴ πλουσίου δ' ἐκείνου, αὐτὴ πλέ. Neque vero Athenis tantum ὁ μετοίκιον pendebant, sed in aliis item vrbibus tota Attica. Lysias ὁ τοῦ ἐξ Φιλωνος, συνεκδιαξάμενος γὰρ τὰ ἑαυτῆς συνάδει, εἰς τὴν Ὠρωπίαν ἀξιώσας, ἡ ἐν Ὠρωπῷ μετοίκιον καταβάλλει, ὅτι προστάτην ἔχει. Nam Oropus terræ erat Atticæ. Scholia Sophoclis ad OEdipum Tyrannum: μεταφέρει ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν τοῖς πόλεσι ξένων πλουσίων τὰ μετοίκια.
units.tr: Others of the Metoikoi, however, paid twelve drachmas each year, which was called the metoikion [μετοίκιον]. Nicephorus, on these words of Synesius about dreams: "that the equal-citizen is one who pays the metoikion; for this is received by the Athenians, and each pays twelve drachmas a year, for foreigners who come to Athens to settle, and this is called the metoikion." Harpocration: a Metoikos is one who lives in a city other than his own, not as a passing foreigner, but who has settled his household there, and who pays twelve drachmas each year, which is called the metoikion, as Euxoulos in Plato shows. Pollux, Book III, chapter 4: the Metoikos is one who pays the metoikion ... [the rest is corrupt]. Hesychius: Metoikoi are foreigners who live together in the city and who, instead of the twelve..., pay into the public treasury; and a little before, the metoikion was levied at twelve drachmas. (So it should be read, not "δίκα".) But concerning this triobolon, which Pollux and Hesychius add, we shall speak below, God willing, in its place. Isaeus, in his speech against Euphiletus and Demophanes, says that men paid twelve drachmas and women only six, and that while the mother paid, the son did not pay the metoikion, and conversely, when the son paid, the mother did not. Harpocration from Isaeus: Isaeus, in his speech against Euphiletus and Demophanes... paid the metoikion, and the woman six... [the rest is corrupt]. Nor did the Metoikoi pay the metoikion only at Athens, but likewise in the other towns of the whole of Attica. Lysias, in his speech for Philon's son... since he has property in Oropus, he pays the metoikion there because he has a patron. For Oropus was land of Attica. Scholia on Sophocles' Oedipus the King: he transfers the metoikia from the rich foreigners in the cities.

units.la: Pendebant autem ὁ μετοίκιον οἱ Μέτοικοι, omniaque alia, priuata, publica, administrabant per Patronum, quem de ciuibus Athenien-sibus eligere Lege iubebantur. Lex hæc est:
units.tr: The Metics, however, paid their metic tax [μετοίκιον] and managed all their other affairs, private and public, through a Patron, whom they were ordered by law to choose from among the Athenian citizens. The law is this:

units.la: Τῶν Μετοίκων ἕκαστον ἕνα τῶν ἀστῶν νέμειν προστάτῃ· καὶ δὲ αὐτὸ ὅ, τι μετοίκιον τ[?]ηλῆς κατ' ἔτος, ἢ τὰ ἄλλα διοικεῖσθαι.
units.tr: "Each of the Metics shall assign one of the citizens as patron; and the same person shall collect the metic tax [μετοίκιον] annually, or manage the other business." [Τῶν Μετοίκων ἕκαστον ἕνα τῶν ἀστῶν νέμειν προστάτῃ· καὶ δὲ αὐτὸ ὅ, τι μετοίκιον τ[?]ηλῆς κατ' ἔτος, ἢ τὰ ἄλλα διοικεῖσθαι.]

units.la: Inquilinorum singuli vnum de ciuibus Patronum eligunto, per illum quotannis tributum pendunto, ceteraque alia administranto.
units.tr: Each of the Inquilines shall choose one of the citizens as patron; through him they shall pay the tribute each year and manage all their other affairs.

units.la: Lege hac cauetur, vt Inquilini eligerent è ciuibus Athenien-sibus quem vellent Patronum, cuius auctoritate se tuerentur & niterentur, ac qui esset quasi vas atque sponsor eorum. Suidas: τῶν μετοίκων ἕκαστος προστάτην ἐχέτω ἀπὸ τῶν ἀστῶν ἕνα, ἡ δὲ αὐτὴ ὅ, τι μετοίκιον πληρῶ κατ' ἔτος, ἐκ τὰ ἄλλα διοικεῖσθαι. Harpocration ex Hyperide ὁ τῷ κατ' Ἀσκληπιάδου ἀπογράφεσθαι ὅτι. φησὶ γὰρ ἕκαστος τὴν μετοίκιαν ἑαυτῷ τῆς πολιτείας τινὰ προστάτην ἀποδέξασθαι τῶν ἰδίων ἢ τὸ χρῆμα. Auctor Etymologici Magni: ἐρώτα γὰρ ἕκαστος τῶν μετοίκων ὅ, τι ἐλεῖ τ' πολίτῃ ἵνα προστάτην, ἥν ἐπιμελούμενον ἢ τῶν ἰδίων, ἐκ δημοσίων ἐπιμελεῖ αὐτὸ, ὡσαύτως ἐπιζητεῖ ὅτι. Harpocration in Προστάτης, οἱ τῶν Μετοίκων Αθηναῖοι προστατεῖς, Προστάτης καλεῖσθαι· ἐνδείξει γὰρ ὡς ἕκαστος τῶν Μετοίκων πολίτην ἵνα Αθηναίων ἢ μὲν προστάτην. Neque tantum Athenis, sed etiam in ceteris Atticæ vrbibus, vt μετοίκιον pendebant, ita Προστάτῃ νέμειν eadem Lege iubebantur[?]. Lysias loco laudato. Καὶ ὁ Ὠρωπῷ μετοίκιον καταβάλλει, ὅτι προστάτην ἔχει.
units.tr: By this law it was provided that the inquilines should choose from among the Athenian citizens whomever they wished as their Patronus, by whose authority they would be protected and supported, and who would be, as it were, their surety and guarantor. Suidas: each of the Metoikoi shall have one protector from among the citizens, and he shall pay the metoikion each year, and the rest shall be managed through him. Harpocration from Hyperides, in his speech against Asclepiades' registration: for each Metoikos, he says, chose for himself a protector from among the citizens for his property or his affairs. The author of the Etymologicum Magnum: each of the Metoikoi asked which citizen he should take as μετοίκιον-protector [προστάτην], who would look after his private affairs and, in public matters, would deal with the state on his behalf. Harpocration on the word Prostates: the Metoikoi at Athens had protectors, who were called Prostatai, for each Metoikos chose one of the Athenian citizens as his protector. Not only at Athens but also in the other towns of Attica, the Metoikoi were ordered by the same law to pay the metoikion and to assign a protector [προστάτῃ νέμειν]. Lysias, in the passage cited: he pays the metoikion at Oropus because he has a protector [προστάτην].

units.la: Manauit ius illud ab eo, quod antiquissimis Athenien-sium temporibus obtinuerat, tenuiores enim ciues patronum aliquem è potentioribus sibi adscis-cebant, cui, non minus quam si ære & libra empti essent, ministrabant, verberibus etiam cædebantur, nisi patroni iussa caperent: Dionysius Halicar-nassensis Lib. II. ὡς καὶ ἀλλαγὴς ἡ ἴσως τοῖς Γαλλικοῖς Romulus τοῖς δημοτικοῖς, ὑπηρέτας ἐκέλευε τῷ ἐν τῷ πλήθους ὃν αὐτὸς ἐξεῦλεν, νέμειν προστάτῃ· ἔτος Ἑλληνικὸν ἡ δραχμὴν, ὢ Θεσσαλοὶ τι μέγιστα πολλοῦ χρώμενοι διεπλεύσαντο, ἡ Ἀθηναῖοι καὶ Ταρραχὰ, ὅτι τὰ κρίτη λαβὼν· ἐκ ἐσοί μὲν γὰρ ἐνδοτονικῶς ἐχρῶντο τοῖς πελάταις, ἔργα τε ὑπηρετοῦντες ἡ ῥωμαῖοι ἐλευθέρας, ἡ ὅπως μὴ προστάτην τὴν ἐλαύνοι αὐτῶν, πλὴν τὰς ἐστὶν ὅτι, ἡ ἐάλα ὥσπερ ἀργυρώνητοι χρώμενοι. Ἀθηναῖοι μὲν Θῆβας τοῖς πελάταις, ὅτι τῆς λαμπρείας· Θεσσαλοί, Πενέστας, οἱ διαζοντες αὐτοῖς ἀρχὴ ἐν τῇ κλήσῃ τῷ τυχῶ. Sed hæc prius fuere apud Athenienses: nam Θη[?]τῆς Solonis longe meliori fuere conditione: in eorumque locum, quem occuparent, venerunt οἱ Μέτοικοι, quibus Lege cogente necessum fuit patronum aliquem è ciuibus Athenien̂sibus sibi eligere, in cuius clientela acquiescerent. Unde apud Terentium Eunucho Thaïs paullo post quam Athenas venisset, ut hinc constat:
units.tr: That right came from what had prevailed in the most ancient times of the Athenians. For the poorer citizens took to themselves some patron from among the more powerful, to whom they rendered service no less than if they had been bought for money and scales; they were even beaten with rods unless they carried out the patron's orders. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book II: as Romulus ordered the plebeians to assign to each of the common people whom he himself had freed a patron [προστάτῃ]... [the rest of this Greek passage, on the clients of the Thessalians, Athenians and others, is too corrupt to restore with confidence]. But these conditions prevailed earlier among the Athenians; for the Thetes under Solon's laws were in a far better position, and in their place, which they had occupied, came the Metoikoi, who by law were bound to choose for themselves some patronus from among the Athenian citizens, in whose clientage they might rest. Whence in Terence's Eunuch Thais, shortly after she had come to Athens, as is clear from this:

units.la: CHÆR. Set istam Thaidem non sciui nobis vicinam. PA. Haud diu est Phœdriæ patrem patronum sibi adoptauit:
