units.tr: CHOREA: But I did not know that this Thais was our neighbour. PAMPHILA: Not long ago she adopted Phaedria's father as her patron.

units.la: CHÆR. Thaïs patri se commendanit in clientelam & fidem: Nobis dedit se.
units.tr: CHOREA: Thais has commended herself to the father's clientage and protection; she has given herself to us.

units.la: Apud Romanos plebs in clientelam potentiorum se dabat, ut è Dionysij laudatis verbis liquet, quæ hic iterum describemus: [?]ἀπέδωκε δὲ ἐδωκε τῆς Πατρικίοις τοῖς δημοτικοῖς, ἐπιτρέψας ἐκείνῳ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐκ τῆς πλήθους οὐ αὐτὸς ἐβούλε-το, νέμειν Πομπάτιο[?]. quod habes etiam apud Plutarchum in Romulo: è cuius Legibus translata hæc XII. PATRONVS SI CLIENTI FRAVDEM FAXIT, SACER ESTO. quam leges apud Seruium ad ista Vergilij Æneidos VI.
units.tr: Among the Romans the plebeians gave themselves into the clientage of the powerful, as is clear from the praise of Dionysius, which we describe again here: [ἀπέδωκε δὲ ἐδωκε τῆς Πατρικίοις τοῖς δημοτικοῖς, ἐπιτρέψας ἐκείνῳ] ... and the rest of that passage, which is garbled in the transcription. You also find this in Plutarch's Romulus, and from its laws these words are translated from the Twelve Tables: "IF A PATRON DEFRAUDS HIS CLIENT, LET HIM BE ACCURSED." The same laws are found in Servius on those lines of Vergil's Aeneid VI.

units.la: Et fraus innexa clienti.
units.tr: And fraud bound up with the client.

units.la: Ex hoc potentiorum patrocinio manauit subsecutis temporibus alterum, quando vicani in patrocinium potentiorum se dabant, in fraudem tributi publici: Sed hoc patrocinium vetitum est Imperatorum sanctionibus: Vide Cod. Vt nemo ad suum patr. & Cod. Th. De patrocinio vicorum: cuius tituli Lex VI. est Imperatorum Honorij & Theodosij A A. ad Aurelianum PF. P. scilicet Orientis: in qua ista leguntur examinanda à nobis, [?]οὐὼ ἐκ ἡ εἰπεῖν, accuratius. Ut in futurum functiones omnes, quas metrocomiæ debent, & publici vici pro antiquæ capitationis professione debent, sciant proculdubio subeundas, nequaquam, cephalæotis, hirenarchis, logographis Chomatum, & ceteris liturgis, sub quolibet patrocinij nomine publicis functionibus denegatis, &c. Nomina ista sunt functionum publicarum, cephalæotis, hirenarchis, logographis Chomatum, liturgis, ut constat ex hoc postremo nomine: nam eadem Lege ista leges, si pro antiquitate census functiones publicas & liturgos, quos homologi coloni præstare noscuntur, pro rata sunt absque dubio cognituri. Maxime autem spectant ista Ægyptios vicanos, quamquam etiam & aliarum regionum, unde scripta est Lex ad Præfectum Prætorio Orientis, sed, ut dixi, maxime ista ad Ægyptios vicanos attinent, argumento est, Chomatum, id est, aggerum Nili mentio, Ecclesiæ item Alexandrinæ: & maxime primora Legis verba: Valerij Theodori & Tharsacij examinatio conticescat, illis duntaxat sub Augustaliano iudicio pulsandis, qui ex Cæsarij & Attici Consulatu possessiones sub patrocinio possidere ceperunt Imperatores Augustalianum iudicium appellant, quod ab Augustali Ægypti Præfecto reddebatur. Sed functiones istas explicemus, cephalæotis: existimo pabula esse iumentorum, quæ vulgo dicuntur capita. ut loquitur Ammianus Marcellinus Libro XXII. Cassiodorus: Ad equos capitum definitum. Hesychius: [?]κεφάλαια, [?]ἄλφιτα ἄλλων[?]. Hac significatione Græce dictum in hac Lege, cephalæotis, quod iumentorum pabula conferebatur. Sequitur, Hirenarchis: Annonas intelligo, quas Irenarchæ consequebantur. Logographis Chomatum sunt item, meo iudicio, annonæ datæ illis, quorum cura erat in tabulas referre diacopos sive fluenta, quæ in chomatis id est, aggeribus Nili, ne quis aut chomata rumperet vel dissolueret, aut diacopos nouos in his aggeribus faceret, quod vnice ca-uebatur, vt testatur Vlpianus Lib. de officio Proconsulis: In Ægypto qui chomata rumpit, vel dissoluit, (hi sunt aggeres, qui quidem solent aquam Niloticam continere) æque plectitur extra ordinem, & pro conditione sua, & pro admissi mensura, quidam opere publico, aut metallo plectuntur, & metallo quidam secundum suam dignitatem, si quis arborem sycaminonem excideriť. nam & hæc res vindicatur extra ordinem non leui pœna, idcirco quod hæ arbores colligunt aggeres Niloticos, per quos incrementa Nili dispensantur, & coercentur, & diminutiones æque coercentur, chomata etiam, & diacopi qui in aggeribus fiunt, plecti efficiunt eos, qui admiserunt. Leg. X. D. de extraordinariis criminibus. Eaque de re extat Imperatorum Honorij & Theodosij AA. Constitutio Leg. vnica Cod. Th. de Nili aggeribus non corrumpendis, in hæc verba.
units.tr: From this patronage of the powerful there later arose another kind, when villagers gave themselves into the patrocinium of the powerful in order to evade public tribute. But this patrocinium was forbidden by the constitutions of the emperors. See the Code, That no one may [enter into patronage] of his own, and the Theodosian Code, On the patronage of villages. The sixth law of that title is a constitution of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius Augusti to Aurelianus, Praetorian Prefect, that is, of the East, in which these words are to be examined by us more carefully: So that in future all the public duties which the metrocomiae owe, and which the public villages owe in return for the old profession of capitation, they will certainly know must be undertaken, and by no patronage in any name are the public functions to be refused: the cephalaeotae, hirenarchs, logographers of the dykes, and the other liturgists, and so on. These are the names of public functions: cephalaeotae, hirenarchs, logographers of the dykes, liturgists, as is clear from the last term; for in the same law they are to learn that the public functions and liturgies which the homologoi coloni are known to render, in proportion to the old census, are to be paid without doubt. These matters chiefly concern the Egyptian villagers, though they also apply to other regions, from which the law was written to the Praetorian Prefect of the East. But, as I said, this chiefly concerns the Egyptian villagers. The evidence is the mention of the chomata, that is, the dykes of the Nile, and likewise the Church of Alexandria; and above all the opening words of the law: Let the examination of Valerius, Theodorus and Tharsacius cease; let them be struck only before the Augustalian court, those who began to possess estates under patronage from the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus. The emperors call it the Augustalian court, because it was held by the Augustal Prefect of Egypt. But let us explain these functions. Cephalaeotis: I think these are fodder for beasts of burden, which are commonly called capita, as Ammianus Marcellinus says in Book XXII. Cassiodorus: a fixed amount for the horses' heads. Hesychius: [κεφάλαια, ἄλφιτα ἄλλων]. In this sense the word cephalaeotis is used in this law in Greek, because fodder for beasts of burden was contributed. Next comes hirenarchis: I understand these to be the rations which the irenarchs received. The logographis chomatum were likewise, in my judgement, the rations given to those whose task was to record in the registers the diacopi or channels, that is, the cuts in the dykes of the Nile, so that no one would break or dissolve the chomata or make new diacopi in these dykes; this was the only thing forbidden, as Ulpian testifies in his book On the Office of the Proconsul: In Egypt whoever breaks or dissolves the chomata (these are the dykes, which usually hold back the Nile water) is punished outside the ordinary order, according to his condition and the measure of the offence: some are punished with public works or the mines, and some, according to their rank, with the mines. Likewise, if anyone cuts down a sycamine tree, for this matter too is avenged outside the ordinary order with no light penalty, because these trees bind the Nile dykes, by which the rising and falling of the Nile are regulated and restrained; and diminutions are equally restrained. Those who make the chomata and the diacopi in the dykes are made to be punished, those who have committed the offence. Digest, Book 10, On extraordinary crimes. There also exists a constitution on this matter of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius Augusti, the single law in the Theodosian Code, On not breaking the dykes of the Nile, in these words.

units.la: Impp. Honor. & Theod. AA. Anthemio P. P.
units.tr: The emperors Honorius and Theodosius Augusti to Anthemius, Praetorian Prefect.

units.la: Si quis posthac per Ægyptum intra duodecimum cubitum fluminis Nili vlla fluenta de propriis ac vetustis vsibus præter fas, præterque morem antiquitatis vsurpauerit, flammis eo loco consumatur, in quo vetustatis reuerentiam, & propemodum ipsius imperij adpetierit securitatem: consciis & consortibus eius Oasenæ deportationi constringendis, ita vt nunquam supplicandi eis, vel recipiendi cuitatem, vel dignitatem, vel substantiam licentia tribuatur. Dat. X. Kal. Octob. Constantinop. Honor. VIII. & Theod. III. AA. Coss.
units.tr: If anyone henceforth in Egypt, within twelve cubits of the river Nile, shall cut any channels for his own private uses, contrary to right and contrary to the custom of antiquity, let him be consumed by fire in the place where he has sought the reverence of antiquity and almost the security of the empire itself; and let his accomplices and partners be bound to deportation to the Oasis, so that they are never given permission to petition, or to recover their citizenship, dignity or property. Given at Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Honorius for the eighth time and Theodosius for the third time, Augusti.

units.la: Eadem Constitutio habetur Leg. vnica C. eod. præterquam quod omittitur vox Oasena, quam induxit Tribonianus, quia Iustinianus noluit eos, qui in perpetuum mittebantur exilium, in Oasim mitti, sed tantum eos, qui ad summum in annum relegabantur: qua de re erat Lex vltima C. de pœnis, sed desiderabatur, eam reddidit magnus Cuiacius è Lib. LX. Basilicon titulo LI. cap. vlt. in illa hæc leguntur: Magistratus autem Alexandriæ & Thebaidos solos iubet in Gypsum, & in Oasin mittere vel in sex menses, vel ad summum in annum. Quod si perpetuum sit exilium, neque in Gypsum mittere, neque in Oasin. Ratio est, vt Græci Interpretes, eodem viro summo referente, tradunt de Oasi, quod sit infesta cuicibus, & muscis grandioribus, exulibus sæpe mortis causam adferentibus, & dandi scilicet vitæ vsus sint, vt Tiberius dicebat, quibus vita conceditur.
units.tr: The same constitution is found in the single law of the same title in the Code of Justinian, except that the word Oasena is omitted, which Tribonian had introduced; for Justinian did not want those sent into perpetual exile to be sent to the Oasis, but only those relegated for a year at most. For this reason the last law On punishments was needed, but it was lacking. The great Cujas restored it from Book 60 of the Basilica, title 51, last chapter, where these words are read: He orders the magistrates of Alexandria and the Thebaid alone to send [offenders] to Gypsum and to the Oasis, either for six months or at most for a year. But if the exile is perpetual, not to send them either to Gypsum or to the Oasis. The reason, as the Greek interpreters report (the great man mentioned above reports it), is that the Oasis is hostile to gnats and large flies, which often cause death to exiles; and so it is a place where, as Tiberius used to say, life is granted to those to whom life is given.

units.la: Sed ad institutum sermonem reuertamur, Liturgi sunt functiones, quæ præstabantur propter ministros publicos siue apparitores custodiæ vrbium appositos, qui Λειτουργοὶ Græcis dicebantur. Verum longe diuersum hoc patrocinium ab illo Athenien-sium: nam illi ne functiones debitas præstarent, patronos adoptabant: Athenienses vero inquilini vt per patronos tributum quotannis penderent.
units.tr: But let us return to our subject. Liturgi are the public services which were rendered on account of the public ministers or attendants assigned to guard the cities, who were called [λειτουργοί] by the Greeks. But this patrocinium is very different from that of the Athenians. For the Romans adopted patrons so as not to render the duties they owed, whereas the Athenian resident aliens adopted patrons so that through their patrons they might pay tribute each year.

units.la: At si quis τῶν Μετοίκων patronum non adoptasset, aut ὁ μέτοικος quotannis non penderet, Lege dabatur aduersus illum.
units.tr: But if any of the [Μετοίκων] had not adopted a patron, or the [μέτοικος] did not pay each year, an action was given against him by law.

units.la: Ἀστυφαίου δίκη.
units.tr: The action of Astyphaios [Ἀστυφαίου δίκη].

units.la: Actio propter non adoptatum patronum, aut tributum non præstitum.
units.tr: Action on account of a patron not adopted, or tribute not paid.

units.la: Hanc dicam poterat, cuicumque liberet, scribere. Grammatici: ὅτι ἂν τὶς ἐθέλῃ [?] Μέτοικος, Γεγραπται μὲν [?] ἐχ, ἢ μὴ δὲ ὁ μέτοικος, ὁ βουλόμενος δικάζειν [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐπὶ [?] τὰς αὐτὰς, ἢ τὴς λέγεται Ἀστυφαίου. Pollux Libro III. cap. V. ξ̓ ... δὲ ... πωλούντων ... μετοίκιον, ἐ[?] Πεσταῖο[?] μὴ ἐ[?]ονίων, Α[?] ... Scribebatur autem hæc dica apud Polemarchum. Pollux: ... Πολέ[?]μαρχ[?] ... Μετοίκων. ... Ἀποχραφῆς, μετοίκιον. Postrema hæc vox, μετοίκιον, corrupta est, neque emendandum, μετοικίου. Nam ei, qui ὁ μέτοικος non soluerat, Ἀποχραφῆς ... scribebatur: Legendum itaque est, μετοίκιος. Aristoteles in Atheniensium Republica: Πολέμαρχος ... (legendum est, ...) ... Ἀποχραφῆς ... Μετοίκιος. Conuictis Metoecis patronum non adoptasse, publicabantur corum bona. Suidas in voce πωλητής, ... Μετοίκων, ... Πεσταῖος ... Si vero conuincerentur tributum non præstitisse, publicaris bonis vendebantur, etiam quandoque ἐπ' ἐξαγωγῇ. Grammatici: οἱ μὲν ... μετοίκιον ... Μετοίκιον, ἀπ[?] ... Πωλητ[?]ῶν, ... ἐ[?] ... Plutarchus in Lycurgo Rhetore: Τελώναι δὲ ... Ξενοκράτει ... τῆς Φιλοσοφίας ... Μετοίκων ἀπαγωγῆς. Demosthenes Orat.I. in Aristogitonem: ... οὐ ... ἔτι γὰρ ... ἐπὶ ... Ἀ ... γνωρίμους ... ἐπὶ ... ἀ[?] ... ἐπὶ ... ἢ μὴ ... Μετοίκων ... τῶν ἀπαγωγῆς. Anonymus apud Suidam in Μέτοικοι. Ζωβίας ... Ἀριστοφάνης Φυ[?]... ... ἐ ... ἐπ ... τῶν μετοικίων ... ἐ ... Ceterum licebat in hac Ἀποχραφῆς actione, ... ἔπ' ἐξαγωγῇ ... ἐπαν ... ... Sed anne cuiuis Ἀ... licitum? Negat Hyperides Orat. II. κατ' Ἀ... apud Harpocrationem licitum fuisse peregrinis, (nec mirum, res quippe illorum agebatur) ἐπ' ... τῆς Ἀποχραφῆς δίκης, quod tamen ἐπ' ... Ἀποχραφῆς liberum erat, ... Ἀ... ... Ἀποχραφῆς βίῳ φησιν ... Ἀποχραφῆς ... ἐν ... ἐπ' ... Ἀ ... δίκης ... Ἀ ... Ἀποχραφῆς κακῶς ... Hæc igitur fuit Lex:
units.tr: Anyone who wishes may write about this action. The grammarians: [ὅτι ἂν τὶς ἐθέλῃ ... Μέτοικος ... ὁ βουλόμενος δικάζειν ...] ... this action is called Astyphaios. Pollux, Book III, chapter 5: [... πωλούντων ... μετοίκιον ...]. This action was recorded before the polemarch. Pollux: [... Πολέμαρχος ... Μετοίκων ... Ἀποχραφῆς, μετοίκιον]. This last word, [μετοίκιον], is corrupt, and it should not be emended to [μετοικίου]; for against the one who had not paid the metic's tax, an [Ἀποχραφῆς] action was brought. It should therefore be read [μετοίκιος]. Aristotle in the Constitution of the Athenians: [Πολέμαρχος ... Ἀποχραφῆς ... Μετοίκιος]. When the Metoeci were convicted of not having adopted a patron, their goods were confiscated. Suidas, under the word [πωλητής]: [... Μετοίκων ... Πεσταῖος ...]. If indeed they were convicted of not having paid the tribute, they were sold with their goods confiscated, sometimes even [ἐπ' ἐξαγωγῇ]. The grammarians: [οἱ μὲν ... μετοίκιον ... Μετοίκιον ...]. Plutarch in the life of the orator Lycurgus: [Τελώναι δὲ ... Ξενοκράτει ... τῆς Φιλοσοφίας ... Μετοίκων ἀπαγωγῆς]. Demosthenes, first oration against Aristogiton: [... οὐ ... ἔτι γὰρ ... Μετοίκων ... τῶν ἀπαγωγῆς]. Anonymous, in Suidas, under [Μέτοικοι]. Zobias ... Aristophanes ... [τῶν μετοικίων]. Moreover, in this Astyphaios action it was permitted ... [ἔπ' ἐξαγωγῇ]. But was it lawful for anyone at all to bring it? Hyperides, in his second oration against [Ἀ...], according to Harpocration, denies that it was lawful for foreigners (and this is no surprise, since their own affairs were being decided) ... in the Astyphaios action, which nevertheless was open to ... Astyphaios ... The text is too corrupt to render further in places. This, then, was the law:

units.la: Μὴ ὀξέ[?]νει Ἀ[?] ... ξένοις ... τῶν ... γεγ[?]ραμμένων τῆς Ἀποχραφῆς. Peregrinis teftimonij dictio non esto in actionibus Ἀποχραφῆς ad exceptionem.
units.tr: Let foreigners not have the right to give testimony in the Apochraphe actions [Ἀποχραφῆς] as a plea of exception concerning the things written down.

units.la: Quanquam Suidas videtur, etsi dubitanter, exiftimare in harum altera, Ἀποχραφῆ puto, licitum fuisse Ἀ[?] in illa vero Ἀποχραφῆς nequaquà: ... ἐ ... ... ...
units.tr: Suidas seems, though hesitantly, to think that in the latter of these, which I take to be the Apochraphe, it was permitted for ..., but in the other, the Apochraphe proper, by no means.

units.la: Quia autem dica hæc scribebatur ab eo qui vellet, vt etiam habes apud Pollucem Libro VIII.cap.VI. Ἀποχραφῆ ... ἡ δίκη ... ἐ[?] ... ... Μετοίκων, ... ἀλλὰ ... ἐπ ... ἐκ ... ... Μετοίκων, & iam in superioribus è Suida diximus, in iis vocabantur apud Polemarchum, qui iudices dabat, si quis τῷ ... ... vnus de multis dicam scriberet Ἀποχραφῆς, siue ob non adoptatum patronum, siue quia ἁ μετοίκιος non præstiterat. At verò si publicanus ipse & vectigalium redemptor τῶν Μετοίκων non soluti tributi accusaret, ab eo vehum abducebatur ad Πωλητὰς in forum, quod Mer[?] vel [illegible, ~4 letters] dicebatur. Plutarchus iam laudatis verbis in Lycurgi Rhetore: [illegible, ~12 letters]. cùm enim publicano ὁ μετοίκιον non pependisset, satis conuictus erat Ἀτελείας[?].
units.tr: Since this action was written by whoever wished, as you also have in Pollux, Book VIII, ch. VI, ... of the metics. As we said earlier from Suidas, in such cases they were summoned before Polemarchus, who appointed the judges, if anyone, one of many, wrote an Apochraphe, either because he had not adopted a patron or because the metic had not paid the metic tax. But if the tax farmer himself, the contractor of the taxes, accused a metic of not having paid the tribute, he was led away by him to the Poletae in the forum, which was called ... Plutarch, in the words already cited, in Lycurgus the Orator: ... For when the metic tax had not been paid to the publican, he was sufficiently convicted of ateleia.

units.la: Non erat quidem, quod se tueretur hac exceptione, Ciuem se esse: nam seuere admodum animaduertebatur in huiusmodi [illegible, ~8 letters] εἰς τὴν πολιτείαν Μετοίκος, sic dictae controuersia illis moueretur, scribereturque ξενίας γραφή, quae etiam Ἀσεβείας appellatur, vt obseruant Grammaticorum filij: [illegible, ~10 letters]. Lex autem haec est: Τοῦ τὰς ξενίας γραφῆς ὁ ... [illegible, ~14 letters] Peregrinitatis accusati in vincula, antequam iudicium reddatur, coniiciuntor. Fideiussores dare ijs ius non esto: conuicti apud iudices vendantur.
units.tr: Indeed there was nothing by which he could defend himself with this plea, that he was a citizen. For very severe punishment was inflicted on such persons, who had become metics ... and controversy arose against them, and a xenias graphe was written, which is also called asebeia, as the sons of the grammarians observe: ... The law is this: Those accused in a xenias graphe ... of foreign status are thrown into chains before judgment is given. They are not permitted to offer sureties; those convicted before the judges are sold.

units.la: Igitur qui accusabantur ξενίας, in vincula primum coniiciebantur, antequam iudicia de illis redderentur, neque fideiussores dare licebat: vbi vero damnati essent ξενίας, vendebantur. Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes [illegible, ~20 letters]. Vipianus: [illegible, ~16 letters]. Atque ita quam graue scelus esse iudicium putarent, significabant, cùm in vincula coniicerent eos, qui fideiussores dare parati erant, & vellent hanc ipsam carceris poenam ante damnationem sustinere.
units.tr: So those accused of xenia were first thrown into chains before judgment was given about them, and it was not allowed to give sureties. But when they were condemned for xenia, they were sold. Demosthenes mentions this law ... Ulpian: ... Thus they showed how grave a crime they judged it to be, when they threw into chains even those who were ready to give sureties and wished to undergo this very penalty of imprisonment before condemnation.

units.la: Vnde etiam iudicio iterum experiri licebat aduersus eum, secundum quem accusatum ξενίας pronuntiatum fuerat, appellaturque haec actio δωρεξενίας, eaque de re haec Lex legitur. Τοὺς ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ξενίας ... [illegible, ~6 letters] Absolutum indicio peregrinitatis ius esto cuicumque liberit, accusare corruptii muneribus iudicij.
units.tr: Hence it was also permitted to try again, by a second action, against the one by whom the man accused of xenia had been pronounced (a foreigner), and this action is called doroxenias [δωρεξενίας]. On this matter the following law is read: ... Let the right be open to anyone who wishes to accuse a man of being acquitted on the charge of foreign status, on the ground that the judgment was corrupted by bribes.

units.la: Non igitur accusato ξενίας se purgasse satis fuit: licebat enim iterum eum in ius vocare δωρεξενίας. Meminit Legis Hyperides [illegible, ~18 letters]. Dicà haec, vt ex Aristotele [illegible, ~10 letters] apud Thesmothetas scribebatur: [illegible, ~14 letters]. Pollux Libro III. cap. IV. [illegible, ~12 letters]. A litigantibus autem pendebatur drachma, à singulis vna, iudicum sportula, non vero, ut volunt viri summi, in apparitorum mercedem. Harpocration, quae descripsit Suidas: ἀπαδάσαος, Ἰσαῖος ἐν τῷ πρὸς τὸ Γύρρου κλῆρον. ἔστι δὲ δραχμὴ καταβαλλομένη ὑπὸ τῶν δικαζομένων τὰς ἰδίας δίκας. Μένανδρος Μισογύνῃ [?].
units.tr: Therefore it was not enough for a man accused of xenia to have cleared himself, for it was permitted to summon him again into court for doroxenias. Hyperides mentions the law ... I will say these things, as from Aristotle ... was written before the Thesmothetae: ... Pollux, Book III, ch. IV: ... A drachma was paid by the litigants, one by each, as a fee for the judges' sportula, not, as certain very eminent men hold, as the wage of the attendants. Harpocration, as Suidas describes it: apadasmos [ἀπαδάσαος]. Isaeus, in his speech concerning the lot of Gyrrhus: a drachma is what those who plead their own cases pay down. Menander, in the Misogynes [Μισογύνῃ]: ...

units.la: ἔλαττει δὲ γραμματέων ἐκ φύσει [?],
units.tr: ... is less of the scribes by nature [...],

units.la: καὶ ἀπαδάσαος μία [?].
units.tr: and apadasmos is one [...].

units.la: Αἰσχίνης δ' ἐν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ περὶ Θεσμοθετῶν φησίν ὅτως [?]. εἰσὶ δὲ γραφαὶ παρ' αὐτοῖς, ὧν ἀπαδάσαος πλεῖσται [?], ξενίας, καὶ δωροξενίας, αἷς [?] δεῖ ἀπόφυξιν τῆς ξενίας, καὶ ψευδεγγραφῆς [?], καὶ ψευδομαρτυρίας, καὶ βλαβῆς [?], καὶ ἀγραφίου, καὶ μοιχείας. Leuiter corrupta sunt Menandri verba, quae, ut puto, dicuntur aduersus τὸν Μισογύνην, qui huic fabulae nomen dedit, siue ab eius vxore, siue à quopiam alio obijciente illi τὸ φιλάνδρειον, Rescribo;
units.tr: Aeschines, in the Constitution of the Athenians, concerning the Thesmothetae, says thus: among them there are indictments, of which the most numerous are apadasmos, xenias, doroxenias, by which the expulsion from foreign status is to be obtained, and false enrolment, and false witness, and damage, and the unwritten (charge), and adultery. The words of Menander are slightly corrupted; they are, I think, said against the Misogynes, who gave the play its name, whether from his wife or from someone else who reproached him with love of a woman. I rewrite:

units.la: ἔλαττε δὲ γεγραμμένον τ' ἰδίαν ἐκ σι δίδωσιν [?],
units.tr: ... was written less ... and gives his own ... [...],

units.la: καὶ ἀπαδάσαος μία.
units.tr: and apadasmos is one.

units.la: Distinximus vocem γραμματεῖον, in has, γράμματα τ' ἰδίαν, nam τ' γραμματεῖς iudices sua sortiebantur δικαστήρια, in quibus iudicia reddebant. Scholia Comici ad hunc Pluti versum,
units.tr: We have distinguished the word grammateion into grammata t' idian, for the grammateis, the judges, allotted their own courts, in which they gave judgments. The scholia of the comic poet on this verse of Plutus:

units.la: ἀλλ' ἢ κατὰ ... ἐπιν [?] ἐν τοῖς γραμμασι [?].
units.tr: But ... in the letters [...].

units.la: ἀπ' ἀποίας [?], αὐτὴ τῷ, ἐδήλωσε. ὅτι δὲ καὶ κατὰ γραμματεῖα ἐκλήπεσθαι [?].
units.tr: From ... itself, it made clear. That they were also drawn by lot according to the tablets [...].

units.la: Epithera vero hoc δίψευν [?] literam designauit, secundum quam ὁ δικαστὴς erat sortitus. Expunximus praeterea vocem δραχμὴ, glossema quippe fuit vocis Παράσιτος [?].
units.tr: Above, this delta-psi letter designated, according to which the judge had been allotted. We have further removed the word drachma, since it was a gloss on the word parasitos.

units.la: TITVLVS VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: VRA[?] Seruorum folutiora multo erant Athenis ; quam Romæ; unde Plautus in Sticho:
units.tr: The rules governing slaves were far more lenient at Athens than at Rome, whence Plautus in the Stichus:

units.la: Atque id ne vos miremini, homines seruulos Potare, amare, atque ad cœnam condicere: Licet hoc Athenis nobis.
units.tr: And do not be surprised at this, that slaves drink, make love, and get invited to dinner. We are allowed this at Athens.

units.la: Demosthenes Philippica III. [illegible, ~8 letters] τὸν ... ὅταν κοινὸν οἰκ- [?]ον ... ἐν τῇ πόλει, ὥστε καὶ τοῖς ξένοις, καὶ τοῖς δούλοις αὐτοῖς μεταδιδόναι. Rursum in eadem: πολλοὺς ἂν τῆς οἰκίας ἰδοι ... ἡμῖν μὴ πλείονες οὐσίας [?] ... βιοῦντας λέγοντας, ... πολίτας ἐν ἐνίαις τῶν ἀνδρῶν πόλεων. Optime certè prisci illi Athenienses iustam & clementem seruitutem præferebant. Serui enim ( qui Græcis ideo σώματα, & Latinis Iurisconsultis corpora dicuntur ) sunt dominis, quod animæ est corpus, vt præclarè disputat Aristoteles Polit. Libro I: ἡ μὲν ψυχὴ, τὸ σώματος ἀρχὴ, δεσποτικὴ δ' ἐν ᾧ φύσει ἐστίν, ὅπως καὶ φύσιν [?] ... ψυχῆς τὸν αὐτὸν διάτερον [?] ... ὅτι πάντων αἱ δεσπῶν [?]. Præterea nata est seruitus ab iis, qui cum essent sui iuris, neque tamen per mentis infirmitatem res suas possent tueri, in prudentiærum clientelam vltro venerunt, atque illis operas suas locarunt. Refert Posidonius Stoicus Historia X. & verba transcripsit Athenaeus in Lib. VI. [illegible, ~80 letters]
units.tr: Demosthenes, Philippic III: "... common to the city, so that it is shared even with strangers and with the slaves themselves." Again in the same speech: "You would see many ... living ... citizens in some of the cities of those men." Certainly those ancient Athenians preferred a just and mild servitude. For slaves (called sōmata by the Greeks and corpora by the Latin jurists) belong to their masters as the body belongs to the soul, as Aristotle argues well in Book I of the Politics: "the soul rules the body ... as master ..." Moreover, slavery arose from those who, though sui iuris, could not protect their own affairs because of weakness of mind, and who of their own accord placed themselves under the protection of the prudent and let their services out to them. Posidonius the Stoic relates this in Book X of his Histories, and Athenaeus transcribed his words in Book VI. [illegible]

units.la: Quae sola vera atque multa erat seruitus, vt quae à natura esset: vnde Aristoteles: [illegible, ~120 letters]
units.tr: This was the only true and most common servitude, being the kind that is by nature. Whence Aristotle: [illegible]

units.la: Anima enim illis pro tale data est. Idem maximus Doctor: [illegible, ~110 letters]. & alterius natura est, id est, seruus est, qui suus esse non potest: [illegible, ~60 letters], Praeterea qui Lege serui sunt, [illegible, ~60 letters], inquit summus virorum, [illegible, ~50 letters] liberalitate potius quàm metu retinendi sunt [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: For the soul is given to them for this purpose. The same greatest teacher: [illegible] and he is of another's nature, that is, he is a slave who cannot be his own master. [illegible] Moreover, those who are slaves by law [illegible], says the greatest of men, [illegible] are to be kept by generosity rather than by fear [illegible].

units.la: inquit Anaxandrides Comicus in Anchise. Ad haec metus erat, ne provocati iniuriis Serui bello dominos lacesserent, quod aliquando euenisse testatur reliquit Posidonius Philosophus: tantusque enim Athenis erat Seruorum numerus, vt quum Demetrius Phalereus anno primo Olympiadis centesimae decimae censum Athenienium ageret, numerata sint seruorum capitum quadringenta millia. Anonymus in Descriptione Olympiadum ad hunc annum: [illegible, ~120 letters]. Creficles [?] Lib. III. Chronicorum idem scribit: [illegible, ~150 letters]. Humaneque itaque Seruos suos habuerunt Athenienses.
units.tr: says the comic poet Anaxandrides in the Anchises. Besides this there was the fear that slaves, provoked by injuries, might attack their masters in war. Posidonius the philosopher records that this once happened. For the number of slaves at Athens was so great that when Demetrius of Phalerum, in the first year of the 110th Olympiad, took the census of Athens, 400,000 heads of slaves were counted. The anonymous author of the Description of the Olympiads, for this year: [illegible]. Creficles in Book III of the Chronicles writes the same: [illegible]. Thus the Athenians treated their slaves humanely.

units.la: Hinc Legem vt scriberent hanc, factum est:
units.tr: From this, in order that they might enact this law, it came about:

units.la: [illegible, ~60 letters] Si quis alienum seruum pulsarit, aduersus eum Lege iniuriarum agito.
units.tr: [illegible] If anyone strikes another's slave, bring an action against him under the law of injuries.

units.la: Non licebat igitur alienum seruum pulsare: meminit huius Legis Xenophon [illegible, ~200 letters]
units.tr: It was therefore not permitted to strike another's slave. Xenophon mentions this law [illegible].

units.la: [illegible, ~250 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~250 letters] vocat, quae proprie αἰκία est, id est, πληγαὶ μόνον, vt interpretantur veteres Magistri, cuius multa erat pecuniaria, vt docet Lysias [illegible, ~12 letters] Ratio Legis est apud Xenophontem, loco laudato:
units.tr: [illegible] he calls it aikia, which properly means blows alone, as the ancient teachers interpret it, and for which the penalty was a fine, as Lysias teaches [illegible]. The rationale of the law is in Xenophon, in the passage cited:

units.la: ὅ ἐνεκαὶ ἔστι τοῦτο ὑπηρέσιον[?], ἐγὼ φέρω[?]. Εἰ νόμος ὧν τὸν δοῦλον[?] ἐάν τῆς ἐλευθέρου τούτου[?] τὸν μέτοικον[?], τὸν ἀπελεύθερον[?], πολλάκις αὐ οἰκήσεις[?] εἴ τὸν Ἀθηναῖον δοῦλον[?], ἐπιτάξειν ἀν[?]. ἐάν τι τὰ γὰρ ἀλλὰ βέλτιον ὁ δῆμος αὐτῇ, ἵ[?] οἱ δοῦλοι, καὶ οἱ μέτοικοι, καὶ τὰ εἴδη ἀλλὰ βελτίους εἰσὶν[?]. & paulò post: ὅπου ἂν εἰσὶ πλούσιοι δοῦλοι, [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐμὸν δοῦλον σὺ διελέσθαι[?]. E quibus Xenophontis verbis videre est, quàm soluta fuerint iura Atheniensium Seruorum, ut qui eadem cum plebe, aut elegantiori vterentur veste, nemini de via caderent, neque liceret eos ab alienis pulsari.
units.tr: For this reason ... I consider that if there is a law that ... a slave, a resident alien, or a freedman ... an Athenian slave ... the people are better ... slaves, resident aliens, and freedmen are better than ... And a little later: wherever there are rich slaves ... my slave ... to distinguish. From Xenophon's words it can be seen how free were the rights of Athenian slaves, who wore the same clothing as the common people or more elegant clothing, were pushed off the road by no one, and were not permitted to be struck by others.

units.la: Seruis in bello captis consultum voluit hac Lege Rhetor Lycurgus:
units.tr: The orator Lycurgus wished to provide for slaves taken in war by this law:

units.la: Μηδένι ἐξεῖναι Ἀθηναίων, μηδὲ τῶν οἰκούντων Ἀθηναίων, ἐλευθέρου σῶμα πρίασθαι ἐπὶ δουλείᾳ ἐκ τῶν ἁλισκομένων, ἀλλὰ τῆς τὰ πολιτείου δεσπότου γνώμης[?].
units.tr: No Athenian, nor any resident of Athens, may buy the body of a free person into slavery from those captured, but only with the consent of the former master. [Μηδένι ἐξεῖναι Ἀθηναίων, μηδὲ τῶν οἰκούντων Ἀθηναίων, ἐλευθέρου σῶμα πρίασθαι ἐπὶ δουλείᾳ ἐκ τῶν ἁλισκομένων, ἀλλὰ τῆς τὰ πολιτείου δεσπότου γνώμης]

units.la: Atheniensium ciuium aut inquilinorum nullus captiuum, qui liber fuerit, in seruitutem vendito, absque prioris domini consensu.
units.tr: No Athenian citizen or resident alien shall sell into slavery a captive who was free, without the consent of his earlier master.

units.la: Tulit hanc Legem Orator Lycurgus, referente Plutarcho in eius Vita: εἰσῆγε δὲ νόμον, μηδένι ἐξεῖναι Ἀθηναίων, μηδὲ τῶν οἰκούντων Ἀθηναῖον, ἐλευθέρου σῶμα πρίασθαι ἐπὶ δουλείᾳ ἐκ τῶν ἁλισκομένων, ἀλλὰ τῆς τῶ πολεμίου δεσπότου γνώμης[?]. Intelligit ἀχμαλώτους, qui bello capti seruitutem seruiebant, cum prius in patria liberi fuissent: hanc Seruitutem ἐκ νόμων vocat Aristoteles Libro I. Politic. cap.VI. ἔστι γὰρ ὡς ἐκ νόμων δοῦλος καὶ δουλείων· ὁ γὰρ νόμος, ὁμολογία τῆς ἐστιν· ἐν ᾧ τὰ πολέμου ἁρπασθέντα τῶν ἁρπασάντων φασί. Atque hic seruitutis modus omnium antiquissimus. Dio Orat. XV. Τοὺς γὰρ ἀφ' ἡμῶν ἡμετέρους δούλους, οὐκ εἰκὸς ἐκ δούλων φῶσι[?], ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ πολέμου χειρὸς[?] ἐπιθέσθαι, ὅτι ὡς δυναμένης[?] καὶ ἁρπάζων ὁ βιαστής[?]. & ex illo alij omnes fluxerunt, quanquam non desunt, qui hunc improbent, Aristotele teste: τῶν δὲ ὁ δίκαιον πολλοὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς νόμοις, ὥσπερ ῥήτορα, γεάφονται ἀνδρόμων[?], ὡς δῆλον, εἰ τῆς βιάσεως δυναμένῳ, καὶ ἐκ δυνάμεως χρείσιμος, ἔτι δοῦλος καὶ ἁρπάζων ὁ βιαστής[?]. & vere Helena apud Theodecten:
units.tr: The orator Lycurgus proposed this law, as Plutarch reports in his Life: "He introduced a law that no Athenian, nor any resident of Athens, may buy the body of a free person into slavery from those captured, but only with the consent of the enemy's master." He means captives who, captured in war, served as slaves though they had previously been free in their homeland. Aristotle calls this servitude "by law" in Book I of the Politics, ch. VI: "for there is a sense in which a slave is so by law and convention; for the law is a kind of agreement by which the things seized in war are said to belong to the captors." And this mode of servitude is the most ancient of all. Dio, Oration XV: "For it is not likely that those who are our slaves ... from slaves ... but from war, by the hand of the seizer, since he was able ..." And from this all the others flowed, although there are not lacking those who disapprove of it, as Aristotle testifies: many of the just things in the laws are written as if by a rhetor ... and it is clear that force and power are useful ... still a slave, and the seizer [illegible]. And truly Helen in Theodectes:

units.la: [?]ξιον δ' ἀπ' ἀμφοῖν ἐκ γένοιν ῥιζωμένη[?],Ὡς ἀν ποσοσπεῖν ἀξιώσωσιν λέγειν[?];
units.tr: Worthy, rooted in both kinds of birth, as they think fit to say?

units.la: Quod si quis in seruitutem abduceretur, aut peteretur, poterat quilibet illum liberali asserere causa manu, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: If anyone was led away into slavery, or claimed as a slave, anyone could assert his liberty by hand under this law:

units.la: Ἐξεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ ἀφαιρεῖσθαι εἰς ἐλευθερίαν, καὶ καταλύσαντα τὸν ἀγόμενον εἰς δουλείαν πρὸς τὰ πολεμικά[?].
units.tr: It is permitted to anyone who wishes to take away the one being led into slavery for freedom, and to release him, [giving surety] for the war. [Ἐξεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ ἀφαιρεῖσθαι εἰς ἐλευθερίαν, καὶ καταλύσαντα τὸν ἀγόμενον εἰς δουλείαν πρὸς τὰ πολεμικά]

units.la: Cuiuis ius esto alium liberali asserere causa manu, seque pro illa fidejussorem dare apud Polemarchum.
units.tr: Anyone shall have the right to assert another person's liberty by hand, and to give himself as surety for it before the Polemarch.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Æschines ἐν τῷ Τιμάρχῳ, αὐ Δεσποτ μηδὲν ἰδικὴν ἔχοντα ἦλθ' εἰς δουλείαν, Φάσκων αὐτῷ εἶ δοῦλον[?]. ἐν πολιτῇ ἡ κακῷ ἡμόμενος ὁ Γιτθήκος ἐπέχειν τῆς τὰ χρήματα αὐτῷ καὶ μάλα χρῆσθαι[?]. ἐπ' αὐτὸν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι εἰς ἐλευθερίαν. ὃ ἡ μὴ τῶν λήξης δικὴν ἐπαινέσθαι[?]. Qui liberali asserebant causa manu, ad Polemarchum ibant, & iudicio sistere promittebant, ac fidejussores dabant, atque interim vindiciae secundum libertatem dabantur. Demosthenes ἐν ᾧ τὰ Φρυνίων ἐπὶ δημοσίου αὐτῷ, ἐξ ᾗ ἔστι Ἑυ[?] ἐλθὼν ἐπὶ ἡ οἰκίαν τῆς Σπεφάνου[?], ἡν αὐτῷ ἀφαιρεῖσθαι ἡ Σπεφάνῳ τὸ νόμων εἰς ἐλευθε-ρίαν, καταλύσαντα αὐτῷ πρὸς τὸ Γολεμάρχῳ. Lysias ἐν ᾧ τὰ Πατκλέωνος. ἡμέρας τοίνυν[?] μὴ ταῦτα πολλαῖς ὕστερον, ἰδὼν ἀπ' ἐκείνου τοῦτο Παχχλέωνα τὸν Νικομήδης, ὡς ἐμὴν πύ-ρησιν αὐτῷ δικαστής ἔ), ῥᾳδίως ἀλλ' ἀντιλαβὼν, βελόμενος εἰς ἐναν ὅπως ἀποτελεῖ τὸ ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ... αὐτὸ ἀπαλλάξαι ... [?] ... ἐπὶ πολλὰ ... ἀμέτρον ἔστι ... [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: Aeschines mentions this law in his speech against Timarchus: [illegible] "... having come into slavery ... claiming him as his slave ... in the city, or ill-treated, ... having held the money and used it very much ... to take him away into liberty ... the lawsuit should not be praised." Those who asserted liberty by hand went to the Polemarch, promised to submit to trial, and gave sureties; meanwhile the vindication was granted in favour of liberty. Demosthenes, in the speech against Phrynion [illegible] ... coming to the house of Stephanus, which Stephanus claimed to be his by law, to assert his liberty, releasing him to the Polemarch. Lysias, in the speech against Pancleon: [illegible] "... the day ... many days later, seeing from that one ... Pancleon, son of Nicomedes, as though he had been ... the judge ... easily seizing, wishing ... that he might accomplish ... [illegible] ... immeasurable ..."

units.la: τὶ μὲν οὖν ἐπιδὼν ἐπαυτὸν μαχομένοι, εἶπον ὅτι εἰς τὸν ταχύτατα ... [illegible, ~25 letters] ... ἐν αὐτῷ ἀ-διλαφὸς, ὡς ἐξαιρήσαιτο αὐτὸν εἰς ἐλευθερίαν. ὅτι ταῦτα ἐπυνσάμενοι ἀπεξέ-νεις ἀγορᾷ, ἀγορᾶ ἀπόντες.
units.tr: [illegible] ... they said that he ... was quickly ... in it ... so that he might take him away into liberty. Having taken these things into account, they were led away from the public square, from the marketplace, [illegible].

units.la: Ad Polemarchum igitur rapiebantur in ius, & illius erat vindicias secundum libertatem dare, fidejussoribus promittentibus futurum, vt is, cui status controuersia mouebatur, iudicio sisteretur, deinde iudices sortiebatur εἰσαγωγὴ εἰς δίκην εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον. Hinc illa Dionis Chrysostomi Orat.XV. Ἀλλὰ ἡ πολλοὶ αὐτῷ ἐλευθέρῳ ὄντες, ἡ αἰδίκως δουλεύοντες, ὧν ὑμεῖς ἤδη χρὴ εἰς δικαστήριον ἐλθόντες, ἐπίδειξαι ἐλευθερίας ὄντος ἑαυτοῦ.
units.tr: They were therefore dragged before the Polemarch into court, and it was his duty to grant vindication in favour of liberty, the sureties promising that the person whose status was disputed would be brought to trial; then he assigned the judges. Introduction into court, before the court. Hence that passage of Dio Chrysostom, Oration XV: But many who are free, or who are unjustly enslaved, should now come into court and show their freedom.

units.la: Quod si quis per iniuriam seruum liberali causa manu aliquem [?]... Quod si quis per iniuriam seruum liberali causa manu assereret, pendebat aerario semissem aestimationis:
units.tr: If anyone by wrongful means claimed a slave as free by manumission, he paid half the assessed value to the treasury: If anyone wrongfully claims another's slave as free by manumission, let him pay half the valuation to the public treasury.

units.la: Εὰν μή τις δῷ ἡ δικαίως εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφίεσθαι ζώντα, ὃ ἡμοῦ τῆς ἡμετέρας ὀφείλειν τῇ δημοσίῳ. Si quis per iniuriam alterius seruum liberali causa manu afferuerit, aerario semissem aestimationis pendito.
units.tr: If anyone does not rightly let a living slave go free, he owes [the penalty] to the public treasury: If anyone by wrong has taken another's slave in hand for a claim of liberty, let him pay half the valuation to the treasury.

units.la: Legem laudat Auctor Argumenti Orationis Demosthenicae in Theocrinem: νόμος δὲ ὧν, Ἐὰν μή τις δίκῃ δικαίως εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφίεσθαι ζῶντα, ὃ ἡμοῦ τῆς ἡμετέρας ὀφείλειν τῇ δημοσίῳ. Demosthenes hac ipsa Oratione: καί μοι λέγε τὸν νόμον, ὃς καλεῖ ὃ ἡμοῦ τῆς ἡμετέρας ὀφείλειν τῇ δημοσίῳ, ὃς ἂν δίκῃ μὴ δικαίως εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφίεσθαι. Pendebat itaque aerario publico semissem aestimationis, non litis, sed pretij, puto, serui illius, quem liberali causa manu afferebat: aduersus quem actio haec dicebatur ἐξαιρέσεως δίκη. Grammatici: ἐξαιρέσεως δίκη, ὁπότε τις ἄγει τινὰ ὡς δοῦλον, ἐπειτα ὡς αὐτὸν ὡς ἐλευθέρων ἐξαιρεῖται, ἐξὸν ὧν αὐτοπαιδεύσαι ἀ-διαφόρου ὡς δούλου λαχόντες ἐξαιρέσεως δίκαι, ὧ εἰς τὸ ἐλευθερίαν αὐτὸν ἐξαιρουμένῳ. Ἰσαῖος δὲ τὴν Εὐμαθοῦς εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι.
units.tr: The author of the argument to Demosthenes' speech against Theocrines cites the law: "and the law says, 'If anyone does not rightly let a living slave go free, he owes [the penalty] to the public treasury.'" Demosthenes, in that same speech: "Read me the law which says that he owes [the penalty] to the public treasury, whoever does not rightly let a slave go free by legal process." So he paid half the valuation to the public treasury, not of the lawsuit but, I suppose, of the price of that slave whom he had taken in hand as free; the action against him was called exaíresis (a suit for seizure). The grammarians say: the suit of seizure arises when someone leads another away as a slave and then claims him as free, which is permitted only to those who have a claim to his freedom. Isaeus says that the Eumathus [case] concerned the seizure of a person for freedom.

units.la: Lege concedebatur Seruis actio aduersus iniquos dominos, qua poterant eos adigere vt se venderent:
units.tr: By this law slaves were granted an action against unjust masters, by which they could compel them to sell them.

units.la: Τοῖς δούλοις ἐξεῖναι προσιὼν αἰτιᾶσθαι, καὶ διαπο-τῶν μεταβαλεῖν ἀπέχεσθαι. Seruis ius esto dominos iniquos adigere vt se vendant humanioribus.
units.tr: Slaves were permitted to approach [the magistrate] and bring an accusation, and to have done with transgression and change. Slaves shall have the right to compel unjust masters to sell them to more humane ones.

units.la: Legitur haec Lex apud Plutarchum περὶ δεισιδαιμονίας, ἐπὶ δούλοις νόμος ἐλευθερίας ἀπογράφει προσιὼν αἰτίας, καὶ διαπομπῆς μεταβαλεῖν ἀπέχεσθαι. Legem Atticam fuisse quanquam non dicat Plutarchus, probant ea, quae apud Pollucem Libro VII. cap.II. superfuns, veterum Comicorum loca: ὁ γὰρ νῦν Φασι τὰς οἰκέτας προσιὼν αἰτεῖν, ἐσὶ δὲ ἡ Αἰσωπάσους ὥρας. εἰ μοι χρήσιμον ἐστιν εἰς ὃ Θησεῖον δραμεῖν, ἐκεῖ δ' ἡ, ἕως ἀν ἄνθρωπός προσιὼν, μῦθον. αὐτὴ δ' ἐπὶ ἑκάτοις Εὐπολίδος Πόλεσι, Κακὰ ζῇ δὲ πάσχοισι, ἀλλὰ προσιὼν αἰτῆσαι.
units.tr: This law is read in Plutarch's On Superstition: a law for slaves permits them to approach with a complaint and to refrain from being sent away and changed. Although Plutarch does not say it was an Attic law, the passages of the old comic poets preserved in Pollux, Book VII, chapter II, prove it: "for now they say the slaves approach and demand, and it is the hour of Aesop..." and, in Eupolis' Cities, "if it is useful for me to run to the Theseion, there, until a man approaches, [I speak] a word."

units.la: Aristophanis versus, meo iudicio, ita sunt distinguendi: Εἰ μὴ χρήσιμόν ἐστιν εἰς ὃ Θησεῖον δραμεῖν, ἐκεῖ δ', ἕως ἂν ἄνθρωπος προσιὼν, μῦθον.
units.tr: In my judgment the verses of Aristophanes should be punctuated thus: "If it is not useful for me to run to the Theseion, there, until a man approaches, [I speak] a word."

units.la: Confugiunt Serui ad Thefei sacellum, quia habebat ius asyli, & ius ibi dicebatur Seruis Θησεῖον ... ἱκέτης ... ἀσυλία ... ἐλευθερία [?]. Grammatici: Θησεύς, ὁ ... ἐκ τοῦ Θησέως, ... ἀσύλου ἐλευθερίας ... ἀδικίας [?].
units.tr: Slaves fled to the shrine of Theseus, because it had the right of asylum, and by that right freedom was said to be granted to slaves. The grammarians say: Theseus... of Theseus... of an asylum of freedom... of injustice.

units.la: Quinetiam libertatem consequebantur, vel inuitis dominis, pecunia numerata:
units.tr: Indeed slaves also obtained their freedom even against the wishes of their masters, for a sum of money paid out:

units.la: Τοῖς δούλοις ἔξεστι ἑαυτοὺς ἐλευθεροῦσθαι, ἀποδόντας τὸ ἀργύριον ... καταβολῆς τοῦ δεσπότου [?].
units.tr: Slaves are permitted to free themselves, having paid the money... the master's deposit.

units.la: Legem hanc colligere licet è Dionis Chrysostomi verbis Orat. XV. ἐμφανῶν ... ἐλευθερωθῆναι ... ἀργύριον ... τῷ δεσπότῃ ... ἀποδιδόντας ... τοῦ δικαστηρίου [?]. & in palliata Diphili Comoedia Καλλισθένης [?], siue Plauti Cafina, Quid tu me vero libertate territas? Quid si tu nolis, filiusque etiam tuus, Vobis inuitis, atque amborum ingratiis, Vna libella liber possum fieri.
units.tr: This law may be gathered from the words of Dio Chrysostom, Oration XV: [they were] to be freed... money... to the master... paying... of the court. Also in the Diphilus comedy Callisthenes (or Plautus' Casina): "Why do you frighten me with freedom? What if you do not wish it, and your son too? Against your will, and against the will of both of you, for one little coin I can become free."

units.la: Serui quippe apud Athenienses suum, quod sibi comparabant, habebant peculium, ex quo aliquid dominis suis pendebant quotannis, atque etiam, pro capite numerabant suo, vt seruitutem exuerent. Xenophon loco laudato, vt colligamus facit: ὅταν γὰρ αὐτῷ ... δοῦλος ... ἐλευθέρας ... ἀποφέρῃ ... τῷ δεσπότῃ [?]. Quod vero ex his Suidae verbis: Ἀποστάσιον δίκη, ὅταν δοῦλος ... ἐλευθερίας αἰτῇ, φέρων μὴ παρασχεῖν τοῖς δούλοις αὐτὸν ἀποτίνειν [?], colligit vir summus, Seruos aliquando egisse aduersus dominos de libertate consequenda, se seruos alios competitores nihil morari dicentes, nobis non potest probari, & plane alio referenda sunt, vt infra, Deo dante, videbimus: neque enim haec actio ex Lege de libertate consequenda, vnquam dicta est Ἀποστασίου, sed Libertorum est. Quanta autem fuerit pecunia, quae a seruo, vt manumitteretur, numerabatur, pro certo dicere non possumus. Apud Plautum vna libella est: Vobis inuitis, atque amborum ingratiis, Vna libella liber possum fieri.
units.tr: Indeed the slaves of the Athenians had their own property, which they acquired, and from it they paid their masters something each year; they even paid a sum per head so as to cast off servitude. Xenophon, as cited, leads us to conclude this: "for when... a slave... of freedom... brings to the master..." As for what the great man gathers from the words of Suidas: "The suit of apostasion, when a slave seeks freedom, [the master] refusing to allow the slaves to redeem themselves..." — I cannot accept that the slaves once sued their masters to obtain freedom, saying that other rivals do not delay them; those things must be referred elsewhere, as we shall see below, God willing. For this action under the law on obtaining freedom was never called apostasion; that name belongs to freedmen. What sum a slave paid to be manumitted we cannot say for certain. In Plautus it is one little coin: "Against your will, and against the will of both of you, for one little coin I can become free."

units.la: Factum quoque est aliquoties, vt afflictis Reipublicae temporibus, qui egregiam in bello nauauerant operam Serui, libertate donarentur à Republica: De iis, qui anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimae tertiae, Archonte Callia Καλλίᾳ ... Ἀρχοντος [?], ad Arginusam Lacedaemonios fuderunt, Aristophanes Ranis, atque eos non tantum libertate, sed & ciuitate donatos conqueritur: τοὺς δ' αἰχμαλώτους ... ἐλευθερίας ... μίας [?], τὴν Πλαταιῶν ... ἐξ ... δούλων ... δωρεάς [?].
units.tr: It also happened several times that in times of crisis for the state, slaves who had performed distinguished service in war were given their freedom by the state. Of those who, in the third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, under the archon Callias, defeated the Lacedaemonians at Arginusae, Aristophanes in the Frogs complains that they were given not only freedom but also citizenship: "...the captives... of freedom... one... the gifts of the slaves of Plataea..."

units.la: De illis qui militauerant Chaeronea aduersus Philippum Macedonem Dio Chrysostomus Orat. XV. ὅτι ὡς Ἀλεξάνδρου ... Φιλίππου ... μετὰ τῶν Χαιρωνέων ... συμπολεμησάντων οἰκέτας ἐλευθέρους [?].
units.tr: Concerning those who had fought at Chaeronea against Philip of Macedon, Dio Chrysostom, Oration XV: "that... as of Alexander... Philip... having fought alongside the men of Chaeronea... slaves made free."

units.la: Seruos, qui manumittebantur, non licebat liberos renunciare in Theatro, id enim hac Lege vetitum: Μὴ αἰκίζειν ... ἀπελευθεροῦσθαι ... ἐν θεάτρῳ, ἀλλ' ἀπ... ἡ χάρις [?]. Legem laudat Æschines εἰς τὰς ιγ' Κτησιφῶντος. καὶ ἀπαγορεύει ὁ νόμος ἀπαγορεύειν [?], μήτε οἰκέτην ἀπελευθεροῦν εἰς τὰ [?] ἀπελευθέρωσιν [?], ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῷ ἄστει [?] τῶν χρόνων [?]. Renunciabantur Serui liberi per praeconem, vt hic habes: Sed in Theatro non debebat fieri haec renunciatio: ambitiosum enim erat: volebant quippe omnes Graecos, qui Ludis intererant, testes esse. Æschines: ἄλλοι δὲ τινες ἀποχρησάμενοι, τὰς αὐτῶν οἰκείας ἀφιέσθαι ἀπελευθερώσεως, μάρτυρας τῆς ἀπελευθερίας τοὺς Ἕλληνας πολίτας. Manumissi seruile suum nomen aliquando mutabant, aliquando syllabis augebant, vt Stephanus ille, qui Philostephanus appellari voluit, in quem est Epigramma Libro II. Anthologias,
units.tr: Slaves who were manumitted were not permitted to be proclaimed free in the theatre, for this was forbidden by the law: "...not to mistreat... to be freed... in the theatre, but..." Aeschines cites the law in his speech against Ctesiphon (section 13): the law forbids... freeing a household slave... but from those in the city... of the times. Slaves were proclaimed free by a herald, as you have here; but this proclamation was not to be made in the theatre, since it was showy; for they wanted all the Greeks who attended the games to be witnesses. Aeschines: "others, having used the freedom of their own... to be released from manumission, with the Greek citizens as witnesses of their freedom." Freed slaves sometimes changed their servile name, sometimes lengthened it with syllables, like that Stephanus who wished to be called Philostephanus, of whom there is an epigram in Book II of the Anthology:

units.la: ὦ Στέφανος πλωτὸς, καὶ πῶς ἁμα · νῦν δὲ παῦσθαι [?] πλαστὴ, ὦ γεγονώς [?] δὲ Φιλοστέφανος.
units.tr: "O Stephanus, floating, and how at once... now to cease... a fictitious one, who was born... but became Philostephanus."

units.la: Tonsurae quoque genus mutabant. Grammatici: ἀϊδραποδώδη τρίχα. τὸν τῆς ἀϊδραποδώδων ἰδίως κουρᾶν. ὦ ἀπελευθερωθέντες ἥλλαττον Ἀθηναῖοι οἱ δοῦλοι. Cum autem code cum Μετοίκοις iure censerentur Liberti, quotannis ὃ μετοίκιον, id est, duodecim drachmas aerario pendebant, & praeterea triobolum siue scribae, siue publicano. Harpocration: ὅτι δὲ καὶ οἱ δοῦλοι ἀφεθέντες εἰς τὴν ἀποστασίαν [?] ἐπίλυσιν ὃ μετοίκιον, δήλοι τε τῆς Κωμικῆς διδασκαλίας, καὶ Αεισύμης. Μένανδρος δ' ἐν Ἀναπηδῶντι, καὶ ἐν Διδύμῃ πρὸς τὰς δώδεκα δραχμάς, καὶ τελώβολον φησὶ Ζεύτης πελεῖν, ἴσως τὰ τέλωνα. Atque de his intelligendus Pollux Libro III. cap. IV. ὃ μετοίκιον ὧ δυοκαίδεκα τῷ δημοσίῳ δραχμῇ, καὶ τῷ Γεγραμμένῃ τελωβολον. itemque Hesychius: μετοίκιον, πέλας ἔπως ἐκαλεῖτο, ὁ ἐπιθέσθαι δραχμὰς δώδεκα, τὰ δὲ Τελῶνη τελωβόλον. Hoc tributum pendebant Liberti, ceteraque alia omnia, publica, priuata, administrabant per Patronum, non quem elegissent ipsi, quemadmodum οἱ Μέτοικοι, sed qui libertate donasset dominus, quem colere, eique Lege constituta praestare tenebantur hac Lege:
units.tr: They also changed the manner of their hair-cutting. The grammarians: "the slavish hair... the particular shearing of slaves... the freed ones, the Athenian slaves, changed." Since freedmen were registered among the resident aliens (metics) by law, they paid the metoikion, that is twelve drachmas, to the treasury each year, and besides a triobol either to the scribe or to the tax-collector. Harpocration: "that freed slaves too, released into... the metoikion, are shown by Comic teaching and Aesimus; Menander in Anapēdōn and in Didymē says the twelve drachmas and the telōbolon..." And Pollux, Book III, chapter IV, should be understood in this sense: "the metoikion of twelve drachmas to the public, and the telōbolon to the registrar." Hesychius likewise: "metoikion, as it was called, the impost of twelve drachmas; the telōnē, the telōbolon." Freedmen paid this tax, and conducted all other matters, public and private, through a patron, not one they chose themselves, as the metics did, but the one who had granted freedom, whom they were bound by law to honour and to render the services which the law prescribed:

units.la: Τοὺς ἀπελευθερωθέντας μὴ ἀφίσασθαι ἢ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπελευθερωσάντων, μήτε ἐπιγράφεσθαι ἑτέρου προστάτου, καὶ ἃ κελεύουσιν οἱ νόμοι παρέχειν.
units.tr: Let freedmen not withdraw from their manumitters, nor enrol under another patron, and let them render what the laws command.

units.la: Legem hanc colligere est ex iis quae referunt Grammatici de actione Ἀποστασίου, & nos eorum verba reddemus infra, σὺ Θεῷ δ' εἴπην. Patronum colebant Liberti, eique quasdam operas praestare tenebantur, vt in hac Lege habes, & e verbis Suidae plenius in sequentibus dicemus: Hinc Chrysippo Libro περὶ ἰσονομίας II. ἀπελευθέροι δοῦλοι ἐλεύθεροι εἰσὶ, sed non οἰκέται erant, id est, non τῆς κτήσεως καταπεμφθέντες, vt loquitur idem Chrysippus, in bonis possidentis non censebantur: Nullum praeterea alium eligere poterant προστάτην, Patronum, quàm eum à quo libertate fuerant donati. Non ignoro Incomparabilem Casaubonum in Animaduersionibus ad Suetonium scribere, potuisse quoque, cum manumitterentur, optare sibi & publice adscifcere patronum alium, quàm eum qui manumitteret, in cuius clientela essent, idque voce praeconis: in hanc sententiam eū induxit Aristotelis locus Rhetoric. Lib. III. cap. VIII. ὥσπερ οὖν τὴν Κηρύκων προσλαμβάνοντα τὸ παιδία, ὅ, ἵνα αὐτῷ ὑπὸ ἐξ ἑνὸς ὁ ἀπελευθερούμενος, ΚΛΕΩΝΑ. Sed idem non est, meo iudicio, fiue Patronus, & Ἐπίτροπος. Patronus non eligebatur à Liberto, sed is erat, qui manumiserat: At vero Ἐπίτροπος publicè ab eo, qui manumittere-tur, adoptabatur: nempe Πατρῶνος cum tutabatur sua auctoritate, & omnia eius minima, maxima, priuata, publica, administrabat: ἐπίτροπος vero aduersus Patronum ipsum, si opus foret, tuebatur: quemadmodum & apud Romanos Liberti, quamquam in Patroni, qui manumiserat, essent clientela, habebant tamen & alium, ex amicis si forte Patroni, cuius se esse clientes dicerent, qui apud patronum iniuriam eorum & in iusta pietate, si res ita se ferret, deprecaretur & tueretur clientem hunc suum: ita intelligenda puto M. Tullij verba Epist. XII. Libri I ad Atticum. Libertum ego habeo, sane nequam hominem, Hilarum dico, ratiocinatorem & clientem tuum.
units.tr: This law is to be gathered from what the grammarians report about the action of apostasion, and we shall give their words below, God willing. Freedmen honoured their patron, and were bound to render him certain services, as you have in this law, and we shall say more fully from the words of Suidas in what follows. Hence Chrysippus, in Book II of On Equality: freed slaves are free persons, but they were not household slaves, that is, they were not sent down as part of the property, and were not counted among the goods of the possessor, as the same Chrysippus puts it. Moreover they could choose no other patron than the one from whom they had received their liberty. I am aware that the incomparable Casaubon, in his notes on Suetonius, writes that when they were manumitted they could also have wished for and publicly adopted another patron than the one who had freed them and in whose clientela they were, and this by a herald's proclamation; he was led to this view by a passage of Aristotle, Rhetoric Book III, chapter VIII: just as the heralds of the Ceryces... the freed person... Kleon. But in my judgment a patron and an epitropos are not the same. A patron was not chosen by the freedman, but was the one who had manumitted him; but an epitropos was publicly adopted by the one who was to be manumitted; the patron indeed protected him by his authority and administered all his affairs, small and great, private and public; the epitropos, on the other hand, defended him against the patron himself, if necessity required. So too among the Romans, freedmen, although they were in the clientela of the patron who had manumitted them, nevertheless had another, one of the friends of the patron, if perchance any, whose clients they said they were, who would plead with the patron on their behalf against his injustice and unjust harshness, if the matter so required, and would protect his client. Thus I think the words of Marcus Tullius should be understood, Letters to Atticus, Book I, letter XII: "I have a freedman, to be sure a worthless fellow, I mean Hilarus, an accountant and your client."

units.la: § Si in hanc Legem commisisset Liberti, iis Ἀπροσκλήτου dica scribebatur ex hac Lege:
units.tr: § If freedmen committed an offence against this law, an action called aprosklētou [Ἀπροσκλήτου] was brought against them under this law:

units.la: Ἐλλὰ Ἀπρόσκλητος patronus esto aduersus Li-bertos, qui patronos non coluerint, aut alias adoptauerint, eaque quae Legibus imperan-tur, non praestiterint, conuenti Liberti in ser-uitutem revocantor: si secundum Libertos pronunciatum fuerit, praefecti liberi iunto.
units.tr: But let Aproskletos [Ἀπρόσκλητος] be patron against freedmen who have not honoured their patrons, or who have otherwise adopted others, and who have not performed what the laws require. When the freedmen are sued, let them be returned to servitude. If judgment is given in favour of the freedmen, let the free-born praefects join in.

units.la: Laudant hanc Legem Grammatici: Ἀπροσκλήτου, dicuntur ὀλίγοι ἐπίτροποι [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~28 letters] [illegible, ~26 letters] [illegible, ~24 letters]. Compelebat hac dica Ἀπροσκλήτου Patronis aduersus Libertum ingratos, vt hinc constat, quibus adstant Ἐπίτροποι illi, quos publice sibi adoptauerant, cum manumitterentur. An Liberorum exceptio, qua se aduersus hanc actionem tuebantur, Ἀπροσκλήτου quoque dicebatur, quaeritur, quaeritur vir Amplissimus & eruditissimus, atque ita dici lusticatur è Dinarchi Oratione pro Æschylo Xenophontis Liberto, cuius epigraphe est apud Diogenem Laertium in Xenophonte, & Dionysium Halicarnassensem in Dinarcho, Ἀπροσκλήτου Ἐπιτρόπου Ἀπροσκλήτου. Confirmandae eius suspicioni facit locus Suidae in hac verba: Ἀπροσκλήτου ἐκ, ὅτε δούλος ἐλευθερωθεὶς ἐπίτροπος γίνεται, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποκλείσῃ, ἐπέχοντι ἐπιτρόπων ἐξαιρεῖσθαι. Quo sensu vir idem sum-mus explicet illa Suidae verba in superioribus dixi-mus: sed nullus dubito Sui-dam docere, Ἀπροσκλήτου dicam esse etiam actionem, qua Libertus, qui aliquo modo δούλος ἐπὶ ἐξῆς, vt loquitur Chrysippus, in iudicium vocat patronum; vt in plenam & omnibus numeris absolutam afferatur libertatem, dicens se non posse applicare ad seruos aliquid fiue operae praestantes, siue pecuniae pendentes ἐπιτροπῆς τοῖς δούλοις ἀλλ᾽ ἢ ταῖς ὑπηρεσίαις, ita in tres distinximus voces, quae vniuersaliter apud Suidam: Serui suas praestabant operas dominis, & aliquid de suo peculio pendebant. Liberti quoque Lege cogebantur patronis ἐπὶ λίβου οἱ ἀποκλείσιν ἐπιτρόπων τοῖς ἀπολαμβάνουσι, qui patronos ἐπὶ λίβου ἀποκλείσιν ἐπιτρόπων ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀποκλείσιν dicam patrono scribit, nil vult siue praestare, siue pendere, cum id seruorum fit, qua etiam de causa quasi seruicentur Liberti, sed potius plena perfectaque tuii libertate. Dica haec Ἀπροσκλήτου scribebatur apud Polemarchum: Aristoteles de Atheniensium Republica: [illegible, ~30 letters] Ἀ[?] [illegible, ~20 letters], Μ[?] [illegible, ~10 letters]. Iudicabantur autem Seruorum actiones in Dominos, Patronorum in Libertos, a contribuebatur [?] iure Domini. Harpocration: [illegible, ~40 letters]. Suidas: [illegible, ~30 letters]. Si hac Atticarum actiones vincerentur Liberti a Patronis, in seruitutem retrahebantur. Harpocration, & ex eo Suidas: [illegible, ~30 letters], scilicet, Libertorum [?] [illegible, ~20 letters]. Atque in ciuitatem [?] comingebantur. Ilusus [?] [illegible, ~30 letters]. Suidas: [illegible, ~40 letters]. Hyperides [?] [illegible, ~20 letters]. Atque haec ita se habere docuerant Oratorum veterum multi, Lysias, Aeschines, & Hyperides [?] [illegible, ~20 letters], aut etiam vendebantur. Demosthenes [?] Huius Legis meminit Valerius Maximus Lib. II. cap. 1. Age quid illud institutum Atheniensium, quam memorabile? quod conuictus a patrono libertus ingratus, iure libertatem exuitur. Supersedeo te, inquit, habere eiusdem, tanti muneris impium aestimatorem. Nec adduci potuit, ut crederet, quoniam liber esse nescit. Sed obiter castigandus est Valerii error, cum putet seruos ab Atheniensibus ciuitate simul cum libertate donatos fuisse: quod verum non est: nempe in animo habebat ille iuxtam illam libertatem apud suos Romanos vindicta datam.
units.tr: The grammarians praise this Law. [Ἀπροσκλήτου] is said to be [few guardians ...]. This action [Ἀπροσκλήτου] served the patrons against ungrateful freedmen, as is clear, and to them were attached those guardians whom they had publicly adopted for themselves when they were manumitted. Whether the plea of the freedmen, by which they defended themselves against this action, was also called [Ἀπροσκλήτου], is a question. A most distinguished and learned man asks it, and he justifies this usage from the speech of Dinarchus for Aeschylus, the freedman of Xenophon, whose title is found in Diogenes Laertius in the life of Xenophon, and in Dionysius of Halicarnassus in the life of Dinarchus: [Ἀπροσκλήτου Ἐπιτρόπου Ἀπροσκλήτου]. The passage of Suidas on these words supports his suspicion: [Ἀπροσκλήτου, when a slave, once freed, becomes a guardian, unless he shuts out...; it is permitted to exempt oneself from the guardians]. In what sense this same man explains those words of Suidas I have said above; but I have no doubt that Suidas teaches that [Ἀπροσκλήτου] is also the name of the action by which the freedman, who in some way is still a slave, [...] as Chrysippus says, summons his patron into court, so that he may be granted full and complete liberty in every respect, saying that he cannot be bound to slaves in any service, whether of labour or of paying money, but only to the services [...]. We have divided these three terms, which Suidas has in general: slaves paid their services to their masters and paid something from their own savings. Freedmen also were compelled by the Law to their patrons [...] who, as the writer says, [...] to the patron wants nothing, neither to render service nor to pay, since that belongs to slaves; for this reason the freedmen were as it were kept in service, but rather were given full and perfect liberty. This action [Ἀπροσκλήτου] was written before the Polemarch; Aristotle writes about the Athenian republic [...]. Actions of slaves against masters, and of patrons against freedmen, were judged, and [...] by the right of the master. Harpocration: [...]. Suidas: [...]. If the Attic actions were won by the patrons against the freedmen, the freedmen were dragged back into slavery. Harpocration, and from him Suidas: [...], namely of the freedmen [...]. And they were brought back into the city [...]. Suidas: [...]. Hyperides [...]. Many of the ancient orators taught that this was so: Lysias, Aeschines and Hyperides [...], or were even sold. Demosthenes [...]. Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 1, recalls this Law: Come now, what of that Athenian custom, how memorable! When a freedman is convicted by his patron of ingratitude, he is stripped of his freedom by law. "I will not trouble you," he says, "to keep him, the impious appraiser of so great a gift." Nor could he be brought to believe it, since he did not know how to be free. But Valerius's error must be corrected in passing, since he thinks that the slaves were given citizenship by the Athenians together with their freedom; this is not true. He clearly had in mind the freedom given by the rod among his own Romans.

units.la: Apud Romanos longe aliud vsurpatum fuit aduersus ingratos Libertos: quanquam subinde mutauit: Nam primo, quod sciam, Patronu concessum Libertum vltra vicesimum lapidem relegare. Quod ab Augusto institutum fuisse suspicatur CL. Lipsius. Augustus enim, vt Dio ait Lib. LV. constituit [illegible, ~20 letters]. Docet id Tacitus Annali XIII. vbi scribit actum in Senatu fuisse de fraudibus Libertorum, effl agitatumque vt aduersus male meritos reuocandae libertatis ius patronis daretur: audaciam, inquit, cohibitam libertate irreuerentiam eo prorupisse fremtibus, vt an aequo cum patronis iure agerent, sententiam eorum consultarent, an verberibus manus vti intenderent, impelleretque patronam ... Quid enim aliud la[?]fo patrono concessum, quam vt vicesimum ultra lapidem, in oram Campaniae libertum releget? Ceteras actiones promiscuas & pares esse. Tribuendum aliquod telum quod sperni nequeat. Occisum esse hunc locum sentit CL. Lipsius: nec nisi vespillones, non enim medicos, ad hoc funus coire, itaque etiam suspiciones suas ludibria appellat. Sed nondum plane depositus est hic locus, quem nullo negotio, sine vlla mutatione, interpretari facile est. Referuntur a Cornelio ea, quae pro sententia dicta sunt in Senatu ab iis, qui aduersus male meritos Libertos reuocandae libertatis ius patronis dari volebant: atque ab his verbis incipiunt, Vt an aequo, &c. quae habentur ad eos, qui contra hanc sententiam differebant: Volunt igitur, ut sententiam Libertorum ipsorum consultent, vi, an aequo cum patronis iure agant: an cum ipsi Liberti manus ultro intendent patronis suis, patronos quoque ut & sibi verbera intendent non impellant, atque ita re ipsa poenam suam dissuadeant, quae admodum levis est: Quis enim aliud, inquiunt, laso patrono concessum, quam ut vicesimum ultra lapidem, in oram Campaniae libertum relegeret? Quid audio, in oram Campaniae relegatos fuisse male meritos Libertos omnes? Vix est, ut credam, solam hanc oram Campaniae delectam fuisse Lege sive Principis Constitutione, in quam omnes male meriti Liberti à patronis relegarentur: & parum prudens, ut cetera mittam, atque in tutum consilium, tot perditos homines, quod sane mores eorum arguebant, eodem convenire: Adde quod poena vix poena fuisset, cum Campania tractus fuerit totius tertiae Italiae amoenissimus atque feracissimus: Contra potius interdictum puto Libertis, qui ultra vicesimum lapidem relegabantur, hoc tractu & agro: Verum insolens loquendi genus ἀσωτίζων[?] fecit, ut Taciti locus corrumperetur. Rescribo: Quid enim aliud laso patrono concessum, quam ut vicesimum ultra lapidem, moram Campaniae, libertum relegeret? Vult Libertum ultra vicesimum lapidem relegari, nec tamen in Campania morari. Sed quare ultra vicesimum lapidem relegantur? An quia, cum vicena millia passuum, ut loquitur Gaius Lib. I. ad Edictum provinciale, in singulos dies dinumerari Praetor iubeat, Leg. I. D. Si quis cautionibus: atque itinere faciendo, inquit Ulpianus Lib. II. ad Edictum, viginti millia passuum in dies singulos peragenda sint, Lib. III. D. de verborum significat. unius saltem dici itinere malemeritum de patrono suo libertum ab eius conspectu abesse voluerunt? Nihil de poena Libertorum ingratorum mutatum hoc Senatusconsulto, valuit enim mitior sententia. Quanquam Claudius paullo ante, Ingratos, & de quibus patroni quererentur, revocauit in servitutem, inquit Suetonius in Claudio cap. XXV. quod absolute non est verum, ut ante nos pridem observarunt viri summi, auctore Marciano Lib. XIII. Institutionum. Nam in servitutem tantum retrahebatur, si patrono delatores summiserat, qui ei de statu controversiam facerent. Divus Claudius libertum, qui probatus fuerit patrono delatores summisisse, qui de statu eius facerent ei quaestionem, servum patroni esse iussit eum libertum. Leg. V. D. de iure patronatus. Commodus Imperator, referente Modestino Lib. singulari de Manumissionibus, constituit postea, ut liberti, qui patronos violaverant contumeliis, aut illata manu pulsaverant, aut non exhibuerant ad paupertatem redactos, cogerentur ad obsequia, ministerium appellat Imperator patronis praestanda, quod si nihil profeceretur, in servitutem alteri à Praeside vendebantur, pretio patroni addicto: nam quod putant viri maximi, addictos fuisse emptori in Libertos, non in servos, nobis non probatur, cum constet nihil profectum, illis administeria patronis praebenda adactis: itaque opus fuit ut in servitutem retraherentur, ut metu coerceantur, quos beneficia non mutauissent. Imperatoris Commodi constitutio talis profertur. Cum probatum sit, contumeliis patronos à libertis esse violatos, vel illata manu atroci esse pulsatos, aut etiam paupertate, vel corporis valetudine laborantes relictos: primum eos in potestatem patronorum redigi, & ministerium dominis praebere cogi. sin autem nec hoc modo admoneantur: vel à Praeside emptori addicentur, & pretium patronis tribuetur. Leg. VI. §. 1. D. de agnoscendis liberis. Mutauit posteaquam illud, ut constat ex his Vlpiani verbis, Lib. IX. de Officio Proconsulis, in quibus habes poenas aduersus male meritos de Patronis Libertos sanctas. Sed si quidem inofficiosus patrono, patronae, liberisve eorum sit libertus, tantummodo castigari eum sub comminatione aliqua seueritatis non dissimulare, si rursum causam querela praebuerit, & demutti oportet. Enim vero si contumeliam fecit, aut conuicium eis dixit, etiam in exilium temporale dari debebit. Quod si manus intulit, in metallum dandus erit. Idem, & si calumniam aliquam eis iniuriam [?], vel delatorem subornauit, dummodo de patroni statu ei quaestionem non fecerit, vel quam causam aduersus eos tentauit. Leg. I. D. de iure patronatus. Quid Vlpianus appellet hic castigari discere est è Modestino Lib. singulari de Manumissionibus, interdum illa poena à liberto ingrato exigitur, vel pars bonorum eius auferitur, & patrono datur, vel fustibus caeditur, & ita absoluitur. Leg. VII. §. 1. D. eod. Nempe castigari est fustibus caedi, quod idem Vlpianus dixit in hoc ipso argumento fustibus castigare. Leg. 1. §. Cum Patronus. D. de officio Praefecti Vrbi. Subsecutis temporibus ex Constitutione Imperatorum Diocletiani & Maximiani A A. ad Veneriam, liberti, qui ingrati probantur, ad ferundi necessitatem redigi possunt. Leg. XII. C. de operis Libertorum. Quod etiam obseruari voluit Constantinus, Lege data ad Maximum Praefectum Vrbi, filiosque etiam, qui post reuocatum in seruitutem patrem nati fuerint, ferituros. Leg. II. C. de Libertis & eorum liberis. Idemque referipsit aliquot post annis ad Concilium Byzantinorum, Leg. I. Cod. Theod. cod.
units.tr: Among the Romans a quite different practice was adopted against ungrateful freedmen, although it was afterwards changed from time to time. For at first, as far as I know, the patron was allowed to banish the freedman beyond the twentieth milestone. Clarissimus Lipsius suspects that this was instituted by Augustus. For Augustus, as Dio says in book LV, decreed [...]. Tacitus teaches this in the Annals, book XIII, where he writes that in the Senate there was debate about the frauds of the freedmen, and it was argued that the right of recalling freedom should be given to patrons against those who had ill deserved: the audacity, he says, held in check by liberty, had burst out into such disrespect that they consulted the opinion of the senators as to whether they should deal with their patrons on equal legal terms, or whether they should raise their hands in blows, and it drove the patron ... For what else was granted to the wronged patron, than that he might banish the freedman beyond the twentieth milestone, to the shore of Campania? The other actions were to be common and equal. Some weapon that cannot be scorned was to be given. Clarissimus Lipsius thinks this passage has been killed off, and that only the undertakers, not the doctors, meet for this funeral; so he calls even his own suspicions mockeries. But this passage has not yet been wholly set aside, and it is easy to interpret without any difficulty and without any change. Cornelius reports what was said in the Senate by those who wanted to give patrons the right of recalling freedom against ill-deserving freedmen; these words begin with Vt an aequo, etc., and they are addressed to those who held back against this opinion. They want, therefore, that the freedmen themselves be consulted, whether they act with equal legal right toward their patrons: whether the freedmen themselves stretch out their hands willingly against their patrons, or whether the patrons likewise do not drive them on to raise blows against themselves, and so by the deed itself they dissuade their punishment, which is very slight. For what else, they say, was granted to the wronged patron, than that he might banish the freedman beyond the twentieth milestone, to the shore of Campania? What do I hear: were all ill-deserving freedmen banished to the shore of Campania? I can hardly believe that this shore of Campania alone was chosen by law or by an imperial constitution as the place to which all ill-deserving freedmen should be banished by their patrons; and it would be unwise, to say nothing of other things, to gather so many lost men in one safe place, which indeed their characters declared. Add that the penalty would scarcely be a penalty, since Campania was the most pleasant and fertile region of all Third Italy. On the contrary, I think a prohibition was placed on the freedmen who were banished beyond the twentieth milestone, from this region and this land. But an unusual way of speaking has corrupted the passage of Tacitus. I restore it: For what else was granted to the wronged patron, than that he might banish the freedman beyond the twentieth milestone, the border of Campania? He wants the freedman banished beyond the twentieth milestone, yet not to remain in Campania. But why are they banished beyond the twentieth milestone? Is it because, when Gaius in book I on the Provincial Edict says that the Praetor orders twenty thousand paces to be counted for each single day (Dig. 2, Si quis cautionibus), and Ulpian in book II on the Edict says, in making a journey, twenty thousand paces are to be covered each day (Dig. 50, de verborum significatione), they wanted the ill-deserving freedman to be kept away from the sight of his patron by at least one day's journey? This Senate decree changed nothing of the punishment of ungrateful freedmen, for the milder opinion prevailed. Although Claudius shortly before, as Suetonius says in Claudius chapter XXV, recalled into slavery those who were ungrateful and of whom their patrons complained, which is not absolutely true, as the greatest men observed long ago on the authority of Marcian, book XIII of the Institutes. For a freedman was dragged back into slavery only if he had sent informers against his patron to bring a suit concerning his status. The divine Claudius ordered that a freedman who was proved to have sent informers against his patron, to bring an inquiry about his status, should be the slave of his patron. (Dig. 37, de iure patronatus.) The Emperor Commodus, as Modestinus reports in his single book on Manumissions, later decided that freedmen who had violated their patrons with insults, or struck them with a hand, or had not shown them due respect, if reduced to poverty, should be compelled to obedience; the Emperor calls this service to be rendered to the patrons; but if nothing was achieved in this way, they were sold to another by the Governor into slavery, the price being assigned to the patron. For what the greatest men think, that they were assigned to the buyer as freedmen, not as slaves, is not approved by us, since it is established that nothing was achieved, as they were compelled to render services to their patrons; so it was necessary that they be dragged back into slavery, that those whom benefits had not changed might be restrained by fear. The constitution of the Emperor Commodus is published as follows: Since it is proved that patrons have been violated by freedmen with insults, or cruelly struck by a hand, or left in poverty or sickness: first, let them be brought back into the power of their patrons, and be compelled to render service to their masters. But if they are not warned in this way, they shall be assigned by the Governor to a buyer, and the price shall be given to the patrons. (Dig. 40, §1, de agnoscendis liberis.) Afterwards it was changed, as appears from these words of Ulpian in book IX, de Officio Proconsulis, in which you have the penalties against freedmen who have ill deserved of their patrons, which are sacred. But if the freedman is disobedient to his patron, patroness, or their children, he must be punished only, and not be spared under some threat of severity, if he again gives cause for complaint; and he must be dealt with. Indeed, if he has done an insult or spoken an abuse against them, he shall also be given temporary exile. But if he has laid hands on them, he shall be given to the mines. The same holds if he has suborned some false accusation or informer against them, provided he has not brought an inquiry about the patron's status, or attempted some cause against them. (Dig. 37, de iure patronatus, law 1.) What Ulpian means here by being punished is to be learned from Modestinus in his single book on Manumissions: sometimes this penalty is exacted from an ungrateful freedman, or part of his goods is taken away and given to the patron, or he is beaten with rods and so released. (Dig. 37, §1, same title.) Indeed, to be punished is to be beaten with rods, which Ulpian also said in this same matter, to punish with rods (Dig. 1, §Cum Patronus, de officio Praefecti Urbi). In later times, by the constitution of the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian Augusti to Veneria, freedmen who are proved ungrateful may be reduced to the necessity of bearing burdens (Cod. XII, de operis Libertorum). Constantine also wished this to be observed, by a law given to Maximus the Prefect of the City, and that the sons also who were born after the father had been recalled into slavery should bear burdens (Cod. II, de Libertis et eorum liberis). And a few years later he rescribed the same to the Council of Byzantium (Cod. Theod., same title, law 1).

units.la: In hac aduersus Libertos Απογραφὴν actione Lege licebat cuiuis ἀξιοῦν, siue is esset ciuis, siue peregrinus.
units.tr: In this action against freedmen, called an apographē [Ἀπογραφή], the law allowed anyone to bring it, whether citizen or foreigner.

units.la: Ἐξῆναι ὑπὸ τῶν γραφαῖς τῶν τὸ Ἀπογραφὴν ... [?] ... ἔξιεν ... [?] τῶν ... [?]
units.tr: It was permitted by the writings ... [the Greek here is too corrupt to render with confidence].

units.la: Cui licebat, siue peregrino, siue ciui, testimonium dicere in actionibus Aduersus Libertos ad exceptionem.
units.tr: Anyone, whether foreigner or citizen, could give testimony in actions against freedmen as an objection to the claim.
