units.la: Licebat igitur cuiuis testimonium dicere, in hac aduersus Libertos actione, antequam iudicium redderetur, ὡς εἰσαγγέλματος ἔστιν ἢ δίκη, ἡ οὐκ εἰσαγγέλματος. Hyperides apud Harpocrationem: Ὑπερίδης ἐν τῷ Ἀπογραφῆς ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ... τῶν ἀπελευθέρων ... [?] ... Ἀπογραφῆς τῆς ... [?] ... ἀπελευθέρων ... [?].
units.tr: Therefore anyone could give testimony in this action against freedmen before judgment was delivered, whether the case was one of an eisangelma or not. Hyperides, in Harpocration: Hyperides, in the ... of the apographē ... of the freedmen ... [the rest is too corrupt to render].

units.la: Census autem Libertorum habebatur, an plenam consecuti essent libertatem. Nonnus in Nazianzeni priorem ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... ea scilicet fini, ut si plenam esse consecuti libertatem censerentur, ab iis quod publico pendebant aerario, exigeretur.
units.tr: A census of freedmen was taken, to determine whether they had obtained full freedom. Nonnus, on Nazianzen's ... [the rest is too corrupt to render]. The purpose, clearly, was that if they were judged to have obtained full liberty, what they owed to the public treasury would be exacted from them.

units.la: Inter seruos censebatur is, qui redemptus ex hostibus, redimias non persoluisset redemptori suo, cui seruitutem seruiebat dum id praestitisset, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Among the slaves was counted a man who, ransomed from the enemy, had not repaid his ransom to his redeemer, and who remained in servitude to him until he had done so, under this law:

units.la: ὁ λυτρωθεὶς ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων ἔστω ... [?] ... ἐὰν μὴ ἀποδῷ λύτρα [?].
units.tr: "The one ransomed from the enemies shall be ... unless he pays the ransom" [ὁ λυτρωθεὶς ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων ἔστω ... ἐὰν μὴ ἀποδῷ λύτρα].

units.la: Redemptus ex hostibus illius esto, qui redemit, nisi redimas ipse persoluerit.
units.tr: He who was ransomed from the enemy shall belong to the one who redeemed him, unless he himself has paid the ransom.

units.la: Legem habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ πρὸς Νικίφρατον[?]. εἶπα δ' ἔφη[?], ὅτι καὶ οἱ νόμοι κελεύουσι, τὸ λυτρωθὲν ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων εἰς τὴν λύτραν[?], ἐὰν μὴ [illegible, ~8 letters] λύτρα. Captiui autem redimi non poterant, nisi à Legatis. Anonymus in Argumento Orationis Demosthenicae περὶ τῆς παραπρεσβείας[?]. ἀπελθὼν δὲ εἰς τὴν πατρίδα πρεσβεύειν, ὥρεν ἐν Μακεδονίᾳ πινὰς τῶν Ἀθηναίων αἰχμαλώτους[?], καὶ [illegible, ~10 letters] ἔφερε[?] ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ γενεᾷ[?] καὶ ῥύσασθαι αὐτὸς[?], οὐκ ἠδύνατο δ' ἂν τὴν ποινὴν[?], εἰ μὴ ἐκ [illegible, ~6 letters] ἀποδοῦναι[?].
units.tr: You have the law in Demosthenes, in the speech against Nicophratus. "And I say," he said, "that the laws also command that one ransomed from the enemy ... unless he ... the ransom" [the Greek is corrupt]. Captives, however, could not be redeemed except through envoys. The anonymous writer in the Argument of Demosthenes' speech On the False Embassy says: going home to act as envoy, he saw some Athenians held captive in Macedonia, and ... he could not redeem them unless ... to pay [the rest is corrupt].

units.la: Seruum autem ociosum atque inertem alere Leges non sinebant: Μὴ ἐξῆναι τρέφειν οἰκέτην[?]. Seruum otiosum ne alito.
units.tr: The laws did not allow a slave who was idle and unemployed to be kept: "It is not permitted to maintain a household slave who is idle" [Μὴ ἐξῆναι τρέφειν οἰκέτην]. Do not keep an idle slave.

units.la: Legem habes apud Ulpianum in Midianam: ἐπὶ δὲ τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις ζῆν τῶν οἰκετῶν[?] τρέφειν οἰκέτην[?] δύο[?] οἱ μὲν, αὐλητρίδες[?] οἱ δὲ, μαχαιροποιοὺς[?] εἶχον τοῖς δού-λους[?]. Serui igitur aliquam artem sciebant, quam exercebant. rum, quod Μετοίκιον, vel πωλητήριον τῆς μετοικίου dicebatur. Plutarchus iam laudatis verbis in Lycurgo Rhetore: πλαὶν δὲ ποτὲ ὑπεδαλάττης Ξενοκράτει τοῦ φιλοσόφου χάριν, τὸν ποιὴς ὁ Μετοίκιον ἀπαγαγόντος. cùm enim publicano ὁ μετοίκιον non pependisset, satis convictus erat [?].
units.tr: You have the law in Ulpian, in the speech against Midias: at Athens ... to keep slaves ... two: the one a flute-girl, the other a sword-maker, they kept as slaves. Slaves therefore knew some trade, which they practised. The tax was called metoikion, or the sale of the metoikion. Plutarch, in the words already cited, in the Life of Lycurgus the orator: "... once, for the sake of the philosopher Xenocrates, ... when the metoikion ..." For when he had not paid the metoikion to the tax-farmer, he was sufficiently convicted.

units.la: Non erat quippe, quod se tueretur hac exceptione, Ciuem se esse: nam seuere admodum animaduertebatur in huiusmodi προεγγεγραμμένους εἰς τὸ πολιτικὸν Μετοίκους, fide statu controuersia illis moueretur, scribereturque ξενίας γραφή, quae etiam Ἀπεσσάτοις appellatur, vt obseruant Grammatic corum filij: ὅταν τις ξενίας [?] Μέτοικος, ἀπὸ [?] Φάσκῃ προεγγεγραμμένος εἰς τὸ πολιτεία. Lex autem haec est:
units.tr: Indeed, he had no means of protecting himself by the plea of being a citizen, for those who had been registered among the citizens as metics were punished very severely; if their status was disputed, an action was brought called xenias graphē, which is also called apesatoi, as the sons of the grammarians observe: "Whenever someone who is a metic, registered in the citizen roll, is accused of xenia ..." The law, moreover, is this:

units.la: { } Left column (Greek, italic): Τοὺς τῆς ξενίας γραφὰς ἐς τὰ οἰκήματα ἐμβάλλειν τοῖς χρήσεως μόνον, καὶ μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἐγγυητὰς καταστῆσαι, κἂν μὴ ἄλλο, καὶ τοῦ δικαστηρίου μεταγράφεσθαι.
units.tr: Those accused in the xenias graphai shall be cast into prison, and they shall not be allowed to appoint sureties, and they shall be transferred to the court [Τοὺς τῆς ξενίας γραφὰς ἐς τὰ οἰκήματα ἐμβάλλειν τοῖς χρήσεως μόνον, καὶ μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἐγγυητὰς καταστῆσαι, κἂν μὴ ἄλλο, καὶ τοῦ δικαστηρίου μεταγράφεσθαι].

units.la: Peregrinitatis accusati in vincula, antequam iudicium reddatur, coniiciuntur. Fidejussores dare ijs ius non esse: conuicti apud iudices venduntur.
units.tr: Those accused of foreignness are thrown into chains before judgment is given. They are not allowed to give sureties; when convicted before the judges, they are sold.

units.la: Igitur qui accusabantur τῆς ξενίας, in vincula primum coniiciebantur, antequam iudicia de illis redderentur, neque fideiussores dare licebat: vbi vero damnati essent τῆς ξενίας, vendebantur. Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτους. ἀλλ' ἔγε' αὐτὸς ἐπὶ τῆς νόμου. οὐδὲ γὰρ οἱ τῆς ξενίας ἁλισκόμενοι ἀγαγοντες ἐκ τῆς οἰκήματι ἔχοντος ἐπ' ἀγορᾷ, ὁ τῶν ἐπὶ ξενίας ... ἀλλ' ἐγὼ ἀξιῶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ὃς εἶναι ἐκπέμπουσι ... πολλοὶ τῆς πολιτείας. Vlpianus: εἰ δὲ ἄλλῳ τῶν ἐπὶ ξενίας τῶν Ἀθηναίων ἀποχρινόμενος εἰς πολίτης μὴ ὢν Ἀθηναῖος ὁ ἀληθὴς, καὶ ταῦτα ποιῶν τῆς πολίτης, ἔχει μὲν χρίσεως, ἔχει δὲ ὁ διομωτήριον. Atque ita quam graue scelus esse istud putarent, significabant, cùm in vincula conijcerent eos, qui fideiussores dare parati erant, & vellent hanc ipsam carceris poenam ante damnationem sustinere.
units.tr: Therefore those accused of xenia were first thrown into chains before judgment was given on them, and they were not allowed to give sureties; but when they had been condemned of xenia, they were sold. Demosthenes mentions this law in the speech against Timocrates: "But let me myself say this about the law. For those caught in xenia, when led out of the prison ... before the ... of xenia ... but I think it right, from his own ..., who are sent out ... many of the citizenship." Ulpian: "But if ... one of the Athenians answering before the judges of xenia is not a true Athenian citizen, and does this ... he has a judgment, and he has ..." And thus they showed how grave a crime they thought this was, since they cast into chains those who were ready to give sureties and who wished to undergo this very penalty of imprisonment before condemnation.

units.la: Vnde etiam iudicio iterum experiri licebat aduersus eum, secundū quem accusatum ξενίας pronuntiatum fuerat, appellabaturque haec actio διωξενίας, eaque de re haec Lex legitur.
units.tr: Hence, too, it was permitted to try the matter again in a second action against the one by whom the accused had been pronounced guilty of xenia; this action was called diōxenias, and concerning it the following law is read:

units.la: { } Left column (Greek, italic): Τοὺς ἀποφυγόντας ξενίας ἐξεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ πάλιν γράφασθαι διωξενίας. Right column (italic): Absolutum iudicio peregrinitatis ius esto cuicumque libuerit, accusare corrupti muneribus iudicij.
units.tr: "Those acquitted of xenia shall be allowed, to whoever wishes, to indict again for diōxenia" [Τοὺς ἀποφυγόντας ξενίας ἐξεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ πάλιν γράφασθαι διωξενίας]. Let anyone whom it pleases have the right to accuse, after acquittal in a judgment of foreignness, those who were corrupted by bribes of the court.

units.la: Non igitur accusato ξενίας se purgasse satis fuit; licebat enim iterum eum in ius vocare διωξενίας. Meminit Legis Hyperides ἐν τῷ κατὰ Αεισταγόρου. ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ τῆς Διωξενίας νόμος ἀρίστην ... ἀποφυγόντας ξενίας εἰρηκει ἐξεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ πάλιν γράφασθαι, ἐὰν μὴ δικῶσι δικαίως ὁ τοῦτον ἀποφυγόντα, πῶς δ' Φαῖσθαι ... κατ' Αεισταγόρου ὁ δικαίου; Dica haec, vt ex Aristotele ἐν τῇ Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ liquet, apud Thesmothetas scribebatur: εἰσὶ ὁ καὶ γραφαὶ τοῖς αὐτοῦ Thesmothetas, ἂν ἀποφύγῃ ἀφ' ἐκάστης ἀρχῆς, ξενίας, καὶ διωξενίας, αὐτοῖς διωξ ... ἀποφυγῆ τῷ ξενίῳ. alibi reperies scriptum fuisse ab Aristotele, ἀποφυγὴ τῷ ξενίῳ. Pollux Libro III. cap. IV. ἐπ' ἀλλὰ τῆς ἀποφευγῶν ξενίας γεγραμμένων ξενίας γραφὴ, καὶ διωξενίας, ἀλλὰ ἀφαιροῦνται τὰς ... ἀπὸ ... [illegible, ~6 letters]. A litigantibus autem pendebatur drachma, à singulis vna, iudicum sportula, non vero, vt volunt viri summi, in apparitorum mercedem Harpocration, quę descripsit Suidas: ἐπὶ δὲ δραχμῇ Ἰσαῖος ἐν τῇ κατὰ Ἐπικράτους ... ἐπὶ δὲ δραχμὴ καταβαλλομένην ὑπὸ τῶν δικαζομένων τὰς ἰδίας δίκας. Μέναδρος Μισογύνῃ.
units.tr: It was therefore not enough for one accused of xenia to have cleared himself, for he could be summoned again to court for diōxenia. Hyperides mentions the law in the speech against Aristogeiton: "since also the law of diōxenia ... has said that those acquitted of xenia may be indicted again by whoever wishes, if ... those acquitted are not rightly prosecuted ..., and against Aristogeiton the ..." As is clear from Aristotle in the Athenian Constitution, this was written before the Thesmothetae: "There are also indictments before the Thesmothetae, if one is acquitted in each office, of xenia and diōxenia ... acquittal from xenia." Elsewhere you will find that Aristotle wrote acquittal from xenia. Pollux, Book III, chapter IV: "... of those who were acquitted of xenia, an indictment of xenia and of diōxenia ... they take away ..." From the litigants a drachma was collected, one from each; this was the judges' fee, not, as some very learned men maintain, the wage of the attendants. Harpocration, whom Suidas copied: "a drachma was paid by those who brought their own private suits." Isaeus in the speech against Epicrates. Menander, in the Misogynes: "a drachma."

units.la: ἐλάττ δὲ γεγραμμένον ἐκ τῶν δίνων, καὶ τὸ Ἡλιαστικὸν μία δραχμή. Αἰσχίνης δ' ἐν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ τῶν Θεσμοθετῶν [?] φησιν ὅτι εἰσὶ δὲ γραφαὶ τοῖς αὐτοῖς, ἐν τῷ Ἡλιαστῶν πόλει, ξενίας, καὶ δωροξενίας, ἀν ὡς δώρα δοῦναι ἀποφυγεῖν τῷ ξενίας, καὶ ψευδεγραφῆς, καὶ ψευδοκλητίας, καὶ βλασφημίας, καὶ ἀγραφίου, καὶ μοιχείας. Leuiter corrupta sunt Menandri verba, quæ, vt puto, dicuntur aduersus <bl>τὸν Μισογύνην</bl>, qui huic fabulae nomen dedit, siue ab eius vxore, siue à quopiam alio obijciente illi <bl>ὁ φιλάργυρος</bl>, Rescribo;
units.tr: The lesser ... of the two, and the Heliastic court, one drachma. Aeschines, in the Athenian Constitution, says that the Thesmothetae ... there are indictments before the same court, in the city of the Heliastae: for xenia, and for dōroxenia, if they gave gifts in order to escape a charge of xenia, and for false registration, false summons, slander, unlawful writing, and adultery. Menander's words are slightly corrupt; I think they are said against the Misogynes, who gave the play its name, whether because of his wife or because someone else reproached him as "the miser." I propose this emendation:

units.la: ἐλάττ δὲ γεγραμμένον τῷ ἰδίᾳ ἐκ σι δίνων, καὶ τὸ Ἡλιαστικὸν μία.
units.tr: "The lesser ... written on ... two obols, and the Heliastic court one drachma."

units.la: Distinximus vocem <bl>γεγραμμένον</bl>, in has, <bl>γράμμα τ' ἰδίαν</bl>, nam <bl>κ' γραμμάτων</bl> iudices sua fortiebantur <bl>δικαστήρια</bl>, in quibus iudicia reddebant. Scholia Comici ad hunc Pluti versum, <bl>ἀλλ' ὁ λαχὼν ἔπινες ἐν τῇ γεγραμμένῃ.</bl>
units.tr: We have separated the word gegrammenon into gramma and idian, for the judges were allotted their courts by letters, and in these courts they gave their judgments. The scholia of the comic poet on this line of the Plutus: "but he who has drawn the lot ... in the marked ..."

units.la: <bl>ἐπὶ ἰωνοῖαις, αὐτὴ τῇ, ἰδιαζοῦς. ὅτι δὲ καὶ κατὰ γεγραμμένα ἐκλεγομένων, παρ' αὐτοῖς [illegible, ~6 letters] ἐπίσκοπος.</bl>
units.tr: "... in the ... of the same, ... private ... that also those who were chosen by written lot, among them ... overseer."

units.la: Epithera verò hoc <bl>δίνων</bl>, literam designauit, secundum quam <bl>ὁ δικαστὴς</bl> erat sortitus. Expunximus praeterea vocem <bl>δραχμὴ</bl>, glossema quippe fuit vocis <bl>Παρασίτης.</bl>
units.tr: Moreover, the letter delta, which I mentioned above, indicated the lot by which the judge had been allotted. We have also removed the word drachma, since it was a gloss on the word parasite.

units.la: DE SERVIS ET LIBERTIS. TITVLVS VI.
units.tr: On Slaves and Freedmen. Title VI.

units.la: VRA Seruorum solutiora multo erant Athenis, quam Romae, vnde Plautus in Sticho:
units.tr: The laws concerning slaves were far more lenient at Athens than at Rome, whence Plautus in the Stichus:

units.la: Atque id ne vos miremini, homines seruulos Potare, amare, atque ad cœnam condicere: Licet hoc Athenis nobis.
units.tr: And do not be surprised at this, that slaves drink, love, and are invited to dinner; we at Athens are allowed this.

units.la: Demosthenes Philippica III. <bl>ὑμεῖς γὰρ τὴν πρὸς ἡμᾶς ... ἐν πάσῃ τῇ πόλει, ὥστε καὶ τοῖς ξένοις, καὶ τοῖς δούλοις αὐτῶν μεταδιδόναι.</bl> Rursum in eadem: <bl>πολλοὶ αὐτῶν τῆς οἰκίας ἰδίᾳ ... ἐν ἐνίοις τῶν ἀνθρώπων πόλεων.</bl> Optime certè prisci illi Athenienses iustam & clementem seruitutem praeferebant. Serui enim (qui Graecis ideo <bl>σώματα</bl>, & Latinis Iurisconsultis corpora dicuntur) sunt dominis, quod animae est corpus, vt præclare disputat Aristoteles Polit. Libro I: <bl>ἀλλὰ ψυχή, τὸ σῶμα ... ἐν ᾧ φύσει ἔστιν, ὅτι καὶ φύσιν καὶ συμφέρον ὁ ἄρχων ... ἀδύνατον.</bl> Præterea nata est seruitus ab iis, qui cùm essent sui iuris, neque tamen per mentis infirmitatem res suas possent tueri, in prudentiærum clientelam vltro venerunt, atque illis operas suas locarunt. Refert Posidonius Stoicus Historia X. & verba transcripsit Athenaeus in Lib. VI. πολλοὺς τινὰς ἑαυτῶν ἀ δωρεαῖς ποιήσασθαι, ὅθεν ὃ τῆς Ἀθηναίας ἐπιδίδωσιν ἑαυτοὺς εἰς τὴν τῶν σιωπώντων τὴν ὑπηρεσίαν, ὅπως ἀφ' ἑκείνων τὴν χορηγίαν τῆς εἰς τὰ αἰσ[?]χρὰ ἐπιμελείας, ὡσὶ πάλιν ἀπολάβωσι ἑκείνοις δ' αὐτὴν ἀφ' ἀὐ ὅσον ὑπηρετοῦ δουλ[?]εύειν. Quae sola vera atque iusta erat seruitus, vt quae à natura esset: vnde Aristoteles: ἐσι μὲν οὖν ἀρχῆς πει ξωοῦ τῶν θεοῦ διεξ[?]αυ, ὅσον ψυχὴ σώματος, καὶ ἀνδρὸς δεσπότης θηρίου, ἀρχικὸν σώματος χρήσιμον ἔχων δ' ὅτι ἐρρυ[?]ῆ τὸ σώματος ζῆσαι, καὶ τὸ τ' ἐσχ' ἀπ' αὐτοῦ βέλτιον. Ἔστι μὲν εἶναι φύσει δοῦλοι, οἷς βέλτιον ἐστὶν ἀρχεσθαι ταύτῃ τῶν ἀρχόντων. Anima enim illis pro tale data est. Idem maximus Doctor: ἐστὶ γὰρ φύσει δοῦλος ἐκείνωλ λόγου ἔμπεσιτοῦ ἀλλὰ αἰσθάνεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἀλλὰ μὴ ἔχει. & alterius natura est, id est, seruus est, qui suus esse non potest: ὁ γὰρ μὴ αὐτὸς φύσει, ἀλλ' ἄλλου, αὐτὸς δὲ αὐτὸς ἔσι φύσει δοῦλός ἐστιν. Praeterea qui Lege serui sunt, si ἔχ' ἡμῶν δοῦλοι, εἰ δ' ἔ, inquit summus virorum, ὅσ' ἔχ' πολέμων ἡ[?]αιροῦνται τῶν ἡ[?]αιτῶν ἔχ' φα-σι, liberalitate potius quam metu retinendi sunt.
units.tr: Demosthenes, Philippic III: "For you show such a disposition towards us ... throughout the whole city, so that one may share it even with foreigners and with their slaves." [ὑμεῖς γὰρ τὴν πρὸς ἡμᾶς ... ἐν πάσῃ τῇ πόλει, ὥστε καὶ τοῖς ξένοις, καὶ τοῖς δούλοις αὐτῶν μεταδιδόναι.] Again in the same speech: "Many of them, in their own households, privately ... in some of the cities of men." [πολλοὶ αὐτῶν τῆς οἰκίας ἰδίᾳ ... ἐν ἐνίοις τῶν ἀνθρώπων πόλεων.] Certainly those ancient Athenians very rightly approved of a just and gentle servitude. For slaves (called by the Greeks "bodies" [σώματα], and by the Latin jurists "corpora") belong to their masters as the body belongs to the soul, as Aristotle argues admirably in Book I of the Politics: "But soul and body ... in which by nature there is, since both nature and advantage the ruler ... impossible." [ἀλλὰ ψυχή, τὸ σῶμα ... ἐν ᾧ φύσει ἔστιν, ὅτι καὶ φύσιν καὶ συμφέρον ὁ ἄρχων ... ἀδύνατον.] Moreover, servitude arose among those who, though they were their own masters, could not, because of the weakness of their minds, protect their own affairs, and so of their own accord came under the protection of the prudent and let out their labour to them. Posidonius the Stoic relates this in Book X of his Histories, and Athenaeus transcribed his words in Book VI: "many of them made themselves ... by gifts, whence ... they gave themselves into the service of those who ... so that from those they might receive provision for ... and again receive it back ... to serve as slaves." [πολλοὺς τινὰς ἑαυτῶν ἀ δωρεαῖς ποιήσασθαι, ὅθεν ... ὑπηρετοῦ δουλεύειν.] This alone was true and just servitude, being the kind that comes from nature. Whence Aristotle: "There is a rule of the living ... as the soul over the body, and the master of a man over a beast ... useful for the body ... for it is better for them to be ruled thus. It is by nature that some are slaves, for whom it is better to be ruled by such rulers." [ἔστι μὲν εἶναι φύσει δοῦλοι, οἷς βέλτιον ἐστὶν ἀρχεσθαι ταύτῃ τῶν ἀρχόντων.] For a soul is given to them in such a role. The same greatest teacher says: "he who is a slave by nature ... does not have reason of his own, but perceives only ... and is another's, and is a slave by nature who is not his own but another's." [ὁ γὰρ μὴ αὐτὸς φύσει, ἀλλ' ἄλλου, αὐτὸς δὲ αὐτὸς ἔσι φύσει δοῦλός ἐστιν.] Furthermore, those who are slaves by law, if they are slaves of ours ... but if not, says the greatest of men, those whom they have taken in war from enemies ... they are to be retained by generosity rather than by fear.

units.la: τύχη δὲ πάντα μεταφέρει τὰ σώματα. πολλοὶ δὲ νῦν μὲν εἰσὶν ἐν ἐλευθέροις, εἰς τ' ἀρχὴν δὲ Σωσίας, εἴτ' εἰς πείτιν ἀπηρὰ χειρὸς ὤλεσ'. τῆ γὰρ ἰδιάνα φέρει δαίμων ἔκαστα.
units.tr: Fortune turns all bodies about. Many are now among the free, and once, Sosias, they lost a hand in war; for the divinity brings each thing to pass by fate.

units.la: inquit Anaxandrides Comicus in Anchise. Ad haec metus erat, ne provocati iniuriis Serui bello dominos lacesserent, quod aliquando euenisse [?] reliquit Posidonius Philosophus: tantusenim Athenis erat Seruorum numerus, vt quum Demetrius Phalereus anno primo Olympiadis centesimae decimae censum Atheniensium ageret, numerata sint seruorum capitum quadringenta millia. Anonymus in Descriptione Olympiadum ad hunc annum: ἐξεδασμὸς τῶν Ἀθηναίων ἡμερῶν κατὰ Δημητρίου τῆς Φαληρέως, ἐκέθησαν μὲν Ἀθηναίων δισμυρίους, οἴκετθ' δὲ μυριάδας πεντακοσίας. Crescicles Lib. ro III. Chronicorum idem scribit: τῇ δεκάτῃ ἀρχῇ τῆς ἑκατοστῆς Ολυμπιάδι, Ἀθηναῖον ἐξεδασμὸν ἡμέραν κατὰ Δημητρίου τῆς Φαληρέως τῆ καλουμένη τῶν Ἀθηνῶν, καὶ ὅρες ἔλεων Ἀθηναῖοι μὲν δισμυρίους περὶ τῆς χιλίας, μετοίκους δὲ μυρίας, εἰσὶν δ' μυριάδας πεντακοσίας. Humane itaque Seruos suos habuerunt Athenienses.
units.tr: So says the comic poet Anaxandrides in the Anchises. Besides this, there was fear that slaves, provoked by injuries, might attack their masters in war, which Posidonius the philosopher reports as having happened once. For the number of slaves at Athens was so great that when Demetrius of Phalerum took the census of the Athenians in the first year of the hundred and tenth Olympiad, 400,000 slaves were counted. An anonymous writer in the Description of the Olympiads on this year: "the enumeration of the Athenians by the days under Demetrius of Phalerum; there were counted 20,000 Athenians, and 500,000 household slaves." Crescicles, in Book III of his Chronicles, writes the same: "In the tenth year of the hundred and first Olympiad, the census of the Athenians was taken under Demetrius of Phalerum, the so-called census of the Athenians; and they found 21,000 citizens, 10,000 metics, and 400,000 slaves [...] 500,000." Thus the Athenians treated their slaves humanely.

units.la: Hinc Legem vt scriberent hanc, factum est: Ἄν τις τύπτῃ τὸν ἀλλότριον δοῦλον, γεγραφας εἴ[?] | Si quis alienum seruum pulsarit, αἰκίας χρὴ τὸ τύπτειν. | aduersus eum Lege iniuriarum agito.
units.tr: From this it came about that they wrote this law: "If anyone strikes another's slave, ... [...] the penalty for beating" [Ἄν τις τύπτῃ τὸν ἀλλότριον δοῦλον, γεγραφας ... αἰκίας χρὴ τὸ τύπτειν]. Let him bring an action for injury against him.

units.la: Non licebat igitur alienum seruum pulsare: meminit huius Legis Xenophon ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ. τῶν δούλων αὖ ἐς τὴν Μετοίκων, πλείστη ἐστὶν Ἀθηναῖον ἀκαλασία, ἐὰν πάσῃ ἐξεῖναι αὐτὸ ἡ, ὅτι ἂν ἐκφεύγῃ ἐστὶ ὁ δοῦλος. Hanc eandem Legem intelligit Athenaeus Libro VI. Ἀθηναῖοι δὲ ἡ τῆς τῶν δούλων ἀρρο[?]οῦ[?] τὸ τύπτειν, ἐκωμωδεῖτο καὶ ἐπὶ δούλων γεγραφὰς ὕβρεως εἴ. Υ ἀφίδης γὰρ ὁ Ρήτωρ ἐν τῇ Μαλθιέᾳ, αἰκίας φησὶν ἐξετάσαι, ὃ μόνον ἐπὶ τῆς ἐλευθέρων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐάν τις εἰς δούλου σῶμα ὑβρίσῃ, γεγραφὰς εἴ καὶ τὸ ὑβρίσασθαι. Ἐλεγον vocat, quae proprie αἰκία est, id est, πληγαὶ μόνοι, vt interpretantur veteres Magistri, cuius multa erat pecuniaria, vt docet Lysias ἐν τῇ πρὸς ἴσοχράτην. Καὶ πῶς τῆς ὅλον ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἡ μὲν αἰκία, ἐκλάμ[?]
units.tr: It was therefore not permitted to strike another's slave. Xenophon mentions this law in his Constitution of the Athenians: "Moreover, among the slaves and the metics there is the greatest licence at Athens, since it is not allowed to strike them, and a slave cannot get out of the way." Athenaeus, in Book VI, understands the same law: "At Athens, the striking of slaves was made a matter of ridicule, and an action for insult was written even concerning slaves. For Hyperides the orator, in the Maltiea, says that an action for assault is brought not only for a free man but also if anyone insults the body of a slave." He calls it ἐλευθέρων ... what properly is aikia, that is, mere blows, as the ancient teachers explain; its penalty was a fine, as Lysias teaches in his speech against Isocrates. And how ... [...] to you, that aikia ... money only to be sold.

units.la: {σ} [?] χρημάτ' ὅτι μόνον πωλῆσαι. Ratio Legis est apud Xenophontem, loco laudato: ὃ δ' ἑνεκέν ... [?] ... Εἰ νόμος λῶ τὸν δοῦλον ... τῆς ἐλευθερίου τύπτε[?]... τὸν μέτοικον, ... τὸν ἀπελεύθερον, πολλάκις ... Ἀθηναίων δοῦλον, ... ἐπιτρέψαι ... καὶ οἱ δοῦλοι, καὶ οἱ μέτοικοι, καὶ τὰ εἴδη ... βέλτιστοι εἰσιν. & paulò post: ὅπου δ' εἰσὶ πλούσιοι δοῦλοι, ... ἐνὶ δούλῳ οἱ δεσπόται. E quibus Xenophontis verbis videre est, quàm soluta fuerint iura Athenienfium Seruorum, vt qui eadem cum plebe, aut elegantiori vterentur veste, nemini de via caderent, neque liceret eos ab alienis pulsari.
units.tr: The reason for the law is given by Xenophon in the passage cited: "But why ... if there were a law striking the slave ... of free ... the metic ... the freedman, often ... of the Athenians' slave ... to allow ... both the slaves and the metics and the ... are the best." And a little later: "where there are wealthy slaves, ... the masters are slaves to one slave." From Xenophon's words it can be seen how lenient were the rights of Athenian slaves: since they used the same dress as the common people, or a more elegant one, no one was to step aside for them in the street, nor was it permitted for them to be struck by strangers.

units.la: Seruis in bello captis consultum voluit hac Lege Rhetor Lycurgus:
units.tr: Lycurgus the orator wished to provide for slaves taken in war by this law:

units.la: Μηδενὶ ἐξεῖναι Ἀθηναίων, μηδὲ τῶν οἰκούντων Ἀθηναῖον, ἐλευθέρων σῶμα πρίασθαι ὅτι δουλεία ἐκ τῶν ἁλισκομένων, ἀλλὰ τῆς τῶ πολεμίου διαπονω γνώμης.
units.tr: "Let it be permitted to no one of the Athenians, nor to any of those dwelling in Athens, to buy the body of a free person into slavery from those captured, but [only] from the enemy's ... opinion."

units.la: Athenienfium ciuium aut inquilinorum nullus captiuum, qui liber fuerit, in feruitutem vendito, absque priores domini confensu.
units.tr: Let no citizen of Athens or resident alien sell into slavery a captive who was free, without the consent of his former master.

units.la: Tulit hanc Legem Orator Lycurgus, referente Plutarcho in eius Vita: εἰσῆγε δὲ νόμον, μηδενὶ ἐξεῖναι Ἀθηναίων, μηδὲ τῶν οἰκούντων Ἀθηναῖον, ἐλευθέρων σῶμα πρίασθαι ὅτι δουλεία ἐκ τῶν ἁλισκομένων, ἀλλὰ τῆς τῶ πολεμίου διαπονω γνώμης. Intelligit ἀχμαλώτους, qui bello capti seruitutem seruiebant, cum prius in patria liberi fuissent: hanc Seruitutem νόμων vocat Aristoteles Libro I. Politic. cap. VI. ἔστι γὰρ ὡς τῶν νόμων δούλος καὶ δουλιῶν ... ὁμολογία τῆς ἔστιν ... ἐν ᾧ πρὸς πόλεμον ... Φασι. Atque hic seruitutis modus omnium antiquissimus. Dio Orat. XV. τοὺς γὰρ ... ἀρχῆς ... δούλους, ... ἀλλὰ ... ληστείας ... πολέμων ... δουλαγωγῶν ... τοῖς λεγομένοις. & ex illo alij omnes fluxerunt, quanquam non desunt, qui hunc improbent, Aristotele teste: τῶν δὲ ... νόμοις, ... δούλων ... χρείτονος ... Βιαίου. & vere Helena apud Theodecten:
units.tr: The orator Lycurgus proposed this law, as Plutarch reports in his Life: he introduced a law that no one of the Athenians, nor any of those dwelling in Athens, should be permitted to buy the body of a free person into slavery from those captured, but [only] from the enemy's ... opinion. He means the captives [ἀχμαλώτους], who, having been taken in war, served as slaves, though before they had been free in their own country. Aristotle calls this servitude of laws in Book I of the Politics, ch. VI: "For there is a sort of slave of the laws ... an agreement ... in which for war ... they say." And this mode of servitude is the most ancient of all. Dio, Oration XV: "For those ... of rule ... slaves ... but ... piracy ... wars ... enslaving ... to those called ..." And from it all the others flowed, although there are not lacking those who disapprove of it, as Aristotle testifies: "of the ... laws, ... of slaves ... better ... violent." And truly Helen in Theodectes:

units.la: Quod si quis in seruitutem abduceretur, aut peteretur, poterat quilibet illum liberali asserere causa manu, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: If anyone were being led off into slavery, or claimed as a slave, anyone could defend him as free by this law:

units.la: Ἐξέναι τῶν βουλομένων ἀφαιρεῖσθαι ἐς ἐλευθερίαν, καὶ καταλύσαντα τὸν ἀγόμενον εἰς δουλείαν, ἐς τῶν πολεμίων.
units.tr: "It is permitted to those who wish to take away and assert into liberty, and to the one who is being led into slavery, to free him..., to the enemies..."

units.la: Cuiuis ius esto alium liberali asserere causa manu, seque pro illa fidejussorem dare apud Polemarchum.
units.tr: Anyone may have the right to claim another as free by hand, and give surety for him before the Polemarch.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Aeschines ἐν τῷ Τιμάρχῳ, ... ἡ ἐλευθερία ... δουλείαν ... Δημοσθένης ... ἐξαρτᾶσθαι ... Ἀθηναίων ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... Qui liberali asserebant causa manu, ad Polemarchum ibant, & iudicio sistere promittebant, ac fidejussores dabant, atque interim vindiciae secundum libertatem dabantur. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ Νεαίρᾳ ... πολλοὺς ... Φρυνίων ... ἐλευθεροῦσθαι ... οἰκίας ... Σπεφαίν ... ἀφαιρεῖ ... κατηγόρησεν αὐτῷ ... ὡς δὲ Γολεμάχω. Lysias ἐν τῷ Παλλήνου. ἡμέρας ... [?] ... Ζ μὴ ταῦτα πολλαῖς ὕστερον, ἰδὼν ἀπόδυμον τοῦτον Παλχλέωνα [?] Νικομήδους, ὡς ἐμ[?]τυ[?] [illegible, ~60 letters] τοὺς Ἀθηναίους, [illegible, ~50 letters] ἀλλ' [?] τὸν [illegible, ~40 letters] τῆς [?]ἐλευθερίας [illegible, ~30 letters] τοῦτο [?] ἀποδοῦναι.
units.tr: Aeschines mentions this law in his speech against Timarchus: "freedom ... slavery ... Demosthenes ... to hang ... of the Athenians ... [illegible]." Those who claimed someone as free by hand went to the Polemarch, promised to bring him before a court, and gave sureties; meanwhile the provisional possession was given in favour of freedom. Demosthenes, in the speech against Neaera: "many ... Phrynion ... to be freed ... houses ... Sphettian ... takes away ... accused him ... as to Golemachus." Lysias, in the speech for Pallenus: "days ... after these things many times later, seeing this man Palchleon [...] son of Nicomedes, as ... [illegible] the Athenians, [illegible] ... but ... [illegible] ... of freedom [illegible] ... to give back this."

units.la: Ad Polemarchum igitur rapiebantur in ius, & illius erat vindicias secundum libertatem dare, fidejussoribus promittentibus futurum, vt is, cui statvs controuersia mouebatur, iudicio sisteretur, deinde iudices sortiebatur εἰσάγων τὸν δίκην εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον. Hinc illa Dionis Chrysostomi Orat.XV. Ἀλλὰ ὑ πολλοὶ αὐτὴν ἐλευθέρους εἶναι, ἢ ἀδίκως δουλεύοντας, ὧν ἔνιοι ἤδη καὶ εἰς δικαστήριον ἐλθόντες, ἀπὸ δὲ ξ ἐλευθέρους ὄντας ἑαυτούς.
units.tr: So they were dragged before the polemarch, and it was his task to grant the claim to liberty (vindicias secundum libertatem), with sureties promising that the person whose status was disputed would be produced at trial. He then assigned the judges by lot, "bringing the case into the court." Hence that passage of Dio Chrysostom, Oration 15: "But many [are] free, or unjustly enslaved, some of whom have already come into court, and [have declared] themselves free." [Ἀλλὰ ὑ πολλοὶ αὐτὴν ἐλευθέρους εἶναι, ἢ ἀδίκως δουλεύοντας, ὧν ἔνιοι ἤδη καὶ εἰς δικαστήριον ἐλθόντες, ἀπὸ δὲ ξ ἐλευθέρους ὄντας ἑαυτούς.]

units.la: Quod si quis per iniuriam seruum liberali causa manu assereret, pendebat aerario semissem aestimationis:
units.tr: If anyone through injustice asserted another's slave by hand in a cause of liberty, he paid half the valuation into the treasury.

units.la: Ἐὰν μή τις δῷ δικαίως εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφιέσθαι ἢ τινα, ὃ ἡμῖν τῆς ὑμῶν μήτε τοὺς δημοσίῳ.
units.tr: "If anyone does not justly [claim] to be released into liberty, or [claims] someone who belongs to us or to the public..." [Ἐὰν μή τις δῷ δικαίως εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφιέσθαι ἢ τινα, ὃ ἡμῖν τῆς ὑμῶν μήτε τοὺς δημοσίῳ.]

units.la: Si quis per iniuriam alterius seruum liberali causa manu asseruerit, aerario semissem aestimationis pendito.
units.tr: "If anyone through injustice asserts another's slave by hand in a cause of liberty, let him pay half the valuation into the treasury."

units.la: Legem laudat Auctor Argumenti Orationis Demosthenicae in Theocrinem: νόμος δὲ ὡ, Ἐὰν μή τις δῷ δικαίως εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφιέσθαι ἢ τινα, ὃ ἡμῖν τῆς ὑμῶν μήτε τοὺς δημοσίῳ. Demosthenes hac ipsa Oratione: καὶ μοι λέγε τὸν νόμον, ὃς καλεῖ ὃ ἡμῖν τῆς ὑμῶν τοὺς δημοσίῳ, ὃς ἂν δόξῃ μὴ δικαίως εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφιέσθαι. Pendebat itaque aerario publico semissem aestimationis, non litis, sed pretij, puto, serui illius, quem liberali causa manu asserebat: aduersus quem actio haec dicebatur ἐξαιρέσεως δίκη. Grammatici: ἐξαιρέσεως δίκη, ὁπότε τις ἀρχὴ τινὰ ὡς δοῦλον, ἐπειτα ὡς αὐτὸν ὡς ἐλευθέρῳ ἀξιώσει, ἐξ ὧν ἀντιπαραλαβὼν ἀπὸ δεσπότου ὡς δοῦλον λαμβάνει ἐξαιρέσεως δίκῃ, ὧν εἰς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν αὐτὸν ἐξαιρευμένῳ. Ἰσαῖος δὲ τῇ Ἐμμαδοῖς εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι.
units.tr: The author of the argument to Demosthenes' speech against Theocrines quotes the law: "The law says: 'If anyone does not justly [claim] to be released into liberty...'" Demosthenes, in the same speech, says: "Read me the law which calls [something] ours and yours, or the public's, whoever shall seem not justly to be released into liberty." So he paid half the valuation into the public treasury, not of the lawsuit but, I think, of the price of that slave whom he asserted to be free. The action against him was called an exaíresis dike (an action of removal). The grammarians say: "An exaíresis dike is when someone first claims a man as a slave and then claims him as free..." [ἐξαιρέσεως δίκη, ὁπότε τις ἀρχὴ τινὰ ὡς δοῦλον, ἐπειτα ὡς αὐτὸν ὡς ἐλευθέρῳ ἀξιώσει...] Isaeus [uses the phrase] "to remove into liberty" in the speech on the Emmadae.

units.la: Lege concedebatur Seruis actio aduersus iniquos dominos, qua poterant eos adigere vt se venderent:
units.tr: By law slaves were granted an action against unjust masters, by which they could compel them to sell them.

units.la: Τοῖς δούλοις ἐξῆν παρέχειν αἰτιᾶσθαι, καὶ δικαστὰς τῶν μεταβαλλόντων ὑπάρχειν.
units.tr: "Slaves were allowed to bring an accusation, and there were judges for those who change hands." [Τοῖς δούλοις ἐξῆν παρέχειν αἰτιᾶσθαι, καὶ δικαστὰς τῶν μεταβαλλόντων ὑπάρχειν.]

units.la: Seruis ius esto dominos iniquos adigere vt se vendant humanioribus.
units.tr: "Let slaves have the right to compel unjust masters to sell them to more humane ones."

units.la: Legitur haec Lex apud Plutarchum περὶ διαδαμονίας, ἐπὶ ἡ δούλοις νόμος ἐλευθερίας ἀπογράφει παρέχειν αἰτιᾶσθαι, καὶ δικαστὰς μεταβάλλειν ὑπάρχειν. Legem Atticam fuisse quamquam non dicat Plutarchus, probant ea, quae apud Pollucem Libro VII. cap.II. supersunt, veterum Comicorum loca: ὁ ἰοὶ νῦν Φασὶ πὰς οἰκέτας παρέχειν αἰτεῖν, ἐστὶν ὅπου ἐν τοῖς Αεισοφάνους Ὧρας.
units.tr: This law is read in Plutarch, On Superstition: "Where the law written for slaves of freedom allows them to bring accusation, and there are judges for those who change masters." [περὶ διαδαμονίας, ἐπὶ ἡ δούλοις νόμος ἐλευθερίας ἀπογράφει παρέχειν αἰτιᾶσθαι, καὶ δικαστὰς μεταβάλλειν ὑπάρχειν.] That this was an Attic law, although Plutarch does not say so, is shown by the passages of the old comic poets preserved in Pollux, Book VII, chapter 2: "Now they say that slaves may bring a charge..., as somewhere in Aristophanes' Hours." [ὁ ἰοὶ νῦν Φασὶ πὰς οἰκέτας παρέχειν αἰτεῖν, ἐστὶν ὅπου ἐν τοῖς Αεισοφάνους Ὧρας.]

units.la: εἰ μὴ χεφίτισι ὅστι εἰς ὃ Θησεῖον δραμεῖν, ἐκ δ᾽, ἐως ἀὐ ἄνθρωπος παρέχειν, μάλιστ᾽. αὐτίκα δὲ ὁ ταῖς Εὐπόλιδος Πόλεσι, Κακὰ ζιαδὲ πάσχουσι, οὐδὲ παρέχειν αἰτεῖν.
units.tr: "...unless there is somewhere to run to the Theseum, ... a man to ... especially. And presently in Eupolis' Cities, they suffer evil things, they do not even ask to be given..." [εἰ μὴ χεφίτισι ὅστι εἰς ὃ Θησεῖον δραμεῖν, ἐκ δ᾽, ἐως ἀὐ ἄνθρωπος παρέχειν, μάλιστ᾽. αὐτίκα δὲ ὁ ταῖς Εὐπόλιδος Πόλεσι, Κακὰ ζιαδὲ πάσχουσι, οὐδὲ παρέχειν αἰτεῖν.]

units.la: Aristophanis versus, meo iudicio, ita sunt distinguendi:
units.tr: In my judgment the verses of Aristophanes should be punctuated as follows:

units.la: Εἰ μὴ χεφίτισι ὅστι εἰς ὃ Θησεῖον δραμεῖν, ἐκ δ᾽, ἐως ἀὐ ἄνθρωπος παρέχειν, μάλιστ᾽.
units.tr: "If there is no ... somewhere to run to the Theseum, ... a man to ... especially." [Εἰ μὴ χεφίτισι ὅστι εἰς ὃ Θησεῖον δραμεῖν, ἐκ δ᾽, ἐως ἀὐ ἄνθρωπος παρέχειν, μάλιστ᾽.]

units.la: Confugiunt Serui ad Thefei sacellum, quia habebat ius asyli, & ius ibi di-cebatur Seruis Γραμματικοί: Θησεῖον, τέμενος πρὸς Θησέα, ὃ τῆς οἰκέτης ἄσυλον ἔστω [?]. Grammatici: Θησεῖον, τὸ [?] τοῦ Θησέως, ὁ τῆς οἰκέτης [?] ἄσυλον [?] ἐλευθερία [?].
units.tr: Slaves took refuge at the shrine of Theseus, because it had the right of asylum, and the right of asylum was declared there for slaves. The grammarians: "Theseion, a precinct of Theseus, where for slaves there is asylum..." [Θησεῖον, τέμενος πρὸς Θησέα, ὃ τῆς οἰκέτης ἄσυλον ἔστω.] The grammarians: "Theseion, the sanctuary of Theseus, where slaves have asylum..." [obscura]

units.la: Quinetiam libertatem consequebantur, vel inuitis dominis, pecunia nu-merata:
units.tr: Indeed they even obtained their liberty against their masters' will, by paying out money.

units.la: Τοῖς δούλοις ἐξῆν ἑαυτοὺς ἐλευθεροῦσθαι, ἀργύριον καταβάλλοντας τῷ δεσπότῃ [?]. Seruis ius esto libertatem consequi numerata domino pecunia proca-pite.
units.tr: "Slaves were allowed to free themselves by paying money to their master." [Τοῖς δούλοις ἐξῆν ἑαυτοὺς ἐλευθεροῦσθαι, ἀργύριον καταβάλλοντας τῷ δεσπότῃ.] Let slaves have the right to obtain liberty by paying their master money counted out per head.

units.la: Legem hanc colligere licet è Dionis Chrysostomi verbis Orat. XV. ἐμφανῶς οὐκ ἂν οἴσει δοκῶ ἐλευθεροῦσθαι [?], εἰς ἀργύριόν ποθεν καταβάλλειν τῷ δεσπότῃ [?]. & in palliata Diphili Comoedia κληρονόμοις, siue Plauti Casina,
units.tr: This law may be gathered from the words of Dio Chrysostom, Oration 15: "clearly would not ... to pay money from somewhere to the master," and from Diphilus' comedy in the palliata style, The Heirs, or Plautus' Casina:

units.la: Quid tu me vero libertate territas? Quid si tu nolis, filiusque etiam tuus, Vobis inuitis, atque amborum ingratiis, Vna libella liber possum fieri.
units.tr: "Why do you frighten me with freedom? What if you do not wish it, and your son too, against your will and both of you unwilling, I may become free for a single little coin."

units.la: Serui quippe apud Athenienses suum, quod sibi comparabant, habebant peculium, ex quo aliquid dominis suis pendebant quotannis, atque etiam, pro capite numerabant suo, vt seruitutem exuerent. Xenophon loco laudato, vt colligamus facit: ὅπου γὰρ ναυλαχῇ διωκούς [?] ὅστις ἐπὶ ξέρμάς [?], ἀρχαῖοι τοῖς αἰ-δραπόδοις δουλάλιφ [?], ἵνα ποιῶσιν μὴ παρῆν τοῖς ἐπιφορὰς [?], καὶ ἐλευθέριος ἐξ ἀγῶνος [?].
units.tr: Among the Athenians, slaves had their own savings, which they acquired for themselves, and from which they paid something to their masters every year; and they even counted out a sum per head to cast off servitude. Xenophon, in the passage cited, as we may gather, says: "For where ... slaves ... were ... and free from the contest..." [ὅπου γὰρ ναυλαχῇ διωκούς...]

units.la: Quod vero ex his Suidae verbis: ὑπομονὴν ἔχειν, ὅταν δούλος ᾖ ἐλευθερίας [?] εἰσὶ-ται, φάσκων μὴ ποιήσιν τοῖς δούλοις αὐτὸν ἀμπρακικῶν [?], colligit vir summus, Seruos aliquando egisse aduersus dominos de libertate consequenda, se seruos alios competitores nihil morari dicentes, nobis non potest probari, & plane alio referenda sunt, vt infra, Deo dante, videbimus: neque enim haec actio ex Lege de libertate consequenda, vnquam dicta est Ἀπογραφή, sed Libertorum est. Quanta autem fuerit pecunia, quae à seruo, vt manumitteretur, numerabatur, pro certo dicere non possumus. Apud Plautum vna libella est:
units.tr: As for the claim that from Suidas' words, "to have patience when a slave is seeking liberty," the great scholar gathers that slaves at some time brought actions against their masters to obtain liberty, saying that other slaves as competitors did not hinder them, we cannot accept; these words must be referred elsewhere, as we shall see below, God willing. For this action from the law on obtaining liberty was never called an apographē, but belongs to freedmen. What the sum was that a slave paid in order to be manumitted we cannot say for certain. In Plautus it is a single little coin.

units.la: Vobis inuitis, atque amborum ingratiis, Vna libella liber possum fieri.
units.tr: "Against your will and both of your ill will, I may become free for one little coin."

units.la: Factum quoque est aliquoties, vt afflictis Reipublicae temporibus, qui egregiam in bello nauauerant operam Serui, libertate donarentur à Republica: De iis, qui anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimae tertiae, Archonte Callia, ἀρχηγὸς Ἀρχῆς [?], ad Arginusam Lacedaemonios fuderunt, Aristophanes Ranis, atque eos non tantum libertate, sed & ciuitate donatos conqueritur: καὶ τὸ αἰχμάλωτα [?] ἐκ Ἀρχειῶν [?] ἐλευθέρους [?], τὴν Πλαταιῶν [?] ἀξίας [?] τῆς δούλων [?] ἐλευθερίας [?].
units.tr: It also happened several times that in the troubled times of the state, slaves who had performed outstanding service in war were granted liberty by the state. Concerning those who, in the third year of the ninety-third Olympiad, in the archonship of Callias, defeated the Lacedaemonians at Arginusae, Aristophanes in Frogs complains that they were given not only liberty but citizenship: [καὶ τὸ αἰχμάλωτα ἐκ Ἀρχειῶν ἐλευθέρους, τὴν Πλαταιῶν ἀξίας τῆς δούλων ἐλευθερίας.]

units.la: De illis qui militauerant Chaeronea aduersus Philippum Macedonem Dio Chrysostomus Orat. XV. ὅτι Ἀλέξανδρος Ἀφιστοκλέους [?] ἐπὶ τῇ Χαιρωνείᾳ μαχόμενοι [?] ἔλαβον τοὺς συμπαλεμένους [?] οἱ ἐλευθέρας [?].
units.tr: Concerning those who had fought at Chaeronea against Philip of Macedon, Dio Chrysostom, Oration 15: "That Alexander... at Chaeronea fighting... they took those who fought with them... free." [ὅτι Ἀλέξανδρος Ἀφιστοκλέους ἐπὶ τῇ Χαιρωνείᾳ μαχόμενοι ἔλαβον τοὺς συμπαλεμένους οἱ ἐλευθέρας.]

units.la: Seruos, qui manumittebantur, non licebat liberos renunciare in Theatro, id enim hac Lege vetitum: Μὴ εἰκάτω ἀπελευθερῶσθαι ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ, ἐὰν ἀπ-μὴ ἔτι [?] ἡ κήρυκα [?]. Legem laudat Æschines [illegible, ~70 letters]. Renunciabantur Serui liberi per præconem, vt hic habes: Sed in Theatro non debebat fieri hæc renunciatio: ambitiosum enim erat: volebant quippe omnes Græcos, qui Ludis intererant, testes esse. Æschines: [illegible, ~60 letters]. Manumissi seruile suum nomen aliquando mutabant, aliquando syllabis augebant, vt Stephanus ille, qui Philostephanus appellari voluit, in quem est Epigramma Libro II. Anthologias,
units.tr: Slaves who were manumitted were not allowed to be proclaimed free in the theatre, for this was forbidden by the law: "Let him not be proclaimed free in the theatre, if ... the herald..." [Μὴ εἰκάτω ἀπελευθερῶσθαι ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ, ἐὰν ἀπ-μὴ ἔτι ἡ κήρυκα.] The law is cited by Aeschines [remainder illegible]. Slaves were proclaimed free through a herald, as you have here; but this proclamation was not to be made in the theatre, for it was ostentatious: they wanted all the Greeks who attended the games to be witnesses. Aeschines: [remainder illegible]. Manumitted slaves sometimes changed their servile name, and sometimes lengthened it with syllables, like that Stephanus who wished to be called Philostephanus, on whom there is an epigram in Book II of the Anthology,

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: [illegible in the original]

units.la: [illegible, ~35 letters]
units.tr: [illegible in the original]

units.la: Tonsuræ quoque genus mutabant. Grammatici: [illegible, ~75 letters]. Cùm autem eodem cum [illegible, ~12 letters] iure censerentur Liberti, quotannis [illegible, ~8 letters], id est, duodecim drachmas ærario pendebant, & prætereà triobolum siue scribæ, siue publicano. Harpocration [illegible, ~70 letters]. [illegible, ~45 letters]. Atque de his intelligendus Pollux Libro III. cap. IV. [illegible, ~60 letters]. itemque Hesychius: [illegible, ~80 letters]. Hoc tributum pendebant Liberti, ceteraque alia omnia, publica, priuata, administrabant per Patronum, non quem elegissent ipsi, quemadmodum oi [illegible, ~6 letters], sed qui libertate donasset dominus, quem colere, eique Lege constituta præstare tenebantur hac Le-ge:
units.tr: They also changed the manner of their haircut. The grammarians: [illegible]. Since with the same ... they were rated as freedmen, each year ... that is, they paid twelve drachmas into the treasury, and besides three obols either to the scribe or to the tax-farmer. Harpocration: [illegible]. Pollux, Book III, chapter IV, is to be understood of these; likewise Hesychius: [illegible]. Freedmen paid this tax, and managed all other affairs, public and private, through a patron, not one they had chosen themselves, but him who had granted them liberty as master, whom they were bound to honour, and to render him services laid down by law, under this law:

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: [illegible in the original]

units.la: Liberti eos, à quibus manumissi sunt, coluntō[?]: neminem alium patronum adoptanto: eaque quæ Legibus imperantur, ijs præstan-to.
units.tr: "Let freedmen honour those by whom they were manumitted; let them adopt no other patron; and let them render those things which the laws enjoin."

units.la: Legem hanc colligere est ex iis quæ referunt Grammatici de actione [illegible, ~12 letters], & nos eorum verba reddemus infra, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Patronum colebant Liberti, eique quasdam operas præstare tenebantur, vt in hac Lege habes, & è verbis Suidæ plenius in sequentibus dicemus: Hinc Chrysippo Libro [illegible, ~12 letters] II. [illegible, ~25 letters], sed non [illegible, ~6 letters] erant, id est, non [illegible, ~20 letters], vt loquitur idem Chrysippus, in bonis possidentis non censebantur: Nullum præterea alium eligere poterant [illegible, ~10 letters] Patronum, quàm eum à quo libertate fuerant donati. Non ignoro Incomparabilem Casaubonum in Animaduersionibus ad Suetonium scribere, potuisse quoque, cum manumitterentur, optare sibi & publice adscifcere patronum alium, quàm eum qui manumitteret, in cuius clientela essent, idque voce præconis: in hanc sententiam eū induxit Aristotelis locus Rhe-toric. Lib. III. cap. VIII. [illegible, ~45 letters] ΚΛΕΩΝΑ. Sed idem non est, meo iudicio, Πατρῶνος[?] sive Patronus, & Ἐπίτροπος, Patronus non eligebatur à Liberto, sed is erat, qui manumiserat: At vero Ἐπίτροπος publicè ab eo, qui manumitteretur, adoptabatur: nempe Ἐπίτροπος cum tutabatur sua auctoritate, & omnia eius minima, maxima, privata, publica, administrabat: Ἐπίτροπος vero aduersus Patronum ipsum, si opus foret, tuebatur: quemadmodum & apud Romanos Liberti, quanquam in Patroni, qui manumiserat, esset clientela, habebant tamen & alium, ex amicis forte Patroni, cuius se esse clientes dicerent, qui apud patronum trahi entem & in iusrapientem, si res ita ferret, deprecaretur & tueretur clientem hunc suum: ita intelligenda puto M. Tullij verba Epist.
units.tr: To gather this law we need only what the grammarians report about the action [illegible], and we shall give their words below [illegible]. Freedmen honoured their patron, and were bound to render him certain services, as you have in this law, and we shall say more fully below from the words of Suidas. Hence Chrysippus, in Book [illegible] II, [illegible], but were not [illegible], that is, were not [illegible], as the same Chrysippus says, were not counted among the goods of the possessor. Moreover, they could choose no other patron besides the one by whom they had been granted liberty. I am not unaware that the incomparable Casaubon, in his Animadversions on Suetonius, writes that when they were manumitted they could also wish for, and publicly adopt by the herald's voice, another patron besides the one who manumitted them, in whose clientele they were; he was led to this opinion by the passage of Aristotle, Rhetoric Book III, chapter VIII, [illegible] Cleon. But in my judgment the patronus and the epitropos are not the same. A patron was not chosen by the freedman; he was the one who had manumitted him. But an epitropos was publicly adopted by the one who was manumitted: the epitropos watched over him with his authority and administered all his affairs, great and small, private and public; and the epitropos defended him even against the patron himself, if need be. Just so among the Romans, freedmen, although the clientela was with the patron who had manumitted them, still had another, perhaps one of the patron's friends, whose clients they said they were, who when the patron dragged his client away and into court, if the matter so required, would entreat and protect this client of his. So I think the words of M. Tullius in Epistle [illegible] should be understood.

units.la: XII. Libri I ad Atticum.
units.tr: XII. Book I of the Letters to Atticus.

units.la: Libertum ego habeo, sane nequam hominem, Hilarum dico, ratiocinatorem & clientem tuum.
units.tr: I have a freedman, a thoroughly good-for-nothing fellow, Hilarus I mean, my bookkeeper and your client.

units.la: ε. Si in hanc Legem commisissent Liberti, iis Ἀπροσαίου dica scribebatur ex hac Lege: [illegible, ~40 letters] | [illegible, ~40 letters] patronis ... aduersus Libertos, qui patronos non coluerint, aut alios adoptauerint, eaque quae Legibus imperantur, non praestiterint, connubii Liberti infer[?] iuniorem renuntiantur, si secundum Libertos pronunciatum fuerit, prefecto liberi iunto.
units.tr: ε. If the freedmen had committed a violation of this Law, an action called Aproseiou was brought against them under it: [illegible] ... against freedmen who did not honour their patrons, or who had adopted others, and did not perform what the Laws prescribe, the freedmen were declared (ineligible) for marriage, if judgment was given for the freedmen, ... the free-born ...

units.la: Λέγος ... [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: Legos ... [illegible]

units.la: Laudant hanc Legem Grammatici: Ἀπροσαίου, [illegible, ~60 letters]. Compecebat hanc dicam Ἀπροσαίου Patronis aduersus Libertos. Ingratos, vt hinc constat, quibus adeant Ἐπίτροποι illi, quos publicè sibi adoptauerant, cum manumitterentur. An Libertorum exceptio, qua leaduersus hanc actionem tuebantur, Ἀπροσαίου quoque dicebatur, quaeritur vir Amplissimus & eruditissimus: atque ita dici suspicatur e Dinarchi Oratione pro Aeschylo Xenophontis Liberto, cuius epigraphe est apud Diogenem Laertium in Xenophonte, & Dionysium Halicarnasseum in Dinarcho, [illegible, ~40 letters] locus Suidae in haec verba: [illegible, ~80 letters]. Quo sensu vir idem summus explicet illa Suidae verba in superioribus dixi-mus: sed nullus dubito Suidam docere, Ἀπροσαίου dicam esse etiam actionem, qua Libertus, qui aliquo modo δούλος ... vt in plenam & omnibus numeris absolutam afferatur libertatem, dicens se non posse applicare ad seruos aliquid siue operae praestantes, siue pecuniae pendentes [illegible, ~50 letters], ita in tres distinximus voces, quae vnicâ legebatur apud Suidam. Serui suas praestabant operas dominis, & aliquid de suo peculio pendebant. Liberti quoque Lege cogebantur patronis ... Ἀπροσαίου ... Atqui Libertus, qui Ἀπροσαίου dicam patrono scribit, nil vult siue praestare, siue pendere, cum id seruorum sit, qua etiam de causa quasi seruicentur Liberti, sed potius plena perfectaque sui libertate. Dica haec Ἀπροσαίου scribebatur apud Polemarchum: Aristoteles de Atheniensium Republica: [illegible, ~30 letters] (ἀγῶν δημόσιος) [illegible, ~25 letters] Ἀ[illegible, ~10 letters] ἀπὸ [illegible, ~20 letters] Ἀ[illegible, ~12 letters], [illegible, ~15 letters] Ἑπιλύτως [illegible, ~20 letters] Μετοίκοις, ὁ [illegible, ~25 letters] Ἀρχων, [illegible, ~10 letters] τῶν Μετοίκων ὁ Παλαίστρα. Iudicabantur autem Seruorum actiones in Dominos, Patronorum in Libertos, à patrono, aut à filiis Patronorum, siue Domini. Harpocration: [illegible, ~20 letters] Suidas: [illegible, ~25 letters] Si hac Ἀπολογίαι actio-nevinterentur Liberti à Patrono, in lerutatem retrahebantur. Harpocra-tion, &c ex eo Suidas: [illegible, ~20 letters]. Atque in [illegible, ~30 letters] coniugebantur. Ifæus [illegible, ~20 letters] Ἐπιγραφή [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters]. Suidas: [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters]. De mofthenes [illegible, ~30 letters] Ἀπολογία [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters].
units.tr: The grammarians praise this Law: Aproseiou, [illegible]. This action, the Aproseiou, was brought by patrons against freedmen, against the ungrateful, as is clear from this: those Epitropoi whom they had publicly adopted for themselves when they were manumitted. Whether the exception of the freedmen, by which they defended themselves against this action, was also called Aproseiou, is asked by that most distinguished and learned man; and he suspects it was so called from the Oration of Dinarchus for Aeschylus, the freedman of Xenophon, whose title is given by Diogenes Laertius in his life of Xenophon, and by Dionysius of Halicarnassus in his life of Dinarchus, [illegible] the passage of Suidas in these words: [illegible]. In what sense that same great man explains those words of Suidas I have said above; but I have no doubt that Suidas teaches that the Aproseiou is also an action by which a freedman, who in some way is a slave ... so that he is brought to full and complete liberty in every respect, saying that he cannot be bound to slaves either to render services or to pay money [illegible]. I have thus distinguished into three words what was read in Suidas as a single word. Slaves rendered their services to their masters and paid something from their own peculium. Freedmen too were compelled by the Law to patrons ... Aproseiou ... But a freedman who writes an Aproseiou against his patron wants neither to render services nor to pay, since that belongs to slaves; for which reason freedmen were, as it were, enslaved, but rather he wants complete and perfect liberty. This action, the Aproseiou, was written at Polemarchus: Aristotle, on the Athenian republic: [illegible] (public contest) [illegible] ... for the Metics, the Archon [illegible] ... of the Metics, the Palaistra. Actions of slaves against masters, and of patrons against freedmen, were tried before the patron, or the sons of the patrons, or the masters. Harpocration: [illegible]. Suidas: [illegible]. If freedmen lost this action of the Aproseiou brought by the patron, they were dragged back into servitude. Harpocration, &c., and from him Suidas: [illegible]. And in [illegible] they were joined in marriage. Isaeus [illegible] inscription [illegible]. Suidas: [illegible]. Demosthenes [illegible] defence [illegible].

units.la: Si vicissent Liberti, perpetua & perfecta libertate fruebantur. Harpocration: [illegible, ~20 letters]. Suidas: [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~15 letters]. Atque hæc ita fe habere docuerant Oratorum veterum multi, Lysias, Aeschines, & Hyperides [illegible, ~15 letters], aut etiam vendebantur. Demosthenes [illegible, ~20 letters].
units.tr: If the freedmen won, they enjoyed perpetual and perfect liberty. Harpocration: [illegible]. Suidas: [illegible]. That these things stood thus, many of the ancient orators taught: Lysias, Aeschines and Hyperides [illegible], or they were even sold. Demosthenes [illegible].

units.la: Huius Legis meminit Valerius Maximus Lib. II. cap. I. Age quid illud institutum Athe-narum, quam memorabile? quod conuictus à patrono libertus ingratus, iure libertatis exuitur. Supersedeo te, inquit, habere eiusdem tanti muneris impium æstimatorem. Nec adducipossum, vt credam vti vitam, quem domi scelefum cerno: abi igitur, & esto ferus, quoniam liber esse nescisti. Sed obiter castigandus est Valerij error, cum patet seruos ab Atheniensibus ciuitate simul cum libertate donatos fuisse: quod verum non est: nempe in animo habebat ille iustam illam libertatem apud suos Romanos vindicta datam.
units.tr: Valerius Maximus mentions this Law in Book II, chapter 1: Come now, what institution of the Athenians is so memorable? A freedman who has been convicted of ingratitude by his patron is stripped of the right of freedom. "I shall spare you," he says, "from having as the impious assessor of so great a favour." Nor can I bring myself to believe that he lives a life of virtue whom I see to be wicked at home: go, then, and be wild, since you did not know how to be free. But Valerius's error must be corrected in passing, since it is clear that slaves were granted citizenship together with liberty by the Athenians, which is not true: he evidently had in mind that just liberty which was granted among his own Romans by the rod.

units.la: Apud Romanos longe aliud viurpatum fuit aduersus ingratos Libertos: quanquam subinde mutauit: Nam primo, quod sciam, Patronus concessum Libertum vltra vicesimum lapidem relegare. Quod ab Augusto institutum fuisse suspicatur CL. Lipsius. Augustus enim, vt Dio ait Lib. LV. constituit [illegible, ~30 letters]. Docet id Tacitus Annali XIII. vbi scribit actum in Senatu fuisse de fraudibus Libertorum, esslagitatumque vt aduersus male meritos reuocandae libertatis ius patronis daretur: quibusdam, inquit, coalitam libertate irreuerentiam eo prorupisse frementibus, vt an æquo cum patronis iure agerent, sententiam eorum consulerent, an verberibus in manus viro intenderent, impellerentur pa-tronos [?] iuam [?] dissuadentes. Quid enim aliud lasso patrono concessum, quam vt vicesimum vltra lapidem, in oram Campaniæ libertum relegeat? Ceteras actiones promiscuas & pares esse. Tribuendum aliquod telum quod spernì nequeat. Occisum esse hunc lo-cum sentit CL. Lipsius: nec nisi vespillones, non enim medicos, ad hoc funus coire, itaque etiam suspiciones suas ludibria appellat. Sed nondum plane de-positus est hic locus, quem nullo negotio, sine vlla mutatione, interpretari facile est. Referuntur à Cornelio ea, quæ prio sententia dicta sunt in Senatu abiis, qui aduersus male meritos Libertos reuocandæ libertatis ius patronis da-ri volebant: atque ab his verbis incipiunt, Vt an æquo, &c. quæ habentur ad eos, qui contra hanc sententiam differebant: Volunt igitur, vt sententiam Libertorum ipsorum consultent, vi, an æquo cum patronis iure agant: an cum ipsi Liberti manus vltro intentent patronis suis, patronos quoque vt & sibi verbera intentent non impellant, atque ita re ipsa poenam suam dissuadeant, quæ admodum leuis est: Quis enim aliud, inquiunt, lafo patrono concessum, quam vt vicesimum vltra lapidem, in oram Campaniæ libertum releget? Quid audio, in oram Campaniæ relegatos fuisse male meritos Libertos omnes? Vix est, vt credam, solam hanc oram Campaniæ delectam fuisse Lege siue Principis Constitutione, in quam omnes male meriti Liberti à patronis relegarentur: & parum prudens, vt cetera mittam, atque in tutum consilium, tot perditos homines, quod sane mores eorum arguebant, eodem conuenire: Addequod poena vix poena fuisset, cum Campania tractus fuerit totius tertiæ Italiæ amœnissimus atque feracissimus: Contra potius interdictum puto Libertis, qui vltra vicesimum lapidem relegabantur, hoc tractu & agro: Verum insolens loquendi genus [illegible, ~8 letters] fecit, vt Taciti locus corrumperetur. Rescribo: Quid enim aliud lafo patrono concessum, quam vt vicesimum vltra lapidem, moram Campaniæ, libertum releget? Vult Libertum vltra vicesimum lapidem relegari, nec tamen in Campania morari. Sed quare vltra vicesimum lapidem relegantur? An quia, cum vicena millia passuum, vt loquitur Gaius Lib. I. ad Edictum prouinciale, in singulos dies dinumerari Prætor iubeat, Leg. I. D. Si quis cautionibus: atque itinere faciendo, inquit Vlpianus Lib. II. ad Edictum, viginti millia passuum in dies singulos peragenda sint, Lib. III. D. de verborum significat. vnius saltem dici itinere malemeritum de patrono suo libertum ab eius conspectu abesse voluerunt? Nihil de poena Libertorum ingratorum mutatum hoc Senatusconsulto, valuit enim mitior sententia. Quanquam Claudius paullo ante, Ingratos, & de quibus patroni quererentur, reuocauit in seruitutem, inquit Suetonius in Claudio cap. XXV. quod absolute non est verum, vt ante nos pridem obseruarunt viri summi, auctore Marciano Lib. XIII. Institutionum. Nam in seruitutem tantum retrahebatur, si patrono delatores summiserat, qui ei de statu controuersiam facerent. Diuus (Claudius libertum, qui probatus fuerit patrono delatores summisisse, qui de statu eius facerent ei quæstionem, seruum patroni esse iussit eum libertum. Leg. V. D. de iure patronatus. Commodus Imperator, referente Modestino Lib. singulari de Manumissionibus, constituit postea, vt liberti, qui patronos violauerant contumeliis, aut illata manu pulsauerant, aut non exhibuerant ad pauperratem redactos, cogerentur ad obsequia, ministerium appellat Imperator patronis praestanda, quod si nihil proficeretur in seruitutem alteri à Præside vendebantur, pretio patronis addicto: nam quod putant viri maximi, addictos fuisse emptori in Libertos, non in seruos, nobis non probatur, cum constet nihil profectum, illis administeria patronis præbenda adactis: itaque opus fuit vt in seruitutem retraherentur, vt metu coërceantur, quos beneficia non mutauissent. Imperatoris Commodi constitutio talis profertur. Cum probatum sit, contumeliis patronos à libertis esse violatos, vel illata manu atroci esse pulsatos, aut etiam pauperate, vel corporis valetudine laborantes relictos: primum eos in potestatem patronorum redigi, & ministerium dominis præbere cogi. sin autem nec hoc modo admoneantur: vel à Præside emptori addicentur, & pretium patronis tribuetur. Leg. VI. §. I. D. de agnoscendis liberis.
units.tr: Among the Romans something quite different was practised against ungrateful freedmen, although it changed from time to time. For first, as far as I know, a patron was permitted to relegate a freedman beyond the twentieth milestone. Clarissimus Lipsius suspects this was instituted by Augustus. For Augustus, as Dio says in Book LV, laid down [illegible]. Tacitus teaches this in Annals XIII, where he writes that a motion was made in the Senate concerning the frauds of freedmen, and it was demanded that the right of revoking freedom be given to patrons against those who had ill deserved: "Some, whose disrespect had broken out from their newly acquired liberty, were so enraged that they were driven to the point of asking the opinion of the freedmen themselves, whether they acted on equal legal terms with their patrons; or whether they should lay hands on their patrons, and should not drive the patrons to strike them in turn, thereby advising against their own punishment." For what else was granted to the wearied patron, except that he may relegate the freedman beyond the twentieth milestone, to the coast of Campania? The other actions are common and equal. Some weapon must be given which cannot be scorned. Lipsius thinks this passage has been destroyed, and that only undertakers, not doctors, were gathered to this funeral; and so he even calls his own suspicions mockeries. But this passage has not yet been fully set aside; it can easily be interpreted without any trouble and without any change. Cornelius reports what was said first in the Senate by those who wished the right of revoking freedom to be given to patrons against ill-deserving freedmen; and they begin with the words Vt an æquo, etc., which are addressed to those who argued against this opinion. They want, therefore, that the freedmen themselves be consulted about their own opinion, whether they act on equal legal terms with their patrons; or whether, when the freedmen themselves lay hands on their patrons, they do not also drive the patrons to strike them in return, and so in fact argue against their own punishment, which is very slight. For what else, they say, has been granted to the wearied patron, except that he may relegate the freedman beyond the twentieth milestone, to the coast of Campania? What do I hear? That all ill-deserving freedmen were relegated to the coast of Campania? I can hardly believe that this coast of Campania alone was chosen by law or imperial constitution as the place to which all ill-deserving freedmen were relegated by their patrons. And it would be unwise, to say nothing of the rest, to gather so many worthless men into one place, though their characters clearly argued for it. Add to this that the punishment would hardly be a punishment, since Campania is the most pleasant and fertile district of the whole of Italy's third region. I think rather that freedmen who were relegated beyond the twentieth milestone were forbidden this district and territory. But an unusual manner of speaking has corrupted the passage of Tacitus. I rewrite it: For what else has been granted to the wearied patron, except that he may relegate the freedman beyond the twentieth milestone, away from Campania? He wants the freedman relegated beyond the twentieth milestone, and yet not to remain in Campania. But why are they relegated beyond the twentieth milestone? Is it because, when Gaius in Book I on the Provincial Edict says that the praetor orders twenty thousand paces to be counted off for each day, Dig. I, If anyone by cautions; and since Ulpian in Book II on the Edict says that twenty thousand paces must be covered in a single day's journey, Dig. III, de verborum significatione: did they wish that the freedman who had ill deserved of his patron should be kept away from his sight by one day's journey at least? This Senatus-consultum changed nothing of the punishment of ungrateful freedmen, for the milder opinion prevailed. Yet Claudius shortly before had, as Suetonius says in Claudius chapter 25, reduced to slavery the ungrateful, and those about whom their patrons complained; which is not absolutely true, as many great men observed before us, on the authority of Marcian in Book XIII of the Institutes. For he was dragged back into servitude only if he had set up informers against his patron, who would bring a suit about his status. The deified Claudius ordered that a freedman who was proved to have set up informers against his patron, who would bring a question about his status, should be the slave of the patron. Dig. V, de iure patronatus. The Emperor Commodus, as Modestinus reports in his single book on Manumissions, later laid down that freedmen who had violated their patrons with insults, or had struck them with a blow, or had not supported them when they were reduced to poverty, or were suffering from illness, were to be compelled to render services to their patrons, which the Emperor calls ministry; and if nothing was achieved in this way, they were sold into servitude to another by the Governor, the price being handed over to the patrons. For the opinion of the great men that they were assigned to the buyer as freedmen, not as slaves, is not approved by us, since it is plain that nothing was achieved, when the services were compelled from them to be rendered to their patrons; so it was necessary that they be drawn back into servitude, so that those whom benefits had not changed might be restrained by fear. The constitution of the Emperor Commodus is cited thus: Since it has been proved that patrons were violated by insults from freedmen, or were fiercely struck by a blow, or were even left in poverty or suffering from ill health: first, they are to be brought back into the power of their patrons and compelled to render ministry to their masters; but if they are not admonished even in this way, they shall be assigned to a buyer by the Governor, and the price shall be given to the patrons. Dig. VI, §1, de agnoscendis liberis.

units.la: Mutauit postea ius istud, ut constat ex his Vlpiani verbis, Lib. IX. de Officio Proconsulis, in quibus habes poenas aduersus male meritos de Patronis Libertos sancitas. Sed si quidem inofficiosus patrono, patrona, liberisve eorum sit libertus, tantummodo castigari eum sub comminatione aliqua seueritatis[?] non defuturae, si rursum causam quaerela praebuerit, & demitti oportet. Enim vero si contumeliam fecit, aut conuicium eis dixit, etiam in exilium temporale dari debebit. Quod si manus intulit, in metallum dandus erit. Idem, & si calumniam aliquam eis instruxit, vel delatorem subornauit, dummodo de patroni statu ei quaestionem non faceret, vel quam causam aduersus eos tentauit. Leg. I. D. de iure patronatus. Quid Vlpianus appellet hic castigari discere est è Modestino Lib. singulari de Manumissionibus, Interdum illa poena à liberto ingrato exiguntur, vel pars bonorum eius auferatur, & patrono datur, vel fustibus caeditur, & ita absoluitur. Leg. VII. §. I. D. eod. Nempe castigari est fustibus caedi, quod idem Vlpianus dixit in hoc ipso argumento fustibus castigare. Leg. I. §. Cum Patronus. D. de officio Praefecti Vrbi. Subsecutis temporibus ex Constitutione Imperatorum Diocletiani & Maximiani A A. ad Veneriam, liberti, qui ingrati probantur, ad seruiendi necessitatem redigi possunt. Leg. XII. C. de operis Libertorum. Quod etiam obseruari voluit Constantinus, Lege data ad Maximum Praefectum Vrbi, filijs etiam, qui post restractum in seruitutem patrem nati fuerint, seruituris. Leg. II. C. de Libertis & eorum liberis. Idemque rescripsit aliquot post annis ad Concilium Byzacinorum, Leg. I. Cod. Theod. eod.
units.tr: Vlpian later changed that law, as is clear from these words of Ulpian in Book IX of On the Duty of the Proconsul, in which you find penalties decreed against freedmen who have behaved badly towards their patrons: "But if a freedman is undutiful towards his patron, his patroness, or their children, he is only to be punished with some threat of severity, which will not be lacking if he again gives cause for complaint, and he ought to be dismissed. Indeed, if he has insulted them or spoken abuse at them, he must be given temporary exile. If he has laid hands on them, he is to be given over to the mines. The same applies if he has devised some false charge against them or suborned an informer, provided he did not bring a question about the patron's status or some other cause against them." Law 1, D. de iure patronatus. What Ulpian means here by "punished" can be learned from Modestinus in his single book On Manumissions: "Sometimes that penalty is exacted from an ungrateful freedman, or part of his goods is taken away and given to the patron, or he is beaten with rods and so released." Law 7, §1, D. eod. Clearly, to be punished is to be beaten with rods, which Ulpian also said in this same matter, "to punish with rods." Law 1, §Cum Patronus, D. de officio Praefecti Urbi. In later times, by a constitution of the Augusti Diocletian and Maximian, addressed to Veneria, "freedmen who are proved ungrateful can be reduced to the necessity of serving." Law 12, C. de operis libertorum. Constantine also wished this to be observed, in a law given to Maximus, Prefect of the City, that even sons born after their father had been reduced to slavery were to be slaves. Law 2, C. de libertis et eorum liberis. He rescripted the same thing some years later to the Council of the Byzacenes, Law 1, Cod. Theod. eod.

units.la: In hac aduersus Libertos Ἀποστασίου actione Lege licebat cuiuis διαμαρτυρεῖν[?], siue is esset ciuis, siue peregrinus.
units.tr: In this action against freedmen for ingratitude [Ἀποστασίου], by law anyone was allowed to give evidence [διαμαρτυρεῖν], whether he was a citizen or a foreigner.

units.la: Ἐξεῖναι δὲ τῆς γραφῆς τῆς τῶν Ἀποστασίου διαμαρτυρῆν τῷ βουλομένῳ ὁμοίως τὴν ξέ-νων καὶ τὴν ἐπιχωρίων.
units.tr: It was permitted to anyone who wished to give evidence in the indictment for apostasy [τῆς γραφῆς τῆς τῶν Ἀποστασίου] in the same way, both foreigners and citizens [Ἐξεῖναι δὲ τῆς γραφῆς τῆς τῶν Ἀποστασίου διαμαρτυρῆν τῷ βουλομένῳ ὁμοίως τὴν ξένων καὶ τὴν ἐπιχωρίων].

units.la: Cui libuerit, siue peregrino, siue ciui, testimonij dictio esto in actionibus Apo-stasiou ad exceptionem.
units.tr: Let it be allowed to whoever wishes, whether foreigner or citizen, to give testimony in actions for apostasy, as an exception.

units.la: Licebat igitur cuiuis testimonium dicere, in hac aduersus Libertos actione, antequam iudicium redderetur, ὡς εἰσαγωγίμως ὅστιν ἡ δίκη, ἡ ὡς εἰσαγώγιμος. Hyperides apud Harpocrationem : Ὑπερίδης δὲ ἐν τῷ κατὰ Αεισαγόρου Ἀποστασίου δικαστηρίῳ φησίν, ὡς οἱ ἐμοὶ μὲν κεκωλυμένοι διαμαρτυρῆν ἐπὶ τὰς γραφὰς τῆς τῶν Ἀποστασίου τῶν βουλομένων, ὁμοίως τὴν ξένων, καὶ τὴν ἐπιχωρίων, μήπου[?] δὲ ὧν οὖ μὲν τὰς τῆς Ἀποστασίου δίκης κεκωλυμένοι διαμαρτυρῆν οἱ ξένοι, οἱ δὲ τῆς Ἀποστασίου κεκωλυμένοι[?].
units.tr: Anyone was therefore permitted to give testimony in this action against freedmen, before judgment was pronounced, whether the case was admissible or not. Hyperides, in Harpocration: "Hyperides, in the court against Leocrates concerning apostasy, says that those who were prevented, as citizens, from giving evidence in the apostasy indictments, and likewise foreigners..." [Ὑπερίδης δὲ ἐν τῷ κατὰ Αεισαγόρου Ἀποστασίου δικαστηρίῳ φησίν, ὡς οἱ ἐμοὶ μὲν κεκωλυμένοι διαμαρτυρῆν ἐπὶ τὰς γραφὰς τῆς τῶν Ἀποστασίου τῶν βουλομένων, ὁμοίως τὴν ξένων, καὶ τὴν ἐπιχωρίων…]

units.la: Censusautem Libertorum habebatur, an plenam consecuti essent libertatem. Nonnus in Nazianzeni ϛηλιτεύσιος priorem. ἐκάλεσε δὲ τῷ Ἀλεξάνδρῳ καὶ τοῖς ἀπελευθέροις ἡμέρᾳ[?] ἐλευθερίας. καὶ οὗτοι δὲ ἐκείνοντο, καὶ ἐδοκιμάζοντο, εἰ ὅλως ἠλευθερώσοντο. ea scilicet fini, vt si plenam esse consecuti libertatem censerentur, ab iis ἀπίκιον[?], quod publico pendebant aerario, exigeretur.
units.tr: A census of freedmen was taken, to determine whether they had won full freedom. Nonnus, on the first (oration) of Gregory Nazianzen: "He summoned Alexander and the freedmen to a day of liberty, and they too were examined and tested, whether they had been wholly set free [ἐκάλεσε δὲ τῷ Ἀλεξάνδρῳ καὶ τοῖς ἀπελευθέροις ἡμέρᾳ ἐλευθερίας. καὶ οὗτοι δὲ ἐκείνοντο, καὶ ἐδοκιμάζοντο, εἰ ὅλως ἠλευθερώσοντο]." The purpose, of course, was that if they were judged to have obtained full liberty, the tax they paid to the public treasury would be exacted from them.

units.la: Inter seruos censebatur is, qui redemptus ex hostibus, redimias non persoluisset redemptori suo, cui seruiturem seruiebat dum id praestitisset, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Among slaves was counted the man who, having been ransomed from enemies, had not paid his redemption price to the one who ransomed him; until he had paid it, he served him, by this law:

units.la: Τοῦ λυτρωθέντος ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων εἶ[?] τὸν λυτρωτὴν, ἐὰν μὴ λυτρώσας λύτρα.
units.tr: "The one ransomed from the enemies belongs to his ransomer, unless he pays the ransom" [Τοῦ λυτρωθέντος ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων εἶναι τὸν λυτρωτὴν, ἐὰν μὴ λύτρα ἀποδῷ].

units.la: Redemptus ex hostibus illius esto, qui rede-mis, nisi redimias ipse persoluerit.
units.tr: The one redeemed from enemies belongs to the one who redeemed him, unless he himself has paid the redemption price.

units.la: Legem habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ πρὸς Νικίαρχον· εἶτα δ᾽ ἔφη, ὅτι καὶ οἱ νόμοι κελεύουσι, τὸν λυτρωθέντα ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων εἰς τὸν λυτρῶνα, ἐὰν μὴ [?] λύτρα. Captiui autem redimi non poterant, nisi à Legatis. Anonymus in Argumento Orationis Demosthenicae περὶ τῆς παραπρεσβείας. ἀπλῶν γὰρ εἰς τὸν [illegible, ~12 letters] παραπρεσβείαν, [?] Μακεδονία τινὰς τῶν Ἀθηναίων αἰχμαλώτους, καὶ [illegible, ~10 letters] φέρει ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας [?] καὶ ῥύσασθαι αὐτούς, ἐὰν ἰδιώτα δὲ τῶν πολιτῶν, εἰ μὴ ἐκ [illegible, ~8 letters] ποιήσας [?].
units.tr: You have the law in Demosthenes, in the speech against Nicarchus: "Then he said that the laws also order that the one ransomed from enemies belongs to the ransomer, unless he pays the ransom" [ἐν τῷ πρὸς Νικίαρχον· εἶτα δ᾽ ἔφη, ὅτι καὶ οἱ νόμοι κελεύουσι, τὸν λυτρωθέντα ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων εἰς τὸν λυτρῶνα, ἐὰν μὴ λύτρα]. Captives, however, could not be ransomed except through ambassadors. The anonymous argument to Demosthenes' oration On the False Embassy says that Philip held some Athenians captive, and that the orator, having been sent as an envoy, was to rescue them, if they were private citizens, unless… [ἀπλῶν γὰρ εἰς τὸν … παραπρεσβείαν, Μακεδονία τινὰς τῶν Ἀθηναίων αἰχμαλώτους… ῥύσασθαι αὐτούς, ἐὰν ἰδιώτα δὲ τῶν πολιτῶν, εἰ μὴ…]

units.la: Seruum autem ociosum atque inertem alere Leges non sinebant:
units.tr: The laws did not allow a slave who was idle and useless to be kept:

units.la: Μὴ ἐξεῖναι δοῦλον τρέφειν οἰκέτην. Seruum otiosum ne alito.
units.tr: "It is not permitted to keep an idle slave" [Μὴ ἐξεῖναι δοῦλον τρέφειν οἰκέτην]. Do not keep an idle slave.

units.la: Legem habes apud Vlpianum in Midianam: εἰσὶ δὲ τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις δοῦλον τρέφειν οἰκέτην· ἀλλ᾽ οἱ μὲν, αὐλοποιοὺς, οἱ δὲ, μαχαιροποιοὺς εἶχον τοὺς δούλους. Serui igitur aliquam artem sciebant, quam exercebant.
units.tr: You have the law in Ulpian's commentary on the speech Against Midias: "The Athenians were permitted to keep a slave…; but some kept slaves who were flute-makers, others who were sword-makers" [εἰσὶ δὲ τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις δοῦλον τρέφειν οἰκέτην· ἀλλ᾽ οἱ μὲν, αὐλοποιοὺς, οἱ δὲ, μαχαιροποιοὺς εἶχον τοὺς δούλους]. Slaves, therefore, knew some craft, which they practised.

units.la: LIBER TERTIVS. DE SENATU QUINGENTORUM ET CONCIONE.
units.tr: BOOK THREE. CONCERNING THE COUNCIL OF FIVE HUNDRED AND THE ASSEMBLY.

units.la: TITULUS PRIMUS.
units.tr: TITLE I.

units.la: CUM eruditissime à præstantissimis viris de Quingentorum Senatu disputatum sit, ne, quod aiunt, actum agere videamur, pauca tantum delibabimus, quæ omnino necessaria sunt ad hunc, quem de illo Senatu instituimus, sermonem.
units.tr: Since the Council of Five Hundred has been discussed most learnedly by most distinguished men, lest, as the saying goes, we seem to be doing what has already been done, we will touch on only a few points, those that are wholly necessary for the discussion of that Council which we have undertaken here.

units.la: Constituit Solon, ut quotannis summæ præesset Reipublicæ Quadringentorum Senatus, non ducto è variis ordinibus numero, quod olim volebat Plato Lib. VI. de Legibus, id quippe denegatum Solonis Legibus [illegible, ~20 letters], vt in hunc Senatum allegerentur: [?] [illegible, ~30 letters] neque postea quoque, aucto numero, concessum, sed è quatuor Tribubus Plutarchus in Solone: [?] [illegible, ~25 letters]. Aucto deinde, siue in ordinem redacto, Tribuum, quæ decem fuerunt, numero, è Quadringentis facti sunt Quingenti Senatores, qui dicti sunt ἡ τῶν Πεντακοσίων βουλή, aut οἱ Πεντακόσιοι. Ex vnaquaque enim Tribu quinginti viri sorte ducebantur: [?] inquit Vlpianus in Androtionam, εἰς ἅπαξ μεσίδας, [?] [?] [?]. Sortiebantur autem, qui ætate essent Senatoria. Libanius in Hypothesi Androtianæ: [?] [?] [?] [?] [?]. Ætatem Senatoriam definitam fuisse puto anno tricesimo: Oportet namque tot annos natum fuisse iudicem, vt constat ex Heliastarum iureiurando: ΚΑΙ ΓΕΓΟΝΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΛΑΤΤΟΝ Η ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΗ. Quinginti autem hi etiam inter iudices: nam vere Plato Lib. VI. de Legibus, [?] [?]. Præterea hoc Senatu noti poterant forte capi in iudices, vt legimus in Græcorum Commentariis [?] [?] [?]. Non potuissent autem, nisi annos minimum triginta nati: & vnus è Tyrannis Triginta Charicles Socrati apud Xenophontem [illegible, ~12 letters] Lib. I. [illegible, ~18 letters], [illegible, ~14 letters], [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters]. Denique Demosthenes in Midiana scribit se ante annum aetatis tricesimum secundum [illegible, ~8 letters], id est, anno aetatis tricesimo primo, qui incidit in annum secundum Olympiadis centesimae sextae, Praetore Athenis Callistrato. Nam vero Plutarchus confert natalem Demosthenis in annum quartum Olympiadis nonagesimae octavae, Dexitheo Athenis Praetore: Neque enim audiendi sunt Dionysius Halicarnasseus & Anonymus in Descriptione Olympiadum, qui adscribunt anno quarto Olympiadis nonagesimae nonae, qui Archontem habuit Demophilum: atque horum sententiam firmari posse putat Vir eruditissimus Demosthenis ipsius verbis Oratione II. adversus Stephanum: [illegible, ~60 letters]. Emendat Vir C L. [illegible, ~10 letters], idque optime, sed male inde probare nititur sententiam Dionysij: Nam ista dicuntur, sive potius scribuntur ab oratore Demosthene, non de Demosthene patre, & aetate sua, sed ex Apollodori, cui hanc Orationem scripserat, persona, de Pasione patre: & proculdubio vera est gravissimi scriptoris Plutarchi sententia, cuius vindicem dabimus & assertorem Demosthenem, qui scribit [illegible, ~30 letters] Aphobum tutorem suum extremo anno Praeturae Polyzeli in uxorem duxisse Onetoris sororem: [illegible, ~40 letters].
