Polyzeli Praetura incidit in annum secundum Olympiadis centesimae tertiae, ut est videre apud Diodorum Siculum, Anonymumque in Descriptione Olympiadum, Cephisodoro, qui Polyzelum excepit, Archonte, Aphobum male administratae tutelae accusavit, qui annus erat tertius Olympiadis centesimae tertiae, cum in viros esset adscriptus, & iam sui iuris, ut legitur ibidem: [illegible, ~45 letters]. Atqui in viros tantum adscribebantur, anno aetatis vicesimo, ut in superioribus diximus, circa Hecatombaeonis initia, quare dixit Demosthenes, [illegible, ~25 letters]. Extremo enim Polyzeli anno sororem Onetoris duxerat in uxorem Aphobus: hunc Polyzelum in Praetura excepit Cephisodorus, quo iam Archonte [illegible, ~12 letters] in viros est transcriptus noster Demosthenes: Neque ante hanc aetatem actionem [illegible, ~12 letters] instituere poterat, ut qui sua ante annum aetatis vicesimum administrare non posset: unde in Graecorum commentariis legimus, [illegible, ~30 letters]. Anno autem primo Olympiadis centesimae quartae, Praetore Athenis Timocrate, iudicium est adeptus adversus Aphobum. Demosthenes ibidem: [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐπὶ Τιμοκράτους. Non igitur conferendus est natalis Demosthenis in annum quartum Olympiadis nonagesimae nonae, sed potius in annum quartum Olympiadis nonagesimae octavae. Atque haec obiter de anno natali Demosthenis, cui cum tam multa debeamus, non potuimus non praestare hanc eius aetati illustrandae operam: sed è diverticulo in viam. Scribit Demosthenes in Midiana, se in Quingentorum Senatum forte captum fuisse, antequam hanc Orationem scriberet, [illegible, ~30 letters]. Orationem scripsit annos natus triginta duos: [illegible, ~60 letters] ἐστιν, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, χειρωνὸς ἐπὶ τῆς [?] πεντήκοντα ἔτη [?] [illegible, ~40 letters] Quare anno aetatis tricesimo, aut tricesimo primo, Demosthenes cooptatus est in Quingentorum Senatum: & cum in illius vitam inquireretur, accusauit eum Midias: an Senatu motus fuerit Demosthenes, ipse de se non dicit, neque verisimile est: nam Aeschines, qui aequa iniqua illi exprobrare ludum iocumque putat, obijcere ei non praetermisisset. imo omnino verum non est. Qui semel in Senatum fuerat cooptatus, poterat rursum non ita multo post legi in eundem: constat id exemplo Demosthenis: nam, vt iam diximus, Senator sorte captus est, siue anno primo Olympiadis centesimae sextae, Elpino Archonte, siue anno sequenti, qui fuit secundus eiusdem Olympiadis centesimae sextae, Callistrato Athenis Praetore, quod verius puto, & nonnisi anno tricesimo peracto in hunc Senatum adscribi potuisse Senatores. Iterum idem Demosthenes anno secundo Olympiadis centesimae octauae, Themistocle Archonte, Senator factus est. [illegible, ~50 letters] Interuallum est à priori fortunione ad posteriorem annorum octo. Non tantum autem sorte ducebantur Quinquaginta ex vnaquaque Tribu viri, sed etiam praeter eos, quinquaginta alij succidanei, in hunc finem, vt si primi illi Quinquaginta sorte lecti, aut ex illis vnus aliquis, vel probaretur minus, vel intra suae [illegible, ~8 letters] annum moreretur, in illorum locum sufficerentur isti, quibus sors obuenerat, ita exponunt proxime laudatum Aeschinis locum Grammatici & Platonis Comici Hyperbolo. [illegible, ~70 letters] Admittebantur in hunc Senatum etiam adscripti ciues, vt è Lege [illegible, ~12 letters] colligere est, vnde Demosthenes [illegible, ~20 letters] de Apollodoro adscripto ciue: [illegible, ~20 letters]. Sortitio haec fiebat quatuor vltimis diebus de trecentis quinquaginta quatuor anni Lunaris. Vlpianus in Androtianam: [illegible, ~60 letters] Quinquaginta illi ex vnaquaque Tribu forte capti Senatores [illegible, ~8 letters] dicebantur. Grammatici: [illegible, ~70 letters] Sorte autem ductae Tribus imperabant sibi inuicem succedentes. Grammatici: [illegible, ~50 letters] Ita singulae Tribus dies triginta quinque imperabant. Vlpianus in Androtianam: [illegible, ~80 letters] [illegible, ~60 letters] δι[illegible, ~40 letters] Supererant anno Lunari perficiendo quatuor illi [illegible, ~12 letters] dies, post regna triginta quinque dierum; quibus quaelibet decem Tribuum ordine forte ducto praefecta fuerat: illi quatuor dies imputabantur quatuor Tribubus, quae primae imperauerant. Suidas: [illegible, ~190 letters] Existimauit Illustris Scaliger vnamquamque Tribum vnum diem per orbem summam rerum gessisse & imperasse, vt, exempli gratia, heri [illegible, ~10 letters] Aiantis Phylae imperabat, hodie [illegible, ~10 letters] Cecropis, cras [illegible, ~10 letters] Acamantis, & ita deinceps totum vertentem annum vnaquaeque suam [illegible, ~8 letters] imperabat, prout forte ducta erat ab ipso anni principio.
units.tr: Solon established that the Council of Four Hundred should preside over the commonwealth each year. The members were not drawn from the various orders, as Plato wished in Book VI of the Laws; Solon's laws refused this, … so that they should be chosen for this Council … nor was it granted afterwards either, when the number was increased, but they were chosen from the four tribes, as Plutarch says in his Life of Solon … Then, when the number of tribes, which had been ten, was increased or reorganised, the Four Hundred became the Five Hundred senators, who were called ἡ τῶν Πεντακοσίων βουλή [the council of the Five Hundred] or οἱ Πεντακόσιοι [the Five Hundred]. For fifty men were drawn by lot from each tribe. Ulpian, in his commentary on the speech against Androtion, says that they were chosen εἰς ἅπαξ μεσίδας [once for each half-tribe]… Those who were of senatorial age cast lots. Libanius, in the Argument to the speech against Androtion: … I think the senatorial age was fixed at thirty years, for a man had to be that old to be a judge, as is clear from the oath of the jurors: "and I have been not less than thirty years old" [ΚΑΙ ΓΕΓΟΝΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΛΑΤΤΟΝ Η ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΗ]. These fifty were also among the judges, for Plato in Book VI of the Laws truly says … Moreover, those who had been selected for this Council could perhaps be chosen as judges, as we read in the Greek commentaries … They could not, however, unless they were at least thirty years old. And one of the Thirty Tyrants, Charicles, speaks to Socrates in Xenophon … Lastly, Demosthenes, in the speech against Midias, writes that before his thirty-second year of age … that is, in his thirty-first year, which fell in the second year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad, when Callistratus was Praetor at Athens. For Plutarch places the birth of Demosthenes in the fourth year of the ninety-eighth Olympiad, when Dexitheus was Praetor at Athens. Nor should Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the anonymous author of the Description of the Olympiads be heard, who assign it to the fourth year of the ninety-ninth Olympiad, when Demophilus was archon. The most learned man thinks their view can be confirmed by Demosthenes' own words in his second speech against Stephanus … The learned man emends the text, and rightly so, but he tries badly to prove from this the opinion of Dionysius. For these things are said, or rather written, by the orator Demosthenes not about his father Demosthenes and his own age, but in the person of Apollodorus, for whom he had written this speech, concerning his father Pasion. And undoubtedly the view of the most serious writer Plutarch is true, whose defender and champion we shall make Demosthenes, who writes that … Aphobus, his guardian, in the last year of the praetorship of Polyzelus, married the sister of Onetor … The praetorship of Polyzelus fell in the second year of the hundred and third Olympiad, as can be seen in Diodorus Siculus and the anonymous author of the Description of the Olympiads. In the archonship of Cephisodorus, who succeeded Polyzelus, Demosthenes accused Aphobus of mismanaged guardianship; this was the third year of the hundred and third Olympiad, when he had been enrolled among the men and was already his own master, as is read in the same place … Yet men were enrolled only in their twentieth year of age, as we said above, about the beginning of Hecatombaeon, which is why Demosthenes said … For in the last year of Polyzelus, Aphobus had married Onetor's sister; Cephisodorus succeeded Polyzelus as praetor, and under him as archon our Demosthenes was transferred among the men. Nor could he bring a suit before this age, since one who could not manage his own affairs before the twentieth year was not competent; hence we read in the Greek commentaries … In the first year of the hundred and fourth Olympiad, when Timocrates was praetor at Athens, he obtained a judgment against Aphobus. Demosthenes in the same place: … under Timocrates. Therefore the birth of Demosthenes should not be placed in the fourth year of the ninety-ninth Olympiad, but rather in the fourth year of the ninety-eighth Olympiad. These things have been said in passing about the year of Demosthenes' birth; since we owe him so much, we could not refuse to offer this labour to illuminate his age, but this is a digression from the road. Demosthenes writes in the speech against Midias that he had perhaps been chosen for the Council of Five Hundred before he wrote this speech … He wrote the speech at the age of thirty-two years … Wherefore in his thirtieth or thirty-first year Demosthenes was co-opted into the Council of Five Hundred. And when an inquiry was made into his life, Midias accused him. Whether Demosthenes was moved from the Council he does not himself say, nor is it likely; for Aeschines, who thinks it a game and a joke to throw such equal and unjust reproaches at him, would not have failed to object this to him. Indeed it is altogether untrue. One who had once been co-opted into the Council could be chosen again not long afterwards for the same body; this is established by the example of Demosthenes. For, as we have already said, he was chosen as senator by lot either in the first year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad, when Elpinus was archon, or in the following year, the second of the same hundred and sixth Olympiad, when Callistratus was praetor at Athens, which I think more likely; and that men could be enrolled in this Council only after completing their thirtieth year. Again, the same Demosthenes was made senator in the second year of the hundred and eighth Olympiad, when Themistocles was archon … The interval from the former lot to the later is eight years. Moreover, not only were fifty men drawn by lot from each tribe, but also fifty others besides them, as substitutes, for this purpose: that if the first fifty chosen by lot, or any one of them, were either found unsatisfactory or died within his year of office, those to whom the lot had fallen should be substituted in their place. The grammarians and the comic poet Plato in his Hyperbolus explain the nearby passage of Aeschines in this way … Citizens who had been enrolled were also admitted to this Council, as can be gathered from the law …, whence Demosthenes … concerning Apollodorus, an enrolled citizen … This sortition was made on the last four days of the three hundred and fifty-four days of the lunar year. Ulpian in the speech against Androtion: … Those fifty senators chosen by lot from each tribe were called … The grammarians: … The tribes that had been drawn by lot governed in turn, each succeeding the other. The grammarians: … Thus each tribe governed for thirty-five days. Ulpian in the speech against Androtion: … To complete the lunar year there remained four days, after the reigns of thirty-five days, over which each of the ten tribes had been placed in charge in an order drawn by lot; those four days were assigned to the four tribes that had governed first. Suidas: … The illustrious Scaliger thought that each tribe governed and held the chief power for one day in turn, so that, for example, yesterday the tribe of Aias governed, today that of Cecrops, tomorrow that of Acamas, and so on; and thus, throughout the whole turning year, each tribe governed on its own day, as it had been drawn by lot from the very beginning of the year.

units.la: Sed huic sententiae aduersantur aliquot veterum Oratorum testimonia, quibus facile probatur vnamquamq; Tribum triginta quinque suos dies continuo imperasse, non singulae suam per orbem [illegible, ~8 letters]. Apud Demosthenem in Timocratea prima Psephismatis vnius verba haec sunt: [illegible, ~45 letters] Timocrates. & paulò post: [illegible, ~50 letters] Nempe quia etiam postridie imperabat Tribus Pandionis, quod etiam constat ex altero Psephismate postridie scripto, quod eadem Oratione legitur: [illegible, ~60 letters] Vides duos continuos dies imperasse Pandionidem, equa Aristocles (nam [illegible, ~8 letters], inquit Stephanus, [illegible, ~10 letters]) [illegible, ~8 letters] populum in suffragia misit. Sed nullum dubitationi locum esse finit Antiphon [illegible, ~20 letters] quin triginta quinque continuos dies singulae Tribus imperarint: haec enim eius verba sunt: [illegible, ~120 letters]. Dicuntur enim ista de iis quae acciderunt die quinto Metagitnionis mensis, vt in superioribus exposuimus. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: But several testimonies of the older orators oppose this view, from which it is easily shown that each Tribe held the government for thirty-five consecutive days, and that not each tribe held it for one day throughout the year. In Demosthenes' Against Timocrates, the first decree reads as follows: ... Timocrates. A little later: ... For the tribe Pandionis was also presiding on the following day, which is also clear from the second decree, written the day after, which is read in the same speech: ... You see that the Pandionid tribe presided for two consecutive days. Aristocles (for ..., says Stephanus, ...) put the matter to the people's vote. But Antiphon leaves no room for doubt that each tribe presided for thirty-five consecutive days: his words are these: ... For these things are said of events that happened on the fifth day of the month Metageitnion, as we explained above. But enough on this.

units.la: Quinquaginta hi vnius Tribus Prytaneis simul non imperabant suam triginta quinque dierum Prytaneiam: sed cum Prytaneia in quinque hebdomades, vt ex Vlpiano liquet, distribueretur: quinquies enim septem faciut triginta quinque; in totidem decurias forte distribuebantur hi quinquaginta, Prytaneis, & prima decuria suam imperabat hebdomadem, secunda secundam, atque ita deinceps ordine forte ducto: dicebantur illi decem, qui in sua hebdomade praerant, [illegible, ~12 letters]. Vlpianus in Androtianam: [illegible, ~110 letters] πληρωσῶσιν αἱ ἐπὶ ἡμέραν. καὶ συνεβαίνε τοῖς ἀρχουσι, ἡμεῖς μὴ ἀρχὴν [?] ἕκαστος ὃ ἀρχὴν ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ, ἐκαλεῖτο Ἐπιστάτης. Ἀρχὴ τί δὲ μίας μόνον ἦρχεν; ὅθεν αὐτὸς ἐκ τῆς Ἀκροπόλεως ἐδησεύετο, καὶ πᾶσα τὰ χρήματα τῆς πόλεως. ἵν' οὖν μὴ ἐγερεθῇ τυραννίδος, ἀρχὴ τὸ τὸ μίαν ἡμέραν ἐποίεσιν αὐτὸν ἀρξαι. ἰσον δ' ὅτι, οἱ ἰδίᾳ πεντήκοντα Πρυτάνεις ἐκαλοῦντο· οἱ δὲ ἕνα, Πεδέδροι· ὁ δὲ εἷς, Ἐπιστάτης.
units.tr: These fifty members of one tribe did not preside together for their whole thirty-five-day Prytany. Rather, since the Prytany was divided into five weeks, as is clear from Ulpian (for five times seven makes thirty-five), these fifty men were distributed by lot into the same number of decuries, the Prytaneis. The first decury held the presidency for the first week, the second for the second week, and so on in the order determined by lot. Those ten who presided in their own week were called ... Ulpian on Androtion: ... [πληρωσῶσιν αἱ ἐπὶ ἡμέραν]. And it happened to the magistrates that each one who held office for a single day was called Epistates. Why only for one day? Because he was entrusted with the keys of the Acropolis and all the city's money; so that he might not be made a tyrant, they allowed him to hold office for one day only. It is the same that the fifty Prytaneis were called ..., but the one, Pededroi, and the one man, Epistates.

units.la: Prytaneia igitur in quinque hebdomadas distribuebatur, vt hic habes, & secundum hanc distributionem Quinquaginta Prytaneis singularum Tribuum, in quinque decurias distinguebantur: vnde intelligenda puto atque emendanda Hesychij verba, ἕδραι βουλῆς ἃ ἐγίνοντο κατὰ πεντημέρων. Referendum existimo, κατὰ ἑπταημέρων [?]. Non enim quinto quoque die Senatus habebatur, vt praeferunt haec verba, sed quotidie, nisi dies esset ἄφετος. Est igitur quod dixi: Decem autem illi singularum decuriarum viri, cum hebdomadem suam imperarent, Πεδέδροι dicebantur, qui ἐκλεγόμενοι τὴν Πρυτανείων καθ' ἑκάστην Πρυτανείων, vt obseruat Grammatici. Hi vero Proedri inter se sortiebantur regna septem illorum hebdomadis dierum, quibus praerant: atque ita fiebat, vt e decem singularum hebdomadum Proedris tres superessent, qui suum non imperarent diem: Proedrus autem, quum suum imperaret diem, Ἐπιστάτης dicebatur: εἷς δὲ, κατὰ κλῆρον μιᾶς ἡμέρας τὴν ἐπὶ [illegible, ~12 letters] ὁμοίως δὲ ἕκαστος τὴν ἀὐλῶ [?] κλῆρον [illegible, ~10 letters] πληρωσῶσιν αἱ ἐπὶ ἡμέραν καὶ συνεβαίνε τοῖς ἀρχουσι, ἡμεῖς μὴ ἀρχὴν ἕκαστος δὲ ἀρχὴν ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ, ἐκαλεῖτο Ἐπιστάτης. Nemini autem licebat Lege, nisi semel Epistatae esse: Δὶς οὐκ ἐξὸν ἡμέας τὸν αὐτὸν Ἐπιστάτην. Nemini bis esse Epistatæ licito.
units.tr: The Prytany was therefore divided into five weeks, as you see here, and according to this division the fifty Prytaneis of each tribe were distinguished into five decuries. From this I think the words of Hesychius should be understood and corrected: ... I think it should be referred to ... (seven-day periods). For the Senate was not held every fifth day, as these words suggest, but every day, unless the day was a holiday. So what I have said stands: the ten men of each decury, when they presided over their week, were called Pededroi, who were chosen ... as the grammarians observe. These Proedroi drew lots among themselves for the (presidency of the) seven days of the week over which they presided. And so it came about that from the ten Proedroi of each week, three remained who did not preside on any day; but a Proedros, when he presided on his day, was called Epistates. One man, by lot, for one day... Likewise each... and it happened to the magistrates that each one who held office for one day was called Epistates. No one was permitted by law to be Epistates more than once: No one may be Epistates twice.

units.la: Memini Pollux Libro VIII. cap. IX. ὁ δὲ Ἐπιστάτης καλούμενος, ἔστιν εἷς τῶν Πρυτανέων, ὁ κληρω λαχὼν δὶς ἢ οὐκ ἐξεστι ἡμέας τὸν αὐτὸν Ἐπιστάτην. Suidas: τῶν Πρυταν-εων εἰς ὁ λαχὼν, Ἐπιστάτης ἐλέγετο. διὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐπιστατοῦν οὐκ ἐξὸν. Habebat enim penes se, quum regnarer, ærarij claues, & tabulari, itemque sigillum publicum, vnde metus erat, ne, si plures fierent Epistatæ, tyrannidem inuaderet. Vlpianus: ἕκαστος ἡ ἀρχὼν εἰς μιᾶ ἡμέρᾳ ἐπαλεῖτο Ἐπιστάτης. Διὰ τὶ δὲ μίαν μόνην ἡμέραν; ὅτι αὐτὸς τὰς κλεῖς τῆς Ἀκροπόλεως ἐπιστεύετο, καὶ πάντα τὰ χρήματα τῆς πόλεως. ἵνα οὖν μὴ ἐσχάτη τυραννίδος, διὰ τοῦτο μίαν ἡμέραν ἐπέτρεπον αὐτῷ ἀρχήν. Pollux loco laudato: ἔχει δὲ ὁ Ἐπιστάτης τὰς κλεῖς τῶν ἱερῶν, ἐν οἷς τὰ χρήματα, καὶ τὰ χρήματα [?]. Suidas: φυλάττει δὲ ὁ Ἐπιστάτης τὸ ἱερὸν τὰς κλεῖς, ἐν ᾧ τε δημόσια χρήματα. ἔτι μὲν καὶ τὴν δημοσίων σφραγῖδα. Quod autem semel fungi Epistatæ munere liceret, intelligendum est de toto vitæ curriculo: nam quod ad annum ipsum, quo Epistatæ fuerunt, referas, ioculare id esset, cum etiamsi nulla id Lex sanciret, aliter fieri non posset. Nemo enim εἷς τῶν Πρυτανείων erat Ἐπιστάτης, nisi πρυτανεύσαντος τῆς Φυλῆς, de qua erat Prytanum vnum, iam vero Prytaneis, vt diximus, distribuebantur sorte in decurias quinque, quarum decuriarum singulæ sorte ductæ suam imperabant ordine hebdomadem, neque vna decuria alterius occupabat vicem & ἐφημείας. An vero ὁ Proëdris decem tres illi, qui Epistatæ non fuerant, sorte non addicente, rursum sortirentur cum aliis, qui supererant, Prytanibus, necdum Proëdri fuerant suam hebdomadem, pro comperto non habeo: inclinat tamen potius animus, vt credam non iterum sortitos fuisse: nam, aut ego valde fallor, aut Prytaneis, incunte Prytania, distribuebantur sorte in has quinque decurias: Προέδρου [?] ἐκληθῆναι τὴν πρυτανείων καὶ ἑκάστῳ πρυτανείαν.
units.tr: Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 9: "The one called Epistates is one of the Prytaneis, the man who obtained the lot; it is not permitted to have the same Epistates twice." Suidas: "One of the Prytaneis who obtained the lot was called Epistates; and because he was Epistates, it was not permitted (a second time)." For while the kingdom lasted he kept in his own possession the keys of the treasury and the records, and likewise the public seal, so there was a fear that if there were several Epistatai, one might seize tyranny. Ulpian: "Each magistrate who held office for one day was called Epistates. Why only one day? Because he was entrusted with the keys of the Acropolis and all the city's money; so, lest he become a tyrant, they allowed him to hold office for one day." Pollux, in the passage cited: "The Epistates holds the keys of the sacred places, in which are the funds." Suidas: "The Epistates guards the keys of the temple in which the public money is, and also the public seal." That it was allowed for an Epistates to serve this office only once must be understood of the whole course of a life; for if you refer it to the year itself in which they were Epistatai, it would be a pointless remark, since even without any law sanctioning it, it could not happen otherwise. No one among the Prytaneis could be Epistates unless his tribe was presiding, of which there was one Prytany; and the Prytaneis, as we said, were distributed by lot into five decuries, and each decury, drawn by lot, held the week in turn, and one decury did not take over the turn and duty of another. Whether those three Proedroi who had not been Epistatai were drawn by lot again, not being assigned by lot, along with the other Prytaneis who had not yet been Proedroi during their week, I do not know for certain. Still, my inclination is rather to believe they were not drawn again. For, unless I am greatly mistaken, the Prytaneis, at the start of the Prytany, were distributed by lot into these five decuries.

units.la: Ab his Proëdris atque Epistatis, alij fuerunt Proëdri atque Epistatæ. Nam quotiescumque habebatur Senatus, aut concio, ὁ ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀρχὼν Ἐπιστάτης legebat nouem Proëdros è singulis vnum Tribubus, excepta Tribu, penes quam erat Prytaneias imperium, vt docuerat Aristoteles ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ. Pollux loco laudato: ἐὰν ὅταν οἱ Πρυτάνεις τὸ δῆμον, ἵνα τῷ βουλῇ συναγάγωσιν, ὁ Ἐπιστάτης ἐξ ἑκάστης φυλῆς (male editur βουλῆς,) Πρόεδροι ἐνα κληθῆ, μόνῳ τῶν πρυτανευόντων ἀφίεις. Suidas: ἐπειδὴ οἱ Πρυτάνεις συναγάγωσι τῇ βουλῇ ἢ τὸν δῆμον, ὁ Ἐπιστάτης κληθῆ Προέδρους ἕνα, ἐξ φυλῆς ἑκάστη ἕνα, πλὴν τῆς πρυτανευούσης. Sed alibi idem Suidas & Harpocration confundunt cum Proëdris illis decem, qui, cum regnarent suum hebdomadis diem, Epistatæ dicebantur, & qui hos nouem forte capiebant, Πρόεδροι, ἐκληθῶντο τὴν Πρυτανείων καὶ ἑκάστῳ πρυτανείας, εἰς δὲ ἑκάστης Φυλῆς, πλὴν τῆς πρυτανευούσης. Confuse haec dicuntur & indistinctè. Nam illi decem erant numero; hi nouem tantum, quia non sorticebatur Tribus illa, cuius erat Prytaneia. Illi erant vnius tantum Tribus, nempe τῆς πρυτανευούσης, hi è nouem aliis, praeter τὴν πρυτανευούσαν, Tribubus capiebantur, è singulis singuli: Illi καθ' ἑκάστην πρυτανείαν, incunte Prytaneia, legebantur: hi quotiescumque habebatur Senatus, aut concio cogebatur. Deniq; distincta erant munia. Horum nouem Proëdrorum vnus Epistata dicebatur, forte ex illis nouem ductus ab Epistata, penes quem erat illius diei regnum.
units.tr: Apart from these Proedroi and Epistatai, there were other Proedroi and Epistatai. For whenever the Senate or an assembly was held, the magistrate who was Epistates read out nine Proedroi, one from each tribe, excluding the tribe which held the Prytany, as Aristotle taught in the Constitution of the Athenians. Pollux, in the passage cited: "When the Prytaneis convene the people or the Senate, the Epistates is called upon to choose one Proedros from each tribe (wrongly printed 'of the Senate'), leaving out only the tribe that is presiding." Suidas: "When the Prytaneis convene the Senate or the people, the Epistates is called upon to choose one Proedros from each tribe, except the presiding tribe." But elsewhere the same Suidas and Harpocration confuse these with those ten Proedroi who, when they presided over their day of the week, were called Epistatai; and those who drew these nine by lot were called Proedroi, who were chosen at the start of the Prytany, one from each tribe, except the presiding one. These things are said confusedly and without distinction. For those ten were a group of ten, while these were only nine, because the tribe whose Prytany it was did not take part in the lot. The former were drawn from the one tribe only, namely the presiding tribe; the latter from the nine other tribes apart from the presiding one, one from each. The former were read out at the start of each Prytany; the latter whenever the Senate was held or the assembly convened. Finally, the duties were distinct. Of these nine Proedroi, one was called Epistates, drawn by lot from those nine by the Epistates, the man who held the kingship of that day.

units.la: Suidas: καὶ πάλιν ἐκ τῆς ἑνάτης ξύντων Ἐπιστάτην ἕνα κληθῆναι. Harpocration: δύο εἰσὶν οἱ καθιστάμενοι Ἐπιστάται, ὁ μὲν ἐκ Πρυτανέων κληρούμενος· ὁ δὲ ἐκ τῆς Πρεσβεῶν. Hi Proëdri Senarui, & populi concioni, praesidebant, vnde nomen inuenerunt: ἐκαλοῦντο δὲ Πρόεδροι, ἐπειδὴ ἐπὶ τὰς ἐκκλησίας προεδρεύοντες τῶν ἡμῶν ἀπέφυγον. Itaque per eos curabatur ea, quae ad τὸ βουλὴ ἢ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν erant: οἱ τινες τὰ ἐκ τῆς ἐκκλησίας διοίκουν, adde, ἐκ τῆς βουλῆ. Nam in hunc finem electi ab Epistata, vt negotio curarent. Suidas ex Aristotele ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ. ὁ Ἐπιστάτης κληθῆ Πρόεδρος ἐνα, ἐξ φυλῆς ἑκάστης ἕνα, πλὴν τῆς πρυτανευούσης. ἡ πάλιν ἐκ τῆς ἑνάτης ξύντων Ἐπιστάτην ἕνα κληθῆ. ἡ δὲ πρᾶγμα ἐξ εἰδὼν. Hi Proëdri relationem faciebant eorum, quorum causa conuenerant: vnde legas in Lege τῆς ἐπιχειροτονίας νόμων. Ἰδ' οἱ Πρόεδροι μὴ ἀρχαιότατον τὴν γνώμην. Vlpianus: οἱ δὲ Πρόεδροι ἀναλαβεῖν εἰς ἕνος σωτηρίαν. Siftebant praeterea in iudicium coram populo. Vlpianus in Timocrateam: εἰ δὲ Πρόεδροι ἐν τῷ δήμῳ εἰσῆγον, εἰ δὲ Ἀρχοντες οἱ Θεσμοθέται, ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ. Quas tamen partes fuisse praecipue τῆς Ἐπιστάτου ἐκ τῶν Προέδρων facile mihi persuadeo: itaque notat de eo Suidas: ὡς εἰσαγγελῆ τὴν δίκην, ὃ ἐπιμελῆσαι τὴν νόμων πάντα ἡμεῖς, ὃ μὴ τὴν ἀλλαφῆν ἡμῶν εἰς ὃ δίδα ἡμῶν τὰς δικαστάς. Quae postrema verba refero ad τὴν εἰσαγγελίαν, aut huiusmodi dicas, quando scilicet ἐν τῇ Συνταξεσίων βουλῇ, aut ἡ ἐκκλησία, reum εἰσαγγελίας, aut alterius criminis, à se condemnatum tradebat ἐκ δικαστηρίῳ, vt grauior multa irrogaretur: Nam alioqui τῶν Προέδρων, aut eorum Epistatæ non erat εἰσαγγελὴν ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, vt habes in laudatis iam ante Vlpiani verbis.
units.tr: Suidas: "And again, from the nine, one of them is chosen as Epistates." Harpocration: "There are two kinds of Epistatai appointed: one drawn by lot from the Prytaneis, the other from the Proedroi." These Proedroi presided over the Senate and over the assembly of the people, and this is where they got their name: they were called Proedroi because they sat in front of the assemblies. Therefore, through them, the business belonging to the Senate or the assembly was managed, that is, those who administered the affairs of the assembly; add, of the Senate. For they were chosen by the Epistates for this purpose, to attend to the business. Suidas, from Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians: "The Epistates is called upon to choose one Proedros from each tribe, except the presiding tribe; or again, from the nine, one of them is chosen as Epistates." These Proedroi made the report concerning those matters for which they had gathered. Hence in the law on the vote of ratification one reads... The Proedroi shall not put the motion first. Ulpian: "The Proedroi shall take up the matter for the safety of ..." They also brought charges before the people in court. Ulpian on Timocrates: "If the Proedroi brought (the matter) before the people, the Thesmothetae, the archons, (brought it) before the court." Yet I easily persuade myself that these functions belonged chiefly to the Epistates among the Proedroi; accordingly Suidas says of him that he brings the prosecution (eisangelia) ... and that he hands over to the jurors. I refer these last words to the eisangelia, or something of the kind, namely when, in the Senate or the assembly, he handed over to the court a man whom he had accused of eisangelia or another crime, so that a heavier penalty might be imposed. For otherwise it was not the function of the Proedroi, or of their Epistates, to bring an eisangelia before the court, as you have in Ulpian's words cited above.

units.la: Vbi forte capti fuerant Quingenti, qui Reipublicæ praeessent, inquirebatur in eorum vitam, morésque, cum probati fuerant, iusiurandum dabát. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ χῷ Νεαίρας· λαχὼν βυλαύων ὁ Απολλόδωρος· δικαιώμα ὅς ἢ ὁμόσας τὸ νομικὸν ὅρκον. Iusiurandi huius Lege imperati, vt hic habes, aliquot Capita hic describemus.
units.tr: Where the Five Hundred who were to preside over the state had been chosen by lot, their life and character were investigated, and once they were approved they took the oath. Demosthenes, in the speech against Neaera: Apollodorus, having been chosen by lot as a senator, and having sworn the senatorial oath. We shall set out here several clauses of this oath, as laid down by the law. ## THE SENATORIAL OATH.

units.la: Ο ΒΟΥΛΕΥΤΙΚΟΣ ΟΡΚΟΣ.
Τὰ βέλτιστα βουλεύσω τῷ δήμῳ τῷ Αθη- ναίων.
units.tr: I will counsel what is best for the people of Athens. [Τὰ βέλτιστα βουλεύσω τῷ δήμῳ τῷ Αθηναίων.]

units.la: Κατὰ τοὺς νόμους βουλεύσω.
units.tr: I will counsel according to the laws. [Κατὰ τοὺς νόμους βουλεύσω.]

units.la: ΟΥΔΕ ΔΗΣΩ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΥΔΕ- ΝΑ ΟΣ ΑΝ ΕΓΓΥΗΤΑΣ ΤΡΕΙΣ ΚΑ- ΘΙΣΤΗΙ ΤΟ ΑΥΤΟ ΤΕΛΟΣ ΤΕ- ΛΟΥΝΤΑΣ, ΓΗΛΗΝ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΕΠΙ ΠΡΟΔΟΣΙΑι ΤΗΣ ΠΟΛΕΩΣ, Η ΕΠΙ ΚΑΤΑΛΥΣΕΙ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΣΥ- ΝΙΩΝ ΑΛΛ,Η ΤΕΛΟΣ ΠΡΙΑΜΕΝΟΣ, Η ΕΓΓΥΗΣΑΜΕΝΟΣ, Η ΕΚΛΕΓΩΝ ΜΗ ΚΑΤΑΒΑΛΗ.
units.tr: I will not bind any Athenian, nor any man who has given surety for three of the same assessment, unless he has conspired to betray the city or to overthrow the democracy, or unless he is a purchaser of the revenues, a surety, or a collector who has not paid the money. [Οὐδὲ δήσω Αθηναίων οὐδένα, ὃς ἂν ἐγγυητὰς τρεῖς καθίστῃ τὸ αὐτὸ τέλος τελοῦντας, πλὴν ἐάν τις ἐπὶ προδοσίᾳ τῆς πόλεως, ἢ ἐπὶ καταλύσει τοῦ δήμου συνίῃ ἄλλ', ἢ τέλος πριάμενος, ἢ ἐγγυησάμενος, ἢ ἐκλέγων μὴ καταβάλῃ.]

units.la: Καθιερώσω δὲ τῷ γράμματι, ᾧ αὐ λέγω- σι.
units.tr: And I will consecrate [this] to the inscription, as they say.

units.la: ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ ΕΝΔΕΙΞΙΝ ΟΥ- ΔΕ ΑΠΑΓΩΓΗΝ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΤΩΝ ΠΡΟ- ΤΕΡΟΝ ΓΕΓΕΝΗΜΕΝΩΝ ΠΛΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΦΕΥΓΟΝΤΩΝ.
units.tr: And I will not accept an indictment, nor a summary arrest, against any of those who formerly have been cast out, except those who have fled. [Καὶ οὐ δέξομαι ἔνδειξιν, οὐδ' ἀπαγωγὴν ἕνεκα τῶν προτέρον γεγενημένων, πλὴν τῶν φευγόντων.]

units.la: IVSIVRANDVM SENATVS.
units.tr: THE SENATE'S OATH.

units.la: Optima quaeque confulam Athe- niensium populo.
units.tr: I will counsel what is best for the people of Athens.

units.la: Secundum Leges confulam.
units.tr: I will counsel according to the laws.

units.la: Neminem vinciam, qui vades dederit tres eiusdem census, nisi quis ad vrbem prodendam, aut popularem statum evertendum conspirarit: aut emptor vectigalium, aut sponsor, aut coactor pecuniam non numerarit.
units.tr: I will not bind anyone who has given surety of three of the same assessment, unless someone has conspired to betray the city or overthrow the popular state; or unless he has not paid the money as buyer of the revenues, surety, or collector.

units.la: Assidebo eo ordine, quem litera fors attribuerit.
units.tr: I will sit in the order which the letter assigned to me by lot shall determine.

units.la: Neminem, nisi exfulum, deferri, ducive finam, praeteritorum caufa.
units.tr: I will not denounce or lead anyone to prison, except an exile, on account of past offences.

units.la: Primum huius iurisiurandi Caput extat apud Demosthenem ἐν τῇ Νεαίρᾳ, de Apollodoro, ὁμολογικῶς ὁ τὰ βέλτιστα βουλεύσω τῷ δήμῳ τῷ Αθηναίων [?]. quod sane ut praestarent Senatores, exigebat ab illis muneris, quod susceperant, ratio.
units.tr: The first clause of this oath is found in Demosthenes, in the speech against Neaera, concerning Apollodorus: "I will counsel what is best for the people of Athens" [?]. The duty which the senators had undertaken certainly required them to keep this promise.

units.la: Secundum Caput describit Xenophon Libro I. Ἀπομνημονευμάτων, de So- crate agens: βουλεύσας γὰρ ποτὲ, ἢ τὸν βουλευτικὸν ὅρκον ὀμόσας [illegible, ~20 letters]. Erat enim Quingentorum Senatus, si cuiusquam, ab institutis patriis, & receptis Legibus, ne latum quidem vnguem discedere, vt qui inter primos in Solonis Leges iurarit. Plutarchus in Solone: [illegible, ~30 letters], primusque Leges, cum feruntur, approbet.
units.tr: Xenophon, in the first book of the Memorabilia, describing Socrates, writes: "for once when he was a member of the council and had sworn the councillor's oath..." For the Five Hundred Senate, if any, held firmly to the ancestral institutions and the received laws, not departing from them by a hair's breadth, since they were among the first to swear to the laws of Solon. Plutarch, in the Life of Solon, says that the Senate first approves the laws when they are proposed.

units.la: Tertium Caput legitur apud Demosthenem in Timocratea, cuius causas aperit ibidem Orator: [illegible, ~40 letters] ΟΥΔΕ ΔΗΣΩ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΥΔΕΝΑ. [illegible, ~50 letters]. Vlpianus: [illegible, ~50 letters]. Senatus igitur neminem vinciebat, nisi quos excipit iusiurandum: de quibus paulo post dicimus, Deo dante.
units.tr: The third clause is read in Demosthenes against Timocrates, whose grounds the orator sets out in the same place: "I will not bind any Athenian..." Ulpian: [the rest is illegible]. The Senate therefore bound no one, except those whom the oath excepts; of these we shall speak a little later, God willing.

units.la: Quartum iurisiurandi Caput a Philochoro defcriptum sequentia declarabunt.
units.tr: The fourth clause of the oath, described by Philochorus, will be made clear by what follows.

units.la: Quintum iurisiurandi Caput habetur apud Andocidem ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν ΜυστηΜυρηείων ἢ ϑ Βυλὴ αὐτὴ εἰ βυλεύοιτο, ἢ ἔμιστι; ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΔΕΧΟΜΑΙ ΕΝΔΕΙ-ΞΙΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΑΠΑΓΩΓΗΝ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΤΩΝ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΩΝ ΓΕΓΕΝΗΜΕ-ΝΩΝ, ΓΑΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΦΕΥΓΟΝΤΩΝ. Quod Kaput additum est, vt ex eodem Andocide constat, post exactos Triginta Tyrannos, cum τῆς μνησικακίας Lex sapientissimo consilio sanciretur.
units.tr: The fifth clause of the oath is found in Andocides, in the speech on the Mysteries: "Let the Council itself, if it deliberates, or the people..." [Ἡ βουλὴ αὐτὴ, εἰ βουλεύοιτο, ἢ ἔμιστι;] "And I will not accept an indictment, nor a summary arrest, on account of past offences, except against the fugitives." As Andocides makes clear, this clause was added after the Thirty Tyrants had been expelled, when the law on remembering past wrongs [τῆς μνησικακίας] was enacted by the wisest counsel.

units.la: Cùm penes Prytanes ius esset habendi Senatum, aut cogendi populum in concionem, si quid noui in Republica accidebat, Prytanibus referebatur, vt prouiderent indicto Senatu, vel concione: Quare deprehensum in re capitali Mnesilochum se Prytanibus delaturam denunciat nescio quae mulier apud Comicum Θεσμοφοριαζούσας,
units.tr: Since the Prytanes had the right to convene the Senate, or to summon the people to an assembly, whenever anything new happened in the state it was reported to the Prytanes, so that they could provide either by calling a Senate or an assembly. Hence, in Aristophanes' Thesmophoriazusae, a certain woman announces that she has caught Mnesilochus in a capital matter and will report him to the Prytanes:

units.la: ἐγὼ δὲ ταῦτα τοῖς Πρυτάνεσιν ἀγγελῶ.
units.tr: I will report these things to the Prytanes. [ἐγὼ δὲ ταῦτα τοῖς Πρυτάνεσιν ἀγγελῶ.]

units.la: Neque quisquam admittebatur petitor in Senatum, nisi ab his Prytanibus, quorum auaritiam carpit Comicus Εἰρήνῃ, vt qui gratis nullum admitteret, induciarum forensium nomen praetexentes: vulgo enim dicebant, ἐκκλησία ἐστὶν, ἡ δυναμένη τιμεῖν εἰσαγγέλλειν, etsi non tam amarent ἐκκλησίας, quam τοὺς ἐγγυητὰς τι ἐν τῆς χειρόν.
units.tr: Nor was any petitioner admitted into the Senate except through these Prytanes, whose greed Aristophanes attacks in the Peace, since they admitted no one for nothing, pretending the excuse of the court holidays. For they commonly said, "An assembly is that which can denounce a man who can pay," though they were not so much fond of assemblies as of the sureties [who paid] for them.

units.la: ἀλλ' ὢ πρυτάνεις δήλαδε πῶς ἡωεῖαν.
units.tr: But, Prytanes, how is it clearly...

units.la: ἐπ' ὡς προξύμως ὁ Πρυτάνεις πρεδίξατο.
units.tr: ...as the Prytanes will readily...

units.la: ἀλλ' οὐκ ἀν εἴ ἢ ταῦτα ἐκκαταγάγειν σ' ἔδει.
units.tr: ...but I should not have had to bring these things...

units.la: ἀλλ' ἔκεγι ἀν' σ' ἐκκεγίειν πῶ ἐκκλησίαν.
units.tr: ...but I have sent up an assembly...

units.la: Vetus Interpres, τοῖς Πρυτάνεσιν ἔθος ὢν προσαγαγεῖν τοὺς δημότας εἰς τὴν βουλήν. καὶ δῆλον ὅτι ἐδωσέχοιντο τῶδε τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τῶν γενομένων προσαγγελλεῖν. καὶ εἰ μὴ τῆς αὐτῆς ἐχρημάτιζε, προσ-ηγεῖμως συνεπέλαμβανοντο. Τοῖς δὲ προσπέφευγαν τοὺς ἐκκλησίας ἐκλεγεῖς ἐπὶ ἡ ἐκκλησία ἀποδοῦς προσσῶνον. δῆλος. Τοῖς πρυτάνεσιν ἔθος προσαγαγεῖν τοὺς δημότας προσόδου ἐπὶ τὴν βουλὴν, ἐδωσ-δοκοῦντο ὁ προσδιαβῆν δημότων. Ὁ δὲ ἐκκλησίαν ἀμφὶ μὲν ὡς προφασιζομένων ὅτι ἐκκλησία ἐστὶν, ἡ δυναμένη τιμεῖν προσαγγεῖν, καὶ μὴ προσαγόντων τῇ βουλῇ, καὶ μὴ ἐδωκοῦντων αὐτοῖς τῆς δημότας.
units.tr: The old interpreter: "It was the custom for the Prytanes to bring the citizens before the Senate." And it is clear that they were accustomed to report to the Senate what had happened in the assembly, and if they did not hold a session, they were promptly brought before the court. Those who had fled to the Senate were arrested on the ground that they were fleeing to the assembly, and the Prytanes did not bring them to the Council nor allowed them into the city. The Prytanes had the custom of bringing the citizens before the Council after the tribal assembly; they were accused of hiding the citizens. Those who were arrested pleaded that an assembly is that which can denounce a man who can pay, and they did not bring them to the Council, nor did they allow them the citizens.

units.la: Senatus quotidie habebatur, nisi dies esset ἀφεσις. Aristoteles ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ apud Harpocrationem & Suidam: εἰ Πρυτάνεις συνάγεσι τὴν Βουλὴν ὀσημέραι, πλὴν ἐαν τῆς ἀφέσιμος ἢ. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. IX. εἰ Πρυτάνεις ἔπι τὴν βουλὴν συνάγεσιν ὀσημέραι, πλὴν ἀν ἀφέσεως τῆς ἢ. Inter dies ἀφεσίμους, fuerunt festi, sed ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀθηναίων ἀγόντων ἐορτῶν, vt est in Lege de Festis: vnde, quod iam diximus, si quos nollent in Senatum admittere Prytaneis, dicebant, Senatum tunc non haberi, quia feriebantur: ἐκκλησία ἐστὶν, ἡ δυναμένη τιμεῖν προσαγγέλλειν.
units.tr: The Senate was held every day, unless the day was a holiday. Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, as cited by Harpocration and Suidas: "The Prytanes convene the Council every day, except on the holidays." Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: "The Prytanes convene the Council every day, unless it is a holiday." Among the holidays there were festivals, which the Athenians kept as public feasts, as stated in the law on festivals. Hence, as we have already said, if the Prytanes wished to exclude anyone from the Senate, they said that the Senate was not then being held, because it was a holiday: "An assembly is that which can denounce a man who can pay."

units.la: Nam τὴν ἐκκληρίαν ad ferias & muneris vacationem referendam puto: πρὸς τὰ ὁ ἑορτῇ ἀφειμένοι ἦσαν, vt legitur in veterum Commentariis, καὶ Θεσμοφορίων συνάγεται εἰς ἐκκλησίαν τῆς βουλῆς. Vnde est apud Demosthenem in Timocratea: ἡ ταῦτα ὄντων Κεφίσων ἀφ' ταῦτα ἀφειμένης τῆς βουλῆς. & paulò post: τῆς βουλῆς μὲν ἀφειμένης, τὴν δὲ δῆμον ἀφ' ἑορτῶν ἐορτίων ἀγόντων. Aristophanes Θεσμοφοριαζούσας.
units.tr: For I think that "the assembly" is to be referred to the holidays and the exemption from public duty, as is read in the old commentaries: "those who were released from duty for the festival," "and at the Thesmophoria the Council is convened to an assembly." Hence in Demosthenes' speech against Timocrates: "since the Council was released from these things" and a little later: "the Council being released, and the people keeping the festivals of the festivals." Aristophanes, Thesmophoriazusae:

units.la: καὶ πῶς; ἐπεὶ νῦν γ' ἂν τὰ δικαστήρια
units.tr: And how so? For now the law courts would not sit...

units.la: μὴ ἐκ δικάζει, ὅτι βουλῆς ἑαδ' ἔσται.
units.tr: ...since it will be a holiday for the Council.

units.la: ἐπεὶ πέντε Θεσμοφορίων ἢ μέσῃ.
units.tr: ...since it is the middle of the Thesmophoria.

units.la: Pfephismate autem cautum est, anno tertio Olympiadis centesimæ tertiæ, Cephisidoro Athenis Prætore, vt Senatus Quingentorum dies quinque feriaretur cum agebantur Apaturia.
units.tr: By a decree it was provided, in the third year of the one hundred and third Olympiad, when Cephisidorus was praetor at Athens, that the Senate of Five Hundred should keep holiday for five days while the Apaturia was celebrated.

units.la: ΦΩΚΟΣ ΕΙΠΕΝ · ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ Η ΒΟΥ-ΛΗ ΑΓΗ͂ ΤΑ ΑΓΑΤΟΥΡΙΑ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΑΛΛΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ. ΕΨΗΦΙΣΘΑΙ ΤΗ͂ ΒΟΥ-ΛΗ͂ ΑΦΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΒΟΥΛΕΥΤΑΣ ΤΑΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ, ΑΣΠΕΡ ΚΑΙ ΑΙ ΑΑ-ΛΑΙ ΒΟΥΛΑΙ ΔΙΑΦΙΕΝΤΑΙ, ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ, ΗΣ ΟΙ ΠΡΟΤΕΝΘΑΙ ΑΓΟΥΣΙ ΓΕΝΤΕ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ.
units.tr: Phocus said: "That the Senate shall celebrate the Apaturia with the other Athenians according to the ancestral customs. It was voted by the Council that the senators should be released on the days on which the other councils are released, from the day on which the Protenthae celebrate the festival." [ΦΩΚΟΣ ΕΙΠΕΝ· ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ ΑΓΗ ΤΑ ΑΠΑΤΟΥΡΙΑ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΑΛΛΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΙΑ. ΕΨΗΦΙΣΘΑΙ ΤΗ ΒΟΥΛΗ ἈΦΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΒΟΥΛΕΥΤΑΣ ΤΑΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ, ΩΣΠΕΡ ΚΑΙ ΑΙ ΑΛΛΑΙ ΒΟΥΛΑΙ ΔΙΑΦΙΕΝΤΑΙ, ΑΠΟ ΤΗΣ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ, ΗΣ ΟΙ ΠΡΟΤΕΝΘΑΙ ΑΓΟΥΣΙ ΓΕΝΕΤΕ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ.]

units.la: Phocus dixit: Senatus Apaturiorum festum agitet cum aliis Atheniensibus secundum instituta patria. Senatores feriantur tot diebus, per quot reliquæ curiæ vacant. quinque nempe diebus, ab eo quem Protenthæ celebrant.
units.tr: Phocus said: the Senate shall keep the Apaturia festival with the other Athenians, according to the ancestral customs. The senators shall be released for as many days as the other councils are released, namely five days, from the day on which the Protenthae keep their festival.

units.la: Senatusconsultum iftud eft, non in Areopago factum, vt volebat Vir Incomparabilis, fed in Senatu Quingentorum, qui fimpliciter ἡ βουλὴ appellatur: Pfephifma effe Senatus indicant ifta eius verba ΕΤΗΦΙΣΘΑΙ ΤΗ͂ ΒΟΥΛΗ. An vero poftea à populo ratum habitum fit Pfephifmate fuo, iuxta cuius ignarifsimus fcio: Tempus Pfephifmatis facti illud effe, quod diximus, indicat Athenæus Libro IV. [illegible, ~60 letters] ΦΩΚΟΣ ΕΙΠΕΝ, &c. Non ignoro Archontem eiusdem nominis fignafse Faltos anni fecundi Olympiadis centefimæ quartæ decimæ, fed magis inclino ad Archontem anni tertij Olympiadis centefimæ tertiæ. Hoc Pfephifmate decernitur, vt Senatus Quingentorum Apaturiorum feftum quinque agitet diebus, quot nimirum celebrabant Protenthæ. Apaturia tribus diebus propiè tranfigebatur: fed tamen fequens μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν dies, quam ἐπὶ τῷ dixerunt, etiam cum feftivitate peragebatur; colligo è Simplicio ad Lib. IV. Phyfic. Κυρίως δὲ [?] ἡ ἑορτὴ Απατουρίων, ὥσπερ ἡ Δορπία, καὶ ἡ Ἀναβρύσεως, καὶ ἡ Ἐπίδαυ[?]. item-que ex Hefychio, Απατούρια, ἑορτὴ Αθηναίων ἐπὶ πεντήκοντα ἡμέρας. ὧν ἡ μὲν ἑορτὴ Δορπία, ἡ δὲ Ἀναβρύσεως, ἡ πέμπτη, Κυρεὼς · ἡ πέμπτη, ἑορτὴ Ἐπίδαυ. Protenthæ vt verò, qui hoc maxime videntur celebraffe feftum, vt verba huius Pfephifmatis indicant, & indicio eft Philyllius in Hercule:
units.tr: This decree was not passed in the Areopagus, as that Incomparable man supposed, but in the Senate of Five Hundred, which is simply called the Council [ἡ βουλή]. That it is a decree of the Senate is shown by these words of it: "It was voted by the Council." Whether it was afterwards ratified by the people, I know not, and I am quite ignorant of it. The time of the decree is shown, as we have said, by Athenaeus in Book IV: [illegible] "Phocus said," etc. I am not unaware that an archon of the same name marks the year of the second year of the one hundred and fourteenth Olympiad, but I incline more to the archon of the third year of the one hundred and third Olympiad. By this decree it is ordained that the Senate of Five Hundred shall keep the festival of the Apaturia for five days, as many as the Protenthae celebrated. The Apaturia was properly completed in three days, but the following day, which they called the "day after" [μεθ' ἡμέραν], was also kept with festivity; I gather this from Simplicius on Book IV of the Physics. Likewise from Hesychius: "Apaturia, a festival of the Athenians lasting fifty days," of which the first was the Dorpia, the second the Anabrysis, the fifth Kyreotis... Protenthae, which seem especially to have kept this festival, as the words of this decree indicate, and as Philyllius in Hercules witnesses:

units.la: βύλεσθ᾽ δῆτ᾽ ἐγὼ φερέσω τίς εἰμ᾽ ἐγώ; / ὦ τῇ Πεγχαίων Δορπία καλυμβῶν.
units.tr: "Will you have me carry it? Who am I? O Dorpia, the cup-bearer of the Pengchaeans [βύλεσθ᾽ δῆτ᾽ ἐγὼ φερέσω τίς εἰμ᾽ ἐγώ; / ὦ τῇ Πεγχαίων Δορπία καλυμβῶν]."

units.la: feftum hoc vno die anteuertebant, quem etiam, vt ex hoc Pfephifmate liquet, genialiter & cum feftiuitate tranfigebant. Quare feftiuiffimus Ariftophanes ὡς ταὐτὸν Νεφέλαις, vno die praecurrere dicit effe Protenthiarum fungi officio: verba eius funt:
units.tr: They used to anticipate this festival by one day, and, as this decree makes clear, they kept it joyfully and with festivity. Hence the most festive Aristophanes, saying that it is the same as in the Clouds, says that the Protenthiae perform the office of running ahead by a single day. His words are:

units.la: πῶς δ᾽ ἡ Δήμητερ δῆτα τὴ ῥαμβοῖα / ἐφαλ᾽ ἰὼ (οὐ πρότερον) ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρα; / ὁ ὅτι εἶ Γεγθέτη (ἠ δὲ ὀδοῦσ᾽ μὴ πάχυς, / ἵ᾽ ὡς ἰδίχι τὰ Πρυτάνεων ἀφελαίας. / ἐφ᾽ ὅ ἐπὶ τὸν ἀνῳ ὑπὸ ἡμέρας μίαν.
units.tr: "But how, Demeter, shall I hurl the rhombos on the day itself, not before? Since you are Gegthetes, and your tooth is not thick, so that it is as though the Prytaneis' ... [πῶς δ᾽ ἡ Δήμητερ δῆτα τὴ ῥαμβοῖα / ἐφαλ᾽ ἰὼ (οὐ πρότερον) ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρα; / ὁ ὅτι εἶ Γεγθέτη (ἠ δὲ ὀδοῦσ᾽ μὴ πάχυς, / ἵ᾽ ὡς ἰδίχι τὰ Πρυτάνεων ἀφελαίας. / ἐφ᾽ ὅ ἐπὶ τὸν ἀνῳ ὑπὸ ἡμέρας μίαν.]"

units.la: Quinque igitur dies Apaturiorum feftô agitado impendebant Protenthæ, quot etiam à Senatoribus feriatos & feftos haberi voluit hoc Pfephifmate Phocus.
units.tr: Therefore the Protenthiae were occupied with keeping the five days of the Apaturia festival, which Phocus in this decree also wished the Senators to hold as holidays and feast days.

units.la: Accipiebant, de publico pecuniam Senatores, honorarium illius operæ, quâ Reipublicæ impendebat. Vlpianus in Timocratea: ὑ μόνοι οἱ ἱκετεύειν ἐλάμβανον μισθόν, ἀλλὰ τῇ βουλῇ. Honorariū hoc erat in diem drachma. Hefychius: βουλῆς λαχεῖν, ὃ λαχεῖν βουλευτὴν, καὶ ἀπαχμὴν τῆς ἡμέρας λαχεῖν.
units.tr: The Senators received a payment from the public treasury, a fee for that service by which they served the commonwealth. Ulpian in the Timocratea: "not only those who supplicated received a wage, but also the Council [ὑ μόνοι οἱ ἱκετεύειν ἐλάμβανον μισθόν, ἀλλὰ τῇ βουλῇ]." This fee was a drachma per day. Hesychius: "to draw a place in the Council, which is to be chosen as a councillor, and to draw the fee for the day [βουλῆς λαχεῖν, ὃ λαχεῖν βουλευτὴν, καὶ ἀπαχμὴν τῆς ἡμέρας λαχεῖν]."

units.la: Cùm Senatum ingressi essent Senatores, Iouì atque Minervæ sacra faciebant. Antiphon τὰς τῆς χρήσεως. Καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ Βουλευτηρίῳ Διὸς Βουλαίου, καὶ Αθηνᾶς Βουλαίας, ἐεφή ὅτι, καὶ εἰσιόντες οἱ βουλευταὶ ἐπεύχοντο. Hoc ipsum est, quod dixit Demosthenes εἰσπήγεια γὰρ τῆς βουλῆς ἱερωποίησαν. Extat locus ἐν τῷ κατὰ Μειδίου, ὡς ἐπαγγειλαμένος με Φόρου, καὶ Τιμοῦτα ἐπαγαγὼν, εἰσπήγεια γὰρ τῆς βουλῆς ἱερωποίησαν. Quibus è verbis colliges Demosthenem Senatorem approbatum, & munere illo functum fuisse, quanquam eum ἐν τῇ δοκιμασίᾳ caedis accusasset Midias. Quid sit ὃ εἰσπήγεια ἱερωποίησαν optime ad hunc locum interpretatur Vlpianus: εἰσπήγεια ἡ ἐκλήσιν, ἰδιώτης εἰσέναι τῆς βουλῆς εἰς ὃ βαλβτηρίον, ὡς κατὰ γνώμην ἀπόντων τῶν πεντακοσίων. Ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ εἰσπήγεια. Proscribebant autem Prytaneis, de quibusnam futura erat relatio in Senatu. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. IX. οἱ Πρυτάνεις προεγράφοντο τῆς βουλῆς, γὰρ ὧν δὴ ἡμέρας. Sumebant vna quotidie cibum Prytaneis singulis suae πρυτανείας diebus. Pollux Libro VIII. cap.XV. ἡ δῆλος, ἐν ᾗ σωσ-διήποιω ἐκάστης ἡμέρας, πεντήκοντα τῆς τῶν Πεντακοσίων βουλῆς, ἡ πρυτανεύουσα φυλή. Athenæus Libro V. σωσεδίηπνων ὁσημέραι εἰ αὐτοὶ Πρυτάνεις σωφρονα καὶ Σωτηρία τὴν πόλεων σωσήσαντα. Harpocration ex Ammonio Lampriensi: ὁ τόπος, ὅπου ἐστὶ σεληνίζονται οἱ Πρυτάνεις, καλεῖται Θόλος.
units.tr: When the Senators had entered the Senate, they performed sacrifices to Jupiter and Minerva. Antiphon, in his work on the use of [such things]: "And in the Council-house itself there is an altar of Zeus Boulaios and of Athena Boulaia, and the councillors, when entering, prayed." This is the very thing Demosthenes meant when he said: "for they consecrated the entrance of the Council [εἰσπήγεια γὰρ τῆς βουλῆς ἱερωποίησαν]." There is a passage in the speech Against Meidias, where he says that he was called up by Phormio and Timotheus was brought in, "for they consecrated the entrance of the Council." From these words you may gather that Demosthenes was approved as a Senator and had discharged that office, although Meidias had accused him in the scrutiny of his eligibility for the killing. What "the entrance" (eisperigeia) means, Ulpian explains very well at this point: "eisperigeia is the calling in, when a private citizen enters the Council at the ballot-box, as though the five hundred were absent and he were acting by decision. Entrance in the assembly." Moreover, they posted to the Prytaneis the matters about which a report was to be made in the Senate. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: "the Prytaneis were posted up before the Council, on the days in question." They took their meal together each day, the Prytaneis of each prytany on their own days. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter XV: "the hall in which the Prytaneis dined every day, the fifty of the Council of Five Hundred, the tribe presiding." Athenaeus, Book V: "the Prytaneis dined daily at public expense, as the saviours of the city." Harpocration, from Ammonius of Lampsacus: "the place where the Prytaneis are accustomed to dine is called the Tholos."

units.la: Quo autem ordine in Senatu sederent οἱ Πεντακόσιοι, sententiamque rogarentur, ac dicerent, quaerendum est. οἱ Πεντακόσιοι in decem classes distribuebantur: classis unaquaeque erat πεντήκοντα ἀνδρῶν ἀπὸ μιᾶς φυλῆς. Quinquaginta illi viri in sua classe singuli sedebant, & sententiam dicebant, nō confuse, ita, ex. gr. qui erat ex Aiantide Tribu sententiam dicebat in sua Aiantidis Tribu classe, non verò inter Senatores, qui erant ex Cecropide, aut Acamantide Tribu. Classes autem, non dubito sedisse, & sententiam dixisse pro eo ordine, quem forsàn ipso anni principio vnicuique attribuerat: ita principem locum obtinebat Tribus illa, quae tunc ἐπρυτάνευε: secundum locum occupabat (nisi post absolutam primam Prytaneiam, videtur enim sedisse post Tribum illam, cuius tunc erat Prytanea, atque ita eodem ordine deinceps) Tribus, cuius erat sequentis πρυτανείας imperium: atque ita deinceps prout ἐπρυτάνευον ἐκ Αἰγεῖδος ἀπὸ Ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἕξ φυλαὶ κλήρῳ λαχοῦσαι κατὰ ἑναυτόν. Quaestio nunc est, de ordine, quo sederent, sententiam rogarentur, & dicerent vniuscuiusque Tribus πεντήκοντα ἄνδρες, siue οἱ Πρυτάνεις. Quod vt intelligatur, sciendum est, & Τοὺς Πεδέδρους τῆς Πρυτανέων, & τὰς ἑνέα Πεδέδρους, ἀπὸ φυλῆς ἑκάστης ἕνα, πλὴν τῆς ἀρχυτανεύσεως, ceteris omnibus praefediile. Quod ad ceteros vero attinet, magna suspicio est habitam esse aetatis rationem, ita vt in vnaquaque Tribu primi sententiam dicerent, rogarenturque, qui aetate essent prouectiores; huc in re non dispari apud Plutarchum in Nicia: λέγεται ἢ ἐν τῇ Σπαρτικῇ ποτε βουλευόμεναι τὴν καινὴν τῆς σωφρονίας, κελεύεις ἵνα αὐτὸς ἔσῃς εἰπεῖν γνώμην Σοφοκλῆς ὁ ποιητὴς, ὡς ἀφιστάμενοι ἐν τῇ συστρατήγων. Itaetiam in Concione, pro aetatis ratione, primi, secundi, tertij, & ita deinceps, orationem habebant ad populū. Alius postea ordo est institutus, Glaucippo Atheniensi Praetore, hoc est, anno tertio Olympiadis nonagesimae secundae: is enim annus hunc habuit Praetorem, vt habent Diodorus Siculus & Anonymus in addicentur, & pretium patronis tribuetur. Leg. VI. §. I. D. de agnoscendis liberis. Mutauit postea ius istud, vt constat ex his Vlpiani verbis, Lib. IX. de Ossicio Proconsulis, in quibus habes poenas aduersus male meritos de Patronis Libertos sancitas. Sed si quidem inofficiosus patrono, patronae, liberisve eorum sit libertus, tantummodo castigari eum sub comminatione aliqua seueritatis non defuturae, si rursum causam querela praebuerit, & demitti oportet. Enim vero si contumeliam fecit, aut conuicium eis dixit, etiam in exilium temporale dari debebit. Quod si manus intulit, in metallum dandus erit. Idem, & si calumniam aliquam eis instruxit, vel delatorem subornauit, dummodo de patroni statu ei quaestionem non faceret, vel quam causam aduersus eos tentauit. Leg. I. D. de iure patronatus. Quid Vlpianus appellet hic castigari discere est è Modestino Lib. singulari de Manumissionibus, Interdum illa poena a liberto ingrato exiguntur, vel pars bonorum eius auferetur, & patrono datur, vel fustibus caeduntur, & ita absoluitur. Leg. VII. §. I. D. eod. Nempe castigari est fustibus caedi, quod idem Vlpianus dixit in hoc ipso argumento fustibus castigare. Leg. I. §. Cum Patronus. D. de officio Praefecti Vrbi. Subsecutis temporibus ex Constitutione Imperatorum Diocletiani & Maximiani A A. ad Veneriam, liberti, qui ingrati probantur, ad seruiendi necessitatem redigi possunt. Leg. XII. C. de operis Libertorum. Quod etiam obseruari voluit Constantinus, Lege data ad Maximum Praefectum Vrbi, filijs etiam, qui post retractum in seruitutem patrem nati fuerint, seruituris. Leg. II. C. de Libertis & eorum liberis. Idemque rescripsit aliquot post annis ad Concilium Byzacinorum, Leg. I. Cod. Theod. eod.
units.tr: In what order the Five Hundred sat in the Senate, and were asked for their opinion and spoke, is a question to be examined. The Five Hundred were divided into ten classes, each consisting of fifty men from a single tribe [πεντήκοντα ἀνδρῶν ἀπὸ μιᾶς φυλῆς]. Those fifty men sat individually in their own class and gave their opinion, not in confusion. Thus, for example, the man from the Aiantid tribe gave his opinion within his own Aiantid class, and not among the senators who came from the Cecropid or Acamantid tribe. I do not doubt that the classes also sat and gave their opinions in a fixed order, which was perhaps assigned to each at the very beginning of the year. So the tribe that was then presiding [ἐπρυτάνευε] held the first place, and the second place was occupied by the tribe whose turn in the next Prytany it was (unless it sat after the first Prytany was over, for it seems to have sat after the tribe whose Prytany it then was, and so in the same order thereafter). The rest followed in the order in which they presided [ἐπρυτάνευον], the six tribes, apart from Aegeis, taking their turns by lot, each for a day [ἐκ Αἰγεῖδος ἀπὸ Ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἕξ φυλαὶ κλήρῳ λαχοῦσαι κατὰ ἑναυτόν]. The question now is about the order in which the fifty men of each tribe, or the Prytanes, sat, were asked for their opinion, and spoke. To understand this, it must be known that the Proedri [Πρόεδροι] of the Prytanes, and the nine Proedri, one from each tribe, except the tribe then presiding, presided over all the others. As for the rest, there is strong suspicion that account was taken of age, so that in each tribe those who were older were asked for their opinion first and spoke first. Plutarch in the life of Nicias says something not unlike this: it is said that once, when the Spartans were deliberating about the new peace, they ordered Sophocles the poet to give his opinion first, as he was one of the generals [λέγεται ἢ ἐν τῇ Σπαρτικῇ ποτε βουλευόμεναι τὴν καινὴν τῆς σωφρονίας, κελεύεις ἵνα αὐτὸς ἔσῃς εἰπεῖν γνώμην Σοφοκλῆς ὁ ποιητὴς, ὡς ἀφιστάμενοι ἐν τῇ συστρατήγων]. So also in the Assembly, the first, second, third and so on spoke to the people in order of age. Later another order was instituted, under Glaucippus the Athenian Praetor, that is, in the third year of the ninety-second Olympiad, for that year had him as Praetor, as Diodorus Siculus and the anonymous writer agree. addicentur, & pretium are assigned to the patrons tribuetur. Leg. VI. §. I. D. de agnoscendis liberis. Later he changed that law, as is clear from these words of Ulpian, Lib. IX. de Officio Proconsulis, in which you will find penalties enacted against freedmen who have behaved badly towards their patrons. But if a freedman has been disrespectful to his patron, patroness, or their children, he is to be punished only, under some threat of severity that will not be lacking, if he again gives cause for complaint, and he ought to be dismissed. Indeed, if he has done an insult or spoken abuse against them, he must also be given temporary exile. If he has laid hands on them, he is to be given to the mines. The same applies if he has contrived some false accusation against them, or suborned an informer, provided he did not thereby raise an inquiry into the patron's status, or attempt some action against them. Leg. I. D. de iure patronatus. What Ulpian means here by castigari (to be punished) is learned from Modestinus, in his single book On Manumissions: Sometimes that penalty is exacted from an ungrateful freedman, or part of his goods is taken away and given to the patron, or he is beaten with rods and so released. Leg. VII. §. I. D. eod. Clearly to be punished is to be beaten with rods, which the same Ulpian called in this very context castigating with rods. Leg. I. §. Cum Patronus. D. de officio Praefecti Vrbi. In later times, by a constitution of the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Augusti, to Veneria, freedmen who are proved ungrateful can be reduced to the necessity of serving. Leg. XII. C. de operis Libertorum. Constantine also wished this to be observed, by a law given to Maximus, Prefect of the City, that children also who were born after their father had been brought back into slavery should be slaves. Leg. II. C. de Libertis & eorum liberis. And some years later he wrote the same rescript to the council of the Byzacenes, Leg. I. Cod. Theod. eod.

units.la: In hac aduersus Libertos Ἀπραξίου actione Lege licebat cuiuis μαρτυρῆσαι, siue is esset ciuis, siue peregrinus.
units.tr: Under this law, in the action of Apraxius against freedmen, anyone was allowed to give evidence, whether he was a citizen or a foreigner.

units.la: Ἐξῆναι ὅτι πάσης γραφῆς τῆς τοῦ Ἀπραξίου διαμαρτυρῆσαι τῷ βουλομένῳ ὁμοίως τὴν ξέ-νων καὶ τὴν ἐπιχωρίων.
units.tr: It was permitted in every indictment of Apraxius for anyone who wished to bear witness against it, equally the foreigner and the citizen [Ἐξῆναι ὅτι πάσης γραφῆς τῆς τοῦ Ἀπραξίου διαμαρτυρῆσαι τῷ βουλομένῳ ὁμοίως τὴν ξέ-νων καὶ τὴν ἐπιχωρίων].

units.la: Cui libuerit, siue peregrino, siue ciui, testimonij dicto esto in actionibus Apraxiou ad exceptionem.
units.tr: Whoever wished, whether a foreigner or a citizen, let him be allowed to give evidence in the actions of Apraxius, as an exception.

units.la: Licebat igitur cuiuis testimonium dicere, in hac aduersus Libertos actione, antequam iudicium redderetur, ὡς εἰσαγώγιμός ἐστιν ἡ δίκη, ἡ οὐκ εἰσαγώγιμος.
units.tr: Anyone therefore was allowed to give evidence in this action against freedmen, before judgment was pronounced, whether the case was admissible to be brought [ὡς εἰσαγώγιμός ἐστιν ἡ δίκη] or not [ἡ οὐκ εἰσαγώγιμος].

units.la: Hyperides apud Harpocrationem: Ὑπερίδης ἐν τῷ κατ᾽ Ἀπραξίου δίκῃ φησίν, ὡς οἱ νόμοι κελεύουσι διαμαρτυρῆσαι τῷ βουλομένῳ, ὁμοίως τὴν ξένων, καὶ τὴν ἐπιχωρίων, μήποτ᾽ οὖν ἐὰν μὴ τῆς τοῦ Ἀπραξίου δίκης κεκώλυται διαμαρτυρῆσαι οἱ ξένοι, ἐὰν δὲ τῆς τοῦ Ἀπραξίου κεκώλυται.
units.tr: Hyperides in Harpocration: Hyperides, in his speech against Apraxius, says that the laws order that anyone who wishes may give evidence, equally foreigners and citizens. Therefore, if foreigners are not prevented from giving evidence in the case of Apraxius, they are prevented from giving evidence in the case of Apraxius [Ὑπερίδης ἐν τῷ κατ᾽ Ἀπραξίου δίκῃ φησίν, ὡς οἱ νόμοι κελεύουσι διαμαρτυρῆσαι τῷ βουλομένῳ, ὁμοίως τὴν ξένων, καὶ τὴν ἐπιχωρίων, μήποτ᾽ οὖν ἐὰν μὴ τῆς τοῦ Ἀπραξίου δίκης κεκώλυται διαμαρτυρῆσαι οἱ ξένοι, ἐὰν δὲ τῆς τοῦ Ἀπραξίου κεκώλυται].

units.la: Census autem Libertorum habebatur, an plenam consecuti essent libertatem. Nonnus in Nazianzeni φιλοπτωχικῷ priorem. ἐκάλυσε δὲ τοὺς Ἀσωίους καὶ τοῖς ἀπλοῖς λόγοις, τόσοι γὰρ καὶ οὗτοι πάσης τοὺς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐλευθερίας. καὶ οὐτινὰς δὲ ἐκείνοντο, καὶ ἐδοκιμάζοντο, εἰ ὅλως ἀληθῶς ἐλευθερώθησαν. ea scilicet fini, vt si plenam esse consecuti libertatem censerentur, ab iis ᾱ μισθῶν, quod publico pendebant aerario, exigeretur.
units.tr: A census of freedmen was also taken, to see whether they had attained full freedom. Nonnus, on the earlier part of Nazianzen's Philoptochicus: he examined the Jews and the simple folk with plain words, for these too were of the same kind as those in full freedom; and they were summoned and tested, to see whether they had been wholly and truly set free [ἐκάλυσε δὲ τοὺς Ἀσωίους καὶ τοῖς ἀπλοῖς λόγοις, τόσοι γὰρ καὶ οὗτοι πάσης τοὺς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐλευθερίας. καὶ οὐτινὰς δὲ ἐκείνοντο, καὶ ἐδοκιμάζοντο, εἰ ὅλως ἀληθῶς ἐλευθερώθησαν]. The purpose, of course, was that if they were judged to have attained full liberty, they should be charged the fee which they paid to the public treasury.

units.la: Inter seruos censebatur is, qui redemptus ex hostibus, redimias non persoluisset redemptori suo, cui seruitutem seruiebat dum id praestitisset, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Among slaves was counted the man who, having been ransomed from enemies, had not paid his ransom to the one who redeemed him. Until he had made that payment he served that redeemer as a slave, under this law:

units.la: Τοῦ λυτρωθέντος ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων εἴη τὸν λύτρα, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποδῷ λύτρα.
units.tr: Let the one ransomed from the enemies belong to the one who ransomed him, if he does not pay the ransom. [Τοῦ λυτρωθέντος ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων εἴη τὸν λύτρα, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποδῷ λύτρα.]

units.la: Redemptus ex hostibus illius esto, qui redemit, nisi redimias ipse persoluerit.
units.tr: Let the one ransomed from the enemies belong to the one who ransomed him, unless he himself has paid the ransom.

units.la: Legem habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ πρὸς Νικίαρχον. εἶτα δ' ἔφη, ὅτι χρὴ οἱ νόμοι κελεύουσι, τὸν λυσαμένου[?] ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων ἐᾶν τὸν λυθέντα, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποδῷ λύτρα[?]. Captiui autem redimi non poterant, nisi à Legatis. Anony-mus in Argumento Orationis Demosthenicæ περὶ παραπρεσβείας. ἀπελθὼν γὰρ εἰς τὴν πόλιν πρεσβείᾳ[?], ὅτι ἐν Μακεδονίᾳ τινὰς τῶν Ἀθηναίων αἰχμαλώτους[?], καὶ ἐπέχειν Φέρῃ[?] ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας [illegible, ~3 letters] καὶ ῥύσασθαι αὐτούς, ἐπὶ ἠδύνατο δὲ τὴν ποινὴν[?], εἰ μὴ ἐν πρεσβείᾳ παρεσθῆτο[?].
units.tr: You have the law in Demosthenes, in the speech against Nicias. Then he said that the laws order that the one who ransomed someone from the enemies should keep the one ransomed, if he does not pay the ransom. [Demosthenes' speech against Nicias, as printed.] Captives, however, could not be ransomed except through envoys. The anonymous writer of the argument to Demosthenes' speech On the False Embassy says that he went to the city on an embassy, because some of the Athenians were captives in Macedonia, and that he was able to bring them back and rescue them from his own [funds], but he could not do so unless he had been sent on an embassy.

units.la: Seruum autem otiosum atque inertem alere Leges non sinebant: Μὴ ἐξεῖναι [?] δοῦλον ἀργὸν τρέφειν οἰκέτην.
units.tr: The laws did not, however, allow a man to keep an idle and unemployed slave: it was not permitted to keep a slave who did nothing. [Μὴ ἐξεῖναι δοῦλον ἀργὸν τρέφειν οἰκέτην.]

units.la: Legem habes apud Vlpianum in Midianam: ἐπεὶ ἐξὸν τῶν Ἀθηναίοις δοῦλον τρέφειν οἰκέτην· ὅτι οἱ μὲν, αὐλοποιοὶ, οἱ δὲ, μαχαιροποιοὶ εἶχον τῶν δούλων. Serui igitur aliquam artem sciebant, quam exercebant.
units.tr: You have the law in Ulpian on Demosthenes' speech Against Midias: since it was permitted for the Athenians to keep a household slave, some of them were flute-makers and others sword-makers, and they had slaves for this work. [ἐπεὶ ἐξὸν τῶν Ἀθηναίοις δοῦλον τρέφειν οἰκέτην· ὅτι οἱ μὲν, αὐλοποιοὶ, οἱ δὲ, μαχαιροποιοὶ εἶχον τῶν δούλων.] Slaves therefore knew some craft, which they practised.

units.la: LIBER TERTIVS. DE SENATV QVINGENTORVM ET CONCIONE.
units.tr: BOOK THREE. CONCERNING THE COUNCIL OF FIVE HUNDRED AND THE ASSEMBLY.

units.la: TITVLVS PRIMVS.
units.tr: TITLE I.

units.la: CUM eruditissime à praestantissimis viris de Quingentorum Senatu disputatum sit, ne, quod aiunt, actum agere videamur, pauca tantum delibabimus, quae omnino necessaria sunt ad hunc, quem de illo Senatu instituimus, sermonem.
units.tr: Since the Council of Five Hundred has been discussed most learnedly by the most distinguished men, I will not, as the saying goes, be doing what has already been done. I will touch on only a few points, those that are wholly necessary for the discussion of that Council which we are undertaking here.

units.la: Constituit Solon, ut quotannis summae praeesset Reipublicae Quadringentorum Senatus, non ducto e variis ordinibus numero, quod olim volebat Plato Lib. VI. de Legibus, id quippe denegatum Solonis Legibus [illegible, ~12 letters] vt in hunc Senatum allegerentur: [illegible, ~30 letters], neque postea quoque, aucto numero, concessum, sed e quatuor Tribubus. Plutarchus in Solone: [illegible, ~40 letters] Quadringentis facti sunt Quingenti Senatores, qui dicti sunt [illegible, ~10 letters] βουλὴ, aut οἱ Πεντακόσιοι. Ex vnaquaque enim Tribu quinginti viri sorte ducebantur: [illegible, ~25 letters], inquit Vlpianus in Androtianam, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Sortiebantur autem, qui aetate essent Senatoria. Libanius in Hypothesi Androtianae: [illegible, ~35 letters].
units.tr: Solon established that the Council of Four Hundred should preside over the commonwealth each year. The members were not drawn from the various orders, as Plato wished in Book VI of the Laws; that method was not allowed by Solon's laws [...] so that they should be chosen for this Council [...]. Nor was it granted afterwards, even when the number was increased, but the members were drawn from the four tribes. Plutarch, in his Life of Solon: [...] From the Four Hundred were made the Five Hundred Senators, who were called [...] the council [βουλή], or "the Five Hundred" [οἱ Πεντακόσιοι]. For fifty men were drawn by lot from each tribe [...], says Ulpian on the Androtion, [...]. Those who were of senatorial age were the ones who drew lots. Libanius, in the Argument to the Androtion: [...].

units.la: Aetatem Senatoriam definitam fuisse puto anno tricesimo: Oportet namque tot annos natum fuisse ludicem, vt constat ex Heliastarum iureiurando: ΚΑΙ ΓΕΓΟΝΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΛΑΤΤΟΝ Η ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΗ. Quingenti autem hi etiam inter iudices: nam vere Plato Lib. VI. de Legibus, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Praeterea hoc Senatu moti poterant forte capi in iudices, vt legimus in Graecorum Commentariis [illegible, ~45 letters]. Non potuissent autem, nisi annos minimum triginta nati: & vnus e Tyrannis Triginta Charicles Socrati apud Xenophontem ἀπομνημονευμάτων Lib. I. ἔστω, εἶπε, χρήσου βουλεύῃ οὐκ ἐξεστιν, ὡς ὕπα Φορμίωνος ἔτι μηδὲ οὐ δηλέξου νεωτέρου πεπαιδευμένα ἐστί. [?]
units.tr: I think the senatorial age was fixed at thirty years. For a man must have been that old to be a judge, as is clear from the oath of the jurors: "and that I have been not less than thirty years old" [καὶ γέγονα οὐκ ἔλαττον ἢ τριάκοντα ἔτη]. These Five Hundred were also among the judges, for Plato truly says in Book VI of the Laws [...]. Moreover, men who had been moved by this Council could perhaps be taken as judges, as we read in the Greek commentaries [...]. But they could not have been so chosen unless they were at least thirty years old. And one of the Thirty Tyrants, Charicles, said to Socrates in Xenophon's Memorabilia Book I: "Let it be," he said, "you are not permitted to deliberate [...], since you have been educated by Phormio... younger [...]. [?]

units.la: Denique Demosthenes in Midiana scribit se ante annum aetatis tricesimum secundum βουλεύειν λαχεῖν, id est, anno aetatis tricesimo primo, qui incidit in annum secundum Olympiadis centesimae sextae, Praetore Athenis Callistrato. Nam vero Plutarchus confert natalem Demosthenis in annum quartum Olympiadis nonagesimae octavae, Dexitheo Athenis Praetore: Neque enim audiendi sunt Dionysius Halicarnasseus & Anonymus in Descriptione Olympiadum, qui adscribunt anno quarto Olympiadis nonagesimae nonae, qui Archontem habuit Demophilum: atque horum sententiam sirmari posse putat Vir eruditissimus Demosthenis ipsius verbis Oratione II. aduersus Stephanum: ὁ δ' πατὴρ ἐπιπελέσθαι τῷ Δυσικίππου Ἀρχοντος. ὁ δὲ Φορμίων Ἀλλωνος ἐλθεῖτο, ὅτι Νικοδήμου Ἀρχοντος, δεκάτῳ ἔτει ἐτέρου, ἢ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν. Emendat Vir C L. ὅτι Νικοφήμου, idque optime, sed male inde probare nititur sententiam Dionysij: Nam ista dicuntur, sive potius scribuntur ab oratore Demosthene, non de Demosthene patre, & aetate sua, sed ex Apollodori, cui hanc Orationem scripserat, persona, de Pasione patre: & proculdubio vera est gravissimi scriptoris Plutarchi sententia, cuius vindicem dabimus & assertorem Demosthenem, qui scribit ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ὀνήτορος ἐξουλάνς Aphobum tutorem suum extremo anno Praeturae Polyzeli in vxorem duxisse Onetoris sororem: ἐγήματο μὲν γὰρ ὅτι Πολυζήλου Ἀρχοντος Σκιρφοφειῶς μιλώς. Polyzeli Praetura incidit in annum secundum Olympiadis centesimae tertiae, vt est videre apud Diodorum Siculum, Anonymumque in Descriptione Olympiadum, Cephisodoro, qui Polyzelum excepit, Archonte, Aphobum male administratae tutelae accusauit, qui annus erat tertius Olympiadis centesimae tertiae, cum in viros esset adscriptus, & iam sui iuris, vt legitur ibidem: ἐγὼ δ' ἀξὺς μὴ τοὺς γάμους, αὐτὴν εἰς δεκαμαστῆς, ἐκεκλόσω. Atqui in viros tantum adscribebantur, anno aetatis vicesimo, vt in superioribus diximus, circa Hecatombaeonis initia, quare dixit Demosthenes, ἐγὼ μὴ τοὺς γάμους δύὴρ εἰς δεκαμαστῆς. Extremo enim Polyzeli anno sororem Onetoris duxerat in vxorem Aphobus: hunc Polyzelum in Praetura excepit Cephisodorus, quo iam Archonte δεκαμαστῆς in viros est transscriptus noster Demosthenes: Neque ante hanc aetatem actionem δίκης instituere poterat, vt qui sua ante annum aetatis vicesimum administrare non posset: vnde in Graecorum commentariis legimus, ἐξαφέντες εἰς ἀνδρας ἐλαχον δίκην ἐπὶ ἔξω. Anno autem primo Olympiadis centesimae quartae, Praetore Athenis Timocrate, iudicium est adeptus aduersus Aphobum. Demosthenes ibidem: ἐλαχον δὲ τὴν δίκην ἐπὶ ἔξω ἐπὶ Τιμοκράτους. Non igitur conferendus est natalis Demosthenis in annum quartum Olympiadis nonagesimae nonae, sed potius in annum quartum Olympiadis nonagesimae octauae. Atque haec obiter de anno natali Demosthenis, cui cum tam multa debeamus, non potuimus non praestare hanc eius aetati illustrandae operam: sed e diuerticulo in viam. Scribit Demosthenes in Midiana, se in Quingentorum Senatum forte captum fuisse, antequam hanc Orationem scriberet. καὶ πελευτῶν βουλεύειν μὲν λαχόντος, δὲ καὶ ἀξιοῦντος κατηγορεῖν. Orationem scripsit annos natus triginta duos: [illegible, ~60 letters] Quare anno ætatis tricesimo, aut tricesimo primo, Demosthenes cooptatus est in Quingentorum Senatum: & cum in illius vitam inquireretur, accusauit eum Midias: an Senatu motus fuerit Demosthenes, ipse de se non dicit, neque verisimile est: nam Æschines, qui æqua iniqua illi exprobrare ludum iocúmque putat, obijcere ei non prætermisisset. imo omnino verum non est. Qui semel in Senatum fuerat cooptatus, poterat rursum non ita multo post legi in eundem: constat id exemplo Demosthenis: nam, vt iam diximus, Senator forte captus est, siue anno primo Olympiadis centesimæ sextæ, Elpino Archonte, siue anno sequenti, qui fuit secundus eiusdem Olympiadis centesimæ sextæ, Callistrato Athenis Prætore, quod verius puto, & nonnisi anno tricesimo peracto in hunc Senatum adscribi potuisse Senatores. Iterum idem Demosthenes anno secundo Olympiadis centesimæ octauæ, Themistocle Archonte, Senator factus est. Æschines [illegible, ~70 letters]
units.tr: Finally, Demosthenes writes in the Midias that before his thirty-second year he was "allotted to deliberate" [βουλεύειν λαχεῖν], that is, in his thirty-first year, which fell in the second year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad, when Callistratus was Praetor at Athens. But Plutarch places the birth of Demosthenes in the fourth year of the ninety-eighth Olympiad, when Dexitheus was Praetor at Athens. Nor should we listen to Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the anonymous author of the Description of the Olympiads, who assign it to the fourth year of the ninety-ninth Olympiad, when Demophilus was Archon. The opinion of these men, a most learned man thinks, can be confirmed by the words of Demosthenes himself in his second Oration against Stephanus: "My father died in the archonship of Diocles... Phormio came of age in the archonship of Nicodemus, in the tenth year after... our father died." The learned editor emends this to "Nicophemus," and does so rightly, but he wrongly strives from this to support the opinion of Dionysius. For these words are spoken, or rather written, by the orator Demosthenes, not about Demosthenes the father and his own age, but in the person of Apollodorus, for whom he had written this Oration, and concern the father Pasion. Without doubt the view of the most weighty writer Plutarch is true, and we will give Demosthenes as its defender and champion. He writes in the Oration against Onetor that Aphobus, his guardian, married the sister of Onetor in the last year of the Praetorship of Polyzelus: "For he married her in the archonship of Polyzelus, in the month of Scirophorion." The Praetorship of Polyzelus fell in the second year of the hundred and third Olympiad, as can be seen in Diodorus Siculus and the anonymous author of the Description of the Olympiads. Under Cephisodorus, who succeeded Polyzelus as Archon, Aphobus was accused of badly administered guardianship. That was the third year of the hundred and third Olympiad, when our Demosthenes had been enrolled among the men and was already his own master, as is read in the same place: "But I, when I had been enrolled among the men [...], brought the suit." For men were enrolled only in their twentieth year, as we said above, around the beginning of Hecatombaeon. That is why Demosthenes said "when I was enrolled among the men." For Aphobus had married the sister of Onetor in the last year of Polyzelus, and Cephisodorus succeeded Polyzelus in office; under his archonship our Demosthenes was transferred into the men's roll. Nor could he bring a legal action before this age, since a man who could not manage his own affairs before his twentieth year could not sue. So in the Greek commentaries we read: "Having been enrolled among the men, they brought the suit..." In the first year of the hundred and fourth Olympiad, when Timocrates was Praetor at Athens, he obtained a judgment against Aphobus. Demosthenes says in the same place: "I brought the suit in the time of Timocrates." Therefore the birth of Demosthenes should not be placed in the fourth year of the ninety-ninth Olympiad, but rather in the fourth year of the ninety-eighth. These remarks on the birth year of Demosthenes, to whom we owe so much, I could not avoid making in order to illuminate his age, but this is a side path rather than the road. Demosthenes writes in the Midias that he was perhaps taken into the Council of Five Hundred before he wrote this Oration: "and when he was allotted to deliberate, and he thought fit to accuse..." He wrote the Oration at the age of thirty-two [...]. Therefore Demosthenes was enrolled in the Council of Five Hundred in his thirtieth or thirty-first year, and when his life was being investigated, Midias accused him. Whether Demosthenes was moved from the Senate he does not say himself, nor is it likely, for Aeschines, who thought it sport and a joke to reproach him with fair and unfair things, would not have let this pass. Indeed, it is altogether untrue. A man who had once been enrolled in the Senate could be chosen again into the same body not long afterwards. This is shown by the example of Demosthenes. For, as we have said, he was perhaps taken as Senator either in the first year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad, under the archonship of Elpinus, or in the following year, the second of the same hundred and sixth Olympiad, when Callistratus was Praetor at Athens. I think the latter is more likely, and that Senators could be enrolled in this Council only once they were thirty years old. Again, in the second year of the hundred and eighth Olympiad, under the archonship of Themistocles, Demosthenes was made a Senator once more. Aeschines [...].

units.la: Interuallum est à priori fortuitone ad posteriorem annorum octo. Non tantum autem forte ducebantur Quinquaginta ex vnaquaque Tribu viri, sed etiam præter eos, quinquaginta alij succidanei, in hunc finem, vt si primi illi Quinquaginta forte lecti, aut ex illis vnus aliquis, vel probaretur minus, vel intra suæ [illegible, ~12 letters] annum moreretur, in illorum locum sufficerentur isti, quibus sors obuenerat, ita exponunt proxime laudatum Æschinis locum Grammatici é Platonis Comici Hyperbolo. [illegible, ~80 letters]
units.tr: The interval from the former lot to the latter is eight years. Moreover, not only were fifty men drawn by lot from each tribe, but also fifty others as substitutes, for this purpose: if those first fifty chosen by lot, or any one of them, were found less fit, or died within his year, these others to whom the lot had fallen should be put in their place. The grammarians explain in this way the passage of Aeschines cited above, and the words of the comic poet Plato in Hyperbolus. [...]

units.la: Admittebantur in hunc Senatum etiam adscripti ciues, vt è Lege [illegible, ~15 letters] colligere est, vnde Demosthenes [illegible, ~20 letters] Neaj-ges de Apollodoro adscripto ciue: [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: Enrolled citizens were also admitted into this Council, as can be gathered from the law [...], whence Demosthenes [...] Neaera [...] concerning Apollodorus, an enrolled citizen [...].

units.la: Sortitio hæc fiebat quatuor vltimis diebus de trecentis quinquaginta quatuor anni Lunaris. Vlpianus in Androtianam: [illegible, ~90 letters]
units.tr: This drawing of lots was made in the last four days of the three hundred and fifty-four days of the lunar year. Ulpian on the Androtion: [...].
