Aristoteles de Republica Athenienfium: ἀπεψηφίσατο ἡ τῶν χειροτονιῶν, (ita rescribendum puto, id est, ἀποψήφισε) ἐκκλησίαν, ἐν ᾗ ἐδὲ τὰς ἀρχὰς ἐπιχειροτονεῖν, οἱ (forte εἰ) ἐδόκουν μὴ καλῶς ἀρχειν. Suidas multum variat ab vsu vocis ἐπιχειροτονίας, itaque vix dubito reponendum esse ἐπιχειροτονία, vbi morem καταχειροτονίας describit. Καταχειροτονία ἢ ἐπιχειροτονία (melius, vti iam diximus ἐπιχειροτονίας, (ἀφ-ερέ). Καταχειροτονία γὰρ ἐγίνετο ὅτως. ἐλεγὼ ὁ κῆρυξ· ὅταν Μέλιας δοκῇ ἀδικεῖν, ἀφέτω τὴν χεῖρα. εἶπα οἱ θέλοντες ἐξέπινον τὰς χεῖρας. καὶ ἐκάλειτο τοῦτο ἀφεῖναι Καταχειροτονία, ἀπαχειροτονία (γ. ἐπιχειροτονία) δὲ ὅτως, ὅταν μὴ δοκῇ ἀδικεῖν Μέλιας, ἀφέτω τὴν χεῖρα, καὶ ἐξέπεινον τινές, καὶ ἐκάλειτο τοῦτο ἀπαχειροτονία. (γ. ἐπιχειροτονία,) λοιπὸν πάσας ἡσθμεῶν τὰς χεῖρας, καὶ εὐθὺς ὁ κῆρυξ ποίαν πλείους εἰσὶ, πότερον τῶν Φασκόντων αὐτὸν ἀδικεῖν (ἐπὶ μὴ, καὶ ὅσαι αὐ ἠσθμ πλείους ἀρεθήσαν, ἐκ] (mallem ἐκεῖνη) τῆ ἡ γνώμη ἐκφέρει. Fiebat tamen aliquando, vt populus, quos ciurare Magistratum & abdicare suo scito iusserat, iuberet iterum Magistratum gerere. Habes exemplum apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ κατὰ Θεοφρίνη. ἀδελφὸς αὐτῷ Θεσμοθέτης, καὶ ταῦτα χρώμενος συμβάλλω, ὅτι οὐδὲς ἔδεξε παρ᾽ ὑμῖν ἀὐδεφος[?] ἵ), ὡς ἡ μόνον αὐτὸς ἀπαχθέσται τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν[?] ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν ἀπέσβη ἐπὶ[?] εἰμὶ δὲ αὐτῷ[?], καὶ ἱκετεύοντας, καὶ λέγοντας, ὡς οὐκ ἐπί[?] Θεοχρίνης [?] ἀρχῆ, ἐπὶ ἡμᾶς καὶ πάλιν ἀπέδοτε τοῖς ἐφέσεως αὐτοῖς. Qui Magistratu mouebantur, etiam apud iudices causam dicere cogebantur. Pollux: τὸν δὲ ἀποχρέ[?]-οντ[?] χρῆσθαι. Harpocration: ἔτος ὧν Ἀθηναι[?] τῆς Ἀργέντων, καὶ ἐν τῇ συνοφάντῃ προσέχοντας ὡς τῷ δήμῳ ἡδεῖαν. Εἰ δὲ ἡς καταχρεσπάνται, ὅπως εἰσιέναι εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον. Alterum Legis Kaput cauet de referendis à Magistratu rationibus apud Scribam & Logistas. Hi Legistae Magistratus erant forte capti, decem numero, apud quos rationes gesti sui Magistratus referebant οἱ ὡς ἀρχῇ intra triginta ab abdicato Magistratu dies. Auctor Etymologici: Λογισταὶ Ἀρχοντες εἰσὶ χειροτονηταὶ δίκας, ἐφ᾽ ὧν πόλιτις οἱ ἀρξαντες ἀρχῇ[?] λίαν, λόγον ἀπίφεσιν τῆς διοικήσεως. Harpocration: Λογισταὶ ἀρχαὶ ἐς Ἀθηναίοις ἐστι καλούμεθα. Εἰσὶ δὲ τὸν ἀριθμὸν δίκας, οἱ ταῖς ἐνθωμένας τῆς διοικήσεων συλλογίζονται ἐν ἡμέραις τειχίσαντες, ὅταν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς ἀποδῶσιν οἱ Ἀρχοντες. Ad hos Legistas non potest referri Pollucis locus libro VIII. cap. IX. δύο δὲ ἦσαν Λογισταὶ, ὁ μὲν τῆς βουλῆς, ὁ δὲ τῆς δικαιότητος, καὶ ταύτης ἐν βουλῇ χειροτονεῖ καταρχήν, ὡς ἀπαγορεύουσιν τοῖς δικασταῖς. Nam diuersi hi Logistae Pollucis ab illis, de quibus iam dictum ex Harpocratione, primum, numero, decem enim illi sunt, hi vero Pollucis, duo, deinde, munere: nam apud illos referebantur rationes: hi affectabantur tantum τοῖς δικαιοῦ[?]ς, & videbant, ne qua fraus fieret, tum à Senatu Quingentorum, cum ab iis omnibus, ἐσει ἀφαιρεῖσθαι τῆς τῆς πόλεως, aut etiam aliquam Reipublicae nauant operam. Verum horum Λογισῶν ταῦτα λόγος in hac Lege, sed illorum tantum decem, οἱ ταῖς ἀθωίας τῆς διοικήσεων συλλογίζονται. De quibus quaeritur an iidem sint cum τοῖς Εὐθύνοις. Eoldem esse negabat Aristoteles ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ, apud Harpocrationem: διὰ λέκτου ταῖς Λογισῶν Αἰσχυτίλης ἐν τῇ Πολιτείᾳ, ἔνθα δείκνυσιν ὅτι ἀφαιρεῖται τῆς Εὐθύνων. At vero Auctor Etymologici putat eosdem fuisse τοῖς Εὐθύνοις cum Logistis: Εὔθυνοι, δίκασται, ἀθῶται οἱ ἡμεῖς Λογισταὶ λέγομεν. Sed rursus est fidem habere Aristoteli, qui etiam horum meminit Polit. Libro VI. cap. vlt. ἐπὶ δὲ ἐνίας τῆς ἀρχῶν, εἰ καὶ μὴ πᾶσαν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι πολλὰ τῆς χειρῶν, αἰσχρὸν ἐπέραν εἰς τὸ λογιστικὸν λογισμόν, καὶ ἀποσυνθωσ[?] αὐτῷ μηδὲν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι ἐπερ. καλοῦσι δὲ τοῦτοι οἱ μὲν Εὔθυνοι, οἱ δὲ Λογισταὶ, οἱ δὲ Ἐξεπαγαὶ, οἱ ὃ Συνηγόροι. Non multum tamen diuersum erat munus Logistarum ab illo Euthynorum, erantque pari numero, decem scilicet. Harpocration: Εὐθῦναι, ὅταμα ἀρχῆς παρ᾽ Ἀθηναίοις, δίκα τὸν ἀριθμὸν αὐδρες ἦσαν, παρ᾽ ἐκ' ἐσίδοσθαί οἱ παρισθώσαντες, ἐκ ἀρξαντες, ἐκ δικαιηταῖς τῇ τῶν δημοσίων τὰς Εὐθύνας. De his Pollux, meo iudicio, Libro VIII. cap.IX. οἱ δ᾽ Εὔθυνοι, ὥσπερ οἱ Παρέδροι τῆς εἰσὶ Ἀρχῆσι, ἀπεσαγεγῶπται. οὗτοι δ᾽ εἰσαγγέλλονται καὶ τὰς ἐφέσεις. Quo ex loco colligi posse puto differitates, quae sunt inter Logistas & Euthynos: nam illi χλαρωτοὶ sunt, hi ἀπεσαγεγῶπται. Logistae sunt tanquam Nouem Archontes, Euthyni sunt, tanquam Paredri Nouem Archontum, & assident Logistis, itaque vbi iudicatum est, Magistratus potestate decedentes aliquid publica debere, Euthyni id ab illis exigunt: εἰσαγγέλλονται καὶ τοὺς ἐφέσεις, id est, τοὺς ἀφειλάσεις τῇ πόλει. units.tr: There are two chapters of this law: one concerning the scrutiny of the magistrates in the court [τὰς τῆς Ἀρχῶν δοκιμασίας ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ], and the other concerning the rendering of accounts for the administration of the magistracy. Before taking up their office, the magistrates therefore underwent a scrutiny [δοκιμασία]. Nor were magistrates who had been chosen by lot exempt from this scrutiny. That the law also covered them is shown by Aeschines, in his speech against Ctesiphon, where, after quoting the words of the law we have described, he inserts these: "...but to be scrutinized for office in the court; since also those chosen by lot ... but they must be scrutinized for office." Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 6: "The scrutiny of the magistrates concerns both those chosen by lot and those elected, and whether a man is fit to hold office or not [δοκιμασία δὲ τῆς Ἀρχῶν ἐπιμελεῖσθαι, καὶ τῆς Κληρωτῆς, καὶ τῆς αἱρέσεως, εἶτ' ἐπιστῆσαι εἶναι ἀρχήν, εἶπε καὶ μή]." From this it came about that anyone who had been rejected by the scrutiny was questioned by those who spoke against him, so that if he was rejected, the one who had been chosen to succeed him would take over the office. Demosthenes, in his speech against Aeschines, says that it is impossible for one who has been rejected to obtain the magistracy by lot [ἀδύνατον ... τοῖς ἀποδεδοκιμασμένοις ἀρχὴν λαχεῖν]. Those undergoing scrutiny were asked whether they had honoured their parents, whether they had performed their military service, whether they had family sacred rites, and whether they had a property qualification. Dinarchus, in his speech against Aeschines, requires that those who speak in public... [the Greek is corrupt here]: "Whether he honours his parents; whether he has served on campaigns on behalf of the city; whether he has a family shrine; whether he pays his taxes [EI ΓΟΝΕΑΣ EY ΠΟΙΕΙ, EI ΤΑΣ ΣΤΡΑΤΕΙΑΣ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΗΣ ΠΟΛΕΩΣ ΕΣΤΡΑΤΕΥΤΑΙ, EI ΙΕΡΑ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΑ ΕΣΤΙΝ, EI ΤΑ ΤΕΛΗ ΤΕΛΕΙ]." The judges, in casting their votes on the scrutiny or rejection [δοκιμασίας vel ἀποδοκιμασίας], used beans. Suidas, from the scholiast on Aristophanes' Knights, says: "for the Senate's overseers voted with beans in the election of the magistrates [ἐν πῶς χειροτονίας τῶν Ἀρχόντων]." Here he calls the scrutinies of the magistrates in court "elections" [χειροτονίαι]. So the Comic interpreter says that those put in office were "elected by show of hands" [χειροτονεῖσθαι τοὺς ἐπὶ Ἀρχαῖς], because they were scrutinized. And the jurors, whom the magistrates call "those who prevent" or "those who are chosen by lot," they nonetheless say they "approve," because they in fact approve. Hence Ulpian, in his commentary on the Timocratean law, teaches that "to hold office" is not only to be allotted the magistracy by lot, but also to receive from the vote of the judge the ballot by which he approves the magistrates in court, so that they may hold office [τῷ ψήφῳ ... ὅτι ὁ ἀρχὴν, id est, calculum iudicis, quo δοκιμάζει τοὺς Ἀρχόντας ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ]. All those magistrates whose life had first to be weighed and inquired into were brought into the court by the Thesmothetae, who presided over the trial. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 9: "The Thesmothetae bring the magistrate in for scrutiny [εἰσφέρεται ἡ εἰ Θεσμοθέται καὶ δοκιμασίας τῆς ἀρχῆς]." Moreover, it was the duty of all nine archons together, not only of the Thesmothetae, to report to the people at the first assembly of each prytany whether the magistrates had governed rightly or not. Pollux in the same place: "and at the assemblies, the archons had to be asked, from the whole body and one by one, whether each seemed to govern well [εἰ δοκεῖ καλῶς ἀρχεῖν]." And a little later: "at the assembly there was a vote (as I said above, this must be read differently) in which the magistrates were voted upon, whether they were governing well [ἐπιχειροτονεῖσθαι]." Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians: "the assembly voted by show of hands, in which they voted on the magistrates, whether they seemed not to govern well [ἀπεψηφίσατο ... ἐν ᾗ ... οἱ ἐδόκουν μὴ καλῶς ἀρχειν]." Suidas departs widely from the ordinary use of the word ἐπιχειροτονία, and I hardly doubt that ἐπιχειροτονία should be restored where he describes the custom of καταχειροτονία. "Katacheirotonia or epicheirotonia [melius, as we have said, ἐπιχειροτονίας]. Katacheirotonia was done thus: the herald cried, 'Whenever Melias seems to do wrong, let him raise his hand'; those who wished raised their hands; and this raising was called katacheirotonia. Apocheirotonia (or epicheirotonia) was done thus: whenever Melias does not seem to do wrong, let him raise his hand; and some raised their hands, and this was called apocheirotonia. Then all lifted their hands, and immediately the herald declared which side was greater, whether of those who claimed he was doing wrong, or of those who did not; and as many as were lifted, that side pronounced its judgment." Yet it sometimes happened that the people, who had ordered that a magistrate be deposed and removed by its decree, ordered him to hold office again. You have an example in Demosthenes, in his speech against Theocrines: "his brother was a Thesmothetes, and I have been told this, that no one among you has received him ... not only was he removed from the office, but also ... and begging and saying that it was not ... to Theocrines' office ... and they returned him to the magistracy again." Those who were removed from office were also compelled to give an account of their conduct before the judges. Pollux: "...to use..." Harpocration: "...was the year of the Archons at Athens, and in the Sycophant they were looking toward the pleasure of the people ... and if they were ..., to enter the court." The second chapter of the law concerns the rendering of accounts by the magistrate before the Scribe and the Logistae. These Logistae were, as it happens, magistrates chosen by lot, ten in number, before whom those who had held office rendered the accounts of their administration within thirty days of laying down their magistracy. The author of the Etymologicum: "The Logistae are magistrates chosen by lot in the courts, before whom those who had held office for a year rendered an account of their administration." Harpocration: "Logistae are called magistrates among the Athenians. They are ten in number, who reckon up the administration of the public affairs, when the archons have handed over to the magistracies." The passage of Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 9, cannot be referred to these Logistae: "There were two Logistae, one of the Senate and one of the court, and this one is chosen by lot in the Senate, as they forbid the jurors..." For these Logistae of Pollux differ from those of whom Harpocration spoke, first in number, since there were ten of the latter and two of Pollux's; and second in function, since accounts were rendered before the former, while the latter were only concerned with the judges and saw to it that no fraud was committed, both by the Council of Five Hundred and by all others, and that no one was deprived of civic rights, or assigned any public service. But the law in this passage refers to the ten Logistae alone, who reckon up the administration of the offices. Here it is asked whether they are the same as the Euthyni. Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, denied that they were the same, as Harpocration reports in the words of Aristotle in the Politics, where he shows that the Logistae were distinct from the Euthyni. But the author of the Etymologicum thinks that the Euthyni were the same as the Logistae: "Euthyni, judges, examiners, whom we call Logistae." Yet we must rather trust Aristotle, who also mentions these in Book VI of the Politics, last chapter: "In some offices, even if not all, it is a fault to be deprived of much of the property, and it is shameful to be taken into the reckoning of the public accounts, and it is nothing to be relieved of them. Some call them Euthyni, others Logistae, others Exetastae, others Synegoroi." Yet the office of the Logistae was not very different from that of the Euthyni, and they were equal in number, namely ten. Harpocration: "Euthynai: when a magistracy among the Athenians ended, ten men were chosen, who were not magistrates, but were appointed to examine the accounts of public affairs." On these, Pollux, in my judgment, Book VIII, chapter 9: "The Euthyni, like the Paredri of the archons, are appointed by lot. These are summoned to the court, and they also hear the appeals." From this passage I think the differences that exist between the Logistae and the Euthyni can be gathered: the former are chosen by lot, the latter are appointed. The Logistae are like the nine archons, the Euthyni are like the Paredri of the nine archons, and they sit beside the Logistae; so when it has been judged that a magistrate, on leaving his office, owes something to the public, the Euthyni exact it from him, and summon him to answer [εἰσαγγέλλονται καὶ τὰς ἐφέσεις], that is, to repay the debt to the city. Est enim [illegible, ~30 letters]. Unde Lysias, [illegible, ~70 letters]. Quomodo autem referendae sint rationes prae-scribebat Lex in hunc modum:
units.tr: Hence it came about that Lycurgus the orator, about to die, had himself brought before the Metroum to the Senate of Five Hundred, wishing to render to them an account of his administration of the Republic. Plutarch [illegible] the Metroum [illegible] Lycurgus [illegible]. These laws, however, exempt no one, but embrace all who are magistrates, [illegible]. For it is [illegible]. Hence Lysias [illegible]. The manner in which the accounts were to be rendered, the law prescribed in this form:

units.la: [illegible, ~60 letters]. [illegible, ~30 letters] Rationes ita referunto: Hoc de publico tantum expendi: nihil. Nihil de publico accepit: nihil expendi.
units.tr: [illegible]. [illegible] They are to render their accounts thus: So much was spent from the public funds: nothing. He received nothing from the public funds: I spent nothing.

units.la: Habes apud Æschinem [illegible, ~40 letters] Κτησιφῶντα, ubi docet etiam eos, qui nihil de publico acceperant, nihil in publicum impenderant, sed tantum ad Rempublicam accesserant. Lege cogi ad referendas rationes [?] apud Lysiam, se scilicet nihil accepisse, nihil expendisse. [illegible, ~90 letters]
units.tr: You have it in Aeschines [illegible] against Ctesiphon, where he also teaches that those who had received nothing from the public funds, and had spent nothing for the public, but had merely come near the Republic, were likewise bound. By law they were compelled to render accounts, namely that they had received nothing and spent nothing, as Lysias shows. [illegible]

units.la: Donec autem rationes retulissent suas Magistratus, fuerunt nihil bonorum in suis potitum habebant potestatem, ex hac Lege: Magistratus ne ferendis rationibus obnoxius de suis bonis nil quicquam Diis consecrare, aut appendere: neque testamentum facere. [illegible, ~50 letters]
units.tr: Until the magistrates had rendered their accounts, they had no power over any of their goods, by this law: Let a magistrate, bound to render accounts, not consecrate or dedicate anything of his own goods to the gods, nor make a will. [illegible]

units.la: Legem habes apud Æschinem [illegible, ~20 letters] Κτησιφῶντα. [illegible, ~120 letters]. Non licet quicquam Diis consecrare, aut appendere, nec licet testamentum facere: ratio est, quia ea, quae consecrant, aut appendunt, aut testamento dant legant [?], oppignerata enim sunt Reipublicae, donec rationes retulerint, vtrobique [?] [illegible, ~50 letters]. Atque haec eadem ratio est, cur non liceat [?] in aliam adoptione transfire familiam: Adoptatus enim familiam mutat & Iitatum, & qui iuris erat sui, alieno subiicitur, quod ab eo, qui reddendis rationibus est obnoxius, fieri non potest, nisi in fraudem Reipublicae. Quare etiam Lege caucebatur, ne quis ἀνεύθυνος[?] peregre proficisceretur.
units.tr: You have the law in Aeschines [illegible] against Ctesiphon. [illegible]. It is not lawful to consecrate or dedicate anything to the gods, nor is it lawful to make a will. The reason is that the things they consecrate or dedicate, or give or bequeath by will, are pledged to the Republic until they have rendered their accounts; on both sides [illegible]. This same reason explains why it was not lawful to pass by adoption into another family: for the adopted person changes his family and rites, and one who was his own master becomes subject to another, which cannot happen for one who is bound to render accounts, except to the defrauding of the Republic. Hence the law also provided that no one [unaccountable, ἀνεύθυνος] should go abroad.

units.la: ΑΡΧΗΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΜΗ ΑΠΟΔΗΜΕΙΝ.
units.tr: That the magistrate who is accountable must not go abroad [ἀρχὴν ὑπεύθυνον μὴ ἀποδημεῖν].

units.la: Ei igitur non licebat peregre extra fines Atticæ proficisci, vt cauetur hac Lege, quæ omnium τῶν ἀδίκων[?] prima legebatur, ne qua fraus fieret. Æschi-nes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος. καὶ ὅτι ἰσχυρῶς ἀπαγεῖ τοὺς ἀνεύθυνους, ὥστε διὰ τοῦτο λέγει[?], ΑΡΧΗΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ (φησί) ΜΗ ΑΠΟΔΗΜΕΙΝ, ὃ Ἡφαιστος[?] (ἐπὶ τῶν Ἀλκιβιάδου[?]) ὅτι ἦρξε, μὴ ἀποδημήσω; ἵνα γε μὴ φαῦλά τι πράξῃ[?] τῆς πόλεως, ἢ ἀποξύς[?] δρᾶσαι[?] χρήματα. Metus scilicet erat, ne quis conuisatus & interceptis publicis pecuniis, aut re male gesta se daret in pedes.
units.tr: It was therefore not lawful for such a man to travel abroad beyond the borders of Attica, as this law provides, which was read first of all the laws concerning wrongdoers, lest any fraud be committed. Aeschines, in his speech against Ctesiphon, and that he strongly forbids the unaccountable, so that for this reason he says: "Accountable magistracy, he says, must not go abroad" [ἀρχὴν ὑπεύθυνον μὴ ἀποδημεῖν]; what Hephaestus [illegible] (concerning the Alcibiades [illegible]) said, that he held office and must not go abroad, lest he do something wrong to the city, or having been [illegible] perform deeds for money. There was clearly fear that someone, having embezzled and intercepted public moneys, or having mismanaged affairs, might take to his heels.

units.la: Præterea Lege caucebatur, ne quis, rationibus non redditis, alium gereret Magistratum: Τὸν αὐτὸν μὴ ἀρχὴν ὑπεύθυνον ὄντα ἐπιέναι[?] ἀρχῆς.
units.tr: Moreover, the law provided that no one, while his accounts remained unrendered, should hold another magistracy: [one who is accountable must not enter another office, τὸν αὐτὸν μὴ ἀρχὴν ὑπεύθυνον ὄντα ἐπιέναι ἀρχῆς].

units.la: Legem hanc partim ex Heliastarum iureiurando, partim ex Vlpiano ad hoc iureiurandum descripsimus. Vlpiani verba diximus in superioribus ita esse concipienda: νόμος τῷ τ' αὐτὸν μὴ ἀρχὴν, μὴ δοῦναι εὐθύνας τῆς τοιαύτης ἀρχῆς. Nō enim negat tantum Lex bis eodem anno licere ὑπεύθυνῳ ἀρχεῖν, sed etiam in genere verat quenquam ἀρχὴν ὑπεύθυνον. præterea-que ita legitur in Heliastarum iureiurando: ΟΥΔΕ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΚΑΤΑΚΤΗΣΩ ΩΣ ΤΕ ΑΡΧΕΙΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΕΡΑΣ ΑΡΧΗΣ. Quæ verba exponit Vlpianus, & ab Heliastis dicuntur, vt & sequentia, quia nullus, nisi δικαστὴς ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, Magistratum gerere quibat.
units.tr: We have described this law partly from the oath of the Heliasts, and partly from Ulpian, who sets it out with reference to that oath. We said in the earlier passages that Ulpian's words are to be understood thus: the law says that the same person must not hold an office while not having given an account of that office. For the law not only denies that an accountable man may hold office twice in the same year, but in general forbids anyone to hold an accountable office. Moreover, it is read thus in the oath of the Heliasts: "Nor will I acquire an office, nor hold office while being accountable for another office." Ulpian explains these words, and they are spoken by the Heliasts, as are the following, because no one could hold a magistracy except as a judge in the court.

units.la: Vnde etiam non licebat Lege, Magistratum, qui rationes suas non retulisset, corona donare.
units.tr: Hence too, by law, a magistrate who had not rendered his accounts could not be crowned with a garland.

units.la: ΑΡΧΗΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΜΗ ΣΤΕ-ΦΑΝΟΥΝ.
units.tr: NOT TO CROWN A MAGISTRATE BEFORE HE HAS RENDERED ACCOUNT [ΑΡΧΗΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΜΗ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΥΝ].

units.la: Frequens huius Legis laudatio occurrit apud Æschinem ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος. ἐπὶ ὁ λύω[?] νομοθέτης, ἐαυτὸς μιᾶς ἀρχῆς τῆς ἐλαχίστης ὑπεύθυνος ἢ, τῶν οὖν ἐά, πρὶν αὐ λόγους καὶ εὐθύνας δοῦναι στεφανοῦν. Iterum: ἐπειδὴ ἀπαγορεύει τοὺς νόμους, ΑΡΧΗΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΜΗ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΥΝ. Rursum: ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν τοὺς νόμους ἀπιδεῖξα ἀπαγορεύοντας μὴ στεφανοῦν τοὺς ὑπευθύνους. Expressit M. Tullius Libro de Optimo genere Oratorum extremo. Cùm esset Lex Athenis, NE QVIS POPVLI SCITVM FACERET VT QVISQVAM CORONA DONARETVR IN MAGISTRATV PRIVS QVAM RATIONES RETVLISSET. Libanius in Argumento Orationis Demosthenicæ ἐπεὶ στεφανῶ νόμων ὁ ἡ κελεύων τοὺς ὑπευθύνους μὴ στεφανοῦν. Anonymus in Argumento eiusdem Orationis: ἀποδείκνυμι[?] εἰ Φάσκων ἐπεὶ τὰς ἡμέρας νόμους ἐν ψηφίσματι· ἕνα μὲν, τ' κελεύοντα τ' ὑπευθύνων μὴ στεφανοῦσθαι, πρὶν αὐ δοῦναι τὰς εὐθύνας. Auctor Argumenti Orationis Æschinis ἐν Κτησιφῶντος. ἐν μὲν, ὅτι ὑπεύθυνον ὄντα τ' Δημοσθένην ἐστεφάνωσεν, τῷ νόμῳ κελεύοντος, μὴ ὀξείᾳ ὑπεύθυνον ἀρχαῖς στεφανοῦν. Cuius Legis Oratio, Legislatorisque consilium fuit, ne qui corona esset à populo donatus, idem cum rationes referret suas, reus peragereatur, & multaretur. Aeschines ibidem: πολλοὶ γὰρ πόλεως ὑπευθύνων ἐπιστρέφεσθαι κέλευσαν τὴν δημοσίων χρημάτων ὅντες ὀξέως ἐχόμενοι δι' ἐφίζασαν ἐκ τῆς δικαστηρίων. Εἰσὶ τοὺς[?] ἀκούοντα δ' (οἷμαι) οἱ δικασταὶ, ἐπὶ Φαινοπταμὸν αὐτῆς ἀλλὰ δὲ τῇ αὐτῇ πόλει, (τυχὸν δὲ καὶ ὁ τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰσαυτοῦ,) σεφίλω μὲν ποτε αὐταρχοῦντες, ὡς ἐλέγοντο, ὅτι σεφανοῦσθαι ἄρετῆς ἕνεκα καὶ δικαιοσύνης τοῦ τῆς δήμου χρυσῷ σεφανῶ, ὁ δὲ αὐτὸς μικρόν ὑπὸ χρῶν ἐξέχει ἐκ τῆς δικαστηρίου κλοπῆς ἕνεκα τὰς εὐθυωρίας ἀφλοχαῖς. ὥσπερ ἰωλαπαζόντο πλὴν ἴπορ φέρει οἱ δικασταὶ ἢ ἀπὸ τῶν πρόσοπος ἀδικήματος, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς αἰχμῆς τοῦ δήμου. κελεῦσαν δὲ ἡ ὡς ἕκαστος ἢ ἐποποιητής, τὸ ἔχει νόμον καὶ μάχῃ καλῶς ἔχοντα, τὸν ἀγαρρήδλιν ἀπαγγελθεῖ ἐπαγγελίας, ὡς ἀπὸ ἐπαγγελμάτων μὴ σεφανοῦν.
units.tr: This law is often praised in Aeschines, in his speech against Ctesiphon. The lawgiver, he says, made himself accountable even for the least of offices, and therefore ordered that no one be crowned before he has given his accounts and audits [ἐπὶ ὁ λύω νομοθέτης, ἐαυτὸς μιᾶς ἀρχῆς τῆς ἐλαχίστης ὑπεύθυνος ἢ, τῶν οὖν ἐά, πρὶν αὐ λόγους καὶ εὐθύνας δοῦναι στεφανοῦν]. Again: since the law forbids it, a magistrate who is still accountable must not be crowned [ἐπειδὴ ἀπαγορεύει τοὺς νόμους, ΑΡΧΗΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΜΗ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΥΝ]. And once more: but I will show that the laws forbid crowning those who are accountable [ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν τοὺς νόμους ἀπιδεῖξα ἀπαγορεύοντας μὴ στεφανοῦν τοὺς ὑπευθύνους]. Marcus Tullius expressed it at the end of his book On the Best Kind of Orator: since there was a law at Athens that no one should propose a decree of the people that anyone be crowned in a magistracy before he had rendered his accounts [NE QVIS POPVLI SCITVM FACERET VT QVISQVAM CORONA DONARETVR IN MAGISTRATV PRIVS QVAM RATIONES RETVLISSET]. Libanius, in the argument to a speech of Demosthenes, says that the law orders those who are accountable not to be crowned [ἐπεὶ στεφανῶ νόμων ὁ ἡ κελεύων τοὺς ὑπευθύνους μὴ στεφανοῦν]. The anonymous writer of the argument to the same speech says: the laws, in a decree, command that those who are accountable not be crowned before they have given their audits [ἀποδείκνυμι εἰ Φάσκων ἐπεὶ τὰς ἡμέρας νόμους ἐν ψηφίσματι· ἕνα μὲν, τ' κελεύοντα τ' ὑπευθύνων μὴ στεφανοῦσθαι, πρὶν αὐ δοῦναι τὰς εὐθύνας]. The author of the argument to Aeschines' speech against Ctesiphon says: the law was that Demosthenes, who was still accountable, had been crowned, and the law ordered that those accountable to offices not be crowned [ἐν μὲν, ὅτι ὑπεύθυνον ὄντα τ' Δημοσθένην ἐστεφάνωσεν, τῷ νόμῳ κελεύοντος, μὴ ὀξείᾳ ὑπεύθυνον ἀρχαῖς στεφανοῦν]. The purpose of this law, and the lawgiver's intention, was that anyone crowned by the people should, when he rendered his accounts, be brought to trial as a defendant and fined. Aeschines says in the same place: many who were accountable to the city were ordered to be brought before the courts, since they were closely held to account for public money [πολλοὶ γὰρ πόλεως ὑπευθύνων ἐπιστρέφεσθαι κέλευσαν τὴν δημοσίων χρημάτων ὅντες ὀξέως ἐχόμενοι δι' ἐφίζασαν ἐκ τῆς δικαστηρίων]. (The rest of the passage, which is corrupt, runs roughly: the jurors, I think, hear the accusation against the one who was crowned with gold for virtue, while the same man, having been accused of theft, is condemned to be bound and beaten; the jurors did not judge by the person of the offence but by the crime itself.)

units.la: Huic Legi vt fraudem facerent, & imponerent, populi scitum faciebant, vt corona donaretur Magistratus, verum sub hac Lege, postquam rationes retulisset suas; (sed & id contra hanc Legem fuisse demonstrat Æschines ibidem: Τούτων γὰρ ἕνεκ' ἡμῖν πᾶς ἀπὸ θυσίας τοῦ τῆς νόμους, οἱ μὲν φύσει μίστεσι εἰσιν, οἱ δὲ ὡς ὄσι μισθοῦ ... ἀλλ' ἔστω πρὸς οὐχ ὁ τῆς αἰχμῆς ...), ἐπεὶ δὲ λόγον καὶ δίκης ἀκούσαι, ἡ πόλις ὅπου ἀδίκημα ἀδικεῖται.
units.tr: To evade this law, and to get around it, they passed a decree of the people that a magistrate be crowned, but under this condition: after he had rendered his accounts. (Aeschines shows in the same place that this too was against the law: For this reason all of us, from the sacrifice of the law, some are in the position of those who are hired, others of those who are paid ... but let it be so, against the one who has the office ...) Once he had given an account and been judged, the city, where the wrong is done, is the one who is wronged.

units.la: Si quis ærarius Magistratum gerebat, capite luebat, vt hac Lege sancitum: Ἐὰν ὡς ὀφείλων ἀρχὴν τὴν δημοσίαν, θανάτῳ ζημίαν ἔστω. Si quis ærarius Magistratum gerat, capitale esto.
units.tr: If anyone who was a treasurer held a magistracy, he paid with his life, as this law enacted: If anyone holds the public office while owing money to the public treasury, let him be punished with death [Ἐὰν ὡς ὀφείλων ἀρχὴν τὴν δημοσίαν, θανάτῳ ζημίαν ἔστω]. If anyone who is a treasurer holds a magistracy, let it be a capital offence.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes in Leptinea: ἐαν δέ ἀλῶ, ἐιορχεῖν ἔγω ὦ νόμω, ὃς κεῖται, ἐαν ὡς ὀφείλων ἀρχὴν τὴν δημοσίαν, θάνατον λέγει· τῶν γὰρ ἐς ἐπ' ἐκείνῳ ὃ ὑπηρέμιον. Nomen eius deferebatur apud Thesmothetas, vt constat ἐκ τῆς τῶν νόμων ὑπηρεσίας, apud Demosthenem in Timocratea: καὶ ἐιδήξις αὐτὸν ἔγω πρὸς τὰς Θεσμοθέτας, καὶ ἀπὸ ἐαν τῆς ἀρχῆς ὀφείλων τῆς δημοσίας.
units.tr: Demosthenes praises this law in his speech Against Leptines: If I am convicted, let me swear by the law which is laid down, which says death for anyone who holds public office while owing money; for the law is directed against that man [ἐαν δέ ἀλῶ, ἐιορχεῖν ἔγω ὦ νόμω, ὃς κεῖται, ἐαν ὡς ὀφείλων ἀρχὴν τὴν δημοσίαν, θάνατον λέγει· τῶν γὰρ ἐς ἐπ' ἐκείνῳ ὃ ὑπηρέμιον]. His name was laid before the Thesmothetae, as is clear from the service of the laws [ἐκ τῆς τῶν νόμων ὑπηρεσίας]. Demosthenes, in the speech Against Timocrates, says: and I laid an information against him before the Thesmothetae, that he was holding public office while owing money [καὶ ἐιδήξις αὐτὸν ἔγω πρὸς τὰς Θεσμοθέτας, καὶ ἀπὸ ἐαν τῆς ἀρχῆς ὀφείλων τῆς δημοσίας].

units.la: Tyrannidem affectare Athenis capital fuit veteri Solonis Lege: Εἴ τις τυραννίδα τυγχάνοι, θάνατον ζημίαν ἔστω. Si quis tyrannidem affectarit, capitale esto.
units.tr: Aiming at tyranny was a capital crime at Athens under the old law of Solon: If anyone should aim at tyranny, let him be punished with death [Εἴ τις τυραννίδα τυγχάνοι, θάνατον ζημίαν ἔστω]. If anyone shall have aimed at tyranny, let it be a capital offence.

units.la: Legem descripsit Plutarchus in Solone, cuius verba in sequentibus reddemus: iam primus instituerat Theseus δημοκρατίαν καὶ ἰσονομίαν, & omnes ἐπὶ τῆς ἴσης in vrbem inuitauerat: verùm non diu obtinuit δημοκρατία apud Athenienses, sed post Theseum Mnestheus, atque insecutis temporibus alij aliquot imperarunt Reges, donec tandem omnino sunt exacti. Apollinis fortes causam exactorum ab Athenienfibus Regum facit Græcus Comici Interpres ad Nubes: τῆς Ἀθηναίοις πυθοχρήστως ἐδώκεν καλλαλᾶσαι μὲν τὰς βασιλείας, μεταπέμψαι δὲ Διὸς βασιλέα. Quod factum puto, quando contendebant inter se de regno Medon & Neleus Codri filij: nam placuit disceptationis arbitrium Apollini permittere, ἀνεξιλαῖς ἐς ὃ χρησμῶν δὲ ἐν Δῆφος, inquit Pausanias Achaicis, qui addit dedisse Μέδοντι τὴν Γυθίαν βασιλείαν τῷ Ἀθηναίων. Sed regnum non fuit. exactum enim videtur tunc Apollinis iussu Regum nomen, vt Iouî cederet; quare Medon Rex non fuit, sed Ἄρχων ἀρχὴ βίς, vt appellatione, ita etiam potestate imminuta. Quanquam & hi, cum nimia viderentur eorum potestas e perpetuis Magistratibus facti sunt Ἄρχοντες Δικαστής. Atque horum quoq; abrogatum est decennale illud imperium metu tyrannidis, & creati sunt Ἄρχοντες ἐπιαύσιοι, qui praesent anno imperio Reipublicæ: Cum autem Solon forte inter hos novem Ἀρχόντας ἐπώνυμος esset allectus, istam adversus tyrannos, aut τυραννίδος ἐπινοοῦντας tulit Legem, neque ipse potuit unquam induci, ut extraordinarium capesseret imperium, & plus Legibus posset, quin contra ultro oblatam recusavit tyrannidem, ut ipse scribit ad Phocum his versibus:
units.tr: Plutarch described this law in his Solon, and I shall give his words in what follows. Theseus had already first established democracy and equality [δημοκρατίαν καὶ ἰσονομίαν], and had invited everyone into the city on equal terms [ἐπὶ τῆς ἴσης]. But democracy did not hold long among the Athenians; after Theseus, Mnesthea, and in the following times several other kings ruled, until at last they were altogether driven out. The Greek commentator on Aristophanes' Clouds gives the reason the Athenians drove out their kings, on Apollo's oracle: [τῆς Ἀθηναίοις πυθοχρήστως ἐδώκεν καλλαλᾶσαι μὲν τὰς βασιλείας, μεταπέμψαι δὲ Διὸς βασιλέα]. I think this happened when the sons of Codrus, Medon and Neleus, were contending with each other for the kingship; for it was agreed to leave the decision to Apollo [ἀνεξιλαῖς ἐς ὃ χρησμῶν δὲ ἐν Δῆφος], as Pausanias says in his Achaica, who adds that Apollo gave Medon the kingship at Athens [Μέδοντι τὴν Γυθίαν βασιλείαν τῷ Ἀθηναίων]. But it was not a kingship, for it seems that by Apollo's command the name of king was then abolished so that it would yield to Zeus; therefore Medon was not king, but an archon [Ἄρχων ἀρχὴ βίς], his power diminished as much as his title. Yet these archons too, since their power seemed excessive, were made magistrates for a fixed term instead of for life [Ἄρχοντες Δικαστής]. And the ten-year rule of these was also abolished, from fear of tyranny, and annual archons were created [Ἄρχοντες ἐπιαύσιοι], who held the government of the commonwealth for one year. When Solon happened to be chosen one of these nine archons, eponymous, he proposed that law against tyrants, or against those who plotted tyranny [τυραννίδος ἐπινοοῦντας]. He himself could never be persuaded to take up an extraordinary power and to have more than the laws, but on the contrary he refused the tyranny when it was offered to him, as he himself writes to Phocus in these verses:

units.la: Εἰ δὲ γῆς ἐφθαμένῳ παιδός[?], Τυραννίδος δὲ καὶ βίης ἀμιλλήσου[?], Οὐ καταλάμψω[?], μιαρὰς καὶ καλλιφυμένας χλέος, Οὐδὲν αἰδούμεθ'[?]. πλέον γὰρ ὧδε νικήσειν δοκέω, Παῖδας ἀνδρὶ[?] δυσεχέπους[?].
units.tr: If I had not thought of the land, and the children, and contended for tyranny and force, I would not have been stained with a foul and shameful reputation; I would not have been ashamed of it. For I do not think I would have gained more by doing so, [and I would have left] children to a man of ill repute.

units.la: His concinit celebratum illius dictum, Ὅ ἔσσι πολέμων ὁ πρὸς[?] atque hac de causa merito gloriatur in Elegiis,
units.tr: Agreeing with this is his well-known saying, which is that [...] and for this reason he rightly boasts in his Elegies:

units.la: Λήμω μὲν γὰρ ἔδωκε τοῦν κέρδος ὅσον ἐπέρχεί[?], Τιμῆς δ' ἀφελῶν, ὅ' ἐπορεξάμενος. Οἱ δ' εἶχον δώματα, καὶ χρήματα ἦσαν ἀγνοί, Καὶ τῆς ἐφεσαμένῳ μηδὲν ἀλλὰ ἔλαν[?]. Ἐξέων δ' ἀμφιβαλὼν χεπτὰς[?] σάχης ἀμφοτέρωσι[?]. Νικᾶν δ' οὐκ εἶλαε[?] ἀδίκεσις ἀδίκως[?].
units.tr: For I gave the people as much honour as was enough, neither taking away nor adding to it. Those who had power and wealth I also guarded, so that they should suffer no wrong; I stood with my strong shield over both sides, and I did not allow the unjust to win unjustly.

units.la: Atque hoc institutum adeo gratum & acceptum fuit Atheniensi populo, ut in illis παιδείοις ἀρχῆς[?], quae fiebant pro concione, ut in superioribus diximus, diris devoueret Praeco, si quis tyrannidem affectaret: morem expressit lepidissimus Aristophanes Θεσμοφοριαζούσαις.
units.tr: This institution was so pleasing and acceptable to the Athenian people that, in those assemblies of the magistracy which were held before the people, as we said above, the herald would curse with dire curses anyone who aimed at tyranny. The most witty Aristophanes expressed this custom in the Thesmophoriazusae.

units.la: Εἴ τις ἐπιβουλεύει τὴν τοῦ δήμου ἀρχήν, Τῷ δὲ γυναικῶν, ἢ τυράννου ἐπαινοῦ, Ἡ τὸν τύραννον συγκατάγειν, Κακῶς ἀπολέσθαι τῶν αὐτῶν καὶ οἰκίαι Ἀρᾶσθε.
units.tr: If anyone plots against the power of the people, or praises a woman's tyranny, or brings back a tyrant, may he perish miserably, both he and his house. [Εἴ τις ἐπιβουλεύει τὴν τοῦ δήμου ἀρχήν, Τῷ δὲ γυναικῶν, ἢ τυράννου ἐπαινοῦ, Ἡ τὸν τύραννον συγκατάγειν, Κακῶς ἀπολέσθαι τῶν αὐτῶν καὶ οἰκίαι Ἀρᾶσθε.]

units.la: Hinc inter cetera iurisiurandi Heliastarum Kapita hoc legitur, KAI TY-PANNON OY ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ EINAI. Qua libertate, quae aequa erat omnibus praecipue gloriabantur Athenae: Hac tamen Lege non licebat τῷ ἐντυχόντι occidere eum, qui tyrannidem affectaret, sed oportebat in iudicio convictum ab Undecimviris capitalibus capite plecti: id liquet ex antithesi, quam instituit Plutarchus, Legum Solonis & Poplicolae: ὃ ὃ μισοτύραννον ἐν τῷ Ποπλικόλᾳ σφοδρότερον. εἰ γὰρ τὶς ἐπιχειρεῖν τυραννίδι, ὁ μὲν Σόλων ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῶν[?] τῷ δίκῃ ἐπιτιμῆσαι, ὁ δ' καὶ πρὸς τῆς κείσεως ἀπέλυσεν[?]. Atque haec quidem quod ad eos qui tyrannidem affectarent: nam Tyrannorum non tanta habebatur ratio: illos enim impune, imo cum spe praemii, licebat occidere. Cicero pro Milone. Graeci homines Deorum honores tribuunt iis viris, qui tyrannos necaverunt. Quae ego vidi Athenis? Quas res divinas talibus institutas viris? Quos cantus? Quae carmina? prope ad immortalitatis, & religionem, & memoriam consecrantur. Aristogitonem & Harmodium intelligit M. Tullius, in quorum honorem Scolia illa scripta, quae ἐν τοῖς τῶν ἑταίρων ᾠδαῖς ἦσαν, ut docet Interpres Comici ad Acharnenses. Hinc in Rhetorum Scholis Lex τυραννοκτόνῳ δίδωσι τιμὴν δωρεάν. Tyrannicidae praemium datur. Honorique Harmodij & Aristogitonis consultum est Lege sive Psephismate isto.
units.tr: Hence, among other clauses of the Heliasts' oath, this is read: AND I WILL NOT VOTE THAT THERE SHALL BE A TYRANT [KAI TYRANNON OU PSEPHIOUMAI EINAI]. Athens prided itself especially on this freedom, which was equal for all. Yet by this law it was not permitted for anyone who met a man aiming at tyranny to kill him; he had to be convicted in court and beheaded by the eleven capital magistrates. This is clear from the contrast Plutarch draws between the laws of Solon and of Publicola: the one is more severe against the tyrant in the Publicola. For if anyone attempted tyranny, Solon ordered him to be punished by a legal sentence, while Publicola allowed him to be killed even without a trial [ὃ ὃ μισοτύραννον ἐν τῷ Ποπλικόλᾳ σφοδρότερον. εἰ γὰρ τὶς ἐπιχειρεῖν τυραννίδι, ὁ μὲν Σόλων ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῶν τῷ δίκῃ ἐπιτιμῆσαι, ὁ δ' καὶ πρὸς τῆς κείσεως ἀπέλυσεν]. So much for those who aimed at tyranny. For the tyrants themselves there was not so great a regard: it was permitted to kill them with impunity, indeed with the hope of reward. Cicero, in the speech for Milo: The Greeks pay divine honours to those men who killed tyrants. What did I see at Athens? What religious rites were instituted for such men? What songs, what poems? They are dedicated almost to immortality, both to religion and to memory. Marcus Tullius means Harmodius and Aristogiton, in whose honour those Scolia were written which were sung at the banquets, as the commentator on Aristophanes' Acharnians teaches. Hence in the schools of the rhetoricians the law gives the tyrannicide a reward: a gift of honour is given to the tyrant-slayer. The honour of Harmodius and Aristogiton was secured by this law or decree.

units.la: Nomina Harmodij & Aristogitonis ne vnquam feruis indere liceto.
units.tr: Let the names of Harmodius and Aristogiton never be given to slaves.

units.la: Id docet Herodes Atticus apud Scriptorem Noctium Atticarum Lib. IX. cap. II. Maiores autem mei Athenienses, Nomina iuuenum fortissimorum Harmodij & Aristogitonis, qui libertatis recuperandae gratia Hippiam tyrannum interficere adorti erant, ne vnquam seruis indere liceret, decreto publico sanxerunt. Quoniam nefas ducerent, nomina patriae libertati devota seruili contagio pollui. Neque tantum in Tyrannos insurgebant, sed etiam in Graecis ciuitatibus Liberi Tyrannorum, oppressis illis, eodem supplicio afficiuntur, vt testatur M. Brutus Epistola ad Ciceronem, & sublata tyrannide, acta rescindebantur: vnde saepius leges: ᾗ ἔξω τῶν ἀνωγεν[?], ὡς ἐπὶ τὴν Τειλαχινην[?].
units.tr: Herodes Atticus teaches this in Book IX, chapter II, of the author of the Attic Nights: Our ancestors the Athenians, by public decree, ordained that the names of the bravest young men, Harmodius and Aristogiton, who set out to kill the tyrant Hippias in order to recover liberty, should never be allowed to be given to slaves. For they judged it wrong that names devoted to the freedom of the fatherland should be polluted by servile contagion. Nor did they rise up only against tyrants. In the Greek states, when the tyrants were overthrown, their children were subjected to the same punishment, as Marcus Brutus testifies in his letter to Cicero, and when the tyranny was abolished, the acts of the tyrants were rescinded; whence the laws often say: [ᾗ ἔξω τῶν ἀνωγεν[?], ὡς ἐπὶ τὴν Τειλαχινην[?]].

units.la: Atque haec quidem Atheniensium communis cum multis aliis populis, in quibus Romani, fuit sententia. Romani tamen, vbi, ita volentibus fatis, omnia vnius arbitrio permissa sunt, Principem Lege Maiestatis tutum & sacrosanctum merito esse voluerunt: & putarunt, quod crimen Maiestatis non solum facto, sed & verbis impiis maxime exacerbatur, vt loquitur Paulus Sententi. Lib. V. Tit. XXIX. quae etiam verba paululum immutata leguntur apud Modestinum Lib. XI. Pandectarum: Crimen Majestatis facto, vel violatis statuis, vel imaginibus, maxime exacerbatur in milites. Leg. VII. §. IV. D. Ad Legem Iuliam Majestatis. Neque enim hic audio virum summum, qui exstimabat Modestinum idem cum Paulo scripsisse. Sed quia ex maledicto non contrahi crimen Maiestatis postea constitutum est, constitutióque relati in Codicem Iustiniani Leg. vnica C. Si quis Imperatori maledixerit. ideo Modestini verba Tribonianum sic immutasse. Ego vero mihi facile persuadeo, Modestinum ita scripsisse, quomodo editum est Crimen maiestatis facto, vel violatis statuis vel imaginibus, maxime exacerbatur in milites: non enim voluit Modestinus maxime exacerbari crimen hoc Maiestatis verbis impiis, cum ipse doceat, nec lubricum linguae ad poenam facile trahendum esse d. Leg. VII. §. III. D. Ad Legem Iuliam Maiestatis. Scribebat autem ista, meo iudicio, Modestinus, occasione eorum, quae in Africa acciderant, cum exauctoratis a militibus Maximinis, Gordiani (quorum aetate floruit Modestinus) Imperatores salutati sunt: nam statuas Maximini deiecerunt, & imagines perfregerunt: quibus exacerbatus Maximini animus, nemini partium Gordiani parcitum voluit: exacerbatum igitur est maxime in milites crimen maiestatis tum facto, quando exauctorarunt milites Maximinum, & Gordianum Imperatorem renunciarunt, cum violatis statuis vel imaginibus: nam etiam crimen Maiestatis contrahebatur, si quid in statuis vel imaginibus Principum admissum, cum cautionibus tamen quibusdam, quas referunt iureconsultorum filij: itaque hoc crimine liberatus est a Senatu, qui statuas Imperatoris reprobatas conflaverit: Leg. IV. §. I. D. eod. Appellat statuas reprobatas, siue, quae a statuario, aut eo qui faciendas locauerat, minus probarentur, vt Imperatoris vultum non referentes: siue quia Imperator eas sibi poni nolebat: (neque enim sine ipsius Imperatoris auctoritate ponebantur) cum itaque neque positae, neque consecratae essent, impune licuit conflare, quemadmodum Seuerus & Antoninus Pontio rescripserunt, non videri contra Maiestatem fieri ob imagines Caesaris non consecratas, venditas. Leg. V. §. II.
units.tr: This, then, was the view of the Athenians, shared with many other peoples, among whom were the Romans. Yet the Romans, when, by the will of the fates, all things were placed at the discretion of one man, wished the Prince to be safe and sacrosanct under the law of majesty, and they thought that the crime of majesty is aggravated not only by deed but also by impious words, as Paulus says in the Sententiae, Book V, Title XXIX. These words, slightly altered, are also read in Modestinus, Book XI of the Pandects: The crime of majesty is aggravated by deed, or by violating statues or images, especially in the case of soldiers. Digest, Law VII, §IV, On the Julian Law of Majesty. For here I do not hear that distinguished man who thought Modestinus wrote the same as Paulus. But since it was later established that a crime of majesty is not incurred by an insult, and this enactment was carried into the Code of Justinian, Single Law, C., If anyone has insulted the Emperor, I think Tribonian therefore altered Modestinus's words in this way. For my part, I readily believe that Modestinus wrote as it has been published: The crime of majesty is aggravated by deed, or by violating statues or images, especially in soldiers. For Modestinus did not wish that this crime of majesty be aggravated by impious words, since he himself teaches that the slip of the tongue is not to be easily drawn into punishment, Digest, Law VII, §III, On the Julian Law of Majesty. In my judgment, Modestinus wrote these things on the occasion of what had happened in Africa, when Gordian (in whose time Modestinus flourished) was hailed as Emperor, after Maximinus had been deposed by the soldiers. For they threw down the statues of Maximinus and broke his images, and Maximinus's anger, roused by this, wished that none of Gordian's party be spared. Therefore the crime of majesty was aggravated especially against the soldiers, both by the deed, when the soldiers deposed Maximinus and proclaimed Gordian Emperor, and by the violation of statues or images. For a crime of majesty was also incurred if anything was done against the statues or images of the Princes, though with certain safeguards which the sons of the jurists report. Hence he was freed of this charge by the Senate, which melted down the statues of the Emperor that had been rejected, Digest, Law IV, §I, ibid. He calls rejected statues those which the sculptor, or the one who had commissioned them to be made, found less acceptable, as not representing the Emperor's face, or because the Emperor did not want them set up for himself (for they were not set up without the Emperor's own authority). Since they had neither been set up nor consecrated, it was lawful to melt them down with impunity, just as Severus and Antoninus rescribed to Pontius that it is not considered to be against majesty to do so concerning the images of Caesar which were not consecrated and were sold. Digest, Law V, §II.

units.tr: Moreover, it was decreed by a decree that after their time had expired, it was lawful to kill with impunity the one who was plotting anything; the Athenians swore to the words of the decree, because it is better that he be killed before he has done anything, than that he should subject the commonwealth to the yoke. The matter is pressed to the utmost, like Merops's subtle arguments in Euripides.

units.tr: Resolved by the Council and the People, Aiantis was prytanis, Kalligenes was secretary, Boethos was epistates, and Demophantos proposed the motion: "In the archonship of ..., on this decree, the Council of Five Hundred, on the day of the Kyamos, when Kalligenes first acted as secretary: if anyone overthrows the democracy, or holds office after the overthrow of the democracy, or conspires to hold it, let him be an enemy of the Athenians, and let his property be public, and let the one who kills him be blameless and holy, and let him be free from the impiety of killing. Let all Athenians, in the sacred rites, and in the phylai and demes, swear an oath to kill the one who did these things." [ΕΔΟΞΕ ΤΗ ΒΟΥΛΗ, ΚΑΙ ΤΩ ΔΗΜΩ ... ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΟΙ ... ΤΑ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΑ, ΑΥΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ ΕΣΤΩ ... ΑΠΑΝΤΑΣ ... ΚΑΙ ΤΟΝ ... ΑΠΟΚΤΕΙΝΕΙΝ ΤΟΝ ... ΤΑ ΠΟΙΗΣΑΝΤΑ.]

units.la: Placuit Senatui, popu-loque Athenien sium: Ariantis Tribus imperabat, Cleogenes erat Scriba: Bacchus praeerat: Demophantus Psephisma scripsit. Incipit tempus huius Psephismatis, ex quo Quingentorum Senatus sit captio, Cleogenes primum Scriba erat. Si quis Atheniensium Respublicam everterit, aut ea euersa Magistratum gerat, Atheniensium hostis esto, impunéque occidatur: bona eius publicantor, subductaque eorum parte decima Minervae sacra. Is qui occiderit, aut occiderit consilium dederit, purus a cade esto: A-[illegible, ~10 letters] [?]
units.tr: It has been resolved by the Senate and the people of the Athenians. The tribe of Antiochis held the presidency, Cleogenes was secretary, Bacchus presided, and Demophantus wrote the decree. The time of this decree begins from when the Senate of Five Hundred was seized, when Cleogenes was first secretary. If anyone overthrows the commonwealth of the Athenians, or holds office after it has been overthrown, let him be an enemy of the Athenians and be killed with impunity. His goods shall be confiscated, and a tenth part of them set aside as sacred to Minerva. Whoever kills him, or gives counsel to kill him, shall be pure of the murder...

units.la: ΔΥΝΑΤΟΣ Ω ΟΣ ΑΝ ΚΑΤΑΛΥ-ΣΗι ΤΗΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΝ ΤΗΝ ΑΘΗΝΗιΣΙ. ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΡΞΗι ΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΚΑΤΑΛΕΛΥΜΕΝΗΣ ΤΗΣ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΣ ΤΟΛΟΙΠΟΝ, ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΤΥΡΑΝΝΕΙΝ ΕΓΑΝΑ-ΣΤΗι Η ΤΟΝ ΤΥΡΑΝΝΟΝ ΣΥΓΚΑ-ΤΑΣΤΗΣΗι. ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΛΛΟΣ ΑΠΟΚΤΕΙΝΗι ΟΣΙΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΝΟ-ΜΙΩ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΠΡΟΣ ΘΕΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΔΑΙΜΟΝΩΝ, ΩΣ ΠΟΛΕΜΙΟΝ ΚΤΕΙ-ΝΑΝΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΚΤΗΜΑΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΟΣ ΠΑΝΤΑ ΑΠΟΔΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΠΟΔΩ-ΣΩ ΤΑ ΗΜΙΣΕΑ· ΤΩ ΑΠΟΚΤΕΙ-ΝΑΝΤΙ ΚΑΙ ΛΟΓΩι ΚΑΙ ΥΗΦΩι, ΚΑΙ ΟΥΚ ΑΠΟΣΤΕΡΗΣΩ ΟΥΔΕΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΚΤΕΙΝΩΝ ΤΙΝΑ ΤΟΥ-ΤΩΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΗι Η ΕΠΙΧΕΙΡΩΝ, ΕΥ ΠΟΙΗΣΩ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΤΕ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΓΑΙΔΑΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΚΕΙΝΟΥ, ΚΑΤΑΓΕΡ ΑΡΜΟΔΙΟΝ ΤΕ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΙ-ΣΤΟΓΕΙΤΟΝΑ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΓΟΓΟ-ΝΟΥΣ ΑΥΤΩΝ. ΟΠΟΣΟΙ ΔΕ ΟΡΚΟΙ ΟΜΩΜΟΝΤΑΙ ΑΘΗΝΗιΣΙΝ Η ΕΝ ΤΩι ΣΤΡΑΤΟΠΕΔΩι Η ΑΛΛΟΘΙ ΠΟΥ Ε-ΝΑΝΤΙΟΙ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗ-ΝΑΙΩΝ ΛΥΩ ΚΑΙ ΑΦΙΗΜΙ.
units.tr: Whoever shall overthrow the democracy of the Athenians, and if anyone shall afterwards begin to overthrow the democracy, and if anyone shall aim at tyranny or help to establish a tyrant, and if anyone else kills such a man, let him be considered pure before the gods and the spirits, as one who has killed an enemy of the Athenians. I will restore all the property of the dead man to the public treasury, but I will give the one who killed him a half-share of it, and I will hide nothing of it. If anyone kills or attempts to kill any of these men, I will do well by him and his children, as by Harmodius and Aristogeiton, and their descendants. Whatever oaths are sworn among the Athenians, whether in the camp or elsewhere, contrary to the people of the Athenians, I declare void and cancel.

units.la: Ταῦτα ὁ ὠμόσαντε Αθηναῖοι πρῶτος καθ' ἱεραῶν πελεί Διονυσίων· καὶ Ἀδ'χεσθε, διορκωῦντι μὴ εἴ πολλὰ καὶ ἀγ-λη αὐτὸν εἴ καὶ ἡμος. [?]
units.tr: The Athenians swore these things first, by the sacred Dionysia; and let them... if they perjure themselves... many and... himself, and...

units.la: Meminit huius tum Pfephismatis, cum iurisiurandi
units.tr: Of this decree he makes mention, when the oath...

units.la: Λεωχάρης. μὴ τοὺς Τειάκοντα οἱ πατῆρες ὑμῶν ἐνηφίσθη, ἡ τὸν πόλιν ποιήσωσι, ἡ τὸν δῆμον κατα-δεῖν εἴ ἀποκτεῖναι. [?] manu, si possim, eum qui euerterit Rempublicam Athenienfium, aut ea euerfa Magistratum gesserit in posterum: & si quis tyrannidem inuadat ipse, aut alteri adstruat, eumque quis alius occiderit, is mihi purus erit à cæde apud Deos & Daemonas, ut qui populi Athenienfium hoftem occiderit: bonáque occisi restituam, ita ut semissis eorum cedat illi qui occidit, me auctore & suffragante: neque quicquam subducam: Si quis autem dum occidit, aut aggreditur illos, percat, honores ei tribuam, eiusque liberu[?], quales Harmodio & Aristogitoni, eorúmque posteris: Quacunque autem iuramenta concipientur Athenis, aut in castris, aut ubicunque fit, contraria Athenienfium populo, irrita habeo & remitto.
units.tr: Leocrates: "Let it not be that your fathers decreed that the Thirty should be..., or that they should make the city..., or that they should bind the people... to kill." I will swear, if I can, by my own hand, against anyone who overthrows the commonwealth of the Athenians, or who holds office after it has been overthrown in future. And if anyone seizes tyranny himself, or helps another to do so, and anyone else kills him, that man shall be pure of murder before the gods and the spirits, as one who has killed an enemy of the Athenian people. I will restore the goods of the one killed, so that half of them goes to the one who killed him, on my authority and by my support, and I will conceal nothing. If anyone dies while killing those men, or while attacking them, I will bestow honours on him and on his children, such as on Harmodius and Aristogeiton and their descendants. Whatever oaths are sworn at Athens, or in the camp, or wherever it may be, contrary to the Athenian people, I hold void and release.

units.tr: ...of the lawful oath, by...

units.la: αῦ· ἐπιορκοῦντι δὲ, ἐξω-
units.tr: ...but to the perjurer, ...

units.la: ndi Lycurgus [?] ὡς τοῦ [?] ο καὶ ὤμοσεν, ἐάν τις πο[?] λίη, τὸν αἰσχανόμενον κα[?] ω ἐγγὺς πεπαιαι μᾶλλον, οντο δεῖν ὅπως ζὴν ἐς πολί[?] ιαχημέν. Ζῶντα, ὦ ἀνδρες, [?] ἐπούμνημα τοῖς καθ' ἐκά[?] ς δεῖ, παρὰ τοιούτες ἐ[?] τὴ ποιῆν, ἀπαυτῆν οἰκω[?] [illegible, ~12 letters] τὰς ἁμαρτίας· παρὰ[?] [illegible, ~14 letters] ὁ ὀ γὸν, [illegible, ~12 letters] μὴ ζῶντα ἄλλο [?] [illegible, ~8 letters] ἀδικωάντων ἁμαρτίας. Quod vero iusiurandum concipiunt omnes in vniuersum Athenienses, cuius alia suis singula quaeque locis adferemus Kapita, Ardetti videntur iurasse: nam is locus erat Athenis, vbi iurare solebant. Hesychius: Ταῖς ῥαδίας ὀπτ' ὅρκοις ἰοῦσας[?], Ἀρδήττιος ἐκάλουν· τόπος δὲ ἦν τῷ πρὸς τὸν Ἰλισσόν[?], ἐξ οὗ τὸ Παναθηναϊκὸν σταδίον[?], ἐν ᾧ τὰς ὅρκους ἐπομνύοντο[?].
units.tr: ...Lycurgus... and he swore that if anyone... rather near... to live in the city... Living, men, ... to each one... such as ... to do, ... to ... their sins... ... not living... of those who do wrong... Now as for the oath which all the Athenians in general take, of which we shall give other particulars in their own places, they seem to have sworn at Ardettos, for that was the place at Athens where they were accustomed to swear. Hesychius: "They called the oaths sworn at Ardettos, the place by the Ilissus, from which comes the Panathenaic stadium, in which they used to swear their oaths."

units.la: Lege non licebat munus eiurare apud alios, quàm qui illud iniunxerant & mandauerant, vt colligere est facile ex hac speciali Lege:
units.tr: By law it was not permitted to refuse a public duty before anyone other than those who had imposed and assigned it, as may easily be gathered from this particular law:

units.la: Ταῖς ἐκ τῆς δήμου χειροτονίας ἐν τῇ βουλῇ μὴ ἐξομνύσθαι.
units.tr: Those chosen by the people's vote shall not excuse themselves in the Council. [Ταῖς ἐκ τῆς δήμου χειροτονίας ἐν τῇ βουλῇ μὴ ἐξομνύσθαι.]

units.la: Legem descripsit Æschines ἐν τῷ πρὸς Κτησιφῶντα περὶ παραπρεσβείας. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ νόμος ἐᾶ τοὺς ἐκ τῆς δήμου χειροτονίας ἐν τῇ βουλῇ ἐξομνύσθαι. Hac eiuratione significabatur id, quod iniungebatur munus, non posse praestari, ob sonticam vel aliam causam. Harpocration: ἐξωμοσία, ὅ μὲν ὅρκου παρέξειν τινὰ ἀπὸ[?] πρᾶξιν[?] ... ἢ τινὰ ἐπέφαν παρέφασιν ἐξωμόσασθαί ἐστιν. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. VI. ἐξωμοσία ἢ, ὅταν τις ἡ πρεσβευτὴς ἀιρεθῇ, ἢ ἐπὶ ἄλλῳ τινὰ δημοσίῳ λειτουργίᾳ, ῥῴωτιν, ἢ ἀδυνατῶν φάσκων ἐξομνύεται αὐτὸς, ἢ δὲ ἐπέφυ. Fiebat namque per alium eiuratio, si is qui munus eiurabat in morbo cubaret: Hinc Æschines per fratrem suum legationem ad Philippum eiurauit, morbum causatus, vt est in Argumento Orationis Demosthenicae περὶ παραπρεσβείας· ἀπεγραψάμενος ὁ Αἰσχίνης, ὡς λέγ(ει) Δημοσθένης, ῥῴωσιν, ἡ τότε ὁ ἀδελφὸς αὐτοῦ Εὔνομος ἦλθεν ἔχων ἰατρὸν, ἐ ὁμνύων ὅτι ῥῴωστῇ Αἰσχίνης.
units.tr: Aeschines described the law in his speech Against Ctesiphon, On the False Embassy. "For the law does not allow those chosen by the people's vote to excuse themselves in the Council." [Οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ νόμος ἐᾶ τοὺς ἐκ τῆς δήμου χειροτονίας ἐν τῇ βουλῇ ἐξομνύσθαι.] By this excuse was signified that the assigned duty could not be performed on account of sickness or some other cause. Harpocration: "To excuse oneself (exomosia) is to swear that one cannot perform some act, or that one has some impediment." [ἐξωμοσία... ἐξωμόσασθαί ἐστιν.] Pollux, Book VIII, chapter VI: "Excuse by oath occurs when someone has been chosen as ambassador, or for some other public service, and is ill, or unable, and excuses himself by oath, or claims a hindrance." [ἐξωμοσία ἢ, ὅταν τις... ῥῴωτιν...] Such an excuse could be made through another person, if the one who was excusing himself was lying ill in bed. Hence Aeschines, citing sickness, excused himself from the embassy to Philip through his brother, as is stated in the argument of Demosthenes' speech On the False Embassy [περὶ παραπρεσβείας]: "Aeschines, having registered himself as ill, as Demosthenes says, then his brother Eunomus came, bringing a doctor, and swore that Aeschines was sick."

units.la: Lege non licebat conuicium facere Magistratui conuentum agenti, qui secus fecisset, multa ei irrogabatur.
units.tr: By law it was not permitted to insult a magistrate while he was holding court; whoever did otherwise was fined.

units.la: Ἐαν τις ἀρχῷ ἐν σιωεδρίῳ λοιδορῇ, ζημιοῦσθαι.
units.tr: If anyone abuses the archon in the council, let him be fined.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Lysias ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ἀγοράτου[?] τῆς Ἀρχοντὸς, οἱ ἢ μὴ Κτησικλέους τῷ ἀρχοντι, ἀπαλλάξαντος ἑνὸς, ὡς ἐγὼ λοιδορῶ, τῷ νόμου ἀπαγορεύοντος, ἐὰν τις ἀρχῷ ἐν σιωεδρίῳ λοιδορῇ τὸν νόμον, ζημιῶσαι ἡξίωσεν, ὑπαλλάττης ὁ ἀρχῶν. capite luisse vult Vlpianus ad Midianam: ὁ δὲ τῆς Ἀρχοντὸς τῆς πόλεως ἀπειλῇ ἡ λοιδορούμενος, ἐφ' οἷς ἢ ἱκανὸς ἀεὶ ἐσται. Sed multam tantum fuisse, testis idem Lysias eadem Oratione non semel: τῆς μὲν νόμου διαφορὰς δὲ ἀρχοντὸς τοῖς ἐν τῷ σιωεδρίῳ λοιδορωμένοις ἡμοιῶ. & paullo post: εἰ γὰρ φανερὸς εἶμι μὴ ἐλθὼν εἰς τὸ σιωέδριον, ὁ δὲ νόμος τοῖς ἐντὸς πολυμελεῖς ἀγορᾶς τὸν δημίου ὀφείλει.
units.tr: Lysias mentions this law in his speech Against Agoratus, concerning the archon: "...Ctesicles... the archon... dismissing... as I abuse... the law forbidding, if anyone abuses the archon in the council, the law demands punishment, the archon being present." Ulpian, in his commentary on Midias, wishes the penalty to have been capital: "...the one who threatens or abuses the archon of the city..." But that it was only a fine, the same Lysias testifies more than once in the same speech: "...the difference between the law and the archon for those who abuse in the council..." and a little later: "For if I am clearly seen not to have gone into the council, the law owes the public executioner to those inside..."

units.la: Quibus è verbis colligas Legem cauisse verbis expressis, ne Magistratui conuicium fieret ἐντὸς τῆς σιωεδρίου, siue ἐν τῷ σιωεδρίῳ, dum forum ageret, id est, apud consilium: verteret Caius, in Ecclesia: nam ita intelligenda sunt eius verba ex Institutionum Lib. I. Tit. de Libertatibus Seruorum, vbi explanat, quinam Liberti ciues Romani sint. Ciues Romani sunt, qui his tribus modis, id est, testamento, aut in Ecclesia, aut ante Consulem fuerint manumissi. Videri posset nonnemini Ecclesiae nomen irrepsisse è Christianorum moribus: nam ex sacris Imperatorum Constitutionibus manumissio procedit in sacrosanctis Ecclesiis: Caio autem Ethnico, vnde Ecclesiae nomen? itaque legunt viri praestantissimi, aut censu, aut ante Consulem. Ego vero existimo vocem Ecclesiae probam esse apud Caium: nam cum cives Romani sint, vt loquitur Vlpianus, liberti, qui vindicta, censu, aut testamento, manumissi sunt: vindicta autem manumittantur apud Magistratum, velut Prætorem, Consulem, Proconsulem: censu vero desitum est manumitti ætate Ulpiani, ut liquido probant hæc eius verba: Censu manumittebantur olim, qui lustrali censu Romæ, iussu dominorum, inter cives Romanos censum profitebantur. Caius tamen etiam tribus modis fieri docet: Uno modorum distributo in duas species: nam cum vindicta fiat apud Magistratum: Caius distinxit. In concilium autem adhibebantur Romæ quinque Senatores & quinque Equites Romani: in Prouincia viginti Recuperatores cives Romani, ut scribit Ulpianus, & docet Theophilus, qui παράδοσις vocat Tit. Quibus ex causis manumittere non possint §. IV. hocque concilium adtribuit tantum Prætori Romæ. ἐγίνετο δὲ ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ ὁ Κυναίλιον[?], ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ τῷ κομιζόντι[?], τῆς Γεραιτωρς[?] καὶ[?] τοῦ οἰκείου[?] δικαστηρίου[?], καὶ συνκαθεζομένων αὐτῷ πέντε Συνκλητικῶν ἐν τίνι[?] Ἰταλιῶν[?] Ῥωμαίων. Quanquam etiam Consul suum habuerit consilium, unde legitur apud Ulpianum Lib. II. de Officio Consulis: Officium Consulis est, consilium præbere manumittere volentibus. Leg. unica D. de Officio Consulis. quemadmodum Iulianus Lib. XLII. Digestorum tum Consuli cum Prætori, & Prouinciarum Præsidibus consilium tribuit: An apud se manumittere possit is, qui consilium præbeat sæpe quæsitum est? Ego quum meminissem Iauolenum præceptorem meum & in Africa & in Syria seruos suos manumisisse, cum consilium præberet, exemplum eius secutus, & in Prætura & Consulatu meo quosdam ex seruis meis vindicta liberaui, & quibusdam Prætoribus consulentibus me, idem suasi. Leg. V. D. de Manumissis vindicta. Non tamen semper concilium cogebat Prætor, aut Consul, quando apud illum manumittebatur: nam Ulpianus Lib. V. ad Edictum testatur se, cum in villa cum Prætore fuisset, passum esse apud eum manumitti, & si lictoris præsentia non esset. Leg. VIII. D. de manumissis vindicta. Itaque definiuit Gaius Lib. I. Rerum Cotidianarum siue aureorum, non esse omnino necesse pro tribunali manumittere: itaque plerumque in transitu serui manumitti solent, cum aut lauandi, aut gestandi, aut ludorum gratia prodierit Prætor, aut Proconsul, Legatusue Cæsaris. Leg. VII. D. eod. Quare obseruandum est, aliquando, apud concilium Consulis siue Proconsulis, siue, Prætoris, siue Præsidis Prouinciæ manumissum fuisse, aliquando apud solum Consulem, aut Prætorem, aut Magistratum, cui huiusmodi jus est: unde titulus Codicis De vindicta libertate, & apud concilium manumissione. & in Imperatoris Antonini Augusti Rescripto ad Tertium concilij tantum mentio, Eorum qui apud concilium manumittuntur, &c. Leg. I. C. eod. & distinguit Imperator Constantius A. ad Maximum Pr. Pr. concilium a Consulibus, Prætoribus, &c. Apud concilium nostrum, (hæc vox nostrum abest a plerisque libris idque merito) vel apud Consules, Prætores, Præsules, Præsides, Magistratusue earum ciuitatum, quibus huiusmodi jus est, adipisci potest patronorum judicio sedula seruitus libertatem. Leg. IV. C. eod. Ex hac igitur obseruatione distinctioneque, dixit Caius, manumitti, aut in Ecclesia, hoc est, apud concilium, aut ante Consulem, id est, non adhibito concilio apud Consulem, aliumue Magistratum, cui huiusmodi jus est. Sed hæc obiter, quæ, quanquam extra rem sint, non ingrata tamen esse æquo Lectori votum sit nostrum.
units.tr: From these words you may gather that the law expressly provided that no insult be offered to a magistrate within the council [ἐντὸς τῆς βουλῆς], or in the council [ἐν τῷ συνεδρίῳ], while he was holding court, that is, before the council. Caius renders it in the Church: for his words in the Institutes, Book I, title On the Liberty of Slaves, must be understood in this way, where he explains who the freed men who are Roman citizens are. "Those are Roman citizens who have been manumitted in one of three ways: by will, in the Church, or before the Consul." It might seem to some that the word Church crept in from Christian customs, for by the sacred constitutions of the emperors "manumission takes place in the sacrosanct churches." But how could the word Church come from Caius, a pagan? Therefore some very distinguished scholars read, by the census, or before the Consul. I, however, think that the word Church is sound in Caius. For since they are Roman citizens, as Ulpian says, freedmen who were manumitted by the rod, by the census, or by will; and those manumitted by the rod are freed before a magistrate, such as the praetor, consul, or proconsul; but manumission by the census had ceased by the time of Ulpian, as these words of his clearly show: "Formerly they were manumitted by the census, those who in the lustral census at Rome, by order of their masters, declared themselves among the Roman citizens." Caius nevertheless teaches that it happens in three ways; having divided the one way into two kinds, since manumission by the rod takes place before a magistrate, Caius made a distinction. For in the council at Rome were present five senators and five Roman knights; in the province, twenty recuperators who were Roman citizens, as Ulpian writes, and Theophilus teaches, who calls it paradosis, in the title On the causes for which they cannot manumit, §4. And this council belonged only to the praetor at Rome. [ἐγίνετο δὲ ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ... καὶ συνκαθεζομένων αὐτῷ πέντε Συνκλητικῶν...] Although the consul also had his own council, whence it is read in Ulpian, Book II, On the Duty of the Consul: "It is the duty of the consul to give counsel to those wishing to manumit." Single law, Digest, On the Duty of the Consul, just as Julian, Book XLII of the Digest, grants a council both to the consul and the praetor and to the governors of provinces: "Whether a person who gives counsel may manumit before himself has often been asked. Since I remembered that my teacher Javolenus manumitted his slaves both in Africa and in Syria while giving counsel, I followed his example, and both in my praetorship and my consulship I freed some of my slaves by the rod, and when some praetors consulted me, I advised the same." Law V, Digest, On Manumission by the Rod. Yet the praetor or consul did not always convene a council when manumission was made before him; for Ulpian, Book V on the Edict, testifies that he himself, when he was at his country house with the praetor, allowed himself to be manumitted before him, even without the presence of a lictor. Law VIII, Digest, On Manumission by the Rod. Therefore Gaius, Book I of his Everyday Matters or Golden Things, defined that it is not at all necessary to manumit from the tribunal: so slaves are commonly manumitted in passing, when the praetor, proconsul, or legate of Caesar has gone out for washing, for being carried, or for the sake of games. Law VII, Digest, same title. Hence it is to be observed that sometimes manumission took place before the council of the consul, proconsul, praetor, or governor of a province, and sometimes before the consul or praetor alone, or before a magistrate who had such a right. Hence the title of the Code, On liberty by the rod, and manumission before the council. And in the rescript of the emperor Antoninus Augustus to Tertius, mention is made only of the council: Of those who are manumitted before the council, etc. Law I, Code, same title. And the emperor Constantius Augustus, in a letter to Maximus, Praetorian Prefect, distinguishes the council from the consuls, praetors, etc.: Before our council (the word our is absent from most books, and rightly so) or before the consuls, praetors, prefects, governors, or magistrates of those cities which have such a right, a slavery diligently serving its patrons may obtain liberty by judgment. Law IV, Code, same title. From this observation and distinction, therefore, Caius said to be manumitted in the Church, that is, before the council, or before the Consul, that is, without a council present, before the consul or another magistrate who has such a right. But these things have been said in passing; though they are beside the point, it is our wish that they will not be unwelcome to the fair reader.

units.la: At vero certum est verbis impijs exacerbari Principes, Maiestatisque crimen contrahi: quanquam Imperatores Augusti Theodosius, Arcadius, & Honorius Rufino Pr. Pr. rescribant, maledictum, si ex levitate processerit, contemnendum esse, si ex insania, miseratione dignissimum, si ab iniuria remittendum. Leg. unica. C. Si quis imperatori maledixerit. Qua de re insignis est Tertulliani locus Lib. de Pallio, cap. IV. qui ita vulgo editur. Physconem & Sardanapalum tacendum est, qui nisi insignes libidinum, alias Reges nemo nosset: tacendum autem, ne quid & illi de Cæsaribus quibusdam vestris obmussitent, propudiosis: nec magnæ forte constantiæ mandatum sit, impuriorem Physcone, molliorem Sardanapalo, Cæsarem designare, & quidem sub Nerone. Optime Vir Incomparabilis arguit mendi hæc verba, nec magnæ forte constantiæ: nam, ut observat illud Literarum μὶ γὰ αὔχημα [?], magnæ atque etiam maximæ constantiæ sit, Cæsarem aliquem Sardanapalo molliorem, & Physcone impuriorem designare: quis enim in illum ausit scribere, qui potest proscribere? aut quis in eum dicere, cui licet, si libet, occidere? E prima Beati Rhenani Editione restituendus est hic locus, in qua ita legitur. Tacendum autem ne quid & illi de Cæsaribus quibusdam vestris obmussitent, pariter propudiosisse ne cane & forte constantiæ mandatum sit, impuriorem Physcon & molliorem Sardanapalo Cæsarem designare, & quidem subneronem. Ita igitur legentes huius editionis vestigia restituimus. Tacendum autem, ne quid & illi de Cæsaribus quibusdam vestris obmussitent, pariter propudiosis: Senecanæ & forte constantiæ mandatum sit, impuriorem Physcone, & molliorem Sardanapalo Cæsarem designare, & quidem sub Neronem. Dixit igitur Tertullianus, tacendum esse Physconem, aut Sardanapalum, ne illi de Cæsaribus quosdam reponant, non minus propudiosos, & nonnemo se componat ad exemplum Senecanæ constantiæ, id est, idem quod Seneca præstet, qui constanter & animose Cæsari impuritiam atque mollitiem ausus est, sive in iis, quæ de Caio scripsit, sive edito Ludo in mortem Claudij, designare, idque imperante Nerone ipso, hoc enim est, quod dicit, sub Neronem, sed Græcatur, ὑπὸ τὸν Νέρωνα.
units.tr: Yet it is certain that Princes are provoked by impious words, and that the crime of treason (maiestas) is incurred. Still, the Emperors Augusti Theodosius, Arcadius and Honorius, in a rescript to Rufinus, Praetorian Prefect, state that a curse, if it has arisen from thoughtlessness, is to be disregarded; if from madness, it deserves the greatest pity; if from injury, it is to be pardoned. Single law, C. Si quis imperatori maledixerit. On this matter there is a notable passage of Tertullian, in the book On the Pallium, chapter IV, which is commonly printed thus: We must be silent about Physco and Sardanapalus, who would be known to no one as kings except for their notorious lusts. We must be silent too, lest some of those scurrilous men of yours should retort with stories about certain of your Caesars. Nor is it perhaps a mandate of great constancy to portray a Caesar as more impure than Physco and softer than Sardanapalus, and indeed under Nero. The incomparable man rightly argues that the words nec magnae forte constantiae are corrupt. For, as the saying of the literati observes [μὴ γὰρ αὔχημα], it would be a matter of great, indeed the greatest, constancy to portray some Caesar as softer than Sardanapalus and more impure than Physco. For who would dare to write against one who can proscribe? Or who would speak against one who may kill whom he pleases? This passage is to be restored from the first edition of Beatus Rhenanus, where it reads: We must be silent too, lest some of those men of yours should retort with stories about certain Caesars, equally shameless; nor is it perhaps a mandate of the constancy of Seneca to portray Physco as more impure, and Caesar as softer than Sardanapalus, and indeed under Nero. Following that edition's traces, then, we restore the text as follows: We must be silent too, lest some of those men of yours should retort with stories about certain Caesars, equally shameless; nor is it perhaps a mandate of the constancy of Seneca to portray a Caesar as more impure than Physco and softer than Sardanapalus, and indeed under Nero. Tertullian therefore says that Physco and Sardanapalus must be passed over in silence, lest some men retort with Caesars no less shameless, and lest someone model himself on the constancy of Seneca, that is, do what Seneca did: he boldly and spiritedly portrayed a Caesar's impurity and effeminacy, whether in what he wrote about Caligula or in his play performed on the death of Claudius, and he did so while Nero himself was emperor. For this is what he means by sub Neronem, though in Greek it is under Nero [ὑπὸ τὸν Νέρωνα].

units.la: Inter præcipuos Atheniensium Magistratus censendi sunt annui illi novem, quorum vnus Archon dicebatur, signabatque Fastos, alter Rex, tertius Polemarchus, reliqui sex Thesmothetæ. Pollux Lib. VIII cap. IX. Ἀρχόντων Ἀθηναίων ὀνόματα. οἱ εἰσὶ Ἀρχοντες. εἰσὶ δ᾽ ὁ τῆς ἐπώνυμος Ἄρχων, Βασιλεύς, Πολέμαρχος, ἡ Θεσμοθέται ἕξ. ἐκ τούτων γὰρ οἱ ἐνία Ἀρχοντες συμπληρωθῶσι. Quos Magistratus cum sortiti essent illi, quos populus designauerat, vt in superioribus diximus, probatque hic ex Oratione aduersus Neæram locum, [illegible, ~40 letters], oportebat in eorum vitam inquiri, antequam Magistratum caperent; idque fiebat prius apud Quingentorum Senatum, deinde apud iudices. Enim, si τῶν Ἀρχόντων Παρέδρος δοκιμασθῶν ἐχέλω ἐν τῇ Πεντακοσίοις, εἴτ᾽ ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, quanto magis ipsos [?] τὰς ἐνία Ἀρχοντας; Sed non finit nos dubitare Pollux loco laudato. ἐκαλεῖτο δὲ τῆς Θεσμοθετῶν ἀδοκιμασίας. ἐπηρώτα ἡ βουλή. Quod ad τὸ ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ δοκιμασίαν attinet, in Lege præcipitur. Vtriusque autem ἀδοκιμασίας, id est, illius quæ apud Quingentorum Senatum; tum etiam, quæ apud iudices, eadem erant Kapita, quorum nonnulla etiam hodie leguntur.
units.tr: Among the chief magistrates of the Athenians must be counted those nine annual officials, of whom one was called the Archon, who signed the calendar (Fasti); another the King; a third the Polemarch; and the remaining six the Thesmothetae. Pollux, Book 8, chapter 9: [Ἀρχόντων Ἀθηναίων ὀνόματα. οἱ εἰσὶ Ἀρχοντες. εἰσὶ δ᾽ ὁ τῆς ἐπώνυμος Ἄρχων, Βασιλεύς, Πολέμαρχος, ἡ Θεσμοθέται ἕξ. ἐκ τούτων γὰρ οἱ ἐνία Ἀρχοντες συμπληρωθῶσι.] That is: "The names of the Athenian archons. These are the archons: the eponymous Archon, the King, the Polemarch, and the six Thesmothetae; for from these the archons are completed." When those whom the people had designated had been chosen by lot to these magistracies, as we said above, and as he proves here from the speech against Neaera [illegible], their lives had to be inquired into before they took office. This was done first before the Council of Five Hundred, and then before the judges. For if [τῶν Ἀρχόντων Παρέδρος δοκιμασθῶν ἐχέλω ἐν τῇ Πεντακοσίοις, εἴτ᾽ ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ], how much more so [the rest of the archons]? But Pollux, in the passage cited, leaves us in no doubt: [ἐκαλεῖτο δὲ τῆς Θεσμοθετῶν ἀδοκιμασίας. ἐπηρώτα ἡ βουλή.] As for the examination before the court, it is prescribed in the law. Moreover, the questions of both examinations, that is, the one before the Council of Five Hundred and also the one before the judges, were the same, and some of them are still read today.

units.la: ΑΝΑΚΡΙΣΙΣ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ.
units.tr: Examination of the Nine Archons [ἀνάκρισις τῶν ἐννέα ἀρχόντων]

units.la: Εἰ Ἀθηναῖοι εἰσὶν ἑκατέρωθεν ἐκ πεντηκοντα[?] ἐκ τειρονίας[?], καὶ τὴν δῆμον πόλει[?]. καὶ εἰ Ἀπόλλων ἔστιν αὐτῆς Πατρῷος[?], καὶ Ζεὺς Ἑρκεῖος[?].
units.tr: [Εἰ Ἀθηναῖοι εἰσὶν ἑκατέρωθεν ἐκ πεντηκοντα[?] ἐκ τειρονίας[?], καὶ τὴν δῆμον πόλει[?]. καὶ εἰ Ἀπόλλων ἔστιν αὐτῆς Πατρῷος[?], καὶ Ζεὺς Ἑρκεῖος[?].] Whether he is an Athenian on both sides, from a family of fifty [?], and of the city's deme; and whether Apollo Patroos and Zeus Herkeios are his.

units.la: Ω ΑΝΘΡΩΠΕ, ΤΙΣ ΗΝ ΣΟΙ ΠΑΤΗΡ; ΕΜΟΙ Ο ΔΕΙΝΑ. ΟΙΚΕΙΟΙ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΟΥΣΙΝ ΑΥΤΩι[?], ΠΑΝΥ ΓΕ, ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΓΕ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ. ΑΝΕΨΙΟΙ[?]· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΟΥΣ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ, ΟΙΣ ΗΡΙΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ· ΕΙΤΑ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ· ΕΙΤΑ ΑΡΟΛΛΩΝΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΔΙΟΣ ΕΡΚΙΟΥ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ ΠΟΛΛΑΚΙΣ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΔΕΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΘΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΑΡΞΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΔΙΕΞΗΦΙΣΜΕΝΟΙ ΦΑΙΝΟΝΤΑΙ.
units.tr: [Ω ΑΝΘΡΩΠΕ, ΤΙΣ ΗΝ ΣΟΙ ΠΑΤΗΡ; ΕΜΟΙ Ο ΔΕΙΝΑ. ΟΙΚΕΙΟΙ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΟΥΣΙΝ ΑΥΤΩι[?], ΠΑΝΥ ΓΕ, ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΓΕ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ. ΑΝΕΨΙΟΙ[?]· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΟΥΣ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ, ΟΙΣ ΗΡΙΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ· ΕΙΤΑ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ· ΕΙΤΑ ΑΡΟΛΛΩΝΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΔΙΟΣ ΕΡΚΙΟΥ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ ΠΟΛΛΑΚΙΣ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΔΕΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΘΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΑΡΞΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΔΙΕΞΗΦΙΣΜΕΝΟΙ ΦΑΙΝΟΝΤΑΙ.] "O man, who was your father? Mine was [?]. Who are the witnesses to this? Tell all of them: first, your own kinsmen; then the members of your clan; then your fellow demesmen; then the phratries; then whether he belongs to Apollo Patroos and Zeus Herkeios; then whether the demesmen have often examined him and he has held office, and whether, being repeatedly voted upon, he appears to have been acquitted."

units.la: Ω ΑΝΘΡΩΠΕ, ΤΙΣ ΗΝ ΣΟΙ ΜΗΤΗΡ; ΕΜΟΙ Η ΔΕΙΝΑ;
units.tr: [Ω ΑΝΘΡΩΠΕ, ΤΙΣ ΗΝ ΣΟΙ ΜΗΤΗΡ; ΕΜΟΙ Η ΔΕΙΝΑ;] "O man, who was your mother? Mine was [?]."

units.la: ΟΙΚΕΙΟΙ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΟΥΣΙΝ ΑΥΤΗ[?]; ΠΑΝΥ ΓΕ, ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΓΕ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΑΝΕΨΙΟΙ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΟΥΣ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ ΤΩΝ ΟΙΚΕΙΩΝ ΑΥΤΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ.
units.tr: [ΟΙΚΕΙΟΙ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΟΥΣΙΝ ΑΥΤΗ[?]; ΠΑΝΥ ΓΕ, ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΓΕ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΑΝΕΨΙΟΙ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΟΥΣ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ ΤΩΝ ΟΙΚΕΙΩΝ ΑΥΤΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ.] "Who are the witnesses to this? Tell all of them: first, her own kinsmen; then the members of her clan; then the phratries of her household and the demesmen."

units.la: Εἰ τοὺς γονέας δὲ ποιοῦσι.
units.tr: [Εἰ τοὺς γονέας δὲ ποιοῦσι.] Whether he honours his parents.

units.la: Εἰ ἐχρατεύοιτο τοῦ τῆς πατρίδος.
units.tr: [Εἰ ἐχρατεύοιτο τοῦ τῆς πατρίδος.] Whether he enjoys the rights of his fatherland.

units.la: Εἰ ὁ ἡμέρα ἔστιν αὐτῆς.
units.tr: [Εἰ ὁ ἡμέρα ἔστιν αὐτῆς.] Whether he [?] of it.

units.la: Εἰ ἀφελεῖς.
units.tr: [Εἰ ἀφελεῖς.] Whether he is unencumbered.

units.la: Καπita ista habes apud Pollucem loco laudato: εὐτὸν ἀρχόντας, εἰσὶ δὲ ὁ τὸ ὠναυ ἐπώνυμος ἀρχῶν, Βασιλεὺς[?] ἐξ, ἐκ τῶν τῶν ἀρχόντων, Ἀθῆναι[?] ἀρχόντες συμπληρωμα πυ[?]· ἐκ οἴκῳ, Ἀθηναῖοι εἰσὶν ἑκάτερωθεν ἐκ τειρονίας, καὶ τὴν δῆμον πόλει. καὶ εἰ Ἀπόλλων ἔστιν αὐτῆς Πατρῷος, καὶ Ζεὺς Ἑρκεῖος, καὶ εἰς τοὺς γονέας δὲ ποιοῦσι. τὸ εἰ ἐχρατεύοιτο ὁ δῆμα ἔστιν αὐτῆς, ἐπηρώτα δὲ ἡ βουλή. Laudat quoque Εὐξυλίδῳ ex Eurythei persona, qui ita iudice
units.tr: You have these questions in Pollux, in the passage cited: [εὐτὸν ἀρχόντας, εἰσὶ δὲ ὁ τὸ ὠναυ ἐπώνυμος ἀρχῶν, Βασιλεὺς ἐξ, ἐκ τῶν τῶν ἀρχόντων, Ἀθῆναι ἀρχόντες συμπληρωμα πυ· ἐκ οἴκῳ, Ἀθηναῖοι εἰσὶν ἑκάτερωθεν ἐκ τειρονίας, καὶ τὴν δῆμον πόλει. καὶ εἰ Ἀπόλλων ἔστιν αὐτῆς Πατρῷος, καὶ Ζεὺς Ἑρκεῖος, καὶ εἰς τοὺς γονέας δὲ ποιοῦσι. τὸ εἰ ἐχρατεύοιτο ὁ δῆμα ἔστιν αὐτῆς, ἐπηρώτα δὲ ἡ βουλή.] He also quotes Euxylides from the persona of Eurytheus, who thus judges [...].

units.la: EXAMEN NOVEM VIRORVM
units.tr: EXAMEN NOVEM VIRORVM

units.la: An ab abauis utrinque ciues essent Athenienses, & ex quo populo: an illis esset Apollo patrius, & Iupiter Hercaeus, necne.
units.tr: Whether the Athenians were citizens on both sides back to their great-grandfathers, and from which deme; whether Apollo Patrius and Zeus Herkeios belonged to them or not.

units.la: Heus tu, quis tibi pater est? Mihine? Ille: Quinam de cognatione testimonium illi dicunt? Multi: primū quidem, hi patrueles, deinde hi patruelum filij: deinde hi, quibus sepulchri ius cum illo commune est: deinde Apollinis Patrij & Iouis Hercaei Genetae. deinde Phratores: deinde populares, qui illi fæpius suis suffragijs Magistratus communiserunt, atque approbarunt.
units.tr: "Hey you, who is your father?" "Mine? So-and-so." "Who bears witness to his kinship?" "Many people: first of all these, his paternal cousins; then these, the sons of his paternal cousins; then those who share the right of burial with him; then the members of the cult of Apollo Patrius and Zeus Genetes Herkeios; then the phratores; then the fellow demesmen, who have often confirmed him in magistracies by their votes and approved him."

units.la: Heus tu, quæ tibi mater est? Mihi ne? Hæc.
units.tr: "Hey you, who is your mother?" "Mine? This one."

units.la: Quinam de cognatione testimonium illi dicunt? Multi: primùm quidem hi, patrueles: deinde hi, patruelum filij: deinde Phratores & populares cognatorum eius.
units.tr: "Who bears witness to her kinship?" "Many people: first of all these, her paternal cousins; then these, the sons of her paternal cousins; then the phratores and fellow demesmen of her kinsmen."

units.la: An parentes honorarint, necne.
units.tr: Whether they honoured their parents or not.

units.la: An pro patria militarint, necne.
units.tr: Whether they served in the army for their country or not.

units.la: An census sit illis, necne.
units.tr: Whether they had a census or not.

units.la: An integri corporis essent, necne
units.tr: Whether they were of sound body or not.

units.la: Ἀρχόντων Ἀθηναίων ὀνόματα, οἱ δὲ, Πολέμαρχος[?], ἢ Θεσμοθέτης[?]
units.tr: The names of the Athenian archons: the first is the Polemarch, or the Thesmothetes.

units.la: [?] δὲ τῆς Θεσμοθετικῆς αἰσχρίας[?], εἰ [illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: ...of the Thesmothetic (office?) ... if ... [the remainder is illegible].

units.la: καὶ εἰ Ἀπόλλων ἔστιν ἄλλος Γα[?]-[illegible, ~10 letters]
units.tr: and whether Apollo is ... [the remainder is illegible].

units.la: [illegible, ~10 letters] κατεῖδες[?]. καὶ εἰ
units.tr: [illegible] ... and if.

units.la: e Demosthenes ἐν τῇ ἐφέσει[?]
units.tr: ...Demosthenes, in the (?) ...

units.la: es alloquitur: ἀλλὰ μηδ[?] ἐκείνων, ἐ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἡ [?]ὸ πολλὰ τῇ διαγράψαι [?] τοὺς ὑμᾶς ἥκω. ὥσπερ γὰρ πρὸς Θεσμοθέτας αἰακρίνεται, ἐγὼ τ' αὐτὸν ἔγνων ἐμαυτὸν ὑμῖν αἰακρίνω.
