Ω ΑΝΘΡΩΠΕ, ΤΙΣ ΗΝ ΣΟΙ ΠΑΤΗΡ; ΕΜΟΙ ΤΟΥΚΡΙΤΟΣ. ΟΙΚΕΙΟΙ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΟΥΣΙΝ ΑΥΤΩ; ΓΑΝΥ ΓΕ, ΓΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΓΕ. πταρές ΑΝΕΨΙΟΙ· ΕΙΤΑ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΟΥΣ. εἶτα οἱ ἀδελφοὶ λέγοντες αὐτῷ. ΕΙ ΓΑ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, ΕΙΤΑ ΑΡΟΛΛΩΝΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΔΙΟΣ ΕΡΚΙΟΥ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ· ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙΣ ΗΡΙΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΕΙΤΑ ΟΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ ΡΟΛΛΑΚΙΣ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΔΕΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΘΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΑΡΞΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΙ ΔΙΕΦΙΣΜΕΝΟΙ ΦΑΙΝΟΝΤΑΙ. τὰ μὲν τοίνυν πρὸς τῆς παλαιᾶς, πῶς ἀὶ ὑμῖν ἀληθῶς πεῖσαι, ἵν' καθαρώτερον ὑπισχίζομαι; καλῶς ὑμῖν τὰς οἰκίας, εἰ βούλεσθε. Τὰ δὲ πρὸς τὸ μητρῷς ἀνούσατε. ΕΜΟΙ γὰρ ἔστι μήτηρ, ΝΙΚΑΡΕΤΗ ΔΗΜΟΣΤΡΑΤΟΥ ΘΥΓΑΤΗΡ ΜΕΛΙΤΕΩΣ. ΤΑΥΤΗΣ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΟΙΚΕΙΟΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΟΥΣΙ. [illegible, ~10 letters] ἀδελφῷ δύο υἱοί. ΕΙΤΑ ΑΝΕΨΙΟΙ αὐτῆς· εἶπε οἱ Πρωτομάχου υἱὸς τὴν λαβοῦσαν τῶν ἐμαυτῷ μητέρα ἐπὶ τῶν ὁ τὼ ἀδελφῷ τὼ ἐμαυτῷ τῶν ἐκ Πρωτομάχου ἐμαυτῷ. Εὐνικες Χολαργεῖς· εἶπα ὡς τῆς ἀδελφῆς, ἀλλὰ μὲν καὶ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ ΓΩΝ ΟΙΚΕΙΩΝ ΑΥΤΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙ. ταῦτα μαρτυρήσαντα. & paullo post, ἐπὶ τίνων, ὡ ἀνδρες ἀκούετε, ὅτις ἐστὶ Ἀρχίας ἀλαχρίνεται, εἰ γένος ἔ πολιτῶν. Dicitur quidem haec ἀλαχρίας Thesmothetarum, quae reuera est omnium Nouemuirorum: itaque quae refert Pollux dici solita ἐπὶ τῇ ἀλαχρίᾳ Thesmothetarum, εἰ τοῖς γένεσι ἔ ποιοῦσι, vsurpari scribit Demosthenes ἐπὶ τῆς τῶν ἐστὶ Ἀρχόντων ἀλαχρίας. Praeterea in Scholiis Aristophanis legimus ad Nubes, ὡς ἀπόγονον οὖν αὐτὸν. Apollinem Patrium, ἐπιμαρτυρῶν οἱ Ἀρχοντες ὑπὸ ἐχέγυνωσαν, siue ἰδικιμάζοντο, quia scilicet interrogabantur, εἰ Ἀπόλλων ἔστι αὐτῆς Πατρῷος. quod factum quoque notat Pollux. Sed singula Kapita paucis expendamus. Primo interrogabantur, an vtrinque ab abauis vsque ciues essent Athenienses, necne: εἰ Ἀλωαχοὶ εἰσιν ἐκ πατρῴων ἐκ τεσσάρων. atque ad iftud Kaput referendum est, quod interrogantur, ex quo fint populo, τῶν δήμων τῆς, itemque an illis esset Apollo Patrius, & Iupiter Hercaeus,necne: εἰ Ἀπόλλων ἔστι Πατρῷος, καὶ Ζεὺς Ἑρκεῖος. Nam quibus non erat Apollo Patrius; aut Iupiter Hercaeus, peregrini & aduenae censebantur: de Apolline quidem Scholiastes Comici loco laudato: ὡς τοῖς αὐτῶν, Apollinem Patrium, εἰ μὲν καὶ οἱ Ἀρχοντες ὅτι ἐχέγυνωσαν. ἐκ γὰρ τῆς μὴ εἰδέναι ξένοις αὐτοῖς ἐκμιζον. Nam, vt inquit Comicus, οὐκ ἔστι βαρβάρος, id est, adscriptitij, ἐκ Πατρῷος ἐστιν. De Ioue vero Hercaeo Harpocration e Dinarcho, Hyperide, & Demetrio, docens illis licere ad Rempublicam accedere, quibus sit Iupiter Hercaeus: Ἑρκεῖος Ζεὺς, Δεῖναρχος ἐκ τῆς ἐπὶ Μοσχίωνος, εἰ Φράτορες αὐτῷ καὶ βωμὸς Διὸς Ἑρκείου, καὶ Ἀπόλλωνος Πατρῷος εἰσιν. ὅτι ἡ Ζεὺς μετὰ τῆς πολιτείας ἐς τὴν Ζεὺς Ἑρκεῖος, διὰ ἀλλὰ τὴν Τριφίδες ἐκ τῆς ἀπὸ τὸ ἀρχαῖος, εἰ γένους, καὶ Δημοτιαι ἐκ τῆς τὴν ἀλλ' ἀπὸ Ἀθηναι ἐξ ἀπὸ ἐλευθεροῦ. Videnturque ij, qui in Phratorum album referebantur, ad Apollinis Patrij & Iouis Hercaei adducti fuisse. Demosthenes loco laudato: ἀλλὰ πεπιστευόμενοι μὲν ἀνθρώπων ἦσαν εἰς τὰς Φράτορας, εἰς Ἀπόλλωνος Πατρῷου ἦσαν, εἰς πάλαι ἱερὰ, vnde in his, quae iam ante defcripfimus: ΕΙΤΑ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, ΕΙΤΑ ΑΡΟΛΛΩΝΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΔΙΟΣ ΕΡΚΕΙΟΥ ΓΕΝΗTAI. Atque ista quidem prioribus seculis ita fuere: nam postea ius istud mutauit, datumque est ciuium adscitorum liberis ciuae matre genitis τῶν ἐπ' Ἀρχόντων ψηφ[?]ίσματι[?], vt è Lege dandae ciuitatis constat. Quinetiam tandem adscriptis ciuibus id concessum fuisse colligo è Plutarcho, qui ciuitate Atheniensi donatus est, & relatus in Tribum Leontidem, vt ipse testatur συμποσιακῶν Libro I. Problemate X. nam Plutarchus ipse Archon creatus est, vt scribit eiusdem Operis Libro II. Problemate vltimo, nam ita habent Codices, quibus vsus est vernaculus noster Interpres voce vna auctiores vulgatis: ἐπὶ τῷ ἐπαινῶμεν [?] ἀρχῷ ἡμῶν [?] A Ἀθηναίων.
units.tr: ...addresses them: "But neither of those..., and I have come to you about many things. For just as the Thesmothetes examine, so I too have examined myself before you. O man, who was your father? Mine was Ktesikles [?]. Did some of your kin bear witness to him? Yes indeed, many, first of all my paternal cousins, then their sons, then my brothers, saying to him: 'Then the phratores, then of Apollo Patrius and Zeus Herkeios, and then the demesmen, who have often approved him and made him magistrate, and who themselves are seen as well-regarded.'" Now as to what concerns the father's side, how I can persuade you truthfully, I promise to explain more clearly; I will also show you my relatives, if you wish. As for the mother's side, hear this: my mother was Nikarete, daughter of Demostratos of Melite. Some of her kin bear witness to this... [illegible] ...she had two sons by her brother. Then the paternal... Eunikes of Cholargos said that she was a sister, but she too was among the phratores and demesmen of her kin. These witnesses have testified. And a little later: "Before whom, men, do you hear, that an archon is examined, whether he is of the citizen stock?" This examination is said to be that of the Thesmothetes, which is in fact that of all the Nine; so what Pollux reports, that the phrase was used of the examination of the Thesmothetes, Demosthenes writes was used of the examination of the archons. Besides, in the Scholia of Aristophanes on the Clouds we read that the archons were examined, or scrutinised, by those who knew them, because they were asked whether Apollo was their Patrius. Pollux also notes this. But let us weigh the individual heads briefly. First they were asked whether they were Athenian citizens on both sides back to their great-grandfathers, or not. To this head should be referred the question from which demes they came, and likewise whether Apollo Patrius and Zeus Herkeios belonged to them or not. For those who did not have Apollo Patrius or Zeus Herkeios were counted as foreigners and aliens. About Apollo the scholiast on the comic poet, in the passage cited, says that the archons were examined concerning this, because those who did not know him were considered strangers. For, as the comic poet says, "he is not a barbarian," that is, a non-citizen, "since he has Apollo Patrius." But about Zeus Herkeios, Harpocration, citing Dinarchus, Hyperides and Demetrius, teaches that only those who had Zeus Herkeios could approach the state: Zeus Herkeios, Dinarchus in the speech against Moschion: "those who are phratores of him, and have an altar of Zeus Herkeios and Apollo Patrius." ...and the Zeus with the citizenship into the Zeus Herkeios ... Those who were enrolled in the register of phratores seem to have been admitted by Apollo Patrius and Zeus Herkeios. Demosthenes, in the passage cited: "but those who were believed to be men were enrolled among the phratores, and were of Apollo Patrius, and of ancient rites," whence among those things which we have already described: "Then the phratores, then of Apollo Patrius and Zeus Herkeios [ΕΙΤΑ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, ΕΙΤΑ ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΔΙΟΣ ΕΡΚΕΙΟΥ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ]." And indeed these things were so in earlier centuries; for afterwards that law was changed, and by decree of the archons it was granted to the children of adopted citizens born of a citizen mother, as is established from the law on the granting of citizenship. Moreover, I gather from Plutarch that this privilege was at length granted to enrolled citizens: he was made a citizen of Athens and enrolled in the tribe Leontis, as he himself testifies in the Symposiacs, Book I, Problem 10. For Plutarch himself was made archon, as he writes in the last Problem of Book II of the same work; for so the manuscripts have it, which our native translator used, and which are richer by one word than the printed texts: "...in the archonship of ... of the Athenians."

units.la: Secundum Kaput Διαχρίσεως spectat cultum parentibus exhibitum: εἰ τιμὴ γονέας [?] ποιοῦσι. Neque enim qui in parentes impius est, potest in patriam bene affectus censeri.
units.tr: The second head of the examination concerns honour shown to parents: whether they honoured their parents. For one who is impious towards his parents cannot be regarded as well disposed towards his country.

units.la: Tertium Kaput est, εἰ ἐστρατεύοντο [illegible, ~6 letters] τῆς παιδείας, Vertimus, An pro patria militauerint, necne: non enim pro comperto habemus, vtrum intelligant de omnibus stipendiis legitime confectis: nam omnia non meruerant stipendia ante quadragesimum aetatis annum: quod si hoc modo de omnibus stipendiis accipiendum est, nonnisi post annum aetatis quadragesimum poterant forte capi Nouemviri.
units.tr: The third head is whether they served in the army [...] for the country. We have translated it: whether they served in the army for their country or not. For we do not know for certain whether this is meant of all the legally completed campaigns; for they had not all served in campaigns before their fortieth year of age. If this must be taken of all campaigns in this way, the Nine could perhaps be chosen only after their fortieth year.

units.la: Quarto interrogabantur, εἰ ὃ τιμημα ἔστιν αὐτῆς. An census sit illis, necne. Intelligit autem Legislator τῶν Γνωσιμεδίμνων censum. Nam cum Theseus Magistratus esse voluisset penes nobiles & potentiores, Nouemviri maxime e nobilibus forte capti: hinc Hieronymus in Chronicis: Nouem Principes ex nobilibus Vrbis electi praefuerunt annuo imperio Reipublicae. Haec vestigia legens Solon Πεντακοσιομεδίμνοις voluit τὰς ἀρχὰς [illegible, ~5 letters] ἀπολιπεῖν. Vnde Demetrius Phalereus in Libro, cui titulum fecit Socrati, vbi de Aristide Lysimachi F. sermo est, existimat esse τὴν μέλιστα τῆς [?] ἀρετῆς τὴν οἴκοι ... [illegible, ~12 letters] πολιτείας, Epimenides ἐξ ἦν ἤρξε τῶν χαλκῶν [?] ... [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐπορεύετο [?]. Quanquam hic ipse Aristides postea suo Pschephismate cauit ἐν τῇ πολιτείᾳ [?], καὶ τὰς Ἀρχὰς ἐξ Ἀθηναίων πάντων αἱρεῖσθαι, nulla census, nulla τῆς δημοκρατίας habita ratione. Sed mox ἡ πάτριος ἐπὶ Περικλέους πολιτεία reuocata est.
units.tr: Fourth, they were asked whether they had the property qualification: whether they had a census or not. The lawgiver means the census of the Pentakosiomedimnoi. For when Theseus wished the magistracies to be held by the nobles and the more powerful, the Novemviri were perhaps chosen mostly from the nobles; hence Jerome in the Chronicle: Nine princes chosen from the nobles of the city presided over the state for a yearly rule. Reading these traces, Solon wished to leave the offices to the Pentakosiomedimnoi. Whence Demetrius of Phalerum, in the book which he entitled Socrates, where he speaks of Aristides son of Lysimachus, thinks that ... [illegible] ... of the state. Epimenides ... [illegible]. Yet this same Aristides later provided by his own decree that the magistracies should be chosen from all Athenians, without regard to census or to the principle of democracy. But soon the ancestral constitution under Pericles was restored.

units.la: Quintum Kaput descripsit Auctor Etymologici: ΕΙ ΑΦΕΛΕΙΣ. An integri corporis essent, necne. Id quidem de Rege tantum in vno è Nouemviris scribit Grammaticus: καὶ οἱ Βασιλεῖς ἐδοκιμάζοντο Ἀθηναῖον, ΕΙ ΑΦΕΛΕΙΣ. addit καὶ ὁλόκληρος, quod est glossema prioris vocis, est enim ΑΦΕΛΗΣ, ὁ ὑγιὴς ὃ σῶμα [?] ἐὰν ὁλόκληρος [?] ἐν τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις. Sed id tamen de omnibus Nouemviris intelligendum esse constat, ex eo quod in bello mutilati, quos ἀδυνάτους Athenienses dixerunt, non poterant forte capi Nouemviri, τῶν ἐπὶ Ἀρχόντων ψηφίσματι. Lysias [?] ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ἀδυνάτων [?] ... Ly-sias ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῆς εἰσαγγελίας [?] ... Ἀδυνάτων ... [illegible, ~15 letters]. & paulò post: οἱ δὲ, ὡς Ἀδυνάτου ὄντα, κληρωθέντες κωλύσουσιν. & infra ex Ἀδυνάτου persona: ὅπῳ γὰρ, ὦ βυλὴ, τῶν μεγίστων ἀρχῶν ὁ δῆμος ἀποστερήσει [?] ... ἡμᾶς. & ibidem: πῶς δὲ ὢν ... ἐὰν τῶν κοσμίων ... συμφέρει ἀπεστερημένος εἶναι. Neque enim à capessendo hoc Magistratu, quod paupertate premantur εἰς τέλων μνῶν κεκτημένοι tantum, arcentur, sed quia sunt σῶμα πεπηρωμένοι, quod manifesto indicant ista Lysiae verba: [illegible, ~45 letters]. Sensus est: non æquum esse, vt qui fraudatur pecunia, quæ τοῖς Ἀδυνάτοις secundum Leges è publico dabatur, ὡς ὑγιαίνων γὰρ τὸ σῶμα δυνάμενος prohibeatur κληροῦσθαι τὴν εἰς Ἀρχόντων, quia scilicet Ἀδυνατος καὶ αἰσχρὸς ἐστ: neque hic quicquam ἀπὸ τῆς ἀπορίας, sed tantum ἀπὸ τῆς τοῦ σώματος δυνάμεως, ἵνα ἢ τὴν Ἀδυνάτων. Negabant enim hunc, cui Orationem scripsit Lysias, ἢ τὴν Ἀδυνάτων, ne pecuniam è publico acciperet: at rursum fatebatur Ἀδυνάτων esse, id est, πεπηρωμένος σῶμα, ne posset κληροῦσθαι τὴν εἰς Ἀρχόντων, additque se ὑπὲρ τοῦ συμφέροντος ἀπέρχεσθαι τῶν εἰς Ἀρχόντων.
units.tr: The fifth head was described by the author of the Etymologicum: whether they were of sound body or not. The grammarian writes this only of the king among the Nine: "the kings also were examined by the Athenians whether they were ... of sound body." He adds "and whole," which is a gloss on the previous word, for the word is aphelēs, meaning healthy in body and whole among the Athenians. But it is agreed that this must be understood of all the Nine, from the fact that those maimed in war, whom the Athenians called adynatoi (the powerless), could perhaps not be chosen as Nine by decree of the archons. Lysias, in the speech on the impeachment [...] of the powerless ... Lysias ... "powerless" ... and a little later: "But they, since he is powerless, having been chosen by lot, will prevent it." And below, in the person of the powerless man: "For how, Council, will the people deprive me of the greatest offices ..., us." And in the same place: "How ... being deprived is advantageous ... for the orderly." For they are excluded from taking this magistracy not because they are oppressed by poverty, having only three hundred drachmas, but because they are of maimed body, which the words of Lysias clearly indicate: [illegible]. The sense is: it is not fair that one who is defrauded of the money which by law was given from the public treasury to the powerless should, as one who is able-bodied, be prevented from being chosen by lot for the archonship; since he is clearly powerless and disgraceful. Here nothing is said of poverty, but only of the strength of the body, so that he may be counted among the powerless. For they denied that the man for whom Lysias wrote the speech was among the powerless, lest he receive money from the public treasury; yet again he confessed that he was powerless, that is, of maimed body, so that he could not be chosen by lot for the archonship, and adds that he is leaving the archonship for the common good.

units.la: Approbati à Senatu, itemque à iudicibus Nouemviri, iurabant in Leges, se eas esse obseruaturos: si secus fecissent, aureā statuam suam pensuros esse.
units.tr: Approved by the Senate, and likewise by the judges, the Nine swore to observe the laws; if they acted otherwise, they would pay a golden statue of their own.

units.la: ΟΡΚΟΣ ΤΩΝ ENNEA ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ.
units.tr: THE OATH OF THE NINE ARCHONS.

units.la: Συμφυλάξειν τοὺς νόμους, ἢ χρυσοῦν αἰδρια-[?]τε ἀποπέσσω ἰσομέτρητον.
units.tr: I will keep the laws; otherwise I will pay a golden statue of equal weight. [Συμφυλάξειν τοὺς νόμους, ἢ χρυσοῦν ἀνδριάντα ἀποτίσω ἰσομέτρητον]

units.la: IVSIVRANDVM NOVEM- VIRORVM
units.tr: THE OATH OF THE NINE

units.la: Leges obseruabo, si secus fecero, auream statuam meam æqui ponderis pendam.
units.tr: I will observe the laws; if I do not, I will pay a golden statue of my own weight.

units.la: Habes apud Pollucem Libro VIII. cap. IX. qui docet quibus in locis ab illis iurari sit solitum: ὤμνυον δὲ οἱ Θεσμοθέται παρὰ τὴν Βασιλείου Σπᾶ, ἐφ' ὧ π συμφυλάξειν τοὺς νόμους ἢ χρυσοῦν αἰδρίαστε ἀποπέσσω. εἶτα οὗτοι ἐν Ἀκροπολιν αἰσλήθητες ὤμνυον ζῶ πα. Plutarchus in Solone: ἰδὼν ὤμνυεν ὅρκον ἕκαστος τῶν Θεσμοθετῶν εἰ ἀρχὴν παρὰ τὸν λίθον καὶ καταφατίζων, εἰ ἢ ἀξιωθαίη τὴν ἡσυχίαν, αἰδριαστὰ χρυσοῦν ἰσομέτρητον αἰα ὄπληνούς, καὶ λαφοῖς. Vbi vides & id à Solone fuisse institutū, & statuam Delphis fuisse ponendam, quod etiam dixit Platonicus Phaedrus, è quo præterea discimus, non tantum Thesmothetarum, sed omnium etiam Nouemvirorum fuisse iusiurandum: χρή σοι ἐγώ, ὥσπερ εἰ εἰναι Ἀρχοντος, ἀνάγκη ... χρυσοῦν εἰκόνα ἰσομέτρητον εἰς Δήφοις ἀναθῆσαι.
units.tr: You have this in Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX, who tells us in which places it was customary for them to swear. The Thesmothetae swore beside the stone of King Spa, pledging to keep the laws, or else to pay a golden statue. Then, having been assembled on the Acropolis, they swore by Zeus [ὤμνυον δὲ οἱ Θεσμοθέται παρὰ τὸν Βασιλείου Σπᾶ]. Plutarch, in the Life of Solon, says that each of the Thesmothetae took the oath standing at the stone, and invoked a curse on himself if he broke it, that he would pay a golden statue of equal weight, and offerings. Here you see both that this was instituted by Solon, and that a statue was to be set up at Delphi. Plato's Phaedrus also says this, and from him we learn further that the oath was taken not only by the Thesmothetae but by all the Nine: it is necessary for you, as if you were an Archon, to dedicate a golden statue of equal weight at Delphi.

units.la: Tantam honestatis curam his Nouemviris voluit esse Solon, vt si quis Archon vino se ingurgitauerit, capital ei fuerit, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Solon wanted these Nine to have such a concern for honour that, by this law, if any Archon gave himself over to drink, it would be a capital offence:

units.la: Τῷ Ἀρχοντι, ἐὰν μέθων λαφῇ, θανάτῳ ἔτω ἡ ξημία.
units.tr: If the Archon, being drunk with wine, is caught, let the penalty be death. [Τῷ Ἀρχοντι, ἐὰν μέθων λαφῇ, θανάτῳ ἔστω ἡ ζημία]

units.la: Si Archon vino madere deprehensus fuerit, capital esto.
units.tr: If an Archon is caught drunk with wine, let it be a capital offence.

units.la: Legem hanc refert Diogenes Laërtius in Solone: Quamuis autem Legis huius verba ad quosuis Magistratus spectare videantur, proprie tamen Legem hanc Archonti π̄ Ἐπωνύμῳ, qui Fastos signabat, scripsisse nobis videtur Solon: Nam ὁ Ἀρχοντα Ἐπωνύμων λαχόντων δίκη ξενοίας, vt docet Iulius Pollux Libro VIII. cap. IX. Quare non oportebat, vt in illum iactaretur istud è veteri Tragœdia:
units.tr: Diogenes Laërtius, in his Life of Solon, reports this law. Although the words of this law seem to apply to any magistrates, it appears to me that Solon wrote this law properly for the Archon eponymous, who signed the public records; for, as Pollux teaches in Book VIII, chapter IX, the Archon Eponymos was the one whom a suit for insolence was brought against. Therefore that line from the old tragedy should not have been thrown at him:

units.la: ἀνδρῶν ἰασξς, αὐτὸς ἔλκεσθαι βρύων.
units.tr: "Himself, roaring, dragged by the hair of men."

units.la: Ne quis verò his Nouemviris iniurius esset, Lege sanxerunt, nam si quis fecisset, ignominiosus erat:
units.tr: Lest anyone should wrong these Nine, they also sanctioned this by law; for if anyone did so, he was to be disgraced:

units.la: Εἰ Θεσμοθέτην, ἢ ἀρχοντα ἱεροφαντῶν, ἢ πινα τούτων, οἷς αὐ ἢ πόλις ὢ[?]
units.tr: If anyone [...] the Thesmothetae, or the Archon crowned, or [...] any of these, to whom the city [...]

units.la: Si quis Thesmothetam, aut Archontē coronatū, aut aliquem eorum, quibus ἀδ́ικαν[?], ἢ στεφανοφορίαν, ἢ ὕβρει ἀμίλω δῶ, ὑ-βεῖν τῆς[?], ἢ παπάξῃ[?], ἢ κακῶς εἴπῃ, ἀτιμος ἔστω καθάπαξ. ciuitas aut immunitatem aliquā, aut coronam ferre, aut honorem aliquem concessit, contumelia affecerit, aut pulsauerit, aut maledixerit, ignominiosus esto.
units.tr: If anyone insults a Thesmothetes, or the crowned Archon, or any of those to whom the state has granted some immunity, or the carrying of a crown, or some other honour, by contumely, or strikes them, or speaks evil of them, let him be disgraced for good. If anyone, having granted the state, or some immunity, or the bearing of a crown, or any honour, has offered insult, or struck, or spoken ill, let him be disgraced.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Μειδίου, docetque ita seuere animaduersum fuisse, quia ciuitati proprie, non priuato alicui, fiebat iniuria: ὅτι τοὺς νόμους ἀδικῶν ὁ τῶν τοιούτων ποιῶν ἀποσυκοφαντῶν, καὶ τὸ ὑμέτερον χείρον ἀποφαίνων, ἐὰν δ᾽ τῆς πόλεως ὄνομα ὁ δὲ Θεσμοθέτης, σύνεδρος αὐτῷ ἐφ᾽ ὁμα, ἀλλὰ τῆς πόλεως.
units.tr: Demosthenes, in his speech Against Meidias, cites this law and shows that the punishment was so severe because the wrong was done properly to the state, not to any private person. He says that the one who, by wronging the laws, makes slanderous accusations and reveals the worse side of you, if he does so against the name of the city, the Thesmothetes shall sit with him as judge on the matter, not as a private person but for the city.

units.la: Lege tenebatur Rex vxorem ciuem atque virginem ducere:
units.tr: By this law the King was bound to take a wife who was a citizen and a virgin:

units.la: Τῶν τῆς Βασιλέως γυναῖκα ἀστὴν εἶναι, καὶ ἀπ-[?] γαμεῖν.
units.tr: The wife of the King must be a citizen, and he must marry a virgin. [Τῶν τῆς Βασιλέως γυναῖκα ἀστὴν εἶναι, καὶ παρθένον γαμεῖν]

units.la: Regis vxor ciuis esto, virgoque ei nu-bito.
units.tr: Let the wife of the King be a citizen, and let him marry a virgin.

units.la: Idque sancitum est propter ea, quæ cum vxore sua Rex curabat, sacra, ne quid secus,& præter ritus patrios in iis fieret. Lex autem perscripta erat in columna lapidea iuxta aram Bacchi ἐν Λίμναις. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Νεαίρας. ὅταν δὲ Θεσμοθέται ἐπὶ ποιῶσι, καὶ ἡ πόλις πολυαῖ, Θεσμὸς ἐξίστατο, τὸν μὲν βασιλέα τοῦτ᾽ ἡ ἡ ὁ δῆμος ἡσυχή ἐκ ἀγεχρίτων κατ᾽ ἀνδραχαῖ χρῆσι[?]. τὸ δ᾽ γυναῖκα αὐτὸ ἑρωῆν ἐπίστατο ἀ[?]ραι[?]: καὶ μὴ ὅτι μεμιγμένον[?] ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ, ἀλλὰ παρθένον γαμεῖν, ἵνα χ᾽ πὰ πόλεως ἡ πόλεως. καὶ ἡ πόλεως, καὶ τὰ ὁμολογούμενα γίγνηται τοῖς θεοῖς ὠρίσαις, καὶ μισθὸν καταλύσῃ μηδὲ χαριστικῶν. καὶ τὸν τῆς τῷ[?] νόμου γεαφθέντες ἐν ξηλότιφ[?] ἐπὶ ἱερῶ τῆς Διονύσου ὡς ἐξ τῶν[?] Λίμναις.Tenebatur quisquis Rex erat, si maritus fieret intra τῆς ἀρχῆς annum, vxorem ducere ciuem, quod illi cum ceteris omnibus Atheniensibus commune erat, & præterea virginem illibatam: aut si iam maritus esset, in ἀναχρίσει interrogabatur an ciuem & virginem in vxorem duxisset.
units.tr: This was enacted because of the sacred rites which the king performed with his wife, so that nothing might be done in them contrary to or apart from the ancestral rites. The law was written on a stone column beside the altar of Bacchus at the Limnae. Demosthenes, in his speech Against Neaera, says that when the Thesmothetae were appointed, and the city was in a state of confusion, the law was set aside, and the king was not to be [...] to marry a woman who had already been with another man, but a virgin, so that the city might be [...] and the agreed rites of the gods be duly performed and not be interrupted. The law was inscribed on a tablet... at the sanctuary of Dionysus among the Limnae. The king was bound, whoever was king, if he became a husband within the year of his office, to take a wife who was a citizen, as was the case for all other Athenians, and besides this a virgin untouched; or if he was already married, he was asked in the examination whether he had taken a citizen and a virgin as wife.

units.la: Quemadmodum Nouemuiri antequam assumerentur ad Magistratū illum, de omni retrorsus vita acta causam dicere solebant, quod si nullam decoris habem[?] perpetua innocentia contraxisse videbantur, ad τὸν ἄρχοντα[?] assumebantur. Deinde Magistratus gesti causam dicentes, rationesque ferētes, si tum quoque innocentes vsquequaque apparuissent, ad Areopagiticum Senatum conscribebantur, Solonis Lege:
units.tr: Just as the Nine, before being admitted to that magistracy, were accustomed to give an account of their whole past life, and if they seemed to have shown no disgrace through a lifelong blamelessness, they were admitted as Archons. Then, when they had given an account of their administration and rendered their accounts, and if they were found blameless in every respect, they were enrolled in the Areopagite Senate, by Solon's law:

units.la: Τῶν δὲ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ Βουλὴν ἐν τῇ κατ᾽ ἐνιαυτὸν Ἀρχόντων.
units.tr: "Of those who are chosen for the Senate of the Areopagus, from the Archons of each year..."

units.la: In Senatum Areopagiticum Nouemuiri cooptantor.
units.tr: The Nine are co-opted into the Areopagite Senate.

units.la: Habes apud Plutarchum in Solone: Συσπαρμὸς δὲ τὸ εἰς Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ Βουλὴν ἐν τῇ κατ᾽ ἐνιαυτὸν Ἀρχόντων, ἧς ἀφ᾽ ὧν ἀρξαι, καὶ αὐτὸς μετεῖχεν. Rursum in Pericle: ἐξῆσαν[?] τῆς ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγου Βουλῆς, ἧς αὐτὸς ἢ μετεῖχε, ἀφ᾽ ὧν μὴ Ἀρχων, μήτε Θεσμο-θέτης, μήτε Βασιλεὺς, μήτε Πολέμαρχος λαχεῖν. αὖται γὰρ αἱ ἀρχαὶ κληρωταὶ τῶν ὄντων ἐκ παλαιοῦ, ἐξ δὲ αὐτῶν οἱ δεκιμασθέντες ἀπεῖσιν εἰς Ἀρείου πάγου. Pollux Libro VIII: οἱ δὲ εἰσὶ Ἀρχοντες οἱ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἐνιαυτὸν, μετὰ δὲ δωδεκα ἔτη τοὺς ἀδ[?]ως δὲ τῆς Ἀρεοπαγίτας προσαπέπεμπτο. Aliis placet sex tantum Thesmothetas post exactum sui Magistratus tempus, in Areopagitarum consilium quotannis adoptari. Libanius in Androtianæ Argumento: ἀξιῶσα ἀξιοφορὸς, ὅτι ἡ μὲν ἐκ τῆς Γειτιακοῖον Βουλὴ ἀξιώσαν ἐν ἐμοῖς αἱ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ, ἀδελφὸν. ὡς γὰρ ἔτος[?] ἡ ῥητορικῶν λέγεται, κατ᾽ ἔτος οἱ ἐνιαυτὸν Ἀρχοντες αὐτῇ αἱ ἀρχῇ ἔστι ἀξιοῦνται ὡς δὲ πινες, ὅτι ἐξ μόνον Θεσμοθέται. οἱ δὲ εἰσὶ Ἀρχοντες ἐν τοῖς. Ἀρχοντες, ἐπιεικῶς μὲν ἦρξαν, ὅσοι τῆς ἀρχῆς χρῶμενοι [?] τῷ μεγαλείῳ πολιτῶν βίῳ [?]· εἰ μὴ ἀρέσκοντο ἐς πάντα δίκαιοι, ἤρξαν ἐπιεικῶς. εἶτα πάλιν μὴ ἐπιεικῶς ἐκ εἶναι [?], εἰ καλὸς ἐν αὐτῷ ἤρξαν, καὶ ἐξ εἰ δικαίως ἀφοδοθὲν ἀρέξαντες [?], [illegible, ~20 letters] τῇ Βουλῇ τῶν Ἀρεοπα-γιτῶν, καὶ ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀχ[?] ἐπιπαῖ ἀριθμῷ [?]. εἰ δὲ μὴ ἐξεδόθησαν. Certo igitur numero Areopagitæ circumscribi non possunt: quanquam quot sint singulis annis dici possit, quemadmodum in veteri illa Inscriptione, quam descripsit Volaterranus: ΤΩΙ ΛΑΜΠΡΟΤΑΤΩΙ ΑΝΘΥΠΑΤΩΙ ΤΗΣ ΕΛΛΑΔΟΣ ΡΟΥΦΩΙ ΦΑΙΣΤΩΙ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΕΙΟΓΑΓΙΤΗΙ, Η ΕΞ ΑΡΕΙΟΠΑΓΟΥ ΒΟΥΛΗ ΤΩΝ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΣΙΩΝ, ΚΑΙ Ο ΔΗΜΟΣ Ο ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΕΥΝΟΙΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΥΕΡΓΕΣΙΑΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ. Neque enim perpetuum hunc esse trecentorum Areopagitarum numerum docet Inscriptio, sed hoc tantum, eo, quo scripta positaque est hæc Inscriptio, anno Areopagitas trecentos fuisse, quod sane mirandum est: Festus autem hic etiam inter Areopagitas, ac proinde de Nomemviris unus, quia adscripti ciues sortiebantur τῶν ἐπὶ Ἀρεοπαγίτῶν [?]. At vero locus è Scholiis ad Æschyli Eumenidas duplici in medo cubat, quorum unum est Scholiorum scriptoris, alterum descriptoris: sita editur: ὁ ἀριθμὸς τῶν Ἀρεοπαγιτῶν λ' καὶ εἰς. Mutauit librarius ὅ ι' in ὅ λ' facili lapsu, itaque rescribendum est: ὁ ἀριθμὸς τῶν Ἀρεοπαγιτῶν ι' καὶ εἰς. atque hoc librarij peccatum est: auctoris vero, quod Areopagitas dicat, qui Ephetæ sunt, nam Ephetæ erant quinquaginta & unus. Pollux: Ἐφέται, τὸ μὲν ἀριθμῶν, εἰς καὶ πεντήκοντα. Nisi dicamus, quod fortasse verius est, in hoc Orestis iudicio, sedisse tantum triginta & unum Areopagitas:
units.tr: You have this in Plutarch's Life of Solon: the enrolment in the Areopagite Senate from the Archons of each year, of whom he himself had also been a member. Again in the Life of Pericles: the Areopagite Senate was entered by those who had been Archons, Thesmothetae, King, or Polemarch by lot; for these offices were, from ancient times, filled by lot, and from among those who had been approved, the members of the Areopagus were drawn. Pollux, Book VIII: the Archons of each year, and after twelve years, those who had been approved were added to the Areopagites. Others think only six Thesmothetae are added each year to the council of the Areopagites after their term of office is completed. Libanius, in the Argument to Androtion: the council of the Areopagus was composed of those who had been Archons, and they were chosen each year... Certainly the number of Areopagites cannot be fixed, although it can be said how many there were each year, as in that old inscription which Volaterranus described: "To the most illustrious Anthypatus of Greece, Rufus, Phaistos, and Areiogagites, the Senate from the Areopagus of the three hundred, and the people of Athens, for goodwill and benefaction." For this inscription shows that the number of three hundred Areopagites was not fixed, but only that in the year in which this inscription was written and set up there were three hundred Areopagites, which is indeed remarkable. This Festus, however, is counted here among the Areopagites, and therefore one of the Nine, because enrolled citizens drew lots among those of the Areopagites. But the passage from the Scholia on Aeschylus' Eumenides exists in a double reading, one by the scholiast and one by the copyist: it is printed thus: "the number of the Areopagites is thirty-one." The copyist changed ι' into λ' by an easy slip, so it must be rewritten: "the number of the Areopagites is eleven." This was a mistake of the copyist; but the author's mention of Areopagites, when he means Ephetae, is his own, for the Ephetae were fifty-one. Pollux: the Ephetae, by number, were fifty-one. Unless we say, which is perhaps more true, that in this trial of Orestes only thirty-one Areopagites sat:

units.la: ἐκλαθῆ ὡς ἕχιστα τυχέων πάλας, ὅσοις δικαιῶν τῶτ' ἐπισταλθῆ πάλας.
units.tr: Let him be forgotten as quickly as possible, having met with misfortune, to whomever this is rightly sent [ἐκλαθῆ ὡς ἕχιστα τυχέων πάλας, ὅσοις δικαιῶν τῶτ' ἐπισταλθῆ πάλας].

units.la: ὁ ἀριθμὸς τῶν Ἀρεοπαγιτῶν λ' καὶ εἰς. Non enim omnes semper Areopagitæ in omnibus causis ius dicebant, sed quidam ex illis tantum, quemadmodum in aliis Tribunalibus factum est: itaque in causa Orestis sedisse fingungur Areopagitæ triginta & unus tantum. Areopagitarum Magistratus erat perpetuus, neque quisquam hoc Senatu mouebatur, qui non grande & inexpiabile admisisset nefas. Libanius loco laudato: ἡ τῶν Ἀρεοπαγιτῶν Βουλὴ ὡς ἀδικήσας εἰ μὴ γλυκῶς ἡμῶν μεγάλως, οὐκ ἐξεδοθῆ. Auctorem huius Senatus Solonem facit Cicero Libro I. de Officiis: Quamuis enim Themistocles iure laudetur, & sit eius nomen, quam Solonis, illustrius, citeturque Salamis clarissimæ testis victoriæ, quæ anteponatur consilio Solonis, ei, quo primum constituit Areopagitas, non minus præclarum hoc, quam illud, iudicandum est. Argumento est, quod nusquam Areopagitarum meminerit Draco in suis Legibus. Plutarchus in Solone: οἱ μὲν οὖν πλέον τῶν ἐξ Ἀρείας πάγου Βουλῶν (ὥσπερ εἰρηταί) Σόλωνα συστήσασθαι φασί, καὶ μάρτυρα αὐτοῖς μάλιστα δοκεῖ ὃ μηδαμοῦ τ' Δράκοντα λέγει μηδ' ὀνομάζειν Ἀρεοπαγίτας, ἀλλὰ τοῖς Ἐφέταις αἰεὶ ἀξιολογίᾳ γε τὴν φονικὴν. At vero Aristoteles Libro II. Politic. extremo affirmat ante Solonem fuisse Areopagitarum Senatum, sed & ipse Solon Lege octaua Axonis tertij decimi auctor est omni exceptione maior Areopagitas iam ante ordinatam à se Rempublicam fuisse, & δίκας φόνου iudicasse. Plutarchus ibid. ὁ δὲ πεισκηδίκας Ἀξων τὰ Σόλωνος ἐν ὀρθοῖ ἐχά[?] [?]ἢ νόμων ὕπως αὐτοῖς ὁ ὁμαίσι γεγεραμμένον. Ἀπὸ μὲν ὅσοι ἀπὸ ἡμῶν ποθὲν ἡ Σόλωνα ἀξίας [?] ὅπῃ πάγῳ ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ καὶ ἀδικήσαντες ὅτι φόνου ἐφυγον, ὅτι δῆμος ἐφάνησαν. Cur enim meminisset Solon eorum, qui Areopagitarum sententia solum verterant propter caedem, si Areopagitarum Senatus ante Solonem non fuisset? Ἐξὸπερ δὲ πάλιν ὡς ἐκ τῆς Σόλωνος ἐρχῆς καὶ νομοθεσίας τὸ ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βυλῇ ὅσον ἐπίσχυσαν. τινὲς γὰρ ἡ πρὸς οἱ ἐκ Σόλωνος ἐν Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ καταδικασάντες, εἰ ἐξ ἕπης Σόλωνι ἔδωκεν τῆς ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βυλῆ ὅχρίσῃ; Sed facile ista coniciari possunt, meo iudicio. Nam ante Draconis νομοθεσίαν Areopagitae de caede iudicia reddiderunt, vt e laudata Solonis Lege constat, neque enim tantum est a Draconis Praetura ad illam Solonis interuallum, vt superesse non potuerint, suas scribentes Leges Solone, qui, antequam Draco Leges ferret, ab Areopagitarum Senatu caedis damati fuerant. Draco vero, Ephetis constitutis, omne Areopagitis abrogauit imperium, nec illi, quamdiu Legibus Draconis stetit Respublica, de caede iudicia reddiderunt: itaque soli Ephetae in quinque illis tribunalibus, de quibus suo loco, Deo dante, dicemus, ius dicebant. Pollux: Ἐφέτας, ἀ μὲν ἐξιθμῶν εἰς ἡ πεντήκοντα. Δεόχων δ' αὖ εἰς καταςῆσαι ἐξισίνδων αἱρεθέντας, εἰς ἐκ ἐφ' ἁμφὶ διωχύμενος, ἐν τῇς πέντε δικαστηρίοις. Sed Solon vetus ius restituit, & Areopagitas cum Ephetis voluit de caede iudicia reddere: addit Pollux, Σόλων δ' αὖ εἰς καταςῆσαι τὸ ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βυλῶ. Itaque quasi de nouo primumq; constituisse hunc Areopagitarum Senatum Solon videtur. Adde quod primus, puto, eum σωίσησιν ἐκ τῶν κατ' ἐναυτὸν Ἀρχόντων, constituit ex annuis Nouemviris: Itemque voluit Lege hunc Senatum Areopagitarum suo regere cōsilio Rempublicam Athenien sium, vt Leges, vt maiorum instituta seruentur:
units.tr: The number of the Areopagites was thirty-one. For the Areopagites did not always all sit in judgment in every cause, but only some of them, as happened in other tribunals; so in the case of Orestes they are imagined to have sat as only thirty-one. The Areopagites were a perpetual magistracy, and no one was removed from this Senate unless he had committed a great and inexpiable crime. Libanius, in the passage cited: the Council of the Areopagites, unless it had greatly wronged us, was not given up. Cicero, in Book I of On Duties, makes Solon the author of this Senate: For although Themistocles is rightly praised, and his name is more illustrious than Solon's, and Salamis is cited as witness of a most famous victory, yet that is to be set above the counsel of Solon, by which he first established the Areopagites, this is to be judged no less distinguished than that. The proof is that Draco, in his Laws, never mentions the Areopagites anywhere. Plutarch, in the Life of Solon: most of those who ascribe the councils of the Areopagus to Solon, as has been said, seem to have as their chief witness the fact that Draco nowhere mentions the Areopagites by name, but always assigns cases of homicide to the Ephetae. But Aristotle, at the end of Book II of the Politics, affirms that the Areopagitarum Senate existed before Solon; and Solon himself, in the eighth law of the thirteenth axon, which is above all exception, is the author of the fact that the Areopagitas had already been in existence, before he had set the Commonwealth in order, and had judged cases of homicide. Plutarch in the same place: the axon concerning homicide, with the laws of Solon in it, was written in the same way for them. For how many of those who were banished from the Areopagus for murder, and were acquitted by the Areopagus sentence, and were then restored, ... Why would Solon have mentioned those who had been exiled by the sentence of the Areopagitarum alone for homicide, if the Areopagitarum Senate had not existed before Solon? Moreover, that the Areopagite council had such force, as if from the rule and legislation of Solon, is shown by these words... Yet these things can easily be conjectured, in my judgment. For before Draco's legislation, the Areopagitae gave judgments on homicide, as is clear from the law of Solon cited above; nor is the interval from Draco's magistracy to that of Solon so great that men who wrote their own laws could not have survived, since Solon, before Draco brought in his laws, had been condemned for homicide by the Areopagitarum Senate. But Draco, when the Ephetae had been appointed, took away all power from the Areopagitis, and while the Commonwealth stood under Draco's laws, they did not give judgments on homicide; so the Ephetae alone, in those five tribunals of which, God willing, we shall speak in their place, gave judgment. Pollux: the Ephetae, who were fifty-one in number. Draco, indeed, chose them from the aristocracy, and they were tried in the five courts. But Solon restored the old law, and wished the Areopagitas together with the Ephetis to give judgments on homicide; Pollux adds that Solon again established the council of the Areopagus. And so it seems that Solon in a sense established this Areopagitarum Senate for the first time and anew. Add that he, I think, first made the annual Archons, that is the nine, from the year's magistrates. Likewise by law he wished this Areopagitarum Senate to govern the Athenian Commonwealth by its counsel, so that the laws and the institutions of the ancestors would be kept.

units.la: Τὼ δὲ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ Βυλῶ ἐξ ὅπισθεν πάντων, καὶ φύλακα τῶν νόμων.
units.tr: "The Council of the Areopagus, the overseer of all, and the guardian of the laws." [Τὴν δὲ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βουλὴν ἐπίσκοπον πάντων καὶ φύλακα τῶν νόμων.]

units.la: Senatus Areopagi Rempublicam consilio suo regito, Legesque seruato.
units.tr: Let the Senate of the Areopagus govern the commonwealth by its counsel, and keep the laws.

units.la: Laudat Plutarchus in Solone: τὼ δὲ αὖ ω Βυλῶ, Areopagi scilicet, ὅπισθεν πάντων, καὶ φύλακα τῶν νόμων ἐκ ἀξίον. Apud Andocidem ἐν ᾧ ἐπεί τὴν μυστήριον in Psephismate, quod factum est post exactos Triginta Tyrannos: ἐπιτάξω ἡ πει- θῶσιν οἱ νόμοι, ὅπως μέλετῶ ἡ Βυλὴ ἡ ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγου τῶν νόμων, ὅπως αἱ αἱ ἐξ αὐτῶν εἰς ἀξιώσεις νόμως. Suidas in Ἀρεὶς πάγος. ἐδίκαζε ὁ καὶ τὰς φονικὰς, ἡ τὰ ἄλλα πολιτικὰ διέκρινε σαφῶς. Neque hic audiendus est Libanius in Androtianæ argumento, qui Rempublicam nonnisi in summo eius discrimine administrasse scribit: ἡ δὲ ἐκ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βυλὴ, τὰ φονικὰ μόνον διέκρινε. εἰ δὲ τις εἴποι, ὅτι καὶ αὕτη δημοσία διέκρινε, λέγομεν ὅτι ἰδίωσα μεγίστη ἀναγκαία ἐγένετο, τότε ἐκ δημοσίων σῴωνται. Atqui nil quicquam, quod alicuius esset momenti, siue in sago, siue in toga, absque huius Areopagitici Senatus auctoritate fiebat. M. Tullius Libro de Natura Deorum II. Vt, si quis dicat, Athenien sium Rempublicam consilio Regi, desit illud Ariopagi: sic cum dicimus, prouidentia mundum administrari, deesse arbitrator, Deorum. Idem Libro I. de Officiis: Quamuis enim Themistocles iure laudetur, & sit eius nomen, quam Solonis, illustrius, cuiusque Salamis clarissimæ testis victoriæ, quæ anteponatur consilio Solonis, ei, quo primum constituit Arcopagitas: non minus præclarum hoc, quam illud, iudicandum est. Illud enim semel profuit, hoc semper proderit ciuitati: hoc consilio Leges Athenien sium, hoc maiorum instituta seruantur. Et Themistocles quidem nihil dixerit, in quo ipse Areopagum iuuerit: at ille adiuuit Themistoclem. Est enim bellum gestum consilio Senatus eius, qui a Solone erat constitutus.
units.tr: Plutarch, in Solon, praises the council, namely that of the Areopagus, as "overseer of all and guardian of the laws, not unworthy." In Andocides, in the decree that follows the mysteries, passed after the Thirty Tyrants were expelled: "I order that the laws be obeyed, so that the council of the Areopagus may watch over the laws, and that those who make them may be ..." Suidas, under Areopagus: it judged cases of murder, and clearly distinguished the other civic matters. Nor should Libanius be heard here, in the argument to Androtion, who writes that the Areopagite council administered the commonwealth only in its greatest peril: "The council of the Areopagus judged only cases of murder. If someone says that it also gave public judgments, we answer that it did so privately, when the greatest necessity arose, and then from public ..." Yet nothing whatever of any importance, whether in war or in peace, was done without the authority of this Areopagite Senate. Marcus Tullius, in Book II of De Natura Deorum: "As, if someone said that the commonwealth of the Athenians is governed by counsel, he would think that the Areopagus was missing; so when we say that the world is administered by providence, we think that the gods are missing." The same, in Book I of De Officiis: "For although Themistocles is rightly praised, and his name is more famous than Solon's, and Salamis is cited as the witness of a most famous victory, yet it must be judged that this counsel of Solon, by which he first established the Areopagites, is no less distinguished than that one. For the former benefited the state once; this will always benefit it. By this counsel the laws of the Athenians are preserved, by this the institutions of the ancestors. Themistocles indeed said nothing in which he helped the Areopagus, but it helped Themistocles. For the war was waged by the counsel of that Senate which had been established by Solon."

units.la: Itaque Isocrates ἐπιμελείας τῆς δικασμάς scripsit in Areopagitico: ὅτι γὰρ οἱ μὲν ἡμῖν [?] ἐν τῷ Θορεσσίῳ ἐσσωδάζον, ὅτι τὸν ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγου βουλῶν ἐπίσκοπον ἐπιμελεῖσθαι τῆς δικασμάς. Hinc memorabile illud Areopagitarum iudicium, quod retulit M. Fabius Libro V. cap.IX. Nec mihi videntur Areopagitae cum damnauerunt puerum coturnicum oculos eruentem, aliud iudicasse, quam id signum esse perniciosissimae mentis, multisque malo futurae, si adoleuisset. Ad hunc quoque Senatum pertinuit cura viarum, ne quis in illis priuatim quicquam aedificii extrueret, aut obstrueret. Heraclides in Fragmento de Politiis: Θεμιστοκλῆς καὶ Αἰσχίδης καὶ ἡ ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγου βουλὴ, πολλὰ ἐδωύασαν, καὶ τὴν ἐδῶν ἐπιμελουμένους, ὅπως μὴ πῆς δικαιοδοκῶσιν αὐτῶς [?] ἐν ἀρυφακίοις [?]. Senatus Areopagi laudes è Minervae persona celebrauit Æschylus versibus, qui non tantùm in eius Eumenidibus, sed hic quoque legi merentur:
units.tr: So Isocrates, in the Areopagiticus, wrote about the care of the courts: that the Areopagite council should oversee the ... Hence the memorable judgment of the Areopagites which Marcus Fabius reports in Book V, chapter 9: "Nor do the Areopagites, when they condemned the boy who put out the eyes of quails, seem to have judged otherwise than that this was a sign of a most pernicious mind, and one that would be a curse to many if he grew up." To this Senate also belonged the care of the roads, so that no one might privately build upon them or obstruct them. Heraclides, in the fragment On the Constitutions: "Themistocles and Aeschines and the council of the Areopagus did many things, and took care of the city, so that ..." The praises of the Senate of the Areopagus were celebrated by Aeschylus in the person of Minerva, in verses that deserve to be read here as well as in his Eumenides:

units.la: κλύοιτ᾽ ἂν ἤδη Ἰσμὸν Ἀθηναίοις λεώς, πειθοῖς δίκας χρίνοντας αἱμάτης χυτῆς. ἔσται ἡ καὶ ὃ λοιπὸν Αἰγέως γραπτός, αἰεὶ δ᾽ ἐκ τῶν βουλευτήριον. * * * * * * * * * * * * πᾶσον δ᾽ Ἀρέου πλῶδε ἀμέζουσαν ἐδρᾶν, σχλωας δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἦλθον Θησέως καὶ φθόνον γραπτὰ ἁπάξῃ, καὶ πόλιν, νέοι σολιν τιμῆ ὑμῖπυργον αὐτεπύργωσθ᾽ ποτ᾽ Ἀρέι δ᾽ ἐξυον. εἴην ἐς᾽ ἐπώνυμος πέτρα, πᾶσας τ᾽ Ἀρέος· ἐν ᾗ τῶν σέβας ἀγῶν, φόβος τε συξκυνῆς ὃ μὴ ἀδικεῖν ῥηθ᾽, ὃ δ᾽ ἡμῖρ, καὶ κατ᾽ ἀφθόνως ὁμῶς, αὐτῷ πολιτῶν μὴ πιτωμένων νόμους, κἂχρᾶς ἐπορόαισ· βερσόρῳ δ᾽ ὕδωρ λαμπρῶ μισῶν, ὑπὸ δ᾽ ἀρήσως πατέρ. ὃ μήτ᾽ ἀναρχὸν μήτε δεσποτούμενον ἀσοῖς ἀξιστέλλεσι βουλεύων σέλης, καὶ μὴ ὃ δῆμος πᾶν πόλεως ἔξω βαλεῖ· ὡς γὰρ δεδοικῶς μηδὲν, ἐνδικὰς βερσᾶ; τοιαύτη τι ταρσοῶντες ἐσδίκως σέβας, ἔρυμά τε χώρας, καὶ πόλεως ὀφτίμιον ἔχει τ᾽ ἀὐ οἷ ἥτις αὐδεῖ πῶν ἔχα ἂτ᾽ ἐς Σκύθησιν, ἥτε Γέλωπος ἐς τόπους· χερδῶν ἀδικῶν τῶ βουλευτήριον, αἰδοῖον, ὀξύθυμον· διὰ δὲ τῶν ὕαξ ἐξεγείρεσθαι Φεύρημα γῆς καλήσαμεν. ἔωτῶ μὲν ἀξέτειν ἐμοῖς πᾶρᾶ ἤσιν αἰτῖσιν ἐς ὃ λοιπὸν. ὀρθαλμὰν δὲ χρή, καὶ ὕφον ἀρχὴ καὶ Δημοσίαν δίκλω, αἰδουμένοις τὸν ὅρκον. εἴρηται λόγος.
units.tr: "Now, you Athenian people, you will hear judges who decide cases by persuasion, judging the shedding of blood. There will be a permanent ... of Aegeus, and always from the council-chamber ... [lacuna in the scan] ... and the city, which all the citizens ... the people, ... a reverence and fear that keeps them from doing wrong ... the laws ... a bulwark of the land and the city's best defence, which no one in the Scythians, nor in the places of Gelon, ... the council, reverend, quick to anger, a guard of the land ... the laws ... this is my speech." [κλύοιτ᾽ ἂν ἤδη Ἰσμὸν Ἀθηναίοις λεώς, πειθοῖς δίκας χρίνοντας αἱμάτης χυτῆς.]

units.la: Areopagitarum tamen maiestatem iuit imminutum Pericles Ephialtis usus opera, quod testatur Aristoteles Lib. Politic. II. extremo: ἢ ὃ γ᾽ μὲν ἐν Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βυλλῶ Ἐφιάλτης σκόλυον[?], καὶ Περικλῆς. Plutarchus in Pericle, & alibi non se-mel. δὲ καὶ μᾶλλον ἰσχύσας ὁ Περικλῆς ἐν τῷ δήμῳ, κατεσκεύασε τὸν ἐξ Ἀρείου πάγου βυλλῶ[?], ὥστε τὸν μὲν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι τὰς πλείστας χρίσεις, ἀλλ' Ἐφιάλτην[?].
units.tr: Yet the majesty of the Areopagites was diminished by Pericles, who used the efforts of Ephialtes. Aristotle attests this at the end of Book II of the Politics: "Ephialtes and Pericles [did this]" [ἢ ὃ γ᾽ μὲν ἐν Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βυλλῶ Ἐφιάλτης σκόλυον[?], καὶ Περικλῆς]. Plutarch also says so in his Life of Pericles, and elsewhere more than once. Pericles, growing even stronger among the people, arranged that the council of the Areopagus should lose most of its cases, and Ephialtes [was the one who ...] [δὲ καὶ μᾶλλον ἰσχύσας ὁ Περικλῆς ἐν τῷ δήμῳ, κατεσκεύασε τὸν ἐξ Ἀρείου πάγου βυλλῶ[?], ὥστε τὸν μὲν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι τὰς πλείστας χρίσεις, ἀλλ' Ἐφιάλτην[?]].

units.la: Adeo honeste autem atque temperanter vitam instituerunt, vt Lege caverunt, ne quis ex illo Senatu Areopagita Comoediam, quam lasciuam nimis credebant, scriberet.
units.tr: The Areopagites, however, lived so honourably and with such restraint that they made a law that no one from that Areopagite senate should write comedy, which they thought too wanton.

units.la: Μηδένα τῶν ἐξ Ἀρείου πάγου κωμῳδίας[?] ἀρεοπαγίτην[?]. Nullus Areopagitarum Comœdiam scribito.
units.tr: "No one of the Areopagites shall write comedy" [Μηδένα τῶν ἐξ Ἀρείου πάγου κωμῳδίας[?] ἀρεοπαγίτην[?]]. "No Areopagite is to write comedy."

units.la: Describit hanc Legem Plutarchus Lib. de Atheniensium Gloria: Καὶ δὴ δραματοποιοῖς, τὸ μὴ κωμῳδοποιίας ὅτως ἀρξόμενον ἡγοῦντο ἐ φερτικὸν, ὥστε νόμος ἐᾶν, Μηδένα ποιεῖν κωμῳδίας Ἀρεοπαγίτην. Quem locum male accepit eruditus Interpres: non enim Areopagitae sunt, qui vetuerunt. Ne quis porro Comoediam scriberet, sed sanctum est, Ne quis Areopagita Comoediam scribat.
units.tr: Plutarch describes this law in his book On the Glory of the Athenians: "And indeed they thought it improper for playwrights to begin with comic writing, so that a law was passed: 'No Areopagite shall make comedies'" [Καὶ δὴ δραματοποιοῖς ... Μηδένα ποιεῖν κωμῳδίας Ἀρεοπαγίτην]. The learned translator has misunderstood this passage. It is not the Areopagites who forbade it; rather, it was enacted that no one should write comedy, namely that no Areopagite should write comedy.

units.la: Si Comoediam autem scribere indignum visum Areopagitarum gravitate, quanto magis mimos agere Senatoriam dignitatem dedecebit? Itaque merito cum in Patricios scenica officia tractantes, tum in populum iis applaudentem, inuehitur Iuuenalis Satyra VII.
units.tr: If writing comedy seemed unworthy of the dignity of the Areopagites, how much more would acting mimes disgrace senatorial rank? Hence Juvenal rightly rails, in Satire VII, against patricians who hired out their services to the stage, and against the people who applaud them.

units.la: Consumptis opibus vocem, Damasippe, locastiSipario, clamosum ageres ut Phasma Catulli, Laureolum velox etiam bene Lentulus egit, Iudice me, dignus vera cruce: nec tamen ipsiIgnoscas populo: populi frons durior huius, Qui sedet, & spectat triscurria Patriciorum.
units.tr: "Damasippus, once you have spent your fortune and hired out your voice to the stage, you would act noisily, like the Ghost of Catullus. Lentulus also acted Laureolus well and swiftly, in my judgment worthy of a real cross. Yet do not pardon the people for this, for the people's brow is harder than his, who sits and watches the patricians' buffoonery."

units.la: Postremo hoc versu magnus Scaliger legebat,
units.tr: Lastly, the great Scaliger read this line:

units.la: Qui sedet, & spectat transcurria Patriciorum.
units.tr: "Qui sedet, et spectat transcurria Patriciorum."

units.la: Interpretabatúrque ludos, ad quos ex Senatu transibant, idque ingratiis nuperi scriptoris, qui vulgatam lectionem tuetur: sunt enim, inquit, triscurria nimiae Patriciorum scurrilitates, quibus mimos agentibus spectator adsidet populus. Sed vulgatam lectionem destruit analogia: neque enim à voce scurra potest formari scurrium: emendatio quoque viri magni probari nobis nequit: itaque aliud quaerendum est. Emendanda igitur vox ista videtur è praecedentibus, quae nonnihil labis contraxerunt ab interpunctione: itaque locus sic est rescribendus, atque interpungendus.
units.tr: He explained it as "the games to which they passed over from the Senate", and he did this against the wishes of a recent writer who defends the common reading: "triscurria" means, he says, the excessive buffooneries of the patricians, to which the people sit and watch while they act mimes. But the common reading is destroyed by analogy, for scurrium cannot be formed from the word scurra. Nor can we accept the emendation of that great man. Something else must therefore be sought. This word seems to need emending from the preceding words, which have suffered some corruption from the punctuation. The passage must therefore be rewritten and punctuated thus.

units.la: Consumptis opibus vocem, Damasippe, locastiSipario, clamosum ageres ut Phasma: CatulliLaureolum velox & iam bene Lentulus egit,Iudice me, dignus vera cruce: nec tamen ipsiIgnoscas populo: populi frons durior huius,Qui sedet, & spectat tricharia Patriciorum.
units.tr: Damasippus, having spent your fortune, you hired out your voice to the curtain, to bawl like a ghost in a noisy play. Quick Lentulus has already performed Catullus' Laureolus well, worthy, in my judgment, of a real cross. Yet do not pardon the crowd for this: the brow of the people who sit and watch the buffooneries of the patricians is harder than that.

units.la: Nemo est veterum, qui Catullo Phasma adscribat, si hunc excipias locum: at vero Laureolum mimum à Catullo fuisse compositum nemo, puto, ambigit, & testis est locupletissimus Tertullianus Lib. aduersus Valentinianos cap. XIV. cuius verba describemus, quia vnice faciunt ad lucem praefcindendam, & mendum tollendum è Poetae Satyrici verbis: Ita depulsa quo minus pergeret, nec habens superuolare crucem, id est, Horon, quia nullum Catulli Laureolum fuerit exercitata, vt destituta Passioni illi suæ in tricha multiplici perplexa, omni ge-nere eius cepit adfligi: Verum ad Iuuenalem redeamus. Refert cum stomacho Poëta, Patricios operam suam locasse scenæ, & de nescio quo, cui nomen facit Damasippo, memorat, cum, vbi sua dilapidauit bona, addixisse suam operam ludicris his artibus, & mimos egisse: ac primo quidem illum, cui nomen Thasma, non minus quam Menandri Comœdiæ: an vero idem argumentum vtrique fuerit, certo non possumus affirmare: primum igitur hunc mimum egit Damasippus;
units.tr: No one among the ancients ascribes the Phasma to Catullus, apart from this passage. But that Laureolus was a mime composed by Catullus, no one, I think, doubts, and the most abundant witness is Tertullian in Book against the Valentinians, chapter XIV. I will quote his words, since they bear directly on clearing up the light and removing the error from the words of the satirist: "Thus, being driven back so that he could not go on, and not able to fly over the cross, that is, Horon, since there was no Catullan Laureolus in which he had practised, he was, as one left behind by that Passion of his in the tangled multiple trichae, begun to be afflicted by every kind of it." But let us return to Juvenal. The poet speaks with disgust of patricians who had hired their services to the stage, and he mentions a certain man named Damasippus, who, after he had squandered his goods, devoted his services to these theatrical arts and acted mimes. And first he acted that mime called Thasma, no less than the comedies of Menander. Whether the same plot belonged to both, we cannot affirm with certainty. So Damasippus first acted this mime.

units.la: (Consumptü opibus vocem, Damasippe, locastiSipario, clamosum ageres vt Thasma:
units.tr: (Having spent your fortune, Damasippus, you hired out your voice to the curtain, to bawl like a ghost:

units.la: Adeo autem profecit in agendis mimis, vt non minus perite atque bene quam Lentulus, cuius nomen magnum in illaudatissima hac arte, meminitque non semel B. Hieronymus & Tertullianus, egerit Catulli mimum, qui Laureolus dicebatur:
units.tr: Yet he made such progress in performing mimes that he acted the mime of Catullus called Laureolus no less skilfully and well than Lentulus, whose name is great in this most disreputable art, and whom St Jerome and Tertullian mention more than once:

units.la: Catulli
units.tr: Catullus

units.la: Laureolum velox & iam bene Lentulus egit.
units.tr: "Laureolum velox et iam bene" Lentulus egit.

units.la: Mimum hunc egit bene peritéque, tanquam iam alter Lentulus, cum tamen magna in eo agendo arte opus esset, cuius argumentum hoc est, vt è Iosepho constat, ςωεφδπω[?] ληφξις[?] ἡγεμὼν[?], crucem autem superuolabat, vt è Tertulliano discimus: vnde Iuuenali velox dicitur egisse Laureolum. Cruciarij autem destituebantur in tricha, vt docet Tertullianus, quo in numero cum fuerit Laureolus, etiam destitutus fuerat in tricha, à qua voce tricharia formauit Iuuenalis, quæ à populo spectari dixit,
units.tr: He acted this mime well and skilfully, as if already a second Lentulus, though great art was needed in its performance. Its plot, as is clear from Josephus, was [the man is led as a prisoner, the leader ...] [ςωεφδπω[?] ληφξις[?] ἡγεμὼν[?]], and he was flying over the cross, as we learn from Tertullian. Hence Juvenal says that Laureolus was acted swiftly. Condemned men were fixed in the tricha, as Tertullian teaches; and since Laureolus was one of that number, he too had been fixed in the tricha. From the word tricha Juvenal formed tricharia, which he says the people watched:

units.la: Qui videt, & spectat tricharia Patriciorum.
units.tr: "Qui videt et spectat tricharia Patriciorum."

units.la: Quia spectabant cruciarium Laureolum in tricha destitutum. Verum, age, cum tam commoda se offerat occasio, gratiam ineamus à Iosepho & Suetonio, illorum locis, vbi agunt de Caij cæde, vel emendatis, vel illustratis. Suetonius prodigia referens, quæ eo ipso, quo cæsus est, die acciderunt. Pantonimus Mnestter Tragœdiam saltauit, quam olim Neoptolemus Tragœdias ludis, quibus Rex Macedonum Philippus occisus est, egerat. Et cum in Laurcolo mimo, in quo actor proripiens se ruina sanguinem vomuit, vt plures secundarum certatim experimentum artis darent, cruore scena abundauit. Iosephus Lib. XIX· ἐξαίδι[?] ἡ σημεῖα δύο ἡμέρας ἐς τὴν Μῖμος εἰσάγαγεν[?], καθ' ὃν σωεφδπω[?] ληφξις[?] ἡγεμών[?], ὅ, τὸ ὀρχήστρα δράμα εἰσαγαγεῖν Κινύγειν[?], ἐν ᾧ αὐτὸς τι ἐκπίπτειν[?], ἢ ἡ ξυγάτηρ Μύρρα[?], αἷμά τι ὡς πεχνητὸν πολὺ ἡ ὃ αἰεὶ τὸν σωεφδπω[?] κακὸν[?], ἡ ὃ αἰεὶ τὸν Κινύγειν. ὁμολογεῖται δὲ ἡ τῷ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκτίνων[?] ἐν ᾗ Φιλίππου τὸν Ἀμύντα Μακεδόνων βασιλέα κτείνῃ Γαυσαρίας εἰς τὴν ἑαυτῶν, εἰς ὃ Ἡαχέσθαι εἰσέ[?]πε. Prodigia ista, vt & cædes Caij, acciderunt nono Kalendas Februarias, vt addit Suetonius, qui dies erat vltimus Ludorum Palatinorum: Miraculum vero auget Iosephus, qui eodem die, quo olim Philippus Macedonum Rex, Caium de medio sublatum fuisse scribit, sed id ingratiis viri magni, qui putat Iosephum rem non satis animo conceptisse. At vero non ista à Iosepho temere siue confícta, siue dicta esse certus sum, idque liquido demonstrabimus ex Diodoro Siculo, cuius hæc sunt verba Lib. XVIII. extremo. Θεοῦ[?] Alexander[?] ὡς δὲ τὸν σεφθαναδὸν[?] ἔπος[?] ἐπαλύπτει[?], βασιλέας ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίας καὶ μιῶν[?] ἐπὶ[?]. Diximus alibi Alexandrum Magnum obiisse ineunte anno primo Olympiadis centesimae quartaedecimae, Hegesia Athenis Praetore, die vicesimo octauo mensis Daesij, qui incidit eo anno in diem vndecimum mensis Augusti: nam vertebat annus quintus Octaëteridis Macedonicae, qui cepit vndecimo Kalendas Nouembris die. Quare dicendum est Alexandrum Magnum imperare cepisse anno Periodi Iulianae quatermillesimo tercentesimo septuagesimo octauo, e cuius diebus aestiuis iniuit Olympias centesima vndecima, vertebatque annus primus Octaëteridis Macedonicae, qui ceperat Nonis Octobribus anni Periodi Iulianae quatermillesimi tercentesimi septuagesimi septimi. Annus erat embolimaeus: adde trium mensium modum. Cepit ergo Apellaeus pridie Nonas Ianuarias anni Periodi Iulianae quatermillesimi tercentesimi septuagesimi octaui: Dies vicesimus secundus πολιτικῶς[?] numeratus Apellaei fuit die nono Kalendas Februarias: eoque die interemptus est Philippus à Pausania: Ergo init imperium Alexandri Magni exante diem octauum Kalendas Februarias anni Periodi Iulianae quatermillesimi tercentesimi septuagesimi octaui, qui dies cadit in vicesimum tertium Apellaei. Quare Alexander, qui rebus humanis exemptus est anno Periodi Iulianae quatermillesimo tercentesimo nonagesimo, mensis Daesij die vicesimo octauo, siue quarto Eidus Augusti, regnauit annos duodecim, menses sex, dies totidem, habita ratione mensium Macedonum, sed dies sunt septemdecim, menses sex, si ab octauo Kalendas Februarias ad quartum Eidus Augusti numeres: Ergo optime dixit Diodorus βασιλεύοντας ἐπὶ δώδεκα, μῆνας ἑπτά[?], quanquam non absolutus erat mensis septimus, sed vertebat. Tragoedia, quam olim Neoptolemus ludis, quibus Philippus occifusus est, egit, est Cinyras: nam eandem saltauit Tragoediam Mnester eo[?] die, quo cæsus est Caius, quam olim egerat Neoptolemus, teste Suetonio: Mnester autem saltauit Tragoediam Cinyram, auctore Iosepho, in cuius verbis pusillum est mendum, sed quod historiam fabularem plane euertit: ὅ, τι ἐρ-χηνὶς δρᾶμα εἰσάγει Κινύραν, ὁ δὲ ἀοτὶς τι ἐκπίνετο[?], ἡ ἡ Μύρρα[?]. Vt verba haec sonant, diceres caesam fuisse Myrrham, quod tamen veterum alius nemo, quod sciam, in literas retulit: certe ipse Iosephus in sequentibus fusi tantum in eo dramate Cinyrae sanguinis meminit: ἀμφὶ τε ὧ τηλιοῦ πολύ[?], ὡς ὃ ἀπὸ τὸν φωρωθέντα ἐκκεχυμένον καὶ ὃ ἀπὸ τὸν Κινύραν[?]. Myrrham vbi pater agnouit, sibi ipse necem conciuit, Myrrha in cognominem mutata est arborem, vt scribit Antonius Liberalis: apud Apollodorum Bibliothecae Lib. III. Panyasis fugisse dicit Myrrham, cumque pene iam à patre retraheretur poenas datura, in arborem fuisse mutatam. De ea ingeniosissimus Poetarum Metamorphoseon Lib. X.
units.tr: Because they watched the condemned Laureolus fixed in the tricha. But come, since such a convenient occasion presents itself, let us gain some grace by clarifying, or correcting, the passages of Josephus and Suetonius where they treat of the murder of Caius. Suetonius, recounting the portents which occurred on the very day he was struck down: "The pantomime Mnester danced the tragedy which Neoptolemus had once acted at the games at which the King of Macedon, Philip, was killed. And when in the mime Laureolus, in which the actor, throwing himself forward in a fall, vomited blood, several of the spectators eagerly gave proof of the art, the stage was swimming with blood." Josephus, Book XIX: [the portents ... the tragedy Cinyras ... Myrrha ... blood ...] [ἐξαίδι[?] ἡ σημεῖα δύο ἡμέρας ... Κινύγειν[?] ... ἐν ᾧ αὐτὸς τι ἐκπίπτειν[?] ...]. These portents, as well as the murder of Caius, happened on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, as Suetonius adds, which was the last day of the Palatine Games. Josephus increases the marvel, for he writes that Caius was removed from the middle on the same day on which Philip, king of the Macedonians, had once been killed; but this is against the wishes of the great man, who thinks Josephus did not conceive the matter sufficiently well. Yet I am certain that Josephus's statements were neither rashly invented nor rashly made, and I will demonstrate this clearly from Diodorus Siculus, whose words in Book XVIII near the end are these: [Alexander ... kings in Judaea ...] [Θεοῦ[?] Alexander[?] ὡς δὲ τὸν σεφθαναδὸν[?] ἔπος[?] ἐπαλύπτει[?], βασιλέας ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίας καὶ μιῶν[?] ἐπὶ[?]]. I have said elsewhere that Alexander the Great died at the beginning of the first year of the 114th Olympiad, under Hegesias as Praetor at Athens, on the twenty-eighth day of the month Daesius, which fell that year on the eleventh day of August; for the fifth year of the Macedonian octaeteris was running, which began on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November. Hence we must say that Alexander the Great began to reign in the year 3378 of the Julian Period, from whose summer days the 111th Olympiad began, and the first year of the Macedonian octaeteris was running, which had begun on the Nones of October of the year 3377 of the Julian Period. It was an embolismic year; add the length of three months. Therefore Apellaeus began on the day before the Nones of January of the year 3378 of the Julian Period. The twenty-second day of Apellaeus, reckoned civilly, was the ninth day before the Kalends of February, and on that day Philip was killed by Pausanias. Therefore the reign of Alexander the Great began on the eighth day before the Kalends of February of the year 3378 of the Julian Period, which day falls on the twenty-third of Apellaeus. Hence Alexander, who was taken from human affairs in the year 3390 of the Julian Period, on the twenty-eighth day of the month Daesius, or the fourth day before the Ides of August, reigned twelve years, six months and as many days, reckoning by Macedonian months; but if you count from the eighth day before the Kalends of February to the fourth day before the Ides of August, the days are seventeen and the months six. So Diodorus rightly said that he reigned "twelve years, seven months" [βασιλεύοντας ἐπὶ δώδεκα, μῆνας ἑπτά[?]], although the seventh month was not completed but was in progress. The tragedy which Neoptolemus once acted at the games at which Philip was killed is Cinyras, for, according to Suetonius, Mnester danced that same tragedy on the day Caius was killed, which Neoptolemus had once acted. Mnester, on Josephus's authority, danced the tragedy Cinyras; there is a small error in Josephus's words, but it entirely overturns the fabulous story: [the actor ... Cinyras ... Myrrha]. As these words sound, you would say that Myrrha was killed, which, so far as I know, none of the other ancients has recorded in writing. Certainly Josephus himself, in what follows, mentions only the blood poured out in that drama of Cinyras: [the blood spilt from the stricken one and from Cinyras]. When Myrrha's father recognised her, he brought about his own death, and Myrrha was changed into a tree of the same name, as Antoninus Liberalis writes. Panyasis, in Apollodorus's Library, Book III, says that Myrrha fled, and when she was nearly dragged back by her father, about to suffer punishment, she was changed into a tree. The most ingenious of poets speaks of her in Metamorphoses Book X.

units.la: Cum tandem Cinyras, avidus cognoscere amantem, Post tot concubitus, illato lumine vidit, Et sceleus, & natam, verbisque dolore retentis, Pendenti nitidum vagina diripit ensem: Myrrha fugit: tenebrisque, & caeca munere noctis, Intercepta neci est: latosque vagata per agros, Palmiferos Arabas, Panchaeaque rura reliquit Perque novem erravit redeuntis cornua Lunae, Cum tandem terra requieuit fessa Sabaea.
units.tr: At last Cinyras, eager to learn who his lover was, after so many couplings, brought in a light and saw both the crime and his daughter. Holding back his words in grief, he snatched a gleaming sword from its hanging sheath. Myrrha fled, and in the dark, shielded by the blessing of the night's concealment, she escaped death. Wandering through the wide fields, she left the palm-bearing Arabians and the Panchaean countryside, and for nine horns of the returning moon she roamed, until at last the weary land of Saba gave her rest.

units.la: Hos versus descripsimus, quia indicio sunt interpunctionem vnius ex illis, qui initio huius fabulae leguntur, mendosam esse ad hunc modum: Gratulor huic terrae, quod abest regionibus illis, Quae tantum genuere nefas. Sit dives amomo, Cinnamaque, costumque suum, sudataque ligno Thura ferat, floresque alios Panchaïca tellus, Dum ferat & Myrrham.
units.tr: We have copied these lines because they show that the punctuation of one of the verses read at the beginning of this tale is faulty, in this way: I congratulate this land, that it lies far from those regions which bore such a crime. Let it be rich in amomum and cinnamon and its own costus, and let it bear incense sweated from the tree and other flowers, the Panchaean land, while it still bears myrrh.

units.la: Interpunctio haec Myrrham adscribit Panchaiae: atqui in sequentibus dicit Panchaïam reliquisse: Palmiferos Arabas, Panchæaque rura reliquit.
units.tr: This punctuation attributes Myrrha to Panchaea; yet in what follows he says she left Panchaea: leaving the palm-bearing Arabians and the Panchaean fields.

units.la: & in Sabæa resedisse: Cum tandem terra requieuit fessa Sabaea.
units.tr: And that she settled in Saba: When at last the weary land of Saba gave her rest.

units.la: Quare existimo in praecedentibus τὸ Panchaïca coniungendum esse cum voce thura, cuius est epitheton, non autem cum voce tellus: itaque distinguo. Sudataque ligno Thura ferat, (floresque alios,) Panchaïca, tellus, Dum ferat & Myrrham tanti noua non fuit arbor.
units.tr: Therefore I think that in the preceding lines the word Panchaïca should be joined with thura, of which it is the epithet, and not with tellus*; so I punctuate: sweated from the tree, (and other flowers,) Panchaean incense, land, while it still bears myrrh; such a great tree was not new.

units.la: Verum ad Myrrham noltra reuertatur oratio. Non igitur occisa est Myrrha, sed euasit: itaque reponendum est apud Iosephum: ὁ, τι ἐρχῆσις δρᾶμα εἰσάγ[?] Κινύρας, ἐν ᾧ ἀντὶς τε ἐκπίνετο, ἡ εἰ Ἰυνάτηρ Μύρρα[?]. in eo dramate peribat Cinyras, abibat siue fugiebat Myrrha. Hactenus de Iosephi verbis disputatum est, pauca dicenda sunt de Laureolo in verbis Suetonij: eius enim oblata occasione huic ista mandauimus chartæ: Et cum in Laureolo mimo, inquit Suetonius, in quo actor proripiens se ruina, sanguinem vomuit, vt plures secundarum certatim experimentum artis darent, cruore scena abundauit. Sed quid illud est? proripiens se ruina: & quo referes? quænam est illa ruina, e qua se proripuit actor? certe id non est pro argumento huius dramatis, nam repræsentabatur eo drama inducebaturque Laureolus latronum antesignanus in crucem actus: in quo Mimo repræsentando, caue putes verum sanguinem vomuisse actorem Laureoli, qui in crucem actus fuerat: nam illa falsis imaginibus, non ex vero à Mimorum actoribus repræsentabantur: itaque hunc, quem vomuit actor Laureoli, ἅμα τεχνίτην [?] τὸν σωματοποιὸν appellat Iosephus in hac historia: unde duo discimus, prius est, sanguinem effusum fuisse, non ab eo qui se ruina proripuerat, sed ab eo qui in crucem fuerat actus fallam, cum partes Laureoli ageret: alterum est, hunc sanguinem fuisse τεχνὴν[?], non verum: atque ex his constat mendosa esse Suetonij verba, quæ ita, me auctore restitues: Et cum in Laureolo Mimo, in quo actor proripiens ceruina sanguinem vomuit, vt plures secundarum certatim experimentum artis darent, cruore scena abundauit. Sensus hic est. Actor primarum partium, id est, is qui Laureolum agebat, cum cruci assigeretur, bis manus, bis pedes, habuit vtriculos de cerrina pelle sanguinis plenos, subduxit ille se, ita vt vtriculi illi affixi clauis sanguinem effuderint, & cruciarius iste falsus subducto paululum capite, ceruino vtre, qui forte appositus erat pectori, tanquam ore, sanguinem vomuerit; quod cum Mimo peracto, alij actores ad dandum certatim artis experimentum, tentare vellent, scena cruore abundavit. Sanguis ille, è ceruino effusus utriculo, id est, quem πηχὺν [?] Iosephus nominat. Sed emansores fumus: ad Areopagitas nostros redeamus.
units.tr: But let my discourse return to Myrrha. Myrrha, then, was not killed but escaped; and so the passage in Josephus must be restored: Cinyras, in whose drama Myrrha was exhibited, in which Cinyras perished, and the daughter, Myrrha, departed or fled. So much has been said about the words of Josephus; a few things must be said about the Laureolus in the words of Suetonius, for it was on this occasion that I committed these matters to paper. Suetonius says: And when in the mime Laureolus, in which the actor, hurling himself from a fall, vomited blood, so that many of the second-rank performers vied to give proof of their skill, the stage was flooded with blood. But what is this? Hurling himself from a fall: and to what will you refer it? What is this "fall" from which the actor hurled himself? Surely it has nothing to do with the plot of this drama, for the play being staged was Laureolus, the captain of robbers, led to the cross. In staging this mime, do not suppose that the actor of Laureolus, who had been led to the cross, really vomited blood, for those things were represented by false images, not by real means, by the actors of mimes. Hence Josephus, in this history, calls the one who vomited, the actor of Laureolus, a mimic artist [τεχνίτην τὸν σωματοποιὸν]. From this we learn two things. First, the blood was poured out not by him who hurled himself from the fall, but by the one who, playing the part of Laureolus, had been led to the cross, a false one. Second, this blood was an artifice [τέχνην], not real. From this it is clear that the words of Suetonius are corrupt, and on my authority they should be restored thus: And when in the mime Laureolus, in which the actor, hurling himself from the stag's hide, vomited blood, so that many of the second-rank performers vied to give proof of their skill, the stage was flooded with blood. The sense is this. The actor of the leading part, that is, the one who played Laureolus, when he was fixed to the cross, had bladders of stag skin full of blood on his hands and feet. He withdrew himself so that the bladders fastened to him poured out blood through the nails. And this false crucified man, with his head drawn slightly aside, vomited blood as if from his mouth through the stag bladder that happened to be placed on his breast. When the mime was finished and the other actors, to give proof of their skill, tried to do the same, the stage was flooded with blood. That blood, poured from the stag's bladder, is what Josephus calls pēchys [πηχύν]. But we have wandered far enough; let us return to our Areopagites.

units.la: Senatus Areopagiticus Lege rationes suas quotannis referebat:
units.tr: The Areopagite Senate by law rendered its accounts every year.

units.la: Τῷ βουλῷ τῷ ἐν Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ ἐγκεκλημένῳ [?] τὰς τῶν Λογισταὶ λόγον ἢ δύναις διδόναι. [?]
units.tr: The Council that is convened on the Areopagus is to receive the accounts of the magistrates and their powers. [Τῇ βουλῇ τῇ ἐν Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ ἐγκεκλημένῃ τὰς τῶν ἀρχόντων λόγον καὶ δύναμιν διδόναι.]

units.la: Describsit Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος [?] ἀγῶνι [?] Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ ἐγκεκλημένῳ τὰς τῶν Λογισταὶ ὁ νόμος κελεύει λόγον καὶ δύναις διδόναι, καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῶν συνεδρίων ἢ τὴν μεγίστων λύσειν ἀγὴν [?] τοῦ τῶν ὑμετέραν ἀρχὴν [?]. Quotannis diximus, quanquam in Lege non habeatur, quia cum Magistratus sit perpetuus, non finito τῆς ἀρχῆς [?] tempore, sed alio definito rationes suas ut referrent, opus fuit.
units.tr: Aeschines, in his speech against Ctesiphon, wrote: The law orders that the Council on the Areopagus receive from the magistrates an account and reckoning, and that the investigation of the greatest matters be conducted from the sessions... [ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος ἀγῶνι ... ἐν Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ ἐγκεκλημένῳ τὰς τῶν ἀρχόντων ὁ νόμος κελεύει λόγον καὶ εὐθύνας διδόναι]. We have said "every year", although the law does not say it, because the magistracy was not bounded by a fixed term but ended at another defined point, and so an annual account was needed.

units.la: Inter præcipuos Magistratus numerandi veniunt Strategi, qui numero decem quotannis bello præficiebantur, ut Grammatici docent ex Hyperide & Aristotele: οἱ καθ' ἕκαστον ἐνιαυτὸν χειροτονούμενοι Στρατηγοὶ δέκα ἀεὶ ἤσαν, ὡς μαρτυ- [?] εἶν ἐκ τε τῆς Ὑπερίδου καὶ Ἀριστοτέλους, καὶ ἐκ τῆς Ἀθηναίων πολιτείας Ἀεισοτέ- [?] λεις. Videtur Plutarchus in Cimone docere è singulis unum Tribubus creatos fuisse, ὡς ἡ Κίμων μὲν τῶν Συγγραφὴν τῶν Τελεσθῶν εἰς ὃ ἡμέραν ἐποίησατο τοῦ ἡμῶν [?] τὰς νενομισμένας ἀποδοῦσι, οὐκ ἀφῆκεν αὐτὸς ἀπολαβεῖν, ἀλλ' ὁρκώσας, ἰωάσκω ἡμᾶς [?] ἔτη καὶ κείνας δίκας ὄντος [?], ἀπὸ φυλῆς μιᾶς ἕκαστον. Quod an verum sit, aut perpetuo usurpatum, necne, pronunciare non audeo: neque multum iuvat Pollux Lib. VIII. qui ita scribit: καὶ γραμματεὺς χειροτονεῖ ἐξ ἀπάντων. potest enim exponi aut de omnibus Tribubus, aut de omnibus Atheniensibus: quod posterius verius puto. Eligebantur autem diebus comitiabus, qui anni verrentis ultimi sunt, à populo. Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος [?]. Κἀκεῖνας ἡ δῆμος εἴωθε χειροτονεῖν ἐν Ἀργαιρεσίαις, Στρατηγοὺς, ἢ Ἱππάρχους, καὶ ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν ἀρχῶν [?]. Idque in Pnyce, etiam, ubi Theatro extructo desitum est ibi concionem habere. Pollux: ἐκκλησιάζειν δὲ πάλαι μὲν ἐν τῇ Πνυκί. αὗτης δὲ τὲ μὲν ἄλλα ἐν τοῖς ἐξυσιαχῷ ἡ κατ' ἐκκλησιά [?], μίνας δὲ τὰς Ἀργαιρεσίας ἐν τῇ Πνυκί. Hesychius: Πνύξ, πόλις Ἀθηνῶν, ἐν ᾗ αἱ ἐκκλησίαι πάλαι μὲν ἦσαν πᾶσαι, νῦν δ' ἀπαξ, ὅταν Στρατηγοὶ χειροτονῶσιν. De Chabria Strategio Demosthenes ἐν τοῖς ἐν τῷ Ἀειστοκράτους. ὡς δ' ἐν Ἀργαιρεσίαις ὑμεῖς Καθεῖλε ὅτι τὸν πόλεμον ἔγωγε κτῆσῆπατε. [?]
units.tr: Among the chief magistrates the Strategoi must be counted; ten were appointed each year to command in war, as the grammarians teach from Hyperides and Aristotle: the Strategoi chosen each year were always ten, as is attested by Hyperides and Aristotle, and by the Constitution of the Athenians of Aristotle [οἱ καθ' ἕκαστον ἐνιαυτὸν χειροτονούμενοι στρατηγοὶ δέκα ἀεὶ ἦσαν]. Plutarch, in his life of Cimon, seems to teach that one was created from each tribe: Cimon, when he had made an agreement with the Tauri, could not bring himself to release the prisoners...; he swore them in and sent them, one from each tribe. Whether this is true, or was used permanently, I do not dare to pronounce; nor does Pollux in Book VIII help us much, who writes: and the secretary is chosen from all [καὶ γραμματεὺς χειροτονεῖ ἐξ ἀπάντων]. For this may be understood either of all the tribes or of all the Athenians, and the latter I think the truer. They were chosen by the people on the days of the elections, which fell in the last months of the year. Aeschines, in his speech against Ctesiphon: and these the people are accustomed to elect at the elections, Strategoi or Hipparchs, and in the case of the magistracies... [κἀκεῖνας ὁ δῆμος εἴωθε χειροτονεῖν ἐν χειροτονίαις]. And this was done in the Pnyx, even after a theatre was built, where they had ceased to hold the assembly. Pollux: In former times they used to assemble in the Pnyx; later, in other places, but the elections were held in the Pnyx. Hesychius: Pnyx, a place in Athens, in which the assemblies were formerly all held, but now only once, when the Strategoi are elected. Demosthenes, on Chabrias the Strategus, in the speech against Aristocrates: and when you elected him at the elections... [ἐν τοῖς ἐν τῷ Ἀριστοκράτους...].

units.la: Nam quod Cleo Boëdromione mense Strategus creatus est, id extra ordinem factum est, suffectus quippe est in locum Niciæ, qui vltro se hoc Magistratu abdicavit. Atque ij sunt, qui dicuntur Στρατηγοὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ὅπλων, ut ab aliis distinguerentur: Neque hic audiendus est Vir Incomparabilis, qui, cum Athenæus Posidonij verba referat Lib. V. ubi de Athenione, qui bello Mithridatico Athenienfium Rempublicam occupavit, agit, εἶλεν τὸν Ἀθηναίων Στρατηγὸν ἐπὶ τὴν ὅπλων, ista animaduertit: Στρατηγὸς est, qui militibus præest, & ut Suetonij vocem usurpem, ducatum habet. Quare igitur addit ἐπὶ τὴν ὅπλων; quia seculo Athenæi Στρατηγοὶ in municipiis dicebantur, etiam ciuiles & urbani Magistratus, ut in Actis S. Apostolorum cap. XVI. & Leg. VI. §. XVI, item Leg. X V. §. IX. D. De excusatione tutorum. Non igitur simpliciter Στρατηγὸς Athenarum creatur Athenio, sed Στρατηγὸς ἐπὶ τὴν ὅπλων, quæ potestas Dictaturæ affinis, ac pæne eadem fuit. Hactenus ὁ Ἰωμβίσιος [?], cui assensum non præbemus, vt qui sciamus iam ab antiquis temporibus, & aliquot retro seculis ante Athenæi ætatem occurrere mentionem τὸ ὅτι τῶν ὅπλων Στρατηγός[?]. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς ἀφανοῦς[?] ex Psephismate Callisthenis: Ἐπικεινέτω ὁ ὅτι τῶν Ὅπλων Στρατηγός[?]. Neque Posidonij verba sunt interpretanda ex usu seculi illius, quo Athenæus scripsit: Nam Athenæi ætate οἱ ὅτι τῶν ὅπλων Στρατηγοὶ fuerunt Ædiles. Philostratus in Lolliano. παρῶτε δὲ ἡ τῆς Ἀθηναίων δήμου[?], γραμματέως αὐτῆς τὸ ὅτι τῶν ὅπλων[?]. ἡ δὲ ἔρχῆ αὐτῆ[?], παλαι μὲν καταλέγειν τε[?], ἡ ἐξῆλθε εἰς τὸ πολέμια[?]· νῦν ὃ ἔφηκεν ἀπαμψάτω[?], καὶ οἴνον ἀγορᾶς[?]. Sed quare ὁ ὅτι τῶν ὅπλων Στρατηγὸς dicebatur? Haec est, meo iudicio, ratio: cum decem essent Strategi, non omnes simul praerant, sed singuli per orbem suum imperabant diem, vt exemplo Miltiadis videre est apud Herodotum, & Cornelium Nepotem, siue Æmilius Probus is est, in Miltiadis vita. Strategus itaque ὅτι τῶν ὅπλων is est, penes quem erat imperium illius diei: atque ita singuli Strategi vicem suam sunt & dicuntur Στρατηγοὶ ὅτι τῶν ὅπλων. Quanquam saepe factum legimus, vt penes eum esset summa auctoritas atque imperium, non in vnum tantum diem & vicem suam, qui auctoritate, aut peritia, aut gratia apud plebem valebat plurimum: Lege autem cauebatur, vt creandus Strategus agrum intra fines Atticæ possideret, & liberos legitimos aut iam haberet, aut suscIperet.
units.tr: For the fact that Cleo was made Strategus in the month of Boedromion was done outside the ordinary order: he was substituted in the place of Nicias, who of his own accord had given up this magistracy. Those are also called Strategoi epi ta hopla, "over the arms", to distinguish them from the others. Nor should we listen here to that incomparable man, who, when Athenaeus quotes the words of Posidonius in Book V, where he deals with Athenion, who seized the government of Athens in the Mithridatic war, notes these things, after the phrase: "he seized the Strategus of the Athenians epi ta hopla": a Strategus is one who commands soldiers, and, to use Suetonius's word, holds the leadership. Why then does he add epi ta hopla? Because in Athenaeus's age, the Strategoi in the municipalities were also called civil and urban magistrates, as in the Acts of the Apostles chapter 16, and in Law VI §16, and likewise Law XV §9 of the Digest, On the excuse of guardians. Therefore Athenion was not simply made Strategus of Athens, but Strategus epi ta hopla, an office akin to the dictatorship and almost the same. So far the Iombisios, to whom we do not give assent, since we know that from ancient times and some centuries before Athenaeus's age, mention of the Strategus of arms occurs. Demosthenes, in the speech on the ..., from the decree of Callisthenes: Let the Strategus of arms be present. Nor are the words of Posidonius to be interpreted by the usage of the age in which Athenaeus wrote, for in Athenaeus's time those who were the Strategoi of arms were the aediles. Philostratus in Lollianus: the secretary of the Athenian people... In former times they were enrolled, and when they went out to war... Now, when the city... But why was the Strategus epi ta hopla so called? This, in my judgement, is the reason. Since there were ten Strategoi, not all led at once, but each in turn commanded for his own day, as can be seen from the example of Miltiades in Herodotus and in Cornelius Nepos, or Aemilius Probus, if that is who wrote the life of Miltiades. Therefore the Strategus epi ta hopla is the one in whose hands the command of that day lay; and so each Strategus, in his turn, is called Strategus epi ta hopla. Yet we often read that the supreme authority and command rested with one man, not for one day and in his turn only, but for whoever was most powerful with the people through authority, skill, or favour. By law, however, it was provided that a Strategus to be created should possess land within the borders of Attica and should already have, or should beget, legitimate children.
