units.la: Τὸν Στρατηγὸν παιδοποιεῖσθαι κατὰ τοὺς νόμους, καὶ γῆν ἐντὸς ὅρων κεκτῆσθαι[?]. | Strategus liberos suscipito è legitimis nuptiis: agrúmque intra fines Atticæ possidero.
units.tr: The Strategus shall beget children according to the laws and possess land within the boundaries [Τὸν Στρατηγὸν παιδοποιεῖσθαι κατὰ τοὺς νόμους, καὶ γῆν ἐντὸς ὅρων κεκτῆσθαι]. The Strategus shall have children from a lawful marriage, and shall possess land within the borders of Attica.

units.la: Meminit Dinarchus ἐν τῷ κατὰ Δημοσθένους[?], καὶ τοὺς μὲν νόμους παρελέγειν τῷ Στρατηγῷ[?], τῷ πῶς δὲ τῆς δήμου πίστιν ἀξιοῦντι λαμβάνειν[?], παιδοποιεῖσθαι κατὰ τοὺς νόμους, γῆν ἐντὸς ὅρων κεκτῆσθαι[?]· πάσας τὰς δικαίας πίστεις ἐπεξεκατελθόντος[?], οὕτως ἀξιοῦν παρεσκευάσθαι τῆς δήμου[?]. Nempe bona oppignerabantur Reipublicæ, liberique erant paternæ fidei obsides: itaque factum aliquando, vt paterna lucrent delicta: atque ex hoc more Sinon Græcus apud Poëtam Latinorum principem de suis liberis,
units.tr: Dinarchus mentions this in his speech against Demosthenes. He says that the laws required the Strategus, when he asked the people for their trust, to beget children according to the laws and to possess land within the boundaries, and that after he had gone through all the lawful pledges of trust, he was to be judged fit for the people's service. Clearly the goods were pledged to the commonwealth, and the children were hostages for their father's loyalty. So it sometimes happened that the fathers' offences fell upon the children, and from this custom Sinon the Greek, in the chief Latin poet, speaks of his own children:

units.la: Quos illi fors ad pœnas ob nostra reposcent Effugia, & culpam hanc miserorum morte piabunt.
units.tr: Whom perhaps chance will demand as punishment for our escapes, and they will atone for this guilt with the death of the wretched ones.

units.la: Cicero Epistola ad Brutum: In qua videtur illud esse crudele, quod ad liberos, qui nihil meruerunt, poena peruenit. Sed id & antiquum est, & omnium ciuitatum. Siquidem Themistoclis etiam liberi eguerunt. Postquam creati fuerant Strategi, ἐδοκιμάζοντο ἐκ Λέγε[?], vt & ceteri Magistratus, atque δοκιμασίας Strategorum meminerunt Grammatici ἐκ Lycurgo ἐν τῷ κατὰ τῆς διοικήσεως[?]. τῆς δοκιμασίας καὶ τῶν νόμων γίνοιτ᾽ ἂν τέλος[?], ὡς οἱ Στρατηγοὶ δοκιμάζονται[?]. Aphthonius cap. vltimo: εἰ πάντα τὰ πρὸ ὑμῶν πολιτευόμενα, κεῖνται[?], ταῖς Στρατηγοῖς[?], ταῖς ἰσρωσιῶν[?], τὰ ψηφίσματα πάντα ὁλίγου δεῖν λέγειν[?], ὅστε καὶ τὸν πόλεμον ἀφίσται[?]. Interrogabantur autem: An agros intra fines Atticæ possiderent, necne: An liberos legitimos iam suscepissent, aut suscepturi essent, necne: colligere est è Dinarcho, qui verbis iam laudatis subiicit: οἱ δὲ τὰ παπέφαι γῆν πεποιηκέναι[?], τὰς δὲ ἡ γνήσι- μίους ὑμῶν[?] ἂν παιδοποιεῖσθαι κατὰ τοὺς νόμους[?], τὴν ἐν ταῖς κείσεσιν ἔνεκα γονέων[?]. ὅρκων. Vbi approbati fuerant, iusiurandum ex Lege concipiebant, cuius hoc extat Kaput.
units.tr: Cicero, in his letter to Brutus: In this case the cruel thing seems to be that the punishment reaches the children, who have deserved nothing. But this is both ancient and common to all states. Indeed the children of Themistocles also were in want. After the Strategi had been created, they were examined, as were the other magistrates, and the Grammarians mention the examination (dokimasia) of the Strategi in Lycurgus, in his speech against the administration. [Greek passage on the examination and the laws, in which it is said how the Strategi are examined.] Aphthonius, in the last chapter: if all the decrees passed before you concern the Strategi and the magistrates, nearly all of them are to be spoken of... Those who were examined were asked whether they possessed land within the boundaries of Attica or not, and whether they had already begotten, or were about to beget, lawful children or not. This may be gathered from Dinarchus, who after the words just cited adds that those who were to be examined had to show that they owned land and had legitimate children, begotten according to the laws. Once they had been approved, they took the oath prescribed by law, of which this chapter survives.

units.la: ΟΡΚΟΣ ΣΤΡΑΤΗΓΩΝ.
units.tr: THE OATH OF THE STRATEGI.

units.la: Δὶς αἱὰ πρὸ [?] εἰς τὴν Μεγαρικὴν [?] ἐμβαλλὼν.
units.tr: Twice every year I will invade the Megarian territory [Δὶς αἰεὶ πρὸ εἰς τὴν Μεγαρικὴν ἐμβαλῶ].

units.la: Bis quotannis in agrum Megarensem irrumpam.
units.tr: Twice a year I will make an incursion into the Megarian territory.

units.la: IVSIVRANDVM STRATEGORVM.
units.tr: THE OATH OF THE STRATEGI.

units.la: Additum est istud Kaput Charino rogante, paulo ante belli Peloponnesiaci initia. Plutarchus in Pericle: ἐπὶ δ᾽ ὁ πεμφθεὶς κῆρυξ [?] Ἀρχιμάχειος αἰτία τῆς Μεγαρέων [?] ἀπονοίας ἔδοξε, γράφει ψήφισμα κατ᾽ αὐτῶν Χαρῖνος, ἀσυνδόν [?] ἀξιῶν [?] καὶ ἀκήρυκτον [?] ἐξεῖναι, ὡς δ᾽ αὖ ὅπως τῆς Ἀττικῆς Μεγαρέων [?] ἐπιπόνου [?] ἐκαλεῖτο. Τοὺς δὲ Στρατηγοὺς, ὅταν ὀμνύωσι τὸν πατρῷον ὅρκον, ἐπομνύειν ὅτι ἡ Ἀττικὴ ἀπὸ πρὸ ἐμβαλλειν εἰς τὴν Μεγαρικὴν ἐμβαλοῦσι. Quemadmodum autem Strategi apud Iudices ἐδικάζοντο, ita etiam rationes referebant, nisi populus Atheniensis esse voluisset αὐτοχειρίας, vt creatus est olim Aristides bello aduersus Barbaros. Plutarchus in Aristide: χειροτονηθεὶς ἦ Στρατηγὸς αὐτοχειρίαν ὅτι τῷ μάχῃ. de Alcibiade, Nicia, & Lamacho Plutarchus ἐγραψε τὴν Ῥήτορων, Δημόσφατος ἢ εἶπεν ὡς χρὴ τοὺς Στρατηγοὺς αὐτοχειρίας εἶναι [?] τῆς [?] ἀδικίας [?] ἐκ τὰ πολέμου πῶς ἢ [?]. αὐτοκράτωρ is est, qui rationes non refert. Suidas: Αὐτοχειρία, πῶς τὰν αὐτοκρατόρων. Atque haec αὐτοχειρία posita erat tum in belli apparatu adornando, tum in bello administrando: id est: militum dilectum habebat, necessaria ad bellum parabat, ipsum denique bellum pro arbitrio αὐτοκράτορος administrabat, quemadmodum apud Romanos Dictator, cuius non tam nomen, quam rem ipsam inuasit Diuus Iulius, & ad posteros transmisit cum Imperatoris titulo, sed maiori longe cum dignatione atque auctoritate: nam vt inquit Vlpianus Lib. XIII. ad Legem Iuliam & Papiam, Princeps legibus solutus est: Augusta autem, licet Legibus soluta non est: Principes tamen eadem illi priuilegia tribuunt, quae ipsi habent. Lib. XXXI. D. de Legibus: vbi interpungendum est, meo iudicio, Augusta autem licet, Legibus soluta non est: Principes, &c. id est, quanquam Augusta sit, Legibus soluta non est, nulla alia veteri Lege, nullo Senatusconsulto: Principes tamen eadem illi tribuunt priuilegia, quae ipsi habent: quemadmodum, exempli gratia, in verbis Vlpiani Lib. LXIII. ad Edictum, Quodcumque priuilegij fisco competit, hoc idem Caesaris ratio, & Augustae habere solet. Leg. VI. §. 1. D. de iure Fisci: quanquam negant viri praestantissimi solere ex Leg. LVII. D. de Legatis II. Sed verum est, quod scribit Gaius Libro XIV. ad Legem Iuliam & Papiam, Quod Principi relictum est, qui antequam dies legati cedat, ab hominibus ereptus est, ex constitutione Diui Antonini, successori eius debetur. Leg. LVI. D. de Legatis II. at tamen, vt scribit Iunius Mauricianus Libro II. ad Legem Iuliam & Papiam, Si Augustae legaueris, & ea inter homines esse desierit, deficit quod ei relictum est, sicuti Diuus Hadrianus in Plotina, & proxime Imperator Antoninus in Faustina Augustae persona constituit, cum ea inter homines esse desiit, quam testator decederet. Leg. LVII. D. eod. habet idem priuilegij ratio Augustae, quod fiscus, sed quamdiu est: non est autem amplius ratio Augustae, vbi ipsa Augusta inter homines esse desiit: at vero fiscus nunquam esse definit.
units.tr: This clause was added at the request of Charinus, shortly before the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. Plutarch, in the Life of Pericles: when Archimachus, the herald sent to the Megarians, seemed to be the cause of their insolence, Charinus proposed a decree against them, that it should be lawful to treat them without truce and without herald, and so the Megarians were called a plague of Attica. And the Strategi, when they swore the ancestral oath, swore also that they would invade the Megarian territory twice a year. As the Strategi were tried before judges, so also they rendered accounts, unless the Athenian people wished them to hold power without accountability, as Aristides was once created Strategus with full powers (autocheiria) in the war against the barbarians. Plutarch in Aristides: elected Strategus with autocheiria, that is with full powers, in the battle. Plutarch wrote of Alcibiades, Nicias and Lamachus that Demosthenes the orator said that the Strategi ought to have full powers in the war, without accountability to the people. A person is autocrator who does not render accounts. Suidas: autocheiria, the power of the autocrators. This autocheiria was granted both in preparing for war and in conducting it: that is, the Strategus raised the soldiers, prepared the things needed for the war, and conducted the war itself at his own discretion, as the Dictator did among the Romans. The divine Julius seized not so much the name as the thing itself, and passed it on to posterity with the title of Imperator, but with far greater dignity and authority. For, as Ulpian says in Book 13 on the Julian and Papian Law: The Prince is released from the laws; but the Augusta, though she is not released from the laws, the princes nevertheless grant her the same privileges that they themselves have. In Book 31 of the Digest, On Laws, the passage should, in my judgment, be punctuated thus: Although the Augusta is not released from the laws, the princes, etc. That is, although she is Augusta, she is not released from the laws, by no other ancient law and no senatorial decree; yet the princes grant her the same privileges that they themselves have, as, for example, in Ulpian's words in Book 63 on the Edict: Whatever privilege belongs to the fisc, the same is usually held by the rank of Caesar and of the Augusta. Digest 6.1, On the Right of the Fisc. Though very distinguished men deny that this holds from Digest 57, On Legacies II. But what Gaius writes in Book 14 on the Julian and Papian Law is true: What is left to the Prince, if it has been taken away by men before the day of the legacy falls due, is owed to his successor by the constitution of the divine Antoninus. Digest 56, On Legacies II. Yet, as Junius Mauricianus writes in Book 2 on the Julian and Papian Law: If you bequeath something to the Augusta, and she has ceased to be among men, what was left to her fails, just as the divine Hadrian decreed in the case of Plotina, and more recently the Emperor Antoninus in the person of the Augusta Faustina, when she ceased to be among men before the testator died. Digest 57, same title: the Augusta has the same privilege as the fisc, but only as long as she lives; the rank of Augusta no longer exists when she herself ceases to be among men, whereas the fisc never ceases to exist.

units.la: Sed ad nostros Strategos reuertamur: Si naues sociorum intercipiebant, aut illos in iuria afficiebant, publica aduersus Strategos [illegible, ~4 letters] instituebantur Lege iudicia.
units.tr: But let us return to our Strategi. If they intercepted the ships of allies, or wronged them, public trials were brought against the Strategi [illegible word].

units.la: Τοῖς Στρατηγοῖς δικὰ ποιοῦντας, καὶ κα- ρίας τὰ πλοῖα τῶν συμμάχων εἰσαγγέλλειν.
units.tr: Against the Strategi who wrong the allies and seize their ships, to bring an impeachment (eisangelein).

units.la: Aduersus Strategos vexantes socios, aut eorum naues intercipientes, publica instituuntur iudicia.
units.tr: Against Strategi who harass the allies or seize their ships, public trials are instituted.

units.la: Meminit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ [?] ἐν Χερρονήσῳ, εἰ γὰρ δικὰ παῖς Διοπείθης Strategus, καὶ καταγὰ τὰ πλοῖα, μικρόν, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, μικρὸν πινάκιον, τῶν πάντα κωλύσαι δυνάμεθ' ἂν. ἡ λέγειν οἱ νόμοι, τῶν τὰς ἀδικουμένας εἰσαγγελλ[?]. Primum itaque aduersus absentem Strategum plebiscito dabatur publicum iudicium, quod ut institueretur, Stratego praesente opus erat: quare arcessebatur: mittebaturque Paralus, aut Salaminia nauis, qua adducheretur. Demosthenes: ἔπι δὲ ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς, ψηφισμα, εἰσαγγελία, Πάραλος· τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἐκεῖνο. Male interpretatur eruditissimus Vvolfius Πάραλον, tribunia iudicia: intelligit namque Orator nauem. Scholia: Πάραλος ἢ Σαλαμινία. αὕτη ἱερὰ τελῆσ δημοσίαν ἔπι δὲ τὰς τῆς πόλεως χρείας πεμπόμεναι ἡ ἐχωνδωτοσην. & narrat Plutarchus in Alcibiade, cùm violatæ religionis accusaretur Alcibiades, qui præerat exercitui in Sicilia, missam esse harum nauium alteram, qua vehereretur: ἡ τέλος ἀπέστελε τῷ Σαλαμινίᾳ πρὸς αὐτὸν, κελεύοντας ἀχολεῖν ἔπι τῷ χείσιν, ἐ πεῖθ[?] τὸν δῆμον. Aristophanes Auibus.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this in his speech on the Chersonese: "For if Diopeithes, the Strategus, wrongs and seizes ships, men of Athens, it would take only a small tablet, a little writ, by which we could prevent all this, if the laws said that one should bring an impeachment against those who are wronged." So first, against an absent Strategus, a public trial was granted by a plebiscite; but in order to institute it the Strategus had to be present, so he was summoned, and the Paralus, or the Salaminia ship, was sent to bring him back. Demosthenes: "Against ourselves, a decree, an impeachment, a Paralus; that is the thing." The learned Wolf mistakenly translates Paralus as "tribunician courts", since the orator means a ship. The scholia: Paralus, or Salaminia. This was a sacred state trireme, sent for the needs of the city. Plutarch also tells in the Life of Alcibiades that when Alcibiades, who commanded the army in Sicily, was accused of violating religion, one of these ships, the Salaminia, was sent to bring him back to the trial. Aristophanes, Birds: [Greek verse, obscure in the scan.]

units.la: μηδαμῶςἩμῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν πλὴν ἁλὸς ἐπὶ ψυχῆς ἀλλήλοις[?]Κλεπτὴρ ἄρχοντες ἐστὶ ἡ Σαλαμινία.
units.tr: [Greek verse from Aristophanes, Birds, obscure in the scan; it refers to the Salaminia as the sacred ship of the Athenians.]

units.la: Lege sanctum erat, Ne cui Syndico iterum fieri liceret creatique à populo: Μὴ ἐξεῖναι χειροτονεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ δήμου, πλέον, ἢ ἅπαξ συνδικῆσαι.
units.tr: By law it was sanctioned that no one should be chosen by the people as Syndic more than once [Μὴ ἐξεῖναι χειροτονεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ δήμου, πλέον, ἢ ἅπαξ συνδικῆσαι].

units.la: Nemo, plus quam semel, Syndicus à populo creator.
units.tr: No one may be chosen as Syndic by the people more than once.

units.la: Ratio Legis est, ne id munus ob publicam utilitatem inventum, uteretur in quæstum compendiúmque priuatum. Habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ πρὸς Λεπτίνην ἔστι ὃ ἡ μάλα ἔχων νόμος ἡμῶν κακῶς, οὐκ ἔπι ζύπους πῆχυς, ἀλλ' ἵνα μὴ ὁ πεζὸς μὲ ἐργασία τῆς ἡ, ἡ συκοφαντία, μὴ ὀξῦναι χειροτονεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τῆς δήμου, πλέον, ἢ ἅπαξ συνδικῆσαι. Vlpianus: ἐστὶ ὁ νόμος ἐκέλευε, μὴ δὶς τὸ ἔργον συνδικεῖν. ἡ γὰρ ἅπαξ τὸ ποιῆσαι, κωλύεται, ἵνα μὴ ἄλλο ὁ κέρδος ψἀ- δεσθαι ἐπιχράσσαν. Idem quoque docet Paulus Lib. I. Sententiarum: Defensionem Reipublicæ amplius quam semel suscipere nemo cogitur. Leg. XVI. §. III. D. de muneribus & honoribus. Defensores enim ciuitatis, vel Reipublicæ, qui ad certam causam agendam, vel defendendam eliguntur, Græci Syndicos appellant, vt notat Arcadius Lib. singulari de muneribus ciuilibus: & defensio ciuitatis est, inquit Hermogenianus Lib. I. Epitomarum, vt Syndicus fiat. Meminit Harpocration, è quo constat, post exactos Triginta Tyrannosid munus esse institutum. συνδικοι. Ἰσαῖος δὲ τοῦ κατ' Ἐλπηρόφου ἡ Δημοφάνους φησὶν. οἱ μὴ τὰ ἐκ Γλαυκίας ἐγὼ ἀκούω, Σωδίκαι ἴσθω, πρὸς οὓς τὰ δημοσιούμενα ἀπεφέρετο. καὶ Λυκοῦργος δὲ τοῦ Καταδεξίππου, εἰ γόνιος, καὶ που ἐπέρωτι δύδρξίος ὅτι οὐκ πρὸς τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας, γραφὰς γραφόμενος, πρὸς τὰς Σωδίκοις ἀπογραφὰς ἀπογραφῶν. μὴ ποτ' ὧν ἀρχὴ τῆς λῶ καὶ ἡσαμῶν μὴ τὸν ἐκ Γλαυκίας χάρδον οἱ Σωδίκοι.
units.tr: The reason for the law is that this office was devised for the public good, and must not be used for private gain and profit. You have it in Demosthenes, in the speech against Leptines: [Greek passage on the law, which says that the office of Syndic was not to be taken twice, so that it should not become a source of profit and sycophancy]. Ulpian: the law ordered that no one should act as Syndic twice; for having done it once, one is prevented, so that the gain from the office may not become a means of private profit. The same is taught by Paulus in Book 1 of the Sentences: No one is compelled to undertake the defence of the commonwealth more than once. Digest 16.3, On Offices and Honours. For those chosen to conduct or defend a particular case on behalf of a city or commonwealth are called Syndics by the Greeks, as Arcadius notes in his single book On Civic Offices; and the defence of the city, says Hermogenian in Book 1 of the Epitomes, is the making of a Syndic. Harpocration mentions this, from whom it appears that the office was instituted after the expulsion of the Thirty Tyrants. [Greek glosses on syndikoi, quoting Isaeus and Lycurgus, on the Syndics to whom public business was referred.]

units.la: Neque item Astynomi munere fungi iterum Lege licebat.
units.tr: Nor was it lawful, by statute, to hold the office of Astynomus a second time either.

units.la: ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΣΤΥΝΟΜΗΣΗι ΔΙΣ. Si quis semel atque iterum Astyno- mus fuerit.
units.tr: If anyone has been Astynomus twice [ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΣΤΥΝΟΜΗΣΗι ΔΙΣ]. If anyone has been Astynomus once or twice.

units.la: Non licuisse, colligere est è Demosthene in Proœmiis: Proœmio LXIV. [?] ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΣΤΥΝΟΜΗΣΗι ΔΙΣ. [?] De his Aristoteles de Republica Athieniensium apud Harpocrationem: Φησὶν [?] τὰς Ἀστυνόμους Ἀριστοτέλης ἐν τῇ Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ· πέντε μὲν ἐν Πειραιεῖ, πέντε δ' ἐν ἄστει. Sed numerus est corruptus: Quindecim enim fuerunt Astynomi, quot & Agoranomi, Metronomi, Sitophylaces: nempe decem in Vrbe, at vero in Piraeo: atque hic numerus semper est reponendus. Emendationis causam petimus ex eo quod Piraeus tertiam Athenarum partem constituebat: Ergo quinque tantum erant in Piraeo: in reliqua vero vrbe decem secundum hanc analogiam.
units.tr: It can be gathered from Demosthenes, in the Proems, that it was not lawful: Proem 64. [?] "If anyone has been Astynomus twice" [?]. Aristotle speaks of these in his Constitution of the Athenians, as quoted by Harpocration: "Aristotle, in the Constitution of the Athenians, says that the Astynomi were five in the Piraeus and five in the city" [Φησὶν τὰς Ἀστυνόμους Ἀριστοτέλης ἐν τῇ Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ· πέντε μὲν ἐν Πειραιεῖ, πέντε δ' ἐν ἄστει]. But the number is corrupt. For there were fifteen Astynomi, as many as there were Agoranomi, Metronomi and Sitophylakes: namely ten in the City and five in the Piraeus, and this is the number that must always be restored. We base the correction on the fact that the Piraeus made up a third part of Athens. Therefore there were only five in the Piraeus, and in the rest of the city ten, by this same proportion.

units.la: Quaestores nonnisi è populi sententia creabantur veteri Athenien-sium Lege:
units.tr: Under the ancient Athenian law, quaestors were appointed only by the vote of the people:

units.la: Γνώμῃ τῆς δήμου χειροτονεῖσθαι τὸν Ταμίαν.
units.tr: "The treasurer shall be elected by the vote of the people" [Γνώμῃ τῆς δήμου χειροτονεῖσθαι τὸν Ταμίαν].

units.la: E populi sententia Quaestores creantur.
units.tr: Quaestors are appointed by the vote of the people.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Vlpianus ad haec Demosthenis ex Androtiana verba: ἀιελόσσα γὰρ ἡ βυλὴ τὸν νόμον, τὸν ἐχεσπόνειν, ista enim adnotat: Καθαφεῖν ἡ βουλὴ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ κελεύοντος χειροτονεῖσθαι τὸν Ταμίαν. Numero erant decem è Pentecosiomedimnis lecti, qui accipiebant coram Senatu, & adseruabant in Minervæ Templo, quod erat in Arce, Minervæ simulacrum, victorias, alium mundum, itemque pecuniam publicam. Pollux Libro VIII. cap.VIII. Ταμίαι τῆς θεοῦ, κληρωτοί, ὧν ἐκ πεντακοσιομεδίμνων ἦσαν. Τὰ δ' χρήματα προελάβοσαν, τῆς βυλῆς παρούσης. Suidas: Ταμίαι Ἀργυρτῆς εἰσιν Ἀθηναίων κληρωτοὶ ἀπὸ πεντακοσιομεδίμνων. οἱ τὰ ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς ἐν ἀκροπόλει χρήματα, ἱερά τε καὶ δημόσια Φυλάττουσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἄγαλμα τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς. Harpocration: ἔρχει τῆς ἰῶν ἐξ' Ἀθηναίοις οἱ Ταμίαι δίκας τῶν ἀρχῶν. ἀναλαμβάνουσι δὲ ὅπου τὸ τε ἄγαλμα τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς καὶ τὰς νίκας, καὶ τὸ δόρυ κόσμου, καὶ τὰ χρήματα ἑκάστου τῆς βυλῆς, ὡς Φησὶν Αἰσχίνης ἐν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ. Hi decem Quaestores sua inter se partiebantur munia, vnius tamen omnes collegij, meo iudicio: quare forte non capiebantur, quemadmodum praeferunt Pollucis & Suidæ codices, quos emendandos itaque ad hunc modum conijcio: apud Pollucem quidem Ταμίαι τῆς θεοῦ, κληρῷ ὅτι μὲν ἐκ Γυπακοσιομεδίμνων. apud Suidam vero Ταμίαι Ἀργυρτῆς εἰσιν Ἀθηναίων κληρῷ ὅτι ἀπὸ Πεντακοσιομεδίμνων. Nam electos fuisse non tantum haec Lex probat, sed etiam quod Pfephisma à Stratocle scriptum honori Oratoris Lycurgi, eadem Lycurgo Quaestori à populo electo adscribit, quae suis Quaestoribus Pollux & Suidas. Pfephismatis verba sunt apud Plutarchum: ἐπὶ δὲ αἱρεθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ δήμου, χειροτονίαν πολλὰ σεινὴν ἀγαθὸν εἰς τὴν Ἀκρόπολιν, καὶ ἀναθέμενος τὴν Θεὸν κόσμου, νίκας τε ἀλληγρύσους, πομπικὰ τε χρυσᾶ καὶ ἀργύρεα, καὶ κόσμον χρυσοῦν εἰς ἑκάτερα χρηματοφέρεα. De eodem Lycurgo Plutarchus in eius Vita: Ταμίας γὰρ ἐλήφθη ὅτι τρεῖς πεντακισχιλίας ταλάντων μυρίων πεντακισχιλίων, ἵ, ὡς ἴσες, μυρίων οκταχιχιλίων ἐξακοσίων πεντήκοντα· καὶ ὁ τὰς ἡμᾶς αὐτῷ ἢ- Φιζόμβος Σταγχής ὁ Ῥήτωρ, ὃ μὲν ἐξ τὴν αἱρεθεὶς αὐτὸς, &c. Sed locus & à mendo & ab interpunctione laborat. Mendum facile est deprehendere: Nam reditus annui Athenien-sium [?]erant sex mille talenta, ducentis quinquaginta minus. Demosthenes sex mille dicit ὡς τὰ περὶ Συμμαχικοῦ. ἐπιδὴ δὲ [illegible, ~30 letters]. Sed defuisse talenta ducenta quinquaginta testis est Polybius Libro II. de Athe-nien-sibus loquens: [illegible, ~70 letters]. Quinquies mille septingenta quinquaginta talenta annua dant in quinque annos viginti octo millia septingenta quinquaginta talenta: Ergo fient in quindecim annos talenta octoginta sex millia ducenta quinquaginta: qui numerus reponendus apud Plutarchū loco laudato, itemque in Phephismate Stratoclis, cuius etiam auctoritate nititur Plutarchus: itaque delenda est [illegible, ~12 letters] in Plutarchi verbis, locusque ita restituendus: Ταμίας γὰρ ἐξήνεγκεν [illegible, ~60 letters]. Scriptum olim fuerat, [illegible, ~40 letters], vnde factum [illegible, ~12 letters], quod fuit ceteris numeris corrumpendis: inter istos autem fuit Stratocles, in cuius Phephismate eundem numerum repone, quibus si addas [illegible, ~20 letters] apud Lycurgum à priuatis intra illud tempus depositae, fient octoginta sex millia, & nongenta talenta, quae Lycurgus administrauit. Sed de his satis est. Quamdiu autem hunc Magistratum gerere licitum Legibus fuerit, videamus: vltra quinquennium Quaestori esse non licebat: Μὴ πλείω πέντε ἐπὶ δεκαπέντε [?] τὰ δημόσια χρήματα. Quaestor vltra quinquennium non esto.
units.tr: Ulpian mentions this law in his comment on the words of Demosthenes from the Androtion: "For the Council, having annulled the law which ordered the treasurer to be elected by vote" [ἀιελόσσα γὰρ ἡ βυλὴ τὸν νόμον, τὸν ἐχεσπόνειν]. His note reads: "The Council annulled the law of the statute which ordered the treasurer to be elected by vote" [Καθαφεῖν ἡ βουλὴ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ κελεύοντος χειροτονεῖσθαι τὸν Ταμίαν]. There were ten of them, chosen by lot from the Pentacosiomedimni, who received the goods in the presence of the Senate and kept them in the temple of Minerva, which stood on the Acropolis: the statue of Minerva, the victories, the other ornaments, and likewise the public money. Pollux, Book 8, chapter 8: "The treasurers of the goddess were chosen by lot, from among the Pentacosiomedimni. They took over the money in the presence of the Council" [Ταμίαι τῆς θεοῦ, κληρωτοί, ὧν ἐκ πεντακοσιομεδίμνων ἦσαν. Τὰ δ' χρήματα προελάβοσαν, τῆς βυλῆς παρούσης]. Suidas: "The treasurers of the Athenians' silver are chosen by lot from the Pentacosiomedimni; they guard the money in the temple of Athena on the Acropolis, both sacred and public, and also the statue of Athena itself" [Ταμίαι Ἀργυρτῆς εἰσιν Ἀθηναίων κληρωτοὶ ἀπὸ πεντακοσιομεδίμνων. οἱ τὰ ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς ἐν ἀκροπόλει χρήματα, ἱερά τε καὶ δημόσια Φυλάττουσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἄγαλμα τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς]. Harpocration: "Among the Athenians the treasurers take account of the magistrates. They receive over the statue of Athena and the victories, and the ornaments of the spear, and the money of each, as Aeschines says in the Constitution of the Athenians" [ἔρχει τῆς ἰῶν ἐξ' Ἀθηναίοις οἱ Ταμίαι δίκας τῶν ἀρχῶν. ἀναλαμβάνουσι δὲ ὅπου τὸ τε ἄγαλμα τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς καὶ τὰς νίκας, καὶ τὸ δόρυ κόσμου, καὶ τὰ χρήματα ἑκάστου τῆς βυλῆς, ὡς Φησὶν Αἰσχίνης ἐν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ]. In my judgement these ten Quaestors divided their duties among themselves, yet all belonged to one college. For this reason, perhaps, they were not chosen by lot, as the manuscripts of Pollux and Suidas seem to say. I therefore propose emending them as follows: in Pollux, "The treasurers of the goddess, chosen by lot, from among the Pentacosiomedimni" [Ταμίαι τῆς θεοῦ, κληρῷ ὅτι μὲν ἐκ Γυπακοσιομεδίμνων]; in Suidas, "The treasurers of the Athenians' silver are chosen by lot from the Pentacosiomedimni" [Ταμίαι Ἀργυρτῆς εἰσιν Ἀθηναίων κληρῷ ὅτι ἀπὸ Πεντακοσιομεδίμνων]. For that they were elected and not chosen by lot is proved not only by this law, but also because the decree written by Stratocles in honour of the orator Lycurgus assigns to Lycurgus, as Quaestor elected by the people, the same duties that Pollux and Suidas assign to their Quaestors. The words of the decree are in Plutarch: "Having been elected by the people to the office of treasurer, he laid up in the Acropolis many sacred and fine things, and dedicated to the goddess the ornaments, the victories of gold and silver, the golden processional objects, and the golden ornament for the two chariots of money" [ἐπὶ δὲ αἱρεθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ δήμου, χειροτονίαν πολλὰ σεινὴν ἀγαθὸν εἰς τὴν Ἀκρόπολιν, καὶ ἀναθέμενος τὴν Θεὸν κόσμου, νίκας τε ἀλληγρύσους, πομπικὰ τε χρυσᾶ καὶ ἀργύρεα, καὶ κόσμον χρυσοῦν εἰς ἑκάτερα χρηματοφέρεα]. Plutarch, in his Life of the same Lycurgus, says: "For he was made treasurer for ten thousand five thousand talents, or, as others say, eight hundred and fifty..." [Ταμίας γὰρ ἐλήφθη ...]. But the passage is faulty both in its text and in its punctuation. The error is easy to detect: the annual revenue of the Athenians was six thousand talents less two hundred and fifty. Demosthenes says six thousand, as in the matter of the Symmachy. [illegible]. But that two hundred and fifty talents were missing is attested by Polybius, Book 2, speaking of the Athenians: [illegible]. Five thousand seven hundred and fifty talents a year make in five years twenty-eight thousand seven hundred and fifty talents; so in fifteen years there would be eighty-six thousand two hundred and fifty talents. This number should be restored in Plutarch at the passage cited, and likewise in Stratocles' decree, on whose authority Plutarch also relies. The [illegible] must therefore be removed from Plutarch's words, and the passage restored thus: "For he brought out [illegible]." It was once written [illegible], whence arose [illegible], which was the corruption of the other numbers; among these was Stratocles, in whose decree the same number is to be restored. If to these you add [illegible] deposited with private persons within that time, as recorded in Lycurgus, you get eighty-six thousand and nine hundred talents, which Lycurgus administered. But enough of this. Let us see how long it was lawful to hold this magistracy under the laws. Beyond five years a man could not remain Quaestor: "Let him not hold the public money more than five years out of fifteen" [Μὴ πλείω πέντε ἐπὶ δεκαπέντε [?] τὰ δημόσια χρήματα]. The Quaestor shall not remain in office beyond five years.

units.la: Legem habes apud Plutarchum in Lycurgo Oratore: Ταμίας γὰρ ἐξήνεγκεν [illegible, ~50 letters] τὰ δημόσια χρήματα. Magistratus hic, aut ego valde fallor, annuus, sed qui, relatis rationibus, & approbatis, iterum, iterumque, in quinquennium vsque, ab eodem geri poterat: vide Plutarchum in Aristide.
units.tr: You have the law in Plutarch's Life of the orator Lycurgus: "For he brought out [illegible] the public money" [Ταμίας γὰρ ἐξήνεγκεν [illegible] τὰ δημόσια χρήματα]. This magistracy, unless I am greatly mistaken, was annual, but one who had had his accounts reported and approved could be re-elected again and again by the same man, up to five years. See Plutarch in his Life of Aristides.

units.la: Inter Quaestores numerandus est is qui administrabat pecuniam illam, quae viritim Athenien-sibus ciuibus distribuebatur ad dies festos, ludos, & spectacula, τὰ θεωρικά dixerunt. Magistratus hic eligebatur circa Dionysia τὰ κατ' ἄγρου, Elaphebolione mense, vt puto: nam tunc maxime solennia spectacula: colligo è verbis Æschinis [illegible, ~80 letters]. Scripsit Phephisma Ctesipho de coronando Demosthene die vicesimo secundo Pyanepsionis: [illegible, ~50 letters]. cum iam septimus ab inito Magistratu mensis ageretur: Ergo Elaphebolione mense τῇ τῆς ὀγδῆς ἀφυτάμιας κυρία ἐκκλησία ἀφέρτη[?], quæ cogebatur die vicesimo Elaphebolionis, creatus est Quæstor τῆς θεωρικῆς Demosthenes, Lysimachida Athenis Prætore, anno secundo Olympiadis centesimæ decimæ. Anno sequenti, qui fuit tertius eiusdem Olympiadis centesimæ decimæ, Archonte Euthycle, Pyanepsionis die vicesimo secundo, Ctesipho populi scitum fecit, vt corona donaretur Demosthenes, cum Tragœdiæ agerentur Dionysiis τῆς κατ' ἄστυ, Elaphebolione mense: Sed hoc ipso anno, paulò antequam hæc Dionysia celebrarentur, die quinto Elaphebolionis mensis Æschines Ctesiphontis nomen apud Archontem detulit, quod populi scitum fecisset παρανόμων, vt corona donaretur Demosthenes in hoc Quæstura Magistratu prius, quam rationes retulisset: ὅτι Χαιρωνίδου Ἀργείος, Ἐλεφηβολιῶνος ἐκτῇ ἱσταμένῳ, Αἰσχίνης [illegible, ~20 letters] Κοθωκίδης [?] παρανόμων γραφὴν, [?] Ctesiphontis [?] [illegible, ~25 letters], ὡς ἀρχὴ δὲ ... [illegible, ~20 letters] Demosthenis [?] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters], τῆς νόμον ... [illegible, ~20 letters]. ἐστὶ Δημοσθένης πιθανὸς, καὶ ὅτι τῆς θεωρικῆς [?]. Eodem, quo populi scitum fecit Ctesiphon, anno Æschines dicam scripsit Ctesiphonti, nam, (vt mittam, si intra annum vertentem dica τῆς παρανόμων non scriberetur, eum qui accusabatur indemnem fuisse καὶ ἐξω κινδύνων, atqui Ctesiphonti scripsit Æschines τιμὴμα τάλαντα πεντήκοντα, ) si non eodem anno dicam scripsisset Ctesiphonti Æschines, neque Elaphebolion mensis, quo nomen Ctesiphontis detulit Aeschines, eiusdem sit anni cum Pyanepsione, quo populi scitum fecit Ctesipho, sed sequentis, proculdubio Demosthenes corona donatus fuisset in theatro ludis Dionysiacis, Elaphebolione mense eiusdem anni, cuius erat Pyanepsion, quo populi scitum fecit Ctesipho: Verum intercessit Aeschines scripta dica τῆς παρανόμων Ctesiphonti: Quare Pyanepsion, quo populi scitum fecit Ctesipho, & Elaphebolion, quo dicam ei scripsit Aschines, sunt eiusdem anni vertentis, qui secundus erat Olympiadis centesimæ decimæ. Sed dices Pyanepsione mense, quo scitum fecit populi Ctesipho, Euthyclem fuisse Archontem, Elaphebolione vero, quo diem dixit Ctesiphonti Aeschines, Chæronidam Archontem fuisse. Nihil tamen est, quod nos deijciat à nostra sententia: nam, aut ego valde fallor; Euthycles Prætor Athenis fuit primis tantum huius anni secundi Olympiadis centesimæ decimæ mensibus, non autem toto anno præfuit, siue fuerit rebus humanis exemptus Euthycles, siue Magistratu motus: in reliquos igitur vertentis anni menses Præturam gessit Chæronyda ὁ Ἔπαλχὼν pro more: & constat quidem è Psephismate Ctesiphontis, Euthyclem Pianepsione affecto Prætorem adhuc fuisse: è dica vero Aeschinis Chæronidam ineunte Elaphebolione iam Archontem fuisse. Sed redeamus ad τῶν ὅτι τῶν θεωρικῶν, de quibus Leges duæ memorantur apud Aschinem ὁ παῖς καὶ Κτησιφῶντος:
units.tr: Among the Quaestors must be counted the officer who administered that money which was distributed man by man to the citizens of Athens for festivals, games and shows, which they called theorica. This magistrate was elected around the Dionysia of the country [τὰ κατ' ἄγρου], in the month of Elaphebolion, as I think: for the shows were then most solemn. I gather this from the words of Aeschines [illegible]. Ctesiphon proposed a decree on crowning Demosthenes on the twenty-second day of Pyanepsion: [illegible], when the seventh month from the start of his magistracy was already being celebrated. Therefore in the month of Elaphebolion, at the main assembly [τῇ τῆς ὀγδῆς ἀφυτάμιας κυρία ἐκκλησία], which was held on the twentieth day of Elaphebolion, Demosthenes was created Quaestor of the theorica, when Lysimachides was Prætor at Athens, in the second year of the hundred and tenth Olympiad. In the following year, which was the third of the same hundred and tenth Olympiad, with Euthycles as Archon, on the twenty-second day of Pyanepsion, Ctesiphon proposed the decree that Demosthenes be crowned, while the tragedies were being performed at the Dionysia of the city [τῆς κατ' ἄστυ], in the month of Elaphebolion. But in this very year, shortly before these Dionysia were celebrated, on the fifth day of the month of Elaphebolion, Aeschines brought against Ctesiphon the charge that he had proposed a decree contrary to the law [παρανόμων], that Demosthenes should be crowned while still holding this Quaestorship before he had rendered his accounts. [Here follow several illegible fragments of the Greek.] Ctesiphon's decree was passed in the same year in which Aeschines brought his suit against him. For, to pass over the point that if the indictment for illegality [τῆς παρανόμων] had not been lodged within the year, the accused would have been acquitted and free from danger, yet Aeschines did bring against Ctesiphon a penalty of fifty talents. If Aeschines had not brought his suit against Ctesiphon in the same year, and if the month of Elaphebolion in which Aeschines brought his charge were not of the same year as Pyanepsion, in which Ctesiphon passed his decree, but of the following year, then undoubtedly Demosthenes would have been crowned in the theatre at the Dionysia in the month of Elaphebolion of the year to which Pyanepsion belonged, in which Ctesiphon passed his decree. But Aeschines intervened by bringing his indictment for illegality against Ctesiphon. Therefore Pyanepsion, in which Ctesiphon passed his decree, and Elaphebolion, in which Aeschines brought his suit against him, belong to the same intercalated year, which was the second of the hundred and tenth Olympiad. But you will object that in the month of Pyanepsion, when Ctesiphon passed his decree, Euthycles was Archon, while in Elaphebolion, when Aeschines brought his charge against Ctesiphon, Chaeronidas was Archon. Nothing here, however, compels me to abandon my view: for, unless I am greatly mistaken, Euthycles was Prætor at Athens only for the first months of this second year of the hundred and tenth Olympiad, and did not hold office for the whole year, whether because Euthycles had departed this life or because he had been removed from office. So for the remaining months of the year Chaeronidas, the son of Epaicho, held the Prætorship as usual. It is certain from Ctesiphon's decree that Euthycles was still Prætor when Pyanepsion was in its final days; and from Aeschines' indictment that Chaeronidas was already Archon at the beginning of Elaphebolion. But let us return to the theorica money, concerning which two laws are cited in Aeschines against Ctesiphon:

units.la: ΝΟΜΟΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΠΙ ΤΟΘΕΩΡΙΚΟΝ ΚΕΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΗΜΕΝΩΝ ΝΩΝ. LEX DE QVÆSTORI- BVS THEORICÆ PECVNIÆ. Ο ΗΓΗΜΟΝΟΣ ΝΟΜΟΣ ΠΕΡΙ LEX HEGEMONIS DE
units.tr: LAW CONCERNING THE QUAESTORS OF THE THEORIC FUND. THE LAW OF HEGEMON CONCERNING THE QUAESTORS OF THE THEORIC FUND [Νόμος περὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τὸ θεωρικὸν κεχειροτονημένων. Νόμος Ἡγήμονος περὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τὸ θεωρικόν]

units.la: Priori illa Lege, quæ in gratiam Eubuli lata est, hi Quæstores Theoricæ pecuniæ, singulis Prytaniis sua populo enumerabant vectigalia, naualia & armamentaria curabant; viarum quoque refectores erant, & Quæstorum cæterorum munera obibant.
units.tr: By the earlier law, which was passed in favour of Eubulus, these Quaestors of the Theoric money used to report the public revenues to the people at each Prytany. They also looked after the naval and armament yards. They were likewise overseers of the roads, and they performed the duties of the other Quaestors.

units.la: Sed Hegemon Lege sua fines rexit, motos restituit terminos, distinctionemque dominiorum fecit: nam solam administrare voluit Theoricam pecuniam, cetera, vt prius fuerant, aliorum curæ commisit. Aeschinis verba sunt: [illegible, ~20 letters] ὦ Ἀθηναῖοι, [illegible, ~30 letters] Εὔβουλον [illegible, ~25 letters] Ἡγήμονος [illegible, ~70 letters] Eubulo Demosthenis & Aeschinis æquali id datum, quia Lege sanxit, vt capital esset ei, qui vellet [?]τὰ θεωρικά, etiam ingruente bello, etiam in militum stipendia impendi: & quidem prior Lex scripta est antequam Demosthenes esset [?]ὅτι ὁ θεωρικὸς χρήματος, obtinebatque adhuc cum in hoc esset Magistratu Demosthenes, vt liquet ex Aeschinis verbis; at vero intra illud tempus, quod est ab anno secundo Olympiadis decimæ supra centesimā, quo Demosthenes Quæstor fuit Theoricæ pecuniæ, ad annum tertiū Olympiadis centesimæ duodecimæ, Archonte Aristophonte, quo Aeschines hanc aduersus Ctesiphontem Orationem habuit, lata est ab Hegemone hæc de Quæstoribus Theoricæ pecuniæ Lex, eius enim hic meminit Aeschines. Horum Quæstorum meminit Pollux Libro VIII. cap. IX. [illegible, ~45 letters]
units.tr: But Hegemon, by his law, defined the boundaries, restored the markers that had been moved, and drew a distinction between their spheres of authority. For he wished the Quaestors to administer the Theoric money alone, and the rest, as before, he left in the care of others. These are the words of Aeschines: [illegible] O Athenians, [illegible] Eubulus [illegible] Hegemon [illegible]. This honour was granted to Eubulus, a contemporary of Demosthenes and Aeschines, because by his law he made it a capital offence for anyone to propose spending the theoric funds on anything else, even when war was pressing, even on soldiers' pay. The earlier law was written before Demosthenes became Quaestor of the Theoric money, and it was still in force while Demosthenes held that office, as is clear from Aeschines' words. But the law on the Quaestors of the Theoric money was passed by Hegemon within the period from the second year of the 110th Olympiad, when Demosthenes was Quaestor of the Theoric money, to the third year of the 112th Olympiad, in the archonship of Aristophon, when Aeschines delivered this speech against Ctesiphon; for Aeschines mentions it here. Pollux mentions these Quaestors in Book VIII, chapter IX. [illegible]

units.la: Lege cautum apud Athenienses erat, Ne quis prima auctoritate à populo, aut Senatu, neque electus, neque creatus, aliquo populi Atheniensis eat Legatus, qui secus faxit, capite luat.
units.tr: Among the Athenians it was provided by law that no one should go as envoy to any place unless he had been chosen or appointed by the people or the Senate. Whoever acted otherwise should pay with his life.

units.la: [?]Ἐάν τίς, ἂν βουλῆς, ἂν δήμου, χειροτονηθῇ αὐτὸν, ἀχθῇ πρεσβεύων, [?]ἰδιότης δὲ ζημία ἔστω.
units.tr: [Ἐάν τίς, ἂν βουλῆς, ἂν δήμου, χειροτονηθῇ αὐτὸν, ἀχθῇ πρεσβεύων, ἰδιότης δὲ ζημία ἔστω.] If anyone, not elected by the Council or the People, is brought forward to go as envoy, let the penalty be a private one.

units.la: Si quis, neque à Senatu, neque à populo creatus, aliquo Legatus eat, capital esto.
units.tr: If anyone, appointed neither by the Senate nor by the people, goes as envoy anywhere, let him be liable to capital punishment.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes [illegible, ~30 letters] τὴν ... [illegible, ~20 letters] Rursum: [illegible, ~40 letters] Graue erat munus πρεσβεία, & seuere in illos animaduertebatur in illos, qui non pro dignitate defungerentur: nec effugio erat locus: Liberos enim suos Legati ad fidem faciendam Athenis futuros obsides relinquebant. Aeschines [illegible, ~20 letters] de liberis suis, quos Athenis reliquerat, [?]ἵν' εἰδῶσι [illegible, ~40 letters] Μακεδονίαν ἐπρεσβεύσα. Post obitam Legationem rationes referebant, & si fidem operamque suam populo probassent, publice conuiuio excipiebantur in Pryraneo, auctore & sciscente Senatu. Anonymus in Argumento Orationis Demosthenicæ τῶν ἀρρεσβείας. ἰσῶν γὰρ ὅτι μὴ τῶν ἀρρεσβείων ἑκάστης τῆς ἀρρεσβείας αἰθωνάς [?] ἑκάστῳ ταῖς ὑπάρχουσι καὶ ἡ μὲν ἀρρεσβεία πρόσεστι ἀνθρώπας ἄλλως κληρώσει, ὥστε τὸν Δημοσθένη γεγραφὴν κλῆσιν αὐτοῖς ἐπὶ ἀεὶ. ἔστω γὰρ ἴσως ὅτι τοῖς κλήρως ἀρρεσβευτὰς μὴ μόνοις ἐπὶ δημοσίου ἀρίστῳ κληθῆναι. Demosthenes hac Oratione: καὶ βουλὴ γὰρ ἡ μὴ κωλύσῃ ἀκούσας πάλιν πρὸς ἐμοῦ ἂν ἐπήνεσε τοὺς, ὅτ᾽ ἐκ τὸ ἀρρυτόμειον ἠξίωσε κληθῆναι. καὶ τοὺς τῆς ἀφ᾽ ἧς γέγονεν ἡ πόλις, σὺν τοῖς πάντα φοβοὶ πάντῃ σύνδοιας ἀρρεσβείας. & paulò post: ὅτ᾽ ἔπαινος, ὅτε κληθεὶς εἰς τὸ ἀρρυτόμειον ὅτι τῶν πρεσβεων ἀπὸ τῆς βουλῆς. Vlpianus: ἀεὶ γὰρ οἱ πρεσβεῖς ἐπιμελούμενοι ἐκ ἀλλωτα πονητῶν ἢ ἑκάστου ἡμῶν χάριν. Pollux Libro IX.cap.V. ὅπως δὲ τῶν πρυτανείων ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως, παρ᾽ ἢ ἐσιτοῦντο, οἱ τὰς δημοσίας πρεσβείας ἡμῶν ἄρτι, Legatiui, quod ex ærario publico accipiebant, modus fuit, binæ in singulos Legationis dies drachmæ. Aristophanes Acharnensibus:
units.tr: Demosthenes praises this law [illegible] [illegible]. Again: [illegible]. The office of envoy was a heavy burden, and those who did not discharge it as their dignity required were severely punished; nor was there any way of escape, since envoys left their children behind at Athens as hostages to guarantee their good faith. Aeschines [illegible] about his children, whom he had left at Athens, [that they might know] that he had gone on embassy to Macedonia. After the embassy was over they rendered accounts, and if they had won the people's approval of their good faith and their labour, they were entertained at public expense in the Prytaneum, by the authority and decree of the Senate. The anonymous writer in the Argument to Demosthenes' speech On the Embassy: [Greek, garbled]. Demosthenes in this speech: [Greek: "And the Council, had it not hindered, would again have praised me, when I was thought worthy to be summoned to the Prytaneum, and those who ... the city ... with all their fear..."]. And a little later: [Greek: "when I was praised, when I was called into the Prytaneum, from the Council..."]. Ulpian: [Greek: "For the envoys always took care of nothing other than the common good, or the favour of each of us."]. Pollux, Book IX, chapter V: [Greek: "Where the public envoys were fed in the Prytaneum, from the city ..."]. The public envoys' allowance, paid from the public treasury, was fixed at two drachmas for each day of the embassy. Aristophanes in the Acharnians:

units.la: ἐπιμελῆ ἡμᾶς ὡς βασιλέα τὸν μέγαν, μαθόν φέρονσας δύο δραχμὰς τῆς ἡμέρας, ἐπ᾽ Εὐξυμάχους Ἀρχῆς.
units.tr: [ἐπιμελῆ ἡμᾶς ὡς βασιλέα τὸν μέγαν, μισθὸν φέρουσας δύο δραχμὰς τῆς ἡμέρας, ἐπ᾽ Εὐξυμάχους ἄρχης.] You treat us with care as if we were the Great King, bringing two drachmas' pay a day, in the archonship of Eusymachus.

units.la: Lege non licebat amplius, quam semel sub eodem Magistratu Scribatus mu-nere fungi:
units.tr: By law it was not permitted to hold the office of Scribe more than once under the same magistrate.

units.la: Ὑπογραμματεῦσαι ὅτι ἔξεστι ἢς τὸν αὐτὸν τῇ ἀρχῇ τῇ αὐτῇ.
units.tr: [Ὑπογραμματεῦσαι ὅτι ἔξεστι ἢς τὸν αὐτὸν τῇ ἀρχῇ τῇ αὐτῇ.] It is not permitted to serve as secretary more than once in the same office.

units.la: Semel tantum sub eodem Magistratu Scriba esto.
units.tr: A man shall be Scribe only once under the same magistrate.

units.la: Legem laudat Lysias ἐν τῇ κατὰ Νικομάχου γραμματείας ἀθωῶν καταγγελία. ὃ δὲ πρῶτος δημόσιος, ὅτι γραμματεύσαι μὴ ὀρχῇ ἔξεστιν εἰς τὸν αὐτὸν τῇ ἀρχῇ τῇ αὐτῇ. Vile erat hoc Scribatus munus apud Athenienses: testatur Vlpianus ad Lepti-neam: εἶπα δὲ ἐπάρχους τῶν Συνεχωρησιῶν ἰσχύει, τὴν χειροτονίαν λίαν πλάτωσε, γραμματέα καὶ ὑπηρέτην τῶν ἐπὶ τοῦ ἄρχοντος, ὀνομάζει παρ᾽ Ἀθηναίοις ἀφορίμμα. & mox subiungit: εἴρηται γὰρ ὑπὸ τῶν ὡς οἱ παρὰ Συνεχωρησίοις Γραμματεῖς σημεῖοί τε εἰσὶ καὶ ἐνδοξοι, καὶ ἡ ὡς οἱ παρ᾽ Ἀθηναίοις. Libanius in Argumento Orationis Demosthenicæ ἐπὶ παρασκευῆς. καὶ Γραμματεὺς τῆς πόλεως, ἥπερ ὡς δῆμος ἐπικουρία. Atque ad hoc munus præcipue adsumebantur Serui publici. Lysias Oratione laudata, de hoc Nicomacho, qui Scriba fuerat: καὶ εἰς τὸ τοῦ ὕβρεως ἥκεις, ὥσπερ ἑαυτὸν νομίζεις εἶ) τὰ τῆς πόλεως, αὐτὸς δημόσιος ὤν. Δημόσιοι Serui publici sunt, qui & Vulgares Iureconsultis dicuntur, & Calones in Glossis. Harpocration, δημοσίους λέγουσι τοὺς τῆς πόλεως δούλους. Vlpianus in II. Olynthiacam: δούλους εἶχον δημοσίους οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι ἀπὸ ἀχμαλώτων ποιησάντες, καὶ εἰσ᾽ ἐδίδασκον τὰ γράμματα, atque ita Scribarum munus defungebantur. Erant autem Scribæ tres, qui sorte creabantur. Suidas: κληρωτοὶ ἦσαν οἱ Γραμματεῖς τὸ ἀρίθμον τῆς, γράφοντες τὰ δημόσια. Οὐδεὶς δὲ ἦσαν οἱ Γραμματεῖς κύριοι, ἀλλ᾽ ἡ τὸ γράφειν, ἡ ἀναγνῶναι. Harpocration: ὁ Γραμματεὺς πῶς τε κληθῆσαι καὶ ἡ ἐπιφανὴς, ὡς τῶν γραμμάτων τὸ ἔστι κύριος καὶ τὰ ψηφίσματα τὰ δημόσια φυλάττειν, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα αὐτὸς ἐγράφειν ἐν τῷ ἀρχεῖῳ τῆς βουλῆς, ὁ δὲ λώκιος Αεισπάλης οἱ Ἀθηναίων πολιτεία. Horum vnus seruabat tabulas & decreta: alter Leges, de quo Lysias Oratione laudata, vbi docet munus illius fuisse, tum Leges describere, cū prælegere atque referre in cōcionibus & iudiciis: ὡς ἐκ γὰρ ὁ Νικομάχῳ τοὺς νόμους ἀναγεγράφθαι. & paulò post: ὑπεδεχόμενος τῆς Ἀρχόντων ὑπεζόλαις ἐκ εἰσαγόντων εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον, ὅτε ἠθέλησε τὸ δόδωμα τοὺς νόμους. Tertius populo ac Senatui prælegebat: Iulius Pollux Lib. VIII. c. IX. Γραμματεὺς, ὁ τῇ πρυτανείαν κληρωθεὶς ὑπὸ τῆς βουλῆς ὅπως ἐν γραμματεῖα φυλάττειν τὰ ψηφίσματα, ἡ ἔπειτα ἐπὶ τοὺς νόμους ὑπὸ τῆς βουλῆς χειροτονήσας ὁ δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς δημοσίας αἱρεῖται Γραμματέως, ἀναγινώσκει τε δήμῳ ἢ τῇ βουλῇ. Priores duo à Senatu legebantur, vt est in his Pollucis verbis, vnde τῆς βουλῆς dicuntur Demostheni ὁ [?]πρὸς[?] τὰς ἀρχὰς [?], tertius à populo, & τῆς πόλεως nuncupabatur, vt est apud Thucydidem Libro VII. ὁ δὲ Γραμματεὺς πόλεως προσελθὼν αἰτήσω τῆς Αθηναίοις, ἀναδοθῆναι [?]. De his Aristophanis Interpres ad hunc Comici versum Equitibus:
units.tr: The law is cited by Lysias in his speech against the scribal office of Nicomachus [Greek: "for it is not permitted to serve as scribe more than once in the same office"]. This scribal office was a lowly one among the Athenians. Ulpian, on Leptines, testifies to this: [Greek: "the secretary and attendant of the archon, called among the Athenians a [lowly thing]"]. And shortly after he adds: [Greek: "for it has been said that the scribes of the Synchorisiai are honoured and conspicuous, but not so the scribes among the Athenians."] Libanius, in the Argument to Demosthenes' speech On the Preparation: [Greek: "and the scribe of the city, which is the people's aid"]. Public slaves were especially employed for this office. Lysias, in the speech cited, speaking of this Nicomachus, who had been Scribe: [Greek: "and you have come to such insolence that you think yourself the affairs of the city, though you yourself are a public slave."] Public slaves (dēmosioi) are the ones the jurists also call vulgares, and the glossaries calones. Harpocration: [Greek: "they call public slaves the slaves of the city."] Ulpian on the Second Olynthiac: [Greek: "The Athenians had public slaves made from captives, and they taught them their letters."] In this way they performed the duties of Scribes. There were three Scribes, chosen by lot. Suidas: [Greek: "The scribes were chosen by lot, three in number, writing the public records. The scribes had no authority except writing or reading."] Harpocration: [Greek: "The scribe was so called, and was eminent, because he was lord of the letters and kept the public decrees, and wrote everything else himself in the archive of the Council."] And [illegible] in the Athenian polity. Of these, one kept the records and decrees, and another the laws. Lysias, in the speech cited, shows that the duty of the latter was to copy out the laws, and then to read them aloud and report them in assemblies and courts: [Greek: "for Nicomachus had been ordered to copy out the laws."] And a little later: [Greek: "He received the laws from the archons' assistants, and did not bring them into the court when he wished to read out the laws."] The third read aloud to the people and the Senate. Julius Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: [Greek: "The Scribe is the one chosen by lot for the Prytany by the Council, to keep the decrees in the archive, or afterwards appointed by the Council to the laws; he is chosen by the public Scribe, and reads aloud to the people or to the Council."] The first two were chosen by the Senate, as these words of Pollux show, and so they are called "of the Council" (tēs boulēs) by Demosthenes [illegible]. The third was chosen by the people and was called "of the city" (tēs poleōs), as in Thucydides, Book VII: [Greek: "The city's Scribe came forward and asked to be given the ..."]. The scholiast on Aristophanes, on this comic line in the Knights: [Greek: "so that the Demos, the Phasis registrars, may bring a suit against us."]

units.la: ὅπως ἡμῖν ὁ [?]Δῆμος[?] οἱ Φασὶς [?]ἀπογραφεῖς[?] δικῆν.
units.tr: [ὅπως ἡμῖν ὁ Δῆμος οἱ Φασὶς ἀπογραφεῖς δίκην.] So that the Demos, the Phasis registrars, may bring a suit against us.

units.la: Φασὶς γὰρ, καὶ τοῖς ἐγγράφων ἐλλήσπον Φιλίππος Γραμματεὺς, ὅτι ὁ δῆμος, ἀπογραφεῖς ἐλλήσπον· ὁ δὲ τῆς βουλῆς Αντιγραφεὺς. δημοσίᾳ ἡ ἀρχὴ, ἐγγράφοι ἀμφότεροι τὰ λεγόμενα. Sed confundit hic Magister errore maximo τοὺς Αντιγραφέας cum Scribis. Legebantur autem Scribæ singulis Prytaniis, vt est apud Pollucem: Γραμματεὺς, ὃς ἐξ ἀρχῆς [?]ἀπογραφῆς[?] κληρωθεὶς ὑπὸ τῆς βουλῆς. Rationesque administrati muneris singulis quoque Prytaniis referebant; ita vt legitimum ministerij tempus diebus triginta verteret; reliqui quinque dies Prytaneiæ reddendis, puto, rationibus dicabantur: Dies triginta ministrasse, & singulis Prytaniis rationes retulisse scribit Lysias Oratione laudata, cuius verba describemus, vt illustremus, atque emendemus: ἢ γὰρ πι, ὦ ἀνδρες δικασταί, ὅτι ἐκείνων δικαίως δίδωκεν, ὅπως καὶ νῦν τὴν ἀρχὴν κατεστήσατο· ἴσως τοσοῦτον μὲν πέντε ἐπ' αὐτῆς ἀπογράψας, ὅσον αὐτοῦ τεσσάρων ἡμερῶν ἀπαλλαχθῶν ἐπιτιμησόμενον. ἐξ ὧν εἶδε αἱ ἀπογραφαὶ αὐτὸν ἀπὸ πάντων χρόνον ἐπιμήσατο, καὶ ὅσα χρείας μῆνες ἔσται τὴν ἀρχὴν ταύτην διδοῦσα ἔδωκεν. ἀλλ' οἱ μὲν δήμοι τῆς αὐτῆς ἀρχῆς τὴν ἀφαίρεσιν λάβων ἀμφέρεσθαι· οὐ δὴ, ὦ Νικόμαχε, οὐκ ἔπαρχον ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐπεφῆλαι, ἀλλὰ μόνον σοὶ τὴν πολιτὴν ἀξίαν νομίζεις ἀρχὴν πολλῷ χρόνον, καὶ μήτε διδόντας ἐσθῆσαι, μήτε τῆς ἐφῶνου ἀναπέμψαι, μήτε τὴν νόμον φαίνεσθαι· ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἐπιφάνεια, τὰ δὲ ἀξιωμένα καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς πόλεως ἦσαν, ὥστε σαυτῷ νομίζεις ἐν τῆς πόλεως, αὐτὸς δημόσιος ὤν. Nicomachus Scriba Leges Solonis intra menses quatuor describere iussus est, at ille non quatuor mensibus, sed totidem annis id præstitit, atque immutauit, abrogauitque, quas describendas acceperat Leges. Lysias: τὰ γραφέντα δὲ αὐτὸν πάντων μηνῶν διαγεγράφθαι τοὺς νόμους τῆς Σόλωνος, αὐτὰ μὲν Σόλωνος αὐτὸν ἑαυτῷ ἐκατέρω, αὐτὰ δὲ πάντων μηνῶν, ἐξ ἑτῶν τῷ ἄρχῳ ἐπαινοῦσι. καὶ ἐκείνων δὲ ἡμέραν ἀρχεῖον λαμβάνων, ἑαυτὸν ἐκ ἀπαλλαχθεὶς ἀπέδωκε. Male editur ἐξ ἐτῶν, nam ex iis, quæ iam ante descripsimus, constat, quatuor tantum annos, non autem sex, huic muneri vacasse Nicomachum: Rescribendum igitur est: αἰτῆ δὲ πεπαρῶν μηνῶν, ἐς ἔτη τῷ ἄρχῳ ἐπαινοῦσι, elegantissime: tot annis Scribatu functus est, quot mensibus imperatum fuerat: quatuor menses præscripti fuerant, totidem ille annos impendit describendis Legibus, cum tamen Scribam munere hoc fungi triginta tantum dies iusesset: atque id est quod his verbis queritur Lysias, ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ ἐκείνου πάντων μηνῶν ἐπὶ τῆς ἀπαλλαχθῆναι, ἐξ ὧν ἐπὶ τῶν ἡμερῶν ἀπαλλαγῆναι. Addit deinde ea, quæ constituta erant, & describenda tantum acceperat, immutasse, & pro arbitrio versasse, perinde ac si ipse Legislator foret, neque rationes retulisse: Lysiæ verba ita legenda & interpungenda sunt: ἐπειτα ἀπαλλαγῆναι διωρισμένων, ἐξ ὧν ἐπὶ αἰαχρέαφθη, αὐτὸν ἀπὸ πάντων χρόνον ἐπιμήσατο, καὶ ὅσα χρείας μῆνες ἔσται τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν διωρισμένων ἔδωκεν.
units.tr: [Φασὶς γὰρ, καὶ τοῖς ἐγγράφων ἐλλήσπον Φιλίππος Γραμματεὺς, ὅτι ὁ δῆμος, ἀπογραφεῖς ἐλλήσπον· ὁ δὲ τῆς βουλῆς Αντιγραφεὺς.] For Phasis says, and Philippus the Scribe, in the written [notes], says that the people's registrars ... but the Council's antigrapheus; both record what is said in public office. But this teacher, through a very great error, confuses the antigraphes with the Scribes. The Scribes were chosen by lot each Prytany, as Pollux says: [Greek: "the Scribe who, from the beginning, was chosen by lot by the Council."] They also rendered accounts of their administration at each Prytany, so that their legal term of service ran for thirty days; the remaining five days of the Prytany were, I suppose, given over to rendering accounts. Lysias, in the speech cited, writes that he served for thirty days and gave accounts at each Prytany. I shall quote his words to illustrate and correct them: [Greek: "For, gentlemen of the jury, you know that he justly ... and that he now established the office; perhaps he indeed, having registered for it, ... as much as he had been given for four days ..."]. From these registrations it is clear that he ... for how many months he had been allotted this office ... Lysias adds that the laws which had been established, and which he had received only to copy, he altered and turned at his own will, just as if he were the lawgiver, and he did not render accounts: [Greek: "then ... the things defined, from which he ... he took for himself ... and gave as many months as there were for the office ..."]. Nicomachus, the Scribe, was ordered to copy out the laws of Solon within four months, but he did this not in four months but in as many years, and altered and repealed the laws he had been given to copy. Lysias: [Greek: "But he had been ordered to copy out all the laws of Solon within four months; yet he took as many years to it, and in the office he was appointed to ..."]. And taking the day of that office, he did not release himself but returned himself. The text is badly edited as [Greek: "ex etōn"], for from what we have described above it is clear that Nicomachus held this office for only four years, not six. It should therefore be rewritten as [Greek: "for as many years as the office had been allotted in months"], which is elegant: he served as Scribe for as many years as he had been ordered to serve in months. Four months had been prescribed, and he spent as many years on the copying of the laws, though he had been ordered to serve as Scribe for only thirty days. This is what Lysias complains of in these words: [Greek: "for the office of the ... which was assigned to him for all months ... from which he was released in the days ..."]. He then adds that he had received only what was established and was to be copied, and that he altered it and turned it to his own will, and that he did not render accounts. The words of Lysias should be read and punctuated thus: [Greek: "then, he was released from the things defined, from which he ... for all time he took for himself, and as many months as the office had been given to him for the defined purposes."]

units.la: Apud Romanos vile quoque hoc Scribarum munus, & Libertorum, quod iudiu [?]monuerunt docti: de Alexándro Persei Filio Plutarch. in Paullo Æmilio: τὸν δὲ εἰπὼν Ἀλέξανδρον, ἀλλ' ἐφ' ὧν [?] ὑμῶν Φασιν· ἐκμα-θόντα δὲ τὰ ῥωμαϊκὰ γεράμματα, καὶ τὴν Ἀφιλέκλεσιν [?] ἐπιγαμμάτων [?] τῆς ἀρχῆς, ἐπι-δείξιον καὶ γεμέντα τῆς [?] τούτου τὴν συνηγορίας ἐξεταζόμενον.
units.tr: Among the Romans this office of scribe was also held cheap, both by freedmen and by others, as learned men have observed. Plutarch, in his Life of Aemilius Paulus, speaks of Alexander, son of Perseus: after learning the Roman letters, he was examined on his skill in them and on the advocacy of this office [ἐκμαθόντα δὲ τὰ ῥωμαϊκὰ γράμματα, καὶ τὴν ἀφηγήσιν ἐπιγραμμάτων τῆς ἀρχῆς, ἐπιδεικνύμενον καὶ γεμέντα τῆς τούτου τὴν συνηγορίας ἐξεταζόμενον].

units.la: DE ORATORIBUS. TITULUS III.
units.tr: ON ORATORS. TITLE III.

units.la: Quanquam inter Magistratus censendi non sint Oratores, tamen ἐν τοῖς ἰδιώταις non sunt numerandi, cum expressis verbis distinguantur ab iis in Aeschinis Oratione aduersus Timarchum: τεῖπον δὲ ἐφε-ξῆς διέξειμι πρὸς ὑμᾶς τοὺς νόμους, καὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἡλικίαν, ἢ μόνον περὶ τῶν ἰδιωτῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τῶν Ῥητόρων. Nemo autem in hunc ordinem cooptabatur, qui esset minor annis triginta, quanquam etiam nonnulli quadragesimum aetatis annum definiant: idque Lege cautum:
units.tr: Although orators are not to be counted among the magistrates, they are not to be numbered among the private citizens [ἐν τοῖς ἰδιώταις] either, since Aeschines distinguishes them expressly from such persons in his speech against Timarchus: "I will go through the laws in order before you, and the age limit, which applies not only to private citizens but also to orators [Ῥήτορες]." No one was admitted to this order who was younger than thirty, although some set the fortieth year of age; and this was provided for by law: Oratores

units.la: Μὴ εἰσελθὴν ἕνα εἰπεῖν μήπω τριάκοντα ἔτη γεγονότα. Ne quis annis triginta minor in Senatu, aut populo, orato.
units.tr: Let no one under thirty years old come forward to speak [Μὴ εἰσελθὴν ἕνα εἰπεῖν μήπω τριάκοντα ἔτη γεγονότα]. No one under thirty years of age shall speak in the Senate or before the people.

units.la: Legem hanc laudat Graecus Aristophanis Interpres ad Nubes: νόμως δὲ ὧν μὴ εἰσελθὴν ἕνα εἰπεῖν μή πω παραγεγονότα ἔτη γεγονότα. ὡς δὲ ἄνδρες, τεσσαράκοντα. Ad Oratores Legem hanc esse referendam dubium esse non potest, cum alioquin liceat apud populum dicere ubi ad annum aetatis vicesimum ventum est: Annum vero tricesimum potius, quam quadragesimum, definiuimus, quia ea aetas est Senatoria, & exempla probant: neque minore debuit esse is, qui re vera erat auctor publici consilij, regendae ciuitatis dux, princeps sententiae in Senatu, in populo, in causis publicis: Nemo autem temere huic Oratorum albo adscribebatur, sed quotannis decem forte legebantur, qui drachmam de publico accipiebant, eo, quo orabant, die, docet Aristoteles apud Scholiastem Aristophanis, ad hunc è Vespis versum,
units.tr: The Greek interpreter of Aristophanes' Clouds approves this law: "by law no one who has not yet reached thirty years of age may come forward to speak, though some say forty." That this law must be referred to orators there can be no doubt, since otherwise one may speak before the people once one has reached the twentieth year of age. We have settled on the thirtieth year rather than the fortieth, because that is the age of the senator, and examples confirm it. Nor should he be younger who in fact was the author of public policy, the leader in governing the state, the chief voice in the Senate, before the people, and in public causes. Nor was anyone enrolled lightly on this list of orators; rather, each year ten were chosen by lot, who received a drachma from the public treasury on the day they spoke. Aristotle, as cited by the scholiast on Aristophanes, teaches this on the line from the Wasps:

units.la: Αὐτὸς ὃ φέρει ὁ σωνηγορικὸν, ὁ ψαχμίλιν.
units.tr: "He himself who brings the summons-fee, the one-drachma man."

units.la: ἐλάμβανον γὰρ οἱ Ῥήτορες ὁ ψαχμίλιν, ὅτι συνηγορεῖν ἐπὶ τῆς πόλεως, ἐὰν ἐπ' ἄλλου τινὸς. ἐκ τούτου δὲ φαίνεται ὅτι μισθοφόρους ἡ ἀρχή. κληρωτοὶ δὲ ἡμερώτατοι δίκῃ Σωνηγόρους Αἰσχύλης φησί. Qui enim Σωνηγόροι hic dicuntur, ii sunt Rhetores, qui forte capti ἐδοκιμάζοντο apud Judices, in vitam illorum inquirebatur, cum è re publica non esset τὸν Ῥήτορας ἡμῶν ὅτι ὁ βῆμα τῆς λόγων ὑπομνηθεὶς ἐκ τῆς πνεύματος, ἀλλ' ἢ τῆς βίας. Atque hanc ob causam dicuntur à Judicibus χρηστέον. Demosthenes in Timocratea: Τοὺς Σωνηγόρους, οὓς χρηστέον, διώκειν δ' ἀπὸ πάσης ὡς σωφρῶν. Judices alloquitur Demosthenes, quos χρηστέον τοὺς Σωνηγόρους docet: docuerat & Antiphon ἐν τῇ Δημοσθένους γραφῇ ἀπολογία, καὶ ἐν τῇ Αἰνίων φόρῳ, ex eo Grammatici: ἐοίκασι πρὸ Ἀθηναίοις ὠνεῖς χρηστέσθαι Σωνηγόροι ὅτι τῆς σωνηγορίας. Examen istud quibusdam continetur Capitibus, quae praescripsit Legislator.
units.tr: For the orators used to receive the drachma because they pleaded on behalf of the city, if they pleaded for someone else. From this it appears that the office was paid. Aeschylus says that the advocates [Σωνηγόροι] were chosen by lot for the days of trial. For those who are here called advocates [Σωνηγόροι] are the rhetoricians who, when they were caught, were examined before the judges; their life was investigated, since it was not fitting for the public that men who had no claim to speak should, by the force of their power, take the platform of speech. And for this reason they are said to be "to be used" [χρηστέον] by the judges. Demosthenes in the speech against Timocrates: "The advocates, whom it is necessary to use [χρηστέον], one should prosecute from every side, as being prudent." Demosthenes addresses the judges, whom he teaches are to be used as advocates [χρηστέον τοὺς Σωνηγόρους]; Antiphon had taught the same in his speech in defence of the case against Demosthenes, and in the speech concerning the Ainians, as the grammarians report from it: "The Athenians seem to have used advocates [Σωνηγόροι] who were bought for the sake of their advocacy." This scrutiny is contained in certain chapters which the lawgiver prescribed.

units.la: ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΙΑ ΡΗΤΟΡΩΝ.
units.tr: The Scrutiny of Orators [ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΙΑ ΡΗΤΟΡΩΝ].

units.la: ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΛΕΓΗ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ, ΤΟΝ ΠΑΤΕΡΑ ΤΥΠΤΩΝ, Ἢ ΤΗΝ ΜΗΤΕΡΑ, Ἢ ΜΗ ΤΡΕΦΩΝ, Ἢ ΜΗ ΠΑΡΕΧΩΝ ΟΙΚΗΣΙΝ.
units.tr: IF ANYONE SPEAKS IN THE ASSEMBLY, WHO BEATS HIS FATHER OR HIS MOTHER, OR DOES NOT FEED THEM, OR DOES NOT PROVIDE THEM A HOME.

units.la: ΕΙ ΤΑΣ ΣΤΡΑΤΕΙΑΣ ΜΗ ΕΣΤΡΑΤΕΥΜΕΝΟΣ, ΟΣΑΙ ΑΝ ΑΥΤΩΙ ΠΡΟΣΤΑΧΘΩΣΙΝ Ἢ ΤΗΝ ΑΣΠΙΔΑ ΑΠΟΒΕΒΛΗΚΩΣ.
units.tr: IF HE, BEING LIABLE FOR MILITARY SERVICE, DOES NOT SERVE, OR CASTS AWAY HIS SHIELD, AS MANY AS ARE ACCUSED OF THIS.

units.la: ΕΙ ΠΕΠΟΡΝΕΥΜΕΝΟΣ Ἢ ΗΤΑΙΡΗΚΩΣ.
units.tr: IF HE HAS PROSTITUTED HIMSELF OR LIVED AS A HIRED MAN.

units.la: ΕΙ Ο ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΑ ΚΑΤΕΔΗ-ΔΟΚΩΣ Ἢ ΩΝ ΑΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝΟΜΟΣ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ.
units.tr: IF HE HAS SQUANDERED HIS PATERNAL ESTATE, OR ANY INHERITANCE HE HAS RECEIVED AS HEIR.

units.la: Εἀν δέ τις [?] ἐπὶ τὴν δικαστήριον [?], ΔΟΚΙΜΑ-ΣΙΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΓΓΕΙΛΑΤΩ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. [?] ἐπὶ τὴν δικαστήριον [?]
units.tr: If anyone wishes, the Athenian who wishes it may give notice of scrutiny to those to whom it belongs, before the court.

units.la: DE ORATORVM VITA QVÆSTIO.
units.tr: A Question concerning the Life of Orators.

units.la: Si quis in populo oret, qui alterum parentum pulsarit, aut non aluerit, aut tectum ad habitandum non praebuerit.
units.tr: If anyone who has struck one of his parents speaks before the people, or has not supported them, or has not given them a roof to live under.

units.la: Si ad militiam vocatus non responderit, aut clypeum abiecerit.
units.tr: If, when called up for military service, he has not answered, or has cast away his shield.

units.la: Si scortetur, aut muliebria patiatur.
units.tr: If he has prostituted himself, or submitted to the passive role of a woman.

units.la: Si paternam, aut aliam quamvis ad se delatam hereditatem, decoxerit.
units.tr: If he has squandered his paternal inheritance, or any other inheritance that has come to him.

units.la: Si, inquam, in populo oret nihilo minus, illius nomen Atheniensium quivis, cui libuerit, & licuerit, deferto: iudicesque ea de re iudicium red-dunto.
units.tr: If, I say, he speaks before the people all the same, let any Athenian who wishes, and is permitted, bring his name forward, and let the judges pass sentence on the matter.

units.la: Habes omnia ista Kapita apud Aeschinem ἐν τῇ πρὸς Τιμάρχου ἐ Solonis Legibus: [?] ἐπὶ τὴν δικαστήριον [?] ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΙΑ (φησί) ΡΗΤΟΡΩΝ ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΛΕΓΗ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ ΤΟΝ ΠΑΤΕΡΑ ΤΥΠΤΩΝ, Ἢ ΤΗΝ ΜΗΤΕΡΑ, Ἢ ΜΗ ΤΡΕΦΩΝ, Ἢ ΜΗ ΠΑΡΕΧΩΝ ΟΙΚΗΣΙΝ. τῶν γὰρ ἐκ λέγει. Sed iam singula Kapita expendamus.
units.tr: You have all these chapters in Aeschines' speech against Timarchus, from the laws of Solon: "Scrutiny of orators. If anyone speaks in the assembly who has beaten his father or his mother, or has not fed them, or has not provided them a home..." (he says) "...for he speaks of those from whom..." But let us now weigh the individual chapters.

units.la: Primum est, de honore parentibus habendo: Nam si quis parentum alterum pulsauerit, aut non exhibuerit, aut in aedes non admiserit, cui, quaeso te, persuadebit, se bene affectum fore in alienos, cum in suos, quibus, tantum Diis, honorem habere debuit, tam impius fuerit. Aeschines: ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΛΕΓΗ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ ΤΟΝ ΠΑΤΕΡΑ ΤΥΠΤΩΝ, Ἢ ΤΗΝ ΜΗΤΕΡΑ, Ἢ ΜΗ ΤΡΕΦΩΝ, Ἢ ΜΗ ΠΑΡΕΧΩΝ ΟΙΚΗΣΙΝ. τῶν γὰρ ἐκ λέγει. νὴ Δία καλῶς γε, ὡς ἔγωγε φημί. [?] ὅτι εἴ τις, οὐ ἐξίσου δεῖ ὑμᾶς τοῖς ἡμῖν, ἐὶς τοὺς δὴ φαύλας, ἢ ποτὲ (φησὶν) [?] οἱ ἄλλοτε, ἡ ἡ πόλις ὅλη;
units.tr: The first concerns the honour owed to parents. For if someone has struck one of his parents, or not supported them, or not admitted them into his house, pray, who will persuade us that he will treat strangers well, when he has been so impious towards his own, to whom he owed honour as much as to the gods? Aeschines: "If anyone speaks in the assembly who has beaten his father or his mother, or has not fed them, or has not provided them a home..." "...for he speaks of those from whom..." Yes indeed, rightly so, as I for my part say. For if someone is not equal to us in these things, shall we entrust the state to him as if he were one of the good? Or (he says) shall we let him be among the bad, as others have been, and the whole city?

units.la: Secundum Kaput militiam spectat: nam qui ad eam vocatus non responderit, aut instructa acie & in pugna clypeum abiecerit, prae ignauia fortis nunquam erit princeps sententiae. Aeschines: Καὶ πῶν δὲ ὑπέρ ἀπίπτε μὴ λέγῃν; ΕΙΣ ΤΑΣ ΣΤΡΑΤΕΙΑΣ φησὶ ΜΗ ΕΣΤΡΑΤΕΥΜΕΝΟΣ ΟΣΑΙ ΑΝ ΑΥΤΩΙ ΠΡΟΣΤΑΧΘΩΣΙΝ Η ΤΗΝ ΑΣΠΙΔΑ ΑΡΟΒΕ-ΒΛΗΚΩΣ δίκην λέγων. ἡ δὲ ποτε; ἀλλ' ἔφη, τῇ πόλει [?] ἵνα τὰ ὅπλα μὴ ῥίπτειν [?], ἡ ἀφὸ δῆλον μὴ δυνατὸς εἰ ἐπαμύνειν, μηδὲ συμβουλεύειν ἀξίου.
units.tr: The second chapter concerns military service. For he who, when called up for it, has not answered, or, when the line was drawn up and in battle, has cast away his shield, out of cowardice will never be a leader of opinion in bravery. Aeschines: "And is it not right that a man who does not speak..." He says: "who, when called for military service, does not serve, or has cast away his shield," speaking as one under judgement. But what then? He says that the man who has thrown away his arms is not fit to defend the city, nor should he be thought worthy to advise it.

units.la: Tertium Caput pudicitiam vindicat: Nam si quis sustinet muliebria pati, quaestumque corpore facere, faciet etiam prostituta Republica. Aeschines: Τέιπον, πῶς ἀλλὰ λέγεις; ΕΙ ΓΕΓΟΡΝΕΥΜΕΝΟΣ, φησὶν, Η ΗΤΑΙΡΗΚΩΣ. τὸν γὰρ ὃ σῶμα ὃ ἑαυτῷ ἐφ' ὕβρει παρέχοιτο, καὶ τὰ καινὰ τὰ τῆς πόλεως ῥᾳδίως ἡγήσαιτο ἀποδώσεσθαι.
units.tr: The third chapter guards chastity. For if someone submits to a woman's role, and makes gain from his body, he will also make the Republic prostitute itself. Aeschines: "Tell me, how do you speak? 'If he has prostituted himself or lived as a hired man.'" For the man who offers his body to outrage for himself will readily think that the city's affairs too may be handed over.

units.la: Quartum denique Caput exigit ab Oratore, ut rem familiarem tueatur, nam si bona sua decoxerit, publicam non multo melius rem tuebitur. Aeschines: Τέταρτον, πῶς ἀξιόλογος; ΕΙ Ο ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΑ, φησί, ΚΑΤΕΔΗΔΟΚΩΣ Η ΩΝ ΑΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝΟΜΟΣ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ, τὸν γὰρ τῷ ἰδίας οἰκίας καὶ χωρὶς οἰκήσομαι, καὶ τὰ καινὰ τῆς πόλεως ἀποδαπλησίως ἡγήσαιτο ἀξιοσοφῆ.
units.tr: Lastly, the fourth chapter requires of the orator that he look after his private property; for if he has squandered his goods, he will look after the public affairs no better. Aeschines: "Fourthly, how is he worthy of mention? 'If he has squandered his paternal estate,' he says, 'or any inheritance he has received as heir.' For the man who has neglected his own household will not be careful of the city's affairs either."

units.la: Atque de iis quaestio habebatur a iudicibus, quando forte capti Oratores ab illis ἐδοκιμάζοντο, εἴτ' ἐπιτήδειοί εἰσι λέγειν, εἴ τι καὶ μή. Meminit illius Lycurgus Rhetor ὁ τὰς δοκιμασίας καὶ τὸν νόμον γινώσκειν· μία μὲν, ὧν οἱ ἐνίοτε Ἀρχῖνις δοκιμάζοντο· ἔπειτα δὲ, ὧν οἱ Ῥήτορες.
units.tr: And the judges held a hearing on these matters, when orators who had been caught were examined by them, to see whether they were fit to speak or not. Lycurgus the rhetorician mentions it: he who knows the scrutinies and the law: one kind, by which some magistrates were examined; then another, by which the Orators were examined.

units.la: Quod si quis alicuius harum rerum reus, latuisset, & oraret in populo, dica illi scribebatur, quam Δοκιμασίαν dixerunt, nomenque eius deferebat Atheniensium quiuis, cui liceret & licerer, iudicesque ea de re iudicium reddebant. Aeschines: Τοῦτος δὲ ὠφέλησε τῆς βήματος, τοῦτος ἀπαγορεύει μὴ δημηγορεῖν. Ἐαν δὲ τις τῷ τοῦτο μὴ μόνον λέγῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ συκοφαντῇ ἡ ἀσελγαίνῃ, καὶ μηκέτι τοιούτου ἀξιώσεται δωρεάν φέρειν ἡ πόλις, ΔΟΚΙΜΑΣΙΑΝ ΜΕΝ, φησὶν, ΕΙΠΑΓΓΕΙΛΑΤΩ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. ὑμᾶς δ' ἤδη καλεῖ ταῦτ' ἐπὶ τῶν δικαστηρίων ἀξιοῦσι. καὶ νῦν ἐγὼ τὴν τῶν ὑμῶν τὸν νόμων ἴσα τοῖς ὑμᾶς. Aeschines sententiam expressit Pollux Lib. VIII cap. VI. δοκιμασία τοῖς Δημαγωγοῖς ἐπηρεάζετο, εἰ ἡμαρτικότες εἶεν, ἡ τὰ παπᾶ κατεδηδοκότες, ἡ τοῖς γονεῦσι κεκακωκότες, ἡ ἄλλως κακῶς βεβιωκότες, ἀτιμοῦς αὐτοὺς ἐχέω ἔτι, καὶ μὴ λέγῃ. Dixit Δημαγωγοί, qui sunt Ῥήτορες, ut e laudaris Aeschinis verbis constat, itemque Aristotele, Graeco Demosthenis Interprete, aliis. Appellabatur quoque haec dica Ῥητεικὴ, Harpocration: Ῥητεικὴ γραφὴ. Ἰσαῖος ὁ τὰ πολεῖς ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΗΣ. ἔοικε Ῥητεικὴ γραφὴ καλεῖσθαι, ἡ τῇ Ῥήτορες γραφῆς ἀξιώσει, ἡ εἰ-πόντες, ἡ ἀποξίαντος ὀδυνῶν· καὶ ὥσπερ λέγεται Πρυτανικὴ ἡ τῇ Γρυτηίως, καὶ Ἐπισατικὴ ἡ κατ' Ἐπισάπου, ἴσως ὁ τῇ τῶν Ῥητεικὴ γραφαί τινες καλοῦνται, ὅτι τῇ ἀφῳφόρους νόμοις αἱ τῶν Ῥητόρων γραφαὶ εἰσάγονται, ὡς Αντιφῶν ὁ τὰ τῇ Γρυ-λεως, εἰ γήσιος, ἀπειπημένῃ. Suidas: Ῥητεικὴ γραφὴ, ὡ ἠγωνίζοντο οἱ Ῥήτορες, οὐ γὰρ πάσας ἠγωνίζοντο τὰς δίκας τὴν παλαιὰν οἱ Ῥήτορες, ἀλλ' εἰσὶ. ἄλλοι δ' Ῥητεικλῷ γραφῷ λέγεσι, ἡ τῇ Ῥήτορες μινωΐλιν, γραφῆντες τι, ἡ εἰπόντες, ἡ ἀποξίαντος ὀδυνῶν. ἴσως ὁ τῇ τῶν Ῥητεικὴ γραφαί τινες καλοῦνται, ὅτι τῇ ἀφῳφόρους νόμοις αἱ τῶν Ῥητόρων γραφαὶ εἰσάγοντα, ὥσπερ λέγεται Πρυτανικὴ γραφὴ ἡ τῇ Πρυτάνεως, καὶ Ἐπισατικὴ ἡ κατ' Ἐπισάπου. Rescribendum est cum apud Harpocrationem, tum apud Suidam, ὅτι τῇ ἀφῳφόρους νόμοις αἱ τῇ τῶν Ῥητόρων γραφαὶ εἰσάγοντα. Dica Oratoribus scribi poterat propter violatas varias Leges, vt ἀσεβείας, ἐνυβρίσεως, &c. Atque haec actio proprie dicebatur ἐπαγγελία. Grammatici: ἐπαγ-γελία, σημαίνει ἡ ἄλλα, ἰδίως δὲ λέγεται τὴν εἰσαγωγὴν τῶν δημηγορῶν ἢ πολιτεύεσθαι οὐκ ἔξον[?]. Siue etiam εἰσαγγελία. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. VI. ἀδικῶ δὲ τῆς ἀλίσκεσθαι[?], ἢ Ἀρχῶν, ἢ Ῥήτωρ, εἰς τὸν βουλὴν εἰσαγγελία δίδοται κατ' αὐτῶν. & paullo post è Theophrasto: ἐγίγνοντο δὲ ἡ εἰσαγγελία[?] ἢ μὴ τὰ ὅρια τῆς δήμου λεγόντων[?], ἢ ποιεῖς τοὺς πολέμους αὐτὸ τῆς πιμφθῶν ἀπαλλάττοντας, ἢ ποιεῖς δόντας Φεύγειν, ἢ γραφαί, ἢ ναῦς, ὡς Θεόφραστος ἐν τῷ νόμῳ. Videtur in his non bene conuenire Polluci cum Æschine: Æschines namque cognitionem defert secundum Legem ad Iudices: Pollux vero ad Quingentorum Senatum. Sed hæc facile inter se conciliari possunt: è Solonis quippe Legibus oportebat τὰς δικαστὰς αἷς ἐν τοῖς τῶν δικαστηρίων ἀμφισβητοῦσιν. Pollux: χίλιοι ὃ ἐξ μὲν τὸν Σόλωνα τὰς Εἰσαγγελίας ἐκεῖνον. Hi mille duo sunt δικαστήρια, quæ in vnum conuenerant, quod sæpe fieri solitum testis Demosthenis Interpres Vlpianus ad hæc è Timocratea verba: δικαστηρίων δυοῖν εἰς ἓν χιλίους ἐψηφισμένων. οἱ τὰς μεγάλας ἢ ἐαυτῶν δικαστήρια, πλεονώντος ἀριθμὸν χιλίων ἢ ἐνὸς. Mutauit & id postea, Demetrio Phalereo Legem ferente, & additi sunt quingenti iudices. idem Pollux: χ' ὁ τὸν Φαληρέα ἢ ταῖς Παισικίδαις[?]. Altera quoque conciliationis ratio iniri potest ex his Pollucis verbis: ἀδικῶ δὲ τῆς ἀλίσκεσθαι[?], ἢ Ἀρχῶν, ἢ Ῥήτωρ, εἰς τὸν βουλὴν εἰσαγγελία δίδοται κατ' αὐτῶν, κἂν μὴ μέτρια ἀδικεῖν ἀξιοῦ, ἡ βουλὴ πιστῶν ζημίας ἐπιβουλὴ[?]. δὲ δὲ μείζω, δικαστήριον.
units.tr: But if anyone was accused of any of these things and had escaped notice and spoke before the people, an action called a scrutiny [Δοκιμασία] was brought against him, and any Athenian who wished, and was permitted, could bring his name forward, and the judges gave judgement on the matter. Aeschines: "This man, having been removed from the platform, is forbidden to address the people. But if someone not only speaks this, but also acts as a sycophant or behaves outrageously, and the city no longer deems him worthy to bring a gift, let any Athenian who wishes give notice of a scrutiny to those to whom it is permitted. You now summon these matters to the courts, and now I too..." Pollux, book VIII, chapter VI, expressed Aeschines' meaning: a scrutiny was brought against demagogues, if they had offended, or had eaten up their patrimony, or had mistreated their parents, or had otherwise lived badly; they were disfranchised and not allowed to speak. He says demagogues [Δημαγωγοί], who are orators, as is clear from the words of Aeschines just quoted, and likewise from Aristotle, a Greek interpreter of Demosthenes, and others. This action was also called a rhetorical indictment [Ῥητεικὴ]. Harpocration: "rhetorical indictment [Ῥητεικὴ γραφὴ]. Isaeus, in the speech on the estate of Euclides: it seems to be called rhetorical indictment, which is a suit brought against orators, either for speaking or for not speaking, or for mistreating parents." And just as the prytanic indictment is so called from the prytanes, and the epistatic from the epistates, perhaps those are called rhetorical indictments because the orators' indictments are brought under the laws concerning the orators, as Antiphon in the speech against Gryllion... Suidas: "rhetorical indictment, which the orators pleaded; for the orators did not plead all the ancient suits, but some. Others speak of a rhetorical indictment [Ῥητεικὴ γραφή] for the orators' wrongdoing, whether for speaking or not speaking, or for mistreating parents. Perhaps those are called rhetorical indictments because the orators' indictments are brought under the laws, just as the prytanic indictment is so called from the prytanes, and the epistatic from the epistates." In both Harpocration and Suidas it should be corrected to read that the orators' indictments are brought under the laws concerning the orators. A scrutiny could be written against orators because of various violated laws, such as for impiety, for outrage, and so on. And this action was properly called an impeachment [ἐπαγγελία]. The grammarians: "impeachment [ἐπαγγελία] signifies one thing, but properly it is said of the introduction of those who speak before the people or engage in public affairs when not permitted." Or also an accusation [εἰσαγγελία]. Pollux, book VIII, chapter VI: "Whoever is caught guilty, whether magistrate or orator, an accusation [εἰσαγγελία] is brought against them before the Council," and a little later from Theophrastus: "accusations [εἰσαγγελία] arose against those who spoke against the boundaries of the people, or who made wars or treaties, or who lured men into exile, or gave them to flee, or against ships, as Theophrastus says in the law." In these matters Pollux seems not to agree well with Aeschines: Aeschines refers the examination according to the law to the judges, while Pollux refers it to the Council of Five Hundred. But these can easily be reconciled: under Solon's laws the cases of accusations had to be heard by the judges of the courts. Pollux: "a thousand judges, under Solon, heard the accusations..." These thousand made up two courts which had met as one, which, as Demosthenes' interpreter Ulpian testifies on these words from the speech against Timocrates, often happened: "when two courts of a thousand had voted together to make one, the great courts of themselves, with a number exceeding a thousand by one." This was later changed too, when Demetrius of Phalerum proposed a law, and five hundred judges were added. The same Pollux: "...under Phalereus and the Paisikides..." Another way of reconciling may be drawn from these words of Pollux: "Whoever is caught guilty, whether magistrate or orator, an accusation [εἰσαγγελία] is brought against them before the Council, and even if they do not seem to have committed a grave wrong, the Council imposes a fine on them; but if the wrong is greater, the court decides."

units.la: Lege præterea Athenienfium cautum erat, vt is qui Orator fore legebatur, agros intra fines Atticæ possideret, & liberos legitimos, aut iam haberet, aut suscepturus esset, qui essent tanquam Reipublicæ oppignerati, & paternæ fidei dati obsides.
units.tr: Moreover, Athenian law required that the man who was to be chosen as an orator should hold land within the borders of Attica and should either already have legitimate children or be about to beget them. These children were, as it were, pledged to the state and given as hostages for their father's good faith.

units.la: Τὸν Ῥήτορα παιδοποιεῖσθαι κατὰ τοὺς νόμους, καὶ γῆν ἐντὸς ὅρων κεκτῆσθαι[?].
units.tr: The orator shall beget children according to the laws and possess land within the borders. [Τὸν Ῥήτορα παιδοποιεῖσθαι κατὰ τοὺς νόμους, καὶ γῆν ἐντὸς ὅρων κεκτῆσθαι]

units.la: Orator liberos suscipito e legitimis nuptiis, agrumque intra fines Atticæ possideto.
units.tr: An orator shall have children from a lawful marriage, and shall possess land within the borders of Attica.

units.la: Legem laudat Dinarchus ἐν τῷ κατὰ Δημοσθένους. Καὶ τοὺς μὲν νόμους παρελθὼν τὴν Ῥήτωρ, τῷ ἀξιοῦν τὸ δῆμον πίστιν ἀξιοῦντι λαμβάνειν, παιδοποιεῖσθαι κατὰ τοὺς νόμους, ἓν εἶπε ὅρων κεκτῆσθαι· πάσας τὰς δίκας πίστῃ ἀποκαταστῆναι, ὅπως ἀξιοῦν παρεσκευάσθαι τὸ δῆμον. οἱ δὲ τῷ πανταχοῦ ἓν πιπαρασκευὴ, τοὺς ὁ οὐ γεγονυῖα μὴ ὁ τὰ τοὺς νόμους, τῶν δὲ τῶν κείσθαι ἕνεκα γενομένων ὅρκων[?].
units.tr: Dinarchus cites this law in his speech against Demosthenes. Passing over the other laws, he says that the orator must beget children according to the laws and possess land within the borders, and that all lawsuits must be settled in good faith. The people, he argues, were prepared to demand such a pledge, and these conditions were laid down for the sake of the oaths that were taken.

units.la: Diligenter autem prouidebant, vt Oratores μετ' δίκης[?], siue in Senatu, siue in populo, orarent, eaque de re extat hæc Lex:
units.tr: The Athenians also took careful provision that orators should speak with right and proper conduct, whether in the Senate or before the people. On this matter the following law survives:

units.la: ΤΩΝ ΡΗΤΟΡΩΝ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΛΕΓΗ ΕΝ ΒΟΥΛΗ Η ΕΝ ΔΗΜΩΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΙΣΦΕΡΟΜΕΝΩΝ, Η ΜΗ ΧΩΡΙΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΥ Η ΔΙΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ Ο ΑΥΤΟΣ ΤΟΙΣ ΑΥΤΟΙΣ, ΟΤΙ Η ΛΟΙΔΟΡΕΙΤΑΙ, Η ΚΑΚΩΣ ΑΓΟΡΕΥΕΙ ΤΙΝΑ, Η ΥΠΟΚΡΟΥΕΙ Η ΧΡΗΜΑΤΙΖΟΝΤΩΝ ΜΕΤΑΞΥ ΑΝΗΚΕΣΤΩΣ ΛΕΓΗ, ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΜΗ ΕΓΙ ΤΟΥ ΒΗΜΑΤΟΣ Η ΠΑΡΑΚΕΛΕΥΤΑΙ Η
