In the decree of the people, which Stratocles son of Euthydemus proposed at Athens, under the archon Anaxicrates, in the second year of the 118th Olympiad, to donate to the orator Lycurgus, the words of the aitesis read: [ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ. ἔδοξε τῷ δήμῳ, ἐπαινέσαι μὲν Λυκοῦργον Λυκόφρονος Βουτάδην ἀρετῆς ἕνεκα καὶ δικαιοσύνης, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτοῦ τὸν δῆμον χαλκῆν εἰκόνα ἐν ἀγορᾷ. γῆν εἴ που ὁ νόμος ἀγορεύει μὴ ἱστάναι, δοῦναι δὲ σίτησιν ἐν Πρυτανείῳ τῶν ἐγγόνων ἀεὶ τῶν Λυκούργου τῷ πρεσβυτάτῳ εἰς ἅπαντα τὸν χρόνον.] (With good fortune. Resolved by the people: to praise Lycurgus son of Lycophron of Boutadae for his virtue and justice, and to set up for him a bronze statue in the agora by the people; if any law forbids erecting it in some place, to grant maintenance in the Prytaneum to the eldest of Lycurgus' descendants for all time.) From these words we learn besides that Solon's law, that a man should not be fed too often in the Prytaneum, was changed; for many were honoured by an aitesis from the people, as Pollux says, and the honour passed to their heirs. So that sometimes, when the dead could not enjoy it, it was requested and granted for them, as happened to Demosthenes, to whom this honour was granted in the first year of the 125th Olympiad, when Gorgias was praetor at Athens. Plutarch, in his Life of Demosthenes, in the book on the Ten Orators, says: [χρόνῳ δὲ ὕστερον Ἀθηναῖοι αἰτησάντι τε ἐκ Πρυτανείου τῆς συγκλήτου τῆς Δημοσθένους ἐδόσθη, καὶ αὐτὸς πεπλεκτικὸς τῷ εἰκόνα ἀνέθηκεν ἐν ἀγορᾷ, ὅτι Γοργίου Ἀρ-γείας.] (Later, the Athenians gave to Demosthenes' descendants the maintenance in the Prytaneum, on his petition, and set up a statue of him in the agora.) There is extant a decree on this matter, written by Demochares son of Laches, in the same Plutarch: [ΔΗΜΟΧΑΡΗΣ ΛΑΧΗΤΟΣ ΛΕΥΚΟΝΟΕΥΣ ΑΙΤΕΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΘΕΝΕΙ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΟΣΘΕΝΟΥΣ ΠΑΙΑΝΙΕΙ ΔΩΡΕΑΝ ΧΑΛΚΗΝ ΕΙΚΟΝΑ ΕΝ ΑΓΟΡΑι, ΚΑΙ ΣΙΤΗΣΙΝ ΕΝ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΩι, ΚΑΙ ΠΡΟΕΔΡΙΑΝ ΑΥΤΩι, ΚΑΙ ΕΚΓΟΝΩΝ ΑΕΙ ΤΩι ΠΡΕΣΒΥΤΑΤΩι ΕΥΕΡΓΕΤΗι, ΚΑΙ ΣΥΜΒΟΥΛΩι ΓΕΓΟΝΟΤΙ ΠΟΛΛΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΚΑΛΩΝ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΗΝ ΤΕ ΟΥΣΙΑΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΚΟΙΝΟΝ ΚΑΘΕΙΚΟΤΙ ΤΗΝ ΕΑΥΤΟΥ.] (Demochares son of Laches of Leuconoe proposes that a bronze statue of Demosthenes be set up in the agora as a gift to Demosthenes son of Demosthenes of Paiania, and maintenance in the Prytaneum, and proedria for him, and for his eldest descendants forever, as a benefactor; and since he has been a councillor and has done many fine things for the people of Athens, and has devoted his property to the common good.) Demochares also recounts Demosthenes' benefactions to the people one by one, as did Demochares' own son Laches in the decree he wrote on this matter, in the archonship of Pytharatus, in the second year of the 127th Olympiad. This decree is extant at the end of the same Plutarch, in the Book on the Ten Orators, in these words: [ΑΡΧΩΝ ΓΥΘΑΡΑΤΟΣ ΛΑΧΗΣ ΔΗΜΟΧΑΡΟΥΣ ΛΕΥΚΟΝΟΕΥΣ ΑΙΤΕΙ ΔΩΡΕΑΝ ΤΗΝ ΒΟΥΛΗΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΔΗΜΟΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΔΗΜΟΧΑΡΕΙ ΛΑΧΗΤΟΣ ΛΕΥΚΟΝΟΕΙ ΕΙΚΟΝΑ ΧΑΛΚΗΝ ΕΝ ΑΓΟΡΑι, ΚΑΙ ΣΙΤΗΣΙΝ ΕΝ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΩι, ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΓΓΟΝΩΝ ΑΕΙ ΤΩι ΠΡΕΣΒΥΤΑΤΩι, ΚΑΙ ΠΡΟΕΔΡΙΑΝ ΕΝ ΠΑΣΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΑΓΩΣΙΝ ΕΥΕΡΓΕΤΗι, ΚΑΙ ΣΥΜΒΟΥΛΩι ΓΕΓΟΝΟΤΙ ΑΓΑΘΩι ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΕΥΕΡΓΕΤΗΚΟΤΙ ΤΟΝ ΔΗΜΟΝ ΤΑΔΕ.] (In the archonship of Pytharatus, Laches son of Demochares of Leuconoe proposes that the Council and the people of Athens grant to Demochares son of Laches of Leuconoe a bronze statue in the agora, and maintenance in the Prytaneum, and to his eldest descendants for ever, and proedria at all games, as a benefactor and as a councillor who has been good to the people of Athens and has benefited the people in these matters.) Even women were granted this honour, as Callisthenes reports in Plutarch's Aristides, concerning Polycrite, granddaughter of Aristides: [ἐπὶ δὲ Αἰσιμάχου γυναικὶ Πολυχρίτῳ ἁπλῶς πάντως, ὡς Καλλισθένης φησί, καὶ ταύτῃ αἰτήσαι ὅσῳ καὶ τοῖς Ὀλυμπιονίκαις ὁ δῆμος ἐψηφίσατο.] (For Polycrite, wife of Aesimachus, the people voted, as Callisthenes says, the same favour as to the Olympic victors.) Also, when Demetrius of Phalerum proposed a decree, the people gave the granddaughters of Aristides a triobol each day: [ὁ δὲ Φαληρεύς ἐν τοῖς Σωκράτει φησὶ μνημονεύειν Αἰσχίδου γυναικῶν δ' μάλιστα πάντα Λεσβίαν· τῇ δὲ μητρὶ καὶ τῇ ταύτης ἀδελφῇ ψήφισμα χαλκᾶς δωρεὰν ἐπιστῶν τὸν δῆμον ἰδίναι, τεσσαρῶν ἑκάστης ἡμέρας· αὐτὸς μάντι φησὶν ὁ Δημήτριος νομοθετῶν ἐψηφίσατο δραχμῶν ἑκατέρᾳ πέντε τὴν γυναῖκα.] (The Phalerean, in his Socrates, says he recalls Aeschides' wives, above all Lesbia; to her mother and her sister the people gave a grant of a bronze coin for each of four days; Demetrius himself, legislating, proposed a vote of five drachmas for each woman.) Socrates, already condemned by the first sentences of the judges, answered this playfully when asked what should be given him: "Since," says Cicero in Book I of De Oratore, "Socrates was asked, he replied that he had deserved to be honoured with the highest distinctions and rewards, and to be given his daily food at public expense in the Prytaneum, which among the Greeks was regarded as the greatest honour."

units.la: Statuae quoque honorem habitum fuisse benemeritis de Republica, non sinunt nos dubitare Pfephismata honori Demosthenis, Democharis, Lycurgi, scripta, quae iam descripsimus: easque statuae, ut plurimum, in foro positae, quanquam & pars quaedam erat fori, in qua statuas ponere Lege non licebat.
units.tr: Statues, too, were given as an honour to those who had deserved well of the Republic. The decrees in honour of Demosthenes, Demochares and Lycurgus, which we have already described, leave no room for doubt. These statues were mostly set up in the forum, although there was a certain part of the forum where the law did not allow statues to be placed.

units.la: DE NON PONENDIS IN ALIQVA FORI PARTE STATVIS LEX.
units.tr: ON THE LAW FORBIDDING STATUES IN A CERTAIN PART OF THE FORUM

units.la: Huius Legis meminit Pfephisma à Stratocle scriptum in honorem Lycurgi: ΑΓΑΘΗΙ ΤΥΧΗΙ ΔΕΔΟΧΘΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ ΕΠΑΙΝΕΣΑΙ ΜΕΝ ΛΥΚΩΥΡΓΟΝ ΛΥΚΟΦΡΟΝΟΣ ΒΟΥΤΑΔΗΝ ΑΡΕΤΗΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΚΑΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΣΥΝΗΣ, ΚΑΙ ΣΤΗΣΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΤΟΝ ΔΗΜΟΝ ΧΑΛΚΗΝ ΕΙΚΟΝΑ ΕΝ ΑΓΟΡΑΙ· ΓΑΗΝ ΕΙ ΠΟΥ Ο ΝΟΜΟΣ ΑΓΑΓΟΡΕΥΕΙ ΜΗ ΙΣΤΑΝΑΙ.
units.tr: The law is mentioned in the decree drawn up by Stratocles in honour of Lycurgus: "It has been resolved by the Council and the People, with good fortune, to praise Lycurgus son of Lycophron of Butadae for his virtue and justice, and to set up for him, at the People's expense, a bronze statue in the agora; but if any law forbids it, let it not be set up." [ΑΓΑΘΗΙ ΤΥΧΗΙ ΔΕΔΟΧΘΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ ΕΠΑΙΝΕΣΑΙ ΜΕΝ ΛΥΚΟΥΡΓΟΝ ΛΥΚΟΦΡΟΝΟΣ ΒΟΥΤΑΔΗΝ ΑΡΕΤΗΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΚΑΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΣΥΝΗΣ, ΚΑΙ ΣΤΗΣΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΤΟΝ ΔΗΜΟΝ ΧΑΛΚΗΝ ΕΙΚΟΝΑ ΕΝ ΑΓΟΡΑΙ· ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΠΟΥ Ο ΝΟΜΟΣ ΑΠΑΓΟΡΕΥΕΙ ΜΗ ΙΣΤΑΝΑΙ.]

units.la: Inter praemia numerandum quoque est monumentum publice extructum. Nam benemeritis de Republica id concedebatur. Plutarchus in Aristide: καὶ μὴν τινι καὶ πάρος ἔδει ἀντὶ Φαληρέως δήκιμος ὃν φασι καταθῆναι τὴν πόλιν αὐτὴν, μηδὲ ἐπιφανὲς καλὸν ἀλλὰ[?] Pfephisma in honorem Zenonis apud Diogenem Laertium in eius vita: ΤΥΧΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΑΓΑΘΗΙ ΔΕΔΟΧΘΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ, ΕΠΑΙΝΕΣΑΙ ΜΕΝ ΖΗΝΩΝΑ ΜΝΑΣΕΟΥ ΚΙΤΤΙΕΑ, ΟΙΚΟΔΟΜΗΣΑΙ ΔΕ ΑΥΤΩΙ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΦΟΝ ΕΠΙ ΤΟΥ ΚΕΡΑΜΕΙΚΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑΙ. Dixit in Ceramico suburbano, in quo sepulcra eorum, qui in bello occubuissent. Grammatici: ΔΥΟ ΔΕ ΟΙ ΚΕΡΑΜΙΚΟΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΙ, Ο ΜΕΝ ΕΝΔΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΠΟΛΕΩΣ, Ο ΔΕ ΕΞΩ, ΕΝΘΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΝ ΠΟΛΕΜΩ ΠΕΠΤΩΚΟΣΙ ΕΠΑΙΝΟΥΜΕΝΑΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΠΙΦΑΝΕΣΙ ΕΛΕΓΟΝ. ΕΙΣΙ ΔΕ ΕΝΘΑ ΚΑΙ ΕΝΘΑΝ ΣΤΗΛΑΙ ΕΠΙ ΤΗΣ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ ΠΕΠΡΑΜΜΕΝΟΙΣ, ΕΧΟΥΣΑΙ ΕΠΙΓΡΑΦΑΙ ΠΑΝΤΑ ΕΝΕΚΑΣ ΤΙΘΕΑΣΙΑ.
units.tr: Among the rewards must also be counted a monument erected at public expense, for this was granted to those who had deserved well of the Republic. Plutarch, in the Life of Aristides, speaks of the city giving a tomb to one who had deserved well of it [καὶ μὴν τινι καὶ πάρος ἔδει ἀντὶ Φαληρέως δήκιμος ὃν φασι καταθῆναι τὴν πόλιν αὐτὴν, μηδὲ ἐπιφανὲς καλὸν ἀλλὰ]. The decree in honour of Zeno, preserved in Diogenes Laertius' Life of him, reads: "It has been resolved by the Council and the People, with good fortune, to praise Zeno son of Mnaseas of Citium, and to build him a tomb at public expense in the Ceramicus." [ΤΥΧΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΑΓΑΘΗΙ ΔΕΔΟΧΘΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ, ΕΠΑΙΝΕΣΑΙ ΜΕΝ ΖΗΝΩΝΑ ΜΝΑΣΕΟΥ ΚΙΤΤΙΕΑ, ΟΙΚΟΔΟΜΗΣΑΙ ΔΕ ΑΥΤΩΙ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΦΟΝ ΕΠΙ ΤΟΥ ΚΕΡΑΜΕΙΚΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑΙ.] He says "in the suburban Ceramicus, in which were the tombs of those who had fallen in war." The grammarians say: "There are two Ceramici at Athens, one inside the city and the other outside, where those who fell in war are publicly praised and are called the public tombs of the illustrious dead. There too stand stelae on the public monuments, bearing inscriptions that always contain praise of the same kind." [ΔΥΟ ΔΕ ΟΙ ΚΕΡΑΜΙΚΟΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΙ, Ο ΜΕΝ ΕΝΔΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΠΟΛΕΩΣ, Ο ΔΕ ΕΞΩ, ΕΝΘΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΝ ΠΟΛΕΜΩ ΠΕΠΤΩΚΟΣΙ ΕΠΑΙΝΟΥΜΕΝΑΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΠΙΦΑΝΕΣΙ ΕΛΕΓΟΝ. ΕΙΣΙ ΔΕ ΕΝΘΑ ΚΑΙ ΕΝΘΑΝ ΣΤΗΛΑΙ ΕΠΙ ΤΗΣ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑΣ ΠΕΠΡΑΜΜΕΝΟΙΣ, ΕΧΟΥΣΑΙ ΕΠΙΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΠΑΝΤΑ ΕΝΕΚΑΣ ΤΙΘΕΑΣΙΑ.]

units.la: Honoris quoque ergo Coronae donabantur viris benemeritis: Diogenes Laertius in Zenone: ἐτίμησαν δὲ τὸν Ἀθηναῖοι σφόδρα τὸν Ζήνωνα ὅτως, ὡς καὶ τὴν πύλην αὐτοῦ τῆς κλῆς ἐξ ἀπεπτάδειαν, καὶ χρυσῷ στεφάνῳ τιμῆσαι, καὶ χαλκῆ εἰκόνι. etiam fato functis hic honos habebatur, ut è populi scito facto in gratiam Zenonis iam mortui constat: ΤΥΧΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΑΓΑΘΗΙ ΔΕΔΟΧΘΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ ΕΠΑΙΝΕΣΑΙ ΜΕΝ ΖΗΝΩΝΑ ΜΝΑΣΕΟΥ ΚΙΤΤΙΕΑ, ΚΑΙ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΣΑΙ ΧΡΥΣΩΙ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΑΡΕΤΗΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΚΑΙ ΣΩΦΡΟΣΥΝΗΣ. Coronae autem istae donabantur ciuibus, vel à Senatu, vel à populo Athenienfi, vel à popularibus, vel à tribulibus, vel denique ab exteris ciuitatibus. Qui à populo corona donabatur, in concione donari debebat, qui à Senatu, itidem in Senatu, idque ex hac Lege: Ἐαν μὴ ἕνα ὁ δῆμος ὁ Ἀθηναίων στέφανοι, ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τὸ στέφανον ἀναγορεύεσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἡ βουλὴ, ἐν τῇ βουλευτηρίῳ· ἀλλαχῇ δὲ, μὴ ἐξεῖναι.
units.tr: Honorary crowns were also given to men who had deserved well. Diogenes Laertius, in the Life of Zeno: "The Athenians honoured Zeno so greatly that they even granted him exemption from ... and honoured him with a golden crown and a bronze statue." [ἐτίμησαν δὲ τὸν Ἀθηναῖοι σφόδρα τὸν Ζήνωνα ὅτως, ὡς καὶ τὴν πύλην αὐτοῦ τῆς κλῆς ἐξ ἀπεπτάδειαν, καὶ χρυσῷ στεφάνῳ τιμῆσαι, καὶ χαλκῆ εἰκόνι.] This honour was also paid to men who had died, as is clear from the decree of the People passed in Zeno's favour after he was already dead: "It has been resolved by the Council and the People, with good fortune, to praise Zeno son of Mnaseas of Citium, and to crown him with a golden crown according to the law, for his virtue and moderation." [ΤΥΧΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΑΓΑΘΗΙ ΔΕΔΟΧΘΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ ΕΠΑΙΝΕΣΑΙ ΜΕΝ ΖΗΝΩΝΑ ΜΝΑΣΕΟΥ ΚΙΤΤΙΕΑ, ΚΑΙ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΣΑΙ ΧΡΥΣΩΙ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΑΡΕΤΗΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΚΑΙ ΣΩΦΡΟΣΥΝΗΣ.] Such crowns were given to citizens either by the Senate, by the Athenian people, by their fellow-demesmen, by their fellow-tribesmen, or finally by foreign cities. A man crowned by the people was to be proclaimed in the assembly; a man crowned by the Senate, likewise in the Senate. This was by the following law: [Ἐαν μὲν ὁ δῆμος ὁ Ἀθηναίων στεφανοῖ, ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τὸν στέφανον ἀναγορεύεσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἡ βουλὴ, ἐν τῷ βουλευτηρίῳ· ἄλλαχῃ δὲ, μὴ ἐξεῖναι.]

units.la: Qui corona à populo donantur, in concione donantor: qui à Senatu, itidem in Senatu: alibi vero ius non esto.
units.tr: Those crowned by the People are proclaimed in the assembly; those crowned by the Senate, likewise in the Senate; elsewhere it shall not be lawful.

units.la: Meminit Legis Aeschines ἐν τῇ κτ' Κτησιφῶντος. δύπερ ὁ ὑμῖν διεξῆλθον τοὺς αὐτὸς τῆς χειρογράφων νόμους, ἐν οἷς ἀρρήτως ἀπείρηται, τὸν ὑπὸ τοῦ δήμου στέφανω- μένον μὴ κηρύττεσθαι ἔξω τῆς ἐκκλησίας. M. Tullius Libro de Optimo genere Oratorum extremo: Cùm esset Lex Athenis, EOS QVI A POPVLO CORONA DONARENTVR, IN CONCIONE DONARI DEBERE. Libanius in Argumento Orationis Demosthenis τῆς τῆ στέφαν. καὶ πάλιν πρεσβύτερος νόμοι, τὸν καλλίονα, Ἐαν μὲν ἕνα ὁ δῆμος ὁ Ἀθηναίων στέφανοι, ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τὸν στέφανον ἀναγορεύεσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἡ βουλὴ, ἐν τῇ βουλευτηρίῳ· ἀλλαχῇ δ', μὴ ἐξεῖναι. Anonymus in Argumento eiusdem: δύπερ δὲ ἀναγινώσκει νόμων, τὸν καλλίονα ἐν Γυμνὶ στεφανοῦσθαι, οὐκ ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ. Pnyx olim locus legitimæ concionis, quod nomen cùm in Lege proculdubio occurreret, optimè interpretatur Anonymus, si αὐτῆ τῆς ἐκκ referibas τοῦ, hoc modo, τὸν καλλίονα ἐν Πνυκὶ στεφανοῦσθαι, ποῦ; ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, Pnyce corona donari: ubi? in concione. Legis ratio est apud eundem Æschinem, ne is qui corona donatur, apud posteros se ostenter, aut in præconiis quæstum aucupetur: ὁ γὰρ νόμος Ἀρρήτως καλλίονα, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΤΙΝΑ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΙ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ, ΕΝ ΤΩι ΒΟΥΛΕΥΤΗΡΙΩι ΑΝΑΚΗΡΥΤΤΕΣΘΑΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ Ο ΔΗΜΟΣ, ΕΝ ΤΗι ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑι, ΑΛΛΟΘΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΑΜΟΥ. ἐξ ὁ νόμος, ὦ Ἀθηναῖοι, καὶ μάλα καλῶς ἔχει. ὁ γὰρ (εἶμαι) ἀεὶ τῆν ὁ νομοθέτης τὸν Ρητορα σιμνιώσαθαι πρὸς τὰς ἐξωθεν, ἀλλ' ἀγαπᾶν ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ πόλει ὑμοίωμα τοῦ δήμου, καὶ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι ἐν τοῖς κηρύγμασιν. ἀκούστε, ὦ Ἀθηναῖοι, ὅτι ὁ μὲν νομοθέτης καλλίονα ΕΝ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι ΕΝ ΠΝΥΚΙ ΤΗι ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑι, ἀναχηρύττην τὸν ὑπὸ τοῦ δήμου στεφανοῦμενον, ΑΛΛΟΘΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΑΜΟΥ. Hæ Coronæ quæ in concione donantur, non consecrabantur, sed domi adseruabantur, futurum posteris paternæ virtutis monumentum, quo ad illam excitarentur. Æschines eadem Oratione: ἀλλ' οὐχ ἐκεῖνον τὸν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀναρρηθέντα στέφανον ἀπολλεγεῖ· ἀλλ' ἔξεστι καὶ τῷ θαυμάζειν, ἵνα μὴ μόνον αὐτὸς, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ ἐξ ἐκείνων, ἔχοντες ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ ὃ ὑπομνῆμα, μηδέποτε κακοὶ τῷ ψυχῷ εἰς τὸν δῆμον γίνωνται. Cum igitur in concione tantum, aut in Senatu corona donari iubeant Leges, sequitur non licere in Theatro, Ludis. Anonymus in Argumento Orationis Æschinis τῆς Κτησιφῶντος. δύπερ δὲ, ὁπὲν τῷ θεάτρῳ αἰκήρυξε τὸν στέφανον, ἀπαγορεύοντος τὸν νόμον μηδένα στεφανοῦσθαι ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ. Ratio est, quia illi qui in Theatro, Ludis, corona donantur, maiorem gloriam consequerentur, cum interfint ex vniuersis Græci nominis populis aliqui, quam ij, qui in concione, in qua solis Athenien sibus interesse ciuibus licebat. Aeschines: ἐκ δὲ τούτου τῆς ἐξόπου στεφθῆναι τοῖς αἰκηρυττομένοις ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ μείζους ὑμῖν ὑμᾶς τῷ ὑπὸ τοῦ δήμου στεφανωθῆναι. Τῆς μὲν γὰρ ἀπολειφθῆναι ὁ τύπος ἡ ἐκκλησία, ἐν ᾗ ἡ ἐξ ἐχει στεφανοῦσθαι, καὶ ἀπίρητο ἀξιῶς μηδαμοῦ κηρύττεσθαι· οἱ δ' αἰσχρῶς ἀποδὲ ἐν τῶν Ἑλλήνων.
units.tr: Aeschines mentions the law in his speech Against Ctesiphon: "just as I have recited to you the laws of the crowns, in which it is expressly forbidden for a man crowned by the People to be proclaimed anywhere outside the assembly." Cicero, in the last book of De optimo genere oratorum: "Since there was a law at Athens that those who were given a crown by the People should be honoured in the assembly." Libanius, in the argument to Demosthenes' speech On the Crown, also cites the law: "If the People of Athens crowns someone, the crown is to be proclaimed in the assembly; if the Council, in the council-chamber; elsewhere, not allowed." [Ἐαν μὲν ὁ δῆμος ὁ Ἀθηναίων στεφανοῖ, ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τὸν στέφανον ἀναγορεύεσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἡ βουλὴ, ἐν τῷ βουλευτηρίῳ· ἄλλαχῃ δὲ, μὴ ἐξεῖναι.] The anonymous writer on the same speech says: "The law states that the man crowned by the People is to be crowned in the assembly, not in the theatre." The Pnyx was formerly the place of the lawful assembly; since this name would certainly occur in the law, the anonymous writer explains it well if one reads the phrase as follows: "Where is a man crowned by the People to be crowned, in the Pnyx? In the assembly," that is, "in the Pnyx, to be crowned in the assembly." The reason for the law is given by Aeschines in the same passage: so that the man who is crowned should not display himself to posterity, nor seek gain from heralds' proclamations. For the law, as he says, orders: [ἐὰν μὲν τίνα στεφανοῖ ἡ βουλή, ἐν τῷ βουλευτηρίῳ ἀνακηρύττεσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ὁ δῆμος, ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἄλλοθι δὲ μηδαμοῦ.] "Gentlemen of Athens, the law is very good indeed. For the lawgiver did not want the orator to show off before foreigners, but to be content with the approval of the People in the city itself, and not to work for proclamations. Hear, Athenians, that the lawgiver wanted the man crowned by the People to be proclaimed among the People, in the Pnyx, in the assembly, and nowhere else." These crowns which were proclaimed in the assembly were not dedicated, but kept at home, as a memorial of their father's virtue for posterity, to stir them to emulate it. Aeschines in the same speech: "But he does not speak of that crown which was proclaimed in the assembly; rather, it is lawful even for the man himself to keep it at home, so that not only he, but also his descendants, may have this reminder in their house and never become ill-disposed towards the People." Since the laws order a crown to be granted only in the assembly or in the Senate, it follows that it was not lawful in the theatre or at the Games. The anonymous writer on Aeschines' speech Against Ctesiphon says: "And indeed, the law forbids anyone to be crowned in the theatre." The reason is that those crowned in the theatre, at the Games, would gain greater glory, since men from all over the Greek world attended, whereas the assembly was open only to Athenian citizens. Aeschines: "For this reason it is more honourable to be crowned in the theatre, but the law forbids it, and rightly so... the crown given by the People in the assembly is the most honourable; the place of the assembly is the Pnyx, where the citizen is crowned, and it is forbidden to proclaim it anywhere else. Those who are proclaimed in the theatre are the ones shown to the Greeks."

units.la: Quando coronæ dabantur à tribulibus aut popularibus, Lege cautum est,ne darentur in Theatro, Ludis, sin fieret secus, praeco, qui praeconium fecisset, infamia notabatur:
units.tr: When crowns were given by fellow-tribesmen or fellow-demesmen, the law provided that they were not to be given in the theatre at the Games; if it were done otherwise, the herald who made the proclamation was marked with infamy.

units.la: Μὴ ἐᾶν τὸν φυλέτην μὲ δήμωσ ἀναγορεῦσαι στεφανωθέντα ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ · μὲ ἀπιμεν ἔτ κήρυκα.[?] Qui corona à tribulibus aut popularibus donantur, ne donantor in Theatro, Ludis; si secus factum, praeco ignominiosus esto.
units.tr: "Let not a fellow-tribesman proclaim a man crowned by the demesmen in the theatre; if he does, let the herald be disgraced." [Μὴ ἐᾶν τὸν φυλέτην μὲ δήμωσ ἀναγορεῦσαι στεφανωθέντα ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ · μὲ ἀπιμεν ἔτ κήρυκα.] Those crowned by fellow-tribesmen or fellow-demesmen are not to be crowned in the theatre at the Games; if it is done otherwise, the herald is to be disgraced.

units.la: Μέμνηται Λέγης Αἰσχίνης Ὀρατιόνε ἰαμ σαπίυς λαυδατα ἐν Κτησιφῶντ. [?] Greek passage continues in the printed Greek, partly illegible at this resolution: Τὴν μὲν τοῦ Τεταρτωδῶν ... ἀνεὶ τοῦ φυλέτου ... [illegible, ~120 letters]. Ἐπειδὰν δὲ ... ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ ... [illegible, ~80 letters].
units.tr: Aeschines the orator mentions this law in his speech against Ctesiphon: "...the first part of the Tetartoidon ... [the tribesman] ... and when ... in the theatre ..." [Μέμνηται Λέγης Αἰσχίνης ... ἐν Κτησιφῶντ. Τὴν μὲν τοῦ Τεταρτωδῶν ... ἀνεὶ τοῦ φυλέτου ... Ἐπειδὰν δὲ ... ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ ...]

units.la: Ita que qui corona donabantur à populae ibus, donabantur in ipso populo. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ στεφάνῳ ... ἐν ἰδίοις δήμοις.[?]
units.tr: Therefore those who were crowned by the People were crowned in the People itself. Demosthenes, in the same crown speech: "... in their own demes."

units.la: At si quis priuatim ab alio corona donaretur, donari non poterat, nisi in Senatu, aut in concione, aut in tribu, aut in populo, ex hac Lege: Μηδὲ ... Ἀ nemine alio q uisquam corona donetur, nisi in Senatu, aut in concione, aut inter tribules, aut inter populares.
units.tr: But if someone was crowned privately by another, he could not be crowned except in the Senate, in the assembly, in the tribe or among the People, according to this law: "Let no one be crowned by anyone except in the Senate, in the assembly, among his fellow-tribesmen, or among his fellow-demesmen."

units.la: Meminit Legis Æschines ἐν τῷ Κτησιφῶντ. παρασαπίπη δὲ ἐν τῷ σ[?]. Μηδὲ ἄλλῳ μηδενὶ ἀναχηρύττεσθαι, ἀπὸ τοῦς βουλῆς, καὶ δήμῳ, καὶ φυλέτῃ, καὶ δημοτῇ.
units.tr: Aeschines mentions the law in his speech Against Ctesiphon: "...and let no one be proclaimed by anyone else, except by the Council, the People, the tribe or the deme." [Μηδὲ ἄλλῳ μηδενὶ ἀναχηρύττεσθαι, ἢ τῇ βουλῇ, καὶ δήμῳ, καὶ φυλέτῃ, καὶ δημότῃ.]

units.la: Verum hospitales coronae ciuibus Athenien-sibus ab exteris ciuitatibus donabantur, idque in Theatro, Ludis, si id sciuisset populus Atheniensis: atque ita hac Lege, quam Διονυσιακὸν νόμον dixit Æschines, cautum est: Μὴ κηρύττεσθαι τὸ ἀλλότριον στέφανον ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ, ἐαν μὴ ψηφίσηται ὁ δῆμος· ἀὐτὸν δὲ τὸν στέφανον ἱερὸν εἶναι τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς. Nemo ab exteris ciuitatibus corona donator in Theatro, Ludis, nisi id sciuerit populus. Corona Mineruae sacra esto.
units.tr: Indeed, hospitality crowns were given to Athenian citizens by foreign cities, and these were proclaimed in the theatre at the Games, provided the Athenian People knew of it. And so the law, which Aeschines calls the Dionysiac law, provides: "A foreign crown is not to be proclaimed in the theatre unless the People has voted for it; the crown itself is sacred to Athena." [Μὴ κηρύττεσθαι τὸ ἀλλότριον στέφανον ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ, ἐὰν μὴ ψηφίσηται ὁ δῆμος· αὐτὸν δὲ τὸν στέφανον ἱερὸν εἶναι τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς.] No one is to be crowned by foreign cities in the theatre at the Games unless the People knows of it. The crown is to be sacred to Minerva.

units.la: Legem laudat Æschines ἐν τῷ Κτησιφῶντ. καὶ ἀλλὰ τῶν παρασ[?] ... νόμου ἐπέγειρ, καλῶσα αἱ ἀναγορεύειν τὸν ἀλλότριον ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ, ἐαν μὴ ψηφίσηται ὁ δῆμος, Αἰχίνης ... ἐπὶ τὴν πολιτικὴν αὐτὸν εἶ φησι, ἀλλὰ ταῦ τὴν ξενικὴν στέφανον (adde ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ) ἐαν ψηφίσηται ὁ δῆμος, ἀπομνημονεύει αὐτοῖς ... ναί· εἶχα οὐ τὴς δὴν πόλις στεφανοῖ. Anonymus in Argumento Orationis Æschinis: ... ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ, ἐαν ψηφίσηται ὁ δῆμος, Αἰχίνης ... ξενικὴν στέφανον. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ στέφανον. ὅσους στεφανοῦσι ἕως τὸν δῆμον, τὰς ...[?] ἀτιμάζεσθαι τὴν στέφανον ποιεῖσθαι ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐκτὸς τῆς ἰδίοις δήμοις, ἐαν μὴ τινας ὁ δῆμος ὁ τῆς Ἀθηναίων, ἢ ἡ βουλὴ στεφανοῖ, τούτους δὲ ἐξεῖναι ἐν τῷ ξένῳ Διονυσίοις ἀναγορεύεσθαι. Sed abutitur Orator hoc Legis Kapite: nam reuera intelligendum est de hospitali corona. Vlpianus: Τούτους ἢ ἀναγορεύεσθαι ἐν τῷ ξένῳ Διονυσίοις ὁ κήρυξ, οὓς ἂν ὁ δῆμος ἕλληται, ἢ ἡ βουλή· ἰσχον ἢ ὅτι τῷ ξενικῷ ὁ νόμος ζῶντα δείρηκεν. Argumento est, quod hae coronae, quae dabantur in Theatro Ludis, hac Lege Mineruae erant sacrae, quia videlicet hospitales erant. Æschines: αὐτὸν τὸν ξεύσων στέφανον, ὃς αἱ ἐν τῷ ἡ ἐν τῷ ἀγῶνι ἐν ἀσφ αἰσχρῆς ἱερὸν ἔτι τῆς Ἀθηναῖς καλῶς ὁ νόμος, ἀφελόμενος τὸν στέφανούμενον. καὶ τοι τῆς ἂν ὑμῖν ἐλλιπῶς ἔ αἰκελώθειαν καταγρακάν τῆς δήμου τῶν Ἀθηναίων· μὴ γὰρ ὅτι πόλις· ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ ἀν ἰδιώτης ὁ ἂν ἐς ἕτως ἀ̣̣χρης γ̣ίο̣ιτο, ὥστε ὃν αὐτὸς ἔδωκε στέφανον, ἀ-μὴ ἀ-ἀκηρύττειν, ἢ ἀφαιρεῖσθαι, ἢ κηδεύειν. ἀλλ᾽, οἶμαι, ἀλλὰ ὁ ξενικὸν ἐὰν τὸν στέφανον, ἢ καθιερῶσ γ̣ώ̣π̣η̣σ̣ιν, ἵνα μ̣υ̣θ̣ι̣ς̣ ἀ̣λ̣λ̣ο̣τ̣ε̣ί̣ο̣υ̣ ἄ̣ν̣ο̣ι̣α̣ν̣ ̣ ... ἐκ κηρύσσω ... Ciuitas, quae vellet ciuem Athenienfem corona donare, id iuris per Legatos sibi concedi petebat. Æschines verbis iam ante laudatis: ἵνα ἡ πόλις βουλομένη τινὰ τῶν ὑμετέρων στεφάνων, ἐπέσχε πυλάσαι, ἐπίσ-τ-η-σ-ε τῆς δήμου.
units.tr: Aeschines praises this law in his speech against Ctesiphon. Among other things, it orders that another's crown is not to be proclaimed in the theatre unless the people has voted for it. Aeschines says it applies to the civic crown, but the foreign crown (add "in the theatre") is to be proclaimed if the people votes for it. Anonymus, in the Argument to Aeschines' speech, [illegible] … [the law of] the foreign crown. Demosthenes, in the same passage, says that those whom the people or the Council crowns are to be proclaimed in the theatre at the Dionysia, and that the crown must not be treated as dishonourable outside their own demes, unless the people of Athens or the Council crowns them. Yet the orator abuses this chapter of the law, for it must in truth be understood of the hospitable crown. Ulpian: the herald is to proclaim in the theatre at the Dionysia those whom the people or the Council has chosen; and the law plainly speaks of the hospitable crown. The evidence is that those crowns given in the theatre at the games were, by this law, sacred to Minerva, because they were of the hospitable kind. Aeschines: [the law] calls the crown of the stranger sacred to Athena, which is given in the theatre or in the contest, and it forbids that a crown be taken away from one who has been crowned [illegible]. And indeed it would be a shameful thing for you to abuse the people of Athens in this way; for not only a city, but not even a private citizen, would be so shameless as to proclaim, take away or dishonour a crown that he himself has given. [Illegible, but it concerns] the crown given to a stranger, or its dedication … to proclaim. The city which wished to give a crown to an Athenian citizen asked, through its envoys, that this right be granted to it. Aeschines, in the words already quoted: that the city, wishing to crown one of your citizens, should be allowed to do so with the people's consent.

units.la: Qui corona donandus erat hospitali, rationem anteactae vitae reddebat, qua probaret dignum se esse, cui hic honos haberetur:
units.tr: The man who was to be given the hospitable crown gave an account of his past life, by which he proved that he was worthy to receive this honour.

units.la: Τὸν στεφανούμενον ξενικῷ στεφάνῳ τὸν λόγον ποιεῖσθαι, εἰς βίον ἀξιόλογεον καὶ ἔπειτα ὠ-φ-ε-ρ-ό--ν-α.
units.tr: The man to be crowned with the hospitable crown should give an account of his life, that it be creditable, and then beneficial. [Τὸν στεφανούμενον ξενικῷ στεφάνῳ τὸν λόγον ποιεῖσθαι, εἰς βίον ἀξιόλογον καὶ ἔπειτα ὠφέλιμον]

units.la: Qui corona donandus est hospitali rationes vitae honeste & temperanter acta reddito.
units.tr: The man who is to be given the hospitable crown must render an account of a life lived honourably and temperately.

units.la: Legis meminit Æschines Orationė laudata: ὅταν οὖν λάβωσι Ῥήτωρ ξενικῷ στεφάνῳ καὶ χρυσῷ ἐν τῇ Ἑλληνι ἀπογεγραμμένα, ἐπιμάλλον αὐτὸν καλὸς εἶναι, καὶ τὸν λόγον, τὰς βεβαιώσεις τῆς χρυσῷ, ὥσπερ ὁ νόμος καλῶς, ποιεῖσθαι, εἰς βίον ἀξιό-λογ-εον, καὶ ἔπειτα ὠ-φ-ε-ρ-ό--ν-α. Si vitam suam approbasset, populus scitum faciebat, quo posset corona, Mineruae postea consecranda, donari in Theatro, Liberalibus τοῖς κατ᾽ ἀγῶν.
units.tr: Aeschines, in the speech cited above, mentions this law: "When therefore an orator receives the hospitable crown and a golden one, inscribed in Greek, it is incumbent upon him to be honourable, and to make the speech, the confirmation of the gold, as the law rightly says, in a life worth recounting, and then beneficial." If the people approved his life, it passed a decree by which the crown, to be dedicated to Minerva afterwards, could be given in the theatre at the Liberalia, at the games.

units.la: Demum inter praemia referenda est excusatio munerum, ἀπαλλαγὴ τῶν λῃτουργιῶν, non quidem omnium, vt praecedenti Titulo à nobis dictum est, sed tantum ποιῆς ἐξῳλῶν, quam impetrabant ab Athenienfibus viri de iis bene meriti: At vero Leptines Legem scripsit, qua cauetur, vt irrita sint populi dona, quibus concesserat ἀπαλλαγὴ benemeritis, neue quis in posterum petat excusationem munerum à populo: qui secus faxit, ignominiosus esto:
units.tr: Finally, among the rewards must be counted exemption from public services, ἀπαλλαγὴ τῶν λειτουργιῶν. This was not, as said in the preceding Title, exemption from all of them, but only from certain of them, which men who had deserved well of the Athenians were accustomed to obtain. But Leptines wrote a law by which the gifts of the people, granting exemption to the well-deserving, were to be made void, and by which no one was to seek exemption from public services from the people in future. Whoever acted otherwise would be disgraced.

units.la: ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΓΑΟΥΣΙΩΤΑΤΟΙ ΛΕΙ-ΤΟΥΡΓΟΥΣΙ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ ΑΤΕΛΗ ΕΙ-ΝΑΙ, ΠΛΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΦ᾽ ΑΡΜΟΔΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΙΣΤΟΓΕΙΤΟΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ, ΜΗΔΕ ΤΟΛΟΙ-ΓΟΝ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΤῷΙ ΔΗΜῷΙ ΑΙΤΗ-ΘΕΝΤΙ ΔΙΔΟΝΑΙ. ΕΙ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΑΛΛῷ ΑΙΤΩΝ ΑΤΙΜΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΓΕΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΟΙΚΙΑΝ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΟΚΕΙ-ΣΘΑΙ ΓΡΑΦΑΙΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΝΔΕΙΞΕΣΙΝ. ΕΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΕΝ ΤΟΥΤΟΙΣ ΑΛΛῷ ΕΝΟΧΟΝ
units.tr: [ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΠΛΟΥΣΙΩΤΑΤΟΙ ΛΕΙΤΟΥΡΓΟΥΣΙ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ ΑΤΕΛΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΠΛΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΠΟ ΑΡΜΟΔΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΑΡΙΣΤΟΓΕΙΤΟΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ, ΜΗΔΕ ΤΟΛΟΙΠΟΝ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ ΑΙΤΗΘΕΝΤΙ ΔΙΔΟΝΑΙ. ΕΙ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΑΛΛΩΙ ΑΙΤΩΝ ΑΤΙΜΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΓΕΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΟΙΚΙΑΝ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΟΚΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΓΡΑΦΑΙΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΝΔΕΙΞΕΣΙΝ. ΕΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΕΝ ΤΟΥΤΟΙΣ ΑΛΛΩ ΕΝΟΧΟΝ] The wealthiest should perform public services, and no one shall be exempt, except the descendants of Harmodius and Aristogeiton and the Nine Archons. Nor shall the people in future grant exemption to anyone who asks for it. If anyone is convicted of asking for it, he and his kin and his household shall be disgraced, and be liable to indictments and denunciations. And if he does in these matters anything that a disgraced man is not allowed to do …

units.la: Ditissimi quique munera obeunto: nemo immunis esto, exceptis Harmodij & Aristogitonis posteris, itemque Nonemuiris. Neque in posterum populus petenti excusationem munerum concedito. Si quis petere conuincatur, ignominiosus esto cum genere suo & familia: eumque si quid, quod ignominioso non licebat, faciat, deferre cui-
units.tr: Let the wealthiest perform public services; no one is to be immune, except the descendants of Harmodius and Aristogeiton, likewise the Nine Archons. Nor is the people to grant exemption in future to one who asks for it. If anyone is convicted of asking, he is to be disgraced together with his kin and family, and let anyone be allowed to lay information against him if he does something that a disgraced man may not do.

units.la: ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΑΥΤΟΙΣ ΟΙΣ- ΠΕΡ ΟΙ ΔΙΚΑΖΟΝΤΕΣ ΟΤΑΝ ΟΦΕΙ- ΛΟΝΤΕΣ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩι ΔΙΚΑΖΩ- ΣΙ. iuis ius esto. Conuictus multator eadem poena, qua ijs, qui inter erarios relati, iudices sedent.
units.tr: The same is to hold for those who judge, when they owe debts to the public treasury. Let the law be the same. A man convicted is to pay a fine, under the same penalty as those who, entered among the debtors to the treasury, sit as judges.

units.la: Legem hanc [illegible, ~9 letters] descripsit Anonymus in Argumento Orationis Demosthenis περὶς Λεπτίνην. Λεπτίνης ἐγραψε νόμον αὐτὸς ῥήματων ὅπως ἔχοντα.
units.tr: The Anonymous writer described this law in the Argument to Demosthenes' speech against Leptines. Leptines wrote a law with the following words:

units.la: ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΟΙ ΠΛΟΥΣΙΩΤΑΤΟΙ ΛΕΙΤΟΥΡΓΟΥΣΙ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ ΑΤΕΛΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ, &c.
units.tr: That the wealthiest should perform public services, and no one be exempt, &c.

units.la: Libanius in Argumento quoque eiusdem. [illegible, ~12 letters] τὴν Λεπτίνης νόμον εἰσηνέγκαν, εἰ μηδένα ἀτέλη, μήτε Ὀλυμπικὸν ἐξὸν εἰ τοῖς δήμῳ δωσεῖ. ἡ δὲ ἀτέλεια αὐτόσυμτε, παρ᾽ ἡν τὰ ἔσχατα. Meminit passim tota hac Oratione, quam dixit Demosthenes, vt hæc Leptinis Lex abrogaretur. Scripta est hæc Lex à Leptine anno primo Olympiadis centesimæ sextæ, qui Prætorem habuit Elpinem: id ita colligo. Orationem aduersus hanc Leptinæ Legem scripsit Demosthenes Archonte Athenis Callistrato. Dionysius Halicarnasseus Epistola ad Ammæum: ἡ ᾿Εξ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον ἐπεγεὶ ὅτι Καλλιστράτου Ἀρχοντος ὁ ἀτέλειαν, ὃν αὐτὸς διέξαγε, χρεῖσαντες ἀπὸ μὲν τῶν λόγων καὶ γραφικῶς. Callistrati Prætura incidit in annum secundum Olympiadis centesimæ sextæ. Anno autem à Lege hac scripta elapso, in Leptinem hanc dixit Orationem Demosthenes. Anonymus in eius Argumento. τὸ νόμου δὲν ὅπως ἔχοντος, ἐγεέ- λατη μὲν ὁ ἀντίπερ Βλλιπης Λεπτίνη, ὃς ἀπέθανε ἀρχὴν εἰσηλθῶν ἡ γραφῶ. κατὰ δὲ τεῖς χρόνος, ἡ γένος Λεπτίνης αἰλ᾽ υἱός. νόμως γὰρ ὧν τὸν γραψάντα νόμον, ἡ ψηφισμα, μὴ σαυτὸν, μὴ εἰ ᾿Ισ᾽ ἀ᾽ υπὸν. ὅμως ὅπως καὶ ὅτω τὸν νόμον ἔχω ποιῆσαι ἐς καὶ πλὴν σπουδῆς, καὶ οἱ γραφόντες ἐξω κινδύνων ὧσι, μὴ τὸν σαυτὸν ἐπίσ- κατάπλης Ἀφείλιον ὡς Βαλίπτου, ᾧ σύννομος Φορμίων ὁ Ῥήτωρ, καὶ Κτήσιππος ὁ ὡς Χαλεῖου, ᾧ σύννομος Δημοσθένης. Orationem hanc, vt diximus è Dionysio, habuit Demosthenes anno secundo Olympiadis centesimæ sextæ, Archonte Callistrato, cum anno ante scripta Lex esset à Leptine. Ergo Leptines Legem hanc scripsit anno primo Olympiadis centesimæ sextæ, Archonte Elpine: Sed diu non obtinuit, nam abrogata est. Dio Chrysostomus Oratione Rhodiaca. Λεπτίνης τὶς εἰσηνέγκε νόμον, ὡς χρῶ τὰς ἀτελείας ἀφέλεας τοῖς ἔχουσι τῶν δῆμον· δίχα τῆ ἀφ᾽ Ἀρμοδίου ἡ Λεισοχείνης Ὀλυμπικὸν ἐξεναι διδόναι μισθὸν ἢ δωρεαὶ ταύτῃ. τί δὲ ἐαὶ ὅπως; προσδεξάντα τὸν νόμον; ὑμῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐάλω γραφῆς. Nempe Demosthene orante, & alteram Legem rogante, hæc Leptinæ Lex abrogata est, anno secundo Olympiadis centesimæ sextæ, Callistrato Athenis Prætore. Aduersabatur enim huic veteri Legi:
units.tr: Libanius likewise, in his Argument to the same speech, [illegible] … that Leptines introduced a law that no one should be exempt, nor should the people grant the Olympic … to anyone. The exemption itself … [illegible]. Demosthenes mentions it throughout this whole speech, which he delivered so that this law of Leptines would be repealed. This law was written by Leptines in the first year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad, when Elpines was archon; I gather this as follows. Demosthenes wrote the speech against this law of Leptines when Callistratus was archon at Athens. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in his Letter to Ammaeus: in the same period, in the archonship of Callistratus, the exemption which he [Demosthenes] delivered, having used speeches and writings… Callistratus' archonship fell in the second year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad. Since the law had been written a year earlier, Demosthenes delivered this speech against Leptines. The Anonymous writer, in the Argument: the law being such as it was, Leptines was accused by Aphobetus, the opponent, who died after entering upon the office, or the indictment… But at the time, Leptines was not the author of the law but his son, for the law and the decree were not written by the man who proposed them … Aphobetus, son of Bulites, with whom Phormion the orator was associated, and Ctesippus, son of Chaleus, with whom Demosthenes was associated. As we have said, from Dionysius, Demosthenes delivered this speech in the second year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad, under the archon Callistratus, when the law had been written by Leptines the year before. So Leptines wrote this law in the first year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad, under the archon Elpines. But it did not last long, for it was repealed. Dio Chrysostom, in the Rhodian Oration: Leptines brought in a law that the exemptions should be taken away from those who had them, and that the Olympic … be given to the people; but by Harmodius' decree … it was not permitted to give the reward or gifts. Why? Did your law [come into force]? No, it was condemned by an indictment. Indeed, while Demosthenes was pleading and asking for another law, this Leptinean law was repealed, in the second year of the hundred and sixth Olympiad, with Callistratus as archon at Athens. For it opposed this old law:

units.la: TAC ΔΩΡΕΑC AC O ΔΗΜΟC EΔΩ- Populi dona rata sunto.
units.tr: The gifts which the people has given shall be valid.

units.la: KE KYPIAC EINAI.
units.tr: and be valid [καὶ κυρίας εἶναι].

units.la: Laudat hanc Legem Demosthenes in Leptinea: τὴν μὲν ὅτι ὧν τῆς ὅτι νόμοις κυρίοις ἀπαρχὴν κυλὸν, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, ἡ ὄφες, TAC ΔΩΡΕΑC, AC O ΔΗΜΟC ΕΔΩΚΕ, ΚΥΡΙΑC ΕΙΝΑΙ. Vlpianus: εἴπω αὐτὸς ἀναγνώσκεσθαι χρῆ ὃ σύνεγχε καὶ ἑτέρων νόμον ὀργάνων ἐν ᾧ χώπα. TAC ΔΩΡΕΑC, AC O ΔΗΜΟC ΕΔΩΚΕ, KYPIAC EINAI. & in Argumento eiusdem. ἔστι ἡ ὃ τοῦ ἀγών μα, ὅτι πρῶτον ὁ νόμος τοῦ, παλαιὸν νόμων, τὸν λέγοντα, τὰς δωρεὰς τῆς δήμου εἰ βεβαίας. Et certè si populum ciui vana spe lactare non licet, quanto minus populo licebit ciues magnis & præclara minantibus donis deludere? in quod tamen incurrerent, si irrita fierent populi dona. Præterea an non hoc esset de mortuis detrahere, dona illis illorumque posteris concessa abrogare? Et quæ, malum, importuna hæc esset religio, nolle populi dona esse rata, quibus, viris optime de Republica Atheniensi meritis honos habetur, cum cuiuis liceat honorem alteri, qui non sit ex eadem familia, ex eadem gente, habere, heredemque supremis testamenti tabulis scribere? At contra Legis huius auctor bono Reipublicæ init consultum, cum enim viros fortes, eorumque posteros, ob præclara edita facinora, maxima maneant præmia, an non ceteri his exemplis in antiquam virtutem animosque viriles excitarentur?
units.tr: Demosthenes praises this law in his speech against Leptines: "… the first of the laws of this kind, men of Athens, which stands as a valid law, … the gifts which the people has given shall be valid." Ulpian: it must be read as the law reads, and in another law of the same kind, where it says: "The gifts which the people has given shall be valid." And in the Argument to the same speech: the purpose of the case is that the first law, an old law, says that the gifts of the people are to be secure. And surely, if it is not lawful to beguile the people with vain hopes of a citizen, how much less will it be lawful for the people to be deluded by citizens promising great and splendid gifts? Yet they would fall into this if the people's gifts were made void. Moreover, would it not be to take away from the dead, to revoke gifts granted to them and their descendants? And what, in heaven's name, would be this troublesome scruple, to refuse that the gifts of the people be valid, by which honour is given to men who have deserved well of the Athenian commonwealth, when anyone may give honour to another who is not of the same family or the same kin, and write an heir in the last tables of his will? On the contrary, the author of this law has taken thought for the good of the commonwealth; for when brave men and their descendants keep great rewards for their outstanding deeds, would not others be roused by these examples to their ancient virtue and manly spirit?

units.la: Huic Legi innitens Demosthenes, Leptineam abrogare suasit, hancque alteram in eius locum rogavit.
units.tr: Relying on this law, Demosthenes urged the repeal of Leptines' law and proposed this second law in its place.

units.la: Τὰς δωρεὰς, ὅσας ὁ δῆμος ἔδωκε, χωρεῖς[?] τὰς δὲ ἔχοντας, κεῖσθαι, ἵν' εἰ μὲν ἀξιοι, ἔχοιεν, εἰ δὲ αἰαξιῶς ἐχὴν δοκιειν, ἐλεγχθέντες ἀφαιρεῖσθαι.
units.tr: The gifts that the people have bestowed: let those who hold them keep them, so that if they are deserving they keep them, but if they are seen to be unworthy, after being convicted they are taken away. [Τὰς δωρεὰς, ὅσας ὁ δῆμος ἔδωκε, χωρεῖς[?] τὰς δὲ ἔχοντας, κεῖσθαι, ἵν' εἰ μὲν ἀξιοι, ἔχοιεν, εἰ δὲ αἰαξιῶς ἐχὴν δοκιειν, ἐλεγχθέντες ἀφαιρεῖσθαι.]

units.la: Dona populi rata sunto. In eorum vitam, quibus concessa sunt, quæstio habetur: Dignis rata; indignis irrita sunto.
units.tr: Let the gifts of the people stand. An inquiry is held into the lives of those to whom they were granted: for the worthy let them stand; for the unworthy let them be void.

units.la: Legem hanc habet Anonymus in Argumento Leptineæ. Ἡ γὰρ ὁ Δημοσθένης βουλεταὶ νόμος· Τὰς δωρεὰς, ὅσας ὁ δῆμος ἔδωκε, χωρίας[?] τὰς δὲ ἔχοντας κεῖσθαι, ἵν' εἰ μὲν ἀξιοι, ἔχοιεν· εἰ δὲ αἰαξιῶς ἐχὴν δοκιειν, ἐλεγχθέντες ἀφαιρεῖσθαι. illamque tota hac Oratione suadet Demosthenes, & quidem merito, cum dignis bene esse, indignis non item, velit; rata enim facit populi dona post quæstionem habitam, & exactam αἰάκειον[?], ita ut indignis adimantur.
units.tr: The Anonymous author has this law in the Argument to the Leptinean: "For the law that Demosthenes proposes: the gifts that the people have bestowed, let those who hold them keep them, so that if they are deserving they keep them, but if they are seen to be unworthy, after being convicted they are taken away." [Ἡ γὰρ ὁ Δημοσθένης βουλεταὶ νόμος· Τὰς δωρεὰς, ὅσας ὁ δῆμος ἔδωκε, χωρίας[?] τὰς δὲ ἔχοντας κεῖσθαι, ἵν' εἰ μὲν ἀξιοι, ἔχοιεν· εἰ δὲ αἰαξιῶς ἐχὴν δοκιειν, ἐλεγχθέντες ἀφαιρεῖσθαι.] Demosthenes urges this law throughout this whole speech, and rightly so, since he wishes it to go well for the worthy but not for the unworthy. For he makes the gifts of the people stand only after an inquiry has been held and fully carried out, so that they are taken away from the unworthy.

units.la: DE GYMNASIIS. TITULUS SEPTIMUS.
units.tr: CONCERNING GYMNASIA. TITLE SEVEN.

units.la: Vanquam inter Magistratus locum non habeant Gymnasiarchæ, cum tamen plurium puerorum cura illis sit commissa, neque inter τοὺς ἰδιώτας[?] sint censendi, hoc loco Legem describemus, quæ de illis lata est, in hæc verba:
units.tr: Although gymnasiarchs do not hold a place among the magistrates, since the care of many boys is entrusted to them and they are not to be counted among private persons (τοὺς ἰδιώτας), I shall set out here the law that was passed concerning them, in these words:

units.la: ΟΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΟΙ ΑΝΟΙΓΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΤΑ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΕΙΑ ΜΗ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΗΛΙΟΥ ΑΝΙΟΝΤΟΣ, ΚΛΕΙΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΔΕ ΠΡΟ ΗΛΙΟΥ ΔΥΝΟΝΤΟΣ. ΚΑΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΤΟΙΣ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑΝ ΟΥΣΙΝ ΕΙΣΙΕΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΕΝΔΟΝ ΟΝΤΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΥΙΟΣ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΟΥ, Ἢ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΥ, Ἢ ΘΥΓΑΤΡΟΣ ΑΝΗΡ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΑΥΤ' ΕΙΣΙΗ, ΘΑΝΑΤΩΙ ΖΗΜΙΟΥΣΘΩ, ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡΧΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΡΜΑΙΟΙΣ
units.tr: "The teachers of the boys shall open their schools not before the sun rises, and shall close them before the sun sets. And no one who is beyond the age of boys shall be allowed to enter while the boys are inside, unless he is the son of a teacher, or a brother, or a son-in-law. If anyone enters contrary to this, let him be put to death. And the gymnasiarchs..." [ΟΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΟΙ ΑΝΟΙΓΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΤΑ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΕΙΑ ΜΗ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΗΛΙΟΥ ΑΝΙΟΝΤΟΣ, ΚΛΕΙΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΔΕ ΠΡΟ ΗΛΙΟΥ ΔΥΝΟΝΤΟΣ. ΚΑΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΤΟΙΣ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑΝ ΟΥΣΙΝ ΕΙΣΙΕΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΕΝΔΟΝ ΟΝΤΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΥΙΟΣ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΟΥ, Ἢ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΥ, Ἢ ΘΥΓΑΤΡΟΣ ΑΝΗΡ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΑΥΤ' ΕΙΣΙΗ, ΘΑΝΑΤΩΙ ΖΗΜΙΟΥΣΘΩ, ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡΧΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΡΜΑΙΟΙΣ]

units.la: Puerorum Præceptores ludum literarium ne aperiunto ante orientem Solem, claudunto vero ante occasum. Nemini liceto ætatem puerilem supergressō in ludum ingredi, quamdiu pueri in illo sunt: excepto filio Præceptoris, aut è fratre nepote, aut genero: si quis aduersus hanc Legem commiserit & in-gressus fuerit, morte luito. Gymnasiarchæ neminem prouectiori[?]
units.tr: Let the teachers of the boys not open the school before sunrise, but close it before sunset. Let no one who is past boyhood enter the school while the boys are in it, except the son of a teacher, or his brother, nephew, or son-in-law. If anyone enters in violation of this law, let him pay with his life. Let the gymnasiarchs allow no one older...

units.la: ΜΗ ΕΑΤΩΣΑΝ ΣΥΓΚΑΤΙΕΝΑΙ ΜΗ-ΔΕΝΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑ͵ ΤΡΟΠΩι ΜΗΔΕΝΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΡΗ͵ ΚΑΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΙΡΓΗ ΤΟΥ ΓΥΜΠΑΣΙΟΥ, ΕΝΟ-ΧΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ Ο ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡΧΗΣ ΤΩι ΤΗΣ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΩΝ ΦΘΟΡΑΣ ΝΟΜΩι. ΟΙ ΔΕ ΧΟΡΗΓΟΙ ΟΙ ΚΑΘΙΣΤΑΜΕ-ΝΟΙ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΕΣΤΩΣΑΝ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑΝ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΕΤΤΑΡΑΚΟΝ-ΤΑ ΕΤΗ.
units.tr: "...to join in, in any age or manner, to the Hermaea [ΜΗ ΕΑΤΩΣΑΝ ΣΥΓΚΑΤΙΕΝΑΙ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑ, ΤΡΟΠΩι ΜΗΔΕΝΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΡΗ, ΚΑΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΙΡΓΗ ΤΟΥ ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΟΥ, ΕΝΟΧΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ Ο ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡΧΗΣ ΤΩι ΤΗΣ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΩΝ ΦΘΟΡΑΣ ΝΟΜΩι. ΟΙ ΔΕ ΧΟΡΗΓΟΙ ΟΙ ΚΑΘΙΣΤΑΜΕΝΟΙ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΕΣΤΩΣΑΝ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑΝ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΕΤΤΑΡΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΗ.] If he permits it and does not expel him from the gymnasium, let the gymnasiarch be liable under the law on the corruption of free men. Let the choregi appointed by the people be over forty years of age."

units.la: ætate Mercurij festis diebus accedere vllo modo sinunto: Si secus fecerit, neque gymnasio expulerit Gymnasiarcha, Lege de ingenuorum corruptela tenetor. Choragi à populo designati annis quadraginta maiores sunto.
units.tr: On the festival days of Mercury let them in no way allow anyone of that age to come; if he does otherwise, and the gymnasiarch does not expel him from the gymnasium, he is bound by the law on the corruption of free-born men. Let the choragi appointed by the people be over forty years old.

units.la: Voluit hac Lege, quæ Legitur apud Æschinem ἐν πρὸς Τιμάρχου [?] statim initio, cautum Legislator puerorum Athenien-sium pudicitiæ: Quare definiuit primum, Ludum literarium aperiendum ad orientem Solem, claudendum esse ante occasum. Æschines: καὶ Διαρρήδην ἀπεδείξατο πρὸς τοὺς διδασκάλους [?] ἐπὶ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας [?] τοὺς παῖδας τοὺς ἐλευθέρους εἰς τὸ διδασκαλεῖον, ἐπειτα μὴ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους πρὸς ἡλίου εἰ-σιέναι· ἡ πρὸς ἡλίου ἀνίσχοντος. καὶ τοὺς διδασκάλους τὰ διδασκαλεῖα, ἡ τοὺς παιδοτρίβας τὰς παλαίστρας, αὐτοῖς μὲν ἀπαγορεύω μὴ πρὸ ἡλίου ἀνίσχοντος ἀνοίγειν, καὶ ἐλείπει δὲ ἡλίου δύσεως, τὰς ἐρημίας, ἡ ὅ σιώπης ἐν πόλει ὑποψία ποιου-μένης.
units.tr: By this law, which is read in Aeschines' speech against Timarchus at the very beginning, the lawgiver took care of the chastity of the boys of Athens. Accordingly he first laid down that the school must be opened at sunrise and closed before sunset. Aeschines says: "And he specified in writing that the teachers should admit the free boys to the school on those days, and then not admit anyone at sunrise or after sunset. And I forbid the teachers of the schools, and the trainers of the wrestling-schools (palaestrae), to open them before sunrise, and to close them after sunset, since in the city lonely places and silence give rise to suspicion." [καὶ Διαρρήδην ἀπεδείξατο πρὸς τοὺς διδασκάλους ἐπὶ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας τοὺς παῖδας τοὺς ἐλευθέρους εἰς τὸ διδασκαλεῖον, ἐπειτα μὴ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους πρὸς ἡλίου εἰσιέναι· ἡ πρὸς ἡλίου ἀνίσχοντος. καὶ τοὺς διδασκάλους τὰ διδασκαλεῖα, ἡ τοὺς παιδοτρίβας τὰς παλαίστρας, αὐτοῖς μὲν ἀπαγορεύω μὴ πρὸ ἡλίου ἀνίσχοντος ἀνοίγειν, καὶ ἐλείπει δὲ ἡλίου δύσεως, τὰς ἐρημίας, ἡ ὅ σιώπης ἐν πόλει ὑποψία ποιουμένης.]

units.la: Verba Legis hæc sunt. ΟΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΓΑΙΔΩΝ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΟΙ ΑΝΟΙΓΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΤΑ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΕΙΑ ΜΗ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΗΛΙΟΥ ΑΝΙΟΝΤΟΣ, ΚΛΕΙΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΔΕ ΠΡΟ ΗΛΙΟΥ ΔΥΝΟΝ-ΤΟΣ. Sed nusquam comparet in hac Lege Kaput, quo itidem cauebatur, ne Gymnasiarcha ante Solem orientem aperiret palæstram, neue post occasum clauderet, quare mutila est hoc Kapite, quod tamen adscriptum fuisse non sinunt nos dubitare hæc Æschinis verba: καὶ τοὺς διδασκάλους τὰ διδασκαλεῖα, ἡ τοὺς παιδοτρίβας τὰς παλαίστρας, αὐτοῖς μὲν ἀπαγορεύω μὴ πρὸ ἡλίου ἀνίσχοντος ἢ ἐπειδὰν ὁ ἥλιος δύῃ, κλείειν δὲ πρὸ ἡλίου ἀνίσχοντος [?]. Sequitur τῆς συμφωνήσεως τῶν παίδων, quos nempe, & qua ætate, iis oporteret in scholam, & in palæstram, qui item exesse iubeantur, quamdiu pueri ill c sunt. Æschines: καὶ Διαρρήδην ἀπεδείξατο τοὺς νεανίσκους τοὺς εἰσφοιτῶντας, οἷς τινας δεῖ εἶναι, καὶ ὡς τινας ἡλικίας ἐ-χοντας. Legis verba sunt: ΚΑΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΤΟΙΣ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΓΑΙΔΩΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑΝ ΟΥΣΙΑΝ ΕΙΣΙΕΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΕΝ-ΔΟΝ ΟΝΤΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΥΙΟΣ ΔΙΔΑΚΑΛΟΥ Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΥ, Η ΘΥΓΑΤΡΟΣ ΑΝΗΡ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΑΥΤ' ΕΙΣΙΗΙ, ΘΑΝΑ-ΤΩι ΖΗΜΙΟΥΣΘΩ. Quod hic habes de Præceptoribus in literis, idem quoque fuisse cautum de Gymnasiarchis nullus dubito, cum ex iis, quæ iam in superioribus obseruauimus, tum ex iis, quæ sequentur. An definitus sit numerus puerorum, qui in eundem ludum literarium, aut in eandem palæstram conuenirent, plane nescio, qui nondum promisi capillum, vt hariolari inciperem: videtur colligi ex his Æschinis verbis, quæ iam ante descripsimus: ἐπειτα μὴ πλειόνων παίδων εἶναι. sed alij legunt, μὴ πλείων παίδων, longe melius, meo quidem iudicio, si attendas ad sequentia, ἡ τοὺς νεανίσκους τοὺς εἰσφοιτῶντας, οἷς τινας δεῖ εἶναι, καὶ ὡς τινας ἡλικίας ἔχοντας. Ibant enim multi in communem ludum literarium eundem, aut palæstram, vt adnotat Plutarchus in Camillo. καίτοι γὰρ ἐχρῶντο πρὸς διδασκάλῳ, ὥσπερ Ἕλληνες, οἱ Φαλίσκοι, βουλόμενοι σωτηρ[?]ίας φεσθαι καὶ συναγωγάζεσθαι μετ' ἀλλήλων ἀδὸς ἐξ ἡχῆς τοὺς παῖδας. Nam δεῖ, inquit Aristoteles Polit. Lib. VIII. cap. I. τὴν κοινὴν χρείαν ποιεῖσθαι καὶ τὴν ἀσκησιν. Definita igitur à Legislatore, vt colliges facile ex eo quod, qui pueritiam supergressi sunt, adire ludum literarium aut palaestram, vetantur, eorum, qui in ludum literarium, aut palaestram, irent, aetas intra pueritiam, conditionis ingenuae & liberae, non seruili; vnde dixit Æschines, καὶ ἀλφαβὴτὸν ὑποδείκνυσι, ὥστε πολλοὺς ἂν ἔχειν... εἶναι τὸν παῖδα τὸν ἐλεύθερον εἰς ὃ διδασκαλον. Terentius Eunucho.
units.tr: The words of the law are these: "The teachers of the boys shall open their schools not before the sun rises, and shall close them before the sun sets." [ΟΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΓΑΙΔΩΝ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΟΙ ΑΝΟΙΓΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΤΑ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΕΙΑ ΜΗ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΗΛΙΟΥ ΑΝΙΟΝΤΟΣ, ΚΛΕΙΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΔΕ ΠΡΟ ΗΛΙΟΥ ΔΥΝΟΝΤΟΣ.] But nowhere in this law does the chapter appear in which it was likewise provided that the gymnasiarch should not open the wrestling-school before sunrise nor close it after sunset. The chapter is therefore mutilated; yet the following words of Aeschines do not allow us to doubt that it was written: "And I forbid the teachers of the schools, and the trainers of the wrestling-schools, to open before sunrise or after sunset, and to close before sunrise..." Next comes the provision about the boys: whom, and of what age, they ought to admit into the school and the wrestling-school, and likewise whom they must order to stay away while the boys are inside. Aeschines: "And he specified in writing the young men who come in, who they must be and of what age." The words of the law are: "And let no one who is beyond the age of boys enter while the boys are inside, unless he is the son of a teacher, or a brother, or a son-in-law. If anyone enters contrary to this, let him be put to death." What you have here about the teachers in letters, the same provision was certainly made about the gymnasiarchs; I doubt this not at all, both from what we have already observed above and from what follows. Whether a fixed number of boys was to meet in the same school or the same wrestling-school, I truly do not know, and I have not yet grown the hair to begin guessing. It seems to be inferred from these words of Aeschines, which we described earlier: "then not to be of more boys." But others read "not of more boys," far better in my judgment if you attend to what follows: "or the young men who come in, who they must be and of what age." For many went into the common school or wrestling-school, as Plutarch notes in the Life of Camillus: "For the Falisci, though they used a teacher as the Greeks did, wished to be saved and to be brought up together with one another, and they led the boys out in a common group." For, says Aristotle in Politics Book VIII chapter 1, "it is necessary to make common use and practice." Therefore the age of those who enter the school or wrestling-school was fixed by the lawgiver, as you may easily gather from the fact that those who have passed boyhood are forbidden to approach the school or wrestling-school. The age within boyhood was that of those of free and noble condition, not servile; whence Aeschines said: "and he prescribes the alphabet, so that many would have... the free boy to be with a teacher." Terence in the Eunuch:

units.la: Fac periculum in literis,
units.tr: Make trial in letters,

units.la: Fac in palaestra, in musicis: quae liberum
units.tr: make trial in the wrestling-school, in music: which it is fitting

units.la: Scire aequum est adolescentem.
units.tr: for a free young man to know.

units.la: At si quis ludum literarium, aut palaestram, dum ibi erant discipuli, praeter ludi magistri aut Gymnasiarchae filium siue generum, aut è fratre nepotem, ingrederetur, capite luebat: & Ludi magistri atque Gymnasiarchae, nisi eiecissent foras, Lege tenebantur τῆς ἐλευθέρων φθορᾶς. Quod vt religiosè obseruaretur ἐχχὴ ὧν ἡ τούτων ἐπιμελησομὴν. Magistratus hic videbat ne quid adversus hanc à Ludimagistris aut Gymnasiarchis committeretur Legem, etiam diebus Musarum festis, quae agitabant pueri in scholis, aut Mercurij, quae celebrabant in palaestris. Æschines : καὶ ἀλφαβὴτὸν ὁ νομοθέτης ὑποδείκνυσι, καὶ τοὺς νεανίσκους τοὺς εἰσφοιτῶντας, οὓς τινας δεῖ εἶ), καὶ ἀς ἡλικίας ἔχοντας, καὶ ἀρχὴν ἡ τῆς ἡλικίας ἢ τούτων ἐπιμελησομὴν· καὶ περὶ παιδαγωγῶν ἐπιμελείας, καὶ περὶ Μουσείων ἐν τοῖς διδασκαλείοις, καὶ περὶ Ἑρμαίων ἐν ταῖς παλαίστραις. Atque ex his vides, quanta labes facta sit in hac Legis descriptione, & quam multa excider-int, hodieque desint, quae olim legebantur. nihil enim hic habes de pueris, qui in palaestram ibant, οὓς τινας δεῖ εἶ), ἢ ἀς τινας ἡλικίας ἔχοντας. Atqui certum est, pueritiam non excessisse: nam hanc Legem scriptam esse περὶ τῆς διδασκαλίας τῶν παίδων, docet Æschines: igitur ista de Ludis literariis & Ludimagistris: ΚΑΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΤΟΙΣ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑΝ ΟΥΣΙΝ ΕΙΣΙΕΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΕΝΔΟΝ ΟΝΤΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΥΙΟΣ ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΟΥ, Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΥ, Η ΘΥΓΑΤΡΟΣ ΑΝΗΡ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΑΥΤ' ΕΙΣΙΗ, ΘΑΝΑΤΩΙ ΖΗΜΙΟΥΣΘΩ. mutato nomine de palaestra & Gymnasiarchis eadem dicenda sunt; praeterea nihil hic iam, quod olim lectum fuit, de Magistratu, qui horum curam gereret, καὶ περὶ παιδαγωγῶν ἐπιμελείας καὶ περὶ Μουσείων ἐν τοῖς διδασκαλείοις, superest tantum περὶ Ἑρμαίων ἐν ταῖς παλαίστραις. ista enim hodie leguntur in Lege: ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡΧΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΡΜΑΙΟΙΣ ΜΗ ΕΑΤΩΣΑΝ ΣΥΓΚΑΤΙΕΝΑΙ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑ, ΤΡΟΠΩ, ΜΗΔΕΝΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΨΗ, ΚΑΙ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΙΡΓΗ ΤΟΥ ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΟΥ, ΕΝΟΧΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ Ο ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡΧΗΣ ΤΩΙ ΤΗΣ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΩΝ ΦΘΟΡΑΣ ΝΟΜΩΙ. Sed etiam cauerat Legislator περὶ Μουσείων ἐν τοῖς Διδασκαλείοις. Agitabant pueri in scholis festum in honorem Musarum, Μούσηα dictum; agitabant & in palaestris in honorem Mercurij Ἑρμαῖα, & quidem per comessationes promiscuasque libidines, vt est in Diogenis Cynici Epistola: ἐν τῷ Γυμνασίοις, ὅταν ἡ πανήγυρις καλουμένῃ Ἑρμαῖα, πίνειν, ἀθύειν, σἰωνοσίας πειρᾶσθαι, ἐκ τῆς σαιτίων παρεχόμενα. Qua de causa noluit Legislator quenquam adultum diebus illis festis in palaestram. Magistratus autem hic, cuius curae erant commissa τὰ διδασκαλεῖα [?] καὶ τὰ γυμνάσια [?], dictus est Κοσμητὴς, de quo vetus Lapis Athenis in Gymnasio. ΕΠΙ ΘΕΩΝΟΣ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ ΚΟΣΜΗΤΟΥ ΔΙΟΝ ΥΣΙΟΥ ΜΑΡΚΟΣ ΑΝΑΦΑΥΣΤΙΟΣ ΓΕΙΜΝΑΣΙΑΡΧΗΣΑΣ.
units.tr: But if anyone entered the school or wrestling-school while the pupils were there, other than the son or the son-in-law of the schoolmaster or of the gymnasiarch, or a nephew from a brother, he paid with his life; and the schoolmasters and gymnasiarchs, unless they had driven him out, were held under the law on the corruption of free men. That this might be scrupulously observed, the magistrate of this, supervised that nothing be committed against this law by the schoolmasters or gymnasiarchs, even on the festival days of the Muses, which the boys celebrated in the schools, or of Mercury, which they celebrated in the wrestling-schools. Aeschines: "and the lawgiver prescribes the alphabet, and the young men who come in, who they must be and of what age, and the magistrate who has the care of these; and concerning the supervision of the paidagogoi, and concerning the Museia in the schools, and concerning the Hermaea in the wrestling-schools." And from this you see how great a corruption has been made in this description of the law, and how many things have fallen out, and are still missing today, which were once read. For here you have nothing about the boys who went into the wrestling-school, "whom they must be, or of what age." Yet it is certain they had not passed boyhood: for Aeschines teaches that this law was written "concerning the instruction of boys." Therefore those words about the schools and schoolmasters: "and let no one who is beyond the age of boys enter while the boys are inside, unless he is the son of a teacher, or a brother, or a son-in-law. If anyone enters contrary to this, let him be put to death." With the name changed, the same must be said of the wrestling-school and the gymnasiarchs. Besides, nothing is here now, as was once read, about the magistrate who had charge of these matters, "concerning the supervision of the paidagogoi and concerning the Museia in the schools"; only "concerning the Hermaea in the wrestling-schools" remains. For these words are read today in the law: "And let the gymnasiarchs not allow anyone of those in that age, in any manner, to join in the Hermaea. If he permits it and does not expel him from the gymnasium, let the gymnasiarch be liable under the law on the corruption of free men." But the lawgiver had also provided "concerning the Museia in the schools." The boys celebrated a festival in honour of the Muses in the schools, called the Mouseia; they also celebrated in the wrestling-schools a festival in honour of Mercury, the Hermaea, and indeed with drinking-parties and promiscuous lusts, as in the Epistle of Diogenes the Cynic: "In the gymnasia, when the festival called the Hermaea is held, to drink, to play, to attempt shameful acts, and to make a show of..." For this reason the lawgiver would not allow any adult into the wrestling-school on those festival days. The magistrate here, to whose care the schools and the gymnasia were committed, was called the Kosmetes, concerning whom an old stone at Athens in the gymnasium reads: "In the archonship of Theon, Dion, son of Ysios, Marcus Anaphaustios, gymnasiarch, [dedicated this] as Kosmetes."

units.la: Qui Gymnasiarcha simpliciter dicitur, τῷ παίδων [?] intelligitur, Magistratus Κοσμητὴς nomen additur, quia curae gymnasiorum erat praefectus. Habebant quoque Ephebi sua gymnasia, & suum Κοσμητὴν [?], de quo Erotianus in Lexico Hippocratis: κόσμου [?], τάξεως [?]. ἁρμονία [?] δὲ ἡ ἐν λέξει [?]. καὶ γὰρ κοσμίους λέγεσθαι τοὺς διὰ ἐξεῖς [?], καὶ Κοσμητὰς [?], τοὺς τῶν Ἐφήβων ὑπαξίας [?] παιδοτρόφους [?]. Sed in his Gymnasiis non eadem habebant μαθηταὶ [?] Ephebi, quas pueri in suis: iam enim sollertes erant in literis, in palaestra, in musicis, ut de Chaerea Ephebo dixit Terentianus Parmeno: neque haec addiscere illis amplius per oclum licebat: nam tunc toto ἐφηβείας [?] suae tempore [?] ἐπεισοδῶ [?] οἱ Ἐφηβοὶ πάνυ χρῶνται [?] ἐπιφυλάττοντες, ὥσπερ ἤδη μαθηταὶ τῶν [?] γραμματικῶν [?]. Quare etiam eorum μαθηταὶ erant γραμματικοὶ in Gymnasiis; unde auctor Axiochi scribit: ἐπειδὴ δὲ εἰς τοὺς Ἐφήβους ἐἰσγάφη [?], καὶ φόβος χείρων εἴη [?], καὶ Λύκειον [?], καὶ Γυμναστιαρχία [?]. Meminit Λυκείου, quia ibi ficiebant μαθηταὶ γραμματικοί. Interpres Comici ad Pacem: Λύκειον δὲ Γυμνάσιον Ἀθήνησιν, ὅπου παρὰ τὸ πολέμου ἐδόκουν γυμνάζεσθαι. Huius Gymnasiarchae Ephebo-rum, & Cosmetae mentio in veteri Lapide Venetiis olim è Græcia adducto. ΑΓΑΘΗ ΤΥΧΗ ΕΠΙ ΚΛ. ΑΤΤΑΛΟΥ ΑΡ ΧΟΝΤΟΣ, ΚΟΣΜΗΤΗΣ ΕΦΗΒΩΝ, ΙΕΡΕΥΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΘΕΑΣ, ΕΙΡΗΝΑΙ ΟΣ ΓΑΙΑΝΙΕΥΣ ΕΦΗΒΕΥΕΝ, ΑΥΤΟΥ ΥΙΟΣ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΙΟΣ ΕΙΡΗΝΑΙΟΥ ΓΑΙΑΝΙ ΕΥΣ ΕΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡ ΧΗΣΕΝ ΤΟΥ ΕΝΙΑΥ ΤΟΥ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΦΗΒΟΥΣ ΦΛ ΣΤΡΑΤΟΛΑΟΣ ΦΥΛΑΣΙΟΣ ΕΓΕΝΟΝ ΤΟ ΕΦΗΒΟΙ ΔΙΑΚΟ ΣΙΟΙ ΚΑΙ ΔΥΟ.
units.tr: One who is called simply Gymnasiarch is understood to be the gymnasiarch of the boys, while the title Cosmetes is added to the magistrate because he was the prefect in charge of the gymnasia. The ephebi also had their own gymnasia and their own Cosmetes. Erotianus, in his Lexicon on Hippocrates, speaks of this: of order, of arrangement; and harmony is the arrangement of words. For those who were called orderly (kosmioi) by their habits, and the Cosmetes, were the tutors of the ephebi in proportion to their rank. But in these gymnasia the ephebi did not have the same pupils that the boys had in theirs, for by then they were already skilled in letters, in wrestling and in music, as Terence's Parmeno says of the ephebe Chaerea, and they were no longer allowed to learn these things in the old way. For throughout their ephebic years the ephebi made much use of the lecture-rooms, as if they were already pupils of the grammarians. Hence the pupils of the grammarians were also in the gymnasia, and the author of the Axiochus writes: when he was enrolled among the ephebi, and fear grew worse, and the Lyceum and the gymnasiarchy... He mentions the Lyceum because the grammarians' pupils gathered there. The commentator on Aristophanes' Peace says: the Lyceum was a gymnasium at Athens, where people seemed to train for war. There is mention of this gymnasiarch of the ephebi and of the Cosmetes in an old inscription that was once brought from Greece to Venice. GOOD FORTUNE. UNDER CLAUDIUS ATTALUS, ARCHON; COSMETES OF THE EPHEBI; PRIEST OF GOD AND GODDESS; EIRENAIOS OF PAIANIA WAS EPHEBARCH; HIS SON DIONYSIUS, SON OF EIRENAIOS OF PAIANIA, WAS GYMNASIARCH; ... PHLAVIUS STRATOLAOS OF PHYLE BECAME... THE EPHEBI, TWO DEACONS.

units.la: Alter Lapis Athenis in Gymnasio. ΑΓΑΘΗ ΤΥΧΗ ΕΠ΄ ΚΛ. ΑΤΤΑΛΟΝ ΑΡ ΧΟΝΤΟΣ ΚΟΣΜΗΤΗΣ
units.tr: Another inscription at Athens, in the gymnasium. GOOD FORTUNE. UNDER CLAUDIUS ATTALUS, ARCHON, COSMETES.

units.la: ΕΦΗΒΩΝ ΙΕΡΕΥΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΘΕΑΣ ΕΙΡΗΝΑΙ ΟΣ ΠΑΙΑΝΙΕΥΣ ΕΦΗΒΕΥΕΝ ΑΝΤΩΝ-ΝΙΟΣ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΙΟΣ ΕΙΡΗΝΑΙΟΥ ΠΑΙΑΝΙ-ΕΥΣ ΕΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡ-ΧΗΣΕΝ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΙΑΝ-ΤΟΝ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΦΗΒΟΥΣ ΦΛ ΣΤΡΑΤΟΛΑΟΣ ΦΥΛΑΣΙΟΣ ΕΓΕΝΟΝ ΤΟ ΕΦΗΒΟΙ ΔΙΑΚΟ-ΣΙΟΙ ΚΑΙ ΔΥΟ.
units.tr: THE EPHEBI; PRIEST OF GOD AND GODDESS; EIRENAIOS OF PAIANIA WAS EPHEBARCH; ANTONINUS DIONYSIUS, SON OF EIRENAIOS OF PAIANIA, WAS GYMNASIARCH; PHLAVIUS STRATOLAOS OF PHYLE BECAME... THE EPHEBI, TWO DEACONS.

units.la: Pluribus paullo de his disputauimus, quia viri magni in his literis nominis non sine errore, confundunt hæc τῶν Ἐφήβων Γυμνασίαρχ cum illis τῶν παίδων. In his τῶν Ἐφήβων Γυμνασίαρχ (quod est satis ad tollendum errorem) versabantur ij homines, quos inanis gloriolæ [?]τitillaret, quo nimirum possent à iunioribus conspici, atque hunc ipsi sui honoris fructum perciperent, dum in se illorum ora conuerterent: hinc Æschines Demosthenem facit σιμινωδ[?]μον ἐν τῇ τῶν μειραχίων διδασκαλίᾳ. Theophrastus: καὶ ἐν ὁροισ[?]ίας, τῶν δὲ Γυμνασίων ἐν τούτοις διδασκαλίαν, ὧν αὐ Ἐφήβοι γυμνάζωνται. At in palæstras τῶν παίδων, ingredi cuiuis, qui hanc ætatem excessisset, erat capital, vt est in hac Lege. Postremum Legis Caput est de Choragis, de quibus præcedentibus titulis à nobis actum est: cautumque, vt quadraginta maiores sint. Æschines: καὶ ὁ τελωνῶν, ἐπὶ τῆς συμφοιτήσεως τῶν παίδων καὶ τῶν χορῶν τῶν ἐγκυκλίων. κελεύει γὰρ τὸν Χορηγὸν τὸν μίσθωτα τῷ οὐσίᾳ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς, διαλίσκειν, ἐὰν πεπαρακόντα ἐτη γεγονότα τὸν παιδοφθίην ἐν ἡλικία ἐν ἔτει ἐπιτρέφειν τοῖς ὑμετέροις παισί. Legis verba hæc sunt: ΟΙ ΔΕ ΧΟΡΗΓΟΙ ΟΙ ΚΑΘΙΣΤΑΜΕΝΟΙ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΕΣΤΩΣΑΝ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΚΙΑΝ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΕΤΤΑΡΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΗ. Harpocration ex Æschine, & Aristotele de Atheniensium Republica: ὅτι νόμος ὅστιν ἐὰν πεπαρακόντα ἐτη γεγονότα παισίν. Atque ita quidem olim: Nam desitum fuisse constat exemplis veterum: Ecce tibi eum, cui Orationem scripsit Lysias Ὑπλοτίας ἀπὸ ἀρχῆς, anno secundo Olympiadis nonagesimæ secundæ, Archonte Theopompo, in viros transscriptus est, annum agens vicesimum sextum, anno quarto Olympiadis nonagesimæ tertiæ, ἐπ' Ἀδεξίου Ἀρχῆς κατὰ τὸν Χορηγὸν παιδικῶν χορῶν, καὶ ἀνήλωσε πλέον ἢ πεντακισχίλια μνᾶς.
units.tr: We have discussed these matters at somewhat greater length, because certain great men in their writings, not without error, confuse the gymnasiarch of the ephebi with the gymnasiarch of the boys. The gymnasiarch of the ephebi (and this is enough to remove the error) was a man whom a vain little glory tickled, since he could no doubt be seen by younger men and gain for himself this fruit of honour, while he turned their eyes upon himself. Hence Aeschines makes Demosthenes a... in the teaching of the youths. Theophrastus: and in the gymnasia, the teaching of those among whom the ephebi exercise. But to enter the wrestling-schools of the boys was a capital offence for anyone who had passed this age, as is stated in this law. The last chapter of the law concerns the choregi, of whom we have spoken in the preceding titles, and it was provided that they should be forty years old or more. Aeschines: and the public contractor, in charge of the assembling of the boys and of the circular choruses. For he orders the choregus, the hired man, to pay with his own property to you, if he is not forty years old and in the prime of life, when he is entrusted with your boys. The words of the law are these: THE CHOREGI WHO ARE APPOINTED BY THE PEOPLE SHALL BE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE. Harpocration, from Aeschines and from Aristotle's work on the Athenian constitution: because there is a law that they must be over forty years old for the boys. And so it was indeed in former times, for the custom is known to have lapsed by the examples of the ancients. Look at the man for whom Lysias wrote the speech On the Hoplite Choregus... he was enrolled among the men in the second year of the ninety-second Olympiad, under the archon Theopompus, at the age of twenty-six; in the fourth year of the ninety-third Olympiad, under the archonship of Adeisios, as choregus of the boys' choruses, he spent more than five thousand minas.

units.la: ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΜΗ ΓΥΜΝΑΖΕΣΘΑΙ, ΜΗΔΕ ΞΗΡΑΛΟΙΦΕΙΝ ΕΝ ΤΑΙΣ ΠΑΛΑΙ-ΣΤΡΑΙΣ.
units.tr: ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΜΗ ΓΥΜΝΑΖΕΣΘΑΙ, ΜΗΔΕ ΞΗΡΑΛΟΙΦΕΙΝ ΕΝ ΤΑΙΣ ΠΑΛΑΙΣΤΡΑΙΣ. [A slave shall not exercise, nor anoint himself with dry oil, in the wrestling-schools.]

units.la: Serui se in palæstra neque exercento, neque unguento.
units.tr: A slave shall not exercise himself in the wrestling-school, nor anoint himself with dry oil.

units.la: Legem laudat Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμάρχου. οἱ πατέρες ὑμῶν ὅτι ἐὰν πεπαρακόντα ἐτη γεγονότα, καὶ τῷ ἐκ φύσεως δυσκινήτων καὶ ἀγαθῶν· ἐνομοθέτουν ἀ τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἡγεμῶνα εἶναι παιδεία, ὥστε τοῖς δούλοις ἀπεῖπον μὴ ποιεῖν. ΔΟΥΛΟΝ Φησὶν ὁ νόμος ΜΗ ΓΥΜΝΑΖΕΣΘΑΙ, ΜΗΔΕ ΞΗΡΑΛΟΙΦΕΙΝ ΕΝ ΤΑΙΣ ΓΑΛΑΙΣΤΡΑΙΣ. Soloni adscribit Plutarchus in Solone; καὶ νόμον ἐχρῆν [?] ἀφαιρεῖσθαι [?] ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΜΗ ΕΠΡΑΟΙΦΕΙΝ [?]. Idem in Amatorio. ὡς ὁ Σόλων δούλοις ξυνεχώρησε [?] φύσιν ἀπιέναι [?]. Qua lege liberos & ingenuos ad hæc studia vocat, quibus Seruis interdixit, vt optime argumentatur Plutarchus, ἡ ἔτι [?] τινὰ τοὺς ἀξίους [?] παρακαλεῖν [?] εἰς τοὺς ἀναξίους [?] ἀπιέναι [?]. quæ est quoque ratio Æschinis loco laudato: καὶ [?] ἐπὶ παρασκευῇ [?] τὸν δὲ ἐλεύθερον ἀλείφεσθαι [?] ἢ γυμνάζεσθαι [?]. ὅπως γὰρ οἱ νομοθέται [?] καλοὶ [?] ἐκ τῆς Γυμνασίων κατηδύνησε [?], ἀπιέναι τοῖς δούλοις μὴ μετέχειν [?], πολλὰ [?] ἀπὸ νόμῳ πρῶτον [?] ὡς ἐκείνους ἐκώλυον [?], τοῖς ἐλευθέροις παρεπέμπειν [?] ἐπὶ τὰ Γυμνάσια. Quinctiam neque pueris peregrinorum id concessum; colligo è populi scito, quod id datum est Coorum liberis propter Hippocratem. καὶ ἐξῆναι πᾶσιν Κῷων παισὶν ἐφοιτᾶν ἐν Ἀθήναις, καὶ ἐξῆναι πᾶσιν Ἀθηναίων.
units.tr: Aeschines cites the law in his speech Against Timarchus: your fathers, because men who were forty years old and naturally fit and good... laid down that education should be the guide of freedom, and so they forbade slaves to do it. The law says: A SLAVE SHALL NOT EXERCISE, NOR ANOINT HIMSELF WITH DRY OIL, IN THE WRESTLING-SCHOOLS. Plutarch, in his Solon, ascribes this to Solon: and it was necessary to take away the law, that a slave shall not anoint himself. The same author, in the Amatorius: since Solon allowed slaves to go away from nature. By this law he invites free and well-born men to these studies, and forbids slaves, as Plutarch argues well: whether still to summon the worthy to go away from the unworthy. This is also the reason in the passage of Aeschines quoted above: and for the preparation, the free man anoints himself or exercises. For the lawgivers, so that the gymnasia might be made honourable, forbade slaves to take part, and had many things first laid down by law, so that they hindered them, while they sent free men to the gymnasia. Nor was this privilege granted to the boys of foreigners; I gather this from the decree of the people, by which it was given to the children of the Coans on account of Hippocrates: and it was allowed to all Coan boys to attend school at Athens, and it was allowed to all Athenians...

units.la: DE MEDICIS ET PHILOSOPHIS. TITVLVS OCTAVVS.
units.tr: On Physicians and Philosophers. Title Eight.

units.la: Veteri olim Atheniensium Lege cautum fuerat, Ne quis seruus, neue qua femina, artem Medicam discerer.
units.tr: By an ancient law of the Athenians it was once provided that no slave and no woman should learn the medical art.

units.la: NE QVIS SERVVS NEVE QVA FEMINA ARTEM MEDICAM DISCITO.
units.tr: That no slave and no woman shall learn the medical art.

units.la: Legis meminit Hyginus in Fabularum Libro, docetque eam tandem antiquatam fuisse, alteramque suffectam fuisse, qua ingenuis feminis medicinam facere concedebatur. Hygini verba sunt: Antiqui obstetrices non habuerunt: unde mulieres verecundia ductæ interierant. Nam Athenienses cauerant, Ne quis seruus aut femina artem medicinam discerct. Agnodice quædam puella virgo concupiuit medicinam discere, quæ cum concupisset, demptis capillis, habitu virili, se Hierophilo cuidam tradidit in disciplinam: quæ cum artem didicisset, & feminam laborantem audisset ab inferiore parte, veniebat ad eam: quæ cum credere se noluissent, æstimans virum esse, illa tunica sublata, ostendebat se feminam esse, & ita eas curabat. Quod cum uidissent Medici, se ad feminas non admitti, Agnodicen accusare ceperunt, quod diceret eum glabrum esse, & corruptorem earum, & illas simulare imbecillitatem. Quo cum Areopagitæ consedissent, Agnodicen damnare ceperunt: quibus Agnodice tunicam alleuauit, & se ostendit feminam esse. & validius Medici accusare ceperunt, quare tum feminæ principes ad iudicium conuenerunt, & dixerunt: Vos coniuges non estis, sed hostes: quia quæ salutem nobis inuenit, eam damnatis. Tunc Athenienses Legem emendarunt, vt ingenuæ artem medicinam discerent. Est igitur prior Lex, quod ad feminas ingenuas spectat, abrogata, & hæc altera ei suffecta.
units.tr: Hyginus mentions this law in his Book of Fables, and he teaches that it was eventually abolished and another put in its place, by which free-born women were permitted to practise medicine. These are Hyginus's words: The ancients had no midwives, so women, held back by modesty, died. For the Athenians had provided that no slave or woman should learn the medical art. A certain maiden named Agnodice longed to learn medicine; and when she had set her heart on it, she cut off her hair, dressed as a man, and placed herself under a certain Herophilus as his pupil. When she had learned the art, and heard that a woman was suffering in the lower parts, she went to her. Since the women were unwilling to trust her, thinking her a man, she lifted her tunic and showed that she was a woman, and so she treated them. When the physicians saw this, seeing that they were no longer admitted to the women, they began to accuse Agnodice, saying that she was a beardless man and a seducer of them, and that the women feigned weakness. When the Areopagites had sat in judgment, they began to condemn Agnodice; whereupon Agnodice lifted her tunic and showed that she was a woman. And the physicians began to accuse her all the more vehemently; then the leading women came together to the court and said: "You are not husbands but enemies, since you condemn her who has found safety for us." Then the Athenians amended the law so that free-born women might learn the medical art. Therefore the earlier law, insofar as it concerns free-born women, was repealed, and this other law was substituted for it.

units.la: INGENVÆ FEMINÆ ARTEM MEDICINAM DISCVNTO.
units.tr: Let free-born women learn the medical art.

units.la: Quare secundum hanc Legem apud Terentium in palliata è Menandro Andria, Lesbia obstetrix quid facto opus sit, imperat:
units.tr: Accordingly, under this law, in Terence's Andria, a play in the Roman style taken from Menander, the midwife Lesbia gives orders about what must be done:

units.la: Adhuc Archillis quæ adsolent, quæque oportet, Signa esse ad salutem, omnia huic inesse video. Nunc primum fac, isthæc vt lauet: post deinde Quod iussi ei dare bibere, & quantum imperani, Date. moxego huc reuertar.
units.tr: So far I see that all the usual signs of a good outcome, as they should be, are present in her. Now first, see that she is washed; then afterwards give her what I told you to drink, and as much as I ordered. I will be back here soon.

units.la: Quin & Romani Obstetrices inter Medicos numerarunt, itaque de illarum, quemadmodum & Medicorum mercedibus, etiam extra ordinem ius dici scripsit Vlpianus Libro VIII. de omnibus Tribunalibus. Sed & obstetricem audiant, quæ vtique medicinam exhibere videtur: Medicos fortassis quis accipiet etiæ cos, qui alicuius partis corporis, vel certi doloris sanitatem pollicentur. vt puta si auricularius, si fistulæ, vel dentium. non tamen si incantauit, si imprecatus est, si (vt vulgari verbo impostorum vtar) si exorcizauit. non sunt istæ medicinæ genera, tamersi sint, qui hos sibi profuisse cum prædicatione adfirment. Lege I. §. II. & III. D. de Extraordinarijs cognitionibus. Pluscula descripsimus, quanquam ea omnia non sint de obstetricibus, vt aliquam illis præferamus lucem. Non enim tantum Christianos perstringit Vlpianus, quod exorcismis Dæmones de hominibus depellerent, sed etiam quia signando, unguendo, & imprecando morbos curabant Christiani. Tertullianus Libro ad Scapulam cap. IV. Ipse etiam Seuerus pater Antonini, Christianorum memor fuit. Nam & Proculam Christianam, qui Torpacion cognominabatur, Euhodea procuratorem, qui eum per oleum aliquando curauerat, requisiuit, & in palatio suo habuit vsque ad mortem eius: quem & Antoninus optime nouerat, lacte Christiano educatus. Putant Viri Clarissimi hunc Proculum Christianum eum esse, cuius meminit Capitolinus in Marco, & Eutychium Græce idem esse Afris Tobracon, siue Topracon, quomodo rescribi voluntapud Tertullianum: Euhodia autem Procuratorem interpretantur, τῆς διοικήσεως ϑησαυρικὸν[?], quod Itinerarij in Orbe Romano Rationarius esset ab Imperatore Marco constitutus, vt honestam functionem sine inuidia, & incommodo, periculoque, obtineret. Quapropter etiam Capitolinus factum affirmat fuisse Proconsulem, videlicet honorarium, itineris cundi causa. Sed ista ab eruditis viris nullo auctore asseruntur. Non negamus aliquando Procuratores appellari Prouinciarum Præsides, sed Itinerarij Rationarium & Procuratorem appellari Proconsulem nobis plane nouum, & hactenus non lectum, non auditum fuit. Appellatur igitur iste Proculus Euhodiæ Procurator, quia Euhodiæ feminæ satis notæ illo seculo res procurabat, & administrabat: tantum abest, vt sit Proculus ille Marci in Grammaticis præceptor, quem in tantum gratus Imperator dilexit, vt vsque ad Proconsulatum prouexerit oneribus in se receptis. Euhodia nomen feminæ esse constat ex hac Inscriptione, quæ Romæ visitur in monte Caballo, & legitur apud Gruterum:
units.tr: Indeed the Romans also counted midwives among the physicians; and so Ulpian, in Book VIII of On All Tribunals, wrote that justice is to be administered outside the ordinary course in matters concerning their fees, as well as those of physicians. Let them also hear a midwife, who certainly seems to provide medical care. One would perhaps accept as physicians even those who promise health for some part of the body or a particular ailment, such as an ear specialist, a specialist in fistulas, or in teeth. But not if someone has used incantations, has invoked, or (to use the common word for impostors) has exorcised. These are not kinds of medicine, even if there are those who boastfully affirm that they have benefited from them. See Digest, law 1, §§ II and III, De extraordinariis cognitionibus. We have quoted more than enough, although not all of it concerns midwives, so that we may throw some light on them. For Ulpian is not only censuring Christians because they drove demons out of people by exorcisms, but also because Christians cured diseases by signing, anointing and invoking. Tertullian, To Scapula, chapter 4: Severus himself, the father of Antoninus, was mindful of Christians. For he also sought out Procula, a Christian woman who was called Torpacion, and Euhodia the procurator, who had once cured him with oil, and kept her in his palace until her death; Antoninus too knew her very well, having been reared on Christian milk. The most distinguished men think that this Christian Proculus is the one mentioned by Capitolinus in his life of Marcus, and that Eutychius in Greek is the same as Tobracon among the Africans, or Topracon, as they wish it to be corrected in Tertullian. Euhodia they interpret as procurator of the administration of the treasury [τῆς διοικήσεως θησαυρικὸν], since he was a travelling accountant in the Roman world, appointed by the Emperor Marcus so that he might hold an honourable office without envy, trouble or danger. Wherefore Capitolinus also affirms that he was made proconsul, that is, an honorary title, for the sake of his travels. But these things are asserted by learned men without any authority. We do not deny that sometimes the governors of provinces were called procurators, but that an itinerant accountant and procurator should be called proconsul is entirely new to us; until now we had neither read nor heard of it. This Proculus, then, is called procurator of Euhodia, because in that age he managed and administered affairs for Euhodia, a woman well known at the time. So far is that Proculus from being the grammar-teacher of Marcus, whom the grateful emperor loved so much that he advanced him to the proconsulship, with the burdens he had undertaken. That Euhodia is a woman's name is clear from this inscription, which is seen at Rome on the Monte Cavallo and is read in Gruter:

units.la: D. M. HERMES EVHODIÆ CONIVGI SVÆ BENE MERENTI.
units.tr: To the spirits of the departed: Hermes, to Euhodia his wife, who well deserved it.

units.la: Et forte Euhodia hæc Tertulliani erat filia Euhodi Imperatoris Seueri Liberti, qui fuit [illegible, ~8 letters], vt appellat Dio, Antonini filij Seueri. Libertum autem Euhodiæ Proculum hunc fuisse suspicor, & ab Euhodia patrona rebus suis administrandis & procurandis admotum: Qui, vt puto, dum seruitutem seruiebat, alipilarij munus implebat: unde ei cognomen Dropacion: ita enim nobis rescribendum videtur apud Tertullianum: Est enim in veteribus Lexicis, [illegible, ~20 letters], Læuabant enim vnguento dropace. Sed ad rem. Idem Tertullianus Scorpiace scorpij virus, quod figendo effudit in vulnus, curari. Nobis, inquit, fides præsidium, si non & ipsa percutitur diffidentia signandi statim, & adiurandi, & vnguendi bestiæ calcem. hoc denique modo etiam Ethnicis sæpe subuenimus. Fiebat hæc adiuratio cum imprecatione: vnde paullo post Tertullianus: At, tu, fides si vigilat, ibidem Scorpio pro solea anathema inlidito, & relinquito in suo sopore morientem. Atque ita imprecabantur exemplo Christi, de quo Lucas IV. 39. cum Petri socrum à febri liberaret: [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters]. Quod verò exi-stimant Viri summi, vsitatum fuisse apud Ethnicos etiam Dæmonas exorcizare, nullo modo probare possumus, nam Tertullianus, quem vnum auctorem laudant, eo loci, de Christiano agit, non de Ethnico. Verba præstantissimi Scriptoris sunt Libro de Idololatria cap. XI. Ipsius fidei conscientiam perrogemus, quo ore Christianus thurarius, si per Templa transfibit, quo ore fumantes aras despuit, & exsufflabit, quibus ipse prospexit? Qua constantia exorcizabit alumnos suos, quibus domum suam cellariam præstat. Thurarij Christiani alumnos vocat Dæ-mones Tertullianus, quia odores, quos vendit, pabula sunt Dæmonum.
units.tr: Perhaps this Euhodia was the daughter of Tertullian's Euhodus, the freedman of the Emperor Severus, who was [illegible], as Dio calls him, of Antoninus, the son of Severus. I suspect that this Proculus was a freedman of Euhodia and was brought in by his patroness Euhodia to manage and administer her affairs. While he was still in servitude, I think, he performed the office of alipilus (depilator), and so he had the surname Dropacion, for that is how I think we must emend the reading in Tertullian. In the old lexicons there is [illegible], because they anointed with the ointment dropax. But to the point.
