The same Tertullian, in the Scorpiace, says that the venom of a scorpion, which it has poured into the wound by its sting, is cured. "For us," he says, "faith is a safeguard, if the very diffidence is not struck down at once by making the sign of the cross, by adjuration, and by anointing the scorpion's heel. Indeed, in this way we have often helped even the heathen." This adjuration was made together with a curse. Hence, a little later, Tertullian says: "But you, faith, if you are awake, strike the scorpion with a curse as with a sandal, and leave it dying in its sleep." And so they cursed, following the example of Christ, of whom Luke writes (4:39) when he freed Peter's mother-in-law from fever, [illegible] [illegible]. But as to what those eminent men think, that it was customary among the heathen also to exorcise demons, we cannot prove this in any way. For Tertullian, the one author they cite, speaks in that passage of a Christian, not of a heathen. The words of that most distinguished writer are in the book On Idolatry, chapter 11: "Let us question the very conscience of the believer: with what mouth will a Christian incense-seller, if he passes through the temples, with what mouth will he spit out and blow away the smoking altars, by which he himself has stood? With what constancy will he exorcise his own clients, for whom he keeps his storeroom?" Tertullian calls the clients of the Christian incense-seller demons, because the perfumes he sells are the food of demons.

units.la: Medici, qui vellent Athenis medicinam artem publice facere, à populo id consequebantur, qui eos eligebat. Xenophon [illegible, ~12 letters] Libro IV. [illegible, ~150 letters]. Sed gratis medicinam faciebant à populo creati: Aristophanes Acharnensibus:
units.tr: Physicians who wished to practise medicine publicly at Athens obtained this right from the people, who chose them. Xenophon [illegible], Book IV [illegible]. But physicians who had been appointed by the people practised medicine for free. Aristophanes, in the Acharnians:

units.la: ΓΕΩΡ. [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: GEORGIUS [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~35 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: ΔΙΚ. Ἀλλ' ὦ πόνηρ' ἢ δημοσίων τυγχάνω, [?]
units.tr: DIKAIOPOLIS: But, you wretch, I happen to be in public service. [Ἀλλ' ὦ πόνηρ' ἢ δημοσίων τυγχάνω]

units.la: ΓΕΩΡ. Ἢ αἰτιοῖλά σ' ὡς πως κομισῶμαί τὸ βοῦς. [?]
units.tr: GEORGIUS: Or I will accuse you somehow, so that I may recover my oxen. [Ἢ αἰτιοῖλά σ' ὡς πως κομισῶμαί τὸ βοῦς]

units.la: ΔΙΚ. Οὐκ ἔστιν, ἀλλὰ χλαῖνε παρὰ τὴς Πιτάλου. [?]
units.tr: DIKAIOPOLIS: No, but take a cloak from Pitalus's [wife]. [Οὐκ ἔστιν, ἀλλὰ χλαῖνε παρὰ τὴς Πιτάλου]

units.la: Scholia: δημόσια χλαμυδηφόροι ἰαβὴ καὶ δημόσιοι [?] ἐπιτιμῶντας ἐπεπάλου. [?] In his, puto, Aristophanis aetate, discipuli Pittali: παρὰ τῆς Πιτάλου. ὁ Πίττα̃λος ἔστ' ἰαβῆς ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀ[?]ως, λείπει δὲ τὰς μαθητάς. [?] Huius Pittali meminit idem Comicus Vespis.
units.tr: Scholia: "public... cloaked... [and] public ... rebuked." In these lines, I think, Aristophanes' time had pupils of Pittalus: "from Pitalus's [wife]. Pittalus is a Iambic [poet] from [illegible], but he lacks the pupils." [Παρὰ τῆς Πιτάλου. ὁ Πίττα̃λος ἔστ' ἰαβῆς ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀ[?]ως, λείπει δὲ τὰς μαθητάς.] The same comic poet mentions this Pittalus in the Wasps.

units.la: Apud Atheniensēs summo, ut par est, in pretio fuit Philosophiae studium, ad quod animum adiungere solebant adolescentuli, ut ex his Terentij Andria constat:
units.tr: Among the Athenians, as is fitting, the study of philosophy was held in the highest esteem, and young men were accustomed to devote themselves to it, as is clear from this passage in Terence's Andria:

units.la: Quod plerique omnes faciunt adolescentuli, Vt animum ad aliquod studium adiungant, aut equos Alere, aut canes ad venandum, aut ad Philosophos, Horum ille nihil egregie praeter cetera Studebat, & tamen omnia haec mediocriter.
units.tr: Most young men do this: they apply their minds to some study, either keeping horses, or dogs for hunting, or to the philosophers. He studied none of these outstandingly beyond the rest, yet he did all of them moderately.

units.la: Factum tamen est aliquando, ut Philosophiam docere Legibus sit interdi-ctum. Sed Critia è Triginta Tyrannis ferocissime dedicatore damnationis suae gloriantur Philosophi. Qui enim scit illum, intelligere potest nonnisi grande aliquod bonum à Critia damnatum, cuius in ceteros odio Socratis Philosophos ferocientis Lex fuit:
units.tr: It did happen, however, at one time that teaching philosophy was forbidden by law. But the philosophers boast of the damnation of Critias, the most fierce of the Thirty Tyrants, who was its author. For whoever knows that man can understand that no great good was condemned by Critias, whose hatred of the others, and of Socrates' philosophers in their boldness, produced this law.

units.la: Λόγον τίχλω μὴ διδάσκειν. Philosophiam ne quis doceto.
units.tr: "Let no one teach words." Let no one teach philosophy. [Λόγον τίχλω μὴ διδάσκειν]

units.la: Legem refert Xenophon Ἀπομνημονευμάτων Libro I. ἐξ ὧν δὴ ἡ ἐμοὶ τῷ Σωκράτει ὁ Κείπας ὥστε ἢ ὅτε τὴν Τειάχνα ὡς Νομοθέτης μ' Χαρικλέους ἐνέμετο, ἀπεμιμνῆσθαι αὐτοῦ ἡ ἐπὶ τῆς ἰδιωτικῆς ἐγκλήσεως, Λόγων τίχλω μὴ διδάσκειν ἐπαρρεάζων ἐκείνῳ, οὐκ ἔχων ὅπως ἀπαλλάσσοιτο, ἀλλὰ ὁ χαλεπῶν τῆς Φιλοσόφοις [?] τῇ πολλοῖς ἐπιλεφθέντων ἐπιφέρειν αὐτοῖς, ἡ Ἀλκιβιάδου πρὸς τοὺς πολλούς. [?]
units.tr: Xenophon, in the first book of the Memorabilia, reports the law. [The Greek text here is too corrupt to render reliably: it recounts that Callias said to Socrates that Charicles, when he was lawgiver among the Thirty, had forbidden him, as a private complaint, to teach words; that he could not escape this, and that the prohibition fell upon many of the philosophers, as Alcibiades did against the many.] [Greek text corrupt]

units.la: Sed ista Critiae Lex abrogata est, cum etiam omnia τὰ ὅσα τὴν Τειάχνα ἀκυρα facta sint: unde iterum Philosophi Athenis docere ceperunt: estque post ea tempora scriptum à Menandro, quem expressit Terentius:
units.tr: But this law of Critias was repealed, since all the acts of the Thirty were declared void. Hence the philosophers began to teach at Athens again. And after that time Menander wrote the passage which Terence rendered:

units.la: Quod plerique omnes faciunt adolescentuli, Ut animum ad aliquod studium adiungant, aut equos Alere, aut canes ad venandum, aut ad Philosophos, Horum ille nihil egregie praeter cetera Studebat, & tamen omnia haec mediocriter.
units.tr: Most young men do this: they apply their minds to some study, either keeping horses, or dogs for hunting, or to the philosophers. He studied none of these outstandingly beyond the rest, yet he did all of them moderately.

units.la: Repertus est tamen post illa Sophocles Suniensis Amphiclidæ Filius, qui Critiæ exemplum æmulatus, Legem tulit, qua Philosophos Athenis exegit, aut certe vetuit scholam habere, nisi Senatui populoque Atheniensi ita videatur.
units.tr: Yet after that there was found Sophocles of Sunium, son of Amphiclides, who, imitating the example of Critias, proposed a law by which he drove the philosophers out of Athens, or at least forbade them to keep a school, unless the Senate and the Athenian people should so decide.

units.la: Μηδένα Φιλόσοφον σχολὴν ἀφηγεῖσθαι, αὖ μὴ τῇ βουλῇ ἢ τῷ δήμῳ δόξῃ · εἰ δὲ μή, θάνατον ζημίαν.
units.tr: No philosopher shall hold a school unless it seems good to the council or the people; otherwise, the penalty is death. [Μηδένα Φιλόσοφον σχολὴν ἀφηγεῖσθαι, αὖ μὴ τῇ βουλῇ ἢ τῷ δήμῳ δόξῃ · εἰ δὲ μή, θάνατον ζημίαν.]

units.la: Nemo Philosophus scholam habeto, nisi Senatui populoque Atheniensi ita videatur: qui secus faxit, capital esto.
units.tr: No philosopher shall keep a school, unless it seems good to the Senate and the Athenian people; whoever does otherwise shall be liable to capital punishment.

units.la: Legem laudat Diogenes Laertius in Theophrasto: ὁ Θεόφραστος οὖν, Theophrastus, ὅμως ἀπεδίδωσι τοῖς λοιποῖς φιλοσόφοις, Σοφοκλέους τὸ Ἀμφικλείδου νόμων εἰσηνεγκίας, μηδένα τὴν φιλοσόφων σχολὴν ἀφηγεῖσθαι, αὖ μὴ τῇ βουλῇ ἢ τῷ δ[?] δήμῳ δέξῃ· εἰ δὲ μή, ἀναγκαῖον [?] εἰς τὴν ζημίαν. Ἀλλὰ αὐτῆς ἐπάνλῃ εἰς τέωτα, Φίλωνος ἢ Σο-φοκλέα γεγαμηκότος ὡς ὀξιῷ νόμον. ὅτι γὰρ τὸν νόμον μὲν ἀχυρῷ ἐπίνοσθ Ἀθηναῖοι, τὸν δὲ Σο-φοκλέα [?] πίντε ζαλάντιος ἐζημίωσθ. καθόδοι πε τῆς Φιλοσόφοις ἐμφίσθμο. Pollux Li-bro IX. cap. V. ἔστι δὲ καὶ νόμος Ἀττικὸς τῶν Φιλοσοφούντων γραφῆς, ἐν Σοφοκλῆς Ἀμφικλείδου Σαμιῶς εἶπεν, ὡς ὧ ἵνα τῷ αὐτῷ πεφυκότων, ἐπήγαγε, μὴ ἐξεῖναι μηδενὶ τῆς Σοφιστῶν ἀλλαταεῖσθαι καὶ ἀσκεῖσθαι. Athenæus Libro XIII. καὶ Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ὡς ψηφίσματα ἐξηλθεν πολλὰς Φιλοσόφους τῆς Ἀθηναίς, nempe illos videri volebat hic Sophocles, vir non sui nominis, lingua Philosophos, sublesta fide, ignaua opera, quo referas ista Pollucis: ἔστι δὲ καὶ νόμος Ἀττικὸς τῶν Φιλοσοφούντων, ἐν Σοφοκλῆς Ἀμφικλείδου Σαμιῶς εἶπεν, ὡς ὧ ἵνα τῷ αὐτῷ πεφυκότων. De hac Lege Alexis Comicus dramate Ἵππων.
units.tr: Diogenes Laertius, in his life of Theophrastus, cites the law: "Theophrastus, however, yet ascribed to the other philosophers the proposal of Sophocles, son of Amphiclides, that no philosopher should hold a school unless it seemed good to the council or the people; otherwise the penalty is [death]. But this law was afterwards repealed by Philo, when Sophocles was [in office], as an unworthy law. For the Athenians repealed the law, and fined Sophocles five talents, and so philosophy again flourished." Pollux, Book IX, chapter 5: "There is also an Attic law concerning the teaching of philosophers; Sophocles, son of Amphiclides, of Sunium, proposed it, and added that no one should be allowed to frequent or practise sophistry." Athenaeus, Book XIII: "Sophocles also brought forward many decrees against the philosophers of Athens." Sophocles, a man not of his own name, wished to be seen as the philosopher of his own tongue, with unsteady faith and idle labour, which you may refer to Pollux's words: "There is also an Attic law on philosophers, which Sophocles, son of Amphiclides, of Sunium, proposed, as also for the same reason..." Alexis the comic poet mentions this law in his play Horses:

units.la: τότ' ἔσην Ἀκαδημία, τότε Ξενοκράτης, πολλ' ἀγαθὰ δοῦναι οἱ θεοὶ Δημητρείῳ, καὶ τοῖς Νομοθέταις, ὅστ᾽ τοὺς τῶν λόγων ὡς φασι δυνάμεις ἀξιοῦσι τοῖς νέοις, ἐς κάθαρας ἀμφὶ φασὶν ἐκ τῆς Ἀθηναῖς.
units.tr: Then there was the Academy, then Xenocrates: may the gods give many good things to Demetrius and to the lawgivers, who, they say, think that the powers of words should be assigned to the young, and ... they do this from Athens.

units.la: Sed diu non obtinuit hæc Lex, nam altero post Olympiadem anno abrogata, ipsique adeo Sophocli multa talentorum quinque irrogata est. Diogenes Laërtius verbis iam laudatis: Ἐν ᾧ αὐτῆς ἐπάνλῃ εἰς τέωτα, Φίλωνος ἢ Σοφοκλέα γεγαμηκότος ὡς ὀξιῷ νόμον. ὅτι γὰρ τὸν νόμον μὲν ἀχυρῷ ἐπίνοσθ Ἀθηναῖοι, τὸν δὲ Σοφοκλέα πίντε ζαλάντιος ἐζημίωσθ. E qua multa colligimus, Philonem eo ipso, quo Legem tulit Sophocles, anno Sophocli dicam scripsisse ἀξιοῦσθ νόμων, ob latâ hanc Legem, alioquin ἀνάξιος fuisset Sophocles. Investigemus vero tempus latæ Legis. Secundum hanc Legem Theophrastus Atticæ finibus excedere iussus est, qui anno tertio Olympiadis centesimæ quartædecimæ, Archonte Philocle, siue Diocle, Aristotelis in Schola successerat: Ergo post annum tertium quartædecimæ supra centesimam Olympiadis hæc Lex lata est: idque cum Athenis Demetrius omnia pro arbitrio versaret: Anno secundo Olympiadis decimæ octauæ, Archonte Anaxicrate, Demetrius Antigoni F. homo prostituti pudoris, Athenas sibi, non in libertatem, quanquam videri vellet, asseruit: eo autem res Athenis imporanter admodum gerente, eius vel suasu, vel gratia Lex hæc rogata lataque est: coniecturam facimus ex his Alexidis,
units.tr: But this law did not hold for long, for in the second year after the Olympiad it was repealed, and Sophocles himself was fined many talents. Diogenes Laertius, in the words already cited: "Afterwards Philo, when Sophocles was [in office], repealed the law as unworthy. For the Athenians repealed the law, and fined Sophocles five talents." From these many passages we gather that Philo, in the very year in which Sophocles proposed the law, wrote [that Sophocles was] worthy of praise for proposing it; otherwise Sophocles would have been unworthy. Let us now investigate the time when the law was proposed. According to this law, Theophrastus was ordered to leave Attica; he had succeeded Aristotle in the school in the third year of the 114th Olympiad, under the archon Philocles or Diocles. So this law was proposed after the third year of the 114th Olympiad. This happened while Demetrius was managing everything at Athens at his pleasure. In the second year of the 118th Olympiad, under the archon Anaxicrates, Demetrius, son of Antigonus, a man of shameless character, claimed Athens for himself, not as a free city, though he wished to seem so. While affairs at Athens were being conducted in a very disordered way, this law was proposed and passed, either at his suggestion or by his favour. We conjecture this from the words of Alexis:

units.la: πολλ' ἀγαθὰ δοῦναι οἱ θεοὶ Δημητρείῳ, καὶ τοῖς Νομοθέταις.
units.tr: May the gods give many good things to Demetrius and to the lawgivers. [πολλ' ἀγαθὰ δοῦναι οἱ θεοὶ Δημητρείῳ, καὶ τοῖς Νομοθέταις]

units.la: Quare existimamus, anno tertio Olympiadis centesimæ decimæ octauæ, Prætore Athenis Coræbo, hanc Legem latam fuisse.
units.tr: Therefore we judge that this law was proposed in the third year of the 118th Olympiad, when Coraebus was praetor at Athens.

units.la: LIBER QUARTUS. DE LEGIBUS.
units.tr: BOOK FOUR. ON THE LAWS.

units.la: TITULUS I.
units.tr: TITLE I.

units.la: CUM Solon in animo haberet æquam omnibus suis ciuibus libertatem constituere, suo maxime instituto facere obseruauit, si à populo iudicia redderentur: Τὰ δὲ δικαστήεια[?], δημοτικὸν, inquit Aristoteles Libro II. Polit. qui verò notat Solonem τὸν δῆμον κολακεῦσαι, τὰ δικαστήρια ποιῆσαι ἐκ πάντων. Qua ratione, videtur ipse Solon temperamentum illud sustulisse, quo miscuerat Democratiam Aristocratiæ & Oligarchiæ, nam plane recidit in Democratiam: δὴ καὶ μέμ-φοιτό τις ἄνες αὐτῷ· λόγον γὰρ ἐτήρει, χρῆσον ποιῆσαι τὸ δικαστήριον πάντων, κληρωτὸν ὅν. Dedit enim Lege prouocationem à Magistratibus ad iudices: Περὶ ἐκείνων, ὅσα αἱ ἀρχαὶ κρίνοιεν, εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον ἐφέσεις ἔδωκε τοῖς βουλομένοις. A Magistratuum sententia ad iudices pronocanto.
units.tr: When Solon meant to establish equal freedom for all his citizens, he saw that it would especially serve his purpose if judgments were given by the people: "The courts were popular," says Aristotle in Book II of the Politics. But Aristotle, who notes that Solon "flattered the people by making the courts out of all of them," [τὸν δῆμον κολακεῦσαι, τὰ δικαστήρια ποιῆσαι ἐκ πάντων] seems to suggest that Solon removed that balance by which he had mixed democracy with aristocracy and oligarchy, for he fell plainly into democracy. Hence someone found fault with him: "for he kept to his plan of making the court out of all men, chosen by lot." [δὴ καὶ μέμφοιτό τις αὐτῷ] For by his law he gave appeal from the magistrates to the judges: "concerning those matters which the magisterial offices decided, he gave appeals to the court for those who wished." [Περὶ ἐκείνων, ὅσα αἱ ἀρχαὶ κρίνοιεν, εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον ἐφέσεις ἔδωκε τοῖς βουλομένοις] That is, appeal lay from the sentence of the magistrates to the judges.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Plutarchus in Solone: καὶ γὰρ ὅσα τοῖς ἀρχαῖς ἐπέξε κρίνειν, ὁμοίως καὶ περὶ ἐκείνων εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον ἐφέσεις ἔδωκε τοῖς βουλομένοις. Rursum in comparatione cum Poplicola: καὶ τοῖς φιλήσει δῆκα, ἐκκαλεῖσθαι τὸν δῆμον, ὥσπερ ὁ Σόλων τοὺς δικαστάς, ἔδωκε. Itaque nouem illi annui Magistratus, qui summi erant ante Solonis Leges iudices, vix reliquam habuerunt ἀρχήν. Suidas: χωρεῖ τε ἢ τὰ πλεῖστα οἱ ἐνέα Ἀρχοντες ὥστε τὰς δίκας αὐτοτελεῖς πεισθαι. ἔτερον δὲ Σόλωνος αὐτοῖς νομοθετήσαντος, οὐδὲν ἕτερον αὐτοῖς ἐπέλειπε, τὸ μόνον αἰσχρὸν τοὺς αἰτιωμένους δίκας. Potestas verò omnis erat penes populum, cum nulla lis incideret, de qua iudicium non redderent τὰ δικαστήρια κληρωτὰ ὄντα ἐκ πάντων. Plutarchus in Solone: τὰ γὰρ πλεῖστα τῶν ἀμφιφόρων ἐπέπιπτεν εἰς τοὺς δικαστάς. maxime cum Leges à Solone data opera scriptæ essent verbis non plane liquidis. Plutarchus ibidem: λέγεται δὲ καὶ τοὺς νόμους ἀσαφεῖς γράψαι, καὶ πολλὰς αἰτιολογίας ἐγγράψαι, αὐξῆσαι τὸ τῶν δικαστηρίων ἰσχύ, μὴ δυναμένους γὰρ ἐκ τῶν νόμων ἀφαιρεῖν[?] ἀμφισβήτημα εἰς ἐκείνους, τὴν νόμων ἔτι ἀπὸ χωρίου[?]. Quo nomine gloriatur in Elegiis Solon ἐξίωσεν induxisse:
units.tr: Plutarch mentions this law in his Life of Solon: "for he gave to those who wished appeals to the court concerning all the matters which the magistrates had power to judge." [καὶ γὰρ ὅσα τοῖς ἀρχαῖς ἐπέξε κρίνειν, ὁμοίως καὶ περὶ ἐκείνων εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον ἐφέσεις ἔδωκε τοῖς βουλομένοις] Again, in the comparison with Publicola: "and he gave the people, as Solon did for the judges, the right to appeal to them." [καὶ τοῖς φιλήσει δῆκα, ἐκκαλεῖσθαι τὸν δῆμον, ὥσπερ ὁ Σόλων τοὺς δικαστάς, ἔδωκε] Hence those nine annual magistrates, who before Solon's laws were the supreme judges, scarcely retained any authority. Suidas: "the nine archons were for the most part in a position to have their cases decided by themselves; but after Solon had legislated otherwise, nothing was left to them except the disgrace of being accused." [χωρεῖ τε ἢ τὰ πλεῖστα οἱ ἐνέα Ἀρχοντες ὥστε τὰς δίκας αὐτοτελεῖς πεισθαι. ἔτερον δὲ Σόλωνος αὐτοῖς νομοθετήσαντος, οὐδὲν ἕτερον αὐτοῖς ἐπέλειπε, τὸ μόνον αἰσχρὸν τοὺς αἰτιωμένους δίκας] Yet the whole power lay with the people, since no dispute arose on which the courts did not give judgment, the courts being drawn by lot from all. Plutarch in Solon: "for most of the disputed matters fell to the judges." [τὰ γὰρ πλεῖστα τῶν ἀμφιφόρων ἐπέπιπτεν εἰς τοὺς δικαστάς] Especially since Solon's laws had been written on purpose in words not wholly clear. Plutarch in the same place: "It is said also that he wrote the laws obscurely, and inserted many qualifying clauses, in order to increase the power of the courts; for since they could not take away the dispute from the laws, they were obliged to refer it to those courts..." [λέγεται δὲ καὶ τοὺς νόμους ἀσαφεῖς γράψαι, καὶ πολλὰς αἰτιολογίας ἐγγράψαι, αὐξῆσαι τὸ τῶν δικαστηρίων ἰσχύ, μὴ δυναμένους γὰρ ἐκ τῶν νόμων ἀφαιρεῖν ἀμφισβήτημα εἰς ἐκείνους] In the elegies Solon boasts that he brought about this result:

units.la: δῆμον γὰρ ἔδωκα τόσον κράτος, ὅσον ἐπαρκεῖ, τιμῆς ὅτ' ἀφελὼν, ὅτ' ἐπορεξάμενος.
units.tr: "For I gave the people as much power as sufficed, taking away from honour, or adding to it, as needed."

units.la: ὅ δ' εἶχεν δυνάμιν, ἐς χρήματα ἦσον ἀγυρεῖ[?],καὶ τῆς ἐφεστάμεν μηδὲν ἀρχὰς ἔχειν[?].ἕτερος δ' ἀμφιδαλλῶν κεφάλῃ σάκος ἀμφοτέρῃ[?],νηχῇ δ' ἅμ' οὐχ εἶας ὀδ' ἐπέρης ἀδίκως[?].
units.tr: "And the one who had power I kept from having more than enough wealth, and I did not allow those who had no office to hold authority over it. And I cast my shield over each side, and I did not allow either to win unjustly over the other."

units.la: Inter iudices autem, vt dicere cepimus, allegabantur omnes ex æquo ciues Athenienses, sine vllo census discrimine: nam etiam Θῆτες[?] Solonis Legè, quam suo loco in superioribus descripsimus, πᾶς ἐκκλησιάζειν καὶ δικάζειν μόνον μετέχειν τῆς πολιτείας[?]. Conditiones tamen hæ exigebantur, vt essent famæ integræ, annos triginta nati, neque inter ærarios relati: sed de hoc tertio capite dicemus, ὧν δ' ἡ' εἰσίν[?], vbi de ærariis agemus. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. X. ἐδικάζον δὲ οἱ ὑπὸ τελευτῶντες ἐπὶ[?], ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑπὲρ[?] τιμῆς[?], siue potius, vt in M S. habetur, ἐπιτίμων[?], καὶ μὴ ἐφεληθέντων τῆς δημοσίας[?]. Cautetur igitur, vt famæ sint integræ, nec ignominiosi; quanquam poterant ex Lege capi in iudices etiam illi, qui Senatu moti fuerant:
units.tr: Now, as I have begun to say, all Athenian citizens without any distinction of property were admitted as judges alike; for even the Thetes were included under Solon's law, which we described in its place among the earlier matters, that all might attend the assembly and only share in the judging of the commonwealth. [πᾶς ἐκκλησιάζειν καὶ δικάζειν μόνον μετέχειν τῆς πολιτείας] Yet these conditions were required: that they should have unblemished reputation, be thirty years old, and not be enrolled among the aerarii; but we shall speak of this third chapter in its place, where we treat of the aerarii. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 10: those who were judges were those who had been... of the honour, or rather, as in a manuscript has it, of those who are full citizens and have not been deprived of public office. [ἐδικάζον δὲ οἱ ὑπὸ τελευτῶντες] It is provided, then, that they should have unblemished reputation and not be disgraced; although, by the law, even those who had been removed from the Senate could be chosen as judges:

units.la: Ἐξεῖναι εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια καθεζέσθαι τοὺς ἐκφυλλοφορηθέντας[?].
units.tr: "It was permitted for those who had been expelled from the leaves to sit in the courts." [Ἐξεῖναι εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια καθεζέσθαι τοὺς ἐκφυλλοφορηθέντας]

units.la: Legem habes in Græcorum Commentariis: ἐξεῖναι μὲν τοῖς εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια καθεζέσθαι τοὺς ἐκφυλλοφορηθέντας[?]. Vnde colligere licet non eos omnes, qui Senatu mouebantur, ignominiosos fuisse: nam alioquin infamia notatos fas non fuisset εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια καθιέναι. At vero apud Romanos Senatu motis, vt testatur Marcellus Libro III. Digestorum, non permittebatur iudicare. Cassius Longinus non putat ei permittendum, qui propter turpitudinem Senatu motus, nec restitutus est, iudicare, vel testimonium dicere: quia Lex Iulia repetundarum hoc fieri vetat. Lege II. D. de Senatoribus.
units.tr: You have the law in the Greek commentaries: "it was permitted for those who had been expelled to sit in the courts." [ἐξεῖναι μὲν τοῖς εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια καθεζέσθαι τοὺς ἐκφυλλοφορηθέντας] From this one may gather that not all who were removed from the Senate were branded with infamy, for otherwise it would not have been lawful for them to enter the courts [εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια καθιέναι]. But among the Romans, as Marcellus testifies in Book III of the Digest, those removed from the Senate were not permitted to judge. Cassius Longinus does not think that one should be allowed to judge, or to give testimony, who has been removed from the Senate on account of disgrace and not restored, because the Julian law on extortion forbids it. Law 2, D., de Senatoribus.

units.la: Alterum Caput est, vt maiores sint annis triginta, de quo in sequentibus videbimus, Deo dante. Iudices autem forte capiebantur è Lege Solonis, qui fecit τὰ δικαστήρια κληρωτά.
units.tr: The second requirement is that they be over thirty years of age, which, God willing, we shall see in what follows. The judges were chosen, perhaps, from Solon's law, which made the courts drawn by lot.

units.la: Γαῖος Ἀθηναίους λαχεῖν εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια.
units.tr: Gaius: "to choose Athenians by lot for the courts." [Γαῖος Ἀθηναίους λαχεῖν εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια]

units.la: Laudat hanc Legem Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Αἰσχίνου α'. ἀλλ' ὑμεῖς ἐπὶ πάντων ἀρχῶν κληρωτῶν Ἀθηναίων, καὶ πάντων δὲ εἰσὶν ὅτι βουλομένων εἰς τοῦτο λαχεῖν ὁ δικαστήριον, μόνοι δικάζεσθ' ἡμῖν[?]. Ἀλλ' τί; ὅτι ἐλάχετε. εἶπα ἀπεκληρώθητε. Ταῦτα γὰρ οἱ νόμοι λέγουσιν[?]. Varia erant apud Athenienses fora atque Tribunalia, nam, vt mittam illa quinque ἐν οἷς ἐδίκαζον περὶ φονικῶν πραγμάτων[?], alia erant Tribunalia, ἐν οἷς ἐδίκαζον περὶ δημοσίων[?]. Decem Tribunalia siue fora fuisse docent Comici Interpretes ad Plutum, inscripta singula vna harum decem literarum, A, B, Γ, Δ, E, Z, H, Θ, I, K, Athenienses qui vellent iudiciis reddundis vacare, nomina sua dabant tabellæ inscripta adscripto patris populique nomine: totidem quoque erant tabellæ, quarum aliæ aliis harū decem literarum essent notatæ, pro numero scilicet eorum, qui in hoc vel illo foro essent iudicaturi: Atque ita fiebat, vt prout quisque hanc aut illâ literam sortiretur, ita huic aut illi foro iudex traderetur: Quicumque autem literæ sortem nactus erat, fori eius præconi ostendebat: Præco tabellam ei dabat, in qua nomen illius itemque fori inscriptum, itemque virgam cum eodem fori nomine: quibus potestatem iudicandi adipiscebatur καὶ ὁ δικαστικὸν. Si quis autem, qui sortitus non esset, inter iudices sedere vellet, multabatur: ἐν τᾶις Ἀθήναις πολλὰ ὧν δικαστήρια, καὶ ἐν ἓξ μὲν, ἐδίκαζον ἀεὶ φονικῶν παραγμάτων· ἐν τῇ δὲ, ἀεὶ δημοτικῶν. καὶ ἑκαστον δὲ τούτων εἶχεν ἐν τῇ τοιχείων εἰδὴν, οἷς, ὡς ἡ τῶν δικαστηρίων λεγόμενον ΑΛΦΑ. ὁμοίως δὲ λεγόμενον ΒΗΤΑ. ἄλλο ΓΑΜΜΑ. καὶ ἐξῆς ὁ Δ, καὶ ὁ Ε, καὶ ἑως τῆς Κ. δίκα γὰρ ὧ τὰ δικαστήρια ἐν Ἀθήναις. ἐ τοῦ ... ἔχοντα τὸ πυρρῷ βάμμα ἐν τῷ τοιχείῳ, ᾧ ἐπὶ τὸ δικαστήριον ὠνομάζετο. ἤρχετο δὲ ἑκάστου εἰς τὸ πίναξιον ἔχων ἐπιγεγραμμένον ὄνομα αὐτῇ καὶ πάξειν καὶ τῷ δήμου, καὶ κληρῳ ἐλάμβανεν. καὶ ὅς ὃς ἂν κληρωτ. ἐκληρώσατο ἐμοῖς τὸ Α, ἀπήρχετο εἰς τὸ Α δικαστήριον. ὁμοίως δὲ εἰς τὸ Β. καὶ ἐφεξῆς. ἀπήρχετο ἢ, καὶ ἑώρων μὲν ἐδίκαζεν τῷ κηρυκι τῆς δικαστηρίῳ τὸν κληρον τῆς τοιχείᾳ. ὁ δὲ κῆρυξ λοιπὸν ἐδίδου αὐτῷ τὸ πιναξιον, ἐν ᾧ ἐπιγεγραμμένον ὧ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς δικαστηρίῳ, ἐδίδου καὶ τῷ ῥάβδον ἅμα τῷ πινακιδίῳ, ᾧ ἐν αὐτῇ ἢ τῇ ῥάβδῳ ὧ τὸ ὄνομα τῆς δικαστηρίῳ ἐ-
units.tr: Demosthenes praises this law in the first speech against Aeschines. But you, who are judged by men chosen from all the Athenian offices filled by lot, and when everyone wants to be chosen for this court, sit alone in judgment over us? "But what?" you say. "They were chosen by lot." I say they were allotted, for the laws say so. Among the Athenians there were various courts and tribunals. Leaving aside the five in which they judged cases of homicide [ἐν οἷς ἐδίκαζον περὶ φονικῶν πραγμάτων], there were other tribunals in which they judged public matters [ἐν οἷς ἐδίκαζον περὶ δημοσίων]. The commentators on Aristophanes' Plutus teach that there were ten tribunals or courts, each marked with one of these ten letters: A, B, Γ, Δ, E, Z, H, Θ, I, K. Athenians who wished to be free to serve as jurors gave their names on a tablet, inscribed with the name of their father and their deme. There were as many tablets as there were letters, each marked with one of the ten, according to the number of jurors who were to sit in this or that court. So it happened that, as each man drew this letter or that, he was assigned to this or that court. Whoever had drawn a letter showed it to the herald of that court. The herald then gave him a tablet on which his name and the name of the court were written, together with a rod bearing the name of the same court [ὁ δικαστικὸν]; by these he gained the power of judging. But if anyone who had not been allotted wished to sit among the jurors, he was fined. In Athens there were many courts: in six they always judged cases of homicide, and in the rest always public matters. Each of these had a sign in the alphabet, so that one court was called Alpha, another Beta, another Gamma, and so on through Delta, Epsilon, up to Kappa [ΑΛΦΑ, ΒΗΤΑ, ΓΑΜΜΑ]. Ten courts there were in Athens, each marked by a letter in red paint, by which the court was named. Each juror came to the tablet bearing his name and that of the court and the people, and drew by lot. Whoever drew the letter A went to court A; likewise for B, and so on in order. The juror then gave the lot to the herald of that letter, and the herald gave him the tablet on which his own name and the name of the court were written, and gave him also the rod, on which the name of the court was written, and so he judged.

units.la: γεγραμμένον, εἴπα ὕπως ἐδίκαζεν. εἰ δὲ ὡς δικαστὴς εἰσιὼν μὴ κληρωθεὶς εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον, ἀλλαφόρως ἐζημιοῦτο. Ad haec alludit Comicus Pluto:
units.tr: To this the comic poet alludes in Plutus:

units.la: ἐν τῇ σοφῷ νῦν λαβὼν τὸ γράμμα οὐ δικάζῃ, οὐ δ' ὁ βασιλεὺς ὁ ἢ Χάρων τὸ ξύμβολον δίδωσιν.
units.tr: Now, having received your letter in the wise [ἐν τῇ σοφῷ νῦν λαβὼν τὸ γράμμα], you do not judge; nor does the king, or Charon, give you the token [τὸ ξύμβολον].

units.la: Ab hoc Tribunalium decem numero putem natum Proverbium: Λύκου δικαστής· ἀπ' Ἡροιμαίδης, ὅτι Λύκος ὁ Ἡρως ὁπ' ὧν ὁ ἐν Ἀθήναις δικαστήριον ἵδρυτο, τὸ δικαστής τὸ μορφῶ ἔχων. ἔνθα εἰ δωρόδοκοι ὄντες καὶ συκοφαντεῖν τὸ δίκα γιγνόμενοι σωσεφόντο. Harpocration: Λύκος ἐστιν Ἡρως ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν Ἀθήναις δικαστηρίῳ τὸ ἡμεῖς μορφῶν ἔχων· ἀπὸ ὧν οἱ δωροδοκοῦντες τὸ δίκα γιγνόμενοι σωσεφόρτο. Hic enim κατὰ ἑκάστην ad decem illa δικαστήρια, ad quorum singula Λύκος ὁ Ἡρως ἵδρυτο, referetur, non autem ad τοὺς δωροδοκοῦντας, quasi decem tantum numero essent. Sed videamus quaenam fuerint haec decem Tribunalia. Olim quinque Tribunalibus καὶ φονικῶν παραγμάτων adscripti erant Ephetae. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. X. Ἐφέται, τὸν μὲν ἀριθμὸν εἰς τὸ πεντήκοντα. Δεκάων δ' αὐτοῖς κατίσταν, ἀρισταῖδῶ αἱρεῖσθαι, ἐδίκαζον ἡ τοῖς ἐφ' ἀμφὶ διαλογυμοῖς, ἐν τοῖς πέντε δικαστηρίοις. Ephetae hi, ut habes in verbis Pollucis, eligebantur ἀπληλίως, non autem sorte capiebantur: sed uni ex his quinque Tribunalibus, nempe Areopagitico adscripsit Solon iudices, qui Areopagitici dicti sunt, ita ut quatuor tantum reliquis Ephetas adscripserit: addit Pollux: Σὸλων δ' Ἐφέτας πρῶτον τῷ ἐξ Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βουλῇ. Sed non multo post Ephetae deridiculo fuerunt: Pollux, κατὰ μικρὸν ἡ καταγελάσθη τὸ Ἐφετῶν δικαστήριον. Itaque his quatuor Tribunalibus alij dati sunt iudices, sorte capti, ut omnino liquet e verbis Scholiastae Comici, quae descripsimus. Inter haec igitur decem Tribunalia, quorum iudices sorte legebantur, recensenda sunt quatuor ista καὶ φονικῶν παραγμάτων, Tribunal τὸ ἐπὶ Πάγαλλο, Tribunal τὸ ἐπὶ Δελφινίῳ, Tribunal τὸ ἐπὶ Πρυτανείῳ, quartum denique Tribunal τὸ ἐν Φρεάτῃ. Superfsunt igitur sex Tribunalia, ἐν οἷς ἐδίκαζον καὶ δημοτικῶν παραγμάτων. Quaenam ista sint, videamus. Occurrit primo longe celeberrimus Heliaea, deinde, Trigonum, tertio Parabystum medium, quarto Parabystum maius: quinto Forum ad Lycum: sexto Tribunal Metichi. Septimum quoque occurrit apud Aristophanem Vespis:
units.tr: From this number of ten tribunals I think the proverb arose: "a judge of Lycus," from Hieromaides, because Lycus the hero, whose image stood in each of the courts at Athens, was... there, those who were bribe-takers and who were false accusers in the judgments were thrown into prison. Harpocration: Lycus is a hero from whose image in the Athenian courts... from which bribe-takers were carried off. For this is to be referred to each of those ten courts, at each of which the hero Lycus was set up, and not to "the bribe-takers," as if there were only ten of them. But let us see which these ten tribunals were. Formerly the Ephetae were assigned to five tribunals for cases of homicide. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 10: "The Ephetae, in number fifty, were appointed by lot from ... the Areopagus, and they judged... in the five courts." These Ephetae, as you have in Pollux's words, were chosen by vote and not drawn by lot; but Solon assigned judges, called Areopagites, to one of these five tribunals, namely the Areopagite court, so that he assigned only four to the remaining Ephetae. Pollux adds: "Solon first assigned the Ephetae to the council from the Areopagus." But not long afterwards the court of the Ephetae became a laughing-stock: Pollux, "gradually the court of the Ephetae was ridiculed." Thus to these four tribunals other judges were assigned, chosen by lot, as is clear from the words of the Comic scholiast which we have quoted. Among these ten tribunals, whose judges were chosen by lot, these four for homicide must be counted: the tribunal at Palladium, the tribunal at Delphinium, the tribunal at the Prytaneum, and lastly the fourth tribunal at the Phrear. The remaining six tribunals, in which they judged also public matters, are therefore left. Let us see what they were. First comes the very famous Heliaea; then the Trigonum; third the Parabystum medium; fourth the Parabystum maius; fifth the Forum at Lycus; sixth the Tribunal of Metichus. A seventh also occurs in Aristophanes' Wasps:

units.la: ὁ δ' αὐτὸ τυμπάνῳ [?] αἴξας, ἐδίκαζεν ἐς τὸ Καμὸν ἐμπεσών.
units.tr: And he, leaping up upon the drum [?], gave judgment, falling into the Camus. [ὁ δ' αὐτὸ τυμπάνῳ αἴξας, ἐδίκαζεν ἐς τὸ Καμὸν ἐμπεσών]

units.la: Scholiastes: τίπος ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ ὅτω λεγόμενος. Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ Παραβύστης, Καιρὸς, Τεί-χανος, Μέσος. Hic habes quatuor Tribunalia, nempe Παραβύστης maius, quod simpliciter dixit Παραβύστης, Parabystum medium, Scholiastae Μέσος, tertium est Καιρὸν δικαστήριον, quartum denique Trigonum: Horum omnium, si Καιρὸν excipias, meminit Pollux Libro VIII. cap.X. ceteraque recenset his verbis: γράμμα δικαστήρια, ἡ Ηλιαία, ὃ Τεῖχανον, ὃ μέμνηται Δεῖναρχος · μεῖζον Παραβύστην, μείζον Παραβύστην. καὶ μείζονος δὲ μέμνηται Λυσίας. ἐν μὲν τῇ τοῦ Παραβύστῳ, οἱ Ἐυδίκα ἐδίκαζον τὰ Μηδίχου κάλλιω, ὃ μιμωσόυσιν Ἀνδροτίων. ὃ ἐπὶ Λύχῳ, καὶ Ηρως δὲ ἰδρύσῃ αὐτὴ ἔχων τῆς Ἀρείας μορφῶ. ὃ δὲ Μηδίχου. Paufanias Atticis: ἔστι δὲ Ἀθηναίοις καὶ ἄλλα δικαστήρια οὐκ ἐς ἔσοδον δίξης ἱκανῶς. Τὸ μὲν οὖν κεκλιμένον Παραβύστων καὶ Τεῖχανον, ὃ μὲν, ἐν ἀφανεῖ πόλεως ἐν καὶ ἐπ' ἐλαχίστης σιωνίαν ἐς αὐτ'. ὃ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς ἐχᾶ τὰ ὀνόματα · βαπταχουῶ ὃ καὶ Φοινικιῶν ἀπὸ χωμῆ. ὃ δὲ καὶ ἐς τὸν Ἀρμαδῖ μονῶν ὁ ἰοματίζοντες. ὃ δὲ μέγιστον, καὶ ἐς ὃ πόλεως σιωνίασιν, Ηλιαίας καλοῦσι. Habes hic de Helixa, de Parabysto, itemque Trigono: quaenam autem haec sint duo Tribunalia, Βαπταχουῶ καὶ Φοινικιῶ, quibus nomen a colore: sed mutuabuntur lucem ab his ὁ τῆ Ἀθηναίων πολιτεία Aristotelis verbis: Τοὺς γὰρ δικαστηρίους χρῆμα ὑπογεγραμμένα ἐφ' ἑκάστῳ ὅτι τοῦ σφηκίσκου τῆς Εἰσόδου. ὁ δὲ λαβὼν τῷ βαχτηρίαν βαδίζει εἰς δικαστήριον ὃ ὁμοίως μὲν τῇ βα-χτηρίᾳ, ἐχῶν δὲ ὃ αὐτὸ χρῆμα ὅτι ὁ τῇ βαλάνῳ. Cuius vero Parabysti, cum duo sint, meminerit Paufanias non dicit, colligere tamen est e Pollucis verbis: Scribit enim Paufanias Παραβύστων ἐν ἀφανεῖ πόλεως, καὶ ἐπ' ἐλαχίστης σιωνίαν ἐς αὐτ'. Tribunal est in obscura urbis parte, in eoque res viles minimique momenti iudicantur. Pollucis verba indicant illud esse Parabystum medium, in quo iudices sedebant Undecimviri: Μέσον Παραβύστων, μείζον Παραβύστων. καὶ μείζονος δὲ μέμνηται Λυσίας. ἐν μὲν τῷ τοῦ Παραβύστῳ οἱ Ἐυδίκα ἐδίκαζον τὰ Μηδίχου κάλλιω, ὃ μιμωσόυσιν Ἀνδροτίων. Pollucis ista, ἐδίκαζον τὰ Μηδίχου κάλλιω, mendosa sunt proculdubio, nam res maioris momenti non iudicabantur in hoc Tribunali, quam in illo, cui à Meticho cognomen, etenim constat, ἐπ' ἐλαχίστης σιωνίαν ἐς Παραβύστων, sed viam non vidit, qua iturad emendationem, Vir eruditissimus, qui rescribit τὰ Μηδίχου κάλλιω. Existimo reponendum esse: ἐν μὲν τῇ τοῦ Παραβύστῳ οἱ Ἐυδίκα ἐδίκαζον τὰ μὴ τῇ χοῦ κάλλιω. In medio Parabysto Undecemviri iudicabant ea, quae ne tantillum quidem pretio unum superabant Choem: Chous est duodecima pars Metreta vini: venibat autem Metretes vini duodecim drachmis: Demosthenes ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ Φαίνιππον. οὐ γὰρ ὁ τῆς ἐχαλκᾶς νῦν πωλεῖ τὰ κειδᾶς ὀκτωκυαδικαδράχμοις, καὶ τὸν οἶνον δωδεκάδραχμον, πλῆτης εἰκότως, ἐπιδὼ ποῦς, οἴτινα μὲν μεδίμνους, πλέον δὲ χιλίους, οἵτινες δὲ Μητρῇς ἔχοντες ὀκταχοσίους. Ego pretium Chois vini erat unius drachmae. Ac proinde res, quae sub iudicium Undecemvirorum in Parabysto cadebant, non excedebant unius pretium drachmae, siue Chois. Atque ex his praeterea liquet, in hoc Parabysto iudices non sedisse, quemadmodum in aliis Tribunalibus sedebant capti, forte. Fuit enim hoc Parabystum Undecemvirorum Tribunal, Γαραξουσιν[?]. ὅτως ἐκαλεῖτο τὸ ἐν Ἀθηναίοις δικαστήριον, ἐν ᾧ ἐδίκαζον οἱ Ἐνδε-κα. Ἀντιφῶν ἐν τῷ πρὸς Νικοκλέα περὶ ὅρων. μνημονεύοι σὴ αὐτῷ ἄλλοί τε τῆς Κω-μικῆς, ἡ Τιμοκλῆς [?] Ὀρεσαυπκλείδη[?]. Ex his igitur septem Tribunalibus, quae recensuimus, expungendum est Parabystum hoc: superierunt itaque sex tantum, quibus adde illa quatuor, in quibus iudicia reddebantur [?], fient decem illa Tribunalia, in quibus ius dicunt forte capti [?] ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀθηναίων iudices. Horum autem Tribunalium sex maximum fuit Heliaea Paufanias. ὁ δὲ μέγιστον, ἡ ἡς ὁ πλεῖστοι σῶμα, καλοῦσιν Ἡλιαίαν. Maximum dixit, meo iudicio, Paufanias, quia de pluribus caufis cognofcebat, eoque nomine ἐς αὐτὸ πλεῖστοι σῶμα. Alioqui par fuisse videtur numerus Iudicum qui in duobus saltem aliis Tribunalibus sedebant, cum numero eorum, qui in Heliaea ius dicebant: nam in Heliaea erant quingenti iudices. Pollux: ἡ Ἡλιαία δὲ πεντακοσίων. Fuit & alterum Tribunal, in quo totidem erant, nam cum fieret aliquando, vt duorum Tribunalium iudices coirent ad ius dicendum, πάλαι δὲ σὺν ἡσθ ἐι σὺν δικάζοντες τὰ δικαστήρια, fiebant mille iudices. Pollux: εἰ δὲ χιλίων δύο δικαστῶν, σύνεισαν δύο δικαστήρια. En tibi exemplum apud Demosthenem in Timocratea. ὡς δὲ Τούτοις, δικαστηρίων δυοῖν εἰς ἓνα ἡ χιλίοις ἐνηφισμένων. Vlpianus: ἐν τῆς μεγάλαις καὶ ἐαυτοῦ δεμένοις ὡς φέρμα, σύνηρχοντο ἐν δύο δικαστηρίων, πληροῦντες ἀριθμὸν χιλίων ἡ ἑνός. Habes tertium quoque Tribunal, in quo erant quoque quingenti: si namque mille & quingentis iudicibus opus foret, tria Tribunalia conueniebant. Pollux: εἰ δὲ πεντακοσίων ἡ χιλίων δύο δικαστῶν, σύνεισαν τὰ τρία δικαστήρια. Exemplum habes apud Dinarchum ἐν τῷ χ̄ Δημοσθένους, ἡ πεντακόσιοι ἐ χίλιοι ὄντες, ἡ ἀπόσης τῆς πόλεως ἐπιτελῶν ἐν τῇ χρόνῳ ἔχειν. item apud Plutarchum in Pericle. Αγων δὲ τῶν μὲν ἀφῆλε τῶν ψηφισμάτων, κείνεσθαι δὲ τῷ δίκῳ ἐγραφῆν, ἐν δικαστῇς χιλίοις ἡ πεντακοσίοις. Non igitur maior fuit numerus iudicum, qui in Heliaea sederent, sed longe plures grauioréfque lites & caufae, quam in aliis Tribunalibus: itaque nemo non optabat forte legi ad hoc Tribunal. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ χ̄ Αεισχίνους α. Ἀλλ᾽ ὑμῖς αὐτοὶ πάντων ἐχῆ κληρουμένων Ἀθηναίων, ἡ πάντων δὲ οἶδ᾽ ὅτι βουλομένων εἰς ἑαυτὸ λαχεῖν ὃ δικαστήριον, μόνοι δικάζειν ἡμῖν. Defignatis ad hunc modum forte Iudicibus, atque Tribunalibus, Iudices porro iusiurandum dabant verbis ex Lege conceptis sic ius secundum Leges vnicuique dicturos: Habes apud Demosthenem in Timocratea ipsam iurisiurandi formulam ὀμόσει repraesentatam.
units.tr: The Scholiast says: "a kind of court, so called from the place." There are the Parabystes, the Kairos, the Teichanos, and the Mesos. Here you have four tribunals: the greater Parabystum, which he simply calls the Parabystes; the middle Parabystum, which the Scholiast calls the Mesos; the third is the Kairos court; and the fourth is the Trigonum. Of all of these, except the Kairos, Pollux mentions in Book VIII, chapter 10, and he lists the rest in these words: "The courts are the Heliaea, the Teichanos, which Deinarchus mentions, the greater Parabystes, and the greater [Parabystes] again. Lysias also mentions a greater one. In the Parabystes the Undecemviri judged the cases of Meticho's (?) lesser sort, which the Androtion [?] imitate. The one by Lycus, and Heros also set up there, having the form of Ares. And that of Meticho." Pausanias in the Attica: "The Athenians also have other courts, not easy to enter. Of these, the Parabystes and the Teichanos lie in an obscure part of the city, and in the lowest places. The one from the market takes its names from the [colour?] ... and the one called the Heliaea is the greatest, where the largest number of people sits." [Παραβύστης, Τεῖχανος, Ἡλιαία] You have here the Heliaea, the Parabystes, and likewise the Trigonum. What the two tribunals are, the Baptachoon and the Phoinikion, named from their colour, will be made clear by the words of Aristotle in the Constitution of the Athenians: "For the courts have a sign written over each one, of the wand... and he who takes his staff goes to the court in the same way as the staff, and having the same mark as the acorn [?]." Pausanias, however, does not say which of the two Parabystes he means, though it may be gathered from Pollux's words. For Pausanias writes of the Parabystes "in an obscure part of the city, and in the lowest places." It is a tribunal in an obscure part of the city, in which trivial matters of little importance are judged. Pollux's words show that this is the middle Parabystes, in which the Undecemviri sat as judges: "The middle Parabystes, the greater Parabystes. Lysias also mentions a greater one. In the Parabystes of the ... the Eudicae judged the cases of Meticho's lesser sort, which the Androtions imitate." These words of Pollux, "judged the cases of Meticho's lesser sort," are doubtless corrupt, for matters of greater importance were not judged in this tribunal than in that one which had its name from Meticho; for it is agreed that it lay "in the lowest part" of the Parabystes. But the most learned man, who rewrites it as τὰ Μηδίχου κάλλιω, did not see the way to the correction. I think it should be restored thus: "In the middle of the Parabystes the Eudicae judged those matters which did not exceed by even a trifle the value of one choinix." A choinix is the twelfth part of a metretes of wine, and a metretes of wine sold for twelve drachmas. Demosthenes, in the speech against Phainippus: "For the man who now sells a choinix of wine for two obols..." I hold that the price of a choinix of wine was one drachma. Accordingly, the matters which came before the Undecemviri in the Parabystes did not exceed the value of one drachma, or one choinix. From this it is further clear that in this Parabystes the judges did not sit, as they sat in the other tribunals, perhaps as captives. For this Parabystes was the tribunal of the Undecemviri, and was so called at Athens, where the Eleven judged. Antiphon in his speech against Nicocles, concerning boundaries, mentions it, as does another [writer] of Comedy... From these seven tribunals, which we have listed, this Parabystes must be struck out; so six only remain, and if we add those four in which judgments were given, there will be ten tribunals in which the Athenian judges perhaps administered justice as captives. Of these tribunals the greatest was the Heliaea, as Pausanias says: "the greatest, where the largest number of people sits, they call the Heliaea." In my judgment Pausanias called it the greatest because it heard cases concerning more people, and for that reason "the largest number of people sits there." Otherwise the number of judges sitting in at least two other tribunals would seem to have been equal to the number of those who dispensed justice in the Heliaea, for in the Heliaea there were five hundred judges. Pollux: "The Heliaea has five hundred." There was also another tribunal in which there were as many; for when it sometimes happened that the judges of two tribunals came together to dispense justice, which in earlier times they did, there were a thousand judges. Pollux: "If there are two thousand judges, two tribunals sit together." Here is an example in Demosthenes' speech against Timocrates: "For when two tribunals had been assigned to one thousand..." Ulpian: "When the large and fixed courts, as they were called, came together in pairs, filling the number of a thousand..." You have a third tribunal too, in which there were also five hundred; for if there was need of fifteen hundred judges, three tribunals came together. Pollux: "If there are five hundred or two thousand judges, the three tribunals sit together." You have an example in Dinarchus, in the speech against Demosthenes, where he says "five hundred or a thousand," and in the whole city... likewise in Plutarch's Pericles: "Anaxagoras, having been accused of impiety, was tried before a thousand or five hundred judges." Therefore the number of judges who sat in the Heliaea was not greater, but the lawsuits and causes there were far more numerous and weightier than in the other tribunals; so everyone hoped to be assigned to this tribunal. Demosthenes, in the speech against Aeschines: "But you yourselves, when all the Athenians draw lots, and I know well that all wish to be allotted to this court, alone judge us..." When the judges and tribunals had been designated in this way, the judges then gave an oath, in words prescribed by law, that they would dispense justice according to the Laws to each man. You have the very formula of the oath set out in Demosthenes' speech against Timocrates, beginning "I will swear."

units.la: ΟΡΚΟΣ ΗΛΙΑΣΤΩΝ. IVSIVRANDVM HELIASTARVM
units.tr: THE OATH OF THE HELIASTS [ὅρκος ἡλιαστῶν]

units.la: ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΤΩΝ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΩΝ. ΚΑΙ ΤΥΡΑΝΝΟΝ ΟΥ ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΟΥΔΕ ΟΛΙΓΑΡΧΙΑΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΚΑΤΑΛΥΗ ΤΟΝ ΔΗΜΟΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ Η ΛΕΓΗ Η ΕΠΙΨΗΦΙΖΗ
units.tr: I will vote according to the laws and the decrees of the people of Athens and of the Council of Five Hundred. I will not vote for a tyranny, nor for an oligarchy, nor, if anyone overthrows the democracy of the Athenians by speech or by vote. [ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΤΩΝ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΩΝ. ΚΑΙ ΤΥΡΑΝΝΟΝ ΟΥ ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΟΥΔΕ ΟΛΙΓΑΡΧΙΑΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΚΑΤΑΛΥΗ ΤΟΝ ΔΗΜΟΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ Η ΛΕΓΗ Η ΕΠΙΨΗΦΙΖΗ]

units.la: Sententiam feram secundum Leges, & populi Atheniensis scita, & Quingentorum Senatusconsulta. Tyrannum, aut paucorum dominatum meo calculo non approbato. neque si quis popularem Athenien-sium statum euertere conetur, aut diΠΑΡΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΟΥ ΠΕΙΣΟΜΑΙ ΟΥΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΕΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΑΠΟΚΟΠΑΣ, ΟΥΔΕ ΓΗΣ ΑΝΑΔΑΣΜΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΟΥΔ' ΟΙΚΙΩΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΦΕΥΓΟΝΤΑΣ ΚΑΤΑΞΩ, ΟΥΔΕ ΩΝ ΘΑΝΑΤΟΣ ΚΑΤΕΓΝΩΣΤΑΙ, ΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΜΕΝΟΝΤΑΣ ΕΞΕΛΩ ΓΑΡΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ. ΟΥΤ' ΑΥΤΟΣ ΕΓΩ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΝ ΟΥΔΕΝΑ ΕΑΣΩ, ΟΥΔΕ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΚΑΤΑΣΤΗΣΩ, ΩΣΤΕ ΑΡΧ[?]ΕΙΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΕΡΑΣ ΑΡΧΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΙΕΡΟΜΝΗΜΟΝΟΣ, ΚΑΙ ΟΣΟΙ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΚΥΑΜΕΥΟΝΤΑΙ ΤΑΥΤΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΗΜΕΡΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΚΗΡΥΚΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΡΕΣΒΕΙΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΣΥΝΕΔΡΩΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΥΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΑΝΔΡΑ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΥΟ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΑΡΞΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΑΥΤΩΙ ΕΝΙΑΥΤΩΙ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΩΡΑ ΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΗΛΙΑΣΕΩΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ, ΟΥΤΕ ΑΥΤΟΣ ΕΓΩ ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΣ ΕΜΟΙ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΙ ΕΙ ΔΟΤΟΣ ΕΜΟΥ, ΟΥΤΕ ΤΕΧΝΗΙ, ΟΥΤΕ ΜΗΧΑΝΗΙ, ΜΗΔΕ ΜΙΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΓΕΓΟΝΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΛΑΤΤΟΝ Η ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΗ. ΚΑΙ ΑΚΡΟΑΣΟΜΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΤΕ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΛΟΓΟΥΜΕΝΟΥ ΟΜΟΙΩΣ ΑΜΦΟΙΝ, ΚΑΙ ΔΙΑΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΟΥ ΑΝ ΗΙ Η ΔΙΩΞΙΣ. ΕΠΟΜΝΥΜΙ ΔΙΑ ΠΟΣΕΙΔΩΝΑ, ΔΗΜΗΤΡΑ ΕΠΑΡΩΜΑΙ ΕΞΩΛΕΙΑΝ ΕΜΑΥΤΩΙ ΚΑΙ ΟΙΚΙΑΙ ΤΗΙ ΕΜΑΥΤΟΥ, ΕΙ ΤΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΒΑΙΝΟΙΜΙ, ΕΥΟΡΚΟΥΝΤΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΔΑ ΠΟΛΛΑ ΚΑΘΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ.
units.tr: I will pass sentence according to the laws, the decrees of the people of Athens and the senate-decrees of the Five Hundred. I will not approve a tyranny or the rule of a few by my vote, nor, if anyone tries to overthrow the popular constitution of the Athenians, or [ΠΑΡΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΟΥ ΠΕΙΣΟΜΑΙ ΟΥΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΕΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΑΠΟΚΟΠΑΣ, ΟΥΔΕ ΓΗΣ ΑΝΑΔΑΣΜΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΟΥΔ' ΟΙΚΙΩΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΦΕΥΓΟΝΤΑΣ ΚΑΤΑΞΩ, ΟΥΔΕ ΩΝ ΘΑΝΑΤΟΣ ΚΑΤΕΓΝΩΣΤΑΙ, ΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΜΕΝΟΝΤΑΣ ΕΞΕΛΩ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ. ΟΥΤ' ΑΥΤΟΣ ΕΓΩ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΝ ΟΥΔΕΝΑ ΕΑΣΩ, ΟΥΔΕ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΚΑΤΑΣΤΗΣΩ, ΩΣΤΕ ΑΡΧ[?]ΕΙΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΕΡΑΣ ΑΡΧΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΙΕΡΟΜΝΗΜΟΝΟΣ, ΚΑΙ ΟΣΟΙ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΚΥΑΜΕΥΟΝΤΑΙ ΤΑΥΤΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΗΜΕΡΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΚΗΡΥΚΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΡΕΣΒΕΙΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΣΥΝΕΔΡΩΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΥΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΑΝΔΡΑ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΥΟ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΑΡΞΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΑΥΤΩΙ ΕΝΙΑΥΤΩΙ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΩΡΑ ΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΗΛΙΑΣΕΩΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ, ΟΥΤΕ ΑΥΤΟΣ ΕΓΩ ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΣ ΕΜΟΙ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΙ ΕΙ ΔΟΤΟΣ ΕΜΟΥ, ΟΥΤΕ ΤΕΧΝΗΙ, ΟΥΤΕ ΜΗΧΑΝΗΙ, ΜΗΔΕ ΜΙΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΓΕΓΟΝΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΛΑΤΤΟΝ Η ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΗ. ΚΑΙ ΑΚΡΟΑΣΟΜΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΤΕ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΛΟΓΟΥΜΕΝΟΥ ΟΜΟΙΩΣ ΑΜΦΟΙΝ, ΚΑΙ ΔΙΑΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΟΥ ΑΝ ΗΙ Η ΔΙΩΞΙΣ. ΕΠΟΜΝΥΜΙ ΔΙΑ ΠΟΣΕΙΔΩΝΑ, ΔΗΜΗΤΡΑ ΕΠΑΡΩΜΑΙ ΕΞΩΛΕΙΑΝ ΕΜΑΥΤΩΙ ΚΑΙ ΟΙΚΙΑΙ ΤΗΙ ΕΜΑΥΤΟΥ, ΕΙ ΤΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΒΑΙΝΟΙΜΙ, ΕΥΟΡΚΟΥΝΤΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΔΑ ΠΟΛΛΑ ΚΑΘΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ.] Neither will I give way beyond these matters, nor will I cancel private debts, nor redistribute the land of the Athenians, nor their houses; nor will I restore exiles, nor condemn those who flee, nor expel those who remain, contrary to the laws in force and the decrees of the people of Athens and of the Council. I myself will not do so, nor will I allow anyone else to do so; I will not establish a magistracy so that one who is accountable in another office, or one of the Nine Archons or the Hieromnemon, or whoever is installed together with the Nine Archons on that day, or herald or envoy or assessor, may hold office; nor will I hold the same office twice, nor hold two offices in the same year. I will not accept gifts on account of my sitting as a judge in the Heliaea; neither I myself nor another for me, nor anyone at my bidding, by any art or device, by no means. I am not less than thirty years old. I will hear both parties alike. I will pass sentence on the matter on which the action is brought. [ΟΥΔΕ ΔΩΡΑ ΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΗΛΙΑΣΕΩΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ]

units.la: Heliastarum hoc fuisse iusiurandum praefert ΤΩΝ, & comprobant illa iurisiurandi verba, C cat, aut decernat aduersus haec, assensum praebebo: neque novas tabulas fieri, aut agrum domosque populi Athenien-sis dividi patiar. Exules non restituam, neque capitis damnatos: neque eos qui urbem incolunt, ea pellain [?], aduersus Leges receptas, & populi Athenienfis scita, Senatusque consulta, neque quenquam alium id aggredi sinam. Neminem Magistratum gerere sinam, qui rationes alterius à se gesti Magistratus non retulerit, sive sit è Nouemviris, sive Hieromnemon, sive quis alius eorum, qui eodem cum Nouemviro die Magistratus sortiuntur, sive Praeco, sive Legatus, sive Assessor: neque eundem bis in eodem esse Magistratu, aut duos Magistratus gerere eodem anno. Munera non accipiam propterea quod iudex in Heliaea sedeo, non ego ipse, neque alter mihi, neque vllus me conscio, nulla arte, nulla fraude. Non sum minor annis triginta. Vtramque partem audiam ex aequo. Sententiam feram de ea re, de qua instituta erit actio. Iouem, Neptunum, Cererem vindices testor, imprecorque exitium ipse mihi & familiae meae, si quid horum non obseruauero: si fidem contra datam libero, omnia prospera atque fausta.
units.tr: Heliastarum hoc fuisse iusiurandum praefert [ΤΩΝ] and confirm it by those oath-words: [if anyone proposes or decrees against these things,] I will give my assent. I will not allow new tablets of debt to be made, nor the land and houses of the people of Athens to be divided. I will not restore exiles, nor those condemned to death; nor will I expel those who dwell in the city, contrary to the laws in force and the decrees of the people of Athens and the Senate, nor will I allow anyone else to attempt it. I will not allow anyone to hold magistracy who has not rendered accounts of his earlier magistracy to another, whether he is one of the Nine, or a Hieromnemon, or any other of those who are chosen for office on the same day as the Nine; whether herald or envoy. I will not accept gifts because I sit as a judge in the Heliaea; neither I myself, nor another for me, nor anyone at my bidding, by any art or fraud. I am not younger than thirty years. I will hear both parties alike. I will pass sentence on the matter on which the trial is held. I call Jupiter, Neptune and Ceres to witness and invoke destruction upon myself and my family if I do not observe any of these things; if I break faith, may all things be prosperous and auspicious.

units.la: titulus, ΟΡΚΟΣ ΗΛΙΑΣ-ΥΔΕ ΔΩΡΑ ΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ
units.tr: Title: THE OATH OF THE HELIASTS; "I accept no gifts" [ὅρκος ἡλιαστῶν; ΟΥΔΕ ΔΩΡΑ ΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ]

units.la: ΤΗΣ ΗΛΙΑΣΕΩΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ. An vero ceteri iudices, qui in aliis Tribunalibus ius erant dicturi, idem iusiurandum iisdem verbis darent, necne, pro certo affirmare non possumus: videtur tamen idem non fuisse: nam Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. X. ita scribit ὄμνυον δὲ ἐν Ἀρείῳ, ΑΠΟΛΛΩ ΓΑΤΡΩΙΟΝ
units.tr: Whether the other judges, who were to sit in other courts, gave the same oath in the same words, we cannot affirm for certain; it seems, however, that it was not the same. For Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 10, writes thus: they swore in the Areopagus [ὄμνυον δὲ ἐν Ἀρείῳ], by Apollo Patrius [ΑΠΟΛΛΩ ΓΑΤΡΩΙΟΝ].

units.la: *ΔΗΜΗΤΡΑΝ [?] ΔΙΑ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΑ. Atqui in Heliaftarum iurciurando Apollo Patrius in tectem atque vindicem non appellabatur, fed Neptunus: neque item Rex Iupiter, fed tantum Jupiter finc vllo cognomine: ΕΠΟΜΝΥΜΙ ΔΙΑ, ΠΟΣΕΙΔΩΝΑ, ΔΗΜΗΤΡΑ. His adde, videri diftingui eos qui Heliaftarum iufiurandum dederint, ab iis qui aliud dederint: ita enim legitur in Lege, quae eft de fecrendis Legibus: [?] ΝΟΜΩΝ [?] ὅτι [?] ΗΛΙΑΣΤΩΝ [?] ὅρκον [?]. Quanquam certum eft, multa fuiffe omnibus Iudicibus communia, in quae iurabant omnes: in his puto fuiffe Kaput Iftud, quod poft exactos Triginta Tyrannos adfcriptum fuit, habeturque apud Andocidem, [illegible, ~12 letters] [?] Ἀνδοκίδης [?], τὰ [?] ὀμώμοσμα [?] τῶν ΗΛΙΑΣΤΩΝ [?].
units.tr: *[by Demeter] [ΔΗΜΗΤΡΑΝ] by Zeus the King [ΔΙΑ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΑ]. Yet in the oath of the Heliasts Apollo Patrius was not called upon as witness and avenger, but Neptune; nor likewise King Jupiter, but only Jupiter without any epithet: [I swear by Zeus, by Poseidon, by Demeter]. Add to this that those who gave the oath of the Heliasts seem to be distinguished from those who gave another oath: for thus it is read in the law which concerns the separating of the laws: [...] of the Heliasts [...] the oath [...]. Although it is certain that many things were common to all judges, which all swore to: among these, I think, was that clause which, after the expulsion of the Thirty Tyrants, was added and is preserved in Andocides, [illegible], the oath of the Heliasts [illegible].

units.la: ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΜΝΗΣΙΚΑΚΗΣΩ ΟΥΔΕ ΑΛΛΟ ΠΕΙΣΟΜΑΙ ΤΗΦΙΟΥ- ΝΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΕΙΜΕ- ΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ. Neque praeteritorum in malum memincro, neque alteri meminenti affen-fum praebebo: fed fententiam feram fe-cundum receptas Leges.
units.tr: I will not remember past wrongs, nor will I give assent to another who does so; but I will pass sentence according to the received laws. [ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΜΝΗΣΙΚΑΚΗΣΩ ΟΥΔΕ ΑΛΛΟ ΠΕΙΣΟΜΑΙ ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ.] Neither will I remember past wrongs, nor will I give assent to another who remembers them; but I will pass sentence according to the received laws.

units.la: Quod hic legitur, ΤΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟ- ΜΟΥΣ. Sed fententiam feram fecundum receptas Leges, referendum eft ad Legem ἀμνηστίας. Praecedentia ita emendo. ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΜΝΗΣΙΚΑΚΗΣΩ, ΟΥΔΕ ΑΛΛΩ ΠΕΙΣΟΜΑΙ. eo fenfu, quo vertimus, Neque praeteritorum in malum meminero, neque alteri meminenti affenfum praebebo. Fuerūt tamen Heliaftarum quaedā propria: in hunc cenfum refero illa quae de Magiftratibus dicuntur, ΟΥΔΕ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΚΑΤΑΣΤΗΣΩ, ΩΣΤΕ ΑΡΧΕΙΝ ΓΡΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΟΝ- ΤΑ ΕΤΕΡΑΣ ΑΡΧΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΙΕΡΟΜΝΗΜΟΝΟΣ, ΚΑΙ ΟΣΟΙ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΚΥΑΜΕΤΟΝΤΑΙ ΤΑΥΤΗ, ΤΗΙ ΗΜΕΡΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΚΗΡΥΚΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΡΕΣΒΕΙΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΣΥ- ΝΕΔΡΩΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΥΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΑΝΔΡΑ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΥΟ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΑΡΞΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΑΥ-TOΝ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΑΥΤΩι ΕΝΙΑΥΤΩι. Nempe Magiftratus à Iudicibus approbabantur, & nonnifi probati Magiftratuum gerebant, ex Lege, [?] Ἀρχαί ἀπαραι [?] ἐν τῷ Διὸς [?] τοῦ ἐν [?] ἔτι, Tribunal illud, in quo ficbat [illegible, ~8 letters] Magiftratuum, antequam munus fuum adirent, erat Heliaea, vt hinc conftat, erat quippe μείζων, ἓς ὁ ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΟΝ [?], vt è Paufania diximus. Cetera, meo iudicio, communia funt omnibus iudicibus. ΤΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΤΩΝ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΩΝ. intelligecum Vlpiano Scholiafte [?] ὑφίσματα τὰ παρὰ [?], τὰ ἰσημέρινα [?] κυκλ. Sequitur, ΟΥΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΕΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΑΠΟΚΟΠΑΣ, ΟΥΔΕ ΓΗΣ ΑΝΑΔΑΣΜΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΑΘΗ- ΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΥΔΕ ΟΙΚΙΩΝ. Optime Vlpianus interpretatur, [?] ἰσωνίζοντα [?] τὰ ἰδιωτικὰ [?] ἐκ [?] ἐκ [?] ἀπο [?]. ὅτι ... [illegible, ~10 letters] ... ΑΝΑΔΑΣΜΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΤ' ΟΙdocuit, cui nomen Τι, vt auctoribus Athenæo & Suida constat, an eodem quoque titulo fuit ista Menandri, cuius meminit Medicus Priscianus? Sed ad iusiurandum Heliastarum redeamus, in quo ista leguntur. ΚΑΙ ΑΚΡΟΑ-ΣΟΜΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΤΕ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΛΟΓΟΥΜΕΝΟΥ ΟΜΟΙΩΣ ΑΜΦΟΙΝ. Virumque partem ex æquo audiam. Non tantum iureiurando Heliastarum habetur, sed etiam hac veteri Solonis Lege imperatur,
units.tr: What is read here, [ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ], but I will pass sentence according to the received laws, must be referred to the law of amnesty. I emend the preceding words thus: [ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΜΝΗΣΙΚΑΚΗΣΩ, ΟΥΔΕ ΑΛΛΩ ΠΕΙΣΟΜΑΙ], in the sense in which we have translated: Neither will I remember past wrongs to their harm, nor will I give assent to another who remembers them. There were, however, some matters proper to the Heliasts: to this category I refer those things which are said about magistrates: [ΟΥΔΕ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΚΑΤΑΣΤΗΣΩ, ΩΣΤΕ ΑΡΧΕΙΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΟΝΤΑ ΕΤΕΡΑΣ ΑΡΧΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΙΕΡΟΜΝΗΜΟΝΟΣ, ΚΑΙ ΟΣΟΙ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΚΥΑΜΕΤΟΝΤΑΙ ΤΑΥΤΗ ΤΗΙ ΗΜΕΡΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΚΗΡΥΚΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΡΕΣΒΕΙΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΣΥΝΕΔΡΩΝ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΥΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΑΝΔΡΑ, ΟΥΔΕ ΔΥΟ ΑΡΧΑΣ ΑΡΞΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΑΥΤΩΙ ΕΝΙΑΥΤΩΙ]. Clearly the magistrates were approved by the judges, and only the approved held magistracies, according to the law [illegible]: that Tribunal in which the examination of magistrates took place before they entered upon their office was the Heliaea, as is evident from this, for it was indeed greater, as we said from Pausanias. The rest, in my judgement, are common to all judges. [ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΤΩΝ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΩΝ], to be understood with Ulpian the scholiast [illegible]. There follows: [ΟΥΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΕΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΑΠΟΚΟΠΑΣ, ΟΥΔΕ ΓΗΣ ΑΝΑΔΑΣΜΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΥΔΕ ΟΙΚΙΩΝ]. Ulpian interprets this well [illegible], [illegible], that [illegible], the law of the Athenians [illegible]: it was called by the title of which, as Athenaeus and Suidas confirm, was this also the title of Menander's work, which the physician Priscian mentions? But let us return to the oath of the Heliasts, in which these things are read: [ΚΑΙ ΑΚΡΟΑΣΟΜΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΤΕ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΛΟΓΟΥΜΕΝΟΥ ΟΜΟΙΩΣ ΑΜΦΟΙΝ.] I will hear both parties alike. This is not only found in the oath of the Heliasts, but is also prescribed by this ancient law of Solon,

units.la: Τοῦ τε κατηγόρου, καὶ τοῦ ἀπολογουμένου ὁμοίως ἀμφοῖν ἀκροᾶσθαι. Virumque partem ex æquo audito.
units.tr: To hear the accuser and the defendant alike, both of them. Hear both parties alike.

units.la: Verfus eft vulgarius Phocylidis:
units.tr: A common verse of Phocylides:

units.la: μήπ' ἤκω δικάσῃς πρὶν ἂν ἀμφοῖν μὴ ἀκούσῃς.
units.tr: "Do not come to judge before you have heard both sides." [μήπ' ἤκω δικάσῃς πρὶν ἂν ἀμφοῖν μὴ ἀκούσῃς.]

units.la: In iureiurando Heliastarum ista quoque leguntur: ΟΥΔΕ ΩΡΑ ΔΕ-ΞΟΜΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΗΛΙΑΣΕΩΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΥΤΟΣ ΕΓΩ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΣ ΕΜΟΙ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΙ ΕΙΔΟΤΟΣ ΕΜΟΥ, ΟΥ ΤΕΧΝΗΙ, ΟΥΤΕ ΜΗΧΑΝΗΙ ΜΗΔΕΜΙΑ. Erat autem muneratio iudici, qui pecuniam accepisse conuictus erat ob ius dicendum, multa irrogata: Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. VI. meminit cautionis. [illegible, ~20 letters] Scholiastes vero Thucydidis ad Lib. VI. multæ. Verba Thucydidis, quæ interpretatur hæc funt, ὅσα ἀπὸ γῆς ἡ ἱκανὸν [illegible, ~30 letters]. Interpretatio ita se habet ut [illegible, ~20 letters].
units.tr: The oath of the Heliasts also contains these words: "I will by no means accept any delay of the Heliaia for the sake of ..., neither I myself, nor another for me, nor others at the instigation of me, nor any of those who know me; not by art, nor by device, by no means." [ΟΥΔΕ ΩΡΑ ΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΗΛΙΑΣΕΩΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΥΤΟΣ ΕΓΩ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΣ ΕΜΟΙ, ΟΥΤ' ΑΛΛΟΙ ΕΙΔΟΤΟΣ ΕΜΟΥ, ΟΥ ΤΕΧΝΗΙ, ΟΥΤΕ ΜΗΧΑΝΗΙ ΜΗΔΕΜΙΑ.] A judge who had been convicted of accepting money for giving a judgment was punished with a fine. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter VI, mentions this security. The scholiast on Thucydides, on Book VI, speaks of the fine. The words of Thucydides, which the scholiast explains, are these: [...]. The explanation runs as follows [...].

units.la: Quanquam nimis remissa erat hæc pœna, si attendas ad summam iudicis illius perfidiam, contra omnia iura diuina atque humana iusiurandum tuum pecunia vendentis: Itaque Romani Decemuiri dignum esse hoc fœlus capitis pœna exiftimarunt, Legemque scripserunt, quae iudicem arbitrumve iure datum, qui ob rem dicendam pecuniam accepisse convictus est, capite punit, ut scribit A. Gellius Lib. XX. cap. I. Sed id postea mutavit, & plerumque Iudices a Praeside aut curia submouentur, aut in exilium mittantur, (quod olim obtinuisse Asconius significat in II. Verrinam.) aut ad tempus relegantur, ut loquitur Paulus Lib. V. Sententi. Tit. XXVIII. ad Legem Iuliam Repetundarum.
units.tr: Yet this penalty was far too lenient, if you consider the great treachery of such a judge, who sells his oath for money, against all divine and human law. Therefore the Roman Decemvirs judged that this crime deserved the penalty of death, and they wrote a law by which a judge or arbiter appointed by law, who was convicted of having accepted money for giving a judgment, was punished by death, as A. Gellius writes in Book XX, chapter I. But this was later changed, and for the most part judges are removed from office by the praetor or the senate, or are sent into exile (as Asconius indicates was once the practice, in his commentary on the second Verrine oration), or are relegated for a time, as Paulus says in Book V of his Sentences, title XXVIII, on the Julian law on extortion.

units.la: [ornamental rule, not transcribed]
DE IN IUS VOCANDO.
units.tr: ON SUMMONING TO COURT (DE IN IUS VOCANDO).

units.la: TITULUS SECUNDUS.
units.tr: TITLE II.

units.la: O[?]MNIUM actionum instituendarum, ut loquitur Iustinianus Institut. Lib. IV. Tit. XVI. de pœna temere litigantium, §. vlt. principium ab ea parte proficiscitur, quæ edicit de in ius vocando. Utique enim in primis adversarius in ius vocandus est, id est, ad eum vocandus, qui ius dicturus sit. Nam in ius vocare, verba sunt Pauli Lib. IV. ad Edictum, est iuris experiundi causa vocare. Leg. I. D. de in ius vocando. Itaque iudicium nullum reddebatur sine in ius vocatione: hæc vero non fiebat sine Magistratus auctoritate. Demosthenes [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] Primum igitur actor adversarium sui nomen deferebat apud Magistratum, cuius erat dicam illam Εἰσαγγελίαν. Huius Magistratus permissu actor adversarium in ius vocabat, sive per apparitores, quos κλητῆρας ἢ κλητῆρας vocant. Aristophanes Avibus.
units.tr: Of all actions to be brought, as Justinian says (Institutes, Book IV, Title XVI, on the penalty for rash litigants, last §), the beginning comes from that part of the edict which deals with summoning to court. For first of all the adversary must be summoned to court, that is, called before the one who is to pronounce judgment. For "to summon to court" (in ius vocare), in the words of Paul (Book IV on the Edict), means to call someone in order to enforce a right. Dig. I, de in ius vocando. Hence no trial was held without a summons to court, and this was not done without the authority of the magistrate. Demosthenes [illegible] [illegible]. First, then, the plaintiff lodged his adversary's name before the magistrate, whose office was that impeachment called Eisangelia. With this magistrate's permission the plaintiff summoned the adversary to court, either through the attendants whom they called klētēres [κλητῆρας] or through ... Aristophanes, in the Birds.

units.la: Μὰ Δία, ἀλλὰ κλητὴρ εἰμι ὑπηρετικός[?].
units.tr: "No, by Zeus, but I am a serving summoner [Μὰ Δία, ἀλλὰ κλητὴρ εἰμι ὑπηρετικός]."

units.la: Scholia: κλητὴρ λέγεται, ὁ καλῶν εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον πολίτας. Ulpianus ad laudata Demosthenis verba. [illegible, ~30 letters] & ad Midianam: [illegible, ~50 letters] Vel in ius vocatio fiebat ab ipso actore cum apparitoribus, aut advocatis testibus, quos etiam κλητῆρας dixerunt. Aristophanes Vespis illustri exemplo repræsentat, quomodo, quibusve verbis in ius vocatio fieret.
units.tr: Scholia: "A klētēr is one who calls citizens to the court [κλητὴρ λέγεται, ὁ καλῶν εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον πολίτας]." Ulpian on the words of Demosthenes just cited, [illegible] and on the Midiana: [illegible]. Or the summons to court was made by the plaintiff himself with the attendants, or with witnesses called in, whom they also called klētēres. Aristophanes, in the Wasps, presents in a famous example how and in what words the summons to court was made.

units.la: Hefychius: κλητήρ, ὁ εἰς δίκην καλῶν, ὁ κλητεύων, καὶ μάρτυρας ἔχων εἰς δίκην[?]. Legeitaque conftitutum eft, vt adferiberetur nomen illius, qui adfuerat cum aduerfarius in ius vocaretur:
units.tr: Hesychius: klētēr, one who calls to a suit, who summons, and who has witnesses for the suit. And so it was established by law that the name of the man who had been present when the adversary was summoned to court should be written down:

units.la: Τὸν τῆς προσκαλέσεως κλητῆρα ὅτι[?] — Eius nomen, qui adfuit cum in ius vocaretur aduerfarius, adfcribito.
units.tr: [Τὸν τῆς προσκαλέσεως κλητῆρα ὅτι] The name of the one who was present when the adversary was summoned to court is to be written down.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demofthenes in Midiana: πίσας τὸν παρυτδμένα[?] ὅδε[?] καὶ τὸν ὅδε ... ἀρχὴν[?] ... ἀλλὰ[?] καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν Διαιτητῶν[?]. Formula haecerat, cum ab apparitore vocatio in ius fiebat, vt ex Vlpiano ad Midianam liquet: ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΩ ΤΟΝ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΤΟΥΔΕ, ΚΑΙ ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΟΥΜΑΙ ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΔΙΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΕΙΝΟΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΗΝΔΕ. Si cum aduocatis testibus his verbis concipiebatur. ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΟΥΜΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΤΟΥΔΕ ΑΔΙΚΗΜΑΤΟΣ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΗΝΔΕ, ΚΑΗΤΗΡΑ ΕΧΩΝ ΤΟΝ ΔΕΙΝΑ. At vero quando femina in ius vocabatur, non tantum illa vocabatur, sed etiam eius maritus: Η ΔΕΙΝΑ ΚΑΙ Ο ΚΥΡΙΟΣ. Scribit id Graecus Comici Interpres ad hos ex Equitibus verfus:
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in the Midiana [πίσας τὸν παρυτδμένα ... ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν Διαιτητῶν]. The formula used when the summons to court was made by the attendant, as is clear from Ulpian on the Midiana, ran: "I accuse this man of [such and such], and I summon him through the attendant to the magistrate [ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΩ ΤΟΝ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΤΟΥΔΕ, ΚΑΙ ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΟΥΜΑΙ ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΔΙΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΕΙΝΟΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΗΝΔΕ]." If it was made with witnesses present, it was phrased in these words: "I summon this man to the magistrate on this charge, and I have the witness [ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΟΥΜΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΤΟΥΔΕ ΑΔΙΚΗΜΑΤΟΣ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΗΝΔΕ, ΚΑΗΤΗΡΑ ΕΧΩΝ ΤΟΝ ΔΕΙΝΑ]." But when a woman was summoned to court, not only she was summoned but also her husband: [Η ΔΕΙΝΑ ΚΑΙ Ο ΚΥΡΙΟΣ]. The Greek commentator on the comic poet explains these verses from the Knights in this way:

units.la: ἐφ' ἁρμάτης[?]Χρυσοῦ Ἱπποξύλ[?] Σιμικλέους[?], ἢ κυκλεύει[?].
units.tr: [Corrupt Greek verse from Aristophanes' Knights, ἐφ' ἁρμάτης Χρυσοῦ Ἱπποξύλ Σιμικλέους ἢ κυκλεύει; not reliably legible in the scan.]

units.la: ὡς αὐτὴ δὲ τῆς ἐλαχαγαμὸς[?] τὴν ἐπιγαμίαν[?] κυρίως ἐπιλογὴν ... ἐπὶ δὲ ἡ γυνὴ ἀνάγκη[?]... ἡ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΚΑΙ Ο ΚΥΡΙΟΣ. ἔντησις, ὁ ἀνήρ. alieno namque iuri, id eft, mariti, fubiecta funt.
units.tr: "As the wife of ... [illegible] ... properly ... but the wife is under necessity ... [the formula]: the woman and her lord [ἡ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΚΑΙ Ο ΚΥΡΙΟΣ]; the husband." For she is subject to another's right, that is, her husband's.

units.la: Fiebat etiam aliquando in ius vocatio manus iniectione. Lucianus ἀκκηπ[?] ... ἴπου, μακρὰ, ... ΑΛ. μὴ ἀῆχ μή. Ita apud Terentium in palliata Apollodori fabula Phormione.
units.tr: Sometimes too the summons to court was made by laying hands on the person. Lucian (...) AL. "No, no!" [μὴ ἀῆχ μή]. So in Terence, in the palliata Phormio, a play based on Apollodorus.

units.la: De. In ius eamus. Ph. In ius? huc, fi quid lubet.
units.tr: Demipho: "Let's go to court." Phormio: "To court? Here, if you like."

units.la: De. Adfequere, acre tine, dum ego huc feruos conoco.
units.tr: Demipho: "Follow him, seize him, hold him fast, while I call my slaves here."

units.la: Ch. Enim folus nequeo: accurre huc. Ph. Vna iniuria'st Tecum. Ch. Lege agito. Ph. Aliera ^ eft tecum, Chreme.
units.tr: Chremes: "I can't manage alone: run here." Phormio: "There is one wrong with you." Chremes: "I shall proceed by law." Phormio: "Another is with you, Chremes."

units.la: De. Rapehunc.
units.tr: Demipho: "Seize him."

units.la: & paullo poft idem Demipho.
units.tr: And a little later the same Demipho [says]:

units.la: Ni fequitur, pugnos in ventrem ingere. Vel oculum exclude.
units.tr: "If he follows, drive your fists into his belly. Or knock out his eye."

units.la: An vero de domo fua aduerfarium in ius vocare permiffum fuerit, pro comperto non habemus: fcimus tamen conceffum fuiffe domum eius adire cum apparitore publico, ad edenda inftrumenta. Demofthenes δὲ πρὸς τὸν Μνησίβουλον ἐν Ἐρέτρᾳ[?] ... ΕΥ[?] ... πρὸς τὸ οἰκίαν τοῦ Θεοφήμου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτοῦ ὁ Δημοσθένης[?] ... ἐκδοῦναι[?].
units.tr: Whether it was permitted to summon an adversary from his own house, we do not have as established; we know, however, that it was allowed to approach his house with a public attendant, in order to produce documents. Demosthenes, against Mnesibulus [ἐν Ἐρέτρᾳ ... πρὸς τὴν οἰκίαν τοῦ Θεοφήμου ... ἐκδοῦναι], and from the man himself ... to surrender.

units.la: Ex hoc Athenienfium iure tranflata eft Decemuiralis haec Lex: SI IN IVS VOCAT. NEI. IT. ANTISTATOR. IGITVR. IM. CAPITO. SI. CALVITVR. PEDEMVE. STRVIT. MANVM. ENDO. IACITO. Neminem autem de domo fua in ius vocari licebat, quique inde vocaret, vim inferre videbatur. Gaius Lib. I. ad Legem XII. Tabularum. Plerique putauerunt nullum de domo sua in ius vocari licere: quia domus tutissimum cuique refugium atque receptaculum sit: eumque, qui inde in ius vocaret, vim inferre videri. Leg. XVIII. D. de in ius vocando. Excipitur tamen, si quis vltro in domum suam aduersario patefecit aditum, aut ex publico conspiciatur, fenestra scilicet domus suae, in qua consistit. Paulus Lib. I. ad Edictum. Sed si aditum ad se praestet: aut ex publico conspiciatur: recte in ius eum vocari Julianus ait. Leg. XIX. D. eod. Neque tamen de domo sua in ius rapi potest: Paulus loco laudato: Sed etsi is, qui domi est, interdum vocari in ius potest: tamen de domo sua nemo extrahi debet. Leg. XXI. D. eod. Leg. CIII. D. de Regulis iuris. Verba Gaij è Lib. I. ad Legem XII. Tabularum, quae leguntur Leg. XX. D. de in ius vocando, & haec sunt: Sed etiam à vinea, & balneo, & theatro nemo dubitat in ius vocari licere, non ab omnibus intelligitur. Vir summus non videt, cur de vinea dicatur potius, quam de alio quocumque genere agri, neque vinea vel qui aliuscumque ager quid faciat ad domum etiam videt. Itaque Basilica maluit sequi, quae habent ἀπὸ πυλῶνος, id est à ianua, siue ianea, vt loquebantur veteres, hoc sensu, vt quemadmodum è fenestra, ita & è ianua domus suae, in qua consistit, in ius vocari quilibet possit. Et sequitur quod est extra domus causam, etiam è medio coetu plurium vnà lauantium vel spectantium in ius vocari posse, puta è balineo publico atque theatro. Ego vero existimo tota hac Lege agi de iis, quae sunt extra domus causam. Messium vindemiarumque tempore ne quis aduersarium cogat ad iudicium venire, oratione Divi Marci exprimitur. Leg. I. D. de feriis: sed maxime celebres erant vindemiales feriae. In Theatra conueniebat populus diebus festis maxime ludorum, qui dabantur, causa. Balinea publica frequentabantur priuatae voluptatis causa. Nullum autem excipi locum, nullum diem priuatae aut publicae laetitiae consecratum docet Gaius, in quo & a quo non liceat in ius vocare, à vinea, scilicet vindemiarum tempore, at quanto magis messium, si his vindemialibus feriis? à theatro, quando ludi dantur, cum publicae, à balneo, cum priuatae indulgetur voluptati. Hanc Legem non descripsit Auctor Eclogae Basilicôn, ceteras ita expressit Lib. VII. Tit. VIII. cap. XVIII. ςοδὶς ἐκ τῆς ἰδίου οἴκου κελεύῃ εἰς ἵκλων. ἑκάστῳ γὰρ ὁ ἰδίος οἶκος, ἀσφαλὲς δὲ καταφύγιον. ἡ δὲ κλῆσις αὐτὸν, βίᾳ ὑποφέρειν εἰ δὲ πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ἰδίωσιν εἴσοδον, ἢ θεωρῆται ἐκ τῆς ἀγορᾶς, κλῆσαι, & cap. XXI. ἐὰν τε μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῆς ἀπὸ τῆς οἴκου κλῆσαι· ὅμως ςοδὶς ἀπὸ τῆς οἴκου ἐλαττ[?].
units.tr: From this Athenian law the Decemviral law was borrowed: "If he summons someone to court and he does not go, let the summoner call witnesses, and then seize him. If he hides or puts off, let him lay hands on him." Nobody, however, was allowed to be summoned to court from his own house, and whoever summoned him from there was considered to be using force. Gaius, Book I on the Law of the Twelve Tables: Most authorities thought that no one may be summoned to court from his own house, because the house is each man's safest refuge and shelter, and whoever summons him from there is considered to use force. Dig. XVIII, de in ius vocando. An exception is made if someone has voluntarily opened access to his house for his adversary, or can be seen from a public place, namely from a window of his house where he stands. Paul, Book I on the Edict: But if he grants access to himself, or can be seen from a public place, Julian says he may rightly be summoned to court. Dig. XIX, eod. Yet a man cannot be dragged out of his own house into court. Paul, in the passage cited: But even if the one who is at home can sometimes be summoned to court, nevertheless no one ought to be dragged out of his own house. Dig. XXI, eod. Dig. CIII, de Regulis iuris. The words of Gaius from Book I on the Law of the Twelve Tables, which are read in Dig. XX, de in ius vocando, are these: But also from a vineyard, from a bath, and from a theatre, no one doubts that one may be summoned to court, and these are not understood by all. The great man does not see why it is said vineyard rather than any other kind of field, nor what a vineyard or any other field has to do with the house. So the Basilica preferred to follow a reading which has "from the gate" [ἀπὸ πυλῶνος], that is, from the door, or doorway, as the ancients said, in the sense that just as from a window, so also from the door of his house, in which he stands, anyone may be summoned. And what follows, that outside the house's sphere one may be summoned to court even from the midst of a crowd of several people bathing or watching together, for example from a public bath or theatre. I, however, think that the whole of this law deals with things outside the house's affairs. At the time of harvest and vintage, let no one compel his adversary to come to trial, is expressed in the speech of the deified Marcus, Dig. I, de feriis; but the vintage holidays were especially celebrated. People gathered in the theatres on festival days, chiefly for the games which were given. Public baths were frequented for private pleasure. Gaius, however, teaches that no place and no day consecrated to private or public joy is excepted, in which and from which it is not permitted to summon to court: from a vineyard, namely at vintage time, and how much more at harvest, if these are vintage holidays; from a theatre, when games are given, for public pleasure; from a bath, when private pleasure is indulged. The author of the Ecloga of the Basilica did not describe this law, but expressed the others thus, Book VII, Title VIII, ch. XVIII: [ςοδὶς ἐκ τῆς ἰδίου οἴκου κελεύῃ εἰς ἵκλων. ἑκάστῳ γὰρ ὁ ἰδίος οἶκος, ἀσφαλὲς δὲ καταφύγιον. ἡ δὲ κλῆσις αὐτὸν, βίᾳ ὑποφέρειν εἰ δὲ πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ἰδίωσιν εἴσοδον, ἢ θεωρῆται ἐκ τῆς ἀγορᾶς, κλῆσαι], that is, one who orders a summons out of his own house [is forced] ..., for each man's own house is a safe refuge; the summons would compel him to be carried off by force; but if he himself grants an entrance, or can be seen from the marketplace, he may be summoned. And ch. XXI: [ἐὰν τε μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῆς ἀπὸ τῆς οἴκου κλῆσαι· ὅμως ςοδὶς ἀπὸ τῆς οἴκου ἐλαττ], even if [a man is] in the house, he should not be dragged out of his house [illegible].

units.la: Porro is qui in ius vocatur, non semper statim sequi debet: nam etiam in ius aliquando vocatur, vt aliquot post diebus iudicio se sistat: habes exemplum apud Aristophanem Auibus:
units.tr: Moreover, the one who is summoned to court (in ius vocatur) does not always have to follow at once, for he is sometimes summoned so that he may present himself before the judge some days later. You have an example in Aristophanes' Birds:

units.la: Καλεῖσθαι Πεισάνδρου Ἔρεως [?] Ἐς τὴν Μοωνυχίαν μιλιᾶν [?]
units.tr: Καλεῖσθαι Πεισάνδρου Ἔρεως [?] Ἐς τὴν Μοωνυχίαν μιλιᾶν [?] (To be summoned by Peisander, son of Erasus, to Munychia.)

units.la: Acta est haec fabula Liberalibus τῆς κατ' ἄστυ, quae agitabantur die sexto decimo Elaphebolionis: ergo intercedit interuallum illud quod est à die sextodecimo Elaphebolionis ad ineuntem sequentem mensem Munychionem: Quare in formula addebatur: ΚΑΛΟΥΜΑΙ siue ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΟΥΜΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΔΕΙΝΑ ΤΟΥΔΕ ΑΔΙΚΗΜΑΤΟΣ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΤΗΝΔΕ, ΕΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΜΕΡΑΝ ΤΗΝΔΕ. Tanta autem cum cura fiebat in ius vocatio, <bl>ἵνα μή</bl>, inquit Auctor Etymologici, <bl>ἀναγράψωσι αἱ ἡμέραι εἰς τὰ</bl> [illegible, ~12 letters] ne iudicium intenderetur in cum, qui in ius vocatus non esset, neve Eremodicij damnaretur.
units.tr: This play was performed at the Liberalia in the city, which were celebrated on the sixteenth day of Elaphebolion. So there is the interval from the sixteenth day of Elaphebolion to the beginning of the following month, Munychion. For this reason the formula added was: "I summon you, or summon you forward, to this suit, before the first (magistrate), for this day." Such care was taken in summoning to court "lest," says the author of the Etymologicum, "the days be entered in the [illegible] ..., so that the suit should not be pressed against the one who had not been summoned to court, nor should he be condemned for eremodicy (default)."

units.la: Erat quippe Eremodicij grauissima poena, vt constat ex hac, quae de Eremodicio scripta est, Lege:
units.tr: Indeed, the penalty for eremodicy (default) was very severe, as is clear from this law which was written about eremodicy:

units.la: Τοῖς ἐμπροσθεν δίκαιον ἔχουσι, εἶτα μὴ [illegible, ~10 letters] εἰς τὸν χρόνον, ἐρημίᾳ ἀλίσκε[?]σθαι· ἡ δὲ ζημία χιλίας δραχμάς. [?]
units.tr: Τοῖς ἐμπροσθεν δίκαιον ἔχουσι, εἶτα μὴ [illegible] εἰς τὸν χρόνον, ἐρημίᾳ ἀλίσκε[?]σθαι· ἡ δὲ ζημία χιλίας δραχμάς. [?] (Those who have a just claim before, then not [...] at the time, are to be condemned by default; the penalty is a thousand drachmas.)

units.la: Cui statutus condictus dies est cum aduersario, nec iuerit, eremodicij damnator, & mille drachmis multator.
units.tr: He for whom a day has been fixed and agreed with his opponent, and who does not go, is to be condemned for default and fined a thousand drachmas.

units.la: Legem laudat Vlpianus ad hæc Demosthenis verba è Midiana: [illegible, ~14 letters] ὅτι μὲν δίκης ... [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: Ulpian cites the law in connection with these words of Demosthenes from the Midiana: [illegible] ὅτι μὲν δίκης ... [illegible]

units.la: Lex haec iubet, vt si quis, cui iudicij dies statutus condictus esset, deseruerit litem contestatam, absens damnaretur, & mille drachmis multaretur: Nam, vt optime obseruat Paulus Libro I. ad Edictum, ex quacumque causa ad Praetorem, vel alios, qui iurisdictioni praesunt, in ius vocatus venire debet, vt hoc ipsum sciatur, an iurisdictio eius sit. Lege II. D. Si quis in ius vocatus non ierit.
units.tr: This law orders that if anyone, for whom a day of trial had been fixed and agreed, abandons the suit already joined, he is to be condemned in his absence and fined a thousand drachmas. For, as Paul very aptly observes in Book I on the Edict, whoever is summoned to court for any cause, whether before the praetor or others who preside over jurisdiction, must come, so that it may be known whether the jurisdiction is theirs. Law 2, D. If anyone summoned to court does not go.

units.la: Constat tamen, inquit Vlpianus Libro XI. ad Edictum, omnis aetatis hominibus restaurationem eremodicii praestari, si se docerent ex iusta causa abfuisse. Lege VII. §. XII. D. de minoribus XXV. annis.
