Itaque intra dies decem licebat ei, qui eremodicij damnatus fuerat, diem aduersario dicere, ad excusandam suam absentiam, & purgandam moram iusiurandum autem dabat se actionem persecuturum:
units.tr: Yet, says Ulpian in Book XI on the Edict, it is established that restoration from eremodicy is granted to people of every age, if they show that they were absent for a just cause. Law 7, §12, D. on minors under twenty-five years. Thus, within ten days, the one condemned for eremodicy was allowed to set a day with his opponent, in order to excuse his absence and purge the delay; he gave an oath that he would pursue the action.

units.la: Τὸ μὴ ἔσται αὐτὸν ἀπλάσθαι ἐξεῖναι.
units.tr: Τὸ μὴ ἔσται αὐτὸν ἀπλάσθαι ἐξεῖναι. (That it be lawful for him not to be [...].)

units.la: Restaurationem eremodicij praestato.
units.tr: Grant restoration from eremodicy.

units.la: Habes apud Demosthenem in Midiana: ἀλλὰ τὸν μὲν ἔσθ' ἀπίστω ἐξ[?]ὸ αὐτὸ δίκην, καὶ τοῦτο μὲν ὅ ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, καὶ τοῖς ἴσον δὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ὑπὸ δίκη. Vlpianus ad hunc locum: Εἰ μὲν ἐδύνατο, φησὶν, ἐκ τοῦ χρόνου ἀπολαβεῖν τὰς ἐνδίκους, ... [illegible, ~18 letters]
units.tr: You have it in Demosthenes in the Midiana: ἀλλὰ τὸν μὲν ἔσθ' ἀπίστω ἐξ[?]ὸ αὐτὸ δίκην, καὶ τοῦτο μὲν ὅ ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, καὶ τοῖς ἴσον δὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ὑπὸ δίκη. Ulpian on this passage: "If he was able, he says, to recover the [...] from the time ..." [illegible]

units.la: Idem Vlpianus paullo ante: [illegible, ~22 letters] Quod si moram non purgasset, mille drachmas datis praedibus persoluebat.
units.tr: The same Ulpian, a little earlier: [illegible] If he had not purged the delay, he paid a thousand drachmas, having given sureties.

units.la: Pollux Libro VIII. cap. VI. ὁ δὲ ἔστι δίκη, ... [illegible, ~24 letters]
units.tr: Pollux, Book VIII, chapter VI: "But this is a suit ..." [illegible]

units.la: Si vero restauratio eremodicij praestabatur, ei, qui in integrum esset restitutus, iudicium refortiri licebat intra duos menses, nisi fecisset, iudicium in rem semel iudicatam translisse credebatur, & praeterea notabatur infamia. Pollux ibidem: ἀπολογεῖν ὁ δίκην ἔξω, ἐπότε τις μὴ πρῶν ἐν δικαστηρίῳ καλῶν [?] ἀποκρίνασθαι ἐπιχειρῶν [?], ἐρημία ὄφλη. ἀπολογεῖν δὲ, εἰς δύο μέρη ἐπάρχει. Εἰ δὲ μὴ τὸν ἀρχὸν [?], ὃ ἐγκαλούμενος ὤφλε, ἡ ἀτιμος ὢ.
units.tr: If, however, restoration from eremodicy was granted, the one restored to his former position could bring the trial again within two months; if he did not do so, the matter was considered to have been transferred into a case already decided, and besides he was marked with infamy. Pollux in the same place: ἀπολογεῖν ὁ δίκην ἔξω, ἐπότε τις μὴ πρῶν ἐν δικαστηρίῳ καλῶν [?] ἀποκρίνασθαι ἐπιχειρῶν [?], ἐρημία ὄφλη. ἀπολογεῖν δὲ, εἰς δύο μέρη ἐπάρχει. Εἰ δὲ μὴ τὸν ἀρχὸν [?], ὃ ἐγκαλούμενος ὤφλε, ἡ ἀτιμος ὢ. (Translation of the Greek is uncertain: to make a defence outside the suit, when someone who had not first been summoned in court tries to answer, he incurs default; and the defence is in two parts. If he did not [...], the accused incurred the penalty, or he was disgraced.)

units.la: Quod si quis in ius vocasse falso diceret, aut adfuisse testaretur, Lege Ψευδοκλητείας actio aduersus illos dabatur: ΤΗΣ ΨΕΥΔΟΚΛΗΤΕΙΑΣ, Actio Ψευδοκλητείας dator χρᾶται [?].
units.tr: If someone said falsely that he had summoned another to court, or testified that he had been present, an action was given against such men under the law of Pseudoklēteia (false summons): ΤΗΣ ΨΕΥΔΟΚΛΗΤΕΙΑΣ, the action of false summons is given ...

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ [?] πρὸς Νικόστρατον. Ἐὰν δὲ [?] τὶς ὁ Αρεσθούσιος ἀ[?]κλήτων [?] δίκῃ [?] δραχμῆς δίκῃ καταδικασάμενος, ὡς ὀφειλόμενος τὸ δημόσιον, κλητῆρας ἐπιχρὰ[?]ειτοις, καὶ εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν βίᾳ, τὸ σκεῦος πτύκτα ἀξιόφορον, πλείστον δὲ εἴκοσι μυρίων ἀξίαν [?], καὶ ὅδ' ὁπόσως κατέλιπεν, ὅτι δὲ ἀμφιεσ-θαι ὤμων δὲν, καὶ ἐκ [?] τὸ δημόσιον ὁ ἐφλημα, ὅπερ ἐπυδόμων τὴν βουλὴν, βάλλον ὅτι τὸν κλητῆρα τὸν ὁμολογουμένως κεκλητευκέναι, τοῦ δὲ Αρεσθούσιος τῆς Ψευδο-κλητείας καὶ τὸν νόμον, Pollux Libro VIII. cap. VI. Ψευδοκλητείας δὲ ἔχρᾶτο, καὶ τῷ δὲ δικαίως κεκλητευκότων. Grammatici: Ψευδοκλητία, ὄνομα δίκης ἔστι, ὡς εἰσὶν οἱ ἐπιχειροῦντες ὀφείλειν τὸ δημόσιον, ἐπιτιθέντες ἀπαιτῆσαι τινας Ψευδῶς κατασκευά-σθαι κλητῆρας καθ' ἑαυτοῦ πρὸς τὸν δίκην ἀφ' ἧς ὤφλον. Atque hæc actio, vt cum è Demosthenis laudato loco, cum è Grammaticorū verbis liquet, actio, inquam, hæc τῆς Ψευδοκλητίας instituebatur, postquam multam, quam publico debebant, qui quasi in ius vocati contestatam litem deseruerant, exsoluissent.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in his speech against Nicostratus: "If anyone from Aresthusia, condemned in a suit for a sum of money as a debtor to the public treasury, employs summoners and enters the house by force, [...] a vessel worth [...], and at most twenty thousand [...], and [...] what he left behind, and [...] for the public treasury, which the Council had decided ..., on the ground that the summoner had summoned him by agreement ... of the action of false summons and the law." Pollux, Book VIII, chapter VI: "They used false summons," and "to those who had summoned rightly." The grammarians: "Pseudoklētia is the name of a suit, against those who undertake to owe a debt to the public treasury, and who press a claim to exact from certain persons that they falsely made summoners against themselves for the suit from which they incurred the penalty." And this action, as is clear both from the passage of Demosthenes cited and from the words of the grammarians, this action, I say, of false summons was brought after the fine, which they owed to the public treasury, had been paid by those who, as though summoned to court, had abandoned the joined suit.

units.la: DE PRÆPARATORIIS IVDICIORVM TITVLVS III.
units.tr: ON THE PREPARATORY STAGES OF TRIALS, TITLE III.

units.la: Egibus instituta est ἀπάχρισις τῶν Ἀρχόντων pro potestate litigantes, siue reos, siue actores, interrogantium, ad quam tenebantur respondere, atque ita his interrogatoriis actionibus, vt loquitur Callistratus Libro II. Edicti monitorij, coguntarante iudicium de suo iure aliquid respondere, Lege I. §.I. D. de interrogationibus in iure faciendis.
units.tr: The interrogation of litigants was introduced in the Attic courts as the questioning of the archons by the litigants [ἀπάχρισις τῶν Ἀρχόντων]. The archon could question either party, defendant or plaintiff, and they were bound to answer him. Callistratus, in Book II of his work on the Edict concerning monitory actions, says that by these interrogatory actions they are compelled to answer the court about their right in some respect, Law 1, §1, D. de interrogationibus in iure faciendis.

units.la: Τοὺς Ἀρχοντας ἀιαχρίνῶν τοῖς σύωτινοῖς εἰς τὸν ἀγῶνα, & τοῖς σύωτινοῦσιν εἰς τὸν ἀγῶνα ἀποκρίνεσθαι.
units.tr: The archons question the litigants on whatever concerns the case, and the litigants answer on whatever concerns the case [Τοὺς Ἀρχοντας ἀιαχρίνῶν τοῖς σύωτινοῖς εἰς τὸν ἀγῶνα, & τοῖς σύωτινοῦσιν εἰς τὸν ἀγῶνα ἀποκρίνεσθαι].

units.la: Magistratus litigantes interrogant: litigantes respondent.
units.tr: The magistrates question the litigants; the litigants reply.

units.la: Legis meminit Isaeus: ἐν τῷ πρὸς τὴν Φιλοκτήμονος κλῆσιν. ἔτι δίκαιον καὶ τοῖς ἀδικοῦσιν ἀπαιτίζων ἔργῳ ὑμῖν ταῦτα μαρτυρίας. ὅτε γὰρ αἱ ἀιαχρίσεις ἦσαν πρὸς τὰς τῆς Ἀρχοῖ, ἃ ἐπὶ τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, ὡς γὰρ γνώσιον τὴν ὅ' Εὐκτήμονος ὄντων, ἐρωτώμενος ὑφ' ὑμῶν, τίς εἴη αὐτῷ μήτηρ, καὶ ὅπου ἰωμᾶτηρ, οὐκ εἴχεν ἀπόδειξαι, ἀ[?]μαρτυρουμένων ἡμῶν, καὶ τὸ ἀρχῶν κελεύοντος ἀποκρίναὶς χ' ἡ νόμων.
units.tr: Isaeus mentions this law in his speech against the claim of Philoctemon: It is also just to demand proof from wrongdoers by deed. For when the apokriseis were held before the archon, in the court, and you asked him who his mother was and where his father was, he could not show it, while we were witnesses; and the archon ordering him to answer, [he did not?] ... the laws. (The Greek is badly garbled in the scan.)

units.la: Est autem duplex ἀιάχρισις, iudiciorum ciuilium vna, & altera iudiciorum criminalium. ἀιάχρισις iudiciorum ciuilium est quasi diuinatio de constituendo iudicio. Grammatici: ἀιάχρισις, ἐξέτασις ὑφ' ἑκάστης ἀρχῆς γινομένη πρὸς τὴν δίκην, αἰεὶ τὴν σιωπῶντων εἰς τὴν ἀγῶνα. ἐξεπάζεσθαι δὲ, καὶ εἰ ὅλως εἰσάγειν χρή. Huiusmodi αἰάχρισις, [?] [?], habetur laudatis Ilxi verbis: nam, quia de haereditate adeunda cognationis iure agitur, in personam fit interrogatoria haec actio, & interrogatur TIΣ ΜΗΤΗΡ, καὶ ΟΤΟΥ ΘΥΓΑΤΗΡ. Praeterea Magistratus, quorum erat εἰσαγεῖν τὰς δίκας εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον, prius adiudicabant, an ὁ διώκων [?] contendentibus esset admittendus, necne, qui item primus. Demosthenes ὁ τοῦ ἐν Ολυμπιοδώρου. καὶ ἔφη αἰσχρίνη [?] τὴν Αρχιππὶ ἀπασαι αἱ ἀμφισβητήσεις, καὶ ἰδὴ ἀγωνίζεσθαι ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, ἀλλ' ἀπόκλισθοι ἡμῶν ὁ πρῶτος ἐκεῖνος ἀγωνίζεσθαι ἐγὼ καὶ Ολυμπιοδώρος ἔφη. & paullo post: καὶ μὴ ζῶν ὁ Αρχέρ αἰσχρίνης πάσαν ἡμῖν τὰς ἀμφισβητήσεις, καὶ αἰσχρίνας εἰσηγάγω εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον. καὶ ἔτι Ολυμπιοδώρος ἠγωνίζετο ταῦτα. Grammatici verbis iam laudatis: αἰάχρισις, ἐξέτασις ὑφ' ἱκέτης ἔχηθ ἠνοιμὴν τὰς δίκας, αὐτὴ τὴν σιωπῶντων εἰς τὸν ἀγῶνα. ἐξεπάζεσθαι δὲ καὶ εἰ ὅλως εἰσάγειν χρή.
units.tr: There are two kinds of apokrisis: one for civil trials, and another for criminal trials. The apokrisis of civil trials is, as it were, a preliminary inquiry into whether a trial should be set up at all. The grammarians define it as an examination made by each magistrate concerning the case, before the litigants enter the contest; and it is to be inquired whether the case should be brought in at all. An apokrisis of this kind is found in the words of Isaeus quoted above: since the inheritance is claimed by right of kinship, this interrogatory action is brought against the person, and he is asked WHO IS HIS MOTHER and WHO IS HIS FATHER. Moreover, the magistrates, whose office was to bring cases into the court, first decided whether the one prosecuting should be admitted against the contenders or not, and who should come first. Demosthenes, in the speech against Olympiodorus, says that Aeschines claimed all the disputes of Archippus and that he himself would plead in court, but that Olympiodorus, who was first, would be the one to plead; and a little later that, though Archippus was not alive, Aeschines brought all the disputes into court, and Olympiodorus still pleaded them. The grammarians, in the words already quoted, say: apokrisis is an examination made by each magistrate who receives the cases, before the contest begins; and it is to be inquired whether the case should be brought in at all.

units.la: In caufis capitalibus αἰάχρισις erat, cum delato rei nomine, actor à Magistratu, apud quem scripta erat dica, interrogabatur, an omnino conftituiffet accufationem profequi, reumque peragere, an teftes aut teftimonia haberet vel exhiberi poftularet, an aliquo euocato ipfi opus effet, necne: ne fcilicet imparatus ad accufandum in iudicium veniret: qui autem actor ἀναχρίσει non aderat, ignominiofus erat. Demofthenes in Midiana: καὶ γὰρ οὔτ' αἰσχρίνεται τοῦτο ὁ συκοφάντης ἐκίνησε. Vlpianus: Ὅτι ἐπλμησι σοφιστὴν [?] τὴν Αρχίππου αἰαχρίσι, διλοῦτι καταγωγὴ ἑαυτῷ. εἰ γὰρ ἀδικεῖσ ὁ Ιιοῦπου, ὅτι τὶς ἀπὸ [?] γεγράφω, αἰάχρισι [?] τῆς δικαστηρίου ἕως τὰς ἀρχῆσιν, ΕΙ ΕΠΕΞΕΙΣΙΝ; ΕΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΣ ΕΧΕΙ; ΕΙ ΧΡΗΖΕΙ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΙΝΑ; ἵνα πρὸς τῶν δὲ τὰς ἐπιτηδευσθέντα, εἰσελθὴν εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον. ὁ δὲ μὴ ἀπωθήσ [?] τὶ τῶν αἰάχρισι, ἐγίγνετο ἄλμος. Rursum Vlpianus ad eandem Midianam: μὴ ὁ ὁ [?] ἐπηκρεωθῶν ὁ δικαστήριον, ἰδίδοντος τὰς Θεσμοθέτας αἰ γραφαί. κἀκεῖνος πρώτων λοιπὸν, ΒΟΥΛΕΙ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΕΙΝ; Ἡ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΑΣ ΕΧΕΙΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΑΣ ΑΠΟ-ΔΕΙΞΕΙΣ ΕΤΟΙΜΟΥΣ; καὶ εἰ σωθῶσι ἵνα ἤδη λοιπὸν εἰσῆλθ.
units.tr: In capital cases there was an apokrisis: once the name of the accused had been reported, the accuser was questioned by the magistrate before whom the indictment had been written. He was asked whether he had firmly resolved to pursue the accusation and carry the defendant through; whether he had witnesses or testimonies, or wished to have them produced; whether he needed to summon anyone; so that he would not come to the trial unprepared to accuse. An accuser who was absent from the apokrisis was disgraced. Demosthenes, in the speech against Midias: For Aeschines did not raise this against the sycophant. Ulpian: if someone is wronged, because someone wrote, in the apokrisis of the court up to the magistrates, DO YOU HAVE AN EXAMINATION? DO YOU HAVE WITNESSES? DO YOU NEED SOMEONE TO BE SUMMONED? so that, having made these preparations, he may enter the court. And one who did not answer the apokrisis was counted as absent. Again Ulpian, on the same speech against Midias: the one who has been summoned before the court, when the Thesmothetae have handed over the indictments, is first asked: WILL YOU PROSECUTE? HAVE YOU WITNESSES READY FOR THE PROOFS? And if they are ready, then he is allowed to enter.

units.la: Verum haec αἰάχρισις, de qua iam agit Vlpianus, non eadem eft cum priore illa, de qua ante diximus: nam prior illa fiebat, antequam Magiftratus iudices fortiretur, πρὸς τὸ δικαστήριον, haec vero prioris iteratio fiebat poft iudicum fortitionem, μὴ ὁ ἐπηκρεωθῶν ὁ δικαστήριον, prior fiebat, vt caueret actori Magiftratus, & poenitentiae locum daret, videretque, an admittenda effet actio, dandique iudices, necne: posterior fiebat, cum datis iam iudicibus accufatio effet instituenda. In priore illa αἰαχεῖ actor iureiurando affirmabat fe accufationem profecuturum, reumque peracturum. Si tempus aliquod poftulaffet, vel ad deliberandum, vel quia parata non haberet omnia ad iudicium, manebat nihilominus accufatio, προθεσμίαν vocant:
units.tr: But this apokrisis, of which Ulpian now treats, is not the same as the earlier one we mentioned. The earlier was held before the magistrate allotted the judges, while the repetition of it, which Ulpian describes as taking place when the judges had been chosen, came after the allotment of judges. The first was made so that the magistrate could secure the accuser and allow him room for repentance, and see whether the action should be admitted, and whether judges should be given or not. The second was made when judges had already been given and the accusation was about to be begun. In the earlier apokrisis the accuser affirmed on oath that he would pursue the accusation and carry the defendant through. If he asked for some time, either to deliberate or because he did not yet have everything ready for the trial, the accusation nonetheless remained; this they call prothesmia.

units.la: Τὸν μέλλοντα κατηγορεῖν, ὅμνυναι, ὡς τὴν ἐπι-ξελφὴν, εἰ πάντα ἐτοιμα ἔχει τῶν ἀγῶν, [?] ἀγῶνα εἰς τὸν ἀγῶ-να ἐὰν ἐτοιμάσας. [illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: The one who is about to accuse swears that, if he has everything ready for the contest, he will press the case; ... [the rest is illegible in the scan].

units.la: Actor iusiurandum dato se actionem profecuturum, si parata omnia habeat ad iudicium: sin minus, iureiurando sibi tempus dari postu-let.
units.tr: The accuser gives oath that he will pursue the action if he has everything ready for the trial; otherwise, by oath, he asks that time be granted to him.

units.la: Habes apud Demosthenem in Midiana : [?πρῶτα μὲν ἥδη διεξελήλυθε τὰ ἐκ τοῦ νόμου] συνωμοσία, [?ἀντιγραφαί]. Ulpianus : [?ἐδὲ τὸν μὲν ἡγούμενον καταγνῶναι, εἰ πρὸς πάντα] [?ἔτι μὲν τὰ πρὸς τὸν ἀγῶνα ἐρωτᾶσθαι, εἰ ὁ σιωπῶν φησιν ἐκεῖνος, ἔρχον ἀπὸ πάντων λαμβάνειν] [?ἐπέλιπον τῆς ἐπιξελῆθη]. [?ἐὰν μὲν οὖν ἐμοῦ ἐρωτήσεις εἰσήγαγο. εἰ δὲ ἢ τινὰ ἄλλα χρόνον ἔχει τὰ ἐπι]- [?σκέψασθαι], [?ἐάν] [?δὲ γραφὴν]. [?ἐκαλεῖτο δὲ ὁ ζητῶν ἐπιγραφὴ] συνωμοσία. Grammatici : [?ἐπι]ωμ- [?υσία], [?ὁ] [?ἐπισκέψασθαι] [?ἐκτὸς] [?ἀλλὰ] [?φάσι] [?χαίρωμεν ἀποδοχῆς], [?ἐὰν] [?ἐν] [?ἀρχῆς], [?ἐὰν] [?τὰ] [?ἐ]- [?πλησίων] [?ἀλλ᾽] [?ἐρχόμενος], [?ὅτι] [?ἐλέγετο], [?καὶ] [?ὁ] [?ποιῇ] [?τὴν] [?ἐπιμυσθαι]. Sed longe differt haec [?ἐπι]ωμ[?υσία], ab illa, de qua Ulpianus : nam haec Grammaticorum fiebat datis iudicibus, illa Ulpiani in [?ἀναχείῳ].
units.tr: You have in Demosthenes, in the speech against Midias, first, indeed, he has already gone through the matters from the law: conspiracy (synomosia), counter-writings (antigraphai). Ulpian: ... to question about the matters pertaining to the contest, whether he says that he will... and if he has other time to consider... the one seeking was called the indictment, synomosia. The grammarians: synomosia, ... [the rest is too garbled to render]. But this synomosia of the grammarians differs greatly from that of which Ulpian speaks: the grammarians' took place when judges had been given, while Ulpian's belonged to the apokrisis.

units.la: Quando suas peregerant in hac [?ἀναχείῳ] partes Magistratus, quorum erat [?εἰσάγειν] [?τὰ] [?γεαφὰς] [?εἰς] [?ὃ] [?δικαστήριον], actor qua actione agere volebat, eam edebat, & certe aequissimum videtur, cum, qui acturus est, ut loquitur Ulpianus Libro IV. ad Edictum, edere actionem, ut proinde sciat reus, utrum agendum, cognita actione, qua conueniatur. Lege D. de edendo: qui libellus, sive in crimen subscriptio ad id inuenta est, inquit Ulpianus Libro VII. de officio Proconsulis, ut caveant singuli, quod crimen obiicient, & praeterea persequeraturos se in crimine usque ad sententiam. Lege VII.D. de accusationibus. Reus vero sibi falso crimen illud obiici libello oppositio testabatur : Αντιγραφῶ dixerunt, idque usurpatum tantum in [?τῆς δίκης τῆς δημοσίας] testantur Grammatici: Αντιγραφὴ κοινὰς δ᾽ ἐν τοῖς δίκαις τοῖς δημοσίαις τὰ τῶν δικαζομένων γράμματα, ἃ ἐκδοῦναι αὐτὸν [?δεῖ], καὶ τὰ τῶν διωκόντων καὶ τὰ τῶν φυγόντος, Αντιγραφὴ, καὶ τὰ μαρτύρια. Δημοσθένης ἐν [?Σπουδαῖς] καὶ [?Τιμαῖος]. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. VI. καὶ ὅτι πρὸς πῶ γεγραφῶ τὸ τῶν φυγόντος γέγραμμα, Αντιγραφὴ οὖν. τὰ ψευδῆ μὲν καταμαρτυρῆσαι Στέφανος, γεγραφὰς τὰ ἐν τῷ γραμματείῳ. qui locus supplendus atque emendandus est e Demosthene ἐν τῷ χ᾽ Στέφανος ψευδομαρτυρίων α᾽. vbi ita legitur.
units.tr: When in this apokrisis the magistrates, whose duty was to bring the indictments into the court, had done their part, the accuser had to set out the action by which he wished to proceed. This seems entirely fair, since the one who is about to act, as Ulpian says in Book IV on the Edict, must produce his action, so that the defendant knows whether to contest it, having learned the action by which he is sued. See D. de edendo. The libellus, in which the accusation was subscribed against the crime, was devised for this purpose, says Ulpian in Book VII on the office of the proconsul, so that each accuser guarantees what crime he will bring, and besides will pursue the crime to sentence. See Law 7, D. de accusationibus. But the defendant, by a written counter-opposition, testified that the crime had been falsely brought against him. They called this antigraphe, and the grammarians testify that it was used only in public trials: antigraphe, and in public trials the writings of the litigants, which each must hand over, both those of the prosecutors and those of the defendants, are called antigraphe, and so are the testimonies. Demosthenes in the speech Against Spoudias and [Timaeus]. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter VI: and because the writing of the one in exile was written against him, it is called antigraphe. Stephanus testified falsely, the writings in the tablet. This passage must be supplied and emended from Demosthenes, in the speech against Stephanus on false testimony, where it reads thus:

units.la: ΑΝΤΙΓΡΑΦΗ : Απολλόδωρος Πασίωνος Αχαρνεὺς, Στέφανος Μενεκλέους, Αχαρνεὺς ψευδομαρτυρίων ἡμῖν ἐμὸν ταλάντων, τὰ ψευδῆ μὲν καταμαρτυρῆσαι Στέφανος, μαρτυρήσας τὰ ἐν τῷ γραμματείῳ γεγραμμένα. πάλιν μαρτύρησα, μαρτυρήσας τὰ ἐν τῷ γραμματείῳ γεγραμμένα. Quanquam & hic ista misere sunt confusa: puto ea ita esse in ordinem aliquem reponenda.
units.tr: ANTIGRAPHE: Apollodorus son of Pasion of Acharnae against Stephanus son of Menecles of Acharnae, on false testimony, of ten talents. Stephanus testified falsely, having testified the things written in the tablet. Again he testified, having testified the things written in the tablet. Although here these things are miserably confused; I think they should be put into some order.

units.la: ΑΝΤΙΓΡΑΦΗ [?Ψ]ΕΥΔΟΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΩΝ ΤΙΜΗΜΑ ΤΑΛΑΝΤΟΝ.
units.tr: Antigraphē of false witnesses: assessed at a talent.

units.la: ΑΠΟΛΛΟΔΩΡΟΣ ΠΑΣΙΩΝΟΣ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΥΣ ΤΑ [?ψ]ΕΥΔΗ ΜΟΥ ΚΑΤΕΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΕ ΣΤΕΦΑ-ΝΟΣ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΑΣ ΤΑ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΙΩι ΓΕΓΡΑΜ-ΜΕΝΑ.
units.tr: Apollodorus, son of Pasion, of Acharnae, says that Stephanus falsely testified against my testimony, having given evidence on the things written in the tablet. [ΑΠΟΛΛΟΔΩΡΟΣ ΠΑΣΙΩΝΟΣ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΥΣ: ΤΑ ΨΕΥΔΗ ΜΟΥ ΚΑΤΕΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΕ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΣ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΑΣ ΤΑ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΙΩι ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ.]

units.la: ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΣ ΜΕΝΕΚΛΕΟΥΣ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΥΣ ΤΑΛΗΘΗ ΜΑΡ-ΤΥΡΗΣΑ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΑΣ ΤΑ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΙΩι ΓΕ-ΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ.
units.tr: Stephanus, son of Menecles, of Acharnae, testified truly, having given evidence on the things written in the tablet. [ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΣ ΜΕΝΕΚΛΕΟΥΣ ΑΧΑΡΝΕΥΣ: ΤΑΛΗΘΗ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΑ, ΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΑΣ ΤΑ ΕΝ ΤΩι ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΕΙΩι ΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΑ.]

units.la: Addunt Grammatici, ἢ τὰ μαρτύρια. Nam edenda sunt omnia, quae quis apud iudicem editurus est. Lege I. §.III. D. de edendo. Quanquam nescio an idem usu venerit Athenien-sibus in edendo, quod Romanis enim Editiones sine die, & Consule fieri debent, ne quid excogitetur e die, & Consule, & praefato die fiat. Diem autem & Consulem excipit Prætor, quo instrumentum conscriptum est, non in quem solutio concepta est: nam dies solutionis, sicuti summa, pars est stipulationis. d. Lege I. §. II. D. eod. vbi quid sit, prælato die, non satis liquet. alij enim legunt, prolato die. alij hanc Florentinam scripturam, prælato, sequuntur, & interpretantur, anticipato: nam Latini præferre diem dixerunt pro anteuertere, & anticipare. Sed neutra lectio aut interpretatio mihi placet: nam, demus agi hic tantum de editione instrumentorum, vt volunt viri summi, non sola prolatione diei, salsi committendi ansa fallariis præbetur: est enim vbi opus sit die prælato: rursum solo die prælato falsum non admittitur: prolato namque opus est, sæpe, vt falsum fabricetur: atqui hic generaliter cautum, ne ex die quocumque tandem modo falsi committendi ansa præbeatur falsariis. Deinde non solas editiones instrumentorum fine die & Consule fieri debere scripsit Vlpianus, neque verum est: nam etiam editio actionis, qua aliquis agere vult, & libellus inscriptionis fit fine die, vt docet Paulus Libro III. de Adulteriis. Libellorum inscriptionum conceptio talis est: CONSVL & DIES APVD illum PRÆTOREM vel PROCONSVLEM LVCIVS TITIVS PROFESSVS EST SE MÆVIAM LEGE IVLIA DE ADVLTERIIS REAM DEFERRE QVOD DICAT EAM CVM GAIO SEIO IN CIVITATE illa DOMO illius, MENSE illo CONSVLIBVS illis ADVLTERIVM COMMISISSE.
units.tr: The grammarians add "or the testimonies" (ἢ τὰ μαρτύρια). For everything that anyone is about to produce before a judge must be put forward. See Law I, §3, D. de edendo. Yet I do not know whether the Athenians in their production of documents followed the same practice as the Romans, for among the Romans the editions must be made without a day and a consul, so that nothing may be devised from the day and the consul, and nothing may be done on the day stated beforehand. However, the praetor receives the day and the consul on which the instrument was drawn up, not the day on which payment was agreed; for the day of payment, like the sum, is part of the stipulation. See the same Law I, §2, D. eod., where it is not quite clear what prælato die means. Some read prolato die (on a deferred day); others follow the Florentine reading prælato and interpret it as anticipato (on an anticipated day), since the Latins used præferre diem to mean anteuertere and anticipare (to go before). But I am satisfied with neither reading nor interpretation. For let us grant that this refers only to the production of instruments, as the great men hold: the mere prolatio diei is not the only opening for forgers to commit fraud; there is a case where die prælato is needed, and again, the fraud is not admitted by die prælato alone. For prolato is needed, often, for a forgery to be made; yet here the law provides in general that forgers are given no opening to commit fraud by any day whatever. Further, Ulpian wrote that not only the editions of instruments must be made without a day and a consul, and this is not true: for the edition of an action, by which someone wishes to sue, and the libel of accusation, are also made without a day, as Paulus teaches in Book III, de Adulteriis. The form of the libel of accusation is this: CONSUL AND DAY, BEFORE that PRAETOR or PROCONSUL, LUCIUS TITIUS HAS DECLARED THAT HE BRINGS A CHARGE UNDER THE LEX IULIA CONCERNING ADULTERY AGAINST MAEVIA, THAT SHE COMMITTED ADULTERY WITH GAIUS SEIUS IN THE CITY, in that HOUSE of that man, IN that MONTH, IN THE CONSULSHIP OF those CONSULS.

units.la: Vtique enim & locus designandus est, in quo adulterium commis-sum est, & persona cum qua admissum dicitur, & mensis. hoc enim Lege Iulia publicorum cauetur, & generaliter præcipitur omnibus qui rem aliquam deferunt. Neque autem diem, neque horam inuitus comprehenderet. Lege III. D. de accusationibus. Vbi quod legitur, CONSVLIBVS illis, obreptitium puto: non enim adscribuntur Consules: & tria tantum Lege Iulia publicorum cauerí dixit hic Paulus, vt locus designetur in quo adulterium admissum est, secundo persona, cum qua commissum est; tertio mensis, quo admissum est. nihil de Consule, nihil de die, vtique cum editiones sine die & Consule fieri debeant, ne quid excogitetur è die & Consule. Lege I. §. II. D. de edendo: vbi rescribe distinctis vocibus, & prælato die, fiat. Latum diem appellat, qui certus non est, quemadmodum lata suga dicitur, quæ relegationi in certum locum opponitur. nihil igitur fieri vult prælato die, id est, præter latum diem. Est autem latus dies, cum mensis tantum adscribitur, non autem quotus mensis dies sit, neque item nomen Consulũ, qui anni illius fastos signant, adponitur: tum enim plane insertus est dies, & vere latus. Quomodo etiam emendandum apud Modestinum Libro IV. Responsorum: Si à debitore, prælato die, pignoris obligatio mentiatur, falsi crimine locus est. Lege XXVIII D. ad Legem Corneliam de falsis. Non enim debitor salsum tantum committit, diem præferendo, sed etiam proferendo: adde quod pignoris obligatio cum sit penes creditorem, ab illo primum editur sine die & Consule: quod si debitor certum diem apponat, falsi crimine se obligat: neque enim adscribere debet præter mensem, id est, latum diem: Rescribe igitur distinctis vocibus in duas: Si à debitore, prælato die, id est, præter latum diem, pignoris obligatio mentiatur, falsi crimine locus est. Fiebant igitur editiones sine die & Consule, sed adscripto MENSE illo, id est, lato die. Sed redeamus ad nostros Athenienses: Post αἰτηγαφὼ[?] scriptam, cum actor, tum reus iusiurandum propter calumniam dabant: ἀντωμοσίαν vocant. Grammatici ἀντωμοσία γράμματα γράφοντες (ea sunt ἀντιγραφὴ ἢ μαρτυρία.) ἐπὶ ἀπογραφὴν [?] ... Οἱ ἀπογραφόμενοι [?] ὀμνύντες, οἱ ἀμφιβάλλοντες, οἱ ἄλλοι ... ἀλλὰ ἀλλ'ἡ ἀληθείᾳ [?] ... ΑΛΗΘΗ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΗΣΕΙΝ. εἰ δὲ, ΑΛΗΘΗ ΑΠΟ-ΛΟΓΗΣΑΣΘΑΙ. iusiurandum actoris dicebatur proprie ἀντωμοσία rei vero ἀντωμοσία. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. VI. ἀντωμοσία μὲν, ὅρκος, ὃν ὁ κατηγορῶν ἀντωμύνει, ἢ ΜΗΝ ΑΛΗΘΗ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΕΙΝ. ἀντωμοσία δὲ, ὅρκος, ὃν ὁ κατηγορούμενος ἀντωμύνει, ἢ ΜΗΝ ΜΗ ΑΔΙΚΕΙΝ. Iustinianus Imperator Lege sanciuit, non aliter neque actorem, neque fugientem in primordio litis exercere certamina, nisi post narrationem & responsionem, antequam utriusque partis aduocati sacramentum legitimum praestent, & ipsae principales personae subeant iusiurandum. Et actor quidem iuret, NON CALVMNIANDI ANIMO LITEM SE MOVISSE, SED EXISTIMANDO BONAM CAVSAM HABERE. Reus autem non aliter suis allegationibus utatur, nisi prius & ipse iurauerit, QVOD PVTANS SE BONA INSTANTIA VTI AD RELVCTANDVM PERVENERIT.
units.tr: For the place where the adultery was committed must surely be stated, and the person with whom it is said to have been committed, and the month. For this is required by the Lex Iulia on public crimes, and it is generally laid down for all who bring any charge. Nor would he be compelled to state the day or the hour against his will. Law III, D. de accusationibus. Here I think the words CONSULIBUS illis are a corruption, for the consuls are not named. Paulus here says that the Lex Iulia on public crimes requires three things: first, the place where the adultery was committed; second, the person with whom it was committed; third, the month in which it was committed. Nothing about the consul, nothing about the day, certainly since editions must be made without a day and a consul, so that nothing may be devised from the day and the consul. See Law I, §2, D. de edendo, where it should be corrected by separating the words, and it should read prælato die, fiat. He calls the latum diem (the broad day) the day that is not fixed, just as a lata fuga is called a flight that is set against relegation to a fixed place. He therefore wants nothing done prælato die, that is, outside the broad day. A day is broad when only the month is written, but not which day of the month it is, nor is the name of the consuls, who mark the year's calendar, added; for then the day is plainly inserted and truly broad. The same passage must also be emended in Modestinus, Book IV of the Responsa: If a pledge of security is falsely claimed by the debtor, with a day set beforehand, there is room for the charge of forgery. See Law XXVIII, D. ad Legem Corneliam de falsis. For the debtor does not commit forgery merely by setting the day beforehand, but also by postponing it. Add that since the pledge of security is in the creditor's keeping, he first produces it without a day and a consul; but if the debtor puts a fixed day, he binds himself to the charge of forgery, for he ought not to add anything beyond the month, that is, the broad day. Therefore separate the words into two: If a pledge of security is falsely claimed by the debtor, with a day set beforehand, that is, outside the broad day, there is room for the charge of forgery. Editions were therefore made without a day and a consul, but with the month that added, that is, the broad day. But let us return to our Athenians. After the αἰτηγαφὼ was written, both the plaintiff and the defendant gave an oath against calumny; they call it antōmosia. The grammarians, writing antōmosia letters (these are the antigraphē or the martyria), at the inscription... Those who inscribe swear, those who are in doubt, the others... but in truth... TO ACCUSE TRULY. And if, TO DEFEND TRULY. Strictly speaking, the oath of the plaintiff was called antōmosia, and that of the defendant likewise antōmosia. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter VI: Antōmosia is the oath which the accuser swears, namely, THAT HE ACCUSES TRULY; antōmosia is the oath which the accused swears, namely, THAT HE DOES NOT WRONG. The Emperor Justinian decreed by law that neither the plaintiff nor the one fleeing may engage in contests at the outset of the suit, unless after the statement and the reply, and before the advocates of each party give the lawful oath, and the principal persons themselves undertake the oath. The plaintiff shall swear THAT HE HAS NOT BROUGHT THE SUIT IN A SPIRIT OF CALUMNY, BUT BELIEVING HE HAS A GOOD CAUSE. The defendant shall not use his pleas unless he too has first sworn THAT, THINKING HE HAS A GOOD CASE, HE HAS COME TO RESIST.

units.la: Lege II.C. de iureiurando propter calumniam dando.
units.tr: See Law II, C. de iureiurando propter calumniam dando (on the oath to be given on account of calumny).

units.la: Peracta hac ἀνάκρισις [?] Magistratus litigantes ad iudicium admittebat, & iudices dabat:
units.tr: When this preliminary examination (anakrisis) was completed, the magistrate admitted the litigants to trial and appointed judges. [Τοὺς ἄρχοντας καλῶν...]

units.la: Τοὺς Ἀρχοντας καλῶν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον τοὺς ὀμόσαντας εἰς τ' ἀγῶνα, ἐ εἰσάγειν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον.
units.tr: Calling the archons to the court, [the litigants] who had sworn to the contest, [the archons] bring them into the court. [Τοὺς Ἀρχοντας καλῶν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον τοὺς ὀμόσαντας εἰς τ' ἀγῶνα, ἐ εἰσάγειν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον.]

units.la: Demosthenes id docet ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ολυμπιοδώρου. Φησὶ δὲ ἐκάλει ὁ Αρχων εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον ἀπὸ τῶν ἀμφισβητούντων τὰς ἡμέρας. & paullo post: καὶ αἰσχρίας εἰσῆγεν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον. Vlpianus in iis, quae proxime descripsimus: εἰδὲ τ' ἡμέρας καταγράφειν, εἰ πάντα ἑτοιμάσεται ἐχρῆν τοῖς ἀγῶσιν ἐρωτᾶσθαι. εἰ δὲ σύνεφθον ἐκ ἔτος, ὅρκον ἀπὸ πάντων λαμβάνειν [?] τῆς ἐπιζελῆς [?]. εἰ μὲν οὖν ὁμοίως εἰσῆγεν.
units.tr: Demosthenes teaches this in his speech against Olympiodorus. He says that the archon summoned the disputing parties to the court by days. And a little later: and he brought the cases into the court. Ulpian, in the passage we have just described: the days must be entered, if everything has been prepared, the contests ought to be asked for; but if there is no year, the oath must be taken from all... then he introduced them in the same way. [Demosthenes, Against Olympiodorus: Φησὶ δὲ ἐκάλει ὁ Ἄρχων εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον ἀπὸ τῶν ἀμφισβητούντων τὰς ἡμέρας. καὶ αἰσχρίας εἰσῆγεν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον.]

units.la: Iudices dabantur sortito à Magistratibus, quorum erat εἰσάγειν τὰς δίκας. Sortiebantur autem quisque iudicum in illo foro, cui iam ante adsignatus erat forte: nempe Heliastes in Heliaea, qui sedebant in Parabysto, in Parabysto, atque ita de ceteris, vt nempe iudicia redderent in iis causis, quae erant cognitionis illorum, siue Tribunalium, in quibus sedebant: hac de re Lex est: Τοὺς δικαστὰς ἀπονέμειν εἰς ὃ δικάζειν.
units.tr: The judges were assigned by lot by the magistrates, whose office was to bring the suits into court. Each of the judges was allotted by lot to the court in which he had previously been assigned: thus the Heliasts in the Heliaea, who sat in the Parabystos, and so on for the others, so that they gave judgment in those cases which fell within the jurisdiction of those tribunals in which they sat. There is a law on this matter: the judges are to be assigned to the courts in which they are to judge.

units.la: Legis meminit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ Αἰσχίνου α'. Ἀλλ' ὑμεῖς αὐτοὶ πάντων ἀπὸ κληρωσάμενοι Αθηναῖοι, ἡ πάντων δὲ οἱ [?] ὅτι βουλομένων εἰς ἔνθα λαχεῖν ὃ δικαστήριον, μόνοι δικάζειν ἡμῖν. Ἀλλ' ἡ, ὅτι ἐλαχέτε, εἶτα ἀπεκληρώσασθε. Ὧν γὰρ οἱ νόμοι λέγουσιν. Describit Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Plutum: ὅτι δὲ σωσέλαμε κρινεῖς τῷ δικαζὴν, ἤρχοντο πάντες οἱ δικασταὶ εἰς τὸ ἀγορὰν· εἶτα πάλιν ἀπεκληρωσάντο οἱ τὰ εἰλημμένα γεγραμμένα ἔχοντες, τίνες δικασταὶ, καὶ ὧν ἡ. Apud Lucianum δικαστηρίοις, habes mores hac in re Athenien-sibus vsurpatos: Praeco Mercurius ad iudicium conuocat litigantes: Iustitia tanquam Magistratus apud quem scriptae sunt dicae, iudices sortitur, praecone Mercurio recitante dicas, pro dignitate atque grauitate criminis plures, vel pauciores. E P M. Ἀκούετε λεὼς, ἀγορᾶι δικῶν ἀλαζὴ τύχη καλέσεσωσθαι τήμερον, Ελαφι-βολιῶνος ἰβδόμῃ ἰσαμῶν. ὁπόσοι γεγραφὰς ἀπηγγεγκαν, ἥκειν εἰς ὃ Αρεῖου πάγον, [?] ἥδη ἡ Δίκη ἀπόκληρωσις δικαστηρίου, ἐ αὐτὴ πρέσα τοῖς δικάζουσιν, οἱ δικασταὶ ἐξ ἀπό-τῶν Ἀθηναίων· ὁ μιαρός, τελώνου ἐκάσης δίκης· ἀριθμὸς τῶν δικαστῶν [?] λόγον τῶ ἐλκ-μάτος. & paullo post: ΕΡ. ΜΕΘΗ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΗΣ ΑΚΑΔΗΜΙΑΣ ΥΠΕΡ ΠΟΛΕΜΩΝΟΣ ΑΝΔΡΑΠΟΔΙΣΜΟΥ. ΔΙΚ. ἐπὶ κλήρωσιν. ΕΡΜ. Η ΣΤΟΑ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΗΣ ΗΔΟΝΗΣ ΑΔΙΚΙΑΣ ΟΤΙ ΤΟΝ ΕΡΑΣΤΗΝ ΑΥΤΗΣ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΙΟΝ ΑΓΕΒΟΥΚΟΛΗΣΕ. ΔΙΚ. πῶτε ἐχμοί. ΕΡΜ. ΠΕΡΙ ΑΡΙΣΤΙΠΠΟΥ ΤΡΥΦΗ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΡΕΤΗΝ. ΔΙΚ. πῶς τε ἡ ζυτίμις δι-καστάτωσιν. ΕΡΜ. ΑΡΓΥΡΑΜΟΙΒΙΚΗ ΔΡΑΣΜΟΥ ΔΙΟΓΕΝΕΙ. ΔΙΚ. τρεῖς ἀπόκληρον μόνοις. ΕΡΜ. Η ΓΡΑΦΙΚΗ ΚΑΤΑ ΠΥΡΡΩΝΟΣ ΛΕΙΠΟΤΑ-ΞΙΟΥ. ΔΙΚ. ὡνέα χρηστότωσθ. ΕΡΜ. ΡΗΤΟΡΙΚΗ ΚΑΚΩΣΕΩΣ ΤΩ ΣΥ-ΡΩ ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ ΤΩ ΑΥΤΩ ΥΒΡΕΩΣ. ΔΙΚ. τίς ἡ ἐπὶ ὅστι; ἡ γὰρ ἐληλεγα-τημένη ξωύματα. ΕΡΜ. ὥστε ἀπόκληρον ΤΩ ΡΗΤΟΡΙ ΣΥΡΩ. κωλύσ[?] γὰρ ἔστιν ἡ αὐτὸ τῆς ὀνόματος. ΔΙΚ. ἀπόκληρον ἑνδέκα, τοσοῦτος ἑκατέρα τῆ δίκη. Nemini, quod sciam, de mendo suspecta sunt postrema haec Luciani verba, at tamen facile fuit & aduertisse mendum, & sustulisse: nam iudicia ista omnia reddenda erant eadem die. Habes paullo ante: οἷσθα ὁ ἀράσσομαι, ὦ Ἑρμῆ; Τῷ μὲν ἄλλας δίκας ἐς τὸν αὐτὸν ὑπεραρχόμενα, σημεῖον ἡ κληρωθῆναι τὰς Θεσμοφόρους, ὅποσον τέ-χναις, ἡ βίοις, ἡ ἐπιστήμης, ἐπὶ τὰς ἀνδρας εἰσὶν ἐππεκλιόμαι. Non igitur iidem poterant iudicium reddere Syro Rhetori & Rhetoricae κακώσεως, eidemque rursum Syro Rhetori & Dialogo ὕβρεως. Rescribe itaque ἀπόκληρον ἑνδέκα, τοσοῦτος ἑκατέρα τῆ δίκῃ. Sortite, inquit, vndecim, totidem vtrique liti.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions the law in his first speech against Aeschines: "But you yourselves, Athenians, draw lots for all, and are all of you willing to be allotted to a court, to judge alone. But you drew lots, and then you were allotted, for so the laws say." The scholiast on Aristophanes' Plutus describes this: when the judges were about to be seated, all the judges came into the agora; then those who held the written tablets with the names of the judges and the courts were allotted again. In Lucian's dialogue, you have the customs used by the Athenians in this matter: the herald Mercury summons the litigants to the court; Justice, as the magistrate before whom the charges were written, draws lots for the judges, Mercury the herald reciting the charges, more or fewer according to the dignity and gravity of the crime. Mercury: "Hear, people, the court of Justice is summoned today, on the seventh day of the month Elaphebolion. As many as have brought charges, come to the Areopagus; now Justice will allot the court, and she herself will sit with the judges, the Athenian judges... each suit one talent..." [Ἀκούετε λεώς...]. And a little later: Mercury: "Of the Academy, concerning the ransom of Polemon." Justice: "By lot." Mercury: "Of the Stoa, concerning the wrong done by Dionysius, who insulted her slave." Justice: "Whence do you know?" Mercury: "Concerning Aristippus, Tryphe against Arete." Justice: "How many judges?" Mercury: "Concerning the Argyrampolic... of the Diogenic." Justice: "Three, allotted alone." Mercury: "The Grammatical, against Pyrrho the Leipotaxian." Justice: "Eleven..." Mercury: "Rhetorical, concerning the ill-treatment of the Syrian Rhetor, dialogue with the same wrong..." Justice: "Who is it, then? For the charge has already been brought." Mercury: "So, allot the Syrian Rhetor, since it is a matter of the same name." Justice: "Eleven, so many for each suit." No one, so far as I know, has suspected these last words of Lucian of corruption; yet it was easy both to notice the error and to remove it, for all these trials had to be decided on the same day. Just before, you have: "Do you know what I suffer, Hermes? When the other suits are brought before the same court, the Thesmophoria are allotted, and so many men are summoned as judges..." Therefore the same men could not give judgment both on the Syrian Rhetor for the ill-treatment of rhetoric and again on the Syrian Rhetor and the Dialogue for wrong. Read therefore "allot eleven, so many for each suit." He says: allot eleven, equally for each suit.

units.la: Lege namque cauebatur, ne quis eadem die duo redderet iudicia.
units.tr: For by law it was provided that no one should pronounce two judgments on the same day.

units.la: Τοὺς δικαστὰς μὴ δικάζειν ἐς ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἡ-μέρᾳ.
units.tr: The judges shall not sit in judgment twice on the same day. [Τοὺς δικαστὰς μὴ δικάζειν ἐς ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ]

units.la: Legem colligere licet partim ἐ Demosthenis verbis ἐν τῷ Τιμοκράτες, partim ex illis quae ad ea adnotat Vlpianus. Demosthenis ista sunt: ὑμεῖς μὲν γὰρ τὰ ὅτι τῷ πλήθει νενομοθετημένα δίκα, ἐάν τις ἐξ ἡμέρας μιᾶς δυοφορῆ, ἐὰν ἄλλο τι ποιῇ, ὧν οἱ νόμοι ἀπαγορεύουσι. Vlpianus: ἐαὶ τῆς δίκης μιᾶς δυοφορῆ, ἐν δυὸ δικαστηρίων· σαλλέ-βαινε γὰρ δύο γίνεσθαι ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ, ἵνα οὖν μὴ ἡ ὥσπερ ἐργασία, χωλύει τῆς. Nam mercedem de publico accipiebant iudices, triobolum scilicet in singulas, quas iudicabant, lites. Lucianus verbis laudatis: ὁ μιαρός, τελώνου ἐκάσης δίκης. Quanquam obolus tantum fuit, Aristophane nebulas docente Olympiade octagesima nona: in eo namque dramate hic legitur versus, οὐ πρῶτον ἔλαβον Ηλιαστικόν.
units.tr: The law may be gathered partly from Demosthenes' words in the speech against Timocrates, and partly from what Ulpian notes on them. Demosthenes' words are these: "You have legislated that a suit may be brought against anyone who, on the same day, takes on a second office, or does anything else that the laws forbid." Ulpian: "if anyone sits as judge in two courts; for it was not allowed for two (cases) to take place on the same day, so that it would not become like a trade, the law forbids it." For the judges received their pay from the public treasury, namely three obols for each case they tried. Lucian, in the words cited: "the wretch, a toll-collector of every suit." Yet it was only one obol, as Aristophanes shows in the Clouds, in the eighty-ninth Olympiad; for in that play this line is read: "I did not first receive the Heliastic (pay)."

units.la: Optime Scholiastes, qui negat quicquam certi constitutum fuisse in τὸ δικαστήριον, quando ista scribebat Comicus: ἀχ ἴσαν ὁ τῆ δικαστῶν ὁ μισθός. Nam omnino certum est, è versu Aristophanis iudices de publico non accepisse plus obolo: quanquam anno proxime elapso triobolum acceperant. Idem tamen Aristophanes, cum anno sequenti, qui erat secundus Olympiadis nonæ supra octagesimam, Vespas committeret, volebat triobolum dari, quot obolorum erat ὁ ἐκκλησιαστικὸν, sed tamen nonnisi vnus dabatur obolus: Aristophanis verba adscribemus, quanquam plusucula sint, vt illustremus & a mendo liberemus. Bdelycleon & Philocleon inter se colloquuntur:
units.tr: The Scholiast is right, who says that nothing certain had been fixed for the court when the comic poet wrote: "Ah, what is the judges' pay?" For it is quite certain, from the line of Aristophanes, that the judges had received from the public treasury no more than one obol, although in the year just before they had received three obols. Yet Aristophanes himself, when in the following year, the second of the ninth Olympiad after the eightieth, he produced the Wasps, wanted three obols to be given, as many obols as the assembly pay came to; but in fact only one obol was given. I shall quote Aristophanes' words, though they are rather long, so that we may illustrate and free them from error. Bdelycleon and Philocleon talk together:

units.la: ΒΔΕ. ἀκρόασαί νῦν ὦ παππίδιον χαλέσας ὀλίγον ὃ μέσπωμεν[?].καὶ ταχύ μὲν λόγοισι Φαῦλως μὲ ψηφοῖς[?], ἀλλ' ἀπὸ χθές,τὸν Φόβον ἡμῖν ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως συλλήβδην τ' ἀφεσποῖνα[?].χαῖρω τούτῳ τὰ τίλη χρεῖς[?], ἡ ταῖς πολλὰς ἐκπέμπεις[?],ταρυτάνεια[?]. μέπαλλ', ἀγρεῖς[?], λιθῆας, μαθοῖς[?], καὶ δημοτρέστα[?].τούτων πλήρωμα, πάλαι τ' ἐγὼ σπιλία[?] ἡμῖν.ἀπὸ τούτων νῦν μαθὼν καταλήξεις τοῖσι δικασταῖς τῆς σπαυᾶς[?],ἐξ χιλιάσιν, κοῦπω πλείους ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ κατέπαυσε.γίγνεσθαι ἡμῖν ἑκατὸν ἴνου καὶ πυτικάσιν[?] πάλαι[?].
units.tr: BDELYCLEON. Listen now, little old father, I call you aside for a little, what we drink. And quickly, in words, not in votes, but from yesterday... fear from the city, and altogether let it go... I rejoice in this... you send out many... (these lines are too corrupt to render with certainty). Of these there is a full supply, and for a long time I... to us. From these things, now learned, you will end the matter for the judges of the ... six thousand, and no more ... has ever quieted in the land. ... to us a hundred (talents) and ... long ago.

units.la: ΦΙΛ. ὦ ἡ δικαστὴ τῆς ἀφοσοῖτων ἡμῖν ἀφ' ἐγίνειν[?] ὁ μαθὼς[?].
units.tr: PHILOCLEON. O judge, of the ... to us ... having learned.

units.la: Scholiastæ verba sunt: Εἰς ἱ μυριάδας λογίζεσθαι τὸν ἐπικωτόν, ὡς τῷ β' εἰς ἑορτὰς παρχωρεῶντων[?]. ἐκέσφ γὰρ τειχοῦσλον τὸ μέλιος[?], ἐ τὸ μέλιος[?] ὑσλεκλα ποιεῖ[?]. Facile subducitur ratio. Centum quinquaginta talentum annuorum si perpendamus sex millibus hominum in singulos menses quindecim talenta tribuenda, nempe tres obolos viritim: sed aduertendum est annum hic accepi decem tantum mensium, non quod non constet duodecim mensibus, sed quia duo saltem in anno menses sunt, quibus nihil iure agi licet. Itaque festis illis diebus non carrebant iudicibus sua stipendia, propterea tanquam decem tantum in annos menses numeret, centum & quinquaginta putat talenta, quem numerum pariunt quindecim decies repetita. Nobis tamen non potest probari obseruatio Scholiastæ: nam non tantum duo sunt menses εἰς ἑορτὰς παρχωρεῶντες, sed etiam sex sunt addendi, ita vt triens anni vix reliquus sit à festis, quibus ius non dicitur, iudicia non redduntur. Xenophon: παρὰ δ' ἐνύτοις οἴεσθαι χρὴ καὶ ἑορτὰς ἀγὰν χελιῶν[?] Αθηναίους ἐν αἷς ἂν χρὴ τὴ δικάζειν[?], καὶ ἄριστοι μὲν ἑορτὰς διπλασίως[?] ἢ οἱ ἄλλοι. Certe nemo, qui attenderit ad festa Athenienfium, quorum mentio occurrit in scriptis veterum, negabit, opinor, duos trientes anni festis his imputari. Præterea nititur obseruatio Scholiastæ verbis Comici; quæ corrupta esse nullus dubito, quasi scilicet sex mille fuerint iudices quotannis:
units.tr: The words of the Scholiast are: "To reckon the (annual) sum at ten thousand, as for the second (days) that fall on festivals..." For it is easy to work out the calculation. If we weigh a hundred and fifty talents a year, and six thousand men are to be paid fifteen talents a month, namely three obols each, but we must note that here he counts only ten months in the year, not because a year does not consist of twelve months, but because at least two months in the year are those on which nothing can lawfully be transacted. So on those festival days the judges did not get their pay; therefore, counting only ten months in the year, he makes it a hundred and fifty talents, which number results from fifteen multiplied by ten. Yet we cannot accept the Scholiast's observation, for there are not only two months that belong to festivals, but six more must be added, so that scarcely a third of the year is left free of festivals, on which judgments are not given and the court does not sit. Xenophon: "Among these, one must suppose that the Athenians also have festivals, on which it is not lawful to judge, and the best (judges) have more holidays than the others." Certainly, I think, no one who has looked at the festivals of the Athenians, which are mentioned in the writings of the ancients, will deny that two-thirds of the year... Moreover, the Scholiast's observation rests on the words of the comic poet, which I have no doubt are corrupt, as if there were six thousand judges each year:

units.la: ἀπὸ τούτων νῦν μαθὼν καταλήξεις τοῖσι δικασταῖς τῆς σπαυᾶς[?],ἐξ χιλιάσιν, κοῦπω πλείους ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ κατέπαυσε.
units.tr: "From these things, now learned, you will end the matter for the judges of the ... six thousand, and no more ... has ever quieted in the land."

units.la: Atqui sex mille non fuerunt. Nouem fuisse Tribunalia, in superioribus diximus, quibus adscribe singulis iudices quingentos, fient quatermille quingenti: adde ἀλφιτοπώλις[?] τοῖς κληρωτοῖς[?] quadringentos quadraginta, singulis namq; Tribunalibus erat quadraginta quatuor Arbitri, fient iudices quatermille nongenti quadraginta: Adde τοῖς ἐκ δήμου δικασταῖς quadraginta, fient in vniuersum quatermille nongenti octoginta; ita vt sint quinquies fere mille, qui numerus reponendus est apud Aristophanem, facileque mutauit, cum litera tantum numeralis esset adscripta, ε' χιλιάσιν, in ἐξ χιλιάσιν, neque peccatur aduersus metri legem, cum referibitur:
units.tr: But there were not six thousand. We said above that there were nine courts, and if you assign five hundred judges to each, you get four thousand five hundred. Add four hundred and forty of those chosen by lot, since each court had forty-four arbitrators; that makes four thousand nine hundred and forty judges. Add forty judges from the demes, and in all there are four thousand nine hundred and eighty. So there are about five thousand, and this number should be restored in Aristophanes; it is easily changed, since only the numeral letter was written, ε' (five) thousand, for ἑξ (six) thousand, and no fault against the metre is committed when it is read:

units.la: ἀπὸ τούτων νῦν μαθὼν καταλήξεις τοῖς δικασταῖς τῆς σπαυᾶς[?],πέντε χιλιάσιν, κοῦπω πλείους ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ κατέπαυσε.
units.tr: "From these things, now learned, you will end the matter for the judges of the ... five thousand, and no more ... has ever quieted in the land."

units.la: Sequens autem versus, qui ita legitur,
units.tr: The following line, which is read thus,

units.la: Γίγνεσθαι ἡμῖν ἑκατὸν δήπου καὶ πεντήκοντα τάλαντα:
units.tr: "Let there be for us a hundred and fifty talents, surely."

units.la: rescribendus est ad hunc modum,
units.tr: should be restored in this way:

units.la: Γίγνεσθε ὑμῖν ἑκατὸν δήπου καὶ πεντήκοντα τάλαντα.
units.tr: "Let there be for you a hundred and fifty talents, surely."

units.la: Nam Philocleonem alloquitur Bdelycleon, sub eiusque persona omnes φιλοδικαςτάς. Vobis igitur, inquit, in mercedem dantur omnibus, qui quinquies mille estis, centum quinquaginta talenta quotannis, nempe triobolum numerat in ὃ δικαστικὸν viritim Philocleon, quemadmodum anno quarto Olympiadis octagesimae octavae, quando ἵππεις in scenam produxit Comicus, triobolum erat ὁ δικαστικὸν, claret ex hoc Aristophanis Equitibus versu:
units.tr: For Bdelycleon is addressing Philocleon, and under his persona all the lovers of the courts. For you, he says, all of you who are five thousand, a hundred and fifty talents are given as pay each year; that is, Philocleon counts out three obols per man for the judicial pay, as in the fourth year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad, when the comic poet brought the Knights onto the stage, three obols was the judicial pay; this is clear from this line of Aristophanes' Knights:

units.la: ὦ θρόντες Ἡλιασταί, θεάτορες τριωβόλου.
units.tr: "O you Heliastic jurors, spectators of the triobol."

units.la: Scholia: οἱ ὃ δικασταὶ ὑπὸ τῆς δημαγωγῶν ἐπείφοντο, τριωβόλου λαμβάνοντες μισθὸν δικαστικὸν μὴ ὃ κείνα. Item eadem fabula paullo ante.
units.tr: The Scholia: "The judges were deceived by the demagogues, receiving as judicial pay three obols, not the (larger sum)." Likewise the same play a little earlier:

units.la: ὦ δῆμε, λούσας πρῶτον ἐκδικάσας μίαν, ἔνθου, ῥόφησον, ἐνπαγ', ἐχὲ τριωβόλου.
units.tr: "O people, first bathe, then judge one case, eat, drink, and go to bed, after the triobol."

units.la: Vbi optime quidem Scholiastes, ἐχὲ τριωβόλου, interpretatur, τὸν δικαστικὸν μισθὸν, ἐπὶ τριωβόλου ἐλάμβανον. Sed tamen male ad praecedentia ἐκδικάσας μίαν, adnotat ista, λείπει ὁ ἡμέραν, imo vero subintelligendum est δίκαν, ὡς γράφω, nam, ut diximus, Lege cautum erat, ὅτι δικαστὰς μὴ δικάζειν δὶς ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ. Anno vero sequenti, qui erat primus Olympiadis octagesimae nonae, cum doceret Nubes Aristophanes, obolus tantum erat ὁ δικαστικὸς μισθὸς, habes eo, quem iam descripsimus, versu Nubium.
units.tr: Here the Scholiast rightly explains "after the triobol" as "they received the judicial pay, after (or for) the triobol." But he badly annotates the preceding words "judge one case" with "the word day is missing," whereas one must rather understand "case", as I write; for, as we said, the law provided "that judges should not judge twice on the same day." In the following year, the first of the eighty-ninth Olympiad, when Aristophanes produced the Clouds, the judicial pay was only one obol; you have this in the line of the Clouds that we have already described:

units.la: ὃν ὠχρὸν ὀβολὸν ἔλαχον Ἡλιαστικήν.
units.tr: "which pale obol I got as Heliastic (pay)."

units.la: & comprobat hic Aristophanis locus, quem illustramus. Annus est Lunaris diebus trecentis quinquaginta quatuor explicatus, huius anni diebus singulis distribue viritim Iudicibus quinquies mille triobolum, annua fiunt centum quadraginta talenta cum triginta minis, quae impenduntur quotannis εἰς τριωβόλον τῶν δικαστικῶν μισθὸν, sed rotunde dixit Aristophanis Bdelycleon esse centum quinquaginta talenta, desunt enim absoluendo numero sesquitalenta quinque.
units.tr: And this passage of Aristophanes, which we are illustrating, confirms it. The year is a lunar year of three hundred and fifty-four days. If you distribute to each of the judges, five thousand in number, three obols for each day of this year, the annual sum comes to a hundred and forty talents and thirty minas, which are spent each year on the triobol, the judicial pay. But Aristophanes' Bdelycleon speaks roundly, saying it is a hundred and fifty talents, for in the full sum five and a half talents are missing.

units.la: Γίγνεσθε ὑμῖν ἑκατὸν δήπου ᾧ πεντήκοντα τάλαντα.
units.tr: "Let there be for you a hundred and fifty talents, surely."

units.la: At vero Philocleon respondet ne decimam quidem partem horum centum quinquaginta talentorum, quae Iudicum esse debebant, iisque procedere in stipendia, mercedulam illorum esse:
units.tr: But Philocleon replies that not even a tenth part of these hundred and fifty talents, which ought to be the judges' due, and which go to their pay, is their paltry wage:

units.la: ΦΙΛ. ἀλλ' εἰ δεκάτη τῆς προσόντων ἡμῖν, ἀρ' ἐγίγνετ' ὁ μισθός.
units.tr: PHILOCLEON. "But if a tenth part of what is ours, would the pay come to that?"

units.la: Scilicet hoc anno secundo Olympiadis octagesimae nonae, quemadmodum & praecedente, ὃ δικαστικὸν fuit obolus tantum: iam vero duo minimum trientes Lunaris anni imputandi sunt festis, quibus sua non currunt Iudicibus stipendia: superest tantum, ac ne vix quidem superest, triens anni, id est, dies centum octodecim, quibus ius dicitur: Si singulis his diebus viritim distribuas Iudicibus quinquies mille unum obolum: fient talenta sedecim, minae viginti tres, drachmae triginta tres, & oboli duo. Decima autem pars talentum centum quinquaginta sunt quindecim talenta. Certe optime observat Aristophanis Scholiastes ex Aristotele de Republica Atheniensium, Iudicum mercedem modo auctam, modo accisam fuisse, pro libidine Demagogorum: τὴν φορὰν λέγει, ἀφ' ὧν ἐδίδοτο ὁ τειχοσκόλων. τοῦτο δὲ ἄλλοτε ἄλλως ἐδίδοτο, τῇ δημαγωγῶν πε πλήθη κολακευόντων, ὡς φησιν Ἀριστοφάνης ἐν πολιτείας. Itaque anno quarto Olympiadis octagesimæ octauæ Iudices triobolum accipiebant: anno sequenti, qui erat primus Olympiadis octagesimæ nonæ, vt & secundo eiusdem Olympiadis, quo Vespas docuit Comicus, ὁ δικαστικὸν erat vnus tantum obolus. Non ignoro Comicum tamen passim Vespis meminisse trioboli. Sed locus, quem interpretamur, omnino nos cogit in hanc sententiam ire, anno secundo Olympiadis nonæ supra octagesimam, quo editum est hoc drama, Iudicum mercedem vnum fuisse obolum, non plures: nam dicit Philocleon, idque cum querela, ὅτι ἡ δικαστὴς τῶν προσοφειλόντων ἡμῖν ἀφ' ἑκάστου ὁ μισθός,
units.tr: Clearly in this second year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad, as in the preceding one, the judicial pay was only one obol. Now at least two-thirds of the lunar year must be counted as festivals, on which the judges' pay does not run; only one third of the year is left, or scarcely even that, namely a hundred and eighteen days, on which justice is administered. If you distribute to the judges, five thousand, one obol for each of these days, the sum comes to sixteen talents, twenty-three minas, thirty-three drachmas and two obols. But a tenth part of a hundred and fifty talents is fifteen talents. Certainly the Scholiast of Aristophanes observes well, from Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians, that the judges' pay was sometimes increased and sometimes reduced, at the whim of the demagogues: he says the amount was given at various times in various ways, as the demagogues flattered the crowds, as Aristophanes says in the Politics. So in the fourth year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad the judges received three obols; in the following year, the first of the eighty-ninth, and likewise in the second year of that Olympiad, when the comic poet produced the Wasps, the judicial pay was a single obol. I am not unaware that the comic poet mentions the triobol here and there in the Wasps. But the passage we are interpreting compels us to this view: in the second year after the eightieth Olympiad, in which this play was produced, the judges' pay was one obol and no more. For Philocleon says, and with complaint, that the judges' pay was from each of those who owe us... (the sentence continues with the next line, quoted in the context).

units.la: quod referendum est ad versum præcedentem, Γίγνεσθαι ὑμῖν ἑκατὸν δήπου καὶ πεντήκοντα ταλάντα.
units.tr: This is to be referred to the preceding verse: "Surely there will be for you a hundred and fifty talents" [Γίγνεσθαι ὑμῖν ἑκατὸν δήπου καὶ πεντήκοντα ταλάντα].

units.la: Nempe queritur Philocleon vix decimam partem eorum centum & quinquaginta talentorum, quæ in mercedem annuam Iudicum, si quidem singulis in singulos anni dies triobolum in stipendium procederet, erant seponenda: Non queritur autem non dari Iudicibus in mercedem decimam partem illorum bis mille talentum annui Atheniensium reditus, quæ pars decima erat talenta ducenta; Credit enim Philocleon cum Iudicibus commode agi, si illis attribuatur triobolum εἰς ὁ δικαστικὸν, hinc illa illius verba: ὁ δὲ γ' ἤδιστον τούτων ὅτι πόντων, ὃ 'γὼ 'πιλελιφομαι, ὅταν οἰκαδ' ἴω τὸν μισθὸν ἔχων καὶ παῖτ' εἰσπονθ' ἅμα πόντες ἀποζῇσθαι ἀξ' ὀργύρειον. ἡ πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἡ Ζυγάτηρ με ἀπονίζῃ· ἡ πόλ' ἀλείφῃ, ἐ πρὸς σκύλα ἀ φιλίου· καὶ παπποζούσ' ἅμα τὴ γλώτῃ πειωόλων ἐκκαλεμίζει.
units.tr: Philocleon complains that he is getting barely a tenth part of those hundred and fifty talents, which had to be set aside for the yearly pay of the judges, if a triobol was paid to each judge for each day of the year. He does not complain that the judges were given no pay at all, though a tenth part of the yearly revenue of Athens, two thousand talents, would have been two hundred talents. Philocleon thinks the judges are well treated if a triobol is assigned to them for their pay. Hence those words of his: "The sweetest thing of all these, which I miss, is when I go home with my pay in hand and my children, along with my wife, are fed with a silver-drachma [?]... Her who was my wife [?] ... and my mother bursts out with delight at the sight of the cakes." [ὁ δὲ γ' ἤδιστον τούτων].

units.la: Quæ non spectant hunc annum, sed ad præcedentia tempora pertinent, quando ὁ δικαστικὸν erat triobolum: Vt & sequentia Bdelycleonis verba non præsens tempus indicant, sed quod antea factum fuerat, & in posterum fieri poterat maxime gratum acceptúmque Iudicibus: σοὶ δ' ἐγὼ τὰς δῶ ταῖς τῆς ἐξολεῖς ἀγαπᾶς.
units.tr: These words do not refer to this year but to earlier times, when the judges' pay was a triobol. Likewise the following words of Bdelycleon do not indicate the present tense but something that had happened before and could happen again, most welcome and acceptable to the judges: "But I will give you ... which you love."

units.la: & paullo post: ἠκιν εἶπη ταρτι, καὶ ὥσπερ δικασταὶ ὡς ὅς τῆς αὖ ὑμῶν ὑστερος ἐλθῇ τῷ σημείου, ὁ τειχοσκόλων ὃ κομιστή.
units.tr: And a little later: "Let him come, for now, and just as judges, when someone comes late after the signal, the wall-keeper's [?] ..."

units.la: Verba autem hæc demonstrant Iudicem, qui sero & signo iam dato aduenisset, cum iam litigantes orare cepissent, mercedem non accepisse, nempe quia ea de lite Iudicium non reddebat: liquet ex his Comici verbis, eodem drama-te. Εἴ τις ὑφεμὸν Ηλιαστὴς, εἰσίτω. ὡς ἰωῖκ' ἀὐ λέγωσιν οὐκ εἰσφρήσομεν.
units.tr: These words show that a judge who had arrived late, after the signal had already been given and the litigants had begun to plead, did not receive his pay, because he did not render judgment in that case. This is clear from these words of the comic poet in the same play: "If any judge of the Heliaea is here, let him come in; for when they begin to speak, we will not let him in."

units.la: Scholia : ἔτος γὰρ ἰῶ, πρὸς μὲν τῆς καταστάσεως τῶν Ρητόρων, κηρύττειν τοῖς δικασταῖς. ὁπότε δὲ ἤρχοντο τῶν δικῶν, οὐκέτι εἰῶν εἰσιέναι τοῖς ὑστεροῦσι δικασταῖς.
units.tr: Scholia: "For he [the herald] was there to proclaim to the judges at the setting up of the orators, and when the trials had begun, he no longer allowed the judges who came late to enter."

units.la: Postquam Iudices sortitus erat Magistratus, Iudices dati ex Lege iurabant se de causa, de qua actio erat, iudicium reddituiros· ΔΙΚΑΣΩ ΓΕΡΙ ΩΝ ΑΝ Η ΔΙΩΞΙΣ Ηι, ΚΑΙ ΓΕΡΙ ΜΕΝ ΩΝ ΝΟΜΟΙ Jus dicam de iis, de quibus actio est: atque sententiam feram secun-
units.tr: After the magistrate had allotted the judges, the judges so appointed swore under the law that they would give judgment on the case that was the subject of the action: "I will judge concerning those matters for which the prosecution is brought [Δικάσω περὶ ὧν ἂν ἡ δίωξις ᾖ], and concerning those matters for which there are laws [καὶ περὶ μὲν ὧν νόμοι]; I will judge the case itself and will pronounce my verdict in accordance with

units.la: ΕΙΣΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ΤΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ, ΠΕΡΙ ΔΕ ΩΝ ΜΗ ΕΙΣΙ ΓΝΩΜΗ ΤΗ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΤΑΤΗ.
units.tr: I will vote according to the laws, and concerning those matters for which there is no law, according to the most just judgment. [ΨΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ, ΠΕΡΙ ΔΕ ΩΝ ΜΗ ΕΣΤΙ ΝΟΜΟΣ, ΓΝΩΜΗ ΤΗ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΤΑΤΗ]

units.la: dum Leges in iis, de quibus Legibus cautum est: de quibus vero Legibus cautum non est, quam iustissime potero.
units.tr: I will give judgment according to the laws in those matters on which the laws have made provision; and in those matters on which no law has been laid down, I will judge as justly as I can.

units.la: Iurasse Iudices, vbi dati erant à Magistratu, se de re illa, cuius iudices sedebant, iudicia reddituros, constat ex his Vlpiani verbis ad Orationem Demosthenis ξ' Τιμοκράτους. ἆρ' ἡ αὐτὴ καλὴ αἰωμοσία; καὶ ὃ εἰσιόντες οἱ δικασταὶ πρὸς ἐκείνου τὸ πρᾶγμα ὤμοσαν, [?] ἡ κείσις ὣ, ἢ μὴ τοι πρὸς τὴν ἤδη κειλκ[?]ν[?]των. Iurisiurandi Lege imperati formulam habes apud Demosthenem partim ἐν ταῖς ξ' ψευδομαρτυρίας α. Ταῦτα ὅτως αὐτὸς αἰτιεγάλατο, ἃ χρὴ μνημονεύειν ὑμᾶς, καὶ μὴ τοῖς ὀξ ἀπάτης νῦν λόγοις ἐπὶ τούτου ρηδ[?]ν[?]σιμοῦμοις, πιστεύεσις ποιήσθαι τὴν νόμων, ἢ τῆς ἐπὶ τούτου γεγραφέντων εἰς τὸ ὑπηρεσίαν. Quas Leges hic intelligat, sequentia comprobant, nempe, δικαστὴν γὰρ ὁμωμοκέναι ὑμᾶς, οὐ [?] ὠν ἂν δὲ ὁ φεύγων ἀξιοῖ, ἀλλ' ἐπ' αὐτοῦ, ΩΝ ΑΝ Η ΔΙΩΞΙΣ Ηι. Idem Demosthenes in Leptinea: ὁμωμοκότες ΠΕΡΙ ΩΝ ΑΝ ΝΟΜΟΙ ΜΗ ΩΣΙ ΓΝΩΜΗι ΤΗι ΔΙΚΑΙΟΤΑΤΗι κεῖνῳ καλῶς. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. X. ὁ ἡ ἀρχὴς τῶ τῆς δικαστῶν, ΠΕΡΙ ΜΕΝ ΩΝ ΝΟΜΟΙ ΕΙΣΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ ψηφίσαται. ΠΕΡΙ ΔΕ ΩΝ ΜΗ ΕΙΣΙ ΣΥΝ ΓΝΩΜΗι ΤΗι ΔΙΚΑΙΟΤΑΤΗι.
units.tr: That the judges, when they had been appointed by the magistrate, swore that they would render judgment in the matter over which they were sitting is clear from these words of Ulpian on Demosthenes' oration against Timocrates: "Is this not the same kind of oath? And the judges who entered swore on that matter [?] ..., either that they would judge it, or not ... according to the laws." You have the formula of the oath imposed by law, in part, in Demosthenes' [speech on false witness]. He explains these things himself, which you must remember, and not be led by the deceitful arguments of the present speakers to trust in the laws or in what has been written about them. Which laws he means here is shown by what follows, namely: "For you have sworn as judges, not concerning whatever the accused demands, but concerning the matter at hand, [concerning which] the action is brought." The same Demosthenes in Leptines: "You have sworn concerning those matters on which the laws make provision, to vote according to the laws; and concerning those on which they make none, by your most just judgment, as is right." Pollux, book VIII, chapter 10: the office of the judges' oath: "concerning those matters on which the laws make provision, they vote according to the laws; concerning those on which they make none, with their most just judgment."

units.la: Iudicabantur autem lites eo ordine, quo in tabulas γραμμάτεων erant relatæ: primo quidem prima inscripta, secundo secunda, atque ita deinceps secundum hanc seriem. Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Vespas. ἡ ὀνμίσων φησὶ τὴν [?] ἀποδειχθέντων τὰ ὀνόματα τῆς εἰσαγγελίας εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον. ποῖον δεινὸς ἀφεῖναι εἰσα[?]ς[?]ν ἐπ' τὴν ξ' τῆς. Sed & ipse Comicus eo alludit Nubibus.
units.tr: Lawsuits were heard in the order in which they had been entered on the lists (γραμματεῖα): first the first one listed, then the second, and so on in this sequence. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Wasps: "He says the names of the cases appointed for the court were entered for that court; what a clever man to let go..." But the comic poet himself alludes to this in the Clouds.

units.la: ΣΩ. ὅπως ἀπαιτέλαις αὖ αἰτιάσεων δίκῶ, μὴ ὀφλήσῃ, μὴ προσόντων μαρτύρων.
units.tr: SOCRATES: "So that you might not, by bringing suits on a new charge, be condemned, when there are no witnesses present."

units.la: ΣΤ. Φαυλότατε καὶ ῥᾳς. ΣΩ. εἶπέ δή. ΣΤ. καὶ δὴ λέγω. εἰ προσᾶδει ἐπὶ μιᾶς ἐνεχύσεως δίκης, παρὰ τὸν ἐμὸν καλῶς ἀπαγξαμένῳ πέχων.
units.tr: STREPSIADES: "Most foolish and wretched man!" SOCRATES: "Speak, then." STREPSIADES: "Well, I say this: if someone is prosecuted on a single charge, he should be ..."

units.la: Vbi sortitus erat Iudices Magistratus, cuius erat ἡγεμονία δικαστηρίου, accepta dica, rursum actorem interrogabat, an paratus esset ad agendum, necne, actore se paratum esse respondente, Iudices sedere ad ius dicendum iubebantur. Vlpianus ad Midianam. μὴ γὰρ ὁ ἀποκληρωθεὶς ὁ δικαστήριον, ἐδίδοτο τῆς Θεσμοθέτας αἱ γεραφαί. καὶ αὐτοὶ ἡρῴων λοιπὸν, ΒΟΥΛΕΙ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΕΙΝ; Η ΜΑΡΤΥΡΑΣ ΕΧΕΙΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΑΣ ΑΠΟΔΕΙΞΕΙΣ ΕΤΟΙΜΟΥΣ; καὶ εἰ σιωπήσῃ ὅτως ἤδη λοιπὸν εἰσίζετο.
units.tr: When the magistrate who presided over the court had allotted the judges, and had accepted the indictment, he again questioned the plaintiff whether he was ready to proceed or not. When the plaintiff replied that he was ready, the judges were ordered to sit down to give judgment. Ulpian on Midias: "For when the judges had been allotted, the thesmothetae handed over the written indictments. And then the herald asked: 'Do you wish to accuse?' or 'Do you have your witnesses ready for the proofs?' And if he remained silent, from then on the case was pursued no further."

units.la: DE IVDICIIS.
units.tr: On Judgments.

units.la: TITVLVS QVARTVS.
units.tr: Title Four.

units.la: VBI confederant Iudices, Praeco dicam recitabat. Aristophanes Vespis, vbi male τῷ Θεοξένου nomen praescribitur, cum proculdubio ὁ κῆρυξ ista pronuntiet.
units.tr: When the judges had taken their seats, the herald read out the charge. In Aristophanes' Wasps, where the name of Theoxenus is wrongly put at the head, the herald is clearly the one who pronounces these words.

units.la: ἀκούετ' ἤδη τῆς γραφῆς ἠξεάλωτο Κύων Κυδαθηναιεύς, Λάσπ' Αἰξωνέα, τὴν τύχην ἀδικεῖν ὅτι μόνος κατέπαυτε τὸν Σικελικὸν τίμημα κλέφος σύκινος.
units.tr: Hear now the indictment: the Cydathenaean dog against Labes of Aixone, for wronging the city by stealing the Sicilian ... and keeping silent about it, a fig-leaf thief.

units.la: A Scriba recitari facit Æschines ὁ παῖς τοῦ Τιμάρχου. εἰδὼς δ' αὐτὸν ἐνοχον ὄντα τὰ οἷς ὀλίγῳ πρεσβύτερον ἠκούσατε αἰαχυνώσκυσθαι τῆς γραμματέως, ἐπὶ ψήφισμα αὐτοῦ τῶν δικαιοσύνων ὠνήσει. Exemplum dicae habes apud Demosthenem ὁ παῖς τοῦ Κτησιφῶντος. ΓΡΑΦΗ ΕΓΙ ΧΑΙΡΩΝΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ ΕΛΑΦΗΒΟΛΙΩΝΟΣ ΕΚΤΗΙ ΙΣΤΑΜΕΝΟΥ. ΑΙΣΧΙΝΗΣ ΑΤΡΟΜΗΤΟΥ ΛΟΘΩΝ. ΚΙΔΗΣ ΑΠΗΝΕΓΚΕ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΝ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΑ ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΩΝ ΓΡΑΦΗΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΚΤΗΣΙΦΩΝΤΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΛΕΩΣΘΕΝΟΥΣ ΑΝΑΦΑΥΣΤΙΟΥ, ΟΤΙ ΕΓΡΑΨΕ ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΟΝ ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ, ΩΣ ΑΡΑ ΔΕΙ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΣΑΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΘΕΝΗΝ ΔΗΜΟΣΘΕΝΟΥΣ ΠΑΙΑΝΙΕΑ ΧΡΥΣΩΙ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΙ, ΚΑΙ ΑΝΑΓΟΡΕΥΣΑΙ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΘΕΑΤΡΩΙ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΙΟΙΣ ΤΟΙΣ ΜΕΓΑΛΟΙΣ ΤΡΑΓΩΔΟΙΣ ΚΑΙΝΟΙΣ, ΟΤΙ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΙ Ο ΔΗΜΟΣ ΔΗΜΟΣΘΕΝΗΝ ΔΙΙΜΟΣΘΕΝΟΥΣ ΠΑΙΑΝΙΕΑ ΧΡΥΣΩΙ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΩΙ ΑΡΕΤΗΣ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΚΑΙ ΕΥΝΟΙΑΣ, ΗΣ ΕΧΩΝ ΔΙΑΤΕΛΕΙ ΕΙΣ ΤΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΛΛΗΝΑΣ ΑΠΑΝΤΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΔΗΜΟΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΑΝΔΡΑΓΑΘΙΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΔΙΟΤΙ ΔΙΑΤΕΛΕΙ ΓΡΑΤΤΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΛΕΓΩΝ ΤΑ ΒΕΛΤΙΣΤΑ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ, ΚΑΙ ΓΡΟΘΥΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΙ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ Ο, ΤΙ ΑΝ ΔΥΝΗΤΑΙ ΑΓΑΘΟΝ ΓΑΝΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΨΕΥΔΗ ΓΡΑΨΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΑ ΤΩΝ ΝΟΜΩΝ ΟΥΚ ΕΩΝΤΩΝ ΓΡΩΤΟΝ ΜΕΝ ΨΕΥΔΕΙΣ ΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΑ ΚΑΤΑΒΑΛΛΕΣΘΑΙ. ΕΙΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΥΠΕΥΘΥΝΟΝ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΥΝ ΕΣΤΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΘΕΝΗΣ ΤΕΙΧΟΠΟΙΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΠΙ ΤΩΝ ΘΕΩΡΙΚΩΝ ΤΕΤΑΓΜΕΝΟΣ. ΕΤΙ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΑΝΑΓΟΡΕΥΕΙΝ ΤΟΝ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΝ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΘΕΑΤΡΩΙ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΙΟΙΣ ΤΡΑΓΩΙΔΩΝ ΤΗΙ ΚΑΙΝΗΙ. ΑΛΛ' ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ Η ΒΟΥΛΗ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΙ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΒΟΥΛΕΥΤΗΡΙΩΙ ΑΝΕΙΡΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ Η ΠΟΛΙΣ ΕΝ ΓΝΥΚΙ ΕΝ ΤΗΙ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΙ ΤΙΜΗΜΑ ΤΑΛΑΝΤΑ ΓΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΚΛΗΤΟΡΕΣ ΚΗΦΙΣΟΦΩΝ ΚΗΦΙΣΟΦΩΝΤΟΣ ΡΑΜΝΟΥΣΙΟΣ ΚΛΕΩΝ ΚΛΕΩΝΟΣ ΚΟΘΩΚΙΔΗΣ. En alterum exemplum apud Diogenem Laërtium in Socrate. ΤΑΔΕ ΕΓΡΑΨΑΤΟ ΚΑΙ ΑΝΘΩΜΟΛΟΓΗΣΑΤΟ ΜΕΛΙΤΟΣ ΜΕΛΙΤΟΥ ΓΙΤΘΕΥΣ ΣΩΚΡΑΤΕΙ ΣΩΦΡΟΝΙΣΚΟΥ ΑΛΩΠΕΚΗΘΕΝ ΑΔΙΚΕΙ ΣΩΚΡΑΤΗΣ, ΟΥΣ ΜΕΝ Η ΠΟΛΙΣ ΝΟΜΙΖΕΙ ΘΕΟΥΣ, ΟΥ ΝΟ-ΜΙΖΩΝ, ΕΤΕΡΑ ΔΕ ΚΑΙΝΑ ΔΑΙΜΟΝΙΑ ΕΙΣΗΓΟΥΜΕΝΟΣ. Α-ΔΙΚΕΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΝΕΟΥΣ ΔΙΑΦΘΕΙΡΩΝ ΤΙΜΗΜΑ ΘΑ-ΝΑΤΟΣ. Sed malim referibere, ΑΝΤΩΜΟΣΑΤΟ, αἰτὴ τὴν ΑΝΘΩΜΟΛΟΓΗΣΑΤΟ. nam est αἰτιμωσίας formula. Habes paullo ante ἡ δ' αἰτιμωσία τῆς δίκης τῆν [?] τὴν [?]. Tertium exemplum dabimus è Plutarcho in Alcibiade. ΘΕΣΣΑΛΟΣ ΚΙΜΩΝΟΣ ΛΑΚΙΑΔΗΣ ΑΛΚΙΒΙΑΔΗΝ ΚΛΕΙΝΙΟΥ ΣΚΑΜΒΩΝΙΔΗΝ ΕΙΣΗΓΓΕΙΛΕΝ ΑΔΙΚΕΙΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩ ΘΕΩ ΤΗΝ ΔΗΜΗΤΡΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΝ ΚΟΡΗΝ ΑΓΟΜΙΜΟΥΜΕΝΟΝ ΤΑ ΜΥΣΤΗΡΙΑ ΚΑΙ ΔΕΙΚΝΥΟΝΤΑ ΤΟΙΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΤΑΙΡΟΙΣ ΕΝ ΤΗ ΟΙΚΙΑ, ΤΗ ΕΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΧΟΝΤΑ ΣΤΟΛΗΝ, ΟΙΑΝ ΓΕΡ ΙΕΡΟΦΑΝΤΗΣ ΕΧΩΝ ΔΕΙΧΝΥΕΙ ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ ΚΑΙ ΟΝΟΜΑΖΟΝΤΑ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΜΕΝ ΙΕΡΟΦΑΝΤΗΝ, ΙΟΛΥΤΙΩΝΑ ΔΕ ΔΑΔΟΥΧΟΝ, ΚΗΡΥΚΑ ΔΕ ΘΕΟΔΩΡΟΝ ΦΥΓΕΕΑ. ΤΟΥΣ Δ' ΑΛΛΟΥΣ ΕΤΑΙΡΟΥΣ ΜΥΣΤΑΣ ΠΡΟΣΑΓΟΡΕΥΟΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΕΦΟΡΤΑΣ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΑ ΝΟΜΙΜΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΚΑΘΕΣΤΗΚΟΤΑ ΥΠΟ ΤΕ ΕΥΜΟΛΠΙΔΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΚΗΡΥΚΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΙΕΡΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΕΞ ΕΛΕΥΣΙΝΟΣ.
units.tr: Aeschines has the clerk read out the charge against the son of Timarchus. Knowing that he himself was liable, and having been a little older than ..., he was called to account before the jurors by the clerk's reading. You have an example of a charge in Demosthenes, against the son of Ctesiphon: "Indictment of Ctesiphon son of Leosthenes of Anaphlystus, brought in the archonship of Chaironides, in the month of Elaphebolion, by Aeschines son of Atrometus of Cothocidae, to the archon, for proposing an illegal decree: that it is right to crown Demosthenes son of Demosthenes of Paeania with a golden crown and to proclaim the crown in the theatre at the Great Dionysia, at the new tragedies, because he is good and benevolent to the people, and because he is zealous to do whatever is best for the people and writes and speaks what is best. Since these things are all falsely written and contrary to the laws, the indictment is brought for the false decree to be entered in the public records. Further, Demosthenes is the wall-builder and appointed overseer of the theoric fund, and the crown must not be proclaimed in the theatre at the new tragedies. If the Council agrees to crown him in the Council-chamber, let the people proclaim it in the theatre; but if the city, in the assembly, the people's crown of gold ... talents ..." Another example, from Diogenes Laertius in the case of Socrates: "This was written and sworn by Meletus son of Meletus of Pithus against Socrates son of Sophroniscus: Socrates is guilty, for he does not believe in the gods the city believes in, but introduces other new divinities; he is also guilty of corrupting the young. The penalty is death." But I would rather read ἀντωμόσατο here, "swore against," than ἀνθωμολογήσατο, because the formula is αἰτιμωσία (the formal claim of disgrace). You have a little earlier the phrase "the disgrace of the suit," ... Let me give a third example from Plutarch in the life of Alcibiades: Thessalus son of Cimon of Laciadae brought an indictment against Alcibiades son of Clinias of Scambonidae for impiety towards the goddess Demeter and Kore, for mocking the mysteries and showing them in his house to his companions, wearing his own robe; for the hierophant, when he displays the sacred things, is called hierophant, the torch-bearer is called Dadouchos, and the herald Theodorus of Phlya. He also brought other companions to initiation and the rites contrary to the lawful and established practice, under the direction of the Eumolpidae, the heralds, and the priests from Eleusis.

units.la: An vero ἀπογραφὴ rei legeretur, nobis non constat, neque certe opus fuit: satis enim liquebat Iudicibus, quae de reius esset dicendum, ex actoris dica. Veteri autem Lege Iudicum singuli tenebantur adnotare & scribere singula, si plura essent, accusationis capita.
units.tr: Whether the defendant's apographe (the written statement of the charge) was read aloud, we do not know for certain, nor was it really necessary: for it was clear enough to the judges what had to be said, from the plaintiff's charge. Under the old law, however, each of the judges was bound to note down and write out the separate heads of the accusation, if there were several.

units.la: Τοὺς κείνους γράφειν τὰ κεφάλαια ἕκαστον. Iudicum singuli actionis, de qua iudicium reddunt,diuersa Kapita in libello adnotanto.
units.tr: Each of the judges writes down the heads (kephalaia) of the matter. Each judge of the action on which they give judgment should note in his little book the separate heads.

units.la: Legem laudat è Boëtho Hesychius. ἐξ πρώτων κείτης. Βοήθος φησὶ ὁ τῆς Πλάτωνος, ὅτι ὁμομοιῆτης ... [?] τοὺς κείνους γράφειν τὰ κεφάλαια ἕκαστον. Vt scilicet iudicium reddere de omnibus possent, & ne qua memoria elaberentur: ita exempli gratia, Iudices illi, qui Socratem capitis damnauerunt, ex hac Lege singuli adnotauerant scripserantque in suum vsum kapita dicæ, quam Melitus Socrati impegerat, nimirum, ὅτι εἰς ἡ πόλις νομίζει θεούς, Σωκράτης δ' νομίζει ὅτι ἕτερα καινὰ δαιμόνια εἰσφέρει ὅτι τοὺς νέους διαφθείρει. Atque haec kapita adnotabantur è dica, quae ante iudicium, & aduersarias τ' ἀντιδίκων orationes apud iudices à Scriba recitabatur. Volebat autem Legislator hac ratione ire consultum Iudicibus, ne illis imponeretur, vel ab actore, vel à reo, & noua crimina, quorum non esset mentio ἐν τῇ γραφῇ, aut affingerentur, aut excusarentur. Debebant enim illi Iudicium reddere de iis tantum, quorum in dica accusabatur reus. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Στέφανον Ψευδομαρτυριῶν α. Δικαίως γὰρ ὁμοίως ὑμᾶς, οὐ [?] ὧν αὐτὸς φύγων ἀξιοῖ, ἀλλ' ἐκ[?] αὐτῶν, ὧν αὐτὸς ἡ [?] ἀξιώσῃ. Quanquam etiam litigatibus aut dicentibus non licebat ἔξω τῶν γραφῶν λέγειν, neq; à subscriptione & tabulis, quae actionis formulam continebant, recedere, aut latius diuagari, quae subscriptio ἀπογραφὴ dicebatur. Quod autem in Iudiciis criminalibus atque capitalibus obseruatum diximus, in ciuilibus quoque vsurpatum videtur.
units.tr: Hesychius quotes the law from Boethus: "From the first law. Boethus, the son of Plato, says that they are alike ... each of them shall write down the heads." So that the judges could give judgment on everything and nothing would slip from memory, for example: those judges who condemned Socrates to death had each, under this law, noted down and written for their own use the heads of the charge which Meletus had brought against Socrates: namely, that "he does not believe in the gods the city believes in, but introduces other new divinities; and that he corrupts the young." These heads were noted from the charge, which was read out before the judges by the clerk before the trial, together with the opposing speeches of the opponents. The lawgiver intended by this method to protect the judges, so that they should not be misled either by the plaintiff or by the defendant, and so that new charges, not mentioned in the indictment, should not be added or excused. For the judges had to give judgment only on those matters with which the defendant was charged in the indictment. Demosthenes, in his first speech against Stephanus on false witness: "For it is just that you judge not the things he himself wishes to escape, but of these things..." Although it was not permitted for litigants or speakers to speak outside the indictments, or to depart from the written statement and the tablets which contained the form of the action, or to range more widely: this written statement was called apographe. What we have said was observed in criminal and capital trials seems to have been used also in civil cases.

units.la: Adesse autem iubebantur litigantes, vt è Vespis Aristophanis palam fit: en tibi de Labete cane reo Bdelycleon.
units.tr: The litigants were ordered to be present, as is plain from Aristophanes' Wasps: here, for example, Bdelycleon speaks about Labes the dog.

units.la: χὴ μὲν ὁ φύγων ἐπὶ Λάβης πάρα.
units.tr: "The accused one is here, at Labes' side."

units.la: De actore Cane Cudatheno Philocleon quaerit, ubi sit: sed locus personis commode non est distinctus, ita editur.
units.tr: Philocleon asks where the Cydathenaean dog, the accuser, is; but the speakers are not properly distinguished in the printed text, so it stands as it is edited.

units.la: ΦΙ. ποῦ δ᾽ ἡ οὐ δώσων, ὁ Κυδαθηναιεὺς κύων;ΚΥ. αὖ, αὖ. ΒΔΕ. πρέσειν ἐπεσς [?] κακῶς, ἀρ᾽ ἔστιν ... λάλης,ἀγαθὸς γ᾽ ὑλακτεῖν καὶ ἀλεξίκακον [?] τὰς χύτρας.
units.tr: PHILOCLEON: Where is the Cydathenaean dog, who will not give...? DOG: Woof, woof. BDELYCLEON: ... badly ..., a good barker, and a warder-off of evil, the pots.

units.la: Canis Cudatheus latratu se hic adesse significat: itaque optime Scholiastes, αὖ, αὖ, ὁ κύων λέγει [?]. ἴσως ὅτι ὧδε εἰμί. μιμεῖται δὲ τῷ φωνῷ τῆς κυνὸς ἀμφί τῆς αὖ, αὖ. quod etiam Bdelycleon verbis his expressit: πρέσειν ἐπεσς [?]. Scholia: αὐτὴ τῆς ὁ κατηγορὸς. ὁ Βδελυκλέων δὲ φησι πρὸς τὸν Κυδαθηναῖα. ὅτι πρέσειν ὁ κατηγορὸς σου οὐ ὧδε. vbi rescribendum est ὁ Βδελυκλέων δὲ φησι πρὸς τὸν Λάκωνα. ὅτι πρέσειν ὁ κατηγορὸς σου, οὐ ὧδε. Sed distinguendum est, nam post ista Bdelycleonis πρέσειν ἐπεσς Canis. distingue & appone personam Canis Cudatheni latrantis, αὖ. cetera sunt Bdelycleonis, non quidem de Labete, sed de Cane Cudatheno: neque Λάκων nomen est Labetis proprium, sed verbum, rescribo.
units.tr: The Cydathenaean dog signals that he is present here by barking; the Scholiast rightly says: "Woof, woof, says the dog: perhaps because I am here." He imitates the dog's voice in the words "woof, woof," which Bdelycleon also expressed in these words: "... badly." The scholium reads: "The accuser himself. Bdelycleon says to the Cydathenaean: 'your accuser is not here.'" This should be corrected to read: "Bdelycleon says to the Laconian: 'your accuser is not here.'" But the punctuation must be changed: after Bdelycleon's words "...badly" the dog speaks; insert a mark and assign to the dog, barking, "woof." The rest belongs to Bdelycleon, not about Labes but about the Cydathenaean dog. Nor is "Laconian" a proper name for Labes, but a verb, so I emend it.

units.la: ΦΙ. ποῦ δ᾽ ἡ οὐ δώσων, ὁ Κυδαθηναιεὺς κύων;ΚΥ. αὖ, αὖ. ΒΔΕ. πρέσειν ἐπεσς [?] κακῶς. ΚΥ. αὖ. ΒΔΕ. λάλης;ἀγαθὸς γ᾽ ὑλακτεῖν καὶ ἀλεξίκακον [?] τὰς χύτρας.
units.tr: PHILOCLEON: Where is the Cydathenaean dog, the accuser? DOG: Woof, woof. BDELYCLEON: ... badly. DOG: Woof. BDELYCLEON: Chatterer? A good barker, and a warder-off of evil, the pots.

units.la: Cani Cudatheno factum nolebat Bdelycleon, itaque dicebat ad patrem, λάλης; attendistine?
units.tr: Bdelycleon did not want this done to the Cydathenaean dog, so he said to his father: "Chatterer? Are you listening?"

units.la: ἀγαθὸς γ᾽ ὑλακτεῖν καὶ ἀλεξίκακον [?] τὰς χύτρας.
units.tr: A good barker, and a warder-off of evil, the pots.

units.la: Latrare saltem & lingere ollas optimus.
units.tr: At least an excellent barker and a licker of pots.

units.la: nempe Canis Cudathenus, non autem Labes, cui impensè fauebat Bdelycleon.
