units.tr: Summoned to court before an Athenian magistrate on account of contracts which were not made in Athens at all, nor bring merchandise into Athens, he uses the exception of the forum.

units.la: Legis meminit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Φορμίωνα. οἱ μὲν οὖν νόμοι, καθ' εἰς ὑμῖς δικάσαι καθῆσθε, ἡ ὅπως λέγουσιν, ἀλλ' ΥΠΕΡ ΜΕΝ ΤΩΝ ΜΗ ΓΕΝΟ-ΜΕΝΩΝ ΟΛΩΣ ΣΥΜΒΟΛΑΙΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΗΣΙ, ΜΗΔ' ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΟΝ ΠΑΡΑΓΡΑΨΑΣΘΑΙ δίδωσιν. & in Argumento eiusdem: Παραγραφὴ ϛ', φησίν, ὁ νόμος δίδωσι τοῖς μὴ γεγονόσιν ὅλως Ἀθηναίοις, μηδὲ εἰς Ἀθηναῖς συμβολαίων. Neque enim propter hos contractus poterat adiri Magistratus, qui Iudices daret: si vero quis eo nomine apud illum in ius vocatus fuisset, exceptione hac fori vtetur: nam etiamsi ex aliena iurisdictione, vt loquitur Vlpianus Lib. V. ad Edictum, ad eum quis vocetur, debes venire Leg. V.D. de Iudiciis, quo saltem forum reuocari postulet. Hac ipsa Exceptione vti posse eos, qui accusantur alicuius criminis, de quo Leges silent, sentit Suidas, quia nempe Legibus cautum non est, quinam Magistratus adeundi sint, itaque nullius videtur esse τοῦτο ἡ δίκῃ εἰσάγειν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον. Suidae verba sunt, καὶ τὸ 'δὲ Παραγραφὴ, καὶ ἐπ' ἐκείνῃ τῇ δίκῃ, ἀλλ' ἡς οὐδὲν [?] ὠφέλει παραγραφὰς [?] τοῖς νόμοις, ὅτι ἔνεστιν αὐτῷ ὁ εἰσάγων ὥσπερ ἡ τὰς ἄλλας δίκας. [?] γὰρ ἄλλων δικῶν παρεγγυᾶν [?] ἐκάτω τὴν ὁ τὰς ἐφ' εἰσαγωγῆν τινα. παραγραφὰς οὖν ἐφῆται καὶ τοῖς ὑπὸ ὑπαγεμένοις, καὶ ὃ τ' ἀ γενομοθέτηται Quod tamen non est simpliciter accipiendum, καὶ ὧν οὐκ εἰσὶ νόμοι, nam ὁ νόμος ὁ εἰσαγωγικὸς contrarium plane probat: quanquam nec ipsa εἰσαγωγή ea est, καὶ ἡς οὖδὲν ὠφέλησαι τοῖς νόμοις, scriptus enim de ea est ὁ νόμος ὁ εἰσαγωγικὸς, sed intelligendum est, καὶ ὧν οἱ νόμοι ὑ συγχωρῆσθαι κείσθαι ἡμέσθαι. In exceptionibus autem prior causam orabat reus, qui exceptione vtebatur. Demosthenes ἐν ᾧ ἐν Σπιφάου ψευ-δομαρτυριῶν α. παραλαβὼν δὲ μὴ ὥστε παρέπεσον λέγειν δῆλο ὃ παραγραφὴ ἔστι, ἐκ μὴ ἐξ ἰδιαίας εἰσάγειν. nam agere etiam is videtur, inquit Vlpianus Lib. I V. ad Edictum, qui exceptione videtur: nam reus in exceptione actor est. Leg. I.D. de exceptionibus. Hunc Demosthenis locum interpretatur Lexicon Rhetoricum apud Auctorem Etymologici. Δυσδικία. ὅταν εἰσάγηταί τις κειμενοῦχος, καὶ ὧν μηδὲν τῷ γράφεσθαι ἡμέρᾳ δικαστηρίου, τὴν δυσδικίαν καλέσαι. καὶ ὧν γὰρ κεκελεῖσθαί τῆς φησί, καὶ ταύτην παραγεγραφέσθαι ἔφηται.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions the law in the speech against Phormio: "The laws, according to which you sit to judge, or however they put it, but in the case of contracts which were not made in Athens at all, nor into the Athenian market, they allow an objection to be lodged." And in the argument to the same speech: "The sixth objection, he says, the law gives to those who were not at all Athenians, nor to contracts into Athens." For on account of these contracts one could not approach the magistrate who appointed judges; but if someone had been summoned to court before him on that account, he would use this exception of the forum: for even if the case is from another jurisdiction, as Ulpian says in Book V on the Edict, one ought to come to the one to whom one is summoned, Digest 5, On judicial matters, at least he may ask that the forum be recalled. Suidas holds that those who are accused of some crime, about which the laws are silent, may use this very exception, because indeed it is not provided by the laws which magistrates are to be approached, and so it seems to belong to no one to bring this case before that court. Suidas's words are: "And paragraphe is also in that action, but for which none of the laws provides an objection, because the one who brings it is in the same position as in other actions. For the lodging of other suits is open to each, as for an eisagoge of some kind. Therefore objections are also allowed to those who are not under the laws, and whatever is not established by law." This, however, is not to be taken simply, and "for which there are no laws"; for the eisagogic law plainly proves the contrary: although the eisagoge itself is not one of those things for which the laws provide nothing, since the eisagogic law was written about it, but it must be understood as "for which the laws have not provided at all." In exceptions, however, the defendant who uses the exception pleads the first case. Demosthenes, in the speech against Spudias on false witness: "Taking up the case, he undertakes to say that it is a paragraphe, as if he were not bringing it by an accusation." For he also seems to act, says Ulpian in Book IV on the Edict, who seems to be using an exception: for in an exception the defendant is the plaintiff, Digest 1, On exceptions. The Rhetorical Lexicon, cited by the author of the Etymologicum, explains this passage of Demosthenes: "Dysdikia: when someone is brought forward under a written charge, and nothing is set down for the day of the court, they call it dysdikia. For he says that it has been announced, and that it is also objected to by paragraphe."

units.la: DE ARBITRIS.
units.tr: ON ARBITRATORS.

units.la: TITVLVS QVINTVS.
units.tr: TITLE FIVE.

units.la: CVM compromissum, vt legitur apud Paulum Lib. II. ad edictum, ad similitudinem iudiciorum redigatur, & ad finiendas lites pertineat, Leg. I. D. de receptu arbitris, Arbitrorum sententiae standum est, nec appellandum, vt hac Lege cauetur.
units.tr: Since a compromise, as is read in Paul, Book II on the Edict, is brought into the likeness of judgments and tends to end lawsuits (Law I, D. de receptis arbitris), the sentence of the arbitrators is to be upheld and not appealed, as this law provides.

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΣΥΜΒΟΛΑΙΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΥΣ ΑΜΦΙΣΒΗΤΩ-ΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ ΕΛΕΣΘΑΙ ΟΝΤΙΝΟΥΝ, ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΑΥΤΟΙΣ ΑΙΡΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΟΝ ΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ, ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ, ΚΑΤΑ ΚΟΙΝΟΝ ΜΕΝΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΓΝΩΣΘΕΙΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΜΗΚΕΤΙ ΚΑΤΑΦΕΡΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ ΕΦ' ΕΤΕΡΟΝ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΕΓΚΛΗΜΑΤΑ, ΑΛΛ' ΕΣΤΩ ΤΑ ΚΡΙΘΕΝΤΑ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΑ.
units.tr: "If certain men dispute with one another about their private agreements, and they wish to submit the matter to an arbitrator, let them be permitted to choose whomever they wish as arbitrator. Since they have wished it, let them abide by the decision of those who have been appointed, and let them no longer bring these charges before another court, but let the judgment of the arbitrator stand as valid." [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΣΥΜΒΟΛΑΙΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΥΣ ΑΜΦΙΣΒΗΤΩΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ ΕΛΕΣΘΑΙ ΟΝΤΙΝΟΥΝ, ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΑΥΤΟΙΣ ΑΙΡΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΟΝ ΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ, ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ, ΚΑΤΑ ΚΟΙΝΟΝ ΜΕΝΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΓΝΩΣΘΕΙΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΜΗΚΕΤΙ ΚΑΤΑΦΕΡΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ ΕΦ' ΕΤΕΡΟΝ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΕΓΚΛΗΜΑΤΑ, ΑΛΛ' ΕΣΤΩ ΤΑ ΚΡΙΘΕΝΤΑ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΑ.]

units.la: Si litigatores de priuatis contractibus in aliquem arbitrum compromittere voluerint, in quemcumque libuerit, compromittunto. Arbitri compromissi sententia stanto, nec ad aliud Iudicium eunto. Sed Arbitri compromissi sententia rata esto.
units.tr: If litigants wish to submit private contracts to some arbitrator, let them submit them to whomever they please. Let the sentence of the compromised arbitrator stand, and let them not go to any other court. But let the sentence of the compromised arbitrator be ratified.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes in Midiana, eamque describit: λέγει δὲ καὶ [?] τὴν τῆς Διαιτητῆς [?] λόγον. EAN ΔE TINES, &c. Arbitri alij sunt forte dati, alij compromissi. Harpocration, quem descripsit Suidas. οἱ ὁ Διαιτητὴς κλήρῳ παρεχόντες [illegible, ~20 letters] τῶν κεκ[?] ἀλλ[?] ληψεῖς. De compromissis Arbitris agitur hac Lege, quod liquet ex his eius verbis. ΚΑΙ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ ΕΛΕΣΘΑΙ ΟΝΤΙΝΟΥΝ. Compromitti autem poterat a litigatoribus in quemcumque illis libuisset: ΚΑΙ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ ΕΛΕΣΘΑΙ ΟΝΤΙΝΟΥΝ, ΕΞΕΣΘΩ ΑΥΤΟΙΣ ΑΙΡΕΙΣΘΑΙ, ΟΝ ΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ. Apud Vlpianum Lib. XIII. ad Edictum, Pedius libro nono, & Pomponius libro trigesimo tertio scribunt, parui referre: ingenuus quis, an libertinus sit, integra famae qui sit arbiter, an ignominiosus. In seruum Labeo compromissi non posse libro vndecimo scribit: & est verum. Leg. VII. D. de receptis Arbitris. Cognoscebant hi compromissi Arbitri de priuatis contractibus. Lex ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΝΕΣ ΠΕΡΙ ΣΥΜΒΟΛΑΙΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΥΣ ΑΜΦΙΣΒΗΤΩΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ ΕΛΕΣΘΑΙ ΟΝΤΙΝΟΥΝ, ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΑΥΤΟΙΣ ΑΙΡΕΙΣΘΑΙ ΟΝ ΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ. Ab his compromissis Arbitris Iudices non appellabantur, sed Arbitrorum sententiae standum erat, vt cauetur hac Lege. ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ, ΚΑΤΑ ΚΟΙΝΟΝ ΜΕΝΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΓΝΩΣΘΕΙΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΜΗΚΕΤΙ ΚΑΤΑΦΕΡΕΤΩΣΑΝ ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in the Midiana and describes it, saying also [?] the word of the arbitrator [?]: "If men..." [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΝΕΣ, &c.]. Arbitrators were perhaps some given, others compromised. Harpocration, whom Suidas copied: those who furnish the arbitrator by lot [...]. This law treats of compromised arbitrators, as is clear from his words: "and they wish to submit to an arbitrator whomever they wish." Litigants could submit to whomever it pleased them: "and they wish to submit to an arbitrator whomever they wish, let it be permitted to them to choose whomever they wish as arbitrator." In Ulpian, Book XIII on the Edict: Pedius in book nine and Pomponius in book thirty-three write that it matters little whether a man is freeborn or a freedman, whether the arbiter is of unimpaired reputation or disgraced. Labeo in book eleven writes that a slave cannot be submitted to compromise, and this is true. (Law VII, D. de receptis arbitris.) These compromised arbitrators took cognizance of private contracts. The law: "If certain men dispute with one another about their private agreements, and they wish to submit the matter to an arbitrator, let them be permitted to choose whomever they wish..." From these compromised arbitrators, judges were not appealed to, but the sentence of the arbitrators had to be stood by, as this law provides: "Since they wish it, let them abide by the decision made among themselves, and let them no longer bring these charges before another court, but let the judgment of the arbitrator stand."

units.la: ΕΦ' ΕΤΕΡΟΝ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΕΓΚΛΗΜΑΤΑ, ΑΛΛ' ΕΣΤΩ ΤΑ ΚΡΙΘΕΝΤΑ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΑ. Lucianus Abdicato.
units.tr: "...before another court; but let the judgments made by the arbitrator be binding." Lucian, Abdicatus.

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters] Quare stari debet, inquit Vlpianus Libro XIII. ad Edictum, sententiae arbitri, quam de re dixerit: siue aequa, siue iniqua sit: & sibi imputet, qui compromisit. Nam & Diui Pij rescripto adiicitur: Vel minus probabilem sententiam aequo animo ferre debet Leg. XXVII. §. II. D. de receptis arbitris. Quod & Antoninus Imperator Nepotiano rescripsit in haec verba. Ex sententia arbitri ex compromisso iure perfecto aditi, appellari non posse, saepe rescriptum est. Leg. I. C. eod.
units.tr: [...] "Therefore, says Ulpian in Book XIII on the Edict, the sentence of the arbitrator, which he has pronounced on the matter, must be stood by, whether it be fair or unfair, and the one who submitted the matter must blame himself. For it is also added in a rescript of the divine Pius: he ought to bear with equanimity a sentence that is less probable." (Law XXVII, §II, D. de receptis arbitris.) Antoninus Imperator also wrote to Nepotianus in these words: It has often been rescinded that an appeal cannot be made from the sentence of an arbiter who has been approached under a compromise made in accordance with law. (Law I, C. eod.)

units.la: Erant alij Arbitri forte capti, quos [illegible, ~12 letters] Diaitetas dixit, Demosthenes: hi sortito dabantur è singulis tribubus, (exagenariis non minores, integri vitae, scelerisque puri: erantque numero quatuor & quadraginta è singulis Tribubus, siue in vniuersum quadringenti quadraginta. Vlpianus in Midianam: [illegible, ~40 letters] Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. X. [illegible, ~60 letters] Suidas: [illegible, ~50 letters] Optime dixit [illegible, ~12 letters]. Nam peregrinis non dabatur apud Arbitros disceptare, vt sequitur ibidem, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Sorte autem illis distribuebantur lites, de quibus sententiam dicerent Arbitri. Pollux verbis iam laudatis. [illegible, ~25 letters] Arbiter autem qui nollet sententiam dicere de controuersia, quae sortito illi obtigerat dirimenda, ignominiosus erat.
units.tr: There were also other arbitrators chosen by lot, whom Demosthenes called Diaitetas. These were given by lot from each tribe, not under sixty years of age, of upright life and pure of crime; there were forty-four from each tribe, or four hundred and forty in all. Ulpian on the Midiana: [...] Pollux, Book VIII, chap. X [...] Suidas: [...] He spoke very well [...], for foreigners were not allowed to plead before arbitrators, as follows in the same place [...]. Cases were distributed to them by lot, on which the arbitrators were to pronounce sentence. Pollux in the words already quoted [...]. An arbiter who refused to pronounce sentence on the controversy that had fallen to him by lot to settle was dishonoured.

units.la: Pollux loco laudato. [illegible, ~50 letters] Atque hi olim de omnibus controuersiis pronunciabant Pollux, [illegible, ~45 letters]. Si nempe rei, qua de disceptabatur, aestimatio esset [illegible, ~20 letters], maior drachmis decem. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. [illegible, ~70 letters] Id intelligit Phauorinus his verbis: [illegible, ~45 letters]. Itaque iudicabant de furto, nullo actoris periculo. Demosthenes in Androtiona. [illegible, ~25 letters]. Sed omnes controuersias non diiudicasse argumento est, quod exceptione fori liceat uti aduersus Arbitros, quasi illorum non sit hanc controuersiam diiudicare. Vlpianus ad Midianam. [illegible, ~60 letters] ΟΥ ΠΡΟΣ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ ΜΕ ΚΡΙΝΕΣΘΑΙ ΔΕΙ, ΑΛΛΑ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΑ Η ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΗΝ. Iurati autem sententiam dicebant Arbitri ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Pollux in the place cited [...]. And these once pronounced on all controversies, Pollux [...], namely if the estimate of the matter in dispute were [...] greater than ten drachmas. Pollux, Book VIII, chap. IX [...] Phavorinus understands this in these words [...]. Accordingly they judged about theft with no risk to the plaintiff. Demosthenes against Androtion [...]. But that they did not decide all controversies is shown by the fact that an exception of forum may be used against arbitrators, as if it were not theirs to decide this controversy. Ulpian on the Midiana: [...] "One must not be judged before an arbitrator, but before an archon or thesmothete." [ΟΥ ΠΡΟΣ ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΗΝ ΜΕ ΚΡΙΝΕΣΘΑΙ ΔΕΙ, ΑΛΛΑ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΑ Η ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΗΝ.] Sworn arbitrators then pronounced sentence under this law:

units.la: Τὸν Διαιτητὴν ὀμόσαντα Διαιτητήν. Arbitri Iurati sententiam dicunto.
units.tr: "The arbitrator, having sworn as arbitrator." [Τὸν Διαιτητὴν ὀμόσαντα Διαιτητήν.] Let the sworn arbitrators pronounce sentence.

units.la: Meminit Legis Demosthenes [illegible, ~4 letters] Ἀθηναίων. Quomodo etiam compromissi Arbitri iurati pronunciabant, vt est in Rescripto Iustiniani Imperatoris ad Demosthenem P P. Si igitur inter actorem & reum, nec non ipsum Iudicem fuerit consensum, vt cum sacramenti religione ls[?] procedat, & ipsi quidem litigatores in scriptis hoc suis manibus, vel per publicas personas scripserint, vel apud ipsum arbitrum in actis propria voce deposuerint, quod sacramentis praestitis arbiter electus est, hoc etiam addito, quod & ipse arbiter iuramentum praestiterit super lite cum omni veritate dirimenda, eius definitionem validam omnimodo custodiri censemus, & neque reum, neque actorem posse discedere, sed tenere omnifariam, quatenus obedire ei compellantur. Leg. IV. C. de receptis Arbitris. Arbitris Sol occasus suprema erat tempestas: quare si is, qui fugiebat, arbitrio se non sisterat ad hanc horam, Arbiter praesenti tunc litem addicebat secundum hanc Legem.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions the law [...] of the Athenians [Ἀθηναίων]. In the same way compromised arbitrators who had been sworn pronounced sentence, as is in the rescript of the Emperor Justinian to Demosthenes, Praefect: If therefore there has been agreement between plaintiff and defendant, and also the judge himself, that the case proceed under the sanction of an oath, and the litigants themselves have written this in their own hands, or through public persons, or have deposed it in the acts before the arbiter himself in their own voice, that the arbiter has been chosen with the oaths sworn, and this being added, that the arbiter himself also took an oath to settle the suit with all truth, we judge that his definition is to be kept valid in every way, and that neither defendant nor plaintiff may withdraw, but both are to be held to it in every respect, insofar as they are compelled to obey him. (Law IV, C. de receptis arbitris.) For the arbitrators the setting of the sun was the final limit; therefore if the one who had fled did not present himself before the arbiter by this hour, the arbiter then adjudged the case to the one present, according to this law.

units.la: Τὸν Διαιτητὴν μὴν ἄχει τῆς ἑαυτῆς, μὴ φανέντος δὲ τῆς φύλης, καταδικάζειν τῷ καταδικάζοντι. Arbitri ad Solem occasum sedento: si reus non adfit, tunc praesenti actori litem addicunt.
units.tr: "Let the arbitrator sit until sunset; if the other party does not appear, let him pronounce against the one who is absent." [Τὸν Διαιτητὴν μὴν ἄχει τῆς ἑαυτῆς, μὴ φανέντος δὲ τῆς φύλης, καταδικάζειν τῷ καταδικάζοντι.] Let the arbitrators sit until sunset; if the defendant is not present, then they award the case to the plaintiff who is present.

units.la: Legem laudat Vlpianus Demosthenis Interpres ad hæc[?] verba: is è Midiana ver-ba. Καὶ τὸν τῆς Διαιτητῆς αὐτοῦ νόμον.] ὅτι μὲν ἀγεῖ τῆς ἐξ ἑτέρας ὀφείλει Διαιτητὴς· μὴ φανέντος δὲ τῆς φύλης, καταδικάζειν, ὡς ὁ νόμος βούλεται, καταδίκω. Hinc Demosthenes hac ipsa Oratione. οὐποτ' ἄρα ἡμῖν ὁ Σπέαπων, ὅτι ποτ' ἦσαν ἡ χωρία, πόσ' αὐτ' ἤδη διεξελαλήσῃ τὰ ἐκ τῶν νόμων, ὑπὸ ωμοσίας, καὶ ἀξ-ἀμφοτέρας· κ[?] ἐπὶ τ[?] καταλειπων. Vlpianus ad hæc verba: τῆς δὲ ὥρας ἐγίγνετο ὀψέ.] Τοῦτ' οὖν δικαίως ὥρα τῆς Διαιτητῆς παρελαβεῖ. Idem Demosthenes in Timocr. ὁ Διαιτητὴς ἡ καταδικαζόντων, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ ὥρας ἀπαλλαττόμενος τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ, ἐαυτῷ ἤδη ὕστις. Arbitrorum sententiae subscribebant Archontes. Vlpianus ad Midianam. ἐὰν γὰρ τῶν Διαιτητῶν δίκας ἐνάτῳ ἀφαιρέσει τῶν Ἀρχόντων. Quare ab iis arbitrium Stratonis inducit postulat Midias apud Demosthenem: ἐὰν δὲ ἐαυτοῖς οὕτως καὶ οἴκοις, ἔρχεται Μιδίας ὑπὸ πάσης ὁ τῶν Ἀρχόντων οἴκημα, καὶ καταλαμβάνει τοὺς Ἀρχόντας ἐξιόντας, καὶ τὸν Σπέατωνα ἀπιόντα ἤδη, τῶν ἑρμῶν δεδικόπε, ὡς ἐγὼ τῶν ἀποξηρομένων ἑνὸς ἐπιωδανόμην. Ὃ μὲν οὖν ἐπὶ τὸ δικαστήριον ἐπὶ πίστει αὐτὸν τῶν Διαιτῶν, ὥς καταλαβόντος ἐκεῖ, ἐπὶ Διαιτητὴν ἀφεθῆναι. Reddebantur autem ab Arbitris iudicia in locis publicis. Demosthenes τῷ Σπεφάνου ἐνδημέροντες ἐνδεὶ α. ἐγίνετο δὲ ἐν διαγεῖς ἐν τῇ ποικίλῃ στοᾷ. & in locis sacris. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ τῷ Νεαίρας, de Arbitris Phrynionis & Stephani. συνελθόντες δὲ οὗτοι ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ. Quinetiam singulis Tribubus assignata videntur fuisse loca, in quibus, eas ἑξαιρεῖ, sederent. Demosthenes τῷ ΕΥέρ-γου καὶ Μνησιβούλου. Ἐ μὲν γὰρ διαμε, ἐν τῇ Ἡλιαία ὡς· οἱ γὰρ τῶν Αἰνιῶν καὶ τῶν ΕΥεξίδα ἑξαιρεῖ, ἐκλεγόντων. Accipiebant Arbitri ab actore drachmam, quam ἀλφάσιον nominant, cum aduersarij nomen deferret apud illos, atque litem æstimaret: drachmam quoque accipiebant ab aduersario ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀντιμοσίας, cum de calumnia iuraret. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. X. ἐχρημάτισαν δὲ οἱ Διαιτηταὶ δραχμὴν ἀπὸ τὸ κεῖνο, τῶν καλουμένων ἀλφάσιον, ἡγεμόνας ἐκ γεμματικῷ ὁ ἕκλημα, καὶ ὁ ἡμυ-μα. ἐχρημάτισαν δὲ καὶ ἐπι[?]ἐχειν τῆς ἀντωμοσίας. Dixerunt quoque hanc ab actore datam drachmam ἀπόδοσιν. Pollux eod. Lib. cap. VI. ἡ ἀπόδοσις δραχμὴ ἦν, ὡ ὁ Διαιτητὴς ἀπολαμβάνειν ἔφερεν. Grammatici è Demetrio Phalereo: Δημήτριος ὁ Φαληρεὺς ἐν τοῖς περὶ νομοθεσίας, τοὺς Διαιτητὰς φησὶ λαμβάνειν τὰς δραχμάς, μίαν μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς λέξεως, ὡ ἀπόδοσιν ἐκάλουν. ἐπεχειρ ἢ ἐχ' ἀπωμοσίας ἐκάλουν. Vbi malim κατ' ἀπωμοσίαν ἐκάλουν. Ab his Arbitris ad Iudices Lege dabatur prouocatio.
units.tr: Ulpian, the interpreter of Demosthenes, cites the law at these words, from the Midiana: "And the law of his arbitrator" [...] "that the arbitrator ought to give the sentence on the basis of the other party; but if the one who has fled does not appear, let him rule against him, as the law wishes." Hence Demosthenes in this same oration: "Never, then, did Spephanus [...] tell us what the places were, how much they then recounted from the laws, under oath, and both parties..." Ulpian on these words: "and the hour was growing late": "Therefore rightly the arbitrator received the hour." The same Demosthenes in Timocrates: the arbitrator did not condemn, but withdrew from the hour of his own accord. Sentences of the arbitrators were subscribed by the archons. Ulpian on the Midiana: "for if an arbitrator's cases are taken away by the archons' decree..." Therefore Midias, in Demosthenes, seeks to draw the arbitration of Stratos from them: "but if they go to their houses, Midias comes to the building of the archons, and catches the archons as they come out, and Stratos already leaving, having struck the herms, as I have heard from one of those who were present..." Then he was brought before the court with a pledge, and as he had been seized there, he was released to the arbitrator. Judgments were given by the arbitrators in public places: Demosthenes [...] it was held in the Painted Stoa. And in sacred places: Demosthenes, about the arbitrators of Phrynion and Stephanus: "and these gathered in the temple." Indeed, places seem to have been assigned to each tribe, in which they sat to hear cases. Demosthenes, about Euergus and Mnesiboulos. For the arbitrators sat in the Heliaia [...]. The arbitrators received from the plaintiff a drachma, which they call alphasion, when the name of the opponent was brought before them and they assessed the suit; they also received a drachma from the opponent for the counter-oath, when he swore concerning calumny. Pollux, Book VIII, chap. X: "The arbitrators took a drachma from each side, which is called alphasion, a payment for the case [...], and they also took a payment for the counter-oath." They also called the drachma given by the plaintiff the apodosis. Pollux, ibid., chap. VI: "The apodosis was a drachma which the arbitrator was accustomed to receive." Grammarians cite Demetrius of Phalerum: Demetrius of Phalerum, in his writings on legislation, says that the arbitrators received drachmas, one from the plaintiff, which they called apodosis, and another from the defendant, which they called [...] of the counter-oath. Where I would prefer "they called it according to the counter-oath." From these arbitrators an appeal to the judges was given by law.

units.la: Ἀπὸ τῶν χληρωτῶν Διαιτητῶν ἐς ἐπέγειν ἐφίσ- Ab Arbitris sortito datis ad Iudices prouocanto. ναι δικαστήριον.
units.tr: From arbitrators chosen by lot, an appeal lies to a court of judges. [Ἀπὸ τῶν κληρωτῶν Διαιτητῶν ἐς ἐφέσιν ἐφίστασθαι δικαστήριον.]

units.la: De his intelligenda omnino est haec Lex apud Lucianum Abdicato, vt ex antithesi Arbitrorum compromissorum constat. ὅρᾶτε γὰρ πού ἡ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις δικαστηρίοις, ὡς ἀπὸ μὲν τῆς κλήρου λαχόντων δικαστῶν, ἐὰν ὡς ἀδικον εἶπαι γεγραμμένην τὴν κεῖσιν, δίδωσιν ὁ νόμος ἐς ἐπέγειν ἐφίναι δικαστήριον. ἐὰν δὲ ἴδιαι ἐκόντες ἐπὶ σώζων- ται δικαστὰς, ἡ αἰρεθέλομαι ὑπεπέλωσι ὀξιπᾶν, οὐκ ἐπί. Habes exemplum apud Demosthenem: hinc Argumentum Orationis eius πρὸς Καλλίππου. αὐτὸς Ἀπολλοδώρου λαξιφὶς δίκῳ τὸ ἀργυρείου Καλλίππου, ἡ ἠξίου πάλιν ὑπεπέλλαι τῶν Λεπτίνου. ὁ ἡ Ἀπολλόδωρος τὸν μὲν Διαιτητὴν ἐδίξατο· πρὸς ἡ τ' ἀρχαῖῳ ἔ νόμου, Λυκοῦργος ἀπελεῖξαι, ἵν', ὡς φησι, ὁμόσας δικάσῃ, ἡ μὴ χωρεῖς ὅρκου ὀξιπέλο τῶν Καλλίππῳ χαρίσηται. ὁ ἡ Λεπτίνης αὐτὸς ἀπορίατο, ἀπεφήνατο, ἐ κατεδήλησε τὴν δίκῃ, ὀξὼ ἔφεσιν δοὺς ὁ Ἀπολλόδωρος, εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον εἰσήρχεσι. At vero Arbitri τὰ ἀσφαλί- σματα, id est, litis instrumenta in echino reponebant & obsignabant, ne qua possent subripi, donec resignarentur apud Iudices. Harpocration, ad cuius exemplum emendandus Suidas. εἰσὶ ἡ οἱ Διαιτηταὶ, ἐπειγοι τῶν δικαστῶν· ὅτι μὲν ἡ ἐν δικαστηρίοις ἐδίκαζον ἀποδεδομένοις, ἡ τὰς ἀπὸ τῶν Διαιτητῶν ἐφεσίμεις ἐκείνον. & paullo post. καὶ ἡ μὲν ἥρεσκε τῆς αὐτὰ δίκαις τίλος εἶχεν ἡ δίκη, εἰ ἡ μὴ, τὰ ἐγ- χλήματα, ἡ τὰς μαρτυρίας, ἐπὶ ἡ ἐν τοῖς νόμοις, ἡ τὰς ἄλλας πί- στεις ἑκατέρων ἐμβαλόντες εἰς καδίσκους, ἡ σημειώμενοι, πρεδίδοσθ τοῖς εἰσαγωγεῦσι τῆς δίκης. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. X. ἡ ἡ ἔφεσις Διαιτητῶν εἰ εἰς δικαστήριον ἐχήχειο, εἰς ἐχῖνον τὰς ψήφους ἐμβαλόντες ἰδία ἑκατέρας τῆ φιλίαις ἡ διώκοντος κατεσημαίνε- το. Aristophanis Interpres ad Vespas. ἐχῖνος. ἄγλος ἡ χαλκῶ, ἡ καὶ ἐκ κεραμὸς, εἰς ὁ καθιᾶσιν οἱ Διαιτηταὶ τὰ γραμματεῖα τῆς μαρτυρίαν, ἃ τινες ἐμμαρτύρησαν, καὶ καταφεμηνάθμοι μὴ ταῦτα, εἰ ἐγκληθὴν ἡ δίαιτα, τοῖς δικαστὰς ἐπεδίδωσιν. Suidas: ἔξεσι ἡ καὶ τοῖς μεμφομένοις ἡξιῶσι, ἐκκαλεῖσθαι ὁ δημόσιον δικαστήριον. Quin etiam aliquando ipsi Arbitri litigantes ad Iudices ire iubebant. Hesychius: Διαιτηταὶ Ἀθηναῖοι ἐπεγοί τινες τῶν δικαστῶν, οἱς ἐπέτρεπον οἱ ἀμφισβητοῦντες τὰ ἐγ- κλήματα, καὶ αὐτοὶ δίκαιοι, εἰ δὲ μὴ, αἰτεῖσθαι ἵνα τοὺς δικαστὰς. Quod si quis Arbitrum vel gratiæ dantem, vel sordibus corruptum, aduersario litem addixisse accusaret, atque apud Iudices probaret, Arbiter notabatur infamia. Grammatici: ἄλλη ἡ εἰσαγωγὴ ὅτι τῆ Διαιτητῆ. εἰ γὰρ τῆς ὑπὸ τῆ Διαιτητῆ ἀδικηθῇ, ἐξὼ τὴν εἰσαγγελίαν ἐποίει τοῖς δικασταῖς, ἐ ἄλλοις, ἡμόσ.. Praeterea rationes suas referebant Arbitri affecto anno apud Logistas mense vndecimo, conuicti pronunciasse aut gratiæ dantes, aut sordibus corrupti, notabantur infamia. Demosthenes in Midiana: βουλόμενος ἡ ὁ μόγον λαβεῖν, φυλάξας τὴν πελταϊάν ἡμέρᾳ τῆ Διαιτητῆ, ἡ τῷ Θαργηλιῶνος ἡ τῷ Χειρροφοιείωνος γεγονότων, εἰς ὧ ὁ μὲν ἦλθε τῆς Διαιτητῆ, ὁ δὲ οὐκ ἦλθε, πίσας τὸν φυτημιόντα δοὺς ἡ ψῆφον τῶν πάντας τοὺς νόμους, κλητεῖα ὑπ' ὀνίνων ὑπηγγελμένος, κατηγόρων ἐ[illegible, ~45 letters]
units.tr: This law must be understood entirely in the sense in which it appears in Lucian's Abdicatus, as is clear from the contrast with arbitrators chosen by agreement. For you see that in the other courts, where the judges were allotted by lot, if a party says that the verdict was unjust, the law allows an appeal to a court. But if the parties have chosen their judges voluntarily and agreed to abide by their decision, no appeal is allowed [ὅρᾶτε γὰρ ... οὐκ ἐπί]. You have an example in Demosthenes, and hence the argument of his speech against Callippus. Apollodorus himself had brought a suit against Callippus over money and asked to appeal again from Leptines' decision. Apollodorus accepted the arbitrator, and against the ancient law Lycurgus, as he says, ... so that, having sworn, the arbitrator might judge, or, if he did not wish to swear, that Callippus might be granted the oath [ἀπελεῖξαι ... χαρίσηται]. Leptines himself was at a loss, gave his decision, and did not settle the case; Apollodorus gave notice of appeal, and they entered the court [ἀπορίατο ... εἰσήρχεσι]. But the arbitrators kept and sealed the instruments of the suit, that is, the written proofs of the case, in an echinus, so that none could be stolen, until they were unsealed before the judges. Harpocration, on whose example Suidas should be corrected, says: arbitrators were a kind of inferior judges; in the courts where cases were decided were the appeals from the arbitrators heard [εἰσὶ ἡ οἱ Διαιτηταὶ ... ἐκείνον]. A little later he adds: if the case had a final ending in the same matters, but otherwise the accusations, or the testimonies, or the other proofs of each side, having been placed in the urns and marked, were handed over to those who introduced the case [καὶ ἡ μὲν ... τῆς δίκης]. Pollux, book VIII, chapter X: if an appeal from arbitrators came to court, the votes were put into the echinus and each was sealed separately by the party or the prosecutor [ἡ ἡ ἔφεσις ... κατεσημαίνετο]. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Wasps: the echinus is a vessel of bronze or of earthenware into which the arbitrators put the written testimonies that some had given, and which were sealed, and these were handed to the judges if the case was challenged [ἐχῖνος ... ἐπεδίδωσιν]. Suidas: it was also permitted to those who found fault to appeal to the public court [ἔξεσι ... δικαστήριον]. Indeed, sometimes the arbitrators themselves ordered the litigants to go to the judges. Hesychius: Athenian arbitrators were certain inferior judges, to whom the disputing parties entrusted their accusations, and who themselves judged; otherwise they demanded judges [Διαιτηταὶ Ἀθηναῖοι ... τοὺς δικαστάς]. If anyone accused an arbitrator of either showing favour or being corrupted by bribes, and proved before the judges that he had decided the case for the adversary, the arbitrator was branded with infamy. The grammarians: there was another introduction of a case against the arbitrator; for if someone was wronged by the arbitrator, he made an accusation before the judges [ἄλλη ἡ εἰσαγωγὴ ... ἡμόσ]. Besides, the arbitrators, at the end of their year, rendered their accounts before the Logistae in the eleventh month; if they were convicted of having pronounced in favour of one side or of being corrupted by bribes, they were branded with infamy. Demosthenes in the Midiana: wishing to take only a bribe, having watched for the day of the arbitrator, and when the Thargelion or the Scirrhophorion came round, on which day the one came to the arbitrator and the other did not come, ... having been summoned by the witnesses, he accused [βουλόμενος ... κατηγόρων [illegible]].

units.la: DE IUREIURANDO.
units.tr: ON THE OATH.

units.la: TITULUS SEXTUS.
units.tr: TITLE SIX.

units.la: MAXIMUM remedium, ut loquitur Gaius Lib. V. ad Edictum Provinciale, expediendarum litium in usum venit Iurisiurandi religio, quia ex pactione ipsorum litigatorum decidantur controversia. Leg. I. D. de iureiurando. Deferebat iusiurandum litigantium alter alteri, eoque praestito controuersiæ decidebantur. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Τιμόθεον [?] βούλομαι ὑμῖν [?], ᾧ ἄνδρες [?], ὅτι ἐπὶ τῆς ἀντωμοσίας [?] μου ὅρκον εἰς τὸν ἐχῖνον [?], ἥξει καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπ' ὀμνύειν ἀπολλάσθαι. ἐγὼ δὲ εἰ μὲν μὴ ἐξεφανῶς αὐτὸν ἡδέως ἐπολλοῖς καὶ μεγάλης ὅρκοις ἐπιωρκηκότα, καὶ πολεμίῳ, καὶ ἰδιώτῃ [?], ἐδωκα ἀν αὐτῷ τόνδε τὸν ὅρκον. νῦν δὲ μὴ δοκεῖ μάρτυρων μὲν ὄντων ἐμοὶ ὡς ἐλάβον ὃ ἀρχὼν [?] ἐπὶ τῆς τεταρτῆς [?], εἰς ἐπὶ ἐκέλευσεν δωσαι, ἐξεφανῶς δὲ τεκμήριον, ὃ πόνον ἐξ, τὸν ὅρκον δωσαι ἐμοῦ [?]. Nam quando prouocatione aduersariorum deferebatur iusiurandum, pactione caucebatur litem iri decisum hoc iureiurando. Argumentum Orationis Demosthenicæ πρὸς Βοιωτὸν περὶ τῆς ὀνόματος. ἐπειτα ἀναλαμβάνεις παῖδας αἰσχυνθεὶς ἀπὸ ἰδίας πρὸς ἐκλήσεως, ὡς ἀπατηθεὶς ἐπιθυμοῦντο. γεύκαλέσατο [?] μὲν γὰρ τῷ Γλαύκωνα ὁμοίως περὶ τῶν παίδων, ἐὰν ὄντως εἰσὶν ἐξ αὐτῆς, ἐπιχειρῶσαι [?] ἐ ἐμόσθεν, ἐμμέμενε τὸν ὅρκον. Veteri autem Solonis Lege, per quos iurare liceret tres sancti sunt DI, per Supplicem, per Procuratorem, per Auerruncatorem, vel triplex, si forte, vnius numinis nomen. Tribus his namque continetur quicquid in votis esse potest:
units.tr: The religion of the oath is the greatest remedy for settling lawsuits, as Gaius says in Book V on the Provincial Edict: it comes into use because disputes are decided by the agreement of the litigants themselves. Law I, D. de iureiurando. One litigant offered the oath to the other, and when it had been given, the controversies were decided. Demosthenes, in his speech against Timotheus [garbled Greek in the scan: "I want to tell you, gentlemen, that when the challenge to the oath was made, he will come himself to swear to clear himself, and I, if I did not know him clearly as a man who had often and gravely sworn falsely, and as an enemy and a private person, would have offered him this oath. But now, since there are witnesses that I received the ... on the fourth ... he ordered me to give the oath, and it is a clear proof that I must give the oath"] [the Greek original is too garbled in the scan to reproduce reliably]. For when the oath was deferred at the challenge of the opposing side, it was secured by agreement that the case would be decided by this oath. Argument of Demosthenes' oration against Boeotus concerning the name: [Greek fragment, garbled in the scan, about Glaucon and the children] "Then, ashamed, he takes the children, as if deceived by his own challenge, for Glaucon had likewise summoned him about the children, whether they were truly his, and he kept to the oath." By the old law of Solon, the gods by whom it was lawful to swear were three holy ones: by the Suppliant, by the Procurator, by the Averruncator, or a threefold name of one deity. For these three contain whatever can be the object of a vow:

units.la: Τρεῖς Θεοὺς ὀμνύω, Ἰκέσιον, Καθάρσιον, Ἐξα-κυνέσιον.
units.tr: I swear by three gods: Suppliant, Purifier, Averter [Τρεῖς Θεοὺς ὀμνύω, Ἰκέσιον, Καθάρσιον, Ἐξακυνέσιον].

units.la: Per tres Deos iuranto, per Supplicem, per Procuratorem, per Auerruncatorem.
units.tr: Swear by three gods: by the Suppliant, by the Procurator, by the Averruncator.

units.la: Habes apud Pollucem Libro VIII. cap. XII. τρεῖς Θεοὺς ὁ μνύω καὶ ἀδέλφ Σόλων, Ἰκέσιον, Καθάρσιον, Ἐξακυνέσιον. Hesychius: τρεῖς Θεοί, τῷ Σόλωνι ἐν τοῖς Ἀξοσι ὄρκῳ πίστεως, ἐπεὶ ἡ ὁ Ὀμηρικόν. Sed ista Hesychij verba, ἡ ὁ Ὀμηρικόν, huc intrusa sunt è proxime praecedenti glossa. Nos in eum locum retrahenda esse existimamus. Sucti erant loci animas eorum, qui in hostico essent mortui, factis sacris ter voce ciere, & secum in patriam vocitare, idque Homeri exemplo, qui praeiuit Odysseias i'.
units.tr: Pollux, in Book 8, chapter 12, has: "I swear by three gods," and Solon, "by Ikesios, Katharsios, Exakynesios" [τρεῖς Θεοὺς ὁ μνύω καὶ ἀδέλφ Σόλων, Ἰκέσιον, Καθάρσιον, Ἐξακυνέσιον]. Hesychius: "three gods; in Solon's Axones, an oath of good faith [ὄρκῳ πίστεως], since [ἐπεὶ ἡ ὁ Ὀμηρικόν]." But these words of Hesychius, "since [ἡ ὁ] Homeric," have been intruded here from the immediately preceding gloss. We think they must be restored to their proper place. The souls of those who had died abroad were thought to be summoned: after sacred rites were performed, the name was called aloud three times and the soul was invited to return home with them. This was done after Homer's example, who set the precedent in the first book of the Odyssey [Odysseias i'].

units.la: ἐπὶ ἕνα τῶν ἄλλων ἑταίρων τοὺς ἑκάστου ἄδοντας.
units.tr: Calling upon one of the other comrades, each of them sings [ἐπὶ ἕνα τῶν ἄλλων ἑταίρων τοὺς ἑκάστου ἄδοντας].

units.la: Didymus: ἐρχαῖον ἔθος τὴν ὅτι ξένης ἀπαλυνόμων τὰς ψυχὰς αἰσχυνθεῖν τείπον τοῖς περιελφθέντας ἐπ' αὐ ὅπίωσιν οἰκαδε. Idem docebat Hesychij Glossa, quæ ad Homeri verba alludit, eaque interpretatur; sed corrupta est; lege: τεῖς ἑκαστον αὐ-τας, τεῖς ἑκαστον φωνήσας, καὶ αἰσχυνθεσάμενος. ἔτος δὲ ὡς τὴν ὅτι τῆς ἀλλοδαπῆς πέμψαντων τας ψυχὰς μετασχηθῆναι καὶ τὸν ἀπόπλεων, καὶ ὁ Ὀμηρικόν. Glossam vero sequentem ita lege: τρεῖς Θεοί, τῷ Σόλωνι ἐν τοῖς Ἀξοσι ὄρκῳ τετάχθαι, ἐν ιϛ cum scriptus esset hic Axonis numerus ad hunc modum ιε ιω, facile mutauit, & coaluit in vnam vocem ἔνοι. Erat igitur, decimus Axon Solonis, in quo de Diis, per quos iurarent, cautum erat. Apud Romanos iuratum non tantum per Deum, sed etiam per salutem suam, item per caput suorum, aut filiorum suorum: sed maxime per salutem, aut genium Principis: de quo iureiurando Vlpianus Libro XXII. ad Edictum: Si quis iurauerit in re pecuniaria per Genium Principis, dare se non oportere, & peieraverit. vel dari sibi oportere: vel intra certum tempus iurauerit se soluturum, nec soluit: Imperator noster cum Patre rescripsit, fustibus eum castigandum dimittere: & ita ei superdici, παρέπεττος μὴ ὄμνυε. Lege XIII. § VI. D. de iureiurando. Imperator, qui Vlpiano hic designatur cum patre, Antoninus est Caracalla cum Seuero, sed eorum Rescriptum obtinere noluit optimus Princeps Alexander Mammææ Filius, qui hæc constituit, vt leguntur Lege II. C. de rebus creditis.
units.tr: Didymus: "an ancient custom: to call the souls of those who had died abroad three times by name, and to make them return home, as Homer also says" [ἀρχαῖον ἔθος τὴν ὅτι ξένης ἀπαλυνόμων τὰς ψυχὰς αἰσχυνθεῖν τείπον τοῖς περιελφθέντας ἐπ' αὐ ὅπίωσιν οἰκαδε]. The gloss of Hesychius, which alludes to Homer's words and explains them, teaches the same, but it is corrupt; it should be read: "calling each of them three times, and calling their names, and invoking [καὶ αἰσχυνθεσάμενος]." The custom was that the souls of those who had been sent away abroad were summoned, as Homer also says. The following gloss, however, should be read thus: "three gods; in Solon's Axones, prescribed for an oath" [τρεῖς Θεοί, τῷ Σόλωνι ἐν τοῖς Ἀξοσι ὄρκῳ τετάχθαι]. Since this number of the Axon was written in this way, ιε ιω (that is, 15 and 10), it was easily changed, and fused into a single word, enoi. So the tenth Axon of Solon was the one in which, concerning the gods by whom they should swear, provision was made. Among the Romans, people swore not only by God, but also by their own safety, likewise by the head of their children, or of their sons; but above all by safety or by the Genius of the Prince. Concerning this oath Ulpian, in Book 22 on the Edict, says: "If anyone has sworn in a monetary matter by the Genius of the Prince that he ought not to give, and has perjured himself, or that it ought to be given to him, or has sworn that he will pay within a certain time and does not pay," our Emperor, together with his Father, rescripted that he be dismissed to be punished with cudgels; and so it was said to him, "Do not swear" [παρέπεττος μὴ ὄμνυε]. Read Digest, de iureiurando, law 13, § 6. The Emperor who is here designated by Ulpian together with his father is Antoninus Caracalla with Severus; but the excellent Prince Alexander, son of Mamaea, was unwilling to uphold their rescript, and he established these provisions, as they are read in Code, de rebus creditis, law 2.

units.la: Imp. Alexander A. Felici.
units.tr: The Emperor Alexander Augustus to Felix.

units.la: Iurisiurandi contempta religio satis Deum vltorem habet. Periculum autem corporis, vel maiestatis crimen secundum constituta Diuorum parentum meorum, etsi per Principis veneratione quodam calore fuerit peieratum, inferri non placet PP. VI. Kal. April. Maximo II. & Æliano Conss.
units.tr: Contempt for the religion of the oath is enough to have God as avenger. But a penalty against the body, or a charge of treason, according to the constitutions of my divine parents, is not to be inflicted, even if the perjury was committed out of some heat of reverence for the Prince. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Maximus (for the second time) and Aelianus.

units.la: In qua Constitutione Alexandri Imperatoris obserua haec verba, etsi per Principis venerationem quodam calore fuerit peieratum, interpretantur enim iste, quæ ex Rescripto Seueri & Antonini Caracallæ superdicebantur ei, qui per Genium Principis peierauerat [?] nam vertendum non est, petulanter ne iurato, sed potius, cum calore ne iurato. Ad hæc quippe alludit Imperator Alexander. Atque non tantum Gentiles, sed etiam Christiani, si viris summis credimus, iurabant per salutem Principis, auctorem laudant Tertullianum Apologetici cap. XXXII. Sed & iuramus, sicut non per Genios Cæsarum, ita per salutem eorum, quæ est augustior omnibus Genijs. Sed aut ego valde fallor, aut Christiani quando per salutem Cæsarum iurabant, Deum ipsum intelligebant, per quem valere se cognoscunt Cæsares, vt paulò ante dicebat Tertullianus, qui addit his, quæ illustramus, Nos iudicium Dei suspicimus in Imperatoribus, qui gentibus illos præfecit. Id in eis scimus esse, quod Deus voluit, & pro magno adiumento habemus; vnde suspicari licet, quod diximus, verbo quidem cum gentibus iurari per salutem Cæsaris, reuera tamen Deum, qui Cæsaris salus est, & per quem valet, à Christianis intelligi: ita longe alio sensu Polycarpus, apud Eusebium Historia IV. illud, ἀγε πῶς ἔχει, dixit, quam dici ab eo volebat Asiæ Proconsul:
units.tr: In this constitution of the Emperor Alexander observe these words: even if the perjury was committed out of some heat of reverence for the Prince. For they explain what was said to the one who had perjured himself by the Genius of the Prince in the rescript of Severus and Antoninus Caracalla. For the words should not be rendered do not swear wantonly, but rather do not swear in the heat of passion, since the Emperor Alexander alludes to this. And not only the Gentiles, but also Christians, if we believe eminent men, swore by the safety of the Prince. They cite Tertullian, Apologeticus, chapter XXXII: But we also swear, not by the Genii of the Caesars, but by their safety, which is more august than all the Genii. But either I am greatly mistaken, or when Christians swore by the safety of the Caesars, they understood God himself, through whom the Caesars know that they prevail, as Tertullian said a little before. He adds, to what we are illustrating: We regard the judgment of God in the emperors, who has set them over the nations. We know that what is in them is what God willed, and we hold it as a great help. Hence one may suspect what we have said: in words, indeed, the oath was sworn among the Gentiles by the safety of Caesar, but in truth God, who is Caesar's safety and through whom he prevails, was understood by Christians. In quite a different sense Polycarp, in Eusebius, Church History IV, said the phrase "come, how is it?" [ἀγε πῶς ἔχει], than the Proconsul of Asia wished it to be said by him:

units.la: λοιπὸν οὖν τῶν παρεστώτων, ἀνήρ ὁ Ἀλυπ[?]ας, [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: Then, of those standing by, the man Alypius [garbled in the scan; approximately: "...the rest of those present..."] [illegible in the scan]

units.la: Ἀλλὰ [?] ἴδε, πᾶς ὁ [?] ἔφη· [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: But look, he said [garbled in the scan] [illegible in the scan]

units.la: DE TESTIBVS.
units.tr: On Witnesses.

units.la: TITVLVS VII.
units.tr: TITLE VII.

units.la: Estimoniorum vsus frequens ac necessarius est, inquit Arcadius, qui & Charisius Libro singulari de Testibus, sed ab his exigendum est testimonium, quorum fides non vacillat, quibusque non interdicitur. Lege I.D. de Testibus. Intestabiles autem erant ii, qui infamia notati fuerant.
units.tr: Arcadius says, and Charisius in his single book On Witnesses, that the use of testimony is frequent and necessary. But testimony must be demanded only from those whose good faith is not in doubt and who are not forbidden to testify. See the law I.D. de Testibus. Those who had been branded with infamy were incapable of giving testimony.

units.la: Μὴ μαρτυρεῖν πρὸς ἀτίμους[?]. Ignominiosi intestabiles sunto.
units.tr: "Let no one give testimony before the dishonoured" [Μὴ μαρτυρεῖν πρὸς ἀτίμους]. Let the infamous be incapable of testifying.

units.la: Habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ κατὰ Νεαίρας[?] de Xenoclide Poeta, qui iudicio publico reus peractus fuerat, & notatus infamia: τὴ μὲν Ξενοκλείδου οὐκ ἀξιοῦσι[?] δικαιοῦσθαι[?] ἐκ μὴ μαρτυρεῖν[?]. Neque item Seruis testimonij erat dictio ex Lege.
units.tr: You have in Demosthenes, in the speech against Neaera, the case of the poet Xenocleides, who was prosecuted in a public trial and branded with infamy. The speaker says they did not think Xenocleides worthy of being admitted to give testimony. Nor was slaves' testimony admitted by law either.

units.la: SERVIS TESTIMONII DICTIO NE ESTO.
units.tr: A SLAVE SHALL NOT BE ALLOWED TO GIVE TESTIMONY.

units.la: Terentius in palliata Apollodori fabula Phormione, Actu II. Scena I.
units.tr: Terence, in the comedy Phormio based on a play by Apollodorus, Act II, Scene I.

units.la: Seruum hominem causam orare Leges non sinunt, Neque testimonij dictio est.
units.tr: The laws do not allow a slave to plead a case, and his word is not admissible as testimony.

units.la: Nisi per tormenta. Demosthenes ἐν τῇ πρὸς Τιμόθεον[?]. ἠξίωσεν αὐτὸν πρὸς τὴν Διαιτητήν[?], εἰ ἐπὶ δούλας εἴη ὁ Αἰχείων αὐτῷ[?], καὶ ἠξίουν αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ δίκῃ τὸν ἐλεγχον διδόναι[?]. Ἀποκρινάμενου δὲ μοι τοῦτο, ὅτι ἐλεύθερος εἴη[?], τῆς μὲν ἐξαιτήσεως ἐπι-γον[?]· μαρτυρεῖν δ' αὐτὸν ἠξίουν ἐμβαλέσθαι[?] τῷ Αἰχείωνος ὡς ἐλεύθερον ὄντα[?]. ὁ δὲ οὕτω μαρτυρίαν πρέσχετο[?], ὅτι ὡς δούλου[?] Αἰχείωνα τῷ δούλου, ἐκ τῆς σώματος[?] ἐλεῖσον ἠξίου ἐμέλησαν[?]. [illegible, ~12 letters]. At qui libertate erant donati, vt hic vides, non poterant torqueri. Verum hæ de seruis quæstiones non habeantur publice in iudicio coram iudicibus. Demosthenes ἐν τῇ πρὸς Σπιφαῖον ψευδομαρτυριῶν α'[?]. εἰμὶ γὰρ ἀπαιτοῦσιν ὑμᾶς εἰδέναι[?], ὅτι ὅσα μὴ δυνατὸν παρὰ τὸ πεπραγμένον[?], τῶν παρὰ[?] χρόνος δίρε[?] ἔτι ἐστὶ[?], ἀνάγκη τοῦτο παρέχειν[?]. Sed apud Arbitrum. Demosthenes ἐν τῇ πρὸς Εὐέργου καὶ Μνησίλαου ψευδομαρτυριῶν[?]. Οὐκ ἐπιλήψεται πραγματῶν[?] Ἀλλὰ τὴν Διαιτητὴν Πυλιδώρα ἐκ Κνίδου ἐπιμαρτυρεῖν[?]. Non tamen sine multis testibus. Demosthenes ibidem: ὅτι γὰρ, εἴπερ ἀγῶν τῶν ἄλλα φασὶν παραγγελθῆναι τὸν Θεόφιλον[?], καὶ ἐμαρτύρησεν[?] ἐστι δέδωκα[?] τὸ σῶμα τῆς Διαιτητῆς, ὑπ' αὐτοῦ δύο μόνον μαρτυρεῖς ἐπαιτοῦσιν[?], ἀπόδειξιν[?] καὶ ἀδελφὸν ἐλευθέρων μαρτυρῶσαν[?], ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλους[?] ἀν πολλοὺς[?]. ἢ μὲν γὰρ διαίτης[?] εἰς τὴν Ἡλίαν[?]· οἱ γὰρ τῶν Οἰνίδα καὶ τὴν Ἐρεχθίδα διαιτῶντες[?]. Atque haec serui in quæstionem postulatio ἀναγκαῖος proprie dicebatur. Grammatici: εἰώθασθ' ὅποτε δικάζειν τυνες[?], ἐξαιτεῖν οἷοτε[?] ἡ ἐφαπτομένας[?], εἰ ἀγαπῶσι εἰς Βάσανον[?], εἰ εἰς μαρτυρίαν τὴν ἀπόλιμας[?]. Qui autem seruum in quæstionem postulabat, pretij æstimati serui fideiussores dabat. Demosthenes ἐν τῇ πρὸς Γνωσίνεον[?]. ἀναγκάσθη μὲν μαρτυρεῖν[?] μασκεσθαι[?], ἀξιοῦν ἢ φαίνοιεν[?] ἀγαθὸν ἀπὸ Φήμης[?]. Idem ἐν τῇ πρὸς Σπιφαῖον ψευδομαρτυριῶν α'. μαρτυρεῖσθαι[?] πρεῖναι, ἔτι Απολλόδωρος προσηχθη Σπιφαῖον παράδοσιν[?] τὸν παιδα τὸν ἀκόλουθον εἰς βάσανον[?] τῆς ὑφαιρέσεως[?] τὸ γεγονός ἔργον[?]. καὶ γὰρ μέλλει[?] ὡς ἔτοιμος γεγόφη Απολλόδωρος, καὶ ἐκ Ἀπολλόδωρος ἀπ' ἐξ ἔτι ἡ βάσμος. Æstimationem serui non dabat, nisi causa caderet; videre est in laudatis Demosthenis verbis: (è quibus hoc amplius discès obsignatam fuisse [illegible, ~9 letters] fidei ergo.) Aristophanes Ranis:
units.tr: Unless under torture. Demosthenes, in the speech against Timotheus, says that he asked the arbitrator whether Aechion was the slave of the other party, and asked that he be examined in the same case. When the other side replied that he was free, they refused to accept the demand for his surrender, but they asked that Aechion give evidence as a free man. He, however, put forward his testimony as that of a slave, and asked that the slave be questioned under torture... [a short phrase is illegible]. But those who had been granted their freedom, as you see here, could not be tortured. Yet these questionings of slaves were not held publicly in court before the judges. Demosthenes, in the first speech against Spudias for false witness: for I ask you to know that whatever cannot be done as things stand, if time still remains, must be provided for... But in the presence of the arbitrator. Demosthenes, in the speech against Euergus and Mnesibulus for false witness: he will not take up the matter, but the arbitrator Pylidora of Cnidus will give evidence... Not, however, without many witnesses. Demosthenes in the same place: for if, as they say, Theophilus was summoned to the contest, and it is evident that he handed over the body of the slave, they demand not merely two witnesses from him, but also many others... Here is the sense that the slave was to be examined. And from this procedure, the demand for a slave to be put to question was properly called anagkaios. The grammarians say that when men were accustomed to judge, they demanded that slaves be surrendered for torture, and if they were unwilling, that they be given up for examination. Whoever demanded a slave for torture gave sureties for the slave's estimated price. Demosthenes, in the speech against Gnosinus: he was compelled to give evidence... and to ask that he be shown to be good with respect to reputation. The same author, in the first speech against Spudias for false witness: Apollodorus was brought before Spudias... the boy, the attendant, was handed over for torture to establish the deed that had been done. For Apollodorus was ready to... [the rest is illegible]. He did not give the estimate of the slave unless the case was lost; this can be seen in the words of Demosthenes quoted above, from which you will learn further that it was sealed... for the sake of faith. Aristophanes, in the Frogs:

units.la: δίκαιος ὁ λόγος. καὶ τῇ πρώτῳ γε [?] Οἱ / τὸν παῖδα τύπτων, ταχέως οἱ κείσεται.
units.tr: That is a just word; and the one who strikes the slave-boy will soon be laid low [δίκαιος ὁ λόγος ... τὸν παῖδα τύπτων ταχέως οἱ κείσεται].

units.la: Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Νεαίρας. παίδι καὶ ἀπολλόδωρος Στέφανον, ὃν ἐπὶ ὠμολόγησεν ἔγραψεν [?], Νεαίραν ξένην ὄντα, ἀγῶνα συνεῖχεν, ἐπειμὲν ὡς τὰς δεσπότας [?] [illegible, ~12 letters] Νεαίρας, ὡς ἐν Μεγάροις ἔγνωσαν ἥλθε, καὶ ἀλλὰ ὑπέρ [?] Στέφανον [illegible, ~10 letters], τὰς εἰδίας ἀκριβῶς τῶν ὄντων Νεαίρα, ὅτι ἐν Στέφανον εἰσὶ, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ ἐπὶ βασάνισαι αὐτὰς. καὶ εἰ ὅλως ὁμολογεῖν ἐν Στέφανον [?] καὶ Νεαίρας ξένης τοὺς παῖδας, πιστεύσαι Νεαίραν τοὺς νόμους, καὶ τοὺς παῖδας ξένους [?]· εἰ ἢ μὴ ὁμολογεῖν ἐν Στέφανον [?] αὐτούς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐξ ἑτέρας γυναικὸς ἀφῆς, ἀφίσασθαι τὰς ἀγῶνας ἠδέλφης Νεαίρας. καὶ εἰ ᾽ἰ ἐν τῷ Βασσῶν βλαφθείσθω ἂν αὐξέσ[?]σι, ἐπιτίνθ᾽ ὁ ἀ βλαβείσθω, Atque, vt plurimum, lis hac [illegible, ~5 letters] terminabatur: habes in his Demosthenis, & clare Pollux Libro VIII. cap VI. [illegible, ~20 letters] ᾠ, ἵ μάρτυρα, ἵ βασάνῳ, ἵ ἄλλῳ πὸ τίσ[?]τω. Varios habendæ quæstionis de seruis modos descripsit Aristophanes Ranis:
units.tr: Demosthenes, in the speech against Neaera. Apollodorus, who had brought the suit against Stephanus, claiming that Neaera was a foreigner, and who had agreed that the slaves were his own... [illegible]... Neaera, as they were examined at Megara, he came and argued on behalf of Stephanus [illegible], exactly as the slaves belonging to Neaera were, that they were to be tortured. And if it was agreed that the slaves belonged to Stephanus and that Neaera was a foreigner, let Neaera trust the laws, and the slaves [be examined]; but if he did not agree that they belonged to Stephanus, but were from another woman, let the case be dismissed for the sister of Neaera. And if [the slaves] were harmed in the examination, let the harm fall on whoever... And, as is most often the case, this dispute was settled in this way. You have this in Demosthenes, and Pollux clearly in Book VIII, chapter VI [illegible]: by a witness, by torture, or by another [means]... Aristophanes described the various ways of holding such an examination of slaves in the Frogs:

units.la: ΞΑΝ. βασάνιζε γὰρ τὸν παῖδα ζυτῶν λαβών.
units.tr: XANTHIAS: Take the boy and torture him with the leek [ΞΑΝ. βασάνιζε γὰρ τὸν παῖδα ζυτῶν λαβών].

units.la: ΔΙΑ. καὶ πῶς βασανίζω; ΞΑΝ πάντα ἕξειν, ἐν κλίμακι / δήσας, χρεμάσας, ὑψηλοῦ μαστιγῶν, δίρων, / ἐρεβλῶν, ὅτι τε τὰς ῥίνας ὄξος ἐγχέων, / πλίνθους ἐπιπθεὶς, πάντα ταῦλα, πλὴν ταχέως / μὴ τύπτε τύπτειν, μὴ δὲ γηθείῳ πέῳ.
units.tr: DIONYSUS: And how am I to torture him? XANTHIAS: In every way: bind him to a ladder, hang him up, flog him, stretch him, pour vinegar up his nostrils, pile bricks on him, do everything, only do not strike him with a leek, nor with a cabbage stalk.

units.la: Quæ postrema facetè adduntur à Comico, quasi diceret, βασάνιζε πάντα χρῶς αὐτὸν, μὴ ἐκ παιδίᾳ, μηδ᾽ ὡς τὶς ἐλευθέρους παῖδας τοῦ ἐκκαυλήματα τῆς ἀγροῦ τύπτοιτο, ἵ᾽ τοῦ γηπίου. Neque iure item Romano Seruis erat testimonii dictio; nam idonei non videntur esse testes, vt scribit Licinius Rufinus Libro II Regularium, quibus imperari potest, vt testes fiant. Lege VI D. de testibus. Sed serui responso, inquit Modestinus Libro III. Regularium, tunc credendum est, cum alia probatio ad eruendam veritatem non est. Lege VII.D. eod. cum Modestino pari ria facit Paulus Libro II.Sententiarum, his verbis: Cum probatio prioris fugæ deficit, serui quæstioni credendum est; in se enim interrogari, non pro domino, aut in dominum, videtur. Lege VII.D. de probationibus. Vir summus existimat reponendum esse, serui responsioni. nam alioquin conflatur ἀντίφασις inexplicabile cum Lege LVIII D. ædilitio edicto, quæ est ex eiusdem Pauli Libro V. Responsorum, Seruum dupla emi: qui rebus ablatis, fugit: mox inuentus præsentibus honestis viris, interrogatus, an & in domo venditoris fugisset, respondit fugisse. quaero, an standum sit responso serui? Paulus respondit: Si & alia indicia prioris fugæ non deficiunt, tunc etiam serui responso credendum est. Vtramque Legem ita conciliare satagit in Interpretationibus ad Pauli Sententiarum Lege II.Tit.XVII. Emptor qui redhibitoria agit, debet probare seruum ex veteri vitio fugisse Lege IV.D. de probat. Deficiente probatione, iudiciis non deficientibus, etiam serui responso credendum est: Lege quaero. §.uli.D.de ædil.edict.quia in se potius interrogari videtur, quam in dominum, vel pro domino, Lege cum probatio D. de probat. Sed non video, quare Vir summus in hac Lege reponendum velit, serui quæstioni, pro serui responsioni, nisi dicas ad tormenta seruorum non veniri, nisi quando alijs argumentis reus urgetur: Lege I.§.I. & Lege XVIII.
units.tr: The comic poet adds this last point wittily, as if he were saying: torture him in every way, but not with a leek or a stalk, so that he is not beaten as a free child would be, nor with such instruments of the field. Nor by Roman law either was testimony allowed to slaves; for they do not seem to be fit witnesses, as Licinius Rufinus writes in Book II of his Regulars, those who can be ordered to become witnesses. See law VI D. de testibus. But the answer of a slave, says Modestinus in Book III of the Regulars, is to be believed only when there is no other proof to bring out the truth. See law VII D. eod. Paulus, in Book II of the Sentences, agrees with Modestinus in these words: When proof of the earlier flight is lacking, the slave's answer under questioning is to be believed; for he is seen to be questioned against himself, not on behalf of or against his master. See law VII D. de probationibus. A very great man thinks that it should be read the slave's answer instead. For otherwise there arises a contradiction that cannot be resolved with Law LVIII D. ædilitio edicto, which comes from Book V of the Responsa of the same Paulus: A slave was bought for double the price; having stolen goods, he fled; soon afterwards he was found in the presence of respectable men, and when questioned whether he had also fled from the house of the seller, he replied that he had fled. I ask whether the slave's answer is to be upheld? Paulus answered: If other indications of the earlier flight are not lacking, then too the slave's answer is to be believed. The same man labours to reconcile both laws in this way, in his Interpretations on Paulus's Sentences, Book II, Title XVII: A buyer who sues for rescission must prove that the slave fled because of an old defect. Law IV D. de probat. If proof is lacking but the indications are not, the slave's answer is also to be believed. See the law quaero, §ult. D. de ædil. edict., because he seems to be questioned in himself rather than in his master or on his master's behalf. See the law cum probatio D. de probat. But I do not see why this great man wants to read the slave's questioning in this law instead of the slave's answer, unless you say that slaves are not put to torture except when the accused is pressed by other arguments. See Law I §I and Law XVIII.

units.la: §.II. at vero hic probatio deficit, itaque non torquetur. Quod vero distinguunt inter probationem, & indicia, non audio: nam etiam indicia certa, quæ iure non respuuntur, non minorem probationis, quàm instrumenta, continent fidem. Lege XIX. C. de rei vindicatione. vide etiam Legem vltimam C. de probationibus. Sed ἀντίωμα [?] sola interpunctione explicari debet. Quæro, an stādum sit responso serui? Paulus respondit: Si & alia indicia priora fugæ, non: Deficiunt, tunc etiam serui responso credendum est. Sensus est: Si sint alia indicia, quæ probationis continent fidem, prioris fugæ, non est standum responso serui. At vero si alia indicia, id est, probatio, deficiant, tunc serui responso credendum est.
units.tr: §II. But here proof is lacking, and so the slave is not tortured. As for the distinction they draw between proof and indications, I do not follow it; for even certain indications, which are not rejected by law, carry no less weight of proof than documents. See Law XIX C. de rei vindicatione. See also the last law C. de probationibus. But the contradiction must be resolved by punctuation alone. I ask whether the slave's answer is to be upheld? Paulus answered: If other indications of the earlier flight are not lacking, then too the slave's answer is to be believed. The sense is this: if there are other indications which carry the weight of proof of the earlier flight, the slave's answer is not to be upheld. But if other indications, that is, proof, are lacking, then the slave's answer is to be believed.

units.la: Peregrinis non interdici testimonium argumento est, quod Libertis, qui Peregrini sunt, & censentur, non interdicitur, vt liquet è laudatis Demosthenis verbis ἐν τῇ πρὸς Τιμόθεον, de Æschrione, qui libertate erat donatus: Ἐπιχρηματίσασθαι δὲ μοι Εὐτυχίδης, ὅτι ἐλευθέρωσ εἰσὶ, τῆς μὲν ἐξαιτήσεως ἐπέσχον, μαρτυρείας δ᾽ αὐτὸν ηξίωσαν ἐμβαδὸν ἔχειν τῆς Αἰσχίνου, ὡς ἐλευθερωθέντος [?]. Quanquam non licebat hospitibus & peregrinis testimonium illud, quod μαρτυρία appellatur, dicere ἐν ταῖς τῆς ἀπογραφῆς δίκαις. Adnotant Grammatici ex Hyperide: Τὰ ... ἀπογραφῆς δίκαις κεκώλυνται μαρτυρῆσαι οἱ ξένοι [?]. Res quippe illorum agebantur.
units.tr: That aliens were not forbidden to give testimony is shown by the fact that freedmen, who were aliens and were counted as such, were not forbidden. This is clear from Demosthenes' words quoted from the speech against Timotheus, concerning Aeschines, who had been granted freedom: "Eutychides argued for me that they were freed. I held back from the demand, but they thought him worthy to give testimony against Aeschines, as one who had been freed" [Ἐπιχρηματίσασθαι δὲ μοι Εὐτυχίδης, ὅτι ἐλευθέρωσ εἰσὶ, τῆς μὲν ἐξαιτήσεως ἐπέσχον, μαρτυρείας δ᾽ αὐτὸν ηξίωσαν ἐμβαδὸν ἔχειν τῆς Αἰσχίνου, ὡς ἐλευθερωθέντος]. Yet foreigners and guests were not permitted to give that testimony which is called martyria in suits concerning registration. The grammarians note from Hyperides: "Foreigners are forbidden to give testimony in suits of registration" [Τὰ ... ἀπογραφῆς δίκαις κεκώλυνται μαρτυρῆσαι οἱ ξένοι]. Naturally, since it was their own affairs that were being decided.

units.la: Nullus præterea, inquit Pomponius Libro I. ad Sabinum, idoneus testis in re sua intelligitur. Lege X. D. de testibus, siue in publico iudicio, siue in priuatis causis, siue in referendis rationibus.
units.tr: "Moreover," says Pomponius in Book I on Sabinus, "no one is regarded as a competent witness in his own cause." See the tenth law in the Digest, de testibus, whether in a public trial, in private causes, or in the rendering of accounts.

units.la: Μὴ μαρτυρεῖν αὐτὸν αὑτῷ, ὅτ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς γραφῆς, ὅτ᾽ ἐν τῆς ἀθωώσεως.
units.tr: Not to give testimony for oneself, whether in the indictment or in the acquittal [Μὴ μαρτυρεῖν αὐτὸν αὑτῷ, ὅτ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς γραφῆς, ὅτ᾽ ἐν τῆς ἀθωώσεως].

units.la: Nemo in re sua idoneus testis esto, siue in publico, siue in priuato iudicio, siue in referendis rationibus.
units.tr: No one is to be a competent witness in his own cause, whether in a public trial, a private trial, or in the rendering of accounts.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes ἐν τῇ πρὸς Σπουδίαν βʹ. μαρτυρεῖν γὰρ οἱ νόμοι οὐκ ἐῶσιν αὐτὸν αὑτῷ, ὅτ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς γραφῆς, ὅτ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς δίκης, ὅτ᾽ ἐν τῆς ἀθωώσεως. Sed aduersarij necesse habebant alter alterius interrogatis respondere, non autem testimonium dicere.
units.tr: Demosthenes quotes the law in the second speech against Spudias: the laws do not allow a man to testify for himself, whether in the indictment, in the trial, or in the acquittal. But the opponents were bound to answer one another's questions, though they were not to give testimony.

units.la: ΤΩΙΝ ΑΝΤΙΔΙΚΩΙΝ ΑΓΕΡΑΝΚΕΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟΚΡΙΝΑΣΘΑΙ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΙΣ ΤΟ ΕΡΩΤΩΜΕΝΟΝ, ΜΑΡΤΥΡΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ.
units.tr: "The opponents must answer one another's questions, but must not give testimony" [Τῶν ἀντιδίκων ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι ἀποκρίνασθαι ἀλλήλοις τὸ ἐρωτώμενον, μαρτυρεῖν δὲ μή].

units.la: Aduersarij alter alterius interrogatis respondere coguntur: testimonium ne dicunto.
units.tr: "Let the opponents be compelled to answer one another's questions; let them not give testimony."

units.la: Descripsit Demosthenes ἐν τῇ πρὸς Σπουδίαν βʹ. ἵνα δὴ εἰδῆτε ἀκριβῶς, αὐτὸν τῷ νόμῳ μὴ ἀπάγεσθαι. ΤΩΙΝ ΑΝΤΙΔΙΚΩΙΝ ΕΠΑΝΑΓΚΕΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΠΟΚΡΙΝΑΣΤΑΙ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΙΣ ΤΟ ΕΡΩΤΩΜΕΝΟΝ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ. Meminit Plato in Apologia Socratis, vbi Socratis Melitum interrogat: Ἀποκρίναι, ὦ ἀγαθέ, καὶ γὰρ ὁ νόμος κελεύει ἀποκρίνεσθαι. Est enim testis definitio hæc apud Demosthenem ἐν τῇ πρὸς Βοίωτον. μάρτυρες μέν εἰσιν ὅ-τι, οἷς μὴ μέτεστι τῆς πραγμάτος, ὥστε ἡ δίκη ἔστιν [?].
units.tr: Demosthenes also described this in the second speech against Spudias: "So that you may know exactly, let him not be led off by the law... The opponents must answer one another's questions, but must not give testimony" [ἵνα δὴ εἰδῆτε ἀκριβῶς, αὐτὸν τῷ νόμῳ μὴ ἀπάγεσθαι. Τῶν ἀντιδίκων ἐπαναγκες εἶναι ἀποκρίνασθαι ἀλλήλοις τὸ ἐρωτώμενον, μαρτυρεῖν δὲ μή]. Plato mentions it in the Apology of Socrates, where Socrates questions Meletus: "Answer, my good man, for the law also commands that one answer" [Ἀποκρίναι, ὦ ἀγαθέ, καὶ γὰρ ὁ νόμος κελεύει ἀποκρίνεσθαι]. Demosthenes gives this definition of witnesses in the speech against Boeotus: witnesses are those who have no share in the matter at issue, so that the suit is…

units.la: Quinetiam familiares & domestici non coguntur inuiti in rem testimonium dicere.
units.tr: Moreover, family members and household servants are not compelled to give testimony against their will in a matter.

units.la: Μὴ ἐπάναγκες ἐξ οἰκίας καταμαρτυρῆσαι ἂν [?] πάλλην [?].
units.tr: It is not compulsory to bear witness against someone from one's own household [Μὴ ἐπάναγκες ἐξ οἰκίας καταμαρτυρῆσαι].

units.la: Familiares testimonium dicere in fa-miliarem suum inuiti ne coguntur.
units.tr: Members of the family are not compelled, against their will, to give testimony against their kinsman.

units.la: Legem collegimus ex his Demosthenis verbis ὃς τὰ ... Τιμοθέου. ὁ μὴ [?] ... ἐφασάμην καταμαρτυρῆσαι ἂν [?] ... εἶχεν [?] ... εἴ). Quod si quis, cui testimonium propter aliquam causam interdicitur, testimonium deferre dicatque, praeter Leges, tum is, cum ille, qui testem aduocauerat, ob id Lege ψευδομαρτυρειῶν postulabatur.
units.tr: We have gathered the law from these words of Demosthenes. If anyone to whom testimony is forbidden for some reason nonetheless offers testimony and speaks, contrary to the laws, then both he and the man who had summoned that witness were, for this reason, liable to prosecution under the law on false witness.

units.la: ΕΣΤΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΟΔΙΚΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΨΕΥΔΟΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΩΝ Ο ΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΑΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ, ΟΤΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΕΙ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ, ΚΑΙ Ο ΠΡΟΒΑΛΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ.
units.tr: Let there also be a prosecutor of false witnesses: whoever bears witness against the law, and whoever is brought forward for these things [ΕΣΤΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΟΔΙΚΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΨΕΥΔΟΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΩΝ Ο ΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΑΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ, ΟΤΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΕΙ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ, ΚΑΙ Ο ΠΡΟΒΑΛΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ].

units.la: Falsi testimonij damnator, qui, praeter quam Legibus licet, testimonium dixerit. In eum, qui hunc testem aduocauerit, sirempse Lege agito.
units.tr: A condemner of false testimony: he who has given testimony otherwise than the laws permit. Against the one who summoned this witness, let him bring action under the law.

units.la: Legem hanc habet Demosthenes ἐν τῷ Σπφαὶς ψευδομαρτυριῶν β'. σκέ-ψασθε τίνων ἐστὶ τὸν νόμον, ὃς καλὸν ἐστί, ὑπὸ δικοῦ ... τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας, ὅ ... ἐν τῷ τόπῳ, ὅ[?] μαρτυρεῖ ... ἐκ τὸν νόμον. ΝΟΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΟΔΙΚΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΨΕΥΔΟΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΩΝ Ο ΜΑΡΤΥΡΗΣΑΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ, ΟΤΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΕΙ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ ΚΑΙ Ο ΠΡΟΒΑΛΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ.
units.tr: Demosthenes has this law in the second speech on false witness against Spudias. "Consider of whom the law speaks, which is fine, ... of false testimony ... in the place, ... bears witness ... according to the law." Let there also be a prosecutor of false witnesses, who bears witness against himself that he testifies against the law, and the one brought forward against these things.

units.la: Testimonium autem vel ipsi coram dicebant testes, quomodo non poterant postulari falsi testimonij Vlpianus ad Orationem Demosthenes ἐπὶ τῷ ... ἀλλ' ἐπιφανὲς ... πολλὰ δὲ ἀλλὰ φορὰ μαρτυρίας καὶ μάρτυρες. ὁ οὖν γὰρ μάρτυς αὐτὸν παρὰ ... ταῖς εἰσὶν ἰμαρτύρῃ, καὶ οὐχ ὧν ... ὑπὸ ... Velut testimonium tabulis inscriptum dabant, idque Lege sanctum, ob hanc causam, ne quis testimonium corrumpat, radat, mutet.
units.tr: The witnesses themselves, however, gave their testimony in person, which is why they could not be charged with false witness. Ulpian, on the speech of Demosthenes, says that testimony was often conveyed by witnesses in writing. Thus they gave testimony inscribed on tablets, and this was made sacred by law, for this reason: that no one should corrupt, scrape or alter the testimony.

units.la: Μαρτυρῆν ἐν τῷ γραμματείῳ.
units.tr: To testify on the writing tablet [Μαρτυρῆν ἐν τῷ γραμματείῳ].

units.la: Scripto testimonium dicito.
units.tr: Give your testimony in writing.

units.la: Laudat Demosthenes ἐν τῷ χ' Σπφαὶς ψευδομαρτυρειῶν α'. Ἀλλ' ... ὁ νόμος μαρτυρῆν ἐν τῷ γραμματείῳ κελεύει, ἵνα μὴ ἀφελῆν ἔξῃ, μήτε παραδιδῶναι τοῖς γεγραμμένοις μηδὲν. Atque etiam, vt aduersus eum, qui testimonium dat, institui possit actio falsi testimonij. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ χ' Σπφαὶς ψευδομαρτυρειῶν β'. οἱ δὲ γε νόμοι, ἃ ταῦτα λέγουσιν, ἀλλ' ἀν εἰδῇ ὡς, καὶ οἷς ἂν ... παραδοθῇ ... γεγραμμένοις ... ἀκολουθεῖ ... μαρτυρεῖν, ἀλλὰ πένεσθαι ... ἀδυνάτων καὶ ... ἐκμαρτυρείων γεγραμμένων ἐν τῷ γραμματείῳ ... ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς ... μαρτυρεῖ, ἵνα ἐαν μὴ αἰ-δεῖσθαι ὁ μαρτυρήσας, ἐκεῖνος ... ψευδομαρτυρειῶν ... ἐὰν ἢ μὴ δύνασθαι, οἱ ἐκ-μαρτυρήσαντες ... Idem ἐν τῷ χ' Εὐέργου ἐΜισθίλου ψευδομαρτυρειῶν. ἔφη γὰρ ἐν τῇ δίκῃ τῆς αἰτίας, ὅτι μὲν μάρτυρας πεὶς ... μαρτυρῶ ... ὡς τὰ ἡμέρα ... ἐν γραμματείῳ ... τὸν νόμον ψευδῆς εἴ). Vlpianus ad Orationem Demosthenis ... ἐπὶ ... καταμαρτυρηθῆναι, ... εἰς τὸ μὴ τὰ ... χρέων. Differebant autem tabulae, quibus testes, qui rebus interfuerant, testimonium domi inscribebat, à tabulis illis, quibus testes, qui interfuerunt rebus non aduocati, sed forte fortuna, testimonium dant: illæ enim exsciatæ sût & expoliatæ: hæ vero è cera, vt è cera, vt si quid adscribere vel delere velint, facile possint. Demosth. ἐν ᾧ ... ψευδομαρτυρειῶν ... ἐπὶ ... ἀπὸ τὸ γραμματείου ... ἐν ᾧ ἡ μαρτυρία γεγραμμένη ... [illegible, ~12 letters]. λθυκωλμῶντε γλγάρ'ὅσι[?], καὶ οἰκοῦν κατεσκευασμένον. καὶ τοῖς μὲν τὰ πράγματα μάρ-τυρεῖν[?], ὥσπερ εἰκότως τοῖς μάρτυσι κατεσκευασμένας μάρτυρεῖν· τοῖς δ' ἐκ τῶν ἐμφάνισιν τῶν μαρτυρίας καὶ εἰ χρὴ ἀπὸ τῶν πραγμάτων (?) καὶ ἐκ μάλιστα γεγραμμένοις τὴν μαρτυρίαν, ἵνα εἴ τι πρὸς γεγράφαι, ἐπὶ ἀπαλλαγὴν βυλὴν, [?]ἀδίδωνι.
units.tr: Demosthenes cites it in the first speech on false witness against Spudias: "But the law orders testimony to be given on the tablet, so that nothing may be removed, nor anything handed over to the written record." And so, that an action for false witness may be instituted against the one who gives testimony. Demosthenes, in the second speech on false witness: the laws which say these things… the one who has testified in writing… if he cannot be shown to have testified falsely… Likewise in the speech on false witness against Euergus and Mnesibulus he says: "…the law commands testimony to be written on the tablet…" Ulpian, on the speech of Demosthenes, says that the tablets differed. The tablets on which witnesses who had been present at the events wrote their testimony at home differed from those on which witnesses who had not been summoned, but happened by chance to be present, gave theirs. The former were scraped and polished; the latter were of wax, so that if anyone wished to add or delete something, he could easily do so.

units.la: Inter testandum aurem imam tangebant. Etymologicographus: λέγοντες λέγοντες, ὅτι μάρτυρόμενοι ἐνὶ, λαμβάνουσιν αὐτήν. At testimonio dicto, in liberorum capita iurabant, se verum dicere. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Ἀφόβον ψευδομαρτυριῶν. ἢ τίνων ἐγὼ μὲν τοῖς ἐπιμελῶς, οἱ δὲ μάρτυρες ἢ πρὸς αὐτὴν μοι γνώμην εἶχον ἄλλα καὶ χαρίεντα ὥσπερ σπεμόνοι τοῖς παῖδας, ὑπὲρ ὧν ἐμαρτύρησεν, πίσιν ὅπωσοῦν ἡλίασθαι ἢ κατ' ἐκείνων. De iureiurando testium Diogenes Laertius in Xenocrate: ὧ ἢ καὶ ἀξιόπιστος σφόδρα, ὥστε μὴ εἶχον αἰώμενον μαρτυρῆν, τοῦτο μόνον σὺν ἐχώρεσιν Ἀθηναῖοι. Cicero Epistolarum ad Atticum Libro I. Epist. XVI. Qua mihi res multo honorificentior visa est, quam aut illa, cum iurare tui cives Xenocratem testimonium dicentem prohibuerunt. Valerius Maximus Libro II.cap.de Majestate: Cum testimonium dicere coactus ad aram accessisset, ut more eius civitatis iuraret, omnia se vero retulisse. Testes, qui in re capitali de homicidio testimonium dicerent, oportebat quoque ad cæsa porrecta suouetaurilij iusiurandum concipere, & si scientes falsa testarentur, sibi & suis totique genti mala omnia imprecari. Antiphon de Herodis cæde: τὴν δὲ, δίον σε δημοσίαν ὅρκον τὸν μίμησιν καὶ ἐμ-ἐστιν, ἐξώλειαν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡλίῳ καὶ οἰκία τῇ σῇ ἐπιθρώμενον, ἤ μὴ μὴ δίκα κατηγορῆσθε ἐμοῦ, ἵ' εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν φόνον, ὡς ἐκπεινα· ἐν ᾧ ὅτ' αἱ καὶ πολλὰ εἰργασμένος ἡλιασμένων δίδωμι ἵ' αὐτοῦ τὰ πραγμάτ, ὅτ' αἱ πολλὰ ἀγαθὰ εἰργασμένος, τούτοις δ' ἐσωζόμεν τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς, ἐ' σὺ πέλεται, αὐτὸς σιαπῶ τοῖς νόμοις ἐξεῦρων, ἀ' ὠμῶπες μὲν αὐτὸς ἐμοῦ κατη-ρήσῃς, ἀ' ὠμῶλοι δ' οἱ μάρτυρες καὶ μάρτυρεῖν ἐμοῦ. Νῦν αὐτὸς τὸν αὐτὸν ὅρκον σοι δημοσαμένους, ἡ ἀπολυμένης τῷ σφαῖρων καὶ μάρτυρεῖν ἐμοῦ. Lege igitur, ut ex his omnibus exemplis colligitur, testes iurati testimonium dicebant.
units.tr: Between giving testimony they touched the lobe of the ear. The Etymologicum: "they touch it, saying that they call the witness to memory." When the testimony was given, they swore on the heads of their children that they spoke the truth. Demosthenes, in the speech against Aphobus on false witness: "…the witnesses who had been carefully… for those for whom they testified, that they would in some way be judged…" Diogenes Laertius, on Xenocrates: he was so trustworthy that, although he had not been sworn, the Athenians permitted him to give testimony. Cicero, in Letters to Atticus, Book I, Letter XVI: Which seemed to me much more honourable than that your citizens swore to prohibit Xenocrates from giving testimony. Valerius Maximus, Book II, chapter on majesty: When he had been forced to give testimony, he approached the altar to swear, as is the custom of that state, that he had reported everything truthfully. Witnesses who gave testimony in a capital case of homicide also had to swear over the sacrificed pig, ram and bull (suovetaurilia), and, if they knowingly testified falsely, to call down every evil upon themselves, their families and their whole race. Antiphon, on the murder of Herodes: "…swearing this oath, and calling down destruction upon himself, his household and his children…" Therefore, as all these examples show, witnesses gave their testimony under oath.

units.la: Τοῖς μάρτυσιν ὅρκον δημοσίας.
units.tr: For the witnesses, the public oath. [Τοῖς μάρτυσιν ὅρκον δημοσίας]

units.la: Testes iurati testimonium dicunto.
units.tr: Let the witnesses give their testimony under oath.

units.la: De iis autem tantum testimonium dicere dareque Lege licebat, quibus testes interfuerant oculati.
units.tr: By law, however, testimony could be given and offered only about those matters at which the witnesses had been present as eyewitnesses.

units.la: Α αἰδῆς, ὡς καὶ οἷς ἀ ἀπαγγείλαν πεπολεμένοις τοῖς μάρτυρσι ἐν γεγραμμένῳ γεγραμμένα.
units.tr: Of those things, the witnesses were to testify in writing, as to those who had been present and had seen them done.

units.la: Eorum, quibus interfuerunt dum fiebant, & fieri viderunt, testimonium scripto dicunto, danto.
units.tr: Those who were present while things were being done, and saw them done, shall give their testimony in writing.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Σπουδίου ψευδομαρτυριῶν β'. οἱ δὲ γε νό-μοι, ἡ τῶν λέγεσιν, ἀλλ' ἀ' ἀ' αἰδῆς, καὶ οἷς δὲ ἀπαγγείλαν πεπολεμένοις, τοῖς μάρτυ-ρεῖν κελεύουσιν ἐν γεγραμμένῳ γεγραμμένοι. Atque hoc testimonium proprie μαρτυρία dicitur.
units.tr: Demosthenes quotes this law in his speech against Spudias on false witness (second). The laws order that witnesses who were present and saw the deeds done shall testify in writing. This kind of testimony is properly called martyria [μαρτυρία].

units.la: Quanquam & de auditione testimonium dabatur, cum testes vidisse quidem se negant, sed audiuisse: verum cum hac cautione, ut rem à mortuo auditam, non à viuente acceptam testari liceat: Præterea aliena fide testimonium dicere licebat de re peregre extra fines Atticæ gesta, & cui interesse non potueris, quod ἐκμαρτυρία dicebatur.
units.tr: Testimony was also given from hearsay, when witnesses deny that they saw something but say that they heard it; yet with this caution, that one might testify to a thing heard from a dead man, not to one received from a living person. Moreover, it was permitted to give testimony on the strength of another's word about a matter done abroad, outside the borders of Attica, and at which one could not have been present; this was called ekmartyria [ἐκμαρτυρία].

units.la: ΑΚΟΗΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΕΙΝ ΤΕ-ΘΝΕΩΤΟΣ. ΕΚΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΑΝ ΔΕ ΥΠΕΡΟΡΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΑΔΥΝΑΤΟΥ.
units.tr: "It is allowed to testify from hearsay about a dead man" [ἀκοὴν εἶναι μαρτυρεῖν τεθνεῶτος]. "Testimony from abroad, for a matter beyond the border and out of reach" [ἐκμαρτυρίαν δὲ ὑπὲρ ὁρίου καὶ ἀδυνάτου].

units.la: De re à mortuo accepta, aut peregre gesta, cui interesse non potuerint, testimonium auriti, non oculati, danto, dicuto. bebatur adversus illum ἀπομαρτυρίου dica, & deponebatur adversus illum drachma ἀπομαρτυρίου nomine.
units.tr: A witness may give and state testimony about a matter received from a dead man, or about something done abroad, at which he could not have been present, provided he heard it and did not see it himself. Against anyone who did so, an action for refusal to testify [ἀπομαρτυρίου] was brought, and a drachma was deposited against him under the name of apomartyria.

units.la: Τιθέναι τας τὸν μαρτυρίας ἀπόντι τῷ δραχμὴν τῷ ἀπομαρτυρίου. Drachmam deponunto adversus eum, qui testimonium defugerit.
units.tr: The drachma of apomartyria is to be deposited against the one who refused to testify. Let them deposit a drachma against the one who shirked giving testimony.

units.la: Legem habes apud Demosthenem ὡς τοῦ κατὰ Τιμάρχου. ὅταν δὲ ἐκκλητεὶς ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκίας, ὁ γὰρ ὧν φανερὸς ἔλιπε τὴν μαρτυρίαν πιστεῖς ὑπὸ ξυνοῦ. τιθέντος δὲ μὲν αὐτοῦ τὴν δραχμὴν τῆς ἀπομαρτυρίου καὶ τὸν νόμον, ὁ Διαρτυρὴς ἢ κλεσιδιήτησαν. Suidas narrat eum, qui ἀπομαρτυρίου damnatus fuerat, multatum fuisse à iudice competenter: at vero is, qui dicam ἀπομαρτυρίου scripserat, si causa caderet, multabatur ea drachma, quam depositerat, id est, sacramento drachmæ. Verba eius sunt, ἀπομαρτυρίου δίκη τῆς ὑπισταμένοις ἢ τὴν περιεχομένων, μαρτυρήσῃ ὑπεγκαλοῦντων (χρ. ἐπαγγελλομένοις.) ὡς δικασταί, εἴπε ἢ ὕστερον ἀποφυγόντων, ἐκάλεσεν ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπὸ ἀλλήλων. καὶ μὲν ἀλλαγῆ, ἐπιμέτρητο κατ' ἀξίαν. εἰ δ' μὴ ἔλαι ὁ διώ-κων, πωλεῖσθαι ἐπέτο δραχμῇ. At vero Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. VI. scribit eum, qui testimonium defugiebat, multatum fuisse drachmis mille: quas si non penderent, eoque nomine in ius vocarentur, ἐκκλητοῦ ἡ ἐκκλησία dicebant. Priusquam autem dicam scriberent ἀπομαρτυρίου, obnagulatum ibant ob portum illius, qui testimonium defugiebat: habes hunc ordinem in laudatis Demosthenis verbis: ὅταν δὲ ἢ διαμεμαρτύρηκε, ἐκκλητεῖς ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκίας· ὁ γὰρ ὧν φανερὸς ἔλιπε τὴν μαρτυρίαν πιστεῖς ὑπὸ ξυνοῦ, λέγεται δὲ μὲν αὐτοῦ τὴν δραχμὴν τῆς ἀπομαρτυρίου καὶ τὸν νόμον. Sed vnice id docet Pollux loco laudato. ἀπομαρτυρίου ἢ, καὶ τὸν ἰδίων μὲν, καὶ μαρτυρήσῃ ὁμολογησάντων, ὡς ἢ τὰς χαρὰς τῆς μαρτυρίας ἐκκλητοῦντων. τὸν δὲ ἃ βουλόμενον μαρτυρῆν, ἐκκλητοῦν, αἰαἴσχιον τῷ μαρτυρῆσαι προσκλήσῃς. ἐάν δὲ αὐτὸν ἢ μαρτυρῇ, ἢ ἐξομόσασθαι ὡς οὐκ εἰδείη ἢ μὴ πεῖσαι, ἢ χιλίας ἀπο-τίνειν. ἐκκλητοῦσθαι μὲν δεῖν ὅτι ὃ κελεύσαι εἰς μαρτυρίαν. ἐκκλητοῦσθαι δ', ὃ δι-καιῶ ὀφείλει, ὅτι ὃ τὰς χιλίας καταβαλεῖν. Ab Athenien-sibus acceperunt Romani Decemuiri, quorum hæc Lex fuit. QVOI. TESTIMONIVM. DEFVGERIT. IS. TERTIIS. DIEBVS. OB. PORTVM. OBVAGVLATVM. ITO. Athenien-sium autem Lex qua is, qui testimonium defugiebat, cogebatur in ius vocatus, aut testimonium, dare, aut eiurare, aut mille drachmas ærario publico pendere, hæc est.
units.tr: You have the law in Demosthenes, Against Timarchus. When someone is summoned from the house, for the one who was evident failed to give testimony in the presence of the others, the drachma of apomartyria is deposited and the law applies. Suidas relates that one who had been condemned in an apomartyria action was fined by the judge according to his standing; but whoever had brought the apomartyria suit, if the case fell, was fined the drachma he had deposited, that is, the sacramental drachma. In Suidas's words, the apomartyria suit was brought against the one who refused to testify, and the case was decided by the court; if the accuser lost, he paid the drachma. But Pollux, Book 8, chapter 6, writes that the one who shirked testimony was fined a thousand drachmas, and if he did not pay them, he was summoned to court, which they called ekklēton [ἐκκλητόν]. Before they wrote an apomartyria action, they went to the house of the one who shirked testimony and called out at his door: you have this procedure in the words of Demosthenes just quoted. Pollux alone teaches this clearly in the passage cited: the one who was summoned to testify, if he refused, or swore that he did not know or could not be persuaded, paid a thousand drachmas. He was summoned to give testimony as one obliged by the law, and summoned as a debtor to pay the thousand. The Roman Decemvirs took this law from the Athenians, and their law read: whoever shirks testimony, on the third day, let him go, summoned by a shout at the door. The Athenian law, by which the one who shirked testimony was compelled, when summoned to court, either to testify, or to swear, or to pay a thousand drachmas to the public treasury, is as follows.

units.la: Τὸν ἐκκλητοῦντα, ἢ μαρτυρῆν, ἢ ἐξομο-σασθαι, ἢ χιλίας δραχμὰς ἀποτίσαι τῷ δημοσίῳ. In ius vocatus testimonium, vel dato, vel eiurato, vel mille drachmis multator.
units.tr: The one summoned to court shall either testify, or swear, or pay a thousand drachmas to the public treasury. Summoned to court, he is to testify, or swear the oath, or be fined a thousand drachmas.

units.la: Meminit Demosthenes ὡς τοῦ κατὰ Τιμάρχου. ὅτι μὲν ὅτε ἐμαρτύρησεν, ὅτ' ἐξωμό-σατο καὶ τὸν νόμον.
