Æschines aduersus Timarchum. ἐπὶ δὲ δικαστηρίῳ ἐσμὲν, γρά-φομαι μαρτυρίαν Μισγόλα. & paullo post, de eodem Misgola, qui testimonium defugiebat: ἐὰν δ' ὁ τοῦ κατὰ τὸν ἐκκλητοῦντα μᾶλλον ἢ ἐλλη μαρτυρῇ, ὑμεῖς δ' ὅλον τῶν ἐγκαλεῖν σιωπᾶσθε. εἰ γὰρ ὁ νόμῳ τοῦ ἀξιοῦσθαι, ἡ τοῦ κατα-ρηκοῦ χιλίας δραχμὰς μᾶλλον ἀποτίσαι τῷ δημοσίῳ, ὥστε μὴ δίκαζε ὁ τοῦ κατὰ τὸν ἑαυτὸν ὑμῖν. & paullo post. ἐὰν δ' ἀρὰ ἐκκλεί-σῃ μόνῃ, πεπληγμένῃ ἢ ὅτι ὁ αἰσχύνεται, ὅτι ὃ ἐξομω-σασθαι τὰς ἀληθείας. Harpocration: λέγεσθαι κλητοῦσθαι καὶ ἐκκλητοῦσθαι ὅτι τὴν μαρτύρων, ὅταν μὴ ἐκκλοῦ-σαι ἐκκλησίαν ἢ τὸν ὅρκον, ἢ ἐκκλη-τοῦσθαι, ἐξ ὧν τὸν ἢ ἐχρησάντο ἑκατὸν χιλίας δραχμὰς, ὡς Ἰσαῖος ἐν τοῖς Ἐνάνδρου καὶ Φύωνος ἀποσασιοῦ. Suidas: ἐκκλητὸν ὃ εἰς κείσει ἀγών, ἵνα ἐπιμαίνηται τῆς μάρτυρος. ἐκκλητοῦσθαι, τὴν ἐγκαταλιπόντων μαρτυρίας τὰ ὀνόματα εἰς τὰς δικαστηρίας κηρύττειν[?].
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions in his speech Against Timarchus that when he testified, when he swore the oath, and the law... Aeschines, Against Timarchus: "Now we are in court; I indict Misgolas for testimony." And a little later, about the same Misgolas, who shirked testimony: if the one who is summoned rather than the other testifies, you remain silent about the accusation. For if by law he must be summoned to testify, or else pay a thousand drachmas to the public treasury, so that he does not judge... And a little later: if he is caught alone, having been struck or being ashamed, to swear the truth. Harpocration: they say "to be summoned" and "to be summoned out" for witnesses who, when they do not give the testimony or the oath, are summoned out, for which they paid a thousand drachmas, as Isaeus says in the speech on the estate of Endrus and Phyon. Suidas: ekklēton is the case brought so that one may be compelled to testify; to be summoned out is to proclaim in the courts the names of those who abandoned their testimony.

units.la: Erat & alia testimonii species, quae διαμαρτυρία proprie haec est Lex. Ἐξῆναι τῆς ἀντιδίκοις ΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝ-ΤΑΙ, ΔΙΑΜΑΡΤΥΡΕΙΝ. Litigantes, si libuerit, διαμαρτυρίᾳ utuntor.
units.tr: There was also another kind of testimony, properly called diamartyria [διαμαρτυρία], whose law reads: "Let it be permitted to the litigants, if they wish, to give diamartyria." Litigants may use diamartyria if they wish.

units.la: Demosthenes laudat ὡς τὰ πρὸς Λεωχάρην[?], ὥστε μὲν γὰρ οὐκ αἰσχύνεσθαι ἔχειν αἱ διαμαρτυρίαι[?], ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ προαιρέσεως καὶ βουλήσεως τῆς διαμαρτυρομένης γίνονται[?]. ἡ γὰρ ὁ νομοθέτης διελέγχειν αὐτὸ ἐποίησε τοῖς ἀντιδίκοις[?]. ἀλλ᾽ AN BOΥΛΩΝ-TAI, ΔΙΑΜΑΡΤΥΡΕΙΝ ἔδωκεν[?]. Est autem διαμαρτυρία, quando quis testatur ad Iudicium non eundum esse, vel eundum esse, de ea re, de qua controuersia mouetur: quo testimonio dicto, agebatur primum de eo aduersus illum, qui dixerat: neque erat rei tantum διαμαρτυρίας, sed etiam actoris, si libuisset. Grammatici: Ἔστιν τῆς ὑπὸ τῶν ἀξιώσεως ἡ διαμαρτυρία[?]. τοῦ γὰρ τὴν εἰσαγωγὴν τῷ δίκῃ εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον, ἐξὸν τοῦ βουλομένου διαμαρτυρήσαι ὡς εἰσαγώγιμος ἔστιν ἡ δίκη, ἡ οὐκ εἰσαγώγιμος[?]. Ibidem alibi: ἐαν ὃς πρέπει τὸν διαμαρτυρομένα μὴ εἰσαγώγιμον ἔστι ἡ δίκη, αὐτὸς μὲν γὰρ σκέπτει ἀγωνίζεται, ὁ γὰρ τὸν διαμαρτυρησόμενα ὁ ἀγὼν ἔστι. Quemadmodum autem necessario non iniungebatur litigantibus διαμαρτυρίᾳ, sed illorum arbitrio permittitur, ira etiam necessario non incumbit inuitis testibus διαμαρτυρίας dicere, neque poterant ἐκκλητὸς ἐξὸς. Demosthenes ὁ τὰ πρὸς Λεωχάρην ἀπελαύνομεν γὰρ ἕκαστος αὐτῶν τὸν ὁ δὲ διαμαρτυρησάμενος κίνδυνον οὐκ αἰσχυνθεὶς εἰσέρχεται[?].
units.tr: Demosthenes, in the speech against Leochares, says that diamartyriai do not bring shame, but arise from the choice and will of the one who testifies: for the lawgiver made them a means of refuting opponents, and granted them to whoever wished to testify. A diamartyria is when someone testifies that a case should or should not be brought to court concerning the matter in dispute. After such testimony had been given, the question was first contested with the one who had spoken, and it belonged not only to the defendant but also to the plaintiff, if he wished. The grammarians say: diamartyria is a challenge to the admissibility of the case, whether the suit can be brought into court or not, as the one who wishes may testify. Elsewhere in the same work: if the case cannot be brought against the one giving diamartyria, he himself contends, for the contest belongs to the one giving diamartyria. Just as litigants were not required to make a diamartyria but were left to their own judgment, so witnesses were not necessarily compelled against their will to give diamartyria, nor could they be summoned to court. Demosthenes, in the speech against Leochares: each of them drives the other away; but the one who gave diamartyria, not ashamed, enters into danger.

units.la: Testes, qui falsum testimonium dixissent, tenebantur falsi testimonii Lege, ii vero, qui eos produxerant, τῆς κακοτεχνίας.
units.tr: Witnesses who gave false testimony were bound by the law on false witness; but those who had produced them were bound by the law on kakotechnia [κακοτεχνία].

units.la: Ὁ μαρτυρήσας τὰ ψευδῆ ὑπόδικος ἔσται τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας[?]· καὶ ὁ παρακαλούμενος τὴν κακοτεχνίαν[?]. Testis, qui falsum dixerit, falsi testimonij Lege, qui vero produxerit, κακοτεχνίας, tenetor.
units.tr: A witness who has said false things shall be liable to the charge of false witness; and the one who urges him on is liable to kakotechnia. A witness who says falsehoods is liable under the law of false witness, and the one who produced him is liable for kakotechnia.

units.la: Post iudicia de re, quae controuertebatur, reddita, Legibus instituuntur actiones ψευδομαρτυρίας aduersus testes, & κακοτεχνίας aduersus illum, cui testimonium dixerant: idque recte atque ordine, cum iudices secundum testium fidem, vt plurimum pronuncient Demosthenes ὁ τὰ πρὸς Ευἐργον ἡ Μιναιθ[?]ν ψευδομαρτυρίας[?]. καλὰς μὲν δικαστὴν οἱ νόμοι ἐῶν, ὦ ἄνδρες δικασταί, ἀπολλύσθαι ἀγῶνα ἀποδιδόντις τῆς δίκης τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας[?], ἵνα, εἴ τις μαρτυρεῖ τὰ ψευδὴ μαρτυρούντως ἀξιοῦ[?] μὴ ἠμέλησε, μαρτυρίας ἀξίαν τῶν νόμων μαρτυρήσας, ἐξέπαυσαν τοῖς δικασταῖς, μηδὲν αὐτῷ πλέον ἡμῖν[?]. ἀλλ᾽ ὑπισκηφάμενος παρακαλούμενος τὰς μαρτυρίας ὁ ἀδικηθεὶς, ἡ εἰσελθὼν ὡς ὑμᾶς, ἡ ὑπαδεικνὺς ὡς ὁ τοῦ ἀγῶνος τοῖς μάρτυρας τὰ ψευδὴ μεμαρτυρηκότας, πρὸς τί τούτων δίκῳ λέξη, καὶ τὸν παρακαλούμενον ἐπὶ ἐκεῖνο ἔχειν τῆς κακοτεχνίας. καὶ ἀλλ᾽ ἔτι τῶν τοῦ μὲν δικαστῶν, ἐκλάπτω ἐπέδειξεν τὰ ὑπαρχόντα ἐαὶ ἡλῆθη[?]· ἵνα μὴ ἀξιῇ ὁ πλῆθος ἀποπέμποιτο διακεῖν τοὺς μάρτυρας τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας ὁ ἀδικούμενος· ταῦτ᾽ ἡ φήσῃ μεγάλας ἐπέδηχθη ἡμῶν ἐμωμείας, ἐαὶ ἀλῷ, καὶ δοκῇ ὑμῖν τὰ ψευδὴ μεμαρτυρηκέναι. καὶ δικαίως, ὦ ἄνδρες δικαστὰς ὑμεῖς γὰρ εἰς τοὺς μάρτυρας βλέποντες ἢ πιστεύοντες, οἷς ἂν ὅτι μαρτυρῶσι, ψηφίζεσθε. ἵνα οὖν μὴ ὑμεῖς ἐξαπατηθῶσι, μηδ' οἱ εἰσιόντες εἰς ὑμᾶς ἀδικήσωσι, δεῖ τοῦτα αὐτοῖς ὑποδικοῖς ἐπίσπον ὁ νομοθέτης. Legibus igitur instituuntur actiones ψευδομαρτυρίας aduersus testes: meminit Pollux Lib. VIII. ψευδομαρτυρίων [?] δίκη ἡ ψευδομαρτυρίας, ψευδομαρτύριον ἐλέγετο. Aduersus testes, inquam, tum μαρτυρῶν, cum συμμαρτυρῶν, vt liquet e verbis Demosthenis ἐν τῷ κατὰ Στεφάνου ψευδομαρτυριῶν β. καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς ὑποκρίσεως, τὸ τε μαρτυρίας, ἡ συμμαρτυρίαν ἀγανίζεσθαι ἅμα, ἵνα, ἐὰν μὲν ἀπαδεχθῇ ὁ μαρτυρήσας, ἐκεῖνος ὑποδίκως ἢ τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἀπαδεχθῇ, οἱ συμμαρτυρήσαντες τὴν συμμαρτυρίαν. Aduersus testes quoque συμμαρτυρῶν. Harpocration ἐπισκέπτεσθαι ὁ ψευδομαρτυρίαν ἡ τῆς συμμαρτυρίας, ὥσπερ καὶ τῆς μαρτυρίας. Isaeus: ἐν τοῖς περὶ τοῦ Διοφάνους κλήρου, μηδόντων δὲ ἡμῶν αἰτιώμενοι, συμμαρτύρησε Λεωχάρης ὅτι μὴ ὑπάδικον εἴη τὸν κλῆρον ἡμῖν. ἐπισκεψαμένων δὲ ἡμῶν, ἡ μὲν λῆξις τοῦ κλήρου διεξήλθη, ἡ δὲ τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας δίκη εἰσῆλ. Idque, cum si illi testi ob aliquam causam interdiceretur testimonium, ( quam Legem iam supra expofuimus. ) cum si falsa testaretur. Actori autem in hoc iudicio non admodum grauis pendenda erat multa, si testes falsi testimonij reos non peregisset: at contra seuere in reos animaduertebatur: nam non tantum de illorum pecunia, sed etiam dignitate agebatur: ignominiosi enim erant. Habes ista non tantum in praecedentibus Demosthenis ex Oratione contra Euergum & Mnesibulum verbis, sed etiam ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ἀφόβου ψευδομαρτυριῶν. ἀλλὰ δίκην δὲ μοι βλέψης ἐλέγχει, εἰ ψευδομαρτυριῶν ὑποδίκει αὐτὸν ἐποίησε τῷ ἀδελφοῦ, ἡ τοῦ ὁμοίου, ἐν τῇ ψευδομαρτυρίᾳ, ἡ τῆς τιμῆς δὲ ἐπιμελεῖ κινδυνεύουσιν. Atque haec primum conuicto ψευδομαρτυριῶν videtur fuisse prima capitis diminutio, ac fortefeterum. Nam demum ter conuicti ψευδομαρτυριῶν ὀλόκληρον ἀπέβαλον. Andocides ἐν τῷ κατὰ μυστηρίων ἐπεμψε ὁ, ὧν τὰ μὲν σώματα ἀτιμα, ἡ δὲ οὐσία ἔχει ἡ σκέπτεσθαι· ὅτι δὲ ἀπ' ἐκείνων, ἀπόσοι τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας ὀφλισκει ἐπὶ τούτων ἀτιμοῦσιν εἶ. Testes, qui in Areopagitarum iudicio testimonium dixerant, si falsi testimonij accusarentur, postulabantur apud Thesmothetas, qui iudices dabant. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. οἱ Θεσμοθέται δίκας τοὺς τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας ἐξ Ἀρείου πάγου εἰσάγειν. Aduersus illos, qui testes produxerant, quos τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας reos peregerant illi, aduersus quos testimonium dixerant, instituebatur ex hac Lege κακοτεχνιῶν actio. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμόθεον φοβούμενος, ἀλλ' μὲν μαρτυρίαν παρὰ-σχηται, ὡς ἐλαθέσθαι ὄντος, μὴ ὑποκρινάμενος ἐγὼ αὐτὸ τῆς ψευδομαρτυρίας, καὶ ἐξελέγξας τὰ ψευδῆ μεταρτυρικὰ Αἰγείωνα, ὅτι ποτὲ τῆς κακοτεχνίας ἐλθοιμι τὴν νόμον. Harpocration. Κακοτεχνιῶν, ὄνομα δίκης, ὡς οἱ ἐλόντες ἵνα ψευδομαρτυρίας τὸ παραχρῆμα αὐτὸ εἰδίδοσαν. Δημοσθένης ἐν ᾧ τῆς Τιμοθέου ποιῶς, εἰ γνώσιος, ἐν ᾧ τῆς ἐΥέρχου τῆς Μνησιβούλου. Pollux Lib. VIII. Αἰσίας ἡ κακοτεχνίας δίκην φησὶν εἶ. Apud Romanos Legibus XII. Tabularum, qui falsum testimonium dixisse conuictus erat, de rupe Tarpeia deiiciebatur. Refert Gellius Lib. XX. cap. I. Anputas, Phauorine, si non illa etiam ex XII. Tabulis de testimoniis falsis poena aboleuisset: & si nunc quoque, vt antea qui falsum testimonium dixisse conuictus esset, è saxo Tarpeio deiiceretur, mentituros fuisse pro testimonio tam multos, quam videmus? Sed id abiit in defuetudinem, vt testatur Gellius, nam neque quisquam de saxo praecipitatus est, ut scribit Modestinus Lib. XII. Pandectarum. Non potest quis sic damnari, ut de saxo praecipitetur. Leg. XXV. §. I. D. de poenis, & praeterea mutauit poenam: nam, ut est apud Paulum Lib. V. Sententiarum, qui falso, vel varie testimonia dixerunt, vel utrique parti prodiderunt: à iudicibus competenter puniuntur. Leg. XVI. D. de testibus. Quanquam istud, competenter, est à mala Triboniani manu: Paulus enim poenas definiuerat, ab eo quippe ita olim scriptum: Qui falso, vel varie testimonia dixerunt, vel utrique parti prodiderunt, aut in exilium aguntur, aut in insulam relegantur, aut curia submouentur. Extat Lib. V. Sententiarum Pauli Tit. XV. de testibus §. V. & eiusdem Libri Tit. XXV. ad Legem Corneliam testamentariam, §. V. Qui ob falsum testimonium perhibendum, vel verum non perhibendum, pecuniam acceperit, dederit, iudicemve ut sententiam ferat, vel non ferat, corruperit, corrumpendumve curauerit, humiliores capite puniuntur, honestiores publicatis bonis cum ipso iudice in insulam deportantur. Sed omnium harum poenarum vicem substituit Tribonianus, à iudicibus competenter puniuntur, id est, competendi poena, & quae veniat ex merito causae; Ratio, cur ita refinxerit Pauli verba Tribonianus, haec est, quod Constitutione Zenonis Imperatoris, quae scripta est ad Arcadium T T & data legitur XII. Kalen. Iun. Decio & Longino Conss. arbitrio iudicum permittitur poena falsi testimonij, pro qualitate videlicet delicti. Sed omnes qui in ciuili scilicet causa suum praebent testimonium, separato, & tanquam ante iudicium interim depositio exceptionis fori priuilegio, huiusmodi praesidio denudatos, ita ad iudicantis intrare secretum, ut quicunque aures eius offenderint, non dubitent sibimet formidandum, data cunctis iudicibus absque vllo praescriptionis obstaculo in testes, quorum voces falsitate vel fraude non carere perspexerint, pro qualitate videlicet delicti, animaduertendi licentia Leg. XIV. C. de testibus. Obtinebat autem haec Zenonis Lex, itaque ad illam Tribonianus Pauli verba refinxit.
units.tr: After the judgment on the matter in dispute has been given, the laws establish actions for false witness (ψευδομαρτυρία) against witnesses, and for trickery (κακοτεχνία) against the party for whom they gave testimony. This is done rightly and in order, since judges for the most part decide according to the credibility of the witnesses. Demosthenes, in his speech against Euergus and Mnesibulus, says: "Men of the jury, the laws rightly allow a suit for false witness to be brought against those who gave testimony, so that if anyone has testified falsely, he may be called to account, and that the judges may not be deceived, nor those who come before you be wronged." Accordingly, the laws establish actions for false witness against witnesses. Pollux, Book VIII: "A suit for false witness (ψευδομαρτυρίων δίκη) was called a ψευδομαρτύριον." I say against witnesses, both those who gave testimony (μαρτυρῶν) and those who gave joint testimony (συμμαρτυρῶν), as is clear from the words of Demosthenes in his second speech on false witness against Stephanus. From the same procedure, the action for giving testimony, or for joint testimony, was brought together, so that if the witness was convicted, he himself was liable to the suit for false witness; and if he was not convicted, those who had given joint testimony were. Harpocration also notes that a suit for false witness is brought against those who gave joint testimony, just as against those who gave testimony. Isaeus, in the speech about the estate of Diophantus: "When we were making our claim, Leocharis gave joint testimony that the estate was not liable to us. When we challenged him, the matter of the estate was carried through, and the suit for false witness was brought." This happened when a witness was forbidden to testify for some cause (which law we have already set out above), and when he testified falsely. In this kind of suit the plaintiff did not need to be very concerned about the fine, if he failed to prosecute the witnesses for false testimony; on the contrary, the guilty were punished severely, for not only their money but also their standing was at stake, since they became infamous. You have these points not only in the words of Demosthenes just quoted from the speech against Euergus and Mnesibulus, but also in his speech against Aphobus. But look at what he says in his speech against... that the man who was convicted of false witness was made liable for it, whether he was a brother or a kinsman, and that they were in danger of losing their honour. And this first conviction for false witness seems to have been the first loss of civic status (capitis diminutio), and perhaps of nothing more. For only after three convictions for false witness did a man lose his full rights. Andocides, in his speech on the mysteries: their bodies are dishonoured, but their property remains intact; and from them, all who are convicted of false witness are deprived of their rights. Witnesses who had given testimony before the Areopagite court, if they were accused of false testimony, were brought before the Thesmothetae, who appointed the judges. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: "The Thesmothetae brought suits for false witness from the Areopagus." Against those who had produced the witnesses, whom the accused had made liable for false witness, the action for trickery (κακοτεχνία) was brought under this same law. Demosthenes, in his speech against Timotheus: "I fear that if he has given testimony, as if it were true, and I have not accused him of false witness, and have not exposed the false testimony of Aegeon, he will be liable to the suit for trickery." Harpocration: "κακοτεχνία, the name of a suit, in which those who lost were at once fined for false witness." Demosthenes, in his speech on the estate of Timotheus, and in his speech against Euergus and Mnesibulus. Pollux, Book VIII: "Aeschines says the suit for trickery..." Among the Romans, under the Twelve Tables, a man convicted of having given false testimony was thrown from the Tarpeian Rock. Gellius reports this, Book XX, chapter I: Do you think, Favorinus, that if the penalty for false testimony had not been abolished by that provision of the Twelve Tables, and if even now, as before, a man convicted of giving false testimony were thrown from the Tarpeian rock, so many would lie in giving testimony as we see? But that custom has fallen into disuse, as Gellius attests. For no one has been hurled from the rock, as Modestinus writes in Book XII of the Pandects: No one can be condemned in such a way that he is thrown from a rock. de poenis, Law XXV, §1. And besides, the penalty has been changed. For, as Paulus has it in Book V of the Sentences: those who have given false or inconsistent testimony, or have betrayed both parties, are punished appropriately by the judges. de testibus, Law XVI. Yet this word "appropriately" comes from the bad hand of Tribonian, for Paulus had defined the penalties himself, since it was once written by him thus: "Those who gave false or inconsistent testimony, or betrayed both parties, are either sent into exile, or relegated to an island, or removed from the senate." This is found in Book V of the Sentences of Paulus, title XV, de testibus, §5, and in the same book, title XXV, ad Legem Corneliam testamentariam, §5: Whoever has received money, or given it, or corrupted a judge to pronounce or not to pronounce sentence, or has arranged for such corruption, to give false testimony or to withhold true testimony, is punished by beheading if he is of lower rank, and if of higher rank is deported to an island with the judge himself, his goods being confiscated. But Tribonian substituted for all these penalties the words are punished appropriately by the judges, that is, a penalty suited to the offence and arising from the merits of the case. The reason why Tribonian altered Paulus's words in this way is this: by a constitution of the Emperor Zeno, written to Arcadius and dated the twelfth day before the Kalends of June in the consulship of Decius and Longinus, the penalty for false testimony was left to the discretion of the judges, according to the nature of the offence. But all who in a civil case give their evidence, separated and as if before the trial, stripped of this safeguard by the privilege of the court of exception, so enter the secret chamber of the judge that whoever offends his ears should not doubt that he has reason to fear; all judges being given, without any obstacle of prescription, the licence to punish the witnesses, whose statements they have found not free from falsehood or fraud, according to the nature of the offence. Law XIV, C. de testibus. This law of Zeno was in force, and so Tribonian recast the words of Paulus to fit it.

units.la: DE RE IUDICATA ET INTEGRI RESTITUTIONE.
units.tr: On a Matter Adjudged and Restitution in Integrum

units.la: TITULUS OCTAVUS.
units.tr: TITLE EIGHT.

units.la: REBUS iudicatis standum esse, rescripsit Imperator Antoninus Augustus Stellatori, Leg. I. C. de re iudicata: alioqui nullus esset litium finis, inquit idem Imperator Pacatiano, Leg. II. C. eod. itaque post rem iudicatam nihil quaeritur, Leg. LVI. D. eod. Res autem iudicata dicitur, inquit Modestinus Lib. VII. Pandectarum, quae finem controuersiarum pronunciatione iudicis accipit, quod vel condemnatione vel absolutione contigit, Leg. I. D. eod. Atque haec quoque fuit Atheniensium Lex:
units.tr: Matters adjudged must stand, as the Emperor Antoninus Augustus rescripted to Stellator (Cod. I, de re iudicata). Otherwise, there would be no end of lawsuits, says the same Emperor to Pacatianus (Cod. II, same title). Therefore after a matter is adjudged, nothing more is sought (Dig. LVI, same title). A res iudicata, says Modestinus in Book VII of the Pandects, is that which reaches an end of disputes by the pronouncement of a judge, which happens either by condemnation or by acquittal (Dig. I, same title). This was also a law of the Athenians:

units.la: ΟΣΩΝ ΔΙΚΗ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΓΕΝΕΤΟ Η ΕΥΘΥΝΑ Η ΔΙΑΔΙΚΑΣΙΑ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΩι Η ΙΔΙΑ, Η ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ, Η
units.tr: Whatever case or arbitration was previously decided before the judges in court, whether private or public [ΟΣΩΝ ΔΙΚΗ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΓΕΝΕΤΟ Η ΕΥΘΥΝΑ Η ΔΙΑΔΙΚΑΣΙΑ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΩι Η ΙΔΙΑ, Η ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ, Η]

units.la: De quibus prius siue priuato, siue publico iudicio à iudicibus pronunciatum est,
units.tr: Concerning those matters which were earlier pronounced upon by judges, whether in a private or a public suit,

units.la: ΤΟ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ ΑΠΕΔΟΤΟ, ΜΗ ΕΙΣΑΓΕΙΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ, ΜΗΔ' ΕΠΙΨΗΦΙΖΕΙΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ, ΜΗΔΕ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΕΙΝ ΕΩΝΤΩΝ, Α ΟΥΚ ΕΩΣΙΝ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΙ.
units.tr: THE PUBLIC DECREE: NOT TO BRING THESE MATTERS INTO COURT AGAIN, NOR TO PUT THEM TO A VOTE, NOR TO ACCUSE ANYONE OVER THEM, WHERE THE LAWS DO NOT ALLOW IT [ΤΟ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ ΑΠΕΔΟΤΟ, ΜΗ ΕΙΣΑΓΕΙΝ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΝ, ΜΗΔ' ΕΠΙΨΗΦΙΖΕΙΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΜΗΔΕΝΑ, ΜΗΔΕ ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΕΙΝ ΕΩΝΤΩΝ, Α ΟΥΚ ΕΩΣΙΝ ΟΙ ΝΟΜΟΙ.]

units.la: aut populus fcitum fecit, de iifdem iterum Magistratus Iudices ne danto, neque in suffragia mittunto, neque eorum, quæ Leges non concedunt, accusare permittunto.
units.tr: Or the people made a decree: concerning the same matters, let the magistrates and judges not hear them again, nor put them to a vote, nor allow anyone to accuse over those things which the laws do not permit.

units.la: Legem ἀξιλεξίᾳ [?] defcripfit in Timocratea Demofthenes : λέγει τὸν μὲν τούτων ἐφεξῆς νόμον. ΟΣΩΝ ΔΙΚΗ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΓΕΝΕΤΟ, &c. Cauet hac Lege Legiflator , femel lite terminata , de eadem re iterum ne detur actio. Eiufdem Legis meminit iterum paullo post ibidem Demofthenes : ὁ μὲν γὰρ οὐκ ἐᾷ, καὶ ὢν ἅπαξ γὰρ ὁ δικαστὴς πάλιν χρῆμα ζητεῖν [?]. Plato in Critone. ἐπὶ γὰρ τούτου τοῦ νόμου ἀπολλύμεθα [?], ὡς ἐξ ἴσης ἐξ δικαιοσύνης [?] ἀποστερήσει ἐξ ἕνεκα [?]. Terentius Phormione Actu II. Scenæ III.
units.tr: Demosthenes, in his speech against Timocrates, quotes this law and says: "He states the first of these laws in sequence: whatever case was previously decided..." [ΟΣΩΝ ΔΙΚΗ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΓΕΝΕΤΟ, &c.] The lawgiver, once a suit is ended, forbids that an action be brought again on the same matter. Demosthenes mentions the same law again shortly after in the same place: "For he does not allow it; once the judge has decided, he may not seek the matter again" [ὁ μὲν γὰρ οὐκ ἐᾷ, καὶ ὢν ἅπαξ γὰρ ὁ δικαστὴς πάλιν χρῆμα ζητεῖν]. Plato in the Crito: "For under this law we perish" [ἐπὶ γὰρ τούτου τοῦ νόμου ἀπολλύμεθα], and so on. Terence, Phormio, Act II, Scene III:

units.la: Attu, qui sapiens es, Magistratus adi,
units.tr: Attat, you who are wise, go to the magistrates,

units.la: Iudicium de eadem causa iterum vt reddant tibi:
units.tr: so that they may give you a hearing again on the same cause;

units.la: Quandoquidem solus regnas, & soli licet.
units.tr: since you alone reign, and only you are permitted.

units.la: Hic de eadem causa bis iudicium adipiscier.
units.tr: Here, on the same cause, you would get a second judgment.

units.la: Quare secundum ius hac Lege constitutum Demiphoni consulebat Hegio, dicebatque Scena sequenti:
units.tr: Hence Hegio, advising Demipho on the right set down by this law, said in the following scene:

units.la: Mihi non videtur, quod fit factum Legibus,
units.tr: It does not seem to me that what has been done by the laws

units.la: Refcindi posse : & turpe incaptu est.
units.tr: can be rescinded; and it is shameful to make a start on it again.

units.la: Donatus ad Terentij Andriam Actu III. Scena I. Hæc res secundum ius simile dicitur, in quo cauetur, ne quis rem actam apud iudices repetat.
units.tr: Donatus on Terence's Andria, Act III, Scene I: This matter is called "according to a similar law," in which it is provided that no one shall seek again a case already tried before the judges.

units.la: ΔΙΚΗ autem in hac Lege est, ἡ περὶ ἐληλυθότων, vt ex gr. Iudicium de adulterio, malæ tractationis, &c. Vlpianus: δίκη κακῶς, τὸν περὶ ἐληλυθότων, ᾗ, περὶ μοιχείας, eaque est, vel ΙΔΙΑ, vt in hac Lege habes, id est, ἰδιωτικὴ, vel ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ, quando κοινὸν ἀπόφυγον ἐλεγχθεὶς ἐστὶ καὶ δημόσιος ἀδίκημα, καὶ πάντων ἐξέστι κατηγορῆσαι τῆς ἀδικούντος. Addit Legislator H ΕΥΘΥΝΑ, id est, interprete eodem Vlpiano , ὑπόλογία ὧν τῶς δημοσίας πεπομένης [?] ἀδικήσει, vt si quis Magistratum gessit, aut legationem obiuit, &c. Sequitur ΔΙΑΔΙΚΑΣΙΑ; Vox proprie significat litem ἡ χρηματῶν, ἡ περὶ κτημάτων. Vlpianus ad hanc Timocrateam paullo ante : Διαδικασία δὲ τῆς ἀναμνήσεως, ἡ ὅτι ὁ ἀνὴρ ἀπὸ δίκης ἡ χρημάτων, ἡ περὶ κτημάτων. Non licebat igitur per hanc Legem eadem de causa , siue ΔΙΚΗ, siue ΔΙΑΔΙΚΑΣΙΑ foret, bis Iudicium adipisci. Demosthenes in Leptinea: οἱ νόμοι δὲ, ὅτι ἐάν δὲ ἐξ τὸν αὐτὸν [?] ἀγὼν, οὔτε δίκῃ, οὔτε Διαδικασίας, οὔτε ἄλλο ξίωσιν οὐδὲν [?]. Vlpianus: δὲς περὶ τὴν αὐτὴν οὐ δὲ δικάζεσθαι. Idem ἐν τοῦ περὶ Νεαιράσθ. οἱ νόμοι δὲ οὐ ζωῦτα λέγεσιν, ἀλλ' ἁπαξ περὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ἀγὼν τῶν αὐτῶν [?] τῆς δίκης. Andocides ἐν τοῦ χ' Ἀλκιβιάδου, ἀλλως τε καὶ τὴν νόμου ἀπο- γραφόντων εἰς περὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἀγῶν, μὴ εἴξειν δικάζεσθαι. At tamen apud eundem Terentium loco proxime laudato Cratinus aduocatus confulenti Demiphoni respondit, nuptias ab Antiphone iudicum sententia damnato contractas cum Phanio non posse confistere:
units.tr: The suit under this law is the one concerning those things that have happened, for example a suit for adultery, for ill-treatment, and so on. Ulpian: "the suit concerning past events, such as concerning adultery" [δίκη κακῶς, τὸν περὶ ἐληλυθότων, ᾗ, περὶ μοιχείας]. And it is either a PRIVATE suit, as you have in this law, that is, idiotike [ἰδιωτικὴ], or a PUBLIC suit, when the offence is a common crime and a public wrong, and it is permitted to accuse the wrongdoer to all. The lawgiver adds "the proceeding" [ΕΥΘΥΝΑ], that is, according to the same Ulpian, the accountability of those who have committed a public wrong, as when someone has held a magistracy or discharged an embassy, and so on. There follows "the arbitration" [ΔΙΑΔΙΚΑΣΙΑ]. The word properly means a suit concerning money or property. Ulpian, a little before, on this Timocratean law: "arbitration is the examination of a man in a suit about money or property." So under this law it was not allowed, in the same matter, whether it was a DIKE or a DIADIKASIA, to obtain a judgment twice. Demosthenes in the Leptinea: "The laws say that if there is a contest over the same thing, neither by suit nor by arbitration nor otherwise may it be contested." Ulpian: "it is not permitted to litigate twice about the same thing." The same, in the speech against Neaera: "The laws do not say this only once, but that a contest over the same matter, of the same suit, is not to be fought." Andocides, in the speech on the Mysteries, that the laws do not permit a suit on the same matter to be fought again once it has been recorded. Yet in the same Terence, in the passage just quoted, Cratinus, the advisor, answered Demipho, who consulted him, that a marriage with Phanium, contracted by Antipho after he had been condemned by the judges' sentence, could not stand:

units.la: --Mihi
units.tr: --To me

units.la: Sic hoc videtur: quod te ab absente hic filius Egit, restitui in integrum æquum est & bonum: Et id impetrabis.
units.tr: It seems so: that since your son sued you in your absence, it is just and good to restore you to your former position; and you will obtain it.

units.la: Istud, inquam, non repugnat Legi, de qua hactenus egimus: nam
units.tr: This, I say, does not contradict the law we have discussed so far, for

units.la: --- si cognata est maxime
units.tr: --- if she is very much a relative,

units.la: Non fuit necesse habere.
units.tr: it was not necessary to have her.

units.la: Sententia Iudicum,
units.tr: The sentence of the judges:

units.la: --- sed, quod Lex iubet,
units.tr: --- but what the law orders,

units.la: Dotem dare.
units.tr: to give a dowry.

units.la: Non potuit enim damnari Antipho ad contrahendas cum Phanio nuptias ἐπικλῆρος[?], sed damnatus fuerat proculdubio à iudicibus, aut Phanium, itidem ut cognata si esset, in uxorem ducere, aut dotem ei dare: cui postremæ parti sententiæ stare vult Antiphonem Demipho, idque à iudicibus impetratu-rum Demiphonem arbitratur Cratinus, non tam, puto, secundum ius Atti-cum, quam ciuile Romanorum: quia nuptiæ consistere non possunt, inquit Paulus Lib. XXXV. ad Edictum, nisi consentiant omnes, id est, qui coëunt, quorum-que in potestate sunt. Leg. II. D. de ritu nuptiarum. itemque nuptiæ, scribente Iuliano Lib. XVI. Digestorum, inter easdem personas nisi volentibus parentibus re-nouatæ iustæ non habentur. Leg. XVIII. D. eod. Id fuisse mentis Demiphonis & sententiæ, cui accedit Cratinus, colligere est è iurgio eius cum Phormione:
units.tr: For Antipho could not have been condemned to contract marriage with Phanium as an heiress [ἐπικλῆρος]; but he had undoubtedly been condemned by the judges either to take Phanium as his wife, if she were a relative, or to give her a dowry. Demipho wishes to hold to this last part of the sentence, and Cratinus thinks the judges would obtain this for Demipho, not, I think, according to Attic law so much as the civil law of the Romans. For, says Paul in Book XXXV on the Edict, marriages cannot stand unless all consent, that is, those who come together and those under whose power they are (Dig. II, de ritu nuptiarum). Likewise, as Julian writes in Book XVI of the Digest, marriages between the same persons, unless the parents are willing, are not held to be valid when renewed (Dig. XVIII, same title). That this was Demipho's mind and opinion, in which Cratinus agrees, may be gathered from his quarrel with Phormio:

units.la: Etsi mihi facta iniuria st, verumtamen Potius quam lites secter[?], aut quam te audiam: Itidem ut cognata si sit, id quod Lex iubet Dotem dare, abduce hanc, minas quinque accipe.
units.tr: Although I have been wronged, yet rather than pursue lawsuits, or listen to you: just as if she were a relative, which the law orders, to give a dowry, take her away, and accept five minae.

units.la: & paullo post Phormioni respondet, & altercatur, quæ omnino hic sunt ad-scribenda sunt, quia sententiam nostram confirmant, & quædam emendan-da sunt:
units.tr: And shortly after he answers Phormio and argues back. All of this must be written out here, because it confirms our opinion, and some things need correcting:

units.la: -- DEM. Non agam? imo haut desinam, Donec perfecero hoc. PHOR. Ineptis. DEM. Sine modo.
units.tr: DEM. Shall I not act? Indeed, I will not stop until I have accomplished this. PHOR. You're being silly. DEM. Just let me.

units.la: PHOR. Postremo tecum nihil rei nobis Demipho'st: Tuus est damnatus gnatus, non tu: nam tua Præterierat iam ad ducendum ætas. DEM. Omnia hæc Illum putato, quæ ego nunc dico, dicere: Aut quidem cum uxore hac, ipsum prohibebo domo.
units.tr: PHOR. In the end, Demipho has nothing to do with you: your son is the one condemned, not you, for your age for marrying had already passed. DEM. Take it that he is the one saying all these things I now say: indeed, I will forbid him my house with this wife.

units.la: GE. Iratus est. PHOR. Tute idem feceris melius.
units.tr: GE. He is angry. PHOR. You yourself would do better to do the same.

units.la: Nam Demipho testatur se Antiphonem, nisi idem secum dicat, ab-dicaturum, & domo prohibiturum cum uxore hac Phanio, quod magis fuit pro Romanorum Legibus, quam Atheniensium institutis. Verum orationi Demiphonis extremæ quod respondet Phormio, Tute idem feceris melius, nemo est, meo quidem iudicio, qui commode possit interpretari è Donati Commentariis: Rescribendum esse puto.
units.tr: For Demipho declares that he will disinherit Antipho, unless he says the same as himself, and will forbid him the house with this wife Phanium. This was more in keeping with the laws of the Romans than with Athenian institutions. But as for Phormio's answer to Demipho's final speech, "You yourself would do better to do the same," no one, in my judgment, can readily explain it from Donatus's commentaries. I think it must be rewritten:

units.la: Tute idem[?] ! feceris melius.
units.tr: You yourself, the same, would have done better.

units.la: Hoc sensu, Tune, id, quod modo interminatus es, Antiphonem tua prohibebis domo cum uxore hac? hem! longe consultius meliusque facies, quam quod minitaris. Sed haec satis, ad Legis enim interpretationem redeundum est.
units.tr: In this sense: "Will you forbid Antipho your house with this wife, which you have just threatened? Hem! You would do far more wisely and better than what you threaten." But enough of this; we must return to the interpretation of the law.

units.la: Cum saepe mutasset Atheniensium status & πολιτεία, factum est, ut quasi de nouo iterumque Lex haec rogaretur ac ferretur.
units.tr: Since the status and polity of the Athenians had often changed, it came about that this law was, as it were, proposed and carried anew, as if for the first time.

units.la: ΤΑΣ ΔΙΚΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΔΙΑΙΤΑΣ ΟΣΑΙ ΕΓΕΝΟΝΤΟ ΕΠΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΟΥΜΕΝΗΙ ΠΟΛΕΙ ΚΥΡΙΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ. ΟΠΟΣΑ Δ' ΕΠΙ ΤΩΝ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΓΡΑΧΘΗ Η ΔΙΚΗ ΕΔΙΚΑΣΘΗ ΙΔΙΑΙ Η ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑΙ ΑΚΥΡΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ.
units.tr: The judgments and arbitrations which were made under the laws while the city was a democracy shall be valid. But whatever was decided, by private or public suit, after the Thirty had been written down, shall be void [ΤΑΣ ΔΙΚΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΔΙΑΙΤΑΣ ΟΣΑΙ ΕΓΕΝΟΝΤΟ ΕΠΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΟΥΜΕΝΗΙ ΠΟΛΕΙ ΚΥΡΙΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ. ΟΠΟΣΑ Δ' ΕΠΙ ΤΩΝ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΕΓΡΑΧΘΗ Η ΔΙΚΗ ΕΔΙΚΑΣΘΗ ΙΔΙΑΙ Η ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑΙ ΑΚΥΡΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ.]

units.la: Legem describsit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτους. λέγει δ' ἐπεγγνόμου νόμου. ΤΑΣ ΔΙΚΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΔΙΑΙΤΑΣ, &c. Partem eius laudat Andocides ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν μυστηρίων. ΤΑΣ ΔΕ ΔΙΚΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΔΙΑΙΤΑΣ ΚΥΡΙΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΟΠΟΣΑΙ ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΟΥΜΕΝΗΙ ΠΟΛΕΙ ΕΓΕΝΟΝΤΟ, ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ. Τὰς δὲ δίκας, ὦ ἄνδρες, [illegible, ~60 letters] Atque in hac, quam descripsit Andocides, parte omisit ista verba, ΕΠΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ, quae non erant omittenda. Est autem verbum ΕΠΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ. Ex legibus, sic accipiendum: tam ex Legum sententia, quam ex verbis. Leg. VI. D. de verborum significatione. Quanquam cum prolatis constitutionibus, inquit Callistratus Lib. III. Cognitionum, contra eas pronunciat iudex, eo quod non existimat causam, de qua iudicat, per eas iuuari: non videtur contra constitutiones sententiam dedisse. Leg. XXXII. D. de re iudicata. Atque haec verbum ΕΠΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ expressit Hegio Terentianus.
units.tr: Demosthenes wrote out this law in his speech against Timocrates, where he says that it was an amended law: "The suits and arbitrations..." [ΤΑΣ ΔΙΚΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΔΙΑΙΤΑΣ, &c.] Andocides quotes part of it in his speech on the Mysteries: "The suits and arbitrations, as many as took place under the laws in the democratic city, shall be valid, and the laws are to be used from the archonship of Euclides. But the suits, gentlemen, [illegible]" [ΤΑΣ ΔΕ ΔΙΚΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΔΙΑΙΤΑΣ ΚΥΡΙΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΟΠΟΣΑΙ ΕΝ ΔΗΜΟΚΡΑΤΟΥΜΕΝΗΙ ΠΟΛΕΙ ΕΓΕΝΟΝΤΟ, ΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ.] But in the part Andocides transcribes he left out those words, "under the laws" [ΕΠΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ], which should not have been omitted. The phrase "under the laws" must be understood thus: both according to the sense of the laws and according to their words. Dig. VI, de verborum significatione. Although, says Callistratus in Book III of the Cognitiones, when constitutions are cited and the judge pronounces against them because he does not think the case he is deciding is helped by them, he does not seem to have given a sentence against the constitutions (Dig. XXXII, de re iudicata). It was this phrase, "under the laws," that Terence's Hegio expressed.

units.la: Mihi non videtur, quod sit factum Legibus Rescindi posse. id est, ἡ δίκη τῷ ἀμφοτέρων ΕΠΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ἄκυρον εἶναι.
units.tr: It does not seem to me that what has been done can be rescinded by the laws, that is, that the judgment is void according to the laws (ἡ δίκη τῷ ἀμφοτέρων ΕΠΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΝΟΜΟΙΣ ἄκυρον εἶναι).

units.la: Lex haec lata est, post exactos Athenis Triginta Tyrannos, in Praetura Euclidis, aut anno si forte sequenti. Duo autem illius sunt Kapita: priori cautur, ne quis rem actam, libera Republica, apud Iudices vel Arbitros repetat. Ulpianus: ἐάν τις ἐν ταῖς δίκαις τὰς κρίσεις ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, εἴτε ἰδιωτικὰς, [?] Διαιτητῶν πρὸς λαβούσας. Alterum Legis Kaput sancit, acta sub Triginta Tyrannis esse irrita, quaecumque demum illa sint: καὶ ἐγὼ τῶν ἄλλων ἄχρι τὰ ὅτι τῆς Τειάκοντα, inquit Æschines ἐν δὲ τῷ Τιμάρχου. Erat namque ἀναρχία Ἀθηναίων, ut signant Fasti. Quare iudicia reddita Triginta Tyrannis rerum Athenis potientibus, irrita sunt, eorumque dantur in integrum restitutiones, sive ἀδίκοι δίκαι, propter maximam illam malitiam, ut Labeonis vocem usurpem, eorum, qui tunc Rempublicam gerebant. Hanc causam restitutionis in integrum ut & alteram expressit Hesychius his verbis. ἀδίκοι. οὕτως ἐλέγοντο οἱ
units.tr: This law was passed after the Thirty Tyrants had been driven out of Athens, in the archonship of Euclides, or perhaps in the year following. It has two chapters. The first provides that no one shall bring again before judges or arbitrators a matter decided while the republic was free. Ulpian: if anyone in lawsuits brings the decisions made in the court, whether private ones [...] having received them from arbitrators [ἐάν τις ἐν ταῖς δίκαις τὰς κρίσεις ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, εἴτε ἰδιωτικὰς, [?] Διαιτητῶν πρὸς λαβούσας]. The second chapter declares void the acts done under the Thirty Tyrants, whatever they may have been. Aeschines says: and I [say] of the others, up to the time of the Thirty [καὶ ἐγὼ τῶν ἄλλων ἄχρι τὰ ὅτι τῆς Τειάκοντα], in the speech against Timarchus [ἐν δὲ τῷ Τιμάρχου]. For there was anarchy at Athens [ἀναρχία Ἀθηναίων], as the Fasti indicate. Hence the judgments delivered while the Thirty held power at Athens are void, and restitutions in integrum are granted against them, as unjust judgments [ἀδίκοι δίκαι], on account of the great wickedness, to use Labeo's word, of those who then governed the state. Hesychius also expressed this ground for restitution in integrum, as well as the other, in these words: unjust: thus were called those [ἀδίκοι. οὕτως ἐλέγοντο οἱ].

units.la: Iudicia arbitriae quacumque, libera Republica, ex Legibus pronunciata, rata sunto. Acta vero, Triginta Tyrannis rerum potientibus, & iudicia, sive privatim, sive publice reddita, rescindunto. [illegible, ~40 letters] εἰς ἀξίωσιν εἰκηπαλμένοι ἢ [?] πολιτικῶν αἰτίας. ἡ τῶν μαρτύρων ἀλλί-[?] τῶν ψευδομαρτυρίων. Postrema ista docent, conuictis atque damnatis testibus falsi testimonij dari integri restitutionem, id est, redintegrandæ causæ actionem, iterumque licebat experiri iudicio: quod & scripsit Harpocration: αἰ-[?]δικίας ἐκίσεως, ὁ ἀ[?]ωγὴν δικαζόμενος, ὅταν ἀλῶσιν οἱ μάρτυρες ψευδομαρτυρεῖν. Eadem habet Suidas, qui é nescio quo scriptore, cuius verba refert, exemplum in hanc rem, si quid iudico, adfert. ἀδίκως τὰ δικαιωθέντα παισὶ, αἰσχροκερδείας ἠσπάσθη. Agit enim de quodam teste, qui conuictus fuerat αἰσχροκερδείας, id est, pecuniam ob falsum testimonium perhibendum accepisse, qua re fecerit iudicium prius redditum irritum, id est, ἀδίκως τὰ δικαιωθέντα. Vide autem diligenter ne confundas, quod viro summo Budæo accidit, cum actione, quæ dicebatur μὴ ἕσα. Nam hæc actio μὴ ἕσα dabatur iis, qui deseruissent litem contestatam ad purgandam moram, & excusandum eremodicium: præstabaturque hac actione restauratio eremodicii. At vero ἀδίκως δίκη, siue redintegrandæ causæ actio dabatur post finitam, iudicio litem, sed iudicium illud irritum fiebat, vel ἐκ πολιτικῶν αἰτίας, ἀπαρχίας scilicet, vel quia testes salsum pro testimonio in ea causa dixisse conuicti fuerant: qua de causa dandam esse integri restitutionem rescripsit Diuus Hadrianus, vt refert Callistratus Lib.V. Cognitionum. Diuus Hadrianus aditus per libellum à Juliano Tarentino, & iudicante (γρ. indicante) eo, falsis testimoniis, conspiratione aduersariorum testibus pecunia corruptis, religionem iudicis circumuentam esse, in integrum causam restituendam in hac verba rescripsit: Exemplum libelli dati mihi à Iuliano Tarentino missi tibi iussi. Tu, si tibi probauerit, conspiratione aduersariorum, & testibus pecunia corruptis oppressum se, & rem seuere vindica, & si qua à iudice tam malo exemplo circumscripto iudicata sunt, in integrum restitue. Leg. XXXIII. D. de re iudicata.
units.tr: Judgments of arbitrators, whatever they were, pronounced under the laws while the republic was free, shall stand. Acts, however, done while the Thirty Tyrants held power, and judgments, whether given in private or in public, shall be rescinded. [illegible, about forty letters] ... of civil causes; or of witnesses ... of false testimonies. These last points show that when witnesses were convicted and condemned for false testimony, restitution in integrum was granted, that is, an action to renew the cause, and it was permitted to try the case again in court. Harpocration also wrote to this effect: the one who brings an action for a judgment, when the witnesses are convicted of giving false testimony [αἰ-[?]δικίας ἐκίσεως, ὁ ἀ[?]ωγὴν δικαζόμενος, ὅταν ἀλῶσιν οἱ μάρτυρες ψευδομαρτυρεῖν]. Suidas has the same, and from some writer whose words he quotes he gives an example to the point, if I am right: unjustly the things adjudged were [overturned], he was caught in shameful gain [ἀδίκως τὰ δικαιωθέντα παισὶ, αἰσχροκερδείας ἠσπάσθη]. He is speaking of a certain witness who had been convicted of shameful gain [αἰσχροκερδείας], that is, of having accepted money for giving false testimony, and by that deed the earlier judgment was made void, that is, unjustly the things adjudged [ἀδίκως τὰ δικαιωθέντα]. Take care, however, not to confuse this with what happened to the most distinguished Budaeus, with the action called mē ... [μὴ ἕσα]. That action was given to those who had abandoned a joined suit in order to clear a delay and excuse their non-appearance, and by this action the restoration of non-appearance was obtained. But the unjust suit [ἀδίκως δίκη], or action to renew the cause, was given after the suit had been finished by judgment, and that judgment became void either on account of civil causes, namely [...], or because witnesses had been convicted of having spoken falsely in that case. For this reason the Divine Hadrian rescripted that restitution in integrum should be granted, as Callistratus reports in Book V of the Cognitiones. The Divine Hadrian, approached by petition from Julianus of Tarentum, and the judge (another reading: indicating) having been circumvented by false testimony, by a conspiracy of the opponents and witnesses bribed with money, and the judge's conscientiousness having been circumvented, rescripted in these words for the cause to be restored in integrum: I have ordered a copy of the petition given to me by Julianus of Tarentum to be sent to you. If it proves to you that he was oppressed by a conspiracy of his opponents and by witnesses bribed with money, vindicate the matter strictly, and whatever has been adjudged by a judge circumvented by such a bad example, restore in integrum. Leg. XXXIII. D. de re iudicata.

units.la: [?]ege veteri erat constitutum, ne duplex reo irrogaretur poena:
units.tr: By an ancient law it was laid down that the accused should not be given a double penalty.

units.la: Μηδὲν ἡμῖν τίμημα ὑπαρχὴν ὅτι χεί-[?] σθαι πλέον, ἢ ἐν, ὑπόπεσον δὲ ὁ δικαστὴς τίμωρον, παλιν, ἢ ὑπόπεσον, ἀμφότερα δὲ, μὴ ἐξεῖναι.
units.tr: Let there be no penalty imposed on us beyond one; the judge may not impose one penalty and then another again, nor both together. [Μηδὲν ἡμῖν τίμημα ὑπαρχὴν ὅτι χεῖσθαι πλέον, ἢ ἕν, ὑπόπεσον δὲ ὁ δικαστὴς τίμωρον, πάλιν, ἢ ὑπόπεσον, ἀμφότερα δὲ, μὴ ἐξεῖναι.]

units.la: Poena plures una ne irrogantor, quancumque instixerint iudices luendam, siue in corpore, siue in ære: vtramque simul ne irrogantor.
units.tr: Let not more than one penalty be imposed, whatever penalty the judges have decided must be paid, whether on the body or in money; let not both be imposed at the same time.

units.la: Legis huius meminit in Leptinea Demosthenes, ὡς γὰρ ἐστιν ἐπίθετον ἡμᾶς ἀδικοῦντα ἐν ἐκείνῳ τίμημα ὑπαρχὴν ἀρχῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου, ὡς ἡ ἐπιθυμία ἔχει, ὡς γὰρ μηδὲν τίμημα ὑπαρχὴν ὅτι χεῖ σθαι πλέον, ἢ ἐν, ὑπόπεσον αἱ ὁ δικαστὴς τίμωρον, παλιν, ἢ ὑπόπεσον ἀμφότερα δὲ, μὴ ἐξεῖναι.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in the speech Against Leptines, where he says that, as the law stands, a penalty for one who wrongs us may not be imposed beyond one thing, nor may a judge impose one penalty and then another, nor both together. [ὡς γὰρ ἐστιν ἐπίθετον ἡμᾶς ἀδικοῦντα ἐν ἐκείνῳ τίμημα ὑπαρχὴν ἀρχῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου, ὡς ἡ ἐπιθυμία ἔχει, ὡς γὰρ μηδὲν τίμημα ὑπαρχὴν ὅτι χεῖσθαι πλέον, ἢ ἕν, ὑπόπεσον αἱ ὁ δικαστὴς τίμωρον, πάλιν, ἢ ὑπόπεσον ἀμφότερα δὲ, μὴ ἐξεῖναι.]

units.la: Lege venia dabatur iis qui inuiti aut per ignorantiam minima admiserant peccata, neque in ius vocabantur, sed officii admonebantur.
units.tr: By this law pardon was granted to those who, against their will or through ignorance, had committed minor offences; they were not summoned to court but were admonished as a matter of duty.

units.la: Τῶν ἀκουσίων ἁμαρτημάτων οὐκ εἰσάγεσθαι εἰς δίκην, ἀλλ' ἰδίᾳ λέγοντα διδάσκειν καὶ νουθετεῖν. [?]
units.tr: For involuntary offences one is not brought to trial, but is taught and admonished in private. [Τῶν ἀκουσίων ἁμαρτημάτων οὐκ εἰσάγεσθαι εἰς δίκην, ἀλλ' ἰδίᾳ λέγοντα διδάσκειν καὶ νουθετεῖν.]

units.la: Peccantes inuite in ius ne rapiantur, sed priuatim officij.
units.tr: Those who sin against their will are not to be dragged into court, but are dealt with privately, as a matter of duty.

units.la: Habes apud Platonem Apologia Socratis apud Iudices : Τῶν ἐκουσίων καὶ ἀκουσίων ἁμαρτημάτων ὁ ἰδίας νόμος εἰσάγειν ἐστὶν, ἀλλ' ἰδίᾳ λέγοντα διδάσκειν καὶ νουθετεῖν. Non enim poena opus est, sed institutione, vt legitur ibidem : [illegible, ~40 letters] Quod intelligendum est de erratis, quae non essent magni momenti, vt ex. gr. in bis, quorum insimulabatur Socrates, & accusabatur: Σωκράτης ἀδικεῖ, καὶ ἐπεργάζεται ζητῶν τὰ [illegible, ~30 letters] in his enim non sunt sitae opes Graeciae, neque ex iis detrimenti quicquam Respublica capit. At in grauioribus criminibus neque ignorantia, neque ἄκουσον omnino excusant, aut metu liberant, sed ad iudices eundum est.
units.tr: In Plato's Apology of Socrates, before the judges, you have: "For voluntary and involuntary offences the law does not bring one to trial, but one is taught and admonished in private." [Τῶν ἐκουσίων καὶ ἀκουσίων ἁμαρτημάτων ὁ ἰδίας νόμος εἰσάγειν ἐστὶν, ἀλλ' ἰδίᾳ λέγοντα διδάσκειν καὶ νουθετεῖν.] For no punishment is needed, but instruction, as is read in the same place: […]. This must be understood of errors which were not of great importance, such as those with which Socrates was charged and accused: […] for in such things the resources of Greece do not lie, nor does the commonwealth suffer any harm from them. But in more serious crimes neither ignorance nor involuntariness at all excuses, or frees from fear; one must go before the judges.

units.la: Inter poenas videtur fuisse, damnari ad remum. Scholiastes Comici id indicat, ad haec eius verba e Ranis:
units.tr: Among the penalties, condemnation to the oar seems to have been one. The commentator on Aristophanes' comedy indicates this, on these words of his from the Frogs:

units.la: [illegible, ~25 letters]

[illegible, ~45 letters], inquit, [illegible, ~30 letters]. Dicit remiges ἀπήμους fuisse; damnati videlicet ad remum publico iudico, capite erant minuti. Neque haec possunt referri ad illos, qui ad remum mercede conducebantur, erant quippe θῆτες, non ἀπήμοι. At hi ἀπήμοι erant, quia publico iudicio damnati erant ad illud opus: ad quod etiam damnatos fuisse ab Athenienstbus hostes bello captos, auctore Philocle, narrat Plutarchus in Lysandro : [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: […] he says […]. He says the rowers were free of infamy (ἀπήμοι); those condemned to the oar by public judgment were, of course, reduced in civic status. These cannot be referred to those who were hired to the oar for wages; they were indeed hired labourers (θῆτες), not men free of infamy. But these were free of infamy, because they had been condemned by public judgment to that work. That enemies taken in war were also condemned by the Athenians to this work, on the authority of Philocles, Plutarch relates in his Life of Lysander: […]

units.la: Fuit quoque inter poenas ad perpetuum carcerem damnari. Plato Apologia Socratis: τί δίσας, ὦ μὴ πάνυ τῶν ἔ Μελήτου μοι ὑμᾶς ἀλλ' οὕτω δ' ἐλωμένῳ [illegible, ~50 letters]; An vero qui in carcere claudebatur, in vinculis quoque erat? Adhibebantur certe eius corpori vincula, vt de Socrate constat apud Platonem Phaedone λύεσθαι, ἔφη, οἱ ἐπὶ τὰ Σωκράτη, & paullo post: [illegible, ~40 letters] & praecedentia ex Apologia euincunt. Continebantur quoque carcere, si multa esset irrogata, quousque eam numerassent. Socrates apud Platonem eadem Apologia, verbis, quae descripsimus, immediate ista subiicit: [illegible, ~50 letters]
units.tr: There was also, among the penalties, condemnation to perpetual imprisonment. Plato, in the Apology of Socrates: […]. But was the man who was shut up in prison also in chains? Certainly chains were put on his body, as is established about Socrates in Plato's Phaedo: "Loose him, he said, the men at Socrates' side…" and a little later: […]; and what goes before, from the Apology, proves it. They were also kept in prison if a fine had been imposed, until they paid it. Socrates, in the same Apology, immediately after the words we have quoted, adds: […]

units.la: Vltimum de damnatis supplicium non videtur sumptum fuisse ante supremam dici tempestatem, id est, Solem occasum. Colliga ex his quae leguntur apud Stobæum Sermone I. [illegible, ~75 letters] ὁρῶν.
units.tr: The final punishment of the condemned does not seem to have been carried out before the last day, that is, before sunset. Gather this from what is read in Stobaeus, Sermon I: […] seeing.

units.la: Athenienium veteri Lege in decennale mittebantur exilium, quorum opes, gratia, & potentia plebi erant inuisæ & suspectæ.
units.tr: By an ancient law of the Athenians, those whose wealth, favour, and power were hateful and suspect to the common people were sent into exile for ten years.

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters]

Legis meminit Aristides [illegible, ~20 letters] apud Photium: [illegible, ~60 letters]. (optime apud ipsum Aristidem Platonica II. scribitur [illegible, ~10 letters]) [illegible, ~50 letters]. Plutarchus in Pericle: [illegible, ~30 letters]. Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Vespas: [illegible, ~25 letters]. Erat autem [illegible, ~15 letters], inquit Plutarchus in Nicia: Hoc enim poenæ genere eluebatur potentiorum inuidia. Plutarchus in Themistocle: [illegible, ~40 letters]. Neque enim poena hæc erat [illegible, ~10 letters], vilium capitum, & hominum improborum, quos feries inhonora parentum Obscuros proauis, & prisca lucis egentes, Plebeia de stirpe tulit.
units.tr: Aristides mentions the law […] in Photius: […]. (It is very well written in Aristides' own Platonic Oration II: […].) Plutarch, in the Life of Pericles: […]. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Wasps: […]. Plutarch, in the Life of Nicias, says: "For by this kind of penalty the envy of the powerful was purged away." Plutarch, in the Life of Themistocles: […]. For this penalty was not [applied to] base and worthless men, and people of bad character, whom "the unhonoured shame of their parents, obscure in their ancestry and lacking the light of ancient renown, brought forth from plebeian stock."

units.la: Plutarchus in Alcibiade: [illegible, ~45 letters]. Vnde dixit Plato Comicus de Hyperbolo: [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: Plutarch, in the Life of Alcibiades: […]. Whence the comic poet Plato said of Hyperbolus: […]

units.la: Neque id tantum Athenis ab Atheniensibus fiebat, sed etiam in subditis ciuitatibus. Aristoteles Polit. Libro III. cap. XIII. [illegible, ~120 letters]. Atque id institutum est, vt possent [illegible, ~20 letters], vt notat hoc ipso capite Aristoteles: [illegible, ~150 letters]. Neque id improbat, siquidem liquido constet suspectos & inuisos esse plebi propter opes, amicos, clientes, & gratiam: [illegible, ~80 letters]. Intra dies decem ab vrbe excedere, & per decennium abesse cogebantur ii, quos, sex millibus, suffragium ferentibus, aut maiore numero, à pluribus damnari contigisset. Ordinem repræsentant Interpres Comici,& Plutarchus: illius verba sunt ad drama Equites: ὁ δὲ Ἔππος τῇ ὀστρα-χισμοῦ [?] ἴουσης, ὡς ἐξ[?] ἐφερ[?]ὴ ἀγορά, ἐκ[?] ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ... [?]ἐφεύλ[?]ο... Plutarchus in Aristide: ὧν δὲ ζίουσιν [?] ὀστρα[?] ... Diodorus Siculus Libro XI. quinquennale facit hoc exilium: ὁ δὲ νόμος ἐπάλ[?]ε ... Pollux Libro VIII. cap. V. ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... Ἀθηναῖος ... Sed male hi Grammatici, Pollux, & Aristophanis Scholiastes scribunt, debuisse damnari sex millibus testularum τῶν ὀστρακιζόντων. imo potius, sex millibus suffragium ferentibus, vt erat solenne in omni graviori causa: mittebantur igitur in exilium quicumque, Athenien-sibus sex mille suffragia ferentibus, plura tulissent puncta, siue maiori testularum numero damnati fuissent. Hunc numerum debuisse esse mille testularum scribit futilis auctor Tzetzes in Chiliadibus, atque in Cynosarge vult cum actum celebra-tum:
units.tr: Nor was this done only at Athens by Athenians, but also in the subject cities. Aristotle, Politics Book III, chapter XIII: […]. And this custom was established so that they might be able […], as Aristotle notes in this very chapter: […]. Nor does he disapprove of it, since it is plain that men were suspected and hated by the people on account of their wealth, friends, clients, and influence: […]. Those whom it happened to be condemned by six thousand voting, or by a greater number, were compelled to leave the city within ten days and to stay away for ten years. The commentators on the comic poet and Plutarch set out the procedure: the words of the former are on the play Knights: […]. Plutarch, in the Life of Aristides: […]. Diodorus Siculus, Book XI, makes this exile last five years: […]. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter V: […]. But these grammarians, Pollux and the scholiast on Aristophanes, wrongly write that one ought to have been condemned by six thousand potsherds of those casting votes by ostracism. Rather, it was by six thousand votes, as was customary in every more serious case: those who had received more votes, when six thousand Athenians voted, were sent into exile, or those condemned by a greater number of potsherds. The trifling author Tzetzes, in his Chiliades, writes that this number ought to have been a thousand potsherds, and he wants the proceeding to have taken place in Cynosarges: […]

[illegible, ~10 letters] ... ἀθηναίας.εἰ δ' ἦσαν ἀπάλιστα πα ὤρα καὶ χιλίων,ὁ τῇ παλιτεία λέγων ... [illegible, ~22 letters] ... συνεγώμενος.
units.tr: The Athenians […] the elder would drive out of the fatherland, […] and writing that name on a potsherd, they threw it into Cynosarges, a place which also drove out the elders of the fatherland by means of potsherds, […] but on the day of the vote, when a thousand were present, he spoke without sympathy […] Athenian. And if there were not […] a thousand, he who speaks in the state […] being gathered together. […]

units.la: Qui ostracismo aberant ab vrbe, bonorum suorum fructus percipiebant: Interpres Comici ad Vespas: ἀλλὰ φέρει γὰρ φυγῆ ἐξωστρακισμοῦ, καὶ τὸ τὴν μὲν φθονοῦντων αἱ διαφθαρμένοι [?] ... ὁ δῆμος, καὶ τοῖς μὲν, ἐχ τὴν τοῦτο ἐπάδον τοιοῦτον. Plutarchus iam laudatis in Aristide: τὸν ἐπὶ τῶ πλείστων ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ... εἰς ἔτη δέκα, καρπούμενον τὰ αὐτῶ.
units.tr: Those who were away from the city through ostracism received the fruits of their property. The commentator on Aristophanes, on the Wasps: "But exile by ostracism brings […] envious […] the people, and to some this was so decreed. Plutarch, in the Life of Aristides, already quoted: "…for ten years, enjoying his own goods."

units.la: E verbis autem Scholiastæ Aristophanis docemur ostracismo pulsis omnium locorum interdictum fuisse praeter certum locum. Quando vero primum sancta sit Ostracismi Lex non liquet in tanto veterum dissensu, constat tantum, quando antiquata: Nam,cum Alcibiades & Nicias, qui tum Athenis rerum potiebantur, consilio inito,fecissent, ut Hyperbolus ostracismo multaretur, desitum est exinde in decennale mittere exilium. Plutarchus in Aristide: Ἀλκιβιάδης καὶ Νικίας, μισήσαντες ἐν τῇ πόλει δυναμένοι, διεσπάσαν[?] · ὡς οὖν ὁ δῆμος ἐμίσησεν[?] ἐκφέρειν τὸν ὀστρακισμὸν, καὶ δῆλος ὢν πρὸς τὴν ἡγεμονίαν[?] , ἀλλὰ ἐξεπέμψαντο Ἀλκιβιάδην[?] , καὶ τὰς ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἐκπέμπειν[?] ἀφῆκε πολυτελῶς καὶ καταλύσαντ[?]. Idem in Nicia,cum hanc ipsam historiam retulisset,addit: ἐξ ὃ πέρας, οὐδὲ ἐπὶ ὁ ἀλλὰ πάντ[?] ἐξωστρακίσθη μὴ Ὑπέρβολον, ἀλλ' ἔσχατος ἐκε�ῖνος.
units.tr: From the words of the scholiast on Aristophanes we learn that those banished by ostracism were forbidden all places except one certain place. When the sacred law of ostracism was first enacted is not clear, given the great disagreement among the ancients; it is only certain when it was abolished. For when Alcibiades and Nicias, who then held power at Athens, had taken counsel and brought it about that Hyperbolus should be punished by ostracism, the practice of sending men into ten-year exile was thereafter abandoned. Plutarch, in the Life of Aristides: "Alcibiades and Nicias, hating […] able to […] when the people began to hate carrying out ostracism, and was clearly […] for leadership, […] they sent away Alcibiades […] and let go of the expulsions from the city […] magnificently and […]." The same author, in the Life of Nicias, after relating this very story, adds: "from that point on, not even […] but all were ostracized, not Hyperbolus, but he was the last."

units.la: Quis vero auctor Ostracismi fuerit,ut dixi,liquido non constat. Nam Thesei primum fuisse qui hanc Legem scripserit,& ostracismo pulsus fuerit,sunt qui scribant. Theophrastus apud Suidam: ὀστρακιζομένων ἠ ἀρετῶν Ἀθηναῖοι Θησέα[?] , ἰσοπληθὲς Θεόφραστος ἐν τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐκ[?] . Eusebius in Chronicis: Θησεὺς Ἀθηναίους[?] , ἐκ μιᾶς πόλεως ἐξ ἑαυτῶν ἐκ[?] , ἐπὶ εἰς μίαν πόλιν, ἔστι ἑαυτῶς δὲ ἐξωστρακίσθη αὐτὸς ἀρετῆς[?] τὸ νόμον. Quae ita vertit B.Hieronymus: Thefeus , cum Athenienfes prius per regionem difperfos primus in unam civitatem congregasset, ignominiose eiectus est per figna testularum, eandem Legem prius ipse constituens. Scholia Pluti: μὴ ὁ ἀρχῆσθαι τῷ δήμῳ μαχεσαμένους τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις τ' Θησέα, Λυκοῦς συνεφιλοτίμους, ἐπαίνων ἐξωστρακισθῶν τ' Ἡρωα. Non defunt,qui putent Ostracifmum inuentum tantum fuisse circa tempora Pififtrati,& Hipparchum Pififtrati cognatum primum omnium hoc exilij genus subiisse. Diodorus Siculus Libro XI. ἐξώστρακον μὲν οὖν αὐτὸν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως μετῳκισμένον τοῦτο τὸ ὄνομα ἀπαγαγόντες αὐτοῦ, ὡς ἐκεῖνον ἐξωστρακίσθη μὲν ἐκ Ἀθηνῶν μὴ τῶν καταλιπόντων τὴν τυραννίδα τῆς Γέλωνος[?] . Plutarchus in Nicia: καὶ ὁ πέρας, οὐδὲ ἐπὶ ὁ ἀλλὰ πάντ' ἐξωστρακίσθη μὴ Ὑπέρβολον, ἀλλ' ἔσχατος ἐκ[?] ἐκεῖνος. ἐξωσπάς δὲ, Ἱππαρχος ὁ Χολαργεὺς συγγνώμης ὡς ὢν τῆς τυραννίδος. Harpocration: Ἱππαρχος ὁ Γέλωνος τοῦ Ἀθηναίου[?] ἄνδρα δὲ ὅτι Ἱππαρχος ὁ Χαρμου, ὡς φησὶ Λυκοῦργος ἐν τῷ Λεωκρατικῷ[?] . τοῦτο δὲ τύπου, Ἀνδροτίων ἐν τῇ Ἀτθίδι φησὶν, ὅτι συγγνώμης μὲν ὢν Γέλωνος τῆς τυραννίδος, ἐξωστρακίσθη τῆς Ἀθηναίους ὀστρακισμὸν νόμον ποτὲ ἐξωστρακισμὸν τοῦ πεθέντος[?] , δι' ἐκεῖνον[?] ἀναιρεῖ τῆς Γέλωνα, ὅτι δημαγωγὸς ὢν καὶ ὑπὸ τυραννίδος ἐτυραννήσειν. Heraclius in Fragmento de Rebuspublicis Hippiam Tyrannum auctorem facit: Ἱππίας ὁ πικρότερος ἐτυράννει. καὶ τ' ἀπὸ ὀστρακισμοῦ νόμον εἰσηγήσατο, ὡς ἐπὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς τυραννίδος. Ælianus Variae Libro XIII.cap.XXIV.Clisthenem : Κλεισθένης δὲ ὁ Ἀθηναῖος ὃν δῆλον ἐξωστρακίζεσθαι ἐξωστρακισμένους, αὐτὸς ἐπὶ τῆς τῆς καταδίκης ἐξωστρακίσθη. At Ptolemaeus Hephaestio ἐπὶ τῆς εἰς πολυμαθίαν ἡγήσεως ἱστορίας, Libro VI.apud Photium, Achillem Lysonis filium ostracismi auctorem laudat: καὶ ὁ τ' ὀστρακισμὸν ἐπαινέσας Ἀθηναῖοι Ἀχιλλέα ἐκ[?] ἐκ[?] ἐγεῖτο, ὡς Λυσωνίας.
units.tr: It is not clear for certain who the author of ostracism was, as I have said. Some writers say that Theseus was the first to write this law and was himself expelled by ostracism. Theophrastus, in Suidas, says that when the Athenians ostracised the men of excellence, Theseus... [Theophrastus in Suidas: ὀστρακιζομένων ἠ ἀρετῶν Ἀθηναῖοι Θησέα ... ] Eusebius in his Chronicle says that Theseus, having gathered the Athenians who had previously been scattered through the countryside into one city, was himself driven out by the potsherd vote, having first established this law himself. St Jerome translates it thus: "Theseus, after he had first gathered the Athenians, who had been scattered through the region, into one city, was ignominiously cast out by the vote of potsherds, having himself first enacted this same law." The scholia on Plutus say that the Athenians, having fought with Theseus, ... were ostracised. Some think that ostracism was invented only about the time of Pisistratus, and that Hipparchus, a kinsman of Pisistratus, was the first of all to undergo this kind of exile. Diodorus Siculus, in Book XI, says that he was driven out of the city by the ostracism... Plutarch, in the Life of Nicias, says: "...and in the end, not Hyperbolus but the last of them was ostracised." Hipparchus of Cholargus was ostracised as a relative of the tyrant. Harpocration: "Hipparchus, son of Gelon the Athenian; but not this Hipparchus son of Charmus, as Lycurgus says in his Against Leocrates. Androtion in the Atthis says that this Hipparchus, being a kinsman of the tyrant Gelon, was ostracised, and that the Athenians once enacted a law of ostracism..." Heraclides, in his fragment on the constitutions, makes the tyrant Hippias the author: "Hippias the elder was tyrant, and he introduced the law of ostracism, as a safeguard for his rule." Aelian, Varia Historia, Book XIII, chapter 24, speaks of Cleisthenes the Athenian, who, when those who were ostracised had been condemned, was himself ostracised. But Ptolemaeus Hephaestion, in the history of the Book of Many Learnings, quoted by Photius in Book VI, names Achilles, son of Lyson, as the author of ostracism: the Athenians, who praised the potsherd vote, honoured Achilles...

units.la: Lege erat vetitum,exulum quemuis apud fe recipere,qui recepisset,exulare cogebatur.
units.tr: By law it was forbidden to receive any exile into one's home; whoever had received one was compelled to go into exile himself.

units.la: Μὴ ἐπιφθονεῖσθαι τῇ φθονήσει[?] φθονοῦντας, ἀλλ' ἐν τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐκχέσθαι τὸν ἐπιφθονοῦντα τοῖς φθονοῦσιν[?] φθονοῦντας.
units.tr: [Greek fragment, corrupt in the scan: roughly, not to be envied by those who envy, but the man who envies is to be cast out among those who envy.]

units.la: Exulam nullum recipito, qui secus faxit, in exilium mittitor.
units.tr: Receive no exile; whoever acts otherwise shall be sent into exile.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Πολυκλέους. οἱ γὰρ νόμοι οὐκ ἐῶσιν ἀπο-δίκεσθαι τὴν φθορὰν [?] τῆς φύσεως [?] καὶ Παύλλο ante dixerat Callicles: οὐ γὰρ [?] ἐάσεις ἐστι τῆς φύσεως ἐάσεως εἰς τὸ ἴσον ἀναβαίνειν. ἃ γὰρ ἐᾶσιν οἱ νόμοι. Hoc iure usi Athenienses, Cimonem, quem in decennale miserant exilium, a ducibus belli noluerunt recipi. Plutarchus in Cimone: ἡ δ᾽ βουλὴ τῆς Πεντακοσίων ἀπηγόρευσε τοῖς Σπαρτιάταις μὴ δίκαιος εἶναι ἀνδρα.
units.tr: Demosthenes praises this law in his speech Against Polycles: "For the laws do not allow the corruption of nature to be pleaded..." And before him Callicles had said in Plato: "For it is not permitted by nature to rise to equality..." (what the laws permit.) By this right the Athenians, who had sent Cimon into ten years' exile, refused to let him be received back among the generals of the war. Plutarch, in the Life of Cimon: "The council of the Five Hundred forbade the Spartans to make Cimon a man..."

units.la: Fragmentum hoc est è Draconis Legibus, quod ad hunc titulum omnino spectat:
units.tr: The following is a fragment of the Laws of Draco, which pertains wholly to this title:

units.la: ΑΠΟΤΕΙΝΕΙΝ ΔΕΚΑΒΟΙΟΝ.
units.tr: To Pay Ten Oxen [ΑΠΟΤΕΙΝΕΙΝ ΔΕΚΑΒΟΙΟΝ].

units.la: Legitur hoc fragmentum apud Pollucem Libro IX. cap. VI. καὶ μέλλω καὶ τῆς Δεξιοκρατῆς νόμοις ἔστιν, ΑΠΟΤΕΙΝΕΙΝ ΔΕΚΑΒΟΙΟΝ. Nummi species erat Athenis bouę (unde nomen invenit) signati. Pollux ibid. ὃ δ᾽ παλαιὸς τῷ τῶν Ἀθηναίων νόμισμα, καὶ ἐκάλεῖτο Βοῦς, ὅτι βοῦν εἶχεν ἐπιτυπωμένον. Illius valor erat duarum drachmarum: & certe haec Pollucis, ὃ δὲ παλαιὸς τῷ refertur ad ὃ Δίδραχμον, de quo ante verba fecerat, docet ὃ Δίδραχμον bouę fuisse signatum: itaque paullo post addit: καὶ ἐν τῇ ᾧδε Δηλίας ἡ ἀρχαία τὴν χάρυκα κηρύττει Φαύν, ὁπότε δυρεαὶ ὑπὲρ ἰδίδοῦ, ὅ̈υ δὲ ἡ ἴσον ἐστιν τὸ κατὰ Βοῦς, καὶ ἑκάστου Βοῦν δύο δραχμὰς Ἀθηναῖα. Primus bouę signauit Theseus. Plutarchus: ἑκαλεῖ δὲ καὶ νόμισμα, βοῶν ἐγγράψας, ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνου δὲ Φασὶ ὃ ἑκατόμβοιον, καὶ ὃ δεκάβοιον ὀνομάζεσθαι. etiam apud Homerum,
units.tr: This fragment is read in Pollux, Book IX, chapter 6: "and in the laws of Dexicrates it is ... to pay ten oxen" [ΑΠΟΤΕΙΝΕΙΝ ΔΕΚΑΒΟΙΟΝ]. It was a kind of coin struck at Athens bearing an ox (whence it got its name). Pollux in the same place: "The old coin of the Athenians was also called the ox, because it bore an ox stamped on it." Its value was two drachmas. Indeed, this passage of Pollux, "the old coin of...", refers to the didrachm, of which he spoke before; he shows that the didrachm was struck with an ox; so shortly afterwards he adds: "and in the Delian ... the ancient herald proclaims ... a fine of ten oxen, and each ox is worth two Attic drachmas." Theseus was the first to strike the ox coin. Plutarch: "He also struck a coin bearing an ox, whence they say the hecatomboion and the dekaboion take their names," as also in Homer: "a hundred-ox and nine-ox..."

units.la: ἑκατόμβοι᾽ ἐννεάβοιαν.
units.tr: "a hundred-ox, a nine-ox [worth]."

units.la: Huius quoque tituli est fragmentum Legis ex Axonibus Solonis, de irroganda multa.
units.tr: Of this same title is a fragment of a law from the Axones of Solon, concerning the imposition of a fine.

units.la: ΜΗ ΓΑΛΕΙΩ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΡΙΤΑΙΑΣ ΤΗΝ ΚΡΙΣΙΝ.
units.tr: The Trial Is Not to Be on the Third Day [ΜΗ ΓΑΛΕΙΩ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΡΙΤΑΙΑΣ ΤΗΝ ΚΡΙΣΙΝ].

units.la: Habetur hoc Legis fragmentum apud Hesychium: τετάρτα ἀπὸ Σόλωνι, ΜΗ ΓΑΛΕΙΩ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΡΙΤΑΙΑΣ ΤΗΝ ΚΡΙΣΙΝ. Æstimatio unius τεί-ταιας est choenicum sedecim: id enim Soloni est τειταία, quam alii τετάς dixerunt: unde verbis Legis addit idem Grammaticus: τετάς γὰρ χοίνικας ἔχει. Sed locus est corruptus: Non enim choenicis, sed medimni tertia pars est. Pollux: ὃ δ᾽ τετάς, χοίνικας ἐκτὸν διχα. & ita rescribendum est apud Hesychium, τετάς γὰρ χοίνικας ς᾽ ἔχει.
units.tr: This fragment of the law is found in Hesychius: "the fourth from Solon," ... The value of one taitaia is sixteen choenices, for this is Solon's taitaia, which others called tetas; whence the same grammarian adds, in the words of the law: "for the tetas holds sixteen choenices." But the passage is corrupt: for it is not the third part of choenices but of the medimnus. Pollux: "the tetas holds sixteen choenices," and so it must be restored in Hesychius, "for the tetas holds 16 choenices."

units.la: Eiusdem generis atque ordinis est Fragmentum istud, de eo, qui habeatur dies decem in nervo ab Undecimviris capitalibus, nisi quid aliud ab Heliastis iudicibus pronunciatum sit.
units.tr: Of the same kind and order is that fragment concerning the man who is to be held for ten days in the stocks by the Eleven, the capital magistrates, unless the Heliastic judges have pronounced otherwise.

units.la: ΔΕΔΕΣΘΑΙ ΕΝ ΤΗ ΠΟΔΟΚΑΚΗ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΔΕΚΑΤΟΝ ΠΟΔΑ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΓΡΟΤΙΜΗΣΗ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ.
units.tr: To be bound in the stocks for ten days, unless the Heliaea should decide otherwise. [ΔΕΔΕΣΘΑΙ ΕΝ ΤΗ ΠΟΔΟΚΑΚΗ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΔΕΚΑΤΟΝ ΠΟΔΑ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΓΝΩΤΙΜΗΣΗ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ]

units.la: Extat apud Lysiam ἐν ᾧ τῷ Θεομνήστου α᾽, qui docet ab Undecimviris capitalibus in nervo habitum fuisse: καὶ μὴ ἀπαγωγὴ τοὺς νόμους τῆς Σόλωνος πολλῶν παλαιῶν. NOMOΣ ΔΕΔΑΙΣΘΑΙ Δ᾽ ΕΝ ΤΗ ΠΟΔΟΚΑΚΗ,
units.tr: It is found in Lysias, in the speech Against Theomnestus (1), where he shows that this was held before the Eleven, the capital magistrates, in the stocks: "and not to bring in the laws of Solon, many of them ancient." The law reads: "to be bound in the stocks for ten days."

units.la: ΗΜΕΡΑΣ ΔΕΚΑ ΤΟΝ ΠΟΔΑ ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΓΡΟΤΙΜΗΣΗ[?]
units.tr: For ten days, to bind the feet, unless he is condemned by the Heliaea.

units.la: ΗΛΙΑΙΑ[?]. ἡ ποδοκάκκη αὕτη ὅτι[?], ὦ Θεόμνηστε[?], ὁ ἰὼν καλεῖ ἐν ᾧ ξύλῳ διδάσκει[?]. Εἰ οὖν ὁ δέσμιος ἐξελθὼν[?], ὡς τῆς Εὐθυωρίας τὴν Εὐδίκης ἀκτηρίαν[?], ὅτι οὐκ ὁ τὴν ποδο-κάκκην εἰλήφθη[?], ἀλλ' ὁ τῆς ξύλου[?], οὐκ ἀλλὰ ἡλίου αὐτὸν νομίζοιεν[?]. Hac voce passim visus erat Solon in suis Legibus, & exstat hodie apud Demosthenem ὁ τῆς ξ[?]υλ[?] Timocratem in Lege [illegible, ~5 letters]. Cum Lysia conuenit in interpretatione huius vocis Interpreti Aristophanis ad hunc Equitum versum:
units.tr: This stocks (podokakke)... Solon used this word in his laws, and it is still found today in Demosthenes, in the law against Timocrates. The interpreter of Aristophanes agrees with Lysias on the meaning of this word, on the line of the Knights where he says that a man is put in the wooden stocks, and the prisoner, when he came out, was thought to be ... not in the stocks but in the sun.

units.la: οὗ σε δίνω τᾶς ξύλας[?].
units.tr: "Of whom I give ... the wooden [stocks]."

units.la: εἶδος δὲ δεσμωτηρίου ὁ ξύλον, ὡ ποδοκάκκλω λέγεται[?]. Est autem constituenda differentia inter ποδοκάκκλω, ποδογράβλω, παυσικάπλω, καὶ πεντεσύελγον[?], quae sunt vincula, quibus vsus erat in carcere. ποδοκάκκλω appellant vinculum, quo pedes impediuntur. Harpocration: ποδοκάκκη, ὃ ξύλον ὃ ἐν δεσμωτηρίῳ οὕτως ἐκαλεῖτο[?], ἡ πεπεβεδέλησθε τὸ ἐπέγυ καππα[?], ποδῶν ὡς κάκωσις ἔσται[?], ἐ καὶ συ-κοπτέω[?], ὡς φησὶ Δίδυμος[?], ᾗ ποδοκάπη[?]. Hesychius: ποδοκάκκη, ὁ ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ δεσμῷ[?], ἐν ᾧ οἱ κακοῦργοι δεσμεύονται[?], ᾗ ποδοκάπη[?]. Τὰ ἀφ' τῶν ποδῶν εἰλήμματα[?]. Suidas: ποδοκάκκη, ξύλον, εἰς ὃ ἐν εἰρκτῇ τοῖς ποδὰς ἐμβάλλοντες σώφρονιζοντες[?]. ἐν εἰρκτῇ τῇ καὶ ποδοκάκκῃ γρεβλοῦμενοι καὶ Θαλαπωφρυΐδμοι ἐώμεν[?]. Hinc in hac Lege apud Lysiam: ΔΕΔΕΣΘΑΙ Δ' ΕΝ ΤΗΙ ΠΟΔΟΚΑΚΗΙ ΤΟΝ ΓΟΔΑ. Plutarchus de Deo Socratis: τοὺς πόδας ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ δεδεμένοι[?]. Lucianus in Toxaris: τὰ σκέλη ἐν ᾧ ξύλῳ καθακκλημένα[?]. Viri Incomparabiles Budæus atque Cuiacius crediderunt idem esse cum mala mansione, de qua Vlpianus Libro XXX. ad Edictum. Si hominem apud se depositum, vt quaestio de eo haberetur, ac propterea vinctum, vel ad malam mansionem extensum. Lege VII. D. Depositi vel contra: & Gaius Libro LXXVII. ad Edictum. Quaestionis verbo etiam ea, quam malam mansionem dicunt, continebitur. Lege XV. §. XLI. D. de iniurijs & famosis libellis. Sed rei, de quibus quaestio habebatur, quique torquebantur, ad malam mansionem erant extensi. At ποδοκάκκη extensio non est, sed ὁ ἐν ᾧ ξύλῳ δισμὸς τῶν ποδῶν[?]. Quin potius respondebit Romanorum neruo Athenien sium ποδοκάκκη. Neruum namque appellamus, inquit Festus, etiam ferreum vinculum, quo pedes vinciuntur. vnde Tertullianus: Nescio an crus de perisceli in neruum se patiatur artari. Certe mala mansio accederet potius ad ποδογράβλω. Nam ποδογράβη est quaestionis siue tormenti genus, quo rei pedes manusque vincti torquentur. Vlpianus ad Timocrateam: Βασανιστήριόν τί ἐστιν ὄργανον, εἰς ὃ ἐμβάλλουσι τὰς δεσμούμενος τὰς χεῖρας καὶ τοὺς πόδας[?], ὅπερ κλεῖσθαι καὶ ποδογράβη[?]. Quanquam idem male confundit cum ποδοκάκκη. Etenim li ποδογράβον luxabat membra illius, qui torquebatur: Vnde à Comicis chirurgicum illud instrumentum, quo luxata membra restituuntur, facete ποδογράβον dicitur. Pollux Libro V.cap. XXV. καὶ ποδογράβον δὲ, τὰ γρέμματα καταδυσῶν ἐν τῇ Κωμῳδίᾳ, ἐργαλεῖον ἰατρικόν[?]. Certe Grammatici notant ποδογράβῳ εἶναι vinculum, & quaestionis genus, quo pedes luxantur: ποδογράβῃ, ὃ γινόμενον ἐπὶ τὰ γρέμματα τῆς ποδῶν ξύλον[?]. Verum & de manibus addidisse debuerant: nam, vt diximus ex Vlpiano, Εἰς τὸν ποδοτράβην τρεβλωμένους οἱ κακοῦργοι διαμελλόμενοι τὰς χεῖρας καὶ τοὺς πόδας. παυσικάπη machina erat, quae inserebatur collo, ne manus ori admoueri possent. Pollux Libro VII.cap.IV. παυσικάπη ὀνομάζεται ξυλίδης μηχάνημα ὄν, τὰς πεάχηλας ἐπιαρμοζόμενον, ὡς ἀδυνατεῖν τὰς χεῖρας τῷ στόματι προσάγειν. Hesychius: παυσικάπη, μηχάνημα ἔχων εἰκὸς, δ' ἂν τὸν πεάχηλον εἴεται, ὡς μὴ δύνασθαι τὰς χεῖρας τῷ στόματι προσάγειν. Suidas: παυσικάπη. μηχάνημα ἔχοις ἐμφερὲς, δ' ἂν τὸν πεάχηλον διεληλυθὼς τὸ στόμα, ὥστε μὴ ἐάνδιψαι, καὶ τὰς αὐχένος, ὡς μὴ δύνασθαι τὰς χεῖρας τῷ στόματι προσάγειν. πεντεσυΐγγον ξύλον est vinculum, quo pedes manusque impediebantur, & praeterea collo inserebatur. Pollux Libro VIII. cap.VII, ἐν δὲ τὰ διαμωτήρια καὶ πεντεσυΐγγον ξύλον ἐκάθιτο. Hesychius : πεντεσυΐγγων ξύλον, πέντε ἐπὰς ἔχων καὶ ὃ διαμωτήριον · τιαπαρᾶς μὲν εἰς ἃς οἱ πόδες καὶ αἱ χεῖρες διφαθῆναι. μίαν δὲ, δ' ἧς ὁ πεάχηλος. Suidas: πεντεσυΐγγων ξύλα. τῇ ποδοκάκκη. πέντε γὰρ ἐπὰς ἔχει, δ' ὧν οἱ πόδες, καὶ αἱ χεῖρες, καὶ ὁ πεάχηλος ἐμβάλλοντες. Eadem est Scholiastae Aristophanis nota ad hunc Equitum versum,
units.tr: The wooden stocks were a kind of prison restraint, and they are called podokakkē. We must distinguish between podokakkē, podograblē, pausikaplē and pentesyngon, which are the fetters used in prison. Podokakkē is the fetter by which the feet are impeded. Harpocration, Hesychius and Suidas all describe it as a wooden device in which the feet of prisoners were held fast. Hence in this law in Lysias: "to be bound in the stocks, the feet." Plutarch, in On the Sign of Socrates, has "with their feet bound in the wood," and Lucian in Toxaris "the legs fixed in the wood." The distinguished scholars Budé and Cujas believed it was the same as the mala mansio, of which Ulpian speaks in Book 30 on the Edict: "if a man deposited with him was bound, so that a question might be put to him, or stretched on the mala mansio" (D. Depositi, law 7), and Gaius in Book 77 on the Edict: "the term 'question' also includes what they call the mala mansio" (D. de iniuriis, law 15, §41). But the defendants who were examined under torture were stretched on the mala mansio, whereas podokakkē is not a stretching but a binding of the feet in wood. Rather, the Athenian podokakkē corresponds to the Roman neruus. For Festus says, "we call even an iron fetter, by which the feet are bound, a neruus," and hence Tertullian: "I know not whether the leg is willing to be compressed into a neruus from the perisceles." Certainly the mala mansio would correspond more closely to podograblē. For podograblē is a kind of question or torture in which the feet and hands of the accused are bound and stretched. Ulpian on the Timocratea says that it is an instrument of torture into which the hands and feet of the bound are put, which is also called podograblē, though he wrongly confuses it with podokakkē. Indeed, the podograblē dislocated the limbs of the one who was tortured; hence the surgical instrument by which dislocated limbs are restored is wittily called podograblon by the comic poets. Pollux, Book 5, chapter 25, mentions it. Grammarians note that podograblē is a fetter and a type of question by which the feet are dislocated. But they ought to have added the hands as well, for, as we said from Ulpian, criminals who were tortured on the podograblē had their hands and feet stretched. The pausikapē was a machine fitted to the neck so that the hands could not be brought to the mouth. Pollux, Book 7, chapter 4, Hesychius and Suidas describe it in the same way. The pentesyngon was a wooden fetter in which the feet and hands were held, and besides this it was fitted to the neck. Pollux, Book 8, chapter 7, and Hesychius and Suidas describe it as having five holes, two for the feet, two for the hands and one for the neck.

units.la: ζῶτοι δῆσαί σ' ἐκέλευε πεντεσυΐγγα.
units.tr: "The Scythian ordered you to bind him in the pentesyngon."

units.la: Sed errant, quod ποδοκάκκω interpretantur: nam ποδοκάκκη pedes tantum arctabat: ποδοτράβη pedes manusque vinctos torquebat: παυσικάπη collo inserebatur: πεντεσυΐγγον ξύλον, non tantum collo inserebatur, sed etiam pedes manusque impediebat.
units.tr: But they are wrong to render podokakkē as ... For podokakkē only confined the feet; podotrabē held the feet and hands fast and stretched them; pausikapē was fitted to the neck; but the pentesyngon was not only fitted to the neck but also impeded the feet and hands.

units.la: Lege firemps[?] irrogabatur multa, siue poena, consultori atque reo:
units.tr: By a law a fine or penalty was imposed on both the adviser and the defendant.

units.la: Τὸν βουλόμενον τὸν συνηγορεῖν τῷ ἀντίδικον καὶ τὸν ἐπὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐργασάμενον.
units.tr: "Whoever wishes may act as advocate for the opponent, and whoever has been in office." [Τὸν βουλόμενον τὸν συνηγορεῖν τῷ ἀντίδικον καὶ τὸν ἐπὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐργασάμενον]

units.la: Legem laudat Andocides ἐν τῷ περὶ τοῦ μυστηρίου. καὶ ἔστιν ὁ νόμος καὶ προσέπεσεν τῷ ὡς κολάσεως ἔχων, καὶ τῶν ὄντων, καὶ χρήσασθαι αὐτῷ, τὸ βουλόμενον ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ἐπιχαρῶς καὶ τῷ τῆς χρήσεως ἐργασάμενον. Nam, vt est in veteri Mimo,
units.tr: Andocides cites this law in his speech On the Mysteries. The law, as it stands, concerns punishment and property, and any person who wishes may take advantage of it, as well as anyone who has worked in the office. For, as is said in an old mime:

units.la: Bis peccat, qui peccanti consilium accommodat.
units.tr: He sins twice who gives counsel to one who is sinning.

units.la: Aristoteles Rhet. Libro I. cap. VII. ὥσπερ ὁ Λεωδάμας κατηγοροῦ Καλλιστράτου, ἔφη, τὸν βουλόμενον τῆς πράξεως μᾶλλον ἀδικεῖν. οὐ γὰρ ἱκανῶς ἐγκαλῶσαι μὴ βουλεύσαμεν.
units.tr: Aristotle, Rhetoric Book 1, chapter 7: as Leodamas said when prosecuting Callistratus, the man who wishes to do a deed sins more than the one who does it, for we have not sufficiently accused the one who merely planned it.

units.la: In confitentes reos, indicta causa, sine vllis iudicum sententiis, animadvertebatur Athenienfium Lege:
units.tr: Against defendants who confessed, without a trial and without any sentence of judges, punishment was inflicted by an Athenian law:

units.la: Τοὺς κακοῦργους τοὺς ὁμολογοῦντας ἀνεῖναι χρίσεως καλάζειν.
units.tr: "Criminals who confess shall be seized without a trial." [Τοὺς κακοῦργους τοὺς ὁμολογοῦντας ἀνεῖναι κρίσεως καλάζειν]

units.la: Legem describsit Demosthenes in Timocratea: ὥσπερ εἶπον, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, τῇ πόλει πάλλα κακούργων τινὲς ὁμολογιῶς, ἀλλὰ χρίσεως καλάζειν οἱ νόμοι καλῶς. Qui sint confitentes rei exponit Vlpianus his verbis: τοὺς κακουργοῦντας ἐπανο-φῶσ λέγειν. & paullo post: τοὺς ὁμολογοῦντας δὲ, ἀ ἀλφὰ τῆς φωνῆς, ἀλλ' εἰς αὐτὴν τὴν πραγμάτων. Quanquam oportebat, etiamsi deprehensi fuissent ἐπανοφῶν, vt crimen faterentur. Aeschines in Timarchum: τίς γὰρ ἐὰν τὸν λωποδύτην, ἐὰν τὴν κλεπτὴν, ἐὰν τὴν μοιχὸν, ἐὰν τὴν ἀγῶν ἀνδροφόνον, ἐὰν τὴν τὰ μίμησα λέγει ἀδικούντων, λέ-ξρα ἢ τῶν πεάζοντων, δύστ ἄχειρ· καὶ γὰρ τούτων οἱ λέγει ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ ἀλωτῆς, ἐὰν μὴ ὁμολογῶσι, ἐπάρχειμα τῆς δυνάπτω ζημιοῦσι. Rapiebantur igitur ad Magistratus confitentes rei, vt plecterentur, non vero, vt in iudicium venirent, quod ἐνδεῖξις dicebatur.
