The grammarians [say] that the money given out for the gods, for sacrifices and festivals was called by this name. I have said that the theorikon was given to individual citizens, namely to those who were present; for no account was taken of those who had gone abroad. Harpocration shows this from Hyperides, teaching that it was not permitted for those who were away from home to receive the theorikon, in the speech against Archestratides. Hence Ulpian said, in the first Olynthiac, that the Athenians made the money paid out into the theorikon, so that each man in the city received two obols. This theorikon was distributed individually among the people whose names were written on the register, and an Alopecian, for example, could not receive this gift among the Paeanians. One may gather this from Demosthenes in the speech against Leochares, where he says that when some men of Oryos had gathered together with a few others, and had entrusted the matter to the secretary of Demophon, they brought it forward; but these men were not allowed to receive the theorikon, as they had been given the public money, and the same ...

units.la: Lege tamen cautum fuerat, vt bello ingruente haec pecunia in militum stipendia numeraretur.
units.tr: Yet the law had provided that, when war broke out, this money should be paid out for soldiers' pay.

units.la: [?]Ὁπότ' ἂν πόλεμος ἢ τὰ ἀξιούντα χρήματα τῆς διοικήσεως γραπτωτικά [?].
units.tr: Whenever there is war, or other pressing needs that require money for the administration, [the theoric money is to be used] [Ὁπότ' ἂν πόλεμος ἢ τὰ ἀξιούντα χρήματα τῆς διοικήσεως γραπτωτικά].

units.la: Ingruente bello è theorica pecunia militum stipendia numerantur.
units.tr: When war breaks out, the theoric money is paid out for soldiers' stipends.

units.la: Legis meminit Demosthenes [?]ὡς τὰ πρὸς Νεαίρας. ἡ μηνόντων γράφειν υμῶν πεμπομένη εἰς τὰ Εὐβοίαν καὶ Ὀλιγοῦν, ἐγραψε ψήφισμα ὁ τῆς βουλῆς Ἀπολλοδώρου [?]βουλῶν καὶ ἐξώστην τα ἐρωτήσας [?] εἰς τὸν δῆμον, λέγων, ἀμφιχθονίου τοῦ δῆμου, εἴτε δοκεῖ τὰ ἀξιούντα χρήματα τῆς διοικήσεως γραπτωτικά [?], εἴτε θεωρικά, κελεύοντων μὴ τὸν νόμον, ὁπότ' ἂν πόλεμος ἢ, τὰ ἀξιούντα χρήματα τῆς διοικήσεως γραπτωτικά [?].
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in his speech Against Neaera. When you were sending men to Euboea and Olynthus, Apollodorus, the son of Pasion, proposed a decree and put it to the people, saying that, whether it seemed good that the money needed for the administration be used for pay, or the theoric fund, the law should order that, whenever there is war, the money needed for the administration be used for pay [ὡς τὰ πρὸς Νεαίρας. ἡ μηνόντων γράφειν υμῶν πεμπομένη εἰς τὰ Εὐβοίαν καὶ Ὀλιγοῦν, ἐγραψε ψήφισμα ὁ τῆς βουλῆς Ἀπολλοδώρου].

units.la: Hanc Legem abrogauit populus, alteramque, Eubulo rogante, tulit, qua cauetur, ne quis theoricam pecuniam in militum stipendia numerari fatagat, & scitum populi faciat. si secus faxit, capite luat.
units.tr: The people repealed this law and, at the proposal of Eubulus, passed another, by which it was provided that no one should try to have the theoric money paid out for soldiers' stipends, or propose a resolution to that effect. If anyone did so, he was to forfeit his life.

units.la: [?]Θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι, εἴ τις ἐπιχειρεῖ μεταποιεῖν τὰ θεωρικὰ γραπτωτικά.
units.tr: To be punished with death if anyone attempts to convert the theoric funds to pay for soldiers [Θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι, εἴ τις ἐπιχειρεῖ μεταποιεῖν τὰ θεωρικὰ γραπτωτικά].

units.la: Si quis adtentet facere, vt theorica pecunia in militum stipendia numeretur, capite luito.
units.tr: If anyone attempts to make the theoric money paid out for soldiers' stipends, he shall forfeit his life.

units.la: Meminit Vlpianus in I.Olynthiacam, ex eoque discimus Eubulum illius auctorem fuisse, & latae Legis tempus colligimus: [?]εἶπε ἐπιχρήσαντος Ἀπολλοδώρου πού νῦν, πάλιν αὐτὰ ποιῆσαι γραπτωτικά, βουλόμενος Εὔβουλος ὁ πολιτευόμενος δημαγωγὸς ἦν, πλείονα ὕσιας ἐπισκοπᾶν τῇ δήμου πρὸς ἑαυτὸν, ἐγραψε νόμον τὸ χειλωτικὸν, ὥστε τὸν ζημιοῦσθαι, εἴτε ἐπιχειρεῖν μεταποιεῖν τὰ θεωρικὰ γραπτωτικά. Cûm Apollodorus, Pasionis is filius fuit, vt ex Oratione contra Neaeram liquet, omni ope niteretur, vt theorica pecunia militum stipendia procederent non id tulit Eubulus, sed antiquata veteri Lege, quæ nitebatur Apollodorus, hanc tulit, & obtinuit. Apollodorus autem hac de re scitum fecerat, [illegible, ~40 letters] vt scribit Demosthenes verbis iam laudatis.
units.tr: Vlpian mentions it in his commentary on the First Olynthiac, and from him we learn that Eubulus was its author, and we gather the time when the law was passed. [The passage runs:] when Apollodorus had once again proposed that these funds be made payable for soldiers' pay, Eubulus, who was a popular leader and wished to draw more of the people's property to himself, proposed the law, so that whoever attempted to alter the theoric funds to be paid out for soldiers' pay would be punished [εἶπε ἐπιχρήσαντος Ἀπολλοδώρου πού νῦν, πάλιν αὐτὰ ποιῆσαι γραπτωτικά, βουλόμενος Εὔβουλος ὁ πολιτευόμενος δημαγωγὸς ἦν, πλείονα ὕσιας ἐπισκοπᾶν τῇ δήμου πρὸς ἑαυτὸν, ἐγραψε νόμον τὸ χειλωτικὸν, ὥστε τὸν ζημιοῦσθαι, εἴτε ἐπιχειρεῖν μεταποιεῖν τὰ θεωρικὰ γραπτωτικά]. Since Apollodorus, the son of Pasion, as is clear from the speech Against Neaera, strove by every means that the theoric money should go to soldiers' stipends, Eubulus did not tolerate this. Instead, with the old law that Apollodorus relied on set aside, he proposed this law and carried it. Apollodorus himself had passed a decree on this matter, [illegible], as Demosthenes writes in the words already cited.

units.la: Annus erat quartus Olympiadis centesimæ septimæ, Callimacho Athenis Prætore, nam eo anno, vt constat è Philochoro Libro VI. [illegible, ~12 letters] Athenis, auxilia ab Atheniensibus è ciuibus Olynthum missa sunt, [illegible, ~70 letters] Athenas, [illegible, ~60 letters] Athenas, [illegible, ~50 letters] sed [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] constat. Neque tantum hæc Eubuli Lex accepta est, sed etiam Apollodorus, postulante Stephano, multatus est, vt è Demosthene [illegible, ~20 letters] constat. Memnit Legis Libanius in Hypothesi I. Olynthiacæ: [illegible, ~40 letters]. Philinus apud Harpocrationem: [illegible, ~50 letters].
units.tr: It was the fourth year of the hundred and seventh Olympiad, with Callimachus as chief magistrate at Athens, for in that year, as is established from Philochorus, Book VI, [illegible] at Athens, auxiliaries were sent from the Athenian citizens to Olynthus, [illegible] to Athens, [illegible] to Athens, [illegible] but [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] is established. Not only was this law of Eubulus carried, but Apollodorus was also fined, at the prosecution of Stephanus, as is established from Demosthenes [illegible]. Libanius mentions the law in the Hypothesis to the First Olynthiac: [illegible]. Philinus, in Harpocration: [illegible].

units.la: Romæ quoque plebi [illegible, ~10 letters] factas fuisse, atque congiaria data, nemo est qui ignoret. Aurelianus primus, vt optime obseruauit Vir Incomparabilis panes distribuit, eosque siligineos, & bilibres, vt à Flauio Vopisco in eius Vita narratur. Postea panes dati sunt non siliginei qui ita dicuntur, sed secundi, qui fiunt è farina cribro valde non discussa: id colligo ex his veteris Persii Interpretis ad hunc eius versum è Satyra III.
units.tr: That at Rome, too, the plebs [illegible] were given largesses and free distributions of grain, no one is unaware. Aurelian was the first, as the distinguished man has rightly observed, to distribute loaves, and these were of fine wheat flour and of two pounds, as is told by Flavius Vopiscus in his Life of Aurelian. Afterwards the loaves given were not of fine wheat, as they are called, but second-grade, which are made from flour not sifted very finely. I gather this from the old commentator on Persius on his verse from Satire III.

units.la: Populi cribro decussa farina.
units.tr: The flour sifted through the people's sieve.

units.la: Farinam, panem non deliciosius cribro discussum, sed plebeium, de populi annona, id est, fiscalem dicit. Panem secundum dixit Horatius Libro II. Epistolarum, Epistola I. quæ est ad Augustum:
units.tr: He speaks of flour, bread not sifted through a fine sieve for luxury, but plebeian bread, from the people's grain allowance, that is, from the treasury. Horace, in Book II of the Epistles, Epistle I, which is addressed to Augustus, called it second-grade bread:

units.la: Viuit siliquis, & pane secundo.
units.tr: He lives on pulse and second-grade bread.

units.la: Vetus Interpres: Pane secundo, non siligineo, non primo, non postremo, sed dispensatorio. Postea nec hunc quidem panem secundum gratis accepit populus, sed sordidum comparabat è fisco pretio, quod Valentinianus & Valens mutarunt, & voluerunt vt mundos panes triginta sex vnciarum gratis acciperent vt habetur Lege V. C. Theod. de annonis ciuicis & pane gradili.
units.tr: The old commentator says: second-grade bread, not of fine wheat, not first-grade, not the very last, but the bread of the distribution. Later the people did not even receive this second-grade bread free; they bought the coarse bread from the treasury at a price. Valentinian and Valens changed this and wished that clean loaves of thirty-six ounces be received free, as is found in the law in the Theodosian Code on the civic grain allowances and on bread of the gradual kind.

units.la: Jmpp. Valentinianus & Valens A A. ad Populum.
units.tr: The Emperors Valentinian and Valens, Augusti, to the People.

units.la: Ciues Romanos qui in viginti panibus sordidis, qui nunc dicuntur Ardinienses, quinquaginta vncias comparabat, triginta & sex vncias in bucellis sex mundis sine pretio consequatur. P P. Roma, Kal. Aug. Valentin. N B. P. & Victore COSS.
units.tr: Roman citizens who used to buy fifty ounces for twenty coarse loaves, now called Ardinienses, shall receive thirty-six ounces free, in six clean loaves. Given at Rome, 1 August, in the consulship of Valentinian and Victor.

units.la: Emendat Vir summus: Ciuis Romanus, qui in viginti panibus sordidis, qui nunc dicuntur Sardinienses. Sed quare dicantur Sardinienses non explicat. Scio equidem ad testatione M. Varronis Libro II. de R. R. aductum fuisse Romam frumentum è Sardinia, quæ pleraque erat [illegible, ~30 letters] ὡσ- [illegible, ~8 letters]ἐώντως[?], inquit Strabo Libro V. Sed nihil ista ad rem. Existimo igitur, panem, qui olim siligineus fuit ex instituto Aureliani, datum fuisse hordeaceum: & quidem primo cribro discussum, ὃ λεπτῷ[?], id est, farinario: unde dicitur panis secundus, id est, non siligineus, neque item ex hordeo primus, id est, cribro pollinario decussus: atque hunc secundum panem etiam mundum dixerunt hac Lege Imperatores, quia farinario cribro erat discussus, opponuntque sordido, id est, cui nihil ademptum est, nec cribro decussus est. Praeterea hac Lege Imperatores adnotauerant, puto, quanti Romani ciues comparárent è fisco panes hos hordeaceos sordidos. Rescribo igitur: Ciuis Romanus, qui in viginti panibus sordidis, qui nunc dicuntur, ordei, mensis quinquaginta uncias comparabat, triginta & sex uncias in buccellis sex mundis sine pretio consequatur. Hic habes, quid factum ante hanc Legem scriptam, quid fieri ex hac Lege velint Imperatores. Viginti panes, unius unciae & semis singulì, hordeacij, quorum farina nullo cribro fuerat decussa, quibus nihil fuerat ademptum, sordidos dixerunt: comparabantur miliarensi & semis, id intelligitur hac nota, mens's[?]. facile autem mutauit m in n & i, unde conflata est vox Ardiniensis. Comparabant igitur è fisco miliarensi & semis in viginti panibus sordidis ordei quinquaginta uncias. At vero Imperatores voluerunt in posterum dari sine pretio in panibus sex hordeaceis farinario cribro discussis, ac proinde non sordidis, sed mundis triginta sex uncias. Habes igitur ex his, quae disputavimus, primo datum fuisse panem siligineum ex instituto Aureliani: deinde hordeaceum, eumque primo mundum, id est, cribro farinario decussum; deinde sordidum, cui nihil ademptum erat. Praeterea bilibres, id est, unciarum viginti quatuor panes dedit Aurelianus: secutis temporibus distributae sunt quinquaginta uncia in panibus viginti hordeaceis sordidis, neque id gratis, sed dato milliarensi & semis. Rursum Imperatores Valentinianus & Valens voluerunt dari sine pretio panes hordeaceos mundos, cribro farinario decussos, atque sex dari iusserunt sex unciarum singulos, id est, in sex panibus mundis uncias triginta sex.
units.tr: The distinguished scholar emends: Roman citizen, who for twenty coarse loaves, now called Sardinienses. But he does not explain why they are called Sardinienses. I know indeed that, by the testimony of Marcus Varro in Book II of On Agriculture, grain was brought to Rome from Sardinia, which was mostly [illegible], as Strabo says in Book V. But these things have nothing to do with the matter. I think, therefore, that the loaf which had once been of fine wheat under Aurelian's arrangement was afterwards given as barley bread: and indeed at first sifted, clean, that is, through a fine sieve, whence it is called second bread, that is, not of fine wheat, nor likewise first of barley, that is, sifted through a sieve for pollard. And the emperors in this law called this second bread also clean, because it had been sifted through a fine sieve, and they set it against coarse, that is, bread from which nothing had been removed and which had not been sifted. Moreover, I think the emperors in this law had noted at what price Roman citizens used to buy these barley loaves, coarse, from the treasury. I therefore rewrite it: Roman citizen, who for twenty coarse loaves of barley, as they are now called, used to buy fifty ounces, shall receive thirty-six ounces free in six clean loaves. Here you have what was done before this law was written, and what the emperors wish to be done under this law. Twenty loaves, each of one and a half ounces, of barley, whose flour had not been sifted through any sieve, from which nothing had been removed, they called coarse; they were bought for a miliarense and a half, as is understood from this mark. The letter m was easily changed into n and i, whence the word Ardiniensis was formed. So they bought from the treasury, for a miliarense and a half, fifty ounces in twenty coarse barley loaves. But the emperors wished in future that thirty-six ounces be given free in six barley loaves sifted through a fine sieve, and accordingly not coarse but clean. From what we have discussed you have, therefore: first, fine wheat bread was given under Aurelian's arrangement; then barley bread, first clean, that is, sifted through a fine sieve; then coarse, from which nothing had been removed. Moreover, Aurelian gave two-pound loaves, that is, loaves of twenty-four ounces. In later times fifty ounces in twenty coarse barley loaves were distributed, and not free, but for a payment of a miliarense and a half. Again the emperors Valentinian and Valens wished clean barley loaves, sifted through a fine sieve, to be given without charge, and ordered that six loaves of six ounces each be given, that is, thirty-six ounces in six clean loaves.

units.la: LIBER QVINTVS. FINIVM REGVNDORVM.
units.tr: BOOK FIVE. OF THE REGULATION OF BOUNDARIES.

units.la: TITVLVS I.
units.tr: TITLE I.

units.la: CVM siticulosa admodum esset terra Attica, vt testatur Dicaearchus ἐν τῷ βίῳ τῆς Ἑλλάδος. ἡ δὲ πόλις, ξηρὰ πᾶσα οὖσα ὕδατος[?], nec perennes essent amnes, aut fontes multi, aut lacus, ita vt oporteret puteos effodere: Legem hac de re scripsit Solon, qua cauit licere publico vti puteo, si intra hippicum sit: vbi maius esset interuallum, priuatum sibi foderent puteum.
units.tr: Since the land of Attica was very dry, as Dicaearchus testifies in his Life of Greece [ἐν τῷ βίῳ τῆς Ἑλλάδος]. The city was entirely without water [ξηρὰ πᾶσα οὖσα ὕδατος], its rivers were not perennial, and there were few springs or lakes, so that wells had to be dug. Solon wrote a law on this matter, by which he allowed the use of a public well if it lay within the hippicum; where the distance was greater, each man was to dig a private well for himself.

units.la: Οπου μὲν ἔστι δημόσιον φρέαρ ἐντὸς ἱππικοῦ, χρῆσθαι τούτῳ· ὅπου δὲ πλεῖον ἀπέχῃ, ἕκαστῳ ὕδωρ ἰδίῳ[?].
units.tr: Where there is a public well within the hippicum, use it; where it is further away, each person has water of his own [Οπου μὲν ἔστι δημόσιον φρέαρ ἐντὸς ἱππικοῦ, χρῆσθαι τούτῳ· ὅπου δὲ πλεῖον ἀπέχῃ, ἕκαστῳ ὕδωρ ἰδίῳ].

units.la: Publico puteo, qui intra hippicum sit, vtuntor: si maius sit interuallum, priuatum sibi quisque effodiunto.
units.tr: They shall use the public well which lies within the hippicum; if the distance is greater, each man shall dig a private well for himself.

units.la: Legem hanc habet Plutarchus in Solone: ἐπὶ δὲ ταῖς ὕδωρ, ὅτε ποταμοῖς ἔστιν ἀεὶ ὕδωρ, ὅτε λίμναις ἔχοιεν, ὅτ' ἀφόνοις πηγὰς ἢ χώρα ξηρὰ ἀρχῆς, ἀλλ' οἱ πλεῖστοι φρέα- σιν ποιητοῖς ἐχρῶντο, νόμον ἔθεντο. Οπου μὲν ἔστι δημόσιον φρέαρ ἐντὸς ἱππικοῦ, χρῆσθαι τούτῳ (τὸ δὲ ἱππικὸν ἀξέσημα, πεντάρων τῷ σταδίων.) ὅπου δὲ πλεῖον ἀπέχῃ, ἕκαστῳ ὕδωρ ἰδίῳ[?]. Hippicum interuallum est stadiorum quatuor, vt inquit Plutarchus. Hesychius vnius tantum stadii facit, ἱππικόν, ὅ ἐστι στάδιον. Quod equidem praetulerim notatione nominis: nam videtur esse illud interuallum, quod sine vlla intermissione equus conficit & decurrit. Temere tamen non licebat intra fines suos sibi puteum fodere, sed ὀργυιὰς latitudinem ab alieno fundo oportebat relinquere ex hac Solonis Lege:
units.tr: Plutarch in his Life of Solon gives this law: when rivers have a constant supply of water, when lakes are available, when springs or dry land lack water, but most people used artificial wells, he laid down the following law: where there is a public well within the hippicum, use it (the hippicum is, as Plutarch says, four hundred and fifty feet... [the figure is garbled in the text]); where the distance is greater, each man shall have water of his own. Plutarch says the hippicum is a distance of four stadia. Hesychius makes it only one stadium, the hippicum being a stadium. I would prefer the latter on the basis of the word's meaning, for that interval seems to be the distance a horse covers without any pause. Nevertheless, one was not permitted to dig a well within one's own bounds without leaving a space of one orgyia's width from the neighbour's land, according to this law of Solon:

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΦΡΕΑΡ ΠΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟ-ΤΡΙΩΙ ΧΩΡΙΩΙ ΟΡΥΤΤΗΙ ΟΡ-ΓΥΙΑΝ ΑΠΟΛΙΠΕΙΝ.
units.tr: IF ANYONE DIGS A WELL NEXT TO ANOTHER'S FIELD, HE MUST LEAVE AN ORGYIA [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΦΡΕΑΡ ΠΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩΙ ΧΩΡΙΩΙ ΟΡΥΤΤΗΙ ΟΡΓΥΙΑΝ ΑΠΟΛΙΠΕΙΝ].

units.la: Si quis puteum iuxta alterius agrum fodiat, orgyæ spadium relinquito.
units.tr: If anyone digs a well beside another's field, he shall leave a space of one orgyia.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis καὶ ἀΒλεξὲι descripsit Gaius Libro IV. ad Legem XII. Tabularum, & Solonis fuisse docet. Sciendum est, in actione finium regundorum illud obseruandum esse, quod ad exemplum quodammodo eius Legis scriptum est, quam Athenis Solon dicitur tulisse: nam illis ita est: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΦΡΕΑΡ ΠΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩΙ ΧΩΡΙΩΙ ΩΡΥΤΤΗΙ ΟΡΓΥΙΑΝ ΑΠΟΛΙΠΕΙΝ. Lege XIII.
units.tr: Harmenopulus mentions this law; Gaius described it in Book IV on the Twelve Tables, and teaches that it was Solon's. It must be noted that in the action for regulating boundaries, the following should be observed, which is written in some way after the example of that law which Solon is said to have passed at Athens: for in that law it reads thus: IF ANYONE DIGS A WELL BESIDE ANOTHER'S FIELD, HE MUST LEAVE AN ORGYIA. Law XIII.

units.la: D. Finium regundorum. Addit Harmenopulus, qui hanc quoque refert Legem, Εἰ μή πω φρέαρ παρ᾽ ἀλλοτρίῳ χωρίῳ ὀρύττῃ, ἐὰν τὶς φρέαρ γὰρ ἀλλοτρίῳ χωρίῳ ὀρύττῃ, εἰ μὴ πω φρέαρ ὁ προὔγραψε τοῦ γείτονος ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἔργου βλαπτεται. Quid sit ΟΡΥΓΙΑ varie exponunt veteres: alij sex pedum ὀργυιὰν esse volunt, alij trium passuum, quidam vnius: Plinius vlnam alicubi vertit. Sed variant multum ab his verbis illa, quae dedit eruditissimus Ioh. Leunclauius in Eclogis Basilicôn. ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΦΡΕΑΡ ΓΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩΙ ΧΩΡΙΩΙ ΟΡΥΤΤΗΙ, ΕΙ ΜΗ ΠΩ ΦΡΕΑΡ Ο ΠΡΟΥΓΡΗΧΕ ΤΟΥ ΓΕΙΤΟΝΟΣ ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΕΝΟΣ ΕΡΓΟΥ ΒΛΑΠΤΕΤΑΙ ΕΠΙ ΤΟΣΟΥΤΟΝ, ΟΣΟΝ ΤΟ ΒΑΘΟΣ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΙ ΑΠΟΦΥΓΕΙΝ. Senfus eft: Si quis puteum effodiat, dummodo puteo, quem iam ante vicinus effodit, nouo hoc opere, (legendum enim puto ἀπὸ τῆς ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΕΝΟΣ ΕΡΓΟΥ, ad hunc modum ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΚΑΙΝΟΥ ΕΡΓΟΥ, vt eft apud Harmenopulum) non noceatur, ad tantundem spatij, quanta fuerit putei profunditas, debet recedere. Nititur haec scriptura altera Solonis Lege qua canit, cum qui παφον ἱ' βοῦ ... ὀρύπῃ, ὅσον τὸ βάθος αὐτὴ, τοσοῦτον ἀπολείπειν, tantum ab alieno agro spacii relinquere, quantum deprimet sepulcrum aut screbem. Quod si quis aquam non inuenisset depresso in altum puteo decem ὀργυιάς, hac Lege voluit Solon licere è vicini puteo bis quotidie aquam extrahere vrna sex choum capace.
units.tr: D. Of the regulating of boundaries. Harmenopulus, who also cites this law, adds: "If anyone digs a well beside another's land, unless he digs it... the well of the neighbour is harmed by the new work, he must withdraw to as great a distance as the depth of the well." The ancient writers explain variously what ORGYIA is: some want it to be six feet, others three paces, some one; Pliny somewhere translates it as an ell. But the words given by the very learned John Leunclavius in his Eclogae Basilicorum differ much from these: IF ANYONE DIGS A WELL BESIDE ANOTHER'S FIELD, UNLESS THE WELL OF THE NEIGHBOUR... IS HARMED BY THE NEW WORK, HE MUST WITHDRAW TO AS GREAT A DISTANCE AS THE DEPTH OF THE WELL. The sense is: "If anyone digs a well, provided that the neighbour's well, which he has already dug, is not harmed by this new work, he must withdraw to as great a distance as the depth of the well" (I think we should read "from the new work" as in Harmenopulus). This second version of the law rests on another law of Solon, by which a man who digs a well to a depth of ten orgyias must leave as much space from the neighbour's field as the depth of the pit... that is, as much as the depth of a tomb or trench. But if someone, having sunk a well to ten orgyias without finding water, by this law Solon allowed him to draw water twice daily from his neighbour's well, in jars holding six choes.

units.la: Ἐαν δὲ ὀρύξαντες ὀργυιὰν δέκα βάθος πρὸς ἑαυτοῖς μὴ ἴδρωσιν ὕδωρ, τότε λαμβάνειν ἀπὸ τοῦ γείτονος, ἐξάγειν ὑδρίας δὶς ἑκάστης ἡμέρας πληγωῆς.
units.tr: If, having dug to a depth of ten orgyias, they do not find water on their own land, then they may take it from the neighbour, drawing twice each day in jars.

units.la: Si quis, depresso in altum puteo decem orgyas, aquam in suo non inueniat, extrahito è vicini puteo bis quotidie aquam vrna sex choum capace.
units.tr: If someone, having sunk his well to a depth of ten orgyias, finds no water on his own land, he may draw water twice daily from his neighbour's well, in a jar holding six choes.

units.la: Legem laudat Plutarchus in Solone: ἐπὶ δὲ πηγὰς ὕδωρ ὅτε ποταμοῖς ... ἀφέσεως ... ἐπὶ δὲ ἀρχάς ... πολίτῃ ... ὅπως ... ἀφεῖναι ... ἰσότιμος. Ratio est ibidem à Plutarcho: ἀπεῖα γὰρ ὤετο ... ἀλλὰ ... ἐφοβοῦντο. Quia vero saepe fiebat, vt controuersiae hac de re mouerentur, hinc Magistratus Athenis, qui ὑδάτων Ἐπισκέπτης dicebatur, cui res haec curae. Colligo é Plutarchi narratione in Themistocle: εἶδι καὶ ἐν Μητρὸς ἱερῷ τῷ κλυσυμένῳ ὑδροφόρῳ κρίνῳ χαλκῷ, μέγεθος διπήχων· ἐν αὐτῇ ὅτι τῆς Ἀθηναίων ὑδάτων Ἐπισκέπτης, ἀρχῶν ὑφηρημένους ὃ ὕδωρ καὶ πηγὴν ... μηνὸς. Eratque praeterea horum Aquarum Curatorum, ita Latinis scriptoribus nominantur, prouidere, ne quis aquam puteorum publicam priua sua auctoritate violaret, deriuaret, aut oletaret. Quia autem, vt diximus, siticulosa admodum erat Attica, factum puto, vt in votis pro impetranda pluuia sui tantum meminissent, & rationem haberent Athenienses. Voti meminit M. Antoninus Libro τῶν εἰς ἑαυτὸν V. ... Ἀθηναίων, ὅσον, ὅσον, ὦ φίλε Ζεῦ, ... τῆς Ἀθηναίων, καὶ τῶν πόλεων.
units.tr: Plutarch in his Life of Solon praises the law: concerning springs, water, when rivers... allowance... concerning the beginnings... citizen... that... to allow... equal in rights. Plutarch gives the reason: for he thought... but they feared... Because such disputes often arose on this matter, the Athenians had a magistrate who was called the Overseer of Waters, to whom this business was entrusted. I gather from Plutarch's account in the Life of Themistocles that there was in the temple of the Mother a bronze urn of two cubits' size, and in it... the Overseer of the Athenian waters... taking away the water and the spring... of the month. There were also, as Latin writers call them, Curators of the Waters, whose task was to see that no one violated, diverted, or fouled the public waters of a well by private authority. Since, as we have said, Attica was very dry, I think it came about that the Athenians remembered their own land in their vows for rain and took account of it. Marcus Antoninus mentions such a vow in Book V of his Meditations... Athenians, how much, how much, O dear Zeus... of Athens and of the cities.

units.la: Lege cauit Solon, Si quis fossam ducere, aut sepulcrum (sepeliebatur enim extra vrbis pomoeria in agris) fodere velit, tantundem spacii relinquat ab alieno agro, in quantam profunditatem deprefferit.
units.tr: Solon provided by law: if anyone wishes to dig a ditch or a grave (for they buried outside the city boundaries in the fields), he shall leave as much space from the neighbour's field as the depth to which he digs.

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΤΑΦΟΝ Η ΒΟΘΡΟΝ ΓΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩι ΧΩΡΙΩι ΟΡΥΤ-ΤΗι, ΟΣΟΝ ΤΟ ΒΑΘΟΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ Ηι ΤΟΣΟΥΤΟΝ ΑΠΟΛΙΠΕΙΝ.
units.tr: IF ANYONE DIGS A GRAVE OR A PIT NEXT TO ANOTHER'S FIELD, HE MUST LEAVE AS MUCH SPACE AS ITS DEPTH IS [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΤΑΦΟΝ Η ΒΟΘΡΟΝ ΓΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩι ΧΩΡΙΩι ΟΡΥΤΤΗι, ΟΣΟΝ ΤΟ ΒΑΘΟΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ Ηι ΤΟΣΟΥΤΟΝ ΑΠΟΛΙΠΕΙΝ].

units.la: Si quis sepulcrum fodiat, aut fossam ducat iuxta vicinum agrum, ab eo tantundem spacij relinquito, in quantam profunditatem deprimet.
units.tr: If someone digs a grave, or leads a ditch beside a neighbour's field, he shall leave from it as much space as he digs down.

units.la: Legem describit Gaius loco laudato. Sciendum est, in actione finium regundorum illud obseruandum esse, quod ad exemplum quodammodo eius Legis scriptum est, quam Athenis Solon dicitur tulisse: nam illic ita est: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΤΑΦΟΝ Η ΒΟΘΡΟΝ ΓΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩι ΧΩΡΙΩι ΟΡΥΤΤΗι, ΟΣΟΝ ΤΟ ΒΑ-ΘΟΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ Ηι, ΤΟΣΟΥΤΟΝ ΑΠΟΛΙΠΕΙΝ. Ita etiam legitur in Eclogis Basilicasn[?]. Plutarchus in Solone: [illegible, ~20 letters] (malim quemadmodum apud Gaium [illegible, ~12 letters]) [illegible, ~45 letters].
units.tr: Gaius describes this law in the passage cited. It must be noted that in the action for regulating boundaries, the following should be observed, which is written in some way after the example of the law which Solon is said to have passed at Athens; for there it reads thus: IF ANYONE DIGS A GRAVE OR A PIT NEXT TO ANOTHER'S FIELD, HE MUST LEAVE AS MUCH SPACE AS ITS DEPTH IS. So it is also read in the Eclogae Basilicorum. Plutarch in the Life of Solon: [illegible] (I would prefer as in Gaius) [illegible].

units.la: Lex est Solonis de sepe ducenda, aut maceria, aut casa inter agrum suum & alienum: & quidem si sepem ducat, limitem ne excedat, si murum, pedem relinquat: si casam, pedes [illegible, ~2 letters]uos.
units.tr: This is Solon's law concerning hedging, or a wall, or a hut between one's own field and another's: if he plants a hedge, he must not go beyond the boundary line; if a wall, he must leave a foot; if a hut, two feet [illegible].

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΙΜΑΣΙΑΝ ΓΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩι ΧΩΡΙΩι ΟΡΥΓΗι, ΤΟΝ ΟΡΟΝ ΜΗ ΠΑΡΑ-ΒΑΙΝΕΙΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΕΙΧΙΟΝ ΠΟΔΑ ΑΠΟ-ΛΙΠΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΟΙΚΗΜΑ, ΔΥΟ ΠΟΔΑΣ.
units.tr: IF ANYONE BUILDS A FENCE NEXT TO ANOTHER'S FIELD, HE MUST NOT TRESPASS ON THE BOUNDARY. IF A WALL, HE MUST LEAVE A FOOT; IF A HOUSE, TWO FEET [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΙΜΑΣΙΑΝ ΓΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩι ΧΩΡΙΩι ΟΡΥΓΗι, ΤΟΝ ΟΡΟΝ ΜΗ ΠΑΡΑΒΑΙΝΕΙΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΕΙΧΙΟΝ ΠΟΔΑ ΑΠΟΛΙΠΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΟΙΚΗΜΑ, ΔΥΟ ΠΟΔΑΣ].

units.la: Laudat [illegible, ~8 letters] Gaius loco laudato. Sciendum est, in actione finium regundorum illud obseruandum esse, quod ad exemplum quodammodo eius Legis scriptum est, quam Athenis Solon dicitur tulisse: nam illic ita est: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΙΜΑ-ΣΙΑΝ ΓΑΡ' ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΩι ΧΩΡΙΩι ΟΡΥΓΗι, ΤΟΝ ΟΡΟΝ ΜΗ ΓΑΡΑΒΑΙΝΕΙΝ· ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΕΙΧΙΟΝ, ΠΟΔΑ ΑΠΟΛΙΠΕΙΝ· ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΟΙ-ΚΗΜΑ, ΔΥΟ ΠΟΔΑΣ. Apud Harmenopulum maius sit interuallum, quam duorum pedum, nempe sex. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΟΙΚΗΜΑ ΕΞ ΠΟΛΑΣ. Existimo autem voce OIKHMA intelligi casam siue tugurium custodiae causa aedificatum earum rerum, quae in agro sunt, aut vt à pluuiis, æstu, ac frigore tueatur. Nam ex eiusdem Solonis Lege sequitur in Eclogis Basilicasn[?].
units.tr: [Illegible] cites the law, as does Gaius in the passage cited. It must be noted that in the action for regulating boundaries, the following should be observed, which is written in some way after the example of the law which Solon is said to have passed at Athens; for there it reads thus: IF ANYONE DIGS A FENCE NEXT TO ANOTHER'S FIELD, HE MUST NOT TRESPASS ON THE BOUNDARY; IF A WALL, HE MUST LEAVE A FOOT; IF A HOUSE, TWO FEET. In Harmenopulus the interval is greater than two feet, namely six. IF A HOUSE, OUT OF THE... I think that by the word OIKHMA is meant a hut or shelter built for guarding the things that are in the field, or for protection from rain, heat and cold. For from the same law of Solon, as it appears in the Eclogae Basilicorum, it follows...

units.la: ΕΙ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΕΝ ΑΓΡΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΙ-ΤΟ ΚΤΙΣΑΙ ΤΟΞΟΥ ΒΟΛΗΝ Α-ΓΟ ΤΟΥ ΑΓΡΟΓΕΙΤΟΝΟΣ ΑΠΕ-ΧΕΤΩ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ΟΡ-ΓΥΙΑΝ.
units.tr: IF ANYONE, IN THE FIELD, WISHES TO BUILD A SHED... LET HIM KEEP AWAY FROM THE NEIGHBOURING FIELD... [gap in the text] ... AN ORGYIA.

units.la: Quibus verbis, ΕΝ ΑΓΡΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΙΤΟ ΚΤΙΣΑΙ, intelligi censeo tum villam rusticam, quam villicus siue colonus habitandam sibi obtinet, & familiae villaticae, atque instrumento omni rustico condendo aut continendo: cum etiam villam vrbanam, quae & Praetorium dicitur, lautius aedificatam, & instar aedificiorum vrbis, & patris familias habitationi relictam. Villam igitur si quis in fundo suo aedificare velit, abesse iussit Solon ab alieno ad arcus vsque iactum. Cetera quae desiderantur ante vocem ΟΡΥΙΑΝ non coniecturis nostris, sed ex integrioribus Libris supplenda sunt.
units.tr: By these words, ΕΝ ΑΓΡΩι ΒΟΥΛΟΙΤΟ ΚΤΙΣΑΙ [in a field, if one wishes to build], I think we should understand both the rustic farmhouse, which the farm manager or tenant holds to live in, along with the farm staff and the storing of all farm equipment, and also the town-style house, which is also called a Praetorium, built more elegantly and in the manner of city buildings, and left for the habitation of the householder. So if anyone wishes to build a house on his own land, Solon ordered that it stand at least a bowshot away from another's property. The rest that is missing before the word ΟΡΥΙΑΝ should be supplied not by my conjectures but from fuller copies of the books.

units.la: Μελιαπῶν σμίλων κεχισμένον, ἀπέχειν τὴν ὑφ' ἑτέρου προσπεσὼν ἰδρυμένων πόδας τετρακοσίους[?].
units.tr: Of a beehive built of ... [the text is corrupt], he must keep away from the neighbour's ... four hundred feet [?].

units.la: Quia apum alucaria facit, ab alucaribus vicini distantia pedes trecentos collocato.
units.tr: Because he keeps beehives, he shall place them three hundred feet away from his neighbour's hives.

units.la: Legem descripsit Plutarchus in Solone: καὶ μελιαπῶν σμίλων κεχισμένον ἐκ-λύσιν, ἀπέχειν τὴν ὑφ' ἑτέρου προσπεσὼν ἰδρυμένων πόδας τετρακοσίους[?]. Sed quia hic fumus, communicabimus cum studiosis nostram super his Vergilij versibus è Lib. IV. Georg. coniecturam.
units.tr: Plutarch describes the law in his Life of Solon: and of a beehive built of ..., let him keep away from the neighbour's ... four hundred feet [?]. But since this is a digression, I will share with my students my conjecture on these verses of Vergil from Georgics Book IV.

units.la: Bis grauidos cogunt foetus: duo tempora messis: / Taÿgete simul os terris ostendit honestum / Pleïas, & Oceani spretos pede repulit amnes. / Aut eadem sidus fugiens ubi piscis aquosi, / Tristior hibernas caelo descendit in undas.
units.tr: They gather their pregnant broods twice a year, two seasons of harvest: when Taygete together with the Pleiad shows her lovely face to the lands, and pushes back with her foot the streams that the Ocean has spurned. Or when the fish of the watery sign, fleeing the same star, descends more sadly into the wintry waves of the sky.

units.la: Locus videtur inextricabilis nupero scriptori, qui hic duo describi mellis metendi tempora obseruat, unum post ortum Pleiadum, verno tempore, alterum autumno, post eorundem occasum matutinum. Sed cur Pleiadem occidendo ait piscem fugere? Seruius Piscem Austrum intelligit, cuius in eos Aquarius aquam infundit: Hic autem oritur eo tempore, quo Pleiades occidunt. Atqui falsum istud est. Nam quo momento Pleias in occasu matutino sita est, in elevatione poli, sub qua Poeta scripsit, os Piscis Australis parum abest à meridiano inferiori. Ceteri quoque Pisces ante Vergilias ortum & occasum faciunt. Ideo quaerendum est, quo sensu Pleias Piscem fugiens occidere dicatur à Vergilio, quod nisi de instanti sidere aliquo non solet vsurpari. Ego vero puto Vergilias dici fugere sidus, non quod instet & insequatur, sed cum auersam & contrariam ab illo insistunt viam. Sideris autem nomine Solem intelligo, quem fugi à Vergilijs dixit Poeta, quia cum Sol è mari emergit, illae in mare descendunt. Pisces vero aquosi vndas, non autem sidus dixit, quia se in vndas immergunt, in quas antea se immerserant Pisces. Quare ita interpungendum est.
units.tr: The passage seems inextricable to a recent writer, who here observes that two times for gathering honey are described: one after the rising of the Pleiades in spring, the other in autumn, after their morning setting. But why does he say that the Pleiad, in setting, makes the fish flee? Servius understands the Fish to be the Southern Fish, on which the Water-Carrier pours water; and this fish rises at the time when the Pleiades set. But that is false. For at the moment when the Pleiad is in its morning setting, at the elevation of the pole under which the Poet wrote, the mouth of the Southern Fish is not far from the lower meridian. The other fishes also rise and set before the Vergiliae. Therefore we must ask in what sense Vergil says that the Pleiad is said to set while the Fish flees, which usually is not said except of some star that is pressing on. I, however, think that the Vergiliae are said to flee the star not because it presses on and pursues them, but because they take a course turned away from and opposite to it. By the name of "star" I understand the Sun, which the Poet says the Vergiliae flee, because when the Sun rises from the sea, they descend into the sea. But he called the watery waves the Fish's, not the star's, because the Fish plunge into the waves into which they had earlier plunged. Hence the punctuation should be as follows.

units.la: Aut eadem sidus fugiens, ubi piscis aquosi / Tristior hibernas caelo descendit in undas.
units.tr: Or when the same star is fled, and where the watery fish, sadder, descends into the wintry waves of the sky.

units.la: Sidus autem de Sole dici testis est Ouidius Lib. IX. Metamorph.
units.tr: That sidus is said of the Sun is attested by Ovid, Metamorphoses Book IX.

units.la: Namque laboriferi cum iam natalis adesset / Herculis, & decimum premeretur sidere signum.
units.tr: For when the birthday of labour-bearing Hercules was at hand, and the tenth sign was being pressed by the star.

units.la: Lex Solonis de plantandis arboribus cauet, ut oleae & ficus serantur nouem pedes ab alieno fundo longe: ceterae vero quinque pedes tantum.
units.tr: Solon's law on planting trees provides that olive and fig trees are to be planted nine feet from another's field, but the other trees only five feet.

units.la: ΕΛΛΙΑΝ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΣΥΚΗΝ ΕΝ-ΝΕΑ ΠΟΔΑΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΑΛΛΟ-ΤΡΙΟΥ ΦΥΤΕΥΕΙΝ, ΤΑ ΔΕ ΑΛΛΑ ΔΕΝΔΡΑ ΠΕΝΤΕ ΠΟΔΑΣ.
units.tr: But that an olive and a fig tree are to be planted nine feet from the boundary of the neighbour, and other trees five feet [ΕΛΛΙΑΝ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΣΥΚΗΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΠΟΔΑΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΟΥ ΦΥΤΕΥΕΙΝ, ΤΑ ΔΕ ΑΛΛΑ ΔΕΝΔΡΑ ΠΕΝΤΕ ΠΟΔΑΣ].

units.la: Oleam & ficum nouem pedes longe ab alieno fundo serito: ceteras vero arbores pedes quinque.
units.tr: Plant an olive and a fig nine feet away from another's field; but other trees five feet.

units.la: Descripsit Gaius loco iam saepius laudato. Sciendum est, in actione finium regundorum illud obseruandum esse, quod ad exemplum quodammodo eius Legis scriptum est, quam Athenis Solon dici ur tulisse: nam illic ita est: ΕΛΛΙΑΝ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΣΥΚΗΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΠΟΔΑΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΟΥ ΦΥΤΕΥΕΙΝ, ΤΑ ΔΕ ΑΛΛΑ ΔΕΝΔΡΑ ΠΕΝΤΕ ΠΟΔΑΣ. Meminit in Solone Plutarchus, & causam addit, quod ficus & olea radices agant longius, neque fit omnibus earum sine damno vicinia, sed & alimentum eripiant, & halitum effient aliquibus infectum: ὥσιπ[?] ἢ καὶ Φυτειῶν μέτρα μάλα ἐμπίπρως[?]. Τὰς μὲν ἄλλο τι Φυτεύοντας ἐν ἀγρῷ πέντε πόδας ἀπέχειν τῆς γείτονος κελεύσας, τὰς δὲ συκῆς ἢ ἐλαίας[?], οὐκέα[?]. προρροιζέστερα[?] γὰρ ἐξικνεῖσθαι ταῦτα τῆς ῥίζης. ἢ δ' ἂν πᾶσι γλυκεῖα τῆς φύσεως ἀσινὰς[?], ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔξω παρέχειν[?], καὶ βλάπτουσαν ἐκείνοις ἀπορρίψαι[?] ἀφίναι[?].
units.tr: Gaius described it in the passage already quoted several times. It must be noted that in an action for determining boundaries, the following point must be observed, which was written somewhat on the model of that law which Solon is said to have passed at Athens: for there it reads thus: ΕΛΛΙΑΝ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΣΥΚΗΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΠΟΔΑΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΑΛΛΟΤΡΙΟΥ ΦΥΤΕΥΕΙΝ, ΤΑ ΔΕ ΑΛΛΑ ΔΕΝΔΡΑ ΠΕΝΤΕ ΠΟΔΑΣ. Plutarch mentions this in his Solon, and adds the reason, that fig and olive trees send their roots further, and their neighbourhood is not harmless to all trees, but they take away nourishment and emit a breath harmful to some [ὥσιπ[?] ἢ καὶ Φυτειῶν μέτρα μάλα ἐμπίπρως[?]. Τὰς μὲν ἄλλο τι Φυτεύοντας ἐν ἀγρῷ πέντε πόδας ἀπέχειν τῆς γείτονος κελεύσας, τὰς δὲ συκῆς ἢ ἐλαίας[?], οὐκέα[?]. προρροιζέστερα[?] γὰρ ἐξικνεῖσθαι ταῦτα τῆς ῥίζης. ἢ δ' ἂν πᾶσι γλυκεῖα τῆς φύσεως ἀσινὰς[?], ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔξω παρέχειν[?], καὶ βλάπτουσαν ἐκείνοις ἀπορρίψαι[?] ἀφίναι[?]].

units.la: Ad Leges de oleis pertinet vox ista à Solone vsurpata:
units.tr: To the laws about olives belongs this word, used by Solon:

units.la: ΣΤΟΙΧΑΔΑΣ.
units.tr: stoichadas [ΣΤΟΙΧΑΔΑΣ].

units.la: Habes apud Pollucem Lib. V. cap. IV. qui docet ita appellasse oleas, quae priuatorum erant, & in illorum agris consitae, quasque opponit publicis & sacris Moeiais dictis. Pollucis verba ista sunt. Σόλων ἡ, ἡ ΣΤΟΙΧΑΔΑΣ τινὰς ἐλαίας ἐκάλεσε, ταῖς Moeiais αἰτίαις[?], ἴσως τὰς ἐπὶ τοῦ τοίχου πεφυτευμένας[?].
units.tr: You have it in Pollux Book V, chapter IV, who teaches that olives were so called, those which belonged to private persons and were planted on their lands, and which he sets against the public and sacred olives called Moriai. Pollux's words are these: Solon called certain olives "stoichades" in contrast to the Moriai, perhaps those planted along the wall [Σόλων ἡ, ἡ ΣΤΟΙΧΑΔΑΣ τινὰς ἐλαίας ἐκάλεσε, ταῖς Moeiais αἰτίαις[?], ἴσως τὰς ἐπὶ τοῦ τοίχου πεφυτευμένας[?]].

units.la: Lege non licebat cuiquam ad priuatos vsus oleas euellere, praeter quam duas quotannis, qui secus fecisset, centum multabatur drachmis in singulas oleas.
units.tr: By the law it was not permitted for anyone to uproot olives for private use, except two each year. Whoever acted otherwise was fined one hundred drachmas for each olive.

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΕΛΑΙΑΝ ΑΘΗΝΗΣΙΝ ΕΞΟ-ΡΥΤΤΗΙ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΙΣ ΙΕΡΟΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ, Η ΔΗΜΟΤΙΚΟΝ, Η ΕΑΥΤΩΙ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΜΕΧΡΙ ΔΥΟΙΝ ΕΛΑΙΑΙΝ ΤΟΥ ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΥ, Η ΕΠΙ ΑΠΟΘΑ-ΝΟΝΤΑ ΔΕΗ ΧΡΗΣΑΣΘΑΙ ΘΦΕΙΑΕΙΝ
units.tr: If anyone uproots an olive in Athens, unless it is for the use of the Athenian temples, public or sacred, or for his own use, up to two olives of each person in a year, or for a funeral, let him ... [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΕΛΑΙΑΝ ΑΘΗΝΗΣΙΝ ΕΞΟΡΥΤΤΗΙ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΙΣ ΙΕΡΟΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ, Η ΔΗΜΟΤΙΚΟΝ, Η ΕΑΥΤΩΙ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΜΕΧΡΙ ΔΥΟΙΝ ΕΛΑΙΑΙΝ ΤΟΥ ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΥ, Η ΕΠΙ ΑΠΟΘΑ-ΝΟΝΤΑ ΔΕΗ ΧΡΗΣΑΣΘΑΙ ΘΦΕΙΑΕΙΝ].

units.la: Si quis oleam Athenis euellat, nisi in vsum Templorum Athenien\sium, aut in priuatum suum duas euellat quotannis, aut in funus, in singulas oleas centum ΕΚΑΤΟΝ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩι ΤΗΣ ΕΛΑΙΑΣ ΕΚΑΣΤΗΣ· ΤΟ ΔΕ ΕΠΙΔΕΚΑΤΟΝ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΟΦΕΙΛΕΤΩ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΙΔΙΩΤΗι ΤΩι ΕΠΕΞΙΟΝΤΙ ΕΚΑΤΟΝ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ΚΑΘ' ΕΚΑΣΤΗΝ ΕΛΑΙΑΝ, ΤΑΣ ΔΕ ΔΙΚΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ [?]ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΑΣ ΩΝ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΙ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΑΙ ΕΙΣΙ. [?]ΠΡΥΤΑΝΕΙΑ ΔΕ ΤΙΘΕΤΩ Ο ΔΙΩΚΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΜΕΡΟΥΣ, ΟΤΟΥ Δ' ΑΝ ΚΑΤΑΓΝΩΣΘΗι ΕΓΓΡΑΦΟΝΤΩΝ ΟΙ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΕΣ [?]ΠΡΟΣ ΟΥΣ ΑΝ Ηι Η ΔΙΚΗ ΤΟΙΣ ΠΡΑΚΤΟΡΣΙΝ Ο ΤΩι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩι, ΓΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΤΑΜΙΑΙΣ ΤΗΣ ΘΕΟΥ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΕΓΓΡΑΦΩΣΙΝ ΑΥΤΟΙ ΟΦΕΙΛΟΝΤΩΝ. drachmas pendito: decimae multa Minervae sacra esto: centum quoque drachmae addicuntor actori. Dicae scribuntor apud Magistratum, cuius est iudices dare. Actor sacramentum deponito. Reo damnato Magistratus exigendam tradito multam, quae in aerarium publicum infertur, exactoribus, decimam vero, quae Minervae cedis. Quaestoribus Deae. Si secus fecerint Magistratus, ipsi de suo pendunto.
units.tr: If anyone uproots an olive in Athens, unless for the use of the Athenian temples, or for his own use, two each year, or for a funeral, let him pay one hundred drachmas to the public treasury for each olive [ΕΚΑΤΟΝ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩι ΤΗΣ ΕΛΑΙΑΣ ΕΚΑΣΤΗΣ]; the tenth part of this belongs to the goddess. Let the one who brings the charge also receive one hundred drachmas for each olive. The lawsuits are to be brought concerning these matters before the magistrates whom each court has as judges. Let the accuser deposit a pledge. If the accused is convicted, let the magistrates hand over the fine to the collectors for the public treasury, and the tenth to the Minerva's sacred treasury. If the magistrates act otherwise, they shall pay from their own pockets.

units.la: Hanc Legem ἰδίως ὀνόμασι[?] reprɛfentat Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Μακάρτατον. Nemini igitur licebat Athenis oleam euellere siue in alieno agro, siue in suo: unde post Legem lectam addit Demosthenes, ὃ ὁ νόμος ἀπαγορεύει μηδὲ ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ χωρίῳ τῷ πατρῴῳ ἐλαίαν ἐξορύττειν. unde suspicari licet ἐ Lege nonnulla excidisse verba statim ab initio, inter cetera haec, ΜΗΔ' ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΧΩΡΙΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΩΟΥ. quae ita suo loco restituenda censeo. ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΕΛΑΙΑΝ ΑΘΗΝΗΣΙΝ ΕΞΟΡΥΤΤΗι, ΜΗΔ' ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΧΩΡΙΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΩΟΥ. At si ex suo ipsius agro, quem à patre acceperat, de quo nemo controuersiam faciebat, oleas euellere licebat, quanto minus ex aliena? Si cuellebat, ærario pendebat publico centum drachmas in singulas oleas, cuius multæ decima Minervæ consecrabatur. centum quoque drachmæ in singulas oleas cedebant & addicebantur actori, qui reum peregisset. Dica autem scribebatur apud Magistratus, quorum erat Iudices dare. Actor vero sacramentum deponebat, quod varie definiunt veteres, nam alij existimant esse decimam multæ, alij vero putant definiri drachmis tribus, vbi controuertitur & agitur de centum drachmis, aut pluribus ad mille vsque, & triginta drachmis, si de mille drachmis, aut pluribus ad decem millia vsque agatur. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. VI.
units.tr: Demosthenes presents this law in its own words in his speech Against Macartatus. No one was therefore permitted at Athens to uproot an olive, whether in another's field or his own. Hence, after reading the law, Demosthenes adds: "which the law forbids, even in one's own ancestral land, to dig up an olive." Hence one may suspect that some words of the law dropped out at the very beginning, among them these: ΜΗΔ' ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΧΩΡΙΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΩΟΥ, which I think should be restored in their place: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΕΛΑΙΑΝ ΑΘΗΝΗΣΙΝ ΕΞΟΡΥΤΤΗι, ΜΗΔ' ΕΚ ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΧΩΡΙΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΩΟΥ. But if it was permitted to uproot olives from one's own land, which one had received from one's father, about which no one raised a dispute, how much less from another's? If anyone uprooted one, he paid one hundred drachmas per olive into the public treasury, of which a tenth was consecrated to Minerva. One hundred drachmas per olive also went to, and were awarded to, the prosecutor who had brought the case against the offender. The lawsuit was lodged before the magistrates, whose duty it was to appoint the judges. The prosecutor deposited the sacred pledge, which the ancients define in various ways; for some think it is a tenth of the fine, others think it is defined by three drachmas where the dispute concerns one hundred drachmas or more up to a thousand, and thirty drachmas if the matter concerns a thousand drachmas or more up to ten thousand. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter VI.

units.la: τὰ μὲν ἀρυτδμφα[?] ὠεισμένα[?], ὅτι ἐδέ[?] κατάβαλλον[?] πρὸς τῆς δίκης τὸν διώκοντα[?], καὶ τὸν διωκόμενον[?]. εἰ ὁ μὲν, διέχαφον[?] ἡ δίκη[?] οἱ εἰσαγαγόντες[?]. ὁ δὲ ῥήτης[?], ἀπαιδοῦ[?] ὁ πρὸς ἀμφοτέρων δόξαν[?]. ἐλαμβάνον[?] ἢ αὐτὸ οἱ δικασταί[?]. οἱ μὲν καὶ ἀπὸ ἑκατὸν δραχμῶν ἀρχόμενοι χιλίων δικαζόμενοι[?], τῆς δραγμὰς[?] καταπίπτοντ[?]. οἱ δ᾽ ἀπὸ χιλίων μέχρι μυρίων, τελέ-χοντα[?]. οἱ δ᾽ οἰόντ[αι][?] ἀρυτδμφα[?] ἐξ ὃ ὅπως δικαστῶν τῆς ὑμέτερας[?], καὶ ἐπὶ ταῦτα[?] ἐν τοῖς γραφομένοις, ὅπῃ μισθοδοσία[?] τῶν δικαστῶν[?].
units.tr: The rest is badly garbled in the scan, but the sense is that the plaintiff and the defendant each made a deposit at the start of the suit, and that the judges took the sum from the parties. Some began their deposits at a hundred drachmas and went up to a thousand, and paid three drachmas; others, from a thousand up to ten thousand, paid thirty; and the rest is too corrupt to recover.

units.la: Initio igitur litis deponebatur sacramentum cum ab actore tum à reo: is vero qui iudicio vicerat, suum sacramentum auferebat, victi sacramentum, & illud quoque, quod victor abstulerat, sed victus reponebat, ad ærarium redibant, vt ex his Aristophanis versibus in Vespis constat.
units.tr: At the start of a suit a deposit (sacramentum) was made both by the plaintiff and by the defendant. The one who had won the case took back his own deposit, and also the deposit of the loser, and whatever the winner had carried off; but the loser repaid it. All of it went back to the treasury, as is clear from these verses of Aristophanes in the Wasps.

units.la: κἀξω Ϝοῦτου τὰ τέλη χωεῖς[?], καὶ ταῖς πολλᾶς ἐκπτοῦς[?], ἀρυτδμφα[?], μέσαν[?], ἀγρεχὶς[?], λιμῶντας[?], μαθοῦς[?], καὶ δημιόφωνα[?]. Ϝοῦτων πλήρωμα ἐλάσιτ[?] εἰγὺς ἀφιλία[?] γῆς ἡμῖν[?]. ἀπὸ Ϝοῦτων νῦν μαθὸν κατάλης[?] Ϝοῖσι δικαστῶν τῆς ἐπιαυτ[?].
units.tr: Of the garbled Greek lines from the Wasps, the recoverable sense is: "and the fees ... and many fines ... the Mede ... the Persians ... from these the total is smaller ... from these the judges of the year are now paid."

units.la: Ad ærarium redibant ἀρυτδμφα[?], vt hic habes, atque ex his merces Iudicibus dabatur, vnde dixit Pollux ἐλάμβανεν ὁ ἀρυτδμφα οἱ δικασταί[?], neque aliter intelligendum puto. De danista, & ex eius persona Strepsiades apud Comicum Nubibus.
units.tr: The deposits went back to the treasury, as you see here, and from them the judges' wages were paid. That is why Pollux says that the judges took the money, and I think it can be understood in no other way. Here is the moneylender, and Strepsiades speaks in his person in Aristophanes' Clouds.

units.la: ὡς ὁ μὲν ταῦτα ἐαδ᾽ εἴπ τε καὶ ἵπα[?]. πᾶς γὰρ ὡς ὅμνυσ᾽, οἷς ὀφείλων τυγχάνω[?], ἡ[?] μοι ἀρυτμφ᾽ ἀπλῶν[?] με φησὶ καξολῆν[?].
units.tr: Thus he spoke, and so on. For everyone to whom I happen to owe money swears by this, and he takes from me the deposit and drives me out.

units.la: Scholia: Ἐὰν γὰρ δικάσας τῆς χρέους κατεβάλλοντες τοῖς Πρυτάνεσιν εἰσῆγεν[?] τοῖς ἐφέσεσιν[?] τῶν ἀρυτδμφα[?] ἐργεῖον τῇ[?], ὅταν καταπίπτωσι[?] οἱ δικαζόμενοι ἀμφότεροι, καὶ ὁ φῦγων, καὶ ὁ διώκων, & ipse Danista Pasias eodem dramate ad Strepsiadem.
units.tr: Scholium: For if, after judgment, they paid the debt to the Prytanes and brought it in before the ... whenever both litigants fall, both the one who flees and the one who pursues; and the moneylender Pasias himself, in the same play, speaks to Strepsiades.

units.la: ἀπαιμι, κἀπὶ ἰαδ᾽, ὅτι ἥνον ἀρυτδμφα᾽, ἡ μηκέτι ζῶν ἐγώ.
units.tr: I go away, and also, because the deposit ... I am no longer alive.

units.la: ΣΤΡ. ἀπαιμι[?] κατὰ ἀπόλαβ[?] ἀρ᾽ αὐτὸ ἔπεισ[?] τὰς δώδεκα.
units.tr: STREPSIADES: I go away, to recover at once the twelve.

units.la: Graecus Interpres, ἀπολαμβάνειν[?]. αὐτὸ τὸ, ἐμμαθῆση καὶ τὰ ἀρυτδμφα[?] ἐπεὶς τὰς δώδεκα μυρίας, ὅ ὅτι ὁ δίκαιον τῆς ἡμέρας τῆς δίκης ἐὰν κελεύῃ σαφῶς ἀπαιτοῦν[?]. Sed male confudit optimus alioqui Magister τῷ ἀπολαμβάνειν[?] καὶ τὰ ἀρυτδμφα[?]. non enim τὰ ἀρυτδμφα omnia possunt τῆς ἀπολαμβάνειν[?] nomine appellari. Nam ἡ ἀπολαμβάνειν[?] proprie dicebatur sacramentum, quod deponebant, vel litigantes cum fisco siue ærario publico de bonis publicatis, aut aliis huiusmodi, vel litigantes alii cum aliis de hæreditatibus, quæ petuntur, aut virginibus dotalibus: Quando litigabatur cum fisco, in facrasacramentum deponebatur quinta pars æstimationis illius rei, de qua litigabatur: in litibus vero, quibus hæreditates petebantur; aut virgines dotales, sacramentum erat decima pars eorum, quæ iudicio petebantur, bonorum. Harpocration : [illegible, ~45 letters] Pollux loco proxime laudato: [illegible, ~70 letters] Erat praterea [illegible, ~12 letters], qua actor multabatur, nisi iudicio vicisset, & reo cedebat, idque in pecuniariis causis, (ne putes cum magno Budæo, in iudiciis ignominiosis tantum.) eratque sexta pars pecuniæ illius, de qua lis erat, & controuerbatur: quanquam nulli decimam esse existiment. Harpocration : ἐπωβελία[?]. [illegible, ~60 letters] Pollux loco proxime laudato: [illegible, ~40 letters] ut& Auctore Etymologici iam laudando, docemur, in pecuniariis causis hac ἐπωβελία multatum fuisse eum, qui pecuniam ab alio in iudicio peteret. ἐπωβελία. [illegible, ~80 letters] Auctor Etymologici ubi hæc, quæ è Suida retulimus, descripsit, addit. [illegible, ~75 letters] [illegible, ~55 letters] Atque hinc intelligendus est Demosthenes [illegible, ~25 letters] Aphobo tutore Demosthenes decem talenta: [illegible, ~50 letters] Atqui, si secundum Aphobum pronunciatum fuisset, Demosthenes tenebatur Aphobo ἐπωβελίας pendere, nempe minas centum, quæ sunt sexta pars decem talentum. E sequentibus vero Demosthenis verbis [illegible, ~60 letters] docemur eum, qui non posset soluere τὴν ἐπωβελίαν ignominiosum fuisse. Nam Demosthenes queritur, siquidem secundum se iudicium non obtinuerit, non habere unde soluat τὴν ἐπωβελίαν, centum minas: ἐμοὶ δὲ ἀτίμητον τοῦτ' ἔστιν, itaque, inquit, & paternis bonis fraudabor, & ignominiosus ero, nisi succurritis, vt qui non habeam domi, vnde τῷ ἐπωβελίαν exsoluam. Hac in voce corruptus Hesychius: ἐπωβελία. ἔστι δὲ ὁ ἀκόλουθον ὃ τῆς καταδίκης, τιμήματι τὸ * ὄλημα ὡς Δίδυμος, ὃ ἕκτον μέρος τῆς τιμήματος, οἱ δὲ ὁ δίκαιον. Rescribo: ἔστι δὲ ὁ ἀκόλουθον ὃ τῆς καταδίκης, τιμήματι ὁ λῆμμα, ὡς Δίδυμος, ὃ ἕκτον μέρος τῆς τιμήματος, οἱ δὲ ὁ δίκαιον. Illud est quod accidit τῷ τιμήματι, id est, pecuniae, de qua lis est; neque enim pecuniam accipiebat actor, secundum quem pronunciatum non fuerat, & praeterea ei, à quo pecuniam in iudicio repetebat, pendebat sextam partem pecuniae, de qua controuertebatur: decimam partem fuisse nonnulli dixerunt, teste Hesychio, cui accedit Eustathius Ad Odyss. A. καὶ ἐπωβελία, ὃ ὑπόδικον τῷ τοῖς παλαιοῖς. Sed sexta pars est Demosthenis, vt è superioribus liquet. Sed non possumus praetermittere sine ingenti piaculo eximium Demosthenis locum ἐν τῷ ἐν Διέρρῳ καὶ Μνησιβούλου ψευδομάρτυ- ριαν. ἐκτίνοντος δὲ μου τῷ Θεοφήμῳ, ὦ ὠφλήκειν τῷ δίκῃ, ὅτι ἐξέτινον πολλαῖς τῶν μαρτύρων χιλίας μὲν καὶ ἑκατὸν δραχμὰς καὶ τῆς καὶ δύο ὀβολὼ τῷ ἐπωβελίαν, τεσσάρακοντα δὲ τὰ ταρυτάμφα. (τῷ γὰρ ἄλλων ἔσθ' αὐτοῦ ὑπερτιμίων ὤφλεν.) ὧν ἐμοῦ ὅτι τῇ τεσσεράζῃ χιλίας τεσσαράκοντα δεκαπέντε δύ' ὀβολὼ ὃ σύμ- πᾶν κεφάλαιον.
units.tr: The Greek interpreter gives apolambanein. The phrase "the deposit and the ..." on the twelve thousand, from the day of the trial, shows clearly that it means a demand for repayment. But this excellent master otherwise confused apolambanein with the deposit, for not all deposits can be called by the name apolambanein. Apolambanein was properly said of the deposit made when litigants contended with the fisc or public treasury over confiscated goods or similar matters, or when litigants contended with one another over inheritances being sought or over dowered maidens. When litigating with the fisc, the sacrament deposited was the fifth part of the value of the thing in dispute; in suits where inheritances or dowered maidens were sought, the sacrament was the tenth part of the goods sought in the trial. Harpocration: [Greek, corrupt]. Pollux, in the passage cited just above: [Greek, corrupt]. There was also another payment, the epobelia, by which the plaintiff was fined if he did not win the case and it went to the defendant. This applied in monetary cases (do not think, with the great Budaeus, that it was only in ignominious trials). It was the sixth part of the money in dispute, though some think it was a tenth. Harpocration: epobelia [ἐπωβελία]. Pollux, in the passage cited just above: [Greek, corrupt]. As the Etymologicum, already cited, also teaches us, in monetary cases the one who sought money from another in court was fined this epobelia. The author of the Etymologicum, where he set down these things, which we have taken from Suidas, adds [Greek, corrupt]. From this we must understand Demosthenes, who owed ten talents to his guardian Aphobus. But if judgment had gone for Aphobus, Demosthenes would have been bound to pay Aphobus the epobelia, namely a hundred minae, which is the sixth part of ten talents. From the following words of Demosthenes we learn that one who could not pay the epobelia was held in disgrace. For Demosthenes complains that if he did not win the case, he would not have a hundred minae from which to pay the epobelia: "For me this is intolerable." So, he says, I shall be cheated of my paternal goods and become infamous, unless you come to my aid, since I have nothing at home from which to pay the epobelia. Hesychius is corrupt in this word: epobelia. It is what follows the condemnation, the valuation (lēmma) of the money, according to Didymus, the sixth part of the valuation; others say it is the right. I rewrite: it is what follows the condemnation, the valuation of the lēmma, according to Didymus, the sixth part of the valuation; others say it is the right. That is what befalls the valuation, that is, the money in dispute. For the plaintiff did not receive the money if judgment was not given in his favour, and besides, he paid to the one from whom he sought money in court the sixth part of the money in dispute. Some have said it was a tenth, as Hesychius reports, and Eustathius agrees in his commentary on the Odyssey. But the sixth part is Demosthenes' figure, as is clear from what has gone before. Yet we cannot pass over without great impiety the outstanding passage of Demosthenes in the speech against Theophemus on false witness. When I paid Theophemus what I had been condemned to pay in the suit, because I had paid many witnesses, I paid one thousand one hundred drachmas and three obols as the epobelia, and forty as the deposit (for he had been condemned to more than the valuation). Of these, I say, the total sum is one thousand five hundred and forty-five drachmas and two obols.

units.la: Is, cui orationem hanc scripsit Demosthenes repetierat à Theophemo secum Leges & Plebiscita Atheniensium armamenta nauium, quae de publico haberet, cum non redderet Theophemus, alter iuit ad Theophemi aedes captum pignora fit rixa, atque vtrinque verbera infliguntur. Noster hic Theophemum ad Senatum Quingentorum defert, dies dicitur: Theophemus damnatur, sed noster satis habuit sibi τὸ δίκαγμα τῆς σκευῆς ἀποδόσθαι δῆμος ἐν τῇ βουλῇ, & Theophemum viginti quinque drachmis multari: actionem vero αἰτίας permitti arbitrio amicorum. Interhaec abiit cum classe noster, redit, nec quicquam aequi impetrat à Theophemo: itaque illum in ius vocat, accusat αἰτίας. Recriminatur Theophemus: fit iudicium, sententiae dicuntur: noster damnatur, cum Euergus & Mnesibulus falsum pro testimonio dixissent: multa illi irrogatur drachmarum mille centum & trium cum duobus obolis ἐπωβελίας nomine, & praeterea drachmarum triginta in τὰ ταρυτάμφα. Poena Legibus non erat constituta, itaque aestimabant litem contendentes: iam vero si τὰ ταρυτάμφα essent ὁ ὑπόδικον τῆς τιμήματος, trecentis tantum drachmis aestimassent litem, quod credibile non est, longe enim pluris aestimarunt. Ergo τὰ ταρυτάμφα fuerunt, quod vult Pollux, triginta drachmae, ὡς οἱ ἀπὸ χιλίων δραχμῶν μέχρι μυρίων δικαζομένοι κατέπεσον. Quod maxime patet ἐκ τῆς ἐπωβελίας. Nam, non tantum ea pendebatur, quando pecunia ab aliquo repetebatur in iudicio, sed etiam, quando lis aestimabatur pecunia, vt ex hoc Demosthenis loco patet, videbatur enim agi de re pecuniaria tantum; Erat autem ἐπωβελία sexta pars τῆς τιμήματος, fuitque in hoc iudicio ἐπωβελία, drachmae mille centum & tres cum duobus obolis. Ergo litem aestimauerat noster drachmis sex mille sexcentis viginti. Æstimauerat quoque proculdubio Theophemus litem: sed nostro irrogata non est alia multa, quam ἡ ἐπωβελία τῆς τιμήματος, quo ipse Theophemo litem aestimauerat, & præterca τὰ ἀρυτὰ[?]. At vero sequitur apud Demosthenem cum de mensa numerasse Theophemo drachmas χιλίας πεντακοσίας δικαστὰς[?] δν' ὀβο-λῶ. Ergo numeravit centum octoginta drachmas plus quam pendere damnatus erat. Definitum erat tempus, intra quod multa soluenda erat, illud à Theophemo proferri postulauerat noster & obtinuerat: τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ Θεοφήμῳ, ἀμφούσης μὲν ἤδη ἐξήκειν τῆς ἀφημείας, ἐδίεμεν οὐκ ἀπαλέσαι τῷ ἀφημείᾳ, ἕως ἂν τῷ ναῷ ἀποτείλω. ὁ δὲ ῥαδίως μὲν χρὴ ἀκοῦσαι ἀποκείνετω· ἔφη, ἀλλ' ἐπεισθῇ τῷ ναῷ ἀποτείλης, πολὺς καὶ ἐμοί. Est autem prolatus dies à Theophemo sub hac Lege, vt nosler fœnus inter ea penderet: & certè benigne hac quidem in re agebat cum eo Theophemus, nam potuisset longe plura ab eo τῷ ἀφημέρῳ exigere. Fœneratus autem est Theophemus, vt puto, τοῦ ἐφικτῷ πέχω, id est, singulis mensibus pendebatur pro drachma obolus: Ergo ἑμμιλως τῶν horum mille centum triginta trium drachmarum fuit, drachmæ centum octoginta octo cum obolis quinque: Adde fortem, fient drachmæ mille trecentæ viginti duæ cum obolo. Itaque corruptus fuit Demosthenis locus: errorque ortus est ex compendiosa scriptura, notisque: ita enim olim scriptum fuit: λα-ξῶν ἔϊπω πρὸ ἐμοῦ ὅτι τῇ πεντέξῃ χιλίας τ' εἰκοσι ζ καὶ τῆς δν' ὀβολῶ. id est, χιλίας πεντακοσίας εἴκοσι μίαν δραχμὰς π καὶ τῆς δν' ὀβολῶ. Unde facilis lapsus, & mutauit in hanc vulgatam scripturam z nota est drachmam significans: Habes in Epistola Cornelij Celsi ad Natalem apud Marcellum, Græci medici pondera medicamentorum ad drachmas redigunt, quæ quia ad denarium nostrum conueniunt, pro nota Græcæ drachmæ, quæ est figura talis z. Vno autem obolo hic tantum minus est. Dixit vero τῆς δν' ὀβολῶ, quia proculdubio tria diobola numerauit, vt summam conficeret, sed vt obscuraret Pollux Lib. IX. cap. VI. ὃ διώβολον ὡς ὑπόπολι λύοντες ἔλαχεν δν' ὀβολῶ. Idem numerus reponendus est semel atque iterum in sequentibus, hac ipsa Oratione. Apud Romanos actione calumniæ tenebatur olim actor, qui temere litem instituerat, in decimam partem litis. §. Hæc autem Inst. de pæn. tem. lit. eam actionem non vtendo extinctam restituit Iustinianus Nou. CXII. & Edicto VII. Atque hæc satis, ad Legis nostræ de non euellendis interpretationem reuertamur. Vbi quis oleas eradicasse conuictus atque damnatus fuerat, Magistratus, apud quem dica scripta fuerat, multam, quam diximus fuisse drachmarum centum in singulas oleas, exigendam tradebat exactoribus, si excipias decimam multæ, Minervæ sacram, quæ exigenda dabatur Deæ Quæstoribus. Si Magistratus suo defuissent officio, ipsi multam de suo pendebant. Excipiuntur tamen hac Lege, si qui oleas euellerint ad vsum Templorum. ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΙΣ ΙΕΡΟΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ Η ΔΗ-ΜΟΤΙΚΟΝ Η. Intelligit Templa, vel quæ erant vniuersi Atheniensium populi, vel priuatim alicuius τῶν ἰδίων Νόμων. Loca enim hæc sacra consita erant oleis. Sophocles OEdipo Coloneo.
units.tr: This is the man to whom Demosthenes wrote the speech. He had demanded back from Theophemus the laws and plebiscites of the Athenians and the ship's fittings that he held on behalf of the public, but Theophemus did not return them. The other man went to Theophemus' house, and the goods were seized as pledges; a quarrel followed, and blows were exchanged on both sides. Our man brought Theophemus before the Council of Five Hundred, and a day was fixed for trial. Theophemus was condemned, but our man was content to recover his equipment by a vote of the Council, and to have Theophemus fined twenty-five drachmas; the action for damages (aitias) was left to the decision of friends. Meanwhile our man went off with the fleet and came back, and got nothing fair from Theophemus. So he summoned him to court and brought an action for damages. Theophemus countercharged; a trial was held and the verdicts were given. Our man was condemned, since Euergus and Mnesibulus had sworn falsely as witnesses. A fine was imposed on him of one thousand one hundred and three drachmas and two obols under the name of epobelia, and besides thirty drachmas as the deposit. There was no penalty fixed by the laws, so the litigants had to estimate the case themselves. Now if the deposit had been the sixth part of the valuation, they would have valued the case at only three hundred drachmas, which is not believable, for they valued it far higher. So the deposit was, as Pollux means, thirty drachmas, as those who litigated for sums from one thousand to ten thousand drachmas paid. This is most clear from the epobelia. For it was paid not only when money was sought from someone in court, but also when the case was valued in money, as this passage of Demosthenes shows; for it seemed that the matter concerned only money. The epobelia was the sixth part of the valuation, and in this trial the epobelia was one thousand one hundred and three drachmas and two obols. So our man had valued the case at six thousand six hundred and twenty drachmas. Theophemus no doubt also valued the case, but no other fine was imposed on our man than the epobelia of the valuation by which Theophemus had himself valued the case, and besides the deposit. But then, according to Demosthenes, he counted out to Theophemus at the table one thousand five hundred drachmas, [Greek, corrupt]. So he paid one hundred and eighty drachmas more than he had been condemned to pay. A time was set within which the fine was to be paid, and our man had asked Theophemus to extend it and obtained this: that for himself, to Theophemus, since the term was already expiring, he should not fail to pay, until he was able to pay the sum; and he should readily hear the answer: but if you are persuaded to pay the sum, it is much for me too. The day was extended by Theophemus under this law, that our man should pay interest in the meantime; and certainly Theophemus was acting kindly in this matter with him, for he could have demanded far more from him for the delay. Theophemus, I think, lent at one per month, that is, one obol was paid each month for each drachma. So the interest on one thousand one hundred and thirty-three drachmas would have been one hundred and eighty-eight drachmas and five obols; add the principal and you get one thousand three hundred and twenty-two drachmas and one obol. So the text of Demosthenes is corrupt, and the error arose from the abbreviated writing and the symbols. For it was formerly written: one thousand five hundred and twenty-one drachmas and two obols, that is, one thousand five hundred and twenty-one drachmas and two obols. From this came an easy slip, and the reading was changed to the common text, since the sign z denotes the drachma. You have in the letter of Cornelius Celsus to Natalis, quoted by Marcellus: Greek physicians reduce the weights of medicines to drachmas, which, since they agree with our denarius, are marked with the sign of the Greek drachma, which is of such a shape z. Only one obol is wanting here. He said and two obols, because he had no doubt counted out three diobols to make up the sum, but Pollux, in Book IX, chapter VI, obscures it: which two obols, paid as a ... they received one obol. The same number must be restored once and again in the following passages of this same speech.

units.la: χωρὶς δὲ ὁ ὁ δὲ ἱερὸς, ὡς ἀπεικάσαι, βρύων
units.tr: The sacred ground, as one may guess, teems [χῶρος δ' ὅδ' ἱερὸς, ὡς ἀπεικάσαι, βρύων]

units.la: δάφνης, ἐλαίας, ἀμπέλου.
units.tr: with laurel, olive, and vine. [δάφνης, ἐλαίας, ἀμπέλου.]

units.la: Peruenerat autem ad Eumenidum sacellum. Itaq; cum sumptum & splendorem, qui in Templis Deorum visebatur, vellent tollere Aues in cognomine Aristophanis dramate, solas arbores, & inter eas oleas relinquunt, quæ in Templis erant satæ.
units.tr: Now he had come to the shrine of the Eumenides. So when they wished to remove the expense and splendour seen in the temples of the gods, the Birds in Aristophanes' play of the same name left only the trees, and among them the olives that had been planted in the temples.

units.la: ὥσ[?]τν μὲν οὐ-[?] χ᾽ νεὼς ἡμᾶς οἰκοδομεῖν δεῖ λιθίνους αὐλῖς. ὅταν [?] χευσαῖσι ὕρεις, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ [?] θαμινοῖς κἀ[?] τεμένεσι οἰκήσειν[?]. Τὰς δ᾽ αὖ σιμοῖς τὴν ὀρνίθων [?] δένδρων ἐλαίας ὁ νεὼς ἔσται[?].
units.tr: "So we must not build temples of stone or gold, but dwell in groves and sacred precincts. Among the birds, the temple will have olive trees [...]." [ὥστ᾽ οὐ χρὴ νεὼς ἡμᾶς οἰκοδομεῖν λιθίνους αὐλῖς. ὅταν χρυσέοις ὕρεις, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ θαμινοῖς κἀν τεμένεσι οἰκήσειν. Τὰς δ᾽ αὖ σιμοῖς τὴν ὀρνίθων δένδρων ἐλαίας ὁ νεὼς ἔσται.]

units.la: Statius Lib. XII. Thebaidos, vbi Misericordiæ Templum Athenis describit:
units.tr: Statius, in Book XII of the Thebaid, where he describes the temple of Mercy at Athens:

units.la: Mite nemus circa, cultúque insigne verendo, Vittata laurus, & supplicis arbor oliuæ.
units.tr: A gentle grove around, notable for its reverent worship: the fillet-wrapped laurel, and the olive, tree of suppliants.

units.la: Ne igitur deficerent, licebat evellere ex agris oleas, ut in Templis fererentur. Mitto præterea olearum vsum in sacris. Excipiuntur quoque ab hac Lege, nec multantur, qui duas tantum quotannis in priuatum suum vsum oleas evellunt: hoc quippe licet ista Lege: ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΑΥΤΩι ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ ΜΕ-ΧΡΙ ΔΥΟΙΝ ΕΛΑΙΑΙΝ ΤΟΥ ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΥ. Excipiuntur quoque, qui oleas evellunt ad mortuorum funera: ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΕΠΙ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΑ ΔΕΗι ΧΡΗΣΑΣΘΑΙ. Nam & cum mortuis oleas efferebant, ut est apud Artemidorum Onirocritici Lib. IV. cap. LIX. Τούτων γ᾽ ὅταν τῶν νοσούντων, ἡ μὲν ἐλαία θανατηφόρος ὅσα πτέρνῃ, αὐτὴ τε ἔ ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῆς καὶ τὰ φύλλα. ἡ γὰρ εἰκὼς, ὡς μὲν γὰρ ἀποθανόντων ἐλαίας σύνεκφέρειν. Præterea cum par propemodum parentibus aut amicis suo fato functis honos, qui Diis immortalibus haberetur, religioneque consecrarentur eorum tumuli & monumenta, (quinetiam Templa iis superstruebant, quod iam aliis obseruatum est.) ad illa quoque ferebantur & superimponebantur oleæ, quas huic vsui licebat ex agris evellere, itémque fruges obserebant. M. Tullius Lib. de Legibus II. extremo. Nam & Athenis iam ille mos à Cecrope, ut aiunt, permansit, hoc ius terra humandi: quam cum proximi iniecerant, obductaque terra erat, frugibus obserebatur, ut sinus & gremium quasi matris mortuo tribueretur, solum autem frugibus expiatum ut vivus redderetur. Ad has oleas ceterasque arbores semper virentes, & quæ nunquam folia amittunt, sepulcris super impositas & satas, respexit Iuuenalis Satyra VII extrema.
units.tr: So that they should not run short, it was lawful to cut olives from the fields to be carried into the temples. I pass over also the use of olives in sacred rites. Exempt from this law, and not fined, are those who cut only two olives a year for their own private use; for the law permits this: "Unless one may use for oneself up to two olives of each man's own per year." Exempt also are those who cut olives for funerals of the dead: "Unless it is for a man who has died." For they also carried olives out with the dead, as is found in Artemidorus, Oneirocritica, Book IV, chapter 59: "Of those who are sick, when the olive is deadly... for it was customary to carry olives out together with the dead." Moreover, since honour almost equal to that paid to the immortal gods was given to parents or friends who had died, and their tombs and monuments were consecrated with religious rites (indeed they built temples over them, as has been noted by others), olives, which it was lawful to cut from the fields for this purpose, were carried to those tombs and laid upon them, and grain was also sown there. Marcus Tullius, On the Laws, Book II, near the end: For at Athens this custom has remained from Cecrops, as they say, the right of burying in the earth: when the nearest kin had cast earth over the body and it was covered, it was sown with grain, so that the bosom and lap of the mother might be given to the dead, and the ground, purified by the crops, given back to the living. Juvenal, in the final part of Satire VII, referred to these olives and other trees that are always green and never lose their leaves, planted and set upon tombs:

units.la: DI maiorum umbris tenuem, & sive pondere, terram, Spirantésque crocos, & in urna perpetuum ver.
units.tr: May the gods grant the shades of our ancestors a light earth, and breathing saffron, and perpetual spring in the urn.

units.la: Sacras multo minus oleas, μορίας[?] dicuntur, cædere aut evellere non licebat, quod ne fierent curæ erat Senatui Areopagitico. Lysias ἐν τῇ Ἀρεοπαγιτικῷ [?]τὰ σίκων. Δῆλον δὲ μοι δοκεῖ[?] ὑμᾶς μὲν, ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς πόλεως τὴν ἀπάν-τα χρόνον [?] μορίας ἐπιμεληθῆναι, μηθ᾽ ὡς ἐπαργαζόμενον[?] πο-[?] ζημιοῦσαι, μηθ᾽ ὡς ἀφανίζοντα εἰς κίνδυνον καταστῆσαι. Qui ausus erat cædere aut evellere, postulabatur apud Areopagitas, quia illorum curæ erat ne fierent, ut iam diximus, & præterea hæc ad religionem spectabant: Vnde hanc Orationem Lysiæ Ὑπὲρ Ἰσοτείας[?] dixit Harpocration. Σηκὸς, [?] λόγος Λυσίου ἐν τῇ τῆς Ἀποτείας [?] τὸ σικοῦ [?]. Multa videtur fuisse fortu-narum publicatio, & exilium. Itaque dixit ille, cui hanc orationem scripsit Lysias, ἐπαιτεῖ τῆς παιδὸς, καὶ ἀπὸ οὐσίας ἀργυρίου ἐαθαι[?]. & paullo post: πρῶτον γὰρ ἀθ-λιώτερος αὐ ἡμεῖς μὲν ... εἰ Φυγαῖς ἀδίκως καταγνώσομαι, ἅπαξ μὲν ὧν τῆς μέρος, ἐρήμου δὲ τῆς οἰ-κίας ἡμελῶς· μηδὲς δὲ πρῶτον ἐνδεῖς, παιδὸς δὲ ἐιῶτης ἐπ' αἰχίσας τερπνὸς αἰτίας. Seruis, qui iudicassent, indicinae praemium libertas. Lysias ibidem: ἐὰν γὰρ εἰ ἀὐ εἰσέλθω ὅτι ἐπ' ἐκείνοις ἐὰν ἐμοῦ ἡμωρήσασθαι. Ἐὰν αὖ ἡμῖς μυΐσασιν, ἐλευθέρας ἡμεῖ-σθαι.
units.tr: Much less was it lawful to cut or pull up the sacred olives, which are called [...]; the Areopagite Council took care that this did not happen. Lysias, in his speech against... [...]. It seems clear to me that you have always taken care of the sacred olives of the city, and that one who damaged them was not punished as a ... but was brought into danger as one who destroyed them. Whoever dared to cut or pull them up was prosecuted before the Areopagites, because it was their care that this should not happen, as we have said, and because these matters pertained also to religion. Hence Harpocration says this speech of Lysias was delivered "On behalf of Isoteles." Much appears to have been confiscation of property and exile. So the man for whom Lysias wrote this speech said that he had been... and a little later: "For first, I am the more wretched... if I am unjustly condemned to exile, I shall lose once my share, and my house will be left desolate..." Lysias in the same place: "For if I enter... for those in power, I shall avenge myself. And if they are informed against, they shall be made free." Slaves who gave evidence were rewarded with freedom for their information.

units.la: DE AGRIS, ARMENTO, atque grege. TITVLVS II.
units.tr: On Fields, Herds, and Flocks. TITLE II.

units.la: CAuit Lege Solon, ne Athenienses sui quantum agri vellent, tantum comparFarent.
units.tr: Solon, by law, provided that the Athenians should not acquire as much land as they wished.

units.la: Μὴ κτᾶσθαι γῆν ὁπόσων αὐ βούλωνται τὴς. Agrum, quantum voluerint, ne possidento.
units.tr: Let no one acquire land beyond whatever amount they wish. Let them not possess land, as much as they wish. [Μὴ κτᾶσθαι γῆν ὁπόσων αὐ βούλωνται τὴς.]

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Aristoteles Polit. Libro II. cap. VIII. causamque illius aperit, nempe bonorum aequalitatem habere vim aliquam ad ciuilem societatem: δῆλον μὲν οὖν ἐν ταῖς ἀνωτάτω... καὶ τῶν παλαιῶν τινες Φαίνονται διεγνωκότες, ὡς καὶ Σόλων ἐνομοθέτησε, καὶ πρὸ δήμου ἔστι νόμος, ὡς κωλύει κτᾶσθαι γῆν, ὁπόσων αὐ βούλωνται τῆς. Est quippe diuitiarum modus, vt aduersus hunc ipsum Solonem disputat virorum maximus eiusdem operis Libro I.cap.VIII. extremo: ἡ γὰρ πλοῦτος κτήσεως ἐκτόπος ... &c, ὥσπερ Σόλων φησὶ ποιῆσαι, πλούτου δὲ οὐδὲν τέρμα πέφυκεν ἀνδράσιν χεῖται.
units.tr: Aristotle mentions this law in Politics Book II, chapter 8, and explains its purpose, namely that equality of goods has some force for civil society: "It is clear from the highest [principles]... and some of the ancients appear to have judged so, as Solon also legislated, and there is a law before the people that forbids acquiring land beyond whatever amount they wish [Μὴ κτᾶσθαι γῆν ὁπόσων αὐ βούλωνται τῆς]." There is indeed a limit to riches, as the greatest of men argues against this very Solon in the same work, Book I, chapter 8, near the end: "For the acquisition of wealth is unlimited... as Solon says he did, but there is no natural end to wealth for men [ἡ γὰρ πλοῦτος κτήσεως ἐκτόπος ... &c, ὥσπερ Σόλων φησὶ ποιῆσαι, πλούτου δὲ οὐδὲν τέρμα πέφυκεν ἀνδράσιν χεῖται]."

units.la: χαῖρε γὰρ, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰς δικαίας τέχνας. Ἔστιν γὰρ ὀργάνων ἀπειρον ἔσται μιᾶς ἐστι τέχνης, οὔτε πλῆθος, ὅτε μεγέθη. ὁ γὰρ πλοῦτος, ὀργάνων πλῆθος ἔστιν οἰκονομικῶν καὶ πολιτικῶν. Sed male est, quod modum agri, de quo Legem tulerat Solon, plane ignoramus. Apud Romanos veteres Lex Stolonis vetabat plus quingentis iugera habere. M. Varro Libro I.de R. R. cap. II. Nam C.Licinium Stolonem & Cn. Tremelium Scrofam video venire: vnum cuius maiores de modo agri Legem tulerunt. Nam Stolonis illa Lex, quae vetat plus D. iugera habere ciuem Romanum. Redeamus ad Graecos, apud quos non licebat rem suam aut haereditatem aut vendere. Aristoteles Polit. Libro II. cap. VII. ὁμοίως γὰρ καὶ τὸν ὑσίαν πωλεῖν οἱ πολῖται κωλύουσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς παλαιοῖς κλήρους ἀξιοῦ... Apud Athenienses decoctores Solonis Lege infamia notabantur. Ο ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΑ ΚΑΤΕΔΗΔΟΚΩΣ, Η ΩΝ ΑΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝΟΜΟΣ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ, ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ. Decoctores paternae, aut alterius cuiusuis haereditatis, ignominiosi sunto.
units.tr: "For wealth, as also the just arts, has no limit: there is no unlimited number of instruments of one art, neither in multitude nor in magnitude; for wealth is a multitude of instruments of household management and of politics [χαῖρε γὰρ, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰς δικαίας τέχνας. Ἔστιν γὰρ ὀργάνων ἀπειρον ἔσται μιᾶς ἐστι τέχνης, οὔτε πλῆθος, ὅτε μεγέθη. ὁ γὰρ πλοῦτος, ὀργάνων πλῆθος ἔστιν οἰκονομικῶν καὶ πολιτικῶν]." But it is unfortunate that we know nothing for certain about the measure of land concerning which Solon passed his law. Among the early Romans the law of Stolo forbade a citizen to have more than five hundred iugera. Marcus Varro, On Agriculture Book I, chapter 2: "For I see that Gaius Licinius Stolo and Gnaeus Tremellius Scrofa are coming: the one whose ancestors passed a law concerning the measure of land. For that law of Stolo, which forbids a Roman citizen to have more than five hundred iugera." Let us return to the Greeks, among whom it was not permitted to sell one's property or inheritance. Aristotle, Politics Book II, chapter 7: "For likewise the citizens forbid the selling of the estate, but to the ancients the allotments..." [ὁμοίως γὰρ καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν πωλεῖν οἱ πολῖται κωλύουσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς παλαιοῖς κλήρους ἀξιοῦ...]. Among the Athenians, by Solon's law, those who squandered their inheritance were marked with infamy: "Those who squander their paternal inheritance, or any other inheritance that they may receive by lot, shall be dishonoured [Ο ΤΑ ΠΑΤΡΩΙΑ ΚΑΤΕΔΗΔΟΚΩΣ, Η ΩΝ ΑΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝΟΜΟΣ ΓΕΝΗΤΑΙ, ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ]." Those who squander a paternal or any other inheritance shall be disgraced.

units.la: Legem descripsit Diogenes Laertius in Solonis, & Aeschines ἐν τῷ Τιμάρχῳ inter ceteros, quos orare Leges non sinunt, recensét ἐπὶ ΤΑ ΠΑ-
units.tr: Diogenes Laertius gives the text of this law in the Life of Solon, and Aeschines, in his speech against Timarchus, lists among the others whom the laws do not allow to speak those who squander [ἐπὶ τὰ πα-]

units.la: ΤΡΩΑ ΚΑΤΕΔΗΔΟΚΩΣ, Η ΩΝ ΑΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝΟΜΟΣ ΓΕΝΗ-TAI.
units.tr: Whoever squanders his paternal estate, or any inheritance that comes to him as heir.

units.la: Cum Attica melior pascendo pecori, quam colendis agris esset, Legem tulit Solon, vt ei qui lupum attulisset, drachmæ quinque darentur, qui lupam, vna.
units.tr: Since Attica was better suited to pasturing flocks than to tilling fields, Solon passed a law that whoever brought in a wolf should receive five drachmas, and whoever brought in a she-wolf, one.

units.la: Τὸ κομιστρὶ λύκου, πέντε δραχμὰς δίδοσθαι· λυκίδα δὲ, μίαν.
units.tr: For bringing in a wolf, five drachmas are to be given; for a she-wolf, one [Τὸ κομιστρὶ λύκου, πέντε δραχμὰς δίδοσθαι· λυκίδα δὲ, μίαν].

units.la: Ei, qui lupum attulerit, quinque drachmæ dantor: vna ei, qui lu-pam.
units.tr: Whoever brings in a wolf is to receive five drachmas; one for a she-wolf.

units.la: Refert hanc Legem Plutarchus in Solone è Demetrio Phalereo: λύκων δ᾽ ὃ κομιστρὶ λύκου, πέντε δραχμὰς ἔδωκε· λυκίδα δὲ, μίαν. ὧν φησὶν ὁ Φαληρεὺς Δημήτριος ὃ μὲν, βοὸς [?]), ὃ δὲ, κακάς πημιῶ. Ἐξαίρον δὲ τῆς Ἀθηναίοις ὃ πολεμεῖν τὰς λύκους, βελτίονα νέμειν [?] γαρ ἀμφὶ χρῆσι ἔχειν. Meminit Legis Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Aues: ἐπὶ τὰς λύκους ἀπέκτεινον ὃ παλαιὸν ἐν τῇ Ἀττικῇ. καὶ νόμος ὧν λυκοκτόνος. δὲ ὁ μὲν Φονίων λύκων τέκνον, ζάλγιτον ἐλάμβανεν· ὁ δὲ πλέον, δύο. Sed in præmio mendum est, vt constat è Plutarcho.
units.tr: Plutarch in his Life of Solon reports this law from Demetrius of Phalerum: "He gave five drachmas for bringing in a wolf, and one for a she-wolf." Demetrius of Phalerum says that the one ... and the other ... Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds mentions the law: "In ancient Attica they killed wolves, and there was a law concerning wolf-slayers; for the one who brought in the young of a wolf received a sixth, and the one who brought more, two." But there is an error in the reward, as is clear from Plutarch.

units.la: Quæ possent vero agrum colere, Lege vetabantur bouem aratorem occidere.
units.tr: Since those who could till the land were forbidden by law to slaughter the plough-ox.

units.la: Βοῦν ἀροτῆρα μὴ ϑύειν.
units.tr: Not to sacrifice the plough-ox [Βοῦν ἀροτῆρα μὴ θύειν].

units.la: Bouem aratorem ne mactato.
units.tr: Do not slaughter the plough-ox.

units.la: Legem laudat Ælianus ποικίλης ἱστορίας Libro V. cap. XIV. νόμος καὶ ἐστὶ Ἀττικὸς, βοῦν ἀροτῆρα, ἢ ὑπὸ ζυγὸν ποιοῦντα γεωργεῖν ἢ ἀροτρεύειν [?] ἐν ἀμάξῃ, μηδὲ τῶν ϑύειν. Quanquam non tantum bouem, qui iam socius hominum esset in rustico opere, & Cereris minister, sed etiam olim nullum omnino bouem mactari voluerunt, & Lege cauerunt.
