units.la: Μὴ δύο τέχνας μετιέναι. Duas artes ne exerceto.
units.tr: Not to pursue two crafts. Let him not practise two crafts.

units.la: Legem hanc alludit in Timocratea Demosthenes: ὑμεῖς μὲν γὰρ τὰ ἐκ τοῦ παλῆς νενομοθετημένα δῆα, ἐὰν τὶς ἢ διχόθεν μαθοφορῇ, ἢ ἄλλο τι ποιῇ, ὧν οἱ νόμοι ἀπαγορεύοιστν, ἃ λύετε. Vlpianus ibidem: ἐαὶ τὶς διχόθεν μαθοφορῇ, ἐκ δύο τεχνῶν. δύο τέχνας μετιέναι πάλιν κωλύεί, ἀφ' ὧ μηδεμίαν καταρξοῦ ἐκ τῆς τῷ γεω-μέλῳ μεείξεσθαι. Eadem ratio apud Aristotelem Politic. Lib. II. cap. XI. ἐν γὰρ ὑφ' ἑνὸς ἔργου ἀρίς' ἀποτελέσθαι. δεῖ δ' ὅπως γίνηταί τῶτ' ἐξῆν τὸν νομοθέτην. καὶ μὴ ὠφελεῖσθαι τὸν αὐτὸν αὐλὴν καὶ σκυτοτομεῖν.
units.tr: Demosthenes alludes to this law in the speech against Timocrates: "For you have the laws long established, that if anyone is convicted of practising two crafts, or of doing anything else that the laws forbid, you annul them." Ulpian, in the same place: "If anyone practises two crafts, the law forbids it again, so that no one may be made to practise a craft or trade." Aristotle, in the Politics, Book II, chapter XI, gives the same reason: a thing is done better when one person does one work, and the lawgiver should not allow the same man to be a farmer and a shoemaker [ἐν γὰρ ὑφ' ἑνὸς ἔργου ἄριστ' ἀποτελέσθαι].

units.la: Lege cauerat Solon, ne quis vir vnguentariam faceret:
units.tr: Solon had provided by law that no man should keep a perfume shop.

units.la: Τοὺς ἀνδρας μὴ μυροπωλεῖν. Ne quis vir vnguentariam facito.
units.tr: Men should not sell perfumes. Let no man keep a perfume shop.

units.la: Legem refert Athenaeus Lib. XIII. extremo: ἀνδρὸς τὴ & τῷ τοιαύτῳ ἀξῆ-σιν τῶν μύρων ἀποδοκιμάσασθαι: Σόλωνος δὲ τὸ νομοθέτου ὑπ' ἐπιτρέποντος ἀνδρὶ τοιαύ-της τῆς ἐργάσασθαι τέχνης. & rursum Lib. XV. Σόλων τε ὁ Ὤφος ἐξ τὸν νόμον κεκώ-λυκε τοὺς ἀνδρας μυροπωλεῖν.
units.tr: Athenaeus, Book XIII, near the end, reports the law: it was thought unworthy that a man should be rejected for selling perfumes, but Solon, the lawgiver, did not permit a man to practise such a craft. And again in Book XV: Solon the Athenian by law forbade men to sell perfumes [Σόλων τε ὁ Ὤφος ἐξ τὸν νόμον κεκώλυκε τοὺς ἀνδρας μυροπωλεῖν].

units.la: Peregrinis non licebat in foro aliquid vendere, aut artem exercere.
units.tr: Foreigners were not permitted to sell anything in the forum, or to practise a craft there.

units.la: Τοὺς ξένους ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι. Peregrini in foro nihil vendunto, neque vllam artem exercento.
units.tr: Foreigners shall not practise a craft in the forum. Let foreigners sell nothing in the forum, and let them practise no craft.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes ἐν τῇ πρὸς ΕΥζουλίσλω ἐφέσῃ, ἡμεῖς ὁ ὁμολογεῖσθαι ἡμῶν. ἐμπορίας πωλῶν, καὶ ἕως ἔχων τινὰ ἔσθ' τὰ βαλλόμενα. ἡ εἰ σοι δοκεῖ τὸ σημεῖον, ὦ ΕΥΒουλίδη[?], ἐγὼ μὴ Ἀθηναίους εἶναι ἡμᾶς, ἐγὼ σοι ξύντυ ὅλως ξυνάστωσ[?] ἑνδεῖξω, ὅτι οὐκ ἔξεστι ξένῳ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐργάζεσθαι[?]. Rursum paullo post: παρασκευὴ τοίνυν ὑμῖν βοηθοῦσι τοῖς νόμοις, μὴ τοὺς ἐργαζομένους, ξένοις νομίζειν. Denique paullo infra: νομίζω γὰρ ἐγὼ ἅ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἡμᾶς ἐργάζεσθαι, μέγιστον σημεῖον τῆς ψυχῆς ἡμῖν αἰτίας τῶν ὑπὸ ἐπιφέρειν. ὦ γὰρ φησι Φαισηνιόπωλιν ἐξ[?], καὶ Φανεροῦν πᾶσι, &c. In foro autem vendebant tenuiores tantum, vt vel ex his Oratoris verbis constat: nam is, cui hanc Orationem scripsit, fatetur matrem esse pauperem, & in foro taenias vendere: quod faciebant sub vmbraculis: vnde mulierum σκιωνὰς καταλαμβανούσων iurgia inter se & ἀκροχειμοί, argumentum dramatis, cui titulum fecit Aristophanes σκιωνὰς καταλαμβανούσης, quod discess vel ex hoc fragmento apud Hesychium.
units.tr: Demosthenes cites this law in his speech against Eubulides: "We, as has been agreed among us, sell goods in trade, and whoever has property... If, Eubulides, it seems to you a sign that we are not Athenians, I will show you that it is not permitted for a foreigner to work in the forum." Again a little later: "Therefore, to assist the laws, you should regard as foreigners those who work in the forum, not..." Finally, a little below: "For I think that the greatest sign of the soul's guilt is our working in the forum..." For in the forum only the poorer people sold, as is clear even from these words of the orator: for the man to whom he addressed this speech confesses that his mother is poor and sells ribbons in the forum, which they did under sunshades; hence the quarrels of the women who took possession of the shade, and the argument of the play which Aristophanes titled Women Taking Possession of the Shade, as is clear even from this fragment in Hesychius [ἡδὴ ἴσως ἀπέλεγχες τοῦτο τῷ δημοσίῳ, ἡ γὰρ ἀχάλμαι].

units.la: ἡδὴ ἴσως ἀπέλεγχες τοῦτο τῷ δημοσίῳ, ἡ γὰρ ἀχάλμαι.
units.tr: Perhaps you will already refute this before the people, for I am not ashamed. [ἤδη ἴσως ἀπέλεγχες τοῦτο τῷ δημοσίῳ, ἠ γὰρ οὐκ αἰσχύνομαι]

units.la: Conuicium enim facit mulier alteri his verbis. Non licebat autem Solonis Legge hanc in foro ἐργασίαν cuiquam, siue mari, siue feminae exprobrare.
units.tr: For the woman makes an insult to the other in these words. By Solon's law, however, it was not permitted for anyone, whether man or woman, to reproach another with this occupation in the forum.

units.la: Ἐνομον εἶ τῇ καταγελείᾳ τῶν τῷ ἐργα- σίας τῷ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἢ τῆς πολιτῶν, ἢ τῆς πολιτῶν ὀνειδίζοντα τινί. Qui ciui siue mari siue feminae exprobrarit, quod in foro merces venales exponat, accufare cum ius esto.
units.tr: "It shall be subject to penalty to mock the occupation of someone in the market, or of a citizen, or to reproach anyone." Whoever reproaches a citizen, man or woman, that he or she sells wares in the forum, let him be liable to prosecution.

units.la: Habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῇ πρὸς ΕΥΒουλίδην ἐφέσει. καὶ τοι, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, ὁ μόνον παρὰ τὰ ψηφίσματα τὰ ἐκ τῶν ἀγορᾶν διέκαλεν ἡμᾶς ΕΥΒουλίδης, ἀλλὰ ἐγὼ τοῖς νόμοις, οἱ κελεύουσιν ἐνόχον εἶ τῇ καταγελείᾳ τῶν τῷ ἐργασίας τῷ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἢ τῆς πολιτῶν ὀνειδίζοντα τινί.
units.tr: You have it in Demosthenes, in his challenge against Eubulides: "And yet, men of Athens, Eubulides does not challenge us only against the decrees made in the assemblies, but I challenge him on the laws, which order that whoever mocks the occupation of someone in the market, or reproaches a citizen, is liable [to penalty]." [ἐνόχον εἶναι τῇ καταγελάσει τῆς ἐργασίας τῆς ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἢ τοῦ πολίτου ὀνειδίζοντα τινί]

units.la: Veteri Athenienfium Lege inter fuos artifices qui peritior habebatur, publice in Prytaneio epulabatur, & primam in Theatris atque concionibus occupabat sedem. Τὸν ἀρίστον ὄντα τῇ ἑαυτοῦ σωτηρίᾳ σίτη- σιν ἐν Πρυτανείῳ λαμβάνειν, ἢ πρωτεδρίας. Peritior in sua arte publice in Prytaneio e- pulator, primamque sedem occupato.
units.tr: By the old Athenian law, whoever among their craftsmen was considered more skilled was publicly feasted in the Prytaneum and occupied the first seat in the theatres and at the assemblies. [Τὸν ἄριστον ὄντα τῇ ἑαυτοῦ τέχνῃ σίτησιν ἐν Πρυτανείῳ λαμβάνειν, καὶ πρωτεδρίας.] The more skilled in his own art was publicly fed in the Prytaneum and occupied the first seat.

units.la: Alludit hanc Legem Aristophanes Ranis, à quo praeterea docemur, non perpetuum fuisse aliquando hunc honorem: nam si quis alius, qui hunc ipsum arte superaret, reperiretur, ei suam σίτησιν, locumque cedebat.
units.tr: Aristophanes alludes to this law in the Frogs, from which we also learn that this honour was not perpetual at some time: for if someone else was found who surpassed him in the same art, he yielded his meals and his place to him.

units.la: νόμος τις εἰσῆλθ' ὅστ' χαίλμος, ἀπὸ τῆς πυρκαῒς, ὅσα μεγάλα καὶ δεξιά, τὸν ἀρίστον ὄντα τῇ ἑαυτοῦ σωτηρίᾳ, σίτησιν αὐτὸν ἐν Πρυτανείῳ λαμβάνειν, ἄξιον τε, τῷ Πλούτωνος ἐξῆς. ΞΑΝ. μανθάνω. ΛΙΑ. ἕως ἀφίκοιτο τῷ πύλῳ ζῷότερος ἕπεσθαι τῆς αὐτὴ. τότε ἡ ἀλκαρψῆν ἐδή.
units.tr: "A law has come in that whoever is the best in his art, from the great and skilful deeds..., should take his meals in the Prytaneum at public expense, and be seated beside Pluto. XANTHIAS: I understand. AEACUS: Until someone better came to the gate to follow [him]; then the seat was taken away." [νόμος τις εἰσῆλθ' ὅστις ἄριστος, ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης, ὅσα μεγάλα καὶ δεξιά, τὸν ἄριστον ὄντα τῇ ἑαυτοῦ σωτηρίᾳ σίτησιν αὐτὸν ἐν Πρυτανείῳ λαμβάνειν, ἄξιον τε τοῦ Πλούτωνος ἐξῆς. ΞΑΝ. μανθάνω. ΑΙΑ. ἕως ἀφίκοιτο τῇ πύλῃ ἄμεινον ἕπεσθαι τῆς αὐτῆς. τότε ἡ ἀλλαχῇ ἔδει.]

units.la: Quanquam enim haec à Comico in inferis fieri dicantur, tamen ab Athenienfibus ex Lege vsurpabantur. Nam quia ab Athenienfibus obferuata funt, adfcribuntur à Comico inferis, vt obferuant veteres ad haec verba Critici. Τῶν τα μεσσοφέρει ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν Ἀθήνῃ ἐῶν εἰς τὰ κατ' Ἅδου. An vero committebantur inter fe vniufcuiufque artis artifices, quo omnium peritiffimus, qui effet, è re auctore haberetur, festo, quod Χαλκεῖα, siue Ηφαίστου, quia ab omnibus artificibus tricesimo Pyanepfionis die agitabatur, dicitur? Atque hinc διξίς, id eft, commissiones, de quibus dicere viri eruditiffimi occuparunt.
units.tr: Although these things are said by the comic poet to happen in the underworld, the Athenians nevertheless used them by law. For since they were observed by the Athenians, the comic poet ascribes them to those below, as the old critics note on these words: "the things carried over from Athens to the regions of Hades." But were craftsmen of each art contested among themselves, so that the most skilled of all, whoever he was, was held to be the expert, at the festival called Chalkeia, or of Hephaestus, because it was celebrated by all craftsmen on the thirtieth day of Pyanepsion? And hence the dixis, that is, the contests, about which the most learned men have laboured to write.

units.la: Lege, si quis portitor, qui Athenis in Insulam Salamina transmittebat, naufragium fecisset, quanquam tempestate actus, non poterat amplius transfretare.
units.tr: By law, if any ferryman who carried passengers from Athens to the island of Salamis suffered a shipwreck, even if driven by a storm, he could not ferry again.

units.la: Ἐὰν δὲ τις τῶν πορθμέων τὴν εἰς Σαλαμῖνα πορθμευόντων ἄχων ἐν τῷ πόρῳ πλοῖον ἀναπέμψῃ, οὕτω μὴ ἐξεῖναι πά-λιν πορθμεῖν ἡμέραν.
units.tr: "If any of the ferrymen who convey [passengers] to Salamis, through carelessness, sends a boat to ruin in the strait, then it shall not be permitted for him to ferry again for a day." [Ἐὰν δέ τις τῶν πορθμέων τὴν εἰς Σαλαμῖνα πορθμευόντων ἄκων ἐν τῷ πόρῳ πλοῖον ἀναπέμψῃ, οὕτω μὴ ἐξεῖναι πάλιν πορθμεῦσαι ἡμέραν.]

units.la: Si quis portitorum, qui in Salamina transmittent, nolens in eo freto naufragium fecerit, neminem in posterum transmittito.
units.tr: If any of the ferrymen who transport [passengers] to Salamis, unwillingly, causes a shipwreck in that strait, let him ferry no one in future.

units.la: Legem retulit Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος. ὅτι μὲν τοῖς πορθμέως τοῖς εἰς Σαλαμῖνα πορθμευουσι νόμων ἐτίθει, ἐάν τις αὐτῶν ἄχων ἐν τῷ πόρῳ πλοῖον ἀναπέμψῃ, οὕτω μὴ ἐξεῖναι πάλιν πορθμεῖν ἡμέραν. Ratio est, ne quis Græcorum capiti impune illudat: ἵνα μηδεὶς ἀλογεσθαι εἰς τὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων σώματα. præsertim in tam augusto freto. Nam Salamis insula erat ἐν κόλπῳ κειμένη, inquit Strabo Lib. IX. ὅτι χερρονησοειδὴς τόπου σύνεγγυς τῷ Ἀττικῷ, ἐ regione Eleusinis sita, ἐν Ἑλευσῖνα, ut est apud Pausaniam Atticis, & testatur Strabo, qui addit fretum fuisse duorum stadiorum: postquam enim Eleusinem descripsit, sequitur. εἶτα ὁ Θεμίστου πύλη, ἢ ὁμώνυμος ἀγχαλὸς ἢ δῆμος· εἶθ' ἡ ἄχεα ἡ Ἀμφιάλη, καὶ ὁ Ἰσχυρίμουν λεπόμιον, καὶ ὁ Σαλαμῖνα πορθμός, ὃν διστόλος.
units.tr: Aeschines reported the law in his speech against Ctesiphon: "that the law established for the ferrymen who ferry to Salamis is that if any of them, unwillingly, sends a boat to ruin in the strait, then it shall not be permitted for him to ferry again for a day." The reason is that no one may harm the bodies of Greeks with impunity, [ἵνα μηδεὶς ἀλογεῖσθαι εἰς τὰ σώματα τῶν Ἑλλήνων,] especially in so sacred a strait. For Salamis, says Strabo in Book IX, is an island lying in a gulf, peninsula-shaped, close to Attica, lying opposite Eleusis, [ἐν κόλπῳ κειμένη, χερρονησοειδὴς τόπου σύνεγγυς τῷ Ἀττικῷ, ἐκ regione Ἐλευσῖνος κειμένη,] as Pausanias also says in the Attics, and Strabo attests, who adds that the strait was two stadia wide. For after describing Eleusis he goes on: "then the gate of Themistocles, or the Attic village of the same name; then the Amphiale cape, and the Isthmus of Ischyrimus, and the strait of Salamis, which is two stadia [wide]."

units.la: DE COLLEGIIS ET pollicitationibus. TITULUS SEPTIMUS.
units.tr: ON ASSOCIATIONS AND PROMISES. TITLE SEVEN.

units.la: NE collegia siue corpora illicita coïrent cauerunt Legislatores & quicumque ad Rempublicam, eius bono atque commodo, accesserunt, metus enim erat, ne hoc prætextu οἱ κακῖκται, quos Aristoteles Lib. II. Politic. vocat τοὺς μὴ τῆς πολιτείας φίλους, mutationem Reipublicæ afferrent: Collegiis vero licitis potestatem faciebat Lex Solonis pactionem, quam vellent, sibi ferre, dum ne quid ex publica Lege corrumperent.
units.tr: Lawmakers, and all who have cared for the welfare and advantage of the commonwealth, took care to prevent unlawful colleges or corporations from assembling. They feared that under this pretext the kakiktai [οἱ κακῖκται], whom Aristotle in Book II of the Politics calls those who are not friends of the constitution [τοὺς μὴ τῆς πολιτείας φίλους], might bring about a change in the state. But Solon's law gave lawful colleges the power to make whatever agreement they wished among themselves, provided they did not corrupt anything in the public law.

units.la: ἘΑΝ ΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΣ Ἢ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, Ἢ ΙΕΡΩΝ ΟΡΓΙΩΝ, Ἢ ΝΑΥΤΑΙ, Ἢ ΣΥΣΣΙΤΟΙ, Ἢ ΟΜΟΤΑΦΟΙ, Ἢ ΘΙΑΣΩΤΑΙ, Ἢ ΕΠΙΛΙΑΝ ΟΙΧΩΜΕΝΟΙ, Ἢ ΕΙΣ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΑΝ, ΟΤΙ ΑΝ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΔΙΑΘΩΝΤΑΙ ΓΡΟΣ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΥΣ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ. ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΠΑΓΟΡΕΥΣΗ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ ΓΡΑΜΜΑΤΑ.
units.tr: If the people [ΔΗΜΟΣ], or the phratries [ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ], or the sacred orgeones [ΙΕΡΩΝ ΟΡΓΙΩΝ], or sailors [ΝΑΥΤΑΙ], or messmates [ΣΥΣΣΙΤΟΙ], or those buried in one tomb [ΟΜΟΤΑΦΟΙ], or the thiasotai [ΘΙΑΣΩΤΑΙ], or those living together [ΕΠΙΛΙΑΝ ΟΙΧΩΜΕΝΟΙ], or those who band together for trade [ΕΙΣ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΑΝ], make binding agreements among themselves, let those agreements stand, unless public writing forbids them.

units.la: Si popula-res, aut Phratores, aut è Sacerdotibus aut Orgeonibus sint, ij, aut coëpulones, aut eodem tumulo qui conduntur, aut thiasotæ, aut ad frumentum coëmendum, aut alias merces profecti, quam velint, pactionem sibi ferunto, dum ne quid ex publica Lege corrumpant.
units.tr: If they are of the common people, or phratores, or of the priests or the Orgeones, or messmates, or those buried in the same tomb, or thiasotae, or have set out to buy grain or other merchandise, let them make for themselves whatever agreement they wish, provided they do not corrupt anything in the public law.

units.la: Legem ἀὐτὸς ὀνόματι[?] descripsit Lib. IV. ad Legem XII. Tabularum Gaius, cuius verba habentur Leg. IV. D. de Collegiis: ea autem hæc sunt. Sodales sunt, qui eiusdem collegij sunt: quam Græci ἑταιρείαν vocant. His autem potestatem facit Lex, pactionem, quam velint, sibi ferre, dum ne quid ex publica Lege corrumpant. Sed haec Lex videtur ex Lege Solonis translata esse: nam inde ita est. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΣ Η ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ Η, &c. Paullo aliter edidit Vir summus in Observationum Libris è Basilicis: ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΣ, Η ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, Η ΙΕΡΩΝ ΟΡΓΙΩΝ ΜΗΝΥΤΑΙ, Η ΣΥΣΣΙΤΟΙ, Η ΟΜΟΤΑΦΟΙ, Η ΘΙΑΣΩ-ΤΑΙ, Η ΕΠΙ ΛΕΙΑΝ ΕΡΧΟΜΕΝΟΙ, Η ΕΙΣ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΑΝ, ΟΤΙ ΑΝ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΔΙΑΘΩΝΤΑΙ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΥΣ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΠΑΓΟΡΕΥΗ· ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ ΠΡΑΓΜΑΤΑ. Sed nos in alia imus, & quidem primo rescribendum putamus ad hunc modum: EAN ΔΕ ΔΗ-ΜΟΣ, Η ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, Η ΙΕΡΩΝ, Η ΟΡΓΕΩΝΩΝ ΗΝ ΑΥΤΟΙ. Sodalitium sive collegium celebrant populares ΔΗΜΟΣ, deinde ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ. Sed veteri populi Atheniensium instituto tota Attica distributa erat in quatuor Tribus, singulae Tribus in tres Φρατρίας in triginta δήμους, vnumquodque δῆμος in triginta hominum capita, inter quos Sacerdotia forte distribuebantur. Grammatici: ἡμῖν [?] ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... Ad Sacerdotes proxime accedebant οἱ ὀργεῶνες dicti: nam sunt οἱ ὅτι ἡμῖν Θεῶν ἢ Ἡρώων σύνοικοντες, vt obseruant Grammaticorum filij, siue οἱ τῆς ἰδίας ἀφιδρυμέ-νοις [?] ἡροῖς ὀργιάζοντες [?] καὶ δήμοις εἰς ταχτῆς ἡμέρας ἥμφρης ἱερας ἥμες [?]. Eorum nomen in hac Lege vsurpasse Solonem, non autem ORGIΩN auctor nobis est Seleucus, qui ἐν τοῦ Ὑπομνήματι τῶν Σόλωνος Ἀξόνων scribit Ὀργεῶνας καλέσθαι, τοὺς συνόδους ἐχόντας [?] περὶ ἥρως ἢ Θεούς. Ad hanc enim Legem omnino alludit Seleucus: Cum igitur οἱ Φρατῆρες non tantum coirent in Φρατρίαν, sed etiam eorum alij essent ἱερεῖς, alij Ὀργεῶνες, potestatem etiam facit celebrandi collegium vel ἱερέων, vel Ὀργεώνων. itaque scripsit Solon, EAN ΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΣ, Η ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, Η ΙΕΡΕΩΝ, Η ΟΡΓΕΩΝΩΝ ΗΝ ΑΥΤΟΙ. Nescio tamen, an Solonis Lege idem constitutum fuerit, quod Diuorum Fratrum Rescriptis, necne. Nam non licet amplius quam vnum collegium licitum habere, vt est constitutum & à Diuis Fratribus. & si quis in duobus fuerit, rescriptum est eligere eum oportere, in quo magis esse velit. Leg. I. §. II. D. eod. Quae paullo post sequuntur, emendauimus: H ΕΠΙ ΛΕΙΟΝ ΟΙΧΟΜΕΝΟΙ Η ΕΙΣ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΑΝ. Quod in Pandectis Florentinis scribitur ΕΠΙ ΛΙΑΝ. mendosum est proculdubio: Quod vero reponunt viri summi è Basilicis ΕΠΙ ΛΕΙΑΝ quasi ad praedandum coirent, nobis non potest probari: nam si maleficij societas coiit, constat, nullam esse societatem: generaliter enim traditur rerum inhonestarum nullam esse societatem Leg. LVII. D. Pro socio. Quare non coit societas ad praedandum, & nihil hic est praedae praedatoribus. At vero societates contrahuntur negotiationis alicuius. Leg. V. D. eod. vt hic, nempe ΕΠΙ ΛΕΙΟΝ, aut ad frumentum coemendum: H ΕΙΣ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΑΝ, aut alias merces. ΛΕΙΟΝ frumentum significare auctor est Hesychius: λεῖον, ὁ ἀπὸ ἀσπ[?]. An vero, quemadmodum apud Romanos, arcam communem haberent, qui collegium celebrabant aut societatem contrahebant Athenis. certo pronunciare non possum. Scio quidem mandatis principalibus permitti apud Romanos, vt loquitur Marcianus Libro III.Institutionum, tenuioribus stipem menstruam conferre, dum tamen semel in mense coeant. Libro I. D. de Collegijs. cum hac stipe conferunt nonnulli † ἐρανοι Atheniensium, quia in veteri Glossario legitur: Ἐρανος, Stipes sodalium: atqui sodales hic non intelliguntur, qui collegium siue sodalitium celebrant, aut societatem contrahunt, siue vniuersorum bonorum, siue negotiationis alicuius, siue vectigalis, siue etiam rei vnius. Lege V. D. Pro socio, sed aequales intelliguntur & amici: quemadmodum apud Terentium in Phormione,
units.tr: Gaius, in Book IV on the Twelve Tables, described this law, and his words are found in Digest 47.22.4 (Of Colleges): they are as follows. Those are fellows who belong to the same college, which the Greeks call hetaireia. The law gives them the power to make whatever agreement they wish among themselves, provided they do not corrupt anything in the public law. But this law seems to have been translated from the law of Solon, for it runs thus. [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΣ Η ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ Η, &c.] The great man [Vir summus] printed it somewhat differently in his Observations, from the Basilica: [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΣ, Η ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, Η ΙΕΡΩΝ ΟΡΓΙΩΝ ΜΗΝΥΤΑΙ, Η ΣΥΣΣΙΤΟΙ, Η ΟΜΟΤΑΦΟΙ, Η ΘΙΑΣΩ-ΤΑΙ, Η ΕΠΙ ΛΕΙΑΝ ΕΡΧΟΜΕΝΟΙ, Η ΕΙΣ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΑΝ, ΟΤΙ ΑΝ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΔΙΑΘΩΝΤΑΙ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΥΣ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΠΑΓΟΡΕΥΗ· ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ ΠΡΑΓΜΑΤΑ.] But we go in another direction, and we think it should first be restored in this form: [EAN ΔΕ ΔΗ-ΜΟΣ, Η ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, Η ΙΕΡΩΝ, Η ΟΡΓΕΩΝΩΝ ΗΝ ΑΥΤΟΙ.] The common people celebrate a fellowship or college, which is called [ΔΗΜΟΣ], then the Phratores. But by the ancient institution of the Athenian people, all Attica was divided into four tribes, each tribe into three phratriai, and into thirty demes, and each deme into thirty men, among whom the priesthoods were apparently distributed by lot. The grammarians [say]: … Next to the priests came those called Orgeones, for they are [those who live with gods or heroes], as the sons of the grammarians observe, or those who celebrate rites for heroes in their own shrines, and for the people on fixed days. That Solon used this name in the law, and not ORGIΩN, is attested by Seleucus, who in his Commentary on the Axones of Solon writes that the Orgeones were so called, those who held meetings concerning a hero or gods. For Seleucus is clearly alluding to this law. Since the Phratores not only gathered in a phratria, but some of them were priests and others Orgeones, the law also gives the power to celebrate a college either of priests or of Orgeones. So Solon wrote: [EAN ΔΕ ΔΗΜΟΣ, Η ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ, Η ΙΕΡΕΩΝ, Η ΟΡΓΕΩΝΩΝ ΗΝ ΑΥΤΟΙ.] I do not know, however, whether the same thing was laid down by the law of Solon as was by the Rescripts of the Divine Brothers, or not. For it is not permitted to have more than one college licit, as was also established by the Divine Brothers; and if someone belongs to two, it was ruled that he must choose the one in which he prefers to be. Digest 47.22.1 §2, same title. What follows shortly after we have corrected: [H ΕΠΙ ΛΕΙΟΝ ΟΙΧΟΜΕΝΟΙ Η ΕΙΣ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΑΝ]. What is written in the Florentine Pandects as [ΕΠΙ ΛΙΑΝ] is without doubt corrupt. But what the great men restore from the Basilica as [ΕΠΙ ΛΕΙΑΝ], as if they assembled for plunder, cannot be approved by us. For if a society for crime was formed, it is established that there is no society at all, since it is generally laid down that there is no partnership in dishonourable matters, Digest 17.2.57, Of Partnership. Therefore a partnership is not formed for plundering, and there is nothing here for plunderers. Rather, partnerships are formed for some kind of business, Digest 17.2.5, same title, as here, namely [ΕΠΙ ΛΕΙΟΝ], that is, for buying up grain, [H ΕΙΣ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΑΝ], or for other merchandise. Hesychius attests that ΛΕΙΟΝ means grain: [λεῖον, ὁ ἀπὸ ἀσπ…]. Whether, however, as among the Romans, those who celebrated a college or contracted a partnership at Athens had a common chest, I cannot say with certainty. I do know that among the Romans, as Marcianus says in Book III of the Institutes, it was permitted to people of modest means to contribute a monthly contribution, provided they met only once a month (Digest 47.22.1, Of Colleges). Some compare with this contribution the Athenian † [ἔρανοι], because in an old glossary we read: [Ἔρανος, a contribution of companions]. But sodales here are not those who celebrate a college or fellowship, or contract a partnership, whether of all goods, or of some business, or of revenue, or even of a single thing (Digest 17.2.5, Of Partnership), but comrades and friends are meant, as in Terence in the Phormio:

units.la: Interea amici, quod polliciti sunt, dabunt; Jnde iste reddet.
units.tr: Meanwhile the friends will give what they promised; from there he will repay.

units.la: Rursum Actu V. Scena VI.
units.tr: Again, Act V, Scene VI.

units.la: Summa eludendi occasio est mihi nunc senes, Ne cuiquam suorum aequalium supplex fiet.
units.tr: Now I have the best chance to make fools of the old men, so that none of my contemporaries will become a suppliant.

units.la: Philemon Comicus:
units.tr: Philemon the comic poet:

units.la: Ἀλλ' ἐᾶσόν ἡ φίλαι σοί, καὶ σιωπῆς τὴν Δία[?], ἐρανον οἴσομεν[?]. ἂν χοῦ μὴ λαβεῖν πῦρα φίλων[?]. ἐὰν ὃ μή, γνώσῃ σαυτὸν ἄλλο μηδὲν, πλὴν σκίαν[?].
units.tr: "But let it be, friends, for you... we will bring a contribution... if you cannot get fire from friends... if not, you will know yourself to be nothing but a shadow." [Ἀλλ' ἐᾶσόν ἡ φίλαι σοί, καὶ σιωπῆς τὴν Δία[?], ἐρανον οἴσομεν[?]. ἂν χοῦ μὴ λαβεῖν πῦρα φίλων[?]. ἐὰν ὃ μή, γνώσῃ σαυτὸν ἄλλο μηδὲν, πλὴν σκίαν[?].]

units.la: E quibus vides eum, cui ἐράνῳ opus erat, factum fuisse supplicem suis aequalibus & amicis:
units.tr: From these lines you see that the man who needed an eranos was made a suppliant to his equals and friends:

units.la: Ne cuiquam suorum aequalium supplex fiet.
units.tr: No one of his equals will he become a suppliant to.

units.la: Nam adibantur amici, & ab iis ἔρανος petebatur. Theophrastus περὶ αὐθαδείας, καὶ φίλῳ ἔρανον χαλεπώτερον εἰσπηγεῖσθαι, εἰπὼν ὅτι σὺ ἂν δοίη, ὑστέρῳ ἡμεῖν φέρων, καὶ λέγων ὅτι ἀπόλλυσι καὶ τῷ ὅ ἀγγέλιον. quod ab illo dictum est valde contumaciter: nam repetebantur atque reddebantur ἔρανοι ab illis, qui huiusmodi collatione fuerant subleuati. Idem Theophrastus περὶ μεμψιμοιρίας καὶ ἐρανὸς εἰσενεγκόντος τῷ φίλων, καὶ Φιλοφρόνως ἔνος. ἱλαρὸς ἔστ' καὶ πῶς, εἰπεῖν, ὅτι δεῖ ὃ ἀγγέλιον ἀπολυώναι ἑκάστῳ, καὶ χρεῖς τούτων, χάριν ὀφείλειν ὡς ἀνθρωπινώτατον[?]; Debebatque restitui collata haec pecunia intra mensem, ex quo collata fuerat. Ita interpretor Grammaticorum verba ista: ἐρανιστὴς ὡς τοῖς κωμῳδοῖς ἐστιν, ὁ τῷ ἐράνῳ μετέχων, καὶ τῷ φόρῳ, ὡ καθ' ἑκάστου μηνὸς ἐδὲ καταβάλλειν, εἰσφέρων. ὃ ὃ ὄνομα ταῦτα λυσίᾳ ἐν τοῖς ἀστεῖς Αἰσχυνέστι ἐν ἔρανος ἐράνῳ, εἰ γάνος. Verba ista, ὡς καθ' ἑκάστου μηνὸς ἐδὲ καταβάλλειν, referenda sunt ad eum, in quem collatus est ἔρανος, non autem ad eum, qui contulit: non enim stipem hanc menstruam siue quoe mensibus semel conferebat, sed quotiescumque exigebat & flagitabat res amicorum aduer-sa: amici vero, in quos collata fuerat haec stipes, debebant eam καθ' ἑκάστου μηνὸς καταβάλλειν, singulis mensibus exsoluere: erat enim quasi credita pecunia, quae singulis mensibus exigitur a creditoribus, vnde Harpocration, Suidas, Pollux: ἐμμῆνοι δίκη, αἱ τι ἐμπεσοῦσαι καὶ ἐρανισταί. Quia scilicet extremo mense reddenda ea est stipes, sicut & credita pecunia: Nam etiam qui hanc stipem conferebant, aliquando a sponsore aliquo sibi caueri volebant: Docet id nos titulus Orationis Lysianæ, si auctorem non menti-tur: ὃ ὄνομα ταῦτα Λυσίᾳ ἐν τοῖς ἀστεῖς Αἰσχυνέστι ταῦτα ἐγίνης ἐράνῳ. Aristocra-res scilicet fideiusserat ἐράνου iri redditum ei, qui contulerat. Ad hanc collatitiam Atheniensium stipem proxime accedit Romanis vsurpatus mos in subleuandis rebus amicorum aduersis, sed sine vlla restitutionis spe aut fidu-cia. Martialis:
units.tr: For it was to friends that people went, and from them an eranos was sought. Theophrastus, in his work on arrogance (peri authadeias), says that it is harder to ask a friend for an eranos, and he adds that the one asked says, "You would give it, bringing it later to us," and says that he is ruined as well... [περὶ αὐθαδείας, καὶ φίλῳ ἔρανον χαλεπώτερον εἰσπηγεῖσθαι, εἰπὼν ὅτι σὺ ἂν δοίη, ὑστέρῳ ἡμεῖν φέρων, καὶ λέγων ὅτι ἀπόλλυσι καὶ τῷ ὅ ἀγγέλιον.] That was said very disdainfully by him, for erana were demanded back and repaid by those who had been relieved by such a collection. The same Theophrastus, in his work on complaining about one's lot (peri mempsimoirias), speaks of one who brings an eranos to a friend and is kindly and cheerful... and how one must release each person from the debt and owe thanks for such a gift as most humane. [περὶ μεμψιμοιρίας καὶ ἐρανὸς εἰσενεγκόντος τῷ φίλων, καὶ Φιλοφρόνως ἔνος. ἱλαρὸς ἔστ' καὶ πῶς, εἰπεῖν, ὅτι δεῖ ὃ ἀγγέλιον ἀπολυώναι ἑκάστῳ, καὶ χρεῖς τούτων, χάριν ὀφείλειν ὡς ἀνθρωπινώτατον[?];] This money collected had to be restored within a month from the time it was collected. I interpret the grammarians' words thus: an erani­stes is, as among the comic poets, one who takes part in the eranos and the contribution, who pays in every month, bringing it in. [ἐρανιστὴς ὡς τοῖς κωμῳδοῖς ἐστιν, ὁ τῷ ἐράνῳ μετέχων, καὶ τῷ φόρῳ, ὡ καθ' ἑκάστου μηνὸς ἐδὲ καταβάλλειν, εἰσφέρων.] The words "to pay in every month" must be referred to the one to whom the eranos was given, not to the one who contributed. For this was not a monthly tax, paid once a month, but a contribution whenever the misfortunes of friends demanded and required it. The friends to whom the contribution had been given were bound to pay it back kath' hekastou mēnos, that is, each month. For it was in effect like a loan, which creditors demand every month; hence Harpocration, Suidas and Pollux: "monthly suits, those into which the contributors and the eranistai fell." Obviously, because this contribution had to be repaid at the end of the month, just like a loan. Indeed, those who made these contributions sometimes wanted security from some surety. The title of a speech of Lysias teaches this, if it does not lie about its author: "Against Aristocrates, that he had been a surety for the eranos..." Aristocrates had evidently guaranteed that the eranos would be repaid to the one who had contributed. Closest to this Athenian contribution among the Romans was the custom, used in helping friends in adversity, of a similar kind, but without any hope or expectation of repayment. Martial:

units.la: Empta domus fuerat tibi, Tongiliane, ducenis: Abstulit hanc nimium casus in Vrbe frequens. Collatum est decies: rogo non potes ipse videri Incendisse tuam, Tongiliane, domum?
units.tr: Your house, Tongilianus, had been bought for two hundred thousand, but a chance event, too common in the city, took it away. A collection of ten thousand was made. I ask, can you not seem, Tongilianus, to have set fire to your own house?

units.la: Iuvenalis Satyra III.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire III.

units.la: Si magna Asturici cecidit domus, horrida mater, Pullati proceres, differt vadimonia Prætor. Tunc geminus casus Vrbis, tunc odimus ignem. Ardet adhuc, & iam accurrit qui marmora donet, Conferat impensas. Hic nuda & candida signa, Hic aliquid præclarum Euphranoris, & Polycleti, Hæc Asianorum vetera ornamenta Deorum, Hic libros dabit, & forulos, mediamque Mineruam, Hic modium argenti: meliora, & plura reponis Persicus orborum lautissimus: & merito iam Suspectus, tanquam ipse suas incenderit ædes.
units.tr: If the great house of Asturicus has fallen, the proud nobles, with their dreadful mother, put off their court appearances, and the praetor too. Then the twin disasters of the city are felt, then we hate fire. It is still burning, and already there runs up the man who will give marble, who will contribute money. Here one gives bare and gleaming statues, here some splendid piece by Euphranor or Polyclitus, here the old adornments of the gods of Asia; here he will give books and bookcases, and a middle-sized Minerva, here a peck of silver. You, Persicus, the most lavish of the childless, offer better and more numerous gifts, and rightly now are suspected, as if you yourself had set fire to your house.

units.la: sed penultimo versu malim,
units.tr: But I would prefer in the penultimate verse:

units.la: vt merito iam Suspectus, tanquam ipse suas incenderit ædes.
units.tr: that rightly now he is suspected, as if he himself had set fire to his own house.

units.la: Ad menstruam illam stipem, quæ in sodalitiis & collegiis conferebatur te-nuioribus apud Romanos accedunt Erani Amisenorum, de quibus Traia-nus in Rescripto ad Plinium Secundum: Amisenos, quorum libellum epistolæ tuæ iunxeras, si legibus istorum quibus de officio sederis vtuntur, concessum est Eranos habere, possumus quominus habeant non impedire, eo facilius, si tali collatione non ad turbas & illicitos cœtus, sed ad sustinendam tenuiorum inopiam vtuntur.
units.tr: Among the poorer Romans, in the associations and guilds, the monthly contribution of which we have spoken was also made in the form of the erani of the Amisenes. Trajan, in his rescript to Pliny the Younger, speaks of them: "As for the Amisenes, whose little book you attached to your letter, it is permitted to them to have erani, if they use the laws of those by whose office you were sitting. We cannot prevent them from having them, the more easily if they use such a collection not for riots and unlawful assemblies, but to support the want of the poorer."

units.la: Adeo autem sibi metuerunt Athenienses, ne aliquo prætextu male asse-cti ciues in Rempublicam inuaderent, vt Lege cauerint eum, qui Reipubli-cæ aliquid pollicitus fuerit, nec præstiterit, capite plecti.
units.tr: The Athenians feared so much that citizens, under some pretext, might attack the state, that they enacted by law that a man who had promised something to the state and did not perform it should be put to death.

units.la: Ἐαὶ ὃς ἐπαγγελλόμενος ᾖ, ἢ δῆμον ἐξαπατήσῃ, εἰσαγγελίαι εἴη τῷ ἀνδρὶ, καὶ αὐτὸν καὶ ἄλλῳ, διαπαν-τὸς ζημιοῦν. Si quis quicquam Reipublicæ pollicitus fuerit, nec præstiterit, publica aduersus eum iudicia instituuntor: conuictus capite luito.
units.tr: "If anyone, promising, deceives the people, let there be an accusation against him, and let him be punished forever, both himself and another." [Ἐαὶ ὃς ἐπαγγελλόμενος ᾖ, ἢ δῆμον ἐξαπατήσῃ, εἰσαγγελίαι εἴη τῷ ἀνδρὶ, καὶ αὐτὸν καὶ ἄλλῳ, διαπαν-τὸς ζημιοῦν.] If anyone has promised something to the state and not performed it, public suits are to be brought against him; if convicted, he shall pay with his head.

units.la: Addit Demosthenes etiam Senatum Quingentorum & Iudices: itaq; Lex integra hæc fuit:
units.tr: Demosthenes adds the Senate of Five Hundred and the judges, and so the whole law read:

units.la: Ἐαὶ τις ἐπαγγελλόμενος ᾖ, ἢ δῆμον, ἢ βουλὴν, ἢ δικαστήριον ἐξαπατήσῃ, εἰσαγγελίαι εἴη τῷ [?] καὶ αὐτὸν καὶ ἄλλῳ, διαπαντὸς ζημιοῦν. Si quis quicquam Reipublicæ, aut Senatui, aut iudicibus pollicitus fuerit, nec præstiterit, publica aduersus eum iudicia instituuntor, conuictus capite luito.
units.tr: "If anyone, promising, deceives the people, or the Council, or the court, let there be an accusation against him, and let him be punished forever, both himself and another." [Ἐαὶ τις ἐπαγγελλόμενος ᾖ, ἢ δῆμον, ἢ βουλὴν, ἢ δικαστήριον ἐξαπατήσῃ, εἰσαγγελίαι εἴη τῷ [?] καὶ αὐτὸν καὶ ἄλλῳ, διαπαντὸς ζημιοῦν.] If anyone has promised something to the state, or to the Senate, or to the judges, and not performed it, public suits are to be brought against him; if convicted, he shall pay with his head.

units.la: Meminit Demosthenes in Leptinea: ἔστι δ' ἠ̓ν δήπου νόμος ὑμῖν, ἐὰν τις ἐπαγγελλόμενος ᾖ, ἢ δῆμον ἢ βουλὴν, ἢ δικαστήριον ἐξαπατήσῃ, τὰ ἔσχατα παθεῖν. Ulpianus: ἀλλ' εἰσὶ νόμοι, οἱ τοὺς ἀπατῶντας κολάζοντες. In eadem Oratione rursum: ἔστιν ὑμῖν νόμος ὃς [?] χρέος, τὴν καλὴν δοκούντων ἔχειν, ἐὰν ὡς ὁ ἀποχειροτονίας ὁ δῆμον ἐξαπατῶσι, χρίνειν· καὶ ἀλλά, ἀναπαύσων ζημιοῦν. Vlpianus: ὅτι τὸ ἀπατῶντα τὸ δῆμον κολάζειν, ἐὰν ἀποχειροτονίας ὁ μὴ ποιῇ. Idem Demosthenes ἐν τοῖς κατὰ Τιμοκράτους· ὅς οὖν ἡμᾶς ὑμᾶς ἡμῶν ἐξαπατήσας ἀποχειροτονίας, νόμων ὄντων, ἐὰν ὡς τὸ δῆμον ἀποχειροτονίας ἐξαπατήσει, εἰσαγγελίαν εἶ ἀπὸ αὐτῶν. Cauet hac Lege auctor, ne quis populum vana spe lactet, & deludat hiantem, vt inde popularem statum euertat. Nulla enim est tam beata ciuitas, in cuius forma omnes ex æquo acquiescant, vel nouarum tabularum, quas σεισάχθειαν appellabant Atheniensis, vel αἰσάδασμον, ac nouæ diuisionis agrorum cupiditate, vel denique nouarum rerum, mutationisq; status spe. Quo consilio vsus est Theseus, vt omnes Atticæ totius cultores in vnam vrbem Athenas cogeret: & post illum Solon: nam Phanias Lesbius auctor est, τὰ Σόλωνα χρησάμενον ἀπάτῃ πρὸς ἀμφοτέρους, ὅτι Φητῆσαι τῆς πόλεως, ἀποχωροῦσαι χρύφα, τῆς ἐν τῇ ἀπὸ ἡμῶν ἐκ μίας χρημάτων, βεβαιῶσαι τὴν συμβο-λαίων. Atque Φησίμαχος praecipua quinque enumerat Aristoteles Polit. Libro IV. cap.XIII.quibus Φίλους ἔστι τὸ δῆμον, qui statum Reipublicæ volunt immutatum, καὶ ἐκκλησίαν, καὶ τὰς ἀρχάς, καὶ δικαστήρια, καὶ ὁπλίτιν, καὶ γυμνασίαν, adde καὶ αἰσάδασμον, καὶ σεισάχθειαν, & si qua sunt huiusmodi. Quare idem Philosophus Polit. Libro V. cap. V. vere pronunciat: αἱ μὲν οὖν δημοκρατίαι μάλιστα μεταβάλλεσι διὰ τὸν τῶν δημαγωγῶν ἀσελγείαν, ὅτι μὲν γὰρ, ἵνα χαρίζωνται ἀδικοῦντες πρὸς γνώσιμους σώσιασιν· ἐὰν δὲ ἀρχὰς ἀναδάσσεις ποιοῦντες, ἐὰν δὲ πατρῷας δὲ τὰς λειτουργίας. Quod vnice caucbant Atheniensis: vnde in iureiurando Heliastarum legitur: ΟΥΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΕΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΑΠΟΚΟΠΑΣ, ΟΥΔΕ ΓΗΣ ΑΝΑΔΑΣΜΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΟΥΔ' ΟΙΚΙΩΝ ΚΑΤΑΞΩ. Negant enim se vnquam permisuros, vt nouæ fiant tabulæ, aut agrorum diuisiones. Vlpianus: ὁσὸν νομοθετήσω τῶν ἰδιωτικῶν χρημάτων, ὥστε μὴ ἀπολαμβάνειν τοὺς ἰδιώτας τὰ χρέα, ἀλλ' ἐδωκάσει. αἰσάδασμος δὲ εἰσὶ γίνεσθαι ἐς τῆς ἀπακλούσας δημοκρατίας· οἱ γὰρ πένητες πολλάκις καὶ ἑαυτοὺς γινώσκουσι ζητοῦσι πρὸς πλουσίους, λέγοντες ὡς ἡ δίκαιον ἔστι τοὺς μὲν ἔχειν χρῆ πολλῶ, αὐτοὺς δὲ μὴ, ἀλλὰ δίκαιον εἶ καὶ αὐτῆς ἐξ ἴσου μεταλαμβάνειν τῶν χρῶν κατ' οἰκίας. quæ postrema verba in superioribus expendimus. Si quis hanc Legem violasset, in ius erat rapiendus πρὸς τὸ βουλῶν εἰς τὸν δῆμον, nam id est, εἰσαγγελίαν εἶ καὶ αὐτῷ. Conuicto poena irrogabatur capitis. Accusator, etsi falso infimulasset, nullum, eo non conuicto, periculo sibi creabat, si, aut ex Atheniensibus sex mille, qui concioni intererant, mille ducenti, aut è Quingentis Senatoribus, centum secundum se pronunciassent: alioqui mille drachmis multabatur.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this in the speech Against Leptines: "There is surely a law among you that if anyone, promising, deceives the people, the Council or the court, he shall suffer the utmost penalty." [ἔστι δ' ἠ̓ν δήπου νόμος ὑμῖν, ἐὰν τις ἐπαγγελλόμενος ᾖ, ἢ δῆμον ἢ βουλὴν, ἢ δικαστήριον ἐξαπατήσῃ, τὰ ἔσχατα παθεῖν.] Ulpian: "But there are laws punishing those who deceive." [ἀλλ' εἰσὶ νόμοι, οἱ τοὺς ἀπατῶντας κολάζοντες.] In the same speech again: "There is a law among you, which the good men of the assembly hold to be of great use, that if anyone deceives the people by a show of promises, they judge him, and also punish him..." Ulpian: "that one who deceives the people is punished, if he does not do what he promised." Demosthenes himself, in the speech against Timocrates: "Whoever, having deceived you by his promises, when the laws exist, deceives the people by his promises, let there be an accusation against him." The author, by this law, guards against anyone deceiving the people with empty hope and beguiling their gaping expectation, so as to overthrow the popular state from within. For there is no state so happy that in its form all are content, whether from the Athenian cancelling of debts, which they called seisachtheia, or aisadasmos, or the desire for a new division of lands, or finally the hope of revolution and change of condition. Theseus used this plan to gather all the inhabitants of Attica into one city, Athens; and after him Solon did too. For Phanias of Lesbos is the authority that Solon, using deceit toward both parties, [...] secretly [...] of the money [...] to confirm the agreements. And Aristotle, in book 4, chapter 13 of the Politics, lists five things by which the people who want the state changed are led: the assembly, the magistracies, the courts, the armed force, the gymnasium; add also aisadasmos and seisachtheia, and whatever else is of this kind. Therefore the same philosopher, in book 5, chapter 5 of the Politics, rightly declares: "Democracies change mostly because of the licence of the demagogues; for by flattering the people they wrong the notables, and by making redistributions of lands they destroy the public service." This the Athenians above all guarded against; hence in the oath of the Heliasts it is read: "Neither will I cut off private debts, nor the redistribution of Athenian land, nor the reordering of houses." For they declared they would never allow new registers of debts or divisions of lands. Ulpian: "to enact a law concerning private money, so that private persons do not recover their debts, but are judged..." Aisadasmos occurs in the most extreme democracy; for the poor often seek from the rich, and themselves demand, saying that it is not just that some have much and they have nothing, but that it is just for them to share equally in the goods of the house. These last words we examined in the earlier passage. If anyone violated this law, he was to be dragged into court before the Council, to the people; for this is the accusation against him. Upon conviction, the penalty of death was imposed. An accuser, even if he had falsely charged someone, did not incur any danger to himself if, although the accused was not convicted, either six thousand Athenians who attended the assembly, or one thousand two hundred, or a hundred of the five hundred senators, acquitted him by their vote; otherwise he was fined a thousand drachmas.

units.la: Neque certe mirum videri cuiquam debet, si voluerint Atheniences eos, qui aliquid Reipublicæ pollicit sunt, obligari ad præstandum, cum etiam Lege sanxerint, eum iniuste fecisse, qui, cum fassus aliquid sit coram ciuibus, fidem fefellerit.
units.tr: Nor should it seem strange to anyone that the Athenians wished those who had promised something to the commonwealth to be bound to perform it, since they also sanctioned by law that he acted unjustly who, having acknowledged something before the citizens, broke faith.

units.la: Εαὶ ὡς ἐναντίον τῶν πολιτῶν ὁμολογήσας τι παράθεσι, τῶν ἐνοχον εἶ πα ἀδικίαν.
units.tr: If anyone, having acknowledged something before the citizens, breaks faith, let him be held to be in the wrong. [Ἐὰν ὡς ἐναντίον τῶν πολιτῶν ὁμολογήσας τι παράθηται, τὸν ἐνοχον εἶναι πρὸς ἀδικίαν]

units.la: Si quis coram ciuibus aliquid fassus insuper habeat, iniuste fecisse pronunciator.
units.tr: If anyone, having acknowledged something before the citizens, nevertheless fails to keep it, let him be pronounced to have acted unjustly.

units.la: Legem laudat Dinarchus ἐν τῇ Φιλοχλέους. καὶ ὁ μὲν χαινὴς τῆς πόλεως νόμος, ἐαὶ τις ἐνδυτῶν τῶν πολιτῶν ὁμολογήσας τι παράθεσι, τῶν ἐνοχον εἶ καλῶς ἐν πα ἀδικίαν.
units.tr: Dinarchus cites the law in his speech against Philocles: "The new law of the city says that if any of the citizens, having acknowledged something, breaks faith, he shall be held guilty of wrongdoing in every respect." [ὁ μὲν καινὸς τῆς πόλεως νόμος, ἐάν τις τῶν πολιτῶν ὁμολογήσας τι παράθηται, τὸν ἐνοχον εἶναι καλῶς ἐν πάσῃ ἀδικίᾳ]

units.la: Etenim si aduersariorum pactiones coram testibus conuentæ, sunt ratæ, quáto magis ius & æquum erit, vt rata sint, quæ ciuibus testibus aliquis falsus est?
units.tr: For if agreements between adversaries, made before witnesses, are upheld, how much more right and fair will it be that those things be upheld which someone has pledged to the citizens in the presence of witnesses?

units.la: At verò si quis dona dederat, aut acceperat ad nocendum populo, vel ciui, ignominiosus erat, & liberi eius, & quicquid eius erat.
units.tr: But if anyone had given gifts, or had received them, to harm the people or a citizen, he was made infamous, and his children, and whatever was his.

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΛΑΜΒΑΝΗΙ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΙΝΟΣ, Η ΑΥΤΟΣ ΔΙΔΩΙ ΕΤΕΡΩΙ, Η ΔΙΑΦΘΕΙΡΗΙ ΤΙΝΑΣ ΕΓΑΓΓΕΛΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΕΠΙ ΒΛΑΒΗΙ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΤΙΝΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΠΟΛΙΤΩΝ ΤΡΟΓΩΙ, Η ΜΗ-ΧΑΝΗΙ, ΗΙΤΙΝΙΟΥΝ ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ, ΚΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ, ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΕΚΕΙΝΟΥ.
units.tr: "If any Athenian receives something from another, or himself gives it to another, or, being an informer, destroys some men by a plot against the people, or wrongs any citizen by bribery or by some device, let him be infamous, and his children, and his property." [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΛΑΜΒΑΝΗΙ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΙΝΟΣ, Ἢ ΑΥΤΟΣ ΔΙΔΩΙ ΕΤΕΡΩΙ, Ἢ ΔΙΑΦΘΕΙΡΗΙ ΤΙΝΑΣ ΕΓΓΕΛΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ἘΠΙ ΒΛΑΒΗΙ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΤΙΝΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΠΟΛΙΤΩΝ ΤΡΟΦΩΙ, Ἢ ΜΗΧΑΝΗΙ, ΗΤΙΝΙΟΥΝ ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ἜΣΤΩ, ΚΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ, ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ἘΚΕΙΝΟΥ]

units.la: Si quis Atheniensium ab alio munera accipiat, aut ipse det alteri, aut pollicitationibus corrumpat alios in perniciem populi, aut alicuius ciuis, aut quocumque alio modo & arte, ignominiosus esto cum liberis & bonis suis.
units.tr: If any Athenian receives gifts from another, or himself gives them to another, or corrupts others with promises to the ruin of the people, or of any citizen, or in any other way and by any art, let him be infamous, with his children and his goods.

units.la: Refert hanc Legem [illegible, ~8 letters] in Midiana Demosthenes: τὸν δὲ νόμον μοι λέγε ἐφιξῆς, ὥσπερ ἡμεῖς λέξαμεν, λέγε· ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΛΑΜΒΑΝΗΙ ΠΑΡΑ ΤΙΝΟΣ, &c. Idem [illegible, ~30 letters]. Vlpianus ad Midianam: ὁ μὲν νόμος ἔστ' ὅτι μὴ ἐξεῖναι δῶρα διδόναι, μήτε λαμβάνειν [?]. Atque idem Vlpianus ibidem scribit capite. in eos sanctum fuisse, [illegible, ~12 letters] quod tamen falsum esse ex ipsius inspectione Legis fit liquido. nam poena hæc est, ATIMOS ESTW KAI PAIDES, KAI TA EKEINOY, quanquam reuera ipsa morte grauior est, in suis quidem sunt bonis, sed cum ὁλόκληροι ἄτιμοι sint, [illegible, ~10 letters], vt cum Vlpiano dicam. Atque hæc quidem sancita sunt in quemuis Atheniensium ciuium. Prima autem Lege caucbatur, vt quicumque eorum, qui ad Rempublicam accederent, munera acceperint ad corruptelam, vel capite luant, vel illius, quod acceperunt, muneris decuplum pendant.
units.tr: Demosthenes quotes this law in the speech Against Midias: "Read me the law in order, just as we have written it, read: If any Athenian receives from anyone, etc." The same [illegible] . Ulpian, in his commentary on the Midian speech, writes: "The law is that it is not permitted to give gifts or to receive them [?]." And the same Ulpian, in the same place, writes that the chapter was [illegible] against those, [illegible], though this is clearly false from the inspection of the law itself. For this is the penalty: "let him be infamous, and his children, and his property." Although in truth it is heavier than death itself: they keep their goods, but since they are wholly infamous [illegible], as I may say with Ulpian. These things were indeed sanctioned against any Athenian citizen. But by the first law it was provided that whoever of those who approached the commonwealth should accept gifts for corruption must either pay with his life or repay ten times the value of the gift he had received.

units.la: Τοὺς δωροδοκοῦντας, ἐὰν θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι, ἐὰν δικαπλοῦν τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς λήμματος ἐκτίνειν.
units.tr: Those who take bribes: if they are punished with death, or else they pay back double the original gain.

units.la: Si quis eorum qui ad Rempublicam gerunt, dona acceperit, capite luito, aut eius, quod accepit, muneris decuplum pendito.
units.tr: If anyone of those who conduct the affairs of the commonwealth accepts gifts, let him pay with his life, or let him pay ten times the value of the gift he has taken.

units.la: Describit hanc Legem Dinarchus ὡς τῷ χ[?] Δημοσθένους. ἀλλ' εἰ νόμοι ταῖς ἄλλαις ἀδικίαις εἰς ὀργυρίου λόγον ἀνακίνητον διπλοῦν τῷ βλάβῳ ἐφείλη κελεύ-ει· καὶ δὲ τῶν δωροδοκούντων δύο μόνον ἡμιμάσκα πεπαίκασιν, ἢ θάνατον, ἵνα τυχὼν τῆς ζημίας [illegible, ~10 letters] ἢ δικαπλοῦν τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς λήμματος ὁ τίμημα τῶν δώρων. ἵνα μὴ λειτυπλὲς ἢ εἰς τοῦτο τὸ ὅλμῶσι ποιεῖν. Meminit idem ὡς τῷ καὶ Αεισχίνης, & docet veteri Lege, de qua suo loco diximus, diris pro concione deuotos fuisse, qui munera ad corruptelam acciperent: πῶς οὖν Νομοθέτης καὶ τὴν δωροδοκούντων ἐσομοθέτησαν; ἐφ' οἷς μὲν ἀρχὴ ἐκ ἐξ ἐπ' ἐμοῦ ἀνθρώπων ποιεῖν δῶρα λαμβάνειν, μὴ ταῦτα λέγειν καὶ γνώσκειν τὴν ἀφεγμάτων, ὀξύλη τῶν ἐπί. ὧν ἐπὶ πω ὅστις Αεισχίνης. ἐπεὶ ὁ βωμοῖς δώρων ζεάφας ποιησάμενος, καὶ καίει μὴν ἕνωτον τὴν ἀδικημ[?] δικαπλασίας ὑπὸ-θέντης θέντις τῇ ψηφίσματος τῷ ἐκποιν[?]. Dica hæc scribebatur apud Thesmothetas. Grammatici: γίγνονται ποιεῖς τὰς Θεσμοθέτας γραφαὶ δώρων[?]. Notabantur autem infamia, & maxima capitis minutione. Andocides ἐν πᾶ ἐκ μυστηρίων[?] ἐπει-γες ἡ, ὧν τὰ ἀλλο σώματα ἀτιμα λῶ[?], τοῦ δὲ ὑπὸ ἔχει, καὶ ἐκέκλωτο[?] · ἐπι δ᾽ ἀν ἤσθη ὑπόσοι δώρων ἐφλοιεν[?] · τοῦτοι ἐδὲ καὶ αὐτοῖς, καὶ τῶν ἐκ τούτων ἀτιμίας[?] ἐ[?]. Meminit Harpocration, è quo hoc amplius discès[?], accusatorem, qui quintam suffragiorum partem non tulisset, non tantum mille drachmis multatum fuisse, sed etiam prima capitis minutione: δώρων γραφὴ, ὅποτε τις αἰτίαν ἔχει τῶν πολιτῶν δῶρα λαβεῖν, ὃ ἐκκλησία ὃ κατ᾽ αὐτῶν δίκης ἐλέγετο, δωροδοκία π[?] ἡ δώρων γραφὴ[?]. ἱσὸν οὖν ἐαυτῷ ἐχ ... μισθοφορᾶς μὴ μισθῶσθαι ὃ πρότερον μέσης τῆ ψήφων, ὀφειλεῖ χιλίας, καὶ ... ἀτιμία ἐς[?]. nempe, puto, illi non licebat in posterum quenquam publico postulare iudicio, ὡς ἐκ αὐτοῦ γράψασθαι[?], vt Andocides loquitur.
units.tr: Dinarchus describes this law in his speech against Demosthenes. But whereas the laws for other wrongs order double the damage to be paid in money reckoning, for those who take bribes they have fixed only two penalties, death, or else repayment of double the original gain, or the value of the gifts, so that it should not be easy for them to attempt such a thing. The same Dinarchus also mentions Aeschines, and teaches that under the old law, of which we have spoken in its place, those who took gifts for corruption were cursed before the assembly. "How then did the lawgiver establish these penalties for those who take bribes?" [illegible passage]. Aeschines likewise [illegible], since he made the altars of the gifts [illegible], and burns [illegible], and under the decree [illegible]. This action was brought before the Thesmothetae. The grammarians: the suits concerning gifts were brought before the Thesmothetae. Such offenders were marked with infamy and the greatest loss of civic rights. Andocides, in his speech [illegible], says that those who had [illegible] were infamous and [illegible]. Harpocration also mentions this, from whom one learns further that an accuser who did not secure a fifth of the votes was not only fined a thousand drachmas but also lost his civic rights from the first. The suit concerning gifts was brought whenever someone was accused of taking gifts from a citizen. Thus it is clear that he could not afterwards bring a public prosecution against anyone, as Andocides says.

units.la: LIBER SEXTUS DE CONNUBIIS
units.tr: BOOK SIX, ON MARRIAGE

units.la: TITULUS I.
units.tr: TITLE I.

units.la: Licenter admodum solutéque vixisse veteres Athenienses, Graecorum literis est proditum, quorum princeps volgivagam Venerem Cecrops hinc Δίφυης dictus, Lege compescuit, & sanxit, ne quis binas nuptias eodem tempore constitutas haberet: Ενα αἰδρα μιᾶς γυναικὸς τυχεῖν. Vnam tantum uxorem ducito.
units.tr: It is reported in Greek writings that the ancient Athenians lived quite licentiously and loosely. Their first king, Cecrops, called Diphyes from this, restrained wandering lust by law and decreed that no one should have two marriages at the same time: That a man should obtain one wife only [Ἕνα ἄνδρα μιᾶς γυναικὸς τυχεῖν]. Take only one wife.

units.la: Athenæus Libro XIII. hanc Legem laudat: ὁ Ἀλωάης ... Κέκροψ μίαν ἐν ἐζύξει [?]. Scholiastes Comici ad Plutum: ἡ αἰδρὶ ὡς ἔτυχε μισγομένων παῖς γυναιξὶ, καὶ ἐκ Ζύπου μὴ γινωσκομένης ... Κέκροψ νόμως ἡ ... ὥστε Φανερῶς συνγίνεσθαι αὐτῆς, καὶ μιᾶς τυχεῖν, καὶ ... ἀνδρῶν ... δύο φύσεις τὸ πατρὸς ... δύο φύσεως ἰδρὶ ἐκ Φύσις ἐχλητ[?].
units.tr: Athenaeus in Book XIII praises this law: Cecrops... allowed one wife in the marriage. The scholiast on the comic poet's Plutus says: the children of a man who mixed indiscriminately with women, and who was not known from a mother, ... Cecrops made a law that, since it was clear that they were of one blood, one should obtain one [wife]... the two natures of father... the offspring of one man and one nature.

units.la: Ὅσοι γυναικῶν ἀνὴρ ἐν ἰωίας ἔχει. ἀλλ' εἷς μίας βλέποντος ὤναιδυ Κύπριν τέρψεται, ὡς ὧς μὴ κακὸς οἶκον θέλει. inquit Euripides Andromacha. Quare etiam vox γάμος originationem accepit, ἀπὸ δὲ δύο ἀμα ἔτ[?]. Huic Legi circa Socratis tempora videtur derogatum fuisse plebiscito, quod descripsit Hieronymus Rhodius: refert enim βουλθεῖσας Ἀλωάης, ἀφ' ὧ λαπὶ ὑδρᾶν, σαυαξῆσαι ὁ πλῆθος, ψηφίσασθαι, γαμεῖν μὲν ἀρ' ὧ μίαν, παιδοποιεῖσθαι δὲ καὶ ἐκ ἑτέρας. Meminit huius plebiscitii Athenæus Libro XIII. vbi docet ex Aristotele Libro περὶ δημοκρατίας, si titulus auctorem non mentitur, Callisthene, Demetrio Phalereo, Satyro Peripatetico, & Aristoxene Musico, Socratem habuisse duas γαμετὰς γυναῖκας, ὅτι συγκεχωρημένον ἦν ψήφισμα τὸ ἐξήνεγκε τότε ἀφ' αὐτῶν αἰσθέσθαι, ὥστ' ἐξῆναι καὶ δύο ἔχειν γυναῖκας τὸν βουλόμενον. Quanquam duas vxores eodem tempore Socratem habuisse negat Panætius Rhodius, qui, vt Plutarchus ait in Pericle, ἐκθῶς ποιὴς τύπος ἐν τῇ πόλει Σωκράτης αἰτίαν. Verùm vna tantùm erat vxor: concedebatur tantùm hoc plebiscito ἀφ' ὧ λαπιδαρεῖν è peregrina & pellice domi, siue nuptiis vxoris loco retenta, παιδοποιεῖσθαι, liberos tollere: Vxorem legitimam imitatur concubina, inquit Iulianus Antecessor, sed vxor legitima non est: neque eius liberi γνήσιοι & ciues è Lege: facti tamen sunt illis temporibus è nothis & naturalibus liberis, huius priuilegij rogatione, Δισ' ἀστῶν ἀνδρῶν [?], cum reuera ciues esse non possent, vt qui matre ciue nati non essent: sola quippe ciuis erat uxor legitima è veteri illa Lege, quæ legitur illo plebiscito, quod retulit Hieronymus.
units.tr: Whatever man has many women in his house is an evil one. But he who looks on one woman alone will enjoy Cypris in her sweetness, and does not wish to be a bad householder. So says Euripides in the Andromache. Hence also the word γάμος (marriage) took its origin, from joining two together. This law seems to have been set aside around the time of Socrates by a plebiscite, which Hieronymus of Rhodes describes. For he reports that, when Aloeus... the people, stirred up, voted that men should marry one wife but might beget children also by another woman. Athenaeus, Book XIII, mentions this plebiscite, teaching from Aristotle's On Democracy, if the title does not mislead, that Callisthenes, Demetrius of Phalerum, Satyrus the Peripatetic and Aristoxenus the musician say that Socrates had two lawful wives, because the decree then brought forward had been agreed upon by them, so that whoever wished might have two wives. Yet Panaetius of Rhodes denies that Socrates had two wives at the same time, for, as Plutarch says in the Pericles, Socrates was a plain example of this in the city. But in truth he had only one wife. By this plebiscite it was only permitted to beget children from a foreign woman or a concubine kept at home, instead of a wife. A concubine imitates a lawful wife, says Julian the Antecessor, but she is not a lawful wife, and her children are not legitimate nor citizens under the law. Nevertheless, in those times, by the proposal of this privilege, they were made from bastard and natural children into citizens, though in reality they could not be citizens, since they were not born of a citizen mother. Only a citizen wife was lawful under that old law, which is read in the plebiscite that Hieronymus reports.

units.la: Γαμεῖν ἀςτῶ μίαν. Vnam vxorem legitimam, eamque ciuem, ducito.
units.tr: Marry one wife who is a citizen [Γαμεῖν ἀστῶ μίαν]. Take one lawful wife, and she a citizen.

units.la: Hac Lege enuptio extra ciuitatem vetita est, & improbatæ cum peregrinis nuptiæ: vnde Terentianus Simo in palliata Menandri Andria Actu III. Sc. I. non sine stomacho dicebat:
units.tr: By this law marriage outside the city was forbidden, and marriages with foreigners were disapproved of. Hence Simo, in Terence's Andria, adapted from Menander, Act III, Scene I, said not without irritation:

units.la: Quid hoc?
units.tr: What is this?

units.la: Adeon' est demens ex peregrina?
units.tr: Is he so mad about a foreign woman?

units.la: Ad quæ verba Donatus: Mulieres enim peregrinæ, inhonestæ, ac meretrices habebantur. Inter ciues peculiari Lege Pallenæi excipiebant Agnusios: nam hi duo populi nuptias inter se non contrahebant. Plutarchus in Theseo: ἐκ τούτου φασὶ τῷ Παλληνέων [?] δῆμῳ τὰς [?] Ἀγκωσίων [?] μὴ εἶ [?]. Vetus istud ius de ducendis in vxores solis ciuibus collapsum restituit Pericles, quod tamen pessimo eius exemplo paullo post obsoleuit, donec tandem Aristophon Euclide Prætore Athenis, scripta Lege solos cives Athenienses esse sanxit, qui vtroque parente ciue nati essent: nam ad ea tempora ciuis censebatur, qui parentum alterutro ciue natus esset. Demosthenes ἐν τῇ πρὸς Εὐβουλίδην ἐφέστ[?]. τῶν γενῶν [?] ὡς ἂν [?] πολίτ[?] ἐκ [?]. Ad hæc tempora, quæ Præturam Euclidis præcesserunt, referendum est argumentum fabulæ palliatæ Plautinæ Epidici: nam in eo dramate Periphanes vxorem duxerat, quæ ciuis non erat: qua in re miror eruditissimorum virorum acumen & diligentiam sugisse ista, quæ sequuntur Actu V. Scena I.
units.tr: On these words Donatus comments: For foreign women were regarded as dishonourable and as prostitutes. By a special law the Pallenians were excepted among citizens, as opposed to the Agnusians, for these two peoples did not contract marriages with each other. Plutarch in Theseus says: from this, they say, the Pallenian people... the Agnusians... This old right, which confined marriage to citizens alone, had fallen into disuse, and Pericles restored it, though under his bad example it soon became obsolete again, until at last Aristophon, in the archonship of Euclides, by written law decreed that only those Athenians were citizens who were born of citizens on both sides, for in those times a citizen was counted as one born of a citizen on either parent's side. Demosthenes, in his speech against Eubulides... of the races... as citizens... To these times, which preceded the archonship of Euclides, must be referred the plot of Plautus' comedy Epidicus, for in that play Periphanes had married a wife who was not a citizen. In this matter I wonder that the keen judgement and diligence of very learned men escaped these lines, which follow in Act V, Scene I:

units.la: E Philippa matre natam, ac Thebis Epidauri fatam, Videon' ego Telestidem te, Periphani filiam?
units.tr: Born of a Philippa mother, and fated at Thebes of Epidaurus, do I see you, Telestis, daughter of Periphanes?

units.la: Hæc tamen ἀσύστατα sunt, ac Thebis Epidauri fatam; Nam si Thebis fata atque nata est, non igitur Epidauri. Atqui in Epidauro nata est; habes Actu IV. Scena I.
units.tr: Yet these words are inconsistent, and fated at Thebes of Epidaurus is wrong. For if she was fated and born at Thebes, then she was not from Epidaurus. But she was born in Epidaurus, as you have in Act IV, Scene I:

units.la: P E. Certe ea est, quam in Epidauro pauperculum memini comprimere.
units.tr: P E. Certainly she is the one whom I remember squeezing as a poor little thing in Epidaurus.

units.la: M V. Plane hic ille est, qui mihi in Epidauro primus pudicitiam pepulit.
units.tr: M V. Plainly this is he who first in Epidaurus stripped me of my modesty.

units.la: Non igitur Thebis Epidauri fata erat Telestis: Adde quod nullæ sunt Thebæ Epidauri. Rescribendum itaque puto:
units.tr: Therefore Telestis was not fated at Thebes of Epidaurus. Add that there are no Thebes of Epidaurus. So I think it should be rewritten thus:

units.la: E Philippa matre natam, ac te Bois Epidauri fatam, Videon' ego Telestidem te, Periphani filiam?
units.tr: Born of a Philippa mother, and fated at Boea of Epidaurus, do I see you, Telestis, daughter of Periphanes?

units.la: Boæ siue Bœa vrbs Laconicæ, cuius meminit Strabo Libro VIII. in descriptione Laconicæ: εἴτε Βοία πόλις, εἴτε Μάγεα [?]. meminit quoque Stephanus: Ab ea non longè abfuit Epidaurus, ἡ Λιμὴν Ἐπιδαύρως Straboni dicta, Laconica vrbs in Argolico sinu. Vide Ptolemæum Libro III. cap. XVI. Ex his autem Plauti verbis colligere est Bœam vrbem fuisse in agro hoc Epidaurensi: vnde dixit, ac te Bois Epidauri fatam. Plinius Libro IV. in descriptione Argolici sinus. Oppida, Boea, Epidaurus Limera cognomine. Atque haec quidem Παρέρια dicta sunto: addemus & alterum eiusdem generis. Nuptiarum celebrandarum legitimum tempus videtur fuisse bruma. Aristoteles Politic. Libro VII. cap. XVI. τὰς δὲ ἀρὰ χρόνοις, δὴ γενέσθαι, ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ χρῶν-ται καὶ νῦν, ἀσιστόρτες χρήσιμος τῶν σιωκαλίας ποιεῖσθαι ταύτην. Hinc apud Terentium in palliata Apollodori fabula Phormione, quam, ut videtur, Apollodorus docuit Dionysiis τῆς κατ' ἄχρι, mense Posideone, ubi de Phormionis cum Phanio nuptiis agitur, spatium apparandis nuptiis sibi concedi postulat, denique ante brumam nuptias celebraturum se negat:
units.tr: Boea, or Boeae, is a town of Laconia, which Strabo mentions in Book VIII in his description of Laconia: whether it is the city of Boea or of Magea... Stephanus also mentions it: not far from it lay Epidaurus, which Strabo called Limen Epidaurus, a Laconian town on the Argolic gulf. See Ptolemy, Book III, chapter XVI. From these words of Plautus it may be inferred that Boea was a town in this Epidaurian territory, whence he said fated at Boea of Epidaurus. Pliny, Book IV, in describing the Argolic gulf: the towns Boea, Epidaurus, surnamed Limera. Let these be counted as digressions. We will add another of the same kind. The proper time for celebrating weddings seems to have been winter. Aristotle, Politics Book VII, chapter XVI: Marriages, it is said, took place at the time of the year when, as most people still do, they fasten the ... of winter. Hence in Terence's Phormio, the comedy of Apollodorus, which Apollodorus, as it seems, produced at the Dionysia in the month of Poseideon, where the marriage of Phormio with Phanium is discussed, Phormio asks for time to prepare the wedding, and finally says he will not celebrate it before the winter solstice:

units.la: Aruspex vetuit ante brumam autem quid noui / Negocij incipere, quae causa est iustissima.
units.tr: The soothsayer has forbidden anything new to be begun before the winter solstice, and that is a most just reason.

units.la: Obiicit scilicet Athenienses religionem, qui nuptias non celebrabant ex instituto, ut credit Eustathius mox laudandus, Cecropis, nisi mense Gamelione, (unde nomen invenit,) id est, diebus brumalibus. Gamelion enim est primus hybernus mensis. Olympiodorus ad Meteora Aristotelis: Γαμηλιῶν ἡ ἐλέγετο μὲν πρὸ Ἀθηναίοις, ὅτε δὲ κατ' ἐκεῖνον τὴν χειμερινὴν γάμους ὑπεπλέξεσθαι. Εὔλογον δὲ ὥστε τότε ἀπὸ ἀρχῆς, ὅτε καὶ ἡ γῆ ἀρόσθεῖσα· ἐπιτήδειος δὲ ὁ χειμὼν πρὸς καρπῶν ἡμέραν. Eusthatius ad Iliad. Σ. ἡ ἀρχιμῶν ὥστε ὁ γαμήλιος λόγος, ὅτε καὶ μὲν Ἀθηναῖος ὁ Γαμηλιῶν, γάμους ἀφωρισμένος. Ἄτας vero hominis, qua nuptiis videtur alligandus, (cum etiam horum non minimam habere debeat curam Legislator, ut est apud Philosophum.) est, è Solonis sententia annus tricesimus quintus. nam fecit Solon humanae vitae terminos hebdomadas decem: in harum autem hebdomadum quinta, ut refert ex eius Elegiis Censorinus de Die Natali, cap. XIV. maturitatem ad stipem relinquendam homini inesse dicebat, quae fere sententia Aristotelis fuit Politic. Libro VII. cap. XVI. annum enim tricesimum septimum definiuit. Certe uxor dignitatis nomen est, non voluptatis, quae liberum quaerendorum voto ducitur: definiuntur enim nuptiae hac Lege.
units.tr: Clearly the Athenians were bound by a religious scruple, who by custom did not celebrate weddings except in the month of Gamelion (from which it takes its name), that is, in the wintry days. For Gamelion is the first winter month. Olympiodorus on Aristotle's Meteorology: Gamelion was so called by the Athenians, because in that winter month they used to hold weddings. It is reasonable that this was so from the beginning, when the land was also ploughed, and the winter was suitable for the harvest day. Eustathius on the Iliad Σ: the Gamelian [month] is so called because in Athens it was set apart for weddings. But the age of man at which he ought to be bound in marriage (since the lawgiver ought to take no small care of this, as the Philosopher says) is, according to Solon's opinion, the thirty-fifth year. For Solon fixed the limits of human life at ten weeks of seven years, and, as Censorinus reports from Solon's elegies in On the Birthday, chapter XIV, he said that in the fifth of these weeks man has maturity to leave seed behind. This is nearly the opinion of Aristotle in Politics Book VII, chapter XVI, where he fixes the age at thirty-seven. Certainly a wife is a name of dignity, not of pleasure, which is undertaken with the desire of begetting children, for marriage is defined by this law.

units.la: ΕΠ' ΑΡΟΤΡΩι ΠΑΙΔΩΝ.
units.tr: Children "for the plough" [Ἐπ' ἀρότρῳ παίδων]

units.la: Refert vir sanctissimus Isidorus Pelusiota Libro III. Epistola CCXLIII. πῶς γὰρ ἀρθένον ὁ ἀνὴρ σιωαπόμβρος, γυναῖκα, ταύτῃσι, χήμεσι ποιεῖ. δίς καὶ πρὸς Αἰγυπτίους ἢ σιωαφία ἢ κατὰ ἰόμον, ΕΓ' ΑΡΟΤΡΩι ΠΑΙΔΩΝ, ἐλέγετο γενέσθαι.
units.tr: The most holy Isidore of Pelusium reports, in Book III, Letter 243: "For how does the man, sowing a virgin, make her a wife with her children?" [πῶς γὰρ παρθένον ὁ ἀνὴρ σπείρων, γυναῖκα, ταῖς τέκνοις, ποιεῖ]. Among the Egyptians too, the union made according to law was said to be "for the begetting of children for the plough" [ἐπ' ἀρότρῳ παίδων].

units.la: Non tamen cuiusvis uxoris civis liberi legitimi erant, sed illius tantum, quae legitime desponsata esset ex hac Lege:
units.tr: However, not every wife's children were lawful citizens, but only those of the wife who had been legitimately betrothed, according to this law:

units.la: ΗΝ ΑΝ ΕΓΓΥΗΣΗ ΕΠΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΙΣ ΑΜΑΡΤΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ, Η ΠΑΤΗΡ, Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ ΟΜΟΓΑΤΩΡ, Η ΠΑ[?]ΡΟΣ Ο ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΕΚ ΤΑΥΤΗΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΥΣ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕΙΣ Η ΤΟΥΤΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΣ ΤΙΣ Η ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ Η, ΟΤΩ ΑΝ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΨΗ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.
units.tr: "If there is a betrothal of an heiress, and if the father, or the brother of the same father, or the paternal grandfather, has betrothed her, the children born of her shall be genuine. If none of these exists, and if there is an heiress who has a kinsman to claim her, and if there is none, then the one who is appointed as her kyrios shall be the kyrios." [ΗΝ ΑΝ ΕΓΓΥΗΣΗ ΕΠΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΙΣ ΑΜΑΡΤΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ, Η ΠΑΤΗΡ, Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΩΡ, Η ΠΑΠΠΟΣ Ο ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΕΚ ΤΑΥΤΗΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΥΣ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕΙΣ Η ΤΟΥΤΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΣ ΤΙΣ Η ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ Η, ΟΤΩ ΑΝ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΨΗ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.]

units.la: Exea, quam in legitimam uxorem desponsarit pater, aut germanus frater, aut avus paternus, legitimos liberos tollunto: si nullus horum superfit: & virgo orba fit, nubito ci, qui iudicio obtinuerit si orba non fit, tutor eam desponsato.
units.tr: The heiress whom her father, or full brother, or paternal grandfather has betrothed as a lawful wife, let them beget lawful children. If none of these survives, and she is an orphan heiress, let her marry the man who has obtained her by judgment. If she is not an orphan, let her guardian betroth her.

units.la: Legem recitauit ἀξίως ὀιόμενον Demosthenes εἰς τὸ φ[illegible, ~6 letters] ἀνδρομάχου, sc. ... Iubet autem Legislator, vt desponsata ducatur vxor. Sponsalia sunt mentio & repromissio futurarum nuptiarum. Leg. I. D. de Sponsalibus. nam moris fuit veteribus stipulari & sponderefibi vxores futuras. Leg. II. D. eod. Desponsare autem patris erat puellæ, aut germani fratris, aut aui paterni, HN AN ΕΓ-ΓΥΗΣΗ ΕΠΙ ΑΙΚΑΙΟΙΣ ΑΜΑΡΤΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ, Η ΠΑΤΗΡ, Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΩΡ, Η ΠΑΠΠΟΣ Ο ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ. Ită sponsalibus etiam consensus eorum exigendus est, quorum in nuptiis desideratur. intelligi tamen semper filiæ patrem consentire, nisi euidenter dissentiat, Iulianus scribit. Leg. VII. §. I. D. eod. in nuptiis autem consensus desideratur, non tantum eorum qui coëunt, sed etiam quorum in potestate sunt. Leg. II. D. de ritu nuptiarum. Pater igitur filiæ eam desponsebat, despondebat quoque frater germanus, si pater non esset, neutro horum superstite, auus paternus: huic enim obseruandum esse ordinem docet verborum series in Lege. Quanquam nullus dubito, si pater peregrè abesset, & filia nubilis esset, sedere eam non opportuisse domi tam grandem, dum pater, 'qui desponderet, qui daret, hinc illinc veniret expectantem: sed in potestate fuit fratris germani despondere: exemplum habes in Trinummo Plauti, nam Lefbonicus despondet Lysiteli suam sororem, Charmide patre absente iamdiu: qui cum peregre rediret, ratum id habebat, vt ex hoc dramate constat.
units.tr: Demosthenes, who rightly thought the law worth citing, quotes it in his speech against ... Andromachus [illegible]. The Lawgiver orders that the betrothed woman be taken as wife. Betrothal is the mention and promise of future marriage. Dig. I, De sponsalibus. For it was the custom of the ancients to stipulate and promise to one another future wives. Dig. II, same title. To betroth a girl belonged to the father, or to the full brother, or to the paternal grandfather: [ΗΝ ΑΝ ΕΓΓΥΗΣΗ ΕΠΙ ΑΙΚΑΙΟΙΣ ΑΜΑΡΤΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ, Η ΠΑΤΗΡ, Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΩΡ, Η ΠΑΠΠΟΣ Ο ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ.] Thus the consent is to be sought in betrothals also from those whose consent is required in the marriage. Yet it is always understood that the father consents to his daughter's betrothal unless he clearly dissents, as Julian writes. Dig. VII, §1, same title. In marriage, consent is required not only from those who come together, but also from those in whose power they are. Dig. II, De ritu nuptiarum. Therefore the father betrothed his daughter; a full brother also betrothed her if there was no father; and, if neither of these survived, the paternal grandfather. For the order of the words in the law teaches that this sequence must be observed. Yet I have no doubt that if the father was abroad and the daughter was of marriageable age, she should not have stayed at home so long while her father, who would betroth and give her, was awaited from here and there. Rather, it was within the power of the full brother to betroth her. You have an example in the Trinummus of Plautus, where Lesbonicus betroths his sister to Lysiteles, Charmides, their father, having been long absent. When he returned, he approved it, as is clear from this play:

units.la: Ch. Filiam meam tibi desponsatam esse audio. Ly. nisi tu ne vis.
units.tr: Ch.: I hear my daughter has been betrothed to you. Ly.: Unless you yourself do not wish it.

units.la: Ch. Imo haud nolo. Ly. Sponden' ergo tuam gnatam vxorem mihi?
units.tr: Ch.: On the contrary, I am by no means unwilling. Ly.: Do you then promise your daughter to me as wife?

units.la: Ch. Spondeo: & mille auri Philippum dotis.
units.tr: Ch.: I promise, and a dowry of a thousand gold pieces.

units.la: Ly. Ifiac lege filiam tuam sponden' mihi vxorem dari.
units.tr: Ly.: Do you promise, by this law, that your daughter be given to me as wife?

units.la: Ch. Spondeo.
units.tr: Ch.: I promise.

units.la: Absentiæ tempus triennio definiuerunt Romani Iurisconsulti: nam si ita patet absit, vt ignoretur, vbi sit, & an sit quid faciendum est, merito dubitatur? Et si triennium effluxerit, postquam apertissime fuerit pater ignotus, vbi degit, & an superstes sit, non prohibentur liberi eius, vtrinsque sexus, matrimonium vel legitimas nuptias contrahere. Leg. X. D. de ritu nuptiarum. imo etiam & ante triennium, si vero sit simile patrem illam conditionem repudiaturum non fuisse. Si filius eius, qui apud hostes est, vel absit, ante triennium captiuitatu, vel absentiæ patris, vxorem duxit: vel si filia nupserit: puto, reëte matrimonium vel nuptias contrahi: dummodo eam filius ducat vxorem, vel filia tali nubat, cuius conditionem, certum sit patrem non repudiaturum. Leg. XI. D. eod. Quibus è verbis colligimus, exacto triennio absentiæ patris, reëte matrimonium vel nuptias contrahere potuisse, etiamsi forte pater conditionem illam repudiaturus fuisset. quanquam semper in coniunctionibus non solum, quid liceat, confideran-dum est, sed & quid honestum sit. Leg. XLII. D. eod. Sed ad Atheniensium Legem redeamus. Si pater, si germanus frater, si auus paternus non supersint, quid faciendum est. EAN ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕΙΣ Η͂ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΣ ΤΙΣ Η͂ ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ Η͂ ΟΤΩ ΑΝ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΨΗ. ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ. Virginum aliæ sunt ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΙ. aliæ sunt ΕΠΙΠΠΟΙΚΟΙ. Eas ΘΗΤΙΚΩΝ?, quæ fratres non habent: Orbas cum veteribus Latinis, dicimus. ΘΗΤΙΚΩΣΙ? sunt, quæ fratres habent, & dotem certam é bonis paternis auferunt. Grammatici: [illegible, ~14 letters], ἡ ἐπὶ μέρει τῆ τῶ κλήρου, ὡς [illegible, ~10 letters] ἔχει ἀδελφοὺς αὐτῆ ὄντως. At vero ΕΠΙΓΡΟΙΚΟΙ duum sunt genera: nam aliae sunt, quae [illegible, ~8 letters] τεκνῶν, vt est in Lege, quam infra suo loco, Deo dante, describemus, egenae, & quibus proximi si nollent eas ducere, dotem liceb int, dabant, οἱ κλῆροι ἔχουσαι πατρῷον. aliae vero sunt dotales virgines, quae totam hæreditatem in dotem adferunt. Grammatici: [illegible, ~12 letters], ἡ ἐπὶ πόσῃ τοῦ κλήρου ὀρφανὴ κεκλεῖσμένη, μὴ ὄντες αὐτῇ ἀδελφοί. De Epicleris iftis virginibus ftatuit Legislator: ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΣ ΤΙΣ Ἡ ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ. Quorum verborum fensus est, eam nubere ei, qui iudicio expertus fuerit, & secundum eum pronunciatum fuerit, nam Lex iubebat [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐπὶ τῆς ἐπικλήρων ἀπαιτῶν. atque hæc quidem de dotalibus virginibus: Egenas quoque qui iudicum sententia damnatus fuerat, aut ducebat ipse, aut alteri elocabat, dote dicta data. id proculdubio significant Legis verba: ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΣ ΤΙΣ Ἡ ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ.
units.tr: The Roman jurists fixed the period of absence at three years. For if a man is absent in such a way that it is unknown where he is, and whether he is alive or what should be done, is it not rightly in doubt? And if three years have passed since the father was clearly known to be missing, where he lives and whether he survives, his children of either sex are not forbidden to contract matrimony or lawful marriage. Dig. X, De ritu nuptiarum. Indeed, even before three years, if it is likely the father would not have rejected such a match. If the son of a man who is among the enemies, or who is absent, has taken a wife before three years of captivity or of his father's absence, or if a daughter has married, I think the marriage or union is rightly contracted, provided that the son takes a wife, or the daughter marries a man whose condition the father would certainly not reject. Dig. XI, same title. From these words we gather that, once the three years of the father's absence had elapsed, a marriage or union could rightly be contracted, even if the father perhaps would have rejected that condition. Yet in alliances one must always consider not only what is permitted but also what is honourable. Dig. XLII, same title. But let us return to the law of the Athenians. If the father, the full brother, and the paternal grandfather do not survive, what is to be done? [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕΙΣ Η͂ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΣ ΤΙΣ Η͂ ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ Η͂ ΟΤΩ ΑΝ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΨΗ. ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.] Some virgins are epiklēroi and others are epipoikoi. Those who have no brothers we call orphans, with the older Latins. Those who have brothers, and who take a fixed dowry from their father's goods, are the [...]. The grammarians [illegible] say: the one who is in turn of the lot, as [illegible] has brothers in reality. But the epigroikoi are of two kinds: some are needy, and for the sake of [illegible] children, as is in the law which, God willing, we shall describe in its place below, and for whom, if the nearest kinsmen were unwilling to marry them, they were permitted to give a dowry; they held the lot from their father. The others are dowered maidens, who bring their whole inheritance as dowry. The grammarians [illegible] say: the orphan heiress who is bound to the lot in her husband's [illegible], her brothers not being present. Concerning these epiklerai the Lawgiver ordained: [ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΣ ΤΙΣ Ἡ ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ.] The sense of these words is that she should marry the man who has won in a judicial proceeding and been declared the winner according to the judgment; for the law required [illegible] concerning the epiklerai. This is said of the dowered virgins. The needy heiresses also, whom a court sentence had condemned, either married the man themselves or gave them to another, with a dowry given. The words of the law, [ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΟΣ ΤΙΣ Ἡ ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ], undoubtedly signify this.

units.la: Quod ad ceteras vero virgines attinet, quas ΕΠΙΓΡΟΙΚΟΥΣ. appellari diximus, ita cauit Legislator. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ Ἡ ΟΤΩ͂ ΑΝ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΨΗ ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ. Tutor eam despon sare iubetur: At vero si sic ΕΠΙΠΡΟΙΚΟΣ, vt esse diximus, ergo fratrem saltem habet: Id certe verum est, sed non ea ætate, vt ad negotia mitti posset; itaque ipse est non minus sub tutorum cura. Apud Romanos tutores soli non possunt sponsalia constituere. Leg. VI. D. de sponsalibus. Hanc ita legitime desponsatam ait Legislator ΕΠΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΙΣ ΔΑΜΑΡΤΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ. Nuptiae namque sunt, consortium omnis vitae, diuini, & humani iuris communicatio. Leg. I. D. de ritu nuptiarum: itaque addit: ΕΚ ΤΑΥΤΗΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΥΣ. ex hac tolluntur liberi, qui germani sint Athenienses cives. Meminit huius Legis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Λεπτίνην, ὅ μὲν γὰρ γένοιτο ὅτι, ὅταν ἡ γυνὴ γένηται. ἐν νόμῳ ζῶντα μαρτυρεῖ λέγων. ΗΝ ΑΝ ΕΓΓΥΗΣΗ ΠΑΤΗΡ Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ Η ΠΑΠΠΟΣ ΕΚ ΤΑΥΤΗΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΥΣ. Verum simpliciter dictum est de quouis fratre, aut auo, sed fratre germano, auo paterno. Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΩΡ Η ΠΑΠΠΟΣ Ο ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ. Praeterea, vt exemplis constat, maritus moriens alteri poterat uxorem elocare: ita Demosthenes Oratoris pater uxorem suam Aphobo clocauit. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ Ἀφόβου α. Δημοφῶντι δὲ τῷ ἐμῷ ἀδελφῷ, ἡ δύο θυγατέρας ἐδωκεν ἐχειν· αὐτὸς δ᾽ οὕτω τῷ μητέρᾳ, ἡ παρὰ ἑαυτῆς ὀδηκοντα μνᾶς, ἐκ τῷ οἰκίαι, ἡ σπλένη ἑαυτῇ ταῖς ἐμαῖς. Phormioni nubit Pasionis uxor, vt supremis Pasionis tabulis caueb atur. Demosthenes ἐν τῇ ἀπολογίᾳ ὑπὲρ Φορμίωνος. ὅτι· Ὁ Πασίων ἐπαλύτικος ὡς Ἀφεσίαν Φορμίων ὑπὸ, τῷ μὲν γυναῖκα λαμβάνει τῷ δὲ ὑπαρχεῖ. Sed & pater moriens filiam desponsare poterat, en tibi exemplum a Demosthene patre. Δημοφῶντι δὲ τῷ ἐμῷ ἀδελφῷ, καὶ δύο θυγατέρας ἐδωκεν ἐχειν. Seuere autem animaduertebatur in eos, qui peregrinam pro ciue elocarent, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: As for the other virgins, whom we said are called epigroikoi, the Lawgiver provided thus: [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ Ἡ ΟΤΩ͂ ΑΝ ΕΠΙΤΡΕΨΗ ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.] The guardian is ordered to betroth her. But if she is an epipoikos, as we have said, then she has at least a brother. This is certainly true, but not at an age when she could be sent to affairs; thus she herself is no less under the care of guardians. Among the Romans, guardians alone cannot make betrothals. Dig. VI, De sponsalibus. The Lawgiver calls such a woman lawfully betrothed [ΕΠΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΙΣ ΔΑΜΑΡΤΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ]. For marriage is the partnership of all life, a sharing of divine and human law. Dig. I, De ritu nuptiarum. And so he adds: [ΕΚ ΤΑΥΤΗΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΥΣ.] From her children are born who are genuine Athenian citizens. Demosthenes mentions this law in his speech against Leptines, where he says: [ὅ μὲν γὰρ γένοιτο ὅτι, ὅταν ἡ γυνὴ γένηται, ἐν νόμῳ ζῶντα μαρτυρεῖ λέγων]: "If a father, a full brother, or a paternal grandfather betroths a woman, children born of her are genuine" [ΗΝ ΑΝ ΕΓΓΥΗΣΗ ΠΑΤΗΡ Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ Η ΠΑΠΠΟΣ ΕΚ ΤΑΥΤΗΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΥΣ]. But it is stated simply of any brother or grandfather; the full brother and paternal grandfather are meant: [Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΩΡ Η ΠΑΠΠΟΣ Ο ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ]. Moreover, as the examples show, a husband dying could give his wife to another in marriage. So Demosthenes the orator's father gave his wife to Aphobus. Demosthenes, In Aphobum I: "To Demophon, my brother, he gave two daughters to have; and himself, to my mother, he gave ... from his own house, the things of my own." Pasion's wife married Phormio, as was provided in Pasion's last will. Demosthenes, In defence of Phormio: "Pasion, when dying, ... gave Apollodorus's ... Phormio, he took the wife, and had the property." And a father dying could also betroth his daughter; here is an example from Demosthenes' father: "To Demophon, my brother, he gave also two daughters to have." Severe punishment was imposed on those who gave a foreigner in marriage as a citizen, by this law:

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΕΚΔΙΔΩΙ ΞΕΝΗΝ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΑΝΔΡΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΙ ΩΣ ΕΑΥΤΩΙ ΠΡΟΣΗΚΟΥΣΑΝ ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ, ΚΑΙ Η ΟΥΣΙΑ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ
units.tr: "If anyone gives a foreign woman in marriage to an Athenian man as though she were related to him, let him be atimos, and let his property be confiscated to the public treasury." [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΕΚΔΙΔΩΙ ΞΕΝΗΝ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΑΝΔΡΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΙ ΩΣ ΕΑΥΤΩΙ ΠΡΟΣΗΚΟΥΣΑΝ ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ, ΚΑΙ Η ΟΥΣΙΑ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ]

units.la: Si quis peregrinam tanquam sibi proximam elocarit Athe-nienfi ciui, ignominiofus esto, ciusque bona publicantor: ΕΣΤΩ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΕΛΟΝΤΟΣ ΤΟ ΤΡΙ-ΤΟΝ ΜΕΡΟΣ, ΓΡΑΦΕΣΤΩ ΔΕ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ, ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙ ΚΑΘΑΠΕΡ ΤΗΣ ΞΕΝΙΑΣ.
