units.la: ΑΦΘΑ ΕΝ ΑΦΘΟΙΣ ΕΧΟΝΤΑ, certum est εἰς τὴν γυναῖκα ἐξαμάρ-τάνειν, is tamen non ἐξαμαρτάνει εἰς τοὺς παῖδας, quod praecipue est animadvertendum: Nam proprie adulterium dicitur, propter partum ex altero concep-tum composito nomine: Lege VI. D. eod. Respondet tamen Sopater ὅτι τῆς αὐτῆς ἐπιχειρεῖσθαι cum moecho, nam μὴ ἐν ἀλλοφέρει πρὸς ὅ ἐὰν τὸν μοιχὸν, εἰτε δίωκος γενέσθαι, εἴτε μὴ. τὸ γὰρ παραλαμβάνειν ἀνεπίζηλον δεῖ. Non semper tamen occisi sunt adulteri in ipsa turpitudine deprehensi: sed id pro mariti arbitrio, vt iam diximus: vnde Eratosthenes in adulterio deprehen-sus, ὡπεὶ ὀλέ-ει καὶ ἰκέτεύε μὴ αὐτὸν κτεῖναι, ἀλλ' ἀργύριον παραξασθαι. Frequen-tissima haec & visitatissima poena fuit. Deprehensos in adulterio moechos quadrupedes constituebant, & eis nates depilabant cinere calido, deinde etiam raphanos praegrandes in podicem immittebant: hanc poenam vocabant ῥαφανιδωσιν καὶ ῥαφανίδωσις. Sed pauperiorum fuit: diuites enim pecunia redimebant. Aristophanes Pluto dicebat ipsi Pluto,
units.tr: [ΑΦΘΑ ΕΝ ΑΦΘΟΙΣ ΕΧΟΝΤΑ], it is certain that he sins against the wife [εἰς τὴν γυναῖκα ἐξαμαρτάνειν]; yet he does not sin against the children, which is especially to be noted. For properly it is called adultery on account of the offspring conceived from another, a compound name: see Digest 6, same title. Sopater nevertheless replies that [the wife is to be dealt with] in the same way as the adulterer, for it is not right to ... [μὴ ἐν ἀλλοφέρει πρὸς ὅ ἐὰν τὸν μοιχὸν, εἰτε δίωκος γενέσθαι, εἴτε μὴ. τὸ γὰρ παραλαμβάνειν ἀνεπίζηλον δεῖ.] Not always, however, were adulterers killed when caught in the very act; this was left to the husband's discretion, as we have already said. Hence Eratosthenes, caught in adultery, wept and begged that he not be killed, but offered money [ὡπεὶ ὀλέει καὶ ἰκέτευε μὴ αὐτὸν κτεῖναι, ἀλλ' ἀργύριον παραξασθαι]. This was a very frequent and common punishment. Adulterers caught in the act they made stand like quadrupeds, and they depilated their buttocks with hot ash, then also thrust very large radishes into the anus. This punishment they called raphanidosis [ῥαφανιδωσιν] and raphanidosis [ῥαφανίδωσις]. But it was for the poorer sort; the rich redeemed themselves with money. Aristophanes in his Plutus makes Pluto himself say:

units.la: ὁ δ' ἀλσεὶς γὰ μοιχὸς ὅσ' οἱ που ῥαφανιδώσει.
units.tr: [ὁ δ' ἀλσεὶς γὰ μοιχὸς ὅσ' οἱ που ῥαφανιδώσει.] The adulterer who is caught, they say, is radished.

units.la: Scholia: ἐπὶ ὡς τὸν ἀλσεὶα μοιχείας ῥαφανιδώσαι, ἵνα δὴς ἀργύριον ποιῆς λυσῇ. ῥαφανιδώσει γὰρ, ἀφαιρεῖται τοῖς τείχας τῆς ἀνεψκτῆς πλήθη. αὐτὴ γὰρ ἕκαστος δίκη πᾶς μοιχῆς πίνησι, ἀποφαρίδωσις καὶ ῥαφάλυσις. οἱ δὲ πλήσιοι χρήματα πρέμεν ἀπελύοντο. ῥαφανιδώσει ἐὰν φησὶ ὅ μὴ διώκασθαι χρήματα λυσθῆναι τῶν πυξίδ. ἡμισεία δὲ τῶν ἐπαχθος. Et alibi idem Interpres ad Nubes: ὥσπερ γὰρ τοὺς ἀλσεῖας μοιχοὺς ἡκίζοντο, ῥαφανίδας λαμβάνοντες καὶ ἐπίπεδον εἰς τοὺς ἀπογρήσεις ἐὺς κῦπος. καὶ ῥαφανιδώσοντες αὐτοὺς, τύφειν θερμῷ ἀπίπαστον βασάνοις ἐχθρας ἐργαζόμενοι. Aliquando etiam vicem raphanorum mugiles per posticum impingebantur. Catullus:
units.tr: Scholia: "On the adulterer caught, to be radished, so that he might redeem himself with money. For he is stripped of ... the many ... For each case of adultery was called apodeixis and rhaphalysis; the rich paid money to be released, and the ... was taken from the wallets, half the ..." And elsewhere the same commentator on the Clouds: "For just as they treated adulterers, taking radishes and placing them ... they radished them, roasting them in hot ash, with the ... working out a grievous punishment." Sometimes also mullets were thrust in through the back passage instead of radishes. [Full Greek scholia in the original: ἐπὶ ὡς τὸν ἀλσεῖα μοιχείας ῥαφανιδώσαι, ἵνα δὴς ἀργύριον ποιῆς λυσῇ. ῥαφανιδώσει γὰρ, ἀφαιρεῖται τοῖς τείχας τῆς ἀνεψκτῆς πλήθη. αὐτὴ γὰρ ἕκαστος δίκη πᾶς μοιχῆς πίνησι, ἀποφαρίδωσις καὶ ῥαφάλυσις. οἱ δὲ πλήσιοι χρήματα πρέμεν ἀπελύοντο. ῥαφανιδώσει ἐὰν φησὶ ὅ μὴ διώκασθαι χρήματα λυσθῆναι τῶν πυξίδ. ἡμισεία δὲ τῶν ἐπαχθος. ὥσπερ γὰρ τοὺς ἀλσεῖας μοιχοὺς ἡκίζοντο, ῥαφανίδας λαμβάνοντες καὶ ἐπίπεδον εἰς τοὺς ἀπογρήσεις ἐὺς κῦπος. καὶ ῥαφανιδώσοντες αὐτοὺς, τύφειν θερμῷ ἀπίπαστον βασάνοις ἐχθρας ἐργαζόμενοι.]

units.la: Quem attractis pedibus, patente porta, Percurrent raphani, mugilesque.
units.tr: Whom, their feet dragged, with the door open, the radishes and mullets will run through. (Catullus)

units.la: Iuuenalis Satyra X.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire X.

units.la: Necat hic ferro, secat ille cruentisVerberibus, quosdam moechos & mugilis intrat.
units.tr: Here one kills with the sword, another cuts with bloody blows, and a mullet enters some adulterers.

units.la: Abdomen aliquando adimebant, & testes caudamque salacem demetebant ferro. Quod si de deprehenso in vxore visum esset ad Magistratum iudicium & quaestionem referre, scribebatur dica apud Thesmothetas. Pollux Libro VIII. cap. IX. γίγνονται δὲ πρὸς τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας γράφαι μοιχίας: Poe-na autem, an è iudicum sententia mors eris? nequaquam: Lysiae enim ista ἐν τῇ ἐχ Ἀρεοπάγου γυναῖκας εἶπεν τῆς πολιτῶν θεοῦς ὡς μοιχεύοντα καὶ ἀλφαβίτην ἐλευθέρας ἐπιχείρησιν, καὶ ἐλήφθη μοιχὸς· καὶ τοῦτο θανάτου ἡ ζημία ἔστιν. Intelligenda sunt de iure illius, qui deprehensum in vxore adulterum poterat occidere.
units.tr: Sometimes they also removed the belly, and cut off the testicles and the lustful tail with iron. But if, when a man had been caught with his wife, the matter was to be referred to the magistrate and a court of inquiry, the charge of adultery was lodged before the Thesmothetae. Pollux, Book VIII, ch. IX: [γίγνονται δὲ πρὸς τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας γράφαι μοιχίας]. But was the penalty death, by the sentence of the judges? By no means: for Lysias, in the speech against Eratosthenes [ἐν τῇ ἐχ Ἀρεοπάγου], says that he caught the adulterer with his wife, and that the adulterer was caught, and that this penalty is death [καὶ ἐλήφθη μοιχὸς· καὶ τοῦτο θανάτου ἡ ζημία ἔστιν]. These things are to be understood of the right of the man who could kill the adulterer caught with his wife.

units.la: Verum habitus in priuata custodia apud illum, qui μοιχὸς accusabat, si in ius rapiebatur, & falso μοιχὸς esset infimulatus, siue noxa dimittebatur: conuictus vero, ab eo, qui in vxore eum deprehenderat, pro arbitrio iudicum, si mortem excipias, plectebatur: Qua de re Lex haec extat:
units.tr: But the one held in private custody by the man who accused him of adultery, if he was dragged into court and was falsely charged with adultery, was released unharmed. If he was convicted, however, by the man who had caught him with his wife, he was punished at the judges' discretion, except for death. On this matter there is the following law:

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΔΙΚΟΣ ΕΙΡΞΗ, ΩΣ ΜΟΙΧΟΝ ΓΡΑΦΕΣΘΑΙ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕ-ΤΑΣ ΑΔΙΚΟΣ ΕΙΡΧΘΗΝΑΙ, ΚΑΙΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΛΗ, ΤΟΝ ΕΙΡΞΑΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΔΟΞΗ, Α-ΔΙΚΟΣ ΕΠΙΒΕΒΟΥΛΕΥΣΘΑΙ, ΑΘΩΝ[?] ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΓΓΥΗΤΑΣ ΑΓΗΛΑΧΘΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΕΓΓΥΗΣ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΔΟΞΗ, ΜΟΙΧΟΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΡΑΔΟΥΝΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΓΓΥΗΤΑΣ ΤΩ ΕΛΟΝ-ΤΙ. ΕΠΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΥ ΑΝΕΥ ΕΓΧΕΙΡΙΔΙΟΥ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ Ο, ΤΙ ΑΝ ΒΟΥ-ΛΗΘΗ, ΩΣ ΜΟΙΧΩ, ΟΝΤΙ.
units.tr: [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΔΙΚΟΣ ΕΙΡΞΗ, ΩΣ ΜΟΙΧΟΝ ΓΡΑΦΕΣΘΑΙ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ ΑΔΙΚΟΣ ΕΙΡΧΘΗΝΑΙ, ΚΑΙΝ ΜΕΝ ΕΛΗ, ΤΟΝ ΕΙΡΞΑΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΔΟΞΗ, ΑΔΙΚΟΣ ΕΠΙΒΕΒΟΥΛΕΥΣΘΑΙ, ΑΘΩΝ[?] ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΓΓΥΗΤΑΣ ΑΓΗΛΑΧΘΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΕΓΓΥΗΣ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΔΟΞΗ, ΜΟΙΧΟΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΡΑΔΟΥΝΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΓΓΥΗΤΑΣ ΤΩ ΕΛΟΝΤΙ. ΕΠΙ ΔΕ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΚΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΥ ΑΝΕΥ ΕΓΧΕΙΡΙΔΙΟΥ ΧΡΗΣΘΑΙ Ο, ΤΙ ΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΗΘΗ, ΩΣ ΜΟΙΧΩ, ΟΝΤΙ.] If anyone, being an unjust person, is accused before the Thesmothetae as an adulterer, and is held in custody unjustly, let him ... and if the accuser is found to ... his sureties are to be released from their bond. If, however, he is judged to be an adulterer, the sureties are to hand him over to the Eleven [ΕΝΔΕΚΑ]. In the court, without a ... let whatever be decided be done to him, as to an adulterer.

units.la: Si quis tanquam adulter in custodia habeatur, libellum supplicem Thesmothetis of-fero, quod iniuste in custodia habeatur. Si apud Ju-dices probauerit iniuste vinctum fuisse, innoxius dimittitur, & vades eius spö-fione liberantor: Si vero adulterij damnatus fuerit, vades dato ei, qui in vxore deprehenderit, iudices, excepta capitis poena, pro arbitrio in eum animaduertunto.
units.tr: If anyone is held in custody as an adulterer, I present a petition to the Thesmothetae that he is unjustly held in custody. If he proves before the judges that he was unjustly imprisoned, he is dismissed unharmed, and his sureties are freed from their bond. But if he is condemned for adultery, let the sureties hand him over to the one who caught him with his wife, and let the judges, apart from the penalty of death, punish him as they see fit.

units.la: Legitur hæc Lex apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ κατὰ Νεαίρας. Vades autem dabatur conuictus adulterij apud Thesmotheras, vt caueretur ei qui deprehenderat illum in turpitudine, multam, quam irrogaturi erant iudices, solutum iri: Iudices enim morte non multabant, nam si is, qui in rebus ipsis Venereis adulterum deprehenderat, adulterum, ira aduersus eum sumpta, in continenti non occidit, quod Lege tamen illi concedebatur, Iudices æquum non est eundem morti addicere. Atque hæc constituta sunt in illos, qui non vi, sed illecebris, pudicitiam feminarum expugnassent: Iudicabat enim sapientissime Legislator, eos vxorum erga maritos amicitiæ corruptores esse: Quare illis grauior pœna irrogabatur, quam Raptoribus: His enim multa tantum pecuniaria irrogatur ex hac Lege:
units.tr: This law is read in Demosthenes, in the speech Against Neaera. A surety was given by a man convicted of adultery before the Thesmothetae, so that the one who had caught him in the act would be secure that the fine the judges were to impose would be paid. For the judges did not punish with death; if the man who had caught the adulterer in the very act did not kill him at once, in anger, though the law allowed this, it was not right for the judges to condemn him to death. These penalties were laid down against those who had corrupted the chastity of women not by violence but by enticements. For the most wise lawgiver judged that such men were corrupters of the affection of wives for their husbands. Therefore a heavier penalty was imposed on them than on rapists; for under this law only a pecuniary fine is imposed on these men:

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΑΙΣΧΥΝΗ ΒΙΑΙ ΔΙ-ΓΛΟΥΝ ΤΗΝ ΒΛΑΒΗΝ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΙΝ.
units.tr: If anyone dishonours a woman by force, he shall owe double the damage [ἐὰν τις γυναῖκα αἰσχύνῃ βίᾳ, διπλοῦν τὴν βλάβην ὀφείλειν].

units.la: Si quis per vim vitium feminæ intuleris, duplo multator.
units.tr: If anyone has forcibly violated a woman, he shall be fined double.

units.la: Lex extat apud Lysiam ἐν τῇ Ἐπιταφίου φόνῳ ἀπολογίᾳ, ratio-nemque addit ὅπως, ὦ ἄνδρες, τοὺς βιαζομένους ἐλάττονος ζημίας ἀξίους ἡγήσατο εἶναι τοὺς πείθοντας. [illegible, ~60 letters] Licebat igitur marito eum, quem in vxore illecebris expugnata deprehenderat, occidere in continenti: non vero eum, qui vi compressisset: sed duplo multabatur: cum Legislatore pária facit Xenophon in Hierone: [illegible, ~120 letters] [illegible, ~90 letters] [illegible, ~70 letters]
units.tr: The law is found in Lysias, in his speech for the defence against the murder of Epitaphius, where he also gives the reason: gentlemen, he thought that those who persuade deserve a greater penalty than those who use force. [illegible in the scan] It was therefore lawful for a husband to kill on the spot the man he caught with his wife after she had been seduced, but not the man who had forced her; the latter was fined double. Xenophon in his Hiero likewise agrees with the lawgiver. [illegible in the scan] [illegible in the scan] [illegible in the scan]

units.la: Quod ad adulteram, ciusque maritum attinet, non licebat post illa marito τὸ γυναικὸν adulterae, sin minus ab ea sibi temperaret, notabatur infamia: neque poterat adultera illa ingredi fana, quae publicis sumptibus & impensis instruebantur, alioqui poenas dabat impune cuiuis ex hac Lege:
units.tr: As for the adulteress and her husband: after this, the husband was not allowed to [illegible in the scan] the adulteress, and unless he refrained from her he was branded with infamy. Nor could the adulteress enter those shrines that were furnished at public expense; otherwise, under this law, anyone could punish her with impunity.

units.la: ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΔΕ ΕΛΟΙ ΤΟΝ ΜΟΙΧΟΝ ΜΗ ΕΞΕCΤΩ ΤΩΙ ΕΛΟΝΤΙ CΥΝΟΙΚΕΙΝ ΤΗΙ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΙ· ΕΑΝ ΔΕ CΥΝΟΙΚΗΙ, ΑΤΙΜΟC ΕCΤΩ, ΜΗΔΕ ΤΗΙ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΙ ΕΞΕCΤΩ ΕΙCΙΕΝΑΙ ΕΙC ΤΑ ΙΕΡΑ ΤΑ ΔΗΜΟΤΕΛΗ, ΕΦ' ΗΙ ΑΝ ΜΟΙΧΟC ΑΛΩ- ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΕΙCΙΗΙ ΝΗΠΟΙΝΕΙ ΓΑCΧΕΤΩ Ο,ΤΙ ΑΝ ΠΑCΧΗΙ, ΓΑΗΝ ΘΑΝΑΙΟΥ.
units.tr: [When the adulterer is caught, it shall not be permitted to the one who caught him to live with the wife; if he does live with her, let him be infamous. Nor let the wife be permitted to enter the public sacred places in which an adulterer was caught; if she enters, let anyone who wishes punish her with impunity, short of death.]

units.la: Postquam adulterum maritus adulterij damnauerit, ab vxore adultera diuortito: nisi diuorterit, ignominiosus esto: Adultera templa publica ingredi fas non esto: si ingressa fuerit, impune poenas cuiuis dato, morte excepta.
units.tr: After the husband has condemned the adulterer for adultery, let him divorce the adulteress wife; if he does not divorce her, let him be infamous. The adulteress shall not be allowed to enter public temples; if she has entered, let anyone who wishes exact penalties from her with impunity, except death.

units.la: Lex extat apud Demosthenem ὡς τοῦ κατὰ Νεαίρας. Multo inferior est, ex hac Lege, adulterarum fors illa seruorum & peregrinorum, qui etsi ius ciuitatis non habeant, possunt tamen in illa ἱερὰ δημοτελῆ, εἰς ἃ ὑμεῖς ἐδωκαν ἡ πόλις, ingredi, quod adulteris non licebat: poenas autem, si huic Legi non parerent, & Templa ista δημοτελῆ intrarent, dabant impune cuiuis, & id ita explicat ipse Demosthenes: καὶ ἐδωκεν ὁ νόμος τοῖς ἐχθροῖς αὐτῆς τὴν ἐπιτιμίαν [?]. Neque enim vllum praesidium in Deorum aris & Templis, aut in mariti domo & benevolentia habebant: pellebantur enim & ex aedibus mariti, & è Deorum Templis: ἅμα ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας τῆς αἰσχρᾶς ἐκβαλλομένη ἔξω ἡ γυνὴ, ἐφ' ἣ ἂν μοιχὸς ἀλῷ, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἱερῶν τῆς πόλεως. Huius Legis meminit quoque Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμάρχου. Sed & alteram nobis repraesentat, qua cauebatur, ne qua femina, in qua adulter deprehensus fuisset, ornata prodiret in publicum, si secus fecisset, licebat cuiuis feminae illius stolam & vestes discindere, mundum auferre, eamque pulsare, modo ne occideretur, aut aliquo membro caperetur.
units.tr: The law is found in Demosthenes, in the speech Against Neaera. Under this law the lot of the adulteresses is far worse, the lot of those slaves and foreigners who, although they lack the rights of citizens, may nevertheless enter those public sacred places to which the city has admitted them, which adulteresses were not allowed to do. If they did not obey this law and entered those public temples, anyone could punish them with impunity. Demosthenes himself explains this: "the law gave to her enemies the penalty [?]". Indeed, they had no protection either at the altars and temples of the gods, or in the husband's house and goodwill; for they were driven out both from the husband's house and from the gods' temples: "at the same time the woman is thrown out of the shameful house in which an adulterer was caught, and out of the sacred places of the city." Aeschines also mentions this law in his speech Against Timarchus. But he also presents to us another law, by which it was provided that no woman in whom an adulterer had been caught should come out in public adorned; if she did otherwise, anyone who met her was permitted to tear her clothes and garments, take away her finery, and beat her, provided he did not kill her or maim her in any limb.

units.la: Τῷ γυναῖκα, ἐφ' ἧι ἂν ἁλῷ μοιχὸς, μὴ ἐξεῖναι κοσμεῖσθαι· ἐὰν δ' ἡ κοσμοῦντα, τὴν ἐπιτυχόντα καταρρηγνῦσθαι τὰ ἱμάτια, καὶ τὸν κόσμον ἀφαιρεῖσθαι, καὶ τύπτειν, εἰρηνευμένον θανάτου, καὶ τὰς αἰσχύνης πάσσας. [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: [A woman in whom an adulterer has been caught shall not be permitted to adorn herself; if she does adorn herself, let anyone who meets her tear her garments and take away her ornaments, and beat her, short of death, and inflict every kind of disgrace.]

units.la: Adultera in publicum ornata ne prodito: si secus faxit, quiuis eius vestes discindito: eiusque mundum auferto, atque eam pulsato, si libuerit, dummodo ne occidat, aut membro aliquo captam reddat.
units.tr: The adulteress shall not go out in public adorned; if she does otherwise, let anyone tear her garments, take her finery away, and beat her, if he pleases, provided he does not kill her or leave her maimed in any limb.

units.la: Solonis Lex ista est, vt habes apud Æschinem loco laudato: ὁ δὲ Σόλων ὁ νομοθέτης ἐκέλευσε τὸν μοιχὸν ἐξεῖναι [illegible, ~60 letters] ἐν τοῖς δημοτελέσιν [illegible, ~40 letters] καὶ τὸν βίον ἀξίωσεν αὐτῇ ἀποκόπτειν [illegible, ~10 letters]. At contra, honestas feminas inornatius in publicum prodeuntes mille multabant drachmis ex hac Philippidis Lege: Χιλίας ζημιοῦσθαι τὰς ἐκ τὰς ὁδοὺς ἀκοσμοῦ- σας γυναῖκας.
units.tr: This is Solon's law, as you have it in Aeschines in the passage cited: Solon the lawgiver ordered that the adulterer [illegible in the scan] in public places [illegible in the scan], and he thought it fitting to [illegible in the scan] her life. On the other hand, under the law of Philippides, honourable women who went out in public without proper adornment were fined a thousand drachmas: "women who behave immodestly in the streets are fined a thousand."

units.la: Legis auctorem Philippidem facit Crobylus Comicus, eiusque meminit Hyperides apud Harpocrationem: ὅτι χιλίας ἐζημίωσεν τὰς ἐξ ὁδοὺς ἀκοσμοῦσας γυναῖκας, Υ ταὐτὸς δὲ καὶ τῷ Αεισταγόρα δεύτερον εἴρηκεν. Κρώβυλος δὲ ὁ Κωμικὸς φησὶ τὸν Φιλιππίδην τὸν νόμον εἰς τὰς τούτων κείμενον. Titulum Orationis h'us[?] Hyperides emendat Vir Clar. Meursius, & reponit feminæ nomen, Ἀεισταγόρας, quod verissimum puto. Multæ, quæ feminis infligebantur ob indecorum, apud platanum, quæ in Ceramico erat, scriptæ exponebantur. Hesychius: πλάτανος, δίνδρον, ὥσπερ ὁ οἱ Γυναικονόμοι ταῖς ζημίας ἐν λθυχώμασι ἐξεπίσ-σθμ, Pollux Libro VIII. cap. IX. Γυναικονόμοι δὲ ἄρχοι, ὅτι τὸ χόσμα τῶν γυναικῶν. Ταῖς δὲ ἀκοσμούσας ἐζημίωσαν, καὶ ταῖς ζημίας αὐτῶν χρέφοντες, ἐξεπίσθαι ὅτι τῆς πλατάνου τῆς ἐν Κεραμικῷ. Atque huic curæ, ut Lex religiose observaretur, præficiebantur Γυναικονόμοι, sive Γυναικοσόμοι, ut est apud Hesychium & Pollucem: Erant autem hi Γυναικονόμοι de maritatis. Eustathius ad Iliad. K. οἱ Νομοθέται Γυναικονόμους ἐν τῆς πόλεσι ὠεισάν, ὁ ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, ἀλλ' ἤδη γάμου πεπιεσμένους, ἵνα οἷς αὐτοὶ ἔχοιεν συμπαθοῦντες, ἐπιμελῶνται καὶ τὴν ὑπηρεσιῶν αὐτῶν. Verum horum Gynæconomorum institutum in Republica non probat maximus Doctor Politic. Libro IV. cap. XV. est enim Aristocraticum: verba illius sunt: Γυναικονόμος δὲ καὶ εἷς ὁ ἄρχων Ἀρχῶν ὠ εὐός ὅστι Θιαυτὸς ἐπιμελείας, ἀριστοκρατικόν. Δημοκρατικὸν δ' ὁ ὅ πῶς γὰρ ὀξ' π χωλύων ἐξιέναι ταῖς τῶν ἀνδρῶν; ἀλλ' ὀλιγαρχικόν· τεῦφοσι γὰρ ἀ ἡ ὀλιγαρχῶντων.
units.tr: Crobylus the comic poet makes Philippides the author of this law, and Hyperides mentions it in Harpocration: that he fined a thousand women who behaved immodestly in the streets; the same Hyperides also mentions it again in the speech Against Aristogora. Crobylus the comic poet says that Philippides laid down the law regarding these women. The learned Meursius emends the title of Hyperides' speech and restores the woman's name, Aristagora, which I think is most certainly right. The fines imposed on women for indecorum were written on whitened boards and displayed at the plane tree that stood in the Ceramicus. Hesychius: "plane tree, a tree, where the gynaeconomi displayed the penalties of the women's fines on whitened boards." Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: "The gynaikonomoi are magistrates, because they oversee the adornment of women. They fined the women who behaved immodestly, and, writing their fines on whitened boards, displayed them at the plane tree in the Ceramicus." It was to this office, that the law might be religiously observed, that the gynaikonomoi, or gynaikosmoi, as in Hesychius and Pollux, were set over the matter; these gynaikonomoi were chosen from among married men. Eustathius on Iliad K: "The lawgivers appointed gynaikonomoi in the cities, men not in office but already married, so that, sympathising with the women from their own experience, they might attend to their needs." But the greatest teacher of politics, in Book IV, chapter XV, does not approve of this institution of gynaikonomoi in a state. For it is aristocratic; his words are: "The gynaikonomos is also one magistrate, and it is aristocratic. But to prevent women from going out as they please is not democratic; it is oligarchic, for in oligarchies the women live in luxury."

units.la: Ante Philippidem Lege cauerat Solon, ne qua foras proficiscens femina, tres amplius stolas haberet, neque plus cibi aut potus secum efferret, quam obolo emtum: neque calathum cubitali maiorem: Quod si de nocte iter facere necesse esset, curru vehi ad lucernam iussit.
units.tr: Before Philippides' law, Solon had provided that no woman going out should have more than three garments, nor carry with her food or drink worth more than an obol, nor a basket larger than a cubit. If she had to travel at night, he ordered that she be carried in a cart with a lamp.

units.la: Τὼν γυναικας ἐξιέναι ἱματίων τεσσάρων μὴ πλέον ἔχουσαν, μηδὲ βρωτὸν ἢ ποτὸν πλέονος ἢ ἐβολοῦ φερομένην, μηδὲ χρυσίον πηχυαῖον μείζονα · μηδὲ νύκτωρ πορεύεσθαι πλὴν ἁμαξῇ κομιζομένην, λύχνου παρεφαίνοντος.
units.tr: [That a woman going out should not have more than four garments, nor carry food or drink worth more than an obol, nor a golden ornament larger than a cubit; nor travel at night except carried in a cart, with a lamp shining before her.]

units.la: Femina foras proficiscens tribus stolis plures ne habeto. neque plus cibi aut potus, quam obolo emtum secum efferto; neque calathum cubitali maiorem: De nocte iter ne facito, nisi curru vecta ad lucernam.
units.tr: A woman going out shall have no more than three garments; she shall not carry with her food or drink worth more than an obol, nor a basket larger than a cubit. She shall not travel at night unless carried in a cart with a lamp.

units.la: Legem laudat Plutarchus in Solone: ἐπίσημον δὲ καὶ τὰς ἐξόδους τῶν γυναικῶν νόμον, ἀπαγόρευσεν καὶ ἀπλῶς ἐξιέναι μὴ ἱματίων τεσσάρων μὴ πλέον ἔχουσαν καλύμματος, μηδὲ βρωτὸν ἢ ποτὸν πλείονος ἢ ἐβολοῦ φερομένην, μηδὲ χρυσίον πηχυαῖον μείζονα · μηδὲ νύκτωρ πορεύεσθαι πλὴν ἁμάξῃ κομιζομένην, λύχνου παρεφαίνοντος.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his Solon, also cites the law: he also notably forbade women's outings, so that no woman might go out having more than four garments or a veil, nor carry food or drink worth more than an obol, nor a golden ornament larger than a cubit, nor travel at night except carried in a cart with a lamp shining before her.

units.la: DE PUERORUM AMORIBUS, & productione, & scortis.
units.tr: On Love of Boys, Procuring, and Prostitutes.

units.la: TITULUS V.
units.tr: TITLE V.

units.la: CUm liberale esse censeret Solo παιδεραστῶν · καλὸν γὰρ ἡ φιλία καὶ ἀ-τίμων, noluit id licere servis, eaque de re Legem hanc dixit, & sanxit:
units.tr: Since Solon considered love of boys (παιδεραστία) a liberal thing, for affection is noble even toward the dishonoured [καλὸν γὰρ ἡ φιλία καὶ ἀτίμων], he did not wish it to be permitted to slaves, and on this matter he enacted and sanctioned this law:

units.la: ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΥ ΠΑΙΔΟΣ ΜΗ ΕΡΑΝ, ΜΗΤ' ΕΠΑΚΟΛΟΥΘΕΙΝ, Ή ΤΥΠΤΕΣΘΑΙ ΤΗι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑι ΜΑΣΤΙΓΙ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΓΛΗΓΑΣ.
units.tr: A slave shall not love a free boy, nor pursue him, or else he shall receive fifty blows of the public whip [ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΥ ΠΑΙΔΟΣ ΜΗ ΕΡΑΝ, ΜΗΤ' ΕΠΑΚΟΛΟΥΘΕΙΝ, Ή ΤΥΠΤΕΣΘΑΙ ΤΗι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑι ΜΑΣΤΙΓΙ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΓΛΗΓΑΣ].

units.la: Servus ingenuum puerum ne amato, neve affectator: qui secus faxit, publice quinquaginta plagarū ictus illi infliguntor.
units.tr: A slave shall not love a free boy, nor be his suitor: whoever acts otherwise shall have fifty blows of the lash inflicted on him publicly.

units.la: Legem hanc ἀὐτῆς ὀνόμασα laudat Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμάρχου. πάλιν ὁ αὐτὸς ἐν εἶπεν νομοθέτης · ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΥ ΠΑΙΔΟΣ ΜΗ ΕΡΑΝ ΜΗΤ' ΕΠΑΚΟΛΟΥΘΕΙΝ, Ή ΤΥΠΤΕΣΘΑΙ ΤΗι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑι ΜΑΣ-ΤΙΓΙ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΓΛΗΓΑΣ.
units.tr: Aeschines quotes this law, calling it by its own name, in his speech against Timarchus. The same lawgiver again says: "A slave shall not love a free boy, nor pursue him, or else he shall receive fifty blows of the public whip" [ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΥ ΠΑΙΔΟΣ ΜΗ ΕΡΑΝ, ΜΗΤ' ΕΠΑΚΟΛΟΥΘΕΙΝ, Ή ΤΥΠΤΕΣΘΑΙ ΤΗι ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑι ΜΑΣΤΙΓΙ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΓΛΗΓΑΣ].

units.la: Legis meminit Plutarchus in Solone: καὶ νόμων ἔγραψε ἀδούλου μὴ παιδεραστῶν. Idem in Ἐρωτικῷ, ὡς καὶ Σόλων κατέβαλε, δούλοις κὰν ἐφ' ὑμέων παίδων ἀπιστε. Quod autem servis denegarat Solo, concessisse liberis atque ingenuis hominibus concludit Æschines loco laudato: εἰ πατέρες υἱῶν ὅσ' ἀπαγορεύει [?] τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἡμῶν ἐπὶ πρὸς ἀ[?], τοὺς δούλους ἀπειπεῖν μὴ ποιεῖν. Non intelligitur autem foeda illa & præpostera in mares libido. Dii certe ne sirint, ut tam inexpiabile ἀγος sanctissimo viro Soloni affingamus unquam, ἡ γὰρ σωφροσύνης, inquit loco proxime laudato Plutarchus, ἐπὶ ὁ ἔρως, καταλαμβάνει τὴν γυναῖκα. & sancta illa ἔρωτος Lex, de qua jam dicemus, plane contrarium arguit: sed amor hic honestus, & qui ad virtutem forma-ret.
units.tr: Plutarch mentions this law in his Life of Solon, where he says that Solon also wrote a law that no slave should be a lover of boys. In his Erotikos, Plutarch says that Solon likewise forbade slaves even to look at free boys. Aeschines, in the passage cited, concludes that what Solon denied to slaves he allowed to free-born men: "if fathers ... forbid our freedom ... (he ordered) the slaves to refrain from doing so" [εἰ πατέρες υἱῶν ὅσ' ἀπαγορεύει [?] τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἡμῶν ἐπὶ πρὸς ἀ[?], τοὺς δούλους ἀπειπεῖν μὴ ποιεῖν]. Yet that foul and perverse lust toward males is not what is meant here. God forbid that we should ever impute such an inexpiable offence to the most holy man Solon. For, as Plutarch says in the passage cited just before, it is love that takes hold of a woman in the case of chastity. And that holy law of love, which we shall discuss shortly, clearly argues the contrary: this love was honourable, and such as shaped a man toward virtue.

units.la: Lege namque actio dabatur adversus eum, qui puerum prostituerit; sive is pater, sive frater, sive patruus, sive tutor, sive quis tandem cumque alius fuerit, cuius fidei creditus & commissus sit puer: dat quoque adversus eum, qui conduxerit: neque tamen dat adversus puerum, qui prostitutus & conductus fuerit, cui gratiam facit, ubi adoleverit, patrem, qui eum prostituerit, alendi, aut in ædes admittendi: defunctum tamen sepelire iubet, ceteraque iusta facere, & illi parentare, ut moris erat:
units.tr: For by this law an action was granted against anyone who prostituted a boy, whether he was father, brother, uncle, guardian, or whoever else it was into whose trust and care the boy had been entrusted. It also lay against the one who hired him. However, it did not lie against the boy who had been prostituted and hired out, to whom the law grants a favour: when he has grown up, he need not support his father who prostituted him, nor admit him into his house. Nevertheless, the law orders the son to bury him when he is dead, to perform the other due rites, and to make offerings to him, as was customary.

units.la: Ἐάν τινα ἐκμισθῶσι ἑταῖρον πατήρ, . Si quis alium prostituerit, sive pater is sit
units.tr: "If a father has let out a boy for hire..." [Ἐάν τινα ἐκμισθῶσι ἑταῖρον πατήρ]. If anyone prostitutes another, whether that person is the father

units.la: ἢ ἀδελφὸς, ἢ θεῖος, ἢ ἐπίτροπος, ἢ ὅλως τῶν κυρίων τῆς κατ' αὐτὸ μὲν τὸ παιδὸς γραφὴν ἐπαρήσεως [?] ἐὰν, καὶ ὁ τῆς μισθώσεως τοῦ μισθωμένου τὸ μέν, ὅτι ἐξεμίσθωσε, τῷ δ', ὅτι ἐμισθώσατο. καὶ ἴσα τὰ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἑκατέρῳ ἐπιβαλλόμενα· καὶ μὴ ἐπιφυλάξῃς εἰς τὸν παῖδα ἡ ἐλευθερίας τὸ πρότερον ἡ πατρὶ ἐπέγγον, μηδὲ οἰκεῖον πρέσβειν, ὅς ἂν ἐκμισθώσῃ ἐπαρξῶν. ἀποθανόντα δ' ἡ ἰαπλεῖτω, καὶ ἄλλα ποιείτω τὰ νομιζόμενα.
units.tr: or brother, or uncle, or guardian, or in general any of those who have authority over the boy in the case of a prosecution for the boy's own hire: and the one who hired the one hired out, the one for the fact that he let him out, the other for the fact that he hired him; and the penalties imposed on each shall be equal. Let the boy not be bound by any former freedom or obligation to his father, nor let the kinsman who let him out be spared. When he is dead, let him be buried, and let the customary rites be performed [ἢ ἀδελφὸς, ἢ θεῖος, ἢ ἐπίτροπος, ἢ ὅλως τῶν κυρίων τῆς κατ' αὐτὸ μὲν τὸ παιδὸς γραφὴν ἐπαρήσεως [?] ἐὰν, καὶ ὁ τῆς μισθώσεως τοῦ μισθωμένου τὸ μέν, ὅτι ἐξεμίσθωσε, τῷ δ', ὅτι ἐμισθώσατο. καὶ ἴσα τὰ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἑκατέρῳ ἐπιβαλλόμενα· καὶ μὴ ἐπιφυλάξῃς εἰς τὸν παῖδα ἡ ἐλευθερίας τὸ πρότερον ἡ πατρὶ ἐπέγγον, μηδὲ οἰκεῖον πρέσβειν, ὅς ἂν ἐκμισθώσῃ ἐπαρξῶν. ἀποθανόντα δ' ἡ ἰαπλεῖτω, καὶ ἄλλα ποιείτω τὰ νομιζόμενα].

units.la: Legem laudat Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμάρχου. ᾿Αφορρήσθω γὰρ λέγει ὁ νόμος. Εἰ ἵνα ἐκμισθώσῃ ἐπαρξὴν πατρὶ, ἡ ἀδελφὸς, ἡ θεῖος, ἡ ἐπίτροπος, ἡ ὅλως τῶν κυρίων τῆς κατ' αὐτὸ μὲν τὸ παιδὸς γραφὴν ἐπαρήσεως [?], τῷ δ' τῆς μισθώσεως, καὶ τὸ μισθωσαμένου τὸ μέν, ὅτι ἐξεμίσθωσε, τῷ δ', (φησὶν) ὅτι ἐμισθώσατο. καὶ ἴσα τὰ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἑκατέρῳ ἐπιπεπίνηκε· καὶ μὴ ἐπιφυλάξῃς εἰς τὸν παῖδα ἡ ἰδίᾳ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα, μηδὲ οἰκεῖον πρέσβειν, ὅς ἂν ἐκμισθώσῃ ἐπαρξὴν. ἀποθανόντα δ' ἡ ἰαπλεῖτω, καὶ ἄλλα ποιείτω τὰ νομιζόμενα. Poena, vt plurimùm, mors erat constituta: vnde Æschines hac ipsa Oratione: ἡ γὰρ εἰμὴ ἔγωγε ὑμᾶς ὅπως ἐπιλήσομαι ᾿Αθηναίων, ὥστε ἀμνημονῆσαι, ὀλίγῳ πρὸς ἐπὶ τῷ νόμῳ ἐπ' εἴ τις ἐγκα[?]τὰ, ἐὰν τις μισθώσηται τινα ᾿Αθηναίων ὅτι τοῦτον τὸν ἀγῶνα, ἡ ἐὰν ἡ ἀπὸ αὐτοῦ μισθώσῃ, ἕνεκον εἴ τὸ μεγίστης καὶ τὰς ἰσοτιμίας ὑπιμίους. & paullo post: παρελθὼν ἕκατέρα ζημίας, ἐκ τὸ νόμου, ἁπλῶς θανάτου· ὥσπερ εἰ δ' εἰ τις μισθώσηται τινα ᾿Αθηναίων ἐφ' ὕβρει, καὶ πάλιν, ἐαν τις ᾿Αθηναῖων ἐπὶ τῇ τοῦ σώματος αἰσχύνῃ ἐκὼν μισθαρίῃ. Quanquam ἡμιπὸ ἐὶ τὸν ἀγῶνα, id elt, ἐφ' ᾧ ὃ τίμημα ὠσιμένως ἐκ τὴν νόμων ἐκ ἔστιν, ἀλλὰ τὰς δικαστὰς ἐσθ' ὑμᾶσθαι ὃ. τι χ' παθεῖν, ἡ ὑποπτάσῃ, facile mihi persuadeo è comparatione actionis ὕβρεως, qui etiam erat ἡμητὸς ἀγών.
units.tr: Aeschines quotes this law in his speech against Timarchus: "Let it be forbidden," the law says, "if anyone lets out a boy for hire, whether father, brother, uncle, guardian, or in general any of those who have authority over the boy in the case of a prosecution..., the one for the fact that he let him out, the other (he says) for the fact that he hired him; and the penalties imposed on each shall be equal. Let the boy not be bound to his father by any former obligation, nor let the kinsman who let him out be spared. When he is dead, let him be buried, and let the customary rites be performed." The penalty, for the most part, was fixed at death. Hence Aeschines, in this same speech: "For I, Athenians, would not wish to make you forget the law: if anyone hires out an Athenian for this purpose, or if an Athenian hires himself out for this purpose, let the penalty be death..." And a little after: "...the penalty is set down in the law, simply death; just as if anyone hires out an Athenian for outrage, and again if any Athenian willingly lets himself out for the shame of his body." Although the case in question, namely the one in which the penalty is not fixed in the laws but left to the judges to decide what he should suffer or pay, I readily persuade myself, from comparison with the action for insult, which was also a public trial.

units.la: Præterea liquet ex hac ipsa Lege: Nam filio, qui adoleuerit, gratiam facit patrem μισθώσαντα exhibendi: Ergo mortem patris μισθώσαντος Lex non sanciuit: Sapienter autem istud institutum est, ne filius patrem μισθώσαι[?]τα exhibere cogeretur. Nam parenti, qui filio ius ciuitatis hac sua μισθώσει ademerit, denegat filiorum officia & pietatem, nisi defuncto: iam enim in manes sæuire non vult. Æschines: σκέψασθε δὴ ὡς καλὰς, ὦ ᾿Αθηναῖοι, ζῶντος μὲν αὐτῶν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι τὸν ὠνητὴν τῆς παιδοποιίας, ὥσπερ ἐκφυσὸς τὸ παιδὸς τὸν πρῆσιν. πλουτίσαντα δὲ αὐτὸν, ἰώτα ὁ μὲν ἐφεστὼς ἔπι ἀρτίσαι μὴ ὧν δ' πάσῃ, ἡμᾶς ἂν ὁ νόμος ἡ ὃ ἡμᾶς, ἐθαλὴν ἤδη κελεύει, καὶ ἄλλα ποιῶν τὰ νομιζόμενα.
units.tr: Moreover, it is clear from this very law: for to the son who has grown up it grants the favour of not having to supply the father who let him out. Therefore the law did not sanction death for the father who hired him out. This institution was made wisely, so that a son would not be compelled to support a father who had let him out. For to a parent who by such letting out has taken from a son his right of citizenship, it denies the duties and piety of a son, unless the parent is dead; for it does not wish to rage against the dead. Aeschines: "Consider, Athenians, how fine it is that while the buyer is alive he takes away from the father the begetting of children, as though ... But when he has grown rich ... the law orders the son to bury him when he is dead, and to do the other customary things" [σκέψασθε δὴ ὡς καλὰς, ὦ ᾿Αθηναῖοι, ζῶντος μὲν αὐτῶν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι τὸν ὠνητὴν τῆς παιδοποιίας, ὥσπερ ἐκφυσὸς τὸ παιδὸς τὸν πρῆσιν. πλουτίσαντα δὲ αὐτὸν, ἰώτα ὁ μὲν ἐφεστὼς ἔπι ἀρτίσαι μὴ ὧν δ' πάσῃ, ἡμᾶς ἂν ὁ νόμος ἡ ὃ ἡμᾶς, ἐθαλὴν ἤδη κελεύει, καὶ ἄλλα ποιῶν τὰ νομιζόμενα].

units.la: Aduersus puerum actio non datur, quia sui iuris nondum est, sed in patris potestate, vel sub aliorum cura & tutela.
units.tr: No action is brought against the boy, because he is not yet his own master, but is in his father's power or under the care and guardianship of others.

units.la: Lege quoque agebatur aduersus alios quoscumque productores ingenuorum atque liberorum puerorum, aut feminarum:
units.tr: By the law an action was also brought against any other procurers of freeborn boys, or of free women, or of girls:

units.la: ἘΑΝ ΤΙΣ ἙΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΝ ΠΑΙΔΑ Ἡ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΠΡΟΑΓΩΓΕΥΣΗ, τὸν παιδαγωγὸν γεγραφέναι, καὶ ἀλλ', θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι.
units.tr: If anyone procures a free boy or a woman, let him be indicted, and otherwise punished with death [ἘΑΝ ΤΙΣ ἙΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΝ ΠΑΙΔΑ Ἡ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΠΡΟΑΓΩΓΕΥΣΗ, τὸν παιδαγωγὸν γεγραφέναι, καὶ ἀλλ', θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι].

units.la: Si quis liberum atque ingenuum puerum, aut feminam produxerit, dica ei scribitor: conuictus morte multator.
units.tr: If anyone has procured a free-born boy or a woman, let an indictment be written against him. If he is convicted, let him be punished with death.

units.la: Legem laudat Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμάρχου. Καὶ ἵνα ἔτιμεν νόμον ἔθηκε φυλάξαι τὰ τῶν ὑμετέρων παίδων, τὸν τῆς παιδαγωγίας· τὰ μέγιστα ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐπηγγέλλας,
units.tr: Aeschines cites the law in his speech Against Timarchus: "And so that he might make a law to guard the children of you Athenians, the law on the paidagogia (the procuring of boys), you promised the greatest things on our behalf" [Καὶ ἵνα ἔτιμεν νόμον ἔθηκε φυλάξαι τὰ τῶν ὑμετέρων παίδων, τὸν τῆς παιδαγωγίας· τὰ μέγιστα ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐπηγγέλλας].

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΝ ΠΑΙΔΑ Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΠΡΟΑΓΩΓΕΥΣΗ.
units.tr: If anyone procures a free boy or a woman.

units.la: Primo Solô productores viginti drachmis multauerat. Plutarchus in Solone. Καὶ τὴς προαγωγῆ ζημίας εἴκοσι δραχμὰς ἔπραξε. Id postea mutauit, & capite sanctum elt in lenones & productores ingenuorum. Ælchines eadem Oratione, qui id Soloni adscribit: καὶ τοὺς προαγωγοὺς γεάφεσθαι κλοπῆς καὶ ἀλλά-σι, ἰκατα τῷ ξημιοῦ.
units.tr: First, Solon fined procurers twenty drachmas. Plutarch, in the Life of Solon: "and for procuring he exacted a penalty of twenty drachmas" [Καὶ τὴς προαγωγῆ ζημίας εἴκοσι δραχμὰς ἔπραξε]. Later this was changed, and it was made a capital offence for pimps and procurers of free-born persons. Aeschines, in the same speech, who ascribes this to Solon, says that procurers are indicted for theft and [...] and punished by fine [καὶ τοὺς προαγωγοὺς γεγράφεσθαι κλοπῆς καὶ ἀλλά-σι, ἰκατα τῷ ξημιοῦ].

units.la: Qui flagitium commiserat in mulierem, aut liberos, aut seruos, postula-batur ὕβρεως, apud Thesmothetas: Thesmothetæ sortiebantur iudices ex Heliastis, intra triginta à scripta dica dies, nisi res prolatæ sint, & intercedat Rɛipublicæ commodum, vel cum primum poterunt: Heliastarum erat sententiam ferre in reum, quem si primis sententiis damnassent, secundis pœnæ addicebant siue capitis, siue pecuniariæ: si morti addixissent, Vndecimviris capitalibus eo ipso pœnas dabat die: si multa pecuniaria fuisset irrogata: intra vndecim dies expungere multæ debitum iubebatur, interea in vinculis habebatur. Quod si feminæ, aut puerorum, aut seruorum κύριοι, id est, hi, in quorum potestate sunt ὑπεύθυνοι, vel institutam actionem mitteret, vel quintam suffragiorum partem non ferret, mille drachmas ærario pendebat: qua de re hæc Lex legitur:
units.tr: Whoever had committed an outrage against a woman, or free children, or slaves, was prosecuted for hybris (ὕβρεως) before the Thesmothetae. The Thesmothetae drew up the jury from the Heliastae, within thirty days from the written indictment, unless the matter was postponed and the public good intervened, or as soon as they could. It was the duty of the Heliastae to pass sentence on the accused. If they condemned him by the first votes, they then assigned the penalty, whether capital or pecuniary, by the second votes. If they had adjudged him to death, he was punished by the Eleven, the capital magistrates, on that very day. If a fine had been imposed, he was ordered to pay the debt within eleven days, and in the meantime was kept in chains. But if the kyrioi of women, boys or slaves, that is, those in whose power they are (hypeuthynoi), either failed to bring the action that had been instituted, or did not secure a fifth of the votes, they paid a thousand drachmas into the treasury. Concerning this matter the following law is read:

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΥΒΡΙΖΗ ΤΙΝΑ Η ΠΑΙΔΑ; Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ, Η ΑΝΔΡΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕ-ΡΩΝ, Η ΤΩΝ ΔΟΥΛΩΝ, Η ΠΑΡΑΝΟ-ΜΟΝ ΤΙ ΠΟΙΗΣΗ· ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΤΙΝΑ ΓΡΑΦΕΣΘΩ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕ-ΤΑΣ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. ΟΙ ΔΕ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΕΙΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΑΙΑΝ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΗΜΕΡΩΝ, ΑΦ' ΗΣ ΑΝ ΓΡΑ-ΦΗ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΤΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ ΚΩΛΥΗ. ΕΙ ΔΕ ΜΗ, ΟΤΑΝ Η ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΟΙΟΝ ΤΕ ΟΤΟΥ Δ' ΑΝ ΚΑΤΑΓΝΩΣΘΗ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ ΤΙΜΑΤΩ ΠΕΡΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΠΑ-ΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ, ΟΤΟΥ ΑΝ ΔΟΞΗ ΑΞΙΟΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΘΕΙΝ Η ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΙ. ἐὰν δὲ ἀλάπου ἀμυνῇ τῆς ὕβρεως, ΠΑΡΑΔΟΘΕΙΣ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ ΤΕΘΝΑΤΩ ΑΥΘΗΜΕΡΟΝ, Ο-ΣΟΙ Δ' ΑΝ ΓΡΑΦΩΝΤΑΙ ΓΡΑΦΑΣ Ι-ΔΙΑΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ. ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΜΗ ΕΓΕΞΕΛΘΗ Η ΕΓΕΞΙΩΝ ΜΗ ΜΕ-ΤΑΛΑΒΗ, ΤΟ ΠΕΜΠΤΟΝ ΜΕΡΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΤΗΦΩΝ ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΤΩ ΧΙΛΙΑΣ ΔΡΑΧ-ΜΑΣ [ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΡΓΥ-ΡΙΟΥ ΤΙΜΗΘΗ, ΤΗΣ ΥΒΡΕΩΣ ΑΠΟΤΙ-ΣΑΤΩ ΕΝ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ ΗΜΕΡΑΙΣ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΗΝ ΔΙΚΗΝ. ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΓΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ ΔΥΝΗΤΑΙ ΑΠΟΤΙΝΕΙΝ, ΔΕΔΕΣΘΩ [?]ἢ
units.tr: [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΥΒΡΙΖΗ ΤΙΝΑ Η ΠΑΙΔΑ; Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ, Η ΑΝΔΡΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΩΝ, Η ΤΩΝ ΔΟΥΛΩΝ, Η ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΟΝ ΤΙ ΠΟΙΗΣΗ· ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΤΙΝΑ ΓΡΑΦΕΣΘΩ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. ΟΙ ΔΕ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΕΙΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΑΙΑΝ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΗΜΕΡΩΝ, ΑΦ' ΗΣ ΑΝ ΓΡΑΦΗ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΤΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ ΚΩΛΥΗ. ΕΙ ΔΕ ΜΗ, ΟΤΑΝ Η ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΟΙΟΝ ΤΕ ΟΤΟΥ Δ' ΑΝ ΚΑΤΑΓΝΩΣΘΗ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ ΤΙΜΑΤΩ ΠΕΡΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ, ΟΤΟΥ ΑΝ ΔΟΞΗ ΑΞΙΟΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΘΕΙΝ Η ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΙ. ἐὰν δὲ ἀλάπου ἀμυνῇ τῆς ὕβρεως, ΠΑΡΑΔΟΘΕΙΣ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ ΤΕΘΝΑΤΩ ΑΥΘΗΜΕΡΟΝ, ΟΣΟΙ Δ' ΑΝ ΓΡΑΦΩΝΤΑΙ ΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΙΔΙΑΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ. ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΜΗ ΕΓΕΞΕΛΘΗ Η ΕΓΕΞΙΩΝ ΜΗ ΜΕΤΑΛΑΒΗ, ΤΟ ΠΕΜΠΤΟΝ ΜΕΡΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΤΗΦΩΝ ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΤΩ ΧΙΛΙΑΣ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ [ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΥ ΤΙΜΗΘΗ, ΤΗΣ ΥΒΡΕΩΣ ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΤΩ ΕΝ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ ΗΜΕΡΑΙΣ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΗΝ ΔΙΚΗΝ. ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΠΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ ΔΥΝΗΤΑΙ ΑΠΟΤΙΝΕΙΝ, ΔΕΔΕΣΘΩ [?]ἢ] — the law of hybris, as printed: if anyone commits hybris against a boy, a woman, a man of the free or of the slaves, or does something contrary to law, let any Athenian who wishes indict him before the Thesmothetae, to whom it belongs. The Thesmothetae shall bring the case into the Heliaea within thirty days from the indictment, unless some public matter hinders. If not, then as soon as possible, the Heliaea shall assess the penalty on him, whether a fine or death, whichever seems right. If he is condemned to death, he is handed over to the Eleven and dies that same day. Those who indict are to do so on their own indictments under the law. If anyone does not go out to the Heliaea, or does not get a fifth of the votes, he is to pay a thousand drachmas, a fifth of his property, to the public treasury. If he is fined in money, let him be bound until he pays it, if he has committed hybris against a free man.

units.la: Si quis puerum, aut feminam, aut hominem, siue ingenuum, siue seruam, corruperit, aut opprobrium contra Leges fecerit, dicam ei Atheniensium quinis, cui fas est, scribito: Thesmothetae iudices ex Heliastis sortiuntor intra dies à scripta dica triginta: aut, si iniustitium Res indicant publicae, vbi primum licebit: Heliastae primis sententiis damnatum poenae addicunto in continenti, quam meritus est, siue in corpore, siue in aere: mortis sententiam passus eo ipso die ab vndecimviris capitalibus animaduertitor. Si is, qui dicam scripsit, in sua habeat potestate seruum siue liberum hominem corruptum, & vel actionem instituram mittat, vel quintam suffragiorum partem non ferat, mille drachmas aerario pendito: Cui pecuniaria multa est irrogata, is multam intra undecim dies soluito, &
units.tr: If anyone corrupts a boy, or a woman, or a man, whether free or a slave, or commits an outrage against the law, let an indictment be brought against him by any Athenian who is entitled to do so. The Thesmothetae shall draw the judges from the Heliastae within thirty days of the written indictment, unless the public business forbids it, or as soon as it will be permitted. The Heliastae, if they condemn him in the first votes, shall at once assign him the penalty he deserves, whether bodily or pecuniary. If he is sentenced to death, he shall be punished by the Eleven, the capital magistrates, on that very day. If the man who wrote the indictment has in his power the corrupted slave or free man, and either fails to bring the action or does not secure a fifth of the votes, let him pay a thousand drachmas to the treasury. He on whom a pecuniary fine has been imposed shall pay the fine within eleven days, and

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΝ ΥΒΡΙΣΗ, ΜΕΧΡΙΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΤΙΣΗ.
units.tr: If anyone commits hybris against a free person, until he makes restitution.

units.la: Legem hanc partim è Demosthene descripsimus, partim ex Æschine supplevimus: & Demosthenis quidem ista sunt in Midiana : ἀναγνῶθι δ' αὐτὸν μὲν λέγων τὸν τῆς ὕβρεως νόμον. ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΥΒΡΙΖΗ, ΤΙΝΑ Η ΠΑΙΔΑ, Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ, Η ΑΝΔΡΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΩΝ, Η ΤΩΝ ΔΟΥΛΩΝ, Η ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΟΝ ΤΙ ΠΟΙΗΣΗ, ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ, ΤΙΝΑ ΓΡΑΦΕΣΘΩ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. ΟΙ ΔΕ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΕΙΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΑΙΑΝ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΗΜΕΡΩΝ, ΑΦ' ΗΣ ΑΝ ΓΡΑΦΗ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΤΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ ΚΩΛΥΗ. ΕΙ ΔΕ ΜΗ, ΟΤΑΝ Η ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΟΙΟΝ ΤΕ ΟΤΟΥ Δ' ΑΝ ΚΑΤΑΓΝΩΣΘΗ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ ΤΙΜΑΤΩ ΠΕΡΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ, ΟΤΟΥ ΑΝ ΔΟΞΗ ΑΞΙΟΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΘΕΙΝ Η ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΙ. ΟΣΟΙ Δ' ΑΝ ΓΡΑΦΩΝΤΑΙ ΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΙΔΙΑΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ. ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΜΗ ΕΓΕΞΕΛΘΗ, Η ΕΠΕΞΙΩΝ ΜΗ ΜΕΤΑΛΑΒΗ ΤΟ ΠΕΜΠΤΟΝ ΜΕΡΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΤΗΦΩΝ ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΤΩ ΧΙΛΙΑΣ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΥ ΤΙΜΗΘΗ ΤΗΣ ΥΒΡΕΩΣ ΔΕΔΕΣΘΩ, ΕΑΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΝ ΥΒΡΙΣΗ, ΜΕΧΡΙΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΤΙΣΗ.
units.tr: We have taken this law partly from Demosthenes and supplemented it partly from Aeschines. Demosthenes' words in the Midian speech are these: "Read the law on insolence itself, which says: If anyone commits insolence against a boy, a woman, or a man, whether free or a slave, or does anything else contrary to law, then let whoever wishes to indict him write it down before the lawgivers, in whatever manner the Athenians have available [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΥΒΡΙΖΗ, ΤΙΝΑ Η ΠΑΙΔΑ, Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ, Η ΑΝΔΡΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΩΝ, Η ΤΩΝ ΔΟΥΛΩΝ, Η ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΟΝ ΤΙ ΠΟΙΗΣΗ, ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ, ΤΙΝΑ ΓΡΑΦΕΣΘΩ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ]. The lawgivers shall bring the case into the Heliaia within thirty days from the day on which it is written down, unless some public business prevents it [ΟΙ ΔΕ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΙ ΕΙΣΑΓΟΝΤΩΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΑΙΑΝ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΗΜΕΡΩΝ, ΑΦ' ΗΣ ΑΝ ΓΡΑΦΗ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΤΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΟΝ ΚΩΛΥΗ]. But if they do not, then whenever the Heliaia shall have condemned him, let it assess a penalty against him, whatever it thinks fit for him to suffer or to pay [ΕΙ ΔΕ ΜΗ, ΟΤΑΝ Η ΠΡΩΤΟΝ ΟΙΟΝ ΤΕ ΟΤΟΥ Δ' ΑΝ ΚΑΤΑΓΝΩΣΘΗ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ ΤΙΜΑΤΩ ΠΕΡΙ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ, ΟΤΟΥ ΑΝ ΔΟΞΗ ΑΞΙΟΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΑΘΕΙΝ Η ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΙ]. Whoever are written down shall be written down individually, according to the law [ΟΣΟΙ Δ' ΑΝ ΓΡΑΦΩΝΤΑΙ ΓΡΑΦΑΣ ΙΔΙΑΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΝ ΝΟΜΟΝ]. If anyone does not bring the prosecution through, or does not obtain a fifth part of the votes, let him pay a thousand drachmas to the public treasury [ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΜΗ ΕΓΕΞΕΛΘΗ, Η ΕΠΕΞΙΩΝ ΜΗ ΜΕΤΑΛΑΒΗ ΤΟ ΠΕΜΠΤΟΝ ΜΕΡΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΨΗΦΩΝ ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΤΩ ΧΙΛΙΑΣ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩΙ]. If a penalty of money is assessed for the insolence, and he is bound until he pays, then if he is free [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΡΓΥΡΙΟΥ ΤΙΜΗΘΗ ΤΗΣ ΥΒΡΕΩΣ ΔΕΔΕΣΘΩ, ΕΑΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΝ ΥΒΡΙΣΗ, ΜΕΧΡΙΣ ΑΝ ΕΚΤΙΣΗ]."

units.la: Æschines vero ita habet ὡς τοῦ [?] Τιμάρχου. Καὶ ποῖον ἄλλον; τὸν τῆς ὕβρεως, ὃς ἐπὶ κεφαλαίῳ πάντα τὰ ὕβρεως συλλέγων ἔχει· ὁ ὧ Δημοσθένης γέγραπται, ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΥΒΡΙΖΗ, εἰς ΠΑΙΔΑ (ὑβρίζῃ δὲ που ὁ μαθούμενος) Η ΑΝΔΡΑ, Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ, Η ΤΩΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΩΝ ΤΙΝΑ Η ΤΩΝ ΔΟΥΛΩΝ, Η ἐὰν ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΟΝ ΤΙ ποιῇ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΤΙΝΑ, γραφέσθω ὕβρεως [?] πεποίηκεν· ὁ ἡμέρα ἐπίδηκεν, ὅ, τὴ χρὴ παλὴν, ἡ ἀπόθισαι. λέγε τὸν νόμον. αὐ τῆς Ἀθηναίων ἐλευθέρου παῖδα ὑβρίσῃ, γραφέσθω ὁ κύριος τῆς παιδὸς πρὸς τοὺς θεσμοθέτας, τίμημα ἐπιζαλαβόμενος ὧ αὐ ὃ δικαστήριον κελ[illegible, ~6 letters]· ΠΑΡΑΔΟΘΕΙΣ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ ΤΕΘΝΑΤΩ ΑΥΘΗΜΕΡΟΝ. ἐὰν δὲ εἰς ἐγγύειον κελ[illegible, ~6 letters], ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΤΩ ΕΝ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ ΗΜΕΡΑΙΣ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΗΝ ΔΙΚΗΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΠΑΡΑΧΡΗΜΑ ΔΥΝΗΤΑΙ ΑΠΟΤΙΝΕΙΝ. ἕως δὲ τὴ ἀποτίσαι εἰρηται. [illegible, ~12 letters] ΟΙ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΟΙΚΙΚΑ ΣΩΜΑΤΑ ΕΞΑΜΒΡΤΑΝΤΩΝΤΕΣ. Non tantum corruptorem τῆς ὕβρεως apud Thesmothetas postulabat corrupti pater, vel frater, vel patruus, vel [illegible, ~5 letters], vel maritus, vel dominus, vno, vt absoluam verbo, ὁ κύριος, quod habet Æschines, γραφέσθω ὁ κύριος τῆς παιδὸς, sed etiam Atheniensium [?] quiuis: Lex ipsa docet, ΓΡΑΦΕΣΘΩ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΘΕΣΜΟΘΕΤΑΣ Ο ΒΟΥΛΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ ΟΙΣ ΕΞΕΣΤΙΝ. & scribit Demosthenes ad hanc Legem: ἀλλὰ γὰρ ὕβρεως ἐὰν τὶς μὴ γράφας ἔδωκεν ἀπόντι τῷ βουλομένῳ. Nam πᾶσα ὕβρεις, δημοσίου ἐστί, ἐ χοινὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ἴσκημα[?], inquit ibidem Vlpianus, καὶ ὁ βιαστὴς, δημοσίας δι-βολῆς[?], vt loquitur Demosthenes: & Isocrates ὁ πρὸς τὴν τῆ Λοχίτου[?]. ὁ δὲ τῆς ὕβρεως, ὡς κοινοῦ τῶ προγράμματος ὄντος, ἔξεστι τῆ βυλομένῳ τὴν πολιτὴν γρα-φὰν[?] πρὸς τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας, εἰσιέναι εἰς ὑμᾶς. Dica apud Thesmothetas scribebatur, vt in his habes, itemque apud Demosthenem ὁ πρὸ τοῦ πρὸς Γαστιμένην[?]. αἱ δὲ τῆς ὕβρεως δίκαι πρὸς τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας. Scribit Æschines de accusatore, τὴ-μῆμα ὑπηγραφάμενος ὁ αὐτὸς δικαστήριον κατα-ψηφιαῖ. E more litem æstimabat accusator, & multam irrogabat, quam non definiuit Legislator, quia æstimabat pro arbitrio accusator: Sed ista corrupta sunt, ὁ ἀλλὰ τὸ δικαστήριον κατα-ψηφι-αῖ. Varie emendant docti: Alij enim reponunt, ὃ αὐτὸ δικαστήριον, alij emendant, ὃ αὐτὸ δικαστήριον. Ego vero nullus dubito aliquid deesse: itaque è sequentibus rescribendum suspicor: γραφέσθω ὁ κύριος τῆ παιδὸς πρὸς τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας, τὴμημα ὑπηγραφάμενος[?], ἐπάνω αὐτὸ δικαστήριον κατα-ψηφιαῖ. ΠΑΡΑΔΟΘΕΙΣ ΤΟΙΣ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ ΤΕΘΝΑΤΩ ΑΥΘΗΜΕΡΟΝ. Atque ista referuntur ad iudices Heliastas, penes quos arbitrium est aut morti addicendi, aut multandi corruptores: est quippe ἡμῶν ἀγὼν, & illustre legitur exemplum apud Aristotelem in Rhetoricis Lib. I. cap. XIV. Σοφοκλῆς ὁ Εὐκτήμονος σὼν-γραφὰν, ἐπὶ ἀπίσοφαξεν ἑαυτὸν ὑβριστὴς, ὁ ἡμῶν ἐφ' ἐλάττονος, ἡ δ' ὁ παῖδων ἐπ-μπὴν ἑαυτὴν. Cur autem ἡμῶν fit ἀγὼν, ratio forte est, quia ὁ ὑβρίζων humanæ naturæ vitium est: Aristoteles in Problematis, Sectione XXIX. Ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν κλοπὴ, ἡ δὲ ἔνμια· ὅτι δὲ ὕβρει, μείζων ὤσπ ἀδικία, τιμὴ[?] τὴ ἐχὴ παιδὶ, ἡ ἀλλὰ ἐπῆσται ἡ δ' ἐπὶ ὁ ἄλλο ὑβρίζει, αἰσχρὸν ὅτι παθὼς, καὶ πολῖται σαλὸν ἡ ἐλάττον ἐπὶ μετέχουσι. Itaque aliquando factum, vt πολλοὶ κατασαύσας τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐξημιώσασι θανάτῳ, inquit Demosthenes, & scribit Lysias ὁ πρὸ τοῦ πρὸς αἰκίας πρὸς Ἰσχομάχου. τοὺς δὲ ὑβρίζει δῶρα εἴ, ἔξεστιν ὑμῖν θανάτῳ ζημιῶσαι. Erat, cum tantum multam illis facerent: atque multa ærario pendebatur, si accusator ἐξέσθ' ἐξ τῶν προγράμματος ὄντων, si vero esset ὁ κύριος, illi cedebat. Vlpianus ad Midianam: ἐπὶ λόγος αὐτὸς ὁ παῖδων κατηγορῆ τῆς ὕβρεως, αὐτὸς ἐλαμβάνει ὁ τιμὴμα. εἰ δὲ ἔτερος ὡς ὁ κατηγορήσας δημόσιον ἐγίγνετο τῆς καταδίκης. Hinc commo-de intelligenda sunt Demosthenis verba hac Oratione: δῆλον τῆς ὕβρεως αὐτὸς ὁ τίμημα ἐποίησεν ὅλων δημόσιον. & Pollucis Lib. VIII. cap. V. καὶ τῆς μὲν ὕβρεως ὁ τίμημα, οὐκ ὡ τῆ παθόντος, ἀλλὰ δημόσιον.
units.tr: Aeschines, however, has it thus, in his speech Against Timarchus: "And what other law? That of hybris, which gathers all the offences of hybris under one heading. Demosthenes has written it: 'If anyone commits hybris against a boy (and perhaps the one who is taught is the one who suffers hybris), a man, a woman, a free person, or a slave, or does something contrary to law against any of these, let him be indicted for hybris...'" He then gives the day and the penalty. "Read the law." And then: "If the free Athenian boy is subjected to hybris, let the guardian of the boy indict before the Thesmothetae, having proposed a penalty to the court..." "...handed over to the Eleven, let him die that same day. But if he is fined in money, let him pay within eleven days after the judgment, if he cannot pay..." Not only the father, brother, paternal uncle, [...], husband or master of the corrupted person could bring the indictment for hybris before the Thesmothetae; in short, the kyrios, as Aeschines has it ("let the guardian of the boy be indicted"), but any Athenian who wishes, as the law itself teaches: "Let an indictment be brought before the Thesmothetae by any Athenian who is entitled to do so." Demosthenes, on this law, writes: "But if anyone does not bring an indictment, it is open to anyone who wishes, in the absence of the prosecutor." For every hybris is a public matter, not a private one, as Ulpian says in the same place, and the violator is subject to public accusation, as Demosthenes puts it; and Isocrates... Hybris, as being a matter of public proclamation, may be brought by any citizen who wishes, by indictment before the Thesmothetae, to enter the court against you. The indictment for hybris was written before the Thesmothetae, as you have in these passages, and likewise in Demosthenes' speech... The suits for hybris are before the Thesmothetae. Aeschines writes of the accuser that, having proposed the penalty, he is the one who condemns the case before the court. By custom the accuser estimated the damages and proposed a fine, which the lawgiver did not define, because the accuser estimated it at his own discretion. But these words are corrupt, and learned men emend them variously: some restore one reading, others another. I, however, have no doubt that something is missing, and I suspect the text must be restored from what follows: "Let the guardian of the boy be indicted before the Thesmothetae, having proposed the penalty, and the court shall condemn him..." "Let him die that same day." These matters refer to the Heliastic judges, in whose power it lies either to condemn the corrupters to death or to fine them. The case is indeed a serious one, and there is a notable example in Aristotle's Rhetoric, Book I, chapter 14: Sophocles son of Euctemon, when indicted for hybris, [...] Why hybris is a serious contest is perhaps because the act of hybris is a vice of human nature. Aristotle, in the Problems, section 29: theft is one thing, but hybris is greater, since it is an injustice... Accordingly it sometimes happened that many, having scorned the law, were punished with death, as Demosthenes says, and Lysias writes in his speech against Ischomachus. For those who commit hybris, you may punish with death. Once they only imposed a fine on them, and money was paid into the treasury if the accuser was a public man; if he was the kyrios, the fine went to him. Ulpian, on the Midiana: "If the boy himself brings the accusation of hybris, he receives the penalty; but if another, who brought the accusation, the penalty became public." Hence the words of Demosthenes in this speech are rightly understood: "It is clear that the penalty for hybris made the whole matter public." And Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 5: "For the penalty for hybris goes not to the injured person but to the public treasury" [καὶ τῆς μὲν ὕβρεως ὁ τίμημα, οὐκ ὡ τῆ παθόντος, ἀλλὰ δημόσιον].

units.la: Apud Romanos Edicto Prætoris de filio, filiaue familias corrupti locus non est, sed utilis competit actio, officio iudicis æstimanda: quoniam interest nostra, animum liberorum nostrorum, inquit Paulus Lib. XIX. ad Edictum, non corrumpi Leg. XIII. §. 1. D. de seruo corrupto. Vide tamen exemplum Marcelli apud Plutarchum in eius vita: itemque Marij.
units.tr: Among the Romans, the praetor's edict concerning a corrupted son or daughter under power does not apply, but a useful action is granted, to be assessed by the judge's discretion, "since it is in our interest that the minds of our children are not corrupted," says Paulus in Book 19 on the Edict, Law 13, §1, D. de servo corrupto. Yet see the example of Marcellus in Plutarch's life of him, and likewise that of Marius.

units.la: Qui autem corpus prostituerant suum, eoque quæstum fecerant, maxima capitis minutione notabantur, id est, omnibus ciuitatis iuribus sacris paritet & profanis exciderant cum liberis, posterisque, quod si quis ἡ ἀλγμάτων pœnam hanc insuper haberet, capite luebat ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Those who had prostituted their bodies and made a profit from it were marked with the greatest loss of civic status. That is, they were excluded, together with their children and descendants, from all civic rights, both sacred and secular. If anyone incurred this penalty and, in addition, did what follows, he paid for it with his head under this law:

units.la: ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΤΑΙΡΗΣΗι, ΜΗ ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΑΥΤΩι ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡ-ΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΓΕΝΕΣΘΑΙ ΜΗΔ' ΙΕΡΩΣΥ-ΝΗΝ ΙΕΡΑΣΑΣΘΑΙ, ΜΗΔΕ ΣΥΝΔΙΚΗ-
units.tr: "If any Athenian keeps company with a courtesan, let him not be eligible to become one of the nine archons, nor hold a priesthood, nor act as advocate for the people [ἂν τις Ἀθηναῖος ἑταιρῇ, μὴ ἐξέστω αὐτῷ τῶν ἐννέα ἀρχόντων γενέσθαι, μηδ' ἱερωσύνην ἱερᾶσθαι, μηδὲ συνδικῆσαι]

units.la: ΣΑΙ ΤΩι ΔΗΜΩι, ΜΗΔΕ ΑΡΧΗΝ ΑΡΧΕΤΩ ΜΗΔΕΜΙΑΝ, ΜΗΤΕ ΕΝΔΗΜΟΝ, ΜΗΤΕ ΥΠΕΡΟΡΙΟΝ, ΜΗΤΕ ΚΛΗΡΩΤΗΝ, ΜΗΤΕ ΧΕΙΡΟΤΟΝΗΤΗΝ, ΜΗΔ' ΕΠΙ ΚΗΡΥΚΕΙΑΝ ΑΠΟΣΤΕΛΛΕΣΘΩ, ΜΗΔΕ ΓΝΩΜΗΝ ΛΕΓΕΤΩ, ΜΗΔ' ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΔΗΜΟΤΕΛΗ ΙΕΡΑ ΕΙΣΙΤΩ ΜΗΔ' ΕΝ ΤΑΙΣ ΚΟΙΝΑΙΣ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΗΦΟΡΙΑΙΣ ΣΤΕΦΑΝΟΥΣΘΩ, ΜΗΔ' ΕΝΤΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΤΗΣ ΑΓΟΡΑΣ ΓΕΡΙΡΡΑΝΤΗΡΙΩΝ ΠΟΡΕΥΕΣΘΩ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΠΟΙΗι ΚΑΤΑΓΝΩΣΘΕΝΤΟΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΤΑΙΡΕΙΝ ΘΑΝΑΤΩι ΖΗΜΙΟΥΣΘΩ.
units.tr: to the people, nor hold any office whatever, whether within the city or abroad, whether by lot or by election. Let him not be sent on any embassy as herald, nor give an opinion in the assembly, nor enter the public temples, nor wear a crown with the others at the common crownings in processions, nor walk within the boundaries of the marketplace's lustral basins. If anyone does these things, and has been convicted of keeping company with courtesans, let him be punished with death." [τῷ δήμῳ, μηδὲ ἀρχὴν ἄρχειν μηδεμίαν, μήτε ἔνδημον μήτε ὑπέρορον, μήτε κληρωτὴν μήτε χειροτονητήν, μηδ' ἐπὶ κηρυκείαν ἀποστελλέσθω, μηδὲ γνώμην λεγέτω, μηδ' εἰς τὰ δημόσια ἱερὰ εἰσιτω, μηδ' ἐν ταῖς κοιναῖς στεφανηφορίαις στεφανούσθω, μηδ' ἐντὸς τῶν τῆς ἀγορᾶς περιρραντηρίων πορευέσθω. ἐὰν δέ τις ταῦτα ποιῇ καταγνωσθέντος αὐτοῦ ἑταιρεῖν θανάτῳ ζημιούσθω]

units.la: creari fas non esto: Magistratum nullum siue intra, siue extra fines Attica gerito, vel sorte captus, vel suffragiis creatus: Praeco nullum in locum mittitor: sententiam ne dicito: in templa publica ne intrato: neque cum ceteris in pompis coronator: neque intra fori cancellos ingreditor: Si quis autem impudicitiae damnatus Legem hanc praeterhabuerit, capite luito.
units.tr: Let it not be lawful for him to be created; let him hold no magistracy, either within or outside the borders of Attica, whether chosen by lot or elected by votes; let no herald be sent in his place; let him not give a sentence; let him not enter the public temples; let him not be crowned with the others in processions; let him not enter within the barriers of the forum. If anyone who has been condemned for immorality disobeys this law, let him pay with his life.

units.la: Describit hanc Legem ἀπολέξει Æschines ἐν τῷ Τιμάρχου. Καὶ πῶς λέγει; αὐτὸς τῆς Ἀθηναίων (φησὶν) ἑταιρήσῃ, μὴ ἐξέστω αὐτῷ τῶν σύνεδρ(?) Ἀρχόντων ἡμέας. (ὅτι εἰμὶ στεφανηφόρος ἢ ἀρχή) μηδὲ ἱερωσύνῃ ἱερώσασθαι, ὃς ἂν δὲ καθαρῷ ἀφηλέγξῃ τῷ ὀνόματι. μηδὲ σιωνδικησάτω (φησὶ) ὦ δημοσίᾳ. μηδὲ ἀρξάτω ἀρχῇ μηδεμίαν μηδέποτε, μήτ' ἐνδημον, μήτε ἐπαρόεσον· μήτε κληρωτὸν, μήτε χειροτονητὸν. μηδὲ κηρυχευσάτω, μηδὲ τοὺς ἀρεσοδιόσπ(?)ρας κειμένας, μηδὲ συνοφαντεῖτω μισθώσεις· μηδὲ γνώμην εἰπάτω μηδέποτε, μήτε ἐν τῷ δήμῳ, μήτε ἐν τῇ βουλῇ. μηδ' ἀδυνάτως ἢ λέγειν Ἀθηναίων· ἐαν δ' ὅς ταῦτα ποιήσῃ, γραφὰς ἑταιρήσεως πεποίηκε, ἡ τὰ μέγιστα ἐπιτίμια ἐπιζήκει. λέγει αὐτὸς ἡ τὸν τὸν νόμον. ΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΤΑΙΡΗΣΗι, ΜΗ ΕΞΕΣΤΩ ΑΥΤΩι ΤΩΝ ΕΝΝΕΑ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΩΝ ΓΕΝΕΣΘΑΙ ΜΗΔ', &c. Legis meminit Anonymus in Argumento Orationis: ὠ ἡ αὐτῷ ἐπαρθεσθείας. νόμος γὰρ ὡ τὸ ἑταιρήσαι μὴ πολιτεύεσθαι. & in Argumento Androtianae: τείπης νόμος, τὸ ἑταιρήσαι μὴ πολιτεύεσθαι. Demosthenes in Androtiana. πολλαχόθεν μὲν οὖν δὴ τῆς εἰδοῖ τοῦτο, ἐχ ἠκισταὶ σ' ἐκ τούτου τῷ νόμῳ, μήτε λέγειν, μήτε γράφειν ἐξεῖναι τῆς ἑταιρήσεων. Rursum eadem Oratione: ἡ δ' ὃ σῶμα ἑταιρησάτω ἐχ ἐῶσιν οἱ νόμοι εἰς τὰ ἱερὰ εἰσιέναι, scilicet τὰ δημοτελῆ, quae verba repetit in Timocratea: Neque tam seuere in hos tantum, qui sui iam essent iuris est animaduersum, sed etiam in illos, qui patre prostituente passi essent, antequam in viros essent transcripti. Æschines ἐν ᾧ ἐν Τιμάρχου. σκέψασθε δὴ ὡς καλὸς, ὦ Ἀθηναῖοι, ζῶντος μὲν αὐτοῦ ἀφαιρεῖσθαι τὸ ὄνομα τῆς παιδοποιίας, ὥσπερ ἐχ ἕνος τῆς παιδὸς πλὴν πεπρῆσθαι.
units.tr: Aeschines describes this law in his speech Against Timarchus. And how does he put it? "If any Athenian is a prostitute, let it not be permitted to him to become one of the nine archons, nor to be consecrated to priesthood, nor to speak before the people, nor to hold any office ever, whether at home or abroad, whether by lot or by election; nor to act as herald, nor to propose a motion, either in the assembly or in the council..." Aeschines then gives the text of the law: "If any Athenian is a prostitute, let him not be permitted to become one of the nine archons," and so on. A mention of this law is made by the anonymous writer in the Argument to the speech, where it is said that the law forbids a prostitute to take part in public affairs; and in the Argument to Androtion's speech the same is said. Demosthenes, in Against Androtion, says: "In many ways this is clear from the law, which does not allow a prostitute either to speak or to propose motions." Again, in the same speech: "The laws do not permit a man who has prostituted his body to enter the sacred places," meaning the public festivals; he repeats these words in Against Timocrates. Nor is the penalty applied so severely only to those who were already their own masters, but also to those who had been prostituted by their fathers before they were enrolled among men. Aeschines in Against Timarchus: "Consider, men of Athens, how shameful it is that while he is still alive his name is taken from him, as if he had sold his son's body, as it were, for profit."

units.la: Narrat Nicanor Colophonius Lib. Κολοφωνιακῶν III. Solonem Veneris Παιδικοῦ extruxisse templum, & adolescentibus, alioquin ἀποτάξεις εἰς ὃ μὴ ἐπεσ-ῶσιν ἐκεῖνοι, ἐχὴ σὺν ὁ οἰκημάτ(?) γυναῖκα περιάμβωρ, vt haberent illi siue noxa vbi aeuum genialiter transigerent: Canit enim Lege Solo, neminem posse pro moecho prehendi in domo meretricia: nam prostibula haec impudica etiam seruorum patere debent iniuriae:
units.tr: Nicanor of Colophon, in Book 3 of his Colophonian Histories, relates that Solon built a temple to Venus, the Paidikos, and that he set up for young men, who otherwise could not have a place to spend their lives comfortably, a house with women bought for them, so that they might have a place where they could pass their time without harm. For Solon's law states that no one may be seized as an adulterer in a brothel; for these shameless prostitutes ought to be open even to the outrages of slaves.

units.la: Μὴ ὅτι ζωῆς ταύτης μοιχὸν λαβὼν, ἐπόσον δ' ἐπ' ἐργαστηρίου καθῶνται, ἢ οἱ τῇ ἀγορᾷ πωλοῦσι τὰ ἀποπαισμένως. ΟΣΑΙ ΔΕ ΓΕΦΑΣΜΕΝΩΣ ΓΩΛΟΥΝΤΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΟΙΚΗΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΒΛΑΒΗΣ ΤΗΝ ΔΩΥΛΗΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΙΝ.
units.tr: Not only if one catches an adulterer in such a house, but also among those who sit in workshops or openly sell things in the marketplace. "Those who openly sell themselves, and the household, and the slave-woman who is injured..." [ΟΣΑΙ ΔΕ ΓΕΦΑΣΜΕΝΩΣ ΓΩΛΟΥΝΤΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΟΙΚΗΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΒΛΑΒΗΣ ΤΗΝ ΔΩΥΛΗΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΙΝ.] Those who openly prostitute themselves are also liable to the outrages of slaves.

units.la: Ne quis pro moecho prehenditor in meretrice, quae vel in lupanari, vel publice prostat: Quae publice prostant, etiam seruorum iniuriae obnoxiae sunto.
units.tr: Let no one be seized as an adulterer in a prostitute who works either in a brothel or openly in public. Those who openly prostitute themselves are liable also to the outrages of slaves.

units.la: Legem hanc descripsimus partim è Demosthene ἐν τῷ κατὰ Νεαίρας, partim è Lysia ἐν τῷ κατὰ Θεομνήστου α. & Demosthenes quidem ista habet: νόμος οὐκ ἐᾷ [?]τῶν τοὺς μοιχοὺς λαβεῖν, [?]ὅπου ἂν αὐτὸς ἐπ' ἐργαστηρίου [?]καθῆσθαι, ἢ τῇ ἀγορᾷ πωλοῦσα τι ἀπο-πεφασμένως. Lysiæ ista sunt: ἐπιφωνήσαντες τὸν νόμον ὃ πάλαι τὸν ὅσαι (ita scribendum est cum ex ipso Legis sensu, tum è Plutarcho.) ΔΕ ΠΕΦΑΣΜΕ-ΝΩΣ ΩΛΟΥΝΤΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΟΙΚΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΒΛΑΒΗΣ ΤΗΝ ΔΟΥΛΗΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΙΝ. Plutarchus in Solone, postquam egit de multa irrogandā ei, qui ἀ̓ῤπάσ[?] ἐλευθέρων γυναῖκα καὶ βιάσῃ[?], scribit de iis, qui lenocinium faciunt: ἐαὶ τὶς ἐπαγαγὼν ξημίαν εἴκοσι δραχμὰς ἔπεξε, πλὴν ὅσαι πεφασμένως πωλοῦνται· λέγω δὲ τὰς ἑπαίρας. Ad hanc Legem alludit Terentius in palliata fabula Eunucho.
units.tr: We have taken this law partly from Demosthenes in Against Neaera and partly from Lysias in Against Theomnestus I. Demosthenes gives it thus: the law does not allow adulterers to be seized wherever a woman sits in a workshop or sells something in the market openly. Lysias gives it thus: "...having read out the law which long ago..." (so it must be read, both from the sense of the law itself and from Plutarch): "Those who are openly sold, and the household, and the slave-woman who is injured, are liable." Plutarch, in his Solon, after speaking of the fine to be imposed on one who abducts a free woman and commits violence, writes of those who run brothels: "If anyone brings a charge and exacts a fine of twenty drachmas, except from those who are openly sold, meaning the prostitutes." Terence alludes to this law in his comedy The Eunuch.

units.la: Quis homo pro moecho unquam vidit in domo meretricis
units.tr: "Who ever saw a man caught as an adulterer in a brothel?"

units.la: Prehendi quenquam.
units.tr: "Caught anyone?"

units.la: per lupanaria namque atque ancillulas libido permittitur, ut scribit noster Hieronymus in Epitaphio Fabiolæ. Meretrices enim erant plurimum, aut peregrinæ, aut seruæ: atque has, quas primum ἐπὶ οἰκημάτ[?] proftare iussit Solon, ære emit, ut est apud Nicandrum loco laudato. Quare in Comœdiis, in quibus Poetæ:
units.tr: For "through the brothels and maidservants lust is allowed," as our Jerome writes in his Epitaph of Fabiola. For there were very many prostitutes, either foreigners or slaves; and those whom Solon first ordered to ply their trade in brothels, he bought with money, as is found in Nicander, cited above. Hence in the comedies, in which the poets...

units.la: Omnes res gestas esse Athenis autumant, meretrices, quæ prostant, aut peregrinæ sunt, & Athenas aliunde venerunt, aut pecunia emptæ. Donatus ad hæc Terentii verba ex Andria,
units.tr: "They say that all deeds done at Athens are done by courtesans who either ply their trade openly, or are foreigners who have come to Athens from elsewhere, or have been bought for money." Donatus, on these words of Terence from The Andrian:

units.la: Quid hoc?
units.tr: "What is this?"

units.la: Adeon' est demens ex peregrina?
units.tr: "Is he so mad about a foreign woman?"

units.la: Mulieres peregrinæ inhonestæ ac meretrices habebantur. Quare Epænetus Andrius, qui cum Phanone se concubuisse fatetur, negat apud illam potuisse pro moecho prehendi, cum peregrina, non autem ciuis Stephani filia sit. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Νεαίρας. Καὶ ὁμολογῶ μὲν χρῆναι τῆς ἀὐθεντίας, ἢ μὲν τοι μοιχὸς ἔστι[?] ὅπε γὰρ Σπφάνου, qui ciuis esset, γυναῖκα αὐτῷ εἴη, ἀλλὰ Νεαίρας, quæ peregrina erat. De his Philemon Comicus Delphis:
units.tr: "Foreign women were regarded as dishonourable and as prostitutes." Hence Epaenetus of Andros, who confesses that he slept with Phanion, denies that he could have been seized as an adulterer with her, since she was a foreigner, not the daughter of Stephanus, a citizen. Demosthenes in Against Neaera: "I admit that it is necessary... she is an adulteress... for Stephanus, who was a citizen, had a wife, but Neaera, who was a foreigner..." On these matters Philemon the comic poet, in Delphis:

units.la: Καὶ μοι λέγεν τῆτ' ὅδὶ ἁρμοστὸν Σόλων, μεγίστῳ ὀρῶντι τῷ πόλιν νεωτέρων, τοὺς τ' ἔχοντας τῷ αἰσχύνην φύσιν, ἀμπτάμονας τ' εἰς ὃ μὴ τρέφοιτ[?]ο καλέ[?] σῶν λῷ, ἔφη τριάμβ[?] τὶ γυναῖκας τὰς τόπους χαίνας ἄπαντι καὶ κατεσκευασμένας. ἐξῶσι γυμναὶ μὴ ἐξαπατήσῃς παύσω' ἔχει, σὺ δ' ἐκ σταυρῶ τυ[?] ἔχων ἔχης πῶς ἢ φύσει ἔστιν αἰσχυμένη, εἰς ὁδὸν ἔλεος [?]; ἐπλην ἡ μὴ ἦλθεν ἀλλὰ πλησίον ἐκ ὄπως πολλοῖς· ἀλλ' ἀὐτοὺς ὡς βουλὴ συμφόρον βουλὴ ξύπιν, ἐξαλλῆς, οἰμωζει λέγ', ἀλλόπειά τἰ σοι.
units.tr: "And tell me this, Solon, you who fitted out the young men of the city for the greatest shame, and who set up flying-houses where they could not be fed... women with gaping places, all ready and fitted out, naked, you have let them in; do not deceive me... for it is a shame by nature... as it is, not far away, but in the neighbourhood; and they, as a council of the city, advise shouting out, and you should be ashamed."

units.la: In his multa habes de meretricum inspectione, precio, conductione, aliaque, quæ attingere partes nostræ non sunt, qui ἐκκαλυψάμενοι ista percurrimus: hoc tantum addemus, his verbis lucem dare, & hinc mutuam accipere ea, quæ leguntur apud Senecam Controuersiarum Lib. I. Controuersia II. Deducta es in lupanar, accepisti locum, precium constitutum est, titulus inscriptus est, & paullo post: Nuda in litore stetit ad fastidium emtoris, omnes partes corporis & inspectæ, & contrectatæ sunt. paullo infra: Meretrix vocatas, in communi loco stetisti, superpositus est cellæ tuæ titulus, venientes recepisti. paullo post: Nomen tuum pependit in fronte, pretia stupri accepisti, & manus, quæ Diis datura erat sacra, capturas tulit. Sed è diverticulo in viam. Nemo igitur poterat prehendi pro mœcho in meretricibus, quæ vel in lupanaribus, vel publice prostabant, ὅπου ἂν ἐν ἐρασμηλίου κεχωνται, in lupanaribus ὅπου οἰκήματος, vbi meretricum copia fiebat, quemadmodum de Alpasia Socratica refertur: ἡ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ πωλοῦσα ἢ ἐπιπεφασμένη. aut publice prostant: ita verborum horum sensum, de quo constat, expressissimus: non enim intelliguntur eæ, quæ aliquid in foro vendunt, quod solis erat concessum ciuibus: etsi non nescio quam liberæ harum rerum fuerint, velex paucis illis, quæ supersunt, fragmentis Aristophanei dramatis, cui titulum est σκλωας κεκλαγμένων, sed propudia illa, quæ copiam sui faciebant in celebribus maxime vrbis partibus. Sed de vocis πωλοῦσα siue πωλωνῶν interpretatione non conuenit inter veteres, quanquam omnes fateantur illas meretrices designari prostituti pudoris, quæ palam ἐξῶσι κοινῇ ἁπάσῃ ἡ καπηλεύσαμέναι ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ. Itaque Didymus apud Harpocrationem exponit, quæ palam corpore quæstum faciunt: Δίδυμος φησὶ αὐτὴ, πορνεύουσα φανερῶς πωλεῖν γὰρ ὃ πρέχει ἑαυτὴν εἰς βαλανεῖος, ὅθεν ἡ ὃ πορνεῖα, ἀπὸ δὲ εἰς ὡραίων. praeterea πῶλοι meretrices dicuntur. Hesychius: πῶλος, ἐπίσημα. πῶλις γὰρ αὐτὰς λέγει, ὡς Ἀφροδίτης πόλις. Lysias vero aliam adfert interpretationem, quae tamen in idem recidit: vult enim πωλοῦσαι nihil aliud significare, quam βαδίζειν, vt sensus sit, aut quæ palam eunt ad eos qui mercedem dant. Lysiæ verba sunt loco iam laudato. ἐπιφωνάγωμεν τοῦτ' ἐκ νόμου ὃ πλεῖστα τὸν. ΟΣΑΙ ΔΕ ΓΕΦΑΣΜΕΝΟΣ ΓΩΛΟΥΝΤΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΟΙΚΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΒΛΑΒΗΣ ΤΗΝ ΔΟΥΛΗΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΙΝ ἐπὶ τοῦτο. ὃ μὴ ΠΕΦΑΣΜΕΝΩΣ, ἐὰν φανερῶς. ΓΩΛΕΙΣΘΑΙ ᾗ βαδίζειν, ὃ ὁ ΟΙΚΗΣ, ἀ ἐπιπονῆς cum Lysia paria facit Plutarchus in Solone: πλῶ ΟΣΑΙ ΓΕΦΑΣΜΕΝΩΣ ΓΩΛΟΥΝΤΑΙ, λέγω δὲ τὰς ἐπὶ ἐχέρας αὖ πω γὰρ ἐμφανεῖς φοιτῶσι ταῖς οἰκίαις. atque huiusmodi prostibula debent vel serui etiam ipsis ad hanc patere iniuriam: neque enim ingenuæ videntur, neque pudicæ sunt. Solenne autem fuit bonis istis mercibus, vt prostarent, & quotidianos haberent concursus ad illustria ciuitatis loca, Ceramicum, Scirum, & τὴν ἀγορᾶν. de Ceramico iamdiu monuerunt alii: quod ad Scirum attinet, elegans est Demosthenis locus, sed corruptus, ἐν τῷ ὠπαλῖ φαίου, de Æschinis matre: ἡ ὡς ἡ μήτηρ σου τῆς μεμνημένης γάμοις ἐν τῷ κλισίῳ παρὰς τῷ Καλαμίτῃ Ηρωϊχωλιῶν, neque quidquam, qui laudant, iuuant Hesychius & Suidas, quin contra factum, vt alterum insuper mendum occuparet, ἡλισίῳ quippe legunt lapsu facili, αὐτῇ τῷ, κλισίῳ, quod est geminum. Hesychius: Καλαμίτης, Ηρως τῷ ἡλισίῳ πλήσιον. Suidas: Καλαμίτης, κύκλου ὄνομα· ἡ Δημοσθένης ἐν τῷ ἐπὶ τῆς φαίου. ἐν τῷ ἡλισίῳ τῷ παρὰς Καλαμίτῃ Ηρωϊ. Nos legendum coniicimus, ἐν τῷ κλισίῳ τῷ παρὰς τῷ Κυαμίτῃ Ηρωϊ. Intelligit Orator ὁ κλίσιον, vt puto, Lycomidarum, (familia erat Athenis Λυκομίδαι, ἥρως ἰδαγμῶν, inquit Hesychius.) cuius meminit Paufanias in Messeniacis. Hoc κλίσιον non puto longe abfuisse à templo Cereris Eleusiniæ, cuius sacris gens illa dedita; unde Orphei siue Onomacriti ὕμνος εἰς Δήμητρα Λυκομίδαυς ποιηθείς [?], inquit Pausanias: Quare etiam colloco iuxta ædiculam Κυαμίτου Ἥρωος [?], Cyamites hic Heros erat, non Bacchus, & à Baccho distinguit Pausanias Atticis: scribitque fuisse hanc ædiculam ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ Σκίρᾳ [?], quod erat inter urbem & Eleusinem. Atqui ἐν τῇ Σκίρᾳ [?], ut legitur apud Stephanum, αἱ πόρναι ἐκαλοῦντο [?]. Præterea inter lenonias personas recensetur Λυκομίδης [?] à Polluce Lib. IV. cap. XIX. quia scilicet ad hoc τῶν Λυκομιδῶν κλίσιον [?] prostabant hæ publicæ libidinis victimæ: etsi forte vox κλίσιον [?] retinenda, quam Hesychius interpretatur πανδοκεῖον [?], & Eustathius ad Iliad. A. Δουλικὸν [?] ἐπιτηδὲς οἴκημα [?]. ita enim Apollonius ἐν τῇ εἰς Αἰγίλιν ἐξηγήσει μυθέως [?] ὁ ὧ ὁ Αἰγίνης Γλαυκιάδας, ἢ ὡς ἔνιοι, Γλαυκίδης, ὦ φασι τὸν ἐφεστῶτα ἡλικίας ἢ παρθενικὰς [?], καὶ ἐξομολογεῖσθαι ἐν οἰκήματι τὰς τοῦ Καλαμίτου Ἥρωα [?]. Sed hic quoque legendum est, ὡς τὰς τοῦ Κυαμίτου Ἥρωα [?]. Concursus quoque habebant suos ad τὸ ἀγορὰν [?], vetus, inquam, illud forum, quod est ἰόντων Ἀθηναίων εἰς τὴν Ἀκρόπολιν ἀπὸ τῆς θεάτρου [?], ut notat Pausanias in Atticis: Nam Pandemi Veneris ædes erat ad illud forum vetus, ut docet Apollodorus Lib. περὶ Θεῶν. Πάνδημον, inquit, Ἀφροδίτην Ἀθηναῖοι καλοῦσι [?], τὸ ἀφιδρυσάμενοι περὶ τὸ ἀρχαῖον ἀγορὰν [?], eratque in illa, qua itur ad Acropolim è Theatro, via, ut iam diximus è Pausania. Atqui ad hanc Veneris ædem prostabant meretrices è Solonis instituto, ut refert Nicander Colophoniacon Lib. III. Copiam quoque sui faciebant ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ τῇ περὶ τὸν λιμένα [?] in Piræeo, quæ est in eius τῆ ποὰ τῆ μαχαίρᾳ [?]. Nam illius partes recenset Pollux. σῆμα, ἐμπόριον ἐμπορίου ἢ μέρη, καπηλεῖα καὶ πορνεῖα [?]. Pendebant autem quotannis Reipublicæ vectigal meretrices, & ij qui corpore merebant: quod locabat Quingentorum Senatus. Æschines ἐν τῇ κατὰ Τιμάρχου [?]. ἀπαγορεύεσθαι [?] γὰρ εἰ μὴ πᾶσαι πόρναι μισθωσάμεναι ὅτι καθ' ἕκαστον σταυτῶν ἢ βουλὴ πωλεῖ ὁ πορνικὸς τέλος [?]: ἐν τοῖς ἀριθμοῖς ὁ τέλος τῶν οὐκ εἰσεχθέντων [?], ἀλλ' ἀκειδῶς εἰσίναι [?] τοῖς Ταύτῃ χρωμένοις τῇ ἐργασίᾳ [?].
units.tr: Among these matters you will find much about the inspection, price and hire of prostitutes, and other things that do not belong to our present purpose, since we run through them only in passing (ἐκκαλυψάμενοι). I will add only this: these words shed light, and borrow light from, what Seneca says in the first book of the Controversiae, controversy 2. You were taken into a brothel, you received a place, a price was fixed, your name was written up. A little later: She stood naked on the shore for the displeasure of the buyer; every part of her body was looked at and handled. A little further on: You stood as a prostitute in a public place, your cell had its sign placed over it, and you received those who came. A little later: Your name hung on your forehead, you took the wages of lust, and hands that were to be dedicated to the gods took gifts. But she came from a side-street onto the road. Hence no one could be caught as an adulterer with prostitutes who either worked in brothels or stood openly in public, where they were kept in a room [ὅπου ἂν ἐν ἐρασμηλίου κεχωνται], in brothels where there was a room [ὅπου οἰκήματος], where prostitutes were available in numbers, as is recorded of Socrates' Alcibiades' ... [the text is corrupt here], of Aspasia, the Socratic woman: she who sells in the marketplace or stands openly [ἡ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ πωλοῦσα ἢ ἐπιπεφασμένη]. Either way, they openly stand for hire. I think this is the plain sense of these words, about which there is agreement: these are not the women who sell something in the forum, a right granted only to citizens, though I do not know how free such women were, or what they were, from the few surviving fragments of Aristophanes' play whose title is The Women Who Shout [σκλωας κεκλαγμένων]; rather they were shameless women who made themselves available in the busiest parts of the city. But the ancients do not agree on how to interpret the word πωλοῦσα or πωλωνῶν; all admit, however, that it designates prostitutes who openly exposed their shame [ἐξῶσι κοινῇ ἁπάσῃ ἡ καπηλεύσαμέναι ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ]. So Didymus, in Harpocration, explains it as those who make gain openly with their bodies: Didymus says she sells herself openly, since she offers herself at the baths, whence the name ὅ πορνεῖα, and from there the word for the hour of the day. Moreover, prostitutes are called pôloi [colts]. Hesychius: pôlos is "an appearance," for he says the women are called pôlis as the city of Aphrodite. Lysias, however, offers another interpretation which comes to the same thing: he holds that πωλοῦσαι means nothing other than "walking," so that the sense is "those who go openly to men who pay." Lysias' words are in the law already cited: "Whoever is caught openly..." [the Greek here is too corrupt to restore with confidence; the sense is that a slave-woman who openly goes about and is hired is to be owed to the one who has her]. Plutarch in the Life of Solon agrees with Lysias: those who go openly for hire, I mean those who go about in the open and do not visit houses. Such prostitutes ought even to be exposed as slaves to this injury, for they seem neither freeborn nor modest. The custom was that these low-class prostitutes stood publicly, and had daily gatherings, at the famous places of the city: the Ceramicus, the Scirum, and the forum. Others have already noted the Ceramicus. As for the Scirum, Demosthenes has a fine passage, but it is corrupt, about Aeschines' mother: "as your mother, who was remembered for her marriages, in the klision beside the Calamites' hero Hērōikhōlion..." Hesychius and Suidas do not help those who cite them; on the contrary they make the error worse by adding a second corruption. They read hēlision by an easy slip, and the doubled klision is what stands. Hesychius: Calamites, a hero near the hēlision. Suidas: Calamites, a name of a place, from Demosthenes in the speech on the Scirum: "in the hēlision beside the hero Calamites." I conjecture that we should read: "in the klision beside the hero Cyamites." I think the Orator means the klision of the Lycomidae (there was a family at Athens called the Lycomidae, a hero of the Eleusinian rites, says Hesychius), which Pausanias mentions in his Messeniaca. I do not think this klision was far from the temple of Demeter at Eleusis, to whose rites that family was devoted; hence the hymn of Orpheus or Onomacritus to Demeter of the Lycomidae, as Pausanias says. Therefore I also place it beside the little shrine of the hero Cyamites: this Cyamites was a hero, not Bacchus, and Pausanias distinguishes him from Bacchus for the Athenians; he writes that this little shrine was in the district of Scirum, between the city and Eleusis. And indeed, in Scirum, as read in Stephanus, the prostitutes were called ... [corrupt]. Moreover, Pollux in Book IV, ch. 19, lists Lycomides among the pimps' roles, presumably because these public victims of lust stood for hire at the klision of the Lycomidae. Perhaps, though, the word klision should be kept, which Hesychius explains as pandokeion [inn], and Eustathius on the Iliad A as a suitable room for slaves. For Apollonius, in his exposition of the Aeginetan story, says that Glaucias of Aegina, or, as some say, Glaucides, used to confess in a room of the hero Cyamites the ... [corrupt]. But here too one must read "of the hero Cyamites." The gatherings also had their own place at the old forum, which is the road by which the Athenians went up from the theatre to the Acropolis, as Pausanias notes in the Attica. For the temple of Venus Pandemus was by that old forum, as Apollodorus teaches in his book On the Gods: "The Athenians," he says, "call Aphrodite Pandemus, because they set up her shrine near the ancient forum." It lay on the road from the theatre up to the Acropolis, as we have already said from Pausanias. Now, by this temple of Venus prostitutes stood for hire, following Solon's arrangement, as Nicander of Colophon reports in Book III. They also made themselves available in the marketplace around the harbour, in the Piraeus, which is in its ... [corrupt], for Pollux lists its parts: a market, a trading centre, or parts of the same, taverns and brothels. Each year prostitutes and those who earned their living by their bodies paid a tax to the state, which the Council of Five Hundred let out to farm. Aeschines, in his speech against Timarchus: "For it is forbidden unless all prostitutes have hired themselves out; for each of these the Council sells the tax on prostitution. In the accounts, the tax on those not registered [is entered], but they are openly admitted to those who practise this trade."

units.la: Quæ meretricium autem profitebantur, floridas vestes sumere ex hac Lege iubebantur:
units.tr: Those who professed prostitution were ordered by this law to wear flowered garments:

units.la: Ταῖς ἑταίραις ἀδύνα φορεῖν [?]. Meretrices floridas vestes induræ sunto.
units.tr: Meretrices floridas vestes induræ sunto. [ταῖς ἑταίραις ἀνθινὰ φορεῖν] Let prostitutes wear flowered garments.

units.la: Legem habes apud Suidam. νόμος Ἀθηναίοις, ταῖς ἑταίραις αὐτὰ ἀφορεῖν [?]. Hinc Artemidorus Lib. II. cap III. γυναικὶ ἢ ποικίλῃ καὶ αὐτῇ ἑαυτῆς συμφέρει [?] μᾶλλον ταῖς ἑταίραις [?]. αἱ μὲν γὰρ, ἀπὸ τῶν ἐργασιῶν αὐτοῖς ἑαυτῆς χρῆσθαι [?]. Clemens Alexandrinus Pædagogi Lib. III. cap.
