II ὡς τὸν ἀρχαῖον τὰ σήματα, ὅτως τῷ μισθαλίδῃ [?] ἐκλείπεται τὰ ἀμείψαματα [?]. Eandem Legem suis Locrensibus posuit Zaleucus, ut auctor est Diodorus Siculus, & usi sunt Syracusani, quod scribit Philarchus apud Athenæum Lib. XII. Quanquam non ferebant, puto, Athenienses, meretrices, non magis quam eas in quibus adulteri deprehensi fuissent, ornatas prodire in publicum, quo alludit Rhetorum illa Lex apud Hermogenem περὶ γάμων [?]. ἐπιτήδες χρυσία εἰ φορεῖν [?], δημόσια ἔσω. Duplex esse ἐκ τῆς ἐκκωμωδίας [?] videtur huius Legis sensus: Si enim προξενητικὸς legas δημόσια, Legislatoris hæc mens est: Meretricem, quæ aurum gestauerit, debere esse publicam: εἰκὸς ἐν βλάβης τῷ δούλῳ ἢ [?] ὀφείλειν [?], id est, permittendam esse ingenuorum & seruorum passim libidini, eiusmodi sunt, ὃν περὶ φασμένας πωλῶν τε [?]. Si [?] scribas [?] δημόσια[?], sensus est, aurum, quo ornata fuerit meretrix, publicum fieri, & in aerarium referri: Vestibus autem & mundo volebant distingui meretrices à pudicis. Hermogenes ibidem, μὴ ὁμοίαν εἶναι τῆς ἐλευθέρας, μηδὲ τὴν αὐτὴν ἀξιοῦσθαι.
units.tr: You have the law in Suidas: a law of the Athenians, that prostitutes should wear flowered garments [νόμος Ἀθηναίοις, ταῖς ἑταίραις ἀνθινὰ φορεῖν]. Hence Artemidorus, Book II, ch. 3: a woman in embroidered or varied clothing suits prostitutes better than herself, for they use such things for their trade. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus III, ch. 2, says that the ancient marks [of prostitution] were abandoned by the hireling, ... [the sense is corrupt]. Zaleucus gave the same law to his Locrians, as Diodorus Siculus reports, and the Syracusans used it, as Philarchus writes in Athenaeus Book XII. Yet I think the Athenians did not allow prostitutes, any more than women caught in adultery, to go out in public adorned, to which the rhetoricians' law in Hermogenes, On Issues, alludes: a prostitute should not wear gold; if she does, it is to be public [δημόσια]. The sense of this law seems to be double. If you read dēmosia (public) as referring to the lawgiver's intention: a prostitute who has worn gold ought to be public, that is, to be open to the lust of freemen and slaves alike, which is the kind of thing that ... [corrupt]. If you write dēmosia differently, the sense is that the gold with which the prostitute was adorned becomes public and is returned to the treasury. Hermogenes in the same place adds that prostitutes were to be distinguished from modest women by their clothing and adornment, and that they should not be treated like the free: not to be like the free woman, nor to be deemed the same.

units.la: DE TESTAMENTIS ET & hereditario Iure.
units.tr: ON WILLS AND HEREDITARY RIGHT.

units.la: TITVLVS VI.
units.tr: TITLE VI.

units.la: ANte Solonem neminem licebat extra gentem & familiam suam heredem scribere:
units.tr: Before Solon, no one was permitted to name as heir anyone outside his own clan and family.

units.la: Ἐν τῷ [?] ἦει τῶ πεπνικότος [?] διὰ τὰ χρήματ[?] τα [?] ἐ [?] εἶκειν [?].
units.tr: In the law of the man who ... because of money ... to yield. [Ἐν τῷ [?] ἦει τῶ πεπνικότος [?] διὰ τὰ χρήματ[?] τα [?] ἐ [?] εἶκειν [?].]

units.la: Extra gentem familiamque heredem ne scribito.
units.tr: Let no one name an heir outside the clan and family.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Plutarchus in Solone: [illegible, ~40 letters] [?] καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ [?] [illegible, ~50 letters] Cuius ratio est apud Platonem Libro XI. de Legibus, quia bona testantis non sunt, sed gentis & familiae: ἐγὼ γ' οὖν, νομοθέτης ὢν, ἐξ ὑμῶν ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς [?] [illegible, ~40 letters] [?].
units.tr: Plutarch mentions this law in his Life of Solon: [passage illegible in the scan] ... Its rationale is given by Plato in Book XI of the Laws, because a testator's goods are not his own but belong to the clan and family: "I, then, being the lawgiver, from you to yourselves ..." [ἐγὼ γ' οὖν, νομοθέτης ὢν, ἐξ ὑμῶν ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς [?] [illegible] [?].]

units.la: Neque tamen omnibus fas fuit indiscriminatim à Solonis Lege, sua testamento dare legare: Feminis namque atque pueris non licet dare legare testamento cuiquam quod excedat pretium medimni hordei.
units.tr: Yet under Solon's law it was not permitted to everyone to give or bequeath his property by will without distinction. Women and boys may not give or bequeath by will to anyone anything exceeding the value of a medimnus of barley.

units.la: Γαμὶ μὴ ἐξεῖναι συμβολὴν μηδὲ γυναιξὶ [?] πέρα μεδίμνων κειλῶν.
units.tr: That it is not permitted to a boy, or to women, to make a contribution beyond medimnoi of barley. [Γαμὶ μὴ ἐξεῖναι συμβολὴν μηδὲ γυναιξὶ [?] πέρα μεδίμνων κειλῶν.]

units.la: Puer aut femina testamento ne danto leganto ultra medimnum hordei.
units.tr: A boy or a woman shall not give or bequeath by will more than a medimnus of barley.

units.la: Lex extat apud Isæum ἐν τῷ ἀπολογισμῷ τῆς Ἀευσάρχου κλήσεως [?]. παιδὸς δὲ ζῶντος ἐξεῖναι ἀρρενικὸν [?] ὁ δὲ νόμος ἀπαρρηδῶν κωλύει, παιδὶ μὴ ἐξεῖναι συμβαλεῖν μηδὲ γυναιξὶ πέρα μεδίμνων κειλῶν. vbi relegendum est, quod iampridem monuit Cl. Meursius πέρα μεδίμνων κειλῶν auctore Harpocratione, cuius haec sunt verba: ὅτι παιδὶ καὶ γυναιξὶ οὐκ ἐξεῖν συμβολὴν πέρα μεδίμνων κειλῶν, Ἰσαῖος ἐν τῷ κατὰ τῆς Ἀλεξάνδρου (ἐκ Ἀευσάρχου) κλήσεως φησί. Causam emendationis, quam non investigavit Vir eruditissimus, in sequentibus aperiemus, Deo dante. Cautum hac Solonis Lege, ne qua femina, neve quis puer, qui annos nondum natus viginti sui non erat iuris, testamento dei leget praeter medimnum hordei, sive quod excedat eius pretium. Quae Lex non solis divitibus, sed etiam pauperibus est scripta: atque pro modulo fuit Legislatori pauperiorum census, ut & in fenore praescribendo, quod penderet mulieri repetita, sed non accepta dos, minimam dotem in animo habuit, quae fuit trium sesquiminarum: Nam cum hic scribit Legislator non licere puero, aut feminae testamento dare legare ultra medimnum hordei, idem est ac si diceret, non licere testamento dare legare quod excedat fenus annuum census illius, qui testamentū[?] scribit: Minimus census fingitur esse Legislator totidem drachmarum, quot est minima dos: Est autem minima dos drachmarum centum quinquaginta: menstruum fenus drachmarum centum est in vnam drachmam, siue obolus sex: itaque centum quinquaginta drachmæ pariunt obolos nouem, quos per duodecim multiplica, fiunt oboli centum & octo, siue drachmæ octodecim, annum centum quinquaginta drachmarum fenus; Atqui his octodecim drachmis vænit hordei medimnus. Demosthenes ὁ πρὸς Φαίνιππον. οὐ δ' ἐκ τῆς ἐχαλκᾶς[?] ... [illegible, ~40 letters] ... πλὴν ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... Quare conceditur impuberi puero, itemque fœminæ ius dandi legandi testamento fenus annuum census sui, nempe pauperi, qui plus centum quinquaginta drachmis non habet in censu, dandi legandi octodecim drachmas, quot vænit medimnus hordei: Nam idem hic plane statuo, quod de dotibus in superioribus dixi, & fenore quod pariunt. Ne autem plura, quam fenus annuum census & facultatum suarum, dent legent, ratio est imbecillitas mentis in feminis, in pueris vero, quod, per ætatem nondum illis creduntur bona, quæ à patribus acceperunt. Dio Chrysostomus Orat. [illegible, ~30 letters] ... [illegible, ~60 letters] ...
units.tr: The law is preserved in Isaeus, in the defence speech concerning the estate of Aristarchus: "While a child is living it is permitted ... but the law, forbidding ... prevents a child from making a contribution, and women beyond medimnoi of barley." [ἐν τῷ ἀπολογισμῷ τῆς Ἀευσάρχου κλήσεως [?]. παιδὸς δὲ ζῶντος ἐξεῖναι ἀρρενικὸν [?] ὁ δὲ νόμος ἀπαρρηδῶν κωλύει, παιδὶ μὴ ἐξεῖναι συμβαλεῖν μηδὲ γυναιξὶ πέρα μεδίμνων κειλῶν.] Here what the most learned Meursius long ago pointed out must be read again: πέρα μεδίμνων κειλῶν, on the authority of Harpocration, whose words are: "that it is not permitted to a child and to women to make a contribution beyond medimnoi of barley, as Isaeus says in the speech against the accusation of Alexander (from that of Aristarchus)." [ὅτι παιδὶ καὶ γυναιξὶ οὐκ ἐξεῖν συμβολὴν πέρα μεδίμνων κειλῶν, Ἰσαῖος ἐν τῷ κατὰ τῆς Ἀλεξάνδρου (ἐκ Ἀευσάρχου) κλήσεως φησί.] The reason for this correction, which that most learned man did not investigate, I shall set out in what follows, God willing. This law of Solon provides that no woman, and no boy who has not yet reached twenty years and is not his own master, may bequeath by will beyond a medimnus of barley, or beyond its value. This law was written not only for the rich but also for the poor, and the lawgiver's measure of the poor man's property was taken by the same scale that governed the interest to be set on a dowry. For the minimal dowry, which a woman could reclaim but not receive, was in his mind the smallest one, of three and a half minae. For when the lawgiver writes that a boy or woman may not give or bequeath by will beyond a medimnus of barley, it is the same as saying that they may not give or bequeath by will more than the annual interest on the property of the one who makes the will. The lawgiver is taken to have set the minimum property at as many drachmas as the minimal dowry, and the minimal dowry is one hundred and fifty drachmas. The monthly interest on one hundred drachmas is one drachma, or six obols. So one hundred and fifty drachmas yield nine obols a month, which multiplied by twelve gives one hundred and eight obols, or eighteen drachmas, as the annual interest on one hundred and fifty drachmas. And a medimnus of barley sold for these eighteen drachmas. Demosthenes, Against Phaenippus: [text illegible in the scan]. Hence it is conceded to a minor boy, and likewise to a woman, the right to give or bequeath by will the annual interest on their property, namely that of a poor person who has no more than one hundred and fifty drachmas in property, the right to give or bequeath eighteen drachmas, which is what a medimnus of barley sold for. For I here hold exactly what I said above about dowries and the interest they yield. And the reason why they may not give or bequeath more than the annual interest on their property and resources is the weakness of women's minds and, in boys, the fact that because of their age they are not believed to be yet in charge of the goods they received from their fathers. Dio Chrysostom, Oration [illegible in the scan].

units.la: Ceteris, qui poterant testamentum facere, concessit Solo necessitudini generis amicitiam præferre, & bona in vniuscuiusque manu posuit, vt possent, quem vellent, heredem scribere, nullis superstitibus liberis masculis, si modo non essent furiosi, aut vi morbi, vel senectutis, vel pharmacorum dementis statu deiecti, aut ab vxoribus circumuenti, aut denique necessitate impulsi, aut in vinculis habiti.
units.tr: To the others, who could make a will, Solon granted that the ties of kinship should come before friendship, and he placed the goods in each man's hands, so that each could name as heir whomever he wished, provided there were no surviving male children, and provided he was not insane, nor deprived of his wits by disease, old age or drugs, nor persuaded by his wife, nor driven by some necessity, nor held in chains.

units.la: ΟΣΟΙ ΜΗ ΕΠΕΠΟΙΗΝΤΟ ΩΣΤΕ ΜΗΤΕ ΑΠΕΙΡΕΙΝ, ΜΗΤ' ΕΠΙΔΙΚΑΣΑΣΘΑΙ, ΟΤΕ ΣΟΛΩΝ ΕΙΣΗΓΕΙ ΤΑ ΕΑΥΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΘΕΣΘΑΙ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΕΘΕΛΗ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΩΣΙ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΑΡΡΕΝΕΣ, ΑΝ ΜΗ ΜΑΝΙΩΝ, Η ΓΗΡΩΣ, Η ΦΑΡΜΑΚΩΝ, Η ΝΟΣΟΥ ΕΝΕΚΕΝ, Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΙ ΠΕΙΘΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΩΝ, Η ΥΠΟ ΑΝΑΓΚΗΣ, Η ΥΠΟ ΔΕΣΜΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΛΗΦΘΕΙΣ.
units.tr: Those who were not made [citizens] ... neither to ... nor to bring suit, when Solon introduced that each may dispose of his own property as he wishes, if they have no legitimate sons who are males ... unless ... driven mad, or ... by a drug, or by disease, or persuaded by a woman ... or under compulsion, or held in bonds. [ΟΣΟΙ ΜΗ ΕΠΕΠΟΙΗΝΤΟ ΩΣΤΕ ΜΗΤΕ ΑΠΕΙΡΕΙΝ, ΜΗΤ' ΕΠΙΔΙΚΑΣΑΣΘΑΙ, ΟΤΕ ΣΟΛΩΝ ΕΙΣΗΓΕΙ ΤΑ ΕΑΥΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΘΕΣΘΑΙ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΕΘΕΛΗ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΩΣΙ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΑΡΡΕΝΕΣ, ΑΝ ΜΗ ΜΑΝΙΩΝ, Η ΓΗΡΩΣ, Η ΦΑΡΜΑΚΩΝ, Η ΝΟΣΟΥ ΕΝΕΚΕΝ, Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΙ ΠΕΙΘΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΩΝ, Η ΥΠΟ ΑΝΑΓΚΗΣ, Η ΥΠΟ ΔΕΣΜΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΛΗΦΘΕΙΣ.]

units.la: Quicumque ciues adscripti non sunt, nemine controuersiam illis faciente de bonis, aut iudicio experiente, quando Præturam adijt Solo, testamento sua danto leganto, cuicumque libuerit, si nullos superstites habeant liberos masculos: neque furiosi sint, vel præ senectute, vel morbi, aut veneficij vi: neque ab vxoribus persuasi: aut necessitate aliqua, vel vinculorum tædio coacti.
units.tr: Whoever are not enrolled as citizens, when no one raises a dispute over their goods or brings them to trial, when Solon held the office of Archon, may give and bequeath by will to whomever they please, provided they have no surviving male children, and provided they are not insane, nor impaired by old age or disease, nor by the force of poison, nor persuaded by their wives, nor compelled by some necessity or by the tedium of chains.

units.la: Legem hanc descripsit & ἀπολέξει expressit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Φιλοκτήμονα β'. Estque proprie scripta ciuibus aboriginibus & indigenis, quibus solis hac Lege conceditur testamentum facere: itaque commode intelligendus est Ilæus ἐν τῷ πρὸς τὸν Φιλοκτήμονος κλῆρον. ὑπὸ ὁ νόμος[?] ... ὦ ἄνδρες, καινὸς ἁπάντων χαίρειν, ἐξεῖναι τὰ ἑαυτῶν ἀποθέσθαι, ἐὰν μὴ παῖδες ὦσι γνήσιοι ἀρρέ- νες. ἐὰν μὴ ἀρα μανεῖς, ἵ' [?] ἀπὸ γένους, ἵ δ' ἄλλο ἢ τῶν ἐκ τῶν νόμων ἀποδιδόναι ἀλ.ζη. [?] Nam ἅπαντες καὶ πάντες καινοὶ ὅσοι ὁ νόμος, nempe indigenis, non autem adscriptis: quo sensu scripsit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Λεπτίνην. Εἰ γὰρ ὁ μὲν Σόλων ἔθηκε νόμον, ἐξεῖναι δωρεῖσθαι τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ὅτῳ ἂν ὡς βούληται, ἐὰν μὴ παῖδες ὦσι γνήσιοι, ἵνα εἰς ὃ μέσον καὶ τὰς ἀπὸ φέλκαι, ἐφάμιλλον ποιῆσαι ὅ πᾶσι ἄλλος δέ. Plutarchus in Solone: δεχίμησε δὲ καὶ τοῖς ἐπὶ Ἀθηναίων νόμῳ· προϊέσθαι γὰρ οὐκ ἔξεσι, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῆς ἡλικίας τὰ χρήματα καὶ τὸν εἶναι καὶ ἀπολιπεῖν· ὁ δ' ᾧ βάλλεται ὡς ἐπιπέσῃ, εἰ μὴ παῖδες εἶεν αὐτῷ, δοῦναι τὰ αὐτοῦ, φιλίας τε συγγενείας ἐπίμονοι μᾶλλον, καὶ χάριν αἰάγκης· καὶ τὰ χρήματα, κτήματα τῆς ἐχόντων ἐπίπονοι. ὁ μὲν αἰσχύνη γὰρ πάλιν, οὐδ' ἁπλῶς τὰ δόσεις ἐφῆκεν, ἀλλ' εἰ μὴ ἰόσων ἐνεχεῖ, ἵ' φαρμάκων, ἵ' ἀνδρῶν, ἵ' ἀνάγκη κατα- γράφεις, ἵ' γυναικὶ πεισθῆμος· δ' πρὸς τοῦ καὶ τοῦ περιτοπαῖ τὸν ἐπανι [?] βάλλεται, οὐδὲ ἠρμένος τῆς βιαίων ἀποδώσωσι, ἀλλ' εἰς ἔαυτὸ τῶν ἀπάτῶν τῇ ἀνάγκῃ, καὶ τὰ πῶς τῶν ἐνδυνῷ θεῖος, ὡς ἡ ἦσαν ἐκεῖνος ἀξιῶσαι λοκισίον ἀξύσσεων [?] δυνάμων. At vero ad- scitis & plebiscito ciuitate donatis, qui orbi essent, hac ipsa Lege denegatum est, vt ex ea colligit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ Σπφαῖς Φιλομύρτυιῶν β'. vbi Legem hanc descripsit, addit namque: ἄξιον δὲ καὶ τῶν συμμαθῶν, ὅτι ΟΣΟΙ ΜΗ ΕΠΕΠΟΙΗΝΤΟ, ἀλλ' ἠσθη πεφυκότες γνήσιοι, τούτοις ὁ νόμος δίδωσιν, ἐὰν ἀπαίδες ὦσι, ἀποθέσθαι τὰ ἑαυτῶν. ὁ δ' εἶπεν πατὴρ ἡμῖν ἐπεπείνη ἑαυτοῦ τῆς δήμου πο- λίτης. ὥστε οὖν ἐκ τῶν δόξων αὐτοῦ ἀποθέσθαι ἀποθέσθαι. Existimo autem ciuium adscriptorum, qui orbi essent, bona in aerarium relata fuisset, cum nulla illis cum aliis ciuibus cognatio & necessitudo intercederet, sed cum Republica tantum: Soli igitur ciui indigenae licebat testamento sua dare legare cui videretur commodum, vt iam è Leptinea Demosthenis laudata conflat. Isæus ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς Ἀγυφίλου κλήρου. νόμον γὰρ ὄντος, ἐξεῖναι ὅτου βούλεται δοῦναι τὰ ἑαυτοῦ. Plato Libro XI. de Legibus: τὸν λόγον τοῦτον, ὦ 'γαθέ, Φοδώνυμος, τὸν νόμον ἐπῇ- σθαι τὸ δίς, ἐξεῖναι τὰ ἑαυτῶν ἀποθέσθαι ἁπλῶς ὅπως ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς ἐθέλῃ ὃ ἀποδοῦναι. Cuius ratio est apud Isæum ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς Αειστάρχου κλήρου, quia sua ipsius sunt: ἐστὶ δὲ δίκαιον τοῦτο, ὦ ἄνδρες· ὁ γὰρ νόμος κελεύει τὰ μὲν ἑαυτῶν ἀποθέσθαι, ὅτῳ ἂν ἐθέλῃ, τῆς δ' ἀλ- λοτρίων ὁσθέντα κέκτηνται. Itaque Legislator non vult quenquam testamento dare legare cuiquam ea bona, de quibus testatori controuersia mouetur, aut iudicio experitur: neque enim eius sunt: hoc sensu verba ista Legis interpretor, ΩΣΤΕ ΜΗΤΕ ΑΠΕΙΠΕΙΝ, ΜΗΤ' ΕΠΙΔΙΚΑΣΑΣΘΑΙ, quae eruditissimo interpreti negotium exhibuerunt.
units.tr: Demosthenes described this law and expressed it almost word for word in the second speech against Philocles. It was written properly for the citizens who were native and indigenous, to whom alone this law granted the right to make a will. So Isaeus, in the speech concerning the estate of Philoctemon, should be read sensibly: "...under this law, gentlemen, everyone who is ... may dispose of his own property, provided he has no legitimate male sons, unless he is mad, or ... from his family, or by some other means ..." For "all" and "everyone" in this law means the indigenous, not the enrolled. In the same sense Demosthenes wrote in the speech against Leptines: "For if Solon made a law that a man may give his own property to whomever he wishes, provided he has no legitimate sons ..., so that ... the same for all." Plutarch in Solon: "He also approved the law of the Athenians: they were not permitted to dispose of their property, but in their lifetime to keep their goods and dispose of them; and he who has no sons may give his property to whom he wishes, preferring friendship and kinship and favour to necessity; and the goods belong to those who possess them. ... Nor did he allow the gift without restriction, but not if one is under the influence of drugs, or chains, or force, or persuaded by a woman, ... nor is he to be subject to violence ..." But on the contrary, to the enrolled and to those given citizenship by a decree of the people, who were childless, this same law denied the right, as Demosthenes gathers from it in the second speech on the estate of Philomyrtis, where he sets out this law and adds: "It is also worth noting that the law grants to those who are not made [citizens], but are born legitimate, that if they are childless they may dispose of their property." He said our father was a citizen by decree of the people, so that ... from his goods. I think, then, that the goods of the enrolled citizens who were childless were carried into the treasury, since they had no kinship or ties of blood with other citizens, but only with the commonwealth. Thus only the native citizen was permitted to give or bequeath by will to whomever seemed fit, as is now clear from Demosthenes' Leptines. Isaeus, in the speech concerning the estate of Hagnias: "For since there is a law that one may give what is one's own to whomever one wishes." Plato, Book XI of the Laws: "This law, good sir, Phoedonymus, allows that what is one's own may be disposed of simply in whatever way one wishes ..." Its reason is given by Isaeus in the speech concerning the estate of Aristarchus, because these goods are their own: "And this is just, gentlemen; for the law orders that what is one's own may be disposed of to whomever one wishes, but what is of others they have acquired by ..." Therefore the lawgiver does not want anyone to give or bequeath by will to anyone those goods over which a dispute is raised against the testator, or which he brings to trial, since they are not truly his. In this sense I interpret these words of the law, "neither to give away, nor to bring suit," which have given the most learned interpreter a great deal of trouble.

units.la: Qui autem heredes scribebantur, etiam in filios adsumebantur, vt liquet e proxime laudata Isæi Oratione: εἰμὴ τοῖνυ πᾶσι ὑμᾶς ὁσθῆναι, ὦ ἄνδρες, ὅτι ἂν ΔΙΚΑΙΟΣ ἡ εἰσαγωγὴ ἡ εἰσηγγελία τὴν εἰσαγωγὴν γίγνονται διδόντων τε αὐτῷ καὶ υἱῶν ποιεῖσθαι τῶν· δικαίως δὲ οὐκ ἔξεστιν. colligere quoque licet e Libro XI. Platonis de Legibus. Vnde sequitur, non simpliciter verum esse, quemuis posse heredem scribi: non enim peregrini poterant heredes scribi ab Athenien. ciue, quia filij loco non poterat censeri, vt qui ciuis non esset, &, vt inquit Plato Libro laudato, τῆς πόλεως ἔστι τὸ, πεῖθος ὅπου καὶ ἡ ἡ ἀδ̈ά. quod etiam apud Romanos obtinuisse colliges ex hoc Rescripto Imper. Titi Ælij Antonini A ad Antestianum. Qui deportantor, si heredes scribantur, tanquam peregrini capere non possunt, sed hereditas in ea causa est, in qua esset, si scripti non fuissent. Lege I. C. de Heredibus instituendis. Vlpianus Tit.
units.tr: Those who were written as heirs were also taken in as sons, as is clear from the oration of Isaeus cited just above: "unless, men, you have all been persuaded that the introduction or the accusation... [εἰμὴ τοῖνυ πᾶσι ὑμᾶς ὁσθῆναι, ὦ ἄνδρες, ὅτι ἂν ΔΙΚΑΙΟΣ ἡ εἰσαγωγὴ ἡ εἰσηγγελία τὴν εἰσαγωγὴν γίγνονται διδόντων τε αὐτῷ καὶ υἱῶν ποιεῖσθαι τῶν· δικαίως δὲ οὐκ ἔξεστιν]." It may also be gathered from Book XI of Plato's Laws. Hence it does not follow that anyone at all may be written as heir. Foreigners could not be written as heirs by an Athenian citizen, because a foreigner could not be counted in the place of a son, since he was not a citizen; and, as Plato says in the book cited, "the city is where the persuasion and the justice are" [τῆς πόλεως ἔστι τὸ, πεῖθος ὅπου καὶ ἡ ἡ ἀδ̈ά]. You will gather that this also held among the Romans from this rescript of the emperor Titus Aelius Antoninus to Antestianus: Those who are deported, if they are written as heirs, cannot take as foreigners, but the inheritance is in the same position it would have been in had they not been written. See the first law, C., De heredibus instituendis. Ulpian, title 22.

units.la: XXII. Qui heredes instituti possunt. §. II. Dedititiorum numero heres institui non po- test, quia peregrinus est, cum quo testamenti factio non est.
units.tr: XXII. Who may be instituted as heirs. §2. A person of the dediticii class cannot be instituted as heir, because he is a foreigner, and with a foreigner there is no capacity to make a will.

units.la: Idem Libro I V. ad Sabinum: Solemus dicere, media tempora non nocere: ut puta ciuis Romanus heres scriptus, viuo testatore factus peregrinus, mox ciuitatem Romanam peruenit, media tempora non nocent. Lege VI. §.II. D. de heredibus instituendis. Neque item nothi heredes scribi poterant: Demosthenes [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐν τῷ κατὰ Εὐβουλίδου [?] de cognatis suis loquitur, qui potuissent, eo excluso, siquidem nothus, ac proinde peregrinus fuisset, hereditatem [illegible, ~8 letters] iure adire. At vero si nothi adoptione in familiam essent adscit, quia ciues, quibus solus eius est bona alterius adipisci, fiebant, poterant heredes scribi, vt constat e Suidae narratione in [illegible, ~10 letters] de Pericle. Sed tamen certae sunt cautiones, quibus coercetur ista libertas sua testamento dandi legandi cuicumque libuerit. Prima cautio est, si sint superstites liberi legitimi masculi, quos ipse genuerit: AN MH ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΩΣΙ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΑΡΡΕΝΕΣ. Hi enim Lege paternorum bonorum sunt heredes, neque vllum est opus testati. Isaeus [illegible, ~30 letters] Δημοσθένης [?] Idem [illegible, ~20 letters] ταῦτα ἐπὶ [?] masculi nempe, vt habes in Lege.
units.tr: The same, in Book IV on Sabinus: We are accustomed to say that intervening times do no harm: for example, a Roman citizen written as heir, who while the testator is alive becomes a foreigner, and soon afterwards reaches Roman citizenship, the intervening times do no harm. See the sixth law, §2, D., De heredibus instituendis. Likewise, illegitimate children could not be written as heirs. Demosthenes, in the speech against Eubulides [?], speaks of his kinsmen, who could have taken the inheritance by law, had he been excluded, since he would have been illegitimate and therefore a foreigner. But if illegitimate children had been received into a family by adoption, since they became citizens, to whom alone it is granted to obtain another's goods, they could be written as heirs, as is clear from Suidas's account of Pericles. Yet there are certain safeguards by which this freedom to give and bequeath by will to whomever one pleases is restrained. The first safeguard: if there are surviving legitimate male children whom he himself has begotten: "if there are no legitimate male children" [AN MH ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΩΣΙ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΑΡΡΕΝΕΣ]. For these, by the law, are heirs of the paternal goods, and no will is needed. Isaeus [...]; Demosthenes [...]; the same [...] these things [...] males, of course, as you have in the law.

units.la: Excipitur praeterea, si furore percitus sui non sit compos, aut deliret, idque vel morbi vi, vel praesenectute, aut si venenum biberit. Demosthenes [illegible, ~40 letters]. Idem [illegible, ~25 letters]. Romani quoque iurisconsulti optime obseruarunt sanitatem mentis esse exigendam. Ineo, qui testatus, inquit Labeo, eius temporis, quo testamentum facit, integritas mentis, non corporis sanitas exigenda est. Lege II.D. Qui testamento facere possint: & Marcellus notat apud Pomponium, Furiosus quoque testamenti factionem habet, licet testamentum facere non poterit. Lege XVI D. cod. nam in aduersa corporis valetudine mente captus, eo tempore testamentum facere non poterit. Lege XVII.D.cod. At vero furiosum in suis inducijs vltimum condere elogium posse, licet ab antiquis dubitabatur, tamen & retro Principibus & nobis placuit, inquit Iustinianus Lege IX.C. cod. Senium autem non obest cuiquam, dummodo mente integer sit, vt habes in Rescripto Diocletiani & Maximiani AA. ad Licinium: Senium quidem aetatis, vel aegritudinem corporis, sinceritatem mentis tenentibus, testamenti factionem certum est non auferre. Lege III. C.cod.
units.tr: Furthermore, an exception is made if a man is not of sound mind because of madness, or is delirious, whether from the force of disease, from old age, or because he has drunk poison. Demosthenes [...]. Idem [...]. The Roman jurists also observed well that soundness of mind must be required. Labeo says of such a man: for one who makes a will, it is the integrity of his mind, not the soundness of his body, that must be required at the time he makes it. Law 2, D. Who may make a will. Marcellus also notes, in Pomponius, that a madman too has the capacity to make a will, though he cannot actually make one. Law 16, D. same title. For a man whose mind is seized during bodily illness cannot make a will at that time. Law 17, D. same title. But that a madman may make a last declaration during a lucid interval, although the ancients doubted it, has nevertheless been approved both by earlier emperors and by us, says Justinian, Law 9, C. same title. Old age, however, harms no one, provided he is sound in mind, as you have it in the rescript of Diocletian and Maximian Augusti to Licinius: "It is certain that old age, or sickness of the body, does not take away the capacity to make a will from those who keep the soundness of their mind." Law 3, C. same title.

units.la: Tertia quoque cautio est: Si quis vxori fuerit obsecutus ab ea persuasus: Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΙ ΠΕΙΘΟΜΕΝΟΣ. Demosthenes ad hanc Legem: [illegible, ~35 letters]. Idem [illegible, ~30 letters] Ὀλυμπιοδώρου [?] nam, vt est ibidem, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Quod sequitur quasi de contextu Legis, ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥ-
units.tr: A third caution also applies: if someone has yielded to his wife, having been persuaded by her [Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΙ ΠΕΙΘΟΜΕΝΟΣ]. Demosthenes on this law: [...]. Idem [...] of Olympiodorus; for, as is there, [...]. What follows, as if it were part of the text of the law, "by the ... " [ΥΠΟ ΤΟΥ-]

units.la: ΤΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΩΝ. non est de Lege ipsa, sed sunt Oratoris verba intercipientis ista, Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΙ ΠΕΙΘΟΜΕΝΟΣ. quia Pasio,si quidem testamentum fecisset, condidisset ab vxore deceptus & persuasus, quam alibi hic Apollodorus à Phormione, viuente Pasione, adulterio pollutam fuisse conqueritur: objicitque hoc ipsorum fuisse facinus, sed leuiter sunt corrupta verba è compendiosa scriptura,cùm enim scriptum fuisset [illegible, ~12 letters] id est, [illegible, ~6 letters], facile expuncta est compendiosa linea, eaque,cui superaddebatur litera: est igitur relcribendum: [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: "...of the lawless" [ΤΩΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΩΝ] is not part of the law itself, but the words of the orator who interjects them: [Η ΓΥΝΑΙΚΙ ΠΕΙΘΟΜΕΝΟΣ]. For Pasion, if he had indeed made a will, would have made it after being deceived and persuaded by his wife, whom Apollodorus elsewhere complains was defiled by adultery with Phormion while Pasion was still alive; and he charges that this was their crime. But the words have been slightly corrupted through the abbreviated script: when [...] had been written, that is [...], the short abbreviating stroke was easily dropped, and the letter to which it was attached was left standing. So it must be rewritten: [...].

units.la: Denique irrita fiunt testamenta, quæ scripserit ciuis Athenien-sis in vinculis,aut aliqua coactus necessitate,Η ΥΠΟ ΑΝΑΓΚΗΣ, Η ΥΠΟ ΔΕΣΜΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΛΗΦΘΕΙΣ, quod etiam laudata è Demosthene atq; Plutarcho confirmant loca: Idemque Plutarch. in Quæstionibus Rom. [illegible, ~20 letters].
units.tr: Finally, wills are void if a citizen of Athens wrote them while in chains, or under some compulsion of necessity [Η ΥΠΟ ΑΝΑΓΚΗΣ, Η ΥΠΟ ΔΕΣΜΟΥ ΚΑΤΑΛΗΦΘΕΙΣ], which the passages quoted from Demosthenes and Plutarch also confirm. Plutarch says the same in his Roman Questions [...].

units.la: In conscribendis testamenti tabulis Magistratum aduocabant,qui præsentia sua illas vel confirmaret & stabiliret, vel soluceret & infringeret. Harpo-crationè Dinarcho : [illegible, ~30 letters]. eadem habet Suidas. Ifæus [illegible, ~40 letters] Κλεωνύμους [illegible, ~40 letters]. Rursum:[illegible, ~20 letters]. Nominatim vero Aftynomum aduocabant, vt est in eadem Oratione: [illegible, ~30 letters]. Amplissimus ideq; eruditissimus vir eiusdem memini sse moris Ifæum vult his verbis [illegible, ~20 letters]. Ei tamen non accedimus: Nam borû verborum sensus est;non commissurum fuisse Nicodemû, vt Phile sororis filia ab Endio adoptiuo Pyrrhi filio clocaretur,tanquà notha,siquidé fuisset è legitimis nuptiis suscepta:sed potius in ius fuisse vocaturum,& de tota hereditate disceptaturû, [illegible, ~20 letters] & iniuriarû, inquit, postulasset Endiû apud Archonté Eponymû,(nam apud hunc [illegible, ~10 letters]) eo quod cötumelia affecisset Philen,què&legitima filia,atq; vnica Pyrrhi heres esset:id docet quæ paulò ante dixerat: [illegible, ~30 letters]. Aliquâdo qui testamenti tabulas scribebant, testes aduocabat,non eorum, quæ testamento suo dabant legabant:signatæ enim erant iam tabulæ,sed vt meminissent & testarentur se testamentum fecisse. Ifæus [illegible, ~30 letters]. Factum etiam est, vt nullæ testamenti tabulæ scriberentur,(quemadmodum apud Romanos calatis comitiis) sed testator voluntatem suam pro concione declararet,& voce nûcuparet: Colligo è Plutarcho Alcibiadê: [illegible, ~45 letters] Quod fiebat, vt puto, quando conuenerat populus [illegible, ~12 letters] calatis comitiis: testamentum nuncupatum Iurisconsulti vocant.
units.tr: In drawing up the tablets of a will they called in a magistrate, who by his presence either confirmed and established them, or dissolved and annulled them. Harpocration, on Dinarchus: [...]. Suidas has the same. Isaeus [...] Kleonymus [...]. Again [...]. Specifically, they called in the Astynomus, as in the same speech: [...]. The most distinguished and most learned man recalls the same custom, and Isaeus means it in these words: [...]. We do not, however, agree with him. For the sense of those words is that Nicodemus would not have allowed Phile, his sister's daughter, to be shut out by Endius, the adoptive son of Pyrrhus, as a bastard, since she had been born of a lawful marriage. Rather, he would have summoned him to court and contested the whole inheritance [...]. And, he says, he would have demanded damages from Endius before the eponymous archon (for before him [...]), because he had insulted Phile, who was both the legitimate daughter and the sole heir of Pyrrhus. This is shown by what he had said a little before: [...]. Sometimes those who wrote out wills called in witnesses, not to attest to the things that they gave or bequeathed in the will, for the tablets were already sealed, but so that the witnesses would remember and testify that the testator had made a will. Isaeus [...]. It also happened that no written tablets were drawn up at all (as among the Romans at the calata comitia), but the testator declared his will before the assembly and dictated it aloud. I gather this from Plutarch's account of Alcibiades: [...]. This was done, I think, when the people had assembled [...] at the calata comitia. Jurists call a will so declared a nuncupative will.

units.la: Quod si pater testamentum conscripserit[?], & liberis masculis heredes substituerit, si ante annum vicesimum aetatis liberi decesserint, testamentum patris ratum erat ex hac Lege:
units.tr: But if a father has drawn up a will and substituted heirs for his male children, and the children die before the age of twenty, the father's will was ratified by this law.

units.la: Ὅ,ΤΙ ΑΝ ΓΝΗΣΙΩΝ ΟΝΤΩΝ ΥΙΩΝ Ο ΠΑΤΗΡ ΔΙΑΘΗΤΑΙ, ΕΑΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΩ-ΣΙΝ ΟΙ ΥΙΕΙΣ ΠΡΙΝ ΕΠΙΔΙΕΤΕΣ ΗΒΑΙΝ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΔΙΑΘΗΚΗΝ ΚΥ-ΡΙΑΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.
units.tr: "Whenever a father makes a disposition while he has legitimate sons, if the sons die before they reach the age of ..., the father's will shall be valid." [Ὅ,ΤΙ ΑΝ ΓΝΗΣΙΩΝ ΟΝΤΩΝ ΥΙΩΝ Ο ΠΑΤΗΡ ΔΙΑΘΗΤΑΙ, ΕΑΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΩΣΙΝ ΟΙ ΥΙΕΙΣ ΠΡΙΝ ΕΠΙΔΙΕΤΕΣ ΗΒΑΙΝ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΔΙΑΘΗΚΗΝ ΚΥΡΙΑΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.]

units.la: Heredes à patre testamento substituti liberis, si liberi ante annum aetatis suae vicesimum decesserint, heredes sunto.
units.tr: Heirs substituted by the father in his will for the children: if the children die before the age of twenty, let them be the heirs.

units.la: Legem hanc nobis descripsit [illegible, ~8 letters] Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Σπουδίας[?] Φιλιππικῷ[?] β'. Superstitibus masculis liberis non poterat pater testamento sua dare legare cuiquam alteri: paternorum quippe bonorum liberi naturae lege sunt heredes, consultum tamen voluit hac Lege Solo patribus: itaque pupillarem, vt iuris Romani, quanquam in annis numerandis non inter vtrumque populum conueniat, substitutionem instituit: idque testamentum, quod sibi impuberibusque liberis fecit pater, ratum esse voluit, quo scribitur heres, si filius ΠΡΙΝ ΕΠΙΔΙΕΤΕΣ ΗΒΑΙΝ, id est, vt alibi diximus, priusquam annos natus viginti, à quo demum anno sui iuris est, & [?] ἐπιτροπῆς[?] cura siue tutela exiit, in vuis esse desierit: Ab anno vicesimo filius sui erat iuris, καὶ ἤδη τὰ πατρῷα ἀπολαμβάνειν[?], vt loquuntur Attici Iurisconsulti: neque amplius quicquam iuris in illius bona erat alteri, neque expectando substitutio; solam enim hanc pupillarem admitti voluit Solo, qui [illegible, ~12 letters] τῶν ἐχόντων[?] ἐπίνοιαν[?]. Atque haec est à Solone instituta, quia eius Lege pueri ante annum aetatis vicesimum non poterant heredem scribere, aut aliquid è bonis suis dare legare alteri, praeter hordei medimnum.
units.tr: This law was reported to us [...] by Demosthenes, in the speech against Spudias, or the second Philippic [ἐν τῷ κατὰ Σπουδίας Φιλιππικῷ β']. While male children survived, a father could not by will give or bequeath anything to anyone else, since by the law of nature the children are the heirs of the paternal property. Yet this law was meant to make provision for fathers alone. So he established a substitution of the kind that Roman law calls pupillary, although the two peoples do not agree on how the years are counted. He wished the will that a father made for himself and his children below the age of puberty to be valid, in which an heir is named in case the son dies "before reaching the age of twenty", that is, as we have said elsewhere, before he has completed his twentieth year, from which year he is his own master and has left guardianship and tutelage [ἐπιτροπῆς] behind him. From the age of twenty the son was his own master, and "now to recover his paternal property" [καὶ ἤδη τὰ πατρῷα ἀπολαμβάνειν], as the Attic jurists put it. Nor did anyone else have any further legal claim on his goods, nor was there any substitution to wait for. For Solon wished only this pupillary substitution to be admitted. And this was instituted by Solon because under his law boys below the age of twenty could not name an heir or give or bequeath anything from their property to another, except a measure of barley.

units.la: Superstite tamen femina prole, licebat testamento sua dare legare alteri sub hac conditione, vt filiam superstitem in vxorem duceret.
units.tr: Even when a woman had surviving children, a man could by will give or bequeath his property to another on this condition: that he marry the surviving daughter.

units.la: Ἐξῆναι [illegible, ~7 letters] ὅπως ἂν εἰθέλῃ τῆς τε αὐτῆς, [illegible, ~10 letters] γυναικὸς καταλίπῃ ΕΠΙ ΤΑΥ-ΤΑΙΣ.
units.tr: It was allowed to leave [his property] to whomever he wished, of the same [woman as] wife, [?] in these [cases] [Ἐξῆναι ... ὅπως ἂν εἰθέλῃ τῆς τε αὐτῆς ... γυναικὸς καταλίπῃ ΕΠΙ ΤΑΥΤΑΙΣ].

units.la: Bona sua cuicumque libuerit testamento danto legunto, etiam superstitibus filiabus, quas in vxores ducunto scripti heredes.
units.tr: Let them give and bequeath their property by will to whomever they please, even if daughters survive, whom the named heirs shall take as wives. [Bona sua cuicumque libuerit testamento danto legunto, etiam superstitibus filiabus, quas in vxores ducunto scripti heredes.]

units.la: Legem hanc laudat Isaeus [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐν τῷ Πύρρου κλήρῳ, [illegible, ~25 letters] Rursum: ὁ γὰρ νόμος ἀξιοῖ ἐξῆναι ὅπως ἂν εἰθέλῃ τῆς τε αὐτῆς, ἐὰν μὴ παῖδας γυναικὸς καταλίπῃ ἄρρενας· ἐὰν δὲ θυγατέρας καταλίπῃ, ΕΠΙ ΤΑΥΤΑΙΣ. [illegible, ~40 letters] Idem δὲ [illegible, ~30 letters] τῷ Ἀεισταρχοῦ κλήρῳ, [illegible, ~45 letters] ἐὰν τῷ βίβλῳ, ταῦτα.
units.tr: Isaeus praises this law in his speech on the estate of Pyrrhus [?]. Again: the law permits a man to dispose of his property as he wishes, of the same wife, provided he leaves no male sons by her; but if he leaves daughters, [it is allowed] on these terms [ὁ γὰρ νόμος ἀξιοῖ ἐξῆναι ὅπως ἂν εἰθέλῃ τῆς τε αὐτῆς, ἐὰν μὴ παῖδας γυναικὸς καταλίπῃ ἄρρενας· ἐὰν δὲ θυγατέρας καταλίπῃ, ΕΠΙ ΤΑΥΤΑΙΣ]. The same [speaker], in the estate of Aristarchus [?] ... [?]

units.la: Adoptatis autem non licebat testamentum scribere: nam aut filios habebat superstites, aut ab intestato hereditatem eius adibant patris adoptantis propinqui.
units.tr: Adopted sons, however, were not allowed to make a will, for either they had surviving sons, or the nearest kin of the adoptive father's father took his inheritance on intestacy.

units.la: [?Τοῖς ποιησιν μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἀληθείαν· ἀλλὰ] [?ζῶντας ἐγκαταλιπόντας τὸν γνήσιον ἐποιήσαντο,] [?ἢ πλουτισθέντας ἀποδιδόναι τῷ κληρονο-] [?μένῳ τοῖς ἐξ ἀρχῆς οἰκείοις ὅσα τῶ ποιησα-] [?μένῳ.] | Adoptati testamentum ne faciunto, sed vel domum patris naturalis redeunto relicto filio legitimo, vel adoptato mortuo hereditatem eius adoptantis patris cognati adeunto.
units.tr: [Τοῖς ποιησιν μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἀληθείαν· ἀλλὰ ζῶντας ἐγκαταλιπόντας τὸν γνήσιον ἐποιήσαντο, ἢ πλουτισθέντας ἀποδιδόναι τῷ κληρονομένῳ τοῖς ἐξ ἀρχῆς οἰκείοις ὅσα τῶ ποιησαμένῳ.] Let an adopted son not make a will; but let him either return to his natural father's house, leaving the legitimate son alive, or, if the adopted son has died, let the cognates of the adoptive father take up his inheritance.

units.la: Legitur hæc Lex apud Demosthenem [?ἐν τῷ κατὰ Λεωχάρους], eaque Solonis est, vt ibidem habes: [?ὁ γὰρ τῶν Σόλωνος νόμος, οὐδὲ ἀδελφὸν τὸ ποιῆσαι ἐὰν τὸ ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας, ὅταν ποιῆται.] sed oportet, vt eo mortuo ad agnatos hereditas devoluatur, si orbus vita excesserit adoptiuus: & certè si propinqui suos subleuare Legibus tenentur, par ratio est, vt in bonorum quoque partem veniant: [?ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ νομοθέτης, οἶμαι, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰς κομιδὰς τῶν οἰκείων, καὶ τὰς ἐκδόσεις τῶν γυναικῶν τῆς ἐγγύης ἡμῖν πρὸς αὐτοῖς παροῦσιν ἡμῖν ἔτι τοὺς ἐπιτροπεύοντας, ὅτω καὶ τὰς κληρονομίας, καὶ τῷ τῶν ἀγαθῶν μετιτοίας τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἀπέδωκε.] Demosthenes ibidem: [?ἐπεὶ δὲ δίκαιον δήπου τὸ ποιητὸν ἡμῖν ποιητέος ἐπερωτᾶν, ἀλλ' ἐγκαταλείπειν μὲν γεγονότος, ὅταν δὲ τῆς ἐπιλείπης τοῖς ἡμῶν ἀποδιδόναι τὰς κληρονομίας.] Itaque pater [?τῇ φύσει] naturalis cernere non poterat hereditatem filij, quem adoptandum dederat in alienam familiam. Demosthenes cad. Orat. [?ἐπὶ δὲ τὰ νομιζόμενα ἐλήφθη, καὶ ποῖον νόμων φανεῖται, ἐρῆμου ὅτις τῶν οἴκων, τοῖς ἐγγυηταῖς ἡμῖν ἐξαγαγὼν ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας; ὅτι μὲν Δίᾳ πατὴρ ὢν τῷ πεπελυτημένῳ ἀπελαυθῶς ἐξ ἐκ πατρῴων οἴκων, καὶ οὐκέτι τῆς οὐσίας, ἐφ' ᾗ ἐγκαταλείπειν τὸν υἱόν,] ἀ̈ὼ̈ εἰς ἂν. neque vllam Lege cognationem cum agnatis patris naturalis habent adoptiui. Isæus [?ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς Ἀγυφίλου κλήρου.] [?ἔστι γὰρ ὁ Κλέων ὑπὸ αἰσχύνης Ἀγυφίλου πατὴρ, ὃς ὁ υἱὸς ὁ Τύπου, ὃν ἐξεποίησε ἐκεῖνα, αἰεὶ μάλιστα ἐξοικῶν·] [?ἐξαπέστησε δ' ἐκ τῶν ὁ πατὴρ ὁ Κλέωνος εἰς ἑαυτὸν οἶκον, καὶ ἐπὶ ἐπὶ εἰσὶν ἐν ἐκείνῳ τοῦ οἴκου, ὥστε ἡμεῖς μὲν ἐξοδ τὸν νόμον κατὰ τὸ τοῦ Ἀγυφίλου.] Neque potest adoptiuus hereditate agnatorum patris naturalis hercisc ere [?καὶ ἡμῖς] siue [?ἐπιχειρίας] iure, nisi eiurata adoptione. Isæus ibidem: [?ἐάν τις γὰρ πολύπαις ἐκποιηθῆς ἡμῶν ἐκληρονομῆσαι τὸ οἶκον, ὅταν ἐξεποιήθη, ἐὰν μὴ ἐπιμείλῃ καὶ τ' νόμον.] Patris dixi, quia à matre per adoptionem nullus alienus esse potest, neque matrem habere, nisi propriam & naturalem, siue in gente maneat, siue inde migret. Isæus [?ἐν τῷ περὶ τοῦ Ἀπολλοδώρου κλήρου.] [?μὴ ἐξ ἡ γὰρ ἐστὶν ἐκποίητος, ἀλλ' ἐμοίως ἐπάρχῃ τῷ αὐτῷ τῆς μητρὸς, καὶ ἐν τοῖς πατρῴῳ μόνῃ τῆς οἰκίας, καὶ ἐκποιητῆς.] Vnde etiam cognatorum matris hereditatem [?καὶ ἡμῖς] potest cernere. Isæus ibidem de Thrasyllo, qui in adoptionem alienæ familiæ datus fuerat, loquens, scribit egisse illum in semissem petitione hereditatis cognati materni: [?ὁ γὰρ καὶ τ' πατρὸς, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸν μητέρα καὶ τὴν Ἀπολλοδώρου τῆς Εὐπολίδος ὑἱὸς ὅ μέσος εἴληφε· καὶ τὴν ἡ ἐξῆν ἀπὸ κατὰ τούτων τὸν συγγένειαν λαχεῖν.] Quod additur in Lege, [?ἀλλὰ ζωντας ἐγκαταλιπόντας γὰρ γνήσιον ἐποιήσαντο,] alibi suo loco expofuimus.
units.tr: This law is read in Demosthenes, in the speech against Leochares, and it is Solon's, as you may see there [ὁ γὰρ τῶν Σόλωνος νόμος, οὐδὲ ἀδελφὸν τὸ ποιῆσαι ἐὰν τὸ ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας, ὅταν ποιῆται]. But it is necessary that, if the adopted son dies childless, the inheritance should pass to the agnates, since, if relatives are bound by law to support their own, it is equally right that they should also share in the goods. [Demosthenes says, in the same place, ...] Thus the natural father could not take up his son's inheritance, since he had given him into another family for adoption. Demosthenes, in the speech ... [?] and adopted sons have no kinship by law with the agnates of their natural father. Isaeus, in his speech on the estate of Agyphilus [?], says that Cleon was the father of Agyphilus ... [?] and it is not possible for an adopted son to divide the inheritance of his natural father's agnates by the law of the ... [?], unless the adoption has been renounced. Isaeus in the same place: [If anyone is adopted...] I have said "father" because through adoption no one can be a stranger to the mother, nor have a mother other than his own natural mother, whether he remains in the clan or migrates from it. Isaeus [in his speech on the estate of Apollodorus]: [...]. Hence he can also take up the inheritance of his mother's kinsmen. Isaeus in the same place, speaking of Thrasyllus, who had been given into adoption into another family, writes that he sued for a half-share of the inheritance of his maternal kinsman. [...] What is added in the law, [but if they have adopted a legitimate son while he is alive,] we have explained elsewhere in its proper place.

units.la: Filij autem inter se hereditatem paternam ex æquo diuidebant ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Sons, moreover, divided the paternal inheritance equally among themselves under this law:

units.la: [?Ἀπολῶσι τοὺς γνησίους υἱοὺς, ἰσομοίρους τὴν τῶν παππῶν.] | Omnes legitimi filij hereditatem paternam ex æquo inter se hercisciunto.
units.tr: [Ἀπολῶσι τοὺς γνησίους υἱοὺς, ἰσομοίρους τὴν τῶν παππῶν.] All legitimate sons shall divide the paternal inheritance equally among themselves.

units.la: Legem laudat Isæus [?ἐν τῷ περὶ τοῦ Φιλοκτήμονος κλήρου.] [?τὸ νόμου κελεύοντος ἀπολῶσι τοὺς γνησίους, ἰσομοίρους τὴν παππῶν.] Quinetiam idem obseruatum est incer legitimum naturalemque, & adoptiuum filium, si quos pater, postquam alterum adoptasset, genuisset, ut ex æquo hereditatem inter se diuiderent ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Isaeus cites the law in his speech on the estate of Philoctemon [τὸ νόμου κελεύοντος ἀπολῶσι τοὺς γνησίους, ἰσομοίρους τὴν παππῶν]. Indeed, the same was observed also between a legitimate son and a natural and adopted son, if the father, after adopting one, had begotten others, so that they divided the inheritance equally among themselves under this law:

units.la: Ἐὰν τοιναυτίω παῖδες ἐπιγνώσωσι, ὁ μὲν ἐκπέπεμπται ἔχει τῆς οὐσίας, καὶ κληρονομεῖν ὁμοίως ἀμφοτέρους.
units.tr: [Ἐὰν τοιναυτίω παῖδες ἐπιγνώσωσι, ὁ μὲν ἐκπέπεμπται ἔχει τῆς οὐσίας, καὶ κληρονομεῖν ὁμοίως ἀμφοτέρους.]

units.la: Si cui, postquam filium adoptauit, alij legitimi nascentur, utrque hereditatem ex æquo inter se herciscunto.
units.tr: If anyone, after adopting a son, has other legitimate sons born to him, both shall divide the inheritance equally between themselves.

units.la: Legem descripsit Isæus loco iam laudato ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς Φιλοκτήμονος κληρου-χίας καὶ Ἀμφίππου ἐν τῷ νόμῳ γέγραπται, ἐὰν τοιναυτίω παῖδες ἐπιγνώσωσι, ὁ μὲν ἐκπέπεμπται ἔχει τῆς οὐσίας, καὶ κληρονομεῖν ὁμοίως ἀμφοτέρους. Quare cautum à Philoctemone, qui Chærestratum adoptabat, testamenti tabulis, si μὴ γένοιτο αὐτῷ παῖδες ἐκ τῆς γυναικός, τότε κληρονομεῖν [?] ἑαυτοῦ.
units.tr: Isaeus has described this law in the passage already cited: [in the estate of Philoctemon and Amphippus, in the law it is written: if children are born in this way, the one who has been sent out has his share of the property, and both inherit equally] [...]. Hence Philoctemon, who was adopting Chaerestratus, provided in his will that, [if sons were not born to him from his wife, then he should inherit ...] of himself.

units.la: Hereditatem vero ab intestato adibant proximi secundum hunc à Lege definitum ordinem.
units.tr: Those nearest, however, took the inheritance on intestacy, in the order defined by the law.

units.la: ΟΣΤΙΣ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΔΙΑΘΕΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΠΟ-ΘΑΝΗ, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΚΑΤΑΛΙ-ΠΗ ΘΗΛΕΙΑΣ ΣΥΝ ΤΑΥΤΗΣΙ· ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΩΝ· ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΟΡΕΣ, ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΓΑ- Si quis intestatus moriatur, relictis filiabus, qui eas in uxores ducent, heredes sunto: si nullæ supersint, hi hereditatem ab intestato cernunto. ex primo quidem fratres defuncti germani & le- ΤΡΟΣ ΜΟΙΡΑΝ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ, Η ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΥΤΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ. ΚΡΑΤΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΡΡΕΝΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΡΕΝΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΑΥΤΩΝ ΩΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΓΕΝΕΙ ΑΓΩΤΕΡΩ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΩΣΙ ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ[?] ΜΕΧΡΙ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΩΝ[?] ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΤΟΥΣ ΜΗΤΡΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΑΝΔΡΟΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗΔ' ΕΤΕΡΩΘΕΝ ΗΝ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΕΓΓΥΤΑΤΩ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ. ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ, ΜΗΤΕ ΙΕΡΩΝ ΜΗΘ' ΟΣΙΩΝ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ.
units.tr: [ΟΣΤΙΣ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΔΙΑΘΕΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΗ, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΚΑΤΑΛΙΠΗ ΘΗΛΕΙΑΣ ΣΥΝ ΤΑΥΤΗΣΙ· ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΩΝ· ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΟΡΕΣ, ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΓΑΤΡΟΣ ΜΟΙΡΑΝ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ, Η ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΥΤΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ. ΚΡΑΤΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΡΡΕΝΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΡΕΝΩΝ, ΕΑΝ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΑΥΤΩΝ ΩΣΙ, ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΓΕΝΕΙ ΑΓΩΤΕΡΩ, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΩΣΙ ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΜΕΧΡΙ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΩΝ ΤΟΥΣ ΜΗΤΡΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΑΝΔΡΟΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗΔ' ΕΤΕΡΩΘΕΝ ΗΝ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΕΓΓΥΤΑΤΩ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ. ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ, ΜΗΤΕ ΙΕΡΩΝ ΜΗΘ' ΟΣΙΩΝ ΑΠ' ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ.] If anyone dies intestate, leaving daughters, let those who will marry them be the heirs; if no daughters survive, let these take the inheritance on intestacy. First, the full brothers of the deceased and the sons of brothers; [Greek] ... Let males, and those born of males, rule, even if they are of more remote kinship; and if no paternal kin survive up to the sons of first cousins, let the maternal kin of the man be the legal heirs by the same [law]. If none survive from either kin within these degrees, let the nearer paternal kinsman be legal heir. [Let there be no inheritance for a bastard, nor for one born of a bastard, neither of sacred nor of ... since the time of Euclides the archon.] [ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ...]

units.la: gitimi fratrum filii heredi-tatem simul adeunto. Si nulli fratres aut fratrum filii superfint, iis geniti eadem Lege hereditatem cernunto: masculi autem, iisque geniti, etiamsi remotiori cognationis sint gradu, praeferuntor. Si nulli superfint paterni proximi ad sobrinorum usque filios, materni defuncti propinqui sirempse Lege hereditatem adeunto: Si è neutra cognatione superfint intra definitum gradum: propior cognatus paternus adito. Noitho nothaeve.
units.tr: The legitimate sons of brothers shall take up the inheritance together. If there are no brothers or sons of brothers, those born of them shall take the inheritance by the same law. Males, and those born of males, are preferred, even if they are of a more remote degree of kinship. If no paternal kin survive as far as the sons of first cousins, the deceased's maternal kin shall take the inheritance by the same law. If no kin from either side survive within the defined degree, the nearer paternal kinsman shall come forward. [A bastard, male or female, ...]

units.la: Legem descripsit [illegible, ~6 letters] Demosthenes [illegible, ~6 letters] Μακαρτάτου. Obscurus autem admodum est huius Legis sensus, eruditissimoque Interpreti negotium exhibuit, vt mirum non sit si forte nos impegerimus. Existimat itaque prima Legis verba, ΟΣΤΙΣ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΔΙΑΘΕΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΓΟΘΑΝΗ, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΚΑΤΑΛΙΓΗ ΘΗΛΕΙΑΣ ΣΥΝ ΤΑΥΤΗΙΣΙ, ita debere cõcipi, ὅστις ἂν μὴ ἀρσθένως ἀποθάνῃ, ἐὰν μὲν παῖδας καταλίπῃ θηλείας, τοὺς εἰρεῖς τούτου ἐὰν δὲ μὴ καταλίπῃ παῖδας θηλείας, τοὺς τοὺς ἡμετέρους [illegible, ~8 letters] ἐς τὴν χρημάτων. & vertit, Quisquis intestatus moritur siquidem liberos muliebris sexus reliquerit, filii cũ bisce, sin minus, hi bona possidento. Verum hic nulla liberorum masculorum mentio, ipso enim naturæ iure, non tantum Solonis Lege in bona patentis veniunt, neque [?] inquit Ifæus, [?] [?] [?] sed sed [?]. Sed feminarum longe alia est ratio, erant enim ex Lege [?] τῆς Ἐπικλήρων. Cauet itaque Legislator, ut is in bona mortui ab intestato veniat, qui eius filias in vxores duxerit, id est, bona habeat ἐπὶ ΤΑΥΤΑΙΣ, vt in superioribus diximus. Quare hæc verba, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΗΜΑ-ΤΩΝ. aliò spectant: Atque Legislatoris mens hæc est: Si etiam femella proles orbus ab intestato decesserit ad hos illius hereditatem deuenire, qui sequuntur. ΕΑΝ Δ' ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ ΟΜΟΓΑΤΟΡΕΣ, ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΜΟΙΡΑΝ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ. Vocantur primum in defuncti bona germani, si quos habet, fratres, & fratrum legitimi filij, eadem ratione, eodemque cognationis iure: Fratrum enim filij, fratres (secundum hanc iuris regulam, Pater & filius pro una habentur persona.) censentur: atque inter eos, vt & inter alios, qui in eodem cognationis gradu, ἐπιχρεία iure hereditatem sibi vindicabant, intestati hereditas ex æquo diuidebatur. Quod si nulli sunt fratres, aut fratribus nati, hoc iure gaudent sorores, sororúmque liberi, & ex æquo fratris hereditatem cernunt. Ifæus [?] ... paullo post: [?] ... Quod si neque vllæ sint sorores, sororumve liberi, ceteri propinqui paterni hereditatem sibi vindicare possunt, ita tamen vt mares, & qui maribus sunt nati in eodem cognationis gradu præferantur, imò etiam genere remotiores, vsque ad sobrinorum paternorum filios. Hac cognatione paterna deficiente, ad maternam itur, atque ad hereditatem vindicandam vocantur eodem ordine & iure cognati materni. Atque in his cognationibus paternis & maternis mares præferuntur, quod locum non habet inter fratrem defuncti, alteriusque fratris liberos, aut si nulli sint fratres fratrúmue liberi, inter sororem sororisue liberos: sed ex æquo tam mares quàm feminæ hereditatem adeunt. Ifæus loco laudato. [?] [?] KPATEIN ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΡ-ΡΕΝΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΡΕΝΩΝ, οἱ αὐ ἐκ τούτων ὦσι, καὶ ΓΕ-ΝΕΙ ΑΠΩΤΕΡΩ τυγχάνοιεν ὄντες. Sed totum ordinem exponit idem Ifæus [?] [?] Ἀγνίου κλήρου. [?] [?] si quos si quos s [?] [?] [?] sed [?] [?] [?] [?] [?]. Atque ex his variis Ifæi locis omnino constat mutilam laudari à Demosthene Legem, quam ita ex Isæo supplebis. ΟΣΤΙΣ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΔΙΑΘΕΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΗΙ [?], ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΚΑΤΑΛΙΠΗΙ ΘΗΛΕΙΑΣ ΣΥΝ ΤΑΥΤΗΙΣΙ [?]. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΩΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΟΡΕΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΓΑΙΔΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΜΟΙΡΑΝ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ Η ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ἡ ἐαὶ ὦσιν ἀδελφαὶ ὁμοπατρίαι, καὶ ἐαὶ παῖδες οἱ ἐκ τούτων, τὴν τῆς παῖδος μοῖραν λαγχάνειν. ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ Η ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΓΑΙΔΕΣ ἡ ἀδελφαὶ, ἢ παῖδες ἐκ τούτων; ΕΞ ΑΥΤΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ, ΚΡΑΤΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΡΡΕΝΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΡΕΝΩΝ, &c. Sensus est: germani fratres eorumque liberi hereditatem sibi vindicent fratris ab intestato defuncti; quod si nulli superstint germani fratres eorumque liberi, germanæ sorores earumque liberi in eius bona veniant: Si vero nullum quoque superstint sorores, aut earum liberi, hereditatem cernunto iis qui nati sunt liberis fratrum vel sororum: ita tamen ut mares maribusque nati præferantur feminis etiam paullo arctiori cognatione coniunctis. Quod si intra hanc cognationem paternam vel maternam ad sobrinorum usque liberos nulli superstint, hereditatem sibi vindicare possunt è ceteris paternis propinquis, qui cognatione coniunguntur arctiori: unde intelligendus Suidas: Χηρωσαί· ὅτι μὴ ἥκοντων ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν, ἀποληξέσθαι τὰς κλήσεις ὁ νόμος συγχωρεῖ τοῖς ἐπιτρόποις ἡμῶν [?]. Atque hi dicuntur in iure Attico Χηρωσαί. Auctor Etymologici: Χηρωσαὶ ἢ λέγονται, οἱ μακρῷ τῆς οὐσίας κληρονόμοι, οἳ Ἐπίκληροι, οἱ τὴν γένεσιν ἐρήμου συγγενῶν οἴκου κληρονόμοι [?]. Hesychius: Χηρωσαί, οἱ μακρῷ τῆς οὐσίας, ἀπαιδεῖς δέ, καὶ οἱ χηρεύοντες τὸ οἶκου τῶν ἀξιῶσι κληρονομουμένων [?]. Corruptum locum corrige, καὶ οἱ χηρεύοντες τὸ οἶκον τῶν ἀξιῶσι κληρονομουμένων [?]. Ceterum, qui hereditatem sibi vindicaverant, videntur transisse in nomen & familiam illius, cuius hereditatem cernebant, quasi adoptati filii, aut ipsi filios, si quos genuerant, illius nomine censentes. Ἰσαῖος ἐν τῷ ὑπὲρ τῆς Ἀπολλοδώρου κλήρου· πάντως γὰρ οἱ πλουτοῦντες μὴ γόντες παιδίοις ποιοῦνται σφᾶς αὐτῶν, ὅπως μὴ ἐξερημώσωσι τοῖς σφετέροις αὐτῶν οἴκοις, ἀλλ᾽ ἔχειν ὡς καὶ ὁ ἐπαγγελλόμενος καὶ πάντα τὰ τοιαῦτα ἀλλοιοῦσι ποιῶσι, δὲ καὶ ἀπαιδὴς πλουτήσωσιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐὰν ποιησάμενοι καὶ ὅταν μόνον ἰδίᾳ τοῦτα γινώσκοιεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ δημοσίᾳ ὅ καινὸν τῆς πόλεως ὅπως τοῦτ᾽ ἔγνωκε· νόμῳ γὰρ τῷ Ἀρχοντι τὴν οἰκῶν, ὅπως αὐ μὴ ἐξερημῶσι, παρασπάσῃ τὸν ἀπομίμημα· ἐκ δὲ τούτου ἐπαγγελλόμενον ἐᾶσθαι, ὅτι εἰ κατελείπετο τὸν κληρον ἐάν τις οἶκος, ἐρήμους ποιοῦ τὸν οἶκον [?]. Ἀλλά τί; παρορᾶντι τοὺς ὡς ἀδελφὰς τὸν μὴ τῷ Ἀπολλοδώρου τῷ ἀδελφοῦ κληρον ἔχουσας, ὧν οἱ οὐκ εἰσαπιοῦσαι, ὅταν αὐλῆς παῖδας [?]. Quod in Lege scriptum est: ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ ΜΗΤΕ ΙΕΡΩΝ, ΜΗΘ᾽ ΟΣΙΩΝ ΑΠ᾽ ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ alibi, suóque loco expositimus: ubi tamen ista, ΑΠ᾽ ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ. sunt apposita post exactos Triginta Tyrannos: imo etiam & eiusdem quoque commatis hæc forte sunt, ΜΗΤΕ ΙΕΡΩΝ, ΜΗΘ᾽ ΟΣΙΩΝ. nam videtur Solo scripsisse tantum, ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ. colligo ex his versibus Aristophanis Avibus. ἐρῶ δὲ δὴ καὶ τὸν Σόλωνος σοι νόμον. Νόθῳ δὲ μὴ ἐξ ἀγχι- ςείῳ, παίδων ὄντων γνη- σίων. ἐαν δὲ παῖδες μὴ ὦσι γνήσιοι, τῆς ἐπιπάτω τῆ ἡμέρας, μεταναι τῆν ἔκγεμί.
units.tr: The law was described by [illegible] Demosthenes [illegible] Makartatos. The sense of this law is very obscure and has caused great difficulty even for a most learned interpreter, so it is no wonder if I too have sometimes stumbled. He thinks, therefore, that the law's opening words, "whoever dies without a will, if he leaves daughters," should be understood as follows: [ὅστις ἂν μὴ ἀρσθένως ἀποθάνῃ, ἐὰν μὲν παῖδας καταλίπῃ θηλείας, τοὺς εἰρεῖς τούτου ἐὰν δὲ μὴ καταλίπῃ παῖδας θηλείας, τοὺς τοὺς ἡμετέρους [illegible] ἐς τὴν χρημάτων]. He translates: "Whoever dies intestate, if he leaves female children, let the heirs with these take the goods; but if he leaves no female children, let these take the goods." Here, however, there is no mention of male children. For by the law of nature itself, and not merely by Solon's law, sons come into their fathers' property. Isaeus says [illegible]. But the case of women is quite different, for they were subject to the law concerning the epiklēros. The lawgiver therefore provides that whoever marries the dead man's daughters comes into the goods of the intestate, that is, holds the goods "in these" women's right, as we said above. Hence the words "but if they are not the kyrioi of the goods" look to something else. The lawgiver's intention is this: if a childless man dies intestate, leaving even a female child, his inheritance is to pass to those who come next. [ΕΑΝ Δ' ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ ΟΜΟΓΑΤΟΡΕΣ, ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΜΟΙΡΑΝ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ.] (If there are brothers of the same mother, and legitimate sons of brothers, let them take the share of the father.) First, the defunct's full brothers, if he has any, and the lawful sons of brothers are called to the goods, on the same principle and by the same right of kinship. For the sons of brothers are counted as brothers, according to this rule of law: Father and son are regarded as one person. Among them, as among others who stand in the same degree of kinship and claimed the inheritance by the epicheireia right, the inheritance of the intestate was divided equally. But if there are no brothers, or sons of brothers, this right belongs to sisters and the children of sisters, who take the brother's inheritance equally. Isaeus [illegible] a little later: [illegible]. But if there are neither sisters nor children of sisters, the other paternal relatives can claim the inheritance for themselves, provided that males and those born of males in the same degree of kinship are preferred, even those more distant in kinship, down to the sons of the paternal first cousins. When this paternal kinship fails, the inheritance passes to the maternal side, and the maternal relatives are called to claim it in the same order and by the same right. In these paternal and maternal lines males are preferred, which does not hold between the defunct's brother and the sons of another brother, or, if there are no brothers or sons of brothers, between a sister and the children of a sister; there, males and females alike take the inheritance equally. Isaeus, in the passage cited. [ΚΡΑΤΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΡΡΕΝΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΡΕΝΩΝ, οἱ αὐ ἐκ τούτων ὦσι, καὶ ΓΕΝΕΙ ΑΠΩΤΕΡΩ τυγχάνοιεν ὄντες.] (To hold [the goods] are the males and those born of males, who in turn are of them, even if they are more remote in kinship.) But the same Isaeus explains the whole order [illegible] in the case of Agnius's estate. [illegible]. From these various passages of Isaeus it is quite clear that Demosthenes cites the law in a mutilated form, which you may supplement from Isaeus as follows: [ΟΣΤΙΣ ΑΝ ΜΗ ΔΙΑΘΕΜΕΝΟΣ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΗΙ [?], ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΚΑΤΑΛΙΠΗΙ ΘΗΛΕΙΑΣ ΣΥΝ ΤΑΥΤΗΙΣΙ [?]. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΤΟΥΣ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΙΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΩΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ ΟΜΟΠΑΤΟΡΕΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΓΑΙΔΕΣ ΕΞ ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΓΝΗΣΙΟΙ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΜΟΙΡΑΝ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ, ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ Η ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΕΣ ἡ ἐαὶ ὦσιν ἀδελφαὶ ὁμοπατρίαι, καὶ ἐαὶ παῖδες οἱ ἐκ τούτων, τὴν τῆς παῖδος μοῖραν λαγχάνειν. ΕΑΝ ΜΗ ΑΔΕΛΦΟΙ ΩΣΙΝ Η ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ ΓΑΙΔΕΣ ἡ ἀδελφαὶ, ἢ παῖδες ἐκ τούτων; ΕΞ ΑΥΤΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΛΑΓΧΑΝΕΙΝ, ΚΡΑΤΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΡΡΕΝΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΡΕΝΩΝ, &c.] The sense is: full brothers and their children claim the inheritance of a brother who died intestate; if there are no full brothers and their children, full sisters and their children come into his goods; but if there are no sisters or their children either, let the inheritance go to those born of the brothers' or sisters' children, provided that males and those born of males are preferred even to females who are related by a somewhat closer kinship. If within this paternal or maternal kinship, down to the children of first cousins, there are none, they may claim the inheritance from the other paternal relatives who are related more closely. Hence Suidas is to be understood: Chērōsai: because the law permits, when those from themselves do not come, that the claims be ended by our guardians [illegible]. And these are called Chērōsai in Attic law. The author of the Etymologicum: Chērōsai are called those who are heirs of the substance without children, who are epikleroi, those who inherit a house of kin left desolate [illegible]. Hesychius: Chērōsai, those who are of the substance but childless, and those who leave the house desolate of those worthy to be inherited [illegible]. Correct the corrupt passage to read: and those who leave the house desolate of those worthy to be inherited. Moreover, those who had claimed an inheritance seem to have passed into the name and family of the man whose estate they were taking, as if they were adopted sons, or themselves counted the sons they had begotten under his name. Isaeus, in his speech on the estate of Apollodorus: For wealthy men who have no children generally adopt for themselves, so that they do not leave their houses desolate, but as the one who makes the claim and all such things they do, and if they are rich and childless, not only privately do they make this known, but also publicly, as the city has decided; for the law commands the archon to take care of the house, lest it be left desolate, and from this the claimant is to be allowed, because if the estate were left to a house, the house would be made desolate [illegible]. But what then? Overlooking those who, as sisters, do not hold the estate of Apollodorus's brother... [illegible]. As for what is written in the law: [ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ ΜΗΤΕ ΙΕΡΩΝ, ΜΗΘ᾽ ΟΣΙΩΝ ΑΠ᾽ ΕΥΚΛΕΙΔΟΥ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΟΣ] (nor may a bastard or one not born of a bastard be near to the sacred things or the holy things, from the archonship of Euclides onward), I have explained it elsewhere and in its proper place, where, however, the words from the archonship of Euclides are added after the thirty tyrants were removed. Indeed, perhaps even the words nor of holy things in the same clause are from a later hand, since Solon seems to have written only: [ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ] (nor may a bastard or one not born of a bastard be near). I gather this from these verses of Aristophanes' Birds: I will also recite for you the law of Solon. To a bastard, not close, while there are legitimate children. But if there are no legitimate children, let the nearest kinsman take it, and the estate go to him. [ἐρῶ δὲ δὴ καὶ τὸν Σόλωνος σοι νόμον. Νόθῳ δὲ μὴ ἐξ ἀγχι-ςείῳ, παίδων ὄντων γνησίων. ἐαν δὲ παῖδες μὴ ὦσι γνήσιοι, τῆς ἐπιπάτω τῆ ἡμέρας, μεταναι τῆν ἔκγεμί.]

units.la: Neque poterant Nothi hereditatem paternam hercisci, extante vel unica filia legitima: Γυναικὸς μὲν ἔσῃς γυναῖκες, νόμου δὲ υἱοῦ, μὴ κληρονομεῖν τὸν νόμον τὰ πατρῷα.
units.tr: Nor could the bastard claim his father's inheritance while even a single legitimate daughter survived: [Γυναικὸς μὲν ἔσῃς γυναῖκες, νόμου δὲ υἱοῦ, μὴ κληρονομεῖν τὸν νόμον τὰ πατρῷα.] (Of a legitimate wife, of a legitimate son, the bastard shall not inherit the paternal estate by law.)

units.la: Laudat hanc Legem Scholiastes Comici ad Aues: νόμος ὧ Ἀθηναίοις, γνη-σίας μὲν ἔσης γυναικὸς, νόθου δ᾽ υἱοῦ μὴ κληρονομεῖν τὸν νόθον τὰ πατρῷα, è quo Sui-das in Ἐπικλῆρος, & hoc spectant Pistheteri ad Herculem verba apud Aristo-phanem:
units.tr: The commentator on Aristophanes' Birds cites this law: There is a law at Athens: when there is a legitimate wife, a bastard son shall not inherit the paternal estate [νόμος ὧ Ἀθηναίοις, γνησίας μὲν ἔσης γυναικὸς, νόθου δ᾽ υἱοῦ μὴ κληρονομεῖν τὸν νόθον τὰ πατρῷα], from which Suidas (under Epiklēros) also quotes it; and to this refer the words of Pistheteros to Heracles in Aristophanes: [illegible].

units.la: τὴν δὲ παπεῶων οὐσὴ ἀχαρῆ μέτεσί σοι τῆς τοῖς νόμοις. νόθος δὲ εἰ καὶ γνήσιος.
units.tr: "Your mother's ... you have no share in the laws. A bastard, even if he is born of a citizen, ..." [τὴν δὲ παπεῶων οὐσὴ ἀχαρῆ μέτεσί σοι τῆς τοῖς νόμοις. νόθος δὲ εἰ καὶ γνήσιος.]

units.la: Ac ne vllo quidem modo aut iure in bona parentis veniebant: Nam cognati ἀνεψιάς iure ab intestato hereditatem cernebant illius, qui decessisset nullo superstite legitimo libero, quanquam Nothos sustulisset, vt è praecedenti Lege constat: Hinc apud Comicum negat Pistheterus Herculem Iouis hereditatem posse adire, quia nothus est, & minatur Neptunum eam sibi ἀνεψιάς iure vindicaturum & asserturum, vt qui sit Iouis frater. Ἔστι ὁ Ποσειδῶν ἀδελφὸς ὡς ἐπαιρῆ σε νῦν ἀὐξεπαῖ σου τῆ πατρῷων κληρονομεῖν, Φάσκων ἀδελφὸς αὐτὸς εἴη γνήσιος.
units.tr: Nor could bastards in any way, by law or otherwise, come into their father's goods. For cousins on the mother's side (ἀνεψιάς) took up his inheritance by right of intestacy when a man died leaving no legitimate child, even though he had raised a bastard, as is clear from the law cited above. Hence in the comedian Pistheterus denies that Heracles can take up the inheritance of Zeus, because he is a bastard, and threatens that Poseidon will claim and assert it for himself by right of kinship (ἀνεψιάς), since he is Zeus's brother: "Poseidon is Zeus's brother, so that he, though he is a bastard, may now claim the paternal inheritance, saying that he himself is the legitimate brother." [Ἔστι ὁ Ποσειδῶν ἀδελφὸς ὡς ἐπαιρῆ σε νῦν ἀὐξεπαῖ σου τῆ πατρῷων κληρονομεῖν, Φάσκων ἀδελφὸς αὐτὸς εἴη γνήσιος.]

units.la: Non tamen omnino expertes erant partis de paternis bonis: nam poterant illis dari ad quinque minas τῆ νοθίων nomine: Τοῖς Νόθοις μέχρι πέντε μνᾶς καταλιμπάνειν νόν.
units.tr: Nevertheless, bastards were not wholly excluded from a share of the paternal goods, for something could be given to them, up to five minas, under the name of "bastard's portion" (τῆ νοθίων). "The law allows one to leave bastards up to five minas." [Τοῖς Νόθοις μέχρι πέντε μνᾶς καταλιμπάνειν νόν.]

units.la: Habes apud Aristophanis Interpretem Auibus, quem descripsit Suidas in Ἐπικλῆρος. νόμος ὧ Ἀθηναίοις, τοῖς Νόθοις μέχρι πέντε μνᾶς καταλιμπάνειν. Suidas alibi ὁ Ἀρχιάτος ὁ τοῖς Νόθοις ἀπὸ ἡμέρας ἐδίδοσθαι, [illegible, ~12 letters] idque τὰ Νόθια dixerunt. Definit Legislator, si Scholiastæ Comici, si Suidæ credimus, τῶν Νόθων summam intra minas quinque: At ille idem Suidas, & is, à quo accepit Harpocration in Νόθια, minas decem definiunt: Νόθια, τὰ τοῖς Νόθοις διδόμενα ἐκ τῆς παρῳκίας ὅτι ἡ ἐκλήσις. ὧ ἡ μέχρι χιλίων δραχμῶν. huiusque rei auctores laudant Lysiam, si titulus non mentitur auctorem ἐν τῷ πρὸς Καλλιφῶντα ξενίας, & Isæum ἐν τῷ πρὸς Λεωσθένη Ἐπικλήσεως. Verum haec, vt puto, facile inter se conciliari possunt. Nam nobis quidem videntur νόθια fuisse in Solonis Legibus minæ quinque, siue quingentæ drachmæ: at postea mutauit, atque decem minas siue mille drachmas in Νόθια dari placuit, vt de Pentacosiomedimnorum dote, quam τῆς Θέσεως dabant, adnotat Aristophanes Grammaticus: Atque hæc certa sunt: iam vero promittam capillum, incipiamque hariolari. Videntur tot in Νόθια datæ drachmæ siue minæ, quot impendebantur à Pentacosiomedimnis, aut Equitibus, aut Zygitis, in elocandis & dotandis orbis puellis. Quare hæ quingentæ drachmæ, quæ Νόθια dicuntur, Pentacosiomedimnorum tantum fuerunt: neque Equites aut Zygitæ hoc modulo, sed eadem illorum analogia, quæ in conferenda orbarum dote. Argumento est, quod Νόθια bonorum paternorum non sint pars decima, sed multo minus: hinc enim ostendit Ifæus ex Endij persona εἰ τοῦ Ἐπα τὰς Γύρρου [?], Phylen notham fuisse, quia bonorum paternorum non decimam partem ei in dotem dedit, sed multo minus, τὰ Νόθια scilicet, drachmas mille: (erat enim Endius è Pentacosiomedimnis.) Cedebat autem, vt ibidem docet Ifæus, decima hereditatis pars in dotem siue legitimam: Quare neque Equites, neque Zygitæ νόθια dabant mille drachmas: non enim tot, vt plurimum, drachmarum erat decima pars bonorum, siue Equitum, siue Zygitarum, vnde neque etiam tot drachmarum erant τὰ νόθια, quæ dabant Equites, aut Zygitæ, cum in τὰ Νόθια non impendatur decima bonorum pars paternorum. Illis autem solis Nothis τὰ Νόθια dabantur, qui illius vere liberi nothi censebantur: vnde Cynosargis conueniebant, quod alibi è Nonno & Diogeniano diximus, vt censerentur. Quod vero negare videtur apud Aristophanem Auibus Pistheterus, Leges non sinere dari à patre moriturô τὰ Νόθια nothis, commode est intelligendum. Comici hi sunt versus:
units.tr: You have this in the scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds, which Suidas copied under Ἐπικλῆρος: "A law of the Athenians: one may leave bastards up to five minas." [νόμος ὧ Ἀθηναίοις, τοῖς Νόθοις μέχρι πέντε μνᾶς καταλιμπάνειν.] Suidas elsewhere says that the bastard's portion was given to bastards from the day ... [illegible, about twelve letters], and they called it "the bastards' things" (τὰ Νόθια). According to the scholiast on the comedian, and to Suidas, the lawgiver fixed the sum for bastards at no more than five minas. But the same Suidas, and the authority from whom Harpocration took his account under Νόθια, put it at ten minas: "Nothia: the things given to bastards out of the inheritance, which is the portion; up to a thousand drachmas." For this they cite Lysias, if the title is right, as author in his speech against Callifon on hospitality (ἐν τῷ πρὸς Καλλιφῶντα ξενίας), and Isaeus in his speech against Leosthenes on the claim to an heiress (ἐν τῷ πρὸς Λεωσθένη Ἐπικλήσεως). But, as I think, these can easily be reconciled. For it seems to me that in Solon's laws the nothia were five minas, or five hundred drachmas; but later the amount was changed, and it was decided that ten minas, or a thousand drachmas, should be given as nothia, as Aristophanes the grammarian notes concerning the dowry of the pentacosiomedimni, which they gave as thesis. These things are certain. Now I will let my hair grow and begin to guess. It seems that as many drachmas or minas were given as nothia as were spent by the pentacosiomedimni, or the knights, or the zeugitae, in marrying off and dowering orphaned girls. Hence these five hundred drachmas called nothia were only those of the pentacosiomedimni; the knights and zeugitae did not use this measure, but the same proportion that applied in providing a dowry for orphans. The evidence is that the nothia were not a tenth part of the paternal goods, but much less. For Isaeus shows, in the person of Endius, that Phyle, the son of Gyrrhus, was a bastard, because he gave her as dowry not a tenth part of the paternal goods, but much less, namely the nothia, a thousand drachmas (for Endius was one of the pentacosiomedimni). Moreover, as Isaeus teaches in the same place, a tenth part of the inheritance went as a legitimate dowry. Therefore neither the knights nor the zeugitae gave the thousand drachmas as nothia; for usually the tenth part of the goods of knights or zeugitae was not that many drachmas, and so the nothia given by knights or zeugitae were not that many drachmas either, since a tenth part of the paternal goods was not spent on nothia. But the nothia were given only to those bastards who were considered the true children of that man; hence they gathered at the Cynosarges, which we have said elsewhere, from Nonnus and Diogenianus, in order to be counted. But as to what Pistheterus in Aristophanes' Birds seems to deny, that the laws did not allow a dying father to give the nothia to bastards, this is to be understood properly. These are the verses of the comedian: [ὑπ. τί δ' ἂν ὦ ὁ πατὴρ ἐμοὶ δίδῳ τὰ χρήματα καὶ Νόθῳ' ... ὑπὸ Διὸς ... ἐπεὶ ὁ νόμος αὐτὸν οὐκ ἐᾷ. ...]

units.la: ὑπ. τί δ' ἂν ὦ ὁ πατὴρ ἐμοὶ δίδῳ τὰ χρήματα καὶ Νόθῳ' ... ὑπὸ Διὸς ... ἐπεὶ ὁ νόμος αὐτὸν οὐκ ἐᾷ. ἐπεὶ ὁ Γοργίας ... ὡς ἐπαίρει σι ... τῷ ἀφίξεται, ... τῷ πατρῴῳ ... χρημάτων, φάσκων ἀδελφὸς αὐτῷ τὴν γένος.
units.tr: [Pistheterus:] "Why should my father give the money to me and to the bastard ..., since the law does not allow it ... Gorgias ... claims ... he will come ... of the paternal ... money, saying that he is his brother by birth." [ὑπ. τί δ' ἂν ὦ ὁ πατὴρ ἐμοὶ δίδῳ τὰ χρήματα καὶ Νόθῳ' ... ὑπὸ Διὸς ... ἐπεὶ ὁ νόμος αὐτὸν οὐκ ἐᾷ. ἐπεὶ ὁ Γοργίας ... ὡς ἐπαίρει σι ... τῷ ἀφίξεται, ... τῷ πατρῴῳ ... χρημάτων, φάσκων ἀδελφὸς αὐτῷ τὴν γένος.]

units.la: Quibus è verbis, si quid iudico, docemur, Leges non sinere, vt nothus, qui à patre, dum erat in viuis, τὰ Νόθια non acceperit, eo mortuo sibi dari postulet ex eius bonis, nam Solonis Lex hic obtinet, ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ. Itaque τὰ Νόθια nothis in manum dabantur à patre, dû adhuc erat in viuis, atque id est, quod his indicat verbis Suidas. Ὁ ἐχρύσιον δὲ τοῖς νόμοις ... ὅπως οὐκ ἐξὸν αὐτοῖς κληρονομεῖν. Sed mittamus hos nothos, qui, quod olim de Megarensibus dictum, ὅτι ἐν λόγῳ, ὅτι ἐν ἀριθμῷ. Qui hereditatem ab intestato adibant, si plures essent eodem cognationis gradu, ex æquo in partem illius veniebant;
units.tr: From these words, if I judge rightly, we learn that the laws did not allow a bastard, who had not received the nothia from his father while he was alive, to demand them from his estate after the father's death; for Solon's law holds here: "Let no bastard have a bastard's portion, nor any bastard be a claimant." [ΝΟΘΩΙ ΔΕ ΜΗΔΕ ΝΟΘΗΙ ΜΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΑΓΧΙΣΤΕΙΑΝ.] So the nothia were handed over to bastards by their father while he was still alive; and this is what Suidas indicates in these words: "...[as he would have given it, were it] not lawful for them to inherit." But let us leave these bastards, who, as was once said of the Megarians, are "in the account, and in the count." Those who took up an inheritance on intestacy, if there were several of the same degree of kinship, came into a share of it equally.

units.la: Τοῦ μέσους ἕκαστον λαχόντος.
units.tr: "Each one obtaining by lot his share of the middle degree." [Τοῦ μέσους ἕκαστον λαχόντος.]

units.la: Legitur Lex ista apud Ifæum ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς Ἀγνίου κλήρου. Διαρρήδην ὁ νόμος κελεύει, τὰ μέσους ἕκαστον λαγχάνειν.
units.tr: This law is read in Isaeus, in the speech on the estate of Agnius. The law expressly orders that each one obtain by lot a share of the middle degree. [Legitur Lex ista apud Ifæum ... Διαρρήδην ὁ νόμος κελεύει, τὰ μέσους ἕκαστον λαγχάνειν.]

units.la: Hereditatem qui sibi vindicabat siue κατὰ δίκην τὴν Ἀφ' ... ἀρχῆς, siue ἐγγυήσεως iure, τῇ κατ' ἄνος, debebat apud Prætorem, apud quem λαγχάνοι ... κλήρων, ... Ἐπικλήρων ... ἀπὸ ... vindicare & sibi asserere, ... ... Solonis hac Lege.
units.tr: Whoever claimed an inheritance for himself, whether by a suit from the beginning (κατὰ δίκην) or by right of a pledge (ἐγγυήσεως), had to do so before the praetor, before whom he would obtain by lot ... claim and assert it for himself, ... by this law of Solon.

units.la: Hereditatem: Ifæus, Oratio de Agnij hereditate.
units.tr: On the inheritance: Isaeus, speech on the inheritance of Agnius.

units.la: ΚΛΗΡΟΥΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝ ΟΣΟΙ ΕΙΣΙ ΜΗΝΕΣ ΠΛΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΣΚΙΡΡΟΦΟΡΙΩΝΟΣ, ΑΝΕΠΙΑΙΚΟΝ ΔΕ ΚΛΗΡΟΝ ΜΗ ΕΧΕΙΝ. De hereditatibus iudicio experiuntor, toto vertente anno, excepto mense Scirrhophorione: hereditatem nisi in iure vindicatam ne adeunto.
units.tr: "Those who are within the degrees shall allot the estate, except in the month Scirrophorion, and no one shall enter an estate that is not claimed in court." [ΚΛΗΡΟΥΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝ ΟΣΟΙ ΕΙΣΙ ΜΗΝΕΣ ΠΛΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΣΚΙΡΡΟΦΟΡΙΩΝΟΣ, ΑΝΕΠΙΑΙΚΟΝ ΔΕ ΚΛΗΡΟΝ ΜΗ ΕΧΕΙΝ.] Inheritances are claimed in court, throughout the year, except in the month Scirrophorion; no one shall enter an inheritance unless it has been claimed in court.

units.la: Legem hanc laudat Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Στέφανον ... β. sed
units.tr: Demosthenes cites this law in the speech against Stephanus, book 2, but

units.la: Legis verba, quæ erant in mendo, ita emendauimus: auctor Demosthenes, qui ante dixerat, ἀποδικάσαι μὲν ἐξεῖναι ἐχθὲς κλήρου[?]. Vult igitur cum, qui hereditatem a se delatam iure credit, iudicio experiri, & sibi apud Prætorem vindicare, (id enim est ΚΛΗΡΟΥΝ ΤΟΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝ) λαχεῖν, inquit Demosthenes, τὸ κλῆρον, εἴτε τῷ δόντι αὐτῷ προσήκει, εἴτε τῷ ἡμῖν. Hæc ἐπιδικασία fiebat apud Prætorem singulis anni mensibus, excepto Scirrhophorione, quia affecto iam anno referendis potius rationibus, quam iuri dicundo vacabant, resque erant prolatæ. Debebat igitur, qui sibi hereditatem vindicabat, ceteros in ius vocare, qui possent de hereditate controuersiam facere. Demosthenes: νόμος κελεύει τὸν ἐπιδικασάμενον ἐὰν ἡ χρῆσις τὸ κλῆρον προσκαλεῖσθαι, ἐάν τις βούλῃ ἀμφισβητεῖν. alioqui ipso iure nulla erat hæc ἐπιδικασία. Demosthenes è Lege mox describenda: ἐὰν ὁ μὴ προσκαλεσάμενος ἐπιδικάσηται, ἀτελὴς ἔσται ἡ ἐπιδικασία. Itaque præco proclamabat, si quis vellet iudicio experiri aduersus eum, qui sibi vindicabat. Demosthenes ὁ ὡς προς Μαχάρταν[?] ἡ τῆς χώρας κληρουχίας, εἴ τις ἀμφισβητεῖ ἡ προσκαλεῖσθαι, βούλεται τὸν κλῆρον τοῦ Ἀγεῖου, ἢ τῷ ἡμῖν, ἢ τῷ δήμῳ[?]. Qui sibi vindicabat ἀμφισβητῶν dicebatur: qui vero contra sibi asserebat, προσκαλεσάμενος[?], quod fiebat cum sponsione & sacramento partis bonorum decimæ, quam pendebat, si causa cecidisset. Pollux Lib VIII ἀμφισβήτησις λέγει, ὅστις ἀμφισβητεῖ, κλῆρου κατέπαυσε, ὡς οὐκ ὄντος τοῦ ὁ πέπαυσαι[?]. Actio hæc proprie dicitur ἀπογραφή. Harpocration, ἀπογραφὴ, ἰδίως λέγει ἐπὶ τῶν τὸ κλῆρον διὰ δικασίας, ἀπογραφὴ ἡ καλουμένη, ὅταν τις ὡς ἁπλοῦς ὢν τῆς τεταλαιπωρημένος, ἐπὶ φάσκει προσήκειν τὸ κλῆρον τοῦ ἡμῖν δόντι. Pollux Lib. VIII. ἀπογραφὴ δ' ἐκαλεῖτο ἐπὶ τὰ κατὰ ἡμᾶς ἀμφισβητούντων. Male idem Harpocratio confundit ἀμφισβήτησιν & ἐξεμαρτυρίαν. Erat enim in hoc negotio ἐξεμαρτυρία, antestatio, neque hunc ἀμφισβητοῦντα, neque illum προσκαλεσάμενον esse audiendos de controuersia quam faciunt, cum defuncto superstites sint liberi. Pollux Lib. laudato ἐξεμαρτυρία ἡ, ὅστις ἐξεμαρτύρησεν ἐπιδικάσει τὴν κλῆρον, ὡς ὄντος ἡμῖν.
units.tr: We have corrected the words of the law, which were corrupt, as follows. The author Demosthenes, who had said before that it is permitted to contest an inheritance ... [ἀποδικάσαι μὲν ἐξεῖναι ἐχθὲς κλήρου[?]]. He means therefore that one who believes an inheritance delivered to him by right should bring a suit and claim it for himself before the praetor (for this is "to allot the estate", ΚΛΗΡΟΥΝ ΤΟΝ ΚΛΗΡΟΝ), "to obtain by lot" the estate, says Demosthenes, "whether it belongs to him who gave it or to us." This claim (epidikasia) was made before the praetor in each month of the year, except Scirrophorion, because at the end of the year they were occupied with rendering accounts rather than with administering justice, and the business was postponed. Therefore whoever claimed the inheritance for himself had to summon the others who might contest the inheritance. Demosthenes: "The law orders that the claimant, if he wishes, shall summon whoever wants to dispute the estate." Otherwise, by law itself, this claim was void. Demosthenes, from the law to be described shortly: "If one who has not summoned the others makes a claim, the claim will be void." So the herald proclaimed if anyone wished to contest by suit against the one who claimed for himself. Demosthenes, in the speech ... on the allotment of land ... if anyone disputes or summons, he wishes to obtain the estate ... for himself, or for us, or for the people. He who claimed for himself was called the disputant (ἀμφισβητῶν); but he who asserted against him was called the one who had summoned (προσκαλεσάμενος), which was done with a sworn deposit from the party of a tenth part of the goods, which he would forfeit if the case went against him. Pollux, book 8: "Amphisbetesis: whoever disputes, having dropped the claim, as though ... ." This action is properly called apographe.
