Harpocration: "Apographe, used especially of those who claim an estate by suit, is the so-called apographe, when someone, being a single person and wearied, says that the estate belongs to him who gave it to us." Pollux, book 8: "Apographe was the name for the claims of those who dispute among us." Harpocration wrongly confuses amphisbetesis and exemartyria. For in this business there was an exemartyria, a calling of witnesses, and neither the disputant nor the one who summoned was to be heard about the controversy they raised, since the deceased had living children. Pollux, in the work cited: "Exemartyria is when one who has called witnesses claims the estate, as though it belonged to us."

units.la: Neque tantum mouebatur controuersia, cum primum apud Prætorem vindicabatur hereditas, sed etiam de asserta atq; adita licebat aduersus illum iudicio experiri, qui sibi vindicauerat: huius actionis ordo præscribitur illa Lege.
units.tr: Nor was the dispute only stirred up when the inheritance was first claimed before the praetor. Once the estate had been claimed and entered upon, it was also permitted to contest it at law against the one who had claimed it for himself. The procedure for this action is laid down in that law.

units.la: ΕΑΝ Δ' ΕΠΙΔΕΔΙΚΑΣΜΕΝΟΥ ΑΜΦΙΣ-ΒΗΤΗΙ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΗΡΟΥ ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΕΙΣΩΙ ΤΟΝ ΕΠΙΔΕΔΙΚΑΣΜΕΝΟΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΝ ΑΡΧΟΝΤΑ, ΚΑΘΑΠΕΡ ΕΠΙ ΤΩΝ ΑΛ-ΛΩΝ ΔΙΚΩΝ, ΠΑΡΑΚΑΤΑΒΟΛΑΣ Δ' ΕΙ-ΝΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΑΜΦΙΣΒΗΤΟΥΝΤΙ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΕΣΑΜΕΝΟΣ ΕΠΙΔΙΚΑ-ΣΗΤΑΙ, ΑΤΕΛΗΣ ΕΣΤΑΙ Η ΕΠΙΔΙΚΑ-ΣΙΑ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΗΡΟΥ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΖΗ-Ο ΕΠΙΔΙΚΑΣΑΜΕΝΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΗΡΟΥ ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΕΙΣΩΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΑΥΤΑ ΩΙ Η ΓΡΟΘΕΣΜΙΑ ΜΗΓΩ. ΕΞΙΚΕΙΤΗΝ Δ' ΑΜΦΙΣΒΗΤΗΣΙΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΑΡΧΟΝ-
units.tr: "But if someone who has been awarded the estate is disputed, the claimant shall summon the awardee before the archon, as in the other suits, and the disputant shall make the deposit. But if the awardee does not summon him and thereby claims the estate, the award of the estate shall be void. And if the awardee of the estate does not live, the summons shall be made against him in accordance with these provisions... the dispute shall go to the archon, whoever holds the property." [ΕΑΝ δὲ ἐπιδικασμένου ἀμφισβητῇ τοῦ κλήρου προσκαλεῖσθαι τὸν ἐπιδικασάμενον πρὸς τὸν ἄρχοντα, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων δικῶν, παρακαταβολὰς δὲ εἶναι τῷ ἀμφισβητοῦντι. ἐὰν δὲ μὴ προσκαλεσάμενος ἐπιδικάζηται, ἀτελὴς ἔσται ἡ ἐπιδικασία τοῦ κλήρου. ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ζῇ ὁ ἐπιδικασάμενος τοῦ κλήρου, προσκαλεῖσθαι κατὰ ταῦτα ... ἐξικέσθαι τὴν ἀμφισβήτησιν εἶναι τῷ ἄρχοντι, ὅτι καθότι ἐπιδικάσατο, οὗ ἂν ἔχῃ τὰ χρήματα.]

units.la: Qui litem mouet ei, qui antea iudicio hereditatem sibi vindicauit, illum in ius ad Prætorem vocato, vt fieri amat in alijs causis: Sacramentio autē qui in ius vocat contendito: nisi in ius vocauerit, iudicium, quo sibi hereditatē vindicauerit, irritū esto: Si decesserit qui hereditatem iudicio creuerat, vocatio tamē in ius fiat ab eo, cui non præscribit tempus. Ius sub Archonte esto, quemadmodū iudiΤΙ ΚΑΘΟΤΙ ΕΠΙΔΙΚΑΣΑΤΟ, ΟΥ ΑΝ ΕΧΗ ΤΑ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΑ.
units.tr: Whoever brings the suit against the one who earlier claimed the inheritance by judgement shall summon him to court before the praetor, as is usual in other cases. The one who summons him to court must make the sacramentum deposit. Unless he summons him to court, the judgement by which he claimed the inheritance shall be void. If the one who claimed the inheritance by judgement has died, the summons to court shall nevertheless be made by the one to whom no time is prescribed. Let the law be under the archon, just as the judgement is, whoever claimed it, whoever holds the property.

units.la: Legem descripsit Demosthenes ὁ τῆς κατὰ Μακαρίαν, de eaque ista forte habet ... [?] ... ἐπιδικασάμενον ... ἔχοντες τὸν κλῆρον ... [?] ... καὶ τῆς βουλήσεως ἀμφισβητῶν. Sed ista potius referenda sunt ad praecedentem Legem, quanquam idem ordo observabatur & ab eo qui primum hereditatem sibi iudicio vindicabat, & ab illo, qui rursum ei, qui hereditatem iudicio creuerat, litem mouebat: Vocare in ius necesse habebat, qui contendebat, alioqui nulla erat haec hereditatis petitio. Pollux Lib. VIII. [illegible, ~20 letters] ... ὁ γὰρ ἀμφισβητῶν ... [?] ... Nimirum idem ordo, vt diximus, observabatur ab eo, qui rursum iudicio vellet experiri aduersus illum, qui in iure iam eam sibi hereditatem asseruerat, qui obseruatus quoque fuerat, qui iudicio hereditatem adierat: ita enim debent postrema haec Legis verba legi: ΚΑΘΟΤΙ ΕΠΕΔΙΚΑΣΑΤΟ ΟΣ ΑΝ ΕΧΗ ΤΑ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΑ. Quod si is qui hereditatem adierat, fato iam esset functus suo, sirempse Lege vocandus erat in ius qui in illius bonis erat, si nondum praescriberet tempus, quod erat annorum quinque. Harpocration: [?] ... Δημοσθένης ... Ῥήτωρ ... Ἰσαῖος ... Μενέστρατον ... Eaque de re haec Lex scripta est.
units.tr: Demosthenes described this law in his speech Against Macartatus, and perhaps he has the following about it ... [?] ... claiming the estate by judgment ... holding the estate ... and of the will disputing [?]. But these words are rather to be referred to the preceding law, although the same order was observed both by the one who first claimed the inheritance for himself by judgment and by the one who in turn brought a suit against the person who had been awarded the inheritance by judgment. The one who contended was bound to summon the other to court; otherwise this claim to the inheritance was void. Pollux, Book VIII. [illegible, about twenty letters] ... for the one who contends ... [?] ... Doubtless, as we have said, the same order was observed by the one who wished in turn to proceed by judgment against him who had already been awarded that inheritance in court, and which was also observed by the one who had entered upon the inheritance by judgment. For the final words of the law should be read thus: "whoever holds the property, as the award was made." If the one who had entered upon the inheritance had already died, then by this law he was to be summoned to court who held his property, provided the time limit had not yet run, which was five years. Harpocration: [?] ... Demosthenes ... the orator ... Isaeus ... Menestratus ... And on this matter this law was written.

units.la: ΓΕΝΤΕ ΕΠΙ ΔΙΚΑΣΑΣΘΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΗΡΟΥ, ΕΠΕΙ-ΔΗ ΠΑΛΙΝ Ο ΚΛΗΡΟΝΟΜΟΣ.
units.tr: [ΓΕΝΤΕ ΕΠΙΔΙΚΑΣΑΣΘΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΗΡΟΥ, ΕΠΕΙΔΗ ΠΑΛΙΝ Ο ΚΛΗΡΟΝΟΜΟΣ.] Whether the estate is to be claimed by judgment, since again the heir ...

units.la: Legem habes apud Isaeum ὁ τῆς ... τῆς Πύρρου κλήρου. ὁ δὲ νόμος πῶς ἐπὶ κλήρου δικάσασθαι τὸν κλῆρον, ἐπειδὴ πάλιν ὁ κληρονόμος.
units.tr: You have the law in Isaeus, in the speech concerning the estate of Pyrrhus. The law: how the estate is to be contested by judgment, since again the heir ... [ὁ δὲ νόμος πῶς ἐπὶ κλήρου δικάσασθαι τὸν κλῆρον, ἐπειδὴ πάλιν ὁ κληρονόμος.]

units.la: DE TVTELIS. TITVLVS SEPTIMVS.
units.tr: On Guardianship. Title Seven.

units.la: Maximam habuit Solo orphanorum pupillorumque curam: cum enim nota sint illa apud Saryricum vota,
units.tr: Solon took the greatest care of orphans and wards. For those well-known prayers of Saryricus are familiar:

units.la: Pupillum vt vtinam, quem proximus heres Impello, expungam.
units.tr: "Would that I might strike off the ward whom my nearest heir is pressing me to remove."

units.la: pupillorum vitae consulere ac cauere voluit hac Lege:
units.tr: By this law he wished to look after and safeguard the lives of wards.

units.la: Μὴ ἐπιτροπεύειν, εἰς ὃν ἡ οὐσία ἔρχεται, τῶν ὀρφανῶν πλουτισμῶν.
units.tr: Not to act as guardian of orphans when the estate passes into one's own hands, for the enrichment of the orphans [Μὴ ἐπιτροπεύειν, εἰς ὃν ἡ οὐσία ἔρχεται, τῶν ὀρφανῶν πλουτισμῶν].

units.la: Tutor is ne esto, qui agnationis iure hereditatem pupilli potest hercisci.
units.tr: Let no one be tutor who, by right of agnation, can claim a share of the ward's inheritance by partition.

units.la: Referunt hanc Solonis Legē Diogenes Laërtius in eius vita: Nolebat igitur, aut consanguineos, aut agnatos [?] , quia mortuis pupillis ante vicesimum aetatis annum, cū non possent [?] , hereditatem adibant, & sibi vindicabant [?] . Non tamē excludūtur à tutela omnes omnino gentiles: nā Auctor Erymologici inter [?] , de quibus in superioribus diximus, recēset tutores siue curatores [?] . κληρονόμοι, οἳ Ἐπίτροποι, οἱ τῆς οὐσίας τῷ ἐρήμου συνήθωλ[?] οἷον κληρονόμοι. Optime, quia, quanquam Solonis Lege ei non liceret ἐπιτροπεύειν, qui si quid pupillis, περὶ ἐπιδικεῖς ἦσαν[?], humanitus accidisset, proximus ἀγχιστεὺς υἱὸς heres in bona veniebat, tamen tam remota cum pupillis cognatione coniungebantur, ut nulla spes esset heredes ἀγχιστεὺς υἱὸς fore. Erant autem hi Ἐπίτροποι, vel testamento, vel ab Archonte dati: Testamento datos fuisse constat è Demosthenis Orationibus contra Aphobum & Onetorem, unde eidem ἐν τῷ Ἐπιφανοῦ ξυνδικῶν[?] α. dicuntur ἐπιτροπεύεσθαι τῷ ἡλικίᾳ[?]. Ab Archonte dari scribit Pollux Lib. VIII. ὁ ἡ Ἀρχων ἐπιμελητὴς Ἐπίτροπων κατέστησε[?]. Lege enim, quam in sequentibus reddemus, Deo dante, orphani Archontis curæ committebantur: quare oportebat Archonti significare hos pupillos esse, & illos testamento tutores esse datos, unde Isæus ἐν τῷ Φιλοκτήμονος κλήσεω[?]. Ἐπηγγέλοντο τῷ παιδὶ τούτῳ πρὸς τὸν Ἀρχοντα, ἐπηγγέλλοντες σφᾶς αὐτοὺς Ἐπίτροπους. Tutores autem isti, siue testamento, siue ab Archonte dati, potestatem habebant in pupillos, qui illis erant crediti: nam tutela est, ut Servius definit, vis ac potestas in capite libero, ad tuendum eum, qui propter ætatem suam sponte se defendere nequit. Leg. I. D. de tutelis. unde Æschines ἐν τῷ Τιμάρχου illos vocat τὴν παίδων κηδεμόνας[?], habebant quoque potestatem in bona, & ea omnia faciebant, quæ pupilli facere tenebantur, donec adoleuissent. Isæus ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς Κλεωνύμου κλήρου. ὁρῶν ἡμᾶς ἐπιτροπεύομένους ὑπὸ Δήμου, καὶ διδοὺς μὴ πλαυτίσας αὐτὸς ἐπὶ παιδὰς ἡμᾶς καταλιπὼν, καὶ τῆς οὐσίας ἡμετέρας ὕσπερ ἠμεῖτο Ἐπίτροπος καὶ κύριος Δήμιας. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ Αφόβου α. de suis tutoribus: εἰς γὰρ τ' συμμαχίαν ἐμοὶ σύνεπεξαιτο τῷ τοῖς πέντε καὶ εἴκοσι μυᾶς, πιλαχωσίας δραχμάς. Quare tutoris patrimonium obligatum erat pupillo. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ Ὀνητορος α. παρέσεσθαι ἢ τῷ πατρὶ κατὰ ἐπίσθηση, ὥσπερ τὰ τῶν ἐπιτροπευόντων χρήματα, ἀποτιμήσασθαι τοῖς ἐπιτροπευομένοις καταλῶσαν[?] τομίζων.
units.tr: Diogenes Laertius reports this law of Solon in his Life. He was unwilling, therefore, to have as guardians either blood relations or agnates, because when wards died before the age of twenty, they could not... and such heirs took up the inheritance and claimed it for themselves. Nevertheless, not all kinsmen were entirely excluded from guardianship. For the author of the Etymologicum, among those of whom we spoke above, lists guardians or curators, the heirs who were, as it were, joined to the deserted estate. This was reasonable, because although by Solon's law the nearest agnate and heir was not permitted to act as guardian, and if anything happened to the wards in a human way, the nearest heir would come into the goods, yet they were bound to the wards by so distant a kinship that there was no hope of their becoming heirs. These guardians were appointed either by will or by the Archon. That those appointed by will existed is clear from Demosthenes' speeches against Aphobus and Onetor, whence in the speech on the guardianship of Ephiphanes they are said to be under guardianship by reason of age. That they were appointed by the Archon Pollux writes in Book VIII: the Archon, as overseer of guardians, appointed them. For by a law, which we shall give in what follows, under God's leading, orphans were committed to the care of the Archon. Hence it was necessary for the Archon to be informed that these were wards and that those had been given as guardians by will. Whence Isaeus, in the speech on the estate of Philoctemon: they announced to the Archon on behalf of this child that they themselves were guardians. These guardians, whether appointed by will or by the Archon, had power over the wards committed to them. For guardianship, as Servius defines it, is power and authority over a free person, for protecting one who, on account of his age, cannot defend himself (Leg. I, D. de tutelis). Whence Aeschines in the speech against Timarchus calls them guardians of the children. They also had power over the goods and did all the things that wards were bound to do until they grew up. Isaeus, in the speech on the estate of Cleonymus: seeing us under guardianship of Demos, and giving nothing, having himself not increased (the property) but leaving us as children, and as our estate's guardian and master, Demos... Demosthenes, in the first speech against Aphobus, on his own guardians: for he joined to me in alliance with the twenty-five minae, drachmas... Hence the guardian's patrimony was bound to the ward. Demosthenes, in the first speech against Onetor: to be present with the father under the agreement, as the property of those under guardianship, thinking it a rebuke to those held under guardianship...

units.la: Inter ceteras autem tutoris curas fuit hæc, locatio ædium pupilli, ut hæc Lex iubet.
units.tr: Among the other duties of the guardian was this one: the letting of the ward's house, as this law orders.

units.la: Τὸν ἐπίτροπον τὸν οἶκον μισθοῦν. Tutor ædes pupilli locato.
units.tr: The guardian shall let out the house. The guardian lets the ward's house.

units.la: Huius Legis meminit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Ἀφόβου ξυνδικῶν. Καὶ τὸν οἶκον οὐκ ἐμίσθωσεν, τῆς νόμων κελεύοντων. & ἐν τῷ ἐκ Ἀφόβου Ἐπιτροπῆς α. Ταύτην γὰρ ἐξῆν, μηδὲν ἐχθὲν τούτων τῆς πατρικῆς, μισθώσασθαι τὸν οἶκον καὶ τούτοισι τοὺς νόμους. Id fiebat in hunc modum. Tutores siue testamento, siue ab Archonte dati, Archonti indicabant locandas esse pupillorum ædes: auctoritate itaque Archontis, & èiudicum, qui adsidebant, consilio, per præconem locabantur. Isæus ἐν τῷ περὶ τῆς Φιλοκτήμονος κλήσεω. Ἐπηγγέλοντο τῷ παιδὶ τούτῳ πρὸς τὸν Ἀρχοντα, ὡς εἰσαποιῆτο τῆς ἐν Ευκτήμονος ἡσυ[?] τῆς πεπλαυτηκὼν, ἐπηγγέλλοντο σφᾶς αὐτοὺς Ἐπίτροπους, καὶ μισθοῦν ἐκέλευον τὸν Ἀρχοντα τοῖς οἰκίαις, ὡς ὀρφανῶν οὖσιν. καὶ ἐπεὶ πρὸς τὸν τὰ δικαιώματα ἐπλήρωσεν, ὁ μὲν Ἀρχων πρὸς ἐξεπρύτειν, εἰ δὲ ἐ-μισθοῦσιν. Pollux Lib. VIII. ἐπιμελητὴς δὲ ὁ Ἀρχων καὶ τοῖς οἰκίαις ἐμισθοῦν τῇ ὀρφανῶν. Ij vero, qui orphanorum ædes ab Archonte conducebant, aliquid pignori opponebant ob obuencionem. Suidas: οἱ μισθούμενοι τοῖς τῶν ὀρφανῶν εἰσὶν τὰς οἰκίας ἐν τῷ Αρχοντα, ἐπείχοντο τῆς μισθώσεως προείχοντο. ἐδί δὲ τὸν Αρχοντα πέμπειν ἡμᾶς ἀποτιμησομένους τὰ ἐπέχοντα. καὶ ἐλέγοντο τὰ μὲν ἐπέχοντα ἀποτιμήματα. οἱ δὲ ἀποτιμησάμενοι, ἀποτιμηταί. ὃ δὲ ἄρχων, ἀποτιμᾶν. Atque hæc locatio fiebat nouo incunte anno, mense Hecatombæone, tunc enim migrabant ex ædibus in alias: vnde Comicus Ἐξληποαζούσας [?].
units.tr: Demosthenes, in the speech against Aphobus' guardians, recalls this law: "And he did not let out the house, though the laws ordered it." And in the first speech from the guardianship of Aphobus: for it was permitted, provided none of these things was contrary to the paternal will, to let out the house and to these the laws. This was done in the following manner. Guardians, whether appointed by will or by the Archon, indicated to the Archon that the wards' houses were to be let. Therefore, by the authority of the Archon and with the advice of the judges who sat with him, they were let out through a herald. Isaeus, in the speech on the estate of Philoctemon: they announced to the Archon on behalf of this child that, as the estate of Euctemon... they had made complaint, they declared themselves guardians, and they asked the Archon to let the houses, since they belonged to orphans. And when he had fulfilled the requirements to the one (who) ... the Archon was to ... otherwise they would let. Pollux, Book VIII: the Archon was overseer and let the houses of the orphans. Those who let the orphans' houses from the Archon pledged something as security for the rent. Suidas: those who let the orphans' houses from the Archon were held back from the letting by the pledge. They sent the Archon to assess the things held. Those who assessed were called appraisers, and the Archon was to assess. This letting took place at the start of the new year, in the month Hecatombaeon, for then they moved from one house to another. Hence the comic poet...

units.la: τί τὰ σκευάρια ταῦτι βούλεται; πότερον μεταικιζόμενος ἐξενιώχας αὖτά; [?]
units.tr: "What does this junk mean? Did you move these things out after changing houses?"

units.la: Dicuntur enim Hecatombæone mense: tunc primum quoque iudices sorte erant capti: vnde dixit Isæus, ὅτι ὠφῶν τὰ δικαστήρια ἐπλήρουν [?]. Qui hæc non fecisset, scribebatur illi δίκη μαθώσεως οἴκου [?], cuius Lib. VIII. meminit Pollux, quod fieri poterat à quolibet Atheniensi: Scribebatur quoque, si tanti non locaretur, quanti debebat locari. Suidas & Auctor Etymologici λέγεται ἡ φάσις καὶ ὅτι τὴν ὀρφανικὴν οἶκον. ὅτε γὰρ μὴ ἐκμισθώσαιεν οἱ Ἐπίζηροι τὸν οἶκον τῶν ὀρφανευομένων, ἔφαγεν αὐτὸν ὁ βουλόμενος πρὸς τὸν Ἄρχοντα, ἵνα μισθωθῇ, ἔφαγε δὲ καὶ εἰ ἐλάττονος ἢ ἐξ τῶν ἀξίας μεμίσθωται [?].
units.tr: For it is said that in the month Hecatombaeon, at that time also the judges were first chosen by lot; hence Isaeus said that they filled the courts. Whoever did not do this was prosecuted by the action for failing to let a house, which Pollux mentions in Book VIII, and which any Athenian could bring. It was also prosecuted if the house was not let for what it ought to be let for. Suidas and the author of the Etymologicum say: the action is also called for the orphan's house. For when the overseers did not let out the house of those who were orphaned, anyone who wished could bring it before the Archon so that it might be let, and he could bring it also if it was let for less than its worth.

units.la: Curæ autem Archonti fuisse orphanos, dotales feminas, & prægnantes post mariti mortem, voluit Solo hac Lege:
units.tr: Solon wished by this law that the Archon should have charge of orphans, of dowered women, and of pregnant women after their husband's death:

units.la: Ο ΑΡΧΩΝ ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΩ ΤΩΝ ΟΡΦΑ-ΝΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΠΙΚΛΗΡΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΟΙΚΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΕΞΕΡΗΜΟΥΜΕΝΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΩΝ, ΟΣΑΙ ΜΕΝΟΥΣΙΝ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΟΙΚΟΙΣ ΤΩΝ ΑΝΔΡΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΤΕ-ΘΝΗΚΟΤΩΝ ΦΑΣΚΟΥΣΑΙ ΚΥΕΙΝ, ΤΟΥ-ΤΩΝ ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΩ, ΚΑΙ ΜΗ ΕΑΤΩ ΥΒΡΙΖΕΙΝ Η ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΤΙ ΠΑΡΑΝΟΜΟΝ, ΚΥΡΙΟΣ Δ' ΕΠΙΒΑΛΛΕΙΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟ ΤΕ-ΛΟΣ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΕΙΖΟΝΟΣ ΖΗΜΙΑΣ ΔΟΚΗ, ΑΞΙΟΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΕΣΑ-ΜΕΝΟΣ ΠΡΟΓΕΜΠΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΙΜΗΜΑ ΕΠΙ-ΓΡΑΨΑΜΕΝΟΣ Ο, ΤΙ ΑΝ ΔΟΚΗ ΑΥΤΩ ΕΙΣΑΓΑΓΕΤΩ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΗΛΙΑΙΑΝ. ΕΑΝ Δ' ΑΛΛΩ ΤΙΜΑΤΩ Η ΗΛΙΑΙΑ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΛΟΝΤΟΣ Ο, ΤΙ ΧΡΗ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΠΑΘΕΙΝ Η ΑΠΟΤΙΣΑΙ.
units.tr: The Archon shall have charge of orphans, of heiresses, of the houses that have been left deserted, and of the women who remain in the houses of dead men, saying they are pregnant; this man shall have charge of them, and he shall not allow them to be abused or to suffer any wrong, and he shall have the power to impose on the wrongdoer the fine that is due. If he seems deserving of a greater penalty, he shall summon him and, having written down the penalty, shall bring him to the court of the Heliaea, and what the court decides shall be done to him or he shall pay. If the Archon fails to assess the penalty, [the court] shall ... [ΟΝ ΑΡΧΩΝ ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΩ ΤΩΝ ΟΡΦΑΝΩΝ ... ].

units.la: Archon orphanorum, dotalium feminarum, familiarum, quæ intercidunt, & prægnatium mulierum, quæ post maritorum obitum in eorum ædibus permanent, curam habeto, neque contumeliam aut aliquid iniustè ijs fieri sinito: multam, quàm potest Magistratus potestate, irrogare ei ius esto. Si maiore pœna dignus videtur, qui aduersus hanc Legem fecerit, Archon in ius vocato in quintum diem, & pœna pro arbitrio irrogata, Heliastis iudicium permittito. Si conuicius fuerit, Heliasta de eo quod tuere in corpore vel in ære debet, iudicium reddunto.
units.tr: The Archon shall have charge of orphans, of dowered women, of families that are dying out, and of pregnant women who remain in the houses of their husbands after the husbands' death; he shall not allow them to be insulted or wronged in any unjust way; he shall have the right to impose a fine, as far as the power of his magistracy allows. If he who breaks this law seems to deserve a heavier penalty, the Archon shall summon him to court within five days, and having fixed the penalty, he shall allow the Heliasts to judge. If he has been insulted, the Heliasts shall give judgment concerning what is owed in person or in money.

units.la: Legem hanc habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῇ πρὸς Μακάρταρ[?]. Καὶ αὐτὸν μὲν τὸν νόμον ὑμῖν ἀναγνῶσαι[?]. Ο ΑΡΧΩΝ ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΣΘΩ ΤΩΝ ΟΡ-ΦΑΝΩΝ, &c. Meminit quoque illius Isæus ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ Ἀπολλοδώρου κλή-σεως[?]. νόμῳ γὰρ τῷ Ἀρχοντι τὴν οἰκίαν, ὅπως αὐτῷ μὴ ἐξεπιμελῆται[?] τὸν ὀρφανόν[?]. Curam mandat & præcipit Legislator Archonti orphanorum. Æschi-nes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμάρχου[?], καὶ τοὺς νόμους λέγων, οἱ κελεύουσι τὸν Ἀρχοντα τῶν ὀρφανῶν ἐπιμελεῖσθαι[?]. Virginum vel feminarum dotalium, familiarum ne prorsus interirent, & mulierum, quæ post maritorum mortem se esse prægnantes asserunt: quod etiam notat Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. IX. ἐπιμελεῖται δὲ ὁ Ἄρχων καὶ τῶν γυναικῶν, ἐὰν αἱ φαίνωνται ἐπ' αὐτοῦ πλου-τῆς οὐσίας[?], quod optime institutum à sapientissimo Legislatore, ne quis per dolum venirer in possessionem hereditatis, etiam à Romanis acceptum est: vide Edictum Praetoris Lege I.§.X.D. de ven-tre inspiciendo. Si quis autem alicui horum iniuriam faceret, vindicabat Praetor, multam ei faciens, [illegible, ~3 letters] quantam poterat, pro Magistratus, quem gerebat, potestate: definita enim erat proculdubio multa, quam irrogare poterat Archon, quemadmodum & alij qui erant ἐν τῇ πόλει, vt ex. gr. Quingentorum Senatus. Quod si maiore poena dignus videretur, Archon in ius ad Heliaeam rapiebat, & vocabat in quintum diem; ita interpretamur Legis verba ΠΡΟΣΚΑΛΕΣΑΜΕΝΟΣ ΠΡΟΓΕΜΡΤΑ, auctore Harpocratione: εἰ μὴ ἄρα [?] ὡς Δημοσθένης πρὸς ἡμᾶς [?] τῆς γὰρ μεγάλης δίκης [?] μία ἡμέρα πρὸς τὸ κείνη, quae Harpocrationis ratio tamen non facit ad institutum nostrum: res tamen est, quam diximus. Tutela autem exibant Athenienses anno aetatis vicesimo, cum Lexiarchico essent inscripti. Antipho ἐν τῷ κατ' Ἀλκιβιάδου λειτουργίας [?] ἐπὶ ἐπιτροπῶν [?] Hinc Astyphilus apud Isaeum, cum Lexiarchico esset inscriptus, vitrici tutela exiit: ἐπὶ [?] τῶν ἐπιτροπῶν [?] tunc enim sui erant iuris, & ad suam mitrebantur negocia, vt docet Pollux, cuius verba iam ante suo loco repraesentauimus: unde Æschines ἐν τῇ κατὰ Τιμάρχου puerum, antequam Lexiarchico inscribatur, sub patris, fratris, aut tutoris cura ac fide esse scribit, in viros vero transcriptum sui facit iuris, ὅτι ἐκ [?] ὁ νόμος θέτης [?] ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐπὶ τὸν παῖδα, παντί, ἀδικάφῳ, ἐπὶ ἐπιτροπῆς, διδασκάλους, καὶ ὅλως τοῖς κυρίοις ἐπιδιδόντες ἐπιγραφὴν εἰς ὃ Ληξιαρχικὸν γραμματεῖον, καὶ πᾶς νόμος γὰρ καὶ εἰδὴ τοῖς τῆς πόλεως, καὶ ἢν δυνῶνται ἀξιοῦσθαι [?] καὶ ἐν τῷ [?] ἐπιτροπῶν, ἀλλ' ἡδὴ αὐτῷ τῷ Τιμάρχῳ. tunc quoque sua administrare scribit eadem Oratione: ὅπως ἐπιγραφὴ Τιμάρχου ἐπὶ εἰς ὃ Ληξιαρχικὸν γραμματεῖον, καὶ κύριος ἐχρήσατο τῆς οὐσίας. Atque ab hinc licebat postulare tutores, qui fuerant, male administratae tutelae: estque scitum veterum iuris Attici Consultorum: ἐγγεγράφθαι εἰς αὐτὰς ἐλαχίστην δίκην ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς. vnde Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Onetoris α'. ἐγὼ δ' ἀξιῶ μὲν τοὺς γάμους αἱρῇ [?] δοκιμασθεῖς, ἐπεγκλήσων, καὶ λόγῳ ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς ἀπήγαγον. Neque pupillis tantum, qui fuerant, sed etiam cuiuis Atheniensi licebat dicam scribere tutoribus. Pollux Libro VIII. ἀλλ' αὐτὴ λῷ δημοσία, ὥσπερ καὶ τῆς ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς. ἐξὸν γὰρ τοῦ βουλομένῳ γράφεσθαι τὸν Ἐπιτροπον, ὧν τὴν ἀδικουμένων ὀρφανῶν. Dica autem apud Archontem scribebatur. Pollux Libro VIII. δίκη πρὸς τὸν Ἀρχοντα λαγχάνοντι ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς ὀρφανῶν. Accusatio autem male administratae tutelae debebat institui intra quinquennium à finita tutela: nam post quinquennium postulari non possunt ex hac Lege:
units.tr: You have this law in Demosthenes, in the speech against Macartatus, where he asks that the law itself be read to you: "The Archon shall have charge of orphans," etc. Isaeus also mentions it in the speech on the action concerning Apollodorus, for by law the Archon has the house, so that he may not neglect the orphan. The lawgiver entrusts and charges the Archon with the care of orphans. Aeschines, in the speech against Timarchus, says the laws order the Archon to care for orphans. It concerned the virgins or dowered women, lest families be utterly lost, and women who claim after their husbands' death that they are pregnant. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX, also notes this: the Archon also has charge of women, if they appear to be in possession of the estate. This was instituted most wisely by the wise lawgiver, so that no one might by fraud gain possession of an inheritance, and it was also adopted by the Romans; see the Praetor's edict, Law I §10, D. de ventre inspiciendo. If anyone did wrong to any of these, the Praetor avenged it, imposing a fine as far as the power of the magistracy he held allowed. For the fine the Archon could impose was certainly defined, as were those of the others who were in the city, for example the Council of Five Hundred. But if he seemed deserving of a heavier penalty, the Archon took him to court before the Heliaea and summoned him within five days. So we interpret the words of the law "having summoned, having written down the penalty," on the authority of Harpocration. Harpocration's explanation, however, does not bear on our purpose; the matter is as we have said. Athenians left guardianship at the age of twenty, when they were enrolled in the Lexiarchic register. Antiphon, in the speech on the public service of Alcibiades: under guardians. Hence Astyphilus in Isaeus, when he was enrolled in the Lexiarchic register, left the guardianship of his stepfather, for then they were their own masters and managed their own affairs, as Pollux teaches, whose words we have already quoted in their place. Hence Aeschines, in the speech against Timarchus, writes that a boy, before he is enrolled in the Lexiarchic register, is under the care and trust of his father, brother, or guardian, but once transferred to the men's roll he becomes his own master, since the law does not forbid... but the enrollment was given to the child under the guardianship of a tutor or teachers, and in general to the masters, into the Lexiarchic register; for every law and custom of the city is such, and if they were able... also under guardians, but now already under Timarchus himself. He writes in the same speech that then too he administered his own affairs: that Timarchus was enrolled in the Lexiarchic register and used the estate as its master. From then on it was permitted to sue guardians for mismanagement of the guardianship, and it was an established rule of the old Attic jurists that a suit against guardians could be brought in those matters. Hence Demosthenes, in the first speech against Onetor: I think it right that marriages be examined, to bring a charge, and I brought him to trial by the guardianship. Not only wards who had come of age, but any Athenian could bring a charge against guardians. Pollux, Book VIII: but it was a public action, as also for guardianship; for anyone who wished might indict the guardian for wronging orphans. The action was brought before the Archon. Pollux, Book VIII: an action before the Archon was brought by one under guardianship of orphans. The accusation for mismanaged guardianship had to be brought within five years from the end of the guardianship, for after five years they could not be sued under this law:

units.la: Εἀν πίντε ἔτι παρέλθη, καὶ μὴ δικάσωνταί, μηκέτι ἐξ [?] τῆς ὀρφανοῖς δίκῶν, ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς ἐγκλημάτων.
units.tr: If five years pass and they do not bring suit, then no longer on the lawsuits of orphans, but on the charges arising from guardianship [Εἀν πίντε ἔτι παρέλθη, καὶ μὴ δικάσωνταί, μηκέτι ἐξ τῆς ὀρφανοῖς δίκῶν, ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς ἐγκλημάτων.]

units.la: Post quinquennium tutores male administratae tutelae à pupillis ne postulantor.
units.tr: After five years, guardians who have administered a guardianship badly may not be prosecuted by their wards.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Ναυσίμαχον. meminit quoque Plato Libro XI. de Legibus: ἅμα δ' ἂν ἐπὶ τῆς ἐπικοινίας ὀρφανῶν, ἐαὶ ἡμῖν κακῶς ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς, μηδὲ πότε ἐπὶ τὴν ἐξικνούμενος τῆς ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς, ἔτω δικίαν λαχεῖν ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπίας.
units.tr: Demosthenes cites this law in his speech against Nausimachus. Plato also mentions it in Book XI of the Laws: "And at the same time, if orphans are wronged by their guardians, let no one who has passed beyond the time of the guardianship bring a suit on this charge against guardians" [ἅμα δ' ἂν ἐπὶ τῆς ἐπικοινίας ὀρφανῶν, ἐαὶ ἡμῖν κακῶς ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς, μηδὲ πότε ἐπὶ τὴν ἐξικνούμενος τῆς ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπῆς, ἔτω δικίαν λαχεῖν ὑπὸ ἐπιτροπίας.]

units.la: Apud Romanos quoque constat potuisse omnes postulare suspectos tutores: Consequens est, inquit Vlpianus Libro XXXV. ad Edictum, vt videamus, qui possunt suspectos postulare? Et sciendum est, quasi publicam esse hanc actionem, hoc est, omnibus patere. Quinimo, & mulieres admittuntur: sed hae sola, quae pietate necessitudinis ductae ad hoc procedunt, ut puta mater, nutrix quoque, & aliae possunt. Potest & soror (nam in soror, & rescriptum extat Diui Seueri) & si qua alia mulier fuerit, cuius Praetor perpensam pietatem intellexerit, non sexus verecundiam egredientis, sed pietate productam, non continere iniuriam pupillorum, admittet eam ad accusationem. Lege I. §. VI. & VII. D. de suspectis tutoribus. Sed quid hic lego, quasi publicam esse hanc actionem? imo re vera erat publica: nam quod nonnulli interpretantur, omnino publicam non esse, quia si vere publica esset, omnibus quidem pateret, praeterquam feminis Lege VIII. D. de accusationibus, quae tamen ad hanc accusationem admittuntur; interpretationem istam, inquam, non admittimus, quia etiam feminis, sed quibusdam tantum, permittitur; publico iudicio aliquem reum facere: Non est permissum, inquit Pomponius Libro I. ad Sabinum, mulieri publico iudicio quemquam reum facere, nisi sc. parentium liberorumque, & patroni & patronae, & eorum filij, filiae, neptis mortem exequatur. Lege I. D. eod. vide & Legem sequentem. At, quia pluribus feminis conceditur hac Lege I. D. de suspectis tutoribus, publica accusatio, putarem rescribendum transpositis vocibus: Et sciendum est, si qua, publicam esse hanc actionem. & certe verum omnino est inter publicas actiones, si qua est publica, hanc unam esse, & longe pluribus patere. Quemadmodum autem, si Archonti videretur puniendus longe gravius, quam ipsi pro Magistratus potestate liceret in eum animadvertere, remittebat ad Heliastas: ita etiam iure Romano solent ad Praefecturam Vrbis remitti, inquit Vlpianus Libro de Officio Praefecti Vrbi, etiam tutores, sive curatores, qui male in tutela sive cura versati, graviore animadversione indigent, quam ut sufficiat ei suspectorum insamia. Lege I. §. VII. D. de off. Praef. Vrbi: quod tamen est intelligendum de plebeijs. Lege I. §. VIII. D. de suspectis tutoribus, & humilioribus. Lege III. §. XVI. D. eod.
units.tr: It is also established that among the Romans anyone could bring a charge against a suspect guardian. It follows, says Ulpian in Book XXXV on the Edict, that we should consider who may bring a charge against suspect guardians. And it should be understood that this action is, as it were, public, that is, open to all. Indeed, women too are admitted, but only those who come forward moved by the duty of close kinship, such as a mother, and also a nurse, and others of that sort. A sister may also do so (for there is a rescript of the Divine Severus concerning a sister), and if any other woman is one whose pious concern the praetor has clearly perceived, who does not overstep the modesty of her sex but is driven by devotion not to tolerate wrong done to the wards, he will admit her to the accusation. See Law 1, §§ 6 and 7, D. de suspectis tutoribus. But what do I read here, as it were public? Indeed it was truly public. For the view that some take, that it was not public at all, because if it really were public it would be open to everyone except women (Law 8, D. de accusationibus), yet women are admitted to this accusation, I say we do not accept that interpretation, since this right is granted even to women, but only to certain ones, to bring someone to trial in a public court. Pomponius says in Book I on Sabinus: "A woman is not permitted to bring anyone to trial in a public court, except that she may pursue the death of her parents and children, of her patron and patroness, and of their sons and daughters and grandchildren." See Law 1, D. eod. and the following law. But since by this law (Law 1, D. de suspectis tutoribus) public accusation is granted to more women, I would think the text should be rewritten with the words transposed: "And it should be understood that if any woman, this action is public." And certainly it is wholly true that among public actions, if there is any public one, this is the only one and is open to far more people. Moreover, just as, if the Archon thought the offender should be punished far more severely than his own magisterial power allowed him to punish, he referred the matter to the Heliasts, so too under Roman law, as Ulpian says in Book on the Office of the Prefect of the City, guardians or curators who have behaved badly in guardianship or curatorship, and who need a punishment heavier than the mere infamy of being suspect, are customarily referred to the Prefect of the City. See Law 1, §. 7, D. de off. Praef. Vrbi: which, however, must be understood of plebeians. See Law 1, §. 8, D. de suspectis tutoribus, and of humbler persons. See Law 3, §. 16, D. eod.

units.la: DE SEPVLCRIS ET Funeribus. TITVLVS VIII.
units.tr: ON TOMBS AND FUNERALS. TITLE VIII.

units.la: Sepulchra fuerunt olim veteribus, quae etiam antea domos praebuerant, speluncae. Auctor Etymologici: ὁ δὲ παλαιὸν ὁ τὰς χολά-[?] μασι τὴς γῆς ἐξαιρεῖσθαι μόνοι ἀνδρῶν μόνοι χαλκῷ κτεγμένοι[?]. Postea ab ipsis Cecropis temporibus ius & Lex fuit terra humandi.
units.tr: In early times, before they provided dwellings, caves served the ancients as tombs. The author of the Etymologicum says that in the old days men alone dug out the earth with bronze tools. Later, from the time of Cecrops himself, burial in the earth was a right and a law.

units.la: MORTVVM TERRA HVMATO.
units.tr: THE DEAD ARE TO BE BURIED IN THE EARTH.

units.la: Habes apud M. Tullium Libro II. de Legibus: Nam & Athenis iam ille mos à Cecrope, ut ajunt, permansit, hoc jus, terra humandi. quàm eum proximi injecerant; obductaque terra erat, frugibus obserebatur, ut sinus & gremium quasi matris mortuo tribueretur, solam autem frugibus expiatum, ut vivis redderetur. Sed semper extra urbis pomoeria. Quare Ἡειάγ portæ ab Atheniensibus appellantur, quod illinc efferebantur mortui ad sepulcra. Auctor Etymologici: Ἡειάγαι, αἱ πύλαι Ἀθῆναι, [?] ὅτι τὰ νεκρὰ ἐκφέρεται ἐκ τῆς πόλεως. Atque ad portas urbis fiebant sepulcra. Plutarchus in Theseo: [?] τὰ πόλεως [?] τὸν Χαλκώδοντα Ἠρῷον, αὐτοῦ Γλαύκου ἱερωμάζει. Idem in Hyperide ex Heliodoro Libro III. [?] μνῆμ[?]. Τοὺς οἴκους [?] ἐν Αἰγίνῃ πυλαῖς. Pausanias Atticis, de Thucydidis monumento: μνῆμά ἐστιν ἡ πρὸς πύλαις Μελιτίδων. Marcellinus in Thucydidis vita: [?] Μελίτης πύλαις Κολωνοῦ [?] Κιμῶνα, [?] Ἡγεσίπου καὶ Θουκυδίδου τάφος. & infra: [?] ἐν αὐτῇ πάρα πολλοί τῆς πύλης, ἐν χωρίῳ τῆς Ἀττικῆς, ὁ Κολωνὸς καλεῖται, καὶ φησὶν Ἀριστοκλῆς. Interemptos vero in acie, honoris ergo, in Ceramico extra urbem sepeliebant. Grammatici: δύο ἦσαν Κεραμεικοί, ὁ μὲν ἔνδον τῆς πόλεως, ὁ δὲ ἔξω. ἔνθα καὶ τοὺς ἐν πολέμῳ πολυτελῶς ἐπιτάφιον δημοσίᾳ. Inde Ceramicum, publicum monumentum dixit Thucydides Libro II. Ἀθέαν δὲ εἰς τὸ δημόσιον σῆμα, ὃ ἔστιν [?] τῆς καλλίστου προαστείου τῆς πόλεως. Scholia: εἰς τὸ δημόσιον σῆμα, ὃ καλοῦμεν Κεραμεικόν. Eorum sepulcra satis bene longa oratione recensuit & prosecutus est Pausanias Atticis. Neque hos tantum, qui in acie occubuissent, sed & alios, quibus honorem habitum vellent, publice in Ceramico sepeliebant. Alij vero de populo in agris sepeliebantur: unde in Legem, quam Titulo Finium regundorum dedimus: [?] τῆς πόλεως [?] βοῦ ἄγειν π᾽ ἀλλοτρίας χωρίου ὁρίζει. Extruebantur autem sepulcra, vel ad vias, ut de monumentis, quæ in Ceramico visuntur, narrat Pausanias Atticis: [?] ὁδὸν κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν τῆς ὁδοῦ [?]. Hinc Artemidorus Oneirocritici Libro I. cap. LXXXIV. [?] μνήματα ἐν τοῖς ἐκτὸς ὁδοῦ [?] ἀποθανόντες, quia scilicet μνήματα καὶ πόλεων τὴν ὁδὸν κατ᾽ ὁδὸν [?]. Plutarchus in Isocrate de Theodecte Phaselita: [?] ὅτι [?] τὸν Κυαμίτην ἐπὶ πολλοῖς, καὶ τὸ ὀνομα τῆς ὁδοῦ, ἐν τῷ ὅτι Ἐλαιῶνα. cuius monumenti meminit quoque Pausanias Atticis: vel extruebantur in agrorum finibus; ut constat è Legis verbis, quæ proxime laudavimus: [?] τῆς πόλεως [?] βοῦ ἄγειν π᾽ ἀλλοτρίας χωρίου ὁρίζει, ὅταν ὁ βαθὺς αὐτῆς ἦ, ἔστω τὸν ὑπάλιμπον. ubi vides sepulchra in extremis agris fieri, neque tamen esse agrorum terminos. Quare hinc lucem accipiet Siculus Flaccus de Conditionibus Agrorum. Inspiciendum erit & illud, quoniam sepulcra in extremis finibus facere soliti sunt: & ei cippos ponere, ne aliquando cippus pro termino errorem faciat. Si quis autem in hostico peregre esset mortuus, in Atticam referebatur, ut in avitis monumentis reconderetur: itaque tot monumenta illorum, qui extra fines Atticæ in bello occubuerant, recensèt Pausanias Atticis, quæ in Ceramico visuntur.
units.tr: You have it in Cicero, Book II of On the Laws: For at Athens too that custom, as they say, has remained from Cecrops: the right of burying in the earth. The nearest kin threw earth over the dead; and when the earth was heaped upon them, it was sown with grain, so that the bosom and lap of a mother might be given to the dead, while the living, purified only by grain, might be restored to life. But this was always done outside the city walls. That is why the gates of Athens were called Eiagai (Heiagai), because the dead were carried out of the city through them to the tombs. The author of the Etymologicum: "Heiagai, the gates of Athens, because the dead are carried out of the city through them." Tombs were also built by the city gates. Plutarch, in the Life of Theseus, speaks of the shrine of Chalcodon and of Glaucus. The same Plutarch, in his Life of Hyperides, drawing on Heliodorus Book III, mentions the houses at the gates in Aegina. Pausanias, in Attica, on the monument of Thucydides: "There is a monument at the gate of the Melitides." Marcellinus, in the Life of Thucydides: "at the Melitan gate, near Colonus, is the tomb of Cimon, Hegesipus and Thucydides." And further on: "there are very many monuments in that place near the gate, in a district of Attica called Colonus," and Aristocles says so. Those who fell in battle were buried outside the city in the Ceramicus, as an honour. The grammarians: "there were two Ceramici, one inside the city and one outside, where those who died in war were honoured with a public funeral oration." Hence Thucydides in Book II calls the Ceramicus the public tomb: "they buried them in the public tomb, which is in the most beautiful suburb of the city." The scholiast: "the public tomb, which we call the Ceramicus." Pausanias, in Attica, recounted and described their tombs at some length. He did this not only for those who had fallen in battle but also for others whom the state wished to honour, whom they buried publicly in the Ceramicus. Ordinary people, however, were buried in the fields. Hence, in the law we gave under the title On the Regulation of Boundaries: the law fixes how far one may drive an ox onto another's land. Tombs were built by the roadsides, as Pausanias tells in Attica about the monuments seen in the Ceramicus. Hence Artemidorus, Oneirocritica, Book I, chapter 84: tombs outside the road, for those who died... because tombs were built beside the roads. Plutarch, in Isocrates on Theodectes of Phaselis: ... Pausanias in Attica also mentions this monument. Tombs were also built within the boundaries of fields, as is clear from the words of the law we quoted just above: the law fixes how far one may drive an ox onto another's land, when it is deep, that is, the distance left as a gap. Here you see that tombs were made at the outermost edges of fields, yet these were not the boundaries of the fields. Hence Siculus Flaccus, On the Conditions of Fields, will be clarified: one should also consider that they were accustomed to make tombs at the outer limits and to set up cippi there, lest a cippus should sometimes cause error as a boundary marker. If anyone died abroad, he was carried back to Attica to be buried in his ancestral tomb. Thus Pausanias, in Attica, lists the many monuments of those who fell in war outside the borders of Attica, which are seen in the Ceramicus.

units.la: Cùm autem nimium ampla & operosa sepulchra fierent, placuit Atheniensibus eorum magnificentiam minui hac Lege:
units.tr: Since the tombs were becoming excessively large and elaborate, the Athenians resolved to restrain their magnificence by this law:

units.la: NE QUIS SEPULCHRUM FACITO OPEROSIUS QUAM QUOD DECEM HOMINES EFFECERINT TRIDUO NEQUE ID OPERE TECTORIO EXORNATO NEC HERMAS IMPOSITO:
units.tr: NO ONE SHALL MAKE A TOMB MORE ELABORATE THAN TEN MEN COULD BUILD IN THREE DAYS, NOR DECORATE IT WITH PLASTER WORK, NOR SET HERMAE UPON IT.

units.la: Legem hanc laudat M Tullius Libro de Legibus II. extremo: Sed post aliquanto propter has amplitudines sepulcrorum, quas in Ceramico videmus, Lege sanctum est; Ne quis sepulcrum faceret operosius, quam quod decem homines effecerint triduo; neque id opere tectorio exornari, nec Hermas hos, quos vocant, litebat imponi. Nimium enim operose sepulcra faciebant Athenienses, Hermas, quia inter infernales Deos credebatur ille animas ad inferos deducere, columnis imponebant, quod hac Lege vetitum est: Columnas quoque statuebant, quibus effigies impositae mortuorum: ita in Isocratis columna Siren erat, cui propter orationis suavitatem comparabatur. Plutarchus in Isocrate: αὐτὴ ὃ Ἰσοκράτης ὅτι τῆς μνήματος ἐπὶ τῷ χρὸς τεῖχοσι πηχῶν, ἐφ᾽ ὃ Σειρῆν πηχῶν ἐστὰ συμβολικῶς. Incidebantur quoque nomen, genus, patria. Diogenes Laertius in Solone: ἀλ-λὰ καὶ αὐτὸς τοῖς τάφοις [?] ἐκ βλέπων [?], καὶ ἀπὸ τὴν δῆμον [?] τοὺς γεγενημένους ἐγκεκ-ρυγμένους, ὧν ἐν ἴδῃς Ἀθηναίων. Pausanias Atticis de iis, qui in Ceramico sunt sepulti: οἱ δὲ ἄλλοι τάφοι [?] τὴν ὁδὸν κεῖσθαι τὴν ἐς Ἀκαδημίαν, καὶ στῆλαι ἐχάσιν ὅτι τῆς τάφοις γράμματα, πεποίηνται, καὶ τὸν δῆμον ἐκείνου λέγουσαι. Antyllus antiquus scriptor de Thucydidis monumento: καὶ γάλα ἡ ἔχει ἐν τῇ Κοίλῃ, Θουκυδίδης Ἀλιμούσιος, ἔχουσα ἐπίγραμμα. idque fiebat cum Elogio. Theophrastus περὶ περιερχίας. καὶ γυναικὸς δὲ πλά τι ποιήσας, ὅπερ γράφει ὅτι ὁ μνῆμα, τῆς πιλύδρου αὐτῆς, καὶ τὰς παξεῖς, καὶ τῆς μνήξεως, καὶ αὐτῆς τῆς γυναικὸς τοῦτο μὲ, καὶ ποταπή ἐστί, ὃ περισπιγράφει ὅτι ἔστι πολύ-τις ζωντοί ἡσθμ. Addebant praeterea mensas, in quibus & ipsi effigiati, & insculpta nomina. Plutarchus in Isocrate: [?] μὲν ὧν τοῦτο μνημεῖ᾽ τε ἀπὸ ζῷ ἐπὶ ἐπ᾽ ἑξ. & paullo post: ὡ δὲ καὶ αὐτὸ τε ἀπ᾽ πλήσιον ἔχουσα ποιησαι τι καὶ τοῖς διδασκάλοις αὐτὸ, ἐν οἷς καὶ Γοργίαν ἐκ σφαγεῖον ἀγροληκὸν βλέπουσα, αὐτὸν τι τὸν Ἰσοκράτει πρέ-σῶτα. Idem Plutarchus in Lycurgo Rhetore: ἐπέφη δὲ αὐτῆς καὶ τὴν εἰκόνων ἴσας δημοσίᾳ, καὶ ἔσιν αὐτῇ τὰ μνήματα ἀντίκρυς τῆς Παμφίας Ἀθηναῖος ἐν πῇ Μελχισιδή τὸ Φιλοσοφικὴν πῶ, πεπίζαι ποιησάμενον, αὐτὴ τι τὴν Λυκούργου καὶ τὸ παιδὸν αὐτῆ ὑπ᾽ ἐκ-γαμιδίᾳ. At in celibum monumentis imponebatur λευξοφόρες, pueri hydriam habentis effigies. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ ἀγορᾷ εἰς Λεωχάρην, ἱππάσηκεν ἐ Ἀρχά-δης, καὶ τὰ λόγου ὅπερ ἐπέ τῆς β[?] τοῦ Μιλιαλίδου, ἄγαμος ὧν τὶ ἐύτη σημεῖον, λευξοφόρες ἐφίζηκεν ἐπὶ τῷ Ἀρχιάδου τάφῳ. Grammatici: ἔχος δὲ ὧ καὶ τῆς ἀγάμως ἀπο-τοῖς λευξοφορῶν, καὶ ὅπο τῇ μνήμα ἐφίζατο, τῆν δὲ ὧ παῖς καὶ ὑδρίαν ἔχων. Neque tamen omnia sepulcra his columnis, mensis, & aliis operibus magno constantibus erant exornata: nam plebis plana fuisse videntur: unde Ηεια appellabatur. Suidas: ἥεια, οἱ τάφοι. Φασὶ δὲ ἵνας χαιρόπεγον μὴ πᾶν τὰς τοὺς τάφους ὑπὸς ὀνομάζε-σθαι, κατ᾽ ἐξαιρετον ἢ τὰς μὴ ὁ ἐν [?] ἀποδήμωθεν. Columnarum vero altitudini modum posuit hac Lege Demetrius Phalereus.
units.tr: Cicero praises this law in Book II, near the end of On the Laws: But after a while, because of the great size of the tombs that we see in the Ceramicus, it was enacted by law that no one should make a tomb more elaborate than ten men could build in three days, nor decorate it with plaster work, nor set up those so-called hermae. The Athenians made their tombs too elaborately: they set hermae on columns, because it was believed that Hermes, among the infernal gods, led souls down to the underworld; this the law forbade. They also erected columns bearing the likenesses of the dead; thus on the tomb of Isocrates there was a Siren on a column, to which he was compared for the sweetness of his eloquence. Plutarch, in Isocrates: ... Names, family, and homeland were also inscribed. Diogenes Laertius, in Solon: ... Pausanias, on those buried in the Ceramicus: the other tombs lie along the road to the Academy, and they have stone slabs with inscriptions and the names of those buried. Antyllus, an ancient writer, on the monument of Thucydides: ... This was done with an epitaph. Theophrastus, On Wealth: ... They also added tables on which the dead themselves were portrayed and their names carved. Plutarch, in Isocrates: ... The same Plutarch, in the Life of Lycurgus the Orator: ... At the tombs of the unmarried was set a figure of a youth carrying a water jar. Demosthenes, in his speech against Leochares: ... sat upon the tomb of Archiades. The grammarians: ... that is, an image of a young man carrying a jar, placed on the tomb. Yet not all tombs were decorated with these columns, tables and other costly works, for the tombs of the common people seem to have been plain; hence they were called heeia. Suidas: "Heeia, tombs. They say that heeia was not applied to all tombs but in particular to those of people who died far from home." Demetrius of Phalerum laid down the height of the columns in this law.

units.la: SVPER TERRÆ TVMVLVM NE QVID STATVITO NISI COLVMELLAM TRIBVS CVBITIS NE ALTIOREM AVT MENSAM AVT LABELLVM.
units.tr: NO ONE SHALL SET ANYTHING UP ON THE EARTH OF A TOMB EXCEPT A SMALL COLUMN NOT TALLER THAN THREE CUBITS, OR A TABLE, OR A BASIN.

units.la: Legem hanc idem Cicero repræsentat Libro laudato II. de Legibus, additque Demetrium Phalereum præfecisse certum Magistratum, qui procuraret, ne quis Atheniensium in hanc Legem committeret. M. Tullij verba sunt: Sed ait rursus idem Demetrius, increbuisse eam funerum, sepulcrorumque, magnificentiam, quæ nunc fere Romæ est: quam consuetudinem Lege minuit ipse. Nam super terræ tumulum noluit quid statui, nisi columellam tribus cubitis ne altiorem, aut mensam, aut labellum: & huic procurationi certum Magistratum præfecerat. Cùm verò sepulcra sancta siue religiosa habita sint: Sepulcrorum enim sanctitas in ipso solo est, quod nulla vi moveri, neque deleri potest: atque vt cetera extinguuntur, sic sepulcra ipsa fiunt sanctiora vetustate. Solonis Lege pœna est iis constituta, qui sepulcra violarent.
units.tr: The same Cicero presents this law in the second book of De Legibus already cited, and adds that Demetrius of Phalerum set a certain magistrate over it, whose task was to see that none of the Athenians transgressed this law. The words of M. Tullius are: But again the same Demetrius says that the magnificence of funerals and sepulchres had grown, such as now is almost at Rome; and he himself reduced this custom by law. For he did not wish anything to be set up above the mound of earth, except a small column of no more than three cubits, or a table, or a basin; and for the oversight of this he had set a certain magistrate. Since sepulchres were regarded as sacred or religious: For the sanctity of sepulchres lies in the very soil, which cannot be moved or destroyed by any force; and while other things are extinguished, sepulchres themselves become more sacred with age. By the law of Solon a penalty was established for those who violated sepulchres.

units.la: NE QUIS SEPULCRA DELEAT NEVE ALIENUM INFERAT; SI QUIS TYMBON, AUT MONUMENTUM, AUT COLUM- NAM VIOLARIT, DEIECERIT, FREGERIT, pœna esto.
units.tr: LET NO ONE DESTROY A TOMB, OR BRING IN ANOTHER'S BODY; IF ANYONE SHALL HAVE VIOLATED, THROWN DOWN, OR BROKEN A TOMBSTONE, A MONUMENT, OR A COLUMN, let there be a penalty.

units.la: Refert Cicero loco laudato: De sepulcris autem nihil est apud Solonem amplius, quam, Ne quis ea deleat, neve alienum inferat: pœnaque est, Si quis bustum (nam id puto appellari tymbon) aut monumentum, inquit, aut columnam violarit, deiecerit, fregerit. Neque tantum violabantur sepulcra & monumenta, si quis ea deleuerit, aut columnam fregerit, sed etiam si quis vestem, quæ cum mortuo condebantur, furaretur: docuit id Synesius Epistola CXLII. extrema: [illegible, ~45 letters] Violari quoque hac Lege scribit Solo sepulcrorum religionem, Si quis alienum intulerit. Habebant enim gentes aut familiæ sua singulæ monumenta: unde Demosthenes [illegible, ~40 letters] Quare Marcellinus cognationem Thucydidis cum Cimone probat hoc argumento: [illegible, ~60 letters] & probro vertebatur maiorum suorum sepulcro priuari, vt è Dinarcho [illegible, ~35 letters] docent Grammatici. [illegible, ~25 letters] Tanta præterea erat horum monumentorum religio, vt inimico ne quidem accedere liceret: vnde ista leges ex hoc more apud Sophoclem Aiacc [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: Cicero, in the passage cited, reports: On sepulchres, however, nothing more is found in Solon than this: "Let no one destroy them, nor bring in another's body." The penalty is: "If anyone shall have violated, thrown down, or broken a burial mound (for I think this is called tymbos) or a monument, or a column." Sepulchres and monuments were violated not only if someone destroyed them or broke a column, but also if someone stole the clothing that was buried with the dead. Synesius shows this in his Epistle 142, at the end: [illegible]. Solon's law also writes that the sanctity of sepulchres was violated by this clause: If anyone shall have brought in another's body. For nations or individual families had their own monuments; whence Demosthenes [illegible]. Hence Marcellinus proves the kinship of Thucydides with Cimon by this argument: [illegible], and it was counted a disgrace to be deprived of the sepulchre of one's ancestors, as the grammarians teach from Dinarchus [illegible]. Moreover, reverence for these monuments was so great that it was not even permitted for an enemy to approach them; whence those laws arose from this custom, as in Sophocles' Ajax [illegible].

units.tr: Indeed, in general, it was provided by a law of Solon that no outsider should approach another's monument, except while going to the funeral.

units.la: Legem refert Plutarchus in Solone: [illegible, ~50 letters] Ne scilicet Deos Manes aliquo modo lacesserent, aut malo carmine terram grauem imprecarentur.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his Life of Solon, reports the law: [illegible]. Namely, so that they should not in any way provoke the Manes gods, or call down a heavy curse on the earth by an evil charm.

units.la: Modum quoque posuit Solo collocationi, elationi, & productioni funerum: eius enim de hac re Lex ista legitur. ΤΟΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΑ ΠΡΟΤΙΘΕΣΘΑΙ ΕΝΔΟΝ, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ. ΕΚΦΕΡΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΑ ΤΗΙ ΥΣΤΕΡΑΙΑ, ΗΙ ΑΝ ΠΡΟΘΩΝΤΑΙ ΠΡΙΝ ΗΛΙΟΝ ΕΞΕΧΕΙΝ. ΒΑΔΙΖΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΝΔΡΑΣ ΠΡΟΣΘΕΝ, ΟΤΑΝ ΕΚΦΕΡΩΝΤΑΙ, ΤΑΣ ΔΕ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑΣ ΟΠΙΣΘΕΝ. ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΕΙΣΙΕΝΑΙ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΟΣ, ΜΗΔ' ΑΚΟΛΟΥΘΕΙΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΙ, ΟΤΑΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΣΗΜΑΤΑ ΑΓΗΤΑΙ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΕΞΗΚΟΝΤ' ΕΤΩΝ ΓΕΓΟΝΥΙΑΝ ΠΛΗΝ ΟΣΑΙ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΩΝ ΕΙΣΙ, ΜΗΔ' ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΟΣ ΕΙΣΙΕΝΑΙ, ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΕΞΕΝΕΧΘΗ Ο ΝΕΚΥΣ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΜΗΔΕΜΙΑΝ, ΠΛΗΝ ΟΣΑΙ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΩΝ ΕΙΣΙΝ.
units.tr: Solon also set a limit on the laying out, carrying out, and processions of funerals; for this law about the matter is read: "Let the dead be laid out indoors, however the family wishes. Let the dead be carried out before sunrise on the day after the laying out, and let them be carried out ahead of the sun's rising. Let the men walk in front when they are carried out, and the women behind. Let no woman who is under sixty years of age, or who is not born of cousins, enter the house of the dead or go to the funeral. Nor is anyone to enter the house of the dead after the body has been carried out, except those born of cousins." [ΤΟΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΑ ΠΡΟΤΙΘΕΣΘΑΙ ΕΝΔΟΝ, ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΒΟΥΛΩΝΤΑΙ. ΕΚΦΕΡΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΑ ΤΗΙ ΥΣΤΕΡΑΙΑ, ΗΙ ΑΝ ΠΡΟΘΩΝΤΑΙ ΠΡΙΝ ΗΛΙΟΝ ΕΞΕΧΕΙΝ. ΒΑΔΙΖΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΝΔΡΑΣ ΠΡΟΣΘΕΝ, ΟΤΑΝ ΕΚΦΕΡΩΝΤΑΙ, ΤΑΣ ΔΕ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑΣ ΟΠΙΣΘΕΝ. ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΕΞΕΙΝΑΙ ΕΙΣΙΕΝΑΙ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΟΣ, ΜΗΔ' ΑΚΟΛΟΥΘΕΙΝ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΙ, ΟΤΑΝ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΣΗΜΑΤΑ ΑΓΗΤΑΙ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΕΞΗΚΟΝΤ' ΕΤΩΝ ΓΕΓΟΝΥΙΑΝ ΠΛΗΝ ΟΣΑΙ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΩΝ ΕΙΣΙ, ΜΗΔ' ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΟΣ ΕΙΣΙΕΝΑΙ, ΕΠΕΙΔΑΝ ΕΞΕΝΕΧΘΗ Ο ΝΕΚΥΣ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΑ ΜΗΔΕΜΙΑΝ, ΠΛΗΝ ΟΣΑΙ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΑΝΕΨΙΑΔΩΝ ΕΙΣΙΝ.]

units.la: Mortuum pro arbitrio intus collocanto. Ante lucem efferunto postridie collocationis: Funus producunto viri quidem primi ordine, feminae subsequuntor. Feminae funestam domum ne intranto, aut exequias cun-to sexagenariis minores, aut quae sobrinis natae non sint: neque item intranto domum, postquam funus elatum est, nisi sobrinis natae sint.
units.tr: Let the dead be laid out indoors as one wishes. Let them be carried out before daylight on the day after the laying out. Let the men walk first in the procession, and the women follow. Let no women go into the house of mourning, or attend the funeral, if they are under sixty years old, or if they are not born of cousins. Likewise, let no one enter the house after the funeral has been carried out, unless they are born of cousins.

units.la: Legem descripsit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Μακαρίας, ibidemque Soloni adscribit, qua cautum primum de collocatione, quae fiebat pro arbitrio a cognatis, ut pater a filio, filius a patre si superstitem haberet; unde probat Isaeus Cleonem Astyphili filium non esse, quia neque eum collocauerit, neque iusta fecerit mortuo: ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἐκομίσθη [?] τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς ἀδελφοῦ, ὁ μὲν [?] πάλαι ὑπὸ [?] ἐξεπέμφθη, [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐπεὶ δὲ ἔθαψεν, οἱ δὲ φίλοι Ἀριστόλου [?] συγχωροῦντες [?] ῥῶντες τὸ πατέρα τῷ μὲν Ἀρρωστῶν, ἐμὲ δὲ [?] [illegible, ~25 letters] λαβὼν τὰ νομιζόμενα ἐπαίνῳ. Aderant huic collocationi promiscue viri & feminae e cognatis. Demosthenes loco laudato: Τοῦτο κελεύει τοὺς σπουδαίους, καὶ πέρας τῆς σωφροσύνης τῆς πολιτικῆς. De elatione autem Solo praescripsit, ut efferrentur ante Solem ortum postridie collocationis: Mutauerat tamen hic mos, quem postea reuocauit Demetrius Phalereus, ut refert M. Tullius Libro illo II. de LL. Sed ait rursus idem Demetrius, increbuisse eam funerum, sepulcrorumque magnificentiam, quae nunc fere Romae est. Quam consuetudinem Lege minuit ipse: ANTE LVCEM enim iussit EFFERRI. Sequitur in Lege de producendo funere, & producendi ordine. Ducebant autem propinqui: Hinc commilitones Astyphili, qui eum iam [illegible, ~25 letters] ἐπὶ πατέρα [?] ἀδελφοῦ, [?] τὰ ἀλλὰ ἀγῶνα. Neque feminae sexagenariis minores, quae sobrinis natae non essent, funestam domum intrare, aut exequias ire poterant. At vero postquam funus elatum fuerat, nemini feminae, quae sobrinis non esset nata minimum, eandem funestam domum intrare non licebat. Quum autem tandem magna hominum celebritas funeribus producendis interesset, eam Lege minuerunt:
units.tr: Demosthenes described this law in his speech Against Macartatus, and he attributes it to Solon as well. It first provided, concerning the laying out, which was done at the discretion of the relatives, such as a father by a son, or a son by a father if he had one surviving. Hence Isaeus proves that Cleon was not the son of Astyphilus, because he neither laid him out nor performed the due rites for the dead: [illegible]. Men and women of the kindred were present together at this laying out. Demosthenes, in the passage cited: "This commands the earnest, and is the limit of civic temperance" [Τοῦτο κελεύει τοὺς σπουδαίους, καὶ πέρας τῆς σωφροσύνης τῆς πολιτικῆς]. Concerning the carrying out, Solon prescribed that the dead be carried out before sunrise on the day after the laying out. This custom had, however, changed, and Demetrius of Phalerum later restored it, as Marcus Tullius reports in the second book of De Legibus: But again the same Demetrius says that the magnificence of funerals and sepulchres had grown, such as now is almost at Rome. He himself reduced this custom by law: for he ordered them to be carried out BEFORE DAWN. The law then goes on about the procession of the funeral and the order of the procession. The relatives led the procession; hence Astyphilus's comrades, who had already [illegible] for the father and brother, and the other contests. Women who were under sixty years old, and not born of cousins, could not enter the house of mourning or attend the funeral. But after the funeral had been carried out, no woman who was not at least born of cousins was permitted to enter the same house of mourning. Yet when at last a great crowd of people attended the funeral procession, they reduced this by law:

units.la: IN FVNERIBVS CELEBRITAS VIRORVM AC MVLIE- RVM PRODVCENDIS NE INTERESTO.
units.tr: AT FUNERALS, MEN AND WOMEN ARE NOT TO ATTEND THE PROCESSION IN LARGE CROWDS.

units.la: Legem laudat è Demetrio Cicero Libro de LL. Sublata etiam erat Lege celebritas virorum ac mulierum, quo lamentatio minueretur, habet enim luctum concursus hominum. Vbi habes causam Legis ferendae. Sumptum quoque sustulit Solo, noluit enim tribus plus vestibus, Ricinis dixerunt Decemviri Romani, mortuum componi, aut condi.
units.tr: Cicero, in his book De Legibus, cites a law from Demetrius: "The gathering of men and women was also removed by law, so that lamentation might be lessened, for a crowd of people brings grief." Here you have the reason for enacting the law. Solon also curbed expense: he did not want the dead laid out or buried in more than three ricinia, as the Roman Decemvirs put it.

units.la: Μὴ πωτιθέναι πλέον ἱματίων τεισῶν [?] Plus tribus ricinis mortuum ne humato.
units.tr: Not to lay out more than three ricinia: "Plus tribus ricinis mortuum ne humato" [Μὴ τιθέναι πλέον ἱματίων τριῶν]. The dead are not to be buried in more than three ricinia.

units.la: Legem laudat Plutarchus in Solone: οὐκ εἴασεν οὐ τιθέναι πλέον ἱματίων τεισῶν [?]. Quam Legem Decemviri in suas Tabulas retulerunt. M.Cicero loco laudato: Posteaquam, ut scribit Phalereus, sumptuosa fieri funera, & lamentabilia cepissent, Solonis Lege sublata sunt. quam Legem eisdem prope verbis nostri Decemviri in undecimam tabulam coniecerunt. Nam de tribus ricinis, & pleraque illa Solonis sunt. Ne autem lamentabilia essent, Solo Lege sustulit lessum & laceratione. hanc ita expresserat Legislator:
units.tr: Plutarch, in his Life of Solon, cites the law: he did not allow the dead to be laid out in more than three garments [οὐκ εἴασεν τιθέναι πλέον ἱματίων τριῶν]. The Decemvirs put this law into their Tables. Cicero, in the passage cited: "Since, as Phalereus writes, funerals had become costly and lamentable, they were abolished by Solon's law. Our Decemvirs put this law into the eleventh table in almost the same words. For the matter of the three ricinia and most of those provisions are Solon's." So that funerals would not be lamentable, Solon abolished by law the wailing and the laceration of the body. The lawgiver expressed this in these words:

units.la: MVLIERES GENAS NE RADVNTO, NEVE LESSVM FVNERIS ERGO HABENTO.
units.tr: WOMEN ARE NOT TO SCRATCH THEIR CHEEKS, NOR TO HOLD A WAILING FOR THE SAKE OF A FUNERAL.

units.la: Habes apud Ciceronem loco laudato: Nam de tribus ricinis, & pleraque illa Solonis sunt. de lamentis vero expressa verbis sunt : MVLIERES GENAS NE RADVNTO, NEVE LESSVM FVNERIS ERGO HABENTO. Sensum huius repræsentauit Plutarchus in Solone verbis istis : ἀμωχαὶ δὲ κοπλο-μένων, καὶ ὃ ἁρῶν πεποιημένα [?], καὶ ὃ κωκύων ἀγὴρ ἐκ ταφῆς ἑτέρων, ἀφεῖλεν [?].
units.tr: You have this in Cicero, in the passage cited: "For the matter of the three ricinia and most of those provisions are Solon's. As for the laments, they are expressed in these words: women are not to scratch their cheeks, nor to hold a wailing for the sake of a funeral." Plutarch, in Solon, gives the sense of this in these words: he removed the beating of the breast by those who mourn, the cutting of the flesh, and the loud wailing of those who lament at another's burial [ἀμωχαὶ δὲ κοπτομένων, καὶ ὁ ἁρῶν..., καὶ ὁ κωκύων ἀγὼν ἐκ ταφῆς ἑτέρων ἀφεῖλεν].

units.la: Hippias Tyrannus Lege præcepit, ut in singulos mortuos Mineruæ Sacerdoti, quæ est in arce, penderetur obolus, hordei duo sextarii, & frumenti totidem.
units.tr: Hippias the tyrant ordered by law that for each dead person an obol be paid to the priestess of Minerva who is in the citadel, along with two sextarii of barley and as many of wheat.

units.la: Τῇ τι ἱερείᾳ τῇ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς, τῆς Ἀκροπόλεῖ, ἐπὶ τῷ ἀποθανόντος, φέρειν χοίνικα χριθῶν, ἢ πυρῶν ἑτέραν, καὶ ὀβολόν [?]. Sacerdoti Minervæ, quæ est in arce, in singulos mortuos; duos hordei sextarios, totidem frumenti, itemque obolum pendito.
units.tr: To the priestess of Athena, who is on the Acropolis, for each dead person, one should pay an obol, a choenix of barley, and another of wheat [Τῇ τῇ ἱερείᾳ τῇ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς, τῆς Ἀκροπόλει, ἐπὶ τῷ ἀποθανόντι, φέρειν χοίνικα χριθῶν, ἢ πυρῶν ἑτέραν, καὶ ὀβολόν]. Pay to the priestess of Minerva, who is in the citadel, for each dead person, two sextarii of barley, as much wheat, and likewise an obol.

units.la: Docet Aristoteles Libro II.Oeconomicon : Ἱππίας ὁ Ἀθηναῖος ἐκέλευσε, τῇ τε ἱερείᾳ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς, τῆς ἐν Ἀκροπόλει, ἐπὶ τῷ ἀποθανόντι, φέρειν χοίνικα χριθῶν, καὶ πυρῶν ἑτέραν, καὶ ὀβολόν.
units.tr: Aristotle, in Book II of the Oeconomica, teaches this: Hippias the Athenian ordered that, to the priestess of Athena in the Acropolis, for the one who has died, one should pay a choenix of barley, another of wheat, and an obol [Ἱππίας ὁ Ἀθηναῖος ἐκέλευσε τῇ τε ἱερείᾳ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς, τῆς ἐν Ἀκροπόλει, ἐπὶ τῷ ἀποθανόντι φέρειν χοίνικα χριθῶν, καὶ πυρῶν ἑτέραν, καὶ ὀβολόν].

units.la: Cùm iusta mortuo fierent, Lege prohibuit Solo, ne boue parentaretur.
units.tr: When rites were being performed for the dead, Solon by law forbade that an ox be sacrificed at the parentalia.

units.la: Μὴ σιαχίζειν βοῦς. Boue ne parentato.
units.tr: Not to slaughter oxen [Μὴ σφάττειν βοῦς]. Do not sacrifice an ox at the parentalia.

units.la: Laudat Plutarchus in Solone: σιαχίζειν ὃ βοῶν οὐκ εἴασεν. Ficbant hæc iusta, ipso clationis die, & ab illa, nono, item tricesimo, anniuersario, & illo quo Natalem eius celebrabant. Pollux Libro III. cap. XIX. σιαγιομαζα, ἐκφοβεῖ, ἐνταπα, τεἰακοντᾳδις, ἡρεισα, νεκύσια [?]. Τῶν τα δὲ ἐπὶ ἡρωικία τῇ ἀπολλαγμένων νόμιμα [?].
units.tr: Plutarch, in Solon, cites: he did not allow oxen to be slaughtered [σφάττειν βοῶν οὐκ εἴασεν]. These rites were performed on the very day of the burial, and from that day on, on the ninth day, likewise on the thirtieth, on the anniversary, and on the day on which they celebrated his birthday. Pollux, Book III, chapter 19, lists the terms for these rites; the customs of those who were honoured in the heroic manner were kept apart [Τῶν δὲ ἐπὶ ἡρωικῇ τιμῇ ἀπολλαγμένων νόμιμα].

units.la: Immolabant vero in effossa scrobe. Porphyrius de Nympharum antro. Τῆς μὲν Ὀλυμπίοις ἡροῖς ναοῖς τι, καὶ ἔδη, καὶ βωμοῖς ἱδρύσαντο [?], ἡρωσίοις δὲ καὶ Ἡρωσιν ἐχάρεις [?], ἐπὶ θυσίαις δὲ βόες [?] καὶ μίαγα [?]. Atque hæc iusta parentibus persoluere cogebantur Lege liberi, aut, si nulli essent liberi, heredes.
units.tr: They used to sacrifice in a dug pit. Porphyry, in On the Cave of the Nymphs: they set up shrines, images and altars for the heroes, and for the heroines and the heroes sacrifices were offered, and oxen and sheep. And these rites were compelled by law to be performed for their parents by the children, or, if there were no children, by the heirs.

units.la: Τοὺς παῖδας ἐκ τοῦ κληρονόμους, ἐπιδιδῶ ἀποδιδόναι οἱ γονεῖς, ὅπως τῷ νομιζομένῳ πύρωσι [?], ἀποδακυάζειν [?]. Liberi, aut heredes, mortuis parentibus iusta faciunto.
units.tr: The children, or the heirs, are to perform the rites for dead parents, in the manner customary [Τοὺς παῖδας ἢ τοὺς κληρονόμους, ἐπιδιδόναι ἀποδιδόναι τοὺς γονεῖς, ὅπως τῷ νομιζομένῳ...]. The children or heirs are to perform the rites for the dead parents.

units.la: Legis, quod ad liberos attinet, meminit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Τιμοκράτους, ὃ νόμῳ καὶ ζωῆς ἀπαγγέλλοντος παῖδας τοῖς γονεῦσι τιμῶν [?], καὶ ἐπιδιδῶ ἀποδιδόναι [?]. ὅπως· τὴν νομιζομένων τύχοι, καὶ ἐκ[?] ... de heredibus colliges ex his Isæi [Greek ?] [Greek ?] Κλεωνύμου κλήρου. ὁρᾷς [?] Κλεώνυμος ἡμᾶς ... Δικαίου[?], καὶ [illegible, ~12 letters] [Greek ?] ἐπὶ παίδας ἡμᾶς καταλιπεῖν, καὶ τῆς οὐσίας ἡμίτεργες [?] ... [Greek ?] Δικαίας, (ἡ γὰρ ... ) τὴν ... οἰκίαν ... καὶ κύριον τὴν αὐτῆς καταλιπεῖν, καὶ ποιεῖ αὐτὰ ... ὁ ζῶν ἀλλοφυεῖς [?] ... ) Quod enim iusta fecisset Dinias mortuo Cleonymo, fecisset heredum vicem, qui eius fidei erant commissi: nam tutores ea omnia faciebant, quæ facere tenebantur pupilli, donec adoleuissent. Inter cetera vero silicernium exhibebant [Greek ?] ... [Greek ?] Græci [Greek ?] vocant, [Greek ?] Circumpotationem vertit M. Tullius, è cuius Libro II. de LL. constat à Solone in Seruorum funere fuisse sublatam.
units.tr: Demosthenes, in the speech against Timocrates, mentions the law concerning children: that by law children are bound to honour their parents and to perform the customary rites for them. From Isaeus's speech on the estate of Cleonymus you may gather who the heirs were. For Dicaeus, who performed the rites for the dead Cleonymus, did so in the place of the heirs to whose trust the estate had been committed; for guardians did all those things which orphans were bound to do until they came of age. Among other things they provided the silicernium, which the Greeks call the circum-potation, a term Marcus Tullius rendered; and from his second Book On the Laws it is clear that Solon abolished it at the funeral of a slave.

units.la: SERVILIS VNCTVRA OMNISQVE CIRCVMPOTATIO
units.tr: THE ANOINTING OF SLAVES AND ALL CIRCUM-DRINKING

units.la: Verba Ciceronis sunt: Iam cetera in XII. minuendi sumptus, lamentationesque funeris, translata de Solonis fere Legibus. addit paulo post: Hæc præterea sunt in Legibus de unctura: quibus Seruilis unctura tollitur, omnisque circumpotatio. Quibus verbis ostendit, fuisse in seruili funere, quia tollitur, & in ciuium concedi: idque iam à Cecrope. Cicero ibidem: Nam & Athenis iam ille mos à Cecrope, ut aiunt, permansit, hoc ius terra humandi: quam cum proximi iniecerant, obductaque terra erat, frugibus obserebatur, ut sinus & gremium quasi matris mortuo tribueretur, solum autem frugibus expiatum, ut vitiis redderetur. Sequebantur epulæ, quas inibant parentes coronati. Nam propinquorum erat, & eorum qui propiori cognatione defunctos contingerent, illud silicernium exhibere. Demosthenes [Greek ?] φησιν· ἀλλὰ δίον ποιεῖν αὐτοὺς ὁ Κεκροπίδης ... τὴν πεπλουτηκότων, ὥσπερ πάλαι εἰωθεῖ γίγνεσθαι, τὸ[?] ἐπίνοσμα [?] ... Hinc fiebat ut in Magistratuum δοκιμασίας, interrogarentur, an parentibus iusta fecissent, & eorum sepulcra exornassent, necne. Xenophon Libro II. [Greek ?] καὶ ἐν Δίᾳ ἐαυτῶν ὡς τὴν ... πολιτῶν [?] ... τῶν τὰς τάφους μὴ κισμῆ, καὶ τῶν ἐξεπιζεῖ ἡ πόλις ... τῶν δοκιμασίας. In his autem epulis iam ab ipso Cecrope celebrabantur defuncti, siquidem laudanda fecissent. M. Tullius: Sequebantur epulæ, quas inibant parentes coronati, apud quas de mortui laude, tum quid veri erat, prædicatum. nā mentiri nefas habebatur. Postea hic honos iis tantum est habitus, qui in bello essent interfecti, aut publice sepeliebantur, eaque orationes habebantur in Ceramico extra vrbem, vbi erant sepulti. Grammatici: Κεραμεικοί. δύο ἦσαν Κεραμεικαί, ὁ μὲν, ἐνδὸν τῆς πόλεως, ὁ δὲ, ἔξω. ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοὺς ἐν πολέμῳ πεπτωκότας τῷ δημοσίᾳ καὶ τοὺς ἐπιταφίους ἔλεγον. Habebant vero orationem ii soli, qui ad eam rem publice erant constituti:
units.tr: Cicero's words are: "The rest, in the Twelve Tables, concerning the reduction of expense and the laments at funerals, is largely taken from the laws of Solon." He adds a little later: "Further, in the laws concerning anointing there are these provisions: by them the anointing of slaves is removed, and all circum-drinking." By these words he shows that it existed at a slave's funeral, since it was removed, and was permitted for citizens; and this from Cecrops onward. Cicero in the same place: "For at Athens that custom from Cecrops, as they say, has lasted, this right of burial in the earth: when the nearest kin had cast earth over, and the earth was heaped up, it was sown with grain, so that the bosom and lap of the mother might be given to the dead, and the soil, purified by the grain, might be returned to its uses. Feasts followed, which the crowned parents entered; for it was the duty of kinsmen, and of those who were bound to the dead by closer relationship, to provide that silicernium." Demosthenes says: "But Cecropides made them ... as those who had grown rich were accustomed to do long ago..." Hence it came about that at the scrutiny of magistrates they were asked whether they had performed the rites for their parents and adorned their tombs or not. Xenophon, in Book II: ... and in the city they were examined concerning the tombs, whether they had neglected them. At these feasts the dead were celebrated from Cecrops' own time, provided they had done praiseworthy deeds. Marcus Tullius: "Feasts followed, which the crowned parents entered; at them the praise of the dead was proclaimed, and whatever truth there was in it, for lying was considered wrong. Afterwards this honour was given only to those who had been killed in war or buried at public expense, and orations were delivered in the Ceramicus outside the city, where they were buried." The grammarians: "Kerameikoi": there were two Kerameikoi, one within the city, the other outside it, where they spoke of those who had fallen in war at public expense and gave the funeral orations [Κεραμεικοί. Δύο ἦσαν Κεραμεικαί, ὁ μὲν ἐντὸς τῆς πόλεως, ὁ δὲ ἔξω, ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοὺς ἐν πολέμῳ πεπτωκότας τῷ δημοσίᾳ καὶ τοὺς ἐπιταφίους ἔλεγον]. Only those who had been publicly appointed for that purpose delivered the oration:

units.la: NEC DE MORTVI LAVDE NISI IN PVBLICIS SEPVLTV- RIS, NEC AB ALIO NISI QVI PVBLICE AD EAM CONSTI- TVTVS SIT, DICITOR.
units.tr: Praise of the dead may be spoken only at public funerals, and only by a person publicly appointed for that purpose.

units.la: Cicero hanc Legem laudat Libro II. de LL. Nec de mortui laude, nisi in publicis sepulturis: (atqui ὁ Κεραμεικῷ πρὸς ἔξω τῆς πόλεως ἐνταῦθα δημοσίᾳ, siue in bello interfectos, siue alios, quibus honorem habitum vellent) nec ab alio, nisi qui publice ad eam constitutus esset, dicit Lege licebat. Neque tantum publice orationem habebant in funere, sed etiam publica erat sepultura eorum, qui in bello occubuissent ex hac Lege.
units.tr: Cicero cites this law in Book II of De Legibus: Praise of the dead is not to be spoken except at public burials (and indeed at the Ceramicus outside the city, where they were publicly buried, whether men slain in war or others whom they wished to honour), nor by anyone other than a person publicly appointed for that purpose, as the law allowed. Not only was the oration delivered publicly at the funeral, but under this law the burial itself was public for those who had fallen in war.

units.la: Δημοσία ταφὰς ποιεῖσθαι τῶν ἐν τῷ πολέμῳ ἀποθανόντων.
units.tr: To hold public burials for those who died in war. [Δημοσία ταφὰς ποιεῖσθαι τῶν ἐν τῷ πολέμῳ ἀποθανόντων]

units.la: Legem laudat Thucydides Lib. II. & morem hunc sepeliendi publice eos, qui in bello occubuissent, & pro concione laudandi describit: οἱ δὲ τὰ αὐτὰ χρώμενοι, οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι τὰ πάτρια νόμῳ χεώμενοι, δημοσία ταφὰς ἐποιήσαντο τῶν ἐν τῷ πολέμῳ ἀποθανόντων, ἔπειτα [?] τοὺς [?] λόγους [?] τῶν ἀποθανόντων [?] ἐπαινοῦντες [?] ἐπιφέρειν [?] τῆς αὐτῆς ἑκάστου [?] τῆς βουλῆς [?] ἐπιδιδόντες δὲ ἡ εὐφορία ἢ λόγοις [?] ἀναξιοι [?] φυλῆς ἑκάστης μίαν. ἔνεστι δὲ τῆς τοῦ ἑκάστου [?] φυλῆς. μία δὲ ἡλίνη [?] ἐκ τῆς φερόμενη [?] ἐγραμμένη τῆς ἀφανοῦς [?], οἱ αὖ μὴ δύρευσιν [?] ἐς αἰσχύνην. ξυνεκφέρεῖ δὲ ὁ βουλόμενος καὶ αὐτῶν καὶ ξένων. καὶ γυναῖκες πρῆσθαι ἃς προσήκουσαι ὅτι τῶν ἔφων, ὀλοφυρόμεναι. πῖπρασιν δὲ ἐς ὅ δημόσιον σῆμα, ὃ ἔστιν ἐπὶ τῆς καλλίστου προαιρέσεως τῆς πόλεως. καὶ ἀεὶ οἱ ἀποτοὶ ἀποθνήσκοντες ἐν τῷ πολέμῳ, πλὴν γὰρ τοὺς ἐν Μαραθῶνι. ἐπιδιδόντες δὲ χρύσωσι γῆ, ὅτε [?] ἡμέρα [?] ὑπὸ τῆς πόλεως, ὃς δὲ γνώμη τε ἀξία μὴ ἀξιώσεως [?] εἶ), καὶ ἀξιώματι προσήκει, λέγει ἐπ' αὐτῶν ἔπαινον τὸν προσήκοντα, μὴ δὲ τῶν ἀπόφθρηνται. ὧδε μὲν θαπτόντων καὶ ἁπὸ πάντως τὸν πολέμου, ὁπότε ξυμβαίη αὐτῆς, ἐχέαντο τοῦ νόμου. Legem autem hanc, qua constitutum est publice in publicis sepulturis de mortuorum laudibus dicere, tulerunt post Romanos nostri Athenienses: etsi enim iam ab ipso Cecrope hic mos permansisset, ut de mortui laude, cum quid veri erat, praedicaretur apud epulas, laudatio haec non publica, sed privata tantum in circumpotatione erat, publica, de qua M. Tullius ex Atheniensium Lege, instituta est, postquam aduersus Persas est pugnatum. Dionysius Halicarnasseus Libro V. εἰώθει γὰρ ποτε Ἀθηναῖοι τεθνηκότων τὸν ἐπιτάφιον ἔπαινον ἐν νόμῳ, εἶτ' ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπὶ Ἀρτεμισίῳ καὶ τῶν Σαλαμῖνι, καὶ ἐν Πλαταιαῖς τῆς πατρίδος ἀποθανόντων ἠξίωσαν [?], εἶτ' ἀπὸ τῶν περὶ Μαραθῶνα ἔργων. Atque ad hanc orationem dicendam constituebatur Lege is, cuius filius in bello ceteris longe fortius cecidisset.
units.tr: Thucydides, in Book II, cites this law and describes the custom of publicly burying those who fell in war and praising them before the assembly. In his words: the Athenians, following their ancestral law, made public burials for those who had died in war; then, in the speeches, they praised the dead, and one speaker was chosen for each tribe. The text is corrupt here, but it describes the gathering of the bones in a common tomb and the funeral oration. Thucydides also says that anyone who wished could join in the procession, both citizens and foreigners, and that women mourned at the tomb; the dead were buried in the public monument in the most beautiful suburb of the city. He adds that the bodies of those who died in the war were always so buried, except those at Marathon, who were buried on the spot. Whoever had shown courage was praised by the speaker, and the speech was fitting to the dignity of the dead. Thus they buried the dead, and at the beginning of the war they kept to this law. [Ὧδε μὲν θαπτόντων...] Moreover, Dionysius of Halicarnassus notes that this law and custom were tulerunt post Romanos nostri Athenienses: the Athenians, our predecessors, passed the law by which it was settled that praise of the dead should be spoken publicly at public burials. Although this custom had existed from the time of Cecrops himself, that praise of the dead, when there was something true to say, should be proclaimed at feasts, this praise was not public but private, within the drinking-circle. The public praise, of which Marcus Tullius speaks from the law of the Athenians, was instituted after the fighting against the Persians. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book V: for the Athenians were once accustomed to deliver an epitaphic praise, by law, for those who had died at Artemisium and at Salamis and at Plataea for their country, and then for the deeds at Marathon. And to deliver this oration the man was appointed by law whose son had fallen in war, excelling all others in bravery.

units.la: Τὸν πατέρα τῆς ἀρίστα ἀποθανόντος ἐν πολέμῳ λέγειν τὸν ἐπιτάφιον.
units.tr: That the father of one who died most nobly in war should deliver the funeral oration. [Τὸν πατέρα τῆς ἀρίστα ἀποθανόντος ἐν πολέμῳ λέγειν τὸν ἐπιτάφιον]

units.la: Legem habes in Polemonis Argumento τῆς ἐπιταφίων λόγων. νόμου ὄντος Ἀθηναῖ, τὸν πατέρα τῆς ἀρίστα ἀποθανόντος ἐν πολέμῳ λέγειν τὸν ἐπιτάφιον, Καλλιμάχου καὶ Κυναγείρου πατέρες δικάζοντο. nam hinc saepe oriebantur controversiae. Quemadmodum autem ceteris iusta persoluebant parentes, aut cognati: ita voluit Legislator parentes constitui, qui de filiorum laudibus dicerent. Polemon ibidem: ὅτι τὰ τε ἄλλα χρὴ καὶ οἰκεῖον εἶ) τῆς κειμηλίοις τὸν ἐγκώμιον τὸν ἐπ' αὐτοῖς λόγῳ. Neque tantum cum terrae mandabantur, pro concione laudabantur, sed etiam is honos in bello interfectis quotannis instaurabatur.
units.tr: You have the law in the argument to Polemon's work on funeral speeches: when there was an Athenian law that the father of one who had died most nobly in war should deliver the funeral oration, the fathers of Callimachus and Cynegeirus went to law. For controversies often arose from this. Just as parents, or relatives, performed the rites for the others, so the lawgiver wished that parents should be appointed to speak of their sons' praises. Polemon in the same place says that it was fitting that the family should make the praise over the dead in a public speech. Not only when the dead were committed to the earth were they praised before the assembly, but this honour was also renewed every year for those slain in battle.

units.la: ORATIO QUA LAUDANTUR IN CONCIONE II QUI IN PROELIIS INTERFECTI SUNT QUOTANNIS ILLO DIE RECITATOR.
units.tr: THE ORATION IN WHICH THOSE WHO WERE SLAIN IN BATTLES ARE PRAISED BEFORE THE ASSEMBLY, AND WHICH WAS RECITED EACH YEAR ON THAT DAY.

units.la: Habes apud Ciceronem Libro de Oratore. Sed in popu[?]lari oratione, qua mos est Athenis laudari in concione eos, qui sint in proelio interfecti, qua sic probata est, ut eam quotannis, ut scis, illo die recitari necesse sit. Plato Menexeno: αὐτὸς δὲ τοὺς πλουτήσαντας ὑμῶν [illegible, ~12 letters] αὐτὴ τὰ νομιζόμενα ποιοῦσα κοινῇ πᾶσιν ἀφ' ἰδίας ἐκάστῳ ἰδίᾳ χήσεται[?].
units.tr: You find it in Cicero's De Oratore: But in a popular oration, in which it is the custom at Athens to praise before the assembly those who have been slain in battle, a custom so approved that, as you know, it must be recited every year on that day. Plato in the Menexenus: the city itself, performing the customary rites for all in common, gives to each of its citizens, rich or poor, a share in the honours of the dead. [Αὐτὸς δὲ τοὺς πλουτήσαντας ὑμῶν...]

units.la: Tanti autem veteres sepulturam exi-stimarunt, vt cum grauissime imprecari vellent, imprecarentur ἐκπέσοι χθονός[?], vt est apud Sophoclem Aiace.
units.tr: The ancients valued burial so highly that when they wished to curse most gravely, they cursed with the words "may he be cast out of the land," as in Sophocles' Ajax.

units.la: Κακὸς κακῶς ἄθαπτος ἐκπέσοι χθονός,
units.tr: A wretch, may he be cast out of the land, unburied and miserably. [Κακὸς κακῶς ἄθαπτος ἐκπέσοι χθονός]

units.la: vt insepulti iacerent. Quare Atheniensium Lege sanctum est, vt si quis in insepultum incidat cadauer, saltem terram ei iniiciat.
units.tr: that is, left lying unburied. Hence it was sanctioned by Athenian law that if anyone should come upon an unburied corpse, he should at least throw earth upon it.

units.la: Ὃς ἂν ἀπάφῳ ταφεὶς τυχῇ σώματι ἀμφὶ [?] πόδας τὸς ἐπιβαλλὴ αὐτὸς γῆ, ζαπτὰ δὲ [?] τοῖς δυσμαῖς βλέπουσας. [illegible, ~10 letters]
units.tr: Whoever happens upon a body lying unburied should cast earth around its feet, and the body should be laid facing the west. [The Greek is largely illegible in the scan.]

units.la: Insepulto hominis cadaueri terram inijcito, & in sepulcro occasum versus condito.
units.tr: Throw earth on an unburied human corpse, and let it be laid to rest facing the west.
