[illegible, ~30 letters]. Grammatici: [illegible, ~20 letters]. Statuit praeterea Legislator impune ei debere esse, qui dum hostem petit, ciui imprudens mortem dedit, quem in hostibus habuit. Demosth. [illegible, ~50 letters]. Denique cauet impune licere occidere moechum,si quis in vxore, vel in matre,vel in sorore,vel in filia,vel in pellice, vel in nuru, & si quas in liberis suis habet,deprehendeLit [illegible, ~40 letters], iure enim hostis censetur. Demosth. [illegible, ~60 letters].
units.tr: Demosthenes describes the law ... by which it was decreed that no one should be condemned for homicide and pay penalty, who unintentionally kills an opponent in the contests: for he did not intend to kill, but to win the victory by strength. Demosthenes in the same place ... If anyone killed another who was lying in ambush, it was lawful for him with impunity: the words of the law are en hodōi kathelōn [ΕΝ ΟΔΩΙ ΚΑΘΕΛΩΝ]. Thus Eustathius, from the ancients, explains on Iliad 1 ... The grammarians ... The lawgiver further established that he ought to be unpunished who, while seeking an enemy, unknowingly gave death to a citizen whom he had regarded as an enemy. Demosthenes ... Finally, he provides that it is lawful with impunity to kill an adulterer if one catches him in one's wife, mother, sister, daughter, concubine, daughter-in-law, or whichever women one has among one's free children, for by right such a man is counted an enemy. Demosthenes ...

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] ἐπεὶ γὰρ ἡ ὅσις ἐστὶ φίλων καὶ πολεμίων, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀφηρπάσμενα ἀξέρχεσθαι τῆς ἐκ[?] πολιτῶν, τοὺς ἐχθρὰ ποιοῦσας ὃν ἐχθρὰ μὴ ἀπέδωκεν ὁ νόμος. Si praeterea vis illata vi repelleretur, impune erat ex hac Lege:
units.tr: For since the law concerns friends and enemies, it does not make enemies of those whom the law has not declared enemies, though it took away from the citizens what had been seized. If force offered was repelled by force, it was lawful without penalty under this law: [ἐπεὶ γὰρ ἡ ὅσις ἐστὶ φίλων καὶ πολεμίων, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀφηρπάσμενα ἀξέρχεσθαι τῆς ἐκ[?] πολιτῶν, τοὺς ἐχθρὰ ποιοῦσας ὃν ἐχθρὰ μὴ ἀπέδωκεν ὁ νόμος.]

units.la: ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΦΕΡΟΝΤΑ Η ΑΓΟΝΤΑ ΒΙΑΙ ΑΔΙΚΩΣ ΕΥΘΥΣ ΑΜΥΝΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΚΤΕΙ-ΝΗ, ΜΗΠΟΙΝΕΙ ΤΕΘΝΑΝΑΙ. Si quis alium iniuste vim inferentem in continenti necassit, iure casus esto.
units.tr: "And if anyone, when someone is carrying off or leading away by force, unjustly and straightway, kills him while defending himself, he shall not be liable to die." If anyone kills another who is unjustly using violence, on the spot, the killing shall be lawful. [ΚΑΙ ΕΑΝ ΦΕΡΟΝΤΑ Η ΑΓΟΝΤΑ ΒΙΑΙ ΑΔΙΚΩΣ ΕΥΘΥΣ ΑΜΥΝΟΜΕΝΟΣ ΚΤΕΙΝΗ, ΜΗΠΟΙΝΕΙ ΤΕΘΝΑΝΑΙ.]

units.la: Habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ κατ' Αἰσχίνην, estque naturae ipsius Lex, cuius causas M. Tullii in Miloniana verbis aperiemus: Est igitur, iudices, haec non scripta, sed nata Lex, quam non didicimus, accepimus, legimus: verum ex natura ipsa arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus. ad quam non docti, sed facti: non instituti, sed imbuti sumus: ut, si vita nostra in aliquas insidias, si in vim, si in tela aut latronum, aut inimicorum incidisset, omnis honesta ratio esset expediendae salutis. Silent enim Leges inter arma, nec se expectari iubent, cum ei, qui expectare velit, ante iniusta poena luenda sit, quam iusta repetenda. Non enim iniuria refertur, sed repellitur, & vi vis illata vindicatur. Quare prima hac de re sancita Lex & scripta Rhadamanthum habet auctorū. Apollodorus Bibliothecae Libro II. vbi de Hercule, qui Linum occiderat: [?] & optime vetus scriptor apud Suidam: [?]. Cautiones tamen adhibet Draco: primum enim cautum, vt statim ac illata fuerit vis & iniuria, vindicetur, tempusque negat struendis insidiis, quibus opprimat eum, qui iniuriam intulerat. Demosthenes: [?]. Deinde illi soli licet, cui vis sit illata, non alteri. Demosthenes: [?]. Atque, qui iure se occidisse fatebantur, causam in foro, [?] Delphinio, dicebant. Demosthenes ibidem: [?]. Vt autem significarent iure se occidisse, Soli gladium ostendebant; liquet Orestis exemplo apud Euripidem, & adnotant Scholia: [?].
units.tr: You have this in Demosthenes, in the speech Against Aeschines [ἐν τῷ κατ' Αἰσχίνην], and it is a law of nature itself. Let us set out its grounds in the words of Marcus Tullius in the Pro Milone: "There is, therefore, judges, this law, not written but born, which we did not learn, receive or read, but which we seized, drew in and absorbed from nature itself. We were not taught it but made for it; we were not instructed but steeped in it: so that if our life had fallen into some ambush, into violence, into weapons of robbers or enemies, every honourable means of securing our safety would be open. For laws are silent amid arms, and they do not bid us wait for what one who wished to wait would have to pay as an unjust penalty before he could recover what is just." For it is not an injury that is being returned, but an attack that is being repelled, and force offered is avenged by force. Therefore this first law, enacted on this matter, is said to have Rhadamanthus as its author. Apollodorus, in Book II of the Library, speaks of Hercules, who had killed Linus; and an excellent old writer in Suidas [?]. Draco, however, adds cautions: first he provides that vengeance be taken at once, as soon as violence and injury have been done, and he denies time for laying ambushes by which to crush the one who had inflicted the injury. Demosthenes: [?]. Next, this right belongs only to the one to whom the violence was done, not to another. Demosthenes: [?]. And those who admitted they had killed rightfully pleaded their cause at the Delphinium [?]. Demosthenes in the same place: [?]. Moreover, to show that they had killed rightfully, they displayed a sword to the sole judge; this is clear from the example of Orestes in Euripides, and the Scholia note it: [?].

units.la: Erat quoque tribunal Φοινικῶν, quod ἐν Φρέατι dicebatur, in quo ius dicebatur illis, qui cum imprudentes aliquem morti dedissent, solum vertebant: si igitur nondum placatis & exoratis occisi cognatis, quibus in ius vocantibus damnati fuerant, accusarentur scientes etiam alium occidisse, de navi causam dicebant, iudicibus in terra sedentibus, quorum sententia si damnarentur, poenas dabant voluntariae caedis, at si secundis absoluerentur suffragiorum calculis, solum nihilominus vertebant ob imprudentem caedem: ita Lege sanctum est. Εαὶ τις ἐπ' ἀκουσίῳ φόνῳ πεφυγὼς, μήπω τὴν ἐκβαλλόντων αὐτὸν ἠδισμένων, αἰτίαν ἔχῃ ἐπίεσυ φόνου ἑκουσίου, τὸν ἐν πλοίῳ πεφυγαπλεύσαντα, ἐν Φρεατοῖ λέγει ἡ γῆς οὐχ ἀπολόμενον. τοὺς δὲ δικαστὰς δικάζειν ἐν τῇ γῇ, καὶ μὴ ἀλῶ, τῷ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐκουσίοις φόνοις δικεῖν διδόναι· ἐαν δ' ἀπόφυγῃ, ταύτης μὲν ἀξίων ἀφιέναι, τῷ δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ πεφυγότι φόνῳ φυγῇ [?] ἐπέχειν. [?] Si quis exulans ob imprudentem cae-dem, nondum exoratis iis, quibus accusantibus damnatus est, postuletur alterius caedis voluntariae, navigio impositus, Phreatte terram non tangens, cansam orato iudices in terra iudicia reddunto: damnatus in poenam volunta-riae caedis incurrito, et dato: absolutus dimittitor, ob priorem tamen caedem exulato.
units.tr: There was also a tribunal of the Phoenicians, which was called en Phreati [at the Well], where judgment was given on those who, having killed someone unintentionally, went into exile. If, therefore, the dead man's kinsmen had not yet been appeased and won over, and they were accused, by those summoning them to court, of having also killed someone knowingly and deliberately, they pleaded their cause from a ship, while the judges sat on land. If they were condemned by their sentence, they paid the penalty for deliberate homicide; but if they were acquitted by a majority of favourable votes, they nevertheless went into exile for the earlier unintentional killing. So the law ordained. [Εαὶ τις ἐπ' ἀκουσίῳ φόνῳ πεφυγὼς, μήπω τὴν ἐκβαλλόντων αὐτὸν ἠδισμένων, αἰτίαν ἔχῃ ἐπίεσυ φόνου ἑκουσίου, τὸν ἐν πλοίῳ πεφυγαπλεύσαντα, ἐν Φρεατοῖ λέγει ἡ γῆς οὐχ ἀπολόμενον. τοὺς δὲ δικαστὰς δικάζειν ἐν τῇ γῇ, καὶ μὴ ἀλῶ, τῷ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐκουσίοις φόνοις δικεῖν διδόναι· ἐαν δ' ἀπόφυγῃ, ταύτης μὲν ἀξίων ἀφιέναι, τῷ δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ πεφυγότι φόνῳ φυγῇ [?] ἐπέχειν.] Translation: If anyone, exiled for unintentional homicide, not yet having been reconciled to those who drove him out, is accused of deliberate homicide, he is to plead from a ship, not touching land, at the Well; the judges shall give judgment on land. If he is condemned, let him pay the penalty for deliberate murder; if he is acquitted, let him be discharged from that charge, but remain in exile for the earlier homicide.

units.la: Legem habes apud Demosthenem in Aristocratem, ἐπὶ ζῶντι, πάμπολλον δικαστήριον ἄλλο ἡ ζευσασθαι, ὃς ἐπονομάζεται, ὃ δὲ Φρεατοῖ. ἐγὼ γάρ, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, καλῶς δίκας ἐπάγειν ὁ νόμος, ἐαν τις ἐπ' ἀκουσίῳ φόνῳ πεφυγὼς, μήπω τὴν ἐκβαλλόντων αὐτὸν ἠδισμένων, αἰτίαν ἔχῃ ἐπίεσυ φόνου ἑκουσίου. [illegible, ~12 letters] ὁ δὲ δικάζων τὸ φονευθὲν μὲν [?] κρίνειν τὸ ἄλλο ἐστὶ [illegible, ~10 letters] τὴν χώραν [?]. De hoc tribunali Aristoteles Polit. Lib. IV. cap. XVI. τέταρτον δὲ, ὅσα τῆς φεύγειν φόνου, ἐπὶ καθόδῳ ἐπιφέρεται, ᾧ Ἀθῆναι λέγεται ὁ ἐν Φρεατοῖ δικαστήριον. Pollux Lib. VIII. ὁ ἐν Φρεατοῖ, ἐν τούτῳ ἐκεῖνο, εἰ τις τῶν φυγόντων ἐπ' ἀκουσίου φόνου αἰτίᾳ, δίκτειναν αἰτίαν ἔχων ἐκείνου, ὅσον πεφυγάδθαι, ὡς δὲ ἐν θαλάττῃ ὁ δικαστήριον. καὶ τὸν ἐν αἰτίᾳ πεφυγαπλεύσαντα, ὅ γῆς δὲ πεφυγαπολοῦσι, ἀπὸ τῆς νεως ἐχεῖ ἀπολογίσαι, μήτε εἰσκωμίσαι εἰς τὸν γῆν βαλλόμενον. Locus hic erat in Piraeco. Pausanias Atticis: ἐσὶ δὲ τὸ Γλαυκιὰς τόπος ἐν θαλάττῃ Φρεατοῖς· ἐκεῖ οἱ πεφυγότες, ὡς ἀπελθόντας ἐπέγειν ἐπιπλέον σῶας ἔσχημα, τοὺς ἀκουσίους ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἀπὸ νεὼς ἀπολογισῶσαι. Helladius: καὶ τέταρτον, ὃ δὲ Φρεατοῖ, ὁ δικάζῃ τὸν χρῆσον μὲν τινα φόνου πρῶτον, αἰτίᾳ γὰρ πεφυγότα ἔχοντα φόνου· ὡς καὶ κειμένους ἔτι νεὼς, ἐξω τὸ Γλαυκιὰς ἀπολωρυμένος ἄλκωσιν καὶ ἁ, ὅτι ὁ νόμος αὐτὸν ἐκ εἰδεῖν τῆς γῆς ἐπιβεῖναι. malè reddidit C.L. Schottus: Quartam Phreaticum, quod iudicat vadimonia deserentes, prius caedis accusatos: nam sensus est: Tribunal hoc de homicidis iudicare, qui iam ante imprudentis caedis damnati deportati fuerant. Iudicabant Ephetae. Harpocratio. Ἐφέται, οἱ δικάζοντες τὰς ἐφ' αἵματι κρίσεις ἔτι Παλλαδίῳ, καὶ ἔτι Πρυτανείῳ, καὶ ἔτι Δελφίνῳ, καὶ ἐν Φρεατοῖ, Ἐφέται σκαλοῦνται. Quod si is, qui caedem fecerat, siue, sciens, siue imprudens, protenus se fugae daret, pedemque struleret, aut omnino ignotus esset, ita ut iudicio se non vadaret, iudicabatur tamen in tribunali, quod ἐπὶ Πρυτανείῳ dicebatur. Pollux Lib. VIII. ὁ ἐπὶ Πρυτανείῳ, δικάζῃ ὁ τὸν ἀποθανόντων, καὶ ἐὰν ἐκ ἀφιῇς. In genere haec obseruari cautum est in quinque illis tribunalibus: primum in ius vocatio, deinde audiebantur testes, sequebatur contendentium διωμοσία, demum ius dicebant iudices. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Αἰσχίνου: ἀλλ' ἐν κεφαλαίῳ λέγω,
units.tr: You have the law in Demosthenes against Aristocrates: "Besides, there is another very large court, which is called the one at the Well, where the law, Athenians, allows a suit to be brought against anyone who, having fled for unintentional homicide and not yet reconciled with those who expelled him, is accused of deliberate homicide." [illegible] ... The judge who tries the slain ... to judge ... the land [?]. Aristotle, Politics, Book IV, chapter 16, speaks of this tribunal: "Fourth, all those who are charged with homicide, being brought back by a recall, are tried before the court at the Well." Pollux, Book VIII: "the one at the Well, in which that is decided, whether one of the exiles for unintentional homicide, accused of deliberate killing of that man, is tried while in exile; and the court in the sea, and the one who has been tried from a ship, and not on land, must plead from the ship, not be carried onto land." This place was in Piraeus. Pausanias, in the Attica: "There is the Glaucias, a place in the sea at the Well; there the exiles, having been... the unintentional killers are pleaded from the ship, not from land." Helladius: "And fourth, the one at the Well, which tries a man first charged with homicide, for he is accused as an exile for homicide; since he is still lying in the ship outside Glaucias, he is pleaded from the ship, because the law does not allow him to set foot on land." C.L. Schottus rendered it badly: "The fourth Phreatic [court], which judges those who abandon their bail, the first accused of killing; for the sense is: This tribunal judges concerning homicides, of those who had already been condemned for unintentional killing and deported." The Ephetae judged. Harpocration: "Ephetae, those who judge cases of bloodshed; they are called Ephetae in the Palladium, in the Prytaneum, in the Delphinium, and in the Well." But if the one who had committed the homicide, whether knowingly or unknowingly, immediately took to flight and fled his foot, or was entirely unknown, so that he did not appear for trial, he was nevertheless judged in the tribunal called epi Prytaneiō [at the Prytaneum]. Pollux, Book VIII: "the one at the Prytaneum, which judges him who killed, even if he does not appear." In general it is provided that these procedures be observed in those five tribunals: first the summons to court, then the witnesses were heard, then followed the oath of the contending parties, and at last the judges pronounced judgment. Demosthenes in the speech against Aeschines: "But to sum up, I say..."

units.la: ὅπόσοι νόμοι περὶ τῶν Φοινικῶν δικαστηρίων εἰσὶ, καλλίστα λέγοντες, ἢ μάρτυρες, ἢ ὀμνυόντες, [?] ἢ ἀγωνιζομένους, ἢ ἀλλ᾽ ὅπως [?] πρὸς [?] εἰρηκε τὸ ψήφισμα τοῦτο, [?] ἡ μὲν ἀρχὴ, ἢ κρίσις, ἢ κείσις, ἢ μαρτυρία συνόδους, ἢ διαμοσία. Ne quid autem mutaretur in his, prouisum est, hac Lege lata:
units.tr: Whatever laws there are concerning the Phoenician courts, speaking most fully of the beginning of the case, the judgment, the summons, the testimony and the oath of the litigants, and of the pleadings: this decree states that the whole procedure is to be observed as it stands, and nothing in it is to be altered.

units.la: ΟΣ ΑΝ ΑΡΧΩΝ Η ΙΔΙΩΤΗΣ ΑΙΤΙΟΣ Ηι ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΘΕΣΜΟΝ ΣΥΓΧΥΘΗΝΑΙ ΤΟΝΔΕ, Η ΜΕΤΑΠΟΙΗΣΗι ΑΥΤΟΝ, ΑΤΙΜΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΑΤΙΜΟΥΣ, ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΕΚΕΙΝΟΥ.
units.tr: "Whoever, whether a magistrate or a private citizen, is responsible for this law being thrown into confusion or altered, let him be deprived of civic rights, and his children likewise, and his property." [ΟΣ ΑΝ ΑΡΧΩΝ Η ΙΔΙΩΤΗΣ ΑΙΤΙΟΣ ΗΙ ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΘΕΣΜΟΝ ΣΥΓΧΥΘΗΝΑΙ ΤΟΝΔΕ, Η ΜΕΤΑΠΟΙΗΣΗΙ ΑΥΤΟΝ, ΑΤΙΜΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ ΑΤΙΜΟΥΣ, ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΕΚΕΙΝΟΥ.]

units.la: Si quis de Magistratibus, aut populo auctor sit has Leges corrumpendi, aut abrogandi, ille, eiusque liberi impune occiduntur, bona publicanto.
units.tr: If anyone among the magistrates or the people is the author of a proposal to corrupt or abrogate these laws, he and his children may be killed with impunity, and his goods shall be confiscated to the public treasury.

units.la: Habetur haec Lex apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ κατ᾽ Αἰσχί[?]νην, qua ceteras τῶν Φοινικῶν ratas esse voluit Legislator, cauet itaque, Ne quis siue priuatus siue Magistratus τὰς Φοινικὰς νόμους corrumpat, antiquetve, illis quicquam deroget, vel abroget: qui secus faxit, ille eiusque liberi impune occidebantur, & bona publicantur. Oportebat igitureo ordine, quo Leges praescribebant, homicidij postulare, & ius dici, in iisque foris, non alibi, de quibus his Legibus cautum est. Si quis iura haec non obseruaret, vel quia sibi non essent nata, vel quia ignoraret, vel quia praescriptum esset tempus, vel aliam ob causam, Lege cautum erat, vt homicidam, quem videret in foro, aut locis sacris versantem in carcerem abduceret, si homicidii reus peragebatur, capite luebat; sin minus, accusator, qui quintam punctorum partem non tulisset, mille multabatur drachmis:
units.tr: This law is found in Demosthenes, in the speech Against Aeschines [ἐν τῷ κατ᾽ Αἰσχί[?]νην], by which the lawgiver wished the other laws of the Phoenicians to be kept valid. He therefore provides that neither a private citizen nor a magistrate shall corrupt the Phoenician laws, or make them older, or derogate anything from them, or repeal them. Whoever acts otherwise, he and his children may be killed with impunity, and his goods are confiscated. It was therefore necessary to bring a charge of homicide in the order which the laws prescribed, and to have judgment given in those courts and nowhere else, which these laws ordain. If anyone did not observe these rights, either because they did not apply to him, or because he was ignorant of them, or because the time limit had passed, or for some other reason, the law provided that a homicide whom he saw in the forum or in sacred places should be led off to prison; if the charge of homicide was pursued against him, he paid with his life; but if not, the accuser, who did not obtain a fifth part of the votes, was fined a thousand drachmas: [illegible]. The law adds that the person who demands to lead off a man-slayer in the sacred precincts may take him to prison; if he is convicted, he is to be punished by death; but if the one who led him away does not receive a share of the vote, he is to pay a thousand drachmas.

units.la: Τὸν ἀνδροφόνον [?] ἀξιοῦντα ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς, ἀπάγειν ἐξεῖναι εἰς τὸ δεσμωτήριον· ἐὰν μὲν ἀλῶ, θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι· ἐὰν δ᾽ ἡ μὴ μεταλάβῃ ὁ πέμ-πων μέρος τῆς ψήφου ὁ ἀπαγαγὼν, χι-λίας πασοφείλειν.
units.tr: Whoever, demanding the killer in sacred places, is permitted to lead him off to prison: if he is convicted, he is to be punished with death; but if the one who led him away does not obtain a share of the votes, he shall owe a thousand drachmas.

units.la: Homicidam in locis sacris, & in foro versantem in carcerem abducito: conuictum morti dato. si vero is qui in carcerem abduxit, quintam suffragiorum partem non tulit, mille drachmis multator.
units.tr: Lead the homicide off to prison when he is found in sacred places or in the forum. Once convicted, he is to be given over to death. But if the one who led him to prison did not obtain a fifth part of the votes, he is to be fined a thousand drachmas.

units.la: Habes apud Demosthenem ἐν ᾧ τῷ Αεισχε[illegible, ~20 letters] ἐν οἷς ἐδὲ τούτων ἕκαστα [illegible, ~30 letters] ἢ ἄλλο τι ἢ βούλεσθαι [illegible, ~40 letters] ἀλῶ, θανάτῳ ζημιωσθήσεται· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ μεταλάβῃ ὁ πέμπων μέρος τῆς ψήφου ὁ ἀπαγαγὼν, χιλίας πασοφείλειν. Sed quid fiet illis homicidis, qui caede perpetrata alio profugiunt? De his ita Lege cautum est:
units.tr: You have it in Demosthenes, in the speech ... where [the text is illegible] ... "if he is convicted, he shall be punished with death; but if the one who led him away does not obtain a share of the vote, he shall owe a thousand drachmas." But what will be done with those murderers who flee elsewhere after the deed is committed? The law provides as follows concerning them:

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΒΙΑΙΩι ΘΑΝΑΤΩι ΑΠΟΘΑ-ΝΗι, ΥΠΕΡ ΤΟΥΤΟΥ ΤΟΙΣ ΠΡΟΣΗ-ΚΟΥΣΙΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΤΑΣ ΑΝΔΡΟΛΗΤΙΑΣ, ΕΩΣ ΑΝ Η ΔΙΚΑΣ ΤΟΥ ΦΟΝΟΥ Υ-ΡΟΣΚΩΣΙΝ, Η ΤΟΥΣ ΑΠΟΚΤΕΙΝΑΝ-ΤΑΣ ΕΚΔΩΣΙ, ΤΗΝ ΔΕ ΑΝΔΡΟΛΗ-ΤΙΑΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΜΕΧΡΙ, ΤΡΙΩΝ ΓΑΕΩΝ[?] ΔΕ, ΜΗ.
units.tr: "If anyone has died a violent death, the relatives of the dead man may have the right of androlepsia on behalf of this against those [who are responsible], until they either submit to a lawsuit for the murder or hand over the killers; and the androlepsia lasts for up to three months, and no longer." [ἐὰν τις βιαίῳ θανάτῳ ἀποθάνῃ, ὑπὲρ τούτου τοῖς προσήκουσιν εἶναι τὰς ἀνδρολη­ψίας, ἕως ἂν ἢ δίκας τοῦ φόνου ὑποσχῶσιν ἢ τοὺς ἀποκτείναντας ἐκδῶσι· τὴν δὲ ἀνδρολη­ψίαν εἶναι μέχρι τριῶν μηνῶν, μὴ πλέον.]

units.la: Si quis violenta morte obierit, cognatis pignerandi homines ius esto, quoad iudicium caedis subierint, vel necis auctores dederint: ius vero in pignus capiendi homines ad tres vsque, nec eo amplius, esto.
units.tr: If anyone dies a violent death, let the relatives have the right to seize men as pledge until they have answered in a trial for the killing or have handed over the perpetrators. But the right of seizing men in pledge shall extend only to three, and no more.

units.la: Legem αὐλάξει[?], vt & praecedentium plerasque, descripsit Demosthenes Oratione sæpius iam laudata Αεισχεφάνης[?] mo, si quis violenta morte obierit, id est, ini[?]licebat. Demosthenes: τοῦτον μὲν δὴ οὕτω ποιῆσαι, πατάξαι, ᾧ γιγνώσκει ὅτι ἀδίκως λέγει[?]. Qui si in externam urbem profugissent, exposceba[?] lent aleam iudicij subire, poscebantur à ciuibu[?] rant, ut dederentur iis, ad quos facinus admissitur, dabatur iniuriam passis capiendi in pignus stas. Demosthenes: σχηπῖδε ὡς καλὸς, ποεῖτες τοῦτα δὲ, ἀλλὰ τῶν μὴ βούλωνται, ποεσείπαξεν ἐκδοῦναι, ὃ ἀνδρολήψιον φησιν εἶ μέχει τείχη, πλέον δὲ nes forte causæ inseruiens, Androlepsiam Leg profugum suscipientes, sed contra eos, apud c νόμως, ἀλλ᾽ μὴ τε δίκας ἐποίωσι πρὸς οἷς ἀλλὰ ὅ παῖς δίδωσι, καλῶς ἂν τούτων εἶ ὃ ἀνδρολήψιον μέχει ratio erat aduersus eos, qui profugum suscepis ciuis Atheniensis morte violenta obiisset, adu[?] ria fuisset cæsus. Harpocratio: ἀνδρολήψια, ὃ ἐκχύεζειν γὰρ τῇ ἔχουσιν πόλιν τὴν ἀνδροφόνον, Auctor Etymologici: ἀνδρολήψια, ἐπλήματος ἐν Ἰωνίας πλούτιον, καὶ μὴ ἐκδιδόσθαι οἱ ἐν ἐκείνῃ αἰτίᾳ εἶ, ἐφέστο ἐκ τῇ νόμου πρὸς τὴν ἐκείνου πολιτείαν ξοντες τὸ φόνου. Vtraque habet Suidas: Pollux a[?] androlepsiam postulanti, vel potius ea vtenti: androlepsia vti: Pollucis verba sunt Lib. VIII. αἰτιῶνται φόνου καταφυγόντας ὡς τινας ἀπαγγεῖν μὴ λαμβάνειν ἄγειν τὴν τείχη ἀπαγαγεῖν. ὁ δὲ ἀδίκως ἀνδρολήψια.
units.tr: Demosthenes, in the oration cited many times already, has described this law, as he has most of the preceding ones: "if anyone dies a violent death" ... "Thus let him do this: strike him whom he knows to be speaking unjustly." Those who had fled to a foreign city were demanded, that is, the citizens of that city were asked to hand them over to those against whom the crime had been committed; and the one who had suffered the injury was permitted to seize men as pledge. Demosthenes: [Greek]. Harpocration: androlepsia is the seizing, from the city holding the murderer, of men who are not handed over. The author of the Etymologicum: androlepsia is what happens when a murder is committed in Ionia and the murderers are not surrendered; the law then permits the seizure of citizens of that state, in the case of the killing. Suidas has both. Pollux, on those who demand androlepsia, or rather use it: the words of Pollux, Book VIII, are that those who accuse fugitives of murder are to be seized and led off to the city... unjustly. Demosthenes is cited on whether the one who harbours the fugitive was to be punished, and the law was directed against those who received a fugitive, when a citizen of Athens had died a violent death.

units.la: Sed Legibus statutum est, quorum ius sit ho
units.tr: But it was established by the laws whose right it was to ho-

units.la: ΠΡΟΣΕΙΠΕΙΝ ΤΩ ΚΤΕΙΝΑΝΤΙ ΕΝ ΑΓΟΡΑ, ΕΝΤΟΣ ΑΝΕΤΙΟΤΗΤΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΑΝΕΤΙΟΥ, ΣΥΝΔΙΩΚΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΚΑΙ ΑΝΕΤΙΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΑΣ, ΚΑΙ ΓΑΜΒΡΟΥΣ, ΚΑΙ ΑΝΕΤΙΟΥΣ, ΚΑΙ ΓΕΝΘΕΡΟΥΣ, ΚΑΙ ΑΝΕΤΙΑΔΟΥΣ, ΚΑΙ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΑΣ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΑΙΔΕΣΑΣΘΑΙ ΔΕΗ, ΕΑΝ ΜΕΝ ΠΑΤΗΡ Η, Η ΑΔΕΛΦΟΣ, Η ΥΙΕΙΣ ΠΑΝΤΑΣ, Η ΤΟΝ ΚΩΛΥΟΝΤΑ ΚΡΑΤΕΙΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΜΗΔΕΙΣ Η[?], ΚΤΕΙΝΗ[?] Δ᾽ ΑΚΩΝ, ΓΝΩΣΙ Δ᾽ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣΩΣΙΝ ΟΙ ΕΦΕΤΑΙ ΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΚΤΕΙΝΑΙ ΕΣΕΣΘΩΝ ΟΙ ΦΡΑΤΟΡΕΣ. ΕΑΝ ΘΕΛΩΣΙ ΔΕΚΑ ΤΟΥΤΟΙΣ ΔΕ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣ ΑΡΙΣΤΙΝΔΗΝ ΑΙΡΕΙΣΘΩΝ Cavetur autem hac Lege pri[?]iuste cæsus sit: secus enim non [?]ηγεδίκας δ̄, ΒΙΑΙΩι, σύμβολαν hanc cædem perpetraverant, [?]ntur ad pœnam: si sicarij nol- s urbis illius, in quam profuge- [?]um pertinebat: si non dederen- ad tres usque homines pote- [?]ν μὲν ἐαυτὸν εἰς δίκας ἀξιοῖ, μετὰ [?]ῶν. ἐὰν δ᾽ ὁ μὴ [illegible, ~4 letters] ἐλλω- μέν. Scribit autem Demosthege esse permissam, non contra quos cædes facta fuisset: ὁ μὲν [?]τειλεῖν, μήτε τοῖς διαφαγοῖς ἐκ- [?]τειλεῖν. Sed revera hæc pigne[?]ent, aut, si extra fines Atticæ [?]rsus eos, in quorum urbe iniu- [?]ἀρπάζῃ ἄνδρας ἐκ ἑνὸς πόλεως· [illegible, ~5 letters] εἰς ἡμέρας. [?]ος. ἐὰν ἐξω τῆς Ἀττικῆς ἀνὴρ Ἀ- τῇ πόλει ὄντες τὸν δικαιοῦντα ἐκ τῆς ῇ ἄλλῃ εἰς Ἀθήνας, δίκην ὑφέ- [?]ddit, multam irrogari iniuria [?]licebat enim priuato consilio [?]προληψιον δὲ, ὅταν τις τῶν ἀνδρο- [illegible, ~6 letters] ἐξεστιν ἐν τῇ οὐκ ἐκδιδόντων [illegible, ~6 letters] ἀδικος ὤν. [?]micidas in ius vocare.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to prosecute the killer in the forum, within the kinship, [kinsmen and relatives]; and the children of kinsmen, and the sons-in-law, and the cousins, and the relatives, and the phratores, may join in the prosecution. The law also provides that the one who was killed was justly slain; otherwise [the killing is not allowed]. If the assassins refuse to be handed over, they are to be held liable to punishment; and if the city to which they fled does not surrender them, the androlepsia extends to as many as three men. Demosthenes writes that this right was granted to be exercised against those who harbour the killers, not against those whom the murder was committed against. But in truth these seizures were made either within the bounds of Attica or, if outside Attica, against those in whose city the injury was done; it was lawful for a private individual to seize, and a fine was imposed on the one who was unjust. It is clear that the androlepsia was a right to bring murderers to trial.

units.la: Homicidam in foro postulanto intra sobrinitatem sobrini: adsunto etiam sobrinorum liberi & generi, itémque sobrinorum soceri, & consobrini, & Phra- tores.Exorantor autem occisi pater, si superfit, aut frater, aut liberi, simul omnes: nam si unus nolit, exorati ne sunto[?]. Si vero nullus horum superfit, cædes autem sit fortuita, & pronuntiarint Ephetæ quinquaginta & unus imprudentem occidisse, adsunto Phratores, si velint, decem, his quinquaginta & unus ex optimatibus eligunter * * Qui ante hanc Legem scriptam ΤΩΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΙ ΘΕΣΜΩΙ ΕΝΕΧΕΣΘΩΝ, ΤΟΥΣ Δ' ΑΠΟΓΙΝΟΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΕΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΔΗΜΟΙΣ, ΟΥΣ ΑΝ ΜΗΔΕΙΣ ΑΝΑΙΡΗ-ΤΑΙ ΕΠΑΓΓΕΛΛΕΤΩ Ο ΔΗΜΑΡΧΟΣ ΤΟΙΣΠΡΟΣΗΚΟΥΣΙΝ ΑΝΑΙΡΕΙΝ, ΚΑΙ ΘΑΠΤΕΙΝ ΚΑΙ ΚΑΘΑΙΡΕΙΝ ΤΟΝ ΔΗ-ΜΟΝ ΤΗΙ ΗΜΕΡΑΙ ΗΙ ΑΝ ΑΓΟΓΕΝΗ-ΤΑΙ ΕΚΑΣΤΟΣ ΑΥΤΩΝ· ΕΓΑΓΓΕΛ-ΛΕΙΝ ΔΕ ΓΕΡΙ ΜΕΝ ΤΩΝ ΔΟΥΛΩΝ ΤΩΙ ΔΕΣΜΟΤΗΙ, ΠΕΡΙ ΔΕ ΤΩΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΩΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΤΑ ΧΡΗΜΑΤ' ΕΧΟΥΣΙΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΗΙ ΧΡΗΜΑΤΑ ΤΩΙ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΙ ΤΟΙΣ ΓΡΟΣΗ-ΚΟΥΣΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΠΟΘΑΝΟΝΤΟΣ ΕΓΑΓ-ΓΕΛΛΕΙΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΑΡΧΟΥ ΕΠΑΓΓΕΙΛΑΝΤΟΣ ΜΗ ΑΝΑΙΡΩΝΤΑΙ ΟΙ ΓΡΟΣΗΚΟΝΤΕΣ, Ο ΜΕΝ ΔΗΜΑΡ-ΧΟΣ ΑΠΟΜΙΣΘΩΣΑΤΟ ΑΜΕΛΕΙΝ ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΑΘΑΤΑΙ, ΚΑΙ ΚΑΘΑΡΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΔΗΜΩΝ ΑΥΘΗΜΕΡΟΝ ΟΠΩΣ ΑΝ ΔΥ-ΝΩΝΤΑΙ ΟΛΙΓΙΣΤΟΥ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΑΓΟΜΙΣΘΩΣΗΙ ΟΦΕΙΛΕΤΩ ΧΙΛΙΑΣ. ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ ΤΩΙ ΔΗΜΟΣΙΩΙ Ο, ΤΙ Δ' ΑΝ ΑΝΑΛΩΣΗΙ ΔΙΓΛΑΣΙΟΝ ΓΡΑ-ΞΑΣΘΩ ΓΑΡΑ ΤΩΝ ΟΦΕΙΛΟΝΤΩΝ. ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΜΗ ΓΡΑΞΗΙ ΑΥΤΟΣ ΟΦΕΙ-ΛΕΤΩ ΤΟΙΣ ΔΗΜΟΤΑΙΣ. cædes perpetrarunt, ea tenentor. Si quis autem in aliquo populo cæsus sit, quem nemo tollat: Demarchus eius cognatis denunciato tollere, & sepelire, & lustra-re populum, ea ipsa die, qua is cæsus est: de seruis autem domino eorum denunciato; de ingenuis vero iis, qui in eorum bona succedunt: Si vero is, qui cæsus est, nihil in bonis habeat, eius cognatis denunciato. Si Dimarcho denunciante, cognati non tollant, Demarchus ipse tollendum & sepeliendum cadauer, eaque ipsa die lustrandum populum, lo-cato, quam minimo poterit: ni locaris, mille drachmas erario publico pendito: Duplum autem eius, quod impenderit, à debentibus exigito: ni exegerit, ipse popularibus suis præstato.
units.tr: *Whoever wishes to prosecute a killer in the forum must be within the degree of cousinship of the slain man: the children and sons-in-law of the cousins are also admitted, likewise the fathers-in-law of the cousins, the cousins themselves, and the phratores. The father of the slain man, if he survives, or his brother, or his children, shall all be asked together to prosecute; for if one of them is unwilling, the others are not to be asked. If none of these survives, but the death was accidental, and the fifty-one Ephetae declare that he killed unintentionally, the phratores are to be admitted, if they wish, ten of them; with these, fifty-one are chosen from the best men. Let them be bound by this law, which was written before. Those who lie unclaimed in the public places, whom no one removes: let the demarch announce to those who are related to them that they should remove them, and bury them, and purify the deme on the same day on which each of them was brought in. He is to announce for the slaves to their master in bonds, and for the free men to those who hold their property. If the dead man has no property, the demarch shall announce to his relatives. If the relatives, when the demarch has given notice, do not remove him, the demarch himself is to hire someone to carry out, bury and purify the deme on the same day, as cheaply as he can. If he does not hire anyone, he shall owe a thousand drachmas to the public treasury; and whatever he spends beyond that, he shall recover at double the amount from those who owe it. If he does not recover it himself, he shall owe it to the people.*

units.la: Legem descripsit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Μακάρτατον. eaque cauetur, quis iure debeat alium cædis postulare & accusare, nempe intra sobrinitatem, siue intra sobrinos: meminit huius Legis idem ἐν τῷ κατὰ Εὐέργου καὶ Μνησιβούλου ψευδομαρτυριῶν. κελεύει γὰρ ὁ νόμος, ὦ ἄνδρες δικασταί, τοὺς ἀποσπονδοῦντας ἐπιξιέναι μεγέθεις [?] [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐν δὲ τῷ ὅρκῳ διαρρείζεται, ὅτι ἀποσπονδὸς ἐστί, καὶ ἂν οἰκέτης ἦ, τῶν [illegible, ~10 letters]. Corruptus est locus, itaque fraudi fuit eruditissimo In-terpreti, qui vertit: iubet enim Lex, iudices, ut cognati caedes persequantur, usque ad sobrinos: & in iureiurando cautetur, debere, si vel seruus sit interfectus, hos eosdem caedem persequi. Sed facile in integritatem restituetur vnius literulæ mutatione, ὅτι συγγενῶν ἐστί, κἂν οἰκέτης ἢ, &c. & ita erit vertendum: & iureiurando affirmatur, quod sit cognatus: quod si sit è seruis, eorum est caedem persequi. Huius nostrae emendationis vadem damus Iulium Pollucem Lib. VIII. cap. X. differentem de iure caedem persequendi: Φόνου δὲ ἔξω ἐπεξιέναι, μέχρις ἀνεψιῶν [?], (legenpum potius e Demosthene, μέχρις ἀνεψιαδῶν.) ἢ ἐν τῷ ὅρκῳ συγγενέσθαι, ὡς συγγενῶν ἐστι τῶν πατέρων, κἂν οἰκέτης ἢ [illegible, ~12 letters]. Postrema ista Pollucis verba in mendo sunt: nam ex iis videtur posse colligi, oportuisse cognatos seruorum caedem eorum persequi. Sed in contrariam sententiam eundum est: Seruorum quippe nulla erat cognatio. Pollucis locus deformaius est è Demosthenis illo, quem iam descripsimus, paullo fusius enarrato. Demosthenis autem hæc est mens, sibi fas non esse, cædem nutricis suæ contra Euergum persequi: cognatus enim non est, ut Leges iubent, & iureiurando affirmandum est: atque cum seruorum cædem persequantur domini, ancilla non est, sed manumissa, temperare itaque mihi nequeo, quin apud Demosthenem rescribendum censeam. κἂν οἰκέτης ᾖ, δεσπότης τὰς ὑποσκ[?]ὴς[?] [?]. & in Pollucis codicibus reponendum: κἂν οἰκέτης ᾖ δεσπότης, ὑποσχεθ[?]ὴ[?] καὶ συνεχώρησαν[?]. Corrumpendo Demosthenis loco fuit, quod supra dixit: ἐπεὶ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ἐστὶ σοι. ἡ γὰρ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ ἑλληνικοῦ σοι ἡ αἰδεσ[?]πότης, ἐπὶ δὲ πραξίαν[?] οἱ γὰρ νόμοι τούτων καλλίστου τῷ διαξιν[?]. Repetitur enim ex hoc loco vox τούτων. Atque hinc potest colligi, cum οἱ Ἐξηγηταὶ dicant, Lege licere cognatorum aut seruorum cædes persequi, & serui sint ἐκ τῆς πολεως τι, & ad dominum referantur, (ut sensus sit, Lege cognatos cognatorum, seruorum dominos cædes debere persequi.) retrahendam esse fugitiuam vocem δεσπότης, & reponendam vicem τούτων. Hanc quoque Legem laudat Demosthenis Scholiastes ad Androtionam. ἐκ ἡδυόατο Ἀνδροτίων φόνου κατηγορίαν καὶ τὰ Διοδώρου ποιήσασθαι μὴ ὧν τῷ προφανεῖ συλλήψεως· αὐτὸς γὰρ μόνοις ἐπιτρέπονται οἱ νόμοι. Itaque in occisi funere publicabatur ad sepulcrum, an quis cognatus sit occiso. Demosthenes ἐκ τοῦ καὶ Εὐέργου καὶ Μνησιβούλου. ἔφησεν μὲν ἐπινεῖκεῖν δὴ ὅτι τῇ ἐκφορᾷ, ἡ προαγορεύεν ὅτι τοῦ μνήματι, εἴ τις προσῆκον ἐστὶ τῆς αἰδελφοῦ, ἐπεὶ δὲ ὁ μνῆμα φυλάττειν ὅτι ἡμᾶς ἡμέρας. Proclamabatur igitur ad sepulcrum, si quis cæso esset cognatus, ut & nomine ciebantur fontes & interfectores, ut sequitur ibidem. ὀνόματι μὲν ὅτι ἀπὸ μὴ προαγορεύει, τῆς διδραχμὸν δὲ ἡ ἐκπίνασι. Sepulcrum obseruabatur triduum, & hasta, cum efferretur cæsus, præferebatur: atque hinc collocarentur ut mortui factum est. Pollux Lib. VIII. δ' ὅτι τῇ ἐκφορᾷ, ὅτι τῶν βιαίως ἀποθανόντων ἐπιφέρετο. καὶ αἱ προσήκοντες ὁ ἀληθὴς τῶν ἐγίνοντο, ὡς ὡγῆτο ὁ νεκρὸς, μή τι βιαίως πέπονθε.
units.tr: Demosthenes quoted this law in the speech against Macartatus, by which it is laid down who has the right to prosecute and accuse another for murder: namely within the kinship, that is, among cousins. The same orator also mentions this law in the speech against Euergus and Mnesibulus on false witness. For the law orders, men judges, that those who are excluded from the libations [may pursue the case], and in the oath it is stated that he is a kinsman, even if he is a slave. The text is corrupted, and so it misled that most learned interpreter, who rendered it: "For the law orders, judges, that the relatives pursue the killing as far as cousins, and in the oath it is provided that they must pursue the killing of the same persons, even if the slain man was a slave." But it is easily restored by changing one little letter: "that he is a kinsman, even if he is a slave", and so it must be translated: "and it is affirmed by oath that he is a kinsman; but if he is one of the slaves, it is for their masters to pursue the killing." In support of this emendation we cite Julius Pollux, Book VIII, chapter X, who discusses the right to pursue a killing: "To pursue a killing outward, as far as cousins" (one should probably read cousins' children, from Demosthenes), "or to be a kinsman by oath, as being of the kin of the fathers, even if he is a slave." These last words of Pollux are corrupt, for from them it might seem that the kin of slaves ought to pursue the killing of their slaves. But the opposite view must be taken: slaves, of course, had no kinship at all. Pollux's passage is a distorted version of the Demosthenes passage I have already transcribed, explained somewhat more fully there. Demosthenes' own meaning is that it was not lawful for him to pursue the killing of his nurse against Euergus: she was not a kinswoman, as the laws require, and must be affirmed by oath; and since masters pursue the killings of slaves, she was not a slave but a freedwoman. I cannot therefore refrain from suggesting that Demosthenes be emended accordingly, and that in the codices of Pollux the reading be altered as well. The corruption of the Demosthenes passage arose from what he said above, where the word "master" has been wrongly inserted into a sentence about the law. The word "these" (τούτων) is repeated from this passage, and from this it can be inferred that, since the Exegetae say that by law the killings of kinsmen or slaves may be pursued, and since slaves belong to the city and are referred to their master (so that the sense is that by law cousins pursue the killing of cousins, and masters of slaves), the fugitive word "master" should be removed and the word "these" restored in its place. The scholiast on Demosthenes also cites this law in his note on Androtion: "Androtion could not bring a charge of murder, nor could Diodorus, except in the case of a manifest arrest; for the laws permit this only to the relatives." Hence at the funeral of the murdered man it was proclaimed at the tomb whether anyone was a kinsman of the dead man. Demosthenes, in the speech against Euergus and Mnesibulus, says that at the carrying out of the body it was proclaimed, at the tomb, whether anyone was a relative of the deceased, since the tomb was guarded for three days. So the proclamation was made at the tomb, if anyone was a kinsman, and the killers were named as well, as follows in the same passage. Thus the proclamation was made, and the spear was carried; the tomb was watched for three days, and with the spear raised, the dead man was carried out, as was done for those who died violently. Pollux, Book VIII, says that the spear was carried at the funeral of those who died a violent death, and the relatives who were present were examined on whether the body was not violently harmed.

units.la: Meminit huius proclamationis ad sepulcrum, & hastæ præla-tæ Harpocratio: ἐπινεῖκεῖν δὴ ὅτι τῆς ἐκφορᾶς, καὶ προσαγορεύειν ὅτι τοῦ μνήματι, Δημοσθένης κατ' Εὐέργου καὶ Μνησιβούλου, ὥσπερ φησίν, ὅτι τῶν βιαίως ἀποθανόντων. Ἴρος δὲ ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ τῶν Ἀττικῶν, ὡς Γεωγεῖδος καὶ Κεφάλου εἶπων γράφει ταῦτ. τινὲς δὲ ὅτι τῆς πάφου δὴν καταπεπηγέναι τὸν Ἐρεχθέα φασί, πεποιῆσθαι ἢ προσκατηγορήμενον· τε καὶ ὁ παῖς σημαίνοντα, ἀλλὰ ὁ νόμων ἐἳ τοῖς προσήκοισι, τῶν τὸν ἔ-πον μετέρχεσθαι τοῖς φονέας.
units.tr: Harpocration also mentions this proclamation at the tomb and the raised spear: "to proclaim at the funeral, and to call out at the tomb," as Demosthenes says against Eubulides and Mnesiboulos, concerning those who died violently. Ieros, in his collection of the Attic (laws), writes these things, reporting on Geogeides and Kephalos. Some say that Erechtheus was fixed to the spear, and that the spear was made a witness; but the law was given to the kinsmen, to pursue the killers by proclamation.

units.la: Auctor Etymologici: ἐπινεῖκεῖν δὴ, ὅτι τῇ ἐκφορᾷ, καὶ προσαγορεύειν ὅτι τοῦ μνήματι. εἰς τοὺς βιαίως ἀποθανόντας τῶν ἐπαγγέλλετο. καὶ Ἴρος δὲ τῇ συναγωγῇ τῶν Ἀττικῶν φησὶν, ὅτι ἴνες δὴν ὅτι τὸ πάφου φασὶ καταπεπηγέναι τὸν Ἐρεχθέα, ὃ παῖς σημαίνοντα, ἀλλὰ ὁ νόμον ἐἳ τοῖς προσήκοισι, τῶν τὸν ἔ-πον μετέρχεσθαι τοῖς φονέας, Ῥητεικά. Ex Harpocratione hausit Auctor Etymologici, quem laudat hoc titulo, Ῥητεικά, ut & alibi sexcenties. Sed ad rem. Partes accusandi dabantur intra sobrinitatem: aderant tamen sobrinorum liberi, & generi, & soceri, (in Lege enim rescribo: ΚΑΙ ΑΝΕΨΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΓΕΝΘΕΡΟΥΣ.) itemque ἀνεψιαδ[?], itemque Phratores occisi: Quare commode intelligendus est Pollux Lib. VIII. in his, γραφὰς φόνου ἐξὼν τῶν βουλομένῳ γράφεσθαι, nimirum τῆς προσήκοισι μέρεις ἀνεψιαδῶν. Sequitur in Lege, quorum ius sit gratiam facere, & de cæde pacisci: Pretium autem, quo homicidæ propinquos occisi placabant, ne eos caedis accusarent, ἀποφόνια dicebatur, vt è Dinarcho & Theophrasto docet Harpocratio. ἀποφόνια, τὰ ὅτι φόνου διδόμενα χρήματα τῆς ψυχῆς [?] τῷ φονεύοντι, ἀπὸ τῆς τοῦ αἰτίας ἐχόντος ὅτι ἀμήρκει, ἵνα μὴ ἐπιξίωσιν ὅτι μὴ ἐπιξεύρεσθαι μηδὲ [?] τῷ τῷ φόνου δίκαιον. Δείναρχος δὲ τὰς Καλλιάδους, ἢ δὲ τὰς Φορμησίου. Θεόφραστος νόμων ἔκτῳ καὶ δικάσαι. Graeci simpliciter ποινὴν dixerunt. Hesychius: ποινὴ ἀντίκτονος ἡ ᾿Αθήνας φόνου διδόμενον. καὶ ἐν Σάμῳ, καὶ τὰ διδόμενα χρήματα ᾿Αθήνης ἀμηρκηθέντος τῆς αὐτοῦ οἰκείοις. In suis Axonibus Solo dixerat ΑΠΟΙΝΑ. Suidas: ΑΠΟΙΝΑ, λύτρα, ἃ διδωσί τῆς φόνου, ἡ σώματος. ὅτω Σόλων ἐν νόμοις, quod etiam videre est in his Legibus. Quod si quis ob imprudentem caedem exulans ἀπηναυλισμόν, interea placare non posset, & exorare eos, qui homicidij illum postulauerant, vt in gratiam cum illis & cum patria rediret, cauet Legislator hac Lege, vt si quis è cognatis, quorum ius & fas erat ἀφιέσθαι, nollet tamen, Ephetæ hac de re cognoscerent, & homicidæ gratiam facerent, si ita videretur: quorum cognitioni & iudicio interesse poterant, si vellent, illius, qui cæsus fuerat, Phratores ad decem vsque: Hic est sensus horum Legis verborum, quæ ita referibo: ΓΝΟΙ Δ᾽ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΕΙϹ ΟΙ ΕΦΕΤΑΙ. nam addita illa ὨϹΙΝ ad vocem ΕΙϹ irrepserunt è margine in contextum. Studiosus enim aliquis adnotauerat, quot essent, qui huic cognitioni interessent, ὡς ιʹ. circiter, inquit, decem, & quinquaginta: nempe quinquaginta & vnus Ephetæ, & Phratores, vt maxime, decem. Ex optimatibus autem eligi debere Ephetas cauit hac Lege Draco, in qua scribo: ΟΥΤΟΙ Δ᾽ ΟΙ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΕΙϹ ΑΡΙΣΤΙΝΔΗΝ ΑΙΡΕΙϹΘΩΝ. Eam intelligit Pollux Lib. VIII. Ἐφέται, τὸν μὲν ἀριθμὸν εἰς ἡ πεντήκοντα. Δεόμεθα δ᾽ αὐτὸς καταξι-σιν, [?] ἀποδίδωσι αἱρεθέντας. Addit Legislator hac sanctione teneri etiam eos, qui prius cædem fecissent. Sequitur alterum Legis Caput, quo præscribitur, quid faciundum sit Demarcho, quando è popularibus suis aliquis occisus est, quem nemo tollit: iubet itaque Draco, vt Demarchus cognatis occisi denuncient, tollant illud cadauer, & sepeliant, populus vero eo ipso die, quo popularis occisus est, lustretur. Denunciet autem de seruis domino: nam domini est, vt supra diximus, seruorum cædes persequi: de ingenuis vero denunciet iis, qui in bona succedunt; æquum enim est, vt eos etiam incommoda, si qua sunt, sequantur. Sin occiso nihil est in bonis, eius cognatis denuncietur. Quod si post Demarchi denunciationem cognati aut domini non fustulerint, Demarchus tollendum cadauer locet, & sepeliendum, & lustrandum eo die populum, quam minimo poterit: Nisi locarit, mille drachmas ærario pendat. Quicquid autem impenderit, duplum à debentibus exigat: nisi exegerit, ipse debeto popularibus: Nam è popularium suorum publica pecunia tollendum sepeliendúmque cadauer, atque lustrandum populum, locabat: Quare æquum est, vt qui Demarchus non exegerit, duplionem eorum, quæ de publica pecunia impenderat, ipse præster, ne quid de iure popularium decedat.
units.tr: The author of the Etymologicum: "to proclaim at the funeral, and to call out at the tomb, against those who died violently." Ieros also says in his collection of the Attic (laws) that some say Erechtheus was fixed to the spear, which was made a witness; but the law was given to the kinsmen, to pursue the killers by proclamation. This is from Harpocration, from whom the author of the Etymologicum, whom he cites under the title "Rhetorica," took it, as he does in many other places. But to the matter. Rights of accusation were granted within the degree of cousins; yet the children of cousins, and sons-in-law and fathers-in-law, were also present (for in the law, I restore the text as: "and of nephews and of kinsmen"), likewise the nephews, and the Phratores of the slain. So Pollux, Book VIII, should be understood in these words: "a charge of murder may be brought by whoever wishes," namely, by those among the relatives within the degree of cousins. The law then states who has the right to grant pardon and to make terms about the killing. The price by which the killer placated the kinsmen of the slain, so that they would not bring a charge of homicide, was called apophonia, as Harpocration shows from Dinarchus and Theophrastus: "apophonia: the money given for murder to the kinsmen of the dead, by the one who killed, so that they would not prosecute." Dinarchus (in the Callias, or in the Phormisius) and Theophrastus, in the sixth book of Laws, also treat this. The Greeks simply called it poine (penalty). Hesychius: "poine: the price given at Athens for a murder, and in Samos, and the money given for killing, which the kinsmen of the slain received." Solon in his Axones had called it apoina. Suidas: "apoina: ransom, what is given for a killing or a wound; so Solon in his laws," which can also be seen in these laws. If someone, exiled for an involuntary killing, could not in the meantime placate those who had brought the charge of homicide, nor persuade them to receive him back into favour and into his country, the lawgiver, by this law, provided that if any of the kinsmen, whose right and duty it was to grant pardon, were unwilling, the Ephetae should take cognisance of the matter and grant the killer pardon if it seemed fit. The Phratores of the slain, up to ten, could attend their examination and judgment if they wished. This is the sense of the words of the law, which I restore as: "gnoi d' hoi pentēkonta kai eis hoi ephetai." For the added word hōsin after eis crept into the text from the margin. For some diligent reader had noted how many would attend this examination, "about ten, and fifty," namely, fifty-one Ephetae and, at most, ten Phratores. Draco ordered in this law that the Ephetae must be chosen from the best men, in which I restore: "these are the fifty and one, chosen from the best." Pollux, Book VIII, understands this: "Ephetae: their number was fifty-one, and they were chosen." The lawgiver adds that by this sanction those who had previously committed murder were also bound. Next follows the second chapter of the law, which prescribes what the Demarch must do when one of his fellow citizens has been killed and no one takes up the body. Draco therefore orders that the Demarch give notice to the kinsmen of the slain, that they remove the corpse and bury it, and that the people be purified on the very day on which the fellow citizen was killed. He is to give notice to the master in the case of slaves, for, as we said above, it is the master's business to pursue the killing of his slaves; but in the case of free men he is to give notice to those who succeed to the goods, for it is fair that they also bear any burdens that may attach. If the dead man has nothing in his goods, notice is to be given to his kinsmen. If, after the Demarch's notice, the kinsmen or masters do not remove the corpse, the Demarch is to contract for its removal and burial, and for the purification of the people, on that day, at the lowest possible cost. If he does not contract for it, he is to pay a thousand drachmas to the treasury. Whatever he has spent, he is to exact double from those who owe it; if he does not exact it, he himself is to owe it to the fellow citizens. For the corpse was removed and buried, and the people purified, at the cost of the public funds of the fellow citizens, and the Demarch contracted for this. Therefore it is fair that the Demarch who does not exact it should himself pay double of what he spent from the public funds, lest anything be taken from the rights of the fellow citizens.

units.la: Atheniensium Lege, qui sibi manus intulisset, manus ei præciderentur eodem tumulo non condenda: Ἐαί ὃς αὐτὸν διαχειρίσηται, ἢ χεῖρα τῆς ... Qui sibi manus intulit, ei manus praeciditor, [illegible, ~10 letters] σώματος θάπτειν. nec eodem tumulo conditor.
units.tr: By an Athenian law, whoever laid violent hands on himself was to have his hands cut off, and was not to be buried in the same tomb. Hands are cut off ... and he is not to be buried in the same tomb [the Greek is too damaged to restore].

units.la: Laudat Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος. Καὶ ἐάν τις αὐτὸν ἀλλαχοῦ [illegible, ~20 letters] τῷ τῶν [illegible, ~12 letters] σώματος θάπτειν. Ratio est apud Iosephum, qui de hac Lege intelligendum est, ἀλλὰ. Lib. III. περὶ ἐτέρας δὲ καὶ τὰς δεξιὰς [illegible, ~25 letters] ἐαυτῷ, ἡγούμενοι, καθάπερ ὁ σῶμα τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπόλειψιν, οὕτω καὶ τῷ χρῆσθαι τὸ σώματος. & certe tantum abest, vt viri fortis & magnanimi talis exitio sit, vt contra timidi & ignaui. Aristoteles Lib. III. Nicomach. cap. VII. ὁ δὲ ἀποθνήσκων φόβου [illegible, ~15 letters] ἤ ἔρωτα, ἤ τι λυπηρὸν, οὐκ Ἀνδρείου, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον δῆλον· μεταξία γὰρ, ὅ φύσιν τὰ ὑπάρχοντα. καὶ ὑχ ὅτι καλὸν ἀποθνήσκειν, ἀλλὰ φύσιν κακόν. Nam sapiens corpus non relinquet inuito Deo: Hinc factum est, vt Lege Thebanorum ἀποχάρες notarentur infamia. refert ex Aristotele Zenobius Cent. VI. Proverb. XVII. Φασὶ δὲ, ὅτι οἱ Θηβαῖοι οἱ ἑαυτοὺς ἀποχρῶντες σώματος [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐπιμων. καὶ Αἰσχύλης δὲ φησι τοὺς Θηβαίων ὁ αὐτὸ τοῦτο, ὅτι τοὺς αὐτοχειρίας ἑαυτοῦ νομίμους οὐκ ἐπίμων.
units.tr: Aeschines cites this in his speech against Ctesiphon: "And if anyone (kills himself) elsewhere ... not to bury ..." The reason is given by Josephus, who must be understood with reference to this law, in Book III Against Apion: they thought the body's leaving the soul, as the soul leaves the body, and so the use of the body, was their own affair, and, as it is, certainly the death of a brave and magnanimous man is not such that it is like that of a timid and cowardly one. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book III, ch. 7: he who dies from fear or love or some grief is not brave, but rather... for nature has made the things that are ours; and it is not that it is noble to die, but that it is a natural evil. "For the wise man will not leave his body against the will of God." Hence it came about that under the law of the Thebans, those who killed themselves were marked with infamy. Zenobius, Centuria VI, Proverb XVII, relates from Aristotle: "They say that the Thebans who killed themselves were ... (and) they did not honour (them with burial)." And Aeschylus also says that the Thebans did not honour with burial those who were lawfully self-killed.

units.la: Diximus in superioribus, quibus arcerentur locis homicidæ, sed pænenos fugerat mouere, Lege cautum fuisse, vt eo loco, in quo excubiæ collocantur, abessent:
units.tr: I said above which places homicides were kept out of, but I had forgotten to mention that the law provided that they should be absent from the place where the guard is posted.

units.la: Ἐκτὸς ἰωέγου ἐξ τοὺς ἀνδροφόνους. Homicidæ intra excubiarum locum ne sunto.
units.tr: "Outside the guard-post, homicides must not (be)." Homicides are not to be within the place of the guard.

units.la: Legem habet Suidas: ἰωέγς. ὁ Ῥυρωρὸς, ὁ Φύλαξ. καὶ πρόμια, οὐδὲ ἐκτὸς ἰωέγου. καὶ ὁ νόμος ὁ περὶ Ἀθηναίοις, ἐκτὸς ἰωέγου ἐκέλευεν ἐξ τοὺς ἀνδροφόνους. E Suida emendanda est Vaticana Proverbiorum Appendix, Cent. III. Proverb. XXV. ἔσθε τὸ ἰωέγου. scribo, οὐδὲ ἐκτὸς ἰωέγου. ὅτι τοὺς φυλάκας ἐκάλυων οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι. καὶ ὁ νόμος ὁ περὶ αὐτοῖς, ἐκ τῆς ἰωέγου, scribe, ἐκτὸς ἰωέγου ἐκέλευσεν ἐξ τοὺς ἀνδροφόνους.
units.tr: Suidas has the law: "guard-post: the watchman, the keeper." And "not outside the guard-post." And the law about the Athenians: "outside the guard-post he ordered homicides to be cast out." The Vatican Appendix of Proverbs, Centuria III, Proverb XXV, should be corrected from Suidas: "...the guard-post." I write: "not outside the guard-post, because the Athenians called the guards by that name." And the law about them: "from the guard-post," I write: "outside the guard-post he ordered the homicides to be cast out."

units.la: Draco Legem quoque Athenien- sibus scripsit, qua sanxit inanimata, quorum casu cædes erat perpetrata, finibus eijci.
units.tr: Draco also wrote a law for the Athenians by which he ordained that inanimate things, by whose falling a killing was committed, should be cast out of the territory.

units.la: Τὰ ἄψυχα, ἐαί τινα ἐμπεσόντα ἀποκτείνῃ, ἐκβαλλέτω. Inanimata, quorum casu cædes alicuius sit facta, finibus eiciunto.
units.tr: [Τὰ ἄψυχα, ἐάν τινα ἐμπεσόντα ἀποκτείνῃ, ἐκβαλλέτω.] Inanimate things, by whose falling someone is killed, are to be cast out of the territory.

units.la: Legem laudat Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος. ἡ γὰρ αὐ εἴη δῆλον, ὦ Ἀθηναῖοι, εἰ τὰ μὲν ξύλα, καὶ τοὺς λίθους, καὶ τὸν σιδηρὸν, τὰ ἄφωνα, καὶ ἀγνώμονα, ἐαί τινα ἐμπεσόντα ἀποκτείνῃ, ὑπαροείζομεν. Meminit Paufanias Eliac. Lib. II. in rebus Theagenis Thasij: καὶ οἱ Θάσιοι καταποντῶσι τῷ εἰκόνι, ἐπακολουθήσας γνώμῃ τῇ Δεξικοντος, ὃς Ἀθηναίοις ἠσμένως χαλκᾶς φονικοῖς, ὑπαρωδεῖσι καὶ τὰ ἄψυχα, εἴ γε ἐμπεσὸν τὸ ἐξ αὐτῆς ἀποκτείνει αἰ ἄνεμον. Eandem narrationem habet Suidas, mutato tantum nomine Theagenis in Niconis: καὶ οἱ Θάσιοι καταποντῶσιν αὐτὸν, τὸν νόμον Δεξικοντος Ἀθηναίου, ὑπαροείζοντος φονικοῦντα καὶ τὰ ἄψυχα. Atque hæ cædes iudicabantur in foro τῷ ὅτι Πρυτανείῳ. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατ' Ἀεισχεγέτας. τέταρτον ἕλκων ἄλλο ἐκ τῶν τοὺς, ὃ ὅτι Πρυτανείῳ, τοῦτο δὲ ὅσ τί; ἐαί λίθος, ἢ ξύλον, ἢ σίδηρος, ἢ τι ζῷον ἐμπεσὸν παταξῆ, καὶ τὸν μὴ βαλόντα ἀγαθὸν τῆς, εἰς δὲ εἰδῇ, καὶ ἔχῃ, ὃ τὸν φόνον ἐργασμένον, τοῖς σῶμα λαγχά- νει. Paufanias Atticis. ὃ δὲ ἐν Πρυτανείῳ κελεύσμων, εἶτα τῷ σιδήρῳ καὶ πᾶ- σιν ὁμοίως τὰς ἀψύχοις δικάζουσιν. λέγεται μὲν δὲ καὶ ἄλλα τῶν ἀψύχων αὐτόματα ὑπάρχειν σὺν τῷ δικαίῳ ὑμφεῖαι ἀλ-ἔφησις. Præerat huic iudicio Rex: Pollux Lib.VIII. Δικάζει δ᾽ ὁ Βασιλεὺς ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς δίκας [?]. Ei adfidebant οἱ Φυλάκων. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. X. Ὁ δὲ Πρυτανεῖα δίκαζε ἐπὶ τῆς ἀλλων τῶν ἐμ-πεσόντων καὶ ἀποκτινάντων [?]. ταῦτα κυρίως ἢ ἐὰν τοῦ [?] δικαστηρίου Φυλάκων, οὓς ἐὰν δ᾽ ἐμπέσοντ᾽ ἀλλων [?].
units.tr: Aeschines cites this law in his speech against Ctesiphon: "For it will be plain, men of Athens, that if we banish wood, stones and iron, things without voice or mind, if they fall on someone and kill him..." Pausanias, Eliaca, Book II, mentions in the story of Theagenes of Thasos that the Thasians threw his statue into the sea, following the opinion of Drakon, who among the Athenians, in a homicide case, judged even inanimate things, when they fell and killed a man. Suidas has the same story, with only the name Theagenes changed to Niconis: "The Thasians drowned him, following the law of Drakon the Athenian, who judged inanimate things too in cases of homicide." These cases of homicide were judged in the Prytaneum. Demosthenes, in his speech against Aristogeiton: "The fourth charge is one brought in the Prytaneum; and what is it? If a stone, or wood, or iron, or some animal falling strikes someone, and the one who threw it is not known, but the one who is known and holds it has committed the killing, he is charged with homicide." Pausanias, Attica: "In the Prytaneum he orders (the case to be heard), then with the iron and all the rest, they judge in the same way the inanimate things. It is said that other inanimate things also, by the right of ..." The king presided over this court; Pollux, Book VIII: "The king judges by his office in cases of ..." The Phylobasileis sat with him. Pollux, Book VIII, ch. X: "The Prytaneum judged the cases of the other things that fall and kill; these were properly (heard) by the court of the Phylobasileis, and if they fall (on) others..."

units.la: Erat quoque αἰκίας Lex, qua iniuriarum dabatur actio ob verbera:
units.tr: There was also a law on aikia (assault), under which an action for injuries was granted on account of blows.

units.la: AN TIC TYΠTHι TINA ΑΡΧΩΝ ΧΕΙΡΩΝ ΑΔΙΚΩΝ αἰκίας δίκην εἴ[?]. Si quis alterum prior pulsarit, iniuriarum postulator.
units.tr: If anyone strikes another first, let him be prosecuted for injury. [ἄν τις τύπτῃ τινὰ πρῶτος ἀδίκως]

units.la: Priora Legis verba descripsit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κ᾽ Ἀεισχρεὶπ. ὀφεὶν γὰρ ὡς ἐὰν πολίτων, ὥσ᾽ ἐὰν τὴν Φονικὴν μόνον, ὅτου τῶν ἐγ[?], AN TIC TYΠTHι TINA ΑΡΧΩΝ ΧΕΙΡΩΝ ΑΔΙΚΩΝ. enim nisi ipse prior pulsasset, αἰκία non erat; sequitur ibidem: ὡς εἴ γε ὑμωθ..., quippe cum iniuriam prior non intulisset, sed vim vi, arma armis repulisset: expresse ἐν ᾧ ΕΥέρ-χου καὶ Μνησίθεου idem Demosthenes: φεύγει δὲ μὲ τὴν ἐλεῖσον ἐκ τῆς αἰ-σχρᾶς αἰκίας, ὅπῃ ἐκ ... ἐφ' ἑαυτοῦ ... idem Demosthenes: ... & ibidem paullo post: ἡ δὲ αἰκία, τῷ τί ἐστι, ὡς ἐὰν ... Legis meminit Demosthenes in Midiana: ὧ ὅ τῆς βλαβῆς ὑμῖν νόμος παῦσαι, ὡ ὅ τῆς αἰκίας. Harpocratio: αἰκίας, εἴδος δίκης ὅτι ἰδιωτικὴς ὅτι πλημμέλειας λεξάνομάζεσ, ἡς ὁ ἡμων ὁ ἐν τοῖς νόμοις ἐστὶν ἀεισχρέον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ ἠλιήτηρες τιμῆμα ὑπογρά-φεται, ὅπου δοκεῖ ἀξιον εἶ[?] ὁ ἀδίκημα, οἱ ἢ δικασταί ἐπικείνουσιν. Dicit Harpo-cratio αἰκίας esse eiusdem speciei: quasi Legislator τῆς αἰκίας ἐξ γεγραφεῖ ἢ δῷ ἀπαρπτὴ τοῦ βουλευτικοῦ. Sed fides sit penes auctorem: nam multo maior apud me auctoritas est, prout debet, grauissimi scriptoris Plutarchi, qui per Solonem scribit, ἐξεῖναι τὴν πλεῖσον ἐπὶ τὸ βουλευτικὸν γεγραφεῖσθαι τὸν ἀδικοῦντα ἢ ἐὰν τὸν ... ἀ ... & ipse sibi it aduerlatum Harpocratio, qui, τῆς αἰκίας ὃ ἡμῆμα ἐκ ... scribit: atqui, vt notat ad Midianam Vlpianus, ὅτι μὲν ... ὅτι δ᾽ ἐν ... ἐστι ... ἐπιτ.
units.tr: Demosthenes quotes the earlier words of the law in his speech against Aeschines: "for if a citizen ... [strikes] anyone, if he strikes first without right" [ἄν τις τύπτῃ τινὰ ἄρχων ἀδίκων]. For there was no aikia unless he had struck first himself; and the same speech continues, "as if indeed ...", since the one who had not inflicted the injury first, but had repelled force with force and arms with arms, was not liable. Demosthenes in the same speech, concerning Euergus and Mnesitheus, says expressly: "he flees from the disgraceful aikia ..." and a little later, "aikia, in what it is, is as if ..." Demosthenes also mentions the law in the speech against Midias: "...the law of injury and the law of aikia." Harpocration says: aikia is a kind of suit, one of those called private and minor offences, in which the law does not fix a penalty, but the plaintiff proposes an estimate of the penalty, and the judges then decide what they think the wrong deserves. Harpocration says aikia belonged to the same class; as if the lawgiver had written the law on aikia in the same way as the law on the council. But let the responsibility rest with the author. For, as is right, I place far greater authority on the most weighty writer Plutarch, who writes through Solon that the offender may be sentenced to a fine ... and Harpocration himself is contradicted by the same, who in saying of aikia ... Vulpian notes on the Midiana that the one thing ... and the other ... is ...

units.la: Quod autem scribit Harpocratio, multam non esse Legibus definitam, recte atque ordine factum est: quippe cum non idem omnibus, qui pulsati essent, datum esset damnum. neque eadem quoque debebat esse multa, quare eam irrogabat, & litem æstimabat actor: Multa erat pecuniaria. Lysias ἐν τῷ κατὰ αἰκίας τῆς Ἰσοκράττεω. κ᾽ ἡ ἐὰν ἐπὶ ... ὅτι ἢ μὲν αἰκία, χρημάτ'; ἐπὶ μὲν ... Scribebatur haec dica apud Quadraginta: Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ Πλυτάρτεω. ἀλλ᾽ ἡ μὲν αἰκία, καὶ τὰ τῆς βίαιων, κατὰ τὸς Τεταρτήτος.
units.tr: As for what Harpocration writes, that the law did not fix the fine, this was rightly and properly done: since the same damage was not owed to everyone who had been struck, and the same fine could not be appropriate in every case. Therefore the plaintiff demanded the penalty and assessed the damages. The fine was a sum of money. Lysias, in his speech against Isocrates' ... on aikia, says that aikia was a matter of money. This suit was brought before the Forty; Demosthenes, in the speech against Plutarchus, says: "but aikia, and the case of violence, [go] before the Forty."

units.la: Totum autem ordinem, quem obseruabant in fanando eo, qui fuerat pulsatus, describit paucis Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κ᾽ ΕΥέρχου ἐν Μνησίθεου. κατ᾽ ἀλ-λ᾽ ... ἐν τῷ Θεοφήμων τὴν ἀγεγεία ... & paullo post: ...
units.tr: Demosthenes, in the speech against Euergus and Mnesitheus, briefly describes the whole procedure they observed in the case of the one who had been struck ... and in the speech on the Theophemus ... and a little after: ...

units.la: Quod si quis alium verberasset, vulnufque inflixisset confulto, & ex destinatione mortem dandi, non scribebatur illi αἰκίας δίκη κατὰ τὸς Τεταρτήτου, sed τιμήματος ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τὴν βουλὴν ἢ ὡς Ἀρείῳ [?]γω. vt constat è Solonis Lege, quam in superioribus descripsimus: Quinetiam longè grauior erat multa: αἰχίας enim pecuniaria tantum erat, neque Legibus definita: At πεπράματος ἐκ πατρίδος multa definita erat Legibus: nempe exilium, bonorumque publicatio: quod si in patriam rediret, delatus morte multabatur:
units.tr: But if anyone had beaten another, inflicting a wound deliberately and with intent to kill, the action was not brought as aikia under the Forty, but a penalty was assessed in the council (the Areopagus), as is clear from Solon's law, which we described above. Moreover, the fine was much heavier: for aikia was only a monetary penalty, and not fixed by law; but for exile from the country (pepramatos ek patridos) the penalty was fixed by law, namely exile and confiscation of goods; and if he returned to his country, when reported he was punished with death.

units.la: Αν μέν τις ἀνδρὸς σῶμα ἢ πεῶσῃ ἐκ πατρίδος, κεφαλὴν, ἢ ὀφθαλμὸν, ἢ χεῖρας, ἢ πόδας, αὐτὸν μὲν φεύγειν τῆς τῆς ἀδικηθέντος πόλιν, τὰ δὲ χρήματα αὐτοῦ δημεύεσθαι. καὶ ἐὰν μὲν κατὰ [?], ἐὰν δὲ [?] θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι.
units.tr: [Ἄν μέν τις ἀνδρὸς σῶμα ἢ πεῶσῃ ἐκ πατρίδος, κεφαλὴν, ἢ ὀφθαλμὸν, ἢ χεῖρας, ἢ πόδας, αὐτὸν μὲν φεύγειν τῆς τῆς ἀδικηθέντος πόλιν, τὰ δὲ χρήματα αὐτοῦ δημεύεσθαι. καὶ ἐὰν μὲν κατὰ, ἐὰν δὲ θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι.]

units.la: Si quis alterius corpus, aut caput, aut vultum, aut manus, aut pedes, destinato laeserit vulnere, exulato à vulnerati patria, & bona eius publicantor: quod si in patriam redierit, delatus morte luito.
units.tr: If anyone with deliberate intent wounds another's body, or head, or face, or hands, or feet, let him be exiled from the country of the one who was injured, and his goods shall be confiscated; and if he returns to the country, let him be punished with death.

units.la: Legem hanc descripsimus è variis Lysiae locis: en tibi ἐν τῇ [?] Κηδίου ἰδιοσυλίας [?] ἀπολογία. αὐ μὲν ὡς ἀνδρὸς σῶμα ἢ πεῶσῃ, κεφαλὴν, ἢ ὀφθαλμὸν, ἢ χεῖρας, ἢ πόδας, αὐτὸς μὲν [?] τῆς [?] τῶν νόμων τῶν ἐξ Ἀρείου φεύξεται τῆς τῆς ἀδικηθέντος πόλιν, ἢ πεπράματος ἐκ πατρίδος καὶ ἐὰν μὲν κατὰ, ἐὰν δὲ [?] θανάτῳ ζημιοῦσθαι. Hinc ille, cui scripsit Lysias Apologiam πεπράματος ἐκ πατρίδος πρὸς Σίμωνα ad Senatum Areopagiticum; dicebat: ἐγὼ ἐἰς τοιοῦτον ἀγῶνα κεκλῆσθαι, εἰ ᾧ καὶ τῆς πατρίδος καὶ τῆς οὐσίας τῆς ἐμῆς ἀπάσης κινδυνεύω. Rursum eadem Apologia extrema: ἀλλὰ δὴ λαν ὅτι καὶ οἱ τῶν νόμων οὐδαμῶς θέντες, οὐκ εἰ' ἂν ἂν [?] μαχοστάμενοι ἔτυχον ἀλλήλων καταξαντες τῶν κεφαλῶν, ὅτι τοῦτο ἠξίωσαν τῆς πατρίδος φυγῇ ποιησασθαι (ἰ' πολλοῦ γ' ἀπέχη) ἀλλ' ὅσοι ἐπεξελθόντες ἀποκτεῖναι ἐναι ἐπώσαν, ἀποκτεῖναι δὲ οὐκ ἠδυνήθησαν, ὡς ἐπὶ τούτων τῶν πιμφείας ἕτερα μεγάλας καταπήσαντο· ἡμῶν μένει ὡς ἐκ ἐξουλλοῦσαι [?] Quare & altera Apologia πεπράματος ἐκ πατρίδος scripsit, ὅτι ὡς τῆς πατρίδος μὴ καὶ τῆς βίου ὁ ἀγών. Non in vitae discrimen veniebat ille qui accusabatur apud Areopagitas πεπράματος ἐκ πατρίδος, verum fortunarum suarum, quibus exuebatur. Quomodo enim, qui Lege iubebatur è patria exulare, τῆς πατρίδος Φυγὴν ποιήσασθαι, cui est ὡς τῆς πατρίδος ὁ ἀγών, in discrimen vitae veniret? Est igitur hic ὡς τῆς βίου ὁ ἀγών idem, quod superiori dixerat Apologia: ὡς τῆς οὐσίας τῆς ἐμῆς ἀπά-σης[?].
units.tr: We have drawn this law from various passages of Lysias: see his speech on the ... [case] of ... In the case of the one who wounds a man's body, or head, or eye, or hands, or feet, let him be exiled from the city of the one who was injured, according to the laws ...; in the case of exile from the country, and if he returns, let him be punished with death. Hence, for the man against whom Lysias wrote his speech on exile from the country against Simon before the Areopagite Council, he said: I am summoned to such a contest that I risk both my country and all my property. Again, the same speech, near its end: But even those who never made laws ... fought against one another and struck each other's heads, did not think it right to be punished with exile from the country (far from it), but those who went out and tried to kill, and did not succeed, suffered the greatest penalties ... Therefore the other speech on exile from the country was also written, where the contest is not for the country but for life. The man accused before the Areopagites on exile from the country was not in danger of his life, but of his fortunes, of which he was stripped. For how could one who by law was ordered to go into exile from his country, to make flight from the country, whose contest is for the country, come into peril of life? So this contest for life is the same as what the earlier speech called my whole property.

units.la: DE ACCVSATIONIBVS. TITVLVS II.
units.tr: ON ACCUSATIONS. TITLE II.

units.la: LEge permisit Solo cuiuis [illegible, ~5 letters] accusare & dicam impingere ei, qui alterum iniuria affecisset:
units.tr: By law Solon permitted anyone at all to accuse and to bring a suit against a man who had wronged another [illegible, about five letters].

units.la: Ἔξεστι παντὶ λαχεῖν δίκην ὑπὲρ [?] ἐκ τῶν κακῶν ποιοῦντος ἔξεναι. Cuinis eum, qui alteri iniuriam intulerit, accusare permissum esto.
units.tr: "Anyone may bring a suit against the one who does wrong [Ἔξεστι παντὶ λαχεῖν δίκην ὑπὲρ ... ἐκ τῶν κακῶν ποιοῦντος]." Let it be permitted to anyone to accuse the man who has inflicted an injury on another.

units.la: Legis meminit Plutarchus in Solone: πρὸ τῆ λεγόμενη πολίτη ... [?] τὰ κακὰ παροικοῦντας [?] ἐδωκε, & species aliquot enumerat: καὶ γὰρ πληγῆς ἐπίεσου καὶ βλαβέντος καὶ βιαζόντας ἐξ αὐτῶν τῆ δυναμένω καὶ βυλευμένα γεάφεσθαι τὸν ἀδικοῦντα καὶ δικαιον. plu-res recenset Pollux, & in vniuersum id pronunciat [?] ... Ratio autem huius Legis eodem legitur loco apud Plutarchum: ὀρῶς ἐπιζοντος τῆ νομοθέτου πρὸς πολίτας, ὥσπερ ἐκ μέσης συναγαγεῖσθαι καὶ συνοχῆν ἀλλήλοις. Praeterea δημόσια ἀδικήματα censentur, quae τῶν πόλιν ἠγεῖτο ἀδικεῖν, ἡ τῶν παθόντα μόνον. & optime Demosthenes: πρὸς ὅσα τῆς βιαζομένους παρείτει, κοινὰ ἀδικήματα, καὶ καὶ τὴν ἔξω τῆς παραγμάτης ὅπου ἠγεῖτο ὁ νομοθέτης, καὶ τὸν βιαζόντα δημοσίας δίκης βοηθείας. Quare cuiuis Atheniensium licet dicam scribere: ita argumentatur Vlpianus ad Midianam: Εἰ γὰρ πᾶσιν ἔξεστι κατηγορεῖν τῶν ἀδικούντων, παρεῖ δλαν ὁλοκλοῦ ἀπαύτων ἐγκλημα καὶ δημόσιον ἀδίκημα. Atque in huiusmodi actionibus, si actor alienus esset, multa, quae iniuria affecto pendi debebat, pendebatur areo aerario publico: At si ipse, qui accusabat, iniuriam esset passus, pendebat illi multam reus. Vlpianus ad Midianam: ἡ πίον οὖν ὅτι, εἰ μὲν αὐτὸς ὁ παθὼν κατηγορεῖ, αὐτὸς ἐλαμβάνοιτο καὶ ὁ δήμημα ὃ οὐκ ἐκ τῆς νόμων. εἰ δὲ ἕτερος ὧν ὁ κατηγορῶν, δημόσιον ἐτίγετο τῆς χαλεπῆς. Neque tenebatur accusator sponsione, quod in aliis tamen iudiciis erat solenne. Isocrates ἐν πρὸ τῆς Λοχίπου. καὶ οἱ θέντες ἡμῖν τοὺς νόμους περὶ τῆς αἰτίας καὶ δίκας καὶ γεαφὰς αὐτῶν παρ' ἐκαστὰ ποιήσαντο, ἵνα ἔτιν ἡμῶν ἕκαστος τυγχάνῃ καὶ δυναμένων καὶ βυλομένων, ὅπως ἐχη ὑμωρείσθαι τοὺς ἀδικοῦντας.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his Life of Solon, mentions this law, and lists several cases: for he gave the right to act on behalf of one who had been struck, or injured, or subjected to violence, and also on behalf of one who was wronged and could not act himself, and to bring suit against the wrongdoer. Pollux lists more, and states the principle in general terms. The reason for this law is given in the same place in Plutarch: the lawgiver wished to bind citizens together, as in one body, with mutual concern for one another. Moreover, those wrongs are reckoned public (δημόσια ἀδικήματα) which the lawgiver judged to harm the whole city and not only the injured person; and Demosthenes puts it very well: the wrongs that the lawgiver wished to be treated as common, not private, are those for which he allowed anyone who wished to bring a public suit. Hence any Athenian may bring an indictment. Ulpian argues this way in his commentary on Midias: "For if everyone is allowed to accuse wrongdoers, it is clearly a common crime and a public wrong." In such actions, if the accuser was not the injured party, the fine that ought to be paid to the injured person was paid into the public treasury; but if the accuser was himself the injured party, the defendant paid the fine to him. Ulpian, again on Midias: "It is clear, then, that if the injured man himself brings the accusation, he receives the fine himself, and if another brings it, the fine goes to the public treasury." Nor was the accuser bound to give a sponsio (a surety), although this was customary in other trials. Isocrates, in his speech Against Lochites: "The lawgivers who set down for us the laws on accusations, suits and indictments made them open to each of us, so that whoever is able and willing may punish wrongdoers."

units.la: DE DAMNIS. TITVLVS III.
units.tr: CONCERNING DAMAGE. TITLE III.

units.la: Lege canetur, ut qui sciens damnum duit, in duplum teneatur, qui imprudens, in simplum:
units.tr: By the law of Lege, whoever causes damage knowingly is liable for double, and whoever causes it unknowingly for single.

units.la: Ἀν μὲν ὡς ἑκὼν βλάψῃ, διπλοῦν· αὐ δ' ἀ-κων, ἁπλοῦν ὃ βλάβος ἐκτίνειν.
units.tr: "If he harms wilfully, he pays double; if unwillingly, he pays single the damage." [Ἂν μὲν ὡς ἑκὼν βλάψῃ, διπλοῦν· ἂν δ' ἄκων, ἁπλοῦν ὃ βλάβος ἐκτίνειν.]

units.la: Si quis prudens sciens damnum duit, in duplum, si imprudens, in simplum tenetor.
units.tr: If anyone knowingly causes damage, he is liable for double; if unknowingly, for single.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes in Midiana: ἀφ' ἑκὼν ἢ εἰ ἐν τοῦ πολιτῶν τῆς βλάβης ὅτι νόμοι πολύτης, ἐν ἐκ τῶν τῶν ἀρξαμένη, δὲ μὲν ἑκὼν βλάψῃ, διπλοῦν· δ' ὁ ἄκων, ἁπλοῦν ὃ βλάβος καλέουσιν ἐκτίνειν. Legis ratio est ibidem, quia ius & aequum est, ut noxia sarciatur: neque tamen eadem esse debet poena illius, qui noxiam fecerit, & damnum dederit, sciens, aut imprudens: ἐμὲν γὰρ πᾶσιν πρὸς παχοῦ βοηθείας δίκαιός ἐστι τυγχάνειν· τῆ δρασθυτὴ δ' οὐκ ἴσον πλεῖ ὀργλύ αἱ δ' ἐκὼν, αἱ τ' ἄκων, ἔταξεν ὁ νόμος.
units.tr: Demosthenes cites this law in the Midiana: "If someone harms another knowingly, he pays double; if unknowingly, he pays single the damage, as the laws of the citizens in many cases provide." The reason for the law, given in the same place, is that it is just and fair that the injury be made good. Yet the penalty of one who causes harm and damage knowingly should not be the same as that of one who does so unknowingly. For it is right that all should receive help in proportion to their need, but the law has not set the same penalty for the wilful and the unwilling offender. [Ἐὰν μὲν ἑκὼν βλάψῃ ... ἐὰν δ' ἄκων ...]

units.la: Legem autem tulit Solo, de eo, qui monoculo oculum, quem unicum habuit, effoderit, ut uterque ei effodiatur.
units.tr: Solon also enacted a law concerning one who gouges out the one eye of a man who has only one: each of his eyes is to be gouged out.

units.la: Ἐὰν μὲν ἑνὰ ὀφθαλμὸν ἔχοντος ἐκκόψῃ τις, ἀμφοτέρων[?] τοὺς δύο.
units.tr: "If someone gouges out the eye of a man who has one eye, let both of his eyes be gouged out." [Ἐὰν μὲν ἑνὸς ὀφθαλμὸν ἔχοντος ἐκκόψῃ τις, ἀμφοτέρων τοὺς δύο.]

units.la: Si quis monoculo oculum effoderit, uter-que ei effoditor.
units.tr: If anyone gouges out the eye of a one-eyed man, let both of his eyes be gouged out.

units.la: Legem descripsit Diogenes Laërtius in Solone, ad quam alludit Aristoteles Libro I. Rhetor. cap. VII. καὶ ὃ ἀγαπητὸν τῆς μὲν μόνον, τῆς δὲ μὴ ἀδικῶν[?] διὰ καὶ ὅτι[?] ἐὰν τις τὸν ἑτερόφθαλμον τυφλώσῃ[?], καὶ τὸ δύο ἐχθρὰ ἀγαπητὸν γὰρ ἀφίρηται[?]. Talionis enim Lex est, uterque caecus: hanc talionis Legem ab his Solonis Axonibus acceperunt Romani Decemviri, SI MEMBRUM NI CUM EO PACIT TALIO ESTO.
units.tr: Diogenes Laërtius, in his life of Solon, records the law, and Aristotle alludes to it in Book I of the Rhetoric, chapter 7: it is an acceptable thing that one who blinds the eye of a man with two eyes should... [Greek as printed garbled]. For this is the law of retaliation, that each is blinded in return. The Roman Decemvirs took this law of retaliation from Solon's axones, and wrote in the Twelve Tables: "If he has broken a limb and does not come to terms with the injured party, let there be retaliation."

units.la: De quadrupedo vero pauperiem faciente, noxae dari proculdubio cauerat Solo; nam de cane haec est eius Lex:
units.tr: Solon did indeed provide that a four-footed animal causing damage should be surrendered to the injured party; for he has this law about a dog:

units.la: Κυὼ δακόντα τὸ δρυοσῶν χλοιῷ τετραπήχει διδυμῶν[?].
units.tr: "A dog that has bitten, let it be bound with a collar of four cubits." [Κύνα δακόντα κλοιῷ τετραπήχει δεδεμένον.]

units.la: Canem, qui momorderit, cathena qua-tuor cubitorum reuinctum noxae da-to.
units.tr: A dog that has bitten someone shall be tied with a chain of four cubits and given up as surrender for the damage.

units.la: Refert Plutarchus in Solone: ἐγὼ δὲ βλάβης τετραπόδων νόμῳ, ὡς ἐκ δὲ καὶ κυνὸς δακόντα ἐπιδιδωῖ κλοιῷ τετραπήχει διδυμῶν[?]. Quod commentum scitum certe est ad securitatem: ὃ μὲν ἐνθύμημα χαρίεν πρὸς ἀσφάλειαν[?], inquit Plutarchus. Meminit autem Canum praecipue, quia ad fores habebant canes catenarios, idque cum ruri, tum in urbe: ruri, ut docet Columella Libro VII.cap.XII. Nunc, ut exordio priore sum pollicitus, de mutis custodibus loquar: quamquam canis falso dicitur mutus custos. in urbe : Eustathius ad Iliad. X. ὡς ἐν ταῖς αὐλαῖς[?] κυνῶν[?].
units.tr: Plutarch reports in his Solon: "Solon's law on damage done by four-footed beasts, namely that a dog which has bitten is to be fastened with a collar of four cubits." This provision is certainly clever for security, as Plutarch says. Solon mentions dogs in particular because at their doors people kept chained dogs, both in the country and in the city. In the country, as Columella teaches in Book VII, chapter 12: "Now, as I promised at the beginning, I shall speak of the dumb guardians; though a dog is wrongly called a dumb guardian." In the city, Eustathius on Iliad X says that it was so in the courtyards of dogs.

units.la: Εἰς οἰκίαν ὅταν ὡς εἰσὴ φίλου, ἐσὴ ζωρεῖν[?], Νικοφῶν, πλὴν τὸ φίλου[?] θύοιαι ἀϑὺς εἰσοίκοι[?] ταῖς κυσίν. ὁ ἰώρως[?] ἰλαχέως πρὸς τὴν ἔστιν. ἢ κυὼν[?] ἔσθμε[?].
units.tr: Whenever you enter the house of a friend, Nicophon, beware of the dogs at the door... (the Greek is much corrupted in the printed text; the sense is a warning to take care of the dogs at a friend's house).

units.la: Quare ut canem caueant praecipitur apud Comicum Lysistrata.
units.tr: Hence the caution to beware of the dog is given by the comic poet in Lysistrata.

units.la: πρὸς γὰρ μύρτοι τῷ κυνὶ[?] παρασαρθὼ μὴ βαδίζῃ τῷ ἱμιλῷ[?].
units.tr: "For take care not to walk past the dog with the myrtle branch..." [πρὸς γὰρ μύρτοι τῷ κυνί παρασαρθὼ μὴ βαδίζῃ τῷ ἱμιλῷ]

units.la: DE VI BONORUM raptorum.
units.tr: ON THE VIOLENT SEIZURE OF GOODS.

units.la: TITULUS IV.
units.tr: TITLE IV.

units.la: Rege, qui per vim aliquid abstulerat, in duplum tenebatur, non tantum ei, à quo per vim abstulerat, sed etiam publico aerario:
units.tr: A person who had taken something by force was liable for double, not only to the one from whom he had taken it by force, but also to the public treasury.

units.la: Τὸν βίᾳ ἐπιῶν[?] ἀφελόντα, ἁπλῶς[?] ἐκ-ἰδιώτη[?], ἢ δ' ἴσον τῆς δημοσίας τιμᾶν[?].
units.tr: [Τὸν βίᾳ ἐπιῶν ἀφελόντα, ἁπλῶς ἐκ-ἰδιώτη, ἢ δ' ἴσον τῆς δημοσίας τιμᾶν] He who, having come upon someone, takes something by force, is simply (liable) to the private person; and (he pays) an amount equal to the public (penalty).

units.la: Qui per vim aliquid abstulerit, in du-plum tenetor ei, à quo per vim abstulit, in duplum quoq; erario publico tenetor.
units.tr: Whoever has taken something by force is liable to double to the one from whom he took it by force; he is also liable to double to the public treasury.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes in Midiana: καὶ πάλιν, τί ἄν ποτε, αὐ μὲν ἐκὼν πρὸς ἑκόντας [?] ὡς λαβὼν [?] ἑλάττων [?] ἐὰν, ἢ δύο, ἢ καὶ δίκας, καὶ ζῶντα ἀποφέρειν, οὐδὲν αὐτῶ [?] τοῖς πόλιν ὅστις. [?] δὲ δὲ μικρόν πάνυ ἡμέρας ἀξίον τῆς λαβῆς, βίᾳ δὲ τὸν ἀφέλπται, ὃ ἴσον τῷ δημοσίῳ φεύγειν εἰ νόμοι κελεύουσιν, ὅσαν ἐξ αὐτοῦ τὰ ἰδιῶτα. Vlpianus ad hæc: ὅτι Εἰ μὲν παρ' ἑκόντος ἑλάσει, ἀκίνδυνον, εἰ δὲ βίᾳ παρ' ἀκόντος, τοῖς διπλασίοις ὑποτιθῶς καταλήγεις. Dixit Vlpianus, τοῖς διπλασίοις ὑποτιθωσ [?], quia, vt iam diximus, duplum reddebat ei, à quo per vim abstulerat, tantumdemque publico pendebat: Pendebat autem publico, quia quæ per vim gesta sunt, tyrannica sunt, & Rempublicam, non priuatos tantum eum euersum. Demo-sthenes ibidem: ὅτι πάντῃ ὅσα ἂν βιάζηται, ἐλαττωθεὶς κοινὰ ἀδικήματα, καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἑξῶ τῶν ἐφεδρικῶν οὗτος ἡγεῖτο ὁ Νομοθέτης. ἐλλύ μὲν γὰρ ἰδιωτικὰ, ἐλίγων, τοῖς δὲ δημοσίοις ἀπολύσεων, καὶ τὸν μὲν πεισθέντα, ἰδίας, τὸν δὲ βιαζόμενον, δημοσίας ἐλάσσα βονηρίας. Atque hæc actio, Βιαίων dicebatur, competens aduersus eos, qui vi aliquid moliebantur: Veteres Magistri: Βιαίων, ὄνομα δίκης. κατὰ τῶν βίᾳ προσθεντῶν ἐποιῶν· ὁ δὲ ἄλλος ἀπαθὴς εἴ ἐπὶ ἐκ τῶν δημοσίων ἴσον τῶ ἐλάττωνι. Scribebantur autem hæ dicæ apud Quadraginta. Demosthenes ἐν τῷ προς Παντατίνον, καὶ γὰρ αἰκίαν, καὶ ἕλεσιν, καὶ Βιαίων, καὶ πρὸς ἐπιχλήσεις ἀδικήματα. Τοῦτον δ' εἶσιν ἐκ ἐκείνου χωρεῖς αἱ δίκαι· καὶ ἐπὶ πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν ἀμφιλέγειν, ἂν ἔ ὑμῖν τὰ αὐτῷ· ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν αἰτία, καὶ τὰ τῶν Βιαίων πρὸς τὰς Τεπαρακοντα. Qui sint hi Quadraginta, vnus, quod ego quidem sciam, docet Pollux Libro VIII. cap.IX. οἱ δὲ Τεπαρακοντα, ποτέ πρὸς τὴν ἀναγωγὴν ἀγχοὺς τὸ ἐχθρῶν ἐκ ἐλε ἄνδρας ἀν δίκης ἐπὶ τὰ πολεμίων, πρὸ μὲν ἐργώ δίκα εἰληχόν. τὰ δὲ ὑπ' ἐκοῦ, Διαιτητῆς προσκλῆσθαι.
units.tr: Demosthenes, in the speech against Meidias, quotes the law: and again, what would be the case if someone, willingly, from willing persons, as if taking, less, if two, or even lawsuits, and carrying off alive, nothing to him, to the city whoever [καὶ πάλιν, τί ἄν ποτε, αὐ μὲν ἐκὼν πρὸς ἑκόντας ὡς λαβὼν ἑλάττων ἐὰν, ἢ δύο, ἢ καὶ δίκας, καὶ ζῶντα ἀποφέρειν, οὐδὲν αὐτῶ τοῖς πόλιν ὅστις]; but he who takes a very small thing, worth a day's wage, and seizes it by force, the law orders him to be prosecuted as for a public offence equal to that, since the private (wrong) is such [δὲ δὲ μικρόν πάνυ ἡμέρας ἀξίον τῆς λαβῆς, βίᾳ δὲ τὸν ἀφέλπται, ὃ ἴσον τῷ δημοσίῳ φεύγειν εἰ νόμοι κελεύουσιν, ὅσαν ἐξ αὐτοῦ τὰ ἰδιῶτα]. Ulpian on these words: that if he takes from a willing person, it is without danger; but if by force from an unwilling one, he is subject to the double penalty [ὅτι Εἰ μὲν παρ' ἑκόντος ἑλάσει, ἀκίνδυνον, εἰ δὲ βίᾳ παρ' ἀκόντος, τοῖς διπλασίοις ὑποτιθῶς καταλήγεις]. Ulpian said subject to the double penalty [τοῖς διπλασίοις ὑποτιθωσ], because, as we have already said, he restored double to the one from whom he had taken it by force, and paid the same amount to the public treasury. He paid to the public because what is done by force is tyrannical, and it subverts the Commonwealth, not merely private persons. Demosthenes in the same place: that all whatever acts of violence, when they are diminished, are common offences, and the Lawgiver so ordered according to the scale of the (penalties) ... for private wrongs are small, but public ones are destructive, and the one who is persuaded (is wronged) privately, while the one who uses violence is (punished) by a public action of great wickedness [ὅτι πάντῃ ὅσα ἂν βιάζηται, ἐλαττωθεὶς κοινὰ ἀδικήματα, καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἑξῶ τῶν ἐφεδρικῶν οὗτος ἡγεῖτο ὁ Νομοθέτης. ἐλλύ μὲν γὰρ ἰδιωτικὰ, ἐλίγων, τοῖς δὲ δημοσίοις ἀπολύσεων, καὶ τὸν μὲν πεισθέντα, ἰδίας, τὸν δὲ βιαζόμενον, δημοσίας ἐλάσσα βονηρίας]. This action was called of violence [Βιαίων], and lay against those who attempted something by force. The old teachers: Biaion, the name of a lawsuit; it was brought against those who acted by force; the other (charge) was equal to the lesser of the public (charges) [Βιαίων, ὄνομα δίκης. κατὰ τῶν βίᾳ προσθεντῶν ἐποιῶν· ὁ δὲ ἄλλος ἀπαθὴς εἴ ἐπὶ ἐκ τῶν δημοσίων ἴσον τῶ ἐλάττωνι]. These suits were brought before the Forty. Demosthenes, in the speech against Pantaenetus [ἐν τῷ προς Παντατίνον]: for both assault, and theft, and violence, and offences against the (state) [καὶ γὰρ αἰκίαν, καὶ ἕλεσιν, καὶ Βιαίων, καὶ πρὸς ἐπιχλήσεις ἀδικήματα]. The suits go before them from that (court), and they are judged before the same (magistrates); but the cause of the actions of violence goes to the Forty [Τοῦτον δ' εἶσιν ἐκ ἐκείνου χωρεῖς αἱ δίκαι· καὶ ἐπὶ πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν ἀμφιλέγειν, ἂν ἔ ὑμῖν τὰ αὐτῷ· ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν αἰτία, καὶ τὰ τῶν Βιαίων πρὸς τὰς Τεπαρακοντα]. Who these Forty were, one author, as far as I know, explains: Pollux in Book VIII, chapter IX: the Forty, in earlier times, when a suit was brought against an enemy's men concerning the ... they took up the suit and were called arbitrators [οἱ δὲ Τεπαρακοντα, ποτέ πρὸς τὴν ἀναγωγὴν ἀγχοὺς τὸ ἐχθρῶν ἐκ ἐλε ἄνδρας ἀν δίκης ἐπὶ τὰ πολεμίων, πρὸ μὲν ἐργώ δίκα εἰληχόν. τὰ δὲ ὑπ' ἐκοῦ, Διαιτητῆς προσκλῆσθαι].

units.la: DE FVRTIS TITVLVS V.
units.tr: ON THEFT, TITLE V.

units.la: Seuera admodum & acria de furtis habuerunt veteres Athenienses iudicia. Draconis enim Lege fures cuiuscumque modi furti supplicio capitis puniebantur:
units.tr: The ancient Athenians had very severe and harsh judgments concerning theft. Under Draco's law, thieves were punished with capital punishment, whatever kind of theft they had committed:
