units.la: FVREM CVIVSCVMQVE MODI FVRTI SVPPLICIO CAPITIS PVNITO.
units.tr: A THIEF OF WHATEVER KIND OF THEFT SHALL BE PUNISHED WITH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT.

units.la: Draconis ista Lex est, de qua A. Gellius Libro XI. cap. XVIII. Draco Athenienses vir bonus multaque esse prudentia existimatus est, iurisque diuini & humani peritus fuit. Is Draco Leges, quibus Athenienses vterentur, primus omnium tulit. In illis Legibus furem cuiuscumque modi furti supplicio capitis puniendum esse, & alia pleraque, nimis seuere censuit sanxitque. Plutarchus in Solone de Draconis Legibus: μία γὰρ ἀλίγου δὴν ἄπασαν ὠσεὶ τοῖς ἀδικήμασιν ζημία, θάνατος. ὥστε καὶ τοῖς λάχανα κλέπτουσι ἢ ὀπώραν, ὁμοίως κολάζεσθαι τῆς ἑσπερι- σύλαις οὐλοῖς τοῖς ἀνδροφόνοις. Id sane è Stoicorum mente, qui ἴσα τὰ ἁμαρτήματα εἶναι dixerunt: Nec enim honesto quicquam honestius esse putarunt, nec turpi turpius: peccata, quia discrepant, æque discrepant: καὶ ὁ πλεῖον καὶ ἔλαττον ἁμαρτάνων, ὅπερ οὐκ εἰσὶν εἰς τὰ καταρθώματα, vt est apud Diogenem Laertium in Zenone: Quare Demosthenes scribebat alicubi, ὅ γ' ἀδικῶν καὶ ὁ δίκαιον, αὐτὸ ὅτι μικρόν ἐστιν, ἀλλ' ὅτι μείζονες ὀφείλουσιν, τὸ αὐτὸ ἐχθρὸν ἡμῖν διωκάμεν. Caufam, cur omnia pœne delicta capitis perfecutus effet supplicio, interrogatus Draco refpondebat, τὰ μὲν μικρὰ ἀδικήματα θανάτου ἄξια νομίζειν. τὰς δὲ μεγάλας οὐκ ἔχειν μείζονα ζημίαν.
units.tr: This is Draco's law, which A. Gellius discusses in Book XI, chapter XVIII: "Draco, an upright man who was thought very wise, was skilled in divine and human law. He was the first of all to draw up laws for the Athenians to use. In those laws he decreed very severely, among many other provisions, that a thief of whatever kind of theft should be punished with capital punishment." Plutarch, in his Life of Solon, on Draco's laws: "For almost all offences had one penalty, death, so that those who stole vegetables or fruit were punished in the same way as murderers" [μία γὰρ ἀλίγου δὴν ἄπασαν ὠσεὶ τοῖς ἀδικήμασιν ζημία, θάνατος]. This is certainly in keeping with the mind of the Stoics, who held that all sins are equal: they thought nothing honourable was more honourable, nor shameful more shameful, and that sins, though they differ, are equally different [ἴσα τὰ ἁμαρτήματα]. And one who sins more or less does not thereby fall into different categories of wrong, as Diogenes Laertius reports in his Life of Zeno. Hence Demosthenes wrote somewhere that the wrongdoer, whether he commits a small or a great wrong, is pursued with the same hostility by us [ὅ γ' ἀδικῶν ... τὸ αὐτὸ ἐχθρὸν ἡμῖν διωκάμεν]. When Draco was asked why he punished almost all offences with death, he replied that he considered small offences deserving of death, and that great ones had no greater penalty [τὰ μὲν μικρὰ ἀδικήματα θανάτου ἄξια νομίζειν. τὰς δὲ μεγάλας οὐκ ἔχειν μείζονα ζημίαν].

units.la: Mutauit postea hæc Draconis de furibus Lex, & Solonis illa lata est, qua dupli pœna vindicandum furtum sanxit,
units.tr: Later this law of Draco concerning thieves was changed, and the law of Solon was enacted, which punished theft with a double penalty.

units.la: Ὅ, τι ἐὰν ἡς πόλεσιν, ἐὰν μὲν αὐτὸς λάβῃ, τὴν διπλασίαν κατα δικάζειν. ἐὰν δὲ μή, τῷ δικαιοπλασίαν παρὰ τὰς ἐπαγωγὰς. διὰ δὲ ταῦτα ἐν τῇ ποδοκίχῃ τὸν τύπον πείθειν ἡμέρας καὶ νύκτας ἴσως, ἐὰν παρειλημμένον ἢ Ἡλιαία. παρειλημμένα δὲ τὸν βυλόμενον, ὅταν περὶ τῶν ἀμαρτημάτων ἡ.
units.tr: Solon's law, as quoted by Demosthenes: "Whoever should be the thief, if he himself is caught, shall pay double; if not, the owner shall recover double from the one who is caught... For this reason, at the ... they shall sit in the stocks for days and nights, if the case is taken to the Heliaea. The one who wishes may take up the case, whenever it concerns offences" [Ὅ, τι ἐὰν ἡς πόλεσιν ... παρειλημμένα δὲ τὸν βυλόμενον, ὅταν περὶ τῶν ἀμαρτημάτων ἡ].

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes in Timocratea: ὅ, τι ἐὰν ἡς πόλεσιν, ἐὰν μὲν αὐτὸς λάβῃ τὴν διπλασίαν κατα δικάζειν. ἐὰν δὲ μή, τῷ διπλασίαν παρὰ τὰς ἐπαγωγὰς. διὰ ταῦτα ἐν τῇ ποδοκίχῃ τὸν τύπον πείθειν ἡμέρας καὶ νύκτας ἴσως, ἐὰν παρειλημμένον ἢ Ἡλιαία. παρειλημμένα δὲ τὸν βυλόμενον, ὅταν περὶ τῶν ἡμαρτημάτων ἡ. Meminit rursum in eadem Oratione: εἰ δὲ ὡς ἰδίαν δίκην κλοπῆς ἀλφά, παρὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν μὲν αὐτὸ δικάζειν ἀπὸ τῶν ἰδίων ὁ ἀμπελὸν παραμένοντος δὲ ἐξίας τῆς δικαστηρίου παρὰ τὸ ἐργεῖον δισμοῦ δὲ κλίσιν, ἐπὶ ἡμέρας, καὶ νύκτας ἴσως, ὅπως ὁρῶν ἀπάντως αὐτὸν διδάξαι. Gellius verbis ad superiorem Legem descriptis subijcit: Eius igitur Leges, quoniam videbantur impendio acerbiores, non decreto iussoque, sed tacito illiteratoque Atheniensium consensu obliterata sunt. Postea Legibus aliis mitioribus à Solone compositis, usi sunt. Is Solon ex septem illis inclytis sapientibus fuit. Is sua Lege in fures, non (vt Draco antea) mortis, sed dupli pœna vindicandum existimauit. Ergo si quis interdiu furtum faxit, resque furtiua intra drachmarum quinquaginta pretium sit (istæ duæ conditiones quanquam in hac Lege non exprimantur, è sequentibus Legibus liquido colliguntur) duplione luebat, si quod furto perierat recepisset Dominus: sin minus decupli pœna vindicandum est furtū, tum in eum qui fecerit, cum in illos, quorum ope & consilio factum est. Præterea habebatur quoque in nervo quinque ipsos dies, & totidem noctes, si de ea re ita pronunciassent Heliastæ: Cauet autem Legislator, vt non iterato iudicio hac de re viderent iudices, sed cum in eo essent, vt sua sententia multarent. Atque id sanxit Solo, si furti tantum, non alterius etiam criminis reus petageretur, ἰδίας δίκης κλοπῆς vocat Demosthenes, quemadmodum alibi ἐν τῷ κοινῷ Κοινῶν αἰτίας, dixit Aristo scripsisse se Cononi ἰδίας δίκης αἰτίας, quia non impegerat ταῖς τῆς ὕβρεως γραφαῖς, neque suo iure τὴν τῶν λωποδυτῶν ἀπαγωγὴν vsus fuerat; quanquam omnibus his teneretur. Duplici vero pœna, dupli scilicet, & vinculorum, vindicandum furtum sanxit Solo, quia nulla aliis esset religio furtum facere, si modo rem tantum, quam furto subripuerant, restituerent, sed poena dupli coercebantur, alias & insuper haec irrogata, qui ignominia vinculorum in officio continebantur. units.tr: Demosthenes cites the law again in his speech Against Timocrates, and in the same speech he mentions it once more: "If someone brings a private suit for theft, the magistrate is to hear it from the private parties ... and if the accused is convicted, he is to be held in the stocks for days and nights..." Gellius adds to his account of the earlier law: "Since these laws seemed unusually harsh, they fell into disuse, not by decree or command, but by the silent and unwritten consent of the Athenians. Afterwards they made use of other, milder laws composed by Solon, who was one of those seven famous wise men. In his law concerning thieves he judged that they should be punished not with death, as Draco had ordered, but with a double penalty." So if anyone stole by day, and the stolen goods were worth no more than fifty drachmae (these two conditions, though not stated in this law, are clearly gathered from the following laws), he paid double, if the owner recovered what had been stolen; but if not, the theft was to be punished with a tenfold penalty, both against the thief and against those by whose help and counsel the theft was done. Moreover, he was also held in the stocks for five days and as many nights, if the Heliastae so pronounced. The lawgiver took care that the judges should not hear the matter again in a second trial, but while they were still considering it, they were to fix the fine by their own sentence. Solon enacted this when the accused was prosecuted for theft alone and not for some other crime; Demosthenes calls this a private suit for theft [ἰδίας δίκης κλοπῆς], just as elsewhere he speaks of a public suit [ἐν τῷ κοινῷ]. Aristo says he wrote to Conon that it was a private suit for injury [ἰδίας δίκης αἰτίας], because he had not brought it under the procedure for outrage [ταῖς τῆς ὕβρεως γραφαῖς], nor had he used his right to have the robbers of clothing arrested [τὴν τῶν λωποδυτῶν ἀπαγωγὴν], although he was liable to all of these. Solon ordained that theft be punished with a double penalty, that is, double payment together with imprisonment, because if they had only to restore the thing they had stolen, there would be no reason for anyone not to steal; they were therefore restrained by the double penalty, and beyond this the additional punishment of imprisonment, by which the disgrace of chains kept them to their duty. units.la: Si rei furtivae aestimatio esset supra drachmas quinquaginta, aut nox furtum factum esset, aut etiam interdiu in balineis, vel aliis publicis locis, capitis supplicio vindicabatur furtum ex hac Solonis Lege:
units.tr: If the value of the stolen thing exceeded fifty drachmas, or if the theft was committed at night, or even by day in the baths or other public places, theft was punished by death under this law of Solon:

units.la: Si lucri furtum, cuius aestimatio sit supra quinquaginta drachmas, faxit, ad Vndecimviros rapitor : si nox furtum faxit, si im aliquis occisit, iure caesus esto, aut vulnerarit fugientem, si fraude esto: aut rapitor ad Vndecimviros : Manifestum huiusmodi furtum qui faxit, etiamsi vades dederit, non noxae facit farcitione, sed morte luito. Si quis item ex aliquo Gymnasio, vestis, aut lecythi, aut alicuius vel minimae rei, aut supellectilis e gymnasio, aut ex balneo, aut e portubus, quod excedat decem drachmarum aestimationem, furtum faxit, morte luito.
units.tr: If someone commits theft for gain, the value of which exceeds fifty drachmae, he is to be taken before the Eleven. If someone commits theft at night, and anyone kills him, let him be lawfully killed; or if he wounds a fleeing thief, let it be without fraud; or let the thief be taken before the Eleven. Whoever commits a manifest theft of this kind, even if he has given sureties, shall not make amends by paying compensation, but shall pay with his life. Likewise, if anyone steals clothing, or an oil flask, or any smallest thing, or household furniture, from a gymnasium, or from a bath, or from the harbours, the value of which exceeds ten drachmae, he shall pay with his life.

[illegible, ~30 letters]. Solonis autem Lex est, ut ex eodem Demosthenis loco constat: cuius tria sunt Capita: primo autem caveret, ut si quis luci furtum faxit, reliquae furtiuae aestimatio sit supra drachmas quinquaginta, rapiatur ad Vndecimviros capitales: nam si intra quinquaginta drachmarum pretium esset, ad Vndecimviros non rapiebatur. Vlpianus ita haec Legis verba, [illegible, ~15 letters] [illegible, ~15 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] interpretatur; [illegible, ~50 letters] [illegible, ~50 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters]: nonenim supplicio capitis puniebantur, sed duplione, atque vinculorum nexu. Alterum caput est de fure, qui nox furtum faxit, cuiuscumque aestimationis res furtiua fuerit: si im aliquis occisit, iure caesus esto, ut vertebant olim Decemviri in suis Tabulis: ius quoque erat ad Vndecimviros rapere, si vellent. Seuerius autem nocturni fures puniuntur, quia noctu facilius furantur: unde Homerus, citante Varrone Libro Rerum Diuinarum XIV.
units.tr: Demosthenes gives the law in this form [illegible in the scan] in Timocrates, but I think he does not describe it fully. The evidence is that [illegible in the scan] said, where Solon [illegible in the scan], as Pollux attests in Book VIII, chapter VII. Solon's law, as is clear from the same passage of Demosthenes, has three heads. First, it provides that if anyone commits theft by day, and the value of the stolen goods exceeds fifty drachmae, he is to be taken before the Eleven, who had the power of capital punishment; for if the value was within fifty drachmae, he was not taken before the Eleven. Ulpian explains these words of the law as follows: [illegible in the scan]; for such thieves were not punished with capital punishment, but with a double payment and the bond of chains. The second head concerns the thief who steals at night, whatever the value of the goods: if anyone kills him, let him be lawfully killed, as the Decemvirs formerly wrote in their Tables; it was also lawful to take him before the Eleven if they wished. Nocturnal thieves are punished more severely, because they steal more easily at night; hence Homer, as cited by Varro in Book XIV of the Divine Antiquities:

units.la: Praeterea non ita facile est noctu, sese aduersus fures tutari, quam interdiu.
units.tr: Moreover, it is not so easy to defend oneself against thieves at night as it is by day.

units.la: Vlpianus: ἐὰν γυναικὶ ἡ μείζονα τῶν πεμφθέντων ἐδήξεν, ἐπειδὴ γὰρ μείζον ὅτι ὁ ἐγκλημα τῆς γυναικὸς· ἐὰν δὲ ἡμέρα, διωθᾶσθαι ὡς καὶ βουλησις καλέσαι ἑαυτῷ· ἐὰν δὲ γυναικὶ, σκέπει. Ab-ducti ad Vndecimviros cum nocturni fures, tum diurni, qui rem pretio drachmarum quinquaginta maiorem subripuissent, capitis supplicio in eos vindicabatur, etiamsi vades dedissent, non autem sarcita noxa quam fecerant: ita interpretor Legis verba, πρὸς δὲ ἀλόντι, ὧν αἱ ἀπαγωγαὶ εἰσιν, ὡς ἐπὶ ἐπιφανῆ ἐκπίνειν τῇ κλεμμάτ-ων, ἀλλὰ διὰ πάντων τὴν ζημίαν. Poterant quidem vades dare; vt habes apud Antiphontem περὶ τῆς Ἡρῳδου φόνου. ἐθέλοιτο γὰρ μὲν ἐγγυητὰς ποιῆσαι τὰς καταγωγὰς τοῦ νόμου, ὅτι γὰρ δὲ μὴ ἐγγενέσθαι ποιῆσαι. τὸ δὲ ἀμῶν ξένων ὁ ὄλης πώποτε ἠθέλησε καταγωγὴν ἐγγυητὰς, ὅτι πώποτε ἐδίδη. Proprie κακουργοί dicuntur, vt est ibidem: ἐπὶ γὰρ τῆς κλεπτῶν ὁ τῆς κακουργῶν νόμος κέται. Aduersus vades dabatur actio ad exhibendum, quae εἰς ἐμφανῆ καταστῆσαι dicitur, οὐ γὰρ ἐστὶν ἀμφισβητησθ... ἐκ φανερῶν. Pollux Lib. VIII. cap. VI. ὧν ἢ δίκη ἡ εἰς ἐμφανῆ καταστῆσαι κλεψίμου, ὁ ποτε τὰς ἐγγύησις τινὰ, ἢ τὰ χρήματα, οἷ τὰ κλοπάσια. Tenebantur enim vades rem furto subreptâ repraesentare. Tertio Legis Kapite sanctum est, vt si quis in balneis, aut gymnasiis furatus sit, vel tantillum, aut in portubus id, cuius aestimatio sit supra drachmas decem, ad Vndecimviros raptus capite luat, quod constat etiam è Lysia ἐν τῷ πρὸς Θεομνήστου. vbi huius Legis verba ista à Solone perscripta, ΘΟΙΜΑΤΙΟΝ ΑΠΟΔΕΔΥΣΘΑΙ, Η ΤΟΝ ΧΙΤΩΝΙΣΚΟΝ ΕΚΔΕΔΥΣΘΑΙ interpretatur. ἀλλ' ἡ ἡ ἀλλ' ἡ ΕΥΔΙΚΑ ὑμνοῦσι, ἀποδίξαιο εἰ τις ἀπαγὼ ἔνα, φάσκων ΘΟΙΜΑΤΙΟΝ ΑΠΟΔΕΔΥΣΘΑΙ, Η ΤΟΝ ΧΙΤΩΝΙΣΚΟΝ ΕΚΔΕΔΥΣΘΑΙ. ἀλλ' ἀφιεὶς τὴν αὐτὸν ἔφην, ὅτι οὐ λωποδύτης ὁμολόγησι. λωποδύται sunt balnearij fures. Hesychius: λωποδύτης, κλέπτης ἀποδύσεως ἐν λουτρῶς κλέ-πτοντες. Meminit huius Legis de manifestis & balnearijs furibus Xenophon Libro I. ἀπομνημονευμάτων. τῷ γὰρ τοῖς νόμοις, ἐαὶ ἡς φανερὸς ἡ ὑπὸ κλέπτων, λ' λωποδύτης, ἔστι ἡ ὑπὸ ζημία. Rationes autem peti possunt ex Aristotele in Problematis, cur in istos adeo seuere animaduertatur: Διὰ τί ποτε, ἐὰν μὲν ὡς ἐν βαλανεῖῳ κλέψῃ, ἢ ἐν παλαίστρᾳ, ἢ ἐξ ἀγορᾶς, ἢ τῶν ἱματίων τῶν ἡμῶν, ἡ ζημία μυσοῦσι· ἐαὶ δὲ ὡς ἐξ οἰκίας, ἁπλοῦν τῆς ἀξίας τῆς κλεμμάτος ἐπιτ-ιμᾷ; Nam primo facillimum est in balineis, & aliis locis publicis furari, & à furibus ne tum quidem recte caueri poterat, cum maxime caucbatur, tam multi erant, tam improbi: ἐν τῷ βαλανείῳ, καὶ ἐν τῇς ἵππων ἀποδιδόναι, ὥσπερ ὁ βαλανεύς, ῥᾷδιον τοῦ βαλανείου κακουργῆσαι. Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἰσχυρὸν ἔχουσι φυλάσ-σειν· οἱ λοιποὶ, ἀλλ' ἐν ᾧ ὅμμα, ὥστε μὲν ὡς τὰ ἀφελέσθαι, ὅτι τὰ κλεπτό-μενα ἡδὲ γῆς. Διὰ ὁ νομοθέτης ὑπὸ ἰσχυρὸς ὁμολογεῖ ἐπὶ φυλακὰς, τὸν νόμον αὐτῆς ἐπίσηση ἀπιλαμβάνοντα σφοδρῶς, ὡς ὁ βιωσαμένοις ἐαὶ ὁ σφετερίζονται τὴν ἀλλοτρίων. Praeterea, non licebat quenquam à balineis, gymnasiis, & locis publicis arcere: quare saltem hac seueritate Legis fures erant coercendi: πρὸς δὲ βαλα-νείῳ ἡμῖν τὸ, ὅτι οὐκ ἐξεστι ὀπλιᾶ κωλύσαι, ὅτι εἰσέλθοι, ὅτι εἰσελθοῖ, μὴ ποτὲ κλέπτειν ὁ αὐτοῦ ἰματίου θέσθαι, ἀποδύσασθαι. ἀλλ' ὡς ἡ βάλετε εἰ τῷ αὐτῷ ἢ τε τῆς κλεπτῆς ἐαῖς, ὁ ἡ τῆς μηνὸς ἀποπλωαί, ἀίαμεμιγμένα χαῖν. Διὰ ὁ νομοθέτης τῆς ἐξ αἰτίας κοινωνοῦσι ἡ εἰς ὁ βαλανεῖον εἰσοδοῦ ὁ ἡ ἀμάμιξεως, μεγάλης ἡμωρίας φανερὸς ὅτι καθῆσθαι τοῖς κλέπτουσι.
units.tr: Ulpian: [ἐὰν γυναικὶ ἡ μείζονα τῶν πεμφθέντων ἐδήξεν... ἐὰν δὲ ἡμέρα, διωθᾶσθαι... ἐὰν δὲ γυναικὶ, σκέπει.] Those who were brought before the Eleven, both night thieves and day thieves, who had stolen goods worth more than fifty drachmas, were punished by death, even if they had given sureties, and not merely made good the damage they had done. I read the words of the law in this way: [πρὸς δὲ ἀλόντι, ὧν αἱ ἀπαγωγαὶ εἰσιν, ὡς ἐπὶ ἐπιφανῆ ἐκπίνειν τῇ κλεμμάτ-ων, ἀλλὰ διὰ πάντων τὴν ζημίαν.] They could, to be sure, give sureties; as you have in Antiphon, On the Murder of Herodes: [ἐθέλοιτο γὰρ μὲν ἐγγυητὰς ποιῆσαι τὰς καταγωγὰς τοῦ νόμου...]. Thieves are properly called criminals, as in the same passage: [ἐπὶ γὰρ τῆς κλεπτῶν ὁ τῆς κακουργῶν νόμος κέται]. Against the sureties there was an action for production, which is called to bring into view [εἰς ἐμφανῆ καταστῆσαι]; for it is not... [οὐ γὰρ ἐστὶν ἀμφισβητησθ... ἐκ φανερῶν]. Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 6: [ὧν ἢ δίκη ἡ εἰς ἐμφανῆ καταστῆσαι κλεψίμου, ὁ ποτε τὰς ἐγγύησις τινὰ, ἢ τὰ χρήματα, οἷ τὰ κλοπάσια.] For sureties were bound to produce the thing that had been stolen. In the third chapter of the law it is laid down that if anyone steals in the baths or the gymnasia, however small the amount, or in the harbours, something valued above ten drachmas, he shall be seized and pay with his life before the Eleven; this is also clear from Lysias, in his speech Against Theomnestus, where he explains the words of this law written down by Solon: [ΘΟΙΜΑΤΙΟΝ ΑΠΟΔΕΔΥΣΘΑΙ, Η ΤΟΝ ΧΙΤΩΝΙΣΚΟΝ ΕΚΔΕΔΥΣΘΑΙ]. If anyone should bring an action, claiming that the cloak was to be stripped off or the tunic taken away, I say he was not a confessed lopodytes. Lopodytai are bath thieves. Hesychius: [λωποδύτης, κλέπτης ἀποδύσεως ἐν λουτρῶς κλέπτοντες]. Xenophon in Book I of the Memorabilia also mentions this law concerning manifest and bath thieves. Reasons for such severe punishment of these men may be sought in Aristotle's Problems: why, if someone steals in a bath, a wrestling school, or the marketplace, or steals clothes, the penalty is severe, but if he steals from a house, he is fined only in proportion to the value of the theft? For, first, it is very easy to steal in baths and other public places, and thieves could not then be guarded against properly even when precautions were greatest, so many and so wicked were they. [ἐν τῷ βαλανείῳ... ῥᾷδιον τοῦ βαλανείου κακουργῆσαι.] Second, [πρὸς δὲ βαλανείῳ ἡμῖν τὸ ὅτι οὐκ ἐξεστι...]; it is not permitted to forbid anyone entry to the baths, nor to keep a man from undressing. Therefore the lawgiver, seeing that the thieves gathered there were mixed in with the crowd and shared the same entrance, judged it clear that a great penalty should be imposed on them.

units.la: Denique fures hi balinearij non tam in priuatos, quàm in ipsam Rempubli-cam committunt: τὸν αὐτὸν ἔχοντα καὶ τὸν ἐν τῇ λιμένι κλέπτοντα, ὃ μόνον τὸν ἰδιώτην βλάπτει, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν πόλιν ἀδικεῖ. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐν τοῖς δημοσίοις, ὃ κοινὴν πᾶσαν σύνεργά-σθαι [?]. Neque tantum in fures, sed etiam in eos, quorum ope & consilio furtum factum fuisset, Lege animaduersum est: ἐπαιτίους dixit Lex superior dupli: De his intelligendum puto fragmentum istud Legis:
units.tr: Finally, these bath thieves do wrong not so much against private persons as against the commonwealth itself: [τὸν αὐτὸν ἔχοντα καὶ τὸν ἐν τῇ λιμένι κλέπτοντα, ὃ μόνον τὸν ἰδιώτην βλάπτει, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν πόλιν ἀδικεῖ.] Likewise also in public matters... Nor was the law concerned only with the thieves, but also with those by whose help and counsel the theft had been committed: the earlier law called them accomplices [ἐπαιτίους]. I think this fragment of the law should be understood of these men:

units.la: ΩΣΤΙΣ ΔΕ ΑΠΙΛΛΗΙ ΤΗ ΘΥ-ΡΑΙ, ΕΝΔΟΝ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΕΠΤΟΥ ΟΝΤΟΣ. Quicumque à ianua prohibuerit, cum fur intus esset.
units.tr: [ΩΣΤΙΣ ΔΕ ΑΠΙΛΛΗΙ ΤΗ ΘΥΡΑΙ, ΕΝΔΟΝ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΕΠΤΟΥ ΟΝΤΟΣ.] Whoever shall keep off from the door, while the thief was inside.

units.la: Refert Lysias ἐν τῷ κατὰ Θεομνήστου α'. ΟΣΤΙΣ ΔΕ ΑΠΙΛΛΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΘΥ-ΡΑΙ, ΕΝΔΟΝ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΕΠΤΟΥ ΟΝΤΟΣ. ὃ ἀπάλλῃ, ὃ ἀποκλείων νομίζε-ται, καὶ μηδὲ εἰς τὴν εἰσφορὰν. Lege hac ἐπαίνοι τῆς κλοπῆς definiunur illi, qui, cum fures sint in aedibus, arcent à ianua, & ingressu prohibent illos, qui suppetias veniebant: videtur enim furtum factum esse illorum ope, & consilio. Veteri autem Lege, qui furem abducebat in carcerem, mille drachmis multabatur, si causa caderet:
units.tr: Lysias reports it in his first speech Against Theomnestus: [ΟΣΤΙΣ ΔΕ ΑΠΙΛΛΗΙ ΤΗΙ ΘΥΡΑΙ, ΕΝΔΟΝ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΕΠΤΟΥ ΟΝΤΟΣ.] [ὃ ἀπάλλῃ, ὃ ἀποκλείων νομίζεται, καὶ μηδὲ εἰς τὴν εἰσφορὰν.] By this law are meant those who, when thieves are inside the house, keep people away from the door and prevent those who were coming to help from entering; for the theft seems to have been committed by their help and counsel. Under the older law, whoever led a man off to prison as a thief was fined a thousand drachmas if the case went against him.

units.la: Τοὺς ἀπάγοντας εἰς τὸ δημωτήριον ὡς ὅτι ἴσχη κλοπῆς, χιλίας δδράχμας τοὺς ἀλόντας. Qui alterum tanquam furem in carcerem abduxerit, ni eum reum peragat, mille multator drachmis.
units.tr: [Τοὺς ἀπάγοντας εἰς τὸ δημωτήριον ὡς ὅτι ἴσχη κλοπῆς, χιλίας δδράχμας τοὺς ἀλόντας.] Whoever has led another away to prison as a thief, and does not carry the prosecution through, shall pay a fine of a thousand drachmas.

units.la: Habes apud Suidam: ἔστι τὸ Ἀθηναῖοι νόμον τὸ τὴν ἀπαγόντων εἰς τὸ δημωτήριον ἄγειν ὅτι ἴσχη κλοπῆς, χιλίας δδράχμας τοὺς ἀλόντας. Itaque varij instituti sunt modi à Legislatore accusandi fures, ὧν αἱ ἀπαγωγαὶ εἰσιν. Poterat enim is, cui furto res periisset, ad Vndecimviros rapere in ius: Quod si viribus minus valeret, poterat indicare Vndecimviris, ut ipsi in ius raperent: Vel apud Vndecimviros dicam scribebat, si nollet furem duci, aut ipse ducere: Sed quoniam is qui accusabat furti, si causa cecidisset, nec tulisset quintam suffragiorum partem, mille drachmis multabatur: si metueret sibi, poterat apud Arbitrum prouocare. Demosthenes in Androtiana: ἐὰν δὲ πολλὰς ἐδιδὼ ἐὰν ... τὸν νόμον ὅτι τοῖς ἰδιωτικοῖς, εἰ τῆς κλοπῆς, ἐρρώσας καὶ σαυτὸν παρεύεις; ἀπα-γωγῆ. ἐν χιλίαις δὲ ὁ κλέπτης, ἀδικήσας ἐς τὰς ἀρχὰς ἔφησεν. τοῦτο ποιήσουσιν ἐκεῖνοι. φοβοῦ καὶ τοῦτο; χρὰ φω. κατάμεμφη σαυτὸν, καὶ πῶς ἂν σὺ ἔχοις χιλίας ἐκτίσαι; δι-καζ κλοπῆς πρὸς Διαιτητὴν, καὶ ἡ κλοπὴ ἀδικήσεις. Vlpianus: τοῦτο δὲ ὁ ἐρρώσας καὶ ὁ ἐξῆς λέγει τῆς ῥώμης καὶ τῆς τῶν σωματῶν ἰσχύος. ἀπαγε δὲ, δηλονότι πρὸς τὸν Ἐνδικα, καὶ τοὺς ὅτι τοῦ δημωτηρίου. Quod si accusatori nihil horum placeret, poterat dicam scribere apud Thesmotheras: vel, si adhuc sibi metueret, indicare Archontibus. Demosthenes ibidem: σιδήρεον βύλει τοῦτο; χρὰ φω. κα-πυκεῖς καὶ τοῦτο; ἐφησέ. τοῦτον οὐδὲν ὅτι ὁ αὐτὸς. Vlpianus: ὃ δὲ σιδήρεον βύλει τοῦ-των· τοῦτ εἶν, ὅτι τ' Διαιτητὴν, ὅτι τὴν πρὸς τὸν Ἐνδικα ἀρχὰς ἀπαγωγὰς χρὰ φω πρὸς τοὺς Θεσμοθέτας, περὶ ὧν εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον εἰσάγειν αἱ χραφαὶ. κα-πυκεῖς καὶ τοῦτο; ἐφησέ, τοῦτ εἶν, ὑπόδηξον τῆς ἀρχῆσαι.
units.tr: You have it in Suidas: [ἔστι τὸ Ἀθηναῖοι νόμον τὸ τὴν ἀπαγόντων εἰς τὸ δημωτήριον ἄγειν ὅτι ἴσχη κλοπῆς, χιλίας δδράχμας τοὺς ἀλόντας.] So the Legislator established various methods of prosecuting thieves, by which they were brought to trial. For the man who had lost goods by theft could drag the thief before the Eleven; if he was too weak for this, he could give information to the Eleven so that they would drag him to court themselves; or he could write a formal accusation before the Eleven, if he did not wish the thief to be led away, or to lead him himself. But since the accuser in a theft case, if he lost his suit and did not win even a fifth of the votes, was fined a thousand drachmas, if he feared for himself he could appeal to an arbitrator. Demosthenes, in the speech Against Androtion: [ἐὰν δὲ πολλὰς ἐδιδὼ... τὸν νόμον ὅτι τοῖς ἰδιωτικοῖς, εἰ τῆς κλοπῆς, ἐρρώσας καὶ σαυτὸν παρεύεις; ἀπαγωγῆ.] Ulpian: [τοῦτο δὲ ὁ ἐρρώσας καὶ ὁ ἐξῆς λέγει τῆς ῥώμης καὶ τῆς τῶν σωματῶν ἰσχύος. ἀπαγε δὲ, δηλονότι πρὸς τὸν Ἐνδικα, καὶ τοὺς ὅτι τοῦ δημωτηρίου.] If the accuser did not like any of these, he could write a formal charge before the Thesmothetae, or, if he still feared, give information to the Archons. Demosthenes in the same place: [σιδήρεον βύλει τοῦτο; χρὰ φω... ἐφησέ.] Ulpian: [ὃ δὲ σιδήρεον βύλει τούτων...] that is, to the arbitrator, or the magistrates, or the Thesmothetae, concerning matters which the written law brought before the court; and, if he still feared, he could give information to the magistrate.

units.la: Legibus quoque morte multabantur manifesti cingulorum incisores βαλλαντιοτόμοι, & sacculari j, qui ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ deprehendebantur.
units.tr: By law, those who were caught in the act, cutters of purses and of belts, and pickpockets [sacculari], were also punished with death.

units.la: Ἐαν δὲ φανερὸς γένηται βαλλαντιοτομῶν, τοῦ θανάτου ... τῷ ζημίας. Manifesti sacularij morte luunto.
units.tr: [Ἐαν δὲ φανερὸς γένηται βαλλαντιοτομῶν, τοῦ θανάτου... τῷ ζημίας.] Caught-in-the-act purse-cutters shall pay with death.

units.la: Légem laudat Xenophon Ἀπομνημονευμάτων Lib. I. ἐχ' δὲ τὰς νόμους, ἐαν τις φανερὸς ἡ βαλλαντιοτομίας[?], τούτῳ θάνατός ἐστιν ἡ ζημία. Horum meminit Aristophanes Ranis, Plato Lib. VIII. de Republ. & Æschines ἐν τῷ κατὰ Κτη-σιφῶντος. Optime describit Plautus Trinummo.
units.tr: Xenophon cites the law in Book I of the Memorabilia: [ἐχ' δὲ τὰς νόμους, ἐαν τις φανερὸς ἡ βαλλαντιοτομίας, τούτῳ θάνατός ἐστιν ἡ ζημία.] If anyone is caught cutting purses, the penalty for him is death. Of these men Aristophanes makes mention in the Frogs, Plato in Book VIII of the Republic, and Aeschines in the speech Against Ctesiphon. Plautus describes them admirably in the Trinummus.

units.la: Mira sunt, Ni illic homo'st aut dormitator, aut sector zonarius. Loca contemplat, circumspectat sese, atque adis noscitat: Credo edepol, quo mox furatum veniat, speculatur loca.
units.tr: Wonderful things! Unless that fellow is either a sleeper or a belt-cutter (sector zonarius). He surveys the places, looks around himself, and takes note of the doorways. I think, by Pollux, he is about to come and steal something; he is spying out the places.

units.la: Sectores Zonarios dixit Plautus, quia τὰ βαλλάντια, vt optime notant veteres ad Comici Ranas, ἐν τῇς ζώσης ἀπομνημονευμένα φέρεσθαι[?] δύο ἐμπορευταί[?]. Sacculari quoque dicuntur, οἱ ἀπὸ σάκκων κλέπτοντες, iisque sunt, teste Vlpiano Lib. IX. de Officio Proconsulis, qui vetitas in sacculo artes exercentes, partem subducunt, partem subtrahunt: id est, aut magicis artibus & carminibus ex alienis sacculis pecunias subducunt & eliciunt, aut subtrahunt, & manu auferunt: Atque cum hi tum illi manifesti & ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ deprehensi capite plectebantur.
units.tr: Plautus called them belt-cutters (sectores zonarios) because purses (τὰ βαλλάντια), as the old commentators rightly note on Aristophanes' Frogs, were carried in the belt [ἐν τῇ ζώνῃ]. They are also called "sacculari", those who steal from bags [οἱ ἀπὸ σάκκων κλέπτοντες]. According to Ulpian, Book IX of On the Office of the Proconsul, these are the people who, practising forbidden arts on a purse, take part of its contents and remove part of it: that is, either by magic arts and spells they draw out and extract money from other people's purses, or they take it away by hand. Both kinds, when caught in the act (ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ), were punished by beheading.

units.la: Capite quoque sanctum est Athenienßium Legibus in vecticularios[?].
units.tr: Under the laws of the Athenians, capital punishment was also decreed against the crowbar thieves (vecticularii).

units.la: Ἐαν τὶς φανερὸς ἡ τοιχωρυχῶν[?], τούτῳ Vecticularij manifesti morte luunto. θάνατος ἐστὶ τῇ ζημίᾳ.
units.tr: Manifest crowbar thieves shall atone with death. [Ἐαν τὶς φανερὸς ἡ τοιχωρυχῶν, τούτῳ θάνατος ἐστὶ τῇ ζημίᾳ.]

units.la: Habes apud Xenophontem loco laudato. ἐχ' δὲ τὰς νόμους, ἐαν τις φανερὸς τοιχωρυχῶν, τούτῳ θάνατός ἐστιν ἡ ζημία. Manifesti effractores & perfossores parictum, vt in alienas aedes irruant, supplicio capitis puniebantur.
units.tr: You have this in Xenophon, in the passage quoted: "And among the laws, if anyone is manifestly a wall-breaker, for him the penalty is death." Manifest housebreakers and wall-piercers, who break into other people's houses, were punished with capital punishment.

units.la: Sirempse quoque Lege plagiarij tenebantur manifesti.
units.tr: Under the law, kidnappers (plagiarii) were also held when caught in the act.

units.la: Ἐαν τὶς φανερὸς ἡ ἀνδραποδιστής[?], Plagiarij manifesti morte luunto. τούτῳ θάνατος ἐστὶ τῇ ζημίᾳ.
units.tr: Manifest kidnappers shall atone with death. [Ἐαν τὶς φανερὸς ἡ ἀνδραποδιστής, τούτῳ θάνατος ἐστὶ τῇ ζημίᾳ.]

units.la: Refert Xenophon loco laudato. ἐχ' δὲ τὰς νόμους, ἐαν τις φανερὸς ἡ ἀνδρα-ποδισμούς, τούτῳ θάνατός ἐστιν ἡ ζημία. Lycurgus ἐν τῷ κατὰ Λυκόφρονος. θαυ-μάζω δ' ἐγώ, τί τὰς ἀνδραποδισμάς, τὴν εἰκὼν ἡμᾶς ἀποστερῶν μόνον, θάνατος ἡμιῶν. Plagiarius is est, qui sine vi, dolo malo, sciens abducit homines liberos & ingenuos, venditque pro seruis, aut supprimit: vel is est, qui alienos seruos abducit sine vi, & plerumque sine furto, & fugam persuader, aut fugitiuos celat. Grammatici: ἀνδραποδιστής, ὁ μόνον ὁ τὰς ἐλευθέρας ἀπάγων εἰς δουλείαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ τὰς δούλους ἀπὸ τῆς δεσποτῶν ἀπαγῶν εἰς ἑαυτόν. Aduersus illum scribebatur ἐλευθερωτικῶν[?]. Pollux Lib. III. cap. VII. ἀνδραποδιστής δέ ἐστιν, ὁ τὸν ἐλεύθερον καταδουλωσάμενος, ἢ τὸν ἀλλότριον οἰκέτην ἀπαγόμενος. καὶ λέγει ὁ χ' τῶν ἀνδραποδιστῶν ἐλευθερωτικόν.
units.tr: Xenophon reports this in the passage quoted: "And among the laws, if anyone is manifestly a kidnapper, for him the penalty is death." Lycurgus, in his speech against Lycophron: "I wonder why, when kidnapping deprives us only of freedom, death is the penalty for us." A plagiarius is one who, without force, by fraud, knowingly leads away free-born men and sells them as slaves, or keeps them back; or one who leads away other people's slaves, usually without theft, and persuades them to flee, or hides fugitives. The grammarians: an andrapodistes is not only one who reduces free people to slavery, but also one who leads slaves away from their masters to himself. A speech called Eleutherotikon was written against him. Pollux, Book III, chapter VII: "An andrapodistes is one who enslaves a free man, or who leads away another's household slave; and the speech of the Eleutherotikon is against kidnappers."

units.la: Attica quoque Lege vindicabatur furtum per licium conceptum. Φωράσοντα γυμνὸν χιτωνίσκον ἔχοντα ἀζωστον Qui furtum it quaerere in domo aliena, εἰσιέναι εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν, ὅπως τὰς ἐρευνήσας. cincticulo amictus intrato.
units.tr: Under Attic law, theft that had been detected by means of the lanx and licium was also prosecuted. The one who wished to search for stolen goods was to enter a house naked, or wearing only a short tunic without a belt [Φωρᾶσαι γυμνὸν χιτωνίσκον ἔχοντα ἄζωστον]. Whoever wishes to seek theft in another's house, let him enter clothed only in a loincloth.

units.la: Si concipiebant in aliquo domo aut res amotas, aut furtum, nudi cincticulo amicti aedes suspectas intrabant, cum prius Deos esse testati, se inveniendi spe quaerere; si invenissent, is, apud quem quaerebant, multabatur.
units.tr: If people suspected that goods had been removed or stolen from someone's house, they went into the suspected premises naked, wearing only a loincloth, after first calling the gods to witness that they were searching in hope of finding the goods. If they found them, the man in whose house they had searched was fined.

units.la: Aristophanes Nubibus.
units.tr: Aristophanes, Clouds.

units.la: ΣΩ. Καπνοῦ ὑοιμάτιον. ΣΤΡ. πίλικινῶν[?] τί;
units.tr: SOCRATES: A smoky cloak. STREPSIADES: What kind of cloak?

units.la: ΣΩ. Οὐκ, ἀλλὰ γυμνὸς εἰσιέναι νομίζεται.
units.tr: SOCRATES: No, but one is accustomed to go in naked.

units.la: ΣΤΡ. Ἀλλ' ἴχ' φαλδαλαν ἐγὼ γ' εἰσέρχομαι[?].
units.tr: STREPSIADES: Well, I at least go in with nothing on [ἀλλ' ἴχ' φαλδαλαν ἐγὼ γ' εἰσέρχομαι].

units.la: Scholia. ἔσος ὣν τοῖς εἰσιοῦσι εἰς οἰκίας τινὸς ὅπως τὰ ἐρύμνησαν, γυμνοὺς εἰσιέναι, ἵνα μὴ τί ἔχοντα τὰ ἱμάτια χρύψαντες λάθωσιν, ἢ ἵνα μὴ τί ἔχοντα ἐχθρὰς λάθωσιν ἐπισαλεύοντες ὃ ξηπυλμον, ᾧ ζημίας αἵτιοι τοῦτο ἡ ῥωνταις[?]. Plato Lib. XII. de Legibus. Φωρᾶν δ᾽ αὖ ἐξελη̃ς τις τὶ πρῶ᾽ ὁπωοῦν γυμνὸς, ἢ χιτωνίσκον ἔχων ἀζωστος παρεσο-μένος τοῖς νομίμοις ἥσεις, ἢ μὲν ἐλπίζων διρῇ̃ν, ὅταν φωρᾷ. Ilæus ὁ τοῦ ἄπελθ ... Sed utrque locus corruptus est; apud Platonem lego: Φωρᾶν δ᾽ αὖ ἐξελη̃ς τις ἢ πρῶ᾽ ὁπωοῦν γυμνὸς ἢ, χιτωνίσκον ἔχων ἀζωστος. apud Ilæum: καὶ ἀξιούντων παρεχέζηκέναι τὴν ἢ φωρᾶν ἐκ τὸν νόμον. De furto per lancem & licium concepto è Decemuirorum Tabulis A. Gellius & Festus.
units.tr: Scholia: Those who go into a house to search for something go in naked, so that they cannot conceal stolen goods under their clothes, or so that they cannot slip something in under their clothes and then "find" it, which made them liable to penalty. Plato, Book XII of the Laws: "If anyone wishes to search for theft in any way, naked, or wearing only a short tunic without a belt, let him go in, hoping to find the thing when he searches." Ilaeus: [the text is corrupt]. But both passages are corrupt; in Plato I read: "If anyone wishes to search for theft in any way, naked, or wearing only a short tunic without a belt." In Ilaeus: "and when they think that the one who searches for theft is to be allowed to enter, according to the law." On the theft conducted by means of the lanx and the licium, Aulus Gellius and Festus write about the Tables of the Decemvirs.

units.la: Tam infesto autem profecuti sunt odio furtum, vt Lege capital sit ei qui rem sustulerit, quam non posuerit.
units.tr: They pursued theft with such hostile hatred that, by law, it was a capital offence to take away something one had not deposited.

units.la: Ο μὴ κατέ-θηκέ τις, μὴ ἀφαρῆσθαι. Εἰ δὲ μὴ, θάνατον ἔξω τῷ ζημίᾳ.
units.tr: [Ὃ μὴ κατέθηκέ τις, μὴ ἀφαιρεῖσθαι. Εἰ δὲ μὴ, θάνατον ἔστω ἡ ζημία.] "Whatever one has not deposited, one must not take away. If one does, the penalty shall be death."

units.la: Si quis tollat, quod non posuerit, capital ei esto.
units.tr: "If anyone takes away what he has not deposited, let it be a capital offence for him."

units.la: Meminit Diogenes Laërtius in Solone, eumque auctorem facit: ἀ μὴ ἔθου, μὴ ἀνύλου· εἰ ὃ μὴ, θάνατος ἰ᾽ ζημία. Videtur accepisse Solo Legem hanc à Iudæis siue Ægyptiis potius, qui ab illis acceperunt. Iosephus totidem pene verbis inter Iudaicas recenseт: ὁ μὴ κατέθηκε τὴς σὰ ἀφαιρούμενος, καὶ ὁ μὴ κατέθηκεν ἀμέλησε, εἰσὶ κολάσεις ὑπ᾽ οὐχ ὅ ἁπλῶς ἐπέγεις, ἀλλ᾽ ἔτι ὃ μείζον. Non enim reuera inuentum est, sed furtum, vt scribit Ælianus qui Variæ Lib. IV. cap. I. hunc Bibliis esse morem memoriæ prodidit. Βιβλίος δύνηρ ἐν ὁδῷ ταπεινῶν ... εἰ μὴ κατέθετο ἀφαιρῆσαι· ἡ γὰρ ἡ μέτα τὸ ἐοδὸν ὕβρημα, ἀλλὰ ἀδικήμα.
units.tr: Diogenes Laertius, in his life of Solon, mentions this and makes him the author: "What you did not deposit, do not take away; if you do, the penalty is death." Solon seems to have received this law from the Jews, or rather from the Egyptians, who had it from them. Josephus records it among the Jewish laws in almost the same words: "He who takes away what he did not deposit, and he who neglects what he did not deposit, are punished not by a simple fine but by something worse." For it was not really an invention; it was theft, as Aelian writes in Varia Historia, Book IV, chapter 1, where he records the memory of this custom among the Byblians [Βιβλίος]: "... unless he had deposited it to take away; for to take what is one's own is not an outrage but a wrong."

units.la: Capital quoque fuit ei, qui ficus furripuisset, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Capital punishment was also the penalty for anyone who stole figs, under this law:

units.la: IN HORTOS IRRVMPERE FICOSQVE DELIGERE CAPITAL ESTO.
units.tr: TO BREAK INTO GARDENS AND PICK FIGS SHALL BE A CAPITAL OFFENCE.

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Festus: Atticos quondam iuuenes solitos aiunt in hortos irrumpere, ficosque deligere, quam ob causam Legem factam, qui id fecisset, capital esset ei. Sed facile mutauit, itaque multati sunt tantum, qui ficus clepserant.
units.tr: Festus mentions this law. He says that young Athenians once used to break into gardens and pick figs, and that for this reason a law was made that whoever did so should be liable to capital punishment. But it was easily changed, and so only those who stole figs were fined.

units.la: Κλέπτοντα σὺκα καλάζεσθαι.
units.tr: Κλέπτοντα σὺκα καλάζεσθαι. [One who steals figs is to be punished.]

units.la: Qui ficus clepserit, multator.
units.tr: Whoever steals figs shall be fined.

units.la: Habes apud Suidam: ὃ γὰρ παλαιὸν τίμια παρὰ τῆς Ἀθηναίοις ὧν τὰ σύκα, καὶ εἴ τις διελαλήσῃ κλέπτων σύκα, ἐκολάζετο. Atque hinc τὴν Συκοφαντῶν nomen.
units.tr: You have it in Suidas: τίμια γὰρ παλαιὸν παρὰ τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις ἦν τὰ σύκα, καὶ εἴ τις διελαλήσῃ κλέπτων σύκα, ἐκολάζετο. [For in ancient times figs were held in high honour among the Athenians, and if anyone was caught stealing figs, he was punished.] Hence the name of the sycophants [συκοφάντης].

units.la: Solonis Lege in fimi fures animaduertebatur.
units.tr: Under Solon's law, thieves of dung were punished.

units.la: Τοὺς βόλιτον ὑφελομένους καλάζεσθαι.
units.tr: Τοὺς βόλιτον ὑφελομένους καλάζεσθαι. [Those who steal dung are to be punished.]

units.la: Fimi fures animaduertuntor.
units.tr: Thieves of dung are punished.

units.la: Ex hac proverbio, βολίτου δίκη, locum dedit: laudat Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Equites: ἢ πρόιμια βολίτου δίκλω παρὰ τοῖς ὅτι μικρᾶς δίκης ἐπέχει-ται. ὁ γὰρ Σόλωνος νόμος ἐστὶ τοὺς βόλιτον ὑφελομένους κολάζει. Suidas totidem verbis. Vaticana Appendix I. Centuria, Prouerbio XXIV. βολίτου δίκη. παρὰ τοῖς ἀξίοις, καὶ ὅτι μικροῦ τιμωρεῖν ἐπέσχεν. ὁ γὰρ τοῖς Αξοσι νόμος ἢ τοὺς βόλιτον ὑφε-λομένους κολάζει, hinc illa Aristophanis.
units.tr: From this came the proverb "the justice of the bolitus" (βολίτου δίκη). The scholiast on Aristophanes' Knights praises it: "Or the proverb 'justice of the bolitus' is used of those who have only a small penalty, for Solon's law punishes those who steal bolitus." Suidas says the same in the same words. The Vatican Appendix, Centuria I, Proverb XXIV, says: "'Justice of the bolitus': among the worthy, and because he came close to punishing a small matter." For the law of the Athenians punishes those who steal bolitus; hence that line of Aristophanes: καὶ γὰρ ἐγών, ὅτι δ᾽ ἐγνων τοὺς βολίτους ἠπημένος. [And I too, because I knew that those who steal dung were ...]

units.la: κἀγών, ὅτι δ᾽ γνων τοὺς βολίτους ἠπημένος.
units.tr: κἀγών, ὅτι δ᾽ γνων τοὺς βολίτους ἠπημένος. [And I, because I knew that the dung-thieves were ...]

units.la: βολίτου voce stercus bubulcum præcipue significatur, quanquam & omne fimi genus in Lege intelligitur: cuius plures quidem differentiæ, verba sunt Plinij Lib. XVII. cap. IX. ipsa res antiqua. Iam apud Homerum regius senex agrum ita suis manibus lætificans reperitur. Augeas Rex in Græcia excogitasse traditur. Maximus autem in Attica fimi erat vfus, quia illius τὰ πλέθρα[?] erant ἀδμῆν[?] καὶ φαῦλα. Itaque stercorabant suos agros: Quare à Solone hac vetitum est Lege fimum subripere.
units.tr: The word bolitus chiefly means ox dung, though every kind of dung is understood in the law. Pliny, Book 17, chapter 9, lists its varieties, and his words are these: "The thing itself is ancient. Already in Homer an aged king is found enriching his field with his own hands. King Augeas is said to have devised it in Greece. But in Attica dung was used most of all, because their fields were unploughed and poor. Therefore they manured their fields, and so Solon forbade by law the stealing of dung."

units.la: DE CONVICIIS. TITVLVS SEXTVS.
units.tr: DE CONVICIIS. TITVLVS SEXTVS.

units.la: LEGE sanxit Solo, ne quis de alio detraheret, in locis sacris, in iudiciis, in Magistratuum consessibus, & in spectaculis: Qui secus faxit, ei, de quo detraxit, multam pendat drachmas tres, & aerario publico duas.
units.tr: By a law, Solon ordained that no one should speak ill of another in sacred places, in courts, in assemblies of magistrates, or at spectacles. Whoever acted otherwise should pay a fine of three drachmas to the man he had slandered and two drachmas to the public treasury.

units.la: Ζῶντα μὴ κακῶς λέγειν τοὺς ἱερεῖς, καὶ δικαστηρίοις, καὶ ἀρχείοις, ἢ θεωρίας ὅσης ἀγῶνων ἢ πρὸς δραχμὰς τοῦ ἰδιώτῃ, δύο δ' ἄλλας ἀποτίνειν εἰς τὸ δημόσιον.
units.tr: Not to speak ill of the living in the temples, the law courts, the magistrates' offices, or at any spectacle of games, under penalty of three drachmas to the private person and two others paid to the public treasury [Ζῶντα μὴ κακῶς λέγειν τοὺς ἱερεῖς, καὶ δικαστηρίοις, καὶ ἀρχείοις, ἢ θεωρίας ὅσης ἀγῶνων ἢ πρὸς δραχμὰς τοῦ ἰδιώτῃ, δύο δ' ἄλλας ἀποτίνειν εἰς τὸ δημόσιον].

units.la: De nemine, qui in vivis superfit, detrahito, inter sacra, in iudicum aut Magistratuum sessimoniis[?], aut in spectaculis: qui secus faxit, multator tribus drachmis, quae convicium passo cedant, & duabus, quae aerario publico inferantor.
units.tr: No one shall slander anyone who is still alive, among sacred things, in the sessions of judges or magistrates, or at spectacles. Whoever does otherwise shall be fined three drachmas, which go to the one who suffered the abuse, and two, which are paid into the public treasury.

units.la: Legis meminit Plutarchus in Solone: ζῶντα δὲ κακῶς λέγειν ἐκώλυσε τοὺς ἱερεῖς, καὶ δικαστηρίοις, καὶ ἀρχείοις, ἢ θεωρίας ὅσης ἀγῶνων ἢ πρὸς δραχμὰς τοῦ ἰδιώτῃ, δύο δ' ἄλλας ἀποτίνειν εἰς τὸ δημόσιον[?]. Non enim tam bene cum hominibus agitur, ut possint temperare sibi, ne omnino irascantur, hic tamen modus esse debet, ut suus sacris, iudiciis, Magistratuum consessibus, & spectaculis, constet honos. ὁ δ' μηδαμῶς, inquit Plutarchus, κεφαλὴν ὀργῆς, ἀπαλλάσσειν καὶ ἀκόλαστον· ὁ ἢ πολλαχοῦ, χαλεπὸν, ἐνίοις δ' ἀδύνατον. διὸ τοῖς δυνατὸν γράφεσθαι τὸν νόμον, εἰ βούλεται ζημίας ὀλίγας, ἀλλὰ μὴ πολλοῖς ἀχθήσας κολάζειν[?]. An vero alibi licet alteri conuicium facere? Non certe: dat enim Lex actionem aduersus eum, qui alium conuiciis incesserit, nec valeat demonstrare manifeste quicquam eorum, quae dixerit.
units.tr: Plutarch in his Life of Solon mentions the law: "Solon forbade speaking ill of the living in the temples, the law courts, the magistrates' offices, or at any spectacle of games, under penalty of three drachmas to the private person and two others paid to the public treasury" [ζῶντα δὲ κακῶς λέγειν ἐκώλυσε τοὺς ἱερεῖς, καὶ δικαστηρίοις, καὶ ἀρχείοις, ἢ θεωρίας ὅσης ἀγῶνων ἢ πρὸς δραχμὰς τοῦ ἰδιώτῃ, δύο δ' ἄλλας ἀποτίνειν εἰς τὸ δημόσιον]. For people do not manage so well with one another that they can restrain themselves and never become angry at all; yet there ought to be this limit, that honour be kept in sacred places, courts, assemblies of magistrates and spectacles. But, says Plutarch, to be wholly free of anger and unrestrained is not easy for many, and for some impossible. Therefore the law was framed so that whoever wished to invoke it might punish with small fines rather than with heavy ones. But may one insult another elsewhere? Certainly not, for the law gives an action against anyone who has attacked another with abuse, unless he can clearly demonstrate any of the things he said.

units.la: Τὸν λέγοντα κακῶς, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποφαίνῃ ὡς ἔστιν ἀληθῆ τὰ εἰρημένα, ζημιοῦσ[?].
units.tr: "The one who speaks ill, unless he shows that what he said is true, shall be fined" [Τὸν λέγοντα κακῶς, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποφαίνῃ ὡς ἔστιν ἀληθῆ τὰ εἰρημένα, ζημιοῦσθαι].

units.la: Qui de alio detraxerit, ni probarit verum esse quod obiecit probrum, multator.
units.tr: Whoever has spoken ill of another, unless he proves true the reproach he cast, shall be fined.

units.la: Legem laudat Lysias ἐν τῇ πρὸς Θεομνήστου β'. ὅτι ὁ νομοθέτης τοὺς ὀργῇ συλλογισμῷ δίδωσιν, ἀλλὰ ζημιοῦν τὸν λέγοντα, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποφαίνῃ ὡς ἔστιν ἀληθῆ τὰ εἰρημένα. Dio Chrysostomus Orat. XV. ζῶντα οἶδα, ἔφη, ὅτι κατηγορεῖας δίδωσιν ὁ νόμος προσφέρεσθαι τὸν, ὃς ἀν βλασφημῇ τινα, οὐκ ἔχων ἀποδεῖξαι ταῖς ὧν λέγει Ἀθηναῖος[?]; Atque haec actio Polluci Lib. VIII. cap. VI. δίκη κακηγορίας dicitur. Quanta autem fuerit multa irrogata, non dicunt: Ego vero existimo duabus multatos fuisse drachmis: nam boue, quod numisma didrachmum est, multari auctores sunt Grammatici. Zenobius: Βοῦς ἐπὶ γλωττῆς. προοιμία ἐπὶ τῶν μὴ δυναμένων προφασίζεσθαι, ἀφ' ὧν ἐν τῇ Ἀθηναίων νόμισμα ἔχει βοῦν εἰκόνα χαρακτῆρα· ἀπὸ γὰρ ἐκτίνειν δεῖ ζῷα πέφυκε ὀρθῶς διὰ ταῦτα προφασιζομένους. Hesychius: βοῦς ἐπὶ γλωσ-σογ. προοιμία ἐπὶ τῶν μὴ δυναμένων προφασίζεσθαι, ἀφ' ὧν ἐν τῇ Ἀθηναίων νόμισμα ἐχ̓ν βοῶν ἐκκεχραγμένον, ὥσπερ ἐκπ[?] [illegible, ~30 letters] Φρυναζομένους ὧν ἔστ, eadem habet Suidas. Atque id multæ fuisse coniicimus, si leue admodum, & non magni momenti esset conuicium: Nam in grauioribus, quando aliquid, quod Legibus damnaretur, alteri, tanquam ab eo factum, obijciebatur, multo longe grauior, quingentæ nimirum drachmæ.
units.tr: Lysias mentions the law in his second speech against Theomnestus: that the lawgiver does not allow those who speak in anger to go unpunished, but fines the speaker unless he shows that what was said is true [ἐν τῇ πρὸς Θεομνήστου β']. Dio Chrysostom, Oration 15: "I know," he said, "that the law gives an action of accusation against anyone who reviles another, if he cannot prove the things he says" [ζῶντα οἶδα, ἔφη, ὅτι κατηγορεῖας δίδωσιν ὁ νόμος προσφέρεσθαι τὸν, ὃς ἀν βλασφημῇ τινα, οὐκ ἔχων ἀποδεῖξαι ταῖς ὧν λέγει Ἀθηναῖος]. Pollux, Book 8, chapter 6, calls this action the "action for abuse" [δίκη κακηγορίας]. The authors do not say how large the fine was. I myself think the convicted paid two drachmas, for the grammarians state that people were fined a "boue," which is the didrachm coin. Zenobius: "An ox on the tongue: a proverb for those who cannot make excuses. The Athenian coin bears the stamp of an ox, for it is right that those who make excuses should pay with living creatures" [Βοῦς ἐπὶ γλωττῆς. προοιμία ἐπὶ τῶν μὴ δυναμένων προφασίζεσθαι, ἀφ' ὧν ἐν τῇ Ἀθηναίων νόμισμα ἔχει βοῦν εἰκόνα χαρακτῆρα· ἀπὸ γὰρ ἐκτίνειν δεῖ ζῷα πέφυκε ὀρθῶς διὰ ταῦτα προφασιζομένους]. Hesychius says the same, as does Suidas, with the same proverb. We suppose the fine was this when the insult was quite slight and of little consequence. For in graver cases, when something punishable by law was thrown at someone as though he had done it, the fine was far heavier, namely five hundred drachmas.

units.la: Τοὶς λέγουσι τὴ ΤΩΝ ΑΠΟΡΡΗΤΩΝ Λεπτολαχανίας δραχμαὶ ὀφείλειν.
units.tr: Those who speak of the forbidden things owe a fine of "leptolachania" drachmas [Τοὶς λέγουσι τὴ ΤΩΝ ΑΠΟΡΡΗΤΩΝ Λεπτολαχανίας δραχμαὶ ὀφείλειν].

units.la: Legem habes apud Isocratem ἐν τῷ Λοχίτου. ὥστε καὶ τῆς κακηγορίας νόμον ἐποίησε, ὡς καλοῦσι τοὺς λέγοντας τὴ ΤΩΝ ΑΠΟΡΡΗΤΩΝ Πεντακοσίας δραχμαὶ ὀφείλειν. Non licebat igitur alteri exprobrare ea, quæ si quis patrasset, in eum insurgebant Leges, & animaduertebant; nisi ἀποφαίνειν ὡς ἔξὸν ἀληθῆ posset apud iudices. Itaque non licebat Lege quanquam homicidam dicere. ΑΝΔΡΟΦΟΝΟΝ μὴ λέγειν.
units.tr: You have the law in Isocrates, in the speech Against Lochites: so the lawgiver also made a law on abuse, under which those who speak of the forbidden things owe five hundred drachmas [ἐν τῷ Λοχίτου. ὥστε καὶ τῆς κακηγορίας νόμον ἐποίησε, ὡς καλοῦσι τοὺς λέγοντας τὴ ΤΩΝ ΑΠΟΡΡΗΤΩΝ Πεντακοσίας δραχμαὶ ὀφείλειν]. It was therefore not permitted to reproach another with those things which, if someone had committed them, the laws would rise up against and punish, unless he could show before the judges that the charge was true. Thus it was not lawful even to call someone a murderer [ΑΝΔΡΟΦΟΝΟΝ μὴ λέγειν].

units.la: Meminit Legis Lysias ἐν τῷ Θεομνήστου α. ὡς οὐκ ἔστι ΤΩΝ ΑΠΟΡΡΗ-ΤΩΝ, ἐὰν τις εἴπῃ τὸν πατέρα ἀπεκτονέναι. τὸν γὰρ νόμον ἡ ζῶντ' ἀπαγορεύειν, ἀλλ' ΑΝΔΡΟΦΟΝΟΝ οὐκ ἐᾶν λέγειν. Nam homicidæ omnibus ciuitatis iuribus, sacris pariter & publicis excidebant, ita vt ne illos quidem alij alloquio dignarentur. Lysias: ὅσοι γὰρ αὐτοὶ διελέγοντο ὡς ἀνδροφόνῳ ὄντι. Vetitum quoque Lege erat, alteri obiicere, quod clypeum abiecisset, qui hoc conuicium fecerat, quingentis drachmis multabatur.
units.tr: Lysias mentions the law in his first speech against Theomnestus: that it is not one of the forbidden things if someone says that another has killed his father, for the law forbids speaking ill of the living but does not allow calling him a manslayer [ἐν τῷ Θεομνήστου α.]. For manslayers were excluded from all the rights of the state, sacred and public alike, so that others would not even deign to address them. Lysias: "For all who conversed with him treated him as a manslayer" [ὅσοι γὰρ αὐτοὶ διελέγοντο ὡς ἀνδροφόνῳ ὄντι]. It was also forbidden by law to reproach someone for having thrown away his shield; whoever made this charge was fined five hundred drachmas.

units.la: ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΦΑΣΚΗ ΑΠΟΒΕ-ΒΛΗΚΕΝΑΙ ΤΗΝ ΑΣΠΙΔΑ Υ-ΓΟΔΙΚΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.
units.tr: "IF ANYONE SAYS THAT SOMEONE HAS THROWN AWAY HIS SHIELD, HE SHALL BE LIABLE TO PROSECUTION" [ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ ΦΑΣΚΗ ΑΠΟΒΕΒΛΗΚΕΝΑΙ ΤΗΝ ΑΣΠΙΔΑ ΥΠΟΔΙΚΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ].

units.la: Laudat Lysias eadem Oratione: ἐὰν τις σὶ εἴπῃ ῥίψαι τὴν ἀσπίδα, ὁ δὲ τὸν νόμον εἴρηται, ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΦΑΣΚΗ ΑΠΟΒΕΒΛΗΚΕΝΑΙ ΥΠΟΔΙΚΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ. Οὐκ ἂν ἐδικάσθη αὐτῷ. & paullo post: ἐπὶ τῆς σὲ ἐρρίφεναι τὴν ἀσπίδα. καὶ τι ἐκεῖ μὴ τῇ ῥίψαι ὠφέλει τὸν νόμον εἴρηται, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ. εἴπῃ ΑΠΟΒΕ-ΒΛΗΚΕΝΑΙ ΤΗΝ ΑΣΠΙΔΑ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΑΣ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ καλεῖ ὀφείλειν. Causa est, quia non illi qui haftam aut gladium, sed qui clypeum abiecerant, Legibus Græcorum multabantur. Plutarchus in Pelopida: οἱ δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων νομοθέτην τὸν ῥίψαντα κολάζειν, ὃ τὸν ξίφος σὺν λόγῳ ... [?] ... Vnde ciuitate Lacedæmoniorum pulsum Archilochum Poëtam narrat Plutarchus, cum in carmine, quod etiam legitur apud Strabonem Lib. XII, quasi re bene gesta gloriaretur de abiecto clypeo.
units.tr: Lysias quotes the same law in the same speech: "If anyone says to you that you threw away your shield, and the law says: IF ANYONE SAYS THAT SOMEONE HAS THROWN AWAY HIS SHIELD, HE SHALL BE LIABLE TO PROSECUTION" [ἐὰν τις σὶ εἴπῃ ῥίψαι τὴν ἀσπίδα, ὁ δὲ τὸν νόμον εἴρηται, ΕΑΝ ΤΙΣ ΦΑΣΚΗ ΑΠΟΒΕΒΛΗΚΕΝΑΙ ΥΠΟΔΙΚΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ]. He would not have been condemned for it. And shortly after, concerning one who said that another had thrown away his shield: where the law is cited, it does not speak of throwing away, but: "IF ANYONE SAYS" THAT ONE HAS THROWN AWAY HIS SHIELD, "HE OWES FIVE HUNDRED DRACHMAS" [ἐπὶ τῆς σὲ ἐρρίφεναι τὴν ἀσπίδα. καὶ τι ἐκεῖ μὴ τῇ ῥίψαι ὠφέλει τὸν νόμον εἴρηται, ΕΑΝ ΔΕ ΤΙΣ. εἴπῃ ΑΠΟΒΕΒΛΗΚΕΝΑΙ ΤΗΝ ΑΣΠΙΔΑ ΠΕΝΤΑΚΟΣΙΑΣ ΔΡΑΧΜΑΣ καλεῖ ὀφείλειν]. The reason is that under Greek laws it was not those who lost a spear or a sword who were punished, but those who had abandoned their shield. Plutarch in the Life of Pelopidas: "The Greek lawgivers punished the one who threw away his shield..." [οἱ δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων νομοθέτην τὸν ῥίψαντα κολάζειν]. Hence Plutarch tells that the poet Archilochus was expelled from the state of the Lacedaemonians, since in a poem, which is also read in Strabo, Book 12, he boasted of the shield he had abandoned as though it were a deed well done.

units.la: ἀσπίδ' μὲν Σαίων τῆς ἀγαλλεται, λὼ σὺ ἐδ' ἀμφίμαντον ... [?] ἐτὸς ἀμφίμητον κάλλιπων οὐκ ἐώλων.
units.tr: "The shield of the Saians he exults in, which I left beside a bush, a fine shield, not unwillingly abandoned" [ἀσπίδ' μὲν Σαίων τῆς ἀγαλλεται, λὼ σὺ ἐδ' ἀμφίμαντον ... ἐτὸς ἀμφίμητον κάλλιπων οὐκ ἐώλων].

units.la: vbi male Strabonis Interpres ἀγαλλόμενον reddidit, eripuit, & Plutarchi alter, iactet: debuerant potius, ornat: alludit enim dubio procul Archilochus ad morem veterum, cuius meminerunt Plutarchus in Pyrrho, Æschylus, Vergilius III. Æneid. alii, qui in ædibus priuatis, in Templis, in locis publicis, arma, quibus hostes exuerant, figebant & appendebant.
units.tr: Where the translator of Strabo renders ἀγαλλόμενον badly as "snatched away" (eripuit), and the other translator of Plutarch as "boasts" (iactet); they ought rather to have rendered it "adorns," for Archilochus undoubtedly alludes to the custom of the ancients, which Plutarch in the Life of Pyrrhus recalls, as do Aeschylus, Virgil in Aeneid III, and others, who fixed and hung up in private houses, in temples and in public places the arms with which they had stripped their enemies.

units.la: TITVLVS SEPTIMVS. DE NEGOTIIS GESTIS.
units.tr: TITLE SEVEN. CONCERNING AFFAIRS CONDUCTED (NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM).

units.la: Ertissimum illud est, quod scripsit Paulus Lib. I. Sententiarum Tit. IV. cum, qui negotia aliena gerit, & bonam fidem, & exactam diligentiam rebus eius, pro quo interuenit, praestare debere: idemque Lege Attica sanctum est: Nam si quis praeuaricando de iure bonisque alterius, pro quo interuenit, cesserat, aut mala fide eius negotia gesserat, bonaque administrauerat, perinde ac si ipse haberet, restituere tenebatur.
units.tr: The most certain rule is what Paul wrote in Book I of the Sentences, Title IV: that one who manages another's affairs must render good faith and exact diligence in the property of the person for whom he acts. The Attic law also sanctioned the same thing. For if anyone, by prevarication, gave up the right and goods of another for whom he had intervened, or managed his affairs in bad faith and administered his goods as if they were his own, he was bound to make restitution.

units.la: Γσεὶ ὢν κλοφῆνα ὡς, ὥσπερ ὁμοίως Qui mala fide bona alterius administrarit,
units.tr: Whoever administers another's goods in bad faith [Γσεὶ ὢν κλοφῆνα ὡς, ὥσπερ ὁμοίως]

units.la: ὀφλισκάνειν, ὥσπερ ἂν αὐτὸς ἔχῃ. ea ipse praestato.
units.tr: shall be liable as if he himself held them; let him make good the loss himself [ὀφλισκάνειν, ὥσπερ ἂν αὐτὸς ἔχῃ].

units.la: Legem habes apud Demosthenem ἐν τῷ πρὸς Ἀφόβου ψευδομαρτυριῶν. ἐὰν μὲν γὰρ ὧν κακούργῃς, νόμος ἐστὶ Δημοσθένους ... ὅς ... ὁμοίως ὀφλισκάνειν, ὥσπερ ἂν αὐτὸς ἔχῃ. Qua Lege obuiam itum est nequitiae tutorum, procuratorum, aliorumque, qui res sibi creditas mala fide administrant. Quare etiam apud Romanos, si pecunia quis negotium gerat, verba sunt Pauli Sententiarum Lib. I. Tit. IV. §. III. vsuras quoque totius temporis praestare cogitur, & periculum eorum nominum quibus collocauit, agnoscere, si lites tempore soluendo non sint. Retulit illa Tribonianus in Legem XXXVII. §. I. D. de negotiis gestis: sed non bona fide: Si pecunia quis negotium gerat, vsuras quoque praestare cogitur, & periculum eorum nominum, quae ipse contraxit: nisi fortuitis casibus debitores ita suas fortunas amiserunt, vt tempore litis ex ea actione contestata soluendo non essent. Expunxit Tribonianus ista verba totius temporis, & de suo addidit, nisi fortuitis casibus debitores ita suas fortunas amiserunt, quae causa sunt, cur priora illa expunxerit: nam vsuras totius temporis praestare non cogitur, si quidem periculum eorum nominum, quibus collocauit negotiorum gestor, agnoscere non tenetur, si debitores fortuitis casibus fortunas suas amiserint, & litis tempore soluendo non sint. At vero Triboniani aevo e Constitutione Diocletiani & Maximiani casum fortuitum praestare non compelluntur negotiorum gestores. Impp. Diocletianus & Maximianus A A. & CC. Eulogio. Negotium gerentes alienum non interueniente speciali pacto, casum fortuitum praestare non compelluntur. Dat. II. Kal. Decemb. CC. Conff. Leg. XXII. C. eod. Ex hac igitur Constitutione negotiorum gestores casum fortuitum non praestabant: itaque Tribonianus addidit, cum Pauli aevo etiam praestaretur casus fortuitus: Nam quod viri praestantissimi putant, Gaium Lib. III. ad Edictum Prouinciale, docere casum fortuitum non praestari a negotiorum gestoribus, non sunt audiendi: nam longe aliud est quod scribit Gaius, ab eo, quod Paulus: nam agit Paulus de actione quae competit ei, cuius negotia geruntur, aduersus eum, qui negotia gerit: Gaius vero scribit de actione, quae competit negotiorum gestori aduersus eum, cuius negotium gessit: Gaij verba sunt. Siue hereditaria negotia siue ea, quae alicuius essent, gerens aliquis, necessario rem emerit, licet ea interierit, poterit quod impenderit, iudicio negotiorum gestorum consequi: velut si frumentum, aut vinum familiae parauerit, idque casu quodam interierit, forte incendio, ruina. Sed ita scilicet hoc dici potest, si ipsa ruina, vel incendium, sine vitio eius acciderit: nam cum propter ipsam ruinam, aut incendium damnandus sit, absurdum est, cum istarum rerum nomine, quae ita consumptae sunt, quicquam consequi. Leg. XXII. D. eod. & vno verbo is, qui negotiorum gestorum agit, inquit Vlpianus Lib. X. ad Edictum, non solum si effectum habuit negotium, quod gesserit, actione ista vtetur, sed sufficit, si vtiliter gesserit, etsi effectum non habuit negotium: & ideo, si insulam fulsit, vel seruum aegrum curauit, etiamsi insula exusta est, vel seruus obijt, aget negotiorum gestorum, idque & Labeo probat. Leg. X. §. I. D. eod. Quando autem casum non praestet is, qui negotium gerit, e sententia veterum Iurisconsultorum habes è Labeone apud Vlpianum Lib. X. ad Edictum: nempe si affectione coactus, ne bona mea distrahantur, negotiis te meis obtuleris, aequissimum esse, dolum dumtaxat te praestare. Leg. III. §. IX. D. eod. Quando autem casum non praestet is, qui negotium gerit, e sententia veterum Iurisconsultorum habes è Labeone apud Vlpianum Lib. X. ad Edictum: nempe si affectione coactus, ne bona mea distrahantur, negotiis te meis obtuleris, aequissimum esse, dolum dumtaxat te praestare. Leg. III. §. IX. D. eod. & de huiusmodi negotiorum gestore, qui sponte & nulla necessitate cogente immiscuit se negotiis alienis, intelligenda est Lex XI. D. cod. Attica Lege feminae non licebat de re contrahere quae maioris esset pretij, quam octodecim drachmarum, siue medimni hordei.
units.tr: You have the law in Demosthenes, in the speech against Aphobus on false witness [ἐν τῷ πρὸς Ἀφόβου ψευδομαρτυριῶν. ἐὰν μὲν γὰρ ὧν κακούργῃς, νόμος ἐστὶ Δημοσθένους ... ὅς ... ὁμοίως ὀφλισκάνειν, ὥσπερ ἂν αὐτὸς ἔχῃ.] By this law provision was made against the wickedness of guardians, agents and others who administer in bad faith the things entrusted to them. Hence also among the Romans, if anyone manages the business with money, these are the words of Paul, Sentences Book I, Title IV, §3: he is also compelled to pay interest for the whole time, and to bear the risk of those debtors to whom he lent, if they are unable to pay when the suit is brought. Tribonian reported these words in Law 37, §1, D. de negotiis gestis, but not faithfully: If anyone manages business with money, he is compelled to pay interest too, and to bear the risk of those debts which he himself contracted, unless the debtors through fortuitous accidents so lost their fortunes that at the time of the suit they were not able to pay. Tribonian removed the words for the whole time, and added on his own account unless the debtors through fortuitous accidents lost their fortunes. These additions are the reason he struck out the earlier words. For the manager of business is not compelled to pay interest for the whole time, if indeed he is not bound to bear the risk of the debts to which he lent, when the debtors have lost their fortunes through chance accidents and are unable to pay at the time of the suit. But in the age of Tribonian, by a constitution of Diocletian and Maximian, business managers were not compelled to answer for chance accidents. The Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Augusti, to Eulogius: those who manage another's business are not compelled to answer for chance accident, unless a special agreement intervenes. Given on the second day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of the Caesars. Law 22, C. eod. Under this constitution, then, managers of business did not answer for chance accident; so Tribonian added the clause, though in Paul's age chance accident was also answered for. For what very distinguished men think, that Gaius in Book III on the Provincial Edict teaches that managers of business do not answer for chance accident, should not be listened to. For what Gaius writes is very different from what Paul writes. Paul treats of the action which belongs to the person whose business is managed, against the one who manages it; but Gaius writes of the action which belongs to the manager of business against the person whose business he managed. Gaius's words are these: If someone, managing inherited business or the affairs of another, has of necessity bought something, and it has perished even so, he may recover by the judgment of business management what he has spent: for example, if he has procured grain or wine for the household and it has been lost by some accident, perhaps by fire or collapse. But this can be said only if the collapse or fire happened without his fault; for since he would be condemned on account of the collapse or fire itself, it is absurd for him to recover anything on account of goods which were so consumed. Law 22, D. eod. And in a single word, the one who brings the action of business management, says Ulpian in Book X on the Edict, will use this action not only if the business he undertook had its effect, but it is enough if he managed it usefully, even though the business had no effect. And so, if he propped up an insula, or cared for a sick slave, even if the insula was burned or the slave died, he will bring the action of business management; and Labeo also approves this. Law 10, §1, D. eod. When the one who manages business is not liable for chance accident, you have, from Labeo through Ulpian in Book X on the Edict, the opinion of the older jurists: namely, if, moved by affection, so that my goods should not be sold, you have taken up my affairs, it is most fair that you answer only for fraud. Law 3, §9, D. eod. And the law in D. eod., Law 11, is to be understood of a manager of this kind, who of his own accord and without any compelling necessity mixed himself into the affairs of others. By an Attic law a woman was not permitted to contract about a matter of greater value than eighteen drachmas, or one medimnus of barley.

units.la: τῶ γυναικὶ μὴ συνάγεσθαι, πλέω ἄργει μεδίμνου κεἰδῶν. Femina plusquam de medimno hordei ne contrahito.
units.tr: A woman shall not contract for more than a medimnus of barley [τῶ γυναικὶ μὴ συνάγεσθαι, πλέω ἄργει μεδίμνου κεἰδῶν]. The Greek words mean: a woman shall not contract for more than one medimnus of barley.

units.la: Legem laudat Dio Chrysostomus Oratione περὶ ἀπιστίας, & rationem reddit, cur feminis non permittantur gerenda negotia, scilicet propter iudicii imbecillitatem. [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐστί, [illegible, ~20 letters] ὡς ἀπίστους [illegible, ~15 letters] γυναικὶ πρὸ Ἀθηναίοις [illegible, ~10 letters] πλέω ἄργει μεδίμνου κεἰδῶν, [illegible, ~12 letters] [?] Erat autem, vt in superioribus diximus, hordei medimnus, idem ac drachmae octodecim, totidem enim veniebat: eratque annuum minimae trium sesquiminarum dotis fenus.
units.tr: Dio Chrysostom cites this law in his Oration On Distrust, and gives the reason why women are not allowed to manage business: namely, because of the weakness of their judgment. [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible]. Now, as we said above, the medimnus of barley was the same as eighteen drachmas, for that was the price it fetched; and this was the yearly interest on the smallest dowry, of three and a half minae.

units.la: DE INGRATIS. TITVLVS OCTAVVS.
units.tr: ON THE UNGRATEFUL. TITLE EIGHT.

units.la: INgrati actio Legibus dabatur aduersus eos, qui bene meritis gratiam non referrent.
units.tr: An action for ingratitude was granted by law against those who did not show gratitude to those who had deserved well of them.

units.la: Ἐξῆναι ἀχαριστίας δικάζεσθαι τοῖς εὐεργέταις μὴ αἰτιοποιούντων.
units.tr: Benefactors were permitted to bring suit for ingratitude against those who had not given them cause [Ἐξῆναι ἀχαριστίας δικάζεσθαι τοῖς εὐεργέταις μὴ αἰτιοποιούντων].

units.la: Ingrati actio dator aduersus eos, qui bene meritis gratiam non rependunt.
units.tr: An action for ingratitude is granted against those who do not repay gratitude to those who have deserved well of them.

units.la: Habes Legem apud Lucianum Abdicato. καὶ μὲν οἱ γὰρ νόμοι ἐξ ἀχαριστίας δικάζεσθαι διδόασιν τοῖς εὐεργέταις μὴ αἰτιοποιούντων. Huius Legis meminit Valerius Maximus Lib. V. cap. III. de Ingratis. Lege itaque Legem, Athenas alloquitur, quae te iureiurando obstrictam tenet, & quia benemeritis debita reddere praemia noluisti, laesis iusta piacula exsoluc. Id autem est institutum, quia [illegible, ~12 letters] verba sunt Xenophontis, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Quanquam idem Xenophon [?] Lib. II. suorum Atheniensium Legibus Ingrati actionem dari negat: [illegible, ~30 letters] (excipit si qui liberi aduersus parentes sint ingrati.) [illegible, ~25 letters].
units.tr: You have the law in Lucian's Disinherited: "For the laws grant benefactors the right to bring an action for ingratitude against those who do not make themselves responsible" [καὶ μὲν οἱ γὰρ νόμοι ἐξ ἀχαριστίας δικάζεσθαι διδόασιν τοῖς εὐεργέταις μὴ αἰτιοποιούντων]. Valerius Maximus mentions this law in Book V, chapter 3, on the ungrateful. Thus the Law, as it were, speaks to Athens: "You are bound by oath to it, and because you have been unwilling to pay the rewards owed to those who deserved well, make due atonement to those you have wronged." This was instituted because [illegible in the scan] are the words of Xenophon, [illegible in the scan]. Yet the same Xenophon, in Book II of his Athenian Laws, denies that an action for ingratitude was given by the Athenian laws [illegible in the scan] (he makes an exception if any children are ungrateful towards their parents) [illegible in the scan].

units.la: DE DESIGNANDIS Atheniensibus.
units.tr: On the Designation of Athenians.

units.la: TITVLVS NONVS.
units.tr: TITLE NINE.

units.la: Ne qua oriretur controuersia, neve qua fraus fieret, Lege sanctum est, vt in tabulis publicis, priuatis, in omni negotio, patris & paterni nomen populi adscriberetur.
units.tr: So that no dispute should arise, and no fraud be committed, the law ordained that in public and private records, in every transaction, the name of the father and the name of the deme should be written.

units.la: [illegible, ~24 letters] Patris & paterni populi nomen adscribunto.
units.tr: The name of the father and of the deme is to be written.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes [Greek, ~60 letters, uncertain], nempe ita adscribebant, exempli gratia, MANTIΘEOΣ MANTIOY ΘΟΡΙΚΙΟΣ. Idque institutum iam a Cecropis temporibus, vt è Varrone B. Augustinus Lib. XVIII. de Ciuitate Dei, cap. IX. vbi de contentione, quae, Cecrope regnante, inter Neptunum & Mineruam fuit, ob imponendum Atheniensium vrbi nomen, agit. Cuius vt iracundia placaretur, triplici supplicio dicit idem auctor ab Atheniensibus affectas esse mulieres: vt nulla vlterius ferrent suffragia: vt nullus nascentium maternum nomen acciperet: vt ne quis eas Ἀλωάδας vocaret.
units.tr: Demosthenes praises the law [the Greek words are unclear in the scan]. Namely, they wrote it in this way, for example, MANTIΘEOΣ MANTIOY ΘΟΡΙΚΙΟΣ [Mantitheos son of Mantias, of Thorikos]. This custom was already in use from the time of Cecrops, as Augustine reports from Varro, in The City of God, book 18, chapter 9, where he deals with the contention between Neptune and Minerva during the reign of Cecrops over the naming of the city of Athens. To appease her anger, the same author says, the women were punished by the Athenians in three ways: that they should no longer cast votes; that no child should take its mother's name; and that no one should call them Aloadae [Ἀλωάδας].

units.la: DE INDICIBVS.
units.tr: DE INDICIBVS.

units.la: TITVLVS DECIMVS.
units.tr: TITLE TEN.

units.la: Indici vera indicanti impunitas Lege erat concessa: in eum vero, qui falsa retulisset, & indicasset, capitis poena sancta erat.
units.tr: By law, an informer who told the truth was granted immunity, but for one who reported falsehoods and gave false information, the penalty was death.

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters] Indici vera indicanti, impune; sin falsa, capital esto. Legem habet Andocides, ὁ τὰ ταῖς θεοῖς τὰ μυστήρια. ὁ γὰρ νόμος ὅτως εἶχεν. Εἰ μὲν ἐλαττοῖ μιλυόντές τις, εἰ τὴν ἀδίκιαν ἐπὶ δὲ τὰ ψυχῆς, πεῖσαι. Atque hanc impunitatem dabat Senatus, penes quem dandi summa erat potestas. Andocides ibidem: Τύχεγος ὡς ὁ ἐσθάλιος μέταιξος, ὃς ἔχων Μεγαράδι ἀποξελθών. ἐκεῖνον δὲ ἐπιτήδεια τῇ βουλῇ, εἰ οἱ ἀδίκαι δοῦεν, μιαυόντι αὐτὸ τὰ μυστήρια, σῶσερχός ὡν, καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους τοὺς ποιοῦντας μὲν ἑαυτὸς, καὶ αὐτὸ τὴν Ἐρμῆ τῆς αἰσχύρος ἐ ἡδή. Ψηφισμάτων ὁ τῆς βουλῆς (ὡς γὰρ αὐτὸς ἀποκρίτωρ) ἄρξατο ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν Μεγαράδι. καὶ κοινωνὸς ἀδίκαι διεμαρτύρηθη, ὑπηρεσία τοὺς μὲν ἑαυτὸς.
units.tr: [illegible, ~30 letters] To an informer who tells the truth, impunity; but if he tells falsehoods, let it be a capital offence. Andocides has the law concerning those who profane the mysteries of the gods: "For the law was thus: if anyone, having been a..., should inform..., let him be..., and let him be..." [ὁ τὰ ταῖς θεοῖς τὰ μυστήρια. ὁ γὰρ νόμος ὅτως εἶχεν. Εἰ μὲν ἐλαττοῖ μιλυόντές τις, εἰ τὴν ἀδίκιαν ἐπὶ δὲ τὰ ψυχῆς, πεῖσαι.] This impunity was granted by the Senate, in whose hands lay the chief power of granting it. Andocides in the same place: "...the Senate, if they were to... and to the others who... the mysteries... and it was voted... the Senate (as he himself reports) began proceedings against him at Megara, and the accuser was convicted of injustice..." [Τύχεγος ὡς ὁ ἐσθάλιος μέταιξος, ὃς ἔχων Μεγαράδι ἀποξελθών. ἐκεῖνον δὲ ἐπιτήδεια τῇ βουλῇ, εἰ οἱ ἀδίκαι δοῦεν, μιαυόντι αὐτὸ τὰ μυστήρια, σῶσερχός ὡν, καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους τοὺς ποιοῦντας μὲν ἑαυτὸς, καὶ αὐτὸ τὴν Ἐρμῆ τῆς αἰσχύρος ἐ ἡδή. Ψηφισμάτων ὁ τῆς βουλῆς (ὡς γὰρ αὐτὸς ἀποκρίτωρ) ἄρξατο ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν Μεγαράδι. καὶ κοινωνὸς ἀδίκαι διεμαρτύρηθη, ὑπηρεσία τοὺς μὲν ἑαυτὸς.]

units.la: DE CONVIVIIS. TITVLVS VNDECIMVS.
units.tr: ON DRINKING PARTIES. TITLE ELEVEN.

units.la: Athenien-sium Lege de conuiuarum numero cautum est, ut in conuiuis triginta consisteret:
units.tr: By the law of the Athenians it was provided concerning the number of guests that a feast should have thirty.

units.la: Τοὺς κεκλημένους μὴ εἶ ὅπι τῶς Conuiuae plures triginta ne sunto.
units.tr: Let there be no more than thirty guests. [Τοὺς κεκλημένους μὴ εἶναι πλείους τριάκοντα]

units.la: Meminit Legis Lynceus Samius in Apophthegmatis. Χαιρεφῶν ὁ παλαιὸς εἰς γάμον ἀκλητος εἰσελθών, καὶ καλαισχύνης ἐχόμενος, καὶ τὴν Γυναικονόμων ἀριθμούντων τοὺς κεκλημένους, καὶ κελεύοντων αὐτὸν ἀποπέμπειν ὡς οὖδὲ τὸν νόμον ὅτι τοῖςπεἰκοντα ἐπόντος, ἀριθμεῖτε δὲ, ἔφη, πάλιν ἀπ᾽ ἐμοῦ ἀρξάμενοι. Atque ut hæc Lex fidelius & seuerius obseruaretur, prouidebant Gynaeconomi, quorum cura erat & muneris, adire conuiuantium domos, & conuiuarum numerum inire: qui si maior esset, quam per Legem licebat, poterant Gynaeconomi illos, qui superessent, & legitimum modum siue numerum, is erat triginta conuiuarum, excederent, è triclinio deturbare: ut ex hac narratione constat: plures igitur quam triginta conuiuæ non poterant interesse conuiuio, siue id nuptiarum, siue alia de causa condiceretur. Philochorus τῆς Ἀτθίδος Lib. VII. εἰ Γυναικονόμοι μὴ τὴν Ἀρεοπαγιτὴν ἐσκήπτοιτο τὰς ἐν τοῖς οἰκίαις σωσίους, ἐν τι τοῖς γάμοις, καὶ τὰς ἄλλας θυσίας. Athenæus Lib. VI. id probat auctoritate Timoclis Comici in Philodicaste. ὅτι ὁ ἐν ἔτος τὰς Γυναικονόμους ἐφοβεῖτο τὸ συμπόσιον, καὶ ἐξεπάζει τὴν κεκλημένων τὸν ἀριθμόν, εἰ ὁ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ἔστι, Τιμοκλῆς ὁ Φιλοδικαστῆ φησὶν ὅτως.
units.tr: Lynceus of Samos mentions this law in his Apophthegms. Chaerephon the old man, having come uninvited to a wedding and being a man of shameless wit, was told by the Gynaeconomi, who were counting the guests and ordering him to be sent away, that the law did not allow more than thirty. "Then count," he said, "starting again from me." And so that this law might be observed more faithfully and strictly, the Gynaeconomi took care to visit the houses of those giving feasts and to take the number of guests. If there were more than the law permitted, the Gynaeconomi could drive out of the dining room those who were over the limit. The lawful measure, or number, was thirty guests. This is clear from the account, so more than thirty guests could not attend a feast, whether it was called for a wedding or for some other reason. Philochorus, in Book VII of his Atthis, says that the Gynaeconomi were to see that the sacred rites in the houses, at weddings and at the other sacrifices, were kept. Athenaeus, in Book VI, supports this with the authority of the comic poet Timocles in his Philodicaste: "The Gynaeconomus is afraid of the drinking party, and examines the number of guests, whether it is within the law. Timocles says in the Philodicaste:" [Ταῖσιν γὰρ ἤδη ἐκ ζυγοῦ ...]

units.la: ταῖσιγαῖ᾽ ἠδὴ ἐκ ζυγὸς, ἵνα τοῖς ὁ φοῖς ὠμὸν καὶ φαρὴς μᾶλλον, ἐφοδεῦων ἐκ βουλῆ᾽ ἀριθμὸν ὅγε Γυναικονόμος λεξεῖ τὴν νόμων τὸν χρηστὸν, ὅταν σίωπα ὁρᾶν τῆν ἐπιωρθῶν.
units.tr: For now, when they are out of the yoke, they fear the feast more than the rain, and when the Gynaeconomus counts the number of guests, as the law says, he sees the guests' seats and is afraid. [Ταῖσιν γὰρ ἤδη ἐκ ζυγοῦ, ἵνα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ὠμὸν καὶ φαρὴς μᾶλλον, ἐφοβεῖτο ἐκ βουλῆς ἀριθμὸν ὅγε Γυναικονόμος λέγει τὴν νόμων τὸν χρηστὸν, ὅταν σιωπᾷ ὁρᾶν τὴν ἐπιωρθῶν.]

units.la: Quibus è Timoclis verbis colligimus aliquid immutatum fuisse eius ætate in hac Lege, circa conuiuarum, puto, numerum: nam, ut videtur, olim tot non fuerūt, sed infra triginta. Ne autē hinc Legi aliqua fraus fieret, altera prouiderunt Athenienses: Cū enim coqui inter priuata seruitia raro haberētur, sed ad nuptias, aut alias folennes epulas conducerentur, Lege cautum est, vt coqui omnes, cum ad aliquas epulas conducerentur, ad Gynæconomos sua nomina deferrent, quo haberent Gynæconomi huic curæ præfecti, quos possent percontari de numero conuiuarum.
units.tr: From these words of Timocles we gather that something in this law was changed in his time, concerning the number of guests, I think. For it seems that formerly there were not so many, but fewer than thirty. Lest any fraud be practised against the law, the Athenians provided another safeguard. Cooks were rarely kept among private servants but were hired for weddings or other solemn feasts. So the law provided that all cooks, when hired for any feast, should register their names with the Gynaeconomi, so that the Gynaeconomi, who were set over this charge, could question them about the number of guests.

units.la: Παῖδας μαγείρους τοὺς ἐν ταῖς πανηγύρεσιν ἀξιου[?]-χοῦς τοὺς ἐκ τῆς Γυναικονόμοις ἀπογρα[?]-φεσθαι.
units.tr: The cooks hired for the festivals should register with the Gynaeconomi. [Παῖδας μαγείρους τοὺς ἐν ταῖς πανηγύρεσιν ἀξιουμένους τοὺς ἐκ τῆς Γυναικονόμοις ἀπογράφεσθαι.]

units.la: Menandro Comico, hanc Legem quod nouimus, imputamus, meminit enim illius in Cecryphalo dramate:
units.tr: We attribute this law, so far as we know, to the comic poet Menander, for we find mention of it in his drama Cecryphalus:

units.la: ταῦτ' ἐς τοῖς Γυναικονόμοις δὲ τοῖς ἐν τοῖς γάμοις ἀπογραφέσθαι πυθόμενος. πῶς τας μαγείρες ἐχ' ὅμως χαλεπόν ἵνα, ἵνα πωλῶνται τοῖς κεκλημένοις ἐαν πλείους τὰς ὧν ἔξεστιν ἑστῶν τύχῃ ἐλάττων.
units.tr: Having learned that at weddings they must register with the Gynaeconomi... how hard it is for the cook, so that they are sold to the guests, if by chance there are more than the law allows, fewer. [Ταῦτ' ἐς τοῖς Γυναικονόμοις δὲ τοῖς ἐν τοῖς γάμοις ἀπογραφέσθαι πυθόμενος. Πῶς τὰς μαγείρες ἔχ' ὅμως χαλεπόν ἵνα, ἵνα πωλῶνται τοῖς κεκλημένοις ἐὰν πλείους τὰς ὧν ἔξεστιν ἑστῶν τύχῃ ἐλάττων.]

units.la: Priores versus tres optime vertes cum Viro Incomparabili Animaduersionum Libro VI. cap.XI. Is, de quo scilicet loquebatur hoc ταῦτ' ἐς Comicum, cum audiuisset omnes coquos, qui ad nuptiales epulas condicebantur, è Lege sua nomina ad Gynæconomos detulisse. Sequentia ita vertit Dalecampius, vt ab inuitatis petant, num quispiam praeter eos quibus licet, ad conuiuium accesserit. male. Non enim in delectu conuiuarum in Legem committebatur, sed in numero, de quo Lege cautum, vt in triginta conuiuis consisteret: praeterea conuiuae non interrogabantur à Gynæconomis, sed coqui, de conuiuarum numero. Interpungendus itaque locus hoc modo:
units.tr: The first three verses were excellently rendered by the incomparable man in his Animadversions, Book VI, chapter XI. He, of whom the comic poet was speaking in these words "ταῦτ' ἐς", had heard that all the cooks who were hired for wedding feasts had registered their names with the Gynaeconomi under the law. The following lines Dalechamps rendered thus: that they ask the invited whether anyone besides those permitted has come to the feast. This is wrong. The law did not concern the choice of guests but their number, which it provided should be thirty. Moreover, the guests were not questioned by the Gynaeconomi; it was the cooks who were questioned about the number of guests. So the passage must be punctuated in this way:

units.la: ἵνα πωλῶνται, τοῖς κεκλημένοις ἐαν πλείους τὰς ὧν ἔξεστιν ἑστῶν τύχῃ, ἐλάττων.
units.tr: So that they are sold, to the guests, if by chance there are more than the law allows, fewer. [ἵνα πωλῶνται, τοῖς κεκλημένοις ἐὰν πλείους τὰς ὧν ἔξεστιν ἑστῶν τύχῃ, ἐλάττων.]

units.la: id est, vt interrogarentur, an ab eo qui epulum praebet plures definito ex Legge numero essent inuitati. Atque hic est interpungendum. Vox ἐλάττων sequentis orationis est principium: is, inquit, qui haec audiuerat, abiit, ad Gynæconomos scilicet. E verbis autem Menandri colliges Legem hanc ea tempestate latam fuisse. Meracam autem potionem in conuiuiis non bibebant, sed dilutum vinum; idque Lege cautum:
units.tr: That is, so that they might be asked whether, by the host of the feast, the guests were more than the number fixed by the law. And here is where the punctuation belongs. The word "fewer" begins the next sentence: the man who had heard these things went away, to the Gynaeconomi of course. From Menander's words you may gather that this law was passed in that period. They did not drink neat wine at feasts but diluted wine, and this too was provided by law:

units.la: Ἐν τοῖς συμποσίοις μὴ πίνειν ἄκρατον.
units.tr: At drinking parties, do not drink neat wine. [Ἐν τοῖς συμποσίοις μὴ πίνειν ἄκρατον.]

units.la: Meminit huius Legis Alexis Comicus in dramate, cui titulus est Æsopo: in eo inter se colloquuntur Æsopus & Solo, quorum verba vulgo male concepta ita à nobis referibuntur, & personis distinguuntur:
units.tr: The comic poet Alexis mentions this law in a play entitled Aesopus. In it Aesop and Solon talk with each other. Their words, commonly misconstrued, are rendered by us as follows, with the speakers distinguished:

units.la: AI. κομψόν γ' τοῦτ' ἔστι πρὸς ὑμῖν, ὦ Σόλων. ἐν τοῖς Ἀθήναις δείξεις δ' ἀρημένον.
units.tr: AE. That is a clever thing you say to them, Solon. In Athens you will show it, but it is forbidden. [ΑΙ. κομψόν γ' τοῦτ' ἔστι πρὸς ὑμῖν, ὦ Σόλων. ἐν τοῖς Ἀθήναις δείξεις δ' ἀρημένον.]

units.la: ΣΟ. ὦ ποῖον; ΑΙ. ἐν τοῖς συμποσίοις ἵν' ἢ πίνετε ἄκρατον. ΣΟ. ἢ γὰρ ῥᾷδιον. πωλοῦσι γὰρ ἐν ταῖς ἁμάξαις διὰ κεκραμένον.
units.tr: SO. What sort? AE. At drinking parties, where you drink neat wine. SO. Oh, that is easy, for they sell it mixed in the carts. [ΣΟ. ὦ ποῖον; ΑΙ. ἐν τοῖς συμποσίοις ἵν' ἢ πίνετε ἄκρατον. ΣΟ. ἢ γὰρ ῥᾷδιον. πωλοῦσι γὰρ ἐν ταῖς ἁμάξαις διὰ κεκραμένον.]
