units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: vapulauerat enim Agoracrito & Equitibus. Inuiti autem cogebantur, & qui hanc militiam detrectabant, fistebantur in iudicium. Xenophon loco laudato. Τοὺς μὲν τοίνυν Ἱππίας δῆλον ὅτι καταλιπεῖν δεῖ [?]τὸν νόμον, τοὺς δυναμένους καὶ [?]χρήματα, καὶ σώματα, ἢ εἰσάγοντα εἰς δικαστήριον, ἢ πείθοντα. Lege praeterea cautum erat, de armis, quibus instructi esse deberent.
units.tr: For Agoracritus had been beaten by the Equites. Those who were unwilling were compelled, and those who shrank from this service were brought before a court. Xenophon, in the passage cited, says: "It is clear, then, that the law must leave out those who are not able, in wealth and in body, and either bring them into court or persuade them." Moreover, the law also provided concerning the arms with which they ought to be equipped.

units.la: Η ΤΩΝ ΙΠΠΕΩΝ ΟΠΛΑΙΣΙΣ. EQVITVM ARMATVRA.
units.tr: The Armour of the Knights: Equitum Armatura

units.la: Legis meminit Xenophon loco laudato. Δωνατοὶ δ' εἰσὶ καὶ τὰ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ΟΠΛΑΙΣΑΙ, ἢ αὐτὸ τῆς αὐτῆς δαπάνης τὰ μεσῷ ἐπιναλισκόντες καὶ τὸν νόμον ΟΠΛΑΙΖΕΣΘΑΙ. Quibus vero armis instructi fuerint, describit Iosephus [?]αλλὼ. Lib. III. cap. III. Τῆς Ἱππέων μάχαιραν μὲν ἐκ δεξιοῦ μακρὰ καὶ κοντὸς ὀπτιμήκης [?]χρὴ. Ξυρεὺς δὲ [?]πλεῖον ἢ ἵππου πλάτος [?]καὶ τῆς γυρυτὸν ἱππόρτωσιν ἢ πλείους ἀκοντες, πλατεῖς μὲν αἰχμαὶ, [?]ἀπόδιοντες ἢ δορατῶν μέγεθος. Χειρὶν ἢ καὶ ξιφαρχες, ὁμοίως τοῖς πεζοῖς, ἅπαν. Cum autem in cute curanda plus æquo operarentur, & comam alerent Equites, Legem tulerunt Cineas & Phri-nus, ne id in posterum facerent.
units.tr: Xenophon, in the passage cited, mentions the law: "Those who are powerful are also those whom the law says must be armed, either by spending the same amount on themselves, or by arming the law" [Δωνατοὶ δ' εἰσὶ καὶ τὰ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ΟΠΛΑΙΣΑΙ]. Which arms they were equipped with, Josephus describes, Book III, chapter III: the knights had a long sword on the right side and a long spear, and a shield wider than the breadth of a horse, and a bow with several javelins; the spear-heads were broad, and the shafts were as long as a spear. They fought with the hand and with swords, like the foot soldiers. But since they took more care than was right over their skin and let their hair grow long, Cineas and Phrynus proposed a law that they should not do so in future.

units.la: Τοὺς νέους μηκέτι ἀβεσθλαίτους εἶ), μη-δὲ κομᾶν.
units.tr: "The young are no longer to go unshod, nor to wear long hair" [Τοὺς νέους μηκέτι ἀβλαύτους εἶναι, μηδὲ κομᾶν].

units.la: Equites posthac plus æquo cutem ne curanto, neue comam alunto.
units.tr: "Knights are not henceforth to care for their skin excessively, nor to keep their hair long."

units.la: Legem laudat Aristophanis Interpres ad Equites. Κινέας δὲ Φεῖνος εἰσηγήσαντο τοῖς νέοις, νόμον γεγράψαντες, μηκέτι ἀβεσθλαίτους εἶναι, μηδὲ κομᾶν. Equites intelliguntur τῶν Νέων nomine in hac Lege: nam Equitum proprium fuit ὁ κομᾶν. Aristophanis Scholiastes ad Equites, & ex eo Suidas: ἐξὼν δὲ τῆς Ἱππάδος ἐ ὁ κομᾶν[?]. hinc Aristophanes Nubibus.
units.tr: The scholiast on Aristophanes' Equites cites this law: "Cineas and Phrynus proposed to the young men, having written a law, that they should no longer go unshod, nor wear long hair" [Κινέας δὲ Φεῖνος εἰσηγήσαντο τοῖς νέοις, νόμον γεγράψαντες, μηκέτι ἀβλαύτους εἶναι, μηδὲ κομᾶν]. The Equites are understood under the name of the young men in this law, for long hair was a peculiar mark of the Equites. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Equites, and from him Suidas, say that long hair was proper to the knights. Hence Aristophanes, in the Clouds:

units.la: ὁ δὲ, κόμην ἔχων,
units.tr: He who has long hair,

units.la: ἱππάζεται τε καὶ ξυγωνεικάζεται.
units.tr: rides and is wrestled with.

units.la: & Equitibus ipsis in cognomine fabula apud eundem dicebat populus,
units.tr: And the people, in the comedy of the same name by the same author, used to say of the Equites themselves:

units.la: τοὺς γὰρ ἐν τῆς κόμης
units.tr: For those of the hair

units.la: ὑμᾶς.
units.tr: you.

units.la: Interpretes. ὅτι ἐκόμων οἱ Ἱππεῖς. idque exemplo, ut puto, Thesei, à quo etiam τῆς κουρᾶς ὁ ἥρως Θησεὺς dicebatur: ἐκείραντο τῆς κεφαλῆς τὸ πρόσθεν μόνον, quod de Abantibus memoriæ prodidit Homerus, at ὄπισθεν ἐκόμων. illud fiebat, nec cum ξιφέων πολύσσονον ἑαυτῷ ἔργον[?], ut cum Archilocho dicam, πρέξιμεν ἐκ τῆς τειχῶν ἀμύνασθαι τοῖς πολεμίοις, inquit Plutarchus in Theseo; hoc vero, quia τοὺς καλοὺς, dicebat olim Lycurgus, ἀπαρέπαισ(?)εις τοὺς δὲ αἰχμητὰς Φοβητέους. Sed hac Lege, (quanquam non videtur diu obtinuisse.) Cineas & Phrynus, cum immutatam vellent Athenienfium Equitum disciplinam, noluerunt illos amplius κομᾶν, ἐν ἀβεσθλαίτοις εἶ). Paullo enim laxior erat horum disciplina, & vita solutior: atque hæc illis ob crebra pericula & improbos labores sunt data quasi diluidia, neque sine exemplo: nam viri omni memoria fortissimi & austeri, Lacedæmonij idem quoque observarunt. Plutarchus in Lycurgo. ποτὲ δὲ καὶ τοῖς νέοις τὰ σκληράγματα τῆς ἀγωγῆς ἐπιφυέντες, οὐκ ἐκώλυον καλλωπίζεσθαι ἀεὶ κομῶντας, καὶ κόσμον ὅπλων καὶ ἱματίων. ὁ γὰρ κομῶντες ἀβύς ἐκ τῆς ἐφήβων ἡλικίας, μάλιστα ἀεὶ τοῖς κινδύνοις ἐπεφέρετο τῷ κόμῳ, λιτῶν τ[?] Φαίπεσθαι καὶ ἡμερησίου[?]. Quod ad stipendium militum attinet, initio duo oboli erant eorum diurnum, qui efficiebant in mensem drachmas decem. Demosthenes Philippica I. ἵνα δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ μίσθος ὁ στρατιώτης δραχμὰς σιτηρέσιον λαμβάνειν[?], quod mutatum postea: nam quatuor obolis meruerunt. Eustathius Ὀδυσσ. A. πεπωλοῦντο βίος[?] Γαυστρία[?], αἱτὶ τὴν στρατιώτην μισθὸς[?], Etiam factum, vt illis oboli sex, id est, drachma in stipendium diurnum procederet. Thucydides: δραχμὴν[?] τῆς ἡμέρας ἕκαστος ἐνέμεσαν. Atque menstruum stipendium erat triginta drachmarum: vnde in palliata Plauti Mostellaria, quae est argumenti Attici.
units.tr: The commentators say that the knights wore their hair long. I think this was after the example of Theseus, from whom the hero Theseus was also called "the shorn one" [τῆς κουρᾶς]. Homer records that the Abantes shaved only the front of the head, but wore their hair long at the back. This was done, as I may say with Archilochus, not for the sake of a close-fought battle with swords, so that they might defend themselves from enemies on the walls, as Plutarch says in his Theseus. But this, because, as Lycurgus used to say, the beautiful should be adorned and the warriors feared. But by this law (though it does not seem to have held for long), Cineas and Phrynus, wishing to change the discipline of the Athenian Equites, did not want them to wear their hair long any more, nor to go unshod. For their discipline was somewhat looser and their life more relaxed; and these privileges were granted to them as a kind of relief because of frequent dangers and harsh labours, and not without precedent: for the most brave and austere men of all memory, the Lacedaemonians, observed the same thing. Plutarch in Lycurgus: "Sometimes, when the hardships of training were imposed on the young, they did not prevent them from taking pride in long hair, and in the adornment of arms and garments; for those who wore long hair from the age of youth were especially eager for dangers, and..." As for the soldiers' pay, at first each foot soldier received two obols a day, which came to ten drachmas a month. Demosthenes, Philippic I: the soldier receives as pay [drachmas] for sustenance; this was later changed, for they were paid four obols. Eustathius on the Odyssey A: [the soldiers were paid...]. It also happened that six obols, that is one drachma, was given as the daily pay. Thucydides: "each man received one drachma a day." The monthly pay was thirty drachmas. Hence in Plautus' Mostellaria, a comedy in the Roman dress set in Attica:

units.la: Vbi sunt isti plagipatidæ, ferritribaces viri, Isti, qui trium nummorum causa subeunt sub falas.
units.tr: Where are those beaten men, those iron-worn men, those who for three coins go under the spears?

units.la: Tres hi Plautini nummi, totidem sunt drachmæ auri, siue ἡμίχρυσοι, id est, triginta drachmæ argenti, quas menstruum fuisse militum terræ Atticæ stipendium diximus: habet ille à Græco Comico, cui apud Pollucem Lib. IV. cap. XXII. quidam milites dicuntur Comica vernilitate τελαμωνοφαχμο-πυργοι, à triginta drachmis argenti menstrui stipendij, & falis, sub quas, vt Plautus indicat, subibant. Præterea extra ordinem, bello Peloponnesiaco, militibus Potidææ præsidiariis duæ drachmæ pendebantur, vt idem Thucydides narrat Lib. III. πλὴν τὶ γὰρ Ποτιδαίαι δίδραχμοι ὁπλῖται ἐφέρουσι, & Polluci sunt δίδραχμοι ὁπλῖται. Atque hæc de pedestri militia. Equites vero drachmam vnam accipiebant in dies singulos. Demosthenes loco laudato. τοῖς δὲ Ἱππεῦσι, δισχιλίοις εἰσὶν, εἰσὶ τελέσαντες δραχμὰς ἕκαστος λαμβάνειν τὴν μίσθος. Neque est mirandum, tam exiguum illis procedere stipendium: nam etiam nullo, vt diximus ex Vlpiano, bello illis è publico data est pecunia. Militibus naualibus stipendium erat oboli diurni tres. Thucydides Lib. VIII. λέγει καλέσων τὸν Τισσαφέρνη πρὸς αὐτοὺς, ὡς Ἀθηναῖοι ἐκ πλείονος χρήματος ἐπιθυμοῦσι τῆς ναυτικῆς τελεσάντων τοῖς ἑαυτῶν ἰδίαν. Excipio vectores triremis Parali, quorum stipendium erat oboli quatuor in dies singulos. Grammatici: οἱ δὲ ἐπιστέλλοντες αὐτὰς, Παράλοι ἐκαλοῦντο, οἱ ἀμφὶ τοῦτο ἡ ἐπαγγελίας τέλεσας τὴν ἐξόλεως ἐλάμβανον, καὶ δ πλοῖον μίσθος ἐστιν ἐξ αὐτῶν εἶναι ἕκαστον.
units.tr: These three Plautine coins are as many drachmas of gold, or half-gold pieces, that is thirty silver drachmas, which we said was the monthly pay of the soldiers of Attica. Plautus took this from the Greek comic poet, in whose work, according to Pollux, Book IV, chapter XXII, certain soldiers are called in comic slang "those with the belts and the sword-hilts" [τελαμωνοφαχμο-πυργοι], from the thirty silver drachmas of monthly pay, and from the spears under which, as Plautus indicates, they went. Besides, outside the regular order, in the Peloponnesian War, the garrison soldiers at Potidaea were paid two drachmas, as Thucydides also relates in Book III: "except that the hoplites at Potidaea receive two drachmas"; and Pollux speaks of the "two-drachma hoplites." So much for the foot soldiers. The knights received one drachma each day. Demosthenes, in the passage cited: "The two thousand knights each received one drachma as pay." Nor is it surprising that so small a pay was theirs, for, as we said from Ulpian, no public money was given to them in any war. The naval soldiers had a pay of three obols a day. Thucydides, Book VIII, says that Tissaphernes called them before himself, since the Athenians desired a greater sum for their naval service. I except the rowers of the trireme Paralus, whose pay was four obols a day. The grammarians: "those who were enrolled were called Paralians; those who took the public pay for this service, and each of whom was a rower of the ship..."

units.la: Cauebatur autem Lege, ne quis miles arma pignori opponeret. Μὴ δῆναι τὰ ὅπλα ἐνέχυρα.
units.tr: It was also provided by law that no soldier should pledge his arms as security. "Let not arms be given in pledge" [Μὴ δῆναι τὰ ὅπλα ἐνέχυρα].

units.la: Legis meminerunt veteres Magistri ad Plutum. Φαίνεται δὲ ἐ ἀπηγορόμενον εἶ, μὴ δῆναι τὰ ὅπλα ἐνέχυρα. λέγ[?] οὖν ὅτι αὕτη (πτία) τὴ ἑαυτῆς βία αἰαλαίζ καὶ τὸς νόμους παλαιῶν τὰς παστρώτας, ὅπλα ἐνέχυρα μὴ λῆκιν. Ad hanc Legem adludit Aristophanes Pluto.
units.tr: The ancient scholiasts on Plutus mention this law. It appears that it was forbidden that arms be given as pledges. The scholiast says that the goddess, by her own force, [...] and that the laws of the ancient [...] forbade arms to be pledged. Aristophanes in Plutus alludes to this law:

units.la: ΒΛΕΨ. ποίοισιν ὅπλοις ἢ δυνάμει πεποίηστε; ποῖον γὰρ ἐ. ἰώγκα, πέλας ἐαυτὰ, οὐκ ἐνέχυρον τὸ ἡμῶν ἢ μιαρωτὰτη;
units.tr: BLEPSIDES. With what arms or power have you been made? For what other [...] is there, near at hand, which is not a pledge, and the most wretched?

units.la: Apud Romanos, arma alienasse, inquit Paulus Lib. singulari de pœnis militum, graue crimen est, & ea culpa desertioni exæquatur, vtique si tota alienauit: sed & si partem eorum, nisi quod interest: nam si tibiale, vel vmerale alienauit, castigari verberibus debet: si vero loricam, scutum, galeam, gladium, desertori similis est. Timori in hoc crimine facilius parcetur: armorumque custodi plerumque ea culpa imputatur, si arma militi commisit non suo tempore. Leg. XIV. §. I. D. de re militari & apud Modestinum Lib. IV. de poenis. Miles, qui in bello arma amisit, vel alienauit, capite punitur: humane militiam mutat. Leg. III. §. XIII. D. eod. Legibus non licebat nisi post septimum mensis diem copias educere.
units.tr: Among the Romans, Paulus, in his single book on the punishments of soldiers, says: To alienate arms is a grave crime, and that fault is equated with desertion, especially if one has alienated the whole; but also if part of them, except what is of no consequence. For if he has alienated a legging or an arm-guard, he ought to be punished with blows; but if a breastplate, shield, helmet or sword, he is like a deserter. Men are more easily spared for this crime, and the keeper of the arms is generally charged with that fault, if he has entrusted arms to a soldier not at the proper time. Digest, Law XIV, §1, De re militari. And in Modestinus, Book IV, De poenis: A soldier who in war has lost or alienated his arms is punished by death; he is leniently dismissed from the service. Digest, Law III, §XIII, same title. By law it was not permitted to lead out the forces before the seventh day of the month.

units.la: Στρατείαν μὴ ἐξάγειν πρὸ τῆς τῶ μη- νὸς ἑβδόμης.
units.tr: To not lead out an army before the seventh day of the month. [Στρατείαν μὴ ἐξάγειν πρὸ τῆς τῶ μηνὸς ἑβδόμης.]

units.la: Legis meminit Hesychius: ἀπείρητο Ἀθηναῖοι στρατιὰν ἐξάγειν πρὸ τῆς τῶ μη- νὸς ἑβδόμης. Zenobius Centuria III. Proverbio LXXIX. ὅτι ἑβδόμης, ἀπείρητο Ἀθηναῖοι στρατείαν ἐξάγειν πρὸ τῆς τῶ μηνὸς ἑβδόμης. Suidas: Ἀθηναῖον ἀπείρητο, ὅτι ἑβδόμης στρατείαν ἐξάγειν. At vero Lacedaemonij τὸν τῆς πανσελήνου νόμον seruabant.
units.tr: Hesychius mentions the law: the Athenians were forbidden to lead out an army before the seventh day of the month. [ἀπείρητο Ἀθηναῖοι στρατιὰν ἐξάγειν πρὸ τῆς τῶ μηνὸς ἑβδόμης.] Zenobius, Century III, Proverb 79: because of the seventh day, the Athenians were forbidden to lead out an army before the seventh day of the month. Suidas: the Athenian was forbidden, because of the seventh day, to lead out an army. The Lacedaemonians, however, observed the law of the full moon.

units.la: Bellum autem indicturi Athenienses in clarigationis signum agnum immittebant in hostium fines ex hac Lege.
units.tr: When the Athenians were about to declare war, they sent a lamb across the borders of the enemy as a sign of the declaration, in accordance with this law.

units.la: Ἄρνα πέμπειν, τὰς πολέμων ἀρχὰς βουλομένους.
units.tr: To send a lamb, for those wishing to begin wars. [Ἄρνα πέμπειν, τὰς πολέμων ἀρχὰς βουλομένους.]

units.la: Legis meminit Diogenianus Centuria II. Proverbio XCVI. Ἄρνα πέμπειν. ὅτι τῶν πολεμίων ἀρχομένων. οἱ γὰρ πόλεμον ἀρχὴν βουλόμενοι, κήρυκα ἔπεμπον ἄρνα ἐπιφερόμενον, ὃν ἡφιέ ἐνδον, ἐσθίειν [?] μυλλόσον [?] ἐπὶ τῆς πόλεως. Hesychius, non in clarigationis, sed pugnae signum, immissum fuisse hunc agnum scribit: Ἄρνα πέμπειν. νόμος ἦν Ἀθηναίοις μὴ ἀποστέλλειν [?], ἀλλ᾽ ἢ τὸν ἄρνα πέμψαντα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῆς πολεμίας.
units.tr: Diogenianus mentions the law, Century II, Proverb 96: to send a lamb, when enemies begin. For those who wished to begin war sent a herald bringing a lamb, which he let loose inside the city... [the Greek here is corrupt in the scan]. Hesychius writes that this lamb was sent not as a sign of declaring war but of battle: there was a law among the Athenians not to send anyone, except the one who sent the lamb, from the office of the enemy. [Ἄρνα πέμπειν. νόμος ἦν Ἀθηναίοις μὴ ἀποστέλλειν, ἀλλ᾽ ἢ τὸν ἄρνα πέμψαντα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῆς πολεμίας.]

units.la: Polemarchus olim veteri Lege in bello, dextro aciei cornu praerat.
units.tr: In former times, under an ancient law, the polemarch commanded the right wing of the battle line in war.

units.la: Τὸν πολέμαρχον ἔχειν χέρας τὸ δεξιόν.
units.tr: The polemarch to hold the right wing. [Τὸν πολέμαρχον ἔχειν χέρας τὸ δεξιόν.]

units.la: Legem habes apud Herodotum Erato. τῶ μὲν δεξιοῦ χέρως ἡγεῖτο ὁ Πολέμαρ- χος Καλλίμαχος. ὁ γὰρ νόμος εἶχε ἔτι τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις τὸν πολέμαρχον ἔχειν χέρας τὸ δεξιόν. Atque etiam inter Stratego sententiam aequo iure ferebat de rebus belli. Herodotus ibidem. ὃ παλαιοὶ γὰρ Ἀθηναῖοι ὁμόψηφον τὸν Πολέμαρχον ἐποιεῦντο τοῖς Στρατηγοῖς.
units.tr: The law is found in Herodotus, Book Erato: "The polemarch Callimachus led the right wing," for the law still gave the Athenians the polemarch holding the right wing. Also, among the generals he had an equal vote with them in matters of war, by the same right. Herodotus in the same place: for the ancient Athenians made the polemarch equal in voting with the generals. [ὃ παλαιοὶ γὰρ Ἀθηναῖοι ὁμόψηφον τὸν Πολέμαρχον ἐποιεῦντο τοῖς Στρατηγοῖς.]

units.la: DE VACATIONE MILITIÆ.
units.tr: DE VACATIONE MILITIÆ.

units.la: TITULUS SECUNDUS.
units.tr: TITULUS SECUNDUS.

units.la: A[?]Τελείαν εἰς τῆς στρατείας τῆς τε- λεῖς ἀφιερωμένοις.
units.tr: Exemption from military service for those dedicated to the rites [Τελείαν εἰς τὴν στρατείαν τοῖς τελεῖς ἀφιερωμένοις].

units.la: Legis meminit Demosthenes ἐν τῷ πρὸς Νεαίρα, vbi agit de Xenoclide Poëta, docetque militiae vacationem ex Lege dari redemptoribus vectigalium, toto sui muneris tempore: nam illos in vrbe adesse erat necesse. ἐπιμελῶς τῶν πεντηκοστῶν τὸ οἶπον ἐν εἰρήνῃ [?] διότι αὐτὸν καταβάλλειν τὰς καταβολὰς εἰς τὸ Βουλευτήριον [?] ἀπολείας ἐκ τῆς νόμου, ὥστε ἐξελ- θὼν ἐκείνῳ μισθώσει. Militia quoque vacabant choreuta veteri Lege.
units.tr: Demosthenes mentions this law in his speech against Neaera, where he deals with the poet Xenocleides, and he shows that by law exemption from military service was granted to the farmers of the taxes for the whole time of their office, since they had to be present in the city: "they must attend carefully to the fiftieth tax, since they must pay the payments into the Council-house..., and so, when they have paid, they are released from the law." Under the old law, dancers also were exempt from military service.

units.la: Τοὺς παὶ Διονύσου χορεύοντας, μὴ στρατεύεσθαι.
units.tr: Those who dance for Dionysus are not to serve in the army [Τοὺς τοῦ Διονύσου χορεύοντας, μὴ στρατεύεσθαι].

units.la: Hac de Lege locus est Demosthenis in Midiana. ἐστα μὲν εἰν ἡ τῶν χορευτῶν, ἀνδυπολύσος ἡμῖν [?], μὴ ἀφεξέλωσι [?] τῆς γραπτίας [?] ἐωσχλήτων [?]. Vlpianus ad hunc locum. ἔως ὧν τοῖς τᾶ Διονύσου χορηγοῖς [?], μὴ γραπτεύεσθαι [?] τὴν τὸν χορὸν [?]. Quamquam intercedebant nonnunquam Hipparchi, vt ex hoc Demosthenis loco colligit Vlpianus. Midias namque Hipparchus. ἡ γὰρ μία ἔκλυμα [?], εἰ τοῖς χορηγοῖς ἐκ ὠλυσιν ἀφεξλωαι [?], καὶ ταῦτα Ἱππαρχος ὤν [?]. Nam etiam saepe Choragi consulto in choreutas capiebant iuuenes aptos bello, quo possent militia vacare. Vlpianus ad haec Demosthenis verba ex Olynthiaca III. οἱ δὲ νόμοι τοῖς ἀτακτοῦσι ἀθῷοις καθίσαν [?]. Vlpianus: τὴν διαφέρειαν οἱ ἀτακτοῦντες τῇ λήμματι [?] κτιῶντων [?], καὶ τὴν ἀγρατῶντων [?]. ἀγρατῶντες μὲν ὅσον ὁ μυλὴποτε ἐξεγαφεὶς εἰς κατάληψιν τῆς γραπτῆς ἀτακτος δὲ, ὁ ἐξεγαφεὶς μὲν, μὴ ὀξιῶν δὲ εἰς τὰς ὑπολειπομένας αὐτῇ γραπτίας [?]. Ληπτακτὴς δὲ, ὁ ἀσκὸς τὸν μάχῳ [?] ὁ ὁ γραπτυπεδὸν τὸν τάξιν ἡ τοῖς σιωπώντες [?] ἀπολιπῶν. νόμοι ἡ ἡσθῇ κελεύοντες ἀφεσθαί τινας τῆς γραπτίας, ὥστε πομπεῖν εἰς τὰ Διονύσια. καὶ χάριν τῶν τῶν ἑαυτῶν, οἱ Χορηγοὶ πρὸς νεωτέρους καὶ τοὺς ἐκ τὴν καλαλόγου μάλιστα ἐπαλείφονται. ὁ δὲ Δημοσθένης, τοὺς μὲν ἐκ καλαλόγου γραπτεύεσθαι ἔφη, ἐκ δὲ τῆς ἀχρῆσου ἡλικίας χρῆσθαι τοὺς χορεύτας. Quare Vlpianus ad Midianam dicit Choragos ius habuisse dandi vacationem militiae choreutis. ἐχὶ χρὴ πινα καὶ ὁ Χορηγὸς ἀδίκως. οἱ ἀφιέναι τῆς γραπτίας τὸν χορὸν, ὅπου τὴν χορηγικὴν καὶ τῆς πολυκυρίως.
units.tr: Demosthenes' passage in the speech against Meidias bears on this law. Ulpian, commenting on this passage, says that the choregoi of Dionysus were not to be enrolled for military service with their chorus. Yet Hipparchs sometimes intervened, as Ulpian gathers from this passage of Demosthenes, since Meidias was a Hipparch. For often the choregoi, deliberately, took young men fit for war into the chorus, so that they might be excused from military service. Ulpian, on Demosthenes' words from the third Olynthiac, "the laws impose penalties on those who fail to attend," explains: those who are absent differ from those who are disorderly, and those who are disorderly from those who are unfit; the absent are those who did not go to the muster, the disorderly those who went but did not obey orders for the rest of the service, and the unfit those who, in the line of battle or in the ranks, left their post. Some laws ordered that certain men be released from military service so that they could take part in the Dionysia, and for the sake of their own honour the choregoi especially sought out younger men and those of the better sort. Demosthenes said that men of mature age served in the army, but that the chorus members were drawn from the unfit age. Hence Ulpian, on the Meidiana, says the choregoi had the right to grant exemption from military service to the chorus members; and some choregoi, acting unjustly, released the chorus from military service, which was a matter of their choregic office and of their power.

units.la: quia scilicet ij, quos Choragi choreutas legebant, militia vacabant.
units.tr: Because, of course, those whom the choregoi enrolled as chorus members were exempt from military service.

units.la: DE PRÆMIIS ET POENIS militum. TITVLVS TERTIVS.
units.tr: On the rewards and punishments of soldiers. Title III.

units.la: QVI egregiam bello operam fortémque nauabant, seque Hipparchis probabant, ad maiora euehebantur, & illorum ratio habebatur in donandis praemiis, conferendisque honoribus, vt puta διπλαδαρχίας, & huiusmodi: at contra ἀτακτοῦντες notabantur ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Those who performed distinguished service in war and showed courage, and who proved themselves to their hipparchs, were promoted to higher posts. Their record was taken into account in awarding prizes and conferring honours, such as the diplarchia and the like. On the contrary, those who were disorderly [ἀτακτοῦντες] were marked down under this law:

units.la: Γλοιεκτῶν μὲν πειθῶν τοῖς ὑπάκτοις, μειονεκτῶν δὲ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἀτακτοῦσι [?].
units.tr: Those who excel should obey their commanders, and those who fall short should be inferior among all the disorderly [Γλοιεκτῶν μὲν πειθῶν τοῖς ὑπάκτοις, μειονεκτῶν δὲ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἀτακτοῦσι].

units.la: Qui egregiam in bello operam praestant, ad maiora prouehuntur; qui secus fecerint, in minorem militiae gradum deiiciuntor.
units.tr: Those who render distinguished service in war are advanced to higher posts; those who act otherwise are demoted to a lower rank of military service.

units.la: Huius Legis meminit Hipparchico Xenophon: εἰς γὰρ μὲν ὃ διπλαρχῶν [?] τοὺς ἀρχομένους, μέγα μὲν καὶ τῷ λόγῳ διδάσκειν ὅσα ἀγαθὰ ἐν τῷ πολιτείᾳ, μέγα δὲ καὶ τῷ ἔργῳ ἐξ τὸν νόμον πλεονεκτῶν μὲν πείθειν τοῖς ὑπάκτοις, μειονεκτῶν δὲ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἀτακτοῦσι [?]. Referebant autem Hipparchi in tabulas illorum nomina, qui nolebant πιθαρχεῖν. Hesychius: Ἱππαρχοὶ δὲ πίναξι τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν ἀτακτοῦντων γράφοντες πρεσμειῶντο [?]. Qui militiam detrectabant, aut in pugna ignaui erant, aut ordinem deserebant suum, infamia notabatur, ex hac Lege:
units.tr: Xenophon mentions this law in his work on the cavalry commander: "For the commander who leads those under him should, by his words, teach greatly what good things there are in the state, and by his deeds, greatly persuade those who excel to obey, and those who fall short among all the disorderly" [εἰς γὰρ μὲν ὃ διπλαρχῶν τοὺς ἀρχομένους]. The hipparchs also used to write the names of those who refused to obey the commander onto tablets. Hesychius: "The hipparchs, writing the names of the disorderly on tablets, ..." [Ἱππαρχοὶ δὲ πίναξι τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν ἀτακτοῦντων γράφοντες]. Those who avoided military service, were cowardly in battle, or deserted their post, were marked with infamy under this law:

units.la: Τὸν ἀσπάτοντα, ἢ τὸ δῆλον, ἢ τὸ λιπόντα τὸ πάξιν, ἀπίχαζ ἀγορᾶς, μήτε στέφων [?], μήτ᾽ εἰσέναι εἰς τὰ ἱερὰ [?] δημοσίαν [?]. ἐὰν δὲ πέσῃ τὰ ποίῃ, εἰπὼν ὅπῃ μὴ χρῇ [?],
units.tr: Whoever throws away his shield, or leaves his rank, is barred from the agora, is not crowned, and may not enter the sacred places [Τὸν ἀσπίδα ... ἀγορᾶς, μήτε στέφων, μήτ᾽ εἰσέναι εἰς τὰ ἱερὰ δημοσίαν].

units.la: Qui militiam detrectat, aut ignauus est, aut ordinem deseris, à foro arcetor, neque coronatur, neq. in publica intrato Tepla [?]: si quis secus faxit, Vndecimviri eum vinciunto, eo ad [illegible, ~60 letters] ἐὰν δὲ ἀλῷ, ὑμᾶτω ἡ Ἡλιαία, ὁ, ᾧ χρὴ παθεῖν αὐτὸν, ἢ ἀποτίσαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἀχρεῖος ὢν ἐμπῆ, ἀποδοῦναι τὸν, ἕως ἂν ἐκτίσῃ. Heliastarum tribunal rapiunto: quicumque voluerit, & ei fas est, accusato. Eo convicto, Heliaste pronuncianto, quam meruerit poenam, aut multam: si multa irrogata sit, in vinculis habetor, donec eam solverit.
units.tr: Whoever avoids military service, or is cowardly, or deserts his post, is barred from the forum, is not crowned, and may not enter public places. If anyone acts otherwise, the Eleven shall bind him and bring him before the court of the Heliaea. If he is convicted, the Heliasts shall pronounce what penalty or fine he deserves. If a fine is imposed and he is unable to pay, he shall be held in chains until he has paid. The Heliasts' tribunal shall be his place of judgement; whoever wishes, and is permitted, may bring the accusation. If he is convicted, the Heliasts shall pronounce what penalty he has earned, or a fine [ἐὰν δὲ ἀλῷ, ὑμᾶτω ἡ Ἡλιαία, ... ἐὰν δὲ ἀχρεῖος ὢν ἐμπῆ, ἀποδοῦναι τὸν, ἕως ἂν ἐκτίσῃ]. Whoever is convicted under this law is held in chains until he pays, as the law requires.

units.la: Legem habent Æschines [illegible, ~20 letters] & Demosthenes [illegible, ~15 letters] Timocratis. Solonis autem ea est, vt docet ibidem Æschines: [illegible, ~70 letters] Ea Lege notabantur infamia primum, qui nondum emeriti militiam detrectabant, [illegible, ~12 letters]. Sequuntur [illegible, ~6 letters]. Deus bone! etiā ignauiæ suæ, quæ forte à natura est, poenas dabunt ignaui: ita est, teste eodem Oratore: [illegible, ~50 letters] vt ex hac Lege constat.
units.tr: This law is found in Aeschines and in Demosthenes against Timocrates. Solon's law is as Aeschines teaches in the same place: [illegible]. Under this law, those who had not yet been discharged from service and still refused military duty were first marked with infamy. [illegible]. Good heavens! Even cowards will pay penalties for their cowardice, which perhaps comes from nature: so it is, as the same orator testifies, [illegible], as is clear from this law.

units.la: Demum hac Lege tenentur [illegible, ~40 letters] qui deseruerant ordinem locumque suum: [illegible, ~80 letters] Meminit huius Legis Lysias: [illegible, ~30 letters] Demosthenes [illegible, ~20 letters] de Xenoclide Poëta: [illegible, ~60 letters] Idem de Rhodiorum libertate: [illegible, ~50 letters] Igitur [illegible, ~20 letters] vt ex hac Lege constat. Quod si quis [illegible, ~25 letters] & damnatus non temperaret sibi ab iis, de quibus hac Lege cautum, rapiebatur ab Vndecimviris ad Heliastarum tribunal, vt ei poena vel multa irrogaretur, vt habetur extremis Legis verbis apud Demosthenem, ad quæ scribit Vlpianus: [illegible, ~90 letters] Heliastæ [illegible, ~15 letters] vt ex hac Lege constat.
units.tr: Finally, those who had deserted their rank and place were bound by this law [illegible]. Lysias mentions this law [illegible]. Demosthenes [illegible] concerning the poet Xenocleides [illegible]. The same concerning the freedom of the Rhodians [illegible]. Therefore [illegible], as is clear from this law. But if anyone, once condemned, did not refrain from those things which this law forbids, he was dragged by the Eleven before the court of the Heliasts, so that a penalty or fine might be imposed on him. This is found in the final words of the law in Demosthenes, on which Ulpian writes: [illegible]. The Heliasts [illegible], as is clear from this law.

units.la: Legem colligere licet ex his Lysiæ verbis [illegible, ~20 letters] Θεσμοῦ-ντων [illegible, ~45 letters] non licet, ergo ignominiosus est; itaque alteri non licebat exprobrasse [illegible, ~20 letters] τὴν ἀσπίδα, vt in superioribus diximus, quod etiam vetat Francorum nostrorum Lex Salica, Tit. XXXII. Lege VI. Siquis alteri imputauerit, quod scutum suum proiecisset in hoste, vel fugiendo prætimore, CXX. den. qui faciunt sol. III. culpabilis iudicetur. Legibus quoque illi, qui nauali bello ordinem suum, id est, nauem deseruissent, aut huic militiæ vocati nomen non dedissent suum, ignominiosi erant:
units.tr: The law may be gathered from these words of Lysias: [illegible] "it is not permitted; therefore he is dishonoured." And so it was not lawful for another to reproach him with having thrown away his shield, as we said above. Our Frankish Salic Law also forbids this, title XXXII, law VI: "If anyone charges another that he threw away his shield in the enemy's presence, or fled for fear, let him be judged guilty and pay 120 denarii, which make three solidi." Those too who in a sea battle had deserted their rank, that is, their ship, or who had not given their name when called to naval service, were dishonoured by the laws.

units.la: Τὸ [illegible, ~40 letters] Qui arma abiecerit, ignominiosus esto.

units.la: In hunc censum etiam veniunt, qui arma abiecerunt.
units.tr: Those who threw away their arms also fall under this censure.

units.la: Τοῦ λιποταξίου καὶ ἀνωμαχίας τὸν ζημίαν τῇ ἀτιμίας. [?]
units.tr: The penalty for desertion and for cowardice in battle is infamy [Τοῦ λιποταξίου καὶ ἀνωμαχίας τὸν ζημίαν τῇ ἀτιμίας].

units.la: Qui nauali bello nauem deseruerit, itemque qui militiae nauali vocatus nomen non dederat, ignominiosus esto.
units.tr: Whoever deserted his ship in a naval battle, and likewise whoever, when called to naval service, had not given his name, shall be dishonoured.

Dicit Pollux in eandem incurrere poenam eos, qui nauali bello, quam qui terrestri, suum deseruissent ordinem: Atqui οἱ λειποταξίαι τῶν ζητῶν ὁλίγου ἀπέμωσ. [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: Pollux, Book VIII, ch. VI: "The one who leaves his ship is a liponautes, as the one who leaves his station is a deserter of rank [λειποταξίας]; while the anomachias is the one who does not leave the ship, and not only fought at sea [ἀνωμαχίας δὲ, ὁ τῶν ναυτῶν μὴ λιπόν]." [illegible]. Pollux says that those who deserted their ship in a naval battle incur the same penalty as those who deserted their post in a land battle. Yet the deserters of rank [λειποταξίαι] nearly [illegible].

And that those who, whenever they left the city, were convicted of desertion, cowardice, or naval defeat (I cite from Suidas: anomachias), or who lost their shield..."

units.la: Mutilatis in bello consulebatur Pisistrati Lege, nam de publico pecuniam accipiebant:
units.tr: Those maimed in war were provided for under the law of Pisistratus, for they received money from the public treasury.

units.la: Τοῖς πηρωθέντας ἐν πολέμῳ δημοσίᾳ τρέφεσθαι. [?]
units.tr: Those maimed in war are to be supported at public expense [Τοῖς πηρωθέντας ἐν πολέμῳ δημοσίᾳ τρέφεσθαι].

units.la: Lex haec non Solonis, sed Pisistrati est, Solonis tamen aemulatione, & explo, vt refert Plutarchus ex Heraclide in Solone: καὶ νόμως αὐτὸς Pisistratus ἐπηγεῖ ἐχαλίμ, ὧν ὅτι καὶ ὁ τοῖς πηρωθέντας ἐν πολέμῳ, δημοσίᾳ τρέφεσθαι κλθέων. τὸν δὲ φησὶν Ἡρακλείδης καὶ παρέ[illegible, ~20 letters]. At non quiuis mutilati in bello debebant publicis sumptibus ali: nam excipiebantur illi, quibus diuitiae domi suppeterent: unde in Lysiana illa ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀδυνάτου, inter cetera, quae adferuntur argumenta, cur non oporteat Ἀδυνάτους λαμβάνειν ὁ τοῦ τῆς πόλεως ἄρχειν, hoc non parui momenti legitur, posse [illegible, ~20 letters] ἀλὰ τῆς ἀπ' ἐκείνου ζωῆ. Itaque soli illi δημοσίᾳ τρέφονται. Lege hac, quorum redditus annuus erat intra tres minas tantum.
units.tr: This law is not Solon's but Pisistratus's, though made in emulation of Solon, as Plutarch reports from Heraclides in the Life of Solon: "Pisistratus himself also made laws, among which was that those maimed in war should be supported at public expense." Heraclides says [illegible]. But not every person maimed in war had to be supported at public expense, for those who had wealth at home were excluded. Hence in the speech of Lysias, among the other arguments adduced why the Adynatoi should not receive from the city's treasury, this point is of no small weight: [illegible]. Thus only those were supported at public expense whose annual income was no more than three minae.

units.la: Harpocratio: Ἀδυνάτοι, οἱ οὐκ ἔχοντες πεῖσαι μίσθωσιν κεκτημένοι ὁ σῶμα πεπηρωμένον. ἐλαμβάνοντο δὲ ἐπὶ δοκιμασίας ἐπὶ τῆς βυλῆς, δύο ἴσολεῖς τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκάσης. corruptus est locus; emendo: οἱ οὐκ ἔχοντες μυρίαν κεκτημένοι, ὁ σῶμα πεπηρωμένοι. Vox enim μισθῶν nihil est: Quare etiam ἀδοκιμάζοντο, inquit Harpocratio, apud Quingentorum Senatum, non tantum, an essent ὁ σῶμα πεπηρωμένοι, & reuera ἀδύνατοι, vt videri volebant, sed etiam an annuus reditus esset intra tres minas, siue trecentas drachmas, vel maior; nulla enim habebatur ratio eorum, quorum prouentus tribus minis maior, neque quicquam è publico accipiebant; mutilus quoque hac de re Hesychij locus: Ἀδυνάτοι, οἱ οὐκ ἔχοντες πεῖσαι τῶν ἀπὸ Ἀθηναίων ἐλαμβάνοντο δὲ τῆς βυλῆς δύο ἴσολεῖς.
units.tr: Harpocration: "Adynatoi are those who do not have [...], possessing a body that is maimed. They were received on examination before the Council, two obols each day." The passage is corrupt; I would emend it to read: "those who do not possess ten thousand [...], possessing a body that is maimed." The word misthōn means nothing here. Hence, says Harpocration, they were examined before the Council of Five Hundred, not only to determine whether they were maimed and truly unable to work, as they wished to appear, but also whether their annual income was within three minae, that is, three hundred drachmas, or more. For no account was taken of those whose income exceeded three minae, and they received nothing from the public. Hesychius' passage on this matter is likewise corrupt: "Adynatoi are those who do not have [...] of the Athenians; they were received on examination before the Council, two obols."

units.la: Referendum puto: οἱ οὐκ ἔχοντες μυρίων τῶν ἀπὸ Ἀθηναίων. Pecunia, quam in dies accipiebant οἱ ἀδύνατοι, obolus erat, vt ex Aristotele docet Harpocratio: ἐλαμβάνοντο δὲ ἐπὶ δοκιμασίας ἐπὶ τῆς βυλῆς ἑβδόλον τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκάστης, ὡς φησὶν Ἀριστοτέλης ἐν Ἀθηναίων πολιτείᾳ. & testatur Lysias loco laudato: καὶ ὑμᾶς ἐμοῦ μὲ ἀφῃρεῖσθαι τὴν ἰδίαν, ὡς ὑγιαίνοντος, οὕτω ἡ ἀφῃρεῖσθαι πολ[illegible, ~10 letters]. ζει, ὡς αἰαπῆμε. & extrem μὴ [?] λόγῳ. At Philoch quaginta quatuor obolo existimant diurnum illor ἐκ τῆς βυλῆς δύο ἰδιῶται. H βουλῆς, δύο ἰδιῶται τῆς ἡμέρ ταπῖ, οἱ πεντηκοσίοι ἑκάστης ἡμέρας, οὐ πεντηκοσίοι ἑκάστης ἡμέρας ἐν ὅτι δικαμαδίστης ἐπὶ τῆς βο ἰδιῶται. Non enim qui è Q los, ceteri verò vnum tar defcripfit Suidas, Harpo aliis in vnum, aliis in duo chmas nouem confentie nem & modum huius vnum fatentur omnes , censendi [illegible, ~6 letters] berent ; necne : itaque C habetur.
units.tr: I think this should be read: "those who do not have ten thousand of the Athenians." The money which the adynatoi received each day was an obol, as Harpocration teaches from Aristotle in the Constitution of the Athenians: "they received, on examination before the Council, a diobol each day." Lysias also testifies in the passage cited. Philochorus, however, thinks the daily pay was two obols. Suidas describes it differently, and not all agree on the amount of this payment, nor whether it was counted by the Council; so the matter remains uncertain.

For then they are sent to their own affairs and enter their paternal inheritance (which happened only in the twentieth year), once they have come out of this care and, as it were, guardianship of the commonwealth. They are also equipped with full armour (panoplia), because Athenian youths at the age of twenty were sent to war equipped in panoply; whence at the Agraulium they bound themselves by oath, [ἐκ κατ... ὄμνυ... τὰ ὅπλα] to swear by the arms.

units.tr: With God's blessing we shall consider under this title those laws which either escaped us or cannot conveniently be reduced to any of their titles, nor were they related under their own titles. I hope the fair reader will pardon the oversight, which human nature has seldom guarded against.

units.la: Absurda nonnemini prima visione Solonis Lex, qua sanxit in seditione alterius utrius-partis esse.
units.tr: To some at first sight the law of Solon seems absurd, by which he enacted that anyone who took neither side in a civil strife should be...

units.la: Ἄτιμος ἔστω ὁ ἐν στάσει μηδετέρας μεί-δος ἡμόωνος[?]. Si qui in seditione non alterius utrius partis fuerit, ignominiosus esto.
units.tr: Let him be without honour who, in a sedition, takes neither side. If anyone in a sedition is not of either party, let him be disgraced. [Ἄτιμος ἔστω ὁ ἐν στάσει μηδετέρας μερίδος ὤν]

units.la: Legem laudat Plutarchus in Solone, ratioque illius ibidem legitur: βάλε[?] ἀλλ' ὡς ἔοικε, μὴ ἀπαξαπᾶς μηδ' ἀναλογίτως ἔχειν πρὸς τὸ κοινόν, ἐν ἀσφαλεῖ τὰ οἰκεῖα, καὶ ὁ μὴ στασιάζειν μηδὲ συνωμοσίαν τῇ παρεισδύσει[?] δικαιότεροι βοηθεῖν μᾶλλον ἀκινδύνως[?]. Meminit Legis idem Plutarchus in vita Solonis, &c. παλαι δὲ Σόλωνος ἐκλέλειπε νόμος, ὃς ἐν στάσει μηδετέρῳ μέρει προσχωροῦντας καλάζειν[?]. & Libro de sera Numinis vindicta: ἀλλ' ὁ λογιώτατος δὲ ὁ τῆς Σόλωνος, ἀλ-λὰ μὴ τὴν ἐν στάσει πόλεως μηδὲ συστασιάσαι[?]. At Cicero capital fuisse dicit: verba illius sunt Libro X. Epist. ad Atticum, Epist. I. Ego vero Solonis, popularis tui, ut puto etiam mei, Legem negligam, qui capite sanxit, si qui in seditione non alterius utrius partis fuisset. Sed puto idem esse Ciceroni capite sanxisse, quod Plutarcho ἀτίμον εἶ). Volebat igitur Solo viros omnes bonos partes illas sequi, quae sunt Reipublicae: nam δικαιότατον εἶ), inquit magnus Doctor Polit. Libro IV. cap. XII. Ὁ βουλόμενος μέρης τῆς πόλεως τῷ μὴ βουλομένῳ μέ-σθαι τῶν πολιτῶν, quod est arcanum imperii, καὶ ὁ μέγιστον στοιχεῖον ἀρχῆς. Atque in hoc argumento versatur tota illa Lysiae oratio, quae est τῷ Φίλωνος δοκιμα-σίας. cias. Philonem hunc ἀτιμοι probat, quia afflictis Atheniensium rebus Reipublicæ defuerat, neque illius partes erat secutus: cum etiam illi deesse non debeant inquilini, vt testatur Lysias: Τοὺς Μετοίκους, ἔλα ἡ ... ἐωντῆς ἐδοκ- ... τῆς πόλεως [illegible, ~12 letters].
units.tr: Plutarch praises this law in his Life of Solon, and the reasoning behind it is given there: that it is not right for a man to be indifferent and detached from the common good, keeping his own affairs safe, and not taking part in the strife or conspiracy of the parties, but rather that it is more just to help the side that is right without danger. The same Plutarch mentions this law in the Life of Solon, etc., and in his book on the delays of divine vengeance, where he says that Solon's law was... not to be indifferent in civil strife. But Cicero says it was punishable by death: his words are in Letter 1 of Book X to Atticus: Indeed I disregard the law of Solon, your popular-party man and, I think, mine too, which punished with death anyone who in a sedition did not take one side or the other. But I think to Cicero "to be punished with death" means what to Plutarch means "to be disgraced." Solon therefore wished all good men to follow those parties which belong to the commonwealth; for, as that great teacher says in Politics Book IV, chapter 12, it is most just that the one who wishes the part of the city should... with the one who does not wish it among the citizens, which is the secret of government and the greatest foundation of power. And that whole oration of Lysias, the one on the scrutiny of Philo, turns on this point. He proves that Philo was disgraced because he had failed the commonwealth in its afflicted state and had not followed its side; since even resident aliens ought not to be absent from it, as Lysias testifies: ...the metics...
