Ἐκ νόμον εἰσαγαγὼν τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς ἄστεος ἐν Πειραιεῖ μείναντα, τοῦτον τιμωρίᾳ. ἔστι γὰρ ... [illegible, ~10 letters] ... καταμείναντα ἐν τῇ Πειραιεῖ. καὶ αὐτὸν οἱ ἐχθροὶ εἰς δίκην ... καταγράψαι. Ratio Legis videtur hæc esse, quia vel metus erat, ne inter se dissiderent, & inde Reipublicæ pestem & exitium crearent: Erant enim magè populares, qui in Piræeo, quam qui in astu habebant: hinc autem sæpe dissidia. Aristoteles Polit. Libro VI. cap.III. καὶ Ἀθηναῖοι γὰρ ὁμοίως εἰσὶν, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον δημοτικοὶ οἱ τὸν Πειραιᾶ οἰκοῦντες τῆς ἂν ἄστυ. & dissidiorum inter eos, qui in astu, & eos, qui in Piræeo habebant, vt & fœderis inter cosdem meminit Lysias ἐν τῇ Υπὲρ Καλλίου ἀπολογία ἐξεγενηθέντος. ἢ γὰρ ἐνεκαν ἐπὶ ἀστεροῦ, ἀλλ' ἐνεκα ἡμῶν τῆς ἐξ ἄστεος καὶ ἐκ Πειραιέως, αἱ συνθῆκαι ἐγένοντο καὶ οἱ ὅρκοι. Sed hoc odium, de quo Lysias, & bellum gestum est, Athenas occupantibus Triginta Tyrannis, vt constat ex eiusdem oratione extrema τῷ Ἐγκωμίῳ. Vel quia metus erat ab incendiariis: Nauale quippe suum habebant in Piræeo Athenienses: atqui apud eos maximum erat rei nauticæ studium, & reuera nihil aliud erat Atheniensium imperium, quam Θαλάσσης ἀρχή.
units.tr: Afterwards the lawgiver himself, when he arrived late and was compelled to stay there, was summoned to court by his opponents. Suidas, more than once, cites this from Aelian: Aelian says that Diopeithes introduced a law that whoever stayed at Piraeus, away from the city, should be punished; for... having stayed at Piraeus, his enemies... indicted him. The reason for the law seems to be this: either there was fear that they would quarrel among themselves and thereby create a plague and ruin for the commonwealth, for those who lived at Piraeus were more popular than those who lived in the city, and disputes often arose from this. Aristotle, Politics Book VI, chapter 3, says: the Athenians are alike, but those who inhabit Piraeus are more democratic than those in the city. Lysias also mentions the disputes between those in the city and those at Piraeus, and the treaty between them, in his Defence on behalf of Callias: for the agreements and oaths were made not for the sake of the city but for us, from the city and from Piraeus. But this hatred, of which Lysias speaks, and the war waged when the Thirty Tyrants occupied Athens, is clear from the closing part of the same oration, the Encomium. Or it was because of fear of incendiaries: the Athenians had their own naval arsenal at Piraeus; and indeed the Athenians had the greatest interest in naval matters, and their empire was nothing other than rule of the sea.

units.la: Lege multa irrogatur ci, qui intra vrbem, tumultu nullo, in publicum prodierit cum armis.
units.tr: By law a fine is imposed on anyone who, within the city and without any tumult, comes into public carrying arms.

units.la: Ὅς τις ἐν ἀστεῖ σιδηροφορεῖν μηδὲν δίον, ἢ ὅπλα ἐξενεγκαι εἰς τὸ δημόσιον, μαθεῖν.
units.tr: Whoever, in the city, without any necessity, carries iron or brings out arms into public, let him be fined. [Ὅς τις ἐν ἄστει σιδηροφορεῖν μηδὲν δέον ἢ ὅπλα ἐξενεγκεῖν εἰς τὸ δημόσιον, ζημιούσθω]

units.la: Si quis intra vrbem, nulla necessitate cogente, ferro accinctus, armisque instructus prodierit, multator.
units.tr: If anyone comes out within the city, under no compelling necessity, girded with iron and equipped with arms, he is to be fined.

units.la: Refert Lucianus in Anacharside è Solonis persona: καὶ ἀσκητὴν γ' ὄντα, ὡς τις ἐν ἀστεῖ σιδηροφορεῖν μηδὲν δίον, ἢ ὅπλα ἐξενεγκαι εἰς τὸ δημόσιον. Ab antiquissi-mis iam temporibus arma non gestarunt in publicum prodeuntes Athenienses, quod etiam reliquos Græci nominis populos docuerunt. Thucydi-des Historia I. καὶ ξυνῆλθον τῶν διαιτῶν μὲν ὅπλων ἐπιπόθησεν, ὥσπερ οἱ βάρβαροι· ἐν τοῖς ἀσφαλῶς δὲ οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι τὸν τε σιδηρον κατέχειν. Hinc enim fiebat, vt cædes patrarentur. Eustathius ad Iliad. A. ὅς δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἡμῖν τὸν Ἀχιλλέα, ὅτι πὸ ὅπλα ἐφόρουν οἱ παλαιοὶ καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἀγορᾶις ... ἀγαθὸν ... ὅτι ... [illegible, ~9 letters] ... ἀκούσῃ. Quo respe-xit hæc Zaleuci Lex: μηδένα φορεῖν ὅπλα ἐν βουλευτηρίῳ.
units.tr: Lucian, in the Anacharsis, quotes this from the persona of Solon: even though he was an ascetic, whoever in the city carries iron without need, or brings arms out into public. From the earliest times the Athenians, when going out in public, did not carry arms, and the other peoples of Greek name followed this custom. Thucydides, Book I: the Greeks in ancient times, like the barbarians, carried arms in their daily life; but the Athenians, as they were safe, kept their iron... Hence killings were committed. Eustathius on Iliad A: the ancients carried arms even in the marketplaces... Hence this law of Zaleucus, which concerns it: let no one carry arms in the council chamber.

units.la: Sacrilegi & proditores morte multabantur Atheniensium Lege, neque intra Atticæ fines sepelicbantnr[?], bonaque eorum publicabantur.
units.tr: Traitors and sacrilegious persons were put to death under Athenian law. They were not buried within the borders of Attica, and their goods were confiscated.

units.la: [illegible, ~70 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Si quis in iudicio proditionis aut sacrilegij damnatus fuerit, intra Atticam ne sepelitor, bona eius publicantor.
units.tr: If anyone is condemned in a trial for treason or sacrilege, let him not be buried within Attica, and let his goods be confiscated.

units.la: Legem retulit Xenophon [illegible, ~35 letters] Libro I. [illegible, ~25 letters] Cùm autem accusati fuerant proditionis, quanquā nondum essent conuicti, in vinculis habebantur, vt constat è iureiurando Senatus Quingentorum apud Demosthenem in Timocratea: [illegible, ~60 letters].
units.tr: Xenophon reports the law [illegible] in Book I [illegible]. When those accused of treason had been charged, although not yet convicted, they were kept in chains, as is clear from the oath of the Senate of Five Hundred in Demosthenes' speech against Timocrates: [illegible].

units.la: Atque id, vt dixi, intelligendum est statim ab accusatione proditionis in vinculis habitos fuisse, antequam criminis illius fuissent conuicti: nam postquam rei peracti fuerant, non est mirum: explicat statim Demosthenes: [illegible, ~30 letters]. Atque hi qui proditionis accusabantur, in vinculis causam dicebant, vt ex his liquet, & Canoni psephismate, quod legitur apud Xenophontem loco laudato, [illegible, ~45 letters]. Morte autem luebant. De sacrilegis manifestis Xenophon Libro I. [illegible, ~40 letters]. De proditoribus constat è Lycurgo [illegible, ~20 letters] corumque cadauera [illegible, ~15 letters]. Thucydides de The-mistocle Libro I. [illegible, ~80 letters]. Cenotaphia tamen poterant illis extrui intra Atticae fines, sed imposita tumulo cruce: idque obseruat Marcellinus in vita Thucydidis profugi ad proditionis crimen: [illegible, ~110 letters]. Quod in hostium tumulis obseruasse videntur Graeci: nam huc refero ea, quae à Tito Quinto Flaminio in Epigrammate dicuntur aduersus Alcaeum Poetam, qui gloriam fugati Philippi Macedonum Regis suis adscribebat Ætolis, hoc item Epigrammate:
units.tr: This, as I have said, must be understood to mean that they were held in chains from the moment of the accusation of treason, before they were convicted of that crime. For once the trial had ended, it is no surprise. Demosthenes explains this immediately: [illegible]. Those accused of treason pleaded their case in chains, as is clear from these passages and from the decree of Canon, which is read in Xenophon at the place cited, [illegible]. They paid with their lives. On manifest sacrilege, Xenophon in Book I [illegible]. On traitors, it is established from Lycurgus [illegible], and their corpses [illegible]. Thucydides on Themistocles, Book I [illegible]. Cenotaphs could nevertheless be erected for such men within the borders of Attica, but with a cross set on the mound. Marcellinus observes this in his life of Thucydides, the exile charged with treason: [illegible]. The Greeks seem to have observed this same practice with the tombs of enemies. For I refer here to what Titus Quinctius Flamininus says in an epigram against the poet Alcaeus, who claimed for his own Aetolians the glory of putting to flight Philip, king of the Macedonians, in this same epigram:

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Rescripsit enim Flaminius in his tumulis paratam esse Alcaeo crucem, nempe propter illa impia, quae hostium tumulis imponebantur, & crucis vicem prae-stare poterant: [illegible, ~50 letters].
units.tr: Flamininus wrote that a cross was prepared for Alcaeus on these tombs, namely because of those impious things that were placed on the tombs of enemies and could take the place of a cross: [illegible].

units.la: [?ἄφλιος] καὶ ἄφυλλος, οὐδ' ἴποτε, τᾶς ἡ' ὅτι νότῳ Ἀλκαίου γαυρὸς πήγυσα ἠλίβατος.
units.tr: [?ἄφλιος] and leafless, nor ever [...] of Alcaeus the proud, lofty [...] (the Greek is too corrupt to render fully).

units.la: Sed in illo Alcaei Epigrammate mendosa est vox ἀθαμπέι in primo versu: quomodo enim erunt ἀθαμπέι, qui se dicunt τᾶς ἡ' ὅτι τύμβῳ Θεσσαλίας χαλκᾶς? nugæ. Rescribo:
units.tr: But in that epigram of Alcaeus the word ἀθαμπέι in the first verse is faulty. For how can they be ἀθαμπέι, who say they lie in the tomb of Thessaly τᾶς ἡ' ὅτι τύμβῳ Θεσσαλίας χαλκᾶς? Trifles. I restore it thus:

units.la: ἄκλαυστοι καὶ ἀπέκτοι, οὐδίποτε, τᾶς ἡ' ὅτι τύμβῳ Θεσσαλίας πειστὰ χαίμὰ μυελάσης.
units.tr: ἄκλαυστοι καὶ ἀπέκτοι, οὐδίποτε, τᾶς ἡ' ὅτι τύμβῳ Θεσσαλίας πειστὰ χαίμὰ μυελάσης. (Unwept and unslain, never [...] in the tomb of Thessaly [...].)

units.la: Quod quidem verum est in confusa hac caesorum hostium sepultura. Sed ad rem οὐκ ἐξεῖ φανερῶς ἀπαγγέλλει ἐν Ἀθήναις τὸ ὅτι προδοσία φιλάνθρωπα, neque item qui capite luerant Athenis. Plutarchus in Phocione, qui proditionis damnatus fuerat: ἐδόξε καὶ ὁ σῶμα τῆς Φωκίωνος ἐκφορὰ, καὶ μηδὲ πῦρ ἐσάψαι μηδὲ ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἀπόλλυσθαι. Qui autem suppetias, vel verbulo, ferebat proditori, eadem quoque multabatur poena. Lycurgus ἐν τῷ κατὰ Λεωκράτους τοὺς λόγῳ μόνον τῷ προδόντι βουλομένῳ ἐπιτιμήσας, ἀλλὰ ἑκάτερον ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἀναγκάσαι μετάλλον. Capite quoque sanctum est in proditores castelli, aut nauis, aut exercitus.
units.tr: This is indeed true of the confused burial of slain enemies. But to the point: [Greek: it is not permitted openly to announce in Athens that...], nor likewise to those who had paid with their heads at Athens. Plutarch, in his life of Phocion, who had been condemned for treason, says: "It was decided that even the body of Phocion should be carried out, that no fire should be applied to it, and that it should not be destroyed from the earth." Whoever gave aid to a traitor, even by a word, was punished with the same penalty. Lycurgus, in his speech against Leocrates, rebuked not only the one who wished to betray, but also forced each of them out of the city into exile. Capital punishment was likewise decreed against traitors of a fortress, a ship, or an army.

units.la: Εαὶ τις Φεύγειν τι προδιδὸν, ἢ ναῦν, ἢ στρατόπεδον, ἢ ἐξ ἀπολωλεκότος ζημίᾳ.
units.tr: Greek: If anyone betrays a fugitive [...] a ship, or a camp, or [...] loss.

units.la: Si quis castellum prodiderit, aut nauem, aut exercitum, morte luito.
units.tr: If anyone betrays a fortress, or a ship, or an army, let him pay with his life.

units.la: Legis meminit Lysias ἐν τῷ κατὰ Φιλώνος ἀδικίας. Εἰ μὲν ὡς Φεύγειν τι προδιδόντι τὴν πόλιν, ὡς ἐπαχθὲς αὖ ζημίας. Quinetiam proditores aliarum civitatum Lege arcebantur finibus Atticae, si intrassent, non secus ac in homicidas animadvertebantur, & capite plectebantur.
units.tr: Lysias mentions this law in his speech against Philo for injustice: [Greek: if he betrays the city, as to one who betrays and flees, it is a heavy penalty]. Moreover, traitors from other states were barred by law from entering the territory of Attica. If they entered, they were treated just like murderers and punished with death.

units.la: Τὸν τῆς αὐτῆς πατρίδος προδότην τῆς Ἀττικῆς χώρας μὴ εἰσβαίνειν· εἰ δὲ μή, οἷς αὖ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ φυγόντων ἐξ Ἀρείου πάγου κατίη.
units.tr: Greek: The traitor of the same fatherland shall not enter the territory of Attica; if he does, let him [...] as those who [...] from the Areopagus.

units.la: Atticam ne intrato patriae suae proditor, si intrarit, eadem Lege tenetor, qua is qui ab Areopagitis damnatus, solum vertere, re-dierit.
units.tr: Let the traitor not enter Attica, his fatherland. If he enters, let him be bound by the same law as one condemned by the Areopagites who, having fled, has returned.

units.la: Legem habes apud Dinarchum ἐν τῷ κατὰ Δημοσθένους, ἢ τὸ γράμμα. Τὰς ... Athenienfium Lege: Τοὺς αὐτομολοῦντας ... ζημιοῦσθαι.
units.tr: You will find the law in Dinarchus, against Demosthenes, or the text. Athenian law: [Greek: those who desert [...] are to be punished].

units.la: Legem colligo ex his Vlpiani verbis ad Timocratem: Εἰ γὰρ ὧν ἀποδιδράσκει, οὐκ ἂν ἐξῆν ἐν Ἀθήναις. Erat igitur ἀποδιδράσκοις, τὸν ἐκ τῆς Ἀθηναίων χώρας ἐκπεσόντα εἰς τοὺς πολεμίους ἀποδιδράσκειν, qui ab Athenienfibus ad hostes defecerant, δίκαιος ἡ ζημία. Is, qui ad hostem confugit, & redijt, torquebitur, ad bestiasque vel in furcam damnabitur: quamuis milites nihil eorum patiantur. Lege III. §. X. D. de re militari: & proditores, transfugae plerumque capite puniuntur, & exauctorati torquentur: nam pro hoste, non pro milite habentur. Lege VII. D. eod. Excipiuntur Scenici artifices, quibus impune erat ἀποδιδράσκειν. Anonymus in Argumento Orationis Demosthenicae ἐκ τῆς Νεοπτολέμου ἐπιστολῆς τοῦ παραγράφου ἐτύγχανον. ὅτι ... τοῖς πολεμίοις.
units.tr: I gather the law from these words of Ulpian on Timocrates: "For if he deserts, it would not be allowed in Athens." So ἀποδιδράσκειν referred to one who had been expelled from Athenian territory and deserted to the enemy, who had defected from the Athenians to the enemy, and the penalty is just. Whoever fled to the enemy and returned will be tortured and condemned to the beasts or to the cross, although soldiers suffer none of these things. See Law III, §10, D. de re militari; traitors and deserters are usually punished with death, and deserters who have been dismissed from service are tortured, for they are regarded as enemies, not as soldiers. See Law VII, D. eod. Stage performers are excepted, for whom desertion was allowed with impunity. The anonymous writer on the argument of Demosthenes' oration says: [Greek: from the letter of Neoptolemus, the marginal note was] [...] to the enemies.

units.la: Aduersus hostes publicos, tanquam aduersus homicidas morti addictos & damnatos, insurrexerunt Atheniensium Leges, quarum hoc Fragmentum legimus.
units.tr: Athenian laws rose against public enemies as against murderers, condemned and doomed to death. We read the following fragment of them.

units.la: ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ ΚΑΙ ΓΟΛΕΜΙΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΣΥΜΜΑΧΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΣ ΓΕΝΟΣ.
units.tr: [Greek: Let him be outlawed and an enemy of the people of the Athenians and of the allies, himself and his kin.]

units.la: Impune occidito, hostisque esto populi Atheniensis, & sociorum, cum is tum eius liberi.
units.tr: Let him be killed with impunity, and let him be an enemy of the Athenian people and of the allies, both he and his children.

units.la: Collegimus hoc Fragmentum è Psephismate, quod, auctore Themistocle, vt habet Plutarchus in eius vita, scriptum est in Arithmium Zelitam: refert Demosthenes III, Philippica: ΑΡΘΜΙΟΣ, φησί, Ο ΠΥΘΩΝΑΚΤΟΣ Ο ΖΕΛΕΙΤΟΣ ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ, ΚΑΙ ΠΟΛΕΜΙΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΣΥΜΜΑΧΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΓΕΝΟΣ. ἐκφανοι ἐχ[?]ἀ[?] αὐτῆ[?] ἀπ[?]ο[?]ἐαλ[?] ἐαν[?] τῇ συμμάχων, αὐτὸν καὶ ἥρως, καὶ ἀτίμους εἶ. τῶτο δ' ἐστὶ, ἡ χωρίς ἀ[?] ἐπιστοῖ[?] ἐ[?] φόσεω ἀπ[?]. (τί γὰρ τῷ Ζῆλειτῃ τῶτ' ἐμωνου, εἰ τῇ Αθηναίων χοινῶν μὴ ἐξέσ[?] ἐ[?]μ[?]φ[?].) ἀλλ' ὁ τῶτο λέγ[?]· ἀλλ' ἐν τοῖς φονεῦσ[?] γεγενημένοις νόμοις, ἐπ[?] ὧν ἀ[?] μὴ ἀ[?]λῶ δῖκας, φόνῳ δικαίσασ[?]. ἀλλ' ἀναγὸς ἐ[?] τ[?] ἀποκτεῖνα. ἐ ΑΤΙΜΟΣ φησὶ ΤΕΘΝΑΤΩ. τῶτο δὲ λέγ[?], καθαιρεῖ τὴν ζωὴν ἡ[?] ἀποκτείνων[?]. Atque hic optime Grammatici è Demosthene ATI-MOΣ, interpretantur ἀτιμώρητος, ἢ ἀ[?] ἡ ἀποκτείνας, ἡ ἐπὶ τοχοῦ ἐπιλυμίᾳ, ἀλλ' ἵνα καθαρὸς αἰτίας. In eos autem omnis homo miles erat, etiam proposito praemio ei qui interfecisset, aut viuentem Athenas adduxisset. Grammatici: ἐπιτρεπονικῶν[?] ἀποχ[?] βάλλω πόλις ἐπ᾽ ἀρχῇ αἰαρεθῶνα[?] ἵνα τὴν μὴ ὄντων ὑφ᾽ ἑαυτῆς, ἐκ[?]ρυπᾶ δώσω χρήματα, εἰ τῆς αὐτῶν αἰτίαν, ποσ[?] τί τῆς. Emendandus Ammonius: ἐπιτρεπρῦξ[?] ἐ[?] λ[?] ἐλεγεν ὁ ἐπιτρέφειν χρήματα δώσω τῇ συλλαβοῦντι, καὶ ἀπαγγείλας ἐ[?] ἀποκτείναντ[?] ἵνα τὴν καταδικαζόντων. Lego, τῇ συλλαβόντι καὶ ἀπαγαγόντι, ἐ[?] ἀποκτείναντι ἵνα τὴν καταδικαζόντων. Cetera apud eundem de Diagora Melio emendanda sunt ex Aristophanis Interprete & Suida. Aristophanes ipse dramate Auibus de Diagora Melio:
units.tr: We have collected this fragment from the decree, which, according to Plutarch in his life of Themistocles, was drawn up against Arithmius of Zeleia: Demosthenes cites it in his Third Philippic: "Arithmius, son of Pythonax, of Zeleia, shall be without honour, and Polemius of the Athenian people and of its allies, he himself and his family [ΑΡΘΜΙΟΣ, φησί, Ο ΠΥΘΩΝΑΚΤΟΣ Ο ΖΕΛΕΙΤΟΣ ΑΤΙΜΟΣ ΕΣΤΩ, ΚΑΙ ΠΟΛΕΜΙΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΔΗΜΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΣΥΜΜΑΧΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΓΕΝΟΣ]. And whoever ... may be an enemy of the Athenian people and its allies, both he and his children." This means: whoever is without honour and kills him, he is unpunished. Both the decree and the word ATIMOS are to be read so. (For what would it matter to the Zeleite that this was enacted, if it was not permitted in the common assembly of the Athenians...) But he who says this: in the laws concerning murderers that were made, against whom ... the case is not heard, [he is condemned] by the sentence of murder. But it is necessary to kill him, and the decree says "atimos" should be "dead". He who says this removes the life of the one who kills. And here the grammarians rightly interpret from Demosthenes "atimos" as "unpunished", the one who kills him, not for the sake of revenge but so that he is free of guilt. Moreover, every man was a soldier against them, even with a reward proposed for whoever had killed them or brought them alive to Athens. The grammarians: ... the city, against whom ... gives money, if ... of the same. Ammonius should be emended: ... he said that money should be given to the one who seized him, and who led him away... and killed... I read: to the one who seized and led away [him], and to the one who killed [him], so that they might condemn... The rest in the same author, about Diagoras of Melos, must be emended from the interpreter of Aristophanes and from Suidas. Aristophanes himself, in his drama The Birds, speaks about Diagoras of Melos:

units.la: τῆδε μὲν ἠ[?] ἡμῖν μᾶλλον ἐπάν[?]ἀγρόστερ[?]. ὡ ἀποκτείνῃ ἡς οὖν Διαγόραν τὸν Μήλιον, λαμβάνειν καλαῦτον. ἐκ[?] τῆς τυ[?]ιγνῶν τῆς ἀπὸ τῆς τιθηνῶν ἀποκτείνῃ, καλάγτων λαμβάνειν.
units.tr: "Whoever kills Diagoras the Melian shall receive a talent; whoever brings him alive shall receive two talents [τῆδε μὲν ἠ[?] ἡμῖν μᾶλλον ἐπάν[?]ἀγρόστερ[?]. ὡ ἀποκτείνῃ ἡς οὖν Διαγόραν τὸν Μήλιον, λαμβάνειν καλαῦτον. ἐκ[?] τῆς τυ[?]ιγνῶν τῆς ἀπὸ τῆς τιθηνῶν ἀποκτείνῃ, καλάγτων λαμβάνειν]."

units.la: Foederis formulam & Leges approbari, priusquam ratum esset, apud Iudices, Legibus est constitutum:
units.tr: The formula of the covenant and the laws were, by the laws, to be approved before the judges before it was ratified:

units.la: Τὰ συμβολα κύρια εἴη, ἐπιδιδῶ δὲ τῆς ἀ[?] ἀκηρίῳ κυρωθῆναι.
units.tr: Greek: Treaties shall be valid, and [...] to be ratified.

units.la: Foedera rata sunto, postquam à iudicibus approbata sunt.
units.tr: Treaties shall be ratified after they have been approved by the judges.

units.la: Legem laudat Demosthenes ὡς Αλινίου. ἐπὶ ὡς συμβόλων φησὶ πέμπο-μένην ταῖς ὑμᾶς τοῖς πεπομένοις ταύτας δὲ κύρια ἔσεσθαι, ἐκ ἐπιδιδῶ δὲ τῆς διαχειρίσεως τῆς πρὸς ὑμῖν κυρωθῆναι, ὡς ὁ νόμος κελεύει· ἀλλ' ἐπιδιδῶ ὡς ἑαυτὸν ἐκδωκεύθη. Ea praecipue Thesmothetarum cura erat, qui ad Iudices referebant: ita capio hunc Pollucis locum Libro VIII. cap. IX. οἱ Θεσμοθέται τὰ συμβόλα τὰ ποτὲς τῆς πόλις κωμῳδεῖ. Atq; secundum has foederis leges & formulam ius Athenis reddebatur sociis, iisdem Thesmothetis in iudicium introducentibus, vt sequitur ibidem apud Pollucem: καὶ δίκης τὰς ἀπὸ συμβόλων εἰσάγοιεν[?]. Cur autem Athenis potius, quam apud socios iudicia redderentur, docet Xenophon [illegible, ~60 letters]. Munychione mense peragebantur hæc iudicia. Aristophanes Avibus.
units.tr: Demosthenes cites the law as that of Aliniu [...] (the Greek is too corrupt to render). He says that the treaties sent to the allies were to be valid, and that they were not to be ratified by any other authority than the judges, as the law commands. This was especially the care of the Thesmothetae, who referred such matters to the judges. So I understand this passage of Pollux, Book VIII, chapter IX: "The Thesmothetae [...] the treaties [...] of the city." And according to these laws of the treaty and its formula, justice was rendered at Athens to the allies, the same Thesmothetae bringing the cases into court, as follows in the same place in Pollux: and they would bring the suits arising from the treaties. Why trials were held at Athens rather than before the allies, Xenophon explains [illegible]. These trials were conducted in the month of Munychion. Aristophanes, in Birds.

units.la: Καλλίμαχος [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: Callimachus [illegible]

units.la: ἐς τὸν Μουνυχιῶνα μῆνα[?].
units.tr: to the month Munychion[?].

units.la: Scholia: παῖ γὰρ Μουνυχιῶνι μηνὶ τὰς ἐάρας δικάζοντας οἱ [?] ξένοις δίκης[?]. Quod commode est intelligendum: non enim hoc vno tantum mense peregrinis iudicia reddebantur, sed etiam à Munychione ad Boëdromionem, interim dum πλεῖμας ἔσῃ ἡ Θαλασσα[?] ab Elaphebolione mense, quem excipiebat Munychion, qui primus est vtilis ad reddenda sociis iudicia.
units.tr: Scholium: for in the month of Munychion they judged the cases of the foreigners [?]. This should be understood sensibly: judgments were given to foreigners not in this one month only, but also from Munychion to Boedromion, in the interval after Elaphebolion, which Munychion followed, and which is the first month useful for rendering judgments to the allies.

units.la: Cum Atheniensium Legibus ij, qui Reipublicæ statum euerterant, aut euerso sustinuissent in ea ciuitate esse, atque Magistratum gerere, ii, inquam, eorumque posteri ignominiosi essent, tamen post exactos Athenis Triginta Tyrannos, Lege, quæ foret in exemplum posteris, omnem memoriam discordiarum obliuione sempiterna delendam sanxit populus, voluitque & hos & illos nullo discrimine haberi, ὃ τῆς ἀμνηστίας ψήφισμα vocat Plutarchus, quanquam Lex reuera fuit, qua cauetur idem iuris esse forcibus & sanatibus, vt verba Legum XII. in [?] negotio vsurpem, eorumque posteris in æternum:
units.tr: Under the laws of Athens, those who had overthrown the constitution, or who had survived the overthrow and held magistracy in that state, were infamous, both they and their descendants. Yet after the Thirty Tyrants were expelled from Athens, the people, by a law that would serve as an example to posterity, decreed that all memory of the discords should be destroyed by everlasting oblivion, and wished both these and those to be held without any distinction. Plutarch calls this the decree of amnesty, although it was really a law by which it was provided that the same right should belong to the exiles and to those who returned, and to their descendants forever. I use the words of the Laws of the Twelve Tables in this matter:

units.la: ΜΗ ΜΝΗΣΙΚΑΚΕΙΝ * * * *
units.tr: not to bear grudges [μὴ μνησικακεῖν] * * * *

units.la: ΜΗΤΕ ΑΔΙΚΟΝ, ΜΗΤΕ ΔΙ-ΚΑΙΟΝ ΛΕΓΕΙΝ.
units.tr: neither to speak of the unjust nor of the just [μήτε ἄδικον μήτε δίκαιον λέγειν].

units.la: Omnem memoriam discordiarum obliuione delento: * * * neque fas neque nefas exprobranto.
units.tr: Let them blot out all memory of discords by oblivion: * * * let them reproach neither right nor wrong.

units.la: Meminit Legis Cicero Philippica I. In quo Templo, quantum in me fuit, ieci fundamenta pacis: Atheniensiumque renouaui vetus exemplum: Græcum etiam verbum vsurpaui, quo tum in sedandis discordiis erat vsa ciuitas illa: atque omnem memoriam discordiarum obliuione sempiterna delendam censui. Atque huius Legis, puto, fragmentum legitur apud Lysiam ἐν τῇ κατὰ Κτησιφῶντος. καὶ τὰς μὲν τῶν ἄλλων Ἀθηναίων παῖδας, ὧν οἱ πατέρες βουλόμενοι ὑμῖν ἐπὶ ζῶσι, ἀπιστεῖν ἐν τοῖς νόμοις, ΜΗΤΕ ΑΔΙΚΟΝ, ΜΗΤΕ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΝ ΛΕΓΕΙΝ. iusiurandum, quod in hanc rem conceptis verbis dabant vniuersus Atheniensium populus, Quingentorum Senatus, iudicesque, extat in Andocidis Oratione, quæ est de Mysteriis. Φέρε δὴ τοίνυν, οἱ ὅρκοι ὑμῖν πῶς ἔχουσιν; ὁ μὲν καινὸς τῇ πόλει ἀπάσῃ, ὃν ὁμομόκασι πάντες μὴ τὰς δίκας[?].
units.tr: Cicero recalls this law in the first Philippic: In this temple, as far as lay in me, I laid the foundations of peace; I renewed the old example of the Athenians; I also used the Greek word which that state then used in quelling discords, and I decided that all memory of discords should be destroyed by everlasting oblivion. I think a fragment of this law is also read in Lysias, in the speech against Ctesiphon: and the children of the other Athenians, whose fathers, wishing to be faithful to you while they lived, were distrustful under the laws, neither to speak unjustly nor justly [μήτε ἄδικον μήτε δίκαιον λέγειν]. The oath which the whole Athenian people, the Senate of Five Hundred, and the judges gave in this matter in set words, is found in the speech of Andocides On the Mysteries: Come now, what do your oaths say? The one which all have sworn to the whole city, not to bear grudges...

units.la: ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΜΝΗΣΙΚΑΚΗΣΩ ΤΩΝ ΠΟΛΙΤΩΝ ΟΥΔΕΝΙ, ΠΛΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΤΡΙΑΚΟΝΤΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΕΝΔΕΚΑ, ΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ, ΟΣ ΑΝ ΕΘΕΛΟΙ ΕΥΘΥΝΑΣ ΔΙΔΟΝΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΑΡΧΗΣ, ΗΣ ΗΡΞΕΝ ἡ ἡ βουλή[?]. αὐτὸν δεῖ βουλεύσασθαι, τί ὁμνυσι[?];
units.tr: And I will bear no grudge against any of the citizens, except the Thirty and the Eleven, nor even against these, if they are willing to give account of the office they held, which the council has ... ; but the council itself must deliberate what he swears.

units.la: ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΔΕΞΟΜΑΙ ΕΝΔΕΙΞΙΝ ΟΥΔΕ ΑΠΑΓΩΓΗΝ ΕΝΕΚΑ ΤΩΝ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΩΝ ΓΕΓΕΝΗΜΕΝΩΝ ΠΛΗΝ ΤΩΝ ΦΕΥΓΟΝΤΩΝ. ὑμῖς δ' αὖ, ὦ Αθηναῖοι τὴν ὁμοσπονδίας δικάζειν; ΚΑΙ ΟΥ ΜΝΗΣΙΚΑΚΗΣΩ, ΟΥΔΕ ΑΛΛΟ ΓΕΙΣΟΜΑΙ ΤΗΦΙΟΥΜΑΙ ΔΕ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΚΕΙΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΝΟΜΟΥΣ. Xenophon Ἑλληνικῶν Lib. II. extremo. [?] ὁμόσπονδοι ὅρκιος ἢ μὴ μνησικακήσῃ, ἐπὶ καὶ νῦν ὁμοῦ γε πολιτευόντα, καὶ τῆς ὅρκιος ἐμμένει ὁ δῆμος. Æschines ἐν τῷ Κτησιφῶντος. νῦν δὲ ἐκ[?]οι μὲν, μεγάλων κακῶν συμβαίνειν, ἵνα [?] τῷ πόλιν, ὃ κέλλισον ἐκ παιδείας ῥῆμα φυγέδα[?]οι, ΜΗ ΜΝΗΣΙΚΑ-ΚΕΙΝ. Huc respexit Aristophanes posteriore Pluto.
units.tr: And I will not admit an accusation or an arrest on account of any of the past events, except against those who fled. But you, Athenians, will you judge the alliance? And I will not bear a grudge, nor will I bring any other charge, but I will act according to the laws in force. Xenophon, at the end of the second book of the Hellenica: the allies swore that they would not bear grudges, and the people abides by the oath. Aeschines in the speech against Ctesiphon: now, great evils are to be feared for the city, unless ... not to bear grudges. Aristophanes in the later Plutus alludes to this:

units.la: μὴ μνησικακήσῃς, εἰ σὺ φυλλὼ κατηλάσεις.
units.tr: Do not bear a grudge, though you yourself drove out Phyllo.

units.la: Scholia: ὅτι μὴ ὁ κατηλθῶν, τοὺς μὴ Θεραμένους Φυλλὼ κελαληθέντας, ἢ ὑ-ποδοῦλας ἐν Γῆρως τῆς Τειάκοντα, ὑπερήσαντα ἔδοξε μὴ μνησικακῆσαι ἀλλήλοις καὶ διαπαξ τῆς πολιτείας. Meminit Isocrates ἐν τῷ ἀγορῷ φθάσαντος πρὸς Καλλίμαχον, τὸ μὲν σιωπηθὲν διαρρηθὲν ἀφιέντων τοῖς σωδίκασι, ἢ φήναντας; ἢ τὴν ἄλλων τι ἱεροῦ-τῶν ἀναξάντας; Quia vero nonnemo hanc Legem temerabat, altera scripta est rogante Archino, qua cautum est ne quis actionem instituat aduersus alterum contra hæc fœdera & iusiurandum:
units.tr: Scholium: because the returnees from Phyle, having sworn to forget the old quarrels, resolved not to bear grudges against one another and to be bound once and for all by the constitution. Isocrates also mentions this in the speech against Callimachus, where those who had been exiled and the rest... Because, however, some men were violating this law, another was written at the proposal of Archinus, by which it is provided that no one shall bring an action against another contrary to these covenants and this oath.

units.la: Ἄν τὶς δικάζηται πρὸς τὰς ὅρκους, ἐξ-ορκῆται παρὰ φύλην ἐπιδαγμάσθαι, τοὺς δὲ Ἀρχοντας πρῶτον εἰσάγειν, λέγειν δὲ πρότερον τὸν ἀπαγγελλόμενον, ὁπότερος δ' ἂν ἡττηθῇ, τῷ ἐπωβελίαν ὀφείλειν.
units.tr: If anyone brings a suit contrary to the oaths, he shall plead an exception; the archons shall first hear the cases; the one who pleads the exception shall speak first; whoever loses the case shall owe the epobelia.

units.la: Si quis in ius vocat aduersus hoc iusiurandum, reus exceptione vtitur: eaque de re Archontes primum iudicia reddunto: prior qui exceptione vtitur dicito: qui causa ceciderit epobelia multator.
units.tr: If anyone summons another to court contrary to this oath, the defendant may use the plea of exception; and on this matter the archons shall first hold the hearings. The one who pleads the exception shall speak first. Whoever loses the case shall pay the epobelia as a fine.

units.la: Legem laudat Isocrates eadem Oratione primore. [?] γὰρ ἐκ Γῆρως κατελθόντες εἰσιοι ἐωσᾶτε τὴν πολιτείαν συνοφαντῶν ὠρμηκότας, καὶ τὰς σὺν ἐπηκοῶς λύει ἐπιχαρῶς, βαλλομένοι τοὺς τε παῖσαν, καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐπιδείξαι ὅτι ἐχὶ αἰτιῶντες ἐπαινοῦσι αὐτοῖς, ἀλλ' ἡμῶν ἡμᾶς τῆ πόλει συμφέρει, εἰπόντος Ἀρχίου, νόμον ἔγραψε, ἀν τὶς δικάζηται πρὸς τὰς ὅρκους, ἐξόρκῃ παρὰ φύλην ἐπιδαγμάσθαι, τοὺς δὲ Ἀρχοντας πρῶτον εἰσάγειν, λέγειν δ' πρότερον τὸν ἀπαγγελλόμενον. ὁπότερος δ' ἂν ἡττηθῇ, τῷ ἐπωβελίαν ὀφείλειν. Nolebat igitur Archinus hac Lege in ius quenquam vocari contra hoc iusiurandum: si quis secus faxit, liceat reo exceptione vti: atque hac de re primum Archontes, apud quos dica scripta est, & quorum est εἰσαγωγὴ εἰς ὃ δικαστήριον, referant ad iudices: prior (quod & in omni exceptione erat solenne) orationem habeat reus, qui exceptione vtitur: Qui causa ceciderit: ἐπωβελίαν pendat.
units.tr: Isocrates praises this law in the same speech, the first one. The men who had returned from Phyle, when they found that certain men were plotting to bring false charges against the constitution and to undo the agreements, and that they were being harassed by informers, showed to the others that they did not blame them but were acting for their own and the city's good. At the proposal of Archinus he wrote a law: if anyone brings a suit contrary to the oaths, the defendant may plead an exception, and the archons shall first hear the case, and the one bringing the charge shall speak first; whoever loses shall owe the epobelia. Archinus therefore did not want anyone to be summoned in violation of this oath: if anyone acted otherwise, the defendant could use the plea of exception. On this matter, the archons, before whom the suit was written and whose office it is to introduce cases to the court, were first to refer it to the judges. The defendant who used the exception was to speak first, as was customary in every exception. Whoever lost the case was to pay the epobelia.

units.la: Legibus caubatur, vt peregrinis & hospitibus in vrbe bene esset, nec iniuria afficerentur.
units.tr: By the laws it was provided that foreigners and guests in the city should be well treated and not wronged.

units.la: Τοὺς ξένους μὴ ἀδικεῖσθαι. Hospites iniuria ne afficiuntor.
units.tr: Strangers are not to be wronged [Τοὺς ξένους μὴ ἀδικεῖσθαι]. Let guests not be wronged or harmed.

units.la: Habes apud Xenophontem [?] Lib. II. Τοὺς γὰρ ξένους, ἐξ οὗ ὁ, τα Σίνης ἢ ὁ Σχίρων ἢ ὁ Γεγρύσεις ἀπίβαλον, ὁ[?]ης ἐπι ἀδικεῖ· ἀλλὰ νῦν οἱ μὲν πολι-τεύόμενοι ἐν ταῖς πατρίσι, καὶ νόμους τίθενται ἵνα μὴ ἀδικῶνται· καὶ φίλους ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀλλήλους καλουμένους ἄλλος κτήσ-θαι βοηθοῦ. Nimirum Ἰσὸς ξένοις, qui & in iu-diciis & apud Magistratum populumque, cum peregrinis ipsis per Leges non liceret, eorum causas agerent: Addit paullo post: ὅσῳ αἱ πόλεις ξένῳ χαρεῖσθαι ἀσφάλειαν καὶ παρασπονδῇ ἡ ἀπιστία. Atque tum hæc cum illa ἰδίως de suis Atheniensibus dixit Socrates ad Aristippum, quem ὃ μὲν ἦμος Κυρηναῖον, ἀφιγμέ-νον δὲ Ἀθηναῖ ἐπὶ κλέος Σωκράτους, narrat Æschines, cum se ibi futurum peregrinum diceret hoc apud Xenophontem loco, Lege hac fretum, ne iniuria à quoquam afficeretur.
units.tr: You have it in Xenophon, Book II: "For the strangers, from whom [names of men] were taken away, ... are wronged; but now those who engage in politics in their own countries make laws so that they are not wronged, and each one seeks helpers among those called friends [Τοὺς γὰρ ξένους ... ἀδικεῖ· ἀλλὰ νῦν οἱ μὲν πολιτεύόμενοι ἐν ταῖς πατρίσι, καὶ νόμους τίθενται ἵνα μὴ ἀδικῶνται· καὶ φίλους ... κτήσθαι βοηθούς]." Namely, Isocrates pleaded the cases of strangers, since by law the foreigners themselves were not permitted to do so in lawsuits, nor before the Magistrate and the people. A little later he adds: "As far as cities provide safety to strangers, faithlessness is a breach of faith [ὅσῳ αἱ πόλεις ξένῳ χαρεῖσθαι ἀσφάλειαν καὶ παρασπονδῇ ἡ ἀπιστία]." Socrates, too, spoke of this, and in the same particular sense about his own Athenians, to Aristippus, whom Aeschines narrates came to Athens from Cyrene for the fame of Socrates. When Aristippus said in this passage of Xenophon that he would be a stranger there, he relied on this law, that no one would wrong him.

units.la: Atheniensium Lege publicisque execrationibus, erranti viam monstrare, & peregrinos tecto excipere, sancitum est.
units.tr: By the law of the Athenians and by public curses it was enacted that one should show the way to a wanderer and receive strangers under one's roof.

units.la: Ὑποφαίνειν ὁδὸν πλανωμένοις, καὶ ξεινωνῶν[?] / χρὴ τὸν βίον ὕδατος ἢ πυρός.
units.tr: "To point out the way to those who wander, and one must share one's life with water or fire [Ὑποφαίνειν ὁδὸν πλανωμένοις, καὶ ξεινωνῶν χρὴ τὸν βίον ὕδατος ἢ πυρός]."

units.la: Erranti viam monstranto : peregrinos tecto excipiunto.
units.tr: Let the wanderer be shown the way; let strangers be received under a roof.

units.la: Meminit M. Tullius Lib. III. de Officiis. Ille vero, inquit Antipater, quid enim est aliud erranti viam non monstrare, quod Athenis execrationibus publicis sancitum est. Diphilus ἐν Παρασίτῳ.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius mentions it in Book III of De Officiis: "Indeed, says Antipater, what else is it than not to show the way to a wanderer, which at Athens was enacted by public curses?" Diphilus, in The Parasite [ἐν Παρασίτῳ].

units.la: ἀγνοεῖς ὅτι τὰς ὁδοὺς[?] / ὅτι ἔστιν, εἰ τῆς μὴ φεύσῃ ὀρθῶς ὁδόν.
units.tr: "Do you not know that there is ... if you do not go wrong on the right road [ἀγνοεῖς ὅτι ... ὅτι ἔστιν, εἰ τῆς μὴ φεύσῃ ὀρθῶς ὁδόν]."

units.la: Hanc autem Legem publicis istis execrationibus sanxit Buzyges: habes in Vaticana Græcorum Proverbiorum Appendice, Centuria I. Proverbio XXI. Βουζύγης. Ὅτι τὴν πολλὰ ἀρωμένων. ὁ γὰρ Βουζύγης Ἀθηναῖον ὁ ὃ ἱερὰν ἄρξειν, ἀλλὰ τε πολλὰ ἀρᾶσθαι[?] καὶ τοῖς μὴ χειρωνοῦσι χρὴ τὸν βίον ὕδατος ἢ πυρός, ἢ μὴ ὑποφαίνοντι ὁδὸν πλανωμένοις[?]. Locum truncatum esse is, cui inter cetera Græcorum omnium Paræmiographorum editionem studiosi debemus, CL. & eruditissimus Andreas Schottus queritur: puto referendum: Βουζύγης, ὅτι τὴν πολ-λὰ ἀρωμένων. ὁ γὰρ Βουζύγης Ἀθηναῖον, ὃ ὃ ἱερὰν ἄρξειν, ἀλλὰ τε πολλὰ ἀρᾶσθαι, καὶ τοῖς μὴ χειρωνοῦσι χρὴ τὸν βίον ὕδατος ἢ πυρός, ἢ μὴ ὑποφαίνοντι ὁδὸν πλανωμένοις. Sensus est, Buzygen Athenis, qui arare docuit, cuius rei monumentum extat in suburbano Buzygio, diris deuouisse inter cetera eos, qui peregrinos hospitio & tecto, id est, aqua & igne non exciperent, aut qui erranti viam non monstrarent: Aqua autem & igni accipere, idem est, quod οἴκῳ δέχεσθαι, nam ii quibus interdictum est igni & aqua, tecto arcentur & prohibentur: atque utrumque coniungit Euripides Oreste, recensetque quasi prima & non deneganda cuiquam hospitii iura, quibus tamen erat interdictum iis, qui cædispiaculo obstringebantur:
units.tr: This law was enacted with those public curses by Buzyges. You have it in the Vatican Appendix of Greek Proverbs, Century I, Proverb 21: "Buzyges: because he called down many curses; for Buzyges, the Athenian, who was the first to teach ploughing, cursed many things, and [cursed] those who would not share water and fire with strangers, or who would not point out the way to wanderers." That the passage is truncated, the learned and most erudite Andreas Schottus, to whom scholars owe, among other things, the edition of all the Greek paroemiographers, complains; I think it should be read: "Buzyges: because he called down many curses; for Buzyges, the Athenian, who was the first to teach ploughing, cursed many things, and [cursed] those who would not share water and fire with strangers, or who would not point out the way to wanderers." The sense is that Buzyges at Athens, who taught ploughing, of which deed a monument stands in the suburban Buzygion, called down curses on, among others, those who did not receive strangers with hospitality and under a roof, that is, with water and fire, or who did not show the way to a wanderer. To receive with water and fire is the same as to receive under one's roof, for those who are forbidden water and fire are kept away from the roof and shut out. Euripides joins the two in Orestes, and lists them as it were the first and undeniable rights of hospitality, which nevertheless were forbidden to those bound by the guilt of bloodshed:

units.la: ἔδοξε δ᾽ Ἀργὰ πῶδε, μήθ᾽ ἡμᾶς ψέγαις / μὴ πυρὶ δίχεσθαι.
units.tr: "It seemed good to the Argives thus, that we should not be received with fire [ἔδοξε δ᾽ Ἀργὰ πῶδε, μήθ᾽ ἡμᾶς ψέγαις / μὴ πυρὶ δίχεσθαι]."

units.la: Nolebat Solo fraudem cuiquam fieri ab annulario, itaque Legem scripsit.
units.tr: Solon did not want anyone to be defrauded by a ring-engraver, and so he wrote a law.

units.la: Δακτυλιογλύφῳ μὴ ἐξεῖναι σφραγῖδα / φυλάττειν τῷ παρέχοντι δακτύλιον.
units.tr: "For the ring-engraver it is not permitted to keep the seal of the ring to the one who gave the ring [Δακτυλιογλύφῳ μὴ ἐξεῖναι σφραγῖδα / φυλάττειν τῷ παρέχοντι δακτύλιον]."

units.la: Annularius expressum annuli, quem vendidit, signum apud se ne habeto.
units.tr: A ring-engraver shall not keep a seal of the impression of the ring he has sold.

units.la: Refert hanc Solonis Legem Diogenes Laërtius in Solonis vita: pertinet autem ad annulum signatorium, eaque cauet Solo, ne possit annularius alio facto simili annulo fraudem ei facere, cui priorem vendidisset.
units.tr: Diogenes Laërtius, in his Life of Solon, reports this law of Solon. It concerns the signet ring, and Solon provides against the engraver defrauding the buyer of the earlier ring by making a similar ring.

units.la: LAVS DEO OPT. MAX.
units.tr: Praise to God, the best and greatest.
